items.name: Petunia axillaris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 18C on the soil surface because they need light to germinate in the UK.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 8cm tall to encourage a bushy, floriferous habit.
Water early in the morning at the base to prevent botrytis grey mould in damp UK summer weather.
Deadhead weekly by pinching off the spent flower and the green seed capsule behind it to prolong blooms.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser from July to September to sustain heavy flowering.
items.description: Petunia axillaris, the large white petunia, wild white petunia or white moon petunia, is an annual herbaceous plant in the family Solanaceae, genus Petunia. It is native to temperate South America comprising southern Brazil, parts of Argentina and Uruguay. The plant's flowers, the only white ones found in the Petunia genus, are 3 to 7 cm long. The commonly-grown garden petunia is a hybrid of P. axillaris and P. integrifolia.

items.name: Maianthemum paniculatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich acidic soil in partial to full shade to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to retain essential soil moisture.
Water regularly during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
items.description: Maianthemum paniculatum is a perennial flowering plant; a species of monocot found from Mexico to Panama. It is often associated with montane environments and is found primarily in forest openings and along roadsides.

items.name: Maianthemum canadense
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn under deciduous trees in acidic, humus-rich soil to mimic its native woodland floor.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the shallow rhizomes moist but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the delicate rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to show.
Plant alongside shade-loving UK natives like wood anemone and hart's tongue fern for ground cover.
items.description:
Maianthemum canadense 
is an understory perennial flowering plant, native to Canada and the northeastern United States, from Yukon and British Columbia east to Newfoundland, into St. Pierre and Miquelon. It can be found growing in both coniferous and deciduous forests. The plant appears in two forms, either as a single leaf rising from the ground with no fruiting structures or as a flowering/fruiting stem with two to three leaves. Flowering shoots have clusters of 12–25 starry-shaped, white flowers held above the leaves.

items.name: Ruscus hypoglossum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained alkaline soil in deep dry shade where other evergreen shrubs struggle
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK summers until their extensive root system establishes
Prune out dead or damaged cladodes at the base in late spring to maintain a tidy green appearance
Propagate by carefully dividing the tough congested root clumps in early spring before new growth
Watch for slugs and snails on the tender new shoots emerging from the soil in damp spring weather
items.description: Ruscus hypoglossum is a small evergreen shrub with a native range from Italy north to Austria and Slovakia and east to Turkey and Crimea. Common names include spineless butcher's-broom, mouse thorn and horse tongue lily. The species name comes from two Greek words ὑπό (hypo) and γλῶσσα (glōssa) meaning under and tongue.

items.name: Dracaena halapepe
items.growersTips:
Grow this Hawaiian native in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive cold UK winters.
Use a very free-draining gritty loam with a pH of 6.0 to 6.5 to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost dries out completely during the winter.
Position in a south-facing room to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight and prevent leaf drop.
Inspect leaf axils weekly for mealybugs which thrive in dry indoor UK heating conditions.
items.description: Dracaena halapepe, synonym Pleomele halapepe, the royal hala pepe, is a species of flowering plant that is endemic to the island of Oʻahu in Hawaiʻi. It inhabits dry, coastal mesic and mixed mesic forests at elevations of 180–610 metres (590–2,000 ft). It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Ruscus hypophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural woodland habitat and prevent leaf burn.
In heavy UK clay mix in coarse grit and leaf mould to ensure the sharp drainage this shrub requires.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep it completely dry during damp UK winters.
Prune out old discoloured three-year-old stems at the base in late spring to encourage fresh shoots.
Watch for slugs and snails on new spring shoots as damp UK weather encourages damage to fresh growth.
items.description: Ruscus hypophyllum is a species of shrub in the family Asparagaceae. They have a self-supporting growth form. Individuals can grow to 0.42 m.

items.name: Beaucarnea goldmanii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of gritty loam-based compost to easily move it indoors for winter.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out, keeping it dry through winter.
Place the pot in your sunniest south-facing patio spot to mimic its native warm, bright habitat.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this plant indoors or in a conservatory.
items.description: Beaucarnea goldmanii is a tree in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to Mexico and northern Central America.

items.name: Beaucarnea hiriartiae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to beat UK chills.
Grow in a greenhouse or south-facing conservatory as this tender species cannot survive UK frosts.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost feels dry to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Blend fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to ensure the rapid drainage this plant demands.
Check leaf undersides weekly for glasshouse red spider mite during dry British summer spells.
items.description: Beaucarnea hiriartiae is a plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Mexico. The species is named for the botanist Patricia Hiriart Valencia.

items.name: Beaucarnea stricta
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October to protect this Mexican native from wet UK winters and frost damage.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Position in your brightest south-facing window or conservatory to maximise scarce UK winter sun.
Repot every three years in spring, keeping the swollen trunk base fully above the soil surface.
items.description: Beaucarnea stricta is a tree in the family Asparagaceae, native to Mexico. The specific epithet stricta means "straight, thin", referring to the leaves.

items.name: Ruscus hyrcanus
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using well-drained, humus-rich soil to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged.
Prune dead or damaged stems at the base in late spring to encourage fresh, healthy new growth.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or compost to protect roots from severe winter frosts.
Position near companion plants like ferns or hostas that thrive in similar damp, shady conditions.
items.description: Ruscus hyrcanus is a perennial evergreen woody shrub-like or small compact bush plant. It is in the asparagus family.

items.name: Dasylirion longissimum
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing brick wall to maximize essential summer heat.
Protect the crown with a fleece jacket or temporary rain shelter from November through March.
Water only during hot dry summer spells and keep completely dry throughout the winter months.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot using a loam-based grit mix to allow easy winter relocation.
items.description: Dasylirion longissimum, common name the Mexican grass tree, is a species of flowering plant native to the Chihuahuan Desert and other xeric habitats in Northeastern Mexico.

items.name: Dracaena cinnabari
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in wet UK winters
Keep in frost-free greenhouse or indoors from October to May as it cannot tolerate UK frosts
Water only when the soil dries out completely during summer and keep almost dry throughout winter
Place in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native hot Socotra island climate
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap spray
items.description: Dracaena cinnabari, the Socotra dragon tree or dragon blood tree, is a dragon tree native to the Socotra archipelago, part of Yemen, located in the Arabian Sea. It is named after the blood-like color of the red sap that the trees produce. It is also the national tree of Yemen.

items.name: Dasylirion texanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised gravel bed with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in your sunniest south facing border against a brick wall to maximize summer heat.
Protect the crown with a fleece jacket or removable cloche from November through to late March.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts and keep completely dry during the winter months.
Grow in a terracotta pot using peat free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for easy winter moving.
items.description: Dasylirion texanum, the Texas sotol and sotol, is a monocot flowering plant native to central and southwestern Texas and in Coahuila state of northeastern Mexico, including the Chihuahuan Desert.

items.name: Dasylirion durangense
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed or gravel mound using fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Protect the crown from winter rot by covering with a temporary glass cloche from November to March.
Water only during dry summer spells once established and never let water sit in the central crown.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing spot to maximize the limited UK summer sunshine.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot with drainage holes so you can move it under cover for winter.
items.description: Dasylirion durangense, common name "sotol," is a perennial plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Durango, Chihuahua and Sonora, Mexico. It is closely related to D. wheeleri S. Wats. and considered a variety of that species by some authors. The plant has a large basal rosette of long stiff leaves over 1 m in length, bearing sharp, curved spines along the margins. The flowering stalk can be up to 3 m tall, bearing small wind-pollinated flowers.

items.name: Dasylirion lucidum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed of 50 percent grit and sharp sand to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in your garden's hottest, most south-facing suntrap against a brick wall to mimic Mexico.
Water only during dry summer spells and keep completely dry from October through to March.
Protect the crown with a fleece jacket or removable rain shelter during freezing winter wet.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot using loam-based John Innes No 3 mixed with extra horticultural grit.
items.description: Dasylirion lucidum is a plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Mexican states of Oaxaca and Puebla. This is a shrub up to 2 m high, with thin, spiny-margined leaves and a scape up to 3 m tall.

items.name: Beaucarnea recurvata
items.growersTips:
Bring the plant indoors by October to protect its trunk from damp UK winter rot and freezing cold.
Water only when the compost dries completely, reducing to once a month during dark winter months.
Blend fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in dull British weather.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the limited winter sunlight hours in the UK.
Wipe the long leaves with a damp cloth in spring to clear dust and prevent red spider mite attacks.
items.description: Beaucarnea recurvata, the elephant's foot or ponytail palm, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. The species is endemic to eastern Mexico; according to IUCN it is now confined to the state of Veracruz, but Plants of the World Online also cites it as occurring in Oaxaca, Puebla, San Luis Potosí, and Tamaulipas. Despite its common name, it is not closely related to the true palms (Arecaceae). It has become popular in Europe and worldwide as an ornamental plant. There are 350-year-old Beaucarneas registered in Mexico.

items.name: Maianthemum stellatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade and moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil to mimic UK woodland edges.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or composted bark every autumn to protect rhizomes and enrich soil.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the emerging shoots with organic grit.
items.description: Maianthemum stellatum is a species of flowering plant, native across North America. It has been found in northern Mexico, every Canadian province and territory except Nunavut, and every US state except Hawaii and the states of the Southeast. It has little white buds in the spring, followed by delicate starry flowers, then green-and-black striped berries, and finally deep red berries in the fall.

items.name: Hyoscyamus niger
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring directly onto well-drained, alkaline soil as they need light to germinate.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to prevent skin absorption of alkaloids.
Watch for the potato flea beetle in early summer, which leaves tiny shot-holes in the foliage.
Leave the distinctive seed pods intact over winter to provide structure and self-seed naturally.
items.description: Henbane is a poisonous plant belonging to tribe Hyoscyameae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. Henbane is native to temperate Europe and Siberia, and naturalised in Great Britain and Ireland.

items.name: Maianthemum bifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, mimicking UK woodland conditions.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate the following spring.
Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained during summer, avoiding waterlogging in heavy clay.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or composted bark to replicate natural forest floor litter.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they can quickly decimate the emerging delicate new shoots.
items.description: Maianthemum bifolium is often a localized common rhizomatous flowering plant, native from western Europe east to Siberia, China and Japan.

items.name: Dracaena sanderiana
items.growersTips:
Keep potted in peat-free compost with perlite and move indoors before autumn temperatures drop below 10C
Water with collected rainwater rather than tap water to prevent brown leaf tips caused by fluoride
Grow in bright indirect light near a west-facing window to avoid scorching the variegated leaves
Wipe leaves monthly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations in dry indoor air
Feed monthly from April to September using a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer diluted to half strength
items.description: Dracaena sanderiana is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Central Africa. It was named after the German–English gardener Henry Frederick Conrad Sander (1847–1920). The plant is commonly marketed as "lucky bamboo," which has become one of its common names, although it is not a species of bamboo.

items.name: Hyoscyamus albus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Place pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic Mediterranean warmth in the damp UK climate.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to avoid fatal root rot in wet winters.
Wear thick gloves when handling or pruning this highly toxic plant to prevent skin absorption.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails which actively target the soft early foliage.
items.description: Hyoscyamus albus, the white henbane or yellow henbane, is a plant in the family of Solanaceae. It is native to Southern Europe, North Africa, West Asia and Macaronesia.

items.name: Beaucarnea gracilis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October to protect the caudex from frost, as it cannot survive wet UK winters.
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp weather.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Position in your brightest south-facing window or conservatory to maximise scarce UK winter sun.
Repot every three years in spring into a shallow pot only slightly wider than the swollen stem base.
items.description: Beaucarnea gracilis is a species of flowering plant in the Asparagaceae family. It is native to Puebla, and northern parts of Oaxaca, in Mexico, where it is endemic to the Tehuacán Valley matorral. It grows primarily in the seasonally dry tropical biome.

items.name: Rohdea
items.growersTips:
Plant Rohdea tubers 10cm deep in late April once the frost risk in your UK region has fully passed
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but not wet
Watch for potato beetles and tomato blight in humid July weather and remove infected leaves quickly
Prune away the lower yellowing leaves in August to improve air circulation and prevent fungal rot
Grow Rohdea alongside basil or marigolds to naturally deter common UK pests like aphids and thrips
items.description: Rohdea is a genus of plants native to eastern Asia. It was long thought to contain only a single species, R. japonica, but recent studies have resulted in several other taxa being transferred into the genus.

items.name: Maianthemum racemosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil to mimic woodland homes.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in autumn to retain moisture and replicate natural forest floor soils.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the shallow rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to show.
items.description: Maianthemum racemosum, the treacleberry, feathery false lily of the valley, false Solomon's seal, Solomon's plume or false spikenard, is a species of flowering plant native to North America. It is a common, widespread plant with numerous common names and synonyms, known from every US state except Hawaii, and from every Canadian province and territory, as well as from Mexico.

items.name: Petunia integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on the soil surface as they need light and UK warmth to germinate.
Water at the base of the plant in the morning to prevent botrytis blight in damp UK summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in May before planting out to encourage a bushy, trailing habit.
Apply a high-potash liquid feed fortnightly from July to September to sustain the purple blooms.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet British spring nights using organic grit.
items.description: Petunia integrifolia, the violet petunia or violetflower petunia, is a species of wild petunia with violet-colored blooms. Petunia integrifolia is native to Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

items.name: Dasylirion serratifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in the brightest, most south-facing spot of your garden to maximize scarce UK sunlight.
Water deeply but infrequently during summer, allowing the compost to dry out completely between times.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a temporary rain shelter or cloche from November to March.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
items.description: Dasylirion serratifolium, or the sandpaper sotol, is a plant species in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Mexican states of Hidalgo and Oaxaca. It is often in cultivation as an ornamental in other places, including in Europe.

items.name: Dracaena fragrans
items.growersTips:
Keep it indoors year-round as it cannot survive UK winter temperatures below twelve degrees Celsius.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in low UK winter light.
Position in bright indirect light near an east or west window to avoid leaf scorch from direct sun.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve light absorption in winter.
Feed with a balanced liquid houseplant fertiliser once a month from April to September only.
items.description: Dracaena fragrans, is a flowering plant species that is native to tropical Africa, from Sudan south to Mozambique, west to Côte d'Ivoire and southwest to Angola, growing in upland regions at 600–2,250 m (1,970–7,380 ft) altitude.

items.name: Dracaena braunii
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots of peat-free compost with grit to move indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Keep indoors in bright indirect light during winter to avoid leaf scorch from direct summer sun.
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and prevent red spider mite infestations.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost growth.
items.description: Dracaena braunii is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It was named after the German collector Braun, Johannes M. (1859–1893). Most plants named Dracaena braunii in cultivation are Dracaena sanderiana, a plant with flowers five times longer than those of D. braunii, while the leaf base is not congested as in D. braunii.

items.name: Dracaena ellenbeckiana
items.growersTips:
Bring containerized plants indoors before October frosts as they cannot tolerate UK winter wet.
Water deeply only when the top five centimeters of soil dries out to prevent root rot in cool weather.
Blend thirty percent grit into peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this species demands.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or bright windowsill to maximize weak UK winter sunlight.
Prune leggy stems in late spring using sterilized shears to stimulate bushier low-level growth.
items.description: Dracaena ellenbeckiana is a species of plant belonging to the Asparagaceae family, subfamily Convallarioideae. Dracaena ellenbeckiana is native to Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, Sudan, and Uganda, and primarily grows in the seasonally dry tropical biome.

items.name: Dracaena aurea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in pots to easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost hits the UK
Plant in a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil dry out, reducing this to monthly in winter
Prune back leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and stimulate fresh new growth
Position in a conservatory or near a south-facing window to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight
items.description: Dracaena aurea, the golden hala pepe, is a species of flowering plant that is endemic to the island of Kauaʻi in Hawaii. It inhabits coastal mesic and mixed mesic forests at elevations of 120–1,070 m (390–3,510 ft). It is a small evergreen tree, usually 4.6–7.6 m (15–25 ft) tall, but sometimes reaches 12 m (39 ft). The gray, straight trunk does not have bark and is 0.3–0.9 m (0.98–2.95 ft) in diameter. The sword-shaped leaves are 20–51 cm (7.9–20.1 in) long and 1–3 cm (0.39–1.18 in) wide.

items.name: Dracaena cantleyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated conservatory as this tropical shrub cannot survive UK winter temperatures below 15C.
Use a well-draining peat-free loam compost mixed with thirty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dry out, using tepid rainwater to avoid leaf burn.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to mimic its rainforest home.
Inspect leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, which thrive on this plant in dry indoor UK winter air.
items.description: Dracaena cantleyi is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to wet tropical areas of Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo. A small tree reaching 1 to 5 m, it has purplish-green leaves with lighter green mottling. Orangutans have been observed masticating its leaves and using the resultant foam as an anti-inflammatory balm.

items.name: Dracaena mannii
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost to survive cold UK winters in a bright draft-free room.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost dries out completely to prevent root rot.
Repot in spring using peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit for sharp drainage.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to stimulate bushy growth and maintain a compact indoor shape.
Wipe leaves monthly with a damp cloth to remove dust and check for hidden mealybugs or scale.
items.description: Dracaena mannii Baker or small-leaved dragon tree, also called Kalala Kabwe, is a small to medium-sized tree, though recorded up to 35 m tall with stem to 2 m in diameter in Cameroon and Gabon. It occurs from Senegal to Angola along the African west coast, is widespread in tropical Africa and is found along the African east coast from Kenya to Kosi Bay in northern KwaZulu-Natal. It prefers lowland, submontane and montane forests which are either moist and evergreen, swampy or on coastal dunes. It is also found along forest edges, in clearings and on river banks from sea level to 1,800 metres.

items.name: Dracaena fernaldii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Solanaceae vegetable in late May after UK frosts pass, spacing them sixty centimetres apart.
Water deeply once a week at the base to prevent blight, avoiding the foliage during damp UK summers.
Apply a high-potassium organic tomato feed every fortnight once the first vegetable fruits set.
Watch for aphids and red spider mites under greenhouse glass, using biological controls in July.
Prune lower yellowing leaves in August to improve air circulation and help the remaining crop ripen.
items.description: Dracaena fernaldii, synonym Pleomele fernaldii, is a species of flowering plant that is endemic to the island of Lānaʻi in Hawaiʻi. It is known by the common name Lanai hala pepe. It can be found in dry forests at elevations of 490–670 metres (1,610–2,200 ft). It is threatened by habitat loss. 400–1000 of these plants remain in the wild, but little recruitment has been observed in the past 10 years. The reasons for the lack of recruitment are unclear.

items.name: Dracaena forbesii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender tropical cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Plant in peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in cool UK light levels.
Keep in a bright conservatory with indirect sun to prevent leaf scorch during long midsummer days.
Check regularly for mealybugs and spider mites which thrive in dry indoor UK heating conditions.
items.description: Dracaena forbesii, synonym Pleomele forbesii, is a species of flowering plant that is endemic to the island of Oʻahu in Hawaiʻi. It inhabits dry, coastal mesic and mixed mesic forests at elevations of 240–730 metres (790–2,400 ft). It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Dracaena transvaalensis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this tender South African shrub cannot survive UK winters.
Grow in a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil feels dry to touch during summer.
Prune back leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and fresh leaf growth.
Position in your brightest south-facing room or conservatory to maximise limited UK winter sunlight.
items.description: Dracaena transvaalensis, the Wolkberg dragon tree, is a medium-sized tree in the genus Dracaena found in the Olifants River Valley near Penge in the Limpopo and the adjacent Wolkberg. It looks similar to Aloe. The plant is considered rare.

items.name: Dracaena serrulata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a free-draining loam-based grit mix to survive damp UK winter roots.
Keep containerized plants in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from October through April.
Water deeply only when the top five centimeters of soil feels dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Prune leggy stems in late spring just as new growth begins to encourage a bushier shrub habit.
Check leaf axils regularly for mealybugs, a common pest in dry indoor winter environments.
items.description: Dracaena serrulata, also called the Arabian or Yemen dragon tree, is a distinctive tree reaching around 5m tall with a single trunk. It is found in the dry escarpment mountains of southwestern Arabia in Oman, South Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

items.name: Dracaena viridiflora
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October as this tender Solanaceae shrub cannot survive wet UK winter frosts.
Grow in a peat-free loam compost mixed with thirty percent grit to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in cool weather.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in late April to encourage a bushier habit for the summer.
Check the undersides of leaves weekly for glasshouse red spider mite during dry summer spells.
items.description: Dracaena viridiflora is a species of shrub or small plant belonging to the family Asparagaceae.

items.name: Eriospermum paradoxum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or sunny windowsill as this South African tuber cannot survive UK frosts.
Plant the tuber in autumn in extremely gritty, free-draining soil with the growing tip just exposed.
Water only from September to April when the fuzzy leaf is active, keeping it totally dry in summer.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic winter sun and prevent leaf stretching.
Watch for mealybugs nestled inside the dense, complex leaf hairs during the winter growing season.
items.description: Eriospermum paradoxum ("haasklossie") is a species of geophytic plant of the genus Eriospermum, indigenous to the Cape region of South Africa. Its habitat is sandy or rocky clay soils in arid winter-rainfall areas. It is a bit peculiar in having a true leaf that is like the scale-leaves of some junipers, from which emerges an enation up to 15 cm (5.9 in) in height and half as wide. but is semisucculent in nature.

items.name: Eriospermum capense
items.growersTips:
Grow this tuberous South African native in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep the soil completely dry during its summer dormancy, starting watering only when leaves emerge.
Provide a minimum winter temperature of 5C in a bright greenhouse or conservatory to prevent frost.
Plant the tuber with its growing tip just below the soil surface in a deep, narrow terracotta pot.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils during the autumn and winter active growing season.
items.description: Eriospermum capense is a species of geophytic plant of the genus Eriospermum, indigenous to the Western Cape Province, South Africa.

items.name: Eriospermum dregei
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this South African tuber is not hardy in the UK climate.
Plant the tuber in a highly gritty, free-draining loam-less compost with the crown at soil level.
Water only from autumn to spring during its active winter growth phase and keep dry in summer.
Position in a south-facing window or under grow lights to prevent leggy winter leaf growth.
Watch for mealybugs in the fibrous leaf sheath and treat with an organic contact insecticide.
items.description: Eriospermum dregei is a species of geophytic plant of the family Asparagaceae.

items.name: Eriospermum cooperi
items.growersTips:
Grow this tuberous South African native in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep the soil completely dry during its summer dormant phase when the single leaf dies back.
Water moderately from autumn to spring only when the leaf is actively growing in a frost-free spot.
Position in a bright, unheated greenhouse or south-facing windowsill to mimic its sunny habitat.
Plant the tuber just below the soil surface in a deep pot to accommodate its extensive root system.
items.description: Eriospermum cooperi is a species of flowering plant of the Asparagaceae family. It is a summer rainfall species found in rocky grassland and open scrub from the Eastern Cape, South Africa to Zimbabwe. It has a solitary erect leaf, white to pale green flowers and grows to 60 cm. The outer tepals are sometimes reddish brown.

items.name: Eriospermum bowieanum
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare South African tuber indoors or in a heated greenhouse to survive wet UK winters.
Plant the tuber just below the soil surface in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mix.
Water only from autumn to spring during its active growth, keeping it completely dry in summer.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise winter sunlight and prevent weak, leggy growth.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils during winter and treat immediately with organic sprays.
items.description: Eriospermum bowieanum is a species of geophytic plant of the genus Eriospermum, endemic to the Robertson Karoo region of the Western Cape Province, South Africa.

items.name: Eriospermum lanceifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African tuber in a gritty, free-draining loam mix under glass to prevent winter rot.
Water only from autumn to spring during its active growth phase, keeping it bone dry all summer.
Provide a minimum winter temperature of five degrees Celsius using a heated greenhouse or cold frame.
Plant the tuber just below the soil surface with the growing tip pointing upwards in late August.
Keep a sharp lookout for glasshouse mealybugs nestled in the base of the lance-shaped winter leaves.
items.description: Eriospermum lanceifolium is a species of geophytic plant of the genus Eriospermum.

items.name: Dasylirion acrotrichum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed of 50 percent grit and loam to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize essential summer heat.
Protect the crown with a fleece jacket or removable glass cloche from November through March.
Water deeply once a fortnight in summer but keep completely dry during the damp winter months.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by cutting close to the trunk to maintain a clean shape.
items.description: Dasylirion acrotrichum, the great desert spoon and green sotol, is a plant native to the Chihuahuan Desert and other xeric habitats in northern and central Mexico.

items.name: Hyoscyamus aureus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining gritty compost during early spring
Grow this tender Mediterranean native in a terracotta pot to move indoors before autumn frosts hit
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in UK damp
Wear gloves when handling to avoid skin contact with its highly toxic tropane alkaloid sap
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to mimic its dry native climate
items.description: Hyoscyamus aureus, the golden henbane or yellow henbane, is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae native to the Eastern Mediterranean and Iraq.

items.name: Maianthemum dilatatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic to neutral woodland soil under deciduous trees to mimic UK forest conditions.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the shallow rhizomes from drying out completely.
Control spreading rhizomes by planting inside buried barriers to prevent it overtaking small borders.
Watch for slug and snail damage on the tender emerging spring shoots during wet British April weather.
items.description: Maianthemum dilatatum is a common rhizomatous perennial flowering plant that is native to western North America from northern California to the Aleutian Islands, and Asia across the Kamchatka Peninsula, Japan, and Korea. It grows in coastal temperate rainforests, and is often the dominant groundcover plant in Sitka Spruce forests.

items.name: Maianthemum trifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic, moisture-retentive peat-free ericaceous compost in a cool, fully shaded woodland spot.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking wet UK bog conditions using rainwater.
Plant the creeping rhizomes shallowly at a depth of two centimeters in early spring as growth starts.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Propagate by carefully dividing the delicate rhizome clumps in autumn after the foliage dies back.
items.description: Maianthemum trifolium is a species of flowering plant that is associated with extremely wet environments and is native to Canada and the northeastern United States as well as St. Pierre and Miquelon and Asia (Siberia).

items.name: Dasylirion leiophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty loam at a depth of fifteen centimeters to ensure rapid drainage in wet UK winters.
Water only once a week in summer and keep completely dry from October to March to prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize heat and protect from cold winds.
Wrap the crown in fleece during prolonged UK frosts below minus eight to prevent freezing damage.
Grow in a terracotta pot using a mix of three parts John Innes number three to one part grit.
items.description: Dasylirion leiophyllum is a species of flowering plant in the asparagus family known by the common names green sotol, smooth-leaf sotol, and smooth sotol. It is native to North America, where it occurs in Chihuahua and Coahuila in Mexico and New Mexico and western Texas in the United States. It was first collected by Valery Havard in 1880 and was described by William Trelease in 1911.

items.name: Beaucarnea pliabilis
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Mexican shrub indoors by October to protect it from wet and freezing UK winters.
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp weather.
Water only when the soil dries out completely in summer, and keep it totally dry throughout winter.
Position in your brightest south-facing window or conservatory to maximise scarce UK winter light.
Prune leggy stems back in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and stimulate fresh new growth.
items.description: Beaucarnea pliabilis is a tree in the family Asparagaceae, native to the Yucatán Peninsula. It grows up to 10 metres (30 ft) tall.

items.name: Dasylirion wheeleri
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised bed of 50% grit and 50% loam to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize summer heat and light.
Water only during dry summer spells and keep completely dry from October through March.
Wrap the crown in fleece during prolonged freezing UK temperatures to prevent frost damage.
Prune dead lower leaves in late spring by cutting close to the trunk to maintain shape.
items.description: Dasylirion wheeleri is a species of flowering plant in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae), native to arid environments of northern Mexico and the southwestern United States.

items.name: Polygonatum odoratum
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes horizontally in autumn five centimetres deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural UK woodland habitat.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to establish roots, keeping the soil consistently damp.
Inspect stems from May to August for sawfly larvae and handpick them to prevent total defoliation.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn every four years to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Polygonatum odoratum, the angular Solomon's seal or scented Solomon's seal, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Europe, the Caucasus, Siberia, the Russian Far East, China, Mongolia, Korea, Nepal and Japan. In the United Kingdom it is one of three native species of the genus, the others being P. multiflorum and P. verticillatum.

items.name: Hyoscyamus muticus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a terracotta pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Water sparingly only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Sow seeds in early spring on the soil surface under glass, as they require light and warmth to sprout.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to avoid absorbing harmful alkaloids.
items.description: Hyoscyamus muticus, the Egyptian henbane, is a shrub in the family of Solanaceae that is native to desert areas of North Africa. It contains alkaloids that are useful in pharmaceuticals. It is used locally as a painkiller and a recreational drug. In high dosages it can be fatal.

items.name: Pleomele
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in cool UK light levels.
Keep in bright indirect light near a south-facing window but shade from intense midsummer midday sun.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and prevent red spider mite attacks.
Repot in spring every two years using a free-draining peat-free loam mixed with one-third perlite.
items.description:
Pleomele is used a common name for several cultivated ornamental plants and may refer to:Species of Pleomele (genus), a former plant genus in the family Ruscaceae now included in Dracaena
Dracaena reflexa (pleomele), a widely cultivated plant previously classified in the genus Pleomele

items.name: Dracaena suffruticosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as UK frost will kill this tender tropical African species.
Use a gritty loam-based potting compost with added perlite to ensure the rapid drainage it requires.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil are dry, reducing to once a month during winter.
Position in bright, indirect light near a south-facing window to prevent leaf scorch in midsummer.
Repot in spring only when roots crowd the pot, using a heavy clay container to prevent tipping.
items.description: Dracaena suffruticosa, synonym Sansevieria suffruticosa is a species of Dracaena native to eastern Africa, from Ethiopia to Malawi. The first description of the species was made in 1915 by N. E. Brown.

items.name: Atropa baetica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Grow in well-drained alkaline chalky soil to mimic its native Spanish limestone habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers but keep soil relatively dry during winter dormancy.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn to prevent rot in wet British winters.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to avoid accidental skin absorption.
items.description: Atropa baetica, commonly known as the Andalusian belladonna, is one of Europe's rarest wildflowers. A close relative of the infamous deadly nightshade, its specific name derives from that of the Roman province of Hispania Baetica, while its common name refers to the Spanish region of Andalucía – both designating the area in the south of Spain where it is most frequently encountered. It is an attractive perennial plant with a herbaceous habit, bearing infundibuliform, yellow or greenish flowers and shiny, black berries. Like the other three species of Atropa, it is an extremely poisonous plant,

items.name: Dracaena goldieana
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical shrub above fifteen degrees Celsius year-round in a heated UK conservatory.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free loam-based compost dry out.
Position in bright filtered light away from direct midday sun to prevent leaf bleaching.
Maintain sixty percent humidity using a wet pebble tray to stop the leaf tips from turning brown.
Wipe the broad patterned leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations.
items.description: Dracaena goldieana, or queen of dracaenas, is a tropical shrub in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to Central Africa and Nigeria. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant, valued for its richly variegated foliage.

items.name: Dracaena surculosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub indoors in the UK as it cannot survive temperatures below ten Celsius.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free loam-based compost dry out.
Wipe the gold-dust spotted leaves monthly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite attacks.
Prune leggy bamboo-like canes back to a leaf node in spring to encourage bushy new basal growth.
Repot every two years in spring using a free-draining mix of houseplant compost and perlite.
items.description: Dracaena surculosa, called the gold dust dracaena and spotted dracaena, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to west and west-central tropical Africa, from Guinea to the Republic of the Congo. Its cultivar 'Florida Beauty' has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Scopolia carniolica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic woodland shade.
Sow seeds in cold frames during UK winter as they require a prolonged cold period to trigger growth.
Keep soil consistently damp during spring but allow it to dry slightly when the plant goes dormant.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to avoid absorbing alkaloids through skin.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the emerging bell-shaped purple flowers.
items.description: Scopolia carniolica, the European scopolia or henbane bell, is a poisonous plant belonging to tribe Hyoscyameae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. It bears dark brownish-violet nodding flowers on long, slender pedicels. It grows to 60 centimetres (24 in) in height. Its toxicity derives from its high levels of tropane alkaloids, particularly atropine. The concentration of atropine is highest in the roots.

items.name: Dracaena aethiopica
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender African plant cannot survive a UK winter outside.
Grow in a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil feel dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Position in a conservatory or south-facing windowsill to maximise crucial UK winter sunlight hours.
Repot in spring every two years using a container only one size larger to avoid waterlogged soil.
items.description: Dracaena aethiopica  is a species of succulent plant widely distributed in Southern Africa. Its binomial name—aethiopica—refers to its origins in Africa. A highly variable species, it grows in desert or dry shrubland and spreads rhizomatically. The leaves grow in rosettes and may be up to 70 centimetres (2.3 ft) tall. Genetically, this species is most closely related to Dracaena ballyi. In Africa, this species has been used to augment poisons for hunting and fishing purposes.

items.name: Dracaena trifasciata
items.growersTips:
Position your snake plant on a bright UK windowsill but shield it from harsh direct summer sun.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, reducing this to once every six weeks during UK winters.
Plant in a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free potting compost to one part horticultural grit.
Keep the plant indoors year-round as it will suffer damage if UK temperatures drop below ten degrees.
Wipe the upright leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve light absorption.
items.description: Dracaena trifasciata is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to tropical West Africa from Nigeria east to the Congo. It is most commonly known as the snake plant, Saint George's sword, mother-in-law's tongue, and viper's bowstring hemp, among other names. Until 2017, it was known under the synonym Sansevieria trifasciata. This plant is often kept as a houseplant due to its non-demanding maintenance; they can survive with very little water and sun.

items.name: Dracaena aletriformis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this tender South African shrub cannot survive UK winter freezes.
Grow in a pot with peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in cool UK weather.
Place in a bright room near an east or west window to avoid leaf scorch from direct summer sun.
Wipe the broad leathery leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and deter red spider mites.
items.description: Dracaena aletriformis is commonly known as the large-leaved dragon tree. These plants are found in forest in the eastern areas of South Africa from Port Elizabeth to northern and eastern Limpopo. They are also found in Eswatini, but are most common in the coastal and dune forests of KwaZulu-Natal.

items.name: Nolana galapagensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic island heat.
Grow this tender Solanaceae in terracotta pots with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK summers.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty compost are dry to prevent root rot in cool climates.
Move pots to a south-facing unheated greenhouse in October to protect the foliage from UK frosts.
Position near marigolds in the greenhouse to deter aphids and whiteflies from the sticky foliage.
items.description: Nolana galapagensis, is a species of flowering plant in the Solanaceae (nightshade) family. It is endemic to the Galapagos Islands.

items.name: Dracaena hyacinthoides
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot with 50% grit to move indoors before the first autumn frost hits your UK garden.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out completely to prevent winter root rot.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight.
Repot in spring using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of horticultural sand.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and check for glasshouse mealybugs.
items.description: Dracaena hyacinthoides, called the African bowstring hemp, Somali hemp, Somali good luck plant, piles root, iguanatail, and mother-in-law's-tongue, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to eastern Africa, from Kenya to South Africa, and it has been introduced to other locales, particularly Florida, the Caribbean, and Central America. An erect shrub reaching 0.9 m (3 ft), it is found in the seasonally dry tropics.

items.name: Disporopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in humus-rich, moist, well-drained acidic soil to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a five-centimetre mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted manure each spring to retain soil moisture.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to show.
items.description: Disporopsis is a genus of plants in the Asparagaceae. It is native to China, Indochina and the Philippines.

items.name: Comospermum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to beat UK chills.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall to maximise essential British summer sunshine.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells to prevent blossom end rot in the fruit.
Support the climbing vines with sturdy bamboo canes or a trellis as soon as active growth begins.
Apply a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser every fortnight once the first flower trusses appear.
items.description: Comospermum is a genus of one species of flowering plant found in southern Japan. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Dracaena kaweesakii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Thai native indoors before October frosts as it cannot survive UK winter wet.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting compost with added perlite to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil feels completely dry to prevent root rot.
Position in a conservatory or south-facing window to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight hours.
Wipe the strap-like leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent red spider mite infestations.
items.description: Dracaena kaweesakii is a species of dragon tree. It can reach 12 metres (39 ft) in both height and crown diameter. It is only found growing atop the limestone mountains in the Loei and the Lop Buri Provinces of Thailand.

items.name: Nicotiana rosulata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the compost surface in early spring as they need UK light to germinate.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy to prevent damping off in our cool British spring weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love chewing the tender young leaves of this Aussie native.
Plant them out in May after the last frost in a sunny, sheltered spot to mimic their warm home.
Feed them weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once they start blooming in midsummer.
items.description: Nicotiana rosulata is a plant in the family Solanaceae, native to Western Australia, South Australia and the Northern Territory.

items.name: Nicotiana forsteri
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March, as they need light and warmth to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently from below to protect the stems.
Watch out for slugs early on, so protect young plants with beer traps or copper tape in spring.
Plant them out in late May after the frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Feed them weekly with high-potash tomato food from July to keep those delicate blooms coming.
items.description: Nicotiana forsteri is a species of wild tobacco in the family Solanaceae, native to Queensland, New South Wales, Lord Howe Island, and New Caledonia. It is a tetraploid.

items.name: Speirantha
items.growersTips:
Plant in early spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil, burying the root crown exactly 5cm deep.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry UK summer spells to prevent blossom end rot.
Watch for potato beetles and aphids from June; handpick them or use organic insecticidal soap.
Prune lower yellowing leaves in late August to improve air circulation and speed up fruit ripening.
Grow alongside basil or marigolds to naturally deter pests and boost pollination in UK plots.
items.description: Speirantha is a genus of one known species of flowering plants found in south-east China. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Aspidistra
items.growersTips:
Keep in frost-free shade outdoors from May to September then bring inside before first autumn frost.
Water only when the top five centimetres of peat-free loam-based compost has dried out completely.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent dust blocking light in dim UK winters.
Repot only every four years in spring as they dislike root disturbance and prefer being congested.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in outdoor pots by checking roots if leaves yellow in chilly spring.
items.description: Aspidistra is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae, native to eastern and southeastern Asia, particularly China and Vietnam. They grow in shade under trees and shrubs. Their leaves arise more or less directly from ground level, where their flowers also appear. The number of species known has increased considerably from the 1980s onwards, with around 100 accepted as of July 2013. Aspidistra elatior is common worldwide as a foliage house plant that is very tolerant of neglect. It and other species can also be grown in shade outside, where they are ge

items.name: Scopolia japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in humus-rich, moist, well-drained alkaline soil to mimic woodland conditions.
Sow seeds in cold frames in autumn, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy for spring.
Water consistently during the spring growing phase, but keep the soil drier during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to prevent skin absorption of alkaloids.
items.description: Scopolia japonica, also Japanese belladonna or Korean scopolia, is a flowering plant species in the genus Scopolia - one of the eight genera in tribe Hyoscyameae of the nightshade family Solanaceae.

items.name: Dracaena ombet
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender African succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Use a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mixed with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, reducing to once a month during the dark winter months.
Place in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native arid, high-light environment.
Repot only every three years in spring as this slow-growing species prefers its roots to be confined.
items.description: Dracaena ombet, commonly known as Gabal Elba dragon tree, is a species of plant belonging to the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae, formerly included in the family Ruscaceae. It is found in northeastern Africa and the western Arabian Peninsula.

items.name: Dracaena tamaranae
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost to survive cold UK winters in a bright conservatory.
Water sparingly in winter, allowing the gritty, free-draining compost to dry out completely.
Repot in spring using a mix of two parts loam-based compost to one part horticultural grit.
Position in a south-facing spot to maximise scarce UK sunlight and prevent leaf drop.
Inspect leaf axils monthly for mealybugs, which thrive in dry indoor winter conditions.
items.description: Dracaena tamaranae, or drago de Gran Canaria, is a species of flowering plant endemic to the island of Gran Canaria, related to the dragon tree, Dracaena draco, and other species of Dracaena from East Africa. Since 1972, specimens of dragon tree have been identified in Gran Canaria with certain peculiarities. These were initially identified as specimens of Dracaena draco. However, a more detailed study concluded that it corresponded to a new species.

items.name: Dracaena angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as this tender tropical shrub cannot survive UK winters.
Keep compost consistently moist but never soggy using tepid rainwater to prevent root rot in winter.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to stop leaf tips turning brown.
Position in bright indirect light near a south-facing window, shielding it from harsh summer sun.
Feed monthly from April to September with a balanced liquid fertiliser diluted to half strength.
items.description: Dracaena angustifolia is a species of Asian tropical forest under-storey plants in the family Asparagaceae; no subspecies are listed in the Catalogue of Life.

items.name: Dracaena draco
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors from October to May as it cannot survive wet UK winters and frost below minus two.
Grow in a pots with fifty percent grit and perlite mixed with peat-free compost to prevent root rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry then drench and drain fully.
Place in the brightest south-facing spot in your garden or conservatory to maximise summer sun.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during winter storage and wipe them off with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Dracaena draco, the Canary Islands dragon tree or drago, is a subtropical tree in the genus Dracaena, native to the Macaronesia archipelago and northwestern mainland Africa.

items.name: Mandragora officinarum
items.growersTips:
Plant your mandrake root deep in a tall pot with gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Keep the soil barely damp in winter but water generously once those large spring leaves appear.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the young foliage.
Position your pot in a sheltered, sunny spot to mimic its native warm Mediterranean climate.
Let the plant die back naturally in summer and keep it completely dry during its dormant phase.
items.description: Mandragora officinarum is the type species of the plant genus Mandragora in the nightshade family Solanaceae. It is often known as mandrake, although this name is also used for other plants. As of 2015, sources differed significantly in the species they use for Mandragora plants native to the Mediterranean region. The main species found around the Mediterranean is called Mandragora autumnalis, the autumn mandrake. In a broader circumscription, all the plants native to the regions around the Mediterranean Sea are placed in M. officinarum, which thus includes M. autumnalis. The names autumn mand

items.name: Dracaena reflexa
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before autumn night temperatures drop below ten degrees to prevent cold damage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost dries out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Repot in spring using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third perlite for sharp drainage.
Prune leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage bushier growth in low UK light.
Wipe leaves monthly with a damp cloth to remove dust and check for mealybugs in heated winter rooms.
items.description: Dracaena reflexa is a tree native to Mozambique, Madagascar, Mauritius, and other nearby islands of the Indian Ocean. It is widely grown as an ornamental plant and houseplant, valued for its richly coloured, evergreen leaves, and thick, irregular stems.

items.name: Reineckea
items.growersTips:
Sow Reineckea seeds indoors in early March at a depth of six millimetres using a heated propagator.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy to prevent damping off in cool British spring weather.
Apply a high-potassium liquid feed every fortnight once the first yellow flowers begin to open.
Watch for tomato hornworms and aphids under leaves during humid UK midsummer afternoons.
Stake the main stem early with a bamboo cane to support heavy fruit during wet and windy Augusts.
items.description: Reineckea is a genus of plants in the Convallarioideae. Several species names have been proposed within the genus, but only one is widely accepted: Reineckea carnea, native to China and Japan.

items.name: Tupistra
items.growersTips:
Grow in a greenhouse or bright conservatory as this tender exotic cannot survive UK winter frosts
Plant rhizomes five centimetres deep in a well-drained loamy compost mixed with plenty of grit
Water moderately in summer keeping soil damp but reduce watering in winter to prevent root rot
Wipe the broad evergreen leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent red spider mite infestations
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer with a balanced liquid fertiliser to encourage spike blooms
items.description: Tupistra is a genus of about 20 species of flowering plants found in south Asia, from southern China to Sumatra and Ambon Island. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Polygonatum verticillatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade and moist, humus-rich, neutral to acid soil to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water regularly during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Watch for sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent complete defoliation.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to retain essential moisture.
items.description: Polygonatum verticillatum or whorled Solomon's-seal is a plant species of the genus Polygonatum. It is widespread in Europe and also in China and the Himalayas though not reported from large sections of western and Central Asia in between those two ranges.

items.name: Dracaena pethera
items.growersTips:
Bring potted plants indoors by October to protect them from wet UK winters and frost damage.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool climates.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining loam mix with added perlite to mimic their native dry soil.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise scarce winter sunlight.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints during humid summer spells and treat with neem oil.
items.description: Dracaena pethera, synonym Sansevieria kirkii, also known as the star sansevieria or the snake plant, is a succulent plant native to Tanzania and the surrounding region in East Africa.

items.name: Datura ferox
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators during March as our UK springs are too cold for germination.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest spot using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent rot.
Water deeply but let the soil dry out completely between waterings to mimic their dry native lands.
Keep a sharp eye out for greenhouse red spider mites which love these plants in dry UK summers.
Wear thick gloves when handling this toxic beauty and avoid planting it near any edible vegetables.
items.description: Datura ferox, commonly known as long spined thorn apple and fierce thornapple, as well as Angel's-trumpets, is a species of Datura. Like all such species, every part of the plant contains deadly toxins that can kill animals that ingest it. Its fruit, red-brown when ripe, has unusually long thorns or spikes.

items.name: Dracaena americana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive cold UK winter frosts.
Plant in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the sharp drainage it requires.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil have dried out completely in summer.
Prune leggy stems back to a node in spring to encourage bushier growth and maintain its shape.
Check leaf axils regularly for mealybugs which thrive in warm indoor UK growing environments.
items.description: Dracaena americana, the Central American dragon tree or candlewood, is a neotropical tree in the genus Dracaena, native to southern Mexico, Guatemala, Panama, Honduras, Belize, Costa Rica, and Colombia. It is one of only two Dracaena species native to the Americas, the other being Dracaena cubensis.

items.name: Dracaena arborea
items.growersTips:
Grow in a loam-based compost with added grit, keeping the pot in a bright, frost-free conservatory.
Water sparingly in winter, only when the top five centimetres of compost has dried out completely.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to stimulate bushy new growth, sealing cuts to prevent rot.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent red spider mite infestations indoors.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost leaf growth.
items.description: Dracaena arborea, the tree dracaena, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to western and west-central wet tropical Africa. It is used as a street tree in a number of African and Brazilian cities.

items.name: Danae racemosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich acidic to neutral soil in deep shade to mimic UK woodlands.
Water weekly during dry UK summers until established to prevent the glossy evergreen foliage drying.
Prune out old damaged stems at the base in late spring to encourage fresh bright green new shoots.
Propagate by dividing the slow-growing rootball in spring or sowing ripe red berries in autumn cold frames.
Watch for slug and snail damage on tender new shoots emerging from the soil in damp British springs.
items.description: Danae is a monotypic genus of flowering plants. The single species, Danae racemosa, is native to west Asia. It is a slow-growing evergreen shrub about 60 cm in diameter and its common names are Alexandrian laurel and poet's laurel. In the APG III classification system, Danae is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Schizanthus pinnatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in late winter indoors at just two millimetres deep to get a head start on spring.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy to prevent damping off disease in our wet British spring.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimetres to encourage a bushier flower display.
Acclimatise them gently to the outdoors in May once the very last frost has safely passed your area.
Watch out for aphids and slugs on the tender young stems during damp early summer mornings.
items.description: Schizanthus pinnatus, called butterfly flower or poor man's orchid, names it shares with other members of its genus, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. It is native to Chile and naturalized elsewhere. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit as an ornamental.

items.name: Dracaena cochinchinensis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this tender evergreen cannot survive UK winter freezes.
Grow in free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil feels dry then water thoroughly and let drain.
Place in a south-facing conservatory or bright windowsill to maximise limited UK winter sunlight.
Repot in spring every two to three years using a heavy clay pot to prevent the plant tipping over.
items.description: Dracaena cochinchinensis is a species of Asian tropical forest under-storey plants in the family Asparagaceae; no subspecies are listed in the Catalogue of Life.

items.name: Peliosanthes
items.growersTips:
Grow under glass in a heated greenhouse as this tropical Asian native cannot survive UK winters.
Use a peat-free compost mixed with one-third perlite to ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British weather.
Keep in dappled shade or indirect light to mimic its natural forest floor habitat and avoid scorch.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius to keep the evergreen foliage alive.
items.description: Peliosanthes is a genus of flowering plants found in eastern Asia. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae.

items.name: Dracaena aubryana
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender African shrub indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow in a free-draining peat-free loam with added perlite to prevent root rot in cool climates.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry, reducing this to once a month in winter.
Place in a bright room with indirect light, avoiding cold draughts from drafty UK windows.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and prevent red spider mite attacks.
items.description: Dracaena aubryana, the lance dracaena, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to west-central Tropical Africa, and it has been introduced to Hawaii. An erect shrub reaching 0.5 to 2.5 m, it is found in the seasonally dry tropics. It is occasionally kept as an ornamental.

items.name: Physalis infinemundi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Grow in pots of peat-free loam-based compost to easily move plants indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in cool summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage bushy growth and increase the yield of lantern fruit.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing under glass in humid UK midsummers.
items.description: Physalis infinemundi is an extinct species of the genus Physalis known from two fossilised fruit found in the Laguna del Hunco Formation of Chubut Province, Argentina dating to the Eocene, around 52 million years old. The species name derives from "in fine mundi" means "at the end of the earth" referring to the fact that it grew in the far south. The fossil was considerably older than the diversification ages predicted by previous molecular clock studies of Solanaceae, which estimated that the family as a whole originated 30 million years ago. The fossils are very similar to modern Physalis sp

items.name: Datura metel
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators around March since our UK spring is too cold for them.
Plant them out in late May only after the final frost, choosing the sunniest, most sheltered spot.
Water them deeply but let the soil dry out completely between times to prevent any root rot.
Wear thick gloves whenever you prune or handle this plant because all its parts are highly toxic.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
items.description: Datura metel is a shrub-like annual or short-lived, shrubby perennial, commonly known in Europe as Indian thornapple, Hindu datura, or metel and in the United States as devil's trumpet or angel's trumpet. Datura metel is naturalised in all the warmer countries of the world. It is found notably in India, where it is known by the ancient, Sanskrit-derived, Hindi name dhatūra (धतूरा), from which the genus name Datura is derived.

items.name: Semele
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at ten millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty-one degrees Celsius.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as this Solanaceae crop demands more summer heat than UK climates.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil moist but prevent blight on the foliage.
Support the climbing vines with sturdy bamboo canes or trellis as soon as active growth begins.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flowers start to open.
items.description: In Greek mythology, Semele, or Thyone, was the youngest daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and the mother of Dionysus by Zeus.

items.name: Petunia ×atkinsiana
items.growersTips:
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in May to encourage bushy growth and more flower buds.
Water at the base in the morning to keep foliage dry and prevent grey mould during damp UK summers.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly by pinching off the flower and the green seed pod base to prolong flowering.
Apply a high-potash liquid feed every fortnight from July to September to sustain heavy blooming.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or wool pellets immediately after planting.
items.description: Petunia × atkinsiana is a Petunia plant "nothospecies" (hybrid), which encompasses all hybrid species of petunia between P. axillaris and P. integrifolia. Most of the petunias sold for cultivation in home gardens are this type and belong to this nothospecies. It is said to have originated with the Quaker plantsman James Atkins at his nursery at Painshill in 1834 but did not spread around the world until the 1990s.

items.name: Maianthemum gigas
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil in partial to full woodland shade.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or composted bark to mimic its native forest floor.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in April.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early autumn after the red berries have finished.
items.description: Maianthemum gigas is a perennial flowering plant. It is found in Mexico and Central America, growing in forest openings and along roadsides or sometimes as an epiphyte on trees.

items.name: Maianthemum scilloideum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native cool woodland habitat.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to protect emerging shoots from late spring frosts.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn after foliage dies back to propagate and maintain vigour.
items.description: Maianthemum scilloideum is a perennial flowering plant. It is a terrestrial forest herb from southern Mexico and Guatemala and also reported from Honduras.

items.name: Dracaena concinna
items.growersTips:
Grow under glass in the UK as this tender tropical shrub cannot survive winter frosts outdoors.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, reducing watering significantly during winter.
Repot in spring using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit for sharp drainage.
Position in bright, indirect light to prevent the narrow, red-edged leaves from scorching in summer.
Wipe the leaves regularly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations in dry indoor air.
items.description: Dracaena concinna is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to Mauritius.

items.name: Dracaena umbraculifera
items.growersTips:
