Bring indoors by October to protect this tender shrub from wet UK winters and frost damage.
Grow in a pot with peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit for essential drainage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil feels dry to prevent root rot in cool climates.
Place in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to mimic its native tropical light.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and deter glasshouse red spider mite.
items.description: Dracaena umbraculifera is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is a tree that was only known from botanical gardens since the end of the 18th century, the original sample was labelled as originating from the island nation of Mauritius. It was declared to be extinct by the IUCN in 1997. This was clearly incorrect, as there are living specimens in botanical gardens around the world. Searches on Mauritius failed to find any trees, however, so it was thought that the IUCN probably should have more correctly assessed the species as 'extinct in the wild'. As such a team of res

items.name: Dracaena steudneri
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this tender African shrub cannot survive wet UK winters.
Grow in a heavy loam-based compost like John Innes No 3 mixed with one-third grit for drainage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil feel dry to prevent root rot in cool climates.
Position in a bright conservatory or south-facing room but shade from scorching midsummer sun.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage branching and propagate the cuttings in warm water.
items.description: Dracaena steudneri, the northern large-leaved dragon-tree, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, found from Ethiopia to southern tropical Africa. It is being investigated for its high-quality fiber content. It is fed upon by larvae of the bush nightfighter, Artitropa erinnys. In the past the name Dracaena steudneri was erroneously assigned to the well-known ornamental and house plant Dracaena fragrans, called the cornstalk dracaena, striped dracaena, compact dracaena, and corn plant, leading to much confusion.

items.name: Dracaena bacularis
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender houseplant indoors before UK autumn night temperatures drop below twelve degrees.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Position in bright indirect light near an east or west window to avoid scorching the thin foliage.
Repot in spring using a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part perlite.
Wipe the cylindrical leaves monthly with a damp cloth to remove dust and check for mealybugs.
items.description: Dracaena bacularis, the rod‑leaved snake plant, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. A rhizomatous geophyte eventually reaching 1.7 m, it can be distinguished from similar members of its genus by its cylindrical leaves, and by the purple sheathes at their bases.

items.name: Nierembergia linariifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this in gritty, sharply draining soil to help it survive wet, cold UK winters without rotting.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your garden to mimic its native warmth.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, letting the top few inches of soil dry out first.
Shear back the faded stems by half in late summer to trigger a fresh flush of those violet blooms.
Bring containers into an unheated greenhouse or porch by October to protect them from hard UK frosts.
items.description: Nierembergia linariifolia, called the narrow-leaved cupflower, is a species of plant described by Robert Graham. Nierembergia linariifolia is part of the genus Nierembergia and the family Solanaceae. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Physaleae
items.growersTips:
Start physalis seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the short UK growing season.
Bury the root ball deep up to the first leaves when planting out in late May to boost root growth.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep drought-proof roots.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite if you are growing them in a UK greenhouse.
Grow them alongside basil and marigolds to help deter pests and boost your harvest naturally.
items.description: Physaleae is a tribe of flowering plants in the subfamily Solanoideae of the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Chamaesaracha
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, sharply draining neutral soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave pots outdoors to experience natural winter chilling for germination.
Plant in your warmest, south-facing border or against a sunny wall to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails which target tender Solanaceae growth in damp UKs.
items.description: Chamaesaracha is a genus of perennial herbs in the nightshade family which are known commonly as five eyes. There are around nine species of five eyes, and they are native to the southwestern and western United States and parts of Mexico. These are hairy plants growing low to the ground and covered in crinkly dull green leaves. The flowers are star-shaped to wheel-shaped and their dried remnants can be found around the fruits, which are spherical berries filled with flat, kidney-shaped seeds.

items.name: Nicandra physalodes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April, barely covered with compost, as they need warmth and light to germinate.
Plant out in late May after the frosts, spacing them 60cm apart because they grow into massive bushes.
Keep them in your sunniest spot and water deeply once a week rather than giving them daily splashes.
Watch out for whitefly and aphids on the soft new leaves, and blast them off with a sharp hose spray.
Deadhead the lantern pods before they turn brown and drop seeds, or they will take over your garden.
items.description: Nicandra physalodes is a species of flowering plant in subfamily Solanoideae of the nightshade family. It is known by the common names apple-of-Peru and shoo-fly plant. It is thought originally to have been native to western South America, including Peru, and is known elsewhere as an introduced and ruderal species – sometimes as a weed – in tropical, subtropical and, to a lesser extent, temperate areas all over the world. It has also long been cultivated as an ornamental plant for its attractive flowers and curious fruits and has been adopted into the traditional medicine of countries far-remo

items.name: Schwenckia curviflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots using free-draining loam to easily move this tender Solanaceae indoors before frost.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Position in your warmest south-facing spot or greenhouse to mimic its tropical light needs.
Prune back leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more purple flowers.
Watch closely for aphids and glasshouse whitefly which target this family in humid UK conditions.
items.description: Schwenckia curviflora is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to southeastern and southern Brazil as well as southeastern Uruguay. It is a perennial plant that grows primarily in seasonally dry tropical biomes. The species belongs to the genus Schwenckia, a group of herbaceous plants and subshrubs mainly distributed in tropical regions of the Americas.

items.name: Hyoscyameae
items.growersTips:
Sow your henbane seeds in spring after chilling them in the fridge to mimic UK winter conditions.
Grow these in poor, well-drained sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Keep a sharp eye out for potato beetles and flea beetles which love munching these leafy nightshades.
Water sparingly once established, letting the top few inches of soil dry out completely between runs.
Wear thick gloves when pruning or handling these plants to protect your skin from their toxic sap.
items.description: Hyoscyameae is an Old World tribe of the subfamily Solanoideae of the flowering plant family Solanaceae. It comprises seven genera: Anisodus, Atropa, Atropanthe, Hyoscyamus, Physochlaina, Przewalskia and Scopolia. The genera Atropanthe and Przewalskia are monotypic, the first being endemic to China and the second to Tibet.

items.name: Withania riebeckii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Grow in pots of gritty, free-draining loam to easily move plants indoors before first autumn frosts
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed fortnightly once the first star-shaped flowers appear
Check foliage weekly for red spider mites which thrive on this plant in dry greenhouse conditions
items.description: Withania riebeckii is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae. It is endemic to the islands of Socotra and Samhah in Yemen's Socotra Archipelago. It is widespread in succulent shrubland and drought deciduous woodland from sea-level to 800 metres elevation.

items.name: Withania
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them into a greenhouse before autumn frosts.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of compost to dry out between drinks.
Watch for greenhouse whitefly and red spider mite, treating early with organic insecticidal soap.
Harvest the roots in October of the second year after the berries turn bright red and leaves yellow.
items.description: Withania is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, with 19 to 23 species that are native to parts of North Africa, western Asia, south Asia, southern Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Canary Islands. Withania was initially included within Physalis by Linnaeus in 1753 but has since become its own genus. This grouping was due to the shared feature of an inflated calyx that surrounds and protects the fruit.

items.name: Fabiana imbricata
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, acidic to neutral soil, adding grit to the planting hole to prevent rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to protect it from cold, drying UK winter winds.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between summer waterings.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in early summer to maintain shape and prevent legginess.
Protect young plants with horticultural fleece during severe, prolonged winter frosts below -5C.
items.description: Fabiana imbricata, vernacular names pichi, palo piche, or false heath, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to dry upland slopes in the foothills of the southern Andes of Chile and Argentina. Growing to 2.5 m tall and wide, it is a frost-hardy, heath-like evergreen mound-forming shrub. It has needle-like leaves and small white, tubular flowers in early summer.

items.name: Nierembergia rivularis
items.growersTips:
Pop this creeping cupflower in a spot with moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that stays damp.
Plant your crowns just level with the soil surface in spring so they do not rot in wet UK winters.
Give it a generous drink twice a week during dry summer spells to keep those white blooms coming.
Slugs love the tender new shoots, so protect them with organic wool pellets in early spring.
Divide the creeping mats every three years in April to keep the centre from dying out and going bare.
items.description: Nierembergia rivularis, the whitecup or water neirembergia, is a species of ornamental plant in the Solanaceae family. The species is also commonly known as chuscho.

items.name: Iochroma grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender shrub cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Grow in pots of loam-based compost with added grit to easily move the plant inside during autumn.
Water copiously in summer but keep the soil barely damp during the dormant winter housing period.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new wood which produces the blue flowers.
Watch closely for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping the plant under cover.
items.description: Iochroma grandiflorum is an Iochroma species found in Ecuador. It was first described in 1845

items.name: Iochroma warscewiczii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot of peat-free loam compost so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Water copiously in summer but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormancy to prevent rot.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to encourage the fresh wood needed for summer flowering.
Check the soft new spring growth regularly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite infestations.
Feed weekly from May to September with a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser to boost blue blooms.
items.description: Iochroma warscewiczii is a shrub in the family Solanaceae. The species, which is native to Peru, was formally described in 1855 by German botanist Eduard August von Regel. It is named for the Polish botanist and explorer Józef Warszewicz Ritter von Rawicz (1812-1866).

items.name: Nolaneae
items.growersTips:
Plant your Chilean bellflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Keep these seaside natives happy by tucking them into a sunny, sheltered gravel garden or rockery.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect the tender young shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps during damp UK springs.
Bring potted Nolana indoors to a frost-free greenhouse before the first autumn frosts hit.
items.description: Nolana is a genus of hard annual or perennial plants in the nightshade family. The genus is mostly native to Chile and Peru. Species in this genus, especially N. paradoxa, serve as a model system for studies on flower color.

items.name: Acnistus arborescens
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender shrub indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from freezing UK winters.
Water generously during dry summer spells but let the compost dry out slightly between soakings.
Feed with a high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight in summer to boost those lovely blooms.
Prune lightly in early spring to shape the plant and encourage bushy new growth for more flowers.
Grow it in a large, well-drained pot using peat-free loam-based compost to easily move it inside.
items.description: Iochroma arborescens is a species of flowering plant in the genus Iochroma, belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Formerly it was considered the single species in the monotypic genus Acnistus. Common names include gallinero, mata-gallina, fruta-de-sabiá, hollowheart, wild tobacco, siyou, bastard sirio, galán arbóreo, tabaco de monte, nigüito, marieneira, güitite, and tabak djab.

items.name: Nierembergia veitchii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in pots of gritty loam so you can move it indoors before the autumn frosts.
Sow the seeds shallowly in early spring on a warm windowsill and keep the compost damp not soggy.
Water your potted plants deeply only when the top two inches of soil feel completely dry to touch.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are overwintering them in your conservatory.
Prune back the straggly stems by half in late winter to encourage bushy new growth for the summer.
items.description: Nierembergia veitchii is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae. The species is commonly called the trailing cup plant.

items.name: Tzeltalia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity this Mexican native needs
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot issues
Support the sprawling stems with canes or a small trellis as the heavy lantern fruits develop
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite under glass and use biological controls early
items.description: Tzeltalia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Withania frutescens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to protect roots from wet UK winter rot.
Move the pot to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to April to survive UK cold.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, mimicking Mediterranean heat.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in late April to stimulate bushy new growth and more flowers.
Inspect the undersides of leaves weekly in summer for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly pests.
items.description: Withania frutescens is a plant species belonging to the family Solanaceae. It is native to the western Mediterranean region, including southern Iberia, the Balearic Islands, Northwest Africa and the Canary Islands.

items.name: Withania somnifera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them indoors before the first autumn frost
Water sparingly once established, allowing the compost to dry out completely between waterings
Prune back by half in late spring to encourage bushy growth and increase root yield for autumn harvest
Check regularly for red spider mites when growing under glass or in warm greenhouse conditions
items.description: Withania somnifera, known commonly as ashwagandha, is an evergreen shrub in the Solanaceae family that is native to the Middle East and North Africa, other African regions, southern Europe, Indian subcontinent, and across Southeast Asia. Several other species in the genus Withania are morphologically similar. Other common names include Indian ginseng and winter cherry.

items.name: Nothocestrum
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Hawaiian tree in a heated greenhouse to survive the damp, chilly British winters.
Use a very free-draining, gritty compost mix to prevent root rot during our cloudy, wet seasons.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out, mimicking its natural volcanic habitat.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites, which love the dry warmth of indoor spaces.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the branches and encourage fresh, healthy tropical growth.
items.description: Nothocestrum is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. It contains four species of large shrubs or small trees that are endemic to Hawaii, where they are known as ʻaiea.

items.name: Mellissia
items.growersTips:
Start your Mellissia seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant them out in late May after the frosts, spacing them forty centimetres apart in rich soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering deeply at the base every three days.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British evenings.
Feed them weekly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertiliser once the first flowers appear.
items.description: Mellissia was formerly a monotypic genus in the family Solanaceae with the single species, Mellissia begoniifolia, endemic to the island of Saint Helena. It was named by Joseph Dalton Hooker in honour of John Charles Melliss, a 19th-century engineer and amateur naturalist who worked on Saint Helena.

items.name: Nolana
items.growersTips:
Sow Nolana seeds indoors in March to get a head start on our short, cool British summers.
Plant them out in May in your sunniest border using gritty soil to ensure excellent drainage.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between soakings.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more blue flowers.
Bring a few potted plants into a frost-free greenhouse by October to overwinter them safely.
items.description: Nolana is a genus of hard annual or perennial plants in the nightshade family. The genus is mostly native to Chile and Peru. Species in this genus, especially N. paradoxa, serve as a model system for studies on flower color.

items.name: Mandragora autumnalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep gritty loam to accommodate the long taproot and prevent winter wet rot in UK soils.
Sow fresh seeds in autumn and expose them to winter cold outdoors to break their natural dormancy.
Position in full sun but protect the delicate autumn blooms from heavy rain using a cloche.
Water sparingly in summer during their dormant phase to mimic their native dry Mediterranean climate.
Protect young foliage from slugs and snails which are highly attracted to the toxic leaves in spring.
items.description: Mandragora autumnalis, known as mandrake or autumn mandrake, is recognized by some sources as a separate species from Mandragora officinarum, although with different circumscriptions. Others regard it as merely part of this very variable species. Plants given the name Mandragora autumnalis consist of a rosette of leaves up to 60 cm (2 ft) across, close to the ground, with a central group of usually purplish flowers followed by yellow or orange berries. The large tap-roots as well as the leaves contain alkaloids and are toxic. They have traditional uses as herbal medicines.

items.name: Withania coagulans
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender shrub cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of sandy, free-draining soil mix have dried out completely.
Prune lightly in late spring to maintain a bushy shape and encourage new berry-bearing growth.
Monitor indoor plants closely for red spider mites and whiteflies in dry summer conditions.
items.description: Withania coagulans is a plant in the Solanaceae or nightshade family, native to Afghanistan and the Indian subcontinent. Within the genus Withania, W. somnifera (Ashwagandha) and W. coagulans are economically significant, and are cultivated in several regions for their use in Ayurveda. It is claimed to help control diabetes. The berries contain a rennet-like protease that can be used to clot milk for cheese production. The plant is prone to leaf spot disease caused by Alternaria alternata.

items.name: Eriolarynx
items.growersTips:
Start Eriolarynx seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant them out in late May after the last frost, spacing them forty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged in damp UK summers.
Feed your plants with a high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight once the first flowers open.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet spells by using organic wool pellets around the stems.
items.description: Eriolarynx is a genus of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae, found in Peru, Bolivia and northern Argentina. Their trumpet-shaped flowers are pollinated by hummingbirds, and to a lesser extent, bees.

items.name: Datureae
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat our short British summers.
Grow them in large, dark pots to absorb maximum sunlight and keep soil temperatures high.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells, keeping leaves dry to prevent grey mould.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first trumpet-shaped flowers appear.
Check the undersides of leaves weekly for glasshouse red spider mites during hot July weather.
items.description: Daturae is a tribe of flowering plants in the subfamily Solanoideae of the family Solanaceae. It comprises three genera: Datura, the Devil's trumpets, Brugmansia, the Angel's trumpets, and the monotypic Trompettia.

items.name: Sansevieria ehrenbergii
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty cactus compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Water only when soil is bone dry, reducing to once every two months from November through March.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK sunlight and maintain a warm microclimate.
Protect from drafts and ensure indoor temperatures never drop below twelve degrees Celsius in winter.
Repot only when the fan-shaped leaves literally begin to crack or push out of the plastic pot.
items.description: Dracaena hanningtonii, synonym Sansevieria ehrenbergii, is a flowering plant which grows in northeastern and eastern tropical Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. It occurs notably in proliferation along the Olduvai Gorge in northern Tanzania.

items.name: Sansevieria trifasciata
items.growersTips:
Position on a bright UK windowsill but keep dry in winter to prevent root rot in unheated rooms
Plant in a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part grit or perlite
Only water when the compost has completely dried out to cope with cool and damp UK climates
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve light absorption
Repot in spring only when the roots start cracking the plastic pot as they prefer being tight
items.description: Dracaena trifasciata is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to tropical West Africa from Nigeria east to the Congo. It is most commonly known as the snake plant, Saint George's sword, mother-in-law's tongue, and viper's bowstring hemp, among other names. Until 2017, it was known under the synonym Sansevieria trifasciata. This plant is often kept as a houseplant due to its non-demanding maintenance; they can survive with very little water and sun.

items.name: Solanum
items.growersTips:
Start aubergines indoors in February with a heat mat to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Bury your tomato stems deep up to the first leaves when planting out to grow a massive root system.
Feed your potatoes weekly with high-potassium liquid seaweed once those first flowers start to open.
Prune away the lower leaves of outdoor tomatoes in August to let the weak British sun ripen fruit.
Keep a sharp eye out for potato blight after warm, humid wet spells in July and strip affected leaves.
items.description: Solanum is a large and diverse genus of flowering plants, which include three food crops of high economic importance: the potato, the tomato and the eggplant. It is the largest genus in the nightshade family Solanaceae, comprising around 1,500 species. It also contains the so-called horse nettles, as well as numerous plants cultivated for their ornamental flowers and fruit.

items.name: Capsiceae
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by late February to beat the short UK growing season.
Keep soil damp but never soggy to prevent root rot, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach twenty centimetres tall to encourage a bushy habit.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food once the first tiny green fruits begin to form in June.
Watch out for aphids and whiteflies under greenhouse glass, using soapy water sprays to clear them.
items.description: Capsiceae is a taxonomic tribe of bell peppers and related plants belonging to the Solanoideae subfamily within the family Solanaceae. The tribe was described by Barthélemy Charles Joseph Dumortier in 1827.

items.name: Tubocapsicum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in February to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow these pepper relatives in a greenhouse or sunny south-facing patio to get enough summer heat.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food once the first tiny star-shaped flowers begin to open.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy, preventing blossom end rot.
Watch out for aphids and glasshouse whiteflies, using yellow sticky traps to catch them early.
items.description: Tubocapsicum is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Leucophysalis
items.growersTips:
Start these tender tomatillo relatives indoors in March to beat the short, cool UK summer season.
Plant them outside in June in a sunny, sheltered spot, spaced fifty centimetres apart in rich soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering at the base to prevent blight on leaves.
Watch out for greenhouse whiteflies and aphids, using yellow sticky traps to catch them early on.
Support their sprawling stems with sturdy bamboo canes and soft twine as the heavy husks develop.
items.description: Leucophysalis is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Datura discolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Plant out in June only after all frost risk has passed into the sunniest, most sheltered spot.
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep soil moist but never waterlogged during dry spells.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect against the highly toxic sap during any leaf tidying.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves in dry summer weather and mist with water to deter them.
items.description: Datura discolor, also called the desert thorn-apple, is an herbaceous annual plant native to the Sonoran Desert of western North America, where it grows in sandy soils and washes. All parts of the plant contain a mix of alkaloids that are potentially lethal when enough is ingested.

items.name: Dyssochroma
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors by October to shield its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in a free-draining, grit-heavy loam to prevent rotting.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as this plant hates soggy feet.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when growing this exotic under glass in dry summer heat.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from May to August to boost growth.
items.description: Dyssochroma is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Calibanus hookeri
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as it is a Mexican succulent, not a Solanaceae vegetable.
Use a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent caudex rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry throughout winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing window or greenhouse spot to mimic its desert habitat.
Watch for mealybugs hiding in the dense, grass-like foliage clumps and treat with isopropyl alcohol.
items.description: One of only two species in its genus, Calibanus hookeri is a member of the family Asparagaceae native to Tamaulipas in Mexico, which can easily be mistaken in the wild for a boulder overgrown with grass tufts.

items.name: Iochroma
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Iochroma indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top two inches of gritty, acidic soil dry out first.
Prune back hard in early spring just as new growth starts to keep this vigorous shrub in bounds.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering your plants in the conservatory.
Feed with a high-potassium tomato fertiliser fortnightly from May to September to boost those blooms.
items.description: Iochroma is a genus of about 34 species of shrubs and small trees belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Species are native from Mexico to south Brazil. They are found in the forests of Mexico and South America. Their hummingbird-pollinated flowers are tubular or trumpet-shaped, and may be blue, purple, red, yellow, or white, becoming pulpy berries. The cupular (cup-shaped) calyx is inflated in some species. The leaves are alternate, simple, and entire.

items.name: Quincula
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early April to give this warm-climate groundcherry enough summer heat.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their dry native soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Keep a sharp eye out for greenhouse whiteflies and red spider mites under the leaves in July.
Grow them alongside basil or French marigolds to help deter pests naturally in your veg patch.
items.description: Quincula is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. The sole species it contains, Quincula lobata, is commonly known as Chinese lantern, lobed groundcherry, or purple groundcherry.

items.name: Sansevieria masoniana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heavy clay pot with gritty, free-draining cacti compost to prevent top-heavy tipping.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once every six weeks during damp UK winters.
Position in bright, indirect light near a south window, keeping temperatures strictly above 10C.
Wipe the single large leaf monthly with a damp cloth to remove dust and maximise winter light.
Propagate in spring by dividing the rhizome with a sterile knife, leaving one leaf per section.
items.description: Dracaena masoniana, synonym Sansevieria masoniana, is a species of Dracaena native to Africa and originally collected in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was initially known in cultivation under the cultivar name 'Mason Congo'. Commonly grown as a houseplant for its striking foliage, it can survive in bright filtered light or shade and with infrequent watering. Often grown as a single large, stiff leaf in pots, the plant's other common names include "whale fin" or "shark's fin".

items.name: Nierembergia scoparia
items.growersTips:
Plant this cup flower in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Give it a sheltered, south-facing spot to soak up every bit of our precious British summer sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between sessions.
Cut the stems back by half in late autumn, then mulch heavily to protect the crown from UK frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love to munch on the fresh new shoots.
items.description: Nierembergia scoparia is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Physalis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early March to give these slow growers enough warmth before the UK summer.
Plant them out in late May after the last frost, burying the root ball deep just like a tomato.
Water them deeply once a week at the base to prevent fruit splitting during dry summer spells.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage bushy growth and get more lanterns per plant.
Watch out for capsid bugs in June, which love to nibble the leaves and ruin the developing husks.
items.description: Physalis is a genus of approximately 75 to 90 flowering plants in the nightshade family (Solanaceae), which are native to the Americas and Australasia. At least 46 species are endemic to Mexico. Cultivated and weedy species have been introduced worldwide. A defining feature of Physalis is a large, papery husk derived from the calyx, which partly or fully encloses the fruit. Many species bear edible fruit, and some species are cultivated.

items.name: Eriolarynx australis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator for UK warmth.
Grow in pots of peat-free compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this plant requires.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as this species cannot survive frost.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing under glass in the UK climate.
items.description: Eriolarynx australis, called mini angel's trumpet or blue angel's trumpet, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Eriolarynx, native to Bolivia and northwest Argentina. It is widely listed in the horticultural literature under the synonym Iochroma australe. It has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Athenaea
items.growersTips:
Start your Athenaea seeds indoors in early March using bottom heat to beat the cool UK spring.
Grow Athenaea in a greenhouse or south-facing border to give them the maximum summer sun they need.
Feed your Athenaea weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first flowers start to open.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and mist the foliage regularly to keep the humidity high.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and get more flowers and fruit.
items.description: The Panathenaic Games were held every four years in Athens in Ancient Greece from 566 BC to the 3rd century AD. These Games incorporated religious festival, ceremony, athletic competitions, and cultural events hosted within a stadium.

items.name: Vassobia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Vassobia indoors before the first autumn frost to keep this tender perennial alive.
Water your Vassobia deeply once a week at the base, letting the top inch of soil dry out between times.
Feed with a high-potassium tomato fertilizer every fortnight in summer to boost its purple blooms.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more potential fruit.
Plant Vassobia in a sheltered, south-facing spot to maximize the limited UK summer sun and warmth.
items.description: Vassobia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Datura quercifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic desert heat.
Grow this tender annual in pots of gritty, free-draining soil placed against a south-facing wall.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in wet summers.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant and prune dead stems only in late autumn.
Position near French marigolds to deter spider mites, which thrive on Datura in dry UK glasshouses.
items.description: Datura quercifolia, commonly known as the oak-leaved thorn-apple and also the Chinese Thorn-Apple, is a small shrub in the genus Datura that is native to Mexico and the Southwestern United States. It grows equally well in dry and moist soils and requires full sun. It contains a mix of alkaloids that are poisonous and can be potentially lethal when ingested.

items.name: Iochroma arborescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in late May after frosts in rich loamy soil mixed with grit for essential winter drainage.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the root zone barely damp during cold winter months.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new wood which produces the best blooms.
Overwinter in a pot indoors or wrap the base in thick fleece to survive wet UK winter freezes.
Check regularly for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping sheltered under glass.
items.description: Iochroma arborescens is a species of flowering plant in the genus Iochroma, belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Formerly it was considered the single species in the monotypic genus Acnistus. Common names include gallinero, mata-gallina, fruta-de-sabiá, hollowheart, wild tobacco, siyou, bastard sirio, galán arbóreo, tabaco de monte, nigüito, marieneira, güitite, and tabak djab.

items.name: Dunalia
items.growersTips:
Start your Dunalia seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short UK growing season.
Plant Dunalia outside in late May only after the final frost, spacing them fifty centimetres apart.
Feed your Dunalia weekly with high-potassium tomato food once the first tiny fruits start to form.
Watch out for greenhouse whiteflies on Dunalia leaves and hang yellow sticky traps to catch them.
Grow Dunalia alongside basil to naturally deter pests and improve the flavour of your harvest.
items.description: Dunalia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Petunia exserta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on the soil surface without covering them as they need light to germinate.
Grow in the sunniest spot possible or under glass to mimic their native warm Brazilian microclimate.
Water at the base in the morning to keep foliage dry and prevent grey mould in damp UK summers.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly to prevent self-seeding and encourage continuous red flowering.
Bring potted plants indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winter freezes.
items.description: Petunia exserta is a rare member of the genus Petunia, endemic to the Serras de Sudeste in southern Brazil. First described in 1987, only fourteen plants were found in the wild during an expedition in 2007. In the wild, the plant is found growing only in shaded cracks on sandstone towers. It is the only Petunia species that is naturally pollinated by hummingbirds, and the only naturally red flowered Petunia species.

items.name: Datura ceratocaula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 5mm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter the cool UK spring.
Grow in a heavy clay soil mix or boggy container to mimic its natural Mexican wetland habitat.
Keep the soil constantly saturated or submerge the pot base in shallow water during summer.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to maximize the short UK heat window.
Wear thick gloves when handling any part of this highly toxic plant to prevent skin absorption.
items.description: Datura ceratocaula is a species of Datura. It is weed-like in its natural habitat, but is grown in gardens and yards as an ornamental plant. The flower has a sweet smell. It is an annual plant that originally came from Mexico.

items.name: Datura leichhardtii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty-one Celsius.
Grow in pots of loam-based John Innes Number Two compost to restrict roots and encourage earlier flowering.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Move pots inside a heated greenhouse or conservatory by mid-September before the first autumn frosts.
Wear thick gloves when pruning seed pods in October to avoid contact with toxic tropane alkaloids.
items.description: Datura leichhardtii is a species of thorn apple in the genus Datura. In 1844, Ludwig Leichhardt discovered this species in Australia. Ferdinand von Mueller gave it the name Datura leichhardtii when he published his first description of it in 1855.

items.name: Fabiana patagonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly loam in full sun to mimic its native dry Andean slopes.
Protect from wet UK winters by planting against a south-facing wall or in a container moved indoors.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prunt lightly after flowering in late summer to maintain its compact, heather-like shape.
Propagate via semi-ripe cuttings in late summer using a gritty, low-nutrient compost mix.
items.description: Fabiana patagonica is a species of plant in the nightshade family, native to Patagonia. This plant species is native to South America.

items.name: Datura wrightii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic desert heat.
Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry, then keep completely dry in winter.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily with bark to protect from frost.
Position in your garden's hottest south-facing spot to ensure enough summer heat for night blooms.
items.description: Datura wrightii, commonly known as sacred datura, is a poisonous perennial plant species and ornamental flower of the family Solanaceae native to the Southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. It is sometimes used as a hallucinogen due to its psychoactive alkaloids. D. wrightii is classified as an anticholinergic deliriant.

items.name: Sansevieria pinguicula
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix with fifty percent pumice to prevent winter root rot.
Keep dry at room temperature in winter and only water when the rosette leaves begin to wrinkle.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK winter sunlight and maintain variegation.
Propagate by letting aerial stolons touch the soil surface in spring to root before cutting free.
Maintain indoor temperatures above twelve degrees Celsius to prevent cold-induced collapse and rot.
items.description: Dracaena pinguicula, synonym Sansevieria pinguicula, also known as the walking sansevieria, is a xerophytic CAM succulent native to the Bura area of Kenya, near Garissa. The species was described by Peter René Oscar Bally in 1943.

items.name: Iochroma fuchsioides
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water copiously daily in summer but keep the soil barely damp from November to March to avoid rot.
Prune back hard by half in early spring just as new growth starts to maintain a bushy shrub shape.
Check the undersides of leaves weekly in summer for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite pests.
Feed weekly with high-potassium liquid tomato fertilizer from May to September to boost flowering.
items.description: Iochroma fuchsioides is an Iochroma species found in Ecuador and Colombia. It was first described in 1848. In addition to the known withanolide D {1}, three new withanolides have been isolated from Iochroma fuchsioides.

items.name: Lycieae
items.growersTips:
Grow your goji berries in a sunny, sheltered spot to help them cope with damp UK summers.
Prune your established bushes in late winter to keep them compact and encourage new fruiting wood.
Water them deeply once a week during dry spells, rather than giving them frequent light sprinkles.
Keep an eye out for powdery mildew in autumn and space your plants well to improve air circulation.
Plant them in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil to mimic their native seaside cliff habitat.
items.description: Lycieae is a tribe of flowering plants in the subfamily Solanoideae of the family Solanaceae. It comprises two genera: Lycium and Grabowskia.

items.name: Sansevieria kirkii
items.growersTips:
Keep this Sansevieria dry in winter by watering only when the potting mix has completely dried out.
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts pumice to one part peat-free compost to prevent root rot.
Position on a bright south-facing windowsill but shade from intense midsummer afternoon sun.
Maintain indoor temperatures above 10C in winter to prevent cold damage and scarring on leaves.
Repot in spring only when the thick rhizomes begin to crack or distort the plastic nursery pot.
items.description: Dracaena pethera, synonym Sansevieria kirkii, also known as the star sansevieria or the snake plant, is a succulent plant native to Tanzania and the surrounding region in East Africa.

items.name: Salpichroa
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous climber in a large pot to stop its invasive roots from taking over your garden.
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator for UK warmth.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp.
Prune the stems back hard to ground level in late autumn to protect the crown from severe UK frosts.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly if you are growing this tender plant inside a British greenhouse.
items.description: Salpichroa is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Datura inoxia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic warm climates.
Grow in pots of free-draining gritty compost placed in the sunniest, most sheltered patio corner.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as wet UK winters will rot the roots.
Wear thick gloves when pruning dead stems in autumn to protect against highly toxic plant sap.
Move pots into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October to overwinter the tender roots.
items.description: Datura innoxia, known as pricklyburr, recurved thorn-apple, downy thorn-apple, Indian-apple, lovache, moonflower, nacazcul, toloatzin, toloaxihuitl, tolguache or toloache, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is more rarely called sacred datura, a common name which is applied more often to the closely related Datura wrightii. It is native to the Southwestern United States, Central and South America, and introduced in Africa, Asia, Australia and Europe. The scientific name is often cited as D. innoxia. When English botanist Philip Miller first described the species in 17

items.name: Sansevieria cylindrica
items.growersTips:
Keep this African succulent in a free-draining cactus compost mix with added grit to prevent rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing this to once every six weeks during UK winters.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light, as UK overcast days slow its growth.
Maintain indoor temperatures above 12C to protect this tender plant from cold draughts and shock.
Wipe the cylindrical leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve photosynthesis.
items.description: Dracaena angolensis, commonly known as African spear or the spear sansevieria, is a succulent plant native to Angola in Southern Africa. For years, it was placed within the genus Sansevieria (snake-plants), a specific name which is still used synonymously by some; in the 21st century, Sansevieria became part of Dracaena (dragon-trees), after improved testing methods, physical comparisons, and other analyses found sufficient commonalities between the two genera to warrant subsumption.

items.name: Aureliana
items.growersTips:
Sow your Aureliana seeds indoors in late March to protect young shoots from the damp UK spring chill.
Plant them out in May in rich, free-draining soil, spaced thirty centimetres apart for good airflow.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs during wet British summers, using beer traps around your patch.
Harvest the leaves from the outside first to keep the plant producing fresh growth until autumn.
items.description: Athenaea is a genus of plants in the family Solanaceae. It includes 14 species native to South America, ranging through Brazil to Bolivia, Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina. The greatest diversity of species is in the Brazilian Atlantic Rainforest.

items.name: Physalis angulata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Harden off and plant out in late May only after the very last frost in a sheltered south-facing spot.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent split lanterns.
Grow in pots of free-draining loam-based compost to restrict root run and encourage earlier fruiting.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under cover and apply biological controls at the first sign.
items.description: Physalis angulata is an erect herbaceous annual plant belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Its leaves are dark green and roughly ovate, often with serrate margins. The flowers are five-sided and pale yellow; the yellow-orange fruits are borne inside a balloon-like calyx. The exact native range is uncertain. The species may be naturally endemic to Australia or the Americas or the native range may encompass both the Americas and Australia. It is now widely distributed and naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

items.name: Liriope muscari
items.growersTips:
Cut back old foliage hard to the ground in March to allow fresh new growth to emerge undamaged.
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winters will rot the crown if the ground remains waterlogged.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they love to eat the emerging new flower spikes.
Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and maintain the plant's vigorous flowering habit.
Plant alongside autumn-flowering cyclamen or ferns for excellent dry shade tolerance in UK gardens.
items.description: Liriope muscari is a species of flowering plant from East Asia. Common names in English include big blue lilyturf, lilyturf, border grass, and monkey grass. This small herbaceous perennial has grass-like evergreen foliage and lilac-purple flowers which produce single-seeded berries on a spike in the fall. In some parts of the United States, it is an invasive species.

items.name: Dasylirion
items.growersTips:
Plant Dasylirion in gritty loam with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep the crown elevated above the soil line when planting to prevent water pooling and crown rot.
Water deeply once a fortnight in dry summer months but keep completely dry from October to March.
Wrap the crown in fleece or use a rain shelter during freezing UK winter wet spells to protect it.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure excellent drainage and move it under a porch for winter shelter.
items.description: Dasylirion is a genus of succulent, rosette-forming plants in the Asparagaceae family, where it is included in the subfamily Convallarioideae. Most species are native to mountainous arid regions of Mexico, with some species also native to the Southwestern United States. The common name sotol is used in English and Spanish to describe various Dasylirion species, as well as giving its name to a distilled spirit made from some species of the genus.

items.name: Sansevieria eilensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this slow-growing Somali succulent in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix with 50% pumice.
Keep the plant completely dry from November to March in a heated room or greenhouse above 10C.
Water only when the cylindrical, channelled leaves begin to slightly wrinkle during summer.
Position on a south-facing UK windowsill to maximise winter light and prevent rot in damp air.
Repot only every three to four years in spring, using a heavy clay pot to prevent tipping.
items.description: Dracaena eilensis, synonym Sansevieria eilensis, is a species of succulent plant native to a small region of Somalia near the town of Eyl. The species was collected in 1973 by John Lavranos.

items.name: Aspidistra elatior
items.growersTips:
Position the plant in a draft-free, north-facing room to mimic its natural deep shade habitat.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and prevent red spider mite attacks.
Repot every three years in spring using a peat-free loam-based compost with added grit for drainage.
Feed monthly from April to September with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer to boost slow growth.
items.description: Aspidistra elatior, the cast-iron-plant or bar-room plant, also known in Japanese as haran or baran (葉蘭) is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Japan and Taiwan. Tolerant of neglect, it is widely cultivated as a houseplant, but can also be grown outside in shade where temperatures remain above −15 °C (5 °F). It is used as training material for the seika form of ikebana.

items.name: Jaltomata lojae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow in large pots of peat-free compost in a sunny greenhouse to protect from cool UK summer nights.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not soggy to prevent blossom end rot in pots.
Support the sprawling stems with a sturdy tripod of bamboo canes as the heavy green berries develop.
Watch closely for aphids and glasshouse whitefly, using yellow sticky traps to catch them early.
items.description: Jaltomata lojae is a plant species native to Peru and Ecuador.

items.name: Polygonatum arisanense
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist, well-drained acidic soil to mimic woodland conditions.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect rhizomes from severe UK winter frosts.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.
Watch for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
items.description: Polygonatum arisanense is a flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. The species is endemic to Taiwan and is found in areas around 1,500 meters in elevation. Its Chinese common name and the species epithet refer to the Alishan Range.

items.name: Jaltomata procumbens
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to combat the cool UK spring before outdoor planting.
Plant out in late May after frosts pass into free-draining soil enriched with well-rotted manure.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly during dry summer spells to prevent blossom end rot in fruit.
Support the sprawling brittle stems with sturdy pea sticks or a low trellis to keep fruit off soil.
Watch for potato aphids and flea beetles in June, using physical barriers or insecticidal soap.
items.description: Jaltomata procumbens, the creeping false holly, is a plant species native to Arizona, USA, Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela. It grows as a weed in agricultural fields and other disturbed locations, but in many places the people protect it because of the edible fruits it produces.

items.name: Nothocestrum latifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Hawaiian native in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive cool UK summers.
Plant seeds 5mm deep in a well-draining, peat-free compost mix with added perlite for drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp British winters.
Inspect leaves regularly for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites, common pests in UK indoor setups.
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer with a high-potassium liquid tomato fertiliser to aid growth.
items.description: Nothocestrum latifolium, commonly known as broadleaf ʻaiea, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, that is endemic to Hawaiʻi. It can be found in dry and mesic forests at elevations of 460–1,530 m (1,510–5,020 ft) on the islands of Maui, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Oʻahu, and Kauaʻi. Broadleaf ʻaiea is threatened by habitat loss. The CDP of ʻAiea on Oʻahu was named after this species.

items.name: Polygonatum
items.growersTips:
Plant Solomon's seal rhizomes 5cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Water deeply weekly during dry UK spring spells to support lush leaf growth and bell-shaped blooms.
Check undersides of leaves from May to July for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae and handpick them off.
Cut the stems back to ground level in late autumn after the foliage has turned yellow and died down.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns in dappled shade to create a classic British woodland border style.
items.description: Polygonatum, also known as King Solomon's-seal, Solomon's seal, or sealwort, is a genus of flowering plants. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae. It has also been classified in the former family Convallariaceae and, like many lilioid monocots, was formerly classified in the lily family, Liliaceae. The genus is distributed throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere. Most of the approximately 63 species occur in Asia, with 20 endemic to China.

items.name: Nolana paradoxa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using free-draining compost to beat UK frosts.
Plant out in late May only after the last frost into a south-facing site with maximum sun exposure.
Incorporate grit or perlite into heavy UK soils to ensure the sharp drainage this coastal plant needs.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings to avoid rot.
Grow in hanging baskets or raised beds to mimic its natural trailing habit and protect from slugs.
items.description: Nolana paradoxa, the Chilean bellflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae, native to central and southern Chile. A spreading half-hardy annual reaching 9 in (23 cm) and useful as an edger or ground cover, it requires full sun. There is a cultivar, 'Blue Bird'.

items.name: Jaltomata chihuahuensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to mimic Mexican heat.
Grow in pots under glass or against a south-facing wall to protect from cool UK summer nights.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, keeping the compost damp but not soggy.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite, treating early with biological controls.
Support the sprawling Solanaceae stems with canes as the heavy green-to-black berries develop.
items.description: Jaltomata chihuahuensis is a plant species native to the Mexican States of Chihuahua and Durango.

items.name: Liriope
items.growersTips:
Plant Liriope muscari in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil, avoiding heavy, waterlogged clay.
Cut back old foliage to the ground in March to allow fresh new growth and autumn flowers to emerge.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells until established, then rely on natural rainfall.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using organic grit barriers around the base.
Divide congested clumps in spring, replanting divisions at the same depth as the original plant.
items.description:
Liriope may refer to:Liriope (nymph), the mother of Narcissus by the river-god Cephissus, according to Ovid's Metamorphoses.
Liriope (plant), a genus of lilioid monocot plants, named for the nymph
Liriope (cnidarian), a genus of hydrozoans in the family Geryoniidae
414 Liriope, a main belt asteroid, also named for the nymph

items.name: Salpichroa origanifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this invasive weed in a sturdy container to prevent its aggressive runners from taking over.
Prune stems hard to ground level in late autumn to control spread and remove frost-damaged growth.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to support its deep, tuberous root system.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in well-drained, poor soil to limit overly vigorous foliage.
Hand-pull emerging suckers in spring, ensuring you dig out the entire deep root to prevent regrowth.
items.description: Salpichroa origanifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names lily of the valley vine, pampas lily-of-the-valley or cock's-eggs.

items.name: Physalis pubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 3mm depth using a heated propagator to combat cool UK spring soil.
Transplant outdoors in late May after frosts, spacing plants 50cm apart in a sheltered, sunny spot.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly during dry summer spells to prevent fruit drop and splitting.
Support the sprawling stems with a short pea brush or low trellis by July to keep husks off damp soil.
Harvest only when the papery calyx turns completely straw-coloured and drops naturally to the ground.
items.description: Physalis pubescens is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by many common names, including husk tomato, low ground-cherry and hairy groundcherry in English, and muyaca and capulí in Spanish. It is native from Brazil, but also found in southern half of the United States, Mexico, Central and much of South America. It can be found elsewhere as an introduced species and sometimes a weed. It can grow in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas. This is an annual herb producing a glandular, densely hairy stem up to about 60 cm (24 in) in maximum height from a taproot.

items.name: Nicotiana paniculata
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March indoors, as they need light to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent damping off in our damp UK spring.
Plant them out in June after the last frost, spacing them forty centimetres apart in full sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young leaves, especially during wet British summer evenings.
Stake the tall flowering stems in July to protect them from strong winds and heavy summer rain.
items.description: Nicotiana paniculata, the small-flowered tobacco, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae, native to western Peru, and introduced to the Canary Islands. It is a parent of the economically important species Nicotiana rustica.

items.name: Nicotiana glutinosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on damp compost but do not cover them, as they need UK spring light to grow.
Plant out in late May after the last frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in fertile soil.
Watch out for aphids and greenhouse whitefly on the sticky leaves, washing them off with soapy water.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the large leaves from wilting.
Wear gloves when handling this plant because the sticky hairs can irritate your skin during pruning.
items.description: Nicotiana glutinosa is a species of tobacco plant that is economically important in tobacco hybrids. N. glutinosa is native to western South America, including Bolivia, Ecuador, and Peru. It is a model organism for the study of Tobacco mosaic virus resistance in tobacco.

items.name: Polygonatum humile
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using moisture-retentive leaf mould soil.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish the running carpet before summer dormancy.
Watch for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Divide congested clumps in autumn after the foliage dies back to propagate and maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns in dappled shade to create a weed-suppressing woodland groundcover.
items.description: Polygonatum humile, the dwarf Solomon's-seal, is a species of plant in the family Asparagaceae. The plant is said to possess scars on the rhizome that resemble the ancient Hebrew seal of King Solomon. This is a perennial species of the genus Polygonatum native to China, Japan, Kazakhstan, Korea, Mongolia and parts of Russia.

items.name: Physalis philadelphica
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early March as they need a long, warm UK summer to actually ripen.
Plant them deep right up to their first leaves in late May to encourage a really strong root system.
You must grow at least two plants close together or you will get empty husks and no fruit at all.
Water them deeply once a week at the base to prevent split fruit, keeping the leaves totally dry.
Stake them early like bush tomatoes because those heavy paper lanterns will weigh the branches down.
items.description: The tomatillo, also known as the Mexican husk tomato, is a plant of the nightshade family bearing small, spherical, and green or green-purple fruit. Tomatillos originated in Mexico and were cultivated in the pre-Columbian era. A staple of Mexican cuisine, they are eaten both raw and cooked in a variety of dishes, notably salsa verde. The tomatillo is a perennial plant, but is generally grown for agriculture each year as if it were an annual.

items.name: Aspidistra yingjiangensis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Yingjiang cast iron plant in a pot of peat-free loam with grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot in our cool damp climate.
Keep this shade-lover indoors or in a sheltered woodland spot to protect leaves from frost burn.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth in spring to clear dust and boost light absorption indoors.
Watch out for slugs and snails during mild UK autumns as they love to shred the fresh new shoots.
items.description: Aspidistra yingjiangensis is a species of Aspidistra that is found in India. The plant's leaves are green with pale yellow spots that are narrowly oblanceolate and it has two or three bracts. The flowers are individual or paired.

items.name: Calibanus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this Mexican desert native cannot survive wet UK winters.
Use a gritty loam-free cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent caudex rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing window or greenhouse spot to mimic its arid habitat.
Watch closely for mealybugs hiding in the dense crown of grass-like leaves during dry summer months.
items.description: Calibanus was a genus of two species of flowering plants, both evergreen succulents from dry areas of northeastern Mexico.The genus was subsumed in the genus Beaucarnea in the year 2014. The APG III classification system places Beaucarnea in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae The now-defunct Calibanus was formerly included in the Agavaceae but was separated from them, for it is polycarpic and dioecious. Its name refers to the monster Caliban, an antagonist in Shakespeare's The Tempest.

items.name: Duboisia hopwoodii
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its roots from wet, freezing UK winters.
Mix fifty percent grit into your peat-free compost to mimic the dry, sandy soils of its homeland.
Water only when the pot feels light, as this desert shrub hates sitting in damp British compost.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and encourage fresh growth.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plant under glass.
items.description: Duboisia hopwoodii is a shrub native to the arid interior region of Australia. Common names include pituri, pitchuri thornapple or pitcheri.

items.name: Brugmansia aurea
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted aurea indoors by late October before the first wet UK frost turns it to mush.
Water daily in summer and feed weekly with high-potash tomato food to boost those huge gold blooms.
Prune your plant back hard in November, cutting just above a node to keep it compact for wintering.
Watch out for red spider mites when you bring it inside, as dry winter radiators encourage them.
Plant it in a heavy, wind-sheltered pot using peat-free John Innes No. 3 with extra grit for drainage.
items.description: Brugmansia aurea, also known as golden angel's trumpet, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae that was native to Ecuador and Colombia, but is now Extinct in the Wild. Despite being declared extinct in its native range, Brugmansia aurea is a popular ornamental and is widely cultivated, like the other members of its genus.

items.name: Jaltomata weberbaueri
items.growersTips:
Start these rare Peruvian treats indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the UK chill.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, especially once those delicate flowers appear.
Watch out for greenhouse whiteflies and aphids, which absolutely love these soft, fuzzy leaves.
Grow them in large, deep pots of rich compost so you can easily move them inside before frost hits.
Gently pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and more berries.
items.description: Jaltomata weberbaueri is a plant species native to Peru. It grows on rocky hillsides at elevations less than 1800 m.

items.name: Sansevieria stuckyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining cactus compost with added grit to prevent root rot in damp UK winter air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once every six weeks during dark winter months.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK sunlight and maintain a warm microclimate.
Wipe the upright cylindrical leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and improve light intake.
Repot in spring only when the thick rhizomes begin to crack or push against the sides of the pot.
items.description: Dracaena stuckyi, synonym Sansevieria stuckyi, is a species of succulent plant native to Africa including Mozambique, Tanzania, and southern Kenya. It is a member of a group of related Dracaena including Dracaena angolensis and Dracaena pearsonii, that grow upright, cylindrical foliage and are native to dry biomes.

items.name: Physalis acutifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 5mm deep using a heated propagator to overcome the cool UK spring.
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam to restrict roots and encourage early summer flowering.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp British summers.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to ensure the green husks ripen fully.
Check weekly for red spider mites and aphids which thrive on this species under glass or fleece.
items.description: Physalis acutifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names sharpleaf groundcherry and Wright's ground-cherry. It is native to the southwestern United States from California to Texas, and northern Mexico, where it can be found in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas. It is sometimes a weed when it springs up in agricultural fields, but it is generally not weedy in wild habitat. This is an annual herb producing a branching stem up to a meter tall. The lance-shaped to oval leaves are up to 12 cm long and have edges lined with shallow, smooth

items.name: Physalis hederifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 6mm, keeping them at 20C before late May planting.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top 5cm of soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn and apply a thick straw mulch to protect roots.
Check plants weekly in June for red spider mites, which thrive in dry UK greenhouse conditions.
items.description: Physalis hederifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common name ivyleaf groundcherry. It is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where it can be found in rocky, dry desert and mountain habitat. This is a rhizomatous perennial herb producing a hairy, branching stem 10 to 80 centimeters long. The gray-green oval leaves are 2 to 4 centimeters long and have smooth or bluntly toothed edges. The flowers growing from the leaf axils are bell-shaped and just over a centimeter long. They are yellow with five brown smudges in the throats. Th

items.name: Physalis peruviana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator for UK warmth.
Grow in pots of poor soil to restrict root space and force the plant to produce fruit over foliage.
Water sparingly once fruit lanterns form to prevent the berries from splitting in damp UK weather.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage branching and speed up ripening before autumn frosts.
Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to get an early harvest next year.
items.description: Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru. Within that region, it is called aguaymanto, uvilla or uchuva, in addition to numerous indigenous and regional names. In English, its common names include Cape gooseberry, goldenberry and Peruvian groundcherry.

items.name: Ruscus
items.growersTips:
Plant Ruscus aculeatus in deep shade under trees where other shrubs struggle in dry UK soils.
Propagate by dividing the tough root clumps in early spring before the new shoots begin to emerge.
Prune out old dull three year old stems at the base in spring to encourage bright new green growth.
Ensure female cultivars like John Redmond have a male partner nearby for winter red berry display.
Grow in heavy clay or chalky soils as this tough evergreen tolerates poor drainage and high pH.
items.description: Ruscus, commonly known as butcher's-broom, is a genus of six species of flowering plants, native to western and southern Europe, Macaronesia, northwestern Africa, and southwestern Asia east to the Caucasus. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae. Like many lilioid monocots, it was formerly classified in the family Liliaceae.

items.name: Liriope spicata
items.growersTips:
Plant your runners just shallowly in spring so the crown sits right at the soil surface to avoid rot.
Give them a hard haircut right down to the ground in March to clear out tatty winter foliage.
Keep them damp during dry UK summers until established, then leave them to cope with dry shade.
Plant them under deciduous trees where they will happily thrive in dry, acidic soil and partial shade.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the fresh new spring shoots as they emerge in April.
items.description: Liriope spicata is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to Cambodia, China, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam. It is sometimes referred to by the common names creeping lilyturf, creeping liriope, lilyturf, and monkey grass. This low-growing, herbaceous perennial has grass-like evergreen foliage and is commonly used in landscaping in temperate climates as groundcover. Creeping lilyturf has white to lavender flowers which produce single-seeded berries on a spike in the fall. It is one of the most popular groundcovers in the southeastern United States and areas wi

items.name: Physalis crassifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot using free-draining sandy loam to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to mimic its arid natural habitat.
Overwinter pots indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this species cannot survive wet UK frosts.
Prune back leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more lantern fruits.
items.description: Physalis crassifolia is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names yellow nightshade groundcherry and thick-leaf ground-cherry. It is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where it can be found in rocky, dry desert and mountain habitat. This is a perennial herb producing a ridged, angular, branching stem approaching 80 cm long, taking a clumped, matted, or erect form. The fleshy oval leaves are 1 to 3 cm long and have smooth, wavy, or bluntly toothed edges. The herbage is glandular and coated in short hairs. The yellow flowers growin

items.name: Jaltomata cajacayensis
items.growersTips:
