Start seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow this rare Andean plant in a greenhouse or south-facing patio container to maximize summer heat.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in damp British weather.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and aphids, which love targeting this nightshade family member.
Stake the sprawling stems early in June to keep the heavy clusters of dark berries off the soil.
items.description: Jaltomata cajacayensis is a plant species native to Peru. The name comes from the Cajacay District, where it was recognized by Mione as a new species.

items.name: Physalis pruinosa
items.growersTips:
Sow indoors in March at 5mm deep using a heated propagator to overcome cool UK spring temperatures.
Grow in pots of peat-free compost on a south-facing patio to maximise essential summer sun and heat.
Water consistently at the base to prevent split fruit, avoiding overhead watering to stop blight.
Support the sprawling, brittle stems with a short cane teepee as the heavy fruit trusses develop.
Harvest only when the papery husks turn completely straw-coloured and drop naturally to the ground.
items.description: Physalis pruinosa is a plant in the genus Physalis in the nightshade family Solanaceae, often referred to as ground cherry or husk tomato. It is a native species in a range extending from northern Mexico through Central America. The plant has a low, spreading habit, and fruits develop in a papery husk, as is characteristic of the genus. While most parts of the plant are toxic to humans due to the presence of solanine and solanidine, the fruit becomes edible once it has ripened to yellow. The fruit's flavor is similar in some respects to that of a ripe tomatillo, but notably has a strong flavor

items.name: Physalis heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 6mm deep using a heated propagator to overcome the cool UK spring.
Plant out in late May in a sheltered, south-facing spot with free-draining, low-nitrogen soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp British summers.
Check regularly for red spider mites under leaves when growing in a UK greenhouse or polytunnel.
Prune the growing tips in July to restrict vegetative growth and force energy into ripening husks.
items.description: Physalis heterophylla, colloquial name clammy groundcherry, is species of herbaceous plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to North America, occurring primarily in the eastern United States and Canada. It is known to occur in all contiguous states except for Nevada and California. It is found mainly in habitats such as dry or mesic prairies, gravel hills and rises, sandy or rocky soils, and waste places such as roadsides.

items.name: Polygonatum pubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in deep shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish rhizomes, keeping the soil damp but not sodden.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut the yellowing stems back to ground level in late autumn once the foliage has completely died.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as the new growth buds begin to show above the soil.
items.description: Polygonatum pubescens, the hairy Solomon's seal or downy Solomon's seal, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to the north-central and eastern US and eastern Canada. It is a forest gap specialist.

items.name: Anthotroche myoporoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian shrub in a container to overwinter indoors when UK temperatures drop.
Plant in a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to maximise essential summer heat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact shape and boost growth.
items.description: Anthotroche myoporoides is a plant species in the family Solanaceae, native to Western Australia. It was first described in 1943 by Charles Gardner.

items.name: Anthotroche pannosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mix inside a terracotta pot to prevent root rot.
Position in the sunniest unheated greenhouse or conservatory to survive damp UK winters and frost.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact, woolly shrub shape.
Monitor closely for aphids and glasshouse whitefly which target the dense, felted silver foliage.
items.description: Anthotroche pannosa is an erect or sprawling shrub in the family Solanaceae. It is found in Western Australia.

items.name: Polygonatum multiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 10cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial or full shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish strong stems before the summer canopy closes.
Check leaves daily in May for Solomon's seal sawfly larvae and handpick them to prevent defoliation.
Cut the dying stems back to ground level in late autumn after the foliage turns yellow and papery.
Mulch annually in March with leaf mould or well-rotted manure to mimic a damp UK woodland floor.
items.description: Polygonatum multiflorum, the Solomon's seal, David's harp, ladder-to-heaven or Eurasian Solomon's seal, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Europe and temperate Asia. In Britain it is one of three native species of the genus, the others being P. odoratum and P. verticillatum.

items.name: Duboisia myoporoides
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie shrub inside for winter or grow it in a pot to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Plant it in a mix of grit and peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as it hates sitting in cold UK wet.
Give it your sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its warm native Australian home.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frosts pass to keep its woody shrub shape neat and bushy.
items.description:
Duboisia myoporoides, or corkwood, is a shrub or tree native to high-rainfall areas on the margins of rainforest in eastern Australia. It has a thick and corky bark.
The leaves are obovate to elliptic in shape, 4–15 cm long and 1–4 cm wide. The small white flowers are produced in clusters. This is followed by globose purple-black berries.

items.name: Beaucarnea
items.growersTips:
Bring Beaucarnea indoors before October frosts as it cannot survive wet UK winters outside.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost is completely dry to prevent stem rot.
Plant in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free multi-purpose compost and horticultural grit for drainage.
Position in the brightest south-facing windowsill to maximise limited UK winter sunlight.
Wipe the long leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent red spider mite infestations indoors.
items.description: Beaucarnea is a genus of flowering plants native to Mexico and Central America. In the APG III classification system, it is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae. Beaucarnea is sometimes treated as a synonym of the genus Nolina, with the species being then transferred to that genus. However, recent research shows that Beaucarnea should be treated as an independent genus.

items.name: Nicotiana plumbaginifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March, as they need light and UK spring sun to sprout.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy while they grow in our cool, wet British summers.
Slugs love these juicy leaves, so protect young plants with copper tape or beer traps in spring.
Plant them near night-scented stock to boost the evening fragrance in your damp UK patio borders.
Wear gloves when handling this wild tobacco relative, as the sticky leaves can irritate your skin.
items.description: Nicotiana plumbaginifolia is a species of tobacco plant known as Tex-Mex tobacco. The species epithet, "plumbaginifolia", is from the leaves bearing similarity to those of the genus Plumbago.

items.name: Atropa bella-donna
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy before spring.
Grow in moist well-drained alkaline soil by adding garden lime to neutral UK garden borders.
Wear heavy gloves when handling to avoid absorbing toxic alkaloids through your skin during pruning.
Cut stems back to the ground in late autumn after the black berries have fallen to prevent self-seeding.
Watch for the deadly nightshade flea beetle which skeletonises foliage in warm UK summer months.
items.description: Atropa bella-donna, commonly known as deadly nightshade or belladonna, is a toxic perennial herbaceous plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, which also includes tomatoes, potatoes and eggplant. It is native to Europe and Western Asia, including Turkey, its distribution extending from England in the west to western Ukraine and the Iranian province of Gilan in the east. It is also naturalised or introduced in some parts of Canada, North Africa and the United States.

items.name: Eriospermum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African tuber in a gritty loam-based compost with at least fifty percent sand.
Plant the tuber in late August with the growing tip positioned just below the gritty soil surface.
Water only from September to April when the single leaf is active, keeping it dry during summer.
Overwinter pots on a sunny indoor windowsill or heated greenhouse keeping temperatures above five C.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which will chew through the tuber and destroy the root system.
items.description: Eriospermum is a genus of tuberous flowering plants. It contains 114 species native to sub-Saharan Africa.

items.name: Capsicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by late February to beat the short UK growing season.
Keep plants in pots rather than open soil to help the roots stay warm in our cool British climate.
Water only when the top inch of compost is dry, as soggy soil causes root rot in UK greenhouses.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are twenty centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Tap the flowers gently with your finger in midsummer to help pollinate them when kept indoors.
items.description: Capsicum is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family Solanaceae, native to the Americas, cultivated worldwide for their edible fruit, which are generally known as "peppers" or "capsicum". Chili peppers grow on five species of Capsicum. Sweet or bell peppers and some chili peppers are Capsicum annuum, making it the most cultivated species in the genus.

items.name: Sansevieria arborescens
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender African plant cannot survive wet UK winters.
Grow in a heavy terracotta pot with 50% grit to prevent root rot in damp British humidity.
Water only once a month from November to March keeping the compost almost entirely dry.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise limited winter sunlight in the UK.
Repot in spring only when roots crack the pot as they thrive when tightly bound.
items.description: Dracaena arborescens, synonym Sansevieria arborescens, is a succulent plant native to Kenya and Tanzania.

items.name: Sansevieria bagamoyensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender African succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Provide bright indirect light on a south-facing windowsill to mimic its native tropical habitat.
Use a free-draining cactus mix with added perlite or grit to ensure excellent drainage in pots.
Repot in spring only when the plant becomes root-bound to encourage upright stem growth.
items.description: Dracaena bagamoyensis, synonym Sansevieria bagamoyensis, also known as snake plant is a succulent plant native to Kenya and Tanzania.

items.name: Maianthemum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil
Position in full or dappled shade to mimic their natural UK woodland habitat and prevent leaf scorch
Water weekly during dry British summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould or composted bark to mimic natural woodland floor decay
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets
items.description: Maianthemum includes the former genus Smilacina and is a genus of perennial herbaceous flowering plants with fleshy, persistent rhizomes. It is widespread across much of North America, Europe and Asia, and may be terrestrial, aquatic or epiphytic. It is characterized by simple, unbranched stems that are upright, leaning or hanging down and have 2–17 foliage leaves. Leaves are simple and may clasp the stem or be short-petiolate. The inflorescence is terminal and either a panicle or a raceme with few to many pedicelate flowers. Most species have 6 tepals and 6 stamens; a few have parts in 4s. Te

items.name: Polygonatum biflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using humus-rich moisture-retentive soil.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish roots before the summer canopy closes in.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut yellowing stems back to ground level in late autumn after the foliage dies back naturally.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth buds begin to show above the soil.
items.description: Polygonatum biflorum is an herbaceous flowering plant native to eastern and central North America. The plant is said to possess scars on the rhizome that resemble the ancient Hebrew seal of King Solomon. It is often confused with Solomon's plume, which has upright flowers.

items.name: Polygonatum ×hybridum
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using humus-rich, moist, acid-to-neutral soil.
Water deeply during dry UK spring spells to keep the woodland soil consistently damp but not soggy.
Check leaves daily in May for sawfly larvae and pick them off immediately to prevent defoliation.
Cut the dying stems back to ground level in late autumn once the foliage turns yellow and collapses.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to mimic a natural forest floor and retain moisture.
items.description: Polygonatum × hybridum, the garden Solomon's-seal, is a hybrid flowering plant, which is a cross between common Solomon's-seal and angular Solomon's-seal.

items.name: Sansevieria
items.growersTips:
Water only when the compost is bone dry, usually every three to four weeks during the UK winter.
Repot in spring using a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part coarse grit.
Keep plants above ten degrees Celsius near bright, indirect light but away from cold UK drafts.
Wipe the upright leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and check for mealybug pests.
Use heavy terracotta pots to prevent top-heavy mature specimens from tipping over on windowsills.
items.description: Sansevieria is a historically recognized genus of flowering plants, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia, now included in the genus Dracaena on the basis of molecular phylogenetic studies. Common names for the 70 or so species formerly placed in the genus include mother-in-law's tongue, devil's tongue, jinn's tongue, bow string hemp, snake plant and snake tongue. In the APG III classification system, Dracaena is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Convallarioideae ; before that it was placed in family Ruscaceae. It has also been placed in the former family Dracaenac

items.name: Physalis longifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Plant out in late May in a sun-baked, south-facing border with poor, sharply draining soil.
Water sparingly once established to restrict leafy growth and encourage heavy fruit production.
Erect a sturdy stake early to support the brittle, sprawling stems against strong UK winds.
Apply a thick straw mulch in late autumn to protect the underground rhizomes from wet winter rot.
items.description: Physalis longifolia, known by the common names common groundcherry, longleaf groundcherry, and wild tomatillo, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. It is native to North America, where it is native to eastern Canada, much of the continental United States, and northern Mexico. It has also been noted as an introduced species in other regions, including parts of the United States outside its native range. In some areas, such as California, it is an occasional noxious weed.

items.name: Nothocestrum breviflorum
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Hawaiian shrub indoors for winter as it cannot survive wet UK frosts below ten degrees.
Grow it in a terracotta pot using a highly gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil dries out completely, then keep it barely damp during winter.
Place your pot on a sunny south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory for maximum light.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the shrub and encourage fresh bushy growth for the summer.
items.description: Nothocestrum breviflorum, commonly known as smallflower ʻaiea, is a species of tree in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, that is endemic to the island of Hawaiʻi. It inhabits dry and mixed mesic forests at elevations of 180–1,830 m (590–6,000 ft). These forests are dominated by ʻōhiʻa lehua and koa or lama, while plants associated with smallflower ʻaiea include wiliwili and uhiuhi. N. breviflorum reaches a height of 10–12 m (33–39 ft). It is threatened by habitat loss. It is federally listed as an endangered species of the United States. There are fewer than 50 individuals remaining.

items.name: Dracaena
items.growersTips:
Bring potted Dracaena indoors by October before UK frosts damage the foliage of this tropical plant.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Wipe the strap-like leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and maximise low UK winter light.
Repot in spring using a free-draining peat-free compost mix with added grit to ensure good drainage.
Place in bright indirect light near an east or west window to avoid leaf scorch from summer sun.
items.description:
Dracaena can mean:Drakaina (mythology), a Greek mythological entity
Dracaena (plant), a genus of plants
Cordyline australis, a plant commonly known as the Dracaena palm
Dracaena (lizard), a genus of lizard
Dracena, a town in Brazil
Dracaena, a fictional dragon-woman in Percy Jackson & the Olympians
Drakaina (model), a French actress and model.

items.name: Aspidistra grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this huge-flowered cast iron plant in a sheltered, deep shade spot to prevent leaf scorch.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out, especially during damp UK winter months.
Keep the bizarre, spider-like purple flowers clear of leaf litter in autumn so you can see them.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer monthly from April to September to boost slow growth.
Protect the foliage from slugs and snails which love hiding under the broad leaves in wet weather.
items.description: Aspidistra grandiflora is a species of flowering plant. A. grandiflora grows in Vietnam in dry broad-leaved lowland forests on karstic limestone outcrops with fissures.

items.name: Physalis coztomatl
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow in pots of peat-free compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this species needs.
Move plants to a sunny greenhouse or south-facing patio only after all risk of May frosts has passed.
Water sparingly once established to prevent root rot and encourage the development of sweet fruit.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing under glass in the humid UK summer.
items.description: Physalis coztomatl is a plant species in the genus Physalis. It produces edible orange-yellow fruits, but is rarely cultivated. The leaves are oval-shaped. It is native to America; the Aztecs used it medicinally. It contains labdane diterpenes, and was the first species in Physalis in which they were found.

items.name: Brugmansia × candida
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted plant indoors to a frost-free conservatory or shed once autumn temperatures drop.
Water heavily daily in summer and feed weekly with high-potash tomato food to boost those blooms.
Prune hard in spring just above a node where the branches fork to encourage maximum flowering wood.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in dry weather and mist the leaves to keep them away.
Plant them in a sheltered, sunny spot using rich John Innes number three compost with extra grit.
items.description: Brugmansia × candida, the angel's trumpet, is a hybrid species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. Its parents are Brugmansia aurea and Brugmansia versicolor, with both listed as extinct in the wild.

items.name: Nicotiana clevelandii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring because they need UK light to germinate, so do not bury them.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy to prevent damping off in our cool, humid British spring.
Watch out for aphids and greenhouse whiteflies which love the sticky leaves of this wild tobacco.
Plant them near potatoes or tomatoes to act as a sacrificial trap crop for common garden pests.
Grow this tender annual in pots so you can easily move it under glass when the autumn chill hits.
items.description: Nicotiana clevelandii is a species of wild tobacco known by the common name Cleveland's tobacco.

items.name: Nicotiana quadrivalvis
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March, as they need light and propagator warmth to grow.
Keep your seedlings on a sunny windowsill, watering from below so you do not wash the tiny roots away.
Plant them out in late May after the frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in fertile soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails in wet June weather, as they absolutely love the tender young leaves.
Feed them weekly with high-potash tomato food from July to keep those white flowers blooming nicely.
items.description: Nicotiana quadrivalvis is a species of wild tobacco known as Indian tobacco. The variety N. quadrivalvis var. multivalvis is known by the common name Columbian tobacco. It is endemic to the western United States, where it grows in many types of habitat. It is a bushy, sprawling annual herb growing up to two meters in maximum height. The lower leaf blades are up to 15 centimetres (6 in) long and are borne on short petioles, the upper smaller and sessile on the stem. The inflorescence is an array of several white, greenish, or purple-tinged flowers with tubular throats up to 5 centimeters long.

items.name: Nicotiana alata
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March; they need light to germinate on your windowsill.
Keep your young plants indoors until late May to protect them from any late British spring frosts.
Water them deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil damp but never soggy during dry spells.
Check the leaves regularly for aphids and slugs, which absolutely love the tender young foliage.
Plant them near your patio or seating area so you can enjoy their lovely evening scent in summer.
items.description: Nicotiana alata is a species of tobacco. It is called jasmine tobacco, sweet tobacco, winged tobacco, tanbaku, and Persian tobacco.

items.name: Lycium brevipes
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert shrub in your sunniest, sheltered UK spot using free-draining sandy soil to avoid root rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drenches in summer.
Prune your shrub in late winter to shape it and remove any frost-damaged stems before new growth.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp British weather.
Grow it in a terracotta pot to keep roots warm and easily move it under glass for winter wet protection.
items.description: Lycium brevipes is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common name Baja desert-thorn. It is native to northwestern Mexico and it occurs in California as far as the Sonoran Desert as well as some of the Channel Islands. It grows in the scrub of desert and coastline. It is also used as a southwestern landscaping plant. This is a bushy, spreading shrub approaching a maximum height of 4 metres (13 ft) with many long, thorny, tangled branches. The branches are lined with small, fleshy green leaves up to 1.5 centimetres (0.59 in) long and coated with glandular hairs. T

items.name: Lycium californicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in your sharpest-draining gritty soil or a pot to survive wet UK winters.
Position your shrub in your garden's hottest, brightest south-facing spot to mimic its home sun.
Water it deeply but very rarely, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks in summer.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frosts to shape it and remove any winter dieback.
Keep a close eye out for snails and slugs who love to feast on the tender new spring shoots.
items.description: Lycium californicum is a spreading shrub in the nightshade family known by the common names California boxthorn and California desert-thorn.

items.name: Lycium cooperi
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough desert shrub in your sunniest spot in sharply draining soil mixed with extra grit.
Water your young plant weekly during dry UK summers, but let the soil dry out fully between drinks.
Prune in late spring after the last frosts to shape the bush and clear out any dead winter wood.
Protect the root zone from winter wet by mulching with gravel rather than moisture-holding bark.
Watch out for aphids on the tender new spring shoots and wash them off with a quick blast of water.
items.description: Lycium cooperi is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common name peach thorn. It is native to the southwestern United States, where it grows in a variety of desert and mountain habitat types. This is a bushy, erect shrub approaching a maximum height of 4 metres (13 ft) with many rigid, thorny branches. The branches are lined thickly with fleshy oval or widely lance-shaped leaves each 1–3 centimetres (0.39–1.18 in) long and coated with glandular hairs. The inflorescence is a small cluster of tubular flowers roughly 1–2 centimetres (0.39–0.79 in) long including th

items.name: Lycium andersonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in your sunniest spot using a very gritty, free-draining cactus compost.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, only soaking the soil once it has dried out completely.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse to survive wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the bush and encourage fresh, berry-producing new growth.
Watch out for aphids on the tender new shoots during our damp, humid British spring days.
items.description: Lycium andersonii is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. Its common names include water-jacket, redberry desert-thorn, Anderson thornbush, Anderson's desert thorn, Anderson boxthorn, Anderson lycium, Anderson wolfberry, and squawberry.

items.name: Lycium chinense
items.growersTips:
Plant your Chinese goji berry in a sunny spot with free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells while the young shrub establishes its roots.
Prune in early spring by cutting back old wood to encourage fresh, fruit-bearing new growth.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp UK summers and space plants well to improve air circulation.
Grow it in a large container if you have heavy clay, using a mix of John Innes No 3 and grit.
items.description: Lycium chinense is one of two species of boxthorn shrub in the family Solanaceae. Along with Lycium barbarum, it produces the goji berry ("wolfberry"). Two varieties are recognized, L. chinense var. chinense and L. chinense var. potaninii. It is also known as Chinese boxthorn, Chinese matrimony-vine, Chinese teaplant, Chinese wolfberry, wolfberry, and Chinese desert-thorn.

items.name: Nicotiana × sanderae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on damp compost but do not cover them, as they need UK spring light to grow.
Plant out only after late May frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in fertile, moist soil.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry summer spells to keep the fragrant blooms from wilting.
Snails love the sticky leaves, so use organic grit barriers or go on damp evening patrols to find them.
Deadhead faded flowers weekly to keep these half-hardy annuals blooming right up to the first frosts.
items.description: Nicotiana × sanderi, also known as Nicotiana × sanderae, is a hybrid of the tobacco species Nicotiana alata and Nicotiana forgetiana. It is the most common ornamental Nicotiana variety found and sold in the United Kingdom. Nicotiana × sanderi requires soft soil mixed with sand to thrive. The plant will grow to heights of 3 feet (0.91 m) and will give off a sweet scent in the evening, like most Nicotiana plants. Nicotiana × sanderi is not hardy against frost and will die if it comes in contact with it; however, it withstands drought. Because of its size, N. × sanderi is used as a house or garde

items.name: Lycium pallidum
items.growersTips:
Plant this pale wolfberry in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy soil to protect it from wet UK winters.
Position your shrub in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to encourage summer flowering.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings to mimic clay.
Prune in late winter by removing dead wood and crossing branches to keep the thorny habit tidy.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with copper tape or beer traps.
items.description: Lycium pallidum is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common names pale wolfberry and pale desert-thorn. It is native to northern Mexico and the southwestern United States. In Mexico it can be found in Sonora, Chihuahua, Zacatecas, and San Luis Potosi. In the United States it occurs from California to Texas and as far north as Utah and Colorado.

items.name: Lycium europaeum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough shrub in your sunniest spot with gritty, free-draining soil to mimic the Med.
Prune in late winter to clear out dead wood and keep its wild, sprawling habit under control.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in its first year, then leave it to fend for itself.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp UK autumns, so space plants well to keep air flowing freely.
Propagate easily by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to get free new plants for friends.
items.description: Lycium europaeum, the European tea tree, European box‑thorn, or European matrimony‑vine, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to the entire Mediterranean region, and has been introduced to the Canary Islands, Madeira, and the Balearic Islands. Its fruit is edible.

items.name: Solanum muricatum
items.growersTips:
Grow pepino melons in pots so you can easily move them indoors before the first autumn frosts hit.
Feed your pepinos weekly with high-potassium tomato food once those purple-striped flowers appear.
Stake the heavy, brittle fruiting branches early to stop them snapping under the weight of melons.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent the ripening fruit from splitting open.
Prune out the leafy side-shoots in summer to let maximum UK sunlight reach and ripen the melons.
items.description: Solanum muricatum is a species of evergreen shrub native to South America and grown for its sweet edible fruit.

items.name: Nicotiana benthamiana
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March, as they need light to germinate indoors.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering from the base to protect delicate stems.
Gradually acclimate your plants to the UK outdoors in late May once all risk of frost has passed.
Watch out for aphids and greenflies, which love the sticky leaves of this Australian native plant.
Grow them in pots on a warm, sheltered patio to mimic the heat they need to thrive in our climate.
items.description: Nicotiana benthamiana, colloquially known as benth or benthi, is a species of Nicotiana indigenous to Australia. It is a close relative of tobacco.

items.name: Nicotiana sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in March as they need light to germinate before planting out in May.
Space plants at least sixty centimetres apart in rich moist soil to allow the huge leaves to expand.
Stake the tall flower spikes early in windy UK gardens to prevent them snapping in summer storms.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells to support the massive foliage and prevent wilting.
Treat as a half-hardy annual in the UK or mulch heavily to protect the crown from wet winter rot.
items.description: Nicotiana sylvestris is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, known by the common names woodland tobacco, flowering tobacco, and South American tobacco. It is a biennial or short-lived perennial plant in the tobacco genus Nicotiana, native to the Andes region in Argentina and Bolivia, in South America.

items.name: Vestia foetida
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean beauty in a sheltered south-facing border to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Give it moist but very well-drained soil, mixing in plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring after the yellow tubular flowers fade to keep its bushy shape tidy.
Watch out for aphids on the lush new spring growth and blast them off with a quick hose spray.
Propagate semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to keep a backup plant in your greenhouse over winter.
items.description: Vestia is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae containing the single species Vestia foetida (syn. V. lycioides). Its principal common names in the Mapudungun language of its native Chile are Huevil (pron. "wayfil" and sometimes redoubled Huevilhuevil) and Chuplín. Other Chilean names include Chuplí, Echuelcún and Palqui (negro) (this last being also applied to Cestrum parqui), while an English common name Chilean box thorn has also been coined recently in reference to a certain similarity of the plant to some species in the box thorn / wolfberry genus Lycium (as refer

items.name: Lycium oxycarpum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough shrub in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic its native warm habitat.
Give it sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winters.
Prune your shrub in late spring after the frosts pass to shape it and encourage fresh new growth.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells once the plant is fully established.
Keep a close eye out for powdery mildew on the foliage during humid, damp British summers.
items.description: Lycium oxycarpum is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to the Karoo regions of South Africa.

items.name: Nicotiana rustica
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March with a light dusting of soil, as they need warmth and light to germinate.
Plant them out in late May after the last frost, spacing them at least forty centimetres apart.
Water the base deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage strong, deep roots.
Watch out for UK slugs and snails early on, using beer traps or physical barriers to protect them.
Pinch out the central flower buds in July if you want to redirect energy into growing larger leaves.
items.description: Nicotiana rustica, commonly known as Aztec tobacco or strong tobacco, known to the Powhatan people as Apooke, is a rainforest plant in the family Solanaceae native to South America. It is a very potent variety of tobacco, containing up to nine times more nicotine than common species of Nicotiana such as Nicotiana tabacum. More specifically, N. rustica leaves have a nicotine content as high as 9%, whereas N. tabacum leaves contain about 1 to 3%. The high concentration of nicotine in its leaves makes it useful for producing pesticides, and it has a wide variety of uses specific to cultures aroun

items.name: Brugmansia arborea
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted angel trumpet indoors by October to protect it from harsh British frosts.
Water daily in summer to keep the soil damp, but let it dry out between waterings in winter.
Prune hard in spring just above a node where the branches form a Y shape to encourage big blooms.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food from May to September to boost those fragrant flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites under the leaves if you overwinter them in a greenhouse.
items.description: Brugmansia arborea, the angel's trumpet, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. The IUCN has classed Brugmansia arborea as extinct in the wild.

items.name: Lycium barbarum
items.growersTips:
Plant your goji berry in full sun and very well-drained, alkaline soil to handle wet UK winters.
Prune established shrubs in early spring by cutting back old wood to encourage fresh fruiting stems.
Water your young shrub deeply once a week, but let it dry out completely between waterings.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp UK summers by spacing plants well to improve air circulation.
Grow them in a large pot if your garden has heavy clay, as they hate sitting in soggy winter soil.
items.description: Lycium barbarum is a shrub native to China, with present-day range across Asia and southeast Europe. It is one of two species of boxthorn in the family Solanaceae from which the goji berry or wolfberry is harvested, the other being Lycium chinense.

items.name: Nicotiana glauca
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender shrub indoors or wrap it in fleece before the first harsh UK frost hits in autumn.
Sow the tiny seeds on the surface of peat-free compost in March, as they need light to germinate.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the gritty, free-draining soil dry out between drinks.
Prune hard in early spring to keep its leggy habit in check and encourage fresh, blue-green leaves.
Watch out for aphids on the lush new shoots and blast them off with a quick spray of your hose.
items.description: Nicotiana glauca is a species of flowering plant in the tobacco genus Nicotiana of the nightshade family Solanaceae. It is known by the common name tree tobacco. Its leaves are attached to the stalk by petioles, and its leaves and stems are neither pubescent nor sticky like Nicotiana tabacum. It resembles Cestrum parqui but differs in the form of leaves and fusion of the outer floral parts. It grows to heights of more than two meters.

items.name: Nicotiana mutabilis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring because they need UK light to germinate, so do not bury them.
Plant them in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect those tall, airy stems from strong UK winds.
Water them deeply at the base once a week rather than spraying the leaves to prevent powdery mildew.
Keep an eye out for green aphids on the sticky stems and wash them off with a gentle hose spray.
Deadhead the fading flowers regularly to keep the magic colour-changing show going right into autumn.
items.description: Nicotiana mutabilis, the colour-changing tobacco plant or flowering tobacco plant, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to northeastern Rio Grande do Sul state in Brazil, and it has been introduced to Great Britain. An erect annual or biennial reaching 1.5 m (5 ft), its flowers start out white and fade to pink and finally dark pink. It is available from commercial suppliers.

items.name: Cestrum
items.growersTips:
Grow Cestrum nocturnum in pots to overwinter indoors at ten degrees Celsius to survive UK frosts.
Prune Cestrum fasciculatum hard in April by cutting back old stems to thirty centimetres from base.
Plant Cestrum in well-drained loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Water Cestrum weekly in summer but keep compost barely damp from November to March to prevent rot.
Check leaf undersides for glasshouse red spider mite when growing Cestrum in UK conservatories.
items.description: Cestrum is a genus of — depending on authority — 150-250 species of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae. They are native to warm temperate to tropical regions of the Americas, from the southernmost United States south to the Bío-Bío Region in central Chile. They are colloquially known as cestrums or jessamines.

items.name: Nicotiana suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of peat-free compost in March, as they need light to germinate.
Plant them out in June after the last frost, choosing a sheltered spot to protect delicate stems.
Water at the base in the morning to keep soil damp but prevent the mildew that damp UK summers bring.
Position them near your patio or seating area so you can enjoy their evening fragrance in summer.
Snick off fading flower stems regularly to keep them blooming right up until the first autumn frosts.
items.description: Nicotiana suaveolens is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is sometimes referred to by the common name Australian tobacco, and is a herb reaching 1.5 meters in height. It is native to New South Wales and Victoria.

items.name: Lycium horridum
items.growersTips:
Plant this thorny South African shrub in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic its home heat.
Use poor, sharply draining soil, mixing in plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid mold.
Prune in late spring after frosts pass, wearing thick gloves to tackle those viciously sharp thorns.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a greenhouse or porch during freezing winters.
items.description: Lycium horridum is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to South Africa as well as southern Namibia and Botswana.

items.name: Salpiglossis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on compost surface without covering as they need light to germinate.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimetres tall to encourage bushy growth.
Plant out in late May after frosts in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect from UK winds.
Water at the base of the plant to keep the sticky foliage dry and prevent botrytis in damp weather.
Stake the slender stems early in June using brushwood support to prevent heavy rain damage.
items.description: Salpiglossis is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the subfamily Cestroideae of family Solanaceae. It is closely related to the genus Reyesia, with which it makes up the tribe Salpiglossideae. Species in the genus Salpiglossis are found in Mexico, Argentina and Chile.

items.name: Lycium cinereum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough South African shrub in your sunniest spot with gravel mixed in to survive UK wet.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry UK summer, then leave it to fend for itself.
Prune your shrub in late winter to keep its wild, sprawling branches tidy and encourage fresh growth.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp British autumns, so space it well to keep the air flowing.
Grow it alongside rosemary or lavender, which love the same sharp drainage and baking hot sun.
items.description:
Lycium cinereum is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to southern Africa. 
It is widespread across South Africa, as well as southern Namibia and Botswana.

items.name: Lycium pumilum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough shrub in your sunniest spot with sharp-draining soil to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave it to survive on rain alone.
Prune your shrub in late winter to remove dead wood and keep its wild, spiny growth under control.
Watch out for aphids on the fresh spring shoots and simply blast them off with a sharp blast of water.
Grow it in a terracotta pot of gritty compost if your garden has heavy, wet UK clay that rots roots.
items.description: Lycium pumilum is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to South Africa and Namibia.

items.name: Solanum melongena
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to ensure a long enough growing season in the UK.
Grow plants in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK outdoor summers are rarely warm enough for success.
Pinch out the main growing tip when the plant reaches thirty centimetres to encourage bushy growth.
Limit each plant to four or five fruits and remove later flowers to ensure the remaining crop ripens.
Water the compost consistently to keep it moist and mist the foliage daily to deter red spider mites.
items.description: Eggplant, aubergine, brinjal, or baigan is a plant species in the nightshade family Solanaceae. Solanum melongena is grown worldwide for its edible fruit, typically used as a vegetable in cooking.

items.name: Brugmansia versicolor
items.growersTips:
Bring it indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by late October before the cold hits.
Water heavily daily in summer and feed weekly with high-potash tomato food to boost the big blooms.
Prune branches hard in November back to the first main Y-junction to keep its size manageable.
Plant in a large pot using John Innes Number 3 compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Watch out for red spider mites under the leaves when you keep it in a warm greenhouse or indoors.
items.description: Brugmansia versicolor is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae, commonly known as "angel's trumpets". They are endemic to Ecuador. Since March 2014, they have been listed as Extinct in the Wild by the IUCN.

items.name: Solanum lycopersicum
items.growersTips:
Plant cordon varieties deep up to their first leaves in May to encourage a strong, deep root system.
Pinch out side shoots of indeterminate types weekly in summer to focus energy on fruit production.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, avoiding wetting the leaves in damp UK weather.
Remove lower leaves up to the first truss in August to improve air circulation and prevent late blight.
Underplant with French marigolds to deter whitefly and glasshouse pests common in UK gardens.
items.description: The tomato is a plant whose fruit is an edible berry that is eaten as a vegetable. The tomato is a member of the nightshade family that includes tobacco, potato, and chili peppers. It originated from western South America, and may have been domesticated there, in Mexico, or in Central America. The Spanish introduced tomatoes to Eurasia in the Columbian exchange in the 16th century.

items.name: Brugmansia sanguinea
items.growersTips:
Grow this one in partial shade because unlike other angels trumpets it hates hot UK greenhouse glass.
Plant the root ball level with the soil in a heavy loam to stop top-heavy wind damage in autumn.
Water deeply twice a week in summer but keep it barely damp in winter to prevent root rot indoors.
Prune back hard in November to fit it inside your frost-free shed or conservatory for the winter.
Watch out for capsid bugs in June which shred the leaves and ruin the winter flower buds.
items.description: Brugmansia sanguinea, the red angel's trumpet, is a species of South American flowering shrub or small tree belonging to the genus Brugmansia in tribe Datureae of subfamily Solanoideae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. It has been cultivated and used as an entheogen for shamanic purposes by the South American Natives for centuries - possibly even millennia.

items.name: Nicotiana tabacum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on compost surface in March without covering, as they need UK spring light to germinate.
Keep young plants indoors until late May to avoid any chance of frost, then space them 50cm apart.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep those massive leaves turgid.
Pinch out the central flower spike in July if you want the plant to focus energy on bigger leaves.
Watch out for slugs and aphids in damp British weather, as they absolutely love the tender foliage.
items.description: Nicotiana tabacum, or cultivated tobacco, is an annually grown herbaceous plant of the genus Nicotiana. N. tabacum is the most commonly grown species in the genus Nicotiana, as the plant's leaves are commercially harvested to be processed into tobacco for human use. The plant is native to Bolivia, commonly grown throughout the world and often found in cultivation. It grows to heights between 1 and 2 metres. Research is ongoing into its ancestry among wild Nicotiana species, but it is believed to be a hybrid of Nicotiana sylvestris, N. tomentosiformis, and possibly N. otophora.

items.name: Lycium intricatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this thorny shrub in your sunniest, well-drained spot to mimic its native Mediterranean heat.
Keep young plants damp, but once established, only water during prolonged dry UK summer spells.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and keep its wild, sprawling habit under control.
Guard against snails and slugs in wet British springs, as they love the tender new shoots.
Grow it in a large terracotta pot if your garden has heavy clay soil to prevent winter root rot.
items.description: Lycium intricatum, the southern boxthorn, is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae (nightshades).

items.name: Brugmansia suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted angel's trumpet indoors by late October before the first frosty UK night hits.
Water heavily daily in summer, but let the compost dry out between light waterings in winter.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food from May to September to boost those massive blooms.
Prune hard in March, cutting back to a node just above the main Y-junction to encourage flowering.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites under the leaves if you overwinter them in a conservatory.
items.description: Brugmansia suaveolens, Brazil's white angel trumpet, also known as angel's tears and snowy angel's trumpet, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, native to south eastern Brazil, but thought to be extinct in the wild. Like several other species of Brugmansia, it exists as an introduced species in areas outside its native range. It is a tender shrub or small tree with large semi-evergreen leaves and fragrant yellow or white trumpet-shaped flowers.

items.name: Lycium afrum
items.growersTips:
Plant this spiny African shrub in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its hot native climate.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because this tough beauty cannot stand winter wet in UK gardens.
Prune your shrub in late spring after the frosts pass to shape it and encourage fresh purple blooms.
Give it a thick mulch of gravel around the base to reflect heat and keep the lower stems dry.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a greenhouse to survive harsh British winters.
items.description: Lycium afrum, the kraal honey thorn is a shrub in the potato family (Solanaceae), indigenous to the Western Cape Province, South Africa.

items.name: Lycium ruthenicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this black goji in free-draining, sandy soil to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Prune your shrub in early spring to remove dead wood and encourage new fruiting lateral branches.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
Grow this hardy shrub in your sunniest, south-facing spot to ensure the berries actually sweeten.
items.description: Lycium ruthenicum, is a flowering plant commonly known as Russian box thorn in the West. It is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family which can be found in Central Asia, southern part of Russia, throughout Northwest China, Northern India and Pakistan. Also commonly known as black fruit wolfberry, siyah goji, black goji and kaokee.

items.name: Nicotiana obtusifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of free-draining compost in March, as they need light to germinate.
Keep this desert native in your sunniest spot and water only when the top two inches of soil dry out.
Watch out for aphids in early summer, washing them off with a gentle spray from your garden hose.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October.
Plant them near carrots or onions to help deter common pests with their sticky, hairy foliage.
items.description: Nicotiana obtusifolia, or desert tobacco, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to the southwestern United States and Mexico.

items.name: Solanum betaceum
items.growersTips:
Grow your tamarillo in a large pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water deeply twice a week in summer, but let the top inch of soil dry out to prevent root rot.
Prune the main stem at one meter high in spring to encourage a bushy habit and more fruiting wood.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food from May to September to boost flower and fruit production.
Watch out for aphids and whiteflies when overwintering your shrub in a greenhouse or conservatory.
items.description: The tamarillo is a tree or shrub in the flowering plant family Solanaceae. It bears an egg-shaped edible fruit. It is common globally, especially in its native South America, and has been introduced in New Zealand, Nepal, Rwanda, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Australia, and Bhutan.

items.name: Espadaea amoena
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Plant them out in late May in free-draining sandy loam enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells to keep the developing roots evenly moist.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots and use beer traps or copper tape to protect them in damp June.
Grow them alongside marigolds to deter whiteflies and boost pollination in your greenhouse or plot.
items.description: Espadaea is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae. The only species is Espadaea amoena.

items.name: Lycium ferocissimum
items.growersTips:
Plant this African boxthorn in a sturdy pot of gritty compost to stop its invasive roots spreading.
Keep it in your sunniest, most sheltered spot because UK frosts will easily nip its tender stems.
Prune hard in late spring after the frosts pass to shape the shrub and keep its sharp thorns tidy.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then let the soil dry out completely before you water it again.
Watch out for spider mites in dry summer spells and blast them off with a sharp spray of water.
items.description: Lycium ferocissimum, the African boxthorn or boxthorn, is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to South Africa.

items.name: Lycium fremontii
items.growersTips:
Plant Fremont barberry in sandy, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out fully between waterings.
Protect young shrubs from slugs and snails in spring by using organic wool pellets around the base.
Prune your bush in late winter to shape it and remove dead wood before the spring growth starts.
Grow this desert native in your sunniest, south-facing spot or against a warm wall to boost berries.
items.description: Lycium fremontii is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, that is native to northwestern Mexico and the southernmost mountains and deserts of California and Arizona in the United States. It often grows in areas with alkaline soils, such as alkali flats.

items.name: Nicotiana langsdorffii
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March, as they need light and propagator warmth to germ
Keep young plants indoors until late May, as even a light UK frost will instantly kill them off
Plant them in a spot sheltered from strong UK winds to protect those tall, nodding lime-green stems
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on their sticky leaves
Snip off faded flower spikes in August to encourage a fresh flush of blooms right up to autumn
items.description:
Nicotiana langsdorffii, Langsdorff's tobacco, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, native to Brazil.
Growing to 1.5 m (4.9 ft) tall by 0.5 m (1.6 ft) broad, it is an annual plant with large sticky leaves up to 
10 in (25 cm) long. It bears 2 in (5.1 cm) long, nodding, tubular bell-shaped flowers that are apple green in colour, with blue anthers. N. langsdorfii lacks fragrance, unlike some of the other tall species. It is grown as an ornamental garden plant.

items.name: Streptosolen
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this tender shrub will not survive UK winter frosts.
Prune back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more orange flowers on new wood.
Water copiously in summer but allow the top inch of compost to dry out before watering again.
Feed weekly from May to September with a high-potash liquid tomato food to boost the bloom cycle.
Plant in a loam-based John Innes No 3 compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure rapid drainage.
items.description: Streptosolen is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae. It is closely related to the genus Browallia, within which it was originally placed. The single species, Streptosolen jamesonii, the marmalade bush or fire bush, is an evergreen shrub bearing loose clusters of flowers which change gradually from yellow to red as they develop, resulting in an overall appearance resembling orange marmalade, found in open woodlands in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Peru. The plant has become naturalized in certain localities in Hawaii.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum
items.growersTips:
Chit seed tubers in a cool, bright frost-free room from February to give crops a head start.
Plant tubers 12cm deep in mid-spring, spacing rows 60cm apart to allow room for earthing up.
Draw soil up around growing stems to block light, preventing green toxic tubers and frost damage.
Water tubers deeply once they reach marble size in June to prevent common scab and boost yields.
Watch for potato blight in warm, wet summer weather and cut infected foliage to ground level.
items.description: The potato is a starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas that is consumed as a staple food in many parts of the world. Potatoes are underground stem tubers of the plant Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family Solanaceae.

items.name: Nicotiana longiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in March indoors, as they need light to germinate.
Plant them out in late May after the frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist but never soggy in our damp summers.
Watch out for slugs on young spring leaves, so use organic beer traps or copper tape to save them.
Plant them near your patio or seating area to enjoy their intense evening fragrance in summer.
items.description: Nicotiana longiflora, the longflower tobacco or long-flowered tobacco, is a species of tobacco native to South America that is sometimes cultivated for its tubular flowers that emit a very sweet odour at night.

items.name: Brugmansia insignis
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted insignis indoors by late October before the first damp UK autumn frost hits.
Water daily in summer to keep the soil moist but never let the pot sit in a soggy saucer.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food from May to September to boost those pink trumpets.
Prune back hard in March just above a node to encourage bushy growth and more flowering wood.
Watch out for red spider mites when overwintering them in your warm conservatory or greenhouse.
items.description: Brugmansia insignis is a South American species of angel's trumpet with large, fragrant flowers. The IUCN has listed this species as Extinct in the Wild, although like the other members of its genus its survival has been ensured by its popularity as an ornamental plant.

items.name: Brugmansia vulcanicola
items.growersTips:
Bring this cool-climate beauty indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in ericaceous compost mixed with grit to give its roots the acidic, sharp drainage it loves.
Water deeply but let the top inch of soil dry out first to prevent root rot in our damp summers.
Prune lightly in early spring just as new growth starts, keeping the canopy open for air circulation.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping it in your greenhouse during dry, warm summer spells.
items.description: Brugmansia vulcanicola is a shrub or tree in the family Solanaceae native to Colombia and Ecuador.

items.name: Lycium australe
items.growersTips:
Plant this Aussie boxthorn in a container with grit-heavy soil to protect it from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry completely between drinks to prevent rot.
Prune in late winter to keep its wild, thorny habit tidy and encourage fresh berry-bearing wood.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots, using organic beer traps in our damp spring weather.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum heat for successful fruiting.
items.description: Lycium australe, the Australian boxthorn, is a native Australian plant with large sharp woody spines, small leaves and very small berries. It is closely related to Lycium ferocissimum, which is listed as an invasive weed in Australia, New Zealand and Cyprus.

items.name: Lycium carolinianum
items.growersTips:
Plant this coastal native in your sunniest spot with free-draining sandy soil to mimic its wild home.
Water your young shrub deeply once a week, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and keep this sprawling, thorny scrambler under control.
Protect the root zone with dry mulch in winter to shield it from cold, wet UK soil which rots roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails on juicy new spring shoots, especially during damp British Aprils.
items.description: Lycium carolinianum, commonly known as Carolina desert-thorn or Christmas berry, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae,

items.name: Lycium berlandieri
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in your sunniest UK spot using extremely gritty, free-draining sandy soil.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the soil dry out completely between sparse drenches.
Protect your plant from winter wet by placing a cloche over it during soggy UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the shrub and encourage fresh berry-bearing wood.
Grow it in a terracotta pot to easily move it under cover when the cold frost hits.
items.description: Lycium berlandieri is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common name Berlandier's wolfberry. It is native to Mexico and the south-western United States from Arizona to Texas.

items.name: Lycium exsertum
items.growersTips:
Plant this thorny desert shrub in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native Arizona heat.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into your soil to ensure the roots never sit in damp UK winter wet.
Keep it in a large terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse before frosts hit.
Prune back the wild arching branches in late spring once you see new green shoots starting to show.
Water deeply but let the compost dry out completely between times to prevent root rot in summer.
items.description: Lycium exsertum, the Arizona desert-thorn, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico. A large shrub reaching 12 ft (3.7 m), it is typically found in deserts and scrublands on slopes and alluvial washes.

items.name: Lycium schweinfurthii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mediterranean native in your sunniest spot in sharply draining, gritty soil to avoid rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Prune your shrub in late winter to shape it and encourage fresh, berry-bearing wood for the autumn.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them with organic grit barriers or copper tape.
Grow it in a terracotta pot to keep roots warm and protect it from wet UK winters in a cold frame.
items.description: Lycium schweinfurthii is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. The plant occurs in the south of the Mediterranean in Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Israel, Cyprus and southern Aegean and Sicily and Pantelleria.

items.name: Lycium shawii
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in your sharpest draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a cold greenhouse before the autumn frosts hit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as this tough shrub hates wet feet more than anything else.
Prune in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and clear out any dead winter wood.
Watch out for aphids on the tender new spring shoots and simply blast them off with a garden hose.
items.description: Lycium shawii, desert thorn or Arabian boxthorn is a species of thorny shrub adapted to desert environments, and can be found throughout the Arabian Peninsula, and some places in Africa. The thin leaved, rigid bush grows up to 3 metres high, with a lot of branches and alternating spines that vary in size, and grow along the branches and on their tips. The leaves narrow towards their base. It produces small whitish-pink or purple flowers from September until April, and red pea-sized seedy berries that are edible. Habitats include gravel plains and foothills up to 4,000 ft (1,200 m), as well as

items.name: Latua
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean native in a sheltered south-facing spot to shield it from cold UK winter winds.
Grow it in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Wear heavy gloves when pruning in spring because every part of this rare shrub is highly toxic.
Feed it weekly with a high-potash liquid seaweed from May to August to boost those purple blooms.
Plant it in ericaceous compost mixed with grit to give it the acidic, free-draining soil it loves.
items.description: Latua pubiflora is the single species of the monotypic genus Latua, endemic to the coastal mountains of southern Chile. A shrub or small tree to 10 m in height, bearing attractive, magenta-to-red, hummingbird-pollinated flowers, it is extremely poisonous – hallucinogenic (deliriant) in smaller doses – due to tropane alkaloid content and is used by Chilean machi (shamans) of the Mapuche–Huilliche people in traditional medicine, as a poison and to enter trance states. Its elegant flowers and yellow tomato-like fruit are attractive enough to merit cultivation as an ornamental.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Bintje’
items.growersTips:
Plant Bintje in mid-April when UK soils warm up, burying tubers 12cm deep with eyes facing upwards.
Keep soil evenly moist as Bintje is prone to common scab if dry during early tuber development.
Earth up the stems regularly to protect the shallow-growing yellow tubers from turning green.
Watch out for late blight in damp UK summers, harvesting early if you spot dark spots on leaves.
Store these high-yielding tubers in a dark, cool, frost-free shed to prevent them sprouting.

items.name: Trianaea
items.growersTips:
Start your Trianaea seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short UK summer window.
Plant them out in June after the last frost, spacing them fifty centimetres apart in rich soil.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged in damp UK weather.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around stems.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first tiny fruits start to form in July.
items.description: Trianaea is a genus of the plant family Solanaceae. It occurs in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. It is placed in the subfamily Solanoideae, tribe Juanulloeae.

items.name: Physalis viscosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this spreading perennial in a buried bottomless bucket to restrict its invasive underground runners.
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep, keeping them at twenty degrees to germinate.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Apply a thick layer of straw mulch in late November to protect the crown from severe British frosts.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves when growing this plant inside a UK greenhouse or polytunnel.
items.description: Physalis viscosa is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by many common names, including starhair groundcherry, stellate ground-cherry and grape groundcherry in English, and arrebenta-cavalo, balãozinho, and camambú in Portuguese and Spanish. It is native to South America, and it is known on other continents as an introduced species and sometimes a weed. It can grow in many types of habitat, including disturbed areas.

items.name: Physalis virginiana
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 5cm deep in spring in well-drained sandy loam to prevent winter root rot in UK clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top 3cm of soil to dry out between.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves in dry greenhouse borders or warm south-facing UK patios.
Cut dead stems back to ground level in late autumn and mulch with leaf mould to protect from frost.
Grow in buried bottomless buckets to restrict the invasive running rhizomes from overtaking borders.
items.description: Physalis virginiana, the Virginia groundcherry, is a rhizomatous perennial with a deeply buried stem base. It is found mostly in eastern North America as far west as Wyoming.

items.name: Solanum abutiloides
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short UK summer season.
Plant them out in late May only after all frost risk has passed, spacing them about one metre apart.
Grow them in large pots against a south-facing wall to trap the maximum amount of British sunshine.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells, keeping the fuzzy leaves completely dry.
Stake the heavy, brittle branches early in summer to protect them from strong autumn wind damage.
items.description: Solanum abutiloides is a species of plant in the family Solanaceae. It is endemic to Argentina and Bolivia, and thrives as a weedy plant in rocky land, on stream banks, and scrub land between 900–3600 metres in elevation. It is also known as dwarf tamarillo, due to superficial similarities with Solanum betaceum. Solanum abutiloides is also sometimes known by the archaic name Cyphomandra abutiloides.

items.name: Goetzea
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Solanaceae shrub indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Grow it in a container with peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH slightly acidic.
Prune your plant in late spring after the frost passes to shape it and encourage new flowering wood.
Feed weekly in summer with a high-potash tomato fertiliser to boost those unusual yellow blooms.
items.description: Goetzea is a genus of plant in the family Solanaceae. It was originally placed by H. Wydler in the family Ebenaceae and named for his teacher the Rev. Johann August Ephraim Goetze. It was for about half a century included in the now defunct family Goetzeaceae Miers ex Airy Shaw.

items.name: Goetzea elegans
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Goetzea indoors by late October to shield it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Plant it in a mix of peat-free compost and perlite to ensure the roots never sit in cold water.
Water it deeply once the top two inches of soil dry out, keeping it drier during dark winter months.
Prune the stems lightly in early spring to shape the plant and encourage fresh, bushy new growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping your plant in a warm conservatory or porch.
items.description: Goetzea elegans, also called beautiful goetzea, mata buey, or matabuey, is a species of plant in the Solanaceae or nightshade family of flowering plants. It is endemic to Puerto Rico. Today it is limited to the northwestern corner of the island because of deforestation and other consumption of its habitat for human use. It is federally listed as an endangered species in the island.

items.name: Calibrachoa
items.growersTips:
Plant your calibrachoa in mid-May once UK frosts pass, keeping the compost level with the pot soil.
Water them only when the top inch of soil feels dry, as they hate soggy British winter-like wet.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food from June to September to keep those blooms coming.
Watch out for aphids in humid June weather; wash them off with a gentle spray from your hose.
Give leggy stems a light haircut in mid-August to encourage a fresh flush of late-summer flowers.
items.description: Calibrachoa is a genus of plants in the Solanaceae (nightshade) family. They are evergreen short-lived perennials and subshrubs with a sprawling habit, with small petunia-type flowers. They are found across much the same region of South America as petunias, from southern Brazil across to Peru and Chile, inhabiting scrub and open grassland.

items.name: Anthocercis
items.growersTips:
Grow this Aussie native in a pot with grit so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Water your plant only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its dry native habitat.
Prune lightly right after flowering in summer to keep its wild shrubby shape neat and compact.
Feed with a low-phosphorus liquid fertiliser in spring to avoid damaging its sensitive root system.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids and spider mites when you bring the pot indoors for the winter cold.
items.description: Anthocercis, commonly known as tailflower, is a genus of shrubs which are endemic to southern temperate Australia with the center of distribution in the South West Botanical Province of Western Australia. All species of Anthocercis contain tropane alkaloids, and have occasionally caused poisoning in children or been suspected of poisoning stock. Anthocercis is known as the only Solanaceous plant known to produce resin compounds on glandular trichomes.

items.name: Solandra
items.growersTips:
Grow your chalice vine in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water heavily during the summer active growth phase, then let the compost dry out completely in winter.
Prune your Solandra hard in early spring to control its massive size and encourage summer flowers.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost to prevent root rot during damp British springs.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plant indoors.
items.description: Solandra is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. It is named after the Swedish naturalist Daniel C. Solander.

items.name: Nicandra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March to get a head start on our short UK summer, planting just 1.5cm deep.
Wait until late May after the last frosts to plant them out in a sunny, sheltered spot.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry spells in July and August.
Plant them near your greenhouse tomatoes to help deter whiteflies with their natural insect repellent.
Shake the dry lantern pods into a paper bag in autumn to easily collect seeds for next spring.
items.description: Nicandra  is a genus of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae, native to western South America. It was first described by Michel Adanson in 1763. The genus is named for Greek poet Nicander of Colophon, who wrote about plants – notably in his poem Alexipharmaca, which treats of poisons and their antidotes.

items.name: Anisodus
items.growersTips:
Plant this toxic Solanaceae cousin in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered, sunny spot.
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at 5mm deep using bottom heat to overcome erratic germination.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, letting the top few inches of soil dry out first.
Cut the faded stems back to ground level in late autumn and apply a thick mulch to protect roots.
items.description: Anisodus is a genus of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Solandra maxima
items.growersTips:
Bring your chalice vine indoors by October as it cannot survive a wet UK winter frost outdoors.
Grow this vigorous climber in a large pot so you can restrict its roots and encourage more flowers.
Water sparingly in winter but drench it once a week in summer when the top inch of soil feels dry.
Prune hard in early spring to keep its massive growth in check and fit your conservatory space.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food from May to September to boost those huge yellow blooms.
items.description: Solandra maxima is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is also known as cup of gold vine, golden chalice vine, Copa de Oro, or Hawaiian lily, is a vigorous vine which is endemic to Mexico and Central America. It has very large yellow flowers and glossy leaves. It is often planted as an ornamental plant.

items.name: Physalis minima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using a heated propagator to offset UK cold.
Transplant outdoors in late May only after the final frost into free-draining soil facing south.
Water the base deeply once weekly to prevent fruit splitting while keeping the foliage dry.
Construct a sturdy bamboo tripod support in June to prevent heavy fruiting stems from snapping.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under leaves and mist with water to raise local humidity.
items.description: Physalis angulata is an erect herbaceous annual plant belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Its leaves are dark green and roughly ovate, often with serrate margins. The flowers are five-sided and pale yellow; the yellow-orange fruits are borne inside a balloon-like calyx. The exact native range is uncertain.
