The species may be naturally endemic to Australia or the Americas or the native range may encompass both the Americas and Australia. It is now widely distributed and naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

items.name: Bouchetia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South American native in a greenhouse or sunny conservatory to beat the UK chill.
Plant your seeds in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam mix with a neutral to acidic pH.
Water sparingly from below to keep the foliage dry, letting the top inch of soil dry out completely.
Watch out for glasshouse whiteflies and red spider mites, using yellow sticky traps to catch them.
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potassium liquid tomato food to encourage healthy growth.
items.description:
Bouchetia is the scientific name of two genera of organisms and may refer to:Bouchetia (gastropod), a genus of molluscs in the family Muricidae
Bouchetia (plant), a genus of plants in the family Solanaceae

items.name: Physalis pumila
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained sandy loam with neutral pH to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep and transplant outdoors after the May frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent shallow sprinkles.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn and mulch with straw to protect roots from frost.
Watch for red spider mites in dry glasshouses and handpick common UK garden snails from young stems.
items.description: Physalis pumila, commonly known as dwarf ground-cherry or prairie ground-cherry, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. It is a perennial or rhizomatous geophyte native to the central and south-central United States. The species grows in open habitats including glades, prairies, sandhills, dunes, sandy floodplains, fields, disturbed habitats, and roadsides.

items.name: Reyesia
items.growersTips:
Sow Reyesia seeds indoors in early April at a depth of 1cm to protect them from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy by watering gently at the base every three days.
Watch out for slugs on young Reyesia shoots during wet British May nights and use beer traps.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your outdoor bed two weeks before transplanting Reyesia.
Plant Reyesia next to French marigolds to naturally deter aphids and boost your crop's growth.
items.description: Reyesia is a small genus of four species of flowering plants belonging to the subfamily Cestroideae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. It is closely related to the genus Salpiglossis, which provides the ornamental species Salpiglossis sinuata. Together, the genera Reyesia and Salpiglossis form the tribe Salpiglossideae within the Cestroideae. Historically, the species now placed in Reyesia have been held by some authors to belong to Salpiglossis, but are currently placed in a genus of their own by virtue of their tiny flowers and peculiar androecium.

items.name: Cyphomandra
items.growersTips:
Start your tamarillo seeds indoors in warm propagators during February to beat the short UK summer.
Grow them in large thirty-centimetre pots so you can easily move them into a greenhouse by October.
Water deeply twice a week in summer, but let the top inch of compost dry out to prevent root rot.
Prune the main tip when it reaches one metre high to force branching and get much more fruit.
Watch out for whiteflies under the leaves in July and use soapy water sprays to keep them away.
items.description: Cyphomandra was a formerly accepted genus in the plant family Solanaceae. It used to contain about 35 species native to the Americas from Mexico southwards to Northern Argentina.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Kerr’s Pink’
items.growersTips:
Pop Kerrs Pink in early April planting tubers twelve centimetres deep to protect from late UK frosts
Give these thirsty heavy yielders a deep weekly soak once they flower to ensure massive tubers
Watch out for late blight in damp British summers by harvesting as soon as the foliage turns brown
Earth up the stems regularly to stop the shallow growing pink skinned tubers from turning green
Store these dry floury spuds in breathable paper sacks in a dark shed to prevent rot and greening

items.name: Brunfelsia
items.growersTips:
Bring your yesterday-today-and-tomorrow indoors by October to protect it from chilly UK frosts.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil acidic, letting the top inch dry out between waterings.
Prune your shrub right after its spring flowering to keep it compact and encourage new blooms.
Feed with an ericaceous fertiliser every fortnight from April to September to boost those flowers.
Watch out for aphids and spider mites when you move your potted plant into the winter conservatory.
items.description: Brunfelsia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to subfamily Petunioideae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. The 50 or so species have been grouped into the three sections: Brunfelsia, Franciscea and Guianenses, which differ significantly in both distribution and characteristics, although molecular data have revealed that only two sections are natural (monophyletic), namely the Caribbean section Brunfelsia and a common section for all South American species. Linnaeus named the genus for the early German herbalist Otto Brunfels (1488–1534).

items.name: Solandra grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Bring this chalice vine indoors by October as it cannot survive a frosty UK winter wet.
Grow it in a large container of peat-free loam-based compost to easily restrict its vigorous roots.
Water it freely from May to September but keep the soil almost bone dry throughout the winter.
Prune the runaway shoots hard in early spring to encourage the flowering spurs to develop.
Place it in your sunniest conservatory spot to mimic its native Mexican heat and trigger blooms.
items.description: Solandra grandiflora, the showy chalicevine, or papaturra is a member of the nightshade (Solanaceae) genus Solandra and, like the other members of the genus, is a climbing plant with large, attractive, trumpet-shaped flowers. It is native to Central America and northern South America and is widely grown in the tropics as an ornamental. The green parts of the plant are highly toxic, due to tropane alkaloid content, and have caused deaths from anticholinergic poisoning, but the flesh of the ripe fruit is said to be edible. The fruits, which are globular and largely enclosed by the accrescent cal

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Ratte’
items.growersTips:
Sprout your Ratte seed tubers in a cool, bright UK room from February to give them a head start.
Plant them eight inches deep in mid-April to protect those delicate French fingerlings from late frosts.
Water your Ratte plants deeply once a week rather than daily to encourage long, smooth tubers.
Earth up the soil around the stems regularly to prevent the shallow-growing tips from turning green.
Harvest these gourmet spuds just as the flowers fade to get that perfect, waxy salad texture.

items.name: Grabowskia
items.growersTips:
Plant this thorny South American shrub in your sunniest, sheltered UK spot to mimic its native heat.
Give it sharply draining soil with plenty of grit to protect its roots from wet British winters.
Prune your grabowskia in late spring after frosts pass to shape it and encourage fresh new growth.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between.
Grow it in a large terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse when winter freezes hit.
items.description: Lycium is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. The genus has a disjunct distribution around the globe, with species occurring on most continents in temperate and subtropical regions. South America has the most species, followed by North America and southern Africa. There are several scattered across Europe and Asia, and one is native to Australia. Common English names for plants of this genus include box-thorn, wolfberry, and desert-thorn. Plants of the World Online currently accepts 101 species. Other estimates are of 70 to 80 species.

items.name: Solanum villosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators in March then plant out after the very last May frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent blossom end rot in dry spells.
Watch out for aphids and flea beetles which love to chew tiny holes in the young spring leaves.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and much more orange fruit.
Grow them alongside marigolds or basil to help deter the pests that naturally plague nightshades.
items.description: Solanum villosum, also known as the hairy nightshade, red nightshade, or woolly nightshade, is a species of sprawling annual weed. It is found in Europe, western Asia, northern Africa and is also naturalized in Australia and North America.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Vitelotte Noire’
items.growersTips:
Plant these deep-blue beauties in mid-April once the cold UK soil warms to at least eight degrees.
Keep them well-watered as tubers form in June, aiming for the damp soil they need to prevent scab.
Earth up the stems regularly to stop the dark skin of shallow tubers from turning toxic green.
Watch out for late blight during warm, wet UK July spells and cut foliage back if you spot spots.
Harvest this late-season variety in October once the leaves yellow and die back naturally.

items.name: Physalis angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Grow in pots of sandy loam to restrict aggressive rhizome spread and facilitate winter shelter.
Water deeply once a week during summer dry spells to prevent fruit drop while avoiding waterlogging.
Handpick three-lined potato beetles and their sticky orange eggs from the foliage in June and July.
Cut the frost-damaged stems back to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect roots.
items.description: Physalis angustifolia, the coastal groundcherry, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to the Gulf Coast shoreline of the Southeastern United States, where it is found on maritime dunes and sands.

items.name: Physalis walteri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to offset UK cold.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.
Check weekly for red spider mites under leaves when growing in UK greenhouses or polytunnels.
Prune the stems back to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect roots from frost.
items.description: Physalis walteri, commonly known as Walter's groundcherry or dune groundcherry, is a species of flowering plant. Its native distribution is Alabama, Florida, Georgia and Virginia in the United States as well as Northeast Mexico. Its habitat is pinelands and open coastal areas.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Irish Whites’
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers late April in the UK at fifteen centimeters deep to avoid any late spring frosts.
Earth up the stems regularly as they grow to protect the shallow tubers from turning green and toxic.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily sprinkles to boost tuber size.
Watch out for late blight in damp UK Augusts, cutting foliage to ground level if you spot brown spots.
Harvest these late-season bakers in October once the foliage has completely died back on its own.

items.name: Physochlaina
items.growersTips:
Plant your Physochlaina orientalis tubers 10cm deep in autumn to protect them from wet UK winters.
Grow this early riser in gritty, alkaline soil to prevent winter rot in damp British climates.
Position it in partial shade under deciduous shrubs so it gets spring sun but stays cool in summer.
Watch out for slugs in early March as the delicate, dark purple shoots first push through the soil.
Let the foliage die back naturally in June as it goes dormant, then mark the spot so you do not dig it up.
items.description: Physochlaina is a small genus of herbaceous perennial flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family, Solanaceae, found principally in the north-western provinces of China although one species occurs in Western Asia, while others occur in Siberia, Mongolia and the Chinese autonomous region of Inner Mongolia. Some sources maintain that the widespread species P. physaloides is found also in Japan, but the species is not recorded as being native in one of the few English-language floras of the country. The genus has medicinal value, being rich in tropane alkaloids, and is also of ornamental

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Atlantic’
items.growersTips:
Chit your Atlantic seed potatoes in February to get a head start before the chilly UK spring soil.
Plant tubers 12cm deep in mid-April to protect early shoots from late frosts in UK gardens.
Water heavily as tubers swell in June to prevent common scab, which Atlantic is prone to.
Harvest Atlantic early as a second early baker because leaving them too long makes them hollow.
Store these high-dry-matter spuds in breathable paper sacks in a dark shed to prevent greening.

items.name: Lycianthes
items.growersTips:
Grow Lycianthes rantonnetii in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top inch of soil dry out to prevent root rot.
Prune back hard in early spring, just as new growth starts, to keep its bushy, flowering shape.
Watch out for aphids and glasshouse whitefly, especially when overwintering your plants indoors.
Mix plenty of grit and well-rotted manure into your compost to give them the rich drainage they love.
items.description: Lycianthes is a genus of plants from the nightshade family (Solanaceae), found in both the Old World and the New World, but predominantly in the latter. It contains over 150 species, mostly from tropical America, with 35-40 species in Asia and the Pacific.

items.name: Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 6mm deep, keeping them on a warm windowsill to beat the UK chill.
Plant outdoors in late May, burying the stem up to the first leaves to grow extra strong roots.
Water the soil directly every morning, never the leaves, to stop late blight in wet UK summers.
Pinch out the side shoots of indeterminate cherry types weekly to channel energy into juicy fruit.
Grow French marigolds nearby to naturally repel aphids and whiteflies from your tomato patch.

items.name: Solanum sessiliflorum
items.growersTips:
Start cocona seeds indoors in warm propagators by February to beat the short, cool UK summer.
Grow them in large pots under glass or in a sunny conservatory to shield them from chilly UK winds.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food once yellow flowers appear to boost the tropical fruit.
Water deeply at the base whenever the top inch of compost dries out, keeping the soil evenly moist.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in hot weather and mist leaves regularly to deter them.
items.description: Solanum sessiliflorum, the cocona, is a tropical shrub of the family Solanaceae. The cocona plant has sturdy branches and huge, serrate and hairy leaves. Cocona closely resembles a number of close relatives, including naranjilla and pseudolulo It can be distinguished from those plants by its lack of spines. It will hybridize with those and other close relatives. Cocona also lacks the characteristic purple coloring usually seen in the naranjilla. Its flowers resemble large potato flowers, with light green petals. Cocona is harvested in parts of South America around the Amazon rainforest such as

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘British Queen’
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers 12cm deep in mid-April to avoid late UK frosts damaging the delicate early shoots.
Earthing up twice is vital for this floury variety to prevent the shallow tubers from turning green.
Water deeply once a week when flowers appear to ensure you get those beautifully fluffy, large spuds.
Keep an eye out for blight in warm, humid July weather and cut foliage back immediately if it hits.
Harvest in August as soon as the skins set, as leaving them in wet autumn soil leads to slug damage.

items.name: Mellissia begoniifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare St Helena native indoors by October to protect it from wet, frosty UK winters.
Sow the seeds shallowly in free-draining, gritty compost to prevent damp dampening-off disease.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this species hates soggy British ground.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse whitefly and aphids when growing them under cover in spring.
Grow them in pots on a sunny south-facing patio to catch every bit of our fleeting summer warmth.
items.description: Mellissia was formerly a monotypic genus in the family Solanaceae with the single species, Mellissia begoniifolia, endemic to the island of Saint Helena. It was named by Joseph Dalton Hooker in honour of John Charles Melliss, a 19th-century engineer and amateur naturalist who worked on Saint Helena.

items.name: Espadaea
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in April, then transplant outside only after late May frosts.
Plant them deep in rich, organic soil with a handful of grit to survive wet, cold UK summers.
Water deeply at the base once a week, keeping the leaves dry to prevent damp-weather powdery mildew.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails during damp June nights, using organic beer traps nearby.
Prune back the lower leaves in late August to let the rare autumn sunshine ripen the remaining crop.
items.description: Espadaea is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae. The only species is Espadaea amoena.

items.name: Solanum bulbocastanum
items.growersTips:
Plant these wild spuds in late April once the soil warms up, burying tubers about ten centimetres deep.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent the tubers from rotting in cool UK rain.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots, though you can relax about late blight as this species is immune.
Grow them in a sunny, sheltered spot or under glass to help them cope with cooler British summers.
Harvest in autumn after the foliage dies back, but handle the small, knobby tubers very gently.
items.description: Solanum bulbocastanum, the ornamental nightshade, is a plant in the family Solanaceae, native to Mexico and parts of the U.S. Southwest. It is closely related to the potato and, as it has evolved strong resistance to all known varieties of potato blight, has been used to genetically engineer resistance into the cultivated varieties of potatoes around the world. The use of genetic engineering is helpful, as efforts to hybridize by traditional methods have so far been unsuccessful, and the use of somatic hybridization to transfer genes is difficult. A resistance to the Columbia root-knot nematod

items.name: Solanum torvum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February on a heat mat at 25C to give them the long hot summer they need here.
Grow this tender perennial in a large pot so you can move it inside a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply once a week to mimic tropical downpours, but let the top inch of compost dry out first.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mites when keeping this plant sheltered indoors.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and keep its thorny spread in check.
items.description: Solanum torvum, also known as pendejera, turkey berry, devil's fig, pea eggplant, platebrush or susumber, is a bushy, erect and spiny perennial plant used horticulturally as a rootstock for eggplant. Grafted plants are very vigorous and tolerate diseases affecting the root system, thus allowing the crop to continue for a second year.

items.name: Alkekengi officinarum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March to beat the UK chill, then transplant outside after the May frosts.
Plant them in a sturdy container to stop their aggressive, invasive roots taking over your beds.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep a sharp eye out for red spider mites during dry UK summers and mist the leaves to deter them.
Cut the stems back to ground level in late autumn and mulch well to protect them from winter rot.
items.description: Alkekengi is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family Solanaceae with a single species Alkekengi officinarum. This species is native to the regions covering Southern Europe to South Asia and Northeast Asia.

items.name: Petunioideae
items.growersTips:
Sow your tomato seeds indoors in March, barely covered with compost, on a warm windowsill.
Water your potatoes deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep root growth.
Keep a sharp eye out for potato blight during warm, wet July spells and cut infected foliage fast.
Plant your peppers alongside basil in well-drained soil to help naturally deter pesky UK aphids.
Pinch out the side shoots of your cordon tomatoes weekly in summer to focus energy on the fruit.
items.description: Petunioideae is a subfamily within the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Witheringia
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short UK growing season.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in our cool British summers.
Watch out for greenhouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing these tender plants under glass.
Feed them weekly with high-potash tomato food once the first delicate star-shaped flowers appear.
Move your pots into a heated greenhouse or bright conservatory by October before the first frost.
items.description: Witheringia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae, with a neotropical distribution. It is closely related to Physalis.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Gala’
items.growersTips:
Chit-grow this early maincrop in April, planting tubers 12cm deep to avoid late UK spring frosts.
Keep soil consistently damp as tubers swell in July to prevent common scab on their yellow skins.
Earth up the stems regularly to stop light turning these shallow-growing Gala potatoes green.
Watch for blight during warm, humid UK July days and cut foliage to the ground if you see it.
Harvest these beauties in August once the leaves yellow, then dry them for top-notch storage.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Desiree’
items.growersTips:
Plant Desiree tubers 12cm deep in mid-April to protect young spring shoots from late UK frosts.
Earth up soil around stems weekly as they grow to prevent these red-skinned tubers turning green.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily sprinkles to avoid scab disease.
Watch out for late potato blight in warm, wet UK Augusts and cut foliage to the ground if it strikes.
Leave harvested Desiree tubers in the autumn sun for a few hours to cure the skins for winter storage.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Anya’
items.growersTips:
Start sprouting Anya tubers in February to give this slow-growing salad potato a vital head start.
Plant them deep in April, about twelve centimetres down, to protect early shoots from late frosts.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkling to encourage those long, nutty-tasting tubers.
Keep a sharp eye out for blight during warm, wet July spells and harvest early if you spot it.
Leave them in the soil until the foliage dies back to let their delicious skin set properly.

items.name: Anthocercis viscosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this Aussie native in a terracotta pot with grit so you can move it indoors before frost hits.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this shrub hates wet feet in UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to keep it bushy and prevent it from getting leggy.
Mix plenty of horticultural sand into your peat-free compost to mimic its coastal habitat.
Watch out for aphids on the sticky yellow flowers and wash them off with a gentle spray of water.
items.description: Anthocercis viscosa, also known as sticky tailflower, is a species of shrub in the family Solanaceae, native to the south coast of Western Australia. It grows up to 3 metres in height and produces white or cream flowers between May and February in its native range.

items.name: Symonanthus
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Australian native in a very sandy, free-draining acidic soil to mimic its home.
Keep watering minimal once established, only dampening the soil when the top two inches are dry.
Protect your plants from harsh UK winter frosts by moving pots into a bright, unheated greenhouse.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to keep its wild, spindly habit neat and bushy.
Watch out for root rot in wet British winters, so always use pots with generous drainage holes.
items.description: Symonanthus is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae. The genus was circumscribed by Laurence Arnold Robert Haegi in Telopea vol.2 on page 175 in 1981.

items.name: Cyphanthera
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Australian native in a container so you can bring it inside before winter frosts hit.
Use a very free-draining, gritty soil mix with low phosphorus to mimic its natural sandy habitat.
Water deeply only when the top few inches of soil are dry, as they hate having soggy roots in winter.
Place your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to maximise summer flowering.
Prune lightly right after flowering in late summer to keep its naturally leggy habit bushy and neat.
items.description: Cyphanthera is a genus of nine species of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae and are endemic to Australia.

items.name: Anthocercis littorea
items.growersTips:
Grow this Aussie native in a pot with grit so you can move it inside before the first autumn frost.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this shrub hates wet feet in UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to keep it bushy, but never cut back into old wood.
Blend fifty percent horticultural grit with peat-free compost to mimic its natural coastal sand.
Watch out for aphids on new spring shoots and blast them off with a sharp spray from your hose.
items.description: Anthocercis littorea, also known as yellow tailflower, is a species of shrub in the family Solanaceae. It is native to Western Australia where it grows on coastal limestone and dunes as well as sandplains.

items.name: Calibrachoa parviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant these mini petunias in mid-May once UK frosts pass, keeping the crown level with the soil.
Water them only when the top inch of compost feels dry, as they hate soggy British winter wet.
Pinch out the growing tips in early June to encourage a bushier habit and way more summer flowers.
Feed weekly with a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser from July to keep the blooms coming.
Watch out for aphids in damp UK Junes, washing them off with a gentle spray from your garden hose.
items.description: Calibrachoa parviflora is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family known by the common name seaside petunia. It is native to much of southeastern South America, Mexico, and the southwestern United States, and it is present as an introduced species in other sections of the Americas, such as the southeastern United States, as well as in Australia, where it is an occasional weed in New South Wales. This herb produces slender, branching stems which creep along the ground and root at nodes. The upright branches are leafy, with fleshy, glandular, oblong or widely lance-shaped leaves. Th

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Kennebec’
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-season baker in mid-April, burying tubers 12cm deep to dodge late UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week when tubers swell, rather than daily sprinkles, to prevent hollow heart.
Keep a sharp eye out for late blight in damp Augusts; harvest early if the leaves turn black.
Earth up the stems twice by June to stop the shallow-growing Kennebec tubers from turning green.
Store these high-starch spuds in dark, breathable paper sacks to keep them perfect for roasting.

items.name: Solanum nigrum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep to give this heat-lover a head start in the UK.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent the shallow roots from drying out in June.
Watch out for aphids and flea beetles in June, washing them off with a gentle spray of soapy water.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage a bushier habit and increase your berry yield.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil before planting to satisfy this heavy feeder.
items.description: Solanum nigrum, the European black nightshade or simply black nightshade or blackberry nightshade, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae, native to Eurasia and introduced in the Americas, Australasia, and South Africa. Ripe berries and cooked leaves of edible strains are used as food in some locales, and plant parts are used as a traditional medicine. Some other species may also be referred to as "black nightshade".

items.name: Anisodus tanguticus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Solanaceae family native in deep, gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its Tibetan home.
Sow seeds in early spring indoors using a heated propagator, as they need warmth to germinate.
Position your pot in full sun but shelter it from wet UK winters, which can rot the fleshy roots.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant to avoid absorbing harmful alkaloids.
Water moderately during the summer active growth phase, then keep it almost dry throughout winter.
items.description: Anisodus tanguticus  is a species of flowering plant belonging to tribe Hyoscyameae of subfamily Solanoideae of the nightshade family Solanaceae. It is thus closely related to Henbane and Deadly Nightshade. Solanaceae is a plant family which includes many important agricultural plants such as the potato and the tomato. It is mostly found growing in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. A. tanguticus is collected and used mostly for its medicinal effects caused by the plant's biologically active nicotine and tropane alkaloids. It has a significant impact in China as one of the 50 fundamental herbs used

items.name: Lycium
items.growersTips:
Plant your goji berry in a sunny, sheltered spot to help the fruits ripen in our cool UK summers.
Prune your bush in late winter by removing low branches to keep the heavy summer berries off the damp soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry spells while the young plant establishes its deep root system.
Grow them in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; add a handful of grit if your garden has heavy clay.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp autumn weather by thinning the centre to improve air circulation.
items.description: Lycium is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. The genus has a disjunct distribution around the globe, with species occurring on most continents in temperate and subtropical regions. South America has the most species, followed by North America and southern Africa. There are several scattered across Europe and Asia, and one is native to Australia. Common English names for plants of this genus include box-thorn, wolfberry, and desert-thorn. Plants of the World Online currently accepts 101 species. Other estimates are of 70 to 80 species.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Marfona’
items.growersTips:
Chit Marfona tubers in February to get a head start before planting them out in mid-April.
Plant tubers 12cm deep in ridges spaced 70cm apart to give these large, waxy spuds room to swell.
Water heavily as the flowers open to ensure your Marfona skins stay smooth and free from common scab.
Earth up the soil around the stems regularly to prevent the shallow-growing tubers from turning green.
Harvest these second early potatoes in July as soon as the foliage begins to turn yellow and die back.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Laura’
items.growersTips:
Chit-grow this red-skinned beauty indoors from February to give it a head start for the UK spring.
Plant tubers 12cm deep in April, spacing them 35cm apart to allow room for those lovely red spuds.
Keep soil consistently damp once flowering starts to stop the tubers from getting unsightly scab.
Earth up the stems regularly as they grow to protect the shallow pink-eyed tubers from greening.
Watch out for late blight in damp UK Augusts, cutting foliage to the ground if leaves turn black.

items.name: Solanum tuberosum ‘Home Guard’
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers early in March, about 12cm deep, as they handle the cool UK spring soil brilliantly.
Protect the early emerging foliage from late frosts by earthing them up with soil or using fleece.
Keep the soil consistently moist once flowers bud to ensure your baby new potatoes swell nicely.
Harvest this first early variety in June as soon as they flower for that perfect waxy texture.
Watch out for slugs in damp British weather by using organic beer traps around your potato patch.

items.name: Lycianthes rantonnetii
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted potato bush indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from UK freezes.
Prune it hard in early spring down to a strong framework to encourage loads of fresh flowering wood.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food from May to September to boost those purple blossoms.
Keep the compost consistently moist during summer but let the top inch dry out before watering again.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it to the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden.
items.description: Lycianthes rantonnetii, the blue potato bush or Paraguay nightshade, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, native to South America. Though related to food plants like the potato and tomato, all parts of the plant are considered toxic to humans.

items.name: Benthamiella
items.growersTips:
Try growing Benthamiella in a gritty, free-draining alpine compost to survive wet British winters.
Keep these tiny cushions dry in winter by covering them with a rain-protecting pane of glass or cloche.
Water sparingly from below in summer to prevent the dense, velvety foliage from rotting at the base.
Position your pots in full sun on a south-facing patio to mimic their native Patagonian habitat.
Topdress the soil surface with horticultural grit to keep the delicate foliage off damp compost.

items.name: Solanum crispum
items.growersTips:
Plant Glasnevin in free-draining soil against a south wall to protect it from cold UK winter winds.
Prune hard in early spring by cutting back the previous year's shoots to a strong bud near the base.
Tie the lax stems to a sturdy trellis or wire support system as this shrub cannot climb on its own.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop and support continuous blooms.
Watch for aphids and potato blight in humid UK summers, removing affected foliage immediately.

items.name: Solanum dulcamara
items.growersTips:
Plant this native scrambler in damp, semi-shaded UK spots like bog gardens or near garden ponds.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in autumn because every part of this woody nightshade is toxic.
Support its weak climbing stems with a sturdy trellis or let it weave through a native hedge.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry British summer spells.
Watch out for the red-and-black capsid bug which loves to feast on the young summer shoots.
items.description: Solanum dulcamara is a species of vine in the genus Solanum of the family Solanaceae. Common names include bittersweet, bittersweet nightshade, bitter nightshade, blue bindweed, Amara Dulcis, climbing nightshade, felonwort, fellenwort, felonwood, poisonberry, poisonflower, scarlet berry, snakeberry, trailing bittersweet, trailing nightshade, violet bloom, and woody nightshade.

items.name: Browallia
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators around March to beat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Sow the tiny seeds on top of damp peat-free compost because they need light to trigger germination.
Pinch out the growing tips when stems reach ten centimetres to encourage a bushy, flower-filled habit.
Water them at the base to keep the soil damp but never soggy, which prevents root rot in damp summers.
Bring your pots inside to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frosts arrive in October.
items.description: Browallia is a small genus of seven species of flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. It is named after Johannes Browallius (1707–1755), also known as Johan Browall, a Swedish botanist, physician and bishop. The genus is closely related to the monotypic genus Streptosolen, the single species of which was published initially under the name Browallia jamesonii.

items.name: Metternichia
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short, cool British growing season.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in our unpredictable UK weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, using beer traps to protect young shoots.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil before planting to give these hungry feeders a boost.
Grow them under a cloche or fleece in May to shield the tender young plants from late British frosts.

items.name: Jaborosa
items.growersTips:
Grow Jaborosa integrifolia in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK rain.
Plant your Jaborosa in a sheltered, south-facing border to trap maximum summer warmth and sun.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep the soil almost dry during our cold, damp winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love devouring the tender emerging nightshade foliage.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn and overwintering them in a frost-free green house.

items.name: Solanum wendlandii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first autumn frost
Provide a sturdy trellis or wires to support the vigorous, scrambling stems armed with sharp thorns
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty soil to dry out completely
Prune hard in late winter to healthy buds to control size and encourage fresh flowering wood
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering in a heated conservatory

items.name: Solanum mammosum
items.growersTips:
Start these frost-sensitive seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short UK summer.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost on your sunniest patio so you can move them inside in autumn.
Water deeply at the base only when the top inch of soil dries, keeping the fuzzy leaves bone dry.
Stake the heavy, fruit-laden stems early in summer to prevent them snapping in wet, windy weather.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap sprays.
items.description: Solanum mammosum, commonly known as nipplefruit, fox head, cow's udder, or apple of Sodom, is an inedible Pan-American tropical fruit. The plant is grown for ornamental purposes, in part because of the distal end of the fruit's resemblance to a human breast, while the proximal end looks like a cow's udder. It is an annual in the family Solanaceae, and part of the genus Solanum, making the plant a relative of the eggplant, tomato, and potato. This poisonous fruit is native to South America, but has been naturalized in Southern Mexico, Greater Antilles, Central America, and the Caribbean. The pl

items.name: Solanum mauritianum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and keep its rapid spread contained.
Wear gloves and a mask when handling to avoid irritation from the fine, dusty hairs on the leaves.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty, free-draining soil to dry.
Check foliage weekly for aphids and glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering indoors.

items.name: Solanum aethiopicum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in February to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow these bitter tomatoes in a greenhouse or polytunnel as they need more heat than UK summers give.
Water the soil deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep a sharp eye out for red spider mites which thrive on these plants in dry greenhouse air.
Feed them high-potash tomato food once the first starry flowers appear to boost your berry yield.
items.description: Solanum aethiopicum, the bitter tomato, Ethiopian eggplant, or nakati, is a fruiting plant of the genus Solanum mainly found in Asia and Tropical Africa. It is also known as Ethiopian nightshade, garden eggs, pumpkin-on-a-stick, and mock tomato. It is a popular vegetable in north-east India, and is known as khamen akhaba in Manipuri and samṭawk in Mizo. They are called Titay bii or simply bii in Darjeeling, Sikkim and Nepal, and are relished with meat, particularly pork. These names are a result of its varied morphology, with ripe fruit often looking like a cross between an eggplant and a toma

items.name: Solanum laxum
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south or west-facing wall in fertile, well-drained soil to survive UK winter frosts.
Prune hard in early spring by cutting back overgrown stems to a strong framework to boost summer bloom.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Tie new shoots regularly to a sturdy trellis or wires as this scrambler lacks self-clinging tendrils.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch around the base in November to protect roots from freezing soil.
items.description: Solanum laxum, commonly known as potato vine, potato climber or jasmine nightshade, is an evergreen vine in the family Solanaceae. It is native to South America and commonly grown as an ornamental garden plant.

items.name: Solanum pyracanthos
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active summer growing season.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning in spring to protect your hands from the sharp orange thorns.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot possible to encourage summer flowering.
Check regularly for aphids and red spider mites which thrive on this plant in dry conservatory air.

items.name: Mandragora
items.growersTips:
Plant mandrake seeds in deep pots of sandy, free-draining loam to let the long taproot grow freely.
Keep your mandrake cosy by overwintering it in a cold frame to protect the roots from UK wet rots.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil dries out, but cut right back when it goes dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love devouring the young emerging leaves.
Sow fresh seeds in autumn outdoors so the natural winter chill can break their stubborn dormancy.
items.description: Mandragora may refer to:

items.name: Solanum nelsonii
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian coastal nightshade indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to mimic its native sandy, free-draining soil.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this wild tomato relative hates soggy roots.
Keep it in your brightest south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to get enough UK summer sunshine.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and mist the leaves occasionally to deter red spider mites.

items.name: Cestrum aurantiacum
items.growersTips:
Bring this orange jessamine indoors to a frost-free conservatory by November to survive UK winters.
Plant your Cestrum in a container using peat-free loam-based compost with added grit for drainage.
Water generously through the summer growing season but keep the soil barely damp during winter.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more orange blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping this plant under cover.

items.name: Solanum pimpinellifolium
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm March, then plant out in June once all UK spring frosts have fully passed.
Give this wild tomato a sturdy trellis or net to support its sprawling, highly vigorous branches.
Water consistently at the base to prevent skin splitting on the tiny, sweet currant-sized fruits.
Do not prune the side shoots, as this wild species fruits best when left to grow as a bushy vine.
Look out for late blight in damp UK Augusts, though this species is tougher than standard tomatoes.
items.description: Solanum pimpinellifolium, commonly known as the currant tomato or pimp, is a wild species of tomato native to Ecuador and Peru but naturalized elsewhere, such as the Galápagos Islands. Its small fruits are edible, and it is commonly grown in gardens as an heirloom tomato, although it is considered to be wild rather than domesticated as is the commonly cultivated tomato species Solanum lycopersicum. Its genome was sequenced in 2012.

items.name: Nicotiana acuminata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in March indoors as they need light and warmth to germinate.
Acclimatise plants gradually before planting out in late May after the very last UK spring frost.
Water the soil directly at the base in the morning to prevent damp foliage and grey mould issues.
Position near seating areas to enjoy the evening scent which is strongest during British summer nights.
Watch out for aphids and tobacco flea beetles which target the sticky leaves of this species.
items.description: Nicotiana acuminata is a species of wild tobacco known by the English common name manyflower tobacco. It is native to Argentina and Chile but it is known on other continents, including North America and Australia, as an introduced species.

items.name: Solanum pseudocapsicum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free windowsill by October as this tender shrub cannot survive UK winters.
Water thoroughly when the top inch of soil dries out, but reduce watering in winter to avoid rot.
Hand-pollinate indoor spring flowers with a soft brush to ensure a heavy crop of autumn berries.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to maintain a bushy shape and encourage fresh fruiting wood.
Watch for aphids and red spider mites when keeping this plant in dry, heated indoor winter air.

items.name: Datura
items.growersTips:
Start your Datura seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short UK summer.
Grow them in pots on a south-facing patio so you can move them into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Feed them weekly with high-potash tomato food from June to September to boost those massive blooms.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping them in dry greenhouse conditions during July and August.
Wear thick gloves when pruning back the stems in autumn because every part of this plant is toxic.
items.description: Datura is a genus of nine species of highly poisonous, vespertine-flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae). They are commonly known as thornapples or jimsonweeds, but are also known as devil's trumpets or mad apple. Other English common names include moonflower, devil's weed, and hell's bells. All species of Datura are extremely poisonous and psychoactive, especially their seeds and flowers, which can cause respiratory depression, arrhythmias, fever, delirium, hallucinations, anticholinergic toxidrome, psychosis, and death, if taken internally.

items.name: Solanum jamesii
items.growersTips:
Plant your small tubers about ten centimetres deep in late April once the UK soil starts to warm up.
Give them a sunny, sheltered spot in well-drained soil to mimic their native dry Southwest home.
Water them deeply but infrequently, letting the soil dry out between waterings to prevent tuber rot.
Watch out for late frosts and cover early shoots with fleece to protect the delicate young foliage.
Harvest the tiny tubers only after the autumn frosts have completely killed off the top growth.

items.name: Solanum rostratum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using bottom heat to mimic warm native soils.
Grow this prickly annual in terracotta pots to restrict roots and prevent invasive garden spreading.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when handling to protect your hands from the extremely sharp spines.
Plant alongside marigolds to deter whiteflies and aphids which are highly attracted to this host.
items.description: Solanum rostratum is a species of nightshade that is native to the United States and northern and central Mexico. Common names include buffalobur nightshade, buffalo-bur, spiny nightshade, Colorado bur, Kansas thistle, bad woman, Mexican thistle, and Texas thistle.

items.name: Grammosolen
items.growersTips:
Start your Grammosolen seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short UK summer.
Grow this vegetable in a polytunnel or under cloches to protect it from cold, damp UK winds.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep root growth.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into your heavy clay soil to prevent winter root rot in wet areas.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around them.
items.description: Grammosolen is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Solanum viarum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in early March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Keep soil consistently damp but not soggy, watering deeply at the base twice a week in midsummer.
Watch out for the potato tuber moth, a common UK pest that loves tunneling into these stems.
Prune the lower leaves in August to let the weak British sun ripen the fruit and prevent rot.
Plant them in fertile, slightly acidic soil enriched with well-rotted manure before transplanting.

items.name: Solanum aviculare
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in early spring at twenty degrees to get a head start on our short summer.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top inch of soil dry out to prevent root rot.
Prune back lightly in mid-spring to keep it bushy and remove any stems damaged by winter chills.
Feed fortnightly with high-potassium tomato food from June to encourage those lovely purple flowers.

items.name: Capsicum chinense
items.growersTips:
Start seeds in January or February on a heated propagator mat to beat the short UK growing season.
Grow them in a sunny greenhouse or polytunnel as UK outdoor summer temperatures are just too cool.
Water only when the pot feels light, as overwatering cold soil causes root rot in British weather.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are twenty centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Feed with high-potassium tomato food only after the first tiny pepper fruits have actually set.
items.description: Capsicum chinense, commonly known as a "habanero-type pepper", is a species of chili pepper native to the Americas. C. chinense varieties are well known for their unique flavors and, in many cases, exceptional heat. The hottest peppers in the world are members of this species, with a Scoville heat unit score of 2.69 million measured in the C. chinense cultivar Pepper X in 2023.

items.name: Solanum erianthum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender potato tree indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from UK cold.
Plant it in a deep container with grit-enriched compost to ensure the roots never sit in soggy soil.
Water deeply once the top two inches of soil dry out, keeping it drier during the dark winter weeks.
Prune back leggy stems in early spring to encourage a bushy shape and more of those velvety leaves.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this tropical beauty in your conservatory.

items.name: Solanum americanum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at five millimetres deep to beat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering at the base to prevent blight issues.
Watch out for aphids and flea beetles, using a horticultural soap spray if you spot leaf damage.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage a bushier habit and more abundant berry clusters.
Grow them alongside basil or marigolds to help deter common pests in your greenhouse or garden bed.

items.name: Capsicum frutescens
items.growersTips:
Start Tabasco seeds indoors in warm propagators by February to beat the short UK summer season.
Grow your plants in pots so you can easily move them into a sunny greenhouse when wet weather hits.
Water only when the top inch of soil dries to avoid root rot in our cool British climate.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and get way more fiery peppers.
Bring your pots inside to a sunny windowsill in October to help them survive the frosty winter.
items.description: Capsicum frutescens is a wild chili pepper that has genetic proximity to the cultivated pepper Capsicum chinense. It is native to Central and South America as well as Mexico. Pepper cultivars of C. frutescens can be annual or short-lived perennial plants.

items.name: Solanum lycocarpum
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in February using a heated propagator to mimic the warm Brazilian climate.
Grow this tender perennial in a large pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep the soil moist but never let the roots sit in soggy mud.
Feed your plant every fortnight with a high-potassium tomato fertilizer once the first flowers open.
Watch out for spider mites in dry greenhouse air by misting the foliage regularly on sunny days.
items.description:
Solanum lycocarpum, or wolf apple, is common in the Brazilian Cerrado ecoregion. In Portuguese, the plant is called lobeira or fruta-do-lobo .
The name "wolf's apple" comes from the fact that its fruit accounts for more than 50% of maned wolves' diet. Likewise, the scientific name "lycocarpum" is formed from Latinized Greek elements "lyco-", meaning "wolf", and "carpum" meaning "fruit".

items.name: Solanum quitoense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to give this slow grower a head start.
Grow it in a large pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October.
Water deeply at the base whenever the top inch of soil feels dry, keeping the large leaves hydrated.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food from June to September to encourage flowering and fruiting.
Wear thick gloves when handling this plant to protect your hands from its sharp, hidden stem spines.
items.description: Solanum quitoense, known as naranjilla in Ecuador, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Panama and as lulo in Colombia, is a tropical perennial plant from northwestern South America. The specific name for this species of nightshade means "from Quito."

items.name: Anthotroche
items.growersTips:
Give this rare Australian native a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a heated propagator to mimic its warm native climate.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil feel bone dry to prevent root rot.
Position your potted plant against a south-facing brick wall to maximise essential summer sun.
Move the container into a frost-free greenhouse by October to protect it from freezing damp.

items.name: Cestroideae
items.growersTips:
Start your peppers and tomatoes indoors in warm February to beat the short, cool British summer.
Bury tomato stems deep up to their first leaves when planting out in May to boost root growth.
Watch for potato blight during warm, wet July spells and cut infected foliage down to the soil.
Water your aubergines deeply once a week at the base rather than giving them daily light sprinkles.
Pinch out the growing tips of your pepper plants in June to encourage a bushier habit and more fruit.
items.description: Cestroideae is a subfamily of the plant family Solanaceae, the nightshades.

items.name: Atropa
items.growersTips:
Sow deadly nightshade seeds in pots of sandy loam during early spring, keeping them barely covered.
Water your established belladonna deeply once a week, letting the top inch of soil dry out first.
Wear thick gloves when pruning back the woody stems in late autumn to avoid skin contact with sap.
Watch out for the flea beetle in May, which loves to chew tiny holes in the dark green leaves.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into your clay soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
items.description: Atropa is a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae: tall, calcicole, herbaceous perennials, bearing large leaves and glossy berries particularly dangerous to children, due to their combination of an attractive, cherry-like appearance with a high toxicity. Atropa species favour temperate climates and alkaline soils, often growing in light shade in woodland environments associated with limestone hills and mountains. Their seeds can remain viable in the soil for long periods, germinating when the soil of sites in which plants once grew is disturbed by human activity or by

items.name: Solanum chilense
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short, cool UK summer growing season.
Grow this wild tomato in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK outdoor nights are just too cold for it.
Water very sparingly once established because this desert native hates wet feet and damp compost.
Provide a sturdy trellis early on to support its naturally sprawling, vigorous vining habit.
Watch out for spider mites in dry greenhouse air and mist the surrounding paths to keep them away.

items.name: Solanum atropurpureum
items.growersTips:
Grow this purple-spined beauty in a pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when handling this plant to protect your hands from its fierce spines.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food from June to September to boost those yellow berry clusters.
Plant it in your sunniest, sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its warm South American homeland.
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to get a crucial head start on UK warmth.
items.description: Solanum atropurpureum, commonly known as malevolence, purple devil and the five-minute plant, is a perennial herbaceous plant native to Brazil. S. atropurpureum contains various toxic tropane alkaloids in its fruit, stems, and leaves, and should not be ingested.

items.name: Symonanthus aromaticus
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian native in a container so you can bring it inside to survive wet UK winters.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into peat-free compost to mimic its natural sandy, dry homeland.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this plant hates soggy British roots.
Keep it in your brightest south-facing spot or a greenhouse to maximize the essential oil scent.
Prune the tips lightly in late spring to keep the woody habit bushy and encourage fresh growth.
items.description: Symonanthus aromaticus is a species of flowering plant in the potato family that is endemic to Australia.

items.name: Fabiana
items.growersTips:
Grow fabiana in acidic, well-drained soil; add some compost and grit to the planting hole.
Keep fabiana damp but not soggy during dry UK summers, watering at the base to avoid rot.
Give fabiana a light trim in late spring after flowering to keep its heather-like shape neat.
Plant your fabiana in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from cold winter winds.
Watch out for root rot in heavy clay; grow fabiana in a raised bed or pot to ensure good drainage.
items.description:
Fabiana may refer to:Fabiana (plant), a genus of evergreen shrubs
Fabiana imbricata
Fabiana (name), a given name

items.name: Solanum incanum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February with a heated propagator to beat the short UK growing season.
Grow this bitter apple in a greenhouse or sunny polytunnel as UK summers are too cold outdoors.
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep soil damp but prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Watch out for spider mites in your greenhouse and mist the leaves regularly to keep them away.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first star-shaped flowers appear.
items.description: Solanum incanum is a species of nightshade, a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to East Africa, West Africa, the Middle East, and eastwards to India. The species was introduced to Taiwan and Vietnam.

items.name: Browallia americana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on damp compost, as they need light and UK spring warmth to germinate.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimeters to encourage a bushier blue display.
Plant them out in late May after the frosts, spacing them twenty-five centimeters apart in borders.
Water your browallia at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist without wetting the foliage.
Watch out for aphids in June and blast them off with a gentle spray from your garden hose.

items.name: Salpiglossis sinuata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March, barely covering them as they need light to germinate well.
Keep young plants in a frost-free greenhouse until late May, as UK spring chills stunt their growth.
Water them at the base in the morning to keep the sticky foliage dry and prevent grey mould issues.
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach ten centimetres high to encourage a much bushier habit.
Stake the slender stems early with birch twigs to protect them from strong British summer winds.

items.name: Acnistus
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Acnistus indoors before the first October frost to survive chilly UK winters.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top two inches of gritty soil dry out between drinks.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more blue flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping your plant in a warm UK conservatory.
Feed with a high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight from May to September to boost blooming.
items.description: Iochroma is a genus of about 34 species of shrubs and small trees belonging to the nightshade family Solanaceae. Species are native from Mexico to south Brazil. They are found in the forests of Mexico and South America. Their hummingbird-pollinated flowers are tubular or trumpet-shaped, and may be blue, purple, red, yellow, or white, becoming pulpy berries. The cupular (cup-shaped) calyx is inflated in some species. The leaves are alternate, simple, and entire.

items.name: Brunfelsia densifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted rain tree indoors before the first autumn frost to protect it from UK chills.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water to keep its sensitive roots happy and warm.
Plant in a peat-free, ericaceous compost mix to provide the acidic soil this Caribbean native loves.
Prune your shrub lightly in late spring after the yellow flowers fade to keep its shape compact.
Check the leaf undersides weekly for spider mites when keeping this plant in a heated conservatory.

items.name: Solanum citrullifolium
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Keep a sharp eye out for UK aphids and flea beetles which absolutely love the spiny foliage.
Plant them in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their native warm Texan climate.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food once the purple, star-shaped flowers start to open.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling this plant to protect your hands from its fierce spines.

items.name: Solanum phureja
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 10cm deep in mid-April to avoid late UK frosts, spacing them 30cm apart in rows.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy, especially when the delicate purple flowers appear.
Watch out for late blight in damp UK summers, harvesting early if you spot dark spots on leaves.
Harvest these speedy spuds just 10 to 12 weeks after planting, as soon as the foliage yellow.
Eat them fresh within a week of digging up, as their thin skins mean they do not store well at all.
items.description: The potato is a starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas that is consumed as a staple food in many parts of the world. Potatoes are underground stem tubers of the plant Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family Solanaceae.

items.name: Solanum aculeastrum
items.growersTips:
Bring this spiny African nightshade indoors before October frosts hit to keep it alive over winter.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when pruning back the ferocious thorns to avoid painful skin punctures.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food from June to September to boost those yellow berries.
Grow it in a heavy terracotta pot to prevent the top-heavy, thorny branches from blowing over.
Sow seeds in February on a heated propagator mat at twenty-two degrees to beat the short UK summer.

items.name: Cyphanthera albicans
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Australian native in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy soil to survive UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are bone dry, as this shrub hates soggy roots.
Place your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum summer heat and ward off frosts.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to keep its wild, upright growth habit neat and bushy.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you overwinter this delicate beauty in your conservatory.

items.name: Solanum centrale
items.growersTips:
Grow this Aussie native in a greenhouse pot of sandy, free-draining soil to mimic its desert home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light waterings.
Sow seeds in early spring using a heated propagator mat at twenty-four degrees to trigger sprouting.
Move pots outdoors only during peak summer heat, placing them against a south-facing brick wall.
Watch out for aphids on young shoots and gently wash them off with a lukewarm water spray.
items.description: Solanum centrale, the kutjera, or Australian desert raisin, is a plant native to the more arid parts of Australia. Like other "bush tomatoes", it has been used as a food source by Central Australia and Aboriginal groups for millennia.

items.name: Capsicum annuum ‘Bird’s Eye’
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors by February using a heated propagator to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Move plants to their final pots in May but keep them in a sunny greenhouse or a south-facing porch.
Water only when the top inch of compost is dry, as soggy soil easily rots these compact roots.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are fifteen centimetres tall to encourage a bushy habit.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food once the first tiny white flowers start to appear.

items.name: Capsicum cardenasii
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in January with a heated propagator to beat the short UK growing season.
Keep this wild species in a pot so you can bring it inside to overwinter before the autumn frosts.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this Andean native hates soggy compost.
Prune the tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and increase your yield of purple flowers.
Watch out for aphids in late spring and blast them off with a gentle spray of lukewarm water.
items.description: Capsicum cardenasii is a plant species in the genus Capsicum and the family Solanaceae. It is a diploid with 2n=2x=24. It is a member within the C. pubescens complex, a group of closely related Capsicum species. It is closely related to C. eximium. It is native to the Andes, and it can be found in Bolivia and Peru. The native name is ulupica.

items.name: Capsicum chacoense
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in January using a heated propagator since this wild species needs extra warmth.
Grow this wild pepper in a greenhouse or sunny conservatory because UK summers are too cold for it.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry as its roots rot easily in wet UK soil.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushy habit and maximize your yield of tiny pods.
Watch out for aphids on young shoots and spray them with diluted organic neem oil immediately.

items.name: Capsicum eximium
items.growersTips:
Sow these wild Bolivian seeds in January on a heated propagator mat to beat the short UK summer.
Keep them in pots of free-draining peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite to prevent rot.
Place your pots in the sunniest spot of a greenhouse or conservatory as they need maximum UK heat.
Overwinter them indoors on a south-facing windowsill because they cannot survive a British frost.
Water only when the pot feels light to mimic their dry, high-altitude native Andean climate.

items.name: Capsicum mirabile
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in January with a heated propagator mat to beat the short UK summer.
Keep this wild Brazilian species in a pot so you can bring it inside before the autumn frosts hit.
Water only when the top inch of compost is dry, as this wild pepper hates soggy, cold roots.
Watch out for aphids in late spring, spraying them off with a gentle hose before they stunt growth.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food once you see the first tiny purple-tinged flowers open.

items.name: Solanum seaforthianum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender climber indoors before autumn frosts hit, as it cannot survive a cold UK winter.
Grow it in a container of peat-free loam-based compost so you can easily move it under glass in winter.
Water freely in summer but keep the soil barely damp during its dormant winter rest in a greenhouse.
Prune back the stems by half in early spring to encourage fresh flowering wood for summer blooms.
Check the soft new spring growth regularly for aphids, especially when kept in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Cestrum elegans
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mexican beauty against a warm, south-facing UK wall to shield it from harsh winter frost.
Water it deeply once a week in summer, but keep the soil barely damp during its chilly winter rest.
Prune your shrub in early spring after frosts pass, cutting back old stems to encourage new blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and aphids, especially if you overwinter your plant in a conservatory.
Feed it weekly with a high-potash tomato food from May to September to boost those crimson flowers.

items.name: Capsicum baccatum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-February to beat the short UK summer growing season.
Keep plants in a greenhouse or polytunnel since our cool UK summers lack the heat they need to ripen.
Stake these tall, floppy plants early on to support their heavy crops of Aji Lemon or Bishop's Crown.
Water deeply but let the compost dry out slightly between times to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Overwinter your favourite plant indoors on a sunny windowsill to get a massive head start next spring.
items.description: Capsicum baccatum, also simply referred to as ají, is a member of the genus Capsicum, and is one of the five domesticated chili pepper species. The fruit tends to be very pungent and registers 30,000 to 50,000 on the Scoville heat unit scale.

items.name: Solanum carolinense
items.growersTips:
This American native is highly invasive in the UK, so grow it only in deep pots to stop root spread.
Wear thick gloves when handling this plant to protect your hands from its sharp, toxic yellow spines.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry, as it thrives in our drier UK summer spells.
Cut the stems back to ground level in late autumn to prevent any berries from dropping and seeding.
Keep a sharp eye out for potato beetles, which love to jump over to this weed-like nightshade cousin.
items.description: Solanum carolinense, the Carolina horsenettle, is not a true nettle, but a member of the Solanaceae, or nightshade family. It is a perennial herbaceous plant, native to the southeastern United States, though its range has expanded throughout much of temperate North America. The plant is considered to be invasive in parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. The stem and undersides of larger leaf veins are covered with prickles.

items.name: Solanum heterodoxum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short UK summer and ensure fruit ripens.
Plant this spiny nightshade in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its native Mexican heat.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when pruning or harvesting to protect your hands from its fierce thorns.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering at the base to prevent blight in damp weather.
Grow them in large terracotta pots so you can easily move them under glass if a wet UK autumn looms.

items.name: Solanum linnaeanum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender nightshade in a greenhouse pot to protect it from unpredictable UK frost.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in autumn to protect your hands from its incredibly sharp thorns.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and treat infestations early with organic insecticidal soap.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium tomato fertilizer once the purple star-shaped flowers appear.

items.name: Solanoideae
items.growersTips:
Start Solanaceae seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short UK summer.
Bury tomato stems deep up to their first leaves when planting out to boost root growth.
Water your peppers at the base in the morning to prevent blight during damp British summers.
Pinch out side shoots of cordons weekly and top the main stem in August to ripen remaining fruit.
Plant French marigolds nearby to deter aphids and whiteflies from your potatoes and aubergines.
items.description: Solanoideae is a subfamily of the flowering plant family Solanaceae, and is sister to the subfamily Nicotianoideae. Within Solanaceae, Solanoideae contains some of the most economically important genera and species, such as the tomato, potato, eggplant or aubergine, chili and bell peppers (Capsicum), mandrakes (Mandragora), and jimson weeds (Datura).

items.name: Solanum elaeagnifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this silverleaf nightshade in a pot so you can bring it inside to survive wet UK winters.
Plant seeds just six millimetres deep in free-draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to mimic its native desert home.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in autumn to protect your hands from its sharp yellow spines.
Keep a close eye out for potato beetles which love to feast on this plant during warm UK summers.
items.description: Solanum elaeagnifolium, the silverleaf nightshade or silver-leaved nightshade, is a species of plant in the nightshade family native to North and South America. It is common in parts of southwestern USA, and sometimes weed of western North America. Other common names include prairie berry, silverleaf nettle, white horsenettle or silver nightshade. In South Africa it is known as silver-leaf bitter-apple or satansbos. More ambiguous names include "bull-nettle", "horsenettle" and the Spanish "trompillo".

items.name: Solanum baretiae
items.growersTips:
Give this rare spud a head start indoors in March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent the tubers from cracking in wet clay.
Watch out for late frosts in May by keeping some horticultural fleece handy to cover young shoots.
Give them a feed with high-potassium tomato fertiliser once flowers appear to boost tuber growth.
Earth up the stems as they grow to protect the shallow tubers from turning green and toxic.

items.name: Solanum sect. Lycopersicon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 6mm deep, keeping them on a warm windowsill until the last spring frost.
Plant them deep in the ground, burying the stem up to the first leaves to grow a stronger root system.
Water the soil directly, never the leaves, to prevent blight in our damp, humid UK summer weather.
Pinch out the side shoots of indeterminate varieties weekly to keep the plant focused on fruiting.
Grow basil nearby to naturally deter pests and boost your crop's flavour as they grow together.

items.name: Nierembergia
items.growersTips:
Plant cup flower in May after frosts pass, burying the root ball level with your soil surface.
Give your plants a good soak once a week, but let the top inch of soil dry out between waterings.
Watch out for slugs during damp British springs, so protect young shoots with beer traps or grit.
Cut your plants back by half in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of beautiful autumn blooms.
Mix lots of grit into your clay soil before planting to keep the roots dry during wet UK winters.

items.name: Juanulloa
items.growersTips:
Bring your gold finger chalice plant indoors by October to protect it from chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow this exotic scrambler in a peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Water generously through summer but let the top two inches of soil dry out completely between drinks.
Prune back the woody stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its wild shape tidy.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this tropical beauty in a heated conservatory.

items.name: Schizanthus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late winter indoors, then transplant outside only after the May frosts pass.
Water them at the base in the morning to keep the soil damp but avoid wetting the delicate blooms.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings are three inches tall to encourage a bushier flower show.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, as they love the tender young stems.
Grow them in pots using peat-free compost mixed with grit to ensure excellent drainage in our rain.
items.description: Schizanthus, also called butterfly flower, fringeflower, poor-man's-orchid, is a genus of plants in the nightshade family, Solanaceae.

items.name: Nicotiana
items.growersTips:
Sow your tiny tobacco seeds on top of compost in March; they need light to germinate on a UK windowsill.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to get a bushier plant with way more of those fragrant flowers.
Watch out for slugs on young plants; they love the juicy leaves of Nicotiana alata in damp British springs.
Plant them near your patio or seating area so you can enjoy their incredible evening scent in summer.
