Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food from July to keep those trumpet blooms coming until frost.
items.description: Nicotiana is a genus of herbaceous plants and shrubs in the family Solanaceae that is indigenous to the Americas, Australia, Southwestern Africa and the South Pacific. Various Nicotiana species, commonly referred to as tobacco plants, are cultivated as ornamental garden plants. N. tabacum is grown worldwide for the cultivation of tobacco leaves that are used for manufacturing and producing tobacco products, including cigars, cigarillos, cigarettes, chewing tobacco, dipping tobacco, snuff, snus, etc.

items.name: Capsicum pubescens
items.growersTips:
Start these black-seeded Rocotos in January indoors with a heat mat to beat the short UK summer.
Grow them in large pots of peat-free compost mixed with perlite to ensure the roots stay damp.
Keep them in a cool greenhouse or shady patio spot as they hate the extreme heat of glasshouses.
Prune the sprawling, vine-like branches in late autumn before bringing them indoors for winter.
Watch out for aphids on the fuzzy leaves and blast them off with a gentle spray of rainwater.
items.description: Capsicum pubescens is a plant of the genus Capsicum (pepper). The species name, pubescens, refers to the hairy leaves of this pepper. The hairiness of the leaves, along with the black seeds, make Capsicum pubescens distinguishable from other Capsicum species. Capsicum pubescens has pungent yellow, orange, red, green or brown fruits.

items.name: Brunfelsia plowmaniana
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender shrub indoors before November to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Keep the compost consistently moist with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water during summer.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid tomato food from May to September to boost blooms.
Prune lightly in late spring just as new growth starts to maintain a compact shape for containers.
Repot every two years in spring using a mix of peat-free ericaceous compost and plenty of perlite.
items.description: Brunfelsia plowmaniana is a species of flowering plant of the nightshade family that is native to the cloud forests of the Bolivian and Argentinian Andes. It was first described in 2012 on the basis of systematic DNA barcoding of specimens from the genus Brunfelsia. Specimens belonging to the new species had previously been placed in the polymorphic species B. uniflora, which a molecular phylogeny revealed as polyphyletic.

items.name: Brunfelsia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical beauty indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a container with ericaceous compost to easily manage the acidic soil pH it craves.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water to keep the sensitive roots happy and warm.
Prune right after the fragrant summer flowers fade to keep its bushy shape neat for your patio.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping it in your conservatory during winter.

items.name: Solanum brevicaule
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild potato relative in mid-April, burying tubers 10cm deep in well-drained, sandy soil.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only when the top 5cm feels dry to prevent tuber rot.
Watch out for late spring frosts in the UK and cover early shoots with fleece to protect them.
Grow this perennial in a large container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse in winter.
Keep an eye out for potato aphids and squash them by hand to prevent the spread of nasty viruses.
items.description: Solanum brevicaule is a tuberous perennial plant of the family Solanaceae. The species is native to South America. It is related to the potato, but unlike the potato which is tetraploid, it has several levels of ploidy: diploid, tetraploid, and hexaploid.

items.name: Scopolia
items.growersTips:
Plant Scopolia carniolica rhizomes five centimetres deep in rich, damp soil under deciduous trees.
Water your plants weekly during dry spring spells to mimic their native damp woodland habitats.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love devouring the emerging tender shoots.
Cut back the yellowing foliage to the ground in midsummer once the plant goes naturally dormant.
Grow them alongside snowdrops and primroses which thrive in the same cool, shady UK garden spots.
items.description:
Scopolia is a genus of four species of flowering plants in the family Solanaceae, native to Europe and Asia. The genus is named after Giovanni Scopoli (1723–88), a Tyrolean naturalist.
The genus has a disjunct distribution, with two recognised species in Central to Eastern Europe,, and two species in East Asia.
The two European species are:Scopolia carniolica Jacq. of Slovenia, Austria and the Carpathian Mountains
Scopolia caucasica Kolesn. ex Kreyer of the Caucasus

items.name: Petunia
items.growersTips:
Pinch out the growing tips of your young plants in May to encourage a really bushy, flower-filled habit.
Water them deeply at the base every morning, as UK summer hanging baskets dry out incredibly fast.
Feed weekly with a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser from July to keep the blooms coming.
Snip off the faded sticky flower heads regularly right back to the stem to prevent seed heads forming.
Watch out for slugs on young spring plantings, and use organic wool pellets to protect the stems.
items.description: Petunia is a genus of 20 species of flowering plants of South American origin. The popular flower of the same name derived its epithet from the French, which took the word pétun, 'tobacco', from a Tupi–Guarani language. A tender perennial plant, most of the varieties seen in gardens are hybrids.

items.name: Solanum pseudolulo
items.growersTips:
Sow your seeds shallowly indoors in early March using a heated propagator to beat the UK chill.
Move your potted plant into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the autumn frosts hit.
Water generously during summer dry spells but let the top inch of compost dry out between drinks.
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potash tomato food to encourage those exotic orange fruits.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and mist the large velvety leaves to keep humidity high.
items.description: Solanum pseudolulo is a subtropical perennial plant from northwestern South America. The pseudolulo is a large herbaceous plant or a small shrub, with heart-shaped leaves. The leaves and stems of the plant are covered in short hairs, and the entire plant is often covered in sharp spines.

items.name: Brugmansia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted angel's trumpet indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from cold.
Feed your plant weekly with a high-potash tomato food from May to September to boost those blooms.
Water heavily every single day during hot summer spells, as these thirsty giants hate drying out.
Prune hard in spring just above a node where the branches fork to encourage more flowering stems.
Watch out for red spider mites under the leaves when keeping them in a warm UK greenhouse or conservatory.
items.description: Brugmansia is a genus of seven species of flowering plants in the nightshade family Solanaceae. They are woody trees or shrubs, with pendulous flowers, and have no spines on their fruit. Their large, fragrant flowers give them their common name of angel's trumpets, adjacent to the nickname devil's trumpets of the closely related genus Datura.

items.name: Solanum sisymbriifolium
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by February to beat the short, cool British summer.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling this beast because the stems and leaves are covered in thorns.
Grow them in large pots against a south-facing wall to trap the maximum amount of British sunshine.
Plant them near your greenhouse tomatoes to act as a sacrificial trap crop for greenhouse whitefly.
Only harvest the red berries when the spiny husk dries up and pulls back naturally from the fruit.

items.name: Brunfelsia portoricensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Puerto Rican native indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a container of ericaceous compost because it hates the alkaline chalky soils of the UK.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH consistently acidic.
Prune your shrub in late spring just as new growth starts to keep its bushy shape manageable.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping it in your conservatory during summer.

items.name: Solanum gilo
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow these bitter berries in a greenhouse or polytunnel as they need more heat than UK summers offer.
Plant them out in late May in large pots filled with rich, free-draining peat-free compost.
Water deeply at the base to keep soil damp, but keep leaves dry to prevent grey mould in damp weather.
Pinch out the main growing tip when the plant is thirty centimetres tall to encourage bushy growth.
items.description: The scarlet eggplant is a fruiting plant of the genus Solanum, related to the tomato and eggplant. Its green fruit is known as gilo. It was once treated as a distinct species, Solanum gilo, but it is now known to be a cultivar group of Solanum aethiopicum.

items.name: Solanum laciniatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this kangaroo apple in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from cold UK winds.
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of six millimetres using a heated propagator.
Water your plant deeply once a week during dry summer spells, letting the topsoil dry out between.
Prune back the stems by a third in late spring to keep its vigorous, bushy shape in check.
Watch out for aphids and potato beetles, which love targeting this plant in warm British summers.

items.name: Nicotianoideae
items.growersTips:
Sow your sweet-smelling Nicotiana seeds indoors in March, but do not cover them as they need light.
Plant out in late May once frosts pass, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in fertile soil.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the large leaves from wilting.
Watch out for green aphids on young shoots and gently wash them off with a diluted soapy spray.
Deadhead faded flowers weekly to keep these half-hardy annuals blooming right up to the autumn frost.

items.name: Solanum glaucophyllum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Argentine native indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it alive over winter.
Grow your waxy-leaf nightshade in a large pot so you can easily move it into a sunny UK greenhouse.
Water it deeply once the top inch of soil dries, but never let the pot sit in soggy winter saucers.
Watch out for aphids and glasshouse whiteflies, blasting them off with a sharp spray of soapy water.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and prevent leggy stems.

items.name: Cestrum parqui
items.growersTips:
Plant your willow-leaved jessamine in a warm south-facing border to shield it from cold UK winds.
Prune the stems hard back to a low framework in early spring to encourage vigorous flowering wood.
Mulch the root area heavily with compost in autumn to protect it from wet and freezing winter soil.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids and glasshouse red spider mites during hot dry UK summer spells.
Water deeply once a week during summer dry spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
items.description: Cestrum parqui, commonly known as palqui, green cestrum, Chilean cestrum, green poisonberry, or willow-leaved jessamine, is a species of flowering plant native to Chile.

items.name: Solanum virginianum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short UK summer and cold spring soil.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent blight in damp UK weather.
Watch out for red spider mites in greenhouse air, so mist the surrounding leaves on hot summer days.
Wear thick gloves when pruning or harvesting to protect your hands from its extremely sharp thorns.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost mixed with grit to ensure the roots stay warm and drain well.
items.description: Solanum virginianum, also called Surattense nightshade, yellow-fruit nightshade, yellow-berried nightshade, Indian nightshade, Thai green eggplant, or Thai striped eggplant, is a medicinal plant used mostly in India. Some parts of the plant, such as the fruit, are poisonous. Solanum surattense Burm. f. and Solanum xanthocarpum Schrad. and Wendl. are synonyms of Solanum virginianum L..

items.name: Browallia speciosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March, barely pressing them into peat-free compost to let light in.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering from the base to protect delicate stems.
Pinch out the growing tips when stems reach ten centimetres to encourage a much bushier habit.
Move pots outside only after mid-May when all risk of frost has passed in your local UK area.
Watch out for aphids and whiteflies when growing them in a typical British greenhouse or conservatory.

items.name: Brunfelsia pauciflora
items.growersTips:
Bring your Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow indoors by October to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Grow it in a pot of ericaceous compost because this plant hates the UK's natural chalky soils.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil damp, but let the top inch dry out before watering again.
Prune the stems back by half in late spring right after the first flush of purple flowers fades.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when you bring the pot inside for winter.

items.name: Brunfelsia latifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring your yesterday-today-and-tomorrow shrub indoors to a bright conservatory before autumn frosts.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost moist but never soggy, especially during active growth.
Feed fortnightly in spring with an ericaceous liquid fertilizer to keep those glossy leaves green.
Prune lightly right after the purple-to-white flowers fade in summer to shape the bush.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air, so mist the foliage regularly to keep them away.

items.name: Nicotiana attenuata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in cool UK climates.
Grow in poor well-drained soil to prevent excessive leafy growth and encourage better flowering.
Water sparingly once established to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent root rot in UK rain.
Watch for slugs and aphids which target young Solanaceae foliage during damp British spring weather.
Plant near night-scented stock to enhance evening fragrance and attract native UK pollinating moths.
items.description: Nicotiana attenuata is a species of wild tobacco known by the common name coyote tobacco. It is native to western North America from British Columbia to Texas and northern Mexico, where it grows in many types of habitat. It is a glandular and sparsely hairy annual herb exceeding a meter in maximum height. The leaf blades may be 10 centimetres (4 in) long, the lower ones oval and the upper narrower in shape, and are borne on petioles. The inflorescence bears several flowers with pinkish or greenish white tubular throats 2 to 3 centimetres long, their bases enclosed in pointed sepals. The flower

items.name: Hyoscyamus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring in well-drained, alkaline soil, barely covering them as they need light to sprout.
Water young plants regularly, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings once established.
Keep a sharp eye out for potato beetles and flea beetles, which love munching on this nightshade.
Wear thick gloves whenever handling this plant, as all parts are highly toxic to touch and ingest.
Grow them in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their favorite warm Mediterranean climate.

items.name: Brunfelsia uniflora
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Brazilian beauty indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winters.
Plant in acidic, ericaceous compost with plenty of grit to ensure the roots never sit in soggy soil.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and leaves healthy green.
Prune lightly in late spring after the first flush of fragrant, colour-changing blooms fades away.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this shrub in a conservatory or greenhouse.

items.name: Jaltomata
items.growersTips:
Start Jaltomata seeds indoors in March with bottom heat to beat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Plant them out in June in a sunny, sheltered spot after all risk of late frost has fully passed.
Grow Jaltomata in pots of rich, free-draining compost to help keep their roots warm in our climate.
Water them at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy, which prevents fruit splitting in rain.
Support their sprawling stems with canes or a small trellis just like you would for bush tomatoes.

items.name: Solanum viride
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the cool British spring weather.
Grow them in a greenhouse or sunny patio container to get the high heat this African nightshade needs.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist but avoid wetting the bitter leaves.
Harvest the young green leaves frequently to stop the plant from flowering and keep growth tender.
Watch out for flea beetles in June and use fine insect netting to protect the delicate foliage.

items.name: Solanum adscendens
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Plant them out in late May after the last frosts, spacing them forty centimetres apart in the soil.
Water deeply at the base twice a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, sturdy roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage bushier growth and get more flowers and berries.
Watch out for potato blight in damp August weather and remove any affected leaves immediately.

items.name: Solanum lasiocarpum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by February to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow this spiny tropical nightshade in a greenhouse or sunny polytunnel to guarantee fruit ripens.
Water deeply at the base to keep soil damp, but avoid wetting leaves to prevent UK tomato blight.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning or harvesting to protect your hands from the sharp thorns.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato fertiliser once yellow star-shaped flowers begin to open.

items.name: Capsicum eshbaughii
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm February using a heated propagator to beat the short UK summer season.
Grow this wild species in a greenhouse or sunny conservatory as it needs more heat than UK patios.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out slightly between drinks to mimic its native habitat.
Watch out for aphids in late spring and use soapy water spray before they damage the delicate new growth.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food once the first tiny white flowers appear in midsummer.

items.name: Solanum africanum
items.growersTips:
Start this tender climber indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Grow it in a large pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse when autumn arrives.
Water deeply once a week to keep the soil damp, but let the top inch dry out so the roots do not rot.
Tie the sprawling stems to a sturdy trellis or obelisk to keep the heavy fruit off damp soil.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food once flowers appear to boost your berry harvest.

items.name: Solanum acerifolium
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators in early March to beat the short UK summer season.
Plant them out in late May only after the last frost, spaced fifty centimetres apart in full sun.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first star-shaped flowers appear.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you are growing them under glass or in a polytunnel.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent blossom end rot in cool British weather.

items.name: Capsicum annuum var. acuminatum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February using a heated propagator to beat the short UK growing season.
Grow them in a greenhouse or sunny conservatory as UK summers are rarely hot enough outdoors.
Water only when the top inch of soil is dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are twenty centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first tiny green peppers begin to form.

items.name: Solanum cheesmaniae
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the cool UK spring and get early fruit.
Plant them in well-drained, slightly acidic soil enriched with plenty of composted organic matter.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist but never soggy in damp British summers.
Watch out for late blight during wet July spells and remove infected lower leaves immediately.
Grow them alongside marigolds to naturally deter aphids and whiteflies in your greenhouse or patio.
items.description: Solanum cheesmaniae is one of two main species of wild tomatoes found on the Galápagos Islands. This species is the one most commonly called the Galapagos tomato. It is a wild tomato that evolved on the Galapagos Islands.

items.name: Solanum retroflexum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short, cool UK summer growing season.
Plant them out in June after the last frost, spaced forty centimetres apart in a sunny, sheltered spot.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent blossom end rot in the berries.
Watch out for aphids and flea beetles in early summer, using organic soap sprays to keep them away.
Harvest only when the berries turn completely dull black, as shiny green ones are highly toxic.

items.name: Solanum aturense
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short, cool United Kingdom summer.
Plant them out in late May only after the last frost, spacing your plants sixty centimetres apart.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering deeply at the base during dry spells.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato fertiliser once the first yellow flowers begin to open.
Provide a sturdy stake or trellis early on to support the heavy, vine-like fruit-bearing stems.

items.name: Solanum arboreum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender shrub in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK winters.
Grow in a large pot with loam-based John Innes No. 3 compost to allow easy moving indoors in autumn.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty soil to dry out completely.
Prune lightly in early spring after frost risk passes to maintain shape and encourage fresh wood.
Monitor indoor plants closely for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly in dry winter conditions.

items.name: Solanum anguivi
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to combat the cool UK spring before outdoor planting.
Plant out in June in a sunny sheltered spot using deep pots to allow for its extensive root system.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but not soggy to prevent blossom end rot in pots.
Watch for aphids and red spider mites under leaves when growing this African nightshade in UK glass.
Prune the growing tips in midsummer to encourage branching and a more abundant harvest of berries.

items.name: Solanum chenopodioides
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot in late May to protect this tender shrub from UK spring frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to support its berry production in free-draining soil.
Prune back hard by one-third in early April to stimulate fresh growth and maintain a compact shape.
Mulch the root zone with well-rotted manure in autumn to insulate roots from wet UK winter freezes.
Monitor leaves in humid July weather for potato blight and pick off affected foliage immediately.

items.name: Solanum crinitum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tender shrub cannot survive UK frosts.
Grow in a large pot of loam-based compost to easily move the plant indoors before autumn chills.
Prune back hard in late winter to manage its vigorous size and encourage fresh purple-veined leaves.
Water generously in summer but keep the soil barely moist during the dormant winter months.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your hands from the sharp spines on stems and leaves.

items.name: Solanum etuberosum
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 10cm deep in late April once UK frosts pass to protect emerging shoots from cold damage.
Grow in acidic to neutral sandy loam to prevent tuber rot in wet, heavy clay British soils.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkles to rot-proof roots.
Watch for late blight in damp August weather and remove affected foliage immediately to save tubers.
Harvest tubers in October after the first light frost has naturally killed off the top foliage.

items.name: Solanum grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot with loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water copiously in summer to support the huge leaves but keep the soil barely damp during winter.
Prune hard in early spring to control size and encourage new flowering wood on this vigorous shrub.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and whitefly when overwintering this plant indoors.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato fertiliser from May to September to boost the blue blooms.

items.name: Solanum plastisexum
items.growersTips:
Start these Australian natives indoors in warm March to beat the short, cool British summer.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure sharp drainage.
Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, watering only when the top two inches feel dry.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are growing them inside a humid UK greenhouse.
Give them a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flowers appear.

items.name: Solanum myriacanthum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to counteract the short, cool UK growing season.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling this plant to protect your hands from its sharp, dense spines.
Grow in large pots of peat-free loam-based compost to easily move them under glass during wet autumns.
Water deeply at the base once the top inch of soil dries, keeping foliage dry to prevent blight.
Prune lower leaves in late August to maximize sunlight exposure and ripen the decorative berries.

items.name: Solanum pachyandrum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or south-facing conservatory to survive cool UK summer temperatures.
Sow seeds indoors in February at twenty-one degrees Celsius using a heated propagator for success.
Water deeply once a week at the base to prevent blossom end rot without wetting the foliage.
Support the heavy climbing stems using sturdy bamboo canes or a trellis system by midsummer.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flower trusses set fruit.

items.name: Solanum pseudoquina
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian nightshade in a large pot so you can move it indoors before autumn frosts.
Sow seeds in early spring on a warm windowsill at a depth of five millimetres in free-draining compost.
Water thoroughly only when the top inch of soil feels dry, as this plant hates soggy winter roots.
Feed weekly in summer with a high-potassium tomato fertiliser to encourage healthy berry production.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering the plant in your conservatory.

items.name: Solanum melissarum
items.growersTips:
Start this rare Brazilian pepino relative indoors in warm propagators by early March for UK success.
Grow them in large pots of rich, peat-free compost kept in a sunny greenhouse or sheltered patio.
Water the soil consistently to keep it damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Stake the heavy, fruit-laden branches early in summer to stop them snapping under their own weight.
Watch out for greenhouse whitefly and spray foliage with organic insecticidal soap at the first sign.

items.name: Solanum trilobatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical nightshade in a pot so you can bring it indoors before the first autumn frosts.
Give it a warm sunny windowsill or greenhouse spot to mimic its native hot south Asian climate.
Plant seeds just five millimetres deep in free-draining peat-free compost kept constantly moist.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites which love the dry indoor air this plant will sit in.
Prune back the woody stems by half in early spring to encourage fresh leafy growth for harvests.

items.name: Solanum stramoniifolium
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short, cool United Kingdom summer.
Plant them out in late May only after the final frost, spacing your plants about sixty cm apart.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food once those first starry purple flowers start to open.
Grow them in a sunny greenhouse or against a south-facing wall to trap vital extra summer heat.
Watch out for aphids and red spider mites under glass, spraying them with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Solanum scabrum
items.growersTips:
Sow your garden huckleberry seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the UK spring chill.
Plant them out in late May after the last frost, spacing your bushes at least fifty centimetres apart.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy to prevent your ripening berries from splitting open.
Net your plants in summer because local UK blackbirds will absolutely love stealing the dark berries.
Only harvest the berries when they lose their shine and turn a dull, matte black, or they will be sour.

items.name: Solanum granulosoleprosum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Brazilian shrub indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it alive over winter.
Grow your plant in a large pot so you can easily move it to a sunny, sheltered patio for the summer.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of compost dry out between waterings.
Prune back the woody stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more flowers.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser from May to September to boost its growth.

items.name: Solanum campechiense
items.growersTips:
Start this tropical spiny nightshade indoors in February using a heated propagator set to 23C.
Grow your southern nightshade in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a warm greenhouse by October.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning this plant to avoid its incredibly sharp, yellow spines.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first purple flowers start to appear.

items.name: Solanum bahamense
items.growersTips:
Start your Bahama nightshade seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the cool UK spring.
Grow this tender Caribbean native in a sunny greenhouse or a very sheltered south-facing patio pot.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil dries, keeping it damp but never soggy to prevent root rot.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium tomato fertiliser once the first purple flowers start to open.
Watch out for glasshouse whiteflies and spray them with organic insecticidal soap immediately.

items.name: Solanum chippendalei
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February using a heated propagator to mimic the warm Australian outback.
Grow this wild spiny bush in a terracotta pot so you can move it under glass when UK rain gets heavy.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining soil have dried out completely.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning this plant to protect your hands from its sharp yellow spines.
Keep a lookout for red spider mites which thrive on this plant in dry greenhouse conditions.

items.name: Solanum caripense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator for UK warmth.
Grow this pepino relative in a greenhouse or sunny patio pot to protect it from cool UK summers.
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy, preventing root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage a bushier habit and more purple flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing this tender climber under glass.

items.name: Solanum ellipticum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant your potato bush in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during rainy summers.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil feel bone dry to mimic its desert home.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and boost purple blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are overwintering this shrub in your conservatory.
items.description: Solanum ellipticum is known as potato bush and under the more ambiguous name of "bush tomato". The Arrernte name of merne awele-awele might refer to this species or to the similar S. quadriloculatum. Native to Australia, the potato bush is a small fruiting shrub in the family Solanaceae.

items.name: Solanum densevestitum
items.growersTips:
Start this rare Australian nightshade indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat UK chills.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost mixed with perlite so you can move them inside if frost looms.
Water deeply at the base only when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent damp-off in cool weather.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and treat early with organic insecticidal soap under the leaves.
Prune the lower yellowing leaves in late summer to help the sunlight ripen those tiny hairy fruits.

items.name: Solanum lanceolatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Plant in peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Water generously through the summer but let the top inch of soil dry out before watering again.
Prune back the woody stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more flowers.
Keep a sharp lookout for glasshouse red spider mite if you overwinter your plant under glass.
items.description: Solanum lanceolatum, with the common names orangeberry nightshade and lanceleaf nightshade, is a species of nightshade. It is native to regions of South America, including the Cerrado ecoregion of the Tropical and subtropical grasslands, savannas, and shrublands biome, primarily in Brazil.

items.name: Solanum furcatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep to beat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent blight in damp UK summers.
Watch out for aphids and flea beetles in June, using physical netting to protect young foliage.
Prune back the leggy stems in mid-July to encourage a bushier habit and more abundant berries.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil before planting to satisfy this heavy feeder.

items.name: Solanum incompletum
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Hawaiian native indoors by October to protect it from wet and cold UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to prevent root rot during damp British summers.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are overwintering it in your greenhouse.
Prune back leggy stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its bushy shape compact.
Water it deeply only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as it hates sitting in soggy compost.

items.name: Solanum ovigerum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the short, cool British summer.
Pot them on into peat-free compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage they crave.
Keep plants in a sunny greenhouse or a very sheltered south-facing patio spot to set fruit.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy, preventing blossom end rot.
Support the heavy, egg-shaped white fruits by tying the main stem securely to a sturdy cane.
items.description: Eggplant, aubergine, brinjal, or baigan is a plant species in the nightshade family Solanaceae. Solanum melongena is grown worldwide for its edible fruit, typically used as a vegetable in cooking.

items.name: Solanum opacum
items.growersTips:
Start these green berry seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant them out in late May once frosts pass, spacing them fifty centimetres apart in rich soil.
Give them a mulch of well-rotted manure to lock in moisture during dry English summer spells.
Watch out for aphids and potato beetles on the leaves, washing them off with a gentle hose spray.
Pick the small green berries only when they turn fully ripe and soft to the touch in autumn.

items.name: Solanum prinophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian native in a pot of gritty loam to move indoors before first autumn frost.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to promote bushy growth and more purple flowers.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your hands from the sharp yellow spines on stems and leaves.
Watch for aphids and glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering the plant in a heated greenhouse.

items.name: Solanum pungetium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to counter the cool UK spring temperatures.
Plant out in late May after the final frost in well-drained soil enriched with organic compost.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to prevent blossom end rot.
Stake the heavy fruiting stems by mid-July to prevent them from snapping in strong UK winds.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first flower trusses set.

items.name: Solanum parishii
items.growersTips:
Plant this purple nightshade in free-draining, gritty soil against a warm, south-facing UK wall.
Water your potted specimens only when the top two inches of compost feel completely dry to touch.
Lightly prune the stems right after its purple summer flowering to keep the shrub neat and bushy.
Protect the root zone with a thick straw mulch in November to help it survive wet UK winters.
Watch out for aphids on new spring shoots and blast them off with a gentle spray from your hose.

items.name: Solanum quadriloculatum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender Australian native indoors as it will not survive UK frosts below five degrees.
Grow in pots of free-draining sandy loam to prevent root rot during wet British summers and autumns.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in spring to protect your hands from its sharp, dense yellow spines.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light waterings.
Position in your hottest, most sun-drenched south-facing spot to encourage purple star-shaped blooms.

items.name: Solanum sandwicense
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or large pot moved indoors by October to survive UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator kept at twenty-one degrees.
Water deeply once a week to keep soil damp but never soggy, preventing root rot in cool UK summers.
Prune lightly in late spring to remove dead wood and maintain a compact shape for patio containers.
Check foliage weekly for aphids and glasshouse whitefly, common pests in humid UK growing spaces.

items.name: Solanum sodiroi
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to counter the short, cool UK growing season.
Grow in large pots of rich, free-draining loam so you can move them under glass when frosts threaten.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil damp but never waterlogged in cool UK summers.
Prune lower leaves in late August to maximize sunlight exposure and ripen the fruit before autumn.
Watch for potato blight during warm, wet July spells and apply copper-based organic sprays early.

items.name: Solanum tampicense
items.growersTips:
Grow this wetland nightshade in a large pot so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Keep the soil constantly wet by sitting the pot in a shallow tray of rainwater during summer.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing spot or a conservatory to mimic its warm native climate.
Wear thick gloves when pruning because the stems are covered in sharp, downward-pointing prickles.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and treat infestations early with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Solanum spirale
items.growersTips:
Bring this Himalayan shrub indoors by October to shield its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in early spring using a heated propagator kept at twenty-one degrees for best germination.
Feed fortnightly with high-potassium tomato food once those yellow star-shaped flowers start to open.
Prune back lightly in late spring to keep its bushy shape and encourage fresh berry-bearing wood.
Plant in free-draining loam mixed with plenty of grit to stop the roots rotting in soggy UK rain.

items.name: Solanum douglasii
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender nightshade in a sunny, sheltered spot by mid-May once all UK frosts have passed.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering deeply at the base during dry spells.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and more white flowers.
Watch out for aphids and potato beetles, washing them off with a gentle spray of soapy water.
Grow it in a large pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for the UK winter.

items.name: Solanum physalifolium
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Plant them out in late May only after all risk of frost has passed, spacing them about fifty cm apart.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent the fruit skins from splitting.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, using fine insect mesh to protect the young leaves.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost placed against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat.

items.name: Solanum marginatum
items.growersTips:
Start this spiny ornamental in February on a warm windowsill using a heated propagator for UK success.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning these thorny stems in late autumn to protect your hands.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than spraying the felted, silvery-grey foliage.
Feed your white-edged nightshade with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once flowers appear in July.
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.

items.name: Solanum robustum
items.growersTips:
Grow this spiny shrub in a big pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.
Give it rich, well-draining soil mixed with plenty of grit to stop the roots rotting in wet winters.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this velvety-leaved beauty sheltered indoors.
Prune back the woody stems in early spring to shape the plant and encourage fresh, dramatic foliage.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between drinks in winter.

items.name: Capsicum annuum ‘Chao Tian Jiao’
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors by mid-February under a heated propagator to beat the short UK growing season.
Grow these upright clusters in a greenhouse or on a south-facing windowsill to get enough hot sun.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food once the first tiny white upright flowers start to set.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, keeping the compost damp but not soggy.
Watch out for aphids on the tender new growth and blast them off with a gentle spray of tap water.

items.name: Capsicum rhomboideum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February with a heated propagator mat to mimic their native warm habitat.
Grow this wild species in a greenhouse or conservatory, as UK summers are too cold for it outdoors.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Prune the tips in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and increase the yield of yellow berries.
Overwinter your plant indoors on a bright windowsill, keeping it above twelve degrees Celsius.

items.name: Capsicum flexuosum
items.growersTips:
Bring your pot indoors over winter because this wild pepper can survive UK frosts if kept dry.
Sow seeds in January using a heated propagator at twenty-five Celsius to kickstart germination.
Water only when the top inch of compost is dry, as this wild species hates soggy roots.
Hand-pollinate the tiny yellow-green flowers with a soft brush since UK pollinators often miss them.
Grow this scrambler in a large pot with a trellis to support its unusually floppy, vine-like habit.

items.name: Solanum triflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at 5mm deep to give this wild nightshade enough summer warmth to grow.
Plant them out in late May once frosts pass, choosing your poorest, sandiest, well-draining soil.
Let the soil dry out completely between waterings as this tough plant hates soggy UK winter roots.
Watch out for potato aphids and flea beetles which love targeting this specific nightshade family.
Grow them alongside tomatoes or potatoes to easily spot and trap shared pests early in the season.

items.name: Solanum umbelliferum
items.growersTips:
Plant this nightshade in a warm, south-facing UK border to shelter it from chilly winds and frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering deeply at the base during dry spells.
Prune back lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and boost new growth.
Watch out for aphids and tomato blight, especially during warm, wet UK summer weather.
Mulch heavily with well-rotted manure in autumn to protect the root system from freezing winters.

items.name: Solanum curvicuspe
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the cool British spring weather.
Plant this climber deep in rich, well-draining soil once the late May frosts have fully passed.
Provide a sturdy trellis or bamboo framework early on to support its vigorous scrambling vines.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the root ball moist.
Mulch heavily around the roots in late autumn to protect this tender perennial from winter wet.

items.name: Solanum ensifolium
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the cool UK spring and get early growth.
Plant this rare nightshade in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Prune back the woody stems by one-third in late autumn to keep the habit bushy for the next season.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly if you are overwintering this tender species in a UK greenhouse.

items.name: Solanum lyratum
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators by mid-March to beat the cool British spring weather.
Grow this tender climber in a greenhouse or south-facing sheltered patio to get enough summer heat.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering at the base to prevent leaf rot.
Tie the sprawling stems to a sturdy trellis or bamboo teepee as they grow to keep foliage dry.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite, spraying with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Solanum diphyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow this exotic twoleaf nightshade in a pot so you can move it indoors before the first UK frosts.
Water deeply only when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Prune back the woody stems in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more orange berries.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites when overwintering your plant indoors.
Mix plenty of grit into your peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.

items.name: Solanum commersonii
items.growersTips:
Plant these wild potatoes in late April, burying tubers 10cm deep in very well-drained, sandy soil.
They love wet UK summers but need a raised bed to prevent tuber rot during heavy August downpours.
Watch out for late blight in damp July weather, and space plants 50cm apart to improve airflow.
Since they are highly frost-sensitive, harvest the small tubers in October before the first frost.
Grow them away from tomatoes to stop the spread of shared pests like the potato cyst nematode.

items.name: Solanum umtuma
items.growersTips:
Start this rare African egg-plant indoors in March using a heated propagator set to 22C for germination.
Grow them in peat-free loam-based compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage they crave.
Move your pots to a sunny greenhouse or south-facing patio only after the late May frosts have passed.
Water the base deeply once a week but let the top soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and mist the leaves on hot days to keep red spider mites at bay.

items.name: Solanum aculeatissimum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian shrub in pots so you can bring it indoors before the autumn frosts hit.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a heated propagator to mimic its native warm climate.
Water deeply once a week but let the well-draining gritty compost dry out between your waterings.
Prune back leggy stems in late winter to keep this thorny bush compact and encourage fresh growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this spiny plant in your conservatory.
items.description: Solanum aculeatissimum, known as Dutch eggplant, and love-apple, is a weedy shrub that bears small, 2–3 cm pale yellow fruit following white flowers with characteristic Solanum yellow stamens.

items.name: Solanum xanti
items.growersTips:
Grow this purple nightshade in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.
Plant in very well-drained, gritty soil with a neutral to alkaline pH to mimic its native scrubland.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between drinks to avoid root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost passes to shape the shrub and encourage fresh purple blooms.
Watch out for aphids and spider mites when keeping it indoors or in a glasshouse during wet UK springs.
items.description: Solanum umbelliferum var. xanti, known commonly as chaparral nightshade, purple nightshade, and San Diego nightshade, is a variety of nightshade. It is native to the western United States in Arizona, California, Nevada, and Oregon, and to north-western Mexico in Baja California.

items.name: Solanum evolvuloides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at 5mm deep using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent drainage.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent stem rot.
Move plants into a sunny greenhouse or polytunnel by late May, as UK summers are too cold outdoors.
Watch out for aphids and red spider mites under glass, washing them off with a gentle water spray.

items.name: Solanum ptychanthum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators in March before transplanting out after the late May frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent blossom end rot in summer heat.
Net your plants early in summer to protect the ripening berries from hungry UK blackbirds and slugs.
Plant alongside basil or French marigolds in a sunny, sheltered spot to naturally deter aphids.
Pinch out the growing tips in July to encourage bushy growth and a much heavier harvest of berries.
items.description: Solanum americanum, commonly known as American black nightshade, small-flowered nightshade or glossy nightshade, is a herbaceous flowering plant.

items.name: Solanum chacoense
items.growersTips:
Start these wild potatoes indoors in March to beat the short UK summer and get a head start.
Grow them in deep containers to easily manage their aggressive, wandering underground runners.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy during the flowering stage to boost tuber size.
Earth up the stems regularly to prevent the tubers from turning green and becoming toxic.
Watch out for late blight in damp August weather and harvest before the first autumn frosts.

items.name: Solanum capsicoides
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators in February to beat the short UK growing season.
Keep plants in a sunny greenhouse or south-facing patio container as they need maximum UK heat.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in cool weather.
Wear thick gloves when pruning or harvesting to protect your hands from its incredibly sharp spines.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry greenhouse air and mist the foliage regularly to deter them.
items.description: Solanum capsicoides, the cockroach berry, is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to eastern Brazil but naturalized in other tropical regions, where it sometimes becomes an invasive weed.

items.name: Solanum interandinum
items.growersTips:
Start seed indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the cool British spring temperatures.
Plant out in late May after the last frosts, spacing them fifty centimetres apart in fertile soil.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to prevent blossom end rot in the UK.
Stake the heavy fruiting stems early in July to protect them from strong British summer winds.
Apply a high-potash liquid tomato feed every fortnight once the first yellow flowers appear.

items.name: Solanum paniculatum
items.growersTips:
Bring your jurubeba indoors by October as this Brazilian native cannot survive wet UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds shallowly in heated propagators by March to give this slow grower a head start in our climate.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food once those tiny purple flowers appear to boost fruit yield.
Watch out for spider mites when growing them in your greenhouse, misting leaves daily to deter them.
Grow them in large pots of peat-free compost so you can easily chase the sun around your UK garden.

items.name: Solanum sarrachoides
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Plant out in late May after frosts, spacing them forty centimetres apart in your sunniest border.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil damp but avoid wetting the hairy leaves.
Keep an eye out for potato aphids and flea beetles which love targeting this nightshade relative.
Pick the ripe green-to-olive berries only when the papery calyx cup completely dries and turns brown.

items.name: Solanum emulans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Plant outside in late May after the final frost, spacing them fifty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil damp but avoid splashing the low foliage.
Keep a sharp eye out for potato aphids and fleabeetles which love targeting this nightshade family.
Feed weekly with a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser once the first tiny star flowers appear.

items.name: Solanum macrocarpon
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by March because UK summers are too short for outdoor sowing.
Grow them in large pots in a sunny greenhouse to give these heat-loving African eggplants enough warmth.
Water the soil deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach thirty centimetres tall to encourage bushier growth.
Watch out for spider mites under the leaves when growing them in dry, warm UK glasshouse conditions.

items.name: Solanum conocarpum
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Caribbean native indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winters.
Sow seeds just five millimetres deep in a heated propagator kept at a steady twenty-four degrees.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp air.
Feed fortnightly in summer with high-potash tomato food to encourage those lovely purple flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering this shrubby nightshade.

items.name: Solanum campylacanthum
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short, cool UK summer season.
Grow this tender African nightshade in a greenhouse or a very sunny, sheltered patio container.
Water deeply at the base once the top inch of soil dries, keeping the prickly foliage bone dry.
Watch out for aphids and red spider mites, which thrive on this plant in dry greenhouse air.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first starry purple flowers appear.

items.name: Solanum brownii
items.growersTips:
Start this rare Australian nightshade indoors in March using a heated propagator set to 22C.
Grow your plants in terracotta pots of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Position your pots against a south-facing brick wall to trap vital summer heat in our cool climate.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this species hates soggy UK winter roots.
Bring the pots into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by mid-October to keep them alive.

items.name: Solanum galapagense
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in February using a heated propagator to mimic the warm Galapagos climate.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are too cold and wet for outdoor success.
Water sparingly once fruit sets to prevent the small orange tomatoes from splitting in damp air.
Prune lower foliage in August to maximize sunlight penetration and airflow in humid UK weather.
Support the sprawling, highly branched wild habit using a sturdy multi-stem stake or cage system.

items.name: Solanum esuriale
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian native in a terracotta pot with 50% grit to survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to meet its high heat requirement.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, then leave to dry out again.
Prune back the dieback in late spring once new shoots appear at the base to keep the habit tidy.
Sow seeds in early spring using a heated propagator set to 22 degrees Celsius to trigger germination.

items.name: Solanum ditrichum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender perennial in a deep container to easily move it indoors before first autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flowers.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage this root-rot prone plant needs.
Watch for aphids on new spring shoots and wash them off with a sharp blast of water from the hose.

items.name: Solanum macoorai
items.growersTips:
Start your Solanum macoorai seeds indoors in warm propagators in early March to beat the UK chill.
Plant them out in late May only after all frosts pass, spacing them fifty centimetres apart.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged in British rain.
Protect them from late blight by growing under a polytunnel or rain shelter during wet Augusts.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser once the first purple flowers begin to open.

items.name: Solanum lichtensteinii
items.growersTips:
Start these tender African nightshades indoors in March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in our cool British spring.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mites if you are growing them under cover in the UK.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food once the first starry purple flowers begin to appear.
Grow them in terracotta pots on a sunny patio so you can easily move them indoors before autumn frost.

items.name: Solanum petrophilum
items.growersTips:
Grow this wild Aussie nightshade in a terracotta pot so you can move it indoors before frosts hit.
Sow the seeds just two millimetres deep in a free-draining sandy loam mix with added grit.
Let the soil dry out completely between waterings to mimic its native arid Australian habitat.
Watch out for glasshouse whiteflies and red spider mites when overwintering your plant indoors.
Prune back the woody stems by one third in early spring to encourage fresh, bushy new growth.

items.name: Cardamine enneaphyllos
items.growersTips:
Plant in late autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moisture-retentive, humus-rich deciduous shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic damp UK woodland soils and prevent early dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut back yellowing foliage to ground level in midsummer once the plant has naturally died back.
Incorporate well-rotted leaf mould into the planting hole to replicate British forest floor soils.

items.name: Lepidium sativum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds every two weeks from March to September for a continuous supply of fresh peppery leaves.
Scatter the tiny seeds thinly on damp compost and just press them down gently without burying them.
Grow them on a cool windowsill indoors in winter using damp kitchen paper instead of garden soil.
Watch out for flea beetles in dry weather by keeping the soil damp and using a fine insect mesh.
Snip the young microgreens at the stem base with scissors just one week after sowing your seeds.
items.description: Cress, sometimes referred to as garden cress to distinguish it from similar plants also referred to as cress, is a fast-growing, edible herb.

items.name: Brassica carinata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April or May at a depth of 1cm to avoid early frosts and ensure rapid germination.
Water deeply once a week at the base to prevent downy mildew in damp UK summer conditions.
Net the crop immediately after planting to protect the leaves from cabbage white butterflies.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles which heavily target young carinata leaves.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into neutral soil before sowing to meet its high nitrogen demand.
items.description: Brassica carinata is a species of flowering plant in the Brassicaceae family. It is referred to by the common names Ethiopian Kale, Ethiopian rape or Ethiopian mustard. It is believed to be a hybrid between Brassica nigra and Brassica oleracea.

items.name: Cardamine bulbifera
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbils in late summer just below the soil surface in moist shaded spots under deciduous trees
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy clay to mimic the ancient woodland soils of the Chilterns and Weald
Collect the dark purple aerial bulbils from leaf axils in July before they drop to propagate easily
Control local slug and snail populations in early spring as they eagerly eat the emerging shoots
Plant alongside native wood anemones and wild daffodils for a synchronized spring woodland display
items.description: Cardamine bulbifera, known as coralroot bittercress or coral root, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a perennial with upright, mostly unbranched, stems to 70 cm (28 in) tall, and leaves made up of between three and 13 leaflets. At the base of each leaf there are bulbils which can fall off and grow into new plants. The flowers have petals that are 10–15 mm (0.4–0.6 in) long collected in corymbose few-flowered racemes and are generally light purple, pink or almost white. It is found in damp places.

items.name: Cardamine trifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under the canopy of deciduous trees or shrubs.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp, mimicking woodland floors.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or immediately after the white flowers fade in late spring.
Plant alongside shade-loving companions like Athyrium ferns, Galanthus, and Hostas for contrast.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the delicate emerging flower buds.

items.name: Lepidium barnebyanum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring just 5mm deep in a cold frame to protect them from unpredictable UK frost.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering gently at the base to avoid stem rot.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using fine insect netting to protect the delicate young leaves.
Mix plenty of sharp sand into your compost to ensure the sharp drainage this rare plant requires.
Grow it alongside radishes to help deter pests and make the most of your vegetable patch space.

items.name: Lepidium dictyotum
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in early spring, just dusting them with five millimetres of fine compost.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering gently at the base every morning.
Watch out for flea beetles in May by using fine insect netting over your young salad greens.
Grow them alongside radishes to help deter pests and maximise your small veg plot space.
Grow this quick crop in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the delicate leaves from cold UK winds.

items.name: Lepidium latipes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in early spring to catch the cool UK growing season.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry British summer spells.
Watch out for flea beetles in June and protect your young leaves with fine insect mesh netting.
Grow this alongside mint or rosemary to help deter common pests in your vegetable patch.
Mix plenty of well-rotted compost into your soil before planting to ensure good drainage.

items.name: Brassica fruticulosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1cm in free-draining, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Grow in full sun but protect young autumn crops from heavy frost using horticultural fleece.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to discourage downy mildew.
Net the crop with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Interplant with mint or sage to mask the scent of the crop from destructive cabbage root flies.
items.description: Brassica fruticulosa, the Mediterranean cabbage or twiggy turnip, is a member of the agriculturally significant genus Brassica. It was described by Domenico Maria Leone Cirillo in 1792.

items.name: Brassica macrocarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 1cm to protect this rare Sicilian wild cabbage from UK frost.
Grow in free-draining limestone-rich soil with a high pH of 7.5 to mimic its native coastal cliffs.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to cope with cool, damp British summer weather.
Protect young plants from cabbage white butterflies and snails using fine insect netting in June.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant brassica is highly prone to winter rot.

items.name: Brassica cretica
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, gritty alkaline soil to mimic its native Greek cliffside habitat in the UK.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in modular trays to protect delicate seedlings.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold, wet winter winds which cause root rot in UK gardens.
Protect young leaves from cabbage white butterflies and pigeons using fine insect netting.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
items.description: Brassica cretica is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly to Greece and the Aegean Islands. It was first described by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1785. A 2021 study suggested that it was the origin of cultivated Brassica oleracea, with later admixture from other Brassica species.

items.name: Brassica narinosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in mid to late summer to prevent bolting caused by the long daylight hours of UK spring.
Plant seeds exactly one centimetre deep in fertile soil enriched with well-rotted garden compost.
Water the soil consistently at the base to keep it moist and prevent the leaves from turning bitter.
Cover crops with fine insect netting immediately after sowing to block cabbage root fly and beetles.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter pests and avoid planting near other brassica family crops.
items.description: Tatsoi is an Asian variety of Brassica rapa grown for greens. Also called tat choy, it is closely related to the more familiar bok choy. This plant has become popular in North American cuisine as well and is now grown throughout the world.

items.name: Lepidium flavum
items.growersTips:
Sow these yellow peppergrass seeds shallowly in early spring under a cloche to beat the UK chill.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, as dry UK summers make them bolt to seed.
Watch out for flea beetles in May; cover your young leafy greens with a fine insect netting.
Grow them alongside radishes to save space and deter pests in your raised vegetable beds.
Harvest the peppery leaves when they are young and tender before the yellow flowers start to open.

items.name: Alyssum chondrogynum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm stone wall to mimic its native Cypriot cliffs.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, keeping the crown completely dry.
Pruneback lightly by one third after summer flowering to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp British springs when tender new growth first emerges.
items.description: Odontarrhena chondrogyna is a species of perennial flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It was previously included in the genus Alyssum, and hence named Alyssum chondrogynum, but was assigned to the newly established Odontarrhena after molecular phylogeny studies from the 2010s. It is endemic to the island of Cyprus, where it grows on rocky serpentinised slopes.

items.name: Alyssum serpyllifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot
Position in full south facing sun to mimic its native dry Mediterranean limestone habitat
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once the established root system is mature
Prune back lightly by one third after summer flowering to maintain a compact tidy cushion habit
Protect from slugs and snails in damp UK springs when young tender shoots are most vulnerable

items.name: Brassica rupestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring at a depth of 1cm in free-draining, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system.
Net plants with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Plant alongside rosemary or mint to deter flea beetles and mask the brassica scent from pests.
Prune yellowing lower leaves in autumn to improve air circulation and prevent grey mould in damp UK winters.

items.name: Brassica hilarionis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Cypriot native in sharply draining, gritty alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in a cold frame to protect young seedlings.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its natural warm cliffside habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells to prevent root rot in the damp British climate.
Protect the evergreen foliage from cabbage white caterpillars and slugs using fine insect netting.
items.description: Brassica hilarionis is a species of perennial cruciferous plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is endemic to Northern Cyprus and is classified as endangered. This species flowers from March to May. Its common name is St. Hilarion Cabbage.

items.name: Alyssum minutum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April using free-draining gritty soil to avoid rot
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells as this alpine Brassicaceae dislikes wet UK winters
Watch for flea beetles in spring by using yellow sticky traps around these low-growing crucifers
Plant alongside carrots to attract predatory hoverflies that naturally control destructive aphids
Avoid rich fertilisers which cause floppy growth and instead topdress with fine limestone grit

items.name: Lepidium montanum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep in spring once the UK frost risk has fully passed
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering gently at the base every few dry days
Watch out for flea beetles making tiny holes in leaves and shield young plants with fine insect mesh
Grow this peppery green in sandy, well-drained soil mixed with compost to mimic its native dry beds
Plant alongside mint or dill to help deter the pests that love targeting your cruciferous greens

items.name: Lepidium ruderale
items.growersTips:
Sow narrow-leaved pepperwort seeds just 2mm deep in free-draining sandy soil from March to May.
Water sparingly once established, as this wild brassica thrives in dry, gravelly UK coastal soils.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring, which chew tiny holes in the peppery, edible green leaves.
Grow it alongside spring onions to help deter common pests with their combined strong scents.
Harvest the young, tangy rosette leaves before the tiny green flowers appear in June for best flavor.

items.name: Alyssum desertorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April to prevent damp-off in cool UK springs.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky soil to prevent the leggy growth caused by rich UK garden loam.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this annual easily rots in damp British conditions.
Position near early-flowering brassicas to attract hoverflies that control spring aphid outbreaks.
Shear back by half after the first June flush to trigger a second wave of blooms before autumn.

items.name: Cardamine hirsuta
items.growersTips:
Hand-pull before spring seed pods explode to stop rapid spread in damp UK borders and gravel paths.
Mulch bare soil with five centimetres of bark in autumn to block light and prevent seed germination.
Hoe young seedlings on a dry breezy UK morning in early spring so the roots dehydrate and die fast.
Grow dense groundcover like Ajuga reptans as a companion to crowd out this light-loving weed.
Check container compost bought from UK garden centres for tiny rosettes before potting up plants.

items.name: Cardamine parviflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a moisture-retentive loam.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged by watering lightly at the base every morning.
Watch for flea beetles in June and protect young leaves using fine insect mesh covers.
Grow alongside mint or chives to deter common brassica pests that target small bittercress.
Hand-weed surrounding soil weekly to prevent fast-growing weeds from smothering this small annual.

items.name: Hesperis matronalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in May or June at five millimetres deep for strong biennial roots before winter.
Grow in moist well-drained soil with garden lime to raise pH and prevent Brassicaceae clubroot.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to stop powdery mildew on leaves.
Cut back faded flowering stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Inspect leaves weekly for caterpillars of the small white butterfly and handpick them off immediately.
items.description: Hesperis matronalis is an herbaceous flowering plant species in the family Brassicaceae. It has numerous common names, including dame's rocket, damask-violet, dame's-violet, dames-wort, dame's gilliflower, night-scented gilliflower, queen's gilliflower, rogue's gilliflower, sweet rocket, and mother-of-the-evening.

items.name: Descurainia paradisa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural UK cold stratification.
Grow in sharply draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells once the deep taproot is fully established.
Prune back the woody stems by one third in late spring to maintain a compact shrubby growth habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Brassica oleracea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1.5cm in firm, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Net plants with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed.
Plant mint or sage nearby to mask the brassica scent and deter destructive flea beetles.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in early spring to boost leafy growth in damp UK weather.
items.description: Brassica oleracea, also known as wild cabbage in its uncultivated form, is a plant of the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Lepidium jaredii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under a cold frame to protect this rare brassica from late UK frosts.
Keep the sandy, free-draining soil consistently damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Watch out for flea beetles in June by using fine insect netting over your young salad greens.
Plant alongside radishes to distract common pests and maximize your small veg plot space.
Harvest the peppery leaves sparingly from the outside of the clump to encourage continuous growth.

items.name: Sinapis alba
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors from March to September at a depth of one centimetre in firm soil.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to prevent early bolting and keep the leaves tender.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring by using fine insect mesh to protect young emerging seedlings.
Incorporate the crop into the soil as green manure before it flowers to boost organic matter.
Grow as a companion plant near brassicas to act as a sacrificial trap crop for cabbage butterflies.
