items.description: White mustard, also called yellow mustard, is an annual plant of the cabbage family. It is sometimes also referred to as Brassica alba or B. hirta. It is native to the Mediterranean region, Europe and Tropical Asia, but is now widespread worldwide. Grown for its seeds, it is used to make the condiment mustard, as a fodder crop, or as a green manure.

items.name: Cardamine amara
items.growersTips:
Grow in permanently wet, poorly drained soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep.
Propagate by division in spring or take stem cuttings in summer to easily increase your stock.
Plant in partial to full shade to mimic its natural UK woodland stream habitat and prevent leaf scorch.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars in spring as this plant is a key larval food source.
Cut back hard after flowering in midsummer to encourage fresh, lush edible foliage for salads.

items.name: Lepidium graminifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just 2mm deep in free-draining sandy soil to match UK wet weather.
Water weekly at the base, letting soil dry out between to prevent damp-off in cool UK summers.
Watch out for flea beetles in June; use fine insect mesh to protect the peppery young leaves.
Cut back the white flower stems in late summer to keep the plant producing tasty salad leaves.
Grow it next to mint or rosemary to help deter pests that love British brassica crops.

items.name: Erysimum jugicola
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Tuck it into a sunny rockery or raised bed where it won't get waterlogged by clay.
Trim the flower stems back by half in July to keep the mound compact and prevent leggy growth.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars in summer, as they love this brassica family member.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to replace these short-lived perennials.

items.name: Erysimum popovii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Spanish wallflower in grit-enriched soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Give it a light trim right after flowering in July to stop it getting woody and encourage fresh growth.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars in summer, as they love this family just like cabbages.
Grow it alongside purple salvias or lavender to beautifully contrast its soft pastel yellow blooms.
Water only during dry spells once established, as this tough plant hates soggy British soil.

items.name: Brassica tournefortii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 6mm in free-draining sandy soil to mimic its native dry habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant weed-like brassica rots in soggy UK clay.
Cover crops with fine insect netting in May to block the inevitable cabbage white butterfly larvae.
Grow in full sun in a dedicated container to prevent its aggressive self-seeding habit in borders.
Harvest the young tender flowering shoots in early summer before the plant becomes tough and bitter.
items.description: Brassica tournefortii is a species of plant known by the common names Asian mustard, pale cabbage, African mustard, Sahara mustard, and Aslooz.

items.name: Lepidium virginicum
items.growersTips:
Sow Virginia pepperweed seeds shallowly at just two millimetres deep in spring as they need light.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry UK summer spells to avoid bolting.
Watch out for flea beetles which chew tiny holes in the leaves and protect young plants with fleece.
Plant this peppery salad green next to onions or garlic to help deter common pests naturally.
Grow them in pots of free-draining compost to easily control their self-seeding habit in your garden.
items.description: Lepidium virginicum, also known as least pepperwort or Virginia pepperweed, is an herbaceous plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae). It is native to much of North America, including most of the United States and Mexico and southern regions of Canada, as well as most of Central America. It can be found elsewhere as an introduced species.

items.name: Lepidium africanum
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in spring, just pressing them into damp soil under a cloche to trap heat.
Give them a quick daily sprinkle of water rather than a deep soak to keep their shallow roots damp.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, so cover your young salad crops with a fine insect mesh early.
Boost your heavy UK clay soil by mixing in plenty of sharp sand and compost before you sow them.
Grow this quick mustardy green next to onions to help keep those pesky aphids off the fresh leaves.

items.name: Lepidium papilliferum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in very free-draining sandy soil to mimic its native dry desert habitat.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the soil dry out completely between light soakings.
Grow this rare plant under a cold frame to protect it from persistent wet UK winter rains.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the delicate young seedlings in damp spring weather.
Sow seeds shallowly, just dusting them with a fine layer of grit to let light trigger germination.

items.name: Descurainia pinnata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring once the UK soil begins to warm.
Grow in well-drained, sandy or chalky soil with a neutral to alkaline pH to prevent root rot.
Water seedlings lightly until established, then allow the soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white butterflies which frequently target this brassica family.
Position in full sun to mimic its native open habitat and ensure strong, upright stem development.

items.name: Cardamine pratensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of damp, peat-free compost as they need winter cold to germinate
Grow in boggy soil or beside a garden pond in partial shade to mimic its natural damp meadow habitat
Leave foliage uncut until July to allow the orange-tip butterfly to lay eggs and caterpillars to feed
Divide established clumps in spring after flowering to maintain vigour and increase your stock easily
Choose the double-flowered Flore Pleno cultivar if you want longer-lasting blooms that do not self-seed
items.description: Cardamine pratensis, the cuckoo flower, lady's smock, mayflower, or milkmaids, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is a perennial herb native to Eurasia.

items.name: Sinapis arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre into poor, well-drained soil to limit wild spread.
Water seedlings weekly until established, then rely solely on UK rainfall to prevent root rot.
Hand-pull plants before yellow flowers fade in July to stop aggressive self-seeding in borders.
Check leaves weekly for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles to protect crops nearby.
Grow as a green manure, digging the foliage into heavy clay soils in autumn to improve structure.
items.description: Rhamphospermum arvense, the charlock, sometimes also called field mustard, wild mustard, or charlock mustard, is an annual or winter annual plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is found in the fields of North Africa, Asia, Europe, and some other areas where it has been transported and naturalised. Pieris rapae, the small white butterfly, and Pieris napi, the green veined white butterfly, are significant consumers of charlock during their larval stages.

items.name: Cardamine flexuosa
items.growersTips:
Hand-weed early in damp spring soil to remove the entire taproot before the explosive seed pods pop.
Sow seeds just 2mm deep in moist, shaded clay-loam borders to mimic natural UK woodland edges.
Water weekly during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars in May and hand-pick them to protect young foliage.
Plant alongside hostas and ferns in damp shade to create a natural ground cover that deters weeds.
items.description: Cardamine flexuosa, commonly known as wavy bittercress or wood bitter-cress, is an herbaceous annual, biennial, or short-lived perennial plant in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae).

items.name: Lepidium latifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial pepperwater in a sturdy pot to stop its invasive roots taking over your garden.
Sow your seeds just half a centimetre deep in spring once the frosty UK winter soil starts to warm.
Keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, mimicking its natural British wild riverbank habitat.
Snip off the white flower heads in summer before they set seed to prevent it invading your lawn.
Harvest the young, mustardy leaves in April before they get too bitter and tough to eat in salads.

items.name: Lepidium didymum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds just half a centimetre deep in early spring as soon as UK soil starts to warm up.
Water the soil consistently but lightly to keep it damp, as dry British summers make it bolt.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, so cover your young plants with a fine insect mesh.
Snip off the outer leaves regularly to encourage fresh, peppery growth all through the autumn.
Grow this low-sprawling herb in a pot of sandy loam to stop it taking over your garden borders.

items.name: Lepidium fremontii
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert pepperweed in sandy, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under a cold frame to protect young shoots from frost damage.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between light soakings.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your garden to mimic its native heat.
Prune back the woody stems by half in late autumn to keep the plant bushy and prevent leggy growth.

items.name: Brassica rapa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep in multi-purpose compost from April to July for reliable UK summer harvests.
Water consistently at the base to prevent bolting during dry spells or sudden UK summer heatwaves.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles using fine insect mesh immediately after sowing outdoors.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs on the leaves.
In wet UK autumns, harvest the leafy greens early as annuals before winter frosts rot the crowns.
items.description: Brassica rapa is an annual to biennial plant species native to Eurasia that is from the Brassicaceae family. The B. rapa subspecies oleifera is an oilseed commonly known as turnip rape, field mustard, bird's rape, and keblock.

items.name: Lepidium draba
items.growersTips:
Start seeds in cold frames in March to protect young roots from unpredictable UK spring frosts.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in a free-draining sandy loam to encourage fast sprouting.
Water the soil deeply once a week rather than daily misting to help those deep taproots establish.
Watch out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars which love munching these peppery leaves in July.
Grow this alongside mint or rosemary to help naturally deter the flea beetles that plague brassicas.

items.name: Lepidium campestre
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly outdoors in late summer at a depth of five millimetres for natural spring blooms.
Grow this field pepperwort in poor, well-drained chalky soil to stop it becoming too floppy.
Water young seedlings weekly during dry UK spring spells, but leave established plants to dry out.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, which love chewing tiny holes in this brassica family member.
Snip off the seed heads in late summer if you want to stop this enthusiastic self-seeder spreading.
items.description: Lepidium campestre, the field pepperwort, field peppercress, field peppergrass, field pepperweed or field cress, is usually a biennial with some form of annual plant in the Brassicaceae or mustard family, native to Europe, but commonly found in North America as an invasive weed. The most notable characteristic of field pepperweed is the raceme of flowers which forks off of the stem. These racemes are made up of first small white flowers and later green, flat and oval seedpods each about 6 mm long and 4 mm wide. Each seedpod contains two brown, 2.5 mm long seeds.

items.name: Descurainia bourgaeana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using free-draining sandy loam.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native hot volcanic habitat.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Grow in containers to easily move indoors or under a cold frame to survive wet winter frosts.
items.description: Descurainia bourgaeana is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae endemic to Las Cañadas del Teide on Tenerife and La Palma in the Canary Islands.

items.name: Descurainia incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer at a depth of two millimetres to mimic natural UK autumn drop.
Grow in sharply draining sandy loam to prevent root rot during wet British winters and springs.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells once the deep taproot has established.
Watch for flea beetles in spring which chew small holes in the greyish felted Brassicaceae foliage.
Position near spring-flowering honesty to attract beneficial pollinators to your wildlife garden.

items.name: Lepidium nitidum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds very shallowly at just two millimetres deep in early spring to catch the cool UK rain.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering gently with a fine-rose watering can.
Watch out for flea beetles in May and protect your young leaves with a lightweight horticultural fleece.
Mix plenty of well-rotted garden compost into your soil beforehand to give it a rich, free-draining base.
Grow this quick salad crop next to radishes as they both love the same cool, damp British weather.

items.name: Lepidium oblongum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in early spring to match cool UK temperatures.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering gently with a fine-rose can at dawn.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using fine insect mesh covers to protect the young leaves.
Grow this quick salad crop next to onions or garlic to help naturally deter hungry garden pests.
Sow small batches every two weeks from April to August for a steady supply of peppery greens.

items.name: Cardamine impatiens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer on moist, weed-free soil to mimic natural autumn germination.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking its native UK damp woodland habitat.
Hand-pull plants in early summer before seed pods explode to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Grow in partial to deep shade under deciduous shrubs where soil remains cool during dry spells.
Watch for orange-tip butterfly caterpillars in spring and tolerate light foliage damage for wildlife.
items.description: Cardamine impatiens, the narrowleaf bittercress or narrow-leaved bitter-cress, is a plant species in the genus Cardamine of the family Brassicaceae. It is a slender, biennial herb, that produces sterile leaves in the first year, one to several flowering stems during the next. Its leaves are pinnate with several pairs of lanceolate, dentate leaflets and a terminal, slightly longer leaflet. The short petals surpass the calyx by half of its length. items.name: Descurainia sophia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at 2mm deep in autumn or early spring directly into well-drained, sandy UK soil.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells, as this plant thrives in dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Hand-pull plants before they set seed in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in borders.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family weed.
Grow alongside spring-flowering bulbs to fill dry, sunny gaps where other plants struggle to survive.
items.description: Descurainia sophia is a species of flowering plant in the cabbage family Brassicaceae. Common names include flixweed, herb-Sophia and tansy mustard. It is an annual plant that reproduces by seeds. It is a dominant weed in dark brown prairie and black prairie soils of southern Alberta. Its stem is erect, branched, and 4–30 in (10–76 cm) high. It was once given to patients with dysentery and called by ancient herbalists Sophia Chirurgorum, "The Wisdom of Surgeons". It is the type species of the genus Descurainia and of the rejected genus Sophia Adans.

items.name: Lepidium densiflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow these dense-flowered peppergrass seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in early spring.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy while the young salad seedlings are establishing.
Watch out for flea beetles in May by using fine insect netting over your outdoor patch.
Harvest the peppery leaves young before the white flowers open to keep the flavour sweet and mild.
Grow them in light, sandy soil with a bit of garden compost to help drainage in wet UK winters.

items.name: Lepidium perfoliatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring just two millimetres deep to catch the cool, damp UK weather they love.
Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, especially during our typical damp British summers.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, so cover your young salad crop with a fine insect mesh net.
Grow this quick salad leaf alongside radishes to help deter common pests from your vegetable plot.
Harvest the peppery leaves when they are young and tender before the yellow flowers start to open.

items.name: Lepidium foliosum
items.growersTips:
Sow these coastal cress seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in early spring as soil warms up.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge to stop this leafy green from bolting.
Grow them in a container of sandy, free-draining compost to mimic their natural seaside cliffs.
Watch out for flea beetles in dry UK summers and use fine insect mesh to protect the foliage.
Harvest the peppery outer leaves regularly to encourage fresh, tender growth throughout autumn.

items.name: Lepidium coronopus
items.growersTips:
Sow these Swinecress seeds just five millimetres deep in early spring as soon as UK frosts ease.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy to mimic its natural damp coastal habitat.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, and protect young leaves with fine horticultural fleece.
Grow it next to mint or rosemary to help deter the pests that love this brassica family herb.
Harvest the peppery outer leaves regularly in summer to stop the plant from self-seeding wildly.

items.name: Lepidium heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring directly into damp, gritty soil, barely covering them with a light tilth.
Water consistently but lightly to mimic UK drizzle, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, using a fine mesh insect net to protect the young green leaves.
Mix in plenty of sharp sand to your vegetable bed to ensure the sharp drainage this wild herb loves.
Harvest the peppery outer leaves regularly throughout summer to encourage fresh, bushy new growth.

items.name: Cardamine concatenata
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 5cm deep in autumn in humus-rich, damp soil under deciduous trees to mimic woodland.
Water weekly during spring active growth if UK rainfall is low, then keep dry during summer dormancy.
Watch for garlic snails and flea beetles in spring, which target Brassicaceae foliage in damp gardens.
Do not prune or cut back dying foliage in summer; let leaves yellow naturally to feed the tuber.
Incorporate leaf mould and grit into heavy UK clay before planting to ensure drainage yet retain moisture.

items.name: Cardamine diphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland perennial in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under deciduous trees.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, barely covering them with compost to mimic forest leaf litter.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking wet UK woodland floors in spring.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in late summer after the foliage dies back to propagate new plants.

items.name: Nasturtium gambellii
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare watercress seeds in late spring in heavy, wet soil right at the edge of your pond.
Keep the soil constantly soggy or submerged in shallow water to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using organic barriers as they love damp UK pond edges.
Grow them alongside native marsh marigolds to help filter the water and provide partial shade.
Clear away dead winter foliage in early spring to encourage fresh, healthy new stems to emerge.
items.description: Nasturtium gambellii is a rare species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common names Gambel's yellowcress and Gambel's watercress. It is known from three or four scattered occurrences in California. It is also native to central Mexico and Guatemala. Its total U.S. population was last estimated at fewer than 300 individuals. It was federally listed in California, as an endangered species of the United States in 1993.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata
items.growersTips:
Plant your cabbages deep up to their lower leaves to stop winter winds rocking and loosening roots.
Firm the soil down with your boots before planting because cabbages love a rock-solid root zone.
Pop a fine mesh net over them from day one to stop the cabbage white butterflies laying eggs.
Tuck a cardboard collar around the stem base at ground level to block hungry cabbage root flies.
Give them a liquid seaweed feed in spring to boost growth after the cold UK winter wet clears out.

items.name: Brassica napus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late August or September at a depth of one to two centimetres for overwintering.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to improve drainage before autumn sowing.
Net young plants immediately to protect them from wood pigeon damage during UK winter months.
Apply a nitrogen-rich organic fertiliser in early spring to boost rapid leafy growth and flowering.
Monitor closely for cabbage stem flea beetle damage on seedlings during dry autumn spells.
items.description: Rapeseed, also known as rape and oilseed rape and canola, is a yellow-flowered member of the Brassicaceae family.

items.name: Nasturtium microphyllum
items.growersTips:
Pop this British native watercress in a damp, shady spot or a shallow pond edge to keep it happy.
Sow the tiny seeds just on the soil surface in spring, keeping the compost constantly soaking wet.
Watch out for mustard beetles and flea beetles, which love to nibble holes in the peppery leaves.
Grow it alongside brooklime or water forget-me-not in your bog garden for a lovely wild UK look.
Harvest the stems regularly through autumn to encourage fresh, tasty new growth for your salads.
items.description: Nasturtium microphyllum, the onerow yellowcress, is an aquatic plant species widespread across Europe and Asia, and naturalized in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Central America, Australia, New Zealand and other places. It occurs in wet locations generally at elevations less than 1500 m. It has been reported from every Canadian province except Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan. In the US, it is fairly common in New England, New York, and Michigan, with scattered populations in the southern and western parts of the country.

items.name: Cardamine maxima
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moist soil rich in leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions for best growth.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged during dry spring spells to prevent early dormancy.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars in May which feed on the foliage but support biodiversity.
Sow seeds immediately after harvesting in summer as they lose viability quickly if stored dry.
Grow alongside wild garlic or primroses in partial shade to create a natural woodland ground cover.

items.name: Cardamine angulata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic to neutral soil enriched with leafmould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Position in partial to full shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in autumn after flowering to control spread and propagate new plants.
Watch for flea beetles in spring and protect young foliage with fine mesh or organic sprays.

items.name: Cardamine heptaphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 8cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic damp UK woodland floors and prevent early dormancy.
Mulch annually in late autumn with leaf mould to replicate natural British beechwood soil conditions.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in late spring before the foliage dies back.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. italica
items.growersTips:
Firm the soil down well with your boots before planting to stop wind rock in wet UK winters.
Cover your crop with fine insect netting immediately to block cabbage white butterflies and birds.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkling to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Add a handful of lime to your soil before planting to raise the pH and ward off nasty clubroot disease.
Harvest the main central head first to trigger lots of delicious, tender side shoots for weeks.

items.name: Alliaria petiolata
items.growersTips:
Uproot garlic mustard manually in early spring before seed pods form to prevent aggressive spreading
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres depth in damp shady spots to mimic natural UK winter chilling
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells to establish healthy leaves for culinary use
Grow in containers to easily contain the vigorous self-seeding habit of this biennial herb
Interplant with wild garlic in moist woodland soil to create a productive native salad corner
items.description: Alliaria petiolata, or garlic mustard, is a biennial flowering plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae). It is native to Europe, western and central Asia, north-western Africa, Morocco, Iberia and the British Isles, north to northern Scandinavia, and east to northern Pakistan and Xinjiang in western China. It has now become a tenacious invasive plant across the northern U.S., in particular because of its earlier springtime emergence than many native species, often in the forest understory.

items.name: Borodinia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of 1.5cm in firm, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Protect young crops from cabbage white butterflies using a fine insect mesh netting from May onwards.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to prevent the plants from bolting.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles and improve the overall health of the crop.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in autumn to protect roots from wet and freezing UK winters.
items.description:
Borodinia may refer to:Borodinia (plant), a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae
Borodinia (protist), a genus of foraminifers in the family Acervulinidae

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. botrytis
items.growersTips:
Firm the soil around your young cauliflowers with your boots to prevent wind rock in breezy UK weather
Sow autumn-harvest varieties like All Year Round in April to avoid the worst of the summer droughts
Fold the inner leaves over the developing white curds to shade them and prevent them turning yellow
Water deeply at the base every week during dry spells to stop the plants buttoning into tiny heads
Net your crop securely from day one to keep the pesky cabbage white butterflies and pigeons away

items.name: Lepidium austrinum
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in early spring just two millimetres deep to catch the cool UK morning moisture.
Keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering gently at the base to avoid any leaf rot.
Watch out for flea beetles in June; use fine insect mesh to keep these tiny pests off the leaves.
Sow a fresh batch every three weeks until August for a steady supply of peppery salad greens.
Grow them next to onions or garlic to naturally deter pests that love this brassica family herb.

items.name: Morettia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under fleece to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and damp.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil with a neutral pH to prevent root rot in wet British winters.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two inches of soil are dry to avoid downy mildew.
Net the crop securely from April onwards to block cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter common Brassicaceae pests naturally in small garden plots.

items.name: Alyssum propinquum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 2mm depth in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent dampening off in UK damp.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings to avoid rot.
Shear back by half after the first summer flush to encourage a second wave of blooms in autumn.
Watch for flea beetles in dry spells, using fine insect mesh to protect the young brassica foliage.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme in sunny, south-facing rockeries to mimic its alpine habitat.

items.name: Cardamine nuttallii
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland perennial in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination in the UK.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring growth but reduce watering when the plant goes dormant.
Apply a leaf mould mulch in autumn to mimic its native forest floor and protect shallow rhizomes.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the tender emerging edible shoots.

items.name: Cardamine douglassii
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous shrubs.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic the damp woodland conditions of its native habitat.
Hand-weed around the delicate spring foliage to prevent vigorous garden grasses from smothering it.
Divide the fibrous root clumps immediately after flowering in late spring to propagate new plants.
Position next to Galanthus or Eranthis as companion plants that share its early damp shade needs.

items.name: Cardamine constancei
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian woodland native in deep shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic forest canopies.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy UK clay to create the damp, acidic, well-drained soil it requires.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Protect the delicate emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early autumn once the summer dormancy period ends.

items.name: Iberis amara
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in spring about half a centimetre deep in well-drained, gritty soil.
Water young seedlings weekly until established, then let the soil dry out to prevent root rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, especially when the shoots are tender.
Deadhead the spent white flowers in midsummer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Grow them alongside carrots to help deter pests and make the most of your vegetable patch space.
items.description: Iberis amara, called wild candytuft, rocket candytuft and bitter candytuft, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to Belgium, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Spain, and Switzerland. It has been introduced to numerous locations including Algeria, Sweden, Eastern Europe, the Caucasus, Iraq, Kazakhstan, the Indian Subcontinent, Korea, Far Eastern Russia, New Zealand, Argentina, Ecuador, Hispaniola, the United States, and Canada. It prefers to grow in warm and sunny conditions, in high-calcium soil.

items.name: Cardamine bellidifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty alpine trough with 50% horticultural grit to mimic UK mountain scree drainage.
Water from below in winter to prevent crown rot in damp, humid UK cold seasons.
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface as they require cold stratification to germinate in spring.
Position in a north-facing rockery or light dappled shade to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Watch for flea beetles in early summer and protect young leaves with fine insect mesh.

items.name: Sisymbrium linifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow these perennial mustard greens in spring or autumn just three millimetres deep in well-drained soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent this leafy brassica from bolting early.
Watch out for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars by using fleece covers over your crop.
Plant alongside rosemary or mint to help deter common UK brassica pests from your salad patch.
Cut back the flowering stems in midsummer to encourage a fresh flush of tender, peppery leaves.

items.name: Brassica rapa subsp. nipposinica
items.growersTips:
Sow Mizuna seeds 1cm deep from April to October, using cloches to extend your autumn harvests.
Keep the soil consistently moist to stop this speedy leaf crop from bolting in dry UK summers.
Pop fine insect netting over your plants to block flea beetles from chewing tiny holes in leaves.
Grow Mizuna next to lettuce or spinach as a trap crop to draw aphids away from your main salads.
Harvest just the outer leaves using cut-and-come-again to get multiple flushes from one plant.

items.name: Cusickiella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep to allow natural UK winter cold to break dormancy.
Grow in a gritty, alkaline scree mix to mimic alpine scree and prevent winter wet root rot.
Water only during dry spring spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between feeds.
Protect young foliage from slugs and snails using copper tape around pots during damp UK springs.
Plant alongside wild thyme in stone troughs to provide excellent drainage and mimic alpine habitats.

items.name: Berteroa incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK self-seeding cycles.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between feeds.
Cut back flowering stems in late summer before seed pods explode to control its invasive spreading.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family weed.

items.name: Coincya monensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just half a centimetre deep in poor, well-drained soil to mimic dunes.
Water young plants weekly, but let established ones dry out to survive dry UK summers.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars, as this cabbage relative is a prime target.
Plant alongside sea kale or wild mustard to create a thriving, coastal-themed veg patch.
Cut back the yellow flower heads in late summer to prevent it from self-seeding everywhere.

items.name: Coincya richeri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cover in free-draining sandy loam to mimic its native coastal soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles since this is a brassica family member.
Plant alongside rosemary or mint to help deter the pests that love this rare leafy green.
Grow this hardy plant in full sun to help it thrive in our cooler, unpredictable British climate.

items.name: Lepidium banksii
items.growersTips:
Sow your coastal cress seeds in early spring under a cold frame to protect them from UK frosts.
Keep the soil constantly damp but not soggy to mimic its natural New Zealand coastal habitat.
Grow this rare plant in a very gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Watch out for slugs and snails, as they absolutely love devouring the tender young salad leaves.
Plant it alongside sea kale or wild cabbage, as they share a love for salty, windy UK seaside spots.

items.name: Lepidium hypenantion
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under fleece to protect young shoots from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged to prevent the taproots from splitting.
Watch out for flea beetles in May by using yellow sticky traps and fine insect mesh over beds.
Grow them alongside radishes to help deter common pests and maximize your vegetable patch space.
Work plenty of well-rotted garden compost into your soil beforehand to ensure a free-draining bed.

items.name: Alyssum alyssoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April directly into poor well-drained UK soils.
Water young seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent dampening off in damp UK springs.
Plant alongside cabbages to attract hoverflies whose larvae voraciously consume brassica aphids.
Hand-weed around the delicate shallow roots instead of hoeing to avoid disturbing the plants.
Collect the small seed pods in August before they split to prevent unwanted self-seeding nearby.

items.name: Selenia aurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of 5mm in free-draining, neutral to alkaline soil.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp UK springs.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter common Brassicaceae pests naturally in UK plots.
Harvest the peppery leaves when young and tender before the yellow flowers appear in summer.

items.name: Brassica elongata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 1cm depth in a sunny, well-drained bed with a high pH of 6.5 to 7.5.
Firm the soil thoroughly around transplant roots to prevent wind rock during wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Protect young spring shoots from cabbage white butterflies using a fine insect mesh.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles which target this specific brassica.
items.description: Brassica elongata, the elongated mustard or long-stalked rape, is a species of the mustard plant that is native to parts of Central Europe, Eastern Europe, the Balkan Peninsula, the Caucasus, Morocco and parts of Central Asia. Through plant invasion this species has become naturalized in many other parts of the world. Some of these naturalized regions include South Africa, North Western Europe, Australia and North America. Given the wide range of climate and ecological conditions of these regions, B. elongata has been able to disrupt the ecosystems of their native plant habitats and has been l

items.name: Phoenicaulis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for successful spring germination.
Grow in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the topsoil to dry out completely.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to deter common Brassicaceae pests like the cabbage white butterfly.
items.description: Phoenicaulis is a monotypic genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae found in western North America. It contains the single species Phoenicaulis cheiranthoides, which is known by the common names daggerpod and wallflower phoenicaulis. The genus name means 'reddish-purple stems', probably in reference to the tendency for the stems to take on such a color, and the species name means 'hand of flowers'.

items.name: Cardamine corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Uproot this highly invasive weed immediately before its explosive seed pods scatter across borders.
Grow it in containers of poor soil if you must cultivate it, to prevent it suffocating alpines.
Hand-pull plants in early spring before white flowers appear to stop rapid self-seeding in damp soil.
Apply a thick organic mulch over cleared soil to block light and stop dormant seeds from germinating.
Check newly purchased nursery pots carefully to avoid accidentally introducing this weed to your garden.

items.name: Cardamine bulbosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp acidic to neutral clay loam in a partially shaded woodland border or bog garden edge.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn or divide the bulbous rhizomes in late summer after dormancy.
Keep the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to mimic its native wet meadow habitat.
Watch for orange tip butterfly caterpillars which feed on the foliage but cause minimal damage.
Position alongside native UK moisture-lovers like Primula vulgaris and Caltha palustris.

items.name: Diplotaxis erucoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep from March to September for a continuous harvest.
Water the soil consistently to keep it damp, as dry ground triggers this spicy rocket to bolt early.
Keep a close eye out for flea beetles, which love eating tiny holes in these peppery salad leaves.
Grow this wild white rocket next to mint or sage to help deter those pesky flea beetles naturally.
Sow in late autumn under a cloche or cold frame to enjoy fresh, peppery winter salad leaves in Kent.

items.name: Thlaspi arvense
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring just five millimetres deep to mimic UK wild germination.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart so these leafy salad greens get plenty of light.
Water gently at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist without waterlogging the roots.
Hand-pull plants before they drop seed to stop this enthusiastic grower taking over your plot.
Harvest the young mustard-tasting leaves early in spring before the bitter white flowers open.

items.name: Barbarea stricta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer to catch the cool, damp autumn weather this biennial needs to establish.
Plant them just five millimetres deep in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soils where they thrive.
Keep the soil consistently damp as dry UK summers will cause this damp-loving plant to bolt early.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring and protect young leaves with fine insect mesh if needed.
Grow them alongside mint or wild garlic to help deter the cabbage white butterflies from laying.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in modules from March to July to stop soil pests eating them before they can germinate.
Plant them out 30cm apart in firm, fertile soil, keeping the stems level with the ground surface.
Water frequently and evenly to stop the swollen stems from splitting or becoming woody and tough.
Cover your crop with fine insect mesh immediately to block cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Harvest when the stems are the size of a tennis ball so they taste sweet and stay beautifully tender.

items.name: Erysimum cheiranthoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or early spring, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit.
Grow this wild wallflower in well-drained, alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Keep a sharp eye out for flea beetles in spring, which love to chew tiny holes in the leaves.
Plant near potatoes or onions as companions to help deter common soil pests in your veg patch.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells in our typical British summers.
items.description: Erysimum cheiranthoides, the treacle-mustard, wormseed wallflower, or wormseed mustard is a species of Erysimum native to most of central and northern Europe and northern and central Asia. Like other Erysimum species, E. cheiranthoides accumulates two major classes of defensive chemicals: glucosinolates and cardiac glycosides.

items.name: Parolinia
items.growersTips:
Sow Parolinia seeds in early spring at a depth of one centimetre in well-drained, gritty compost.
Grow this tender Canary Island native in pots to easily move indoors before the first UK frosts.
Water sparingly, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings to prevent root rot.
Position containers in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its hot homeland.
Watch for cabbage white caterpillars and flea beetles, which target this Brassicaceae family member.

items.name: Cardamine californica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 5cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous tree shade.
Water weekly during dry spring active growth, then stop watering completely when it goes dormant.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper tape.
Propagate by dividing the fragile rhizomes in late summer while the plant is fully dormant.
Grow alongside early shade-lovers like Galanthus or Hepatica to mark its spot during dormancy.

items.name: Lepidium howei-insulae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cover to protect this rare Lord Howe peppergrass from UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to mimic its native damp coastal habitat.
Grow in a very free-draining sandy loam mixed with compost to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Watch out for slugs and snails which absolutely love devouring the tender young peppery leaves.
Plant alongside radishes and mustards to help deter common brassica pests in your veg patch.

items.name: Barbarea verna
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in damp soil from July to September for a steady winter supply of peppery leaves.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers to stop this biennial from bolting to seed.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring and use fine insect netting to protect the young foliage.
Plant this land cress next to mint or rosemary to help deter those pesky cabbage white butterflies.
Grow it in partial shade rather than full sun to keep the leaves tender and prevent bitter tastes.
items.description: Barbarea verna is a biennial herb in the family Brassicaceae. Common names include land cress, American cress, bank cress, black wood cress, Belle Isle cress, Bermuda cress, poor man's cabbage, early yellowrocket, early wintercress, scurvy cress, creasy greens, and upland cress. It is native to southern Europe and western Asia, and naturalized elsewhere It has been cultivated as a leaf vegetable in England since the 17th century. As it requires less water than watercress, it is easier to cultivate.

items.name: Coincya wrightii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into the gritty, well-drained soil of a sunny rockery.
Keep watering to a absolute minimum once established, as this Lundy cabbage hates soggy UK winter wet.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the plant base.
Avoid adding rich compost or manure to the soil, as this rare native thrives on low-nutrient grit.
Grow them alongside thrift or sea campion to mimic their natural breezy, coastal cliff environment.
items.description: Coincya wrightii, known as Lundy cabbage, is a species of primitive brassicoid, endemic to the island of Lundy off the southwestern coast of England, where it is sufficiently isolated to have formed its own species, with its endemic phytophagous beetles. Coincya wrightii grows natively only on the eastern cliffs and slopes of the island and nowhere else in the world and is a protected species. It reaches up to a metre in height and with its yellow flowers it looks a little similar to oil seed rape. Although it is a member of the cabbage family, it tastes unpleasant – it has been described as "

items.name: Teesdalia nudicaulis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on a free-draining sandy loam to mimic its natural UK acidic heathland habitat.
Keep watering minimal and let the soil dry out fully between feeds to prevent damp-off root rot.
Leave this tiny annual unpruned so it can self-seed naturally in your gravel garden every spring.
Watch out for slugs early on, as they love to munch the delicate rosettes before they can flower.
Plant them alongside sheep-bit or early hair-grass to recreate a thriving British coastal community.

items.name: Moricandia arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in spring once UK soil warms to fifteen degrees.
Grow in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to mimic its native Mediterranean limestone habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant brassica dislikes wet winter roots.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to deter pests and match its preference for dry sunny spots.
items.description: Moricandia arvensis, the purple mistress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It has a broadly western Mediterranean distribution, from the Canary Islands to northern Africa including Mauritania and Chad, the Iberian Peninsula, Italy and as far as Greece, and has been introduced to France, Corsica, and Sardinia. It has an intermediate C3–C4 carbon fixation system, known as C2 photosynthesis.

items.name: Alyssum wulfenianum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun against a stone wall to mimic its alpine scree habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, as damp soil will kill the plant.
Trim back by half after the yellow spring blooms fade to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic grit barriers.
items.description: Alyssum wulfenianum, the madwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the southeastern Alps. Preferring dry, porous soils, it is hardy in USDA zones four through nine. There is a cultivar, 'Golden Spring'.

items.name: Barbarea orthoceras
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer for a winter crop, barely covering them with five millimetres of damp soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy to prevent this American wintercress from bolting.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring and cover your young plants with a fine insect mesh to block them.
Grow this leafy green in light shade to mimic its natural damp UK woodland edge habitat.
Plant next to mint or rosemary to help deter the cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs.

items.name: Notoceras
items.growersTips:
Sow Notoceras seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in free-draining, sandy loam soil.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings to prevent rot.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter the cabbage white butterfly from laying eggs on the foliage.
Do not prune this annual vegetable, but harvest the seed pods when they turn yellow in late summer.

items.name: Nasturtium floridanum
items.growersTips:
Sow these Florida yellowcress seeds very shallowly in spring, just pressing them into damp compost.
Keep the soil consistently boggy and wet, mimicking their native damp habitats in your UK garden.
Grow them in partial shade to mimic forest canopies and prevent the delicate leaves from scorching.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love the tender young damp-loving stems.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost mixed with sand to easily move them indoors before winter frost.
items.description: Nasturtium floridanum, common names Florida yellowcress and Florida watercress, is an aquatic plant species endemic to Florida, though widely distributed within that state. It is found in wet places at elevations less than 50 m.

items.name: Cardamine breweri
items.growersTips:
Grow this UK-hardy bittercress in wet, acidic soil or shallow pond edges to mimic its stream habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn just under the soil surface in a cold frame to benefit from winter stratification.
Keep the soil constantly saturated or water daily during dry summer spells to prevent early bolting.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper barrier tape.
Plant alongside water mint or marsh marigold in boggy areas to create a natural damp-loving community.

items.name: Cardamine micranthera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn 5mm deep in damp, acidic to neutral soil to mimic UK stream-side habitats.
Keep soil constantly wet but not stagnant, watering daily with rainwater during dry summer spells.
Grow in partial to deep shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching in midday UK sun.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Plant alongside water forget-me-not or marsh marigold in bog gardens for natural shade and support.

items.name: Brassica juncea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in July or August at a depth of 1cm to prevent premature bolting in summer heat.
Net crops immediately with 7mm mesh to exclude cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged, preventing a bitter taste.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter pests, avoiding planting near other brassicas to limit disease.
Harvest outer leaves continuously when 10cm long to encourage fresh, tender growth through winter.
items.description: Brassica juncea, commonly mustard greens, brown mustard, Chinese mustard, Indian mustard, Japanese mustard, Korean green mustard, leaf mustard, Oriental mustard and vegetable mustard, is a species of mustard plant.

items.name: Cardamine pensylvanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in damp, humus-rich soil during early spring.
Keep soil consistently wet by watering twice weekly to mimic its natural UK wetland habitat.
Position in partial shade to prevent the delicate edible leaves from scorching in summer sun.
Hand-weed surrounding soil regularly as this species easily gets choked out by aggressive grasses.
Harvest the peppery leaves before white flowers appear in May to prevent self-seeding and bitterness.

items.name: Erysimum × cheiri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in June or July for strong bare-root plants ready to transplant into autumn beds.
Plant out in October in free-draining chalky or alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage bushy growth and more fragrant flowers.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and clubroot disease as they are brassicas.
Remove spent flower spikes in July to encourage a potential second flush of blooms.
items.description: Erysimum cheiri, syn. Cheiranthus cheiri, the wallflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae (Cruciferae), native to Greece, but widespread as an introduced species elsewhere. It is also treated as a hybrid under the name Erysimum × cheiri. It is widely cultivated as a garden plant.

items.name: Cardamine glara
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking its native UK woodland edge habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn at 2mm depth in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Hand-weed around the base in spring to prevent aggressive garden grasses from smothering the crown.
Divide mature clumps in early autumn every three years to maintain plant vigour and increase stock.
items.description: Cardamine glara is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to New Zealand. A rhizomatous perennial herb, its specific epithet refers to the scree that it is often found growing in.

items.name: Cardamine lyrata
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic bittercress in a garden pond margin or boggy soil at a depth of 0 to 10cm.
Plant in partial shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching in hot UK summer sun.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and pushing them directly into wet, muddy pond edges.
Watch for aphids and flea beetles in summer, rinsing them off with pond water to avoid chemicals.
Trim back aggressive runners in late autumn to keep the plant from overtaking smaller pond plants.
items.description: Cardamine lyrata, known commonly as Japanese cress and Chinese ivy, is a species of aquatic plant in the mustard family. It is native to the marshes of eastern China and Siberia, as well as Korea and Japan. It flowers from May to June in the wild, with seeds ripening through September. The flowers are bisexual and are pollinated by insects, but are also self-fertile.

items.name: Alyssum montanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural sand to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in spring once the risk of frost has passed.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Cut back the foliage by half immediately after flowering in July to maintain a neat, compact mound.
Position in full south-facing sun next to lavender or rosemary to thrive in poor, alkaline soils.

items.name: Cardamine pentaphyllos
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland soil rich in leaf mould and organic matter
Keep soil consistently moist but free-draining during spring growth using a thick bark mulch layer
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in late spring before the foliage dies back
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Associate with Galanthus and Erythronium for a synchronized early spring shade garden display
items.description: Cardamine pentaphyllos, the five-leaflet bitter-cress or showy toothwort, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to Western and Central Europe in Slovenia and Croatia. It is an herbaceous perennial, growing to 30–50 cm (12–20 in), with palmate leaves and racemes of purple, pink or white flowers in late Spring and early Summer.

items.name: Nasturtium officinale
items.growersTips:
Grow this watercress in a container of compost submerged in a bucket of water to mimic stream beds.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring and keep the soil constantly wet to prevent the leaves going bitter.
Watch out for flea beetles in summer, using fine mesh covers to protect the peppery young leaves.
Cut the stems back regularly to encourage bushy new growth and stop the plant from flowering early.
Grow watercress alongside mint in a shady, damp spot where they can both enjoy boggy UK soil.
items.description: Watercress or yellowcress is a species of aquatic flowering plant in the cabbage family, Brassicaceae.

items.name: Armoracia rusticana
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring placing root cuttings at a forty-five degree angle under five centimetres of soil.
Grow in large heavy-duty pots to prevent the invasive taproots from taking over your garden borders.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to prevent the roots from becoming woody.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family member.
Lift and replant the main roots every autumn to maintain the best pungent flavour for horseradish sauce.
items.description: Horseradish is a perennial plant of the family Brassicaceae. It is a root vegetable, cultivated and used worldwide as a spice and as a condiment. The species is likely native to Southeastern Europe and Western Asia.

items.name: Turritis glabra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on well-drained, sandy soil to mimic its native UK shingle habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this hardy biennial thrives in dry, gravelly cottage borders.
Watch out for the rare striped flea beetle which loves munching on this wild brassica relative.
Leave the tall flower spikes to self-seed naturally in late summer for a display the next year.
Plant alongside wild marjoram or thyme to create a perfect drought-tolerant UK pollinator haven.

items.name: Leavenworthia torulosa
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare annual seeds in late autumn to mimic the cool, wet UK winter they need to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during their active spring growing period.
Plant them in a gritty, alkaline soil mix to replicate their natural limestone glade habitat.
Position your pots in full sun to ensure these delicate, low-growing wildflowers get enough light.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring, as they love to devour the tender young seedlings.
items.description: Leavenworthia torulosa, the necklace gladecress, is a species of plant in the mustard family. It is native to the eastern United States where it is only found near limestone cedar glades of Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, and Tennessee. It is considered rare in all states it is found except Tennessee, where it is common in the Nashville Basin due to the abundance of available habitat.

items.name: Capsella bursa-pastoris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in early spring just 2mm deep so the UK light can trigger quick germination.
Give them a quick splash of water only when the top inch of your gritty soil feels completely dry.
Keep a sharp eye out for white rust pustules on the leaves during damp British autumn weather.
Harvest the heart-shaped seed pods regularly to stop this speedy grower from taking over your plot.
Plant them near your spring onions to help deter pests while keeping their roots happy and shallow.
items.description: Capsella bursa-pastoris, commonly known as shepherd's purse or lady's purse, is a small flowering plant in the mustard family. It has been described as a protocarnivore because its seeds contain mucilage, which traps nematodes.

items.name: Rhamphospermum pubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, alkaline soil to mimic UK chalk downland habitats.
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells, but keep established roots dry in winter.
Hand-pull competing perennial weeds around the base to prevent this wild brassica being choked out.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars in summer and net plants with fine insect mesh.
Prune back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to encourage healthy basal growth for spring.

items.name: Matthiola
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into heavy UK clay to give Matthiola the sharp drainage and neutral to alkaline soil it loves.
Plant plug plants in spring just level with the soil surface to prevent damp UK weather rotting stems.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as these plants hate sitting in soggy winter mud.
Snip off faded flower spikes right down to the base in summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, protecting young leaves with a fine mesh or organic insect spray.
items.description: Matthiola is a genus of flowering plant in the mustard family Brassicaceae. It is named after Italian naturalist Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577). The genus contains about 50 species of annual, biennial and perennial herbaceous plants and subshrubs. Many are cultivated for their heavily scented, colorful flowers.

items.name: Descurainia tanacetifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in early spring just beneath the soil surface so they get light to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent young seedlings from damping off.
Watch out for flea beetles in late spring and use fine insect netting to protect the foliage.
Grow this tansy mustard alongside onions or garlic to help deter common UK garden pests.
Harvest the young peppery leaves regularly before the yellow flowers appear to keep them tasty.

items.name: Leavenworthia stylosa
items.growersTips:
Sow these dainty annuals in autumn using gritty, well-drained soil to mimic their limestone habitat.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy during their active winter and spring growth.
Position your pots in full UK winter sun to encourage those lovely yellow flowers to open up.
Protect the delicate winter rosettes from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Let the plants self-seed naturally in your gravel garden to enjoy a fresh display next spring.

items.name: Heliophila pusilla
items.growersTips:
Sow these delicate South African annuals directly outdoors in May once the UK frosts have passed.
Choose your sunniest, most sheltered spot with gritty, fast-draining soil to mimic their homeland.
Water sparingly only when the top inch of soil is dry, as they hate sitting in damp UK winter wet.
Sow seeds just two millimetres deep and keep them moist until they sprout in about two weeks.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme to help support their thin, floppy stems in breezy weather.

items.name: Cochlearia anglica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a boggy, saline-mimicking soil mix to trigger natural winter cold dormancy.
Keep the soil constantly wet using harvested rainwater to mimic its natural British saltmarsh home.
Position your pots in partial shade because this coastal native dislikes our hot inland summer sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love eating the tender, vitamin-C rich leaves in damp weather.
Harvest the outer fleshy leaves sparingly in spring to keep the perennial root system productive.
items.description: Cochlearia anglica is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae known by the common names English scurvygrass and long-leaved scurvy grass. It is a plant of the coastlines of Europe, especially the British Isles. It is edible, and as its name suggests, it is rich in vitamin C. It has spade-shaped leaves and white flowers.

items.name: Rapistrum rugosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres into poor, well-drained soil to limit wild spread.
Water seedlings weekly until established, then withhold water entirely to prevent leggy, weak stems.
Hand-pull plants in June before the yellow flowers set seed to stop aggressive self-seeding in lawns.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary in pots to contain its invasive roots and mask cabbage white butterflies.
Check foliage weekly in June for flea beetles and crush them to protect nearby vegetable brassicas.

items.name: Isatis tinctoria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in spring about one centimetre deep in a sunny spot with alkaline soil.
Water young seedlings weekly but leave established woad alone as it loves dry, well-drained UK soil.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars and clubroot since woad is in the brassica family.
Cut the leaves for dyeing in July of its first year before the plant loses its rich blue pigment.
Deadhead the yellow flowers in spring of year two to stop this self-seeding plant taking over.
items.description: Isatis tinctoria, also called woad, dyer's woad, dyer's-weed, or glastum, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae with a documented history of use as a blue dye and medicinal plant. The double use of woad is seen in its name: the term Isatis is linked to its ancient use to treat wounds; the term tinctoria references its use as a dye. It is occasionally known as Asp of Jerusalem. Woad is also the name of a blue dye produced from the leaves of the plant. Woad is native to the steppe and desert zones of the Caucasus, Central Asia to Eastern Siberia and Western Asia but is now also found i

items.name: Morisia
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained gritty soil or scree to prevent winter wet from rotting the deep taproot.
Plant in full sun in an alpine trough or raised bed to mimic its native Mediterranean grit habitat.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the gritty topsoil to dry fully.
Protect the crown with a layer of horticultural grit or gravel to stop damp soil touching leaves.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the low-growing rosettes of yellow blooms.

items.name: Diplotaxis viminea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep from April to June once UK frosts have passed.
Grow this wild rocket relative in poor, well-drained soil to stop the leaves from losing flavour.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells as this Mediterranean native hates soggy UK roots.
Watch out for flea beetles making tiny holes in the leaves and use fine mesh netting to stop them.
Harvest the peppery young leaves frequently before the yellow flowers appear to keep them tender.
items.description: Diplotaxis viminea also known by the common name Vineyard wall rocket is a species of annual herb in the family Brassicaceae. They have a self-supporting growth form and simple, broad leaves. Individuals can grow to 5.8 cm tall. It forms a basal rosette of leaves and flowering stems with or without leaves. It blooms June through October in western Europe, but may have an extended flowering period of up to eight months elsewhere in its range. This species grows in fields and vineyards and It is considered by some to be a weed of vegetable crops, vineyards, and gardens.

items.name: Malcolmia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep directly into well-drained soil from March to May.
Water sparingly once established as this Mediterranean native dislikes waterlogged UK winter soil.
Watch for flea beetles in spring which chew tiny holes in the leaves of this brassica family member.
Sow in successive batches every fortnight until July to extend the short three-week flowering window.
Grow alongside carrots to help deter carrot rust fly with the strong scent of these flowers.

items.name: Peltaria alliacea
items.growersTips:
Pop this perennial garlic cress in a moist, semi-shaded spot to mimic its native woodland edge.
Divide your clumps in early spring or autumn to easily propagate and keep the growth vigorous.
Watch out for flea beetles in dry UK summers, keeping the soil damp to deter these tiny pests.
Snip off the white flower stalks in summer to keep the garlic-mustard flavored leaves tender.
Grow it in a container if you want to stop its eager, spreading root system from taking over.

items.name: Noccaea caerulescens
items.growersTips:
This zinc-loving alpine thrives in UK gardens if you mix plenty of grit and gravel into your soil.
Sow the tiny seeds in autumn just on the soil surface as they need winter cold and light to sprout.
Water them gently from below during dry UK springs to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who love chewing the young foliage in damp British weather.
Plant them near metal-tolerant alpines in a sunny rockery or scree bed for the best display.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. viridis
items.growersTips:
Net your spring greens early to stop the pesky cabbage white butterfly laying eggs on the leaves.
Sow seeds outdoors in April at a depth of two centimetres in firm, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot.
Water your collard greens deeply once a week at the base rather than giving them daily light sprinkles.
Plant dwarf kale next to mint or rosemary to help distract hungry pests with those strong scents.
Harvest the outer leaves first in winter to keep the plant producing fresh new growth from the centre.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep from April to August, as summer heat makes them bolt and go to seed too quickly.
Cover your crop with fine insect mesh immediately after planting to block cabbage white butterflies.
Give them a fast-acting organic nitrogen feed like seaweed liquid to boost those tender green stems.
Harvest the main central stem just before the white flowers open to trigger lots of tasty side shoots.
Grow them alongside mint or rosemary to help confuse the pests that love this Chinese broccoli.

items.name: Barbarea vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer just below the soil surface to match the UK autumn rain for easy sprouting.
Grow this biennial in damp, nitrogen-rich soil near your compost heap where it thrives best.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring, so cover young leaves with fleece to keep them pristine.
Plant alongside cabbages as a clever trap crop to draw hungry white butterflies away from your veg.
Cut back the yellow flower spikes in July before they drop seeds to stop it invading your lawn.
items.description: Barbarea vulgaris, also called wintercress, or alternatively winter rocket, rocketcress, yellow rocketcress, yellow rocket, wound rocket, herb barbara, creases, or creasy greens, is a biennial herb of the genus Barbarea, belonging to the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Heliophila variabilis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in May after the last frosts, just barely covering them with fine soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering gently at the base on dry summer mornings.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using a fine insect mesh to protect these delicate seedlings.
Grow them alongside carrots or radishes to help deter common pests and maximize your veg patch space.
Add plenty of well-rotted compost to your patch before sowing to give these quick growers a boost.

items.name: Heliophila africana
items.growersTips:
Sow these Cape rain daisies in late spring after frosts, just pressing seeds lightly into the soil.
Give them a spot in your sunniest, most sheltered bed to mimic their warm South African homeland.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty soil dry out fully between light soakings.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme or sedums to help support their delicate, floppy stems.
Protect young shoots from slugs during wet UK springs using copper tape or beer traps.

items.name: Polyctenium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its Great Basin home and prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat and protect from UK damp.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the root zone completely dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain a compact shape and prevent woody legginess.
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate Brassicaceae foliage first emerges.

items.name: Capsella rubella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the soil surface in early spring, as they need light to germinate in UK weather.
Water lightly but consistently at the base to prevent downy mildew in our damp British summers.
Watch out for flea beetles in May and protect young leaves with fleece or a fine insect mesh.
Grow them alongside onions or garlic to naturally deter aphids and thrips from the tender foliage.
Harvest the heart-shaped pods early before they split and self-seed aggressively across your plot.

items.name: Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in July to stop early bolting caused by chilly UK spring temperatures.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy to prevent the heads from splitting open.
Pop a fine insect mesh over them immediately to block cabbage root fly and flea beetles.
Mix in plenty of well-rotted manure before planting to satisfy their hunger for nitrogen.
Harvest in late autumn before the first hard frosts turn their tender leaves to mush.
items.description: Brassica rapa is an annual to biennial plant species native to Eurasia that is from the Brassicaceae family. The B. rapa subspecies oleifera is an oilseed commonly known as turnip rape, field mustard, bird's rape, and keblock.

items.name: Brassica rapa var. parachinensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in August for a autumn crop to avoid the worst flea beetle damage in the UK climate.
Keep soil consistently moist by watering at the base to prevent this fast grower from bolting.
Protect your young plants with fine insect netting to block cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Grow them alongside mint or rosemary to help deter pests with their strong, aromatic scents.
Harvest the tender flowering stems just as the first yellow buds begin to open for the best taste.

items.name: Sinapidendron
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep in early spring using cloches to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Grow in fertile well-drained soil with a pH above 6.5 to prevent the devastating clubroot disease.
Net the crop securely from May to September to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to stop the plants bolting to seed.
Interplant with mint or sage to help deter flea beetles which riddle the leaves with tiny holes.

items.name: Microstigma
items.growersTips:
Sow your seeds indoors in early April at a depth of one centimetre to beat the chilly UK spring.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently at the base every three days.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using a fine mesh fleece to protect the young green leaves.
Mix plenty of well-rotted garden compost into your soil a week before planting to boost growth.
Plant next to mint or sage to help deter pests naturally and improve the flavour of your harvest.

items.name: Nasturtiopsis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of one centimetre once the risk of hard frost has passed
Keep the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to prevent this brassica from bolting early
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white caterpillars using fine insect netting
Grow in moderately fertile well-drained soil with a neutral pH to encourage healthy leaf growth
Plant alongside mint or sage to help deter common brassica pests in the damp UK climate

items.name: Cardamine angustata
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 5cm in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic woodlands.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep soil damp but avoid waterlogging during winter dormancy.
Hand-pick orange-tip butterfly caterpillars in early summer rather than using chemical pesticides.
Clear away fallen autumn leaves from the crown to prevent crown rot in damp UK winter conditions.
Grow alongside Galanthus nivalis and Primula vulgaris which share its early spring shade preferences.

items.name: Cardamine flagellifera
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Propagate by dividing the creeping runners in autumn or early spring to control its spreading habit.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil damp but avoid waterlogged conditions.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
Grow alongside shade-loving Astilbe or Hostas to complement its delicate white spring blooms.

items.name: Cardamine rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this native of wet woods in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics UK stream banks.
Plant divisions in early autumn at a depth where the crown sits level with the damp soil surface.
