Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently boggy and cool.
Watch for flea beetles in spring, protecting young leaves with fine insect mesh if damage occurs.
Cut back faded flowering stems in midsummer to encourage fresh green foliage and prevent self-seeding.
items.description: Cardamine rotundifolia, also known as American bittercress or mountain bittercress, is a perennial herbaceous brassica native to eastern North America. It was first described by André Michaux in his publication Flora Boreali-Americana (1803).

items.name: Cardamine depressa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring to match cool UK temperatures.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged by watering lightly every two to three days.
Protect young leaves from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets during damp British springs.
Grow in partial shade to mimic its natural alpine habitat and prevent the delicate foliage burning.
Plant alongside wild garlic or mint to help deter common Brassicaceae pests like flea beetles.

items.name: Cardamine quinquefolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland perennial in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic its native damp forest floor.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould into clay soils to create the humus-rich, moist conditions it loves.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp before summer dormancy.
Leave the dying foliage alone in early summer as it naturally dies back to underground rhizomes.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly devour the emerging tender shoots.

items.name: Erysimum scoparium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Canary Island wallflower in the poorest, sharpest-draining soil you have to avoid rot.
Pop it in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic its native hot, dry volcanic cliffs.
Trim the flower spikes back by half in late summer to keep this short-lived woody perennial bushy.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots and shield the crown from wet winter waterlogging.
Grow it next to rosemary or thyme in a raised bed so they can all share the same dry, gritty soil.
items.description: Erysimum scoparium is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to the Canary Islands. It is a shrubby species of wallflower with purplish flowers found at high altitudes.

items.name: Brassica rapa var. hakabura
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in July or August to avoid early bolting triggered by the long UK midsummer days.
Sow directly at a depth of one centimetre and thin the seedlings to twenty centimetres apart.
Keep the soil consistently damp to prevent woody stems and stop the roots from splitting.
Cover immediately with ultra-fine insect mesh to block cabbage root fly and flea beetles.
Grow them next to mint or rosemary to help deter local UK pests with strong herbal scents.

items.name: Iberis saxatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rock-dwelling gem in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure its roots never sit in wet.
Prune the stems back by half right after spring flowering to keep its neat, cushion-like shape.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to mimic its native limestone cliffs and prevent winter rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs, as they love to feast on the tender new shoots.
Water sparingly once established, only giving it a drink during prolonged dry spells in summer.

items.name: Notothlaspi australe
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a gritty compost mix to let winter cold naturally break their dormancy.
Plant them in a sharply draining rock garden or scree bed to mimic their native alpine habitat.
Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the gravelly topsoil to dry out completely between drinks.
Protect the young rosettes from damp UK winters with a glass cloche to prevent crown rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails, which love to feast on the tender leaves during wet spring nights.

items.name: Notothlaspi rosulatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this alpine penwiper plant in a scree bed with 70% grit to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the seeds shallowly in autumn and leave the pot outdoors to get winter chills for germination.
Water only from below during the growing season to keep the hairy rosette from rotting in damp air.
Protect the precious taproot at all costs by sowing seeds directly into deep, biodegradable pots.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the succulent, low-growing leaves.

items.name: Erysimum asperum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Siberian wallflower in free-draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winter dampness.
Sow seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep in late spring for strong autumn transplanting.
Water young plants weekly, but let established ones dry out to prevent root rot in soggy weather.
Cut back the faded flower stems by half in late summer to keep your wallflowers neat and compact.
Watch out for clubroot disease, especially if you grow them near cabbages or other brassicas.

items.name: Cochlearia groenlandica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into cool, damp, gritty soil to mimic coastal cliffs.
Keep the soil consistently moist but free-draining, mimicking the damp sea spray of the UK coast.
Plant alongside sea thrift or wild thyme in a rockery to recreate their natural seaside community.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love the fleshy, vitamin-C rich leaves during damp UK springs.
Harvest only the outer leaves in winter to allow this hardy biennial to keep growing through frosts.
items.description: Cochlearia groenlandica, known in English as polar scurvygrass or Greenland scurvy-grass, is a flowering plant of the scurvy-grass genus in the cabbage family.

items.name: Orychophragmus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer directly into moist, free-draining soil to establish winter-hardy rosettes.
Plant seeds at a depth of five millimetres in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to prevent early bolting and keep the leaves tender.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and use fine netting to protect the brassica foliage.
Grow alongside early spring bulbs like daffodils to create a vibrant purple and yellow colour contrast.

items.name: Iberis umbellata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly into well-drained UK soil in April, just five millimetres deep, for summer blooms.
Water these Mediterranean natives sparingly, only during dry spells, as damp UK soil causes rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimetres to encourage a bushier habit.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during wet British weather.
Cut the faded flower stems back by half in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.

items.name: Erysimum repandum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn directly into gritty, free-draining soil to mimic UK gravel paths.
Water young plants sparingly only during dry spells as this wild wallflower hates soggy winter soil.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles since it belongs to the brassica family.
Prune back lightly after its spring yellow blooms fade to keep the habit neat and prevent legginess.
Grow it alongside native UK wildflowers like red campion to create a charming cottage garden look.

items.name: Erysimum crepidifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this pale yellow wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in your sunniest border, as it hates damp shade and needs full sun to thrive.
Trim the stems back by half after flowering in July to keep the habit neat and bushy.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during wet British Mays.
Sow seeds shallowly in pots during June to get strong young plants ready for autumn planting.

items.name: Erysimum capitatum
items.growersTips:
Plant these wallflowers shallowly, just level with the soil, in autumn for a brilliant spring show.
Give them super sharp drainage by mixing plenty of grit into your soil to survive wet UK winters.
Clip them back by half right after flowering in summer to stop them getting woody and leggy.
Keep a sharp eye out for cabbage white caterpillars, as they love munching these brassica cousins.
Grow them next to tulips in sunny borders; the purple and yellow contrast looks absolutely stunning.

items.name: Maresia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to match cool UK germination temperatures
Grow in well-drained sandy loam with a neutral pH to prevent clubroot common in Brassicaceae crops
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged to prevent early bolting
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles and slugs using fine insect mesh or cloches in spring
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs on the foliage

items.name: Brassica rapa subsp. sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly outdoors from April to August at a depth of one centimetre in firm, fertile soil.
Net your crop immediately after sowing to block cabbage root fly and hungry wood pigeons.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry summer spells to prevent the plants from bolting.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to help deter flea beetles from chewing holes in the leaves.
Harvest the tender flower buds and young leaves regularly in spring or autumn to prolong cropping.

items.name: Erysimum odoratum
items.growersTips:
Plant this wallflower in autumn in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Keep watering minimal once established, only soaking during dry spells to mimic its rocky habitat.
Cut back the spent flower stems by half in late summer to keep the plant bushy and prevent legginess.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and slugs, which love chewing these sweet-scented leaves.
Grow it alongside purple salvias or tulips in sunny borders for a classic spring colour contrast.

items.name: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from July to avoid early summer bolting triggered by long British daylight hours.
Keep soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge to stop the plants from running to seed early.
Drape ultra-fine insect netting over your crop immediately to block flea beetles and cabbage moths.
Sow a pinch of seeds every two weeks until September for a steady supply of fresh leaves into winter.
Grow them next to mint or sage to help deter those pesky pests that love munching on the leaves.

items.name: Leavenworthia alabamica
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare Alabama gladecress seeds in autumn just under the surface of gritty, alkaline soil.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy during our wet UK winters to prevent root rot.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot possible to mimic their native open limestone glades.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the delicate new growth.
Grow them in shallow alpine pans rather than deep pots to suit their fibrous, shallow root system.
items.description: Leavenworthia alabamica is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is commonly known as Alabama gladecress. It is endemic to Alabama.

items.name: Leavenworthia uniflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late autumn as this winter annual needs cold UK wet weather to trigger germination.
Plant seeds just two millimetres deep in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its limestone habitat.
Keep the soil damp through winter but avoid waterlogging during our heaviest January downpours.
Watch out for slugs in early spring when the tiny, delicate white flowers first begin to emerge.
Let the plants self-seed in summer by leaving the dry, seed-filled pods to burst open naturally.
items.description: Leavenworthia uniflora, called Michaux's gladecress or one-flowered gladecress, is a plant species native to the southeastern and Midwestern parts of the United States. It is reported from northwestern Georgia, northern Alabama, Tennessee, northern Arkansas, southern Missouri, Kentucky, southeastern Indiana, southwestern Ohio, and northwestern Virginia. It grows in open, sun-lit locations at elevations less than 500 meters.

items.name: Iberis linifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this biennial in late summer using gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds just three millimetres deep in pots of free-draining compost during June or July.
Grow this alongside lavender or thyme in a sunny, south-facing border to match its dry needs.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer to keep the plant neat and encourage fresh growth.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, especially during damp British April weather.

items.name: Thlaspi californicum
items.growersTips:
Sow these alpine seeds in autumn so chilly UK winter temperatures can naturally break their dormancy.
Grow them in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to mimic their native Californian serpentine cliffs.
Water sparingly from below to keep the foliage dry and prevent rot in damp British winter weather.
Protect the delicate young leaves from hungry slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape.
Plant them near creeping thyme to create a beautiful, well-drained rock garden display.

items.name: Thlaspi caerulescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they need winter cold to germinate well in our cool UK climate.
Plant them in zinc-rich or poor, gritty soil because they actually hate overly fertile garden beds.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, mimicking the wet but free-draining upland areas of Britain.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during wet UK April mornings.
Grow them near brassicas as companion plants to help draw away pests from your main vegetable crops.
items.description: Noccaea caerulescens, the alpine penny-cress or alpine pennygrass, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is found in Scandinavia and Europe.

items.name: Thlaspi alpestre
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine pennycress in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its native UK limestone screes.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill can trigger germination.
Position it in full sun, perhaps tucked into a rock garden or a crevice in a raised alpine bed.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails, which love to munch on the young spring foliage in wet weather.

items.name: Heliophila coronopifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late May when the UK soil warms up, just three millimetres deep.
Water these South African beauties sparingly, letting the top inch of soil dry out between drinks.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to mimic their native sandy soils and prevent winter root rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, as they love the tender young shoots.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to help support their delicate, floppy stems.

items.name: Farsetia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 5mm deep in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in damp UK climates.
Grow in full sun and shelter from cold winds using a south-facing wall or cold frame in winter.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, as this Mediterranean native hates wet feet.
Protect young shoots from cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and slugs using fine insect netting.
Prune lightly after flowering in late summer to maintain a compact shape and prevent leggy growth.

items.name: Raffenaldia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of one centimetre in free-draining, slightly alkaline soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent the taproot from splitting.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cover the crop with fine insect netting to exclude cabbage root fly and cabbage white butterflies.
Harvest the peppery leaves and young seed pods regularly to encourage continuous fresh growth.

items.name: Noccaea montana
items.growersTips:
Grow this alpine in gritty, free-draining limestone soil to mimic its native scree habitat.
Plant seeds in autumn just below the surface so winter cold can naturally break their dormancy.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as wet UK winters are this plant's main enemy.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails which love to feast on its delicate mountain foliage.
Position it in your rock garden where it gets full sun but stays safe from damp, stagnant air.

items.name: Noccaea rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine gem in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its scree habitat.
Water sparingly, only during dry summer spells, as it absolutely hates having wet winter feet.
Protect the delicate rosettes from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Avoid pruning, but gently clear away fallen autumn leaves so the crown does not rot in the damp.
Grow it in a raised bed or alpine trough to ensure it gets the maximum winter drainage it needs.

items.name: Conringia orientalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in early spring, just five millimetres deep, to avoid taproot damage.
Grow this brassica relative in poor, well-drained chalky soil to prevent floppy, weak stem growth.
Keep a sharp eye out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars, which love these blue-green leaves.
Water sparingly once established, as this hardy annual thrives in dry UK summer spells.
Sow alongside quick-growing radishes to help mark the rows and deter flea beetles naturally.

items.name: Iberis sempervirens
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet root rot in damp UK climates.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in June to maintain a neat mound and prevent leggy stems.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in raised beds or rockeries to ensure good air circulation.
Water newly planted Iberis weekly during dry spring spells, but leave established plants dry.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, especially during wet UK April weather.
items.description: Iberis sempervirens, the evergreen candytuft or perennial candytuft, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to southern Europe. The species is often used as an ornamental garden shrub because of its decorative flowers. Iberis is so named because many members of the genus come from the Iberian Peninsula in south west Europe. Sempervirens means "always green", referring to the evergreen foliage.

items.name: Erysimum ‘Chelsea Jacket’
items.growersTips:
Plant this lovely wallflower in autumn so its roots settle before the damp UK winter chill sets in.
Pop your Chelsea Jacket in a spot with gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Trim the stems back by half right after spring flowering to keep its bushy shape and stop it woody.
Keep an eye out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars which love munching these leafy greens.
Grow it alongside spring-flowering tulips to create a stunning, classic British cottage border.

items.name: Erysimum baeticum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Spanish wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a sunny spot next to lavender to keep its roots dry and attract early UK pollinators.
Cut the faded flower stems back by half in July to keep the plant bushy and prevent woodiness.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars in summer, as they love this brassica family member.
Avoid overwatering once established, as damp UK soil is this alpine beauty's biggest enemy.

items.name: Erysimum franciscanum
items.growersTips:
Plant this California wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a sunny spot by a south-facing wall to mimic its native coastal warmth and prevent rot.
Cut the faded flower stems back by half in July to keep the plant bushy and stop it getting leggy.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars and clubroot, as this beauty is in the brassica family.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to replace these short-lived perennials.

items.name: Erysimum menziesii
items.growersTips:
Pop this coastal wallflower in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow your seeds shallowly, just barely covered with grit, in a cold frame during late spring.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot.
Plant alongside sea thrift and sedums in a sunny rock garden to mimic its natural dunes.
Protect the young foliage from slugs and snails during damp British spring evenings.

items.name: Erysimum insulare
items.growersTips:
Plant this coastal wallflower in extremely sharp-draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in your absolute sunniest spot to mimic its native California cliffs and boost blooms.
Avoid overwatering once established, as damp UK soil easily rots this dry-loving shrubby perennial.
Trim the flower stems back by half in late summer to keep its naturally tidy, mounded habit neat.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and snails, which love targeting its brassica-family leaves.

items.name: Erysimum mediohispanicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Spanish wallflower in grit-enriched, alkaline soil to survive wet British winters.
Cut the faded flower stems right back in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy green leaves.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing border to mimic its hot, dry native Mediterranean home.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and their caterpillars, as they love this family of plants.
Sow seeds in late spring in free-draining compost and just lightly cover them with fine vermiculite.
items.description: Erysimum mediohispanicum is a perennial short-lived monocarpic herb found in many montane regions of eastern Spain where it is distributed between 800–2,000 m above sea level and inhabits forests, scrublands, and shrublands. It occupies two main regions in the Iberian Peninsula, one in the north and the other in the south-east. Erysimum mediohispanicum may be treated as one of a group or complex of six closely related species, or as Erysimum nevadense subsp. mediohispanicum.

items.name: Erysimum nevadense
items.growersTips:
Plant this Sierra Nevada wallflower in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native hot, dry Spanish mountain home.
Trim the spent flower stems back by half in late summer to keep its neat, mounded shape for winter.
Water sparingly, only during prolonged dry spells, as this alpine beauty hates soggy root zones.
Grow it alongside creeping thymes or sedums in a raised bed or rockery to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Erysimum caboverdeanum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cape Verde wallflower in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position in your absolute sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its volcanic island origin.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to prevent rot.
Take stem cuttings in late summer as insurance because this species is short-lived in our climate.
Protect it with fleece during hard UK frosts, as it only tolerates temperatures down to freezing.

items.name: Cochlearia danica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer directly into well-drained, sandy grit to mimic UK coastal cliffs.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drenches.
Grow this salt-tolerant plant alongside sea kale or thrift in a sunny, gravel-filled container.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love targeting the tender, vitamin-C-rich spoon-shaped leaves.
Harvest the peppery leaves sparingly in winter and spring before the tiny pink flowers appear.
items.description: Cochlearia danica, or Danish scurvygrass, is a flowering plant of the genus Cochlearia in the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Noccaea fendleri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic their native alpine winter chill.
Keep watering minimal once established, only soaking them during prolonged dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using beer traps to protect the foliage.
Plant them alongside thyme or sedums in a sunny rock garden to ensure they get maximum light.
Avoid rich composts; instead, mix plenty of horticultural grit into your beds to prevent root rot.

items.name: Rytidocarpus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at 1cm depth in fertile, well-drained soil with a neutral to alkaline pH.
Protect young seedlings from cabbage white butterflies and slugs using fine insect netting.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil evenly moist, preventing premature bolting in dry spells.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter common brassica pests and improve overall crop health.
Harvest the outer leaves continuously in autumn to encourage fresh growth before the first hard frost.

items.name: Cochlearia tatrae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the UK winter cold naturally breaks their dormancy for spring growth.
Grow this alpine spoonwort in a gritty, free-draining limestone soil mix to mimic its mountain home.
Keep the soil damp with rainwater rather than tap water to match its native cool, moist rock crevices.
Position your pots in a partially shaded, north-facing spot to protect them from hot UK summer sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love targeting the tender, vitamin-C rich leaves.
items.description: Cochlearia tatrae, the Tatra scurvy-grass, is a flowering plant of the genus Cochlearia in the family Brassicaceae. The plant is endemic to and named after the Tatra Mountains, which in northern Slovakia and southern Poland.

items.name: Barbarea intermedia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep from March to August for a steady salad crop.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to stop this peppery biennial bolting early.
Watch out for flea beetles making tiny holes in the leaves, especially during dry spring spells.
Plant alongside rosemary or mint to help deter the cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs.
Grow this hardy winter cress in partial shade to keep the leaves tender and prevent bitter tastes.
items.description: Barbarea intermedia is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to northern Africa and many parts of Europe, and naturalized in some parts of Asia, Africa and Europe.

items.name: Diplotaxis tenuifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in spring just five millimetres deep in well-drained soil for quick germination.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy to stop this peppery rocket from bolting in dry spells.
Cut back the yellow flowers in summer to encourage fresh, tasty leaves and prevent self-seeding.
Grow it next to carrots or onions to naturally deter those pesky flea beetles from eating the leaves.
Protect your plants with fleece during wet UK winters to keep harvesting fresh leaves all year round.
items.description: Diplotaxis tenuifolia is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name perennial wall-rocket. It is native to Europe and western Asia, where it grows on disturbed ground and roadsides, and it can now be found throughout much of the temperate world where it has naturalized. In recent years it has increasingly been cultivated to produce salad leaves, which are marketed as wild rocket in Britain or arugula in the US. It is easily confused with garden rocket, which has similar uses.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. sabauda
items.growersTips:
Firm the soil down well with your boots before planting to stop winter winds rocking the roots.
Net your crops early with a fine mesh to keep the cabbage white butterflies and pigeons away.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving them frequent light sprinkles.
Plant them near mint or rosemary to help confuse pests, but keep them away from your tomatoes.
Sow in late spring and transplant by July so they establish before the cold UK winter sets in.

items.name: Neslia paniculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just 1cm deep directly into well-drained, alkaline soil to mimic UK chalk downs.
Water young seedlings weekly to establish, but let the soil dry out fully between sessions later.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using fine insect netting to protect the delicate young leaves.
Grow this brassica relative alongside mint or dill to naturally deter common UK cabbage pests.
Harvest the young mustard-tasting leaves before the yellow flowers bloom in midsummer for best flavor.
items.description: Neslia is a monotypic plant genus in the family Brassicaceae. The only species is Neslia paniculata (L.) Desv.

items.name: Enarthrocarpus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under fleece to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and flea beetles.
Plant seeds exactly one centimeter deep in well-drained, alkaline soil to ensure rapid germination.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-resistant roots.
Interplant with mint or sage to deter the cabbage white butterflies that plague UK brassicas.
Harvest the pods when young and green before they turn woody in the damp British autumn weather.

items.name: Sterigmostemum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under fleece to protect young shoots from unpredictable late UK spring frosts.
Grow this in well-drained, sandy loam with a neutral pH to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep a sharp lookout for flea beetles in June and use fine insect mesh to protect the young foliage.
Plant alongside radishes to help deter common pests and maximize your vegetable patch space.

items.name: Fibigia clypeata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained grit to let UK winter frosts naturally break their dormancy.
Plant this Mediterranean native in your sunniest border using poor, alkaline soil to avoid rot.
Water seedlings sparingly during damp UK springs, letting the soil dry out fully between drinks.
Leave the gorgeous, papery seed pods intact through winter to feed local birds and add structure.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the fuzzy, silvery young leaves in wet weather.

items.name: Diplotaxis muralis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to September just five millimetres deep in sunny, well-drained patches.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy to prevent this wild rocket relative from bolting too quickly.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring by covering young seedlings with a fine insect mesh.
Harvest the peppery leaves cut-and-come-again style when they reach about ten centimetres long.
Grow it next to mint or sage to help deter those pesky pests that love eating brassicas.

items.name: Boechera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining gritty compost to mimic UK winter.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two centimetres of soil are completely dry to avoid rot.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps in damp UKs.
Grow in a raised bed or rockery with added horticultural grit to survive wet British winters.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to maximise growth during short UK summer days.
items.description: Boechera (rockcress) is a genus of the family Brassicaceae. It was named after the Danish botanist Tyge W. Böcher (1909–1983), who was known for his research in alpine plants, including the mustards Draba and Boechera holboellii. According to recent molecular-based studies, Boechera is closely related to the genus Arabidopsis which also includes the widely known model plant Arabidopsis thaliana.

items.name: Eremobium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under fleece to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and flea beetles.
Grow in sandy, sharply draining soil with a neutral pH to prevent clubroot in wet UK winters.
Water sparingly at the base only during dry spells to avoid crown rot in humid summer weather.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter the cabbage white butterflies that target this brassica.
Harvest the outer leaves progressively in autumn to encourage continuous fresh growth before frost.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. ramosa
items.growersTips:
Sow Daubentons seeds indoors in March then plant out in deep, firm, alkaline soil spaced one meter apart.
Keep young plants damp but once established only water during dry spells to encourage deep roots.
Nets are essential from May to October to stop cabbage white butterflies laying eggs on the leaves.
Take stem cuttings in spring to easily propagate this perennial kale as it rarely produces seeds.
Plant mint or sage nearby to help confuse the pests that are always hunting for your brassicas.

items.name: Thlaspi perfoliatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn onto bare, chalky soil to mimic the UK's natural limestone habitats.
Keep watering minimal once established, as this hardy annual thrives in dry, well-drained gravel.
Watch out for slugs on young spring seedlings, especially during damp UK April mornings.
Leave the tiny white flowers to self-seed naturally in summer to ensure they return next spring.
Grow them alongside wild pansies or salad burnet in rockeries for a lovely native wildflower display.
items.description: Noccaea perfoliata is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is an annual native to southern, central, and southeastern Europe, North Africa, and western and central Asia from the eastern Mediterranean to the Altai, Xinjiang, and Pakistan.

items.name: Lobularia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using free-draining peat-free compost.
Water the soil at the base weekly during dry UK summers to prevent mildew on the dense foliage.
Shear back the plants by half in mid-July to stimulate a second flush of autumn flowers.
Watch for flea beetles in spring, which chew tiny holes in the leaves of this brassica family member.
Plant alongside carrots to attract hoverflies whose larvae will voraciously consume local aphids.

items.name: Lepidium monoplocoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a cold frame to protect them from unpredictable UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy, mimicking the damp riverbeds of its native habitat.
Mix plenty of grit into your heavy UK clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage this wild herb craves.
Watch out for slugs and snails in May, as they absolutely love devouring the tender young leaves.
Grow this rare pepperweed alongside mint in pots to keep its vigorous, sprawling habit contained.

items.name: Lepidium nanum
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare alpine cushion in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its Great Basin home.
Keep it in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to shield the tight foliage from persistent UK winter wet.
Water from the base or use a gravel mulch to prevent the dense cushion from rotting in damp weather.
Position your pot in full sun with maximum airflow to keep the delicate green mound compact and healthy.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to hide under the tight foliage during damp British springs.

items.name: Lepidium phlebopetalum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cover using a gritty, free-draining compost to combat UK dampness.
Water sparingly from below once established, allowing the soil to dry out to prevent root rot.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot of your patio to mimic its native hot, dry environment.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British summers, as they love the tender young leaves.
Grow this brassica relative near mint or sage to help deter common UK pests like cabbage white flies.

items.name: Brassica rapa var. perviridis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to August at a depth of one centimetre to avoid transplant shock.
Keep the soil consistently damp to prevent bolting during dry, warm UK summer spells.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring by covering your young plants with a fine insect mesh.
Grow them alongside mint or rosemary to help deter hungry pests with their strong scents.
Harvest the outer leaves first to encourage a steady, continuous supply of fresh greens.

items.name: Leavenworthia crassa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late autumn as this rare annual needs chilly UK winter temperatures to trigger growth.
Grow them in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic their natural limestone glade habitat in your garden.
Keep the soil consistently damp during winter and spring, but avoid letting them sit in soggy mud.
Protect the delicate spring flowers from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic grit barriers.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme or sedums to provide support and keep the soil cool.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. palmifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Tuscan kale seeds 1cm deep in late spring to avoid the worst of the UK's damp cold.
Firm the soil well around the roots with your boots to stop winter winds rocking the tall stems.
Drape fine netting over your plants by June to block cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Pick the tender lower leaves first in winter, leaving the top crown to keep growing through frosts.

items.name: Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera
items.growersTips:
Firmly tread down the soil before planting to stop wind rock from loosening their shallow roots.
Net your crops early to keep greedy cabbage white butterflies and woodpigeons off the tender leaves.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving them frequent light sprinkles.
Stake the tall stalks in autumn to help them survive wet, windy British winters without toppling.
Pick the lowest sprouts first from the bottom of the stem upward to encourage a continuous harvest.

items.name: Iberis gibraltarica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Gibraltar candytuft in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Tuck it into a south-facing stone wall crevice where it mimics its native limestone cliff home.
Cut back the spent flower stems by half in July to keep the mound tight and prevent leggy growth.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh, drying easterly winds with a temporary fleece wrap.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn so they get the winter chill they need to sprout.
items.description: Iberis gibraltarica, the Gibraltar candytuft, is a flowering plant of the genus Iberis and the family Brassicaceae. It is the symbol of the Upper Rock Nature Reserve in Gibraltar, but is a native of North Africa. Gibraltar is the only place in Europe where it is found growing in the wild. The candytuft grows from crevices in the limestone, and is often seen growing in abundance from the north face of the Rock of Gibraltar. Its flowers range from pale violet to almost white, and can reach up to 8 cm (3.1 in) across.

items.name: Thlaspi rotundifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in a gritty, free-draining scree mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly from below in summer, keeping the foliage dry to prevent rot in damp British air.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the delicate leaves during mild, wet spring nights.
Grow it alongside saxifrages in a raised bed or alpine trough for a stunning, natural companion.
Avoid rich soil as too many nutrients make this gravel-loving plant grow leggy and lose its shape.

items.name: Aethionema saxatile
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun next to limestone rock garden companions like Campanula carpatica.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in cold frames during early spring.
Cut back the spent flowering stems by half in late summer to maintain a compact, bushy habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic ferrous phosphate pellets.

items.name: Halimolobos jaegeri
items.growersTips:
Try sowing these seeds in early spring under a cold frame to protect them from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering gently at the base to avoid rot.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, using fine insect mesh to keep these pests off the foliage.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to ensure the sharp drainage this plant loves.
Grow them alongside radishes to help deter pests and make the most of your veg plot space.

items.name: Hornungia alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply drained, gritty soil or scree to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to allow natural winter cold stratifying.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the grit mulch around the crown bone dry.
Shear back lightly by half after spring flowering to maintain a tight, cushion-like growth habit.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK gardens.
items.description: Hornungia alpina is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to the mountains of Southern and Central Europe, as far south as northern Spain, central Italy and North Macedonia , and is sometimes grown as an ornamental plant in gardens .

items.name: Physaria thamnophila
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic their native dry habitat.
Keep watering minimal, letting the soil dry out fully between drinks to prevent any root rot.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot possible, or use a cold frame to shield them from UK rain.
Protect the young foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the pot rims.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than the open ground to easily manage winter wet and drainage.

items.name: Physaria tumulosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare chalk-loving gem in a raised bed filled with gritty, alkaline limestone chippings.
Keep watering to a minimum, mimicking dry limestone cliffs by only soaking them during dry spells.
Protect the crown from wet winter rot by placing a glass cloche over the plant from November to March.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the low-growing rosettes in damp spring.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to let the natural UK winter chill trigger germination.

items.name: Bunias orientalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just 1cm deep in a sunny spot, as Turkish rocket loves UK sunshine to thrive.
Water deeply once a week during dry English summers to help its massive taproot establish quickly.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and slugs, which love chewing these mustard-family leaves.
Cut back the flowering stems in July to stop this vigorous self-seeder from taking over your plot.
Plant it next to fruit trees as a dynamic accumulator that brings up nutrients from deep soil.
items.description:
Bunias orientalis, the Turkish wartycabbage, warty-cabbage, hill mustard, or Turkish rocket, is an edible wild plant species in the genus Bunias.
It is classified as an invasive neophyte in most of Middle Europe and parts of North America.

items.name: Braya humilis
items.growersTips:
Sow Braya humilis seeds in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic their cold alpine habitat.
Water these little plants from below to keep their crowns dry and prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, as they love to devour the tender, low-growing foliage.
Grow them in a raised bed or alpine trough to ensure they get the sharp drainage they absolutely need.
Plant them alongside dwarf saxifrages to create a beautiful, thrive-together alpine community.

items.name: Polyctenium fremontii
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a super-gritty alpine mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, mimicking its natural Great Basin arid cycle.
Keep it in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield it from relentless British rain.
Never prune this slow grower; just gently tease away any dead foliage in late spring.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into the sunniest spot in your garden.
items.description: Polyctenium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It contains a single species, Polyctenium fremontii, the desert combleaf, a small and compact plant native to the northern Great Basin region of the Western United States. The plants are known by the common name combleaf, owing to the resemblance of their deeply lobed leaves to a comb. It grows in sagebrush shrub steppe in northeastern California, southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho, and northwestern Nevada.

items.name: Noccaea perfoliata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn directly into gritty, well-drained soil to mimic UK chalk downs.
Keep watering minimal once established, only dampening the soil during unusually dry spring spells.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and slugs, as this crucifer family plant is a tasty snack.
Do not prune this annual, but let it self-seed naturally in your gravel paths for next spring.
Grow it alongside wild marjoram or thyme which thrive in the same poor, alkaline UK soils.

items.name: Braya longii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare northern rock-cress in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native limestone barrens.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only when the top inch dries out to prevent root rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill can trigger germination.
Watch out for slugs and snails, as they love to devour the delicate rosettes in damp UK weather.
Grow them in containers so you can move them under glass to protect against excessive winter rain.

items.name: Braya pilosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to let the UK winter chill naturally break their dormancy.
Plant this rare arctic beauty in very gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native limestone home.
Water sparingly from below to keep the crown dry and prevent rot during damp British winters.
Protect the delicate white flowers from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around pots.
Grow them in terracotta alpine pans so you can move them under glass to shelter from heavy rain.
items.description: Braya pilosa is a long-lived perennial flowering plant of the mustard family known by the common name hairy braya. It was first found by Sir John Richardson in 1826 during an expedition in search of the Northwest Passage. It wasn't found for 154 years, between 1850 and 2004.

items.name: Streptanthus albidus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic native scree.
Keep them in a cold frame to protect the young roots from wet UK winters and prevent rotting.
Water sparingly from below, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid damp-off.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the tender young leaves during damp British spring nights.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot in your garden to help these California natives thrive.
items.description: Streptanthus glandulosus subsp. albidus is a subspecies of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name Metcalf Canyon jewelflower. It is endemic to California, where it is known only from the Central Coast Ranges in the San Francisco Bay Area. It grows in open areas such as grasslands, often on serpentine soils.

items.name: Streptanthus bracteatus
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare bracted jewelflower seeds in autumn to let UK winter cold naturally break dormancy.
Grow them in sharply draining, gritty limestone soil to mimic their native Texas Edwards Plateau.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty compost dry out completely between soakings.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot possible to cope with cool, damp UK summer afternoons.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love chewing the delicate flowering stems in damp spring weather.

items.name: Streptanthus diversifolius
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in early spring under glass to protect these delicate annuals from late UK frosts.
Plant them in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water sparingly around the base only when the top inch of soil feels dry to mimic their dry habitat.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the tender young leaves of this annual jewel.
Grow them alongside hardy succulents or thyme in sunny gravel beds to match their dry soil needs.
items.description: Streptanthus diversifolius is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name variableleaf jewelflower, or varied-leaved jewelflower. It is endemic to California, where it is limited to the Sierra Nevada foothills. It is a resident of woodlands and other foothill habitat. It is an annual herb producing a hairless, waxy stem up to a meter tall. The basal leaves are variable in shape and are often divided into narrow, threadlike segments. Leaves higher on the stem are also variable, having round to lance-shaped blades which clasp the stem at their bases. Flowers occur

items.name: Streptanthus callistus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Water the young plants at the base twice a week to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails which love to munch on the tender young leaves in spring.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into your clay soil to ensure the roots get the drainage they need.
Grow them alongside carrots or onions to help deter common pests naturally in your veg patch.

items.name: Rapistrum perenne
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil at a shallow depth of five millimetres.
Grow in full sun and avoid watering once established, as this plant thrives in dry UK soils.
Cut back the flowering stems to the base in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Check regularly for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles in damp UK springs.
Plant alongside drought-tolerant UK natives like wild marjoram to create a resilient gravel garden.

items.name: Physaria bellii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic their native rocky limestone soil.
Keep pots in a cold frame over winter to give them the cold period they need to germinate in spring.
Water sparingly from below once established, as this alpine native easily rots in damp UK winters.
Plant them alongside thyme or sedums in a sunny, raised scree bed to ensure excellent drainage.
Protect the young silvery foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps during wet spring nights.

items.name: Brassica napus rapifera
items.growersTips:
Sow Swede seeds direct in June at a depth of one centimetre to avoid transplant shock in dry soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist during August and September to prevent your Swedes from splitting.
Net your crop early with fine mesh to protect the young leaves from hungry UK cabbage white flies.
Dust wood ash around the base of the plants to deter slugs and snails during wet British summers.
Leave your Swedes in the ground until after the first autumn frosts to sweeten up their flavour.

items.name: Aethionema grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full south-facing sun, tucked into a raised bed, rockery, or gravel garden crevice.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the crown dry to mimic alpine conditions.
Prune back by half immediately after summer flowering to keep the plant compact and prevent legginess.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers in damp weather.

items.name: Erucastrum nasturtiifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just five millimetres deep in free-draining soil to mimic UK wayside habitats.
This wild brassica loves a sunny spot in poor, alkaline soil, so add lime if your garden is acidic.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars in summer; use fine netting to protect the peppery leaves.
Water young plants weekly during dry spells, but let established ones dry out to prevent root rot.
Grow it alongside mint or sage to help deter those pesky flea beetles from chewing the foliage.

items.name: Crambe maritima
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep gritty free-draining soil to mimic UK shingle beaches and prevent winter root rot.
Sow seeds outdoors in autumn at 2cm depth so winter cold naturally breaks their dormancy.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers.
Force early tender stems in January by covering the crown with a dark bucket or forcing pot.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of blue-green foliage.
items.description: Crambe maritima, common name sea kale, seakale or crambe, is a species of halophytic (salt-tolerant) flowering plant in the genus Crambe of the family Brassicaceae. It grows wild along the coasts of mainland Europe and the British Isles.

items.name: Succowia balearica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres directly into well-drained, gritty soil.
Grow this Mediterranean annual in full sun to mimic its native Balearic light levels in the UK.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Harvest the edible leaves before the plant produces its distinctive spiny, spherical seed pods.
items.description: Succowia is a monotypic genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It only contains one known species, Succowia balearica (L.) Medik.

items.name: Lepidium amissum
items.growersTips:
This extinct New Zealand herb needs sandy, free-draining soil to mimic its coastal home.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under a cold frame to protect them from damp UK frosts.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out to prevent root rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails, which love eating the tender young leaves in spring.
Grow this in a sunny container so you can move it indoors during wet winter months.

items.name: Crambe cordifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant taproots deeply in autumn or spring to accommodate their massive, carrot-like root systems.
Stake the giant flowering stems early in May to prevent heavy summer winds from snapping them.
Apply a thick layer of well-rotted manure in late winter to satisfy this heavy feeder's appetite.
Watch out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and slugs which target this brassica family giant.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the ground in August to encourage fresh basal foliage.

items.name: Aethionema retsina
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Plant in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Greek habitat and ensure compact flowering cushions
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established as this alpine dislikes wet foliage
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate new shoots first begin to emerge
Trim back lightly by one third after summer flowering to maintain a tight habit and prevent legginess

items.name: Physaria filiformis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare yellow mustard in very shallow, gritty soil to mimic its natural limestone glades.
Give it a sunny, sheltered spot in your UK garden to protect the delicate winter rosette from rot.
Water very sparingly only when the top inch of gritty compost is bone dry to prevent root damage.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the tender young flowering stems.
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late summer so they get the winter cold they need to germinate.

items.name: Physaria globosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic their native limestone soils.
Keep these little brassicas safe from winter wet by placing pot-grown plants under a cold frame.
Watch out for slugs and snails early in spring, as they love to munch on the young rosettes.
Water sparingly around the base, only when the top few centimetres of soil feel completely dry.
Plant them alongside dwarf campanulas or saxifrages in a sunny, raised rock garden or scree bed.

items.name: Physaria didymocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine gem in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters.
Keep watering to a minimum, only soaking the soil when it has dried out completely.
Protect the grey-green rosettes from slugs and snails during damp British spring nights.
Grow this brassica family beauty in a raised bed or alpine trough to ensure perfect drainage.
Position your pots in full sun to mimic its native dry, rocky calcareous hillsides.

items.name: Physaria chambersii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic their native dry soils.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the gritty soil dry out completely between soakings.
Protect these alpine beauties from wet UK winters by using a rain shelter or cold frame.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the low-growing rosettes in damp weather.
Grow them in terracotta pots to help the roots breathe and prevent waterlogging in rainy areas.

items.name: Physaria obcordata
items.growersTips:
Tuck seeds just half a centimetre deep in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic their rocky home.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this alpine dislikes wet UK winters.
Protect the crown from rot by mulching with horticultural grit rather than damp bark or compost.
Grow this rare beauty in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a cold frame during wet spells.
Watch out for slugs in spring, as they love to munch the tender new rosettes in damp British weather.

items.name: Zilla spinosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to mimic its native desert heat and prevent winter rot
Use a potting mix of three parts coarse grit to one part loam to ensure the rapid drainage it needs
Water only when the soil is completely dry then drench thoroughly and never let the pot sit in water
Position in the absolute brightest south-facing spot possible to maximise scarce UK summer sunlight
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
items.description: Zilla is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Zilla spinosa, that grows in the Sahara-Arabian deserts of northern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula.

items.name: Streptanthella longirostris
items.growersTips:
Sow these longbeak streptanthella seeds shallowly in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam.
Keep soil barely damp to mimic its dry native habitat, as UK dampness quickly rots the taproot.
Grow this wild mustard relative under a cold frame or cloche to shield it from heavy UK autumn rain.
Watch out for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which love targeting this brassica family member.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter pests and match its preference for dry, sunny spots.
items.description: Streptanthella is a genus of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Streptanthella longirostris, which is known by the common name longbeak streptanthella, or simply streptanthella. It is native to western North America, where it occurs throughout the western United States and the northwestern states of Mexico. It grows in many types of habitat, including deserts, sagebrush, foothill woodlands, sandy flats, chaparral, and scrubby canyons.

items.name: Hornungia petraea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on well-drained gravelly soil to mimic UK limestone habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this winter annual dislikes damp summer soil.
Grow alongside limestone lovers like wild thyme to provide the sharp drainage and low competition.
Leave seed heads intact in late spring to allow natural self-seeding before the plant dies back.
Clear surrounding weeds in autumn to give the tiny overwintering rosettes enough light to grow.

items.name: Chorispora tenella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring just 5mm deep to catch the cool, damp UK weather this plant loves.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent this fast grower from bolting to seed.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, using fine insect mesh to protect the tender young leaves.
Grow this mustard relative alongside radishes as a trap crop to draw pests away from your mains.
Harvest the peppery leaves when young and small, before the purple flowers appear and turn them bitter.

items.name: Physaria congesta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to mimic the cold winter stratification this alpine needs.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining compost mix with added limestone chippings to match its alkaline origin.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this hardy plant hates winter wet and rot.
Top-dress your pots with a thick layer of grit to keep the low foliage off wet winter soil.
Protect the delicate yellow spring blooms from slugs using beer traps or pet-friendly wool pellets.

items.name: Ionopsidium acaule
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the soil surface in late summer so autumn rain triggers quick germination.
Give this little annual a gritty compost mix in a shady UK crevice where it can happily self-seed.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during dry spring spells to prolong those lilac winter blooms.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK winters, as they love devouring the tender young leaves.
Plant them alongside winter pansies or early bulbs to fill bare gaps with a low carpet of flowers.

items.name: Brassica juncea subsp. tsatsai
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer to avoid the summer heat and stop this spicy mustard bolting in UK rain.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy to prevent the leaves from getting too bitter to eat.
Cover your crop with fine insect netting early on to block flea beetles and hungry pigeons.
Mix plenty of well-rotted compost into your soil beforehand to feed this leafy green's rapid growth.
Harvest the outer leaves first to keep the plant producing fresh new growth right through autumn.

items.name: Coincya monensis subsp. monensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring 5mm deep in well-drained, sandy soil to mimic its native UK coastal habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully between waterings.
Protect young leaves from cabbage white butterflies and slugs using fine mesh netting in summer.
Grow in full sun and avoid acidic soils by adding lime to reach a neutral to alkaline pH of 7.0.
Do not over-fertilize this wild cabbage relative, as rich soil causes floppy, weak growth.
items.description: Coincya monensis subsp. monensis, the Isle of Man cabbage, is a species of plant in the family Brassicaceae that is found in coastal habitats on the west of the island of Great Britain and around the coasts of the Isle of Man.

items.name: Eruca vesicaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from March to September at a shallow depth of one centimetre to avoid taproot damage.
Water plants consistently at the base in summer to prevent premature bolting caused by dry UK soil.
Cover young crops with fine insect mesh to block flea beetles, a major pest in British gardens.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter pests and mask the peppery scent of the foliage.
Harvest the outer leaves regularly when young to encourage continuous growth and milder flavour.
items.description: Eruca vesicaria is a species of Eruca native to Spain, Morocco, and Algeria. Some botanists consider Eruca vesicaria and E. sativa (arugula) to be conspecific. However, they are different in many morphological aspects such as sepal persistence, silique shape, and habit. Most importantly, they do not hybridize freely with each other as there is partial reproductive isolation between them. Plants of the World Online has accepted them as two distinct species.

items.name: Cordylocarpus muricatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at 1cm depth in well-drained, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot in UK gardens.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil moist but not waterlogged, avoiding powdery mildew.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in damp weather.
Cover plants with fine insect netting to exclude cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into the bed a month before planting to provide essential nitrogen.
items.description: Cordylocarpus is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Cordylocarpus muricatus, which is native to Algeria and Morocco.

items.name: Calepina irregularis
items.growersTips:
Sow these white-flowered salad greens in early autumn to match the cool, damp UK winter growing cycle.
Grow them in moist, alkaline clay soils, adding garden lime if your UK plot is naturally acidic.
Space seedlings ten centimetres apart in partial shade to stop the leaves from turning too bitter.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and use fine netting to protect the foliage from caterpillars.
Harvest the peppery outer leaves continuously before the white flowers appear in early spring.

items.name: Physaria fendleri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in spring using a free-draining sandy compost.
Keep this desert native dry by watering only when the top five centimetres of soil is dusty dry.
Grow it in your sunniest gravel garden or a terracotta pot to mimic its dry Colorado home climate.
Protect the crown from wet UK winters by mulching with grit rather than moisture-holding bark.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around pots.

items.name: Erucastrum gallicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just five millimetres deep into any poor, well-drained soil to mimic UK roadsides.
Water young seedlings weekly until established, then leave them to brave the British rain on their own.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer by checking the leaves for tiny, characteristic shot-holes.
Grow this wild mustard alongside mint to help deter the cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs.
Snip off the yellow flower heads before they set seed in late summer to stop it taking over your plot.

items.name: Camelina sativa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at about one centimetre deep in April once the cold UK spring soil warms up.
Keep the soil damp until they sprout, then only water during prolonged dry British summer spells.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, using fine mesh nets to protect the young green leaves.
Mix in some compost to ensure your soil drains well, as this crop hates sitting in soggy clay.
Harvest the seed pods in late August once they turn a golden-brown colour and feel dry to touch.
items.description: Camelina sativa is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae usually known as camelina, gold-of-pleasure, or false flax, but also occasionally as wild flax, linseed dodder, German sesame, or Siberian oilseed. It is native to Europe and areas of Central Asia, but cultivated as an oilseed crop mainly in Europe and in North America. It is not related to true flax, which is in the family Linaceae.

items.name: Raphanus sativus subsp. acanthiformis
items.growersTips:
Sow your mooli seeds directly in late summer to stop them bolting in the cooler UK autumn weather.
Sow seeds exactly two centimetres deep in stone-free, loose soil so the long white roots grow straight.
Water them deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage the taproots to push downward.
Cover your crop with fine insect mesh immediately after sowing to block greedy UK cabbage root flies.
Harvest your mooli before the first hard winter frost of the year turns the crunchy flesh to mush.

items.name: Streptanthus glandulosus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under cover, barely pressing them into gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep young plants on the dry side to mimic their native scrubland, watering only when soil is dry.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, as they love targeting the tender young foliage.
Plant them alongside drought-tolerant UK natives like wild thyme to help replicate their dry habitat.
Avoid rich garden composts; instead, mix in plenty of horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
items.description: Streptanthus glandulosus is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name bristly jewelflower. It is native to California and southwestern Oregon, where it grows in many types of habitat, including grassland, chaparral, and woodlands. Genetic and other analyses indicate that it is a species complex with ten subspecies which evolved as populations were isolated from each other. The complex includes subspecies previously considered separate species, such as the rare Tiburon jewelflower endemic to the San Francisco Bay Area. Plants in the complex are variable. In gen

items.name: Cakile edentula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring directly into extremely sandy, free-draining soil to mimic UK beaches.
Water sparingly once established, letting the sandy substrate dry out completely between pours.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps during damp UK spring nights.
Plant alongside sea kale or samphire in a sunny, wind-exposed spot for a coastal veggie bed.
Harvest the peppery leaves sparingly before the plant flowers in midsummer to keep them tasty.

items.name: Camelina alyssum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in April when soil warms, just five millimetres deep to get quick germination.
Give them a sunny, well-drained spot and avoid heavy clay by mixing in plenty of grit first.
Water gently once a week during dry spells, keeping the soil damp but never soggy or waterlogged.
Keep a sharp eye out for flea beetles in spring, using fine insect mesh to protect young leaves.
Harvest the seed pods in late summer once they turn golden brown but before they split open.

items.name: Muricaria prostrata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres into free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil are completely dry.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and cabbage white caterpillars using fine insect netting.
Grow in full sun in a south-facing border or container to mimic its native Mediterranean light.
In wet UK winters move container-grown plants under a cold frame to protect roots from waterlogging.

items.name: Crambe abyssinica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late April at a depth of 1.5cm once the UK spring soil has warmed up.
Grow in free-draining, low-nitrogen soil to prevent excessive leaf growth at the expense of seeds.
Water young plants weekly during dry spells, but let established plants rely on natural UK rainfall.
Net the crop early in summer to protect the young brassica foliage from cabbage white butterflies.
Harvest the seed pods in late August once they turn a dry golden-brown color before autumn rains.

items.name: Physaria parvula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic their rocky wild home.
Protect these alpine beauties from wet UK winters by placing a layer of gravel around the collar.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil dries out to prevent the crown from rotting away.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp British springs as they love the tender young foliage.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame during heavy downpours.

items.name: Orychophragmus violaceus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of 2mm in late summer for natural winter vernalisation in UK soils.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland edge habitat in the UK.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to prevent premature bolting and prolong the purple blooms.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars in summer and net plants to protect the foliage.
Plant alongside early spring bulbs like daffodils to mask their fading foliage as this plant grows.

items.name: Camelina microcarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in early spring to catch the cool UK rains for sprouting.
Keep soil barely damp as this little gold-of-pleasure plant hates soggy roots in our wet winters.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, so pop a fine mesh cover over your young plants to protect them.
Grow them alongside carrots or onions to help deter the pests that love this brassica family member.
Harvest the seed pods when they turn a lovely golden brown, just before our autumn damp sets in.

items.name: Aurinia saxatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full, baking sun next to south-facing stone walls or in gravel scree beds.
Cut back by half immediately after spring flowering to keep the mound compact and neat.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer rather than sowing seeds in wet soil.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which attack this brassica.
items.description: Aurinia saxatilis is an ornamental plant native to Asia and Europe.

items.name: Psychine stylosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under fleece to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and slugs.
Grow in well-drained, alkaline soil, adding grit and lime to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-resistant roots.
Net the plants from May to September to exclude cabbage white butterflies and prevent caterpillar havoc.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles, which frequently target this brassica family member.
items.description: Psychine is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Psychine stylosa, which is native to Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia.

items.name: Cakile maritima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in sandy, well-drained soil in April, just a centimetre deep, on a sunny border.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, as this seaside native thrives on dry, salty neglect.
Watch out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars, as this plant is in the brassica family.
Harvest the peppery young leaves and seed pods regularly in summer to keep the plant bushier.
Mix plenty of grit and horticultural sand into your soil to mimic its natural UK shingle habitat.

items.name: Cardamine occulta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of two millimetres in damp compost to match UK winter stratification.
Water the soil consistently to keep it moist but never waterlogged during dry spring spells.
Hand-weed surrounding soil early in spring before this invasive brassica flings its seeds.
Grow it in partial shade alongside damp-loving companion plants like hostas and astilbes.
Watch for the cabbage white butterfly caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.

items.name: Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus
items.growersTips:
Sow your mooli seeds directly from mid-July to August so they do not bolt in the midsummer heat.
Prep your soil by digging deep and removing stones so the long roots can grow straight and true.
Water them deeply and consistently to prevent the roots from splitting and becoming woody to eat.
Keep a sharp eye out for flea beetles and cover your young plants with fine insect netting.
Harvest them before the first hard winter frost, usually around October, to stop them rotting.

items.name: Armoracia sisymbrioides
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in deep fertile soil to allow the taproot to establish during the wet UK winter.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent the root from becoming woody and bitter.
Grow in large heavy containers to prevent this vigorous Brassicaceae root from invading your lawn.
Watch for cabbage white caterpillars and use fine insect netting to protect the foliage in summer.
Harvest roots in late autumn after the first UK frost has concentrated the pungent mustard oils.

items.name: Aethionema armenum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining, grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to mimic its native dry alpine habitat.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in July to maintain a compact, bushy shrub habit.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp spring weather when tender new shoots first emerge.

items.name: Sibaropsis
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare seeds indoors in early April to protect the young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Plant them out in late May in well-drained, sandy loam enriched with plenty of organic compost.
Space your plants thirty centimetres apart in a sunny, sheltered spot to maximise their growth.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering them deeply at the base twice a week.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British summers by using beer traps around your crop.

items.name: Thelypodiopsis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of 5mm in well-drained, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not soggy, avoiding overhead dampness.
Protect young brassica foliage from cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Apply garden lime to UK acidic soils before planting to achieve the preferred pH of 6.5 to 7.5.
Grow alongside mint or sage to help deter common UK brassica pests like aphids and flea beetles.

items.name: Polypsecadium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under fleece to protect young brassica foliage from late UK frosts.
Grow in firm, moisture-retentive, alkaline soil incorporated with well-rotted manure beforehand.
Net the crop securely from May to September to exclude cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Apply garden lime to the bed before planting to raise soil pH above 6.5 and prevent clubroot disease.

items.name: Hesperidanthus
items.growersTips:
Sow these hardy winter greens in August to ensure they establish before the cold UK damp sets in.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent the taproots from splitting.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies in autumn and use fine netting to protect the foliage.
Grow them alongside mint or sage to help deter those persistent UK garden slugs and snails.
