Harvest the outer leaves gradually in winter to encourage fresh, tender growth through spring.

items.name: Ptilotrichum
items.growersTips:
Pop this little alpine in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Tuck it into a sunny rockery or raised bed where it can soak up every bit of British sunshine.
Water your young plants weekly until established, then leave them to thrive on natural rainfall.
Give it a light haircut with shears right after flowering to keep its neat, cushion-like shape.
Watch out for slugs in damp spring weather, protecting the tender new growth with organic grit.

items.name: Stenopetalum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm in free-draining sandy loam to prevent winter waterlogging.
Water sparingly at the base once established to avoid crown rot in damp UK summer conditions.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and flea beetles using fine mesh netting or organic grit barriers.
Grow in full sun and shelter from cold winds using a south-facing wall to mimic its native warmth.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils before planting to ensure the rapid drainage this plant needs.

items.name: Menkea
items.growersTips:
Sow your menkea seeds indoors in early April to protect the young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Grow this mustard-family veggie in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil to prevent clubroot issues.
Water the base of your menkea plants deeply once a week rather than giving them daily light sprinkles.
Keep a close eye out for flea beetles in June and use fine insect mesh to protect the tender leaves.
Plant menkea alongside companion herbs like dill or mint to naturally deter common garden pests.

items.name: Warea
items.growersTips:
Sow Warea seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres in well-drained, alkaline UK soil.
Water young seedlings weekly at the base, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged in wet winters.
Protect young Brassicaceae shoots from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Grow Warea alongside mint or sage to help deter common UK garden pests naturally without chemicals.
In late autumn, clear away dead foliage to prevent clubroot fungal spores from overwintering in soil.

items.name: Sisymbrium erysimoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in early spring once the UK frosts have passed.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent this wild mustard from bolting early.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using fine insect mesh to protect the young, tender leaves.
Grow this fast crop alongside mint or rosemary to help deter common cabbage white butterflies.
Harvest the peppery leaves frequently from the outside to encourage continuous fresh green growth.

items.name: Erysimum arenicola
items.growersTips:
Plant this sand-loving wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in your sunniest border or a raised bed to mimic its natural coastal habitat.
Clip the faded flower stems back in July to keep the plant compact and prevent it getting leggy.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp British April weather.
Grow it alongside alpine pinks or sedums in a rockery where its roots won't sit in soggy soil.

items.name: Erysimum cazorlense
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cazorla wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Place it in your garden's brightest, most sun-drenched spot to mimic its native Spanish cliffs.
Water sparingly once established, only drenching the soil during prolonged dry UK summer spells.
Trim back the spent flower stems in late summer to keep your plant bushy and prevent leggy growth.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape.

items.name: Erysimum collinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial wallflower in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Trim the stems back by half after flowering in July to prevent the plant from becoming woody.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry, rocky habitat.
Avoid watering once established, as damp soil is the quickest way to kill this drought-lover.
Take softwood cuttings in summer to easily propagate and replace these short-lived beauties.

items.name: Thelypodieae
items.growersTips:
Sow your wasabi seeds in autumn using a gritty, wet compost mix kept in deep shade to mimic streams.
Grow your land cress in moist, nitrogen-rich soil under fleece to stop flea beetles in spring.
Plant sea kale crowns ten centimetres deep in sandy soil, then cover with a bucket to blanch them.
Water your winter radish crops consistently at the base to stop the roots from splitting open.
Keep your cabbage family crops netted from July to October to block the hungry cabbage white butterfly.

items.name: Rorippa gigantea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a moisture-retentive compost.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged to mimic its natural wet woodland habitat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Grow alongside water-loving companion plants like native ferns and marsh marigolds in partial shade.
Clear away the dying annual foliage in late autumn to prevent rot and encourage self-seeding.

items.name: Rorippa sessiliflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a moist seed compost under glass
Keep the soil constantly wet or boggy to mimic its natural UK riverbank and wetland habitat
Grow in full sun to partial shade in acidic to neutral clay soil to ensure rapid leaf development
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member
Harvest the peppery leaves continuously before the yellow flowers appear in midsummer to stop seeding

items.name: Pachyphragma macrophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp shade under deciduous trees where autumn leaves naturally mimic its woodland habitat
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chill to germinate in UK climates
Divide congested clumps immediately after the white spring flowers fade to maintain plant vigour
Keep soil consistently moist during dry UK summers but ensure good drainage to prevent winter rot
Pair with hostas and ferns to cover the bare ground when those companion plants die back in winter
items.description: Pachyphragma is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Pachyphragma macrophyllum, a perennial or rhizomatous geophyte native to eastern Turkey and the Caucasus.

items.name: Brassica
items.growersTips:
Firm the soil thoroughly by treading before planting to prevent wind rock in wet UK winters.
Cover crops with ultra-fine insect netting immediately after planting to block cabbage root fly.
Apply garden lime in autumn to raise soil pH above 6.8 to prevent the devastating clubroot fungus.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Plant companion nasturtiums nearby to act as a trap crop for hungry large and small white butterflies.
items.description: Brassica is a genus of plants in the cabbage and mustard family (Brassicaceae). The members of the genus are informally known as cruciferous vegetables, cabbages, mustard plants, or simply brassicas. Crops from this genus are sometimes called cole crops—derived from the Latin caulis, denoting the stem or stalk of a plant.

items.name: Raphanus raphanistrum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in well-drained UK soil at a depth of 1.5cm from March to August for continuous harvests.
Water consistently at the base twice a week to prevent the roots from splitting or becoming woody.
Net crops early in spring to protect against cabbage white butterflies and flea beetle damage.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy UK clay soils before planting to prevent root fanging.
Grow alongside mint or rosemary to deter common Brassicaceae pests like the cabbage root fly.
items.description: Raphanus raphanistrum, also known as wild radish, white charlock or jointed charlock, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. The species is native to western Asia, Europe and parts of Northern Africa. It has been introduced into most parts of the world and is regarded as a habitat threatening invasive species in many areas, for example, Australia. It spreads rapidly and is often found growing on roadsides or in other places where the ground has been disturbed. The cultivated radish, widely used as a root vegetable, is sometimes considered to be one of its subspecies as Raphanus rapha

items.name: Tropidocarpum californicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late frost damage.
Grow in well-drained, gritty soil with neutral pH to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of soil are completely dry.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.
Position in full sun to maximise warmth and mimic its native dry Californian habitat.

items.name: Rytidocarpus moricandioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cloches to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and slugs.
Grow in fertile, well-drained alkaline soil, adding garden lime if your UK garden has acidic soil.
Net plants securely from transplanting onwards to exclude cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed.
Interplant with mint or sage to help deter flea beetles, which heavily target Brassicaceae crops.
items.description: Rytidocarpus is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Rytidocarpus moricandioides, which is endemic to Morocco.

items.name: Lunaria annua
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late spring at a depth of six millimetres for naturalised growth.
Water seedlings weekly during dry UK summer spells to establish strong roots before winter dormancy.
Watch for caterpillars of the small white butterfly and protect young foliage with fine netting.
Cut stems at the base in late August once seed pods turn brown and papery to dry them indoors.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic their natural British woodland edge habitat.
items.description: Lunaria annua, commonly called honesty or annual honesty, is a species of flowering plant in the cabbage and mustard family Brassicaceae. It is native to southern Europe, and cultivated throughout the temperate world.

items.name: Coincya
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1cm in free-draining sandy soil to mimic UK coastal habitats.
Protect young plants from cabbage white butterflies and slugs using fine insect netting.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Grow alongside mint or sage to help deter common Brassicaceae pests in your vegetable plot.
Avoid waterlogged winter clay by planting in raised beds or incorporating grit before sowing.

items.name: Sinapis
items.growersTips:
Sow Sinapis alba seeds directly from March to September at a depth of one centimetre in firm soil.
Grow mustard as a quick green manure to dig into clay soil before it flowers in autumn.
Watch for flea beetles in dry spring weather by using yellow sticky traps near the young seedlings.
Water the crop consistently at the base to prevent premature bolting during dry UK summer spells.
Interplant Sinapis with potatoes to help suppress soil-borne pests and wireworms naturally.
items.description:
Sinapis is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. As of July 2025, three species are accepted by Plants of the World Online:Sinapis alba L. – white mustard, formerly Brassica alba
Sinapis flexuosa Poir.
Sinapis pubescens L.

items.name: Dimorphocarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow these quirky mustard-family seeds indoors in March to beat the chilly UK spring soil.
Plant them out in May in a sunny spot with sandy, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, watering only at the base during dry summer spells.
Watch out for flea beetles in June; use fine insect mesh to protect the young, tender leaves.
Gently harvest the unique twin-podded seed crops in late autumn once they turn completely dry.

items.name: Sibara
items.growersTips:
Sow sibara seeds shallowly in early spring under a cloche to protect them from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy to prevent this peppery salad leaf from bolting.
Watch out for flea beetles in June by using yellow sticky traps and fine insect mesh over beds.
Grow sibara alongside radishes and spring onions to naturally deter common UK vegetable pests.
Harvest the outer leaves continuously from May to October to encourage fresh, tender new growth.

items.name: Thysanocarpus
items.growersTips:
Sow fringepod seeds shallowly in autumn to mimic the cool UK winter wetness they need to germinate.
Plant these dainty annuals in sandy, well-drained soil to prevent root rot during soggy UK springs.
Position them next to low-growing rockery herbs like thyme to give their delicate stems wind shelter.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty soil dry out fully between light soakings.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using organic grit barriers to protect the tiny leaves.

items.name: Moricandia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in spring using free-draining grit-amended compost.
Grow in full sun and alkaline soil to mimic Mediterranean cliffs, adding lime to acidic UK soils.
Protect young plants from slugs and cabbage white butterflies using fine netting or organic bait.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Overwinter container-grown plants in a cold greenhouse to protect them from excessive winter wet.

items.name: Streptanthus carinatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late summer outdoors so they overwinter as rosettes to flower the following spring.
Grow them in gritty, free-draining soil with added lime to mimic their natural limestone habitat.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as these plants hate sitting in winter wet.
Protect young winter rosettes from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Plant them alongside native UK rockery plants like Sedums to help support local pollinators.
items.description: Streptanthus carinatus, the lyreleaf jewelflower, is an annual to biennial plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae) found in the Arizona Upland of the Sonoran Desert. Subspecies S. carinatus arizonicus has white to cream colored flowers in its western range, becoming strongly yellow eastward. Subspecies S. carinatus carinatus has purple flowers.

items.name: Rorippa aquatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this semi-aquatic plant in a shallow pond margin with the crown submerged under 5cm of water.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet, muddy ericaceous soil.
Keep containerized plants in a water-filled tray to mimic UK wetland conditions and prevent drying.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars in summer, as they target this brassica.
Divide the root clumps every three years in March to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding.

items.name: Hirschfeldia incana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or spring just below the soil surface in poor, well-drained chalky or sandy soil.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK spells, then leave established plants to survive on rainfall.
Cut back the tough flowering stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your borders.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles which target this brassica family member.
Grow alongside rosemary or thyme in sunny, dry gravel gardens to mimic its natural maritime habitat.
items.description: Hirschfeldia incana is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by many common names, including shortpod mustard, buchanweed, hoary mustard and Mediterranean mustard. It is the only species in the monotypic genus Hirschfeldia, which is closely related to Brassica. The species is native to the Mediterranean Basin but it can be found in many parts of the world as an introduced species and often a very abundant noxious weed. This mustard is very similar in appearance to black mustard, but is generally shorter. It forms a wide basal rosette of lobed leaves which lie flat on the gro

items.name: Arabidopsis lyrata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the soil surface in spring, as they need light to germinate in our UK climate.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering gently from the base to avoid washing tiny seeds away.
Plant them in gritty, free-draining alkaline soil to mimic their natural British limestone habitat.
Watch out for hungry slugs and snails in damp weather, as they love to devour the delicate rosettes.
Grow them alongside wild thyme or stonecrop in a sunny rockery to help suppress aggressive weeds.

items.name: Raphanus sativus var. niger
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds from July to August so they mature in the cool autumn and do not bolt in the summer heat.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart to give these large, heavy roots room to swell up.
Water deeply once a week to keep the soil damp, which stops the roots from splitting and woody flesh.
Throw a fine mesh net over them immediately after sowing to block the pesky UK cabbage root fly.
Leave them in the cold winter ground and dig them up as you need them, they love a frost.

items.name: Thelypodium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under cover to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and damp.
Grow them in fast-draining, alkaline soil to mimic their native dry, rocky western habitats.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in our wet climate.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, using fine insect mesh to protect the tender young leaves.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter pests and match their preference for dry soil.

items.name: Paysonia
items.growersTips:
Sow Paysonia seeds in early spring under cloches to protect young greens from wet UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp British summers.
Net your Paysonia crops early in the season to stop cabbage white butterflies laying their eggs.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your clay soil to give these leafy veg the nitrogen they crave.
Plant Paysonia alongside mint or sage to help deter those pesky flea beetles from chewing the leaves.

items.name: Raphanus sativus var. sativus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds just one centimetre deep in small batches every fortnight from March to September.

Harvest them young when they are the size of a marble so they stay wonderfully crunchy and sweet.

items.name: Rorippa palustris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK riverbank conditions

Cut back spent flowering stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your lawn

items.name: Rorippa austriaca

Control this highly invasive weed by digging up the deep taproots entirely in early spring.
Smother persistent patches with thick black polythene sheeting for at least two full growing seasons.
Never compost the roots or stems; dispose of them in council green waste to prevent re-sprouting.
Grow only in sturdy, submerged containers if you must cultivate this aggressive spreader in the UK.
Mow or cut back the yellow flowers in May before they set seed to stop wind-blown garden invasion.

items.name: Eruca

items.name: Dithyrea
items.growersTips:

items.name: Crambe

items.name: Raphanus

items.name: Sisymbrium officinale

items.description: Rapistrum, the bastard cabbages, is a genus of the family Brassicaceae with a distinctive cross like arrangement of its petals. It is also known as wild-turnip or turnipweed. Species of Rapistrum are annual to perennials. The yellow petals are accompanied by sepals that stand vertically at near right angles (erecto-patent). Leaf shape and arrangement varies from rough toothed (dentate) to a configuration of opposingly lobed pairs along the plant stalk, pinnately lobed.

Harvest the tender top shoots regularly before the yellow flowers appear to keep the flavour sweet.
Grow them alongside onions or garlic to help naturally deter common British pests from the crop.
items.description: Sisymbrium altissimum is a species of Sisymbrium. The plant is native to the western part of the Mediterranean Basin and is widely naturalized throughout most of the world, including all of North America. After maturity it forms a tumbleweed. Common names of the plant include Jim Hill mustard, tall tumblemustard, tall mustard, tumble mustard, tumbleweed mustard, tall sisymbrium, and tall hedge mustard.

items.name: Lunaria rediviva
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial honesty in moist, dappled shade to mimic its native European woodland home.
Sow the seeds in autumn because they need a cold UK winter chill to trigger spring germination.
Mulch with leaf mould in spring to keep the soil consistently damp and cool during dry spells.
Watch out for caterpillars of the orange-tip butterfly, so leave some foliage for these beauties.
Cut back the flowered stems in late winter if you want to collect those lovely translucent seedpods.
items.description: Lunaria rediviva, known as perennial honesty, is a species of plant in the cabbage family Brassicaceae. This hairy-stemmed herbaceous perennial is found throughout Europe. It often grows in damp woods on lime substrates. Growing up to 1 m (3.3 ft) tall, it has large, pointed oval leaves with marked serrations. Clusters of fragrant, pale pink flowers are borne in spring, followed by translucent oval seedheads, often used in flower arranging. It is cultivated as a garden plant, and has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Eudema
items.growersTips:
Start your Eudema seeds indoors in early April to protect young shoots from late UK spring frosts.
Plant Eudema in deep, well-drained sandy loam with a neutral pH to encourage strong root systems.
Water Eudema deeply once a week at the base rather than overhead to prevent damp-loving UK slugs.
Feed Eudema with a high-potassium organic fertilizer in July to boost your late-summer harvest.
Sow companion dill nearby to naturally deter aphids and hoverflies from your Eudema crop.

items.name: Raphanus sativus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep every two weeks from March to August for a continuous UK harvest.
Water evenly to prevent woody roots and splitting during dry spells in the British summer.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetle damage by using fine insect mesh immediately after sowing.
Sow alongside lettuces to act as a trap crop for pests and save valuable vegetable patch space.
Grow winter cultivars like Black Spanish from July to August to harvest during cold UK winters.
items.description: The radish is a flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae. Its large taproot is commonly used as a root vegetable, although the entire plant is edible and its leaves are sometimes used as a leaf vegetable. Originally domesticated in Asia, radishes are now grown and consumed globally. The radish is sometimes considered to form a species complex with the wild radish and instead treated as the subspecies Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus.

items.name: Alyssoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to mimic UK winter chill for successful spring germination.
Grow in sharply draining chalky or gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat and encourage flowering.
Prune lightly after summer flowering to maintain a compact habit and prevent the stems from splaying.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in damp weather.

items.name: Arabidopsis thaliana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of damp peat-free compost in spring, as they need light to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy by watering gently from below to avoid washouts.
Watch out for common UK garden pests like aphids and flea beetles that love these tiny brassicas.
Grow them in small pots on a sunny windowsill or cold frame to shelter them from heavy UK rain.
Sow a fresh pinch of seeds every three weeks from March to September for a continuous supply.
items.description: Arabidopsis thaliana, the thale cress, mouse-ear cress or arabidopsis, is a small plant from the mustard family (Brassicaceae), native to Eurasia and Africa. Commonly found along the shoulders of roads and in disturbed land, it is generally considered a weed.

items.name: Sisymbrium loeselii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in early spring once your UK soil starts to warm up.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy while these fast-growing salad greens establish.
Watch out for flea beetles in June; use fine insect mesh covers to protect the delicate leaves.
Harvest the young peppery leaves before the bright yellow flowers appear to keep the flavour sweet.
Grow them in light, free-draining soil with a bit of garden compost dug in to boost leaf growth.

items.name: Alyssum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April on a sunny windowsill for sturdy UK plugs.
Water the soil base weekly in dry summer spells to prevent mildew on the dense Brassicaceae foliage.
Shear back the faded stems by half in July to stimulate a second flush of late summer UK blooms.
Plant alongside carrots to attract hoverflies that voraciously consume destructive garden aphids.
Sow the robust cultivar Carpet of Snow in gritty, well-drained soil to survive wet UK winters.
items.description: Alyssum is a genus of over a hundred species of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae, native to temperate Europe, Asia, and northern Africa, with the highest species diversity in the Mediterranean region. The genus comprises annual and perennial herbaceous plants or (rarely) small shrubs, growing to 10–100 cm tall, with oblong-oval leaves. Alyssum flowers are characteristically small and grouped in terminal clusters; they are often yellow or white colored but can be pink or purple.

items.name: Rorippa sinuata
items.growersTips:
Grow in damp, heavy clay or alluvial soil to mimic its native UK riverbank habitat.
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface at a depth of two millimetres.
Keep the soil constantly wet by watering daily during dry British summer spells.
Watch for flea beetles in spring and protect young leaves with fine insect mesh.
Plant alongside watercress or mint in a dedicated bog garden to control its spreading roots.

items.name: Rorippa curvipes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using moist, peat-free compost.
Grow in a boggy garden border or damp container to mimic its natural UK wetland habitat.
Water daily during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently wet and prevent early bolting.
Net the crop in spring to protect the young leaves from cabbage white butterfly caterpillars.
Harvest the peppery leaves regularly from May to October to stimulate fresh, tender new growth.

items.name: Rorippa curvisiliqua
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just 2mm deep in damp, heavy clay or silt soils to mimic UK riverbank conditions.
Keep soil consistently wet by watering daily, as this wetland native cannot tolerate drying out.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK spring weather.
Grow in partial shade to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching during hot southern UK summers.
Harvest the peppery leaves regularly before yellow summer flowers appear to maintain leaf quality.

items.name: Rorippa subumbellata
items.growersTips:
Grow in saturated sandy soil mimicking UK lake margins using a mix of sharp sand and peat-free compost
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they require light and constant moisture to germinate
Water daily from beneath to keep the pot permanently waterlogged during the active summer growing phase
Protect young plants from slugs and snails which target Brassicaceae in damp British spring weather
Overwinter in a cold frame to protect the roots from freezing solid during severe UK winter frosts

items.name: Arabidopsis arenosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on gritty, well-drained soil to mimic UK shingle beaches they love.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells as this wild crucifer hates sitting in soggy British wet.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring, which chew tiny holes in the delicate rosettes of leaves.
Plant alongside wild thyme or stonecrop in a sunny rockery to match its natural gravelly habitat.
Avoid rich compost and instead mix plenty of sharp sand into your beds to keep the soil poor and open.

items.name: Murbeckiella
items.growersTips:
Plant Murbeckiella seeds in early spring just two millimetres deep to let UK light trigger growth.
Water your Murbeckiella only at the base once a week to prevent damp UK rot on its low foliage.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs during wet British Junes as they love these tender young leaves.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure excellent drainage during soggy UK winter months.
Grow Murbeckiella alongside rosemary to help deter pests and share the same free-draining soil.

items.name: Lyrocarpa
items.growersTips:
Start lyrocarpa seeds indoors in April to beat the cool UK spring before transplanting in late May.
Plant these lyrocarpa brassicas in firm, alkaline soil with added lime to prevent clubroot disease.
Space your lyrocarpa plants forty centimetres apart to allow their unique lyre-shaped pods to expand.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Net your lyrocarpa crop early in the season to protect the tender leaves from hungry wood pigeons.

items.name: Sisymbrium orientale
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep in early spring to match cool UK weather.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry spells to stop early bolting.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles which love this brassica family plant.
Grow this alongside mint or sage to help deter the pests that are attracted to its mustard scent.
Harvest the young peppery leaves frequently before the yellow flowers appear to keep them tasty.

items.name: Cakile
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring 1cm deep in a mix of sharp sand and grit to mimic their native UK shingle habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the sandy substrate to dry out completely between waterings.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails, which target tender Brassicaceae leaves in damp UK weather.
Plant alongside sea kale or samphire in a dedicated coastal bed to match their high salt tolerance.
Harvest the peppery seed pods and young leaves in summer before the plant sets seed and dies back.
items.description: Cakile is a genus within the flowering plant family Brassicaceae. Species in this genus are commonly known as searockets, though this name on its own is applied particularly to whatever member of the species is native or most common in the region concerned, the European searocket Cakile maritima in Europe, and the American searocket C. edentula in North America. The genus is native to Europe, Asia and North America, but the European searocket has been introduced into North America and has spread widely on both east and west coasts; in many places it is replacing the native C. edentula, and is

items.name: Physaria
items.growersTips:
Plant these hardy alpine brassicas in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winter rot.
Sow your bladderpod seeds shallowly in spring, just barely covering them with a fine layer of grit.
Water them deeply but infrequently, letting the gritty compost dry out fully between each drink.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp British mornings.
Grow them alongside thymes or sedums in a raised bed or rockery to match their dry soil needs.

items.name: Zilla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring at a depth of one centimetre once the UK soil has warmed to fifteen degrees
Grow in free-draining sandy soil mixed with grit to mimic its native desert-like arid conditions
Water sparingly only at the base once the soil dries out completely to prevent root rot in UK damp
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during wet UK summers
Position in the absolute brightest spot of your garden to maximise essential daily summer sunlight
items.description: Zilla may refer to:

items.name: Cochlearia
items.growersTips:
Sow Cochlearia officinalis seeds in autumn directly into damp, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
Water consistently to mimic coastal salt marshes, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Grow scurvy grass alongside mint or wild garlic in damp, cool corners of a UK woodland garden.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets in spring.
Harvest the vitamin C-rich leaves sparingly in winter when other fresh garden greens are scarce.

items.name: Lunaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in late spring at a depth of five millimetres for best root development.
Grow in moist, well-drained soil with partial shade to mimic their natural UK woodland edge habitat.
Watch for caterpillars of the orange-tip butterfly and cabbage white on the leaves in midsummer.
Leave the seed pods on the plant until autumn turns them papery, then harvest for dry arrangements.
Plant alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to mask fading bulb foliage as the Lunaria grows.
items.description:
Lunaria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It is native to Europe and has been introduced to North America and elsewhere. Species include:L. annua, annual or biennial
L. rediviva, perennial
L. telekiana. rare Balkan species

items.name: Teesdalia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring into very sandy, free-draining soil to mimic UK gravelly banks.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as this native plant is highly adapted to dry, acidic soils.
Grow in full sun and keep the surrounding area weed-free to prevent taller plants from shading it.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres and do not cover them deeply as they need light.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic grit barriers.

items.name: Macropodium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful UK germination.
Grow in deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of 6.5 to 7.
Net plants securely from spring to autumn to protect the brassica foliage from cabbage white butterflies.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in early spring to feed the hungry roots and retain moisture.

items.name: Matthiola maderensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Madeiran beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep young plants in a cold frame over winter to protect them from harsh British frosts and damp.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as they hate soggy roots in our cool climate.
Prune back lightly in late spring after flowering to keep its woody, shrubby habit neat and bushy.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic the bright cliffs of its native Madeira.

items.name: Descurainia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early spring once UK soil reaches ten degrees.
Water seedlings sparingly only when the top two centimetres of gritty, well-drained soil feels dry.
Net young plants in May to block the cabbage white butterfly and prevent devastating caterpillar loss.
Sow alongside mint or sage to deter flea beetles which frequently target UK brassica crops.
Harvest the peppery young leaves before yellow flowers appear in June to prevent bitter tasting crop.

items.name: Aurinia
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your heavy UK clay soil to give Aurinia the sharp drainage its roots absolutely crave.
Cut the stems back by half right after flowering in June to keep the mounds neat and bushy for winter.
Sow seeds just one millimetre deep in spring, using a cold frame to protect them from damp UK frost.
Water only during dry spells, as our wet winters are this drought-tolerant plant's biggest enemy.
Plant next to rosemary or thyme in a sunny rockery, as they all love the same dry, alkaline soil.

items.name: Eudema nubigena
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at a depth of 1cm to protect young shoots from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering deeply at the base every three days.
Watch out for slugs during wet British springs by placing beer traps around your young plants.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your vegetable bed a week before planting to boost growth.
Grow these alongside carrots to help deter common pests naturally without using harsh chemicals.
items.description: Borealandea nubigena is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. It is found only in Ecuador. It is native to very high elevation superpáramos from 4,000 to 4,500 meters elevation, where it grows on cliffs and in rocky areas. It is threatened by habitat loss.

items.name: Nasturtium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in May after frosts, 1.5cm deep in poor soil to encourage flowers instead of just leaves.
Water young plants weekly, but once established only water during dry spells to avoid root rot.
Check under leaves weekly for large white butterfly caterpillars and hand-pick them off immediately.
Plant near runner beans or brassicas as a sacrificial trap crop to lure aphids away from vegetables.
Grow the compact cultivar Tom Thumb in pots to easily control its spread in damp UK weather.
items.description:
Nasturtium may refer to:Tropaeolum, a plant genus in the family Tropaeolaceae, commonly known as nasturtium
Nasturtium , a plant genus in the family Brassicaceae, which includes watercress
Nasturtiums  a 1912 painting by E. Phillips Fox
Nasturtiums, a 1903 painting by Tudor St. George Tucker
Nasturtium (horse) (1899–1916), an American Champion Thoroughbred racehorse
Senecio tropaeolifolius, a succulent plant that is known as "false nasturtium"

items.name: Draba norvegica
items.growersTips:
Plant this arctic-alpine in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its native mountain scree home.
Water sparingly in winter to prevent root rot, as wet UK winters are its biggest enemy.
Position your pot in full sun but keep it sheltered from heavy, persistent British downpours.
Surround the collar with a thick layer of horticultural grit to stop damp soil touching foliage.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on these compact cushions in early spring.

items.name: Petrocallis
items.growersTips:
Grow Petrocallis pyrenaica in a gritty alpine trough with fifty percent horticultural grit for drainage
Water only during dry spring active growth and keep completely dry in winter using a rain shelter
Topdress the soil surface with limestone chippings to prevent the foliage rotting from wet soil
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow winter chilling for natural spring germination in the UK
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they quickly destroy the delicate cushion of foliage

items.name: Eutrema penlandii
items.growersTips:
This rare alpine needs a gritty, free-draining acidic scree mix to mimic its cold Rocky Mountain home.
Keep the soil constantly moist but never waterlogged by using a deep, gravel-mulched terracotta pot.
Position your pot in a cool, north-facing spot to shield this cold-loving plant from hot UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, as they love the tender young foliage.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave them outdoors so the natural winter frost triggers germination.

items.name: Malcolmia africana
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep in sunny, well-drained borders come April.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during spring germination to prevent damp-off in cool UK weather.
Watch out for flea beetles in May by using fine insect netting over your young salad greens.
Harvest the peppery leaves when they are young and tender before the summer heat makes them bitter.
Grow this quick crop next to radishes to maximise your small vegetable patch space this season.

items.name: Turritis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Grow in poor, sharply draining chalky soil to mimic native UK downs and prevent winter root rot.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, letting the top five centimetres of soil dry completely.
Watch for orange-tip butterfly caterpillars in spring and avoid spraying to support UK biodiversity.
Plant alongside wild marjoram or thyme to provide structural support for the tall, slender stems.

items.name: Schizopetalon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with neutral to alkaline pH to prevent Brassicaceae clubroot rot.
Water sparingly at the base once established to prevent damp-off in cool, humid British summers.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp spring nights.
Plant near sweet alyssum to attract beneficial predators that control cabbage white caterpillars.

items.name: Bunias
items.growersTips:
Sow Turkish rocket seeds in autumn in deep pots to accommodate the long taproot before transplanting.
Grow Bunias orientalis in well-drained, poor soil to prevent the plant from becoming too invasive.
Cut back flowering stems in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh, edible spring leaves.
Protect young spring shoots from cabbage white butterfly caterpillars using fine insect netting.
Plant Bunias alongside mint or sage to deter common brassica pests in damp UK spring weather.

items.name: Biscutella
items.growersTips:
Sow Biscutella seeds in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic UK alpine scree conditions.
Water sparingly, allowing the soil to dry completely between waterings to prevent root rot.
Watch for flea beetles in spring, which target this Brassicaceae family member in UK gardens.
Grow Biscutella in full sun to prevent the stems from becoming leggy in the weak UK winter light.
Avoid rich organic fertilizers; instead, top-dress with fine limestone grit to keep soil alkaline.

items.name: Parrya
items.growersTips:
Sow Parrya seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow winter chilling for successful spring germination.
Grow Parrya in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native limestone scree and prevent winter rot.
Water Parrya only during dry summer spells, keeping the crown dry in winter with a gravel mulch.
Protect young Parrya shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps during damp UK spring nights.
Plant Parrya alongside alpine saxifrages in raised beds to ensure the sharp drainage they require.

items.name: Calepina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early autumn or spring at 1cm depth to match the cool UK growing season.
Grow in free-draining, alkaline to neutral soil, adding grit to heavy clay to prevent root rot.
Water moderately at the base to keep soil damp, avoiding waterlogging during wet British winters.
Hand-weed early to prevent fast-growing Calepina from being smothered by aggressive garden weeds.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and use fine netting to protect the young foliage.

items.name: Myagrum
items.growersTips:
Sow Myagrum perfoliatum seeds in March at 1cm depth in free-draining soil to avoid winter wet rot.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent early bolting in dry UK summers.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles and cabbage white butterflies using fine insect netting.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter brassica pests that are common in damp British gardens.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils before planting to ensure the sharp drainage they need.
items.description: Myagrum, muskweed or musk weed, is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It has only one species, Myagrum perfoliatum, native to Europe and the Middle East, and an introduced weed in North America, South America, Australia and other places in Asia. It is sister to Isatis.

items.name: Clypeola
items.growersTips:
Sow Clypeola seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in early April once UK frosts begin to ease.
Grow this brassica family crop in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Water sparingly but deeply once a week, letting the topsoil dry out completely between sessions.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, using fine mesh netting to protect the young foliage.
Plant alongside thyme or rosemary to help deter pests naturally in your sunny UK vegetable plot.

items.name: Kernera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to mimic UK winter chill for successful spring germination.
Grow in gritty, alkaline soil with sharp sand to prevent winter root rot in wet British weather.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty substrate to dry out completely between feeds.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic wool pellets.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to replicate its native European alpine habitat.

items.name: Capsella
items.growersTips:
Sow Capsella bursa-pastoris seeds in early spring at a shallow depth of just two millimetres.
Keep the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged to prevent early bolting in dry UK summers.
Watch out for flea beetles in May and protect young seedlings with fine insect mesh covers.
Grow Capsella near onions or garlic to naturally deter common Brassicaceae pests from the crop.
Incorporate well-rotted garden compost into light sandy soils to retain essential spring moisture.
items.description:
Capsella may refer to:Capsella (bivalve), a mollusc genus in the family Donacidae
Capsella (plant), a plant genus in the family Brassicaceae

items.name: Arabidopsis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they need light and winter cold stratification to sprout.
Water from the base to keep the tiny rosette dry and prevent dampening off in damp UK spring weather.
Watch for cabbage stem flea beetle and aphids which target this Brassicaceae family member in June.
Grow in low-nutrient, well-drained sandy loam to mimic its natural UK wayside and wall habitats.
Harvest seed pods when they turn yellow but before they shatter to easily collect next years crop.
items.description: Arabidopsis (rockcress) is a genus of small flowering plants in the cabbage and mustard family, Brassicaceae. Arabidopsis species are native to temperate and subarctic Eurasia and North America, North Africa, and the mountains of eastern tropical Africa. This genus is of great interest since it contains thale cress, one of the model organisms used for studying plant biology and the first plant to have its entire genome sequenced. Changes in thale cress are easily observed, making it a very useful model.

items.name: Alliaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in moist, shady spots to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, mimicking damp British spring weather.
Watch for green veined white butterfly caterpillars which feed heavily on Alliaria leaves in summer.
Harvest leaves in early spring before the white flowers appear to prevent bitter tasting foliage.
Grow alongside wild garlic in damp clay soils as they share identical light and moisture needs.

items.name: Caulanthus inflatus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring because this desert native needs extra warmth to get started.
Grow them in a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to mimic their dry California home in wet UK weather.
Water very sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely to prevent root rot.
Position your pots in the absolute sunniest spot of your garden to help the yellow stems swell up.
Protect the young shoots from slugs and snails which love the succulent-like stems in damp springs.

items.name: Clausia
items.growersTips:
Sow Clausia seeds in early spring at a depth of one centimetre in moist, well-drained alkaline soil.
Water the base weekly during dry UK summers to prevent early bolting and woody stem development.
Protect young Clausia shoots from cabbage white butterflies using a fine insect mesh netting.
Grow Clausia alongside mint or sage to naturally deter common Brassicaceae pests in your plot.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in autumn to insulate roots from wet UK winter freezes.

items.name: Erysimum
items.growersTips:
Chop back your Bowles Mauve by half in late summer to keep it from getting woody and leggy.
Plant them in gritty, free-draining soil so their roots do not rot during our wet UK winters.
Take stem cuttings in July as backup because these short-lived perennials often tire out after three years.
Position them in your sunniest spot to prevent downy mildew from dampening their lovely grey leaves.
Grow them alongside rosemary and thyme which love the same dry, alkaline soil as your wallflowers.

items.name: Matthiola longipetala
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April, just covering them with a light sprinkling of fine compost.
Plant these night-scented stocks right under your patio windows to enjoy the evening perfume.
Water gently at the base to keep the soil damp but never soggy, preventing damp-off in cool spring.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, which leave tiny holes in the leaves of young seedlings.
Sow a fresh batch every three weeks until July for a continuous supply of lovely evening scent.

items.name: Thlaspi
items.growersTips:
Sow your field pennycress seeds in autumn so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep the soil damp but not soggy as this cabbage-family green hates sitting in heavy winter wet.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring by using fine insect mesh over your young salad leaves.
Grow them alongside onions or garlic to help deter the pests that love this brassica relative.
Harvest the peppery leaves when they are young and tender before the white flowers open in May.

items.name: Megadenia
items.growersTips:
Sow Megadenia seeds in early spring under glass at a depth of one centimetre to beat UK frosts.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never waterlogged using a fine-rose watering can.
Grow them in a partially shaded spot to mimic their native cool, damp woodland habitat.
Blend plenty of leaf mould into your sandy loam soil to provide the rich, loose structure they love.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs as they adore the tender young shoots.

items.name: Heliophila
items.growersTips:
Sow these Cape rain daisies in April under glass to protect them from late British spring frosts.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to mimic their native sandy soils and prevent winter root rot.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy UK ground.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings are three inches tall to encourage a bushier flowering.
Plant them alongside poached egg plants to attract hoverflies that will devour any aphid outbreaks.

items.name: Matthiola sinuata
items.growersTips:
Plant this seaside native in free-draining sandy soil to mimic its natural UK coastal dunes.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring and keep them just moist until they establish their deep taproots.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, which love chewing tiny holes in crucifer leaves.
Give it a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the delicate pale purple flowers from harsh UK winds.
Avoid overwatering once established, as this biennial is highly prone to root rot in wet UK winters.

items.name: Draba nemorosa
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of free-draining gritty compost in autumn to let winter cold trigger germination.
Position your pots in a bright, south-facing spot to mimic the sunny, open banks of their native habitat.
Water sparingly from below to keep the soil damp but never soggy, preventing winter rot in damp UK weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, as they love to devour the tender young rosettes.
Plant them alongside slow-growing alpine sedums in a shallow stone trough to prevent faster weeds smothering them.

items.name: Draba incana
items.growersTips:
Plant this arctic-alpine in gritty, free-draining limestone soil to mimic its native UK uplands.
Keep watering minimal, only drenching the gritty soil once it is completely dry to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors in UK cold frames so winter chills can naturally trigger germination.
Position your pots in full sun but shield them from heavy, persistent winter rain with a cloche.
Grow this compact beauty alongside low-growing saxifrages in a raised scree bed or alpine trough.

items.name: Stanleya pinnata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Prince's Plume in your sunniest, sharpest-draining spot to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds shallowly in grit-heavy compost during spring, keeping them on a warm windowsill to start.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to prevent rot.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit and lime into your soil to mimic its native alkaline scrublands.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, which absolutely love devouring the young spring shoots.

items.name: Peltaria
items.growersTips:
Plant Peltaria alliacea in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter stratification for spring germination.
Divide established clumps in early spring to control its vigorous, invasive-leaning root spread.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to prevent the leaves from becoming excessively bitter.
Watch for flea beetles in spring, protecting young foliage with fine insect mesh or fleece.

items.name: Draba muralis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of free-draining gritty soil as they need winter cold to sprout.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during winter, then let it dry out slightly between spring waters.
Watch out for slugs eating the delicate young rosettes in early spring and use beer traps to protect.
Grow this little wall-cress alongside sempervivums in a sunny, raised rock crevice or stone trough.
Leave the faded flower stems alone in summer so it can self-seed and return in your gravel garden.
items.description: Drabella is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Draba muralis, an annual or biennial known as wall whitlowgrass. It is native to southern, central and northern Europe, northwestern Africa, Turkey, Crimea, and the Caucasus.

items.name: Isatis
items.growersTips:
Sow Isatis tinctoria seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil.
Water young plants weekly until established, then only during prolonged dry UK summer spells.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and flea beetles, netting the crop in midsummer.
Cut back flowering stalks in July before they set seed to prevent invasive self-seeding in lawns.
Grow alongside rosemary or mint to help deter the brassica pests that commonly attack Isatis.

items.name: Aubrieta
items.growersTips:
Cut back hard with shears right after spring flowering to keep it compact and prevent woody gaps.
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to stop winter wet from rotting its shallow roots.
Sow seeds in late spring on top of damp compost because they need light to germinate successfully.
Tuck them into dry stone walls or rock crevices where they can cascade down and stay dry at the base.
Watch out for flea beetles in dry UK summers, which leave tiny, unsightly holes in the foliage.
items.description: Aubrieta is a genus of flowering plants in the cabbage family Brassicaceae. The genus is named after Claude Aubriet, a French flower painter. It includes over 20 species native to southeastern Europe and Western Asia. Some species have escaped from gardens throughout Europe. It is a low, spreading plant, hardy, evergreen and perennial. It has small violet, pink, or white flowers, and it inhabits rocks and banks. It prefers light, well-drained soil, is tolerant of a wide pH range, and can grow in partial shade or full sun.

items.name: Subularia
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare aquatic annual in shallow, acidic pond margins or cold water tanks in early spring.
Keep the compost constantly waterlogged to mimic the damp mud of its native Scottish loch habitats.
Anchor seeds just under a thin layer of fine, washed silica sand to keep them from floating away.
Watch out for pond snails in summer, as they can quickly devour the delicate, needle-like foliage.
Sow seeds in March indoors before placing pots in your outdoor garden pond once frosts have passed.

items.name: Caulanthus cooperi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring to beat the UK chill, planting them just five millimetres deep.
Grow this desert native in a gritty, free-draining mix to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this plant hates soggy roots.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape in damp British springs.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its hot homeland.

items.name: Caulanthus amplexicaulis
items.growersTips:
Start this California native early indoors in March to beat the short, damp UK growing season.
Sow seeds just three millimetres deep in free-draining, gritty compost to prevent winter rotting.
Grow this brassica relative in your sunniest spot with sharp drainage to mimic its dry scrub home.
Watch out for UK slugs and cabbage white caterpillars which love devouring these unusual leaves.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between light waterings.

items.name: Caulanthus crassicaulis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early spring to give this wild cabbage relative a head start on UK chill.
Plant them in free-draining sandy loam to mimic their native dry soil and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings in summer.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and protect your young plants with fine insect netting.
Grow them alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter common brassica pests in your veg patch.

items.name: Caulanthus glaucus
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare wild cabbage seeds in spring using a free-draining, gritty compost to prevent rot.
Keep the soil barely damp, watering only when the top two inches feel dry to mimic desert homes.
Protect young leaves from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp UK springs.
Grow them in your sunniest, south-facing spot or a greenhouse to get enough heat for good growth.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your garden beds to ensure the roots never sit in wet soil.

items.name: Caulanthus coulteri
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March to shield young plants from cold, unpredictable UK spring weather.
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in free-draining compost to prevent winter rotting.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy to stop this wild cabbage relative from bolting early.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and use fine netting to protect the leaves from caterpillars.
Grow them alongside mint or sage to help deter those pesky brassica pests in your veg patch.

items.name: Caulanthus pilosus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early spring to give this desert-native wild cabbage a warm head start.
Grow it in poor, sharply draining gritty soil to mimic its natural dry Great Basin habitat.
Water very sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Protect the young rosettes from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Position your pots in the absolute sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to trap heat.

items.name: Caulanthus heterophyllus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring to beat the cool UK weather, planting them just five millimetres deep.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently at the base to prevent stem rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, using beer traps to protect young shoots.
Grow them alongside mint or sage to help deter those pesky cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs.
Add well-rotted manure to your patch a few weeks before planting to give these hungry feeders a boost.

items.name: Camelina
items.growersTips:
Sow your gold-of-pleasure seeds in April just one centimetre deep to catch the spring showers.
Keep the soil relatively poor as rich UK borders make these plants floppy and reduce seed yields.
Watch out for flea beetles in May and use a fine mesh netting to protect the young seedlings.
Water only during dry spells once established because this hardy crop absolutely hates soggy roots.
Harvest the seed pods in August when they turn a lovely paper-brown but before they split open.
items.description: Camelina is a genus within the flowering plant family Brassicaceae. The Camelina species, commonly known as false flax, are native to Mediterranean regions of Europe and Asia. Most species of this genus have been little studied, with the exception of Camelina sativa, historically cultivated as an oil plant. Heinrich Johann Nepomuk von Crantz was the first botanist to use the genus Camelina in his classification works in 1762.

items.name: Malcolmia maritima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly directly into raked soil in spring, just five millimetres deep, for easy success.
Water the soil gently at the base rather than overhead to prevent these delicate stems from rotting.
Watch out for flea beetles, which love eating tiny holes in these leaves during dry UK summers.
Sow a new batch every three weeks from April to July to keep their lovely sweet scent going all summer.
Grow them alongside your vegetable patches to attract helpful pollinators that boost your crop yields.

items.name: Lepidium
items.growersTips:
Sow garden cress seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in moisture-retentive, fertile soil.
Grow pepperwort in partial shade during hot UK summers to prevent premature bolting and bitter leaves.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent damping off disease in damp British weather.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles using fine insect netting or fleece from early spring.
Sow seeds every two weeks from March to September for a continuous harvest of fresh salad leaves.
items.description:
Lepidium is a genus of plants in the mustard/cabbage family, Brassicaceae. The genus is widely distributed in the Americas, Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia. It includes familiar species such as garden cress, maca, and dittander. General common names include peppercress, peppergrass, pepperweed, and pepperwort. Some species form tumbleweeds.
The genus name Lepidium is from Greek meaning 'small scale', which is thought to be derived from a folk medicine usage of the plant to treat leprosy, which cause small scales on the skin. Another meaning is related to the small scale-like fruit.

items.name: Caulanthus californicus
items.growersTips:
Start this rare California native in pots under glass in March to protect from cold UK spring rain.
Sow seeds just barely covered with a three-millimetre layer of fine grit to prevent damping off.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining soil are bone dry to avoid root rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love targeting these tender young rosettes in damp UK weather.
Grow them alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to match their strict need for dry, sunny spots.

items.name: Leavenworthia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of two millimetres to mimic their natural winter-annual life cycle.
Grow in shallow, gritty limestone soil to replicate the alkaline cedar glades they naturally inhabit.
Keep the soil consistently damp during winter and spring but allow it to dry out completely in summer.
Position in full sun in a cold frame to protect the delicate winter rosettes from heavy UK frosts.
Watch for flea beetles in early spring and protect young seedlings with fine insect mesh covers.

items.name: Draba aretioides
items.growersTips:
Grow this alpine gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes No.1, grit, and sand.
Keep your plant in an unheated greenhouse or alpine house to shield it from wet UK winter rain.
Water only from the base or plunge the pot to keep the tight, hairy cushion from rotting.
Top-dress the soil with a thick layer of fine granite grit to keep the foliage off damp earth.
Watch out for aphids in early spring, gently brushing them off the tight rosettes with a soft brush.

items.name: Solms-laubachia
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare alpine in a hyper-drained, gritty scree mix to survive wet British winters.
Shelter your plants in an unheated alpine house or cold frame to keep winter rain off the crown.
Water from below or around the base in spring to prevent the delicate foliage from rotting.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing through the fleshy root systems.
Keep these high-altitude beauties in a cool, north-facing spot out of harsh afternoon UK sun.

items.name: Idahoa
items.growersTips:
Sow your Idahoa seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres in free-draining sandy loam.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent your delicate seedlings from rotting.
Watch out for slugs during wet UK springs by using organic wool pellets around your young plants.
Grow Idahoa alongside radishes and salad leaves to make the most of your small vegetable plot space.
Grow them in a cold frame to protect the early spring blooms from harsh British frosts and winds.

items.name: Draba lactea
items.growersTips:
Plant this arctic alpine in gritty, sharply draining scree mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as damp soil quickly rots its taproot.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs, as they love the tight rosettes.
Plant next to low-growing saxifrages or sedums which share its love for sunny, exposed rockeries.
Gently top-dress the soil around the collar with fine granite grit to prevent winter wet rot.

items.name: Coronopus
items.growersTips:
Sow swinecress seeds just 2mm deep in autumn so the damp UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry British spring spells to stop bolt.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, as they love chewing tiny holes in Coronopus rosette leaves.
Clear competing weeds from your patch early on, as this low-growing annual is easily smothered.
Grow them next to taller mint or chives to provide light dappled shade during hot July afternoons.
items.description: Coronopus is a synonym for the accepted genus name Lepidium. It was applied to some species of flowering plants in the cabbage and mustard family Brassicaceae known commonly as swinecress or wartcress. These are generally low spreading annual herbaceous plants with many long stems, deeply lobed leaves and small white flowers. They have a strong scent, smelling like garden cress, Lepidium sativum, when crushed. Lepidium squamatus may be native to the Mediterranean but Lepidium didymum may be native to South America. Both species are widespread weedy introduced species in other areas.

items.name: Cardamine
items.growersTips:
Sow Cardamine hirsuta in damp, shady borders during autumn for a continuous supply of winter salad.
Water container-grown bittercress daily in summer to prevent early bolting and woody leaf texture.
Hand-weed before the seed pods explode in May to stop aggressive self-seeding across damp lawns.
Grow Cardamine pratensis in boggy, acidic soil to attract the orange-tip butterfly to your garden.
Interplant with wild garlic in damp shade to create a pest-resistant, edible ground cover.
items.description: Cardamine is a large genus of flowering plants in the mustard family, Brassicaceae, known as bittercresses and toothworts. It contains more than 200 species of annuals and perennials. Species in this genus can be found in diverse habitats worldwide, except the Antarctic. The name Cardamine is derived from the Greek kardaminē, water cress, from kardamon, pepper grass.

items.name: Eruca vesicaria subsp. sativa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds just one centimetre deep in spring and autumn to avoid the hot midsummer bolting weather.
Water your salad rocket consistently at the base to stop it getting too peppery and tough to eat.
Cover young plants with fine insect netting to block those pesky UK flea beetles from eating holes.
Pinch out any yellow flowers immediately to keep the plant producing tasty, tender leaves for longer.
Grow rocket next to mint or dill to help deter pests naturally in your damp British garden plot.

items.name: Draba fladnizensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pot in full sun but shield it from heavy winter rain using a glass pane or cloche.
Water sparingly from below in summer to keep the tight rosette dry and prevent rot.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the natural UK winter cold can trigger spring germination.
Grow it in a raised scree bed alongside slow-growing saxifrages to prevent it being smothered.

items.name: Braya
items.growersTips:
Sow your Braya seeds in early spring when UK soils reach eight degrees, just half an inch deep.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently at the base every dry morning.
Watch out for slugs and cabbage white caterpillars, using organic barriers to protect young leaves.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your patch a few weeks before planting to feed these greens.
Grow your Braya alongside mint or sage to help deter those pesky pests naturally in your garden.

items.name: Hornungia
items.growersTips:
Sow your sweet-scented Hornungia seeds shallowly in autumn to mimic British wild limestone habitats.
Keep the soil gritty and free-draining using horticultural grit to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Position these tiny annuals in full sun near paths so their delicate honey fragrance is easy to enjoy.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between your waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the tender young spring shoots during damp British mornings.

items.name: Iberis
items.growersTips:
Plant your perennial Iberis sempervirens in autumn to let the roots settle before the UK winter.
Cut the stems back by half right after flowering in June to keep the mounds neat and bushy.
Grow them in gritty, free-draining soil because wet UK winter clay will rot their roots.
Water newly planted Iberis once a week, but leave established clumps alone to brave dry spells.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with beer traps or wool pellets.
items.description: Iberis, commonly called candytuft, is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It comprises annuals, evergreen perennials and subshrubs native to the Old World. Species are native to the Mediterranean basin, Western Asia, the Caucasus, and western Europe. The name "candytuft" is not related to candy, but derives from Candia, the former name of Iraklion on the Island of Crete.

items.name: Neslia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in April when UK soil warms, just five millimetres deep in a sunny, open spot.
Water young seedlings weekly to establish, then only during dry spells to prevent root rot.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, using insect netting to protect the delicate leaves.
Grow next to potatoes or onions to help deter common pests naturally in your veg patch.
Harvest the young leaves before the yellow flowers appear to keep the flavor mild and sweet.

items.name: Draba aizoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a spot in full, baking sun, ideally tucked into a south-facing rock crevice or trough.
Water very sparingly, only during dry spring active growth, and never let water sit in the rosette.
Protect the crown from winter rot by mulching with a thick layer of sharp grit or alpine gravel.
Keep a watchful eye out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the tight, spiny cushions.
items.description: Draba aizoides is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, known as yellow whitlow-grass. It is native to Europe where it is found on limestone rocks and walls. In the British Isles it is found only on the Gower Peninsula in Wales.

items.name: Didymophysa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic alpine scree.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Protect the foliage from winter wet using an open-ended cloche while maintaining maximum airflow.
Plant alongside other alpine brassicas in raised scree beds to ensure rapid drainage of rainwater.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet spring nights as they target the tender young rosettes.

items.name: Conringia
items.growersTips:
Sow your hare's-ear mustard seeds directly in April once the chilly UK spring soil begins to warm.
Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, watering only during dry spells in June and July.
Watch out for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars which love chewing these blue-green leaves.
Grow them in poor, well-drained chalky soil to stop these wild brassicas from getting too floppy.
Plant them alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter those pesky flea beetles from your crop.

items.name: Armoracia
items.growersTips:
Plant horseradish in spring in deep, fertile, moist soil, burying root cuttings at a 45-degree angle.
Grow armoracia in large, buried pots or root barriers to prevent it from aggressively taking over.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent the roots from becoming woody and losing flavor.
Watch for the cabbage white butterfly and flea beetles, as this brassica is highly susceptible.
Lift and replant the roots annually in late autumn after the first frost for the best flavor.

items.name: Draba
items.growersTips:
Plant your Draba in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, keeping the foliage dry to prevent mildew.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp British springs, as they love the tender green rosettes.
Grow Draba alongside alpine saxifrages in a raised rock garden or gravel bed for perfect drainage.
Tuck Draba into a stone trough or alpine house to shield its delicate spring blooms from heavy rain.

items.name: Galitzkya
items.growersTips:
Sow your Galitzkya seeds in early spring under fleece to protect young shoots from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering deeply at the base every Tuesday morning.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into heavy UK clay to give these roots the sharp drainage they crave.
Watch out for slugs during wet British Junes by placing beer traps around your leafy Galitzkya crop.
Plant Galitzkya alongside onions to naturally deter the pests that love to munch on its foliage.

items.name: Rorippa
items.growersTips:
Grow watercress in pots of compost submerged in water trays to mimic UK streams and prevent drying out.
Sow seeds outdoors from April to July at a shallow depth of five millimetres in moisture-retentive soil.
Protect young plants with fine mesh to prevent damage from flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars.
Harvest outer leaves regularly from June to October to encourage fresh growth and delay flowering.
Grow alongside mint or celery in boggy garden areas to share similar high-moisture soil conditions.

items.name: Streptanthella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under glass to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts and damp.
Grow this brassica relative in free-draining, sandy loam to prevent root rot during wet summers.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to stop the plants from bolting prematurely.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and use fine netting to protect the foliage from caterpillars.
Grow them alongside mint or sage to help deter common UK pests like aphids and flea beetles.

items.name: Sisymbrium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep in early spring to match the cool UK weather.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently at the base during dry spells.
Watch out for flea beetles in May, protecting young leaves with a fine insect mesh cover.
Grow these greens next to mint or sage to help deter those pesky cabbage white butterflies.
Harvest the peppery young leaves regularly from the outside to keep the plant producing fresh growth.
items.description: Sisymbrium is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. Many of the common names for species in this genus include rocket, mustard, or hedge mustard.

items.name: Hesperis
items.growersTips:
Sow sweet rocket seeds outdoors in late spring directly where you want them to bloom next summer.
Keep young plants damp but avoid waterlogging during wet UK winters by adding grit to your soil.
Watch out for flea beetles in June, as they love chewing tiny holes in this cabbage family member.
Cut back faded flower spikes in July to stop self-seeding and encourage a second flush of blooms.
Plant them near your patio or seating area so you can enjoy their lovely evening scent in July.

items.name: Selenia
items.growersTips:
Sow Selenia seeds in early spring at a depth of 1cm in fertile, well-drained soil to avoid damp-off.
Protect young Selenia crops from UK slugs using beer traps or organic wool pellets around stems.
Water Selenia deeply once a week at the base to prevent powdery mildew in humid British summers.
Interplant Selenia with mint or sage to deter the common cabbage white butterfly from laying eggs.
Harvest Selenia leaves early in the morning during cool autumn days to ensure the best crisp texture.
items.description:
Selenia may refer to:Selenia (company), an Italian electronics company merged into Alenia Aeronautica
Selenia (moth), a genus of moths
Selenia (plant), a genus of plants
Selenia, a character from the film Arthur and the Invisibles

items.name: Caulanthus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early March to beat the cool UK spring, then transplant them out in May.
