Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil to give these hungry brassicas a rich, fertile bed.
Water deeply at the base once a week to keep the soil damp, especially during dry summer spells.
Net your crop early to protect the leaves from hungry cabbage white butterflies and pigeons.
Plant them alongside mint or sage to help deter those pesky aphids and flea beetles naturally.
items.description: Caulanthus is a genus of plants in the family Brassicaceae. Plants of this genus may be known as jewelflowers. They are also often referred to as wild cabbage, although this common name usually refers to wild variants of Brassica oleracea, the cabbage plant. Jewelflowers are native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where they are often found in warm, arid regions. Many species have an enlarged, erect stem rising from a basal rosette of leaves. Flowers arise directly from the surface of the stem; many species have colorful, bell-shaped flowers. The best-known of the fourtee

items.name: Arabis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Arabis in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Cut the stems back by half right after spring flowering to keep the mound tight and bushy.
Water newly planted Arabis weekly during dry spells, but leave established clumps to fend for themselves.
Watch out for downy mildew in damp UK summers and space plants thirty centimetres apart for airflow.
Tuck them into south-facing rockies or raised beds where they get maximum British sunshine.
items.description: Arabis, or rockcress, is a genus of flowering plants, within the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Lesquerella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in autumn so they get the winter chill they need.
Grow this brassica relative in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native limestone scree habitat.
Water only during dry spells in summer, as our wet UK winters are the biggest threat to its roots.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring, protecting young leaves with fine insect mesh or cloches.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme in your sunniest gravel garden spot to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Ionopsidium
items.growersTips:
Sow violet cress seeds in late summer for a lovely splash of winter colour in damp UK rockeries.
Scatter the tiny seeds directly onto moist, weed-free soil without burying them as they need light.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy, especially during dry spells in autumn and spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the tender young leaves in damp British weather.
Let this little annual self-seed naturally in gravel paths to create a charming, permanent carpet.

items.name: Athysanus
items.growersTips:
Sow this leafy green in early spring under a cloche to protect young shoots from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy by watering gently at the base every dry morning.
Mix plenty of well-rotted garden compost into your soil beforehand to give it a rich, crumbly bed.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp British spells, using organic beer traps to save leaves.
Plant next to mint or sage to help deter common pests that love to munch on leafy brassica relatives.
items.description:
Athysanus may refer to:Athysanus (leafhopper), a true bug genus in the subfamily Deltocephalinae
Athysanus (plant), a plant genus in the family Brassicaceae
Pleistodontes athysanus, a fig wasp species native to Australia

items.name: Noccaea
items.growersTips:
Grow Noccaea caerulescens in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native UK limestone habitat.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn, barely covering them, so winter cold can naturally break dormancy.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry British summer spells.
Watch out for flea beetles in spring, protecting young leaves with a fine insect mesh cover.
Plant them near wild thyme or marjoram to create a beautiful, bee-friendly rock garden display.

items.name: Draba verna
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn onto gritty compost, barely covering them so winter light can trigger growth.
Water very sparingly from below to keep the tiny rosettes dry and prevent damp-off in wet UK winters.
Tuck them into a raised scree bed or alpine trough to ensure the sharp drainage they absolutely crave.
Watch out for garden snails in early spring as they can devour these tiny plants in a single night.
Pair them with miniature sedums that won't crowd them out in your cold frame or gravel garden.
items.description: Draba verna, common whitlowgrass, is a species of plant in the cabbage family. It is a small spring-flowering annual which is widely dispersed around the world, and which is found on walls, pavements and patches of bare ground. It has a complex taxonomy which is not yet fully elucidated.

items.name: Matthiola fruticulosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild stock in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native Mediterranean limestone cliffs.
Keep watering to a minimum once established because this dry-loving plant absolutely hates wet feet.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a cold frame to protect young seedlings from damp UK weather.
Snip off faded flower spikes in late summer to keep the plant tidy and encourage fresh new growth.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, especially if you grow them near vegetable brassicas.

items.name: Euclidium syriacum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in early April once the UK frosts begin to ease.
Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, watering only when the top centimetre feels dry.
Watch out for flea beetles in late spring, as they love to chew tiny holes in this plant's leaves.
Grow this fast annual alongside hardy geraniums to help fill in any gaps as it starts to fade.
Mix plenty of grit into your garden bed to give this wild mustard the sharp drainage it craves.
items.description: Euclidium is a genus of flowering plants in the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Euclidium syriacum, a white-flowered annual herb native to Eurasia. It ranges from southeastern Europe to Ukraine and European Russia, the Caucasus, western and Central Asia, the western Himalayas, Xinjiang, and Mongolia.

items.name: Iodanthus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn 5mm deep in moist, alkaline soil to mimic UK woodland edges for spring growth.
Water consistently at the base to keep soil damp but not waterlogged during dry UK summer spells.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside wild garlic or mint to deter common Brassicaceae pests like flea beetles.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in late autumn to encourage healthy crown development.

items.name: Eutrema
items.growersTips:
Grow Eutrema japonicum in deep shade using a highly porous, gritty compost to mimic mountain streams.
Water daily with cold rainwater to keep the soil constantly wet but never stagnant or waterlogged.
Protect plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape, as they love the damp shade.
Grow in pots that can be moved indoors or to a cold frame to protect roots from freezing in winter.
Incorporate slow-release organic fertilizer into the soil mix before planting in early spring.

items.name: Strigosella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in late April once UK soils warm, just five millimetres deep to ensure light.
Water gently at the base twice a week, increasing to three times during dry British summer spells.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots; use beer traps or organic wool pellets around your patch.
Mix plenty of well-rotted garden compost into your soil before planting to improve clay drainage.
Grow these next to carrots or radishes to deter pests and make the most of your vegetable plot.

items.name: Conringieae
items.growersTips:
Sow hare's-ear mustard seeds directly in April, just five millimetres deep in well-drained chalky soil.
Keep seedlings damp but never soggy, watering only at the base when the top inch of soil feels dry.
Watch out for flea beetles in June; use fine insect mesh to protect the young, tender leaves.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter the cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs.
Harvest the peppery greens early in summer before the plant bolts and the stems become too woody.

items.name: Pennellia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres in free-draining, neutral to alkaline soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during wet British springs.
Grow alongside mint or sage to deter the cabbage white butterflies that target Brassicaceae crops.
Apply a garden lime treatment to acidic UK soils before planting to prevent clubroot disease.

items.name: Physaria repanda
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Grow this in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural sand to prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly around the base only when the top two inches of soil feel completely dry to touch.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British summers by using organic copper tape on pots.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot of your patio to mimic its natural dry, rocky habitat.

items.name: Arabis allionii
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine gem in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters without rotting.
Position your pots in full sun but tuck them where they get light shade during hot July afternoons.
Trim the foliage back by half right after spring flowering to keep its neat, cushion-like shape.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, letting the top few inches dry out completely.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with beer traps or organic pellets.

items.name: Ochthodium aegyptiacum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April after frosts at a depth of 5mm directly into free-draining, gritty soil.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Watch for flea beetles and cabbage white caterpillars which target this Brassicaceae family member.
Clear dying plants in autumn to prevent self-seeding and maintain neat borders in wet winters.
items.description: Ochthodium is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Brassicaceae. It includes a single species, Ochthodium aegyptiacum, an annual native to Cyprus, Egypt, the Levant, and Turkey in the eastern Mediterranean.

items.name: Arabis scabra
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare native in gritty, free-draining limestone soil to mimic its Avon Gorge home.
Keep watering to a minimum, only dampening the soil when the top two inches are bone dry.
Position your pot in full sun but shield it from heavy, persistent winter rain to prevent rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the delicate young foliage.
Propagate by taking soft stem cuttings in early summer to secure next year's plants.

items.name: Physaria lepidota
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine yellow salad in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its rocky home.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under a cold frame to protect them from wet UK winter rot.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two inches of gritty soil have dried out completely.
Watch out for slugs and snails that love to feast on these low-growing rosettes in damp weather.
Grow them alongside wild thyme in raised beds or rockeries to ensure they get maximum British sun.

items.name: Matthiola fragrans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent damp winter rot in damp UK climates.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out fully between watering to mimic dry hills.
Protect the young grey-green foliage from slugs and snails during wet British spring nights.
Plant near a patio or seating area so you can enjoy the sweet evening scent during summer nights.
Avoid heavy clay soils by mixing plenty of horticultural grit into your planting beds or pots.
items.description: Matthiola fragrans is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to Ukraine, south, east and central European Russia, and Kazakhstan. It is confined to chalk outcrops.

items.name: Sibara filifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under a cold frame to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Grow this rare island native in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells rather than spraying the foliage.
Keep a sharp eye out for cabbage white caterpillars and protect your crop with fine insect netting.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter common pests naturally in your kitchen garden.

items.name: Degenia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring at a depth of five millimetres in free-draining, gritty alkaline compost.
Position containers in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic dry, rocky Croatian scree.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Protect plants from slugs and snails in spring using copper tape around the pots or gravel mulches.
Avoid rich organic fertilisers to maintain the compact, cushion-like habit of this alpine herb.
items.description: Degenia is a monotypic plant genus in the family Brassicaceae containing the single species Degenia velebitica. The yellow-flowered plant is endemic to the Velebit and Kapela mountain ranges of Croatia. It is an endangered species and has had protected status since 1964. It grows in open stony grasslands, settled scree slopes, and rock crevices fully exposed to sun and stormy northeasterly (Bora) winds, from 300 to 1300 meters elevation.

items.name: Streptanthus longisiliquus
items.growersTips:
Sow these wild cabbage seeds indoors in early spring at a shallow depth of just five millimetres.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy to prevent young seedlings from rotting in our cool spring.
Watch out for cabbage white caterpillars and use fine netting to protect the leaves in summer.
Grow them in alkaline, well-drained soil to mimic their natural limestone cliff habitat.
Plant them alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter common brassica pests in your veg patch.

items.name: Streptanthus niger
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect them from wet UK frosts before planting out.
Grow this rare beauty in very sharply draining, gritty soil to mimic its native serpentine habitat.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love targeting the tender young foliage in damp British springtimes.
Position in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to maximise the chances of those dark purple blooms.
items.description: Streptanthus glandulosus subsp. niger is an endangered subspecies of flowering plant within the family Brassicaceae. Like other genus members, this herb has wavy petal margins with perimeter calluses that discourage larval herbivory. This plant is endemic to the Tiburon Peninsula of Northern California, and occurs at elevations below 150 m on serpentine grasslands. The common name for this subspecies is Tiburon jewelflower or black jewelflower. This annual herb blooms in May and June and displays dark purple sepals. The etymology of this genus scientific name derives from the Greek word strept

items.name: Streptanthus vernalis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic rocky scree.
Keep these delicate annuals safe from damp UK winters by growing them in pots you can move inside.
Water only when the top inch of soil is dry, as they hate soggy roots in cool British summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the tender young leaves during wet spring spells.
Plant them alongside low-growing thymes to help suppress weeds while keeping the soil quite dry.

items.name: Streptanthus tortuosus
items.growersTips:
Sow these shieldplant seeds thinly in spring just under the soil surface using a cold frame.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, letting the top inch dry out between light waterings.
Watch out for cabbage white butterflies and slugs, as they love munching on this brassica relative.
Grow them alongside native UK wildflowers in sandy, well-drained soil to mimic their rocky home.
Avoid rich fertilisers; this hardy plant thrives in poor, alkaline soils with plenty of sunshine.

items.name: Streptanthus howellii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic their native scree.
Keep them in an unheated greenhouse over winter to protect the foliage from persistent UK wet.
Water sparingly from below once the rosette is established to prevent crown rot in damp weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails during mild British springs as they love the tender young leaves.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than open borders to easily control soil moisture and drainage.

items.name: Stanleya viridiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in deep pots of gritty compost to accommodate their long, taproot-like habit.
Plant this prince's plume in your sunniest spot with sharp drainage to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for cabbage white butterflies, as they love this brassica family relative.
Avoid rich fertilisers, as this wild perennial thrives best in poor, alkaline, chalky soils.

items.name: Stanleya elata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring in deep pots to protect the long taproot before planting out in gritty soil.
Position this desert native in your sunniest south-facing border to mimic its hot homeland.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged UK dry spells to prevent root rot.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in damp British springs using beer traps or grit.
Leave the architectural seed heads over winter to provide structure and feed local garden birds.

items.name: Abdra
items.growersTips:
Sow your draba seeds in autumn in gritty, free-draining compost to let winter cold break dormancy.
Keep these alpine beauties in a raised bed or scree garden to protect them from wet UK winters.
Water them only at the base during dry spells to prevent their tight, hairy rosettes from rotting.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate yellow flower cushions first emerge.
Tuck sharp grit around the collar of the plant to shield it from damp soil and prevent winter damp.

items.name: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Shanghai'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly under cloches in early April or wait until July to prevent early bolting.
Sow seeds just one centimetre deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil to ensure rapid germination.
Water plants consistently at the base to keep the soil damp and prevent them going to seed early.
Protect young leaves from flea beetles by using a fine insect mesh immediately after sowing.
Harvest the outer leaves first for a continuous supply, or take the whole head when it is compact.

items.name: Boechera laevigata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to let the UK winter naturally break their dormancy for you.
Plant them in very gritty, alkaline soil to mimic their native rocky limestone woodland habitat.
Water only during dry spells in summer as this plant hates having wet feet in damp British winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails early in spring when the delicate young rosettes start to emerge.
Position them in dappled shade under deciduous trees to protect them from the harsh midday sun.
items.description: Borodinia laevigata is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name smooth rockcress. It is native to many areas of the eastern United States and Canada, where it grows in calcareous rocky woods and bluffs. It is moderately common throughout its range, although it is absent from the southeastern coastal plain and the far north.

items.name: Boechera lemmonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters without rot.
Position your Lemmon's rockcress in full sun, ideally tucked into a south-facing raised gravel bed.
Water very sparingly, only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between.
Protect the delicate rosettes from slugs and snails during damp UK spring nights using copper tape.
Propagate by sowing seeds in cold frames during autumn to let winter frosts naturally trigger growth.

items.name: Boechera missouriensis
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in autumn in a cold frame to let the UK winter chill naturally break their dormancy.
Plant them in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this plant hates soggy British weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the tender new rosette leaves.
Grow them alongside wild thyme or sedums in a sunny rock garden to mimic their natural rocky habitat.
items.description: Borodinia missouriensis, commonly called Missouri rockcress, is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae). It is native to the eastern United States, where it has a highly fragmented range localized in the Northeast, the Upper Midwest, the Interior Highlands, and the Southeast. Its natural habitat is typically on rocky or sandy woodlands and bluffs, in areas of acidic soil. It is generally uncommon throughout most of its range, with exception for the Interior Highlands region.

items.name: Boechera pulchra
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in autumn in a gritty, free-draining mix to let UK winter cold trigger germination.
Water very sparingly once established, only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails during wet British springs as they love the young shoots.
Plant them alongside thyme or sedums in a sunny rock garden to mimic their natural dry habitat.
Avoid rich fertilizers entirely because this alpine beauty thrives best in poor, alkaline soil.

items.name: Bivonaea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early autumn to match UK cool-season germination.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot during wet British winters.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the limited light levels of UK spring months.
Water sparingly only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to avoid damping off disease.
Plant alongside early-flowering Aubrieta to attract pollinators to this low-growing annual.

items.name: Dilophia
items.growersTips:
Start these high-altitude Asian greens in a cold frame by April to protect them from damp UK spring.
Sow your seeds shallowly at just five millimetres deep in free-draining, gritty compost mixes.
Water them lightly but consistently at the base to prevent waterlogging in cool British summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love targeting the tender young leaves of these rare brassicas.
Grow them alongside radishes to help deter common pests while maximizing your small vegetable plot.

items.name: Siraitia grosvenorii
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 25C and 2cm deep using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK outdoor summer temperatures are too cold for fruit set.
Provide a strong trellis for the vigorous vines and hand-pollinate the female flowers at midday.
Water deeply at the base keeping soil moist but not soggy to prevent root rot in humid glasshouses.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato fertilizer weekly once the first female flowers appear.

items.name: Gynostemma pentaphyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a container of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before winter frosts.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Provide a trellis or netting for the tendrils to climb up to two metres high in a sheltered spot.
Prune the vine back hard to ground level in late autumn before overwintering it in a greenhouse.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers.

items.name: Cucurbiteae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on their edge 2cm deep indoors in April to prevent rot before planting out in late May.
Water deeply at the base, never over the leaves, to prevent powdery mildew in humid UK summers.
Sink a plastic pot next to the plant base to direct water straight to the roots and save water.
Pinch out the main growing tip of pumpkins after four fruits form to focus energy before autumn.
Place a slate or tile under developing squash to stop them rotting on damp UK soil in late summer.

items.name: Cucumis metuliferus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using a heated propagator to ensure the required 21C minimum.
Grow inside a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are too cold and wet for outdoor survival.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent powdery mildew on the highly sensitive foliage.
Train the vigorous vines up sturdy trellises and pinch out the growing tips to encourage lateral fruiting.
Harvest only when the spikes turn bright orange as unripe green fruits lack the signature banana flavor.

items.name: Cucumis melo
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April on their sides 1.5cm deep in 9cm pots using a heated propagator set to 21C.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK summers are rarely warm enough for outdoor success.
Pinch out the main growing tip at the fifth leaf to encourage side shoots that bear the fruit.
Water the soil around the base of the plant daily but keep the main stem dry to prevent rot.
Place a tile or piece of wood under developing melons to stop them rotting on the damp soil.

items.name: Cucumis sativus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on their edge 2cm deep in April indoors to prevent rotting in damp UK spring compost.
Water the soil around the base daily, never the leaves, to prevent powdery mildew in humid weather.
Grow all-female greenhouse varieties like Carmen to avoid bitter fruits caused by cross-pollination.
Pinch out the main growing tip at the top of the support to encourage heavy-fruiting side shoots.
Plant alongside dill or marigolds to deter aphids and attract pollinators to your outdoor crops.

items.name: Momordica cochinchinensis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 25C using a heated propagator to survive the short UK summer.
Plant in a deep container of rich, free-draining loam and place in your warmest, sunniest greenhouse.
Hand-pollinate the distinct male and female yellow flowers daily as UK insects ignore them.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil damp but never let the roots sit in cold mud.
Provide a sturdy trellis or overhead netting to support the heavy, vigorous climbing vines.

items.name: Thladiantha dubia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers ten centimetres deep in spring using large pots to restrict their highly invasive roots.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to support the rapid growth of this vigorous climber.
Provide a sturdy two-metre trellis or wires against a south-facing wall to maximise summer sun.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers in August as UK native insects often ignore this dioecious plant.
Cut all vines back to ground level in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect tubers from hard frost.

items.name: Momordica charantia
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2.5cm deep using a heated propagator set to 22C to ensure germination.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing brick wall to survive the cool UK summer nights.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip when it reaches 1.5 metres to encourage productive side branches.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers using a small paintbrush because UK pollinator activity can be low.

items.name: Trichosanthes kirilowii
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 20C in deep pots to protect the taproot before late May planting.
Grow against a south-facing wall or in a greenhouse to provide the high summer heat this vine needs.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells to keep the moisture-loving roots damp.
Provide a sturdy trellis at least two meters high to support the heavy climbing vines and fruits.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in June to feed the plant and retain soil moisture.

items.name: Cucumis maderaspatanus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator to survive chilly UK springs.
Grow this climber against a warm south-facing wall on a trellis to maximise scarce UK summer sun.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to avoid wetting leaves and preventing powdery mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip at 1.5 metres to encourage fruiting side shoots to develop.
Plant alongside radishes to deter cucumber beetles and conserve precious greenhouse border space.

items.name: Trichosanthes tricuspidata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator to overcome cool UK spring soils.
Grow this vigorous climber inside a polytunnel or greenhouse to ensure the high heat it requires.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent rot.
Train vines onto strong trellis support and pinch out growing tips to encourage lateral fruiting.
Hand-pollinate the nocturnal white flowers using a small brush since UK night pollinators are rare.

items.name: Telfairia pedata
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at 25C to ensure germination.
Grow this tender vine inside a greenhouse or conservatory to protect it from cool UK summer nights.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during summer, keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Provide a sturdy trellis or overhead netting to support the heavy, vigorous climbing vines.
Prune lateral shoots back to two leaves in late summer to redirect energy into ripening the fruit.

items.name: Dendrosicyos socotrana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender desert tree in a gritty loam-based cactus compost with fifty percent perlite.
Keep the plant above twelve degrees Celsius year-round in a heated greenhouse or bright indoors.
Water only when the soil is bone dry in summer and keep completely dry throughout the winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic the intense light of Socotra.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite under glass and treat immediately with biological controls.

items.name: Inodorus Group
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep using individual pots on a warm windowsill.
Plant out in late May after frosts, spacing sixty centimetres apart in rich, moisture-retentive soil.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil damp but avoid wetting the leaves to prevent rot.
Pinch out the main growing tip after five leaves to encourage lateral fruiting branches to develop.
Support developing melons on raised tiles or nets to prevent ground rot in damp British summers.

items.name: Cucumis melo ‘Montreal Market’
items.growersTips:
Sow indoors in April at 2cm deep using individual pots on a heated propagation mat set to 21C.
Grow on in a greenhouse or polytunnel as the UK climate is too cool for outdoor success.
Train the main stem up a vertical support and pinch out the growing tip at the fifth leaf.
Support the heavy, netted melons in individual net bags tied to the frame to prevent vine breakage.
Water deeply at the base keeping foliage dry, then reduce watering when fruits reach full size.

items.name: Herpetospermum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Plant out in June against a south-facing wall to maximise sun exposure and shelter from cold winds.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil moist without wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy trellis or A-frame to keep the heavy fruits off damp UK soil.
Prune the main growing tip when it reaches two metres to encourage fruiting lateral branches.

items.name: Telfairia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 3cm depth using bottom heat of 25C to overcome the cool UK spring.
Grow in a greenhouse or south-facing polytunnel to meet the high heat demand of this African vine.
Provide a sturdy trellis at least two meters high to support the heavy, vigorous climbing tendrils.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil moist but never waterlogged in damp UK summers.
Prune the main shoot at one meter to encourage lateral branching and increase leaf yield.

items.name: Trichosanthes scabra
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 20C in deep pots to protect taproots before late May planting.
Grow against a south-facing wall under glass or polytunnel to survive cool UK summer nights.
Water deeply at the base weekly keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK weather.
Prune lateral shoots after the fifth leaf to encourage female flowers and improve fruit set.
Incorporate well-rotted manure and grit into soil to ensure rich nutrients with sharp drainage.

items.name: Trichosanthes pentaphylla
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 20C in deep pots to avoid disturbing the sensitive taproot system
Grow this tender climber inside a polytunnel or greenhouse to ensure the high heat it needs in the UK
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot
Train vines up a sturdy trellis and prune side shoots after the first flower to boost fruit yield
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and use organic wool pellets around the base to protect them

items.name: Trichosanthes cochinchinensis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at 22C to ensure germination
Grow in a greenhouse or south-facing polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity this vine needs
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot
Train the vigorous vines up sturdy trellises and hand-pollinate the white night-blooming flowers
Protect young plants from slugs in May using organic beer traps or copper tape around container rims

items.name: Cucumis argenteus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool British springs.
Plant out in late May in a sunny, sheltered spot using raised mounds to improve cold soil drainage.
Water deeply at the base twice weekly to keep soil damp but avoid wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip at five leaves to encourage lateral fruiting branches to develop.
Grow alongside radishes to deter cucumber beetles and under fleece until flowers need pollination.

items.name: Citrullus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep in individual pots using a heated propagator.
Grow plants in a greenhouse or polytunnel to ensure they get the high heat and humidity they need.
Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but keep the foliage dry to avoid rot.
Place a slate or tile under developing fruit to protect it from damp soil and prevent rotting.
Hand pollinate female flowers using a small brush with pollen from male flowers on a sunny morning.

items.name: Cucumis melo var. cantalupensis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel to provide the high heat and humidity these melons require in the UK.

items.name: Benincaseae

items.name: Doyerea emetocathartica

items.name: Gynostemma

items.name: Alsomitra

items.name: Cucumis melo ‘Sprite’

items.name: Ecballium elaterium

items.name: Kedrostis nana

items.name: Ibervillea sonorae

items.name: Melothria

Sow seeds indoors in April at two centimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty-one degrees Celsius.

items.name: Benincasa hispida var. chieh-qua

Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall in fertile soil rich in well-rotted manure.

items.name: Cucumis anguria

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.

items.name: Momordica foetida

Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at a steady 22C to 25C.

items.name: Fevillea cordifolia

items.name: Trichosanthes dioica

items.name: Cucumis melo var. flexuosus

items.name: Momordica dioica

items.name: Momordica cymbalaria

items.name: Cucumis melo Makuwa Group

items.name: Coccinia sessilifolia

Apply a high-potassium tomato fertiliser weekly once yellow flowers appear to boost fruit set.

items.name: Cucurbita moschata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep on their sides in 9cm pots to prevent rotting in cold UK soil.

items.name: Gerrardanthus lobatus

items.name: Gerrardanthus macrorhizus
items.growersTips:
Grow this caudiciform in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with the tuber sitting on top.

Water only when the soil dries out fully during summer, avoiding wetting the exposed swollen base.

Check the underside of leaves weekly in summer for red spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor air.

items.name: Praecitrullus fistulosus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to survive the cool UK spring.

Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent mildew.
Hand-pollinate the yellow flowers using a cotton bud because UK pollinator activity can be low.

items.name: Acanthosicyos
items.growersTips:
Grow Acanthosicyos horridus in a heated greenhouse with sandy, free-draining cactus compost.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, mimicking desert conditions to prevent root rot.
Sow seeds individually in deep pots at a depth of two centimeters to protect the long taproot.
Install a sturdy trellis early to support the heavy, sprawling, extremely thorny green stems.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of twelve degrees Celsius to keep this desert melon alive.

items.name: Benincasa
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2.5cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to survive the cool UK spring.
Grow in a greenhouse or against a south-facing wall in fertile soil with a pH of 6.0 to 6.8.

Train the heavy vines up a sturdy trellis and support swelling winter melons with net hammocks.
Water deeply at the base to keep soil moist but avoid wetting leaves to prevent powdery mildew.

items.name: Momordica

Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using a heated propagator to maintain the vital 22C minimum.

Water daily at the base to keep soil moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in cool UK nights.

Hand pollinate the yellow flowers using a small paintbrush because UK greenhouse pollinators are scarce.

items.name: Cayaponia tayuya
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at twenty-one degrees Celsius using deep pots to protect taproots.
Grow this tender vine inside a greenhouse or polytunnel to ensure the high heat and humidity needed.

Water deeply at the base twice a week to keep soil moist but prevent waterlogging and root rot.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato feed every two weeks once the vine reaches two meters tall.

items.name: Lagenaria sphaerica
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.

Pinch out the main growing tip at 2 metres to encourage lateral fruiting branches in short summers.
Hand-pollinate the white evening flowers using a paintbrush as UK nocturnal pollinators are scarce.

items.name: Trochomeria

Grow this tender African caudiciform in a greenhouse or sunny windowsill to protect from UK frost.
Plant seeds 1cm deep in a free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two and horticultural grit.
Water deeply only when the soil is dry, then keep completely dry in winter to prevent tuber rot.
Watch for red spider mite under glass and treat early with biological controls like Phytoseiulus.
Train the climbing annual vines up a small trellis or moss pole during the active summer growth.

items.name: Schizocarpum parviflorum

Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Grow this tender climber inside a polytunnel or greenhouse to ensure the high humidity it craves.
Water the base deeply twice a week keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK summers.
Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy trellis or netting to keep the small fragile fruits off wet soil.
Apply a high-potassium liquid tomato fertilizer every fortnight once the first yellow flowers appear.

items.name: Citrullus afer

items.name: Sicana odorifera

items.name: Zehneria

items.name: Apodanthera undulata

items.name: Lagenaria rufa

items.name: Cayaponia espelina

items.name: Diplocyclos

items.name: Lagenaria siceraria

items.name: Citrullus ecirrhosus

items.name: Melothria scabra
