Plant this California native in a raised bed with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only during severe summer droughts once established, as damp soil will quickly rot the roots.
Position your pot in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to mimic its hot desert habitat.
Protect the crown from winter wet by top-dressing the surrounding soil with a thick layer of gravel.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer rather than trying to divide its delicate taproot.

items.name: Eriogonum nidularium
items.growersTips:
Plant this birdnest buckwheat in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Keep watering to a absolute minimum, only drenching it during prolonged summer droughts in July.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most south-facing spot you have to mimic its native desert heat.
Protect the delicate, papery winter skeletons from harsh gales by placing them near a house wall.
Top-dress the soil with gravel rather than organic mulch to prevent the crown from rotting in rain.

items.name: Eriogonum ochrocephalum
items.growersTips:
Plant this ochre buckwheat in a raised bed or rockery with gritty, free-draining alkaline soil.
Protect it from wet winter rot by placing a layer of gravel mulch right around the plant collar.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as this hardy herb absolutely hates soggy roots.
Give it a light trim after summer flowering to keep its neat, low-growing cushion habit tidy.
Position it in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its native hot, dry scrubland home.

items.name: Eriogonum ovalifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a raised bed or scree garden with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Protect the woolly foliage from winter rain by placing a pane of glass or cloche over it from November.
Water only during dry spring spells, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Surround the collar with a deep layer of granite chippings to prevent rot at the base of the plant.
Grow it in a terracotta pot using a loam-less alpine compost mix so you can move it out of the rain.

items.name: Eriogonum nudum
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sunniest spot with gritty, sharp-draining soil to survive UK wet.
Keep watering to an absolute minimum once established, only soaking during prolonged summer droughts.
Protect the crown from winter rot by mulching with gravel or horticultural grit rather than compost.
Grow it alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme or oregano which love the same dry, sunny conditions.
Sow seeds in pots during early spring, barely covering them with a very thin layer of fine grit.

items.name: Eriogonum nummulare
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mojave native in a raised bed with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, letting the soil dry out completely between times.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its hot, arid desert home.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a cold glass greenhouse when winter rain hits.
Avoid rich soils and fertilisers entirely, as nutrient-poor ground keeps its growth tight and neat.

items.name: Eriogonum parishii
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate annual in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure the sharp drainage it craves.
Water very sparingly only during dry summer spells as this California native hates wet roots.
Sow seeds in early spring under cover using a gritty seed compost and barely cover them with grit.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its desert home.
Keep a close eye out for slugs and snails when the tiny seedlings first emerge in the spring.

items.name: Eriogonum parvifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sunniest spot using a very gritty, free-draining cactus compost.
Avoid summer watering entirely once established to prevent root rot in our damp British climate.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to keep its low, mounding shape neat and tidy.
Protect it from winter wet with a rain shelter or by keeping it in a moveable terracotta pot.
Grow it alongside sedums and thymes which thrive in the same dry, nutrient-poor soil conditions.

items.name: Eriogonum palmerianum
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate annual buckwheat in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the seeds shallowly in early spring, barely covering them with a thin layer of fine grit.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot possible, ideally against a warm south-facing brick wall.
Water only when the soil is dry to the touch, as this desert native hates soggy roots.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using copper tape around your containers.

items.name: Eriogonum panamintense
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mojave native in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure it survives wet UK winters.
Mix two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to mimic its natural free-draining desert soil.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most wind-sheltered spot of your patio to maximize summer heat.
Avoid watering entirely during damp UK winters to prevent the crown from rotting in the cold.
Surround the base with a thick layer of granite chippings to keep wet soil away from the foliage.

items.name: Eriogonum pelinophilum
items.growersTips:
Give this rare clay-loving beauty a raised bed with heavy clay mixed with plenty of sharp grit.
Keep it dry in our wet UK winters by using a rain shelter or planting it in a cold alpine house.
Water it deeply once a week during hot dry summers but let the soil dry out completely between times.
Surround the base with a thick layer of slate chippings to keep damp soil off its low foliage.
Prune very lightly after its yellow summer blooms fade to keep its tight mounded shape tidy.

items.name: Eriogonum pendulum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Oregon native in a raised bed or gravel scree to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs.
Keep watering to an absolute minimum once established, only soaking it during prolonged dry spells.
Surround the base with a thick layer of grit to prevent wet soil from rotting the lower foliage.
Grow it alongside hardy sedums or thyme which thrive in the same poor, alkaline, sun-baked soils.
Leave the dried flower heads on through winter to provide structure and seeds for local UK birds.

items.name: Persicaria lapathifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in damp clay or boggy soil near UK ponds at a depth equal to the original nursery pot size.
Water heavily during dry summer spells to mimic its natural British canal and riverbank habitat.
Watch for dock beetles in June and handpick them to prevent severe foliage damage in wet weather.
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn after the first frost to keep the crown healthy.
Divide the root clump in early spring using a sharp spade to control its vigorous spreading habit.

items.name: Persicaria arifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in boggy soil or pond edges where the roots can remain constantly wet during UK summers.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring when the young, tender triangular leaves first emerge.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous root clumps in early spring just as new growth begins.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris or Iris pseudacorus which thrive in the same wet conditions.

items.name: Coccoloba caracasana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before UK frosts.
Water thoroughly once the top two inches of soil dry out, reducing this to a minimum in winter.
Prune in late spring after new growth starts to maintain its shape and remove frost-damaged stems.
Position in a conservatory or south-facing room to maximise light during dull UK autumn months.
Repot every two years in spring using a grit-heavy mix to ensure the sharp drainage it requires.

items.name: Persicaria dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in boggy soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep.
Propagate by division in mid-spring to control its vigorous spread in small UK garden ponds.
Cut back the decaying foliage to the base in late autumn to keep the water clear and tidy.
In colder UK regions, mulch the crown heavily in November to protect it from hard winter frosts.
Pair with Caltha palustris to provide early spring colour before this foliage fully emerges.

items.name: Muehlenbeckia hastulata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean climber against a warm south-facing UK wall to shield it from harsh winter frost.
Water your young plant deeply once a week during dry British summers until its roots are established.
Prune the vigorous tangled stems hard in early spring to keep its growth shape under control.
Mix plenty of grit into your clay soil before planting to ensure the roots never sit in winter wet.
Grow it alongside winter-flowering clematis to create a lovely year-round evergreen screen.

items.name: Muehlenbeckia sagittifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this climber in well-drained soil enriched with grit to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Position it against a south-facing wall to shield its delicate arrow leaves from cold British winds.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Prune hard in early spring to control its vigorous spread and encourage lush new green growth.
Mulch the base heavily with bark chips in late autumn to protect the crown from hard frosts.

items.name: Coccoloba padiformis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical in a warm conservatory or heated greenhouse to survive cold UK winters.
Plant in a very free-draining, acidic peat-free compost mix with added perlite to prevent root rot.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top two inches of soil have completely dried out.
Position in bright, indirect light near a south-facing window but shade from scorching summer sun.
Mist the leaves daily or use a gravel tray to mimic the high humidity of its native rainforest home.

items.name: Fallopia convolvulus
items.growersTips:
Hand-pull young black-bindweed seedlings in May before their taproots anchor deeply in damp UK soil.
Hoe hoeable beds weekly in spring to sever the delicate stems of emerging seedlings at soil level.
Unwind the twining stems from your cultivated plants early in summer before they strangle growth.
Mulch borders with a five-centimetre layer of bark in March to suppress light-stimulated seeds.
Bag and dispose of mature plants in August before they drop hundreds of viable seeds into the soil.

items.name: Eriogonum cedrorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine buck-wheat in a raised gravel bed or scree garden to mimic its dry native slopes.
Mix equal parts grit and peat-free compost to give its roots the sharp, fast drainage it craves.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells, as wet winter soil is this plant's biggest enemy.
Protect the crown with a slate collar to keep damp winter mulch from rotting the base of the herb.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill can trigger germination.

items.name: Eriogonum soredium
items.growersTips:
This dwarf buckwheat needs sharp grit mixed into your UK soil to survive wet winter root rot.
Plant it in your sunniest, windiest rock garden spot to mimic its native dry Utah ridges.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Protect the crown with a layer of pea gravel to keep damp winter wet away from the foliage.
Grow this alpine gem in a terracotta alpine pot so you can move it under glass for winter.

items.name: Persicaria odorata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pot to easily move this frost-tender herb indoors to a sunny windowsill before October.
Keep the soil constantly soggy by placing the pot in a shallow saucer filled with rainwater.
Plant in moisture-retentive, peat-free compost mixed with well-rotted manure for rich nutrients.
Harvest the young leaf tips weekly in summer to encourage bushy growth and prevent leggy stems.
Overwinter at temperatures above five degrees Celsius to prevent the tropical plant from dying.
items.description: Persicaria odorata is a species of flowering plant in the knotweed family, Polygonaceae. It is sometimes referred to by the common names Vietnamese coriander, rau răm, laksa leaf, Vietnamese cilantro, phak phai, praew leaf, hot mint, Cambodian mint and Vietnamese mint, is an herb whose leaves are used in Southeast Asian and Northeast Indian cooking.

items.name: Ruprechtia salicifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South American shrub in a large pot with loam-based compost to move indoors for winter.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to mimic its habitat.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormant period.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to shape the shrub and remove winter dieback.
Provide grit-heavy, free-draining soil to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK autumns and winters.

items.name: Koenigia
items.growersTips:
Pop Koenigia in moisture-retentive clay soil that never dries out, ideally near a UK garden pond.
Plant container-grown Koenigia campanulata at the exact same depth as its pot in early spring.
Give it a hard chop right down to the ground in late autumn after the first frost hits your plot.
Watch out for slugs devouring the tender new spring shoots, so use beer traps around the crown.
Divide your Koenigia clumps every three years in March to keep this vigorous herb from taking over.

items.name: Persicaria capitata
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink knotweed in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water young plants weekly until established, then only during prolonged dry British summer spells.
Cut back frost-damaged foliage in early spring to encourage fresh bronze-leaved ground cover.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using beer traps or organic grit barriers.
Grow alongside blue-flowered Campanula or dwarf conifers to contrast the pink globe-like blooms.

items.name: Systenotheca
items.growersTips:
Tuck your Systenotheca into free-draining sandy loam to stop winter wet rotting its delicate crown.
Give it a cozy fleece wrap by late October to shield this tender herb from harsh UK frosts.
Water deeply at the base only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent mildew.
Snip back the spent summer flowering stems in September to keep its growth compact and bushy.
Plant it alongside rosemary or thyme to help deter local slugs from munching the young shoots.

items.name: Fallopia aubertii
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in a sturdy spot where its rampant growth won't crush weaker fences.
Prune it hard in late winter or early spring to keep its massive size under control in UK gardens.
Water young plants weekly until established, then let the UK rain do the work as it tolerates drought.
Plant in poor or average soil to naturally restrict its speed, as rich soil makes it grow too wild.
Watch out for aphids on fresh spring shoots, and simply blast them off with a quick hose spray.

items.name: Rumex
items.growersTips:
Sow Rumex sanguineus seeds in spring at five millimetres deep in moisture-retentive, neutral soil.
Water container-grown sorrel twice weekly in dry UK summers to stop leaves turning bitter and tough.
Cut back flower spikes in July to prevent invasive self-seeding and encourage fresh salad leaves.
Watch for green dock beetles in May and handpick them to prevent skeletonisation of the foliage.
Divide established clumps in March using a sharp spade to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.

items.name: Persicaria mitis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam near pond edges to mimic its native UK wetland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 5mm to allow natural winter chilling to break seed dormancy.
Water weekly during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp, mimicking bog conditions.
Cut back dead stems to ground level in late autumn to prevent self-seeding and tidy the winter plot.
Plant alongside Marsh Marigold or Water Forget-me-not to create a cohesive native UK wetland display.

items.name: Persicaria orientalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or cold-stratify in the fridge for six weeks to break dormancy in UK climates.
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade to prevent leaf scorch.
Water deeply twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp.
Stake the tall, hollow stems by mid-spring using hazel twigs to prevent wind damage in UK gales.
Deadhead spent pink tassels in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your borders.

items.name: Polygonum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring after the last frost, barely covering them with five millimetres of fine soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry spells in UK summer months.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in late May to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Watch for aphids and slugs on tender new growth, using organic barriers or beer traps in damp weather.
Clear dead annual plants completely in autumn to prevent excessive self-seeding across your borders.

items.name: Coccoloba pubescens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Caribbean native in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors by October
Water thoroughly only when the top three inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in cool weather
Wipe the massive leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations indoors
Prune in late spring just as new growth starts to control its size for indoor winter housing
Keep winter temperatures strictly above twelve degrees Celsius to prevent leaf drop and dieback

items.name: Coccoloba uvifera
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water deeply once the top two inches of soil dry out, reducing this to once a month during winter.
Prune in late spring to control size, cutting just above a leaf node to encourage bushier growth.
Position in your brightest south-facing room or heated conservatory to meet its high light needs.
Feed fortnightly from April to September using a balanced liquid fertiliser diluted to half strength.

items.name: Rheum
items.growersTips:
Plant your crown in autumn with the growing tip just visible at the soil surface, never buried deep.
Mulch heavily with well-rotted manure in late winter, keeping it clear of the central crown buds.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to keep those thick stalks juicy, avoiding the crown itself.
Pull stalks with a firm twist and pull at the base rather than cutting them to prevent crown rot.
Stop harvesting by late June to let the plant build up its energy reserves for next year's crop.

items.name: Stenogonum
items.growersTips:
Plant this little Mexican herb in a gritty, free-draining loam to survive damp British winters.
Keep your potted plants on a sunny south-facing windowsill to mimic its native warm habitat.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this species hates soggy roots.
Sow the seeds shallowly indoors in early April using a heated propagator to boost germination.
Watch out for greenhouse aphids in May and gently wash them off with a organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Fallopia baldschuanica
items.growersTips:
Prune this vigorous climber hard in late winter to keep its rapid growth from overtaking your patio.
Plant it in poor, well-drained soil to naturally restrict its otherwise rampant, invasive spread.
Grow it in a sturdy container to stop the aggressive roots from colonising your flowerbeds.
Water deeply only during dry summer spells once established, as it easily tolerates UK rainfall.
Watch out for aphids on fresh spring shoots, blasting them off with a quick spray from your hose.

items.name: Persicaria wallichii
items.growersTips:
Grow this highly invasive plant only in a large, sturdy container to prevent spread via rhizomes.
Submerge the pot in a bog garden or keep soil constantly wet to mimic its native damp habitat.
Cut stems to the ground in late autumn and bag the debris to prevent self-seeding in your garden.
Plant in partial shade to protect the foliage from scorching during hot UK summer afternoons.
Wear gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from the sap when cutting back the hollow stems.

items.name: Reynoutria sachalinensis
items.growersTips:
Do not plant Giant Knotweed in the UK as it is highly invasive and illegal to cause it to grow.
Report any wild sightings to the Environment Agency to prevent further spread in UK waterways.
If present on your property hire a certified specialist to treat it with systemic glyphosate.
Dispose of all plant material at licensed landfills rather than composting to prevent regrowth.
Eradicate infestations before selling your home to avoid severe legal and mortgage issues.

items.name: Duma
items.growersTips:
Plant Duma florulenta in well-drained, gritty loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Prune back woody stems by one-third in early spring to encourage fresh, bushy growth and more flowers.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails in damp British springs using organic beer traps or grit.
Propagate this perennial by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to overwinter in a cold frame.

items.name: Reynoutria japonica
items.growersTips:
Inject glyphosate into stems at the base in late summer when nutrients flow down to the rhizomes.
Dig out the entire root system down to three metres deep and sift the soil to remove all fragments.
Cover the infested area with heavy-duty root barrier membrane extending two metres past the stems.
Dispose of all cut stems at a licensed landfill site rather than composting them in your garden.
Monitor the soil weekly from March to October for emerging reddish-purple asparagus-like shoots.

items.name: Muehlenbeckia platyclada
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender ribbon bush indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter frost.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp air.
Prune leggy stems back by a third in April to encourage that unique, flat, ribbon-like green growth.
Repot in spring using a free-draining mix of peat-free compost with plenty of added horticultural grit.
Keep a close eye out for spider mites when you bring it inside your warm, dry home for the winter.

items.name: Coccoloba gigantifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring this giant indoors by mid-October as it cannot survive a damp, freezing British winter.
Grow your specimen in a large pot so you can easily move it inside a heated conservatory for winter.
Keep the compost consistently moist with tepid rainwater but never let the pot sit in cold water.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed from April to August to boost those massive leaves.
Wipe the giant leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and maximize scarce UK winter sunlight.

items.name: Eriogonum bicolor
items.growersTips:
Plant this little buckwheat in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure it gets the sharp drainage it needs.
Keep watering to an absolute minimum once established, only soaking it during prolonged dry spells.
Protect the foliage from excessive winter wet by placing a cloche over it from November to March.
Prune the spent flower stems back to the base in late summer to keep the mounded shape tidy.
Surround it with low-growing thymes or sedums which thrive in the same poor, gritty soil conditions.

items.name: Eriogonum tiehmii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Nevada gem in a mix of seventy percent grit and alpine compost to mimic its dry home.
Keep it under a cold glass frame or alpine house over winter to shield it from relentless UK rain.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, using a tray from below to keep the foliage completely dry.
Top-dress the pot with a thick layer of limestone chippings to prevent wet soil rotting the neck.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums in a raised scree bed for the perfect dry-loving companions.

items.name: Reynoutria multiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant the tuberous roots fifteen centimetres deep in autumn using well-drained soil to avoid rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to support the vigorous climbing stems.
Provide a strong trellis or obelisk in spring before the rapid twining growth begins.
Lift tubers in late autumn and store in dry peat in a frost-free shed over UK winters.
Grow in large pots to contain the vigorous root system and prevent it overtaking borders.

items.name: Muehlenbeckia australis
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in a sturdy container to easily control its highly invasive UK spread.
Prune hard in late winter to keep its rampant, tangled growth from smothering nearby garden shrubs.
Grow it in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet, cold British winters.
Water young plants weekly in summer, but let established ones dry out to curb excessive growth.
Watch out for aphids on fresh spring shoots, blasting them off with a sharp blast from your hose.

items.name: Hollisteria
items.growersTips:
Since Hollisteria is a rare US desert annual, grow it in a greenhouse to mimic that dry warmth.
Sow the seeds shallowly in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent UK damp from rotting them.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, using a tray underneath to keep the foliage completely dry.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites, which love the hot, dry air this herb prefers.
Place your pots on the sunniest south-facing windowsill you have to catch every bit of UK sunshine.

items.name: Nemacaulis
items.growersTips:
Sow woolly cabbage seeds in late spring using a very sandy, free-draining soil mix to mimic dunes.
Keep these desert annuals in your sunniest south-facing spot to cope with cool British summers.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil is bone dry to prevent the delicate stems from rotting.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under cover when heavy autumn rain starts.
Avoid feeding these low-nutrient specialists, as rich UK composts will quickly kill their roots.

items.name: Muehlenbeckia ephedroides
items.growersTips:
Grow this leafless NZ native in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Plant it in your sunniest, south-facing gravel garden or container to mimic its dry riverbed home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings in summer.
Prune back any wayward, tangled grey stems in late spring after the last frost to keep it tidy.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of gravel in autumn to shield it from freezing UK winter damp.

items.name: Eriogonum gracilipes
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in a raised bed or scree garden with fifty percent grit to survive UK wet.
Give it a deep pot with a thick gravel mulch to keep the foliage dry during damp British winters.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Protect the crown from winter rot by placing a glass cloche over the plant from November to March.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums and sedums in full sun to recreate its native mountain home.

items.name: Brunnichia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot using deep gritty loam to mimic its native riverbank habitat
Provide a sturdy trellis or pergola to support its vigorous woody tendrils as it climbs in summer
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep soil relatively dry throughout winter
Prune hard in late winter to restrict spread and encourage fresh flowering wood for the summer
Mulch the root zone heavily with straw in November to protect the crown from severe UK frosts

items.name: Dodecahema
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.
Position in full sun next to low-growing Sedums to mimic its natural dry, open habitat.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, as this annual dislikes UK dampness.
Protect young seedlings from slugs using organic grit barriers during wet British spring nights.
Collect seeds in late summer before autumn rains rot the seed heads to ensure next year's crop.

items.name: Fagopyrum tataricum
items.growersTips:
Sow Tartary buckwheat seeds in late May once UK frosts pass, about two centimetres deep in the soil.
This tough herb thrives in poor, acidic UK soils, so do not add any rich compost or fertilisers.
Water young seedlings weekly if the British summer is dry, but let established plants dry out.
Watch out for slugs and snails when the shoots first emerge, as they love the tender young leaves.
Harvest the nutrient-rich seeds in autumn once the hulls turn a deep, rustic brown colour.

items.name: Rheum ribes
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, fertile, free-draining soil with a pH of 6.0 to 6.8 to mimic its native rocky slopes.
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of 1.5cm, keeping temperatures around 15 to 20 Celsius.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the crown dry to prevent rot in damp weather.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Do not harvest any stalks in the first two years to allow the deep taproot system to establish.

items.name: Rheum rhabarbarum
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns in autumn with the buds just at the soil surface to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Feed generously with well-rotted manure in late winter, keeping it clear of the emerging crowns.
Stop harvesting by mid-June to let the plant build up its energy reserves for next spring.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to stop the stalks from becoming tough, stringy and woody.
Watch out for crown rot in soggy winters, and split congested clumps every five years in spring.

items.name: Chorizanthe
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a cold frame to protect them.
Grow in a sharply draining, gritty soil mix with added perlite to survive wet UK spring weather.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp air.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to mimic their native arid environment.
Plant alongside drought-tolerant sedums or sempervivums to create a compatible dry gravel garden.

items.name: Coccoloba
items.growersTips:
Bring your sea grape indoors by October because UK frosts will quickly kill this tender Caribbean shrub.
Plant in a very free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to stop winter root rot in damp UK weather.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, then let the pot drain completely.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs in winter when your indoor heating makes the air dry and stagnant.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring just as new growth starts to keep its shape compact indoors.

items.name: Fagopyrum esculentum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring after the last frost at a depth of two centimetres in well-drained soil.
Water young seedlings weekly during dry spells but avoid waterlogging to prevent root rot.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender young shoots during damp UK spring nights and use barriers.
Incorporate organic matter into poor sandy soils before sowing to help retain essential moisture.
Grow alongside brassicas as a green manure to suppress weeds and attract beneficial pollinators.

items.name: Polygonella
items.growersTips:
Grow this coastal US native in sharply drained, sandy soil to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass, barely covering them with a fine grit layer.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic its hot, dry natural habitat.
Leave the dried seed heads on over winter to provide structure and protect the crown from frost.

items.name: Pterostegia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring just under the soil surface to match chilly UK temperatures.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, especially during our cool, wet British spring months.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young shoots, using organic beer traps to protect them.
Grow this delicate herb in a sheltered, partially shaded spot to mimic its native woodland edge.
Mix plenty of grit into your garden beds to ensure the roots do not rot in heavy clay soils.

items.name: Symmeria
items.growersTips:
Plant this Brazilian river-dweller in a heated pond or water-logged acidic bog garden at 20C minimum.
Keep the soil constantly submerged in rainwater to mimic its natural Amazonian flooding cycle.
Overwinter your potted specimens indoors under bright grow lights as they cannot survive UK frosts.
Feed weekly with an acidic liquid seaweed fertilizer during spring to mimic rich river silt deposits.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late summer and rooting them directly in warm, muddy water.

items.name: Antigonon
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican vine in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant in free-draining gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet British autumns and winters.
Prune stems back to the base in late winter to encourage vigorous new flowering growth in spring.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during summer to support the intense pink blooms.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or conservatory to meet its high heat and light needs.

items.name: Chorizanthe brevicornu
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 2mm in a gritty, sharply draining soil mix to prevent root rot.
Grow in containers under a cold frame to protect this desert annual from excessive UK winter wet.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is bone dry, mimicking its native arid habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximize limited UK summer heat.
Sow alongside Sedums in rockeries to provide the ultra-dry, low-nutrient soil conditions it needs.

items.name: Chorizanthe douglasii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn using a cold frame to mimic winter chill.
Grow in a gritty, sharply draining soil mix with added perlite to survive wet UK winter rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry, keeping foliage dry to prevent mildew.
Position in the brightest, south-facing spot of your garden to maximise limited UK summer sun.
Plant alongside low-growing sedums or thymes which share its need for dry, nutrient-poor soil.

items.name: Chorizanthe corrugata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under glass at a depth of two millimetres using a gritty, free-draining compost
Grow in terracotta pots placed in full sun to mimic its native arid habitat and prevent root rot
Water sparingly from below only when the soil is dry to the touch, keeping the foliage bone dry
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to ensure the rapid drainage it needs
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using copper tape around pots during wet UK spring days

items.name: Chorizanthe cuspidata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a cold frame to protect them
Grow in a sharply draining sandy loam mix with added grit to mimic its native coastal dune habitat
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in wet UK summers
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to maximise essential light levels
Plant alongside low-growing sedums or thrift to provide structural support for its sprawling stems

items.name: Chorizanthe membranacea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn under cold frames to survive wet UK winters.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix with fifty percent horticultural sand to prevent root rot.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry, mimicking dry California summers.
Position pots in the brightest south-facing spot to maximise sunlight during short UK summer days.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots as damp UK weather makes them highly vulnerable.

items.name: Chorizanthe fimbriata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn under glass to mimic its native dry winter cycle before spring planting
Grow in a gritty scree bed or terracotta pots with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp British climates
Position in the most sun-baked south-facing spot in your garden to encourage the pink fringed blooms
Plant alongside hardy sedums and sempervivums which share its extreme drought and drainage needs

items.name: Chorizanthe parryi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn under a cold frame to mimic winter wet then dry out for spring planting.
Grow in a gritty mix of five parts sharp sand to one part loam to survive wet UK winter dampness.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry to prevent root rot in humid UK summers.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or gravel garden to maximise scarce UK summer heat.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs using copper tape as damp UK weather brings heavy infestations.

items.name: Chorizanthe orcuttiana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface of a sharply draining, gritty, low-nutrient sandy mix.
Grow in pots under a cold frame to protect this winter-annual from excessive UK winter wetness.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil dries completely, mimicking its arid native habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to maximise scarce UK summer warmth and light.
Avoid all fertilisers as high nutrient levels will quickly kill this specialized coastal plant.

items.name: Chorizanthe pungens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained sandy soil to mimic its native dry Mediterranean-style habitat.
Grow in terracotta pots with a grit-heavy compost mix to ensure the roots never sit in UK winter wet.
Place in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise warmth and prevent damping off.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully.
Position near low-growing Sedums to provide physical support and prevent wind damage to weak stems.

items.name: Chorizanthe staticoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn under a cold frame to survive wet UK winters before spring planting.
Grow in a mix of three parts grit to one part peat-free compost to mimic dry native scree soils.
Water only during prolonged dry spring spells, allowing the gritty growing medium to dry fully.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to maximise scarce UK summer heat.
Plant alongside low-growing Sedums or Thymus which share its need for sharp drainage and low nutrients.

items.name: Chorizanthe robusta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of three millimetres in a free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Place in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native California dunes in the damp UK climate.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells once established as this annual hates wet roots.
Sow directly into final pots to avoid transplant shock which easily kills its delicate taproot.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using copper tape around pots during wet UK springs.

items.name: Chorizanthe valida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres depth in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost mix.
Position pots in a south-facing cold frame to protect overwintering seedlings from heavy UK rain.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two centimetres of soil has dried out completely.
Grow in containers of pure horticultural grit and peat-free compost to mimic native sandy soils.
Place copper tape around pots to protect the delicate young foliage from nocturnal slug damage.

items.name: Chorizanthe watsonii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn using cold frames to mimic winter chill.
Grow in a sharply draining mix of five parts grit to one part loam to prevent winter wet root rot.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to maximise scarce UK sunlight.
Plant alongside low-growing Sedums which share its need for dry soil and won't crowd its tiny frame.

items.name: Chorizanthe stellulata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn using a cold frame to mimic winter chill.
Grow in a sharply draining gritty soil mix to prevent root rot during wet UK winters and springs.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to replicate its arid habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise limited UK summer warmth.
Plant alongside low-growing sedums or sempervivums which share its need for dry, nutrient-poor soil.

items.name: Chorizanthe uniaristata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under glass in a gritty, free-draining compost mix at a depth of just two millimetres
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to mimic its dry native habitat
Grow in terracotta pots alongside Sedums to easily move them shelter during heavy autumn downpours
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings as damp UK gardens pose a high risk to shoots

items.name: Chorizanthe xanti
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of three millimetres in a free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or under a cold frame to protect from wet UK summers.
Grow in terracotta pots with added grit to ensure rapid drainage and prevent winter waterlogging.
Sow alongside drought-tolerant Sedum or Festuca glauca which share its strict low-water needs.

items.name: Koenigia alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous herb in moist, clay-heavy soil to mimic its native damp subalpine UK habitat.
Divide the dense root clumps in early spring to keep its spreading habit from overtaking borders.
Position it in partial shade to prevent the lush green foliage from scorching in hot southern sun.
Cut the flowering stems right back to the ground in autumn after the white blooms fade to brown.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails which love to feast on the tender new spring shoots.

items.name: Rheum webbianum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan rhubarb in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil to mimic its mountain home.
Give it plenty of space in a damp, partially shaded spot where its massive leaves can spread out.
Mulch heavily with well-rotted manure in autumn to keep the roots cool and damp through UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the emerging young crown buds.
Divide the large root clumps in early spring just as the soil warms up to propagate new plants.

items.name: Atraphaxis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Atraphaxis in gritty, sharply draining soil to help it survive wet UK winters.
Give it a sheltered, south-facing spot in full sun to mimic its native dry, rocky habitats.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the woody stems and encourage fresh, compact growth.
Grow it alongside companion plants like lavender or rock roses that share its love of dry soils.

items.name: Oxytheca perfoliata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic dry habitats.
Keep watering to a minimum, letting the gritty soil dry out completely between sparse waterings.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your patio to trap essential summer warmth.
Protect these delicate annuals from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the stems.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums in shallow containers to create a beautiful, drought-tolerant display.

items.name: Aconogonon
items.growersTips:
Plant Aconogonon campanulatum in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that does not dry out in summer.
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges to control its vigorous spread.
Cut the hollow stems back to ground level in late autumn after the first frosts blacken the foliage.
Grow in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges, preventing leaf scorch during dry summer spells.
Combine with moisture-loving Astilbe or Hostas to mask the bare lower stems of taller varieties.

items.name: Muehlenbeckia
items.growersTips:
Plant your wire vine in free-draining soil with grit to survive wet, cold UK winters without rotting.
Keep it in a container if you want to stop its vigorous, scrambling stems from taking over borders.
Give it a hard haircut in early spring to shape the messy tangle and encourage fresh, glossy leaves.
Watch out for frost damage on young shoots in May, and throw some fleece over it if a freeze looms.
Water it deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the top inch of soil dry out first.

items.name: Koenigia islandica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring on the surface of damp, gritty compost because they need light to sprout.
Keep the soil constantly wet to mimic its native Scottish mountain bogs, so never let it dry out.
Grow this tiny annual in a shallow alpine trough rather than open borders so it does not get lost.
Position your pot in a cool, north-facing spot to protect this arctic plant from hot UK summers.
Watch out for aggressive garden weeds that will easily smother this delicate three-inch herb.

items.name: Centrostegia thurberi
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic desert soils.
Keep watering very sparse, only dampening the soil when it has dried out completely to prevent rot.
Grow this delicate annual in a terracotta pot so you can move it under glass during wet UK summers.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to maximise summer warmth.
Watch out for slugs and snails early on, as they will quickly devour the tender young seedlings.

items.name: Koenigia weyrichii
items.growersTips:
Plant this robust perennial in moist, clay-heavy UK soil to keep its vigorous roots happy.
Give it plenty of space in a damp border alongside large ferns or Rodgersia to balance its spread.
Cut the leafy stems right back to ground level in late autumn once the UK frosts turn them brown.
Divide the clump in early spring using a sharp spade to easily control its enthusiastic growth.
Water deeply during dry British summers to prevent the large, lush leaves from drooping and drying.

items.name: Koenigia ×fennica
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous hybrid in moisture-retentive clay soil to keep its lush foliage happy.
Give it plenty of room in a partially shaded border, as it can easily crowd out smaller neighbours.
Divide the root clump in early spring to control its spread and share new plants with friends.
Cut the stems right back to ground level in late autumn once the bronze foliage dies down.
Keep an eye out for slugs on tender new spring shoots, especially during damp UK April weather.

items.name: Rheum officinale
items.growersTips:
Give this giant rhubarb plenty of elbow room in deep, rich soil packed with well-rotted manure.
Plant the crown just at the soil surface in autumn so winter cold stimulates next spring's buds.
Thirsts for water in dry UK summers, so drench it weekly to keep those massive leaves from wilting.
Cut back the thick flower spikes in early summer to keep the plant's energy in the roots and leaves.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, and clear dead winter debris to stop crown rot setting in.

items.name: Rheum palmatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil, burying the crown just at ground level.
Give it a bucket of water weekly during dry UK summers to keep those massive leaves from wilting.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs; protect the emerging pink buds early on.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in July to direct energy back into the roots for next year.
Divide the massive root clump in late autumn using a sharp spade to easily make new free plants.

items.name: Mucronea
items.growersTips:
Pop Mucronea in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Water your Mucronea only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy roots.
Plant Mucronea alongside thymes or sedums in a sunny rockery for a thriving dry-loving community.
Keep an eye out for slugs during damp British springs, as they love the tender young foliage.
Propagate your Mucronea by taking soft stem cuttings in midsummer to ensure backup plants for winter.

items.name: Eriogonum longifolium var. gnaphalifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this scrubby buckwheat in a raised bed or rockery with sharp grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native warm, open pine-scrub habitat.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts once established, as wet roots will quickly rot it.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums and thymes which share its love for nutrient-poor, dry soil.
Protect the winter crown from heavy rain using a cloche or a pane of glass angled over the plant.

items.name: Brunnichia ovata
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous US native in a large container to control its aggressive, spreading root system.
Plant your redvine in a south-facing spot with a sturdy trellis to support its heavy woody vines.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.
Prune the vine hard in late winter to manage its size and encourage fresh, healthy spring growth.
Protect the root area with a thick mulch of bark chips before the first harsh UK winter frosts hit.

items.name: Gilmania luteola
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Mojave native in a container with ninety percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, mimicking desert rain with a light misting only once a month.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximize British sun.
Watch out for damp-loving UK greenhouse pests like glasshouse red spider mite on the tiny leaves.
Use a top dressing of fine limestone gravel to keep the collar dry and prevent winter rot.

items.name: Oxytheca
items.growersTips:
Grow this dry-loving annual in a gritty, free-draining gravel bed to survive wet UK winter rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in April under a cold frame to protect young seedlings from late spring frosts.
Water very sparingly only at the base once established, keeping foliage dry to prevent mildew.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to match its strict low-nutrient soil needs.
Watch out for slugs during damp UK springs, as they will quickly devour the tender young shoots.

items.name: Rheum australe
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, fertile soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure or compost
Position in full sun or partial shade, ensuring the crown sits just at the soil surface level
Water copiously during dry summer spells to support the massive, dramatic leaf development
Apply a thick mulch of organic matter in autumn to protect the crown from severe UK winter wet
Watch for slugs and snails on emerging spring shoots and clear away dead winter foliage promptly

items.name: Fallopia scandens
items.growersTips:
Plant this climber in a sturdy pot of loam-based compost to stop its vigorous roots from spreading.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill breaks their dormancy.
Give it a trellis against a south-facing wall to shield the delicate white flowers from cold winds.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the top soil dry out completely before watering again.
Cut the dying stems right back to the ground in late autumn to keep the garden neat and tidy.

items.name: Calligonum polygonoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert shrub in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it dry during wet winters.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, only dampening the soil when the pot feels completely weightless.
Place your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum summer heat and block cold winds.
Do not prune this slow grower at all, just gently snip off any frost-damaged tips in late spring.
Mix a handful of limestone chippings into your compost to mimic its native alkaline desert soil.

items.name: Rheum maximowiczii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rhubarb relative in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil to support its huge leaves.
Keep it happy in the UK by watering deeply at the base during dry spells, especially in midsummer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs as they love to shred the emerging foliage.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late summer to keep the plant tidy and prevent unwanted seeding.
Grow it alongside damp-loving shuttlecock ferns or hostas for a stunning, lush foliage contrast.

items.name: Fallopia ciliinodis
items.growersTips:
Plant this fringed bindweed in partial shade to mimic its native cool, woodland-edge UK habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep its shallow root system from drying out.
Sow seeds in autumn just five millimetres deep in pots kept outdoors for natural winter chilling.
Give it a sturdy trellis or obelisk to climb so its delicate twining stems do not smother neighbours.
Watch out for slugs early in spring as they love to munch on the tender new emerging shoots.

items.name: Fagopyrum cymosum
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial buckwheat in deep, moist soil during April to help it survive dry UK summers.
Give it a thick mulch of leaf mould in November to protect the crown from wet British winter rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on the tender young spring shoots as they emerge in April.
Cut the stems right back to the ground in late autumn once the first frosts turn the foliage black.
Grow it in partial shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat perfectly.

items.name: Rheum palaestinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert rhubarb in a raised gravel bed to mimic its dry Middle Eastern home in wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in deep pots of gritty compost so their long, delicate taproots have plenty of room to grow.
Keep water entirely off the crinkled leaves to prevent rot during damp British spring days.
Surround the crown with a thick layer of horticultural grit to stop slugs hiding under the foliage.
Do not water at all during its summer dormancy period to prevent the root from rotting in your soil.

items.name: Eriogonum
items.growersTips:
Plant your wild buckwheat in sharply draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet British winters.
Give them a sunny spot next to a south-facing brick wall to mimic their hot native hillside home.
Water newly planted herbs once a week then leave them alone to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Trim off faded summer flower papery heads in late autumn to keep the neat mounded shape tidy.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or copper tape around your pots.

items.name: Rheum undulatum
items.growersTips:
Plant your crowns in autumn with the growing tip just below the soil surface to prevent frost rot.
Dig in plenty of well-rotted manure before planting to satisfy this plant's greedy appetite.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep those huge leaves lush and prevent the plant bolting.
Cut back the flower spikes in late spring so the plant puts all its energy into tasty stems.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or organic pellets to protect them.

items.name: Rheum nobile
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine giant in deep, scree-like soil with grit to mimic its dry Himalayan scree home.
Protect the crown from wet winter rot by covering it with a cloche or pane of glass from November.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame, barely covering them with a thin layer of sharp grit or sand.
Keep it in your coolest, most wind-sheltered spot to prevent the delicate translucent tower tearing.
Watch out for slugs early in spring as they love to devour the emerging, highly prized flower spike.

items.name: Chorizanthe rigida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring under glass in a gritty, free-draining mix to prevent UK damp rot.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the soil dry out completely between light mistings.
Position pots in the brightest, south-facing spot possible to mimic their native desert sun.
Grow in terracotta pots rather than open UK soil to ensure excellent drainage and root warmth.
Do not fertilise this plant, as nutrient-rich UK multi-purpose composts will cause it to collapse.

items.name: Dedeckera
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare buckthorn relative in extremely sharp-draining, gritty soil to mimic its desert home.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for UK winters.
Water very sparingly, only when the top few inches of grit are bone dry, to prevent root rot.
Position your pot in the brightest, most sun-baked spot in your garden to get enough light.
Feed once in spring with a highly diluted, low-nitrogen fertilizer to avoid soft, weak growth.

items.name: Rheum rhaponticum
items.growersTips:
Plant your crowns in late autumn with the buds just 2cm below the soil surface to avoid crown rot.
Give them a bucket of water weekly in dry UK summers, especially while the stalks are swelling.
Watch out for slugs in damp spring weather and clear away old leaves to stop crown rot setting in.
Pull stalks with a gentle twist-and-pull action in May rather than cutting them to prevent rot.
Mulch heavily with well-rotted manure in late winter, keeping it clear of the central growing bud.

items.name: Mucronea californica
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sharpest-draining gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors in pots so the natural winter cold breaks their dormancy.
Keep watering to a absolute minimum once established, as damp soil will quickly rot the roots.
Grow it in a container you can move under a cold frame or greenhouse to shield it from winter rain.
Give it your hottest, most south-facing gravel bed to mimic its sunny desert home.

items.name: Reynoutria
items.growersTips:
Inject a dose of liquid seaweed into the soil around young stems in spring to boost early growth.
Try planting dwarf Fallopia compacta in a heavy clay pot to stop its vigorous roots from spreading.
Snip back the hollow stems right to the ground in late autumn once the frost turns them brown.
Grow this thirsty herb in damp, semi-shaded UK spots, watering deeply twice a week in dry summers.
Pair this vigorous grower with tough woodrush or hostas that can handle its dense summer shade.

items.name: Enchylaena tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of grit and peat-free compost to mimic its dry desert home.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but never let the pot sit in a saucer of water.
Prune the leggy stems by one third in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more red berries.
Grow it in a terracotta pot alongside potted rosemary or thyme for a lovely, drought-tolerant display.

items.name: Chenopodium quinoa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in mid-April about two centimetres deep once the soil starts to warm.
Give young plants a weekly deep soak at the base rather than light daily sprinkles to build roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails when seedlings are small, using organic grit barriers to stop them.
Grow quinoa alongside French beans to help anchor the tall stalks against strong British winds.
Harvest the seed heads in late August once they turn red or yellow and the lower leaves fall off.

items.name: Maireana sedifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet winters and move indoors by November
Water only when the soil is bone dry from May to September and keep completely dry during winter
Prune lightly in late spring after frost to shape the shrub but never cut back into old woody stems
Position in the hottest south facing spot to maximise intense summer sun and prevent foliage rotting
Plant alongside hardy sedums or sempervivums in a raised gravel bed to ensure rapid water drainage

items.name: Maireana aphylla
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty soil with added perlite to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or a greenhouse to mimic its native Australian heat.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to zero watering from November through February.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to maintain its compact, tangled shrub shape.
Overwinter in a pot to easily move indoors before autumn frosts dip below minus five Celsius.

items.name: Maireana georgei
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian desert native in a pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Bring your potted plant indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill from October to April.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, reducing to once a month during the cold winter months.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to maintain a compact shape and prevent legginess.
Position in your garden's hottest, most south-facing spot to maximise essential summer sun exposure.

items.name: Chenopodium giganteum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring after the last frost, as they need light and warmth to germinate.
Give this thirsty giant a deep soak weekly at the base, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage a bushier habit and prevent it blowing over.

items.name: Acacia moirii

items.name: Acacia myrtifolia

Drench it deeply once a week in summer, but let the pot dry out completely before watering again.

Wrap it in double-thickness fleece during frosty UK snaps, as it only tolerates down to minus five.

items.name: Acacia nigricans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre using a heated propagator to sprout.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy to prevent damping off in our damp UK spring.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their warm native home.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser once flowers bud to boost those yellow blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are starting them early in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Acacia obtusifolia

Start your seeds indoors in March using hot water scarification to break their tough outer coats.

Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil are dry, as wet roots will rot in UK damp.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in spring using copper tape or beer traps.
At the end of autumn, dig up and compost this annual before the first hard frost kills it.

items.name: Acacia olgana
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March using a deep pot to give the long taproot plenty of room to grow.
Pour boiling water over the seeds and soak them for a day before planting to break their dormancy.
Plant them outside in late May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic the hot Australian sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving them frequent light sprinkles.
Grow them in very free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer weeks.

items.name: Acacia oxycedrus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in spring after a hot water soak to break dormancy before planting out in May.
Keep this Aussie native in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic its warm home climate.
Grow it in a container with gritty, free-draining soil so you can move it under cover for winter.
Water your potted acacia deeply once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out between drinks.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you bring your potted shrub indoors for the winter.

items.name: Acacia paradoxa
items.growersTips:
Grow this spiny shrub in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse during wet UK winters.

Let the compost dry out completely between waterings to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Prune lightly right after spring flowering to keep it compact and manage those vicious thorns.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping this plant indoors or in a conservatory over winter.

items.name: Acacia pendula
items.growersTips:
Bring this weeping wattle indoors by October as it cannot survive a typical wet UK winter frost.
Plant your seeds in free-draining sandy loam with grit added to prevent waterlogged winter roots.
Pour boiling water over the seeds and soak for a day before sowing to break their tough dormancy.
Position your potted tree against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum summer heat and light.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged stems.

items.name: Acacia penninervis
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in March to give this fast grower a head start before the last spring frost.
Plant them out in May in a sheltered, south-facing spot to mimic their sunny native Australian home.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out in between.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are starting them early in a warm UK conservatory.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil bed to ensure the sharp drainage this species absolutely demands.

items.name: Acacia plicata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 5mm using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Grow this Australian native in a terracotta pot filled with gritty, free-draining loam-based soil.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as this plant hates soggy roots.
Place your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot on your patio to mimic its warm habitat.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you overwinter your potted acacia in a conservatory.

items.name: Acacia podalyriifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Australian beauty in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free green house.
Water it sparingly in winter but keep the soil consistently moist during its active summer growth.
Plant in extremely free-draining, acidic to neutral soil mix to prevent dreaded winter root rot.
Prune lightly immediately after its winter yellow blooms fade to keep its bushy shape compact.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and mealybugs if you overwinter it under glass.

items.name: Acacia pravissima
items.growersTips:
Plant your Oven's wattle against a south-facing brick wall to shield it from harsh UK winter winds.
Prune right after spring flowering to keep it compact and prevent it from getting too leggy.
Mix plenty of grit into your clay soil to ensure excellent drainage, as wet winter roots will kill it.
Water deeply once a week during its first hot UK summer, then leave it to be completely drought-tolerant.
Wrap the main stem in fleece during severe winter frosts if you live in the colder north of the UK.
items.description: Acacia pravissima, commonly known as Ovens wattle, Oven wattle, wedge-leaved wattle and Tumut wattle, is a species of flowering plant in the legume family, Fabaceae. It is an evergreen shrub native to southeastern Australia.

items.name: Acacia prominens
items.growersTips:
Start your golden shower wattle in pots indoors during March to protect seedlings from late UK frosts.
Plant them in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during our wet British winters.
Water your young acacia deeply once a week, letting the topsoil dry out completely between sessions.
Prune lightly right after its spring yellow blooms fade to keep this vigorous grower neat and bushy.
Wrap the main stem in fleece during November to shield it from harsh, freezing UK winter winds.

items.name: Acacia pulchella
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in spring using hot water scarification to break their tough dormancy coats.
Plant this Australian native in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy, free-draining ericaceous soil.
Keep your potted plant in a sunny, sheltered spot to shield it from cold, wet UK winter winds.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between light waterings.
Prune lightly right after flowering in late spring to maintain its bushy, compact shape.

items.name: Acacia pycnantha

Plant this Australian native in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Sow the seeds in spring after soaking them in poured boiled water overnight to break their dormancy.

Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings to prevent rot.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to soak up the maximum amount of UK summer sun.

items.name: Acacia redolens

Plant this Australian native in your sunniest, sheltered spot with super gritty, free-draining soil.

Grow it alongside rosemary or lavender which love the same dry, sunny conditions in British gardens.

items.name: Acacia restiacea
items.growersTips:
Grow this Aussie native in a pot with 50% grit so you can move it indoors before the UK frost hits.
Sow the seeds in spring after soaking them in hot water overnight to break their tough outer shell.

Place your pot against a south-facing brick wall to soak up every bit of precious UK summer sun.
Snip off the spent yellow flower heads in late summer to keep this wiry shrub looking tidy.

items.name: Acacia retinodes

Grow this tender evergreen in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.

Water thoroughly once the top few inches of soil dry out, but keep it barely damp during winter.
Prune lightly right after flowering in summer to keep its shape and stop it getting too leggy.
Position your pot against a warm, south-facing brick wall to maximize essential summer sunshine.

items.name: Acacia rostellifera
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian wattle in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Sow the seeds in spring after soaking them in hot water for twenty-four hours to break dormancy.

Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to keep its fast-growing, bushy shape in check.

items.name: Acacia salicina

Position your pots against a south-facing wall to maximise the limited UK summer sunshine.

items.name: Acacia saligna

Plant this Australian native in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to protect it from cold UK winds.
Use a very free-draining, gritty soil mix to prevent root rot during our wet British winters.
Water your young acacia deeply once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between.
Prune lightly right after its spring yellow blooms fade to keep its vigorous growth in check.
Grow this tender shrub in a large container so you can easily move it into a greenhouse for winter.

items.name: Acacia shirleyi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using deep pots to protect the taproot before the last frost.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent damping off.
Blend plenty of grit into your compost to mimic its native drainage and survive wet UK summers.
Place your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to maximise crucial summer heat.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you are starting these seedlings in a warm greenhouse.

items.name: Acacia spectabilis
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian beauty in a large pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse.
Sow the seeds in spring after soaking them in hot water overnight to break their tough dormancy.
Feed weekly with a low-phosphorus liquid fertiliser through summer to boost those yellow blooms.
Water deeply once a week when dry, but always let the top two inches of gritty soil dry out first.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you keep your potted acacia indoors during the winter.

items.name: Acacia stenophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre after soaking them in warm water.
Plant this Aussie native in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic its warm home climate.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty, free-draining soil dry out between drinks.
Protect young plants with fleece during cold snaps, as UK frosts can easily damage new growth.
Grow it in a large container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.

items.name: Acacia suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early spring using hot water scarification to break their tough dormancy.
Plant out in a sunny, sheltered spot with extremely free-draining sandy soil to survive wet winters.
Water young plants deeply once a week, but let them dry out completely to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Prunings are rarely needed, so just lightly pinch out the tips in late spring to encourage bushiness.
Protect your potted acacia in a cold greenhouse or unheated conservatory when winter frosts arrive.

items.name: Acacia tetragonophylla
items.growersTips:
Bring this Australian wattle indoors by October to protect its roots from wet UK winter freezes.
Sow seeds in spring exactly five millimetres deep after soaking them in boiled water for a day.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost feels bone dry to mimic its desert home.
Prune lightly right after flowering in summer to keep its spiky needle-like foliage compact.
Mix three parts horticultural grit with one part peat-free compost to ensure ultra-sharp drainage.

items.name: Acacia tortilis
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre after soaking them in warm water.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy to prevent your young seedlings from rotting at the base.
Place your pots on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic their native African sunshine.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites which thrive in the dry indoor air these plants prefer.
Plant them alongside French marigolds in pots to help naturally deter pests in your greenhouse.

items.name: Acacia truncata
items.growersTips:
Since this Australian native is actually a tender perennial shrub, grow it in a pot to overwinter.
Sow the seeds in spring after soaking them in hot water overnight to break their hard outer coat.
Plant them in a very free-draining, grit-heavy acidic compost mix to prevent winter root rot.
Keep the pot on a sunny, sheltered south-facing patio to mimic its warm coastal homeland.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are dry, as this plant hates sitting in soggy compost.

items.name: Acacia vestita
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in a warm, sheltered spot against a south-facing wall to block UK wind.
Grow it in a container of gritty, free-draining loam so you can move it indoors before winter frosts.
Water thoroughly once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between each watering.
Prune very lightly right after spring flowering to keep it bushy, avoiding cutting into old wood.
Protect your potted shrub in a cold greenhouse from November to March to survive wet British winters.

items.name: Acacia xanthophloea

You need to grow this tender African tree in a large pot so you can move it indoors for winter.
Plant seeds 1cm deep in free-draining sandy loam after soaking them in warm water for 24 hours.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry, as this tree hates soggy UK winter soil.
Place your pot by a south-facing wall to trap maximum summer heat and shield it from cold winds.

items.name: Acaciella

Sow your seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to beat the cool UK weather.

Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are starting them off in your greenhouse.

items.name: Acanthephippium
items.growersTips:
Keep these terrestrial orchids in pots of bark and moss to survive the damp UK winter indoors.
Water them heavily from spring to autumn, but let the compost dry out completely during winter.
Place your pots in bright, filtered light but shield them from harsh direct summer afternoon sun.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser every two weeks only when you see active new leaf growth.
Repot in spring right after flowering, taking care not to damage their highly sensitive roots.

items.name: Acanthocarpus
items.growersTips:
Bring this Australian native indoors or to a heated greenhouse before the first autumn UK frosts.
Plant in extremely free-draining sandy loam with added grit to survive wet British winters.

Position in your sunniest south-facing border or against a warm wall to mimic its desert home.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to maintain a neat tufted shape.

items.name: Acanthocarpus canaliculatus

Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize warmth and mimic its native habitat.

Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to avoid waterlogging the roots.

items.name: Acanthocarpus preissii
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender Australian native in a terracotta pot using free-draining gritty loam-based soil.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it will not survive wet UK winter frosts below zero.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, allowing the compost to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in the brightest spot possible, such as a south-facing conservatory or sun-baked patio.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your hands from the sharp, needle-like leaf tips.

items.name: Acanthoideae

Plant Acanthus spinosus in deep, fertile loam to accommodate its incredibly long, thirsty taproot.

Cut the spent flower spikes right back to the base in October to keep the crown tidy for winter.
Watch out for snails hiding in the deep leaf folds; use organic wool pellets around the base.
Divide your congested clumps in spring using a sharp spade to slice through the tough rootstocks.

items.name: Acanthopale

Bring your potted Acanthopale indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from UK cold.
Water your Acanthopale only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot.

Prune back leggy stems by one-third in late March to encourage a bushier, more compact shape.
