items.name: Acanthophyllum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of three millimetres in free-draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic their dry native habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise scarce UK summer warmth.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps during damp British spring nights.
Incorporate plenty of horticultural grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Acanthophyllum cerastioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in grit-rich, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters without rotting.
Position it in your sunniest, most wind-exposed rockery or gravel garden to mimic its mountain home.
Water sparingly, only during dry summer spells, keeping the foliage dry to prevent winter damp damage.
Trim the spent flower cushions lightly in late summer to keep its tight, moss-like habit neat.

items.name: Acanthopsis
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK frosts.
Plant in gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot during our damp British winters.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, then soak it thoroughly and let drain.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense sunshine of its natural habitat.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in spirit.

items.name: Acanthorrhinum
items.growersTips:
Plant these snapdragon cousins in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on a sunny windowsill, just pressing them into the compost.
Water them deeply at the base once a week during dry spells, keeping the spiny foliage dry.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in autumn to keep the plant neat and encourage fresh spring growth.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps to protect them in damp UK weather.

items.name: Acanthus

Plant your Acanthus deep in fertile, well-drained soil in spring to help its fleshy roots settle.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to stop the large leaves from wilting in the heat.
Cut the faded flower spikes right down to the base in autumn to keep the clump looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, as they love the soft new growth.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or spring using a sharp spade to slice through the tough roots.

items.name: Acanthus arboreus
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Acanthus arboreus indoors before November to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant this shrubby bear's breeches in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to ensure fast drainage.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy during its active spring and summer growing phase.
Wear thick gloves when pruning back dead stems in spring to avoid painful pricks from its sharp leaves.
Position your pot in the brightest, most sheltered spot on your patio to mimic its native sunshine.

items.name: Acanthus balcanicus
items.growersTips:
Plant your bear's breeches in deep, well-draining soil to accommodate its massive taproot.
Give it a generous drink during dry UK summers to keep those dramatic flower spikes upright.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh new shoots.
Cut the faded flower stems right down to the base in autumn to keep the clump looking tidy.
Position it in full sun or partial shade where it has plenty of room to spread without crowding.

items.name: Acanthus dioscoridis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Syrian bear's breeches in a raised bed with sharp grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water it deeply once a week during dry spring spells, but keep it bone dry during winter dormancy.
Watch out for slugs chewing the emerging pink-flushed spring shoots before they can establish.
Cut the faded flower spikes right to the base in late summer to keep the rosette looking tidy.
Sow seeds in a cold frame in autumn so the natural winter chill triggers spring germination.

items.name: Acanthus ebracteatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this seaside holly in moist, clay-rich soil near a pond edge to mimic its mangrove home.
Give it a thick mulch of bark in autumn to protect its roots from hard UK winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love chewing the tender new emerging shoots.
Grow it in a warm, sheltered greenhouse if your local UK garden gets frequent freezing temperatures.
Wear thick gloves when pruning dead leaves because those jagged, holly-like edges are incredibly sharp.

items.name: Acanthus hirsutus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Turkish native in your sunniest, sharpest-draining spot to survive wet UK winters.
Dig in plenty of grit and organic matter to keep its roots dry and prevent cold-weather rot.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry UK summer, then leave it to establish.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the emerging fuzzy spring foliage.
Cut the faded flower spikes right down to the base in late autumn to keep the clump tidy.

items.name: Acanthus hungaricus
items.growersTips:
Plant this bear's breeches in deep, fertile, well-drained soil to accommodate its taproot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Cut the spent flower spikes right down to the base in autumn to keep the clump looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when the fresh, deeply lobed leaves start to emerge.
Divide mature clumps in spring or autumn using a sharp spade to slice through the tough roots.

items.name: Acanthus ilicifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant this seaside holly in a sheltered, boggy pond edge or wet clay soil to mimic its wild home.
Wrap the crown with fleece in late autumn because UK frosts can easily kill this tender perennial.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning dead leaves in spring to protect your hands from its spines.
Water it deeply twice a week in dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently wet and muddy.
Sow seeds in a heated propagator at twenty degrees Celsius in early spring for reliable germination.

items.name: Acanthus mollis
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winters will rot the fleshy roots of Acanthus mollis.
Control spread in small gardens by planting inside a deep root barrier to restrict invasive runners.
Cut flower spikes to the base in October and clear dead foliage to prevent overwintering snails.
Grow in partial shade to prevent the large leaves from wilting during dry UK summer spells.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its winter dormant phase.

items.name: Acanthus montanus
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors or to a heated conservatory before the first autumn frost hits.
Plant your Acanthus montanus in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter root rot in UK rain.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of compost dry out between drinks.
Cut back faded flower spikes to the base in late autumn to keep the prickly foliage looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs, as they love to shred the young leaves.

items.name: Acanthus spinosus
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, well-drained soil as their taproots hate wet winter clay common in UK gardens.
Position in full sun or partial shade, allowing plenty of space as they easily crowd out neighbours.
Cut flower spikes to the base in late summer to prevent prolific self-seeding across your borders.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in winter when the plant is dormant to guarantee new stock.

items.name: Achetaria azurea
items.growersTips:
Plant this Brazilian beauty in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frosts.
Water your plant deeply once the top two inches of compost feel dry, avoiding any waterlogging.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a much bushier shape and more blue flowers.
Mix plenty of grit into your peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering your plant indoors.

items.name: Achimenes
items.growersTips:
Start your rhizomes indoors in March at a depth of two centimetres in a warm, bright propagator.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water to avoid shocking their delicate roots.
Keep them in a sheltered, semi-shaded spot outdoors once the UK summer night temperatures stay above ten degrees.
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach eight centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Bring the pots back inside by October and keep the compost completely dry over the winter months.

items.name: Achimenes erecta
items.growersTips:
Plant these little rhizomes just one inch deep in early April using a peat-free compost with grit.
Keep them on a warm UK windowsill until June, then move them to a sheltered, semi-shaded patio spot.
Water them from the bottom to keep the soil damp but never soggy, which prevents rhizome rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when they are three inches tall to get a really bushy, flower-filled plant.
Bring them indoors before the first autumn frost and let the pots dry out completely for winter.

items.name: Achimenes grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Start your rhizomes indoors in March at one inch deep in a peat-free compost with added perlite.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering with tepid rainwater to avoid root shock.
Place them in bright, indirect light, as hot UK summer afternoon sun will easily scorch the leaves.
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach three inches tall to encourage a bushier, trailing habit.
Bring containers inside before autumn frosts, then store the dry rhizomes at ten degrees Celsius.

items.name: Achimenes longiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant your small scaly rhizomes about two centimeters deep in pots from late March to start them off.
Keep the compost consistently moist with tepid rainwater but never let the pot sit in soggy runoff.
Place them on a bright windowsill out of direct midday sun to prevent the delicate leaves burning.
Bring your pots indoors before the first autumn frosts hit as these tropical beauties cannot cope.
Let the plants dry out completely in October then store the dormant rhizomes in a dry, frost-free shed.

items.name: Achlydosa
items.growersTips:
Tuck this orchid into a damp, peat-free ericaceous compost mix mimicking its native boggy home.
Keep it cozy in a cool, shady greenhouse or cold frame to shield it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Water with rainwater only to keep the soil consistently wet, as tap water is far too alkaline.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the tender emerging shoots.
Propagate by very careful division in early spring just as the new growth begins to show.

items.name: Achlys
items.growersTips:
Grow this shade-lover in moist, acidic woodland soil rich in leaf mould under a canopy of trees.
Plant rhizomes shallowly just five centimetres deep in autumn so they can establish over winter.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the tender emerging triple leaves.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Achlys triphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland native in deep shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural damp canopy.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or composted bark to create the acidic, humus-rich soil it loves.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins.
Protect the delicate, vanilla-scented leaves from slugs and snails using beer traps in spring.

items.name: Achyrocalyx
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender perennial in a south-facing, sheltered spot using grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Overwinter your plants in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to survive wet UK winter cold.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the soil dry out completely between each watering.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer as insurance against harsh British winter losses outdoors.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertilizer in spring to encourage stronger, more resilient stems.

items.name: Achyronychia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using a gritty, free-draining seed compost.
Grow in a terracotta pot to prevent waterlogging during wet and cool UK summer spells.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to mimic its native arid habitat.
Position in your garden's hottest, most south-facing spot to maximise scarce UK summer sun.
Plant alongside Sedums in gravel beds to ensure the soil remains low in nutrients and dry.

items.name: Acianthella
items.growersTips:
Grow these tiny Australian orchids in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame to mimic UK winter sun.
Plant the small tubers just two centimetres deep in a very free-draining, gritty orchid compost.
Water them gently from autumn to spring, then keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the single, heart-shaped ground leaf.
Repot your tubers every second year in late summer before the autumn growing cycle kicks off again.

items.name: Acianthinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these terrestrial orchids in a gritty, free-draining compost of peat substitute, sand and perlite.
Keep tubers completely dry during their summer dormancy from June to August to prevent them rotting.
Water sparingly from September when new shoots emerge, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Protect these frost-tender orchids by overwintering them in a cold greenhouse kept above five degrees.
Repot the small tubers annually in late summer at a shallow depth of two centimetres below the soil.

items.name: Acianthus
items.growersTips:
Grow these tiny terrestrial orchids in a gritty, free-draining compost mix of bark, loam and perlite.
Keep the tubers completely dry during their summer dormant phase to prevent them from rotting away.
Place pots on a cool, bright UK windowsill or in a frost-free greenhouse during winter flowering.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, allowing the top inch of compost to dry out between drinks.
Watch out for slugs and snails in autumn, as they will quickly devour the emerging single leaves.

items.name: Acokanthera
items.growersTips:
Bring your bushkanthera indoors to a bright conservatory before the first cold autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to avoid root rot in our damp UK climate.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in spring to protect your skin from its highly toxic milky sap.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer from May to September to boost those blooms.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for red spider mites when keeping this plant in a greenhouse.

items.name: Acokanthera oblongifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African beauty in a large pot so you can move it indoors before frost hits.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy from spring to autumn, then water sparingly in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape it and keep its sap off your bare skin.
Use a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Watch out for mealybugs and scale insects when you bring your plant inside for the cold UK winter.

items.name: Acokanthera oppositifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring this toxic beauty indoors by October because UK frosts will quickly kill it.
Grow it in a loam-based potting compost like John Innes No 3 mixed with plenty of grit.
Water thoroughly when the top two inches of soil dry out, then let it drain completely.
Prune it in late spring after flowering, always wearing thick gloves to avoid the deadly sap.
Watch out for mealybugs and scale insects when you bring the pot indoors for the winter.

items.name: Acokanthera rotundata
items.growersTips:
Bring your bushman's poison indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters.
Water this toxic beauty only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining compost are dry.
Prune your shrub in late spring wearing thick gloves to avoid skin contact with its deadly sap.
Repot in spring using a mix of peat-free compost, perlite, and orchid bark for perfect drainage.
Check the leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, which love the warm indoor winter spots this plant needs.

items.name: Acomis
items.growersTips:
Sow Acomis seeds shallowly indoors in March, then transplant out in late May once frosts are over.
Grow these Australian annuals in your sunniest, sheltered border in free-draining, sandy soil.
Let the soil dry out between waterings to mimic their dry native habitat and prevent root rot.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with gravel barriers or beer traps.
Deadhead the yellow button flowers regularly through summer to keep new blooms coming until autumn.

items.name: Aconitum
items.growersTips:
Always wear thick gloves when handling monkshood because all parts of this plant are highly toxic.
Plant your aconitum in rich, moisture-retentive soil that mimics a damp UK woodland edge.
Keep the soil consistently damp during dry summer spells to prevent the leaves from browning.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the ground in autumn to encourage healthy return next spring.
Grow them alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade where their deep blue hoods really pop.

items.name: Aconitum anthora
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers five centimetres deep in autumn so they establish well before the UK winter frost.
Give this yellow monkshood moist but sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet clay.
Wear thick gloves whenever you handle or prune this highly toxic beauty to keep your skin safe.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and healthy.
Grow it in light dappled shade to mimic its native woodland edge and prevent the leaves scorching.

items.name: Aconitum carmichaelii
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-flowering beauty in rich, damp soil that stays cool and moist during dry UK summers.
Wear thick gloves when handling any part of this highly toxic plant, especially when dividing it.
Position it in partial shade to keep the roots cool, mimicking its native woodland edge habitat.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the ground in late autumn once the gorgeous blue blooms finish.
Stake the tall stems of cultivars like Wilsonii early in spring to protect them from UK wind gusts.

items.name: Aconitum columbianum
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood in damp, rich soil mimicking UK woodlands, adding plenty of leaf mould first.
Wear thick gloves when handling this toxic beauty, especially when dividing the roots in autumn.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, as it hates drying out around the roots.
Position it in partial shade to protect the delicate blue hooded flowers from strong afternoon sun.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the ground in late autumn to encourage healthy spring growth.

items.name: Aconitum coreanum
items.growersTips:
Plant this pale yellow monkshood in moist, well-drained soil rich in leaf mould to mimic woodland.
Wear thick gloves whenever handling this highly toxic beauty, especially during division or planting.
Position it in partial shade to keep the soil cool, as hot UK summer sun can scorch its delicate leaves.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to help the tuberous roots establish and support summer blooms.
Propagate by dividing the root clumps in autumn once the foliage has completely died back.

items.name: Aconitum degenii
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood three inches deep in rich, damp soil that mimics a cool UK woodland edge.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry British summers, but never let the roots sit in bog.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant, especially during spring division.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the ground in autumn to keep the clump tidy for next spring.
Watch out for delphinium moth caterpillars and aphids, which love to feast on the tender new shoots.

items.name: Aconitum firmum
items.growersTips:
Plant this toxic beauty in rich, damp soil in partial shade, mimicking its native woodland edge.
Always wear thick gloves when handling it to protect your skin from its highly poisonous sap.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, as it hates drying out around its roots.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the ground in autumn using dedicated, well-washed secateurs.
Divide the tuberous roots in spring every three years to keep the plant vigorous and flowering well.

items.name: Aconitum fischeri
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-blooming monkshood in moist but well-drained soil rich in leaf mould or compost.
Always wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant, especially during division.
Position it in partial shade to keep the soil cool and mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to prevent the lower leaves from yellowing and dropping off.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the ground in late autumn once the foliage dies down.

items.name: Aconitum henryi
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers horizontally five centimetres deep in rich, damp soil during autumn or early spring.
Wear gloves whenever handling this highly toxic plant, especially when dividing it in autumn.
Grow it in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges, keeping the soil consistently moist.
Cut the faded flower stems back to ground level in late autumn after the foliage dies down.
Stake these tall, floppy stems early in spring using hazel twigs to support the heavy blooms.

items.name: Aconitum heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native alpine home.
Always wear gloves when handling this highly toxic plant, especially during division in autumn.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in spring to retain moisture and keep the roots cool in summer.
Propagate by dividing the tubers in late autumn once the top growth has completely died back.

items.name: Aconitum lamarckii
items.growersTips:
Wear thick gloves when planting this monkshood in damp, humus-rich soil to block its toxic sap.
Plant the crowns just below the surface in partial shade to mimic its native cool woodland edge.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Cut the faded yellow flower spikes down to the base in autumn to keep the clump tidy and healthy.
Grow it alongside hostas or ferns which love the same cool, damp shade and mask its lower stems.

items.name: Aconitum lasiostomum
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood in damp, heavy UK clay improved with leafmould to mimic its native woodland.
Wear thick gloves when handling these toxic roots, planting them just three centimetres deep in autumn.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp, as dry roots cause leaf drop.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the base in late autumn to keep your borders tidy for winter.
Plant it alongside ferns and hostas in partial shade where the soil stays cool and moist all day.

items.name: Aconitum lycoctonum
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood in moist, dappled shade to mimic its natural European woodland habitat.
Always wear thick gloves when handling it because every single part of this beauty is highly toxic.
In dry UK summers, water deeply at the base once a week to prevent the leaves from crisping up.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the ground in autumn to keep the clump tidy for next spring.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth starts, wearing gloves of course.

items.name: Aconitum napellus
items.growersTips:
Wear thick gloves and long sleeves when handling to avoid absorbing its highly toxic alkaloids.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial woodland shade.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut faded flower spikes to the ground in autumn to encourage healthy regrowth the following spring.
Watch for delphinium moth caterpillars and treat infestations by hand-picking with sturdy gloves.

items.name: Aconitum plicatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood in damp, rich soil with the crown just below the surface to mimic alpine woods.
Wear thick gloves whenever you handle it because every part of this plant is extremely poisonous.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, as it hates drying out around its roots.
Cut the faded flower stems down to the ground in autumn using dedicated, thoroughly washed shears.
Grow it in partial shade alongside hostas or ferns to keep its roots cool in the summer heat.

items.name: Aconitum reclinatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this white monkshood in deep, moisture-retentive soil enriched with well-rotted leaf mould.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Wear thick gloves when handling this highly toxic plant, even during simple autumn division.
Position it in cool, dappled shade to mimic its native woodland home and prevent leaf scorch.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the ground in late autumn once the foliage dies down naturally.

items.name: Aconitum tauricum
items.growersTips:
Plant this monkshood in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics a cool UK woodland edge.
Wear thick gloves when handling any part of this highly toxic plant, especially during division.
Position it in partial shade to keep the soil cool and prevent the deep blue flowers from fading.
Propagate by dividing the tubers in autumn or late winter while the plant is completely dormant.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in spring to lock in the moisture your aconitum craves during summer.

items.name: Aconitum uncinatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this climber near a sturdy shrub like yew to let its weak stems scramble up naturally.
Wear thick gloves whenever handling this highly toxic beauty, especially when dividing in autumn.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, mimicking cool, moist UK woodland conditions.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in spring to keep its shallow roots cool and replicate forest soil.
Watch out for delphinium moth caterpillars in May, which love to shred the delicate blue blooms.

items.name: Aconitum variegatum
items.growersTips:
Wear sturdy gloves when planting this toxic beauty, placing tubers five centimetres deep in autumn.
Give it a spot in damp, dappled shade to mimic its native European woodland edge in your garden.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, as dry roots trigger early yellowing.
Cut the spent flower stems back to ground level in autumn, but always wash your tools afterwards.
Plant it alongside hostas or ferns to hide its bare lower stems and enjoy the contrasting foliage.

items.name: Acosmium
items.growersTips:
Start Acosmium seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short, cool UK summer.
Plant your young Acosmium out in late May, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water these annuals deeply at the base once a week, avoiding wet foliage to prevent powdery mildew.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on tender new growth during damp British spring nights.
Feed them weekly with a high-potassium liquid tomato fertiliser from July to boost summer blooms.

items.name: Acrocarpus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of 1cm using bottom heat of 20C to boost germination.
Grow in a sheltered south-facing spot or greenhouse to protect from cool UK summer night chills.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily light sprinkles to encourage deep rooting.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 15cm high to promote a bushier flowering habit.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer once the first flower buds begin to form.

items.name: Acrodon
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African succulents in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water them only when the soil is bone dry, keeping them completely dry from November to March.
Bring your potted Acrodon indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints; dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Propagate them by taking stem cuttings in late spring, letting the cut end callous before potting.

items.name: Acrodon bellidiflorus
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and sharp sand to survive UK rain.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter to prevent root rot.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs hiding in the dense, fleshy leaves during damp autumn days.
Position your pot in the brightest, most sun-drenched spot in your garden to trigger summer blooms.

items.name: Acrosanthes anceps
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African succulent in a grit-heavy, free-draining soil mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to almost nothing during the cold winter months.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing patio to mimic the intense light of its native habitat.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in late spring, letting them callus over before potting in sand.

items.name: Acrosorus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical fern in a warm, humid conservatory or heated greenhouse to survive UK cold.
Plant in a very loose, chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild tree-top home.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, avoiding cold tap water shocks.
Mist the fronds daily or use a gravel tray to recreate the high humidity of its native rainforest.
Keep it in bright, filtered light but shield it from direct midday sun to prevent frond scorch.

items.name: Acrostichum
items.growersTips:
Grow Acrostichum in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to protect it from chilly UK winters.
Plant this swamp fern in a rich, peat-free loam kept constantly wet, even boggy, all year round.
Position your fern in bright, filtered light but shield it from direct, scorching midday sun.
Water only with lukewarm rainwater to avoid shocking the roots during cold British winters.
Watch out for scale insects and mealybugs on the undersides of those massive fronds in spring.

items.name: Acrostichum aureum
items.growersTips:
Bring your golden leather fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive frosty UK temperatures.
Grow this coastal swamp fern in a rich, peat-free compost kept constantly wet, even waterlogged.
Place your potted fern on a deep tray of water to mimic its native mangrove habitat humidity.
Keep the plant in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to get enough daily sunlight.
Feed it with a diluted seaweed fertilizer during summer to replicate its natural saline environment.

items.name: Acrostichum danaeifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring this giant leather fern indoors before October to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Keep the soil constantly wet by placing its pot in a shallow tray filled with rainwater.
Mix plenty of composted bark and leaf mould into the soil to mimic its native swampy habitat.
Position your fern in a bright conservatory or steamy bathroom to provide the high humidity it craves.
Feed it weekly with a diluted liquid seaweed fertilizer during the active spring and summer growth.

items.name: Acrostichum speciosum
items.growersTips:
Bring this mangrove fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive a frosty UK climate below five degrees.
Grow it in a heavy clay and peat-free compost mix to mimic its natural muddy coastal swamp habitat.
Keep the pot sitting in a shallow tray of rainwater year-round to ensure the soil never dries out.
Position your fern in a humid, warm conservatory or bathroom that gets bright but indirect sunlight.
Gently wipe the large leathery fronds with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and prevent red spiders.

items.name: Actaea
items.growersTips:
Plant your Actaea in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil in a sheltered, dappled shade spot.
Water them deeply and regularly during dry UK summers to prevent their beautiful leaves from crisping.
Leave the spent flower spikes over winter as their seed heads look lovely in frosty UK gardens.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when the tender new dark shoots first emerge from the soil.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to keep them vigorous and healthy.

items.name: Actaea asiatica
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, neutral to acidic soil.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate in spring.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted manure each spring to retain essential moisture.
Keep soil consistently damp during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch and berry drop.
Wear gloves when handling or cutting back in autumn, as all parts of this plant are highly toxic.

items.name: Actaea biternata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded woodland border.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn to undergo natural UK winter chilling for spring germination.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Mulch annually in early spring with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to retain crucial moisture.
Cut the faded flower stems and foliage back to ground level in late autumn after the first frost.

items.name: Actaea elata
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding leafmould to mimic woodland conditions.
Position in dappled shade to prevent leaf scorch from the intense midday summer sun in southern UK.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in autumn to maintain a tidy habit and promote vigor.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they can quickly decimate the emerging new shoots.

items.name: Actaea heracleifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded spot.
Incorporate leaf mould deeply into the planting hole to mimic its native woodland floor habitat.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the large leaves from crisping at edges.
Cut the spent flower spikes to the base in late autumn, leaving foliage to die back naturally.
Watch for slugs and snails on emerging spring shoots, using beer traps or organic pellets early on.

items.name: Actaea japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh winds that dry out the delicate foliage.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch and ensure late-season flowering.
Cut the spent flower stems back to the ground in late autumn after the foliage dies back naturally.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Actaea matsumurae
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leafmould before planting.
Set the crown just at the soil surface in autumn or spring, avoiding planting too deeply in heavy clay.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the foliage from scorching and drying at the edges.
Cut the faded flower spikes and foliage down to the ground in late winter before new spring growth.
Divide congested clumps in early spring every four years to maintain vigour and increase flower size.

items.name: Actaea pachypoda
items.growersTips:
Plant in shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, watering weekly during dry British summer spells.
Plant bare roots in autumn or spring with the crown positioned just below the soil surface.
Cut back the dead foliage to ground level in late winter before the new spring shoots emerge.
Wear gloves when handling this highly toxic plant, especially during autumn berry harvest.

items.name: Actaea podocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in dappled woodland shade to mimic UK forest floors.
Incorporate leafmould or well-rotted manure deeply into the planting hole to retain summer moisture.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to support the development of the tall autumn flower spikes.
Cut the spent flower stems down to the ground in late autumn after the white berries have fallen.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Actaea racemosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leafmould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in dappled shade to prevent the delicate white bottle-brush flowers from scorching in July.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the large foliage from crisping at the edges.
Cut the spent flower spikes down to the base in late autumn once the foliage dies back naturally.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp weather.

items.name: Actaea rubifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating leaf mould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Position in deep or dappled shade to prevent the delicate, pale green foliage from scorching in summer.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted compost each spring to retain moisture and feed the crown.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Actaea rubra
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in deep or partial shade to mimic UK woodland floors.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they need winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the delicate compound foliage from crisping.
Wear gloves when handling or pruning in autumn, as all parts of this native-relative are highly toxic.
Combine with ferns and hostas in damp shade to contrast the bright red autumn berries safely.

items.name: Actaea simplex
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade, incorporating leafmould before planting.
Keep soil consistently damp, watering deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in late autumn, leaving foliage to die back naturally.
Position dark-leaved cultivars like Brunette near pale green ferns to highlight the foliage contrast.

items.name: Actaea spicata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in deep or partial shade to mimic UK woodlands.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Keep soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, watering deeply at the base to prevent drying out.
Wear gloves when handling or pruning in autumn, as all parts of this native plant are highly toxic.
Plant alongside ferns and hostas in shade borders to provide contrasting texture and foliage depth.

items.name: Actiniopteris
items.growersTips:
Grow this little eyelash fern in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam, peat-free compost and perlite.
Keep it in a humid, warm spot indoors or in a heated conservatory, away from cold UK drafts.
Water from below with rainwater to keep the soil barely damp, letting the top dry out between drinks.
Watch out for glasshouse spider mites in dry winter air, misting nearby to keep humidity high.
Never prune the delicate fronds; just gently snip off any fully dead, brown ones at the very base.

items.name: Actiniopteris radiata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny fern in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts peat-free compost and perlite.
Keep it in a humid, warm spot indoors as our chilly UK winters will easily kill this exotic beauty.
Water sparingly from below once the fronds start to curl slightly, avoiding a soggy crown at all costs.
Place your pot on a shallow tray of wet pebbles to boost the local humidity without rotting the roots.
Group it with small fittonias or mosses in a bright terrarium to mimic its natural tropical home.

items.name: Actinostephanus enpingensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare shade-lover in a sheltered, frost-free greenhouse or warm conservatory over winter.
Plant it in a highly free-draining, acidic ericaceous compost mix with plenty of added perlite.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil consistently damp, not wet.
Position it in dappled woodland shade away from the drying winds and harsh afternoon UK summer sun.
Feed monthly in spring with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser to boost its delicate foliage growth.

items.name: Actinostrobus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Aussie native in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to ensure the sharp drainage this conifer needs.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep it completely dry over the wet winter.
Prune very lightly in late spring, only cutting soft new growth as it won't regrow from old wood.
Grow it in a patio pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse or conservatory for the winter.

items.name: Actinostrobus arenarius
items.growersTips:
Give this Aussie native a super gritty, free-draining sandy soil to survive wet British winters.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Water it deeply but let the compost dry out completely before you even think about watering again.
Place it in your hottest, most sun-drenched patio spot to mimic its warm Western Australia home.
Do not prune back into the old wood because this cypress relative will not regenerate from it.

items.name: Actinostrobus pyramidalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this cypress in well-drained, sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position it in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to protect it from harsh, freezing winds.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Avoid pruning the old wood, as this slow-growing conifer will not regenerate from bare branches.
Grow it in a large terracotta pot so you can move it into a greenhouse during severe frosts.

items.name: Adelocaryum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan beauty in moist, dappled shade to mimic its native woodland edge habitat.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the UK winter chill can naturally break their dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love eating the tender new shoots.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or compost into your soil to keep it rich, acidic, and free-draining.
Mulch the crown heavily in late autumn to protect its roots from severe, wet British frosts.

items.name: Adelonema
items.growersTips:
Bring your Adelonema indoors by October as they cannot survive chilly UK winters below fifteen degrees.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free, bark-rich compost feels dry to prevent root rot.
Position your plant in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to avoid leaf scorch.
Mist the leaves regularly or use a pebble tray to mimic the humid rainforests they love so much.
Feed with a diluted balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September for lush growth.

items.name: Adelonema wallisii
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical beauty indoors year-round as it cannot survive a chilly British winter outdoors.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid leaf burn.
Position in a bright room but well away from south-facing windows to prevent the leaves scorching.
Repot in spring using a peat-free mix packed with orchid bark and perlite for excellent drainage.
Wipe the broad, patterned leaves weekly with a damp cloth to boost humidity and clear away dust.

items.name: Adenanthera
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to mimic their native warmth.
Plant them out in late May in well-drained, gritty soil located in your sunniest, sheltered spot.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil dries out, keeping them damp but never soggy in our cool wet.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you keep them under cover during a damp British summer.
Grow them alongside potted marigolds to help deter pests and add a lovely splash of contrast color.

items.name: Adenanthera bicolor
items.growersTips:
Start this tropical beauty indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to beat the UK chill.
Soak the hard seeds in warm water for twenty-four hours before sowing them one centimetre deep.
Grow it in a container of free-draining sandy loam so you can move it inside when autumn hits.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping your plant indoors over winter.

items.name: Adenanthera pavonina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in spring after soaking them in hot water overnight to break their hard coats.
Grow this tropical beauty in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to protect it from UK frosts.
Water your potted red sandalwood tree only when the top two inches of compost feel completely dry.
Feed your young plant with a diluted balanced liquid fertiliser once a fortnight through summer.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier shape in your container plant.

items.name: Adenium
items.growersTips:
Bring your desert rose indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK autumn nights.
Water only when the grit-heavy soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November to March.
Repot in spring using a mix of half cactus compost and half perlite to prevent root rot in our damp.
Prune leggy stems in early spring just as new growth starts, to encourage a bushier flowering shape.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when keeping them on warm conservatory sills.

items.name: Adenochilus
items.growersTips:
Keep these delicate terrestrial orchids in a chilly, unheated greenhouse to survive damp UK winters.
Plant the fragile rhizomes just two centimetres deep in a loose, airy mix of chopped sphagnum moss.
Water with rainwater only, keeping the compost damp in summer but barely moist during winter rest.
Guard the tender emerging spring shoots from slugs using organic wool pellets around your pots.
Grow them alongside shade-loving native ferns or mosses that thrive in the same cool, humid spots.

items.name: Adenophora
items.growersTips:
Plant your ladybells in deep, fertile, neutral to alkaline soil so their long taproots can settle.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love eating the tender new shoots.
Leave the stems alone in autumn then cut them back to the ground in early spring to protect crowns.
Avoid moving established plants because their sensitive taproots hate being disturbed or divided.

items.name: Adenophora divaricata
items.growersTips:
Plant this ladybell in moist but well-drained neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its woodland home and protect the delicate blue bell flowers.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn as they need winter chill to germinate in the UK.
Slugs love the young spring shoots so protect them early with organic pellets or copper barriers.
Avoid moving it once established because its deep taproot hates being disturbed by transplanting.

items.name: Adenophora liliifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this ladybells root crown just below the soil surface in moist, well-draining UK loam.
Water deeply once a week during dry English summers, keeping the soil damp but never soggy.
Protect the young spring shoots from hungry UK slugs using organic grit or beer traps.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the base in autumn to keep the clump tidy for winter.
Grow them alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade to mimic their natural woodland edge.

items.name: Adenophora triphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial in moist, well-drained soil during autumn so roots settle before UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the tender emerging shoots.
Prune the flower stems right back to the ground in late autumn after the foliage dies down.
Grow it alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.

items.name: Adenophorus
items.growersTips:
Bring your delicate Adenophorus ferns indoors before the first damp UK autumn frost chills them.
Grow this Hawaiian epiphyte in a moist, bark-rich orchid mix rather than standard UK garden soil.
Mist the fronds daily with soft rainwater to mimic tropical humidity in dry British centrally heated rooms.
Keep them in bright, indirect light near a north-facing window, away from harsh afternoon sun.
Water only when the top layer of bark feels dry, ensuring the pot never sits in stagnant water.

items.name: Adenophorus periens
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate Hawaiian fern in a warm, humid terrarium to mimic its native tropical canopy.
Mist your fern daily with rainwater to keep humidity high without waterlogging the mossy compost.
Mount it on a piece of damp bark with sphagnum moss rather than planting it in standard garden soil.
Keep your terrarium in bright, indirect light but shielded from harsh, direct British summer sun.
Watch out for indoor fungus gnats and gently wipe the tiny fronds with a damp cotton bud if needed.

items.name: Adenophorus tamariscinus
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate Hawaiian fern in a terrarium to mimic its native tropical humidity in the UK.
Plant it in a highly acidic, loose orchid bark and sphagnum moss mix rather than standard soil.
Keep the compost consistently damp using tepid rainwater instead of harsh UK tap water.
Position your glass vessel in bright, indirect light but shield it from cold winter windowsill drafts.
Never prune its tiny fronds; just gently snip off any dead, brown stems at the base in spring.

items.name: Adenopodia
items.growersTips:
Sow these annual seeds indoors in warm April, planting them exactly one centimetre deep in pots.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent any damp-off rot.
Plant them out in sunny, sheltered UK borders only after the very last frost of late May has passed.
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach ten centimetres tall to encourage a much bushier shape.
Watch out for hungry slugs on new spring growth, using beer traps or copper tape to protect them.

items.name: Adenostyles
items.growersTips:
Try sowing Adenostyles seeds in early spring under cover to beat the damp UK frost.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to mimic their damp alpine meadow habitat.
Mix plenty of grit into your heavy UK clay soil to ensure their roots do not rot during wet winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the tender young spring shoots of these plants.
Plant them alongside ferns and hostas in a partially shaded spot for a beautiful woodland look.

items.name: Adesmia
items.growersTips:
Sow Adesmia seeds in early spring under glass, barely covering them with a light grit or compost.
Place your pots on a south-facing windowsill to give these sun-lovers maximum warmth and light.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light soakings.
Plant them alongside thrift or sedums in a gritty, free-draining rockery to mimic their dry home.
Watch out for damp UK autumns, as these annuals will rot quickly if left in waterlogged soil.

items.name: Adesmia aconcaguensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March using a gritty compost to protect seedlings from damp UK spring weather.
Plant out in May in your sunniest border, ensuring the soil is extremely free-draining and sandy.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this Andean native hates sitting in wet mud.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, which love targeting the tender young spring foliage.
Grow alongside hardy succulents or sedums in a gravel garden to match its dry-land requirements.

items.name: Adesmia balsamica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Grow this Chilean native in a gritty, free-draining soil mix to mimic its dry habitat and prevent rot.
Place your pots on a south-facing patio to maximise the summer sun and warmth this plant craves.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light soakings.
Watch out for damp UK autumn days, as excessive moisture will quickly ruin the aromatic foliage.

items.name: Adesmia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep to give this Chilean native a head start.
Plant out in May in your sunniest border using gritty soil to mimic its dry Andean habitat.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Sow alongside poached egg plants to attract the pollinators needed for seed production.

items.name: Adesmia muricata
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds indoors in March at a depth of five millimetres to beat the chilly UK spring soil.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy while they germinate on a sunny windowsill in your home.
Plant them out in May in your grittiest, fastest-draining soil to mimic their native dry habitat.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry to prevent root rot in damp summers.
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach ten centimetres tall to encourage a much bushier habit.

items.name: Adhatoda zeylanica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse before winter frost.
Water thoroughly when the top inch of compost feels dry, but cut back drastically during winter.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage a bushier habit and prevent it getting leggy.
Use a peat-free loam-based potting compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent drainage.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this plant indoors over winter.

items.name: Adiantopsis
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate fern in a pot of peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering only with harvested rainwater.
Place your pot in a draught-free room or a sheltered, shady UK porch that stays above five degrees.
Snip off any dead or tatty fronds right at the base of the plant during the active spring growth.
Group your pot with maidenhair ferns and fittonias to naturally boost the local humidity levels.

items.name: Adiantum
items.growersTips:
Plant your maidenhair fern in a sheltered, shady spot with moist, neutral to alkaline soil.
Water regularly with stored rainwater to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Cut back all the dead, brown fronds right to the base in early spring before new growth starts.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or compost into the planting hole to mimic a damp woodland floor.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the delicate new spring fronds.

items.name: Adiantum aethiopicum
items.growersTips:
Bring this maidenhair indoors for winter as it cannot survive a wet, freezing UK frost outside.
Keep the compost damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering from below to avoid rotting the crown.
Mix plenty of leafmould and perlite into your peat-free compost to mimic its wild forest floor.
Snip away any brown, crispy fronds right at the base in early spring to welcome fresh green growth.
Position your pot in a steamy, north-facing bathroom to give it the high humidity it craves.

items.name: Adiantum aleuticum
items.growersTips:
Plant this maidenhair fern in a sheltered, north-facing spot with damp, leaf-mould enriched soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Leave the dead fronds on over winter to protect the crown from hard frosts, then tidy in spring.
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new fiddleheads emerge to propagate them easily.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the delicate new fronds early.

items.name: Adiantum atroviride
items.growersTips:
Plant this maidenhair fern in a sheltered, draft-free spot with moist, humus-rich, alkaline soil.
Water consistently to keep the soil damp but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Tuck it next to hostas or astilbes in a shady border where they can share damp, dappled conditions.
Snip away any frost-damaged or brown fronds right at the base in early spring to welcome new growth.
Protect the crown with a thick mulch of leaf mould in autumn to insulate it from wet winter cold.

items.name: Adiantum bellum
items.growersTips:
Keep this delicate Bermuda maidenhair fern damp but never soggy by watering from the base in winter.
Grow it in a pot of peat-free compost mixed with perlite so you can move it indoors for UK frosts.
Place your potted fern on a tray of wet pebbles to boost humidity in dry, centrally heated rooms.
Cut back old, tattered fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh green growth.
Position it in a north-facing window or dappled shade to prevent the soft leaves from scorching.

items.name: Adiantum capillus-veneris
items.growersTips:
Plant this maidenhair fern in a sheltered, chalky spot with moist but well-drained alkaline soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp using harvested rainwater, but never let the roots sit in water.
Cut back old, tattered fronds right to the base in early spring just as the new fiddleheads emerge.
Grow it in a container so you can bring it into a humid conservatory to protect it from UK frosts.
Pair it with shade-loving hostas or wild ginger to help maintain the high humidity it craves.

items.name: Adiantum caudatum
items.growersTips:
Keep this trailing maidenhair in a hanging pot so its runners can cascade down and root freely.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy, especially in winter.
Place it in a steamy UK bathroom with bright, indirect light to mimic its humid jungle home.
Snip off dead, brown fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, vibrant green growth.
Repot in spring using a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for excellent drainage.

items.name: Adiantum chilense
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean maidenhair in a sheltered spot with moist, alkaline to neutral chalky soil.
Water regularly in summer to keep the soil damp, but never let it sit in soggy winter wet.
In our chilly UK winters, mulch the crown heavily with leaf mould to protect it from hard frosts.
Cut back the old, dead fronds right to the ground in early spring before the new growth uncurls.
Grow it alongside hostas or bleeding hearts in a dappled woodland border or a shady rock garden.

items.name: Adiantum concinnum
items.growersTips:
Bring your brittle maidenhair indoors by October to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Keep the compost consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering only with tepid rainwater.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and leaf mould to mimic its native forest floor.
Snip away any brown, dried-out fronds right at the base in early spring to spur fresh growth.
Position the pot in a steamy, north-facing bathroom to provide the high humidity it craves.

items.name: Adiantum cunninghamii
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate maidenhair fern in a sheltered, draft-free spot with moist, acidic soil.
Water regularly with stored rainwater to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Protect it from harsh winter frosts by moving container-grown plants into a cool greenhouse.
Snip away any brown or damaged fronds at the base in early spring to encourage fresh new growth.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into the planting hole to mimic its woodland home.

items.name: Adiantum diaphanum
items.growersTips:
Keep this delicate fern cosy indoors or in a heated greenhouse, as it cannot survive UK frosts.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, as tap water is too harsh for it.
Pot it in a peat-free, free-draining mix of leaf mould and perlite to mimic its forest home.
Place it in bright, indirect light, avoiding harsh midday sun which easily burns the fronds.
Snip off any brown, dying fronds at the base in spring to encourage fresh, healthy new growth.

items.name: Adiantum edgeworthii
items.growersTips:
Plant this walking fern in a hanging pot indoors to let its fronds root and spread naturally.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, as UK tap water is too alkaline.
Grow it in a mix of peat-free compost, perlite, and orchid bark for the perfect airy drainage.
Keep it in a humid, draft-free spot like a bright bathroom away from direct British radiators.
Watch out for sneaky fungus gnats in winter by using yellow sticky traps near the soil surface.

items.name: Adiantum formosum
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant maidenhair fern in a deep, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil that mimics woodland.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering less often during damp UK winters.
Grow it in a large container so you can easily move it indoors before the first harsh winter frosts.
Snip away any frost-damaged or brown fronds right at the base of the plant in early spring.
Position your pot in dappled shade away from dry, cold winds which quickly scorch the delicate foliage.

items.name: Adiantum hispidulum
items.growersTips:
Keep this rosy maidenhair in a pot so you can move it indoors before the first sharp UK winter frost.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost damp, but never let the pot sit directly in a puddle.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into peat-free compost to mimic its natural woodland floor home.
Snip away old, tatty fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for the new pink growth.
Position it in a north or east-facing room to give it bright light without burning the delicate fronds.

items.name: Adiantum jordanii
items.growersTips:
Plant your California maidenhair fern in a sheltered, frost-free spot with moist, alkaline soil.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering less in winter to prevent the roots from rotting.
Cut back old, tatty fronds in early spring just as the fresh new green fiddleheads start to emerge.
Protect your fern from dry winds and strong summer sun by placing it in dappled or deep shade.
Sow spores in late summer using sterile compost kept under a clear cover in a warm, bright room.

items.name: Adiantum latifolium
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender fern indoors in a bright room but safely out of any direct hot UK afternoon sun.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy or waterlogged.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and orchid bark to mimic its native tropical soil.
Mist the fronds daily or place the pot on a wet pebble tray to mimic humid rainforest conditions.
Snip away any brown or dying fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, tidy new growth.

items.name: Adiantum lunulatum
items.growersTips:
Bring this walking fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive frosty UK temperatures below ten degrees.
Plant it in a shallow, wide pot using peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering from below to avoid crown rot.
Position your pot in a humid, draft-free spot with bright but indirect light, away from radiators.
Snip off old, brown fronds at the base in early spring to encourage fresh, vibrant green growth.

items.name: Adiantum pedatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this maidenhair fern in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered, shady spot.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or composted bark to mimic its natural woodland floor.
Cut back the dead fronds to ground level in late winter before the new fiddleheads start to emerge.
Protect young spring fronds from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Adiantum peruvianum
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender Peruvian maidenhair indoors year-round as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost barely damp, never letting the pot sit in a puddle.
Repot in spring using a peat-free, free-draining mix enriched with plenty of leaf mould or coir.
Snip off any brown, dying fronds right at the base in early spring to encourage fresh green growth.
Place your pot on a wet pebble tray in a steamy bathroom to mimic its native humid rainforest home.

items.name: Adiantum philippense
items.growersTips:
Bring this maidenhair fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive a frosty UK climate outdoors.
Water with tepid rainwater keeping the compost consistently damp but never soggy to prevent rot.
Pot it up in a peat-free ericaceous mix blended with plenty of perlite for that vital drainage.
Snip off any brown or dying fronds right at the base in early spring to encourage fresh growth.
Place your pot on a tray of wet pebbles to boost humidity in dry, centrally heated UK homes.

items.name: Adiantum polyphyllum
items.growersTips:
Bring this giant maidenhair indoors by October as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter frost.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy by watering from below with lukewarm rainwater.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and perlite into your peat-free compost to mimic its native forest floor.
Snip away any brown or tatty fronds right at the base in early spring to welcome fresh green growth.
Position your pot in a steamy bathroom or on a wet pebble tray to beat dry UK central heating.

items.name: Adiantum raddianum
items.growersTips:
Keep your delta maidenhair fern in a humid bathroom or kitchen to mimic its tropical home.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the compost damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and perlite into peat-free compost to create the perfect drainage it needs.
Snip away any brown or dying fronds at the very base of the stem in early spring to boost new growth.
Place it in bright, indirect light near a north-facing window to prevent the delicate leaves burning.

items.name: Adiantum reniforme
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender fern in a pot of gritty, lime-rich compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Water from the bottom to keep the delicate, kidney-shaped fronds dry and prevent crown rot.
Place it on a tray of wet pebbles in winter to mimic the humid microclimate of its native islands.
Keep it in bright, indirect light away from drafty UK radiators that dry out the precious foliage.
Repot only in spring when roots peek through the bottom, using a shallow pan rather than a deep pot.

items.name: Adiantum silvaticum
items.growersTips:
Plant this forest maidenhair in a sheltered, draft-free spot with moist, humus-rich, acidic soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, using rainwater rather than tap water.
Protect it from harsh UK winter frosts by applying a thick mulch of leaf mould around the base.
Snip away any dead or tattered fronds right at the base in early spring to encourage fresh growth.
Grow it in deep shade alongside hostas or astilbes, away from drying winds and direct hot sun.

items.name: Adiantum tenerum
items.growersTips:
Keep this delicate maidenhair indoors or in a heated conservatory as it cannot survive UK frosts.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost damp but never let the pot sit directly in water.
Repot in spring using a peat-free loam mixed with plenty of perlite and leafmould for drainage.
Snick off any brown, dying fronds right at the base in early spring to encourage fresh new growth.
Position in a humid, draft-free spot with bright indirect light, away from drying radiators.

items.name: Adiantum trapeziforme
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender giant maidenhair indoors or in a heated conservatory to keep it safe from UK frosts.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy to prevent root rot.
Mix leaf mould and perlite into peat-free compost to mimic its natural tropical forest floor soil.
Keep it in a humid room like a bathroom or place the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to stop brown tips.
Snip off old tattered fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh bright green growth.

items.name: Adiantum venustum
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen maidenhair fern in moist, humus-rich soil mixed with plenty of leaf mould.
Position it in dappled or deep shade, ideally tucked under a north or east-facing garden wall.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during dry UK summer spells to avoid browning.
Cut back the old, tattered fronds right to the ground in February before the new pink growth emerges.
Divide established clumps in spring using a sharp spade to easily propagate and spread your stock.

items.name: Adiantum viridimontanum
items.growersTips:
Plant this green mountain maidenhair in a gritty, alkaline soil mix to mimic its native UK limestone.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering with rainwater rather than hard tap water if you can.
Position your fern in a sheltered, damp spot that gets bright but indirect light, avoiding hot sun.
Snip away any dead or tatty fronds in early spring just as the fresh new fiddleheads start to emerge.
Protect your young plants from slugs and snails in spring, as they love the tender new growth.

items.name: Adinandra
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender acid-lover in ericaceous compost and keep it in a pot so you can move it inside.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent yellowing leaves.
Position your pot in a sheltered, semi-shaded spot to mimic its natural woodland canopy home.
Bring your potted shrub into a frost-free conservatory or greenhouse before the first autumn frost.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove any dead wood.

items.name: Adinandra integerrima
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender evergreen indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from freezing.
Plant it in ericaceous compost to give it the acidic, lime-free soil it needs to thrive.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil chemistry perfectly acidic.
Position it in a bright conservatory or on a sunny windowsill to mimic its warm native climate.
Prune lightly in late spring after any new growth starts to maintain a neat, compact shape.

items.name: Adinandra lasiopetala
items.growersTips:
Plant this acid-loving shrub in ericaceous compost mixed with pine needles to mimic its forest home.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent leaf yellowing.
Grow it in a container so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse during harsh UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape it without losing next year's flower buds.
Mulch with composted bark in spring to keep the shallow roots cool and damp during dry spells.

items.name: Adonis
items.growersTips:
Plant Adonis vernalis in autumn in well-drained, gritty, alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters.
Give these slow growers a spot in full sun but keep the soil consistently damp during spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love eating the tender new shoots of Adonis amurensis in spring.
Divide your established clumps carefully in late summer only when they get too crowded to flower.
Plant them near snowdrops or hellebores to create a stunning, early spring woodland display.

items.name: Adonis aestivalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in autumn because UK winter cold naturally triggers their germination.
Grow them in your sunniest spot with gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water seedlings weekly during dry spring spells, but let the soil dry out completely between times.

Flush the central urn with fresh rainwater weekly, but keep the peat-free compost barely damp.
