Position your plant on a bright south-facing windowsill to mimic the tropical canopy light.
Slice off offsets with a sharp knife in spring once they reach a third of the parent plant's size.

items.name: Aechmea tayoensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this Ecuador native in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild home.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but let the potting compost dry out between waterings.
Bring your potted plant indoors to a warm, bright windowsill before October frosts hit the UK.
Flush the central reservoir with fresh water monthly to prevent stagnation and smelly rot indoors.
Wipe the broad, leathery leaves with a damp cloth in winter to maximize weak UK sunlight levels.

items.name: Aechmea tessmannii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark and perlite, never in heavy garden soil.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnant rot.
Bring your plant indoors by October as it cannot survive UK frosts and needs a warm winter home.
Position it on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the bright canopy light of its native jungle.
Feed during summer by spraying a very weak liquid orchid fertiliser directly onto the leaves.

items.name: Aechmea tillandsioides
items.growersTips:
Grow this bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark so you can bring it indoors before winter frosts hit.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnant rot.
Position it on a bright UK windowsill but shield it from scorching direct midsummer afternoon sun.
Mist the leaves regularly in winter to counteract dry indoor heating and keep humidity high.
After the main rosette flowers and dies, carefully slice off the pups to pot up as new plants.

items.name: Aechmea tocantina
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark and peat-free compost so you can move it inside.
Water by filling the central leafy rosette cup with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to keep it fresh.
Place it on a bright south-facing windowsill indoors from October to May to survive UK winter cold.
Feed during summer by spraying a very weak liquid orchid fertilizer directly onto the leaves monthly.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints when you bring the plant indoors for winter.

items.name: Aechmea tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this Brazilian bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark and peat-free compost to easily move it inside.
Water into the central urn with rainwater, keeping it topped up but flushing it out weekly to stop rot.
Keep it on a bright windowsill but shield it from direct summer sun to prevent leaf scorch.
Bring it indoors before October as it will not survive UK frosts and needs a minimum of ten degrees.
Once the main plant flowers and dies, slice off the basal pups with a sharp knife to pot up new ones.

items.name: Aechmea vanhoutteana
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian beauty indoors for winter as it cannot survive frosty UK temperatures.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but let the potting compost dry out between waterings.
Pot it in a very free-draining orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to prevent root rot.
Place it on a bright windowsill with indirect light to mimic its natural canopy home.
Flush the central reservoir with fresh water every few weeks to stop the water from stagnating.

items.name: Aechmea victoriana
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian beauty indoors for winter as it will not survive a frosty UK garden freeze.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but empty and flush it every month to prevent rot.
Plant in a very free-draining orchid bark mix rather than heavy, water-retaining UK compost.
Place it on a bright east or west windowsill where it gets gentle morning sun but no midday scorch.
Feed it by misting a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser onto the leaves during the active summer months.

items.name: Aechmea warasii
items.growersTips:
Grow this Brazilian bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark and peat-free compost to ensure fast drainage.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnant rot indoors.
Bring your potted plant inside by October, as it cannot survive UK winter frosts below ten degrees.
Wipe the arching, spiny leaves with a damp cloth to prevent indoor dust buildup and spider mites.
Propagate by slicing off the offsets or pups with a sharp knife once they reach half the parent size.

items.name: Aechmea weilbachii
items.growersTips:
Bring your Aechmea indoors by October because UK frosts will quickly kill this tender Brazilian gem.
Water into the central rosette cup using rainwater, keeping it topped up but flushing it weekly.
Plant it in a free-draining orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to prevent root rot in our damp.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf axils, especially during dry winter indoor heating.
Cut the parent rosette at the base with sharp shears once it dies back after its purple bloom.

items.name: Aechmea winkleri
items.growersTips:
Grow this bromeliad in a gritty, free-draining orchid bark mix rather than standard garden soil.
Keep the central rosette cup filled with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnation.
Bring your potted specimen indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts and rot.
Position it in bright, filtered light near a south window to mimic its natural canopy habitat.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Aechmea woronowii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark and peat-free compost to easily move it indoors.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but flush it out weekly to prevent stagnant rot in winter.
Place your pot on a bright, south-facing windowsill to mimic the tropical sun it needs to flower.
Wipe the broad, leathery leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and help it photosynthesise.
Wait until spring to slice off offsets with a sharp knife once they reach a third of the parent size.

items.name: Aechmea zebrina
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark mix so you can bring it indoors before autumn frost.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but let the potting compost dry out between waterings.
Place it in your brightest room or a heated conservatory to mimic the intense South American sun.
Flush the central reservoir with fresh water every month to prevent stagnant rot and smelly buildup.
Wipe the zebra-striped leaves with a damp cloth to keep dust from blocking essential winter light.

items.name: Aegonychon
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland soils rich in leaf mould and organic matter.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to establish roots, then rely on natural UK rainfall patterns.
Prune back hard to ground level in late autumn to prevent the spreading stems from becoming woody.
Position alongside native Primula vulgaris as companions to create a classic British woodland floor.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they target the tender new emerging foliage.

items.name: Aeonium
items.growersTips:
Bring your aeoniums inside before the first autumn frost, as they cannot survive a wet UK winter.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, and stop watering completely in winter.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit with peat-free compost to stop their roots rotting in our rain.
Snip off leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and propagate the cuttings easily.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots, especially if you grow your shrubs in containers.

items.name: Aeonium arboreum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to prevent rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty, free-draining compost is completely dry.
Take stem cuttings in May or June by letting the cut end calloused for a week before potting.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which eat the roots and cause the rosette to collapse.
Plant in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of John Innes number two and horticultural grit.

items.name: Aeonium aureum
items.growersTips:
Bring your green goddess inside by October because wet UK winters will quickly rot this Canary native.
Plant your golden rosette in a gritty mix of half John Innes number two and half coarse perlite.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep it completely dry during its summer dormancy.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots, especially if you grow it in a terracotta pot.
Snip off the main rosette after it flowers to encourage the side pups to take over the show.

items.name: Aeonium balsamiferum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender succulent indoors on a south-facing windowsill to survive damp UK frosts.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining loam-sand mix are bone dry to stop rot.
Propagate in spring by snipping leggy stems and letting them callus for three days before potting.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container compost and pick off mealybugs with alcohol-soaked buds.
Position in full summer sun to stimulate the balsam-scented oils and encourage yellow spring blooms.

items.name: Aeonium canariense
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to May to survive UK winters.
Grow in a gritty mix of equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural sand for sharp drainage.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry during spring and summer.
Position in full sun on a south-facing patio to encourage the natural red leaf margins to develop.
Check leaf rosettes weekly for vine weevil grubs and mealybugs which thrive in damp UK conditions.

items.name: Aeonium ciliatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in early spring at eighteen degrees to offset its tender annual habit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to a bare minimum during damp winters.
Move pots to a south-facing unheated greenhouse or porch by October to survive frost and damp cold.
Check leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium cuneatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is dry, then keep completely dry from November through March.
Bring pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Propagate by detaching side rosettes in late spring, allowing the stem to callus before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium dodrantale
items.growersTips:
Bring your green rose indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive a wet UK winter.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, keeping it completely dry during summer dormancy.
Blend half peat-free compost with half perlite or horticultural grit to prevent fatal root rot.
Propagate by gently detaching the small offsets or chicks that cluster around the base in spring.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf rosettes.

items.name: Aeonium glandulosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring on well-drained gritty compost, barely covering them with a fine grit layer.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to almost nothing during winter dormancy.
Bring pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill by October to survive wet UK winters.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the roots and treat with nematodes in late summer to prevent collapse.
Grow in terracotta pots with 50 percent perlite to ensure rapid drainage in damp British weather.

items.name: Aeonium glutinosum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a mix of equal parts John Innes number two and horticultural grit to ensure rapid drainage.
Water thoroughly only when the compost dries out completely, then keep almost dry through winter.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings, letting the wounds callous for three days before potting.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to develop the characteristic sticky stems.

items.name: Aeonium gorgoneum
items.growersTips:
Bring your gorgoneum indoors by October before UK frosts hit, as it cannot survive freezing wet soil.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry, and keep it completely dry during winter.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost and coarse grit to ensure the fast drainage this shrub needs.
Snip off leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier, more compact shrubby growth habit.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf rosettes during dry indoor winter storage.

items.name: Aeonium haworthii
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to prevent wet rot.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free grit to one part John Innes number two for essential drainage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, keeping completely dry in winter.
Take stem cuttings in May by letting the wound callous for three days before potting in sharp sand.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which eat the roots and cause the rosette head to topple over.

items.name: Aeonium hierrense
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost to ensure drainage.
Water only when the soil dries out completely in summer, and keep almost bone dry throughout winter.
Position in a terracotta pot on a south-facing patio to maximise summer sun and prevent root rot.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf rosettes and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium holochrysum
items.growersTips:
Bring pots indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from wet UK winter frosts and rot.
Grow in a mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in damp air.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Inspect the leaf rosettes weekly for vine weevil grubs and mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices.
Take stem cuttings in May to propagate new plants as backups against cold British winter losses.

items.name: Aeonium lancerottense
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this tender Canary Island succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Plant in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maintain the pink leaf margins in summer.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.

items.name: Aeonium leucoblepharum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive cold UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or patio to bring out the distinctive red leaf stripes.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous for three days before potting.

items.name: Aeonium lindleyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Protect from frost by overwintering indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings, letting the wounds callous for three days before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils during winter and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Aeonium nobile

Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a heated propagator at twenty degrees to kickstart growth
Grow in ninety percent grit mixed with loam to prevent root rot during wet British winters
Water only when the rosette leaves feel soft then drench fully and let dry out completely
Bring indoors to a frost free windowsill by October as this tender succulent cannot survive frost
Protect the single large rosette from slugs and snails which disfigure the foliage in damp weather

items.name: Aeonium sedifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty 50:50 mix of John Innes No 2 and perlite to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Bring indoors to a frost-free windowsill or heated greenhouse from October to April to avoid frost.

Prune leggy stems in spring by pinching out growing tips to encourage a bushy, compact shrubby habit.

items.name: Aeonium smithii
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender perennial cannot survive wet UK winters outside.
Grow in a gritty mix of fifty percent John Innes number two and fifty percent horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost which chew the roots and cause the rosette to topple.

items.name: Aeonium tabuliforme

Plant this flat rosette on a slight slope in gritty soil so rainwater drains away from its crown.
Water only from the base during winter to prevent rot in the tight, plate-like leaf rosettes.

items.name: Aeonium undulatum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter your Aeonium indoors in a bright frost-free room as UK winters will kill this succulent.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty, free-draining soil mix has dried out completely.

Position in full sun on a south-facing patio to prevent the large rosettes from becoming leggy.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in late spring and letting the wound callous before potting up.

items.name: Aeonium urbicum
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts John Innes number two to one part horticultural grit.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Inspect the leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations with organic insecticidal soap.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in late spring, allowing the cut end to callous before potting.

items.name: Aequatorium

Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Plant out in late May in well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.

Pinch out the growing tips in June to promote a bushier habit and increase the number of flowers.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Aerangidinae

Grow these African orchids on bark mounts in your bathroom to mimic their natural humid canopy life.
Water them with tepid rainwater only when the roots turn silvery-grey to prevent winter crown rot.

Hang them in bright, indirect east-facing windows to avoid scorching their delicate green leaves.
Feed them with a highly diluted orchid fertiliser every third watering during the active summer.

Grow these orchids in slatted baskets with chunky bark to let UK winter air circulate around roots.
Hang them in a bright south-facing conservatory but use a light shade cloth during hot July days.

Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf axils during dry indoor heating months in winter.
Feed with a weak high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer weekly only during their active spring growth spurt.

items.name: Aeschynanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your lipstick plant indoors for winter as our chilly UK climate will easily damage them.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Hang them in a bright bathroom where natural steam mimics their native humid rainforest home.
Prune the stems back by a third in spring to encourage bushy growth and way more colorful blooms.
Repot into a free-draining orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to keep their roots breathing.

items.name: Aeschynanthus acuminatus
items.growersTips:
Hang this lipstick plant in a bright bathroom to mimic its native humid forests in the dry UK air.
Water it only when the top two inches of peat-free compost dry out to prevent root rot in winter.
Keep it indoors year-round as it hates UK cold and needs temperatures to stay strictly above 15C.
Trim back the trailing stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more blooms.
Feed with a diluted high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight from April to September.

items.name: Aeschynanthus buxifolius
items.growersTips:
Keep this lipstick plant cozy indoors during UK winters, as it cannot cope with frost or cold drafts.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free orchid compost feel dry.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where high humidity and indirect light mimic its native rainforest.
Snip back leggy stems by a third in spring right after flowering to boost next year's red blooms.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them off with a cotton bud dipped in spirit.

items.name: Aeschynanthus longicaulis
items.growersTips:
Bring your zebra basket vine indoors by October as it cannot cope with chilly UK winter drafts.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp air.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the natural steam mimics its native humid tropical rainforest.
Trim back leggy stems by a third in spring to encourage bushy growth and more yellow-green flowers.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints during winter when indoor central heating dries the air.

items.name: Aeschynanthus pulcher
items.growersTips:
Hang this lipstick plant in bright, indirect light away from cold winter drafts near a UK window.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost dry out, using lukewarm rainwater.
Feed with a diluted high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight from April to September.
Prune stems back by a third in late autumn after flowering to encourage bushier spring growth.
Keep the room above fifteen degrees Celsius to prevent the buds dropping off during winter.

items.name: Aeschynanthus radicans
items.growersTips:
Hang this lipstick plant in a bright bathroom where steamy UK showers mimic its tropical home.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to avoid deadly root rot.
Prune stems back by a third in spring to encourage bushy growth and more scarlet blooms.
Keep it indoors year-round as our chilly UK nights below twelve degrees will stunt its growth.
Feed with a diluted high-potassium tomato fertiliser fortnightly from April to September.

items.name: Aeschynanthus speciosus
items.growersTips:
Keep this lipstick plant indoors or in a warm conservatory to protect it from chilly UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to avoid rotting the roots.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where high humidity and indirect light mimic its native jungle home.
Snip back leggy stems by a third in spring to encourage bushy growth and more brilliant blooms.
Feed with a diluted high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight from April to September.

items.name: Afrofittonia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African perennial in a warm conservatory to protect it from chilly UK winters.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid root shock.
Blend plenty of leaf mould and grit into your peat-free compost to mimic its native forest floor.
Snip back the leggy stems in early spring to encourage a bushier, more compact growth habit.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites during dry summer spells and mist the foliage regularly.

items.name: Afrosolen
items.growersTips:
Plant your Afrosolen bulbs in gritty, free-draining soil to stop them rotting in wet UK winters.
Tuck these South African bulbs into a warm, south-facing border or pot to soak up the British sun.
Keep watering them regularly through spring, but let the soil dry out completely over the summer.
Bring your pots indoors or lift the bulbs before the first frost, as they cannot survive UK freezes.
Grow them in terracotta pots to easily manage soil moisture and move them away from cold winter rain.

items.name: Afzelia africana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty-four Celsius
Grow this tropical legume in pots of free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool wet UK summers
Position containers in your warmest south-facing suntrap or greenhouse to maximise summer heat units
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite under leaves when growing under glass in midsummer

items.name: Afzelia bipindensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK springs.
Grow in pots of gritty, free-draining loam to easily move shelter during wet British summers.
Water only when the top 5cm of soil dries out to prevent root rot in humid UK weather.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to maximise limited UK summer heat.
Feed weekly with a low-nitrogen fertiliser to support pod development without overproducing foliage.

items.name: Afzelia quanzensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African tree as a summer annual in pots using loam-based compost with extra grit.
Sow the thick-coated seeds in March after nicking the seed coat and soaking in warm water for 24 hours.
Bring pots indoors by September before UK night temperatures drop below 10C to prevent frost death.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil are dry to mimic dry-season conditions.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot in your garden to maximise summer heat.

items.name: Afzelia rhomboidea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Grow in large containers of free-draining loam-based compost to allow easy moving indoors for winter.
Water deeply once a week during summer, allowing the top five centimeters of soil to dry out fully.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to maximize limited UK summer warmth.
Apply a potassium-rich liquid fertilizer monthly from June to August to support container growth.

items.name: Afzelia xylocarpa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical annual in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK cool summers.
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth after soaking them in warm water for 24 hours to break dormancy.
Water deeply once a week to mimic monsoonal patterns, allowing the sandy potting mix to dry out fully.
Feed fortnightly with a low-nitrogen potassium fertilizer to encourage sturdy stems without excess sap.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mites under leaves and mist daily to maintain high local humidity.

items.name: Agalmyla
items.growersTips:
Bring your agalmyla indoors before October frosts as this tropical climber hates UK winter chills.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of peat-free compost dries to prevent root rot.
Position your plant in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to mimic forest canopies.
Feed with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertilizer every two weeks during the active summer growth.
Grow agalmyla in a free-draining orchid bark and perlite mix to keep its epiphytic roots happy.

items.name: Aganonerion
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before UK frosts.
Water generously through the summer active growth phase but keep the soil barely damp over winter.
Prune back unruly stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more blooms.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing patio to maximise the high light levels it needs.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry greenhouse air and mist the foliage regularly to deter them.

items.name: Aganosma
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant it in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the roots never sit in wet soil.
Water thoroughly once the top inch of soil dries out, but keep it nearly dry throughout winter.
Prune your vine in early spring just as new growth starts, cutting back unruly stems to a strong bud.
Watch out for red spider mites and mealybugs which thrive on this plant in dry conservatory air.

items.name: Agatea
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender climber against a south-facing UK wall to shield it from cold northerly winds.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot.
Prune back the woody stems by a third in early spring to encourage fresh, vigorous flowering shoots.
Mulch the root zone with five centimetres of compost in November to protect it from hard UK frosts.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are overwintering your plant in a conservatory.

items.name: Agave
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your soil to ensure fast drainage so the roots do not rot during wet UK winters.

Watch out for agave snout weevil in summer and drench with systemic insecticide if you see damage.
Give this giant plenty of space away from paths so its sharp leaf tips do not snag passersby.

items.name: Agave xylonacantha
items.growersTips:
Plant this agave in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it under glass for wet UK winters.
Keep it in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its native Mexican light levels and heat.
Stop watering completely from October to March to prevent the root rot caused by cold British damp.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing through the roots of potted agaves.
Protect the gorgeous, lethal leaf spines from frost damage by wrapping the crown in fleece in winter.

items.name: Agavoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant your agaves in a fifty-fifty mix of grit and peat-free compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep them bone dry in unheated greenhouses from November to March to prevent lethal winter rot.
Look out for agave snout weevil damage on your Yuccas and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Plant hardy Agave americana on a south-facing slope or raised bed to maximize scarce UK sunshine.
Prune dead lower leaves of Cordylines in late spring only after the worst winter frosts have passed.

items.name: Ageratina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of three millimetres to beat the cool UK weather.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and more abundant autumn flowers.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to build strong, deep roots.
Grow them alongside taller cosmos or dahlias to provide natural support against strong UK winds.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around stems.

items.name: Aglaodorum
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare aquatic aroid in a heated greenhouse pool to survive chilly UK winter temperatures.
Plant your specimen in heavy clay loam enriched with well-rotted leaf mould to mimic muddy swamps.
Keep the rhizome constantly submerged under at least ten centimetres of warm, still water.
Boost low UK light levels with a warm-spectrum LED grow light from October through to April.
Propagate by carefully dividing the thick rhizomes during their active growth phase in midsummer.

items.name: Aglaomorpha
items.growersTips:
Grow your Aglaomorpha in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild tree home.
Water your fern only when the top inch of soil dries out, using tepid rainwater to avoid leaf shock.
Place this beauty in a humid bathroom or mist it daily to beat dry UK central heating in winter.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light, keeping it safe from harsh, direct midday sun.
Keep your home above fifteen degrees Celsius to protect this tropical fern from chilly UK drafts.

items.name: Aglaomorpha coronans
items.growersTips:
Bring it indoors for winter as this tropical fern cannot survive UK frosts below ten degrees.
Plant in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its natural epiphytic home.
Water from the top into the nest-like crown but let the pot drain fully to prevent root rot.
Position in bright, indirect light like an east window to keep those glossy fronds from scorching.
Wipe the wide fronds with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and check for hidden scale insects.

items.name: Aglaomorpha heraclea
items.growersTips:
Grow this giant fern in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild tree home.
Keep it cozy indoors or in a heated conservatory as it will not survive a chilly UK winter frost.
Water thoroughly once the top inch of soil dries, using tepid rainwater to avoid brown leaf tips.
Wipe those massive fronds with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and keep pests like scale at bay.
Give it bright, filtered light near a north window, avoiding harsh direct summer afternoon sun.

items.name: Aglaomorpha meyeniana
items.growersTips:
Grow this epiphytic fern in a chunky orchid bark mix rather than standard compost to prevent rot.
Keep it cozy indoors year-round as it cannot survive frosty UK winters below ten degrees Celsius.
Water from the top into the fuzzy rhizome but let the pot drain fully so it never sits in water.
Place it in bright, indirect light near a north or east window to mimic its natural canopy home.
Mist the exposed creeping rhizomes daily during dry winter heating months to keep humidity high.

items.name: Aglaomorpha novoguineensis
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical fern cozy indoors during UK winters as it cannot survive temperatures below 15C.
Grow it in a chunky, bark-rich orchid compost mix to mimic its natural tree-dwelling habitat.
Water thoroughly only when the top inch of soil feels dry, using tepid rainwater if you can.
Position your fern in bright, indirect light near a north or east-facing window to avoid leaf burn.
Mist the fronds daily or use a gravel tray to mimic the high humidity of its native rainforests.

items.name: Aglaonema
items.growersTips:
Keep your Chinese evergreen warm and away from chilly drafts near UK windows during winter.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to avoid root rot.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and boost low light absorption.
Feed with a weak liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September for lush growth.
Choose red-variegated cultivars like Crete for brighter spots, but keep green types in shade.

items.name: Aglaonema commutatum
items.growersTips:
Keep your Chinese evergreen in a draft-free spot above 15C, away from chilly UK winter windows.
Water only when the top half of the compost is dry, as damp UK winters easily cause root rot.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and boost light absorption in winter.
Repot in spring using a peat-free houseplant mix with extra perlite to ensure sharp drainage.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Aglaonema costatum
items.growersTips:
Keep this slow-growing beauty in a warm draft-free room above fifteen degrees all winter long.
Water only when the top half of the peat-free compost dries out to prevent soggy root rot.
Wipe the dark glossy leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and maximize low UK light.
Repot only every three springs into a snug pot using a mix of houseplant soil and extra perlite.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the leaf stems and dab them off with organic neem oil.

items.name: Aglaonema modestum
items.growersTips:
Keep your Chinese evergreen warm and draft-free indoors, especially during damp UK winter months.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost dry out to prevent root rot in cool rooms.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to remove dust and help them photosynthesise.
Repot in spring using a mix of houseplant compost, perlite, and orchid bark for perfect drainage.
Keep this plant away from cold windowsills in winter as temperatures below fifteen degrees hurt it.

items.name: Aglaonema simplex
items.growersTips:
Keep your Chinese evergreen snug indoors at 18C, shielding it from cold UK windowsill drafts.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost dry out to prevent soggy root rot.
Wipe those broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and boost winter light absorption.
Feed with a weak liquid fertiliser monthly from April to September to encourage lush green growth.
Repot every two years in spring using a free-draining mix of houseplant compost and perlite.

items.name: Agrostemma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in March or April at a depth of five millimetres to avoid root damage.
Support the tall stems of Agrostemma githago with hazel twigs or brushwood before they start to flop.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile soil; overly rich soil produces lush foliage but fewer flowers.
Water seedlings weekly until established, then only during prolonged dry spells in the UK summer.
Deadhead regularly to prolong the blooming season and prevent aggressive self-seeding in borders.

items.name: Agrostemma githago
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in March or April at a depth of five millimetres into poor, gritty soil.
Support the tall, floppy stems using hazel twigs or brushwood link stakes before flowers open in June.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells and completely avoid feeding to prevent excessive foliage.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in summer to prolong flowering and prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Wear gloves when handling seeds and seed pods as all parts of this British native are highly toxic.

items.name: Agrostophyllinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these epiphytes in a heated greenhouse or conservatory keeping winter temperatures above twelve C
Pot in a free-draining medium of fine bark and perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Water with tepid rainwater only when the bark dries out to mimic their natural tropical wet-dry cycle
Position in bright indirect light avoiding direct summer sun which easily scorches the thin leaves
Inspect the dense clumps regularly for mealybugs hiding in the tightly overlapping leaf sheaths

items.name: Aichryson
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted tree houseleek indoors to a frost-free windowsill before the first autumn chill.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel bone dry, then soak it and let it drain fully.
Mix equal parts John Innes number two compost and coarse grit to keep their shallow roots rot-free.
Take stem cuttings in early summer, letting them dry for a few days before popping them in grit.
Snip off the yellow flower heads once they fade to keep the main plant from dying back completely.

items.name: Aichryson ×aizoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender succulent in pots of gritty, free-draining loam to easily move indoors by October.
Water sparingly from below only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry to prevent stem rot.
Position in a bright, unheated porch or south-facing windowsill to mimic its native Canary Islands.
Pinch out the yellow spring flowers if you want to delay the plant dying after its monocarpic bloom.
Inspect the dense leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations with organic neem oil.

items.name: Aichryson bollei
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost without burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to a bare minimum during damp winters.
Bring pots indoors to a bright windowsill by October to protect this tender annual from UK frosts.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost which chew through the delicate roots of this succulent.
Grow in shallow terracotta pots rather than deep plastic ones to prevent waterlogging in UK damp.

items.name: Aichryson divaricatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on free-draining gritty compost under glass to start them early.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Sow alongside Sedum album in shallow stone troughs to create a complementary dry-tolerant display.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in May to encourage a bushier habit before they flower.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which destroy the roots of these succulents in container soil.

items.name: Aichryson dumosum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Madeira native indoors to a bright windowsill before the first UK autumn frost.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost are completely dry.
Snip off the yellow star-shaped flowers after blooming to keep this short-lived shrub leafy.
Check the tight leaf rosettes regularly for vine weevil grubs and wipe away any fuzzy mealybugs.
Propagate easily by taking stem cuttings in spring and letting them callous over before potting.

items.name: Aichryson villosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty compost without covering them as they need light to sprout
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are bone dry to prevent winter rot in damp UK air
Bring pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October before the first autumn frosts arrive
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in late spring to encourage a bushier branching habit
Discard the plant after it finishes flowering in summer as this species is a strict annual here

items.name: Aizoanthemopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African native in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by late October.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely during damp winter months.
Position your pots on a south-facing patio to maximise the precious British summer sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the fleshy leaf joints, and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Aizoanthemopsis hispanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the soil dry out completely between sparse summer drinks.
Overwinter this tender Spanish succulent indoors on a sunny windowsill to protect it from UK frosts.
Pair it with hardy sedums in a gravel garden to mimic its natural dry Mediterranean habitat.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs as they love the fleshy, moisture-rich leaves.

items.name: Aizoanthemum
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage these plants need to survive damp UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, mimicking their natural desert cycle.
Keep them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October.
Position your pots on a south-facing patio to maximise every bit of scarce British summer sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints, especially when overwintering them indoors.

items.name: Aizoanthemum hispanicum
items.growersTips:
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to ensure this succulent survives wet UK winters.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or porch by October.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep the foliage completely dry during damp autumn days.
Position your pot in the absolute sunniest spot of your patio to coax out those delicate blooms.
Sow the tiny seeds on the soil surface in spring, pressing them in gently without burying them.

items.name: Aizoon
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your soil to help these succulent-like plants survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep them in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic their native warm and dry environments.
Protect them from winter frost by moving potted plants into a cold frame or unheated greenhouse.
Water sparingly, only when the soil is dry, as damp British weather is their biggest enemy.
Propagate them easily by taking stem cuttings in late spring when the active growing season starts.

items.name: Aizoon canariense
items.growersTips:
Bring this Canary Island native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant in a gritty cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite to ensure rapid drainage in rain.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, then soak it thoroughly and let it drain.
Position your pot on a south-facing patio to maximise the limited UK summer sunshine it craves.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs on the fleshy leaves when you bring the plant inside for winter.

items.name: Aizoon hispanicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Spanish succulent in your sunniest spot using a gritty, free-draining alpine compost mix.
Keep it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly but never let the pot sit in water.
Sow the tiny seeds on the soil surface in early spring, pressing them in gently without burying.
Watch out for damp-loving slugs and snails during wet UK summers, as they love the fleshy leaves.

items.name: Aizoon secundum
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing ice plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Position your pot in full south-facing sun to encourage the tiny yellow flowers to open fully.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, keeping it completely dry from November through March.
Bring container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse or bright windowsill before the first UK frost.
Propagate easily in spring by snipping stems and letting them dry for a day before potting up.

items.name: Alafia
items.growersTips:
Bring your Alafia indoors by October to protect this tender tropical climber from chilly UK frosts.
Grow Alafia in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure the fast drainage it needs.
Position your Alafia in a conservatory or south-facing windowsill to get maximum daily sunlight.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, keeping it much drier in winter.
Prune back any unruly twining stems in early spring just as the new growth starts to show.

items.name: Alangium
items.growersTips:
Plant your Alangium in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to prevent winter stem dieback.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the woodland-style soil consistently damp.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove damaged wood and shape the shrub before new spring growth.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your soil to mimic their native forest floor.
Watch out for late spring frosts which can scorch the delicate emerging star-shaped leaves.

items.name: Alangium chinense
items.growersTips:
Plant this in a sheltered, south-facing spot to shield its delicate leaves from harsh UK winds.
Wrap the young trunk in fleece during wet UK winters to protect it from severe, bark-splitting frost.
Grow it in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil, mixing in plenty of leaf mould before planting.
Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead wood, as it dislikes heavy, hard renovation cuts.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, using beer traps to protect them early on.

items.name: Alangium javanicum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical beauty indoors for winter as it will not survive a frosty UK garden freeze.
Plant it in a deep pot using ericaceous compost mixed with grit to mimic its native acidic soil.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet.
Position your pot in a conservatory or bright windowsill that gets indirect morning sunlight.
Feed it monthly from April to September with a diluted liquid seaweed fertilizer to boost growth.

items.name: Alangium platanifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil that mimics its native forest.
Position it in a sheltered, dappled shade spot to protect those large, maple-like leaves from wind.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead wood and maintain its elegant, multi-stemmed shape.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to replicate forest floor nutrients.

items.name: Alangium salviifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Asian shrub in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant it in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the roots never sit in wet soil.
Water it generously throughout the summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost passes to shape it and remove any winter-damaged wood.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping the plant indoors during winter.

items.name: Alantsilodendron
items.growersTips:
Start these annuals indoors in March to beat the late UK frosts, sowing seeds just five millimetres deep.
Water them at the base early in the morning to prevent damp rot during humid British summer spells.
Plant them alongside dwarf marigolds to deter the aphids that love targeting their tender new stems.
Mix plenty of gritty sand into your garden soil to keep their roots dry during wet English summers.
Snip off the faded flower heads weekly in July and August to keep new blossoms coming until autumn.

items.name: Albizia
items.growersTips:
Start your Albizia seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator to mimic warmer climates.
Plant them out in May after the last frost in a south-facing spot sheltered from cold UK winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving them daily light sprinkles.
Prune your young Albizia in late spring to encourage a strong central leader and bushy growth.
Mulch the root area with well-rotted manure in autumn to protect them from wet winter cold.

items.name: Albuca
items.growersTips:
Plant your Albuca bulbs shallowly in autumn so the bulb tops are just showing above the soil level.
Give them a gritty, free-draining compost mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting away.
Water your Albuca only when the soil is dry, then stop completely during their summer dormancy.
Keep them on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect them from harsh UK frosts.
Place them near low-growing succulents like Echeveria to complement their quirky, spiralled leaves.

items.name: Albuca abyssinica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African bulb in a pot so you can easily bring it inside before the first UK frost.
Plant the bulbs in spring with their necks just showing above a very gritty, free-draining compost.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, then keep the soil almost bone dry during its winter dormancy.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or sunny patio to mimic its native bright sunlight.
Watch out for slugs on the tender new shoots in spring, using copper tape around your pots to stop them.

items.name: Albuca acuminata
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water it only when active growth appears in autumn, then keep it dry during summer dormancy.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill by November.
Plant the bulbs shallowly in autumn, leaving the very top of the bulb neck just above the soil.
Watch out for aphids on the winter foliage and gently wipe them off with a damp cloth.

items.name: Albuca bracteata
items.growersTips:
Grow your pregnant onion in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive damp UK winters.
Keep it on a bright, south-facing windowsill indoors as it will not survive a frosty British winter.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, and keep it completely dry throughout winter.
Peel away the papery outer layers gently to reveal the tiny green baby bulbs forming on the side.
Repot the baby bulblets in spring by pressing them halfway into the soil rather than burying them.

items.name: Albuca cooperi
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep them bone dry during their summer dormancy, restarting watering only when autumn shoots appear.
Move pots to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill by October to survive wet UK winters.
Do not cut back the quirky, corkscrew foliage while green as it feeds the bulb for next year.
Group them with hardy sempervivums in shallow stone troughs for a stunning, drought-tolerant display.

items.name: Albuca fastigiata
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Set the bulbs just below the soil surface, leaving the very tips exposed to prevent rotting.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, then keep them almost completely dry during winter dormancy.
Bring potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill before the first frost.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to feast on the emerging strap-like leaves.

items.name: Albuca foetida
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African bulb indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant the bulbs shallowly in spring with the top third exposed above the soil to prevent rotting.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, then stop completely during its summer dormancy.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to mimic its native rocky habitat.
Keep an eye out for aphids on the spring flower spikes and gently wipe them off with a damp cloth.

items.name: Albuca humilis
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs in autumn about five centimetres deep in gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep them on a sunny windowsill or in a cold greenhouse to shield them from wet UK winters.
Water them weekly during their spring growth, but let the soil dry out completely in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the delicate, onion-scented white flowers.
Group them with hardy succulents like Sempervivum in shallow alpine pans for a lovely display.

items.name: Albuca juncifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters without rot.
Keep your pot on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse, as it cannot tolerate UK frosts.
Water it only when the soil dries out completely, then stop watering when it goes dormant in summer.
Plant the bulbs shallowly in autumn, leaving the top third of the bulb exposed above the soil.
Watch out for aphids on the curly leaves, and gently wash them off with a splash of soapy water.

items.name: Albuca longipes
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it completely dry during its summer dormant phase to prevent the bulb from rotting.
Place your pot on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse as it grows during our winter.
Plant the bulbs shallowly with their tops just showing at the soil surface for best growth.
Watch out for slugs and snails during the damp UK autumn when the new winter leaves emerge.

items.name: Albuca setosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb shallowly in UK soil with the top third of the bulb exposed to the air.
Use a gritty, free-draining cactus mix to prevent bulb rot during wet British winters.
Water it only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely during its winter dormancy.
Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it indoors to a bright windowsill before the first frost.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the succulent-like leaves in damp UK spring weather.

items.name: Albuca shawii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in spring about 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet winters.
Keep them bone dry during their winter dormancy by moving containers into a cold greenhouse or shed.
Water them regularly but lightly in summer, only when the top few centimetres of soil feel dry.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to munch on the emerging aniseed-scented leaves.
Grow them in pots alongside hardy succulents like Sempervivums to match their drainage needs.

items.name: Albuca spiralis
items.growersTips:
Keep your frizzle sizzle on a sunny UK windowsill, as it needs direct light to curl its leaves.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely when it goes dormant in summer.
Plant the bulb with the top third exposed above a very gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix.
Move it indoors by October because this South African beauty cannot survive wet, freezing UK winters.
Avoid cutting back yellowing summer leaves, as the bulb needs to suck back that energy to regrow.

items.name: Albuca viscosa
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs shallowly in autumn with their tops just peeking out of a gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep them on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.
Water them only when the soil is dry to the touch, then stop watering completely during summer dormancy.
Watch out for aphids on the sticky, scented leaves and gently wash them off with a lukewarm spray.
Pair them with small succulents in terracotta pots to give their quirky, curling foliage center stage.

items.name: Alcantarea brasiliana
items.growersTips:
Bring this giant bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant in a highly free-draining mix of orchid bark and perlite to mimic its rocky native home.
Keep the central leafy cup filled with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnation.
Position your pot in the brightest spot possible, like a south-facing patio, for optimal color.
Feed during active summer growth by spraying a very weak liquid seaweed fertilizer onto the leaves.

items.name: Alcantarea edmundoi
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian giant indoors by October to protect its tender leaves from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a very free-draining mix of orchid bark and perlite rather than standard garden soil.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but let the potting compost dry out between waterings.
Position your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing patio to mimic its native sunny cliffs.
Wipe the broad leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent indoor dust and watch for mealybugs.

items.name: Alcantarea extensa
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Alcantarea indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and peat-free compost to prevent wet feet.
Fill the central urn with rainwater, flushing it weekly in summer but keeping it dry in winter.
Position your container in a bright conservatory or south-facing patio to get maximum summer sun.
Look out for mealybugs in the leaf crevices and wipe them away using a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Alcantarea geniculata
items.growersTips:
Bring this giant inside by October as it cannot survive a wet UK winter frost below five degrees.
Grow it in a heavy clay pot with free-draining orchid bark to stop the top-heavy rosette toppling.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but flush it out weekly to prevent stagnant rot.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot of your patio to coax out those lovely red leaf flushes.
Feed only during June and July with a weak foliar seaweed spray misted directly onto the leaves.

items.name: Alcantarea glaziouana
items.growersTips:
Bring this giant bromeliad indoors to a bright conservatory before the first cold UK autumn frosts.
Plant it in a very free-draining orchid bark and perlite mix rather than heavy garden soil.
Water by filling the central rosette cup with rainwater, keeping it topped up during warm summers.
Feed during active summer growth by spraying a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer directly onto leaves.
Watch out for scale insects and mealybugs hiding deep inside the leaf joints during winter indoors.

items.name: Alcantarea heloisae
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian beauty indoors by mid-October to protect its tender leaves from UK frosts.
