Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to prevent root rot in wet British winters.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Wear thick gloves when handling to protect your skin from the irritating, bristly hairs.
Deadhead immediately after flowering in July to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your borders.

items.name: Amsinckia vernicosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to mimic UK wildflower meadow regeneration.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet British climates.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between feeds.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms in late summer to control aggressive self-seeding in small gardens.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise flowering and prevent leggy growth in overcast weather.

items.name: Amsinckiopsis kingii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in free-draining gritty soil to mimic its native dry habitat in UK winters.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine trough to prevent root rot from heavy UK winter rainfall.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, allowing the soil to dry out completely between.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the crown.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its winter dormancy.

items.name: Amsonia
items.growersTips:
Pop your amsonia in well-drained soil with plenty of grit to survive our wet UK winters without rotting.
Cut the stems back by a third after flowering in June to keep the plant bushy and stop it flopping.
Plant them alongside spring bulbs like tulips to hide the dying bulb foliage as the amsonia grows.
Give your young plants a deep soak once a week during dry spells until their roots are established.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh new shoots when they first emerge in early UK spring.

items.name: Amsonia ciliata
items.growersTips:
Plant this fringed bluestar in your sunniest spot with gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its home.
Water it weekly during its first UK summer, then leave it alone as it is highly drought-tolerant.
Cut the stems back to the ground in late autumn once the gorgeous golden foliage display finishes.
Watch out for slugs on tender new spring shoots, using beer traps or organic wool pellets to deter.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth starts, keeping the root ball intact.

items.name: Amsonia hubrichtii
items.growersTips:
Plant this thread-leaf star in full sun and free-draining soil to get that gorgeous autumn gold.
Give it a deep weekly soak during its first UK summer to help those deep, drought-busting roots bed in.
Cut the stems back to the ground in early spring just as the new green shoots start to peep through.
Divide established clumps in autumn using a sharp spade to get free plants for your borders.
Pair it with dark purple salvias or autumn asters to make those delicate blue flowers pop.

items.name: Amsonia orientalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare beauty in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soil to keep its roots happy in UK summers.
Position it in full sun or light dappled shade to ensure those starry blue flowers open fully in June.
Cut the stems back to the ground in late autumn once the foliage turns its lovely buttery yellow.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer rather than trying to divide its tough crown.
Keep an eye out for slugs on young spring shoots, but otherwise enjoy its excellent pest resistance.

items.name: Amsonia tabernaemontana
items.growersTips:
Plant this blue star in deep, moisture-retentive soil to help it survive dry UK summers.
Give it a hard chop by a third after flowering in June to stop stems flopping in British rain.
Watch out for slugs on tender new spring shoots, especially during damp April and May weather.
Pair it with yellow autumn-fruiting grasses to contrast beautifully with its golden October foliage.
Plant the crown just level with the soil surface in autumn so winter wet doesn't rot the roots.

items.name: Amsonia tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this woolly bluestar in your sharpest-draining, grit-amended soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to mimic its native desert home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between occasional drenchings.
Cut the faded stems back to the ground in early spring just as the fresh new growth starts to peep up.
Plant it alongside silver-leaved artemisia or hardy sedums which love the same dry, sunny conditions.

items.name: Anacamptis
items.growersTips:
Plant your pyramidal orchids in autumn using a very shallow depth, just covering the tuber with soil.
Mix plenty of crushed limestone or grit into your soil to mimic the chalky downs they love in the UK.
Avoid watering them at all during their summer dormancy period to prevent the tubers from rotting.
Plant them alongside fine native grasses like fescues to provide crucial structural support.
Never use chemical fertilisers nearby as they destroy the vital soil fungi these orchids need.

items.name: Anadenanthera
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to mimic their warm native climate.
Grow this tender annual in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them under glass in rain.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to avoid root rot in damp UK weather.
Keep a close eye out for spider mites when keeping these plants in warm, dry indoor windowsills.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertilizer once the first true leaves appear.

items.name: Anadenanthera colubrina
items.growersTips:
Bring your pots inside by October because this tropical beauty cannot survive a British frost.
Sow seeds in spring just below the soil surface after soaking them in warm water for 24 hours.
Use a very gritty cacti compost mix to prevent root rot during our damp UK autumn months.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry to mimic its native dry season.
Keep a close eye out for spider mites when you bring your potted plant indoors for the winter.

items.name: Anadenanthera peregrina
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical Fabaceae tree indoors by October to protect it from the chilly UK winter frost.
Sow your seeds at a depth of one centimetre in free-draining sandy loam with a heat mat set to 25C.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry to prevent lethal root rot disease.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry conservatory air and mist the leaves weekly to deter them.
Feed your young tree with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month through summer.

items.name: Anaphalioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass, barely covering them to let UK light spark growth.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering gently at the base during dry spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young shoots during damp British spring nights and use barriers.
Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage a much bushier habit and more summer flowers.
Mix grit into your heavy UK clay soil before planting to ensure the roots don't rot in winter wet.

items.name: Anaphyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare tropical aroid in a warm greenhouse or conservatory to survive chilly UK winters.
Plant the tubers in a free-draining mix of orchid bark, peat-free compost, and plenty of perlite.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy during the active spring and summer growth.
Move your potted plant into a shaded spot away from direct midday sun to prevent leaf scorching.
Reduce watering significantly in autumn and keep the tuber dry and frost-free over the winter.

items.name: Anaphyllum beddomei
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Indian aroid indoors by October to protect its tuber from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant the tuber five centimetres deep in a free-draining mix of orchid bark, peat, and perlite.
Water generously in summer to mimic monsoons, but keep it barely damp during winter dormancy.
Position in bright, filtered light to mimic forest understoreys and prevent leaf scorch in June.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air, so mist the leaves daily to keep humidity high.

items.name: Anaphyllum wightii
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare tropical aroid in a warm conservatory, keeping it above fifteen degrees all year.
Use a very chunky, well-draining peat-free orchid compost mix to prevent its delicate roots rotting.
Keep the compost consistently moist with tepid rainwater, but never let the pot sit in deep water.
Position your plant in bright, indirect light, shielding its soft leaves from harsh midday sun.
Mist the foliage daily or use a gravel tray to mimic the high humidity of its native rainforest.

items.name: Anchietea
items.growersTips:
Protect this Brazilian climber from UK frosts by growing it in a container to move indoors for winter
Plant your butterfly vine in peat-free loam with grit to ensure the sharp drainage it needs to thrive
Water deeply once a week in summer but let the top inch of soil dry out completely between waterings
Provide a sturdy trellis in a warm south-facing spot to support its vigorous twining woody stems
Prune lightly in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its scrambling habit under control

items.name: Anchietea pyrifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Brazilian climber in a conservatory or heated greenhouse to survive cold UK winters.
Plant in loam-based compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this exotic vine demands.
Water freely during the active summer growth but keep the soil barely damp throughout winter.
Provide a sturdy trellis or wires for its twining stems to scramble up toward the glasshouse light.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every two weeks from spring to late summer for blooms.

items.name: Anchomanes
items.growersTips:
Grow this exotic aroid in a large pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frosts.
Plant the tuber deep, about fifteen centimetres down, in rich, free-draining ericaceous compost.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during summer, then stop watering completely when it goes dormant.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping your plant indoors over the chilly winter.
Wear thick gloves when handling it because those stems have sharp thorns that will easily prick you.

items.name: Anchomanes difformis
items.growersTips:
Keep this tuberous aroid in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first UK autumn frost.
Plant the tuber at least fifteen centimetres deep in a rich, loamy mix to support its heavy stem.
Water heavily during the summer growth spurt but keep the soil almost bone-dry throughout winter.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this plant in a heated conservatory.
Wait until the single giant leaf naturally dies back in autumn before cutting it off at the base.

items.name: Anchusa
items.growersTips:
Plant Anchusa in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in spring under cover for reliable germination.
Cut back Anchusa azurea Loddon Royalist to ground level after flowering to encourage fresh growth.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry UK summers and water the soil directly at the base to prevent it.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its winter dormant phase.

items.name: Anchusa arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or spring just five millimetres deep in poor, sandy soil to mimic UK dunes.
Let the soil dry out completely between waterings to prevent this wild borage from rotting.
Watch out for capsid bugs in summer; just hand-pick them off to keep the blue flowers pristine.
Chop the stems down to ground level in autumn once the seeds have dropped to keep it tidy.
Grow it alongside wild poppies and cornflowers in a sunny, gravelly border for a cottage look.

items.name: Anchusa azurea
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep-rooted beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rot.
Sow seeds just half a centimetre deep in spring, keeping them on a sunny, warm windowsill to start.
Cut the faded flower stems right down in July to trigger a second flush of brilliant blue blooms.
Take root cuttings in late autumn to propagate new plants, as the main clump often dies after three years.
Watch out for powdery mildew in dry UK summers, so water the base of the plant, not the hairy leaves.

items.name: Anchusa capensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass, as they need light and UK warmth to germinate well.
Plant them in your poorest, sharp-draining soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Keep watering minimal once established, only giving them a drink during prolonged dry UK spells.
Cut back faded flower stems in July to encourage a second flush of those brilliant blue blooms.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with beer traps or wool pellets.

items.name: Anchusa crispa
items.growersTips:
Give this rare coastal gem very sharp drainage by mixing lots of grit and sand into your soil.
Keep watering to a minimum once established, as it hates wet winter feet in our damp UK climate.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in pots of gritty compost during early spring.
Protect the young rosettes from slugs and snails which love to munch the hairy leaves in spring.
Grow it in your sunniest gravel garden or a raised bed to mimic its natural sandy habitat.

items.name: Anchusa officinalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just 5mm deep in free-draining soil, as they need a bit of light to germinate.
Plant this alkanet in your poorest, grittiest soil to prevent it from getting too floppy and tall.
Cut the faded flowering stems right back to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of leaves.
Watch out for powdery mildew in dry UK summers; water the soil directly, never splash the foliage.
Grow it next to rosemary or thymes in full sun to create a perfect, dry-tolerant bee haven.

items.name: Anchusa strigosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep-rooted borage relative in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds just five millimetres deep in spring, keeping pots on a sunny windowsill or in a cold frame.
Position it in your brightest, most sun-baked border alongside drought-loving English lavender.
Avoid summer watering once established, as damp soil will quickly rot its thick, fleshy taproot.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the base in July to encourage a second flush of blue blooms.

items.name: Ancistrocarya japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare borage family gem in deep, humus-rich, acidic soil to mimic its woodland home.
Find a sheltered, damp, fully shaded spot in your garden to protect its leaves from UK sun scorch.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summers.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould every autumn to protect the crown from harsh UK winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love targeting the tender new emerging shoots.

items.name: Ancistrochilus
items.growersTips:
Grow this African orchid in a warm conservatory, keeping it above fifteen degrees during winter.
Pot your orchid in a chunky bark and perlite mix to ensure the roots dry out quickly after watering.
Water heavily while the new pseudobulbs grow, then stop watering completely when leaves drop in autumn.
Watch out for red spider mites during hot UK summers by misting the air around the leaves daily.
Repot only when the new growth starts in spring, taking care not to damage the delicate new roots.

items.name: Ancylobothrys
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical climber indoors for winter as it will not survive a frosty British winter outside.
Grow it in a container with grit-heavy, free-draining compost to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Water it deeply only when the top three inches of soil are dry, mimicking its native dry seasons.
Prune the vigorous vines in late spring after the frost passes to keep it tidy in your greenhouse.
Position it in your brightest south-facing conservatory to maximise the limited UK summer sunshine.

items.name: Andersonglossum boreale
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to let winter chill break dormancy naturally in the UK climate.
Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil, adding grit to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water moderately during dry spring spells, but keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, protecting young emerging shoots with grit barriers.
Position in partial shade mimicking woodland edges, pairing with native ferns or wild primroses.

items.name: Andira
items.growersTips:
Start Andira seeds indoors in April to get a head start on our short, cool UK growing season.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering deeply at the base every dry morning.
Pinch out the growing tips when your plants reach fifteen centimeters to encourage a bushier habit.
Sow them alongside marigolds to help deter the aphids and slugs that love tender young annuals.
Feed your plants with a high-potash liquid fertilizer every two weeks once the first buds appear.

items.name: Andrographis
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March with bottom heat, as this tropical herb needs warmth to germinate.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top inch of soil feels dry, as damp UK soil will quickly rot its roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more medicinal leaves.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to mimic the free-draining sandy soils of its native habitat.

items.name: Andrographis paniculata
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep using a heated propagator to beat UK chills.
Grow this tender herb in pots of gritty, free-draining soil so you can bring it inside for winter.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach fifteen centimetres high to encourage a bushy habit.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its native warmth.

items.name: Androstephium breviflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of grit and loam to ensure drainage
Keep your bulbs completely dry during their summer dormancy to mimic their native arid US habitat
Plant the bulbs quite deep at about ten centimetres down to protect them from cold UK winter frosts
Position your pot in the brightest spot possible like a south facing patio or a sunny greenhouse
Water sparingly only from late autumn to spring when you see active green growth beginning to show

items.name: Androstephium coeruleum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs three inches deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to survive UK wet.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormancy to prevent the bulbs from rotting in your soil.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame or greenhouse during wet winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the emerging flower spikes.
Pair them with low-growing thymes in a sunny rock garden to provide essential support and drainage.

items.name: Anemarrhena asphodeloides
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring in free-draining sandy loam with grit added to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry Asian hillsides, ensuring maximum summer warmth
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep almost dry throughout the damp winter
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so winter chill naturally breaks their physical dormancy
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails which target the new growth in damp weather

items.name: Anemocarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under cover to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts.
Water your everlastings at the base in the morning to prevent damp and rot in our humid summers.
Blend plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage these Australian natives need.
Snails love the tender young foliage, so set organic beer traps around them in damp spring weather.
Pick the papery flowers just as they start to open so they dry beautifully for winter displays.

items.name: Anemonastrum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edge conditions
Sow fresh seed in cold frames in autumn as they require winter chilling to break dormancy in spring
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to retain moisture and protect shallow fibrous roots
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges to maintain plant vigour
Watch for caterpillars and slugs in damp UK springs which rapidly damage the delicate new foliage

items.name: Anemonastrum baicalense
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil to mimic Siberian woodland edges.
In dry UK summers, water weekly at the base to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect rhizomes from severe British winter frosts.
Propagate by careful root division in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Anemonastrum canadense
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous spreader in moisture-retentive clay or loam in partial shade to mimic woodland.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp and prevent early dormancy.
Divide the dense rhizomatous root clumps in early spring just as new green growth begins to emerge.
Plant alongside aggressive companions like Matteuccia struthiopteris to contain its invasive habit.

items.name: Anemonastrum flaccidum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry spring spells to mimic the damp woodland floor of its native habitat.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in November to protect rhizomes from severe UK winter frosts.
Propagate by dividing the delicate rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has died down.
Plant alongside Galanthus and Hepatica for a continuous early spring shade-garden display.

items.name: Anemonastrum narcissiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its alpine woodland home.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to trigger UK spring growth.
Mulch annually in early spring with leafmould to retain moisture and keep roots cool in dry summers.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK weather.

items.name: Anemone
items.growersTips:
Soak dry Anemone coronaria tubers in water for twenty hours before planting in autumn or spring.
Plant wood anemone rhizomes horizontally just two centimetres deep in moist, humus-rich shade.
Mulch autumn-flowering Japanese anemones in November to protect crowns from severe UK winter frosts.
Water newly planted anemones weekly during dry UK spring spells to establish deep, resilient roots.
Divide congested clumps of Japanese anemones in early spring to maintain vigour and control spread.

items.name: Anemone apennina
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers five centimetres deep in autumn, soaking them in water overnight first to wake them up.
Give them a spot under deciduous trees where they get spring sun but cool shade during hot UK summers.
Keep the soil moist but well-drained by mixing in plenty of leaf mould before you plant them.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in May so the tubers can store energy for next year.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they love to munch on the fresh new shoots.

items.name: Anemone berlandieri
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers five centimetres deep in autumn, placing them on their sides if you cannot find the eyes.
Give them sharp-draining, gritty soil to prevent the tubers from rotting during wet UK winters.
Water them weekly during their spring growing phase, then let them dry out completely when dormant.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the delicate emerging spring foliage.
Plant them near early-flowering primroses to create a beautiful, naturalised woodland display.

items.name: Anemone biflora
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep them dry during their summer dormancy to mimic their native dry Middle Eastern hillsides.
Grow them in a cold frame or alpine house to protect the delicate early spring blooms from UK rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in February as the fresh new shoots begin to push through the soil.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to ensure the sharp drainage these alpines crave.

items.name: Anemone blanda
items.growersTips:
Soak the shrivelled tubers in tepid water for twenty-four hours before planting in autumn.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous trees or shrubs.
In heavy UK clay, mix grit into the planting hole to prevent winter waterlogging and tuber rot.
Leave the dying foliage to wither naturally in late spring to feed the tubers for next year.
Associate with snowdrops and early daffodils for a layered spring display in partial shade.

items.name: Anemone caroliniana
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, well-draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep them dry during their summer dormancy to mimic their native dry prairie habitat in the UK.
Grow them alongside dwarf spring bulbs like crocus to fill the gaps when they die back in July.
Protect the early spring buds from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers.
In wet UK winters, grow them in raised beds or alpine troughs to ensure they never sit in boggy soil.

items.name: Anemone coronaria
items.growersTips:
Soak the claw-like tubers in tepid water for twelve hours before planting to kickstart UK growth.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep with the pointed ends facing downwards in autumn or early spring.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter rot in wet British garden borders.
Apply a thick mulch of bracken or leaf mould in November to protect tubers from hard UK frosts.
Grow alongside early flowering dwarf narcissi to mask the anemone foliage as it dies back in June.

items.name: Anemone crassifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Tasmanian native in acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics moist UK woodland conditions.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summers.
Position your plant in partial shade to protect its delicate white summer blooms from scorching.
Apply a thick leaf mould mulch in late autumn to protect its roots from severe UK winter frosts.
Propagate by carefully dividing the fibrous root clumps in early spring just as new growth starts.

items.name: Anemone cylindrica
items.growersTips:
Plant this thimbleweed in well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural winter chill triggers spring germination.
Space them thirty centimetres apart in full sun to mimic their native open meadow habitat.
Cut the dried, cotton-like seed heads back in late winter to keep your borders looking tidy.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers until their deep taproots are fully established.

items.name: Anemone drummondii
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Tuck the tiny tubers just five centimetres deep in autumn, spacing them about ten centimetres apart.
Keep soil barely damp in summer, as this mountain native hates soggy roots during its dormant phase.
Place them in a spot that gets full morning sun but stays cool and sheltered from harsh afternoon heat.
Grow them in a raised bed or alpine trough so they do not get swamped by larger, aggressive plants.

items.name: Anemone flaccida
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes shallowly, about two centimetres deep, in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil.
Position them under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge and catch the spring sun.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth, but let it dry out slightly when dormant.
Mulch with leaf mould in autumn to protect the shallow roots from harsh UK winter frosts.
Plant them alongside snowdrops and primroses for a beautiful, naturalised spring display.

items.name: Anemone hortensis
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers five centimetres deep in autumn, soaking them in warm water first to wake them up.
Give them sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent the tubers from rotting during wet UK winters.
Position them in a sunny, sheltered spot to mimic their native warm Mediterranean hillside home.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh shoots.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in spring to feed the tubers for next year.

items.name: Anemone multifida
items.growersTips:
Plant this buttercup family gem in free-draining, gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill breaks their dormancy.
Keep the soil moist but never soggy during spring, then reduce watering once it dies back in summer.
Plant them alongside dwarf hardy geraniums or alpine phlox which love the same sunny, gritty spots.
Avoid moving them once established as their deep taproots really hate being disturbed in your borders.

items.name: Anemone narcissiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, free-draining, humus-rich soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent winter rot.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames during autumn, as they require winter chilling to germinate in spring.
Position in partial shade or dappled woodland light to mimic their natural alpine meadow habitat.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, replanting them immediately.

items.name: Anemone nemorosa
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes horizontally in autumn five centimetres deep in leaf-mould-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water only during dry spring spells to keep soil damp, then leave completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the brittle rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has completely died back.
Plant alongside wild garlic and primroses to mimic natural UK woodland communities and extend color.

items.name: Anemone parviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this northern native in damp, gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its favourite limestone crevices.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural winter chill triggers spring germination.
Protect the delicate emerging spring shoots from hungry slugs using beer traps or copper tape.
Divide the fibrous roots gently in early spring just as new growth begins to propagate your clump.

items.name: Anemone sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in moist, well-drained soil with leaf mould added to mimic its native woodlands.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during dry UK summers to stop it going dormant.
Cut back the faded foliage and spent flower stems in autumn to keep the clump tidy for next spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love chewing the tender new shoots.
Divide overcrowded clumps in early spring or autumn to control its spread and get free new plants.

items.name: Anemone trifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in autumn beneath deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural canopy shelter.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted compost into your soil to keep it moist but free-draining.
Plant the delicate rhizomes shallowly, about two centimetres deep, and space them ten centimetres apart.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth, but let it dry out slightly once it goes dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tender new shoots first start to emerge.

items.name: Anemone tuberosa
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn five centimetres deep in very gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent rot.
Give them a warm, dry summer baking by keeping potted plants under a glass pane during wet Augusts.
Position them in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic their native hot desert conditions.
Protect the early spring emerging buds from slugs using organic grit barriers around the crown.
Plant them alongside hardy succulents or sedums that share their love for dry, sun-drenched spots.

items.name: Anemone virginiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in partial shade with moist, leaf-mould enriched soil to mimic UK woods.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural winter chill triggers spring germination.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut the faded stems back to the ground in late autumn to keep the clump tidy for next spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using beer traps to protect them.

items.name: Anemone vitifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan native in partial shade to mimic its woodland home and prevent leaf scorch.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted manure to recreate the rich, damp soil it loves.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, especially while the roots establish.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in late autumn to keep the clump looking tidy.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Anemoneae
items.growersTips:
Plant your wood anemone rhizomes shallowly, just two centimetres deep, in damp, leaf-mould-rich soil.
Water your autumn-flowering Japanese anemones weekly during dry summer spells to stop buds dropping.
Slice through thick roots of Japanese anemones in spring to easily propagate free new plants.
Cut back faded stems of Anemone hupehensis right to the ground in late autumn to keep them tidy.
Watch out for foliar nematodes in wet UK summers, which turn the leaves of your anemones black.

items.name: Anemonoides
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes of wood anemone horizontally just two centimetres deep in rich, damp leaf mould.
Tuck them under deciduous shrubs like hazel to mimic their natural British woodland canopy habitat.
Mulch with well-rotted leaf mould every autumn to keep the soil moist and mimic a forest floor.
Avoid watering once they go dormant in midsummer, as wet summer soil will rot the resting rhizomes.
Plant them alongside early emerging ferns and hostas to hide the anemone foliage as it dies back.

items.name: Anemonoides nemorosa
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 2-5cm deep in autumn, laying them horizontally in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil.
Incorporate leafmould or well-rotted manure to mimic UK woodland soils before autumn planting.
Water during dry spring spells but leave soil dry during their summer dormancy to prevent rot.
Plant alongside early bulbs like Galanthus or under deciduous shrubs to match their light needs.
Leave dying foliage intact in late spring to naturally feed the rhizomes for next year's blooms.

items.name: Anemonoides oregana
items.growersTips:
Plant this Oregon anemone five centimetres deep in autumn under deciduous shrubs for summer shade.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your soil to mimic their native damp woodland floor.
Water these beauties weekly during dry spring spells, but let them go completely dormant in summer.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails in early spring as the delicate new shoots first emerge.
Plant them alongside snowdrops and hostas to fill the bare gaps when the anemones die back in July.

items.name: Anemonoides quinquefolia
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes horizontally three centimetres deep in autumn, ensuring they do not dry out before.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould to mimic UK deciduous woodland soil before planting in shade.
Water weekly during dry spring spells, but allow soil to dry slightly once summer dormancy begins.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside native UK woodland companions like Primula vulgaris and Galanthus nivalis.

items.name: Anemonoides ranunculoides
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn using leaf mould to mimic UK woodlands.
Water weekly during dry spring active growth but keep soil relatively dry during summer dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the emerging young foliage.
Do not prune or cut back dying summer foliage to allow the rhizomes to naturally store energy.
Plant under deciduous shrubs alongside Galanthus nivalis for a sequential spring woodland display.

items.name: Anemonoides trifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes 2cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep soil barely damp once foliage dies back in summer.
Mulch annually in January with leafmould to mimic British woodland soil and protect emerging buds.
Plant alongside Galanthus nivalis and Hepatica nobilis for a synchronized early spring display.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic iron phosphate pellets.

items.name: Anemonopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral leafmould-rich soil in full or dappled shade.
Water weekly with rainwater during dry UK summers to keep the woodland soil consistently damp.
Shelter from strong winds to protect the delicate, nodding flower stems from snapping in summer.
Apply a thick mulch of decayed leafmould or composted bark every spring to mimic forest floor soils.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in April.

items.name: Angadenia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant your pinwheel jasmine in peat-free loam compost mixed with plenty of grit for sharp drainage.
Water generously through the summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings in winter.
Prune back the woody stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more blooms.
Keep a close eye out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in a dry, warm conservatory.

items.name: Angelonia angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots to easily move indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winters.
Plant out in late May only after all risk of frost has passed and soil has warmed to fifteen degrees.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep roots in dry summer spells.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in June to promote a bushier habit and more flower spikes.
Mix grit into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage required to prevent root rot.

items.name: Angelonia biflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet, cool UK summer spells.
Plant out only after late May frosts pass, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-tolerant roots.
Deadhead spent flower spikes in midsummer to stimulate a second flush of blooms before autumn.
Overwinter potted plants indoors at minimum ten degrees Celsius as they cannot survive UK frosts.

items.name: Angelonia salicariifolia
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender perennial cannot survive UK frosts.
Plant out in late May in free-draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its drought-tolerant nature.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more purple flower spikes.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer to guarantee new plants for the following spring season.

items.name: Angianthus
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in March to give these Aussie annuals enough warmth before the May frost.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to mimic their native dry beds and prevent winter root rot.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy British wet feet.
Plant them alongside gravel-loving sedums and thymes which share their need for baking hot sun.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with copper tape or beer traps.

items.name: Angkalanthus oligophylla
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Arabian perennial indoors before the first autumn frost to keep its roots warm.
Plant in very free-draining grit-heavy soil to prevent winter rot in wet British weather.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, as this plant hates soggy feet.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory for maximum light.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring when the plant is actively growing.

items.name: Angolluma
items.growersTips:
Bring your Angolluma indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from damp UK winter rot.
Plant in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part peat-free compost to ensure fast drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep it completely dry from November through to March.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem joints and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Keep it on a south-facing windowsill to get the maximum possible sunlight during dull British summers.

items.name: Angraecinae
items.growersTips:
Bring your angraecoids indoors by October to protect them from chilly, damp UK autumn nights.
Grow them in chunky bark or mounted on cork to keep their thick roots well-aerated and rot-free.
Water with tepid rainwater weekly in summer, but let them dry out completely during dark winters.
Hang them in a bright east-facing window where they can catch the gentle British morning sun.
Mist the aerial roots daily during dry summer spells to mimic their humid forest home.

items.name: Ania
items.growersTips:
Tuck your terrestrial Ania orchid into a well-drained, leafy compost mix to mimic its forest home.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during summer, then cut back on watering once autumn arrives.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on those tender new orchid shoots.
Grow your Ania in a pot so you can easily bring it inside a cool greenhouse before winter frosts.
Give it dappled shade under taller shrubs to protect the delicate leaves from strong UK summer sun.

items.name: Anisacanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your desert hummingbird bush indoors or to a frost-free greenhouse before the first UK freeze.
Plant this Texan native in your sunniest, south-facing spot in extremely sharp-draining gravelly soil.
Prune your bush back hard by half in late spring once you spot the very first signs of new green growth.
Water deeply but let the compost dry out completely between sessions to mimic its native dry habitat.
Pot it up in a terracotta container rather than the open ground to help keep its roots warm and dry.

items.name: Anisacanthus quadrifidus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mexican native in your sunniest, sheltered south-facing border to mimic its warm home.
Give it sharply draining soil by mixing plenty of grit into the planting hole to prevent winter rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep it almost dry throughout the winter.
Prune the stems back hard to about fifteen centimetres in spring to encourage bushy new flowering growth.
Protect the root zone with a thick autumn mulch of bark to help it survive wet UK winter frosts.

items.name: Anisocarpus madioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts before outdoor transplanting.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet, unpredictable UK summers.
Water sparingly at the base once established, allowing the topsoil to dry out between waterings.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing border to maximise the limited British summer sunshine.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly through August to prolong the flowering display until autumn.

items.name: Anisocarpus scabridus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April using a well-drained gritty compost mix.
Place pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry, rocky Californian habitat.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during wet springs.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to ensure shared needs for sharp drainage are met.

items.name: Anisopappus
items.growersTips:
Sow these tender annual seeds shallowly indoors in March to beat the short UK summer growing season.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in our cool, unpredictable spring weather.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a much bushier shape and far more yellow flowers.
Plant them out in June alongside purple salvias for a gorgeous, high-contrast colour combination.
Deadhead the spent blooms weekly through August to keep the plant producing fresh flowers until autumn.

items.name: Anisopus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant in a very gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet UK autumns and winters.
Water generously only when the soil dries out completely, then keep it bone dry throughout winter.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk in late spring to support its vigorous twining perennial stems.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry summer glasshouses and mist the foliage to deter them.

items.name: Anisotes
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African shrub in pots of loamy grit mix so you can move it indoors before frost.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out, keeping it barely damp through winter.
Prune your plant by a third in late spring to encourage bushy growth and more tubular red flowers.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering your pots.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertiliser every two weeks from May to August to boost blooming.

items.name: Anisotes diversifolius
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Yemeni shrub indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry, then let the pot drain fully.
Prune the stems back by a third in late April to encourage a bushier shape and more summer blooms.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping it in your conservatory.

items.name: Anisotoma
items.growersTips:
Plant your Anisotoma in gritty, well-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, letting the topsoil dry out between waterings.
Protect the crown with dry bracken or fleece during hard frosts in colder northern UK regions.
Prune back the faded flower stems in late autumn to keep the perennial clump neat and compact.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn to naturally break dormancy over the UK winter.

items.name: Anna
items.growersTips:
Plant your Anna in well-drained UK loam enriched with leaf mould to mimic its woodland origins.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering deeply during dry summer spells.
Mulch with composted bark in late autumn to protect its roots from hard British winter frosts.
Prune back dead stems in early spring just as new green shoots begin to peek through the soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, using organic grit barriers around the base.
items.description: Anna may refer to:

items.name: Anodendron
items.growersTips:
Bring your Anodendron indoors by October to protect this tender evergreen from chilly UK frosts.
Grow this climber in a pot of peat-free loam compost so you can easily move it into a conservatory.
Water thoroughly when the top inch of soil feels dry, but keep it barely damp during winter.
Prune your plant in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its vigorous vines in check.
Watch out for red spider mites and mealybugs which thrive on this plant in warm glasshouse air.

items.name: Anoectochilus
items.growersTips:
Keep jewel orchids in a terrarium with damp sphagnum moss to survive dry UK winter central heating.
Water with room-temperature rainwater only when the top centimetre of their moss or bark feels dry.
Grow them under bright indirect light on a north windowsill to mimic their natural forest canopy.
Check weekly under the velvet leaves for mealybugs and wipe them away with a damp cotton bud.
Repot every spring into a loose mix of fine orchid bark, perlite, and chopped sphagnum moss.

items.name: Anogramma
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate annual fern in a sheltered, damp glasshouse to survive cold British winters.
Sow the dust-like spores on sterilized, moist peat-free compost kept constantly humid in shade.
Keep the growing medium damp but never soggy by watering from below with tepid rainwater.
Protect the tiny, overwintering prothallus stage from slugs by using organic wool pellets.
Position your pots in deep shade away from drying winds and direct, scorching summer sun.

items.name: Anogramma ascensionis
items.growersTips:
This critically endangered fern needs a warm terrarium to survive the chilly UK climate.
Keep its volcanic-style grit mix constantly damp with rainwater, never letting the soil dry out.
Place your glass container in bright, indirect light but far away from cold winter draughts.
Watch out for tiny fungus gnats in the humid soil, using yellow sticky traps to catch them early.
Sow its dust-like spores on sterilized compost inside sealed plastic tubs to help them sprout.

items.name: Anogramma leptophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate annual fern in moist, sheltered rock crevices using acidic, gritty leafmould.
Sow its dust-like spores on damp peat-free compost in late summer, keeping them in a warm propagator.
Keep the soil constantly damp but never soggy, using harvested rainwater instead of tap water.
Protect this frost-sensitive species by overwintering it in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse.
Position it alongside small liverworts or filmy ferns in deep shade to mimic its damp woodland home.

items.name: Antegibbaeum
items.growersTips:
Bring this succulent indoors by October to protect its delicate roots from wet UK winter rot.
Plant in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part John Innes number two for perfect drainage.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, focusing moisture on the base during its autumn growth spurt.
Position on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sunshine.
Check the tight leaf crevices weekly for mealybugs, dabbing them away with an alcohol-dipped cotton bud.

items.name: Antennaria
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty well-drained soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Water newly planted pussytoes weekly until established then leave to rely entirely on UK rainfall.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain the dense silver carpet and promote fresh growth.
Position as a groundcover companion next to Campanula carpatica or dwarf spring bulbs in rockeries.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots during wet British weather and protect with organic grit.

items.name: Anthemideae
items.growersTips:
Sow your chamomile seeds in March on a sunny windowsill, just pressing them gently into the compost.
Water your young corn marigolds only when the top two inches of soil feel completely dry to the touch.
Keep a sharp eye out for blackfly aphids on the tender new stems of your yellow chamomile plants.
Deadhead your annual feverfew weekly in July to keep those cheerful white daisy blooms coming.
Mix plenty of grit into your heavy clay soil before planting to give these Mediterranean roots drainage.

items.name: Anthericum
items.growersTips:
Plant your St Bernard's lily in free-draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position them in full sun or very light dappled shade to encourage those delicate white summer blooms.
Water regularly during their first spring growing season, then let them become quite drought-tolerant.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth starts, rather than in the autumn chill.
Protect the tender new spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Anthericum liliago
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 10cm in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position in full sun, ideally next to dark-leaved Heuchera to contrast the white star-like blooms.
Water weekly during the spring growing season, but keep dry once the summer flowering period ends.
Cut dead flower stems to the base in October and mulch with grit to protect crowns from wet frost.
Watch for slugs and snails on emerging spring shoots, using organic wool pellets around the clump.

items.name: Anthericum ramosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky soil or add grit to heavy UK clay to prevent winter root rot.
Position in full sun to replicate its native European meadows for the best summer flowering.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to trigger spring germination.
Cut the spent flower stems back to the base in autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent self-seeding.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate and maintain vigour.

items.name: Anthonotha
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres to protect young roots from late UK frosts
Grow in acidic to neutral sandy loam to mimic native soils and prevent root rot in wet UK winters
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkles to boost roots
Position in a south-facing sheltered spot to maximise solar heat and shield from cold northern winds
Interplant with brassicas to benefit from the nitrogen-fixing nodules on these legume roots

items.name: Anthurium
items.growersTips:
Keep your plant warm and draft-free indoors, as UK winter windowsills get too cold for them.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free orchid compost mix feels dry to your touch.
Mist the leaves daily or use a pebble tray to mimic the humid rainforests in dry UK central heating.
Snip off yellowing leaves and faded flower spathes at the very base using sterilized secateurs.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid orchid food diluted to half-strength every fortnight in summer.

items.name: Anthurium acaule
items.growersTips:
Keep this strap-leaved plant in a warm, draft-free room above fifteen degrees to survive UK winters.
Water only when the top half of the peat-free, orchid-bark potting mix feels completely dry.
Wipe the long, leathery leaves with a damp cloth monthly to prevent spider mites in dry radiator heat.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser every two weeks from April to September to boost foliage growth.
Repot into a shallow, wide pot in spring to accommodate its spreading, nest-like root system.

items.name: Anthurium alcatrazense
items.growersTips:
Grow your Alcatrazense in a chunky orchid bark, perlite and peat-free compost mix for drainage.
Keep this Colombian native indoors year-round, as it cannot survive UK winter temperatures.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid leaf burn.
Place it in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to mimic its natural canopy home.
Mist the leaves regularly or use a pebble tray to counter dry UK central heating in the winter.

items.name: Anthurium alluriquinense
items.growersTips:
Keep this Ecuadorian beauty warm indoors year-round, ideally above sixteen degrees Celsius in winter.
Plant in a chunky, bark-heavy orchid mix to prevent root rot in our damp, low-light UK winters.
Water only when the top half of the compost feels dry, using tepid rainwater to avoid leaf burn.
Position in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window, away from cold draughts and radiators.
Wipe the large leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and check for sneaky spider mites.

items.name: Anthurium amoenum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical perennial indoors by September to shield it from chilly UK autumn nights.
Pot your plant in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild rainforest home.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top two inches of compost feel completely dry to touch.
Keep it in a humid bathroom or on a wet pebble tray to stop the leaf tips from turning brown.
Wipe the broad leaves weekly with a damp cloth to clear dust and check for sneaky spider mites.

items.name: Anthurium andicola
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant indoors by October to protect it from cold UK winters, keeping it above fifteen degrees.
Grow it in a chunky mix of orchid bark, perlite, and peat to mimic its natural cloud forest home.
Water with lukewarm rainwater when the top two inches of soil dry out, as tap water causes leaf burn.
Place it in a bright bathroom or near a humidifier to combat dry indoor air from central heating.
Wipe the broad leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mites from settling in.

items.name: Anthurium andraeanum
items.growersTips:
Pop your anthurium in a peat-free orchid compost mix to keep those roots breathing and draining well.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, using tepid rainwater to avoid brown tips.
Keep them on a pebble tray filled with water to boost humidity in our dry central-heated UK homes.
Place them in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to mimic their rainforest canopy.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid orchid food every fortnight from April to September for blooms.
items.description: Anthurium andraeanum, also known as Édouard François André's Tailflower, is a flowering plant species in the family Araceae that is native to Colombia and Ecuador. It is a winner of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Anthurium argyrostachyum
items.growersTips:
Keep this rare Andean beauty in a warm, humid bathroom to mimic its native tropical cloud forest.
Pot your plant in a chunky orchid bark, perlite, and peat mix to prevent waterlogging in UK winters.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of soil dry out to avoid cold root shock.
Wipe the velvety leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations indoors.
Position it in bright, indirect light near an east window, keeping it safe from harsh summer sun.

items.name: Anthurium bakeri
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical epiphyte in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to drain wet UK rain.
Water only when the top two inches of moss feel dry, using tepid rainwater to avoid brown tips.
Hang its long, strap-like leaves near a bright east window, shielded from harsh afternoon sun.
Mist the roots daily in winter to counter dry radiator heat, aiming for high indoor humidity.
Snip off faded red berries in autumn with sterile shears to keep the mother plant vigorous.

items.name: Anthurium bonplandii
items.growersTips:
Keep this leafy beauty snug indoors year-round because UK drafts and cold windows will stunt it.
Water only when the top two inches of bark-heavy orchid mix dry out to prevent soggy root rot.
Wipe those leathery leaves with a damp cloth weekly to stop UK house dust blocking its light.
Feed with half-strength orchid fertiliser monthly from April to September to boost leaf growth.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight central crown where the new upright leaves emerge.

items.name: Anthurium brownii
items.growersTips:
Keep this big-leafed beauty in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to prevent root rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, using tepid rainwater to avoid leaf scorch.
Place your pot on a wet pebble tray near a bright east window to mimic tropical jungle humidity.
Wipe those massive ruffled leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and deter spider mites.
Feed with a diluted half-strength liquid seaweed fertiliser only during the active spring growth.

items.name: Anthurium camposii
items.growersTips:
Keep your Anthurium camposii warm indoors year-round, as it cannot survive UK winter drafts.
Pot it in a chunky, bark-heavy orchid mix to mimic its natural epiphytic growing conditions.
Water only when the top two inches of moss feel dry, using tepid rainwater to avoid brown tips.
Position it in bright, indirect light near an east window to prevent UK winter leaf yellowing.
Wipe the large, velvety leaves weekly with a damp cloth to stop spider mites in dry radiator heat.

items.name: Anthurium clarinervium
items.growersTips:
Keep this Mexican beauty warm indoors, never letting UK winter room temperatures drop below fifteen.
Water only when the top half of the peat-free bark and perlite compost mix feels completely dry.
Mist the velvety leaves daily or use a gravel tray to mimic tropical humidity in dry British homes.
Wipe the heart-shaped foliage with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and prevent spider mites.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost those white veins.

items.name: Anthurium clavigerum
items.growersTips:
Keep this climber warm indoors or in a heated conservatory as UK winters will easily kill it.
Plant it in a super chunky orchid bark and perlite mix to mimic its natural epiphytic home.
