items.name: Artia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Artia crowns five centimetres deep in well-drained soil during the mild autumn months.
Water your Artia deeply once a week at the base to keep the roots damp but never waterlogged.
Watch out for slugs on young Artia shoots in damp spring weather and use organic wool pellets.
Cut back the faded Artia stems right to the ground in late October to prevent winter crown rot.
Mix plenty of composted bark into heavy clay soils to give your Artia the sharp drainage it needs.

items.name: Arum
items.growersTips:
Plant your Arum tubers deep, about fifteen centimetres down in moist, dappled woodland shade.
Wear gloves when handling Arum as all parts, especially those bright red autumn berries, are toxic.
Grow them alongside hostas and ferns to hide the Arum's messy, yellowing summer dieback phase.
Keep the soil consistently damp during winter and spring, but let it dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the fresh, arrow-shaped spring foliage.

items.name: Arum besserianum
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 15cm deep in autumn to protect them from hard UK winter frosts in well-drained soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist during their active winter growth phase, but dry in summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails eating the early emerging foliage during damp British spring days.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs to provide summer shade and crucial winter light in your garden.
Add plenty of leaf mould to your soil before planting to mimic their native woodland habitat.

items.name: Arum concinnatum
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres to protect them from hard UK frosts.
Give them a mulch of leaf mould in spring to mimic their natural damp woodland soil preference.
Keep the soil consistently moist during winter and spring but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails eating the fresh autumn foliage as soon as it emerges in September.
Grow them under deciduous trees so they get winter sun and summer shade when they go dormant.

items.name: Arum creticum
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers eight inches deep in autumn to protect them from hard UK winter frosts.
Give them a sunny, sheltered spot against a south-facing wall to mimic their warm Cretan home.
Let the soil dry out completely in summer when the plant goes dormant and the leaves die back.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure sharp drainage so the tubers do not rot in wet winters.
Watch out for slugs in early spring when those beautiful yellow spathes first start to emerge.

items.name: Arum cylindraceum
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland native in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres to protect it from UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during its active spring growth.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted compost into your soil to mimic its natural forest home.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when those fresh, glossy green leaves first emerge.
Plant it alongside shade-loving wood anemones or wild ginger to create a beautiful woodland carpet.

items.name: Arum dioscoridis
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers deep at about fifteen centimeters to survive the wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Give them a rich, damp soil in spring, but let them dry out completely once they go dormant in July.
Watch out for slugs chewing the gorgeous, smelly spathes as they emerge in late spring or early summer.
Grow them in a warm, sheltered spot like a south-facing wall to mimic their native Mediterranean home.
Plant them near early-rising hostas to hide the messy, yellowing foliage when it dies back in summer.

items.name: Arum hygrophilum
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers deep at about fifteen centimeters to shield them from harsh UK winter frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp during their winter growing phase but let them dry out in summer.
Feed them with a high-potash fertilizer in late winter to boost those lovely green-tipped spathes.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the fresh new foliage first starts to emerge.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs to give them winter sun and dry summer shade which they love.

items.name: Arum idaeum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cretan tuber five inches deep in autumn using gritty, sharply draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep it completely dry during its summer dormancy by sheltering it from heavy UK summer downpours.
Position your pot in a sunny, sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its warm Mediterranean home.
Watch out for slugs eating the early spring shoots and protect the emerging foliage with gravel.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the leaves emerge in late winter to boost blooms.

items.name: Arum italicum
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers about ten centimetres deep in autumn to protect them from harsh UK winter frosts.
Grow them under deciduous shrubs so they get winter sun but shade when they go dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the beautiful marbled leaves during damp British springs.
Cut the faded flower spathes back in May if you want to prevent them seeding all over your lawn.
Pair them with snowdrops and hostas for a seamless, year-round foliage display in damp shade.

items.name: Arum korolkowii
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers eight inches deep in autumn to protect them from hard UK winter frosts.
Give them a dry summer rest by stopping all watering once the leaves naturally die back in June.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they love to munch the emerging exotic-looking spathes.
Mix plenty of grit and leaf mould into heavy UK clay to ensure the sharp drainage they crave.
Grow them alongside early snowdrops to fill the bare ground while the arum is still dormant.

items.name: Arum maculatum
items.growersTips:
Plant the tubers about fifteen centimetres deep in autumn to protect them from harsh winter frosts.
Grow them under deciduous shrubs to mimic their natural British woodland home and keep them happy.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in summer so the tubers can store energy for next year.
Wear thick gloves when handling them because every single part of this plant can irritate your skin.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during their active spring growing season.

items.name: Arum nigrum
items.growersTips:
Plant this black-flowered arum tuber about ten centimetres deep in rich, damp soil in autumn.
Position it in dappled woodland shade to mimic its native habitat and protect the dark spathes.
Water regularly during its winter and spring growing phase, then let it dry out when dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging fresh shoots.
Wear gloves when handling this plant or clearing old foliage because all parts can irritate your skin.

items.name: Arum orientale
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers eight centimeters deep in moist, dappled shade to mimic their native woodlands.
Keep the soil consistently damp during winter and spring, but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the emerging spring foliage by using organic wool pellets.
Mulch the soil heavily with leaf mould in autumn to replicate the rich forest floors they love.
Plant them alongside snowdrops and primroses which share their love for damp, shady UK spring spots.

items.name: Arum palaestinum
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers eight centimeters deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep them damp during their winter growth but let them dry out completely once they go dormant in summer.
Grow them in a warm, sheltered spot or pot to protect the exotic winter foliage from harsh UK frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the emerging spathes and leaves in early spring.
Plant them near deciduous shrubs so they get winter sun but are shaded during their summer dormancy.

items.name: Arum pictum
items.growersTips:
Plant this autumn gem in late summer in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter tuber rot.
Bury the tubers about ten centimetres deep in a warm, south-facing spot to mimic Mediterranean sun.
Let the soil dry out completely in summer when the plant goes dormant and leaves die back.
Watch out for slugs chewing the gorgeous silver-veined autumn foliage as it first emerges.
Pair it with autumn crocus or cyclamen for a stunning, low-growing late season border display.

items.name: Arum purpureospathum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cretan beauty in a sheltered, south-facing spot to shield it from harsh UK winter winds.
Plant the tubers deep, about fifteen centimeters down, in sharply draining soil to prevent rot.
Give it a thick mulch of organic matter in autumn to protect the tender tubers from hard UK frosts.
Water it regularly during its winter growing phase, but keep it bone dry when it goes dormant in summer.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it into a cold greenhouse during freezing wet weather.

items.name: Arundina
items.growersTips:
Bring this bamboo orchid indoors by October to protect it from wet and freezing UK winter weather.
Grow your Arundina in a bark-based orchid compost mix rather than standard British garden soil.
Water generously with tepid rainwater in summer, but let the potting mix dry out between waterings.
Feed weekly in spring with a high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer to boost those tall, leafy stems.
Propagate by gently detaching the small plantlets, or keikis, that form along the mature canes.

items.name: Asarina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the short UK summer and get early blooms.
Grow them in pots with a trellis so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids and glasshouse whitefly when growing them in humid UK conservatories.
Mix plenty of grit into your multi-purpose compost to ensure the roots never sit in cold winter wet.

items.name: Ascidieria
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical orchid in a warm conservatory or heated greenhouse to survive UK winter cold.
Pot in a free-draining medium of fine bark and sphagnum moss to prevent root rot in humid conditions.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the potting mix dries out, reducing frequency during winter.
Position in bright, filtered light but shield from direct mid-summer sun to avoid leaf scorch.
Maintain high humidity above fifty percent by placing the pot on a wet pebble tray year-round.

items.name: Asclepias
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late winter then cold-stratify them in your fridge for four weeks to break dormancy.
Plant taproots deeply in gritty, free-draining soil to help them survive wet British winters.
Water young plants weekly until established, then leave them dry so they do not rot at the crown.
Watch out for bright yellow aphids in July and simply blast them off with a sharp jet of water.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in March just as the new red shoots begin to emerge.

items.name: Asclepias albicans
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Keep your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot or a conservatory to mimic Mexico.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely from November.
Sow seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator mat set to twenty-one degrees Celsius.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you overwinter your plant in a greenhouse or indoors.

items.name: Asclepias angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this narrow-leaved milkweed in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a greenhouse for winter.
Sow seeds in early spring after chilling them in your fridge for four weeks to break dormancy.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining compost mix to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Water deeply but infrequently, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings in summer.
Check the narrow leaves regularly for yellow aphids and simply wash them off with a gentle hose.

items.name: Asclepias asperula
items.growersTips:
Plant this taprooted beauty in deep, gritty soil so its long roots can stretch and survive UK wet.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pots outdoors all winter; they need that cold UK chill to sprout.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drenches in summer.
Watch out for slugs on tender spring shoots and protect the crown from winter wet with a gravel mulch.
Avoid moving it once planted, as the deep taproot hates being disturbed and won't recover easily.

items.name: Asclepias californica
items.growersTips:
Give this California native your sharpest-draining gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a cold glass frame when winter rains start.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pot outside to let UK winter frosts naturally break dormancy.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, mimicking its native desert home.
Avoid rich fertilisers as this plant thrives in poor, low-nutrient soils and will rot in rich compost.

items.name: Asclepias cinerea
items.growersTips:
Plant Carolina milkweed in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet, cold UK winters.
Sow seeds in late winter, barely covering them, then cold-stratify in your fridge for four weeks.
Keep young plants damp, but let established roots dry out between waterings to prevent root rot.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic their warm home.
Bring container-grown plants into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from October to April.

items.name: Asclepias cordifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using deep pots to accommodate the long taproot, then leave them outside to chill.
Plant in your sunniest spot with extremely gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between occasional soakings.
Protect the vulnerable young spring shoots from slugs using beer traps or copper tape barrier rings.
Avoid moving this beauty once planted because its deep taproot hates being disturbed or relocated.

items.name: Asclepias curassavica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender milkweed in pots so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frosts hit.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on compost with a light grit cover, keeping them warm on a windowsill.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil dries out, but keep it much drier during its winter dormancy.
Watch out for bright yellow aphids in summer and simply wash them off with a gentle hose spray.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more nectar-rich blooms.

items.name: Asclepias erosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in your sharpest grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pots outdoors so winter cold naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep young plants damp in spring but let established ones dry out completely between waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs as they love to devour the tender new shoots.
Grow this milkweed in a deep terracotta pot so you can move it under a cold frame for winter shelter.

items.name: Asclepias fascicularis
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sunniest spot in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet winters.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors in pots so the natural UK winter cold can break their deep dormancy.
Water sparingly once established because this tough cookie prefers drought to soggy British roots.
Watch out for bright yellow aphids in summer, but leave them be so ladybirds can have a feast.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in early spring just as the new shoots begin to emerge.

items.name: Asclepias hirtella
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep-taprooted milkweed in a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pot outdoors to let winter cold naturally break their dormancy.
Water young plants weekly, but once established, leave them dry to prevent root rot in damp clay.
Grow them in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic the hot, open North American prairies.
Avoid moving them once planted because their long, delicate taproot absolutely hates disturbance.

items.name: Asclepias humistrata
items.growersTips:
Grow this sandhill milkweed in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pot outdoors because they need a cold winter chill to germinate.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, as this plant hates soggy roots.
Place your pot in the sunniest, hottest spot of your garden to mimic its native Florida warmth.
Check the fleshy leaves regularly for aphids and gently wipe them off with a damp cloth in summer.

items.name: Asclepias lanuginosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this woolly milkweed in a raised bed with lots of grit to survive wet British winters.
Keep watering to a minimum once established, only soaking during prolonged summer dry spells.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape.
Avoid moving this beauty once planted because its deep taproot hates being disturbed.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame to let the UK winter chill naturally break their dormancy.

items.name: Asclepias latifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late winter using deep pots to accommodate the long taproot this plant will develop.
Keep watering to a absolute minimum once established because this species hates wet winter soil.
Plant in your sunniest south-facing spot with lots of grit to survive wet UK autumns and winters.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails which absolutely love the tender new growth.
Leave the seed pods on over winter to enjoy the architectural shapes in your frosty UK garden.

items.name: Asclepias longifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this longleaf milkweed in a deep pot to protect its long taproot from wet UK winter rot.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to mimic its natural damp boggy grassland home.
Watch out for bright yellow aphids in June and just blast them off with a gentle hose spray.
Do not prune the fading autumn stems too early as they provide vital frost protection for the crown.
Mix plenty of acidic peat-free compost and grit into your soil to keep it damp yet free-draining.

items.name: Asclepias meadii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pots outside to get the winter chill they need to germinate.
Plant them in deep, gritty, free-draining soil to mimic their native dry midwestern prairies.
Keep young plants damp but let established ones dry out to survive wet British winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love eating the tender new shoots.
Avoid moving them once planted because their long taproots hate being disturbed or damaged.

items.name: Asclepias mexicana
items.growersTips:
Grow this Mexican milkweed in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.
Sow seeds in February using a heated propagator, as they need consistent warmth to germinate well.
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil mixed with horticultural sand to prevent root rot in wet winters.
Water deeply but infrequently, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings to mimic dry climates.
Watch out for aphids on the tender new shoots in spring and simply blast them off with a garden hose.

items.name: Asclepias oenotheroides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late winter using deep pots to accommodate the long taproot this wildflower develops.
Plant them in your sunniest spot in extremely free-draining soil mixed with plenty of grit or sand.
Water only when the soil is completely dry to prevent root rot in our damp UK autumn weather.
Protect young shoots from slugs in spring and watch out for aphids on the stems as they grow.
Leave the stems intact over winter to protect the crown then cut back to the base in early April.

items.name: Asclepias pedicellata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using deep pots to protect the long taproot from root disturbance.
Plant out in late May in a sheltered, south-facing spot with gravel mixed in to survive wet winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids in June, brushing them off by hand to protect the delicate stems.
Leave the faded stems intact over winter to shield the crown, then cut them back in early April.

items.name: Asclepias purpurascens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they need winter chill to germinate in the UK climate.
Plant your purple milkweed in deep, fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full, warm sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help its deep taproot establish properly.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Leave the decorative seed pods on over winter then cut stems back to the ground in early spring.

items.name: Asclepias ruthiae
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot filled with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Place your pot in the hottest, sunniest spot of your patio, ideally against a south-facing wall.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then give it a light splash, keeping it dry through winter.
Protect the fleshy roots from rot by top-dressing the compost with a thick layer of pea gravel.
Sow seeds in early spring on a heated propagator mat at twenty-one degrees to trigger germination.

items.name: Asclepias speciosa
items.growersTips:
Plant your showy milkweed seeds in autumn so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy.
Grow them in your sunniest spot in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Watch out for bright yellow aphids in June and simply blast them off with a sharp jet of water.
Leave the seedpods on in autumn for winter structure, then cut stems to the ground in early spring.

items.name: Asclepias subulata
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it indoors for winter.
Water it only when the soil is bone dry, as damp UK winters will quickly rot its fleshy roots.
Position your pot in the hottest, brightest spot in your garden, ideally against a south wall.
Prune the rush-like stems back by half in late spring to encourage fresh, vigorous new growth.
Watch out for aphids on the tender tips and simply blast them off with a sharp spray of water.

items.name: Asclepias subverticillata
items.growersTips:
Grow this toxic milkweed in a sink or deep pot to stop its aggressive runners invading your borders.
Keep the soil gritty and sharply drained, as damp UK winter wet will quickly rot its taproot.
Sow seeds in cold frames in January to give them the essential winter chill they need to germinate.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between your waterings.
Position in your hottest, brightest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry Arizona home.

items.name: Asclepias texana
items.growersTips:
Bring this Texas native indoors for winter as it cannot survive wet UK frosts and freezing soil.
Grow it in a terracotta pot filled with gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry, keeping it barely damp during winter.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic Texan heat.
Watch out for aphids on the fresh summer shoots and blast them off with a sharp spray of water.

items.name: Asclepias tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this sandhill milkweed in a deep pot with gritty, free-draining soil to protect its long taproot.
Keep watering to an absolute minimum once established, as our damp UK winters will easily rot them.
Position your pot in the hottest, most south-facing sun trap in your garden to mimic its home desert.
Sow seeds in early spring using a heated propagator, as they need consistent warmth to germinate.
Watch out for slugs on the tender new spring shoots, so use beer traps or grit barriers early on.

items.name: Asclepias tuberosa
items.growersTips:
Plant them in your sunniest spot with gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in pots in February, then cold-stratify them in your fridge for a month to boost growth.
Mark their spot with a cane because they stay dormant and invisible until late spring in the UK.
Water newly planted roots deeply once a week, but stop watering completely once they are established.
Leave the gorgeous seed pods on over winter to feed local birds and create beautiful frost displays.

items.name: Asclepias variegata
items.growersTips:
Plant your redring milkweed seeds in autumn so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy.
Give this deep-taprooted beauty at least thirty centimetres of soil depth so it can establish well.
Water sparingly once established, as our damp UK winters can easily rot its delicate crown.
Watch out for yellow aphids in summer, but leave some for the ladybirds to feast on naturally.
Grow it in a terracotta pot to help drain away heavy British rain and keep its roots happy.

items.name: Asclepias verticillata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames so the natural UK winter chill breaks their deep dormancy.
Plant these deep taproots in very gritty, free-draining soil to stop winter wet rotting the crown.
Water newly planted plugs weekly until established, then leave them to thrive in dry summer spells.
Watch out for slugs devouring the tender new needle-like shoots as they emerge quite late in May.
Leave the decorative seed pods on over winter for structure, then cut stems to the ground in March.

items.name: Asclepias viridiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn and leave pots outdoors to let winter cold naturally break their deep dormancy.
Plant in your sunniest spot with sharp sand mixed into the soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply but rarely, letting the soil dry completely to mimic their native dry grasslands.
Watch out for slugs in spring as they absolutely love the tender new shoots of emerging milkweed.
Leave the stems alone in autumn so the beautiful, silky seed pods can develop for winter interest.

items.name: Asparagoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns in trench thirty centimetres wide and fifteen deep, spacing them forty centimetres apart.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in autumn to protect crowns from wet UK winter freezes.
Stop harvesting spears by mid-June to allow ferns to grow and recharge the crown for next spring.
Cut yellowed autumn foliage down to ground level in November to prevent asparagus beetle overwintering.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, sensitive root systems with a hoe.

items.name: Asparagus
items.growersTips:
Prep your bed with lots of well-rotted manure to keep these hungry perennials happy for decades.
Plant bare-root crowns in April, twenty centimetres deep in trenches, spreading the roots like spiders.
Resist the urge to harvest any spears for the first two years so the roots can get really strong.
Keep a sharp eye out for the asparagus beetle and its grubs, which will quickly strip the foliage.
In autumn, when the beautiful ferny foliage turns yellow, cut it right down to the ground.

items.name: Asparagus acutifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in free-draining sandy loam with grit added to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Bury crowns 15cm deep in trenches, covering with 5cm of soil, then backfill as shoots grow in spring.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, brittle root system of this wild species.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late autumn to protect the crown from severe UK winter frosts.
Cut the yellowing, spiny fern-like foliage back to ground level in October to prevent rust disease.

items.name: Asparagus aethiopicus
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this South African native cannot survive UK winters outside.
Water thoroughly when the top two centimetres of compost feel dry but never let the pot sit in water.
Repot in spring using a loam-based John Innes No 2 compost mixed with one-third grit for drainage.
Prune yellowing or tangled stems at the base in spring to encourage fresh bright green fronds.
Watch closely for scale insects and mealybugs which hide in the dense thorny foliage indoors.

items.name: Asparagus africanus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of loam-based compost so you can move it indoors before UK frosts.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently damp during the active spring and summer growth.
Provide a sturdy trellis or moss pole early in spring to support its vigorous, scrambling stems.
Prune yellowing or dead woody stems at the base in late autumn to encourage fresh spring shoots.
Check regularly for red spider mites and scale insects, which thrive in dry indoor winter air.

items.name: Asparagus albus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy soil with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre in deep pots to protect the long taproots.
Grow in a south-facing sheltered spot or unheated greenhouse to shield from hard UK frosts.
Prune the spiny white stems back to the base in late autumn once they turn yellow and die back.
Water sparingly once established as this Mediterranean native prefers dry conditions over damp.

items.name: Asparagus aphyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Prune dead tangled stems back to the base in late autumn to prevent fungal diseases from overwintering.
Grow in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Mediterranean habitat.

items.name: Asparagus asparagoides
items.growersTips:
Grow in containers to easily overwinter indoors as it is not frost-hardy in typical UK winters
Plant tubers 5cm deep in free-draining loam mixed with grit to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil
Water moderately in summer but keep compost barely moist during its semi-dormant winter phase
Provide a trellis or netting for the twining stems to climb up to three metres in a conservatory
Prune dead tangled scramblers to the base in late winter before new spring shoots emerge

items.name: Asparagus capensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty free-draining loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Overwinter in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as it cannot survive UK ground freezes.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during the active summer growing season.
Prune back dead woody stems in late autumn to encourage fresh thorny shoots next spring.
Propagate by dividing the tuberous root clump in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Asparagus cochinchinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent crown rot.
Sow seeds in spring at 1cm depth in a heated propagator at 20C before transplanting outdoors in May.
Protect young shoots from late spring frosts using horticultural fleece or cloches in northern UK.
Cut back the climbing, thorny stems to ground level in late autumn after foliage turns yellow.
Watch for asparagus beetle larvae in summer and hand-pick them to prevent severe defoliation.

items.name: Asparagus dauricus
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, well-drained sandy loam with a pH of 6.5 to 7.5, adding grit to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds in spring at 1.5cm depth in pots before transplanting to permanent beds the next year.
Water young plants weekly in dry UK summers, but keep established crowns dry to avoid crown rot.
Cut the yellowing fern-like foliage back to 5cm above ground level in late autumn after first frost.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, spreading root system of the crowns.

items.name: Asparagus declinatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African native in a pot with grit-heavy soil to move indoors before frost.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during its active autumn and winter growth phase.
Sow seeds 1cm deep in spring using a heated propagator kept at a constant 15 to 20 degrees Celsius.
Cut back yellowing scrambling stems to the base in late spring as the plant enters summer dormancy.
Watch closely for red spider mite when keeping this delicate climber in a dry UK greenhouse.

items.name: Asparagus densiflorus
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this South African native cannot survive UK winter temperatures.
Water thoroughly once the top two centimetres of compost feels dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Repot in spring only when the vigorous tuberous roots begin to push the plant up out of its pot.
Prune yellowing stems at the very base in spring using sharp shears to encourage fresh green growth.
Grow in a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure essential fast drainage.

items.name: Asparagus falcatus
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this South African native cannot survive UK winters.
Water thoroughly when the top two inches of compost dry out, then let it drain completely.
Repot in spring using a loam-based John Innes No 2 compost mixed with one-third grit for drainage.
Prune old yellowing climbing stems at the base in spring to encourage vigorous new shoots.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling to protect your hands from its sharp, hooked thorns.

items.name: Asparagus fallax
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Canary native in free-draining gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rot.
Grow in a container to easily move indoors to a greenhouse before the first autumn frosts hit.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently moist during the active spring growing season.
Propagate by carefully dividing the tuberous root clump in spring just as new shoots start to emerge.
Position in bright filtered light rather than direct UK sun to prevent the delicate foliage burning.

items.name: Asparagus horridus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with 50% grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Place in your garden's hottest south-facing spot or a cold greenhouse to mimic Mediterranean sun.
Water deeply only when the soil dries out completely, then keep dry throughout the winter months.
Prune back dead or crossing woody stems in late spring once the risk of hard UK frosts has passed.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when handling this shrub to protect your hands from its brutal thorns.

items.name: Asparagus krebsianus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with a pH of 6.5 to 7.5 to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to protect from frost damage.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the compost barely damp during damp UK winter months.
Prune back dead woody stems to the base in late spring after the risk of hard frost has passed.
Mulch the root zone with well-rotted manure in April to boost leafy growth of this shrubby species.

items.name: Asparagus lignosus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters in deep pots to accommodate the taproot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back the woody stems to ground level in late autumn after they turn yellow to prevent pests.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in November to protect the crown from severe UK winter frosts.

items.name: Asparagus maritimus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy soil with added grit to mimic its native UK coastal shingle habitat.
Plant crowns 15cm deep in trench systems during early spring to protect them from frost damage.
Water young plants weekly in dry summer spells but keep established beds dry to prevent root rot.
Cut yellowing autumn foliage back to 5cm above ground level to prevent overwintering of pests.
Hand-weed beds carefully to avoid damaging the shallow, spreading root systems of the crowns.

items.name: Asparagus mucronatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with grit to mimic Mediterranean soils and prevent winter root rot.
Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frosts, keeping the root crown level with the soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep completely dry during wet UK winters.
Prune back dead woody stems in late winter to encourage fresh, ornamental needle-like growth.
Protect young plants from slugs in spring and shield from harsh, freezing winds using fleece.

items.name: Asparagus nesiotes
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent crown rot.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre in deep pots to accommodate the taproot.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Cut back dead foliage to ground level in late autumn to prevent overwintering pests.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails in spring using grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Asparagus officinalis
items.growersTips:
Prepare a permanent bed by digging in well-rotted manure and grit to ensure excellent winter drainage
Plant bare-root crowns in April fifteen centimetres deep in trenches on a ridge of loose soil
Apply a thick mulch of garden compost in late autumn after the ferns have turned yellow and died back
Cut all yellowed foliage down to ground level in autumn using sharp shears to prevent asparagus beetle
Stop harvesting spears by the twenty-first of June to allow the plant to build energy for next year

items.name: Asparagus prostratus
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy soil or shingle to mimic its wild UK maritime cliff habitat.
Water sparingly once established as this native coastal plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using grit barriers during damp UK spring weather.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomatous rootstock in early spring just as new growth begins.
Do not harvest spears for eating as this rare native species is grown purely for conservation.

items.name: Asparagus racemosus
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots using free-draining gritty compost so you can move them indoors before autumn frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the soil almost dry during the cold winter dormancy.
Prune the thorny climbing stems back by half in late winter to encourage vigorous new spring shoots.
Repot every two years in spring using a mix of John Innes No 3, coarse grit, and well-rotted manure.
Watch for red spider mites under leaves in dry summer weather and mist regularly to boost humidity.

items.name: Asparagus retrofractus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winters.
Bring container-grown plants indoors to a bright, frost-free conservatory before November frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of compost feels dry to the touch.
Prune out old, yellowing woody stems at the base in spring to encourage fresh, vibrant growth.
Inspect the dense, needle-like foliage regularly for spider mites in dry, heated indoor air.

items.name: Asparagus rubicundus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy loam with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect delicate shrubby stems from cold UK winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, keeping the soil barely damp in winter.
Prune back dead woody stems to the base in late autumn to prevent fungal diseases like rust.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in early spring to boost growth without touching stems.

items.name: Asparagus scandens
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors or protect with fleece in winter as this South African native cannot survive UK frosts
Grow in pots of loam-based compost with added grit to ensure the sharp drainage this plant demands
Water moderately in summer but keep the soil barely moist during the cold dormant winter months
Position in bright indirect light or partial shade to prevent the delicate fern-like foliage scorching
Prune out yellowing or dead climbing stems at the base in early spring to encourage fresh green growth

items.name: Asparagus setaceus
items.growersTips:
Keep indoors year-round as a houseplant or move outside only during warm frost-free UK summer months
Water thoroughly once the top two centimetres of compost dry out then empty the drainage saucer
Position in bright indirect light near an east or west window to prevent the delicate fronds burning
Mist the foliage regularly or place on a wet pebble tray to combat dry centrally heated indoor air
Prune yellowing or bare stems right back to the soil level in spring to stimulate fresh green growth

items.name: Asparagus simulans
items.growersTips:
Grow in a warm greenhouse or conservatory as this tender South African native will not survive UK frost
Use a free-draining loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot indoors
Water moderately in summer but keep the soil almost dry during the cold dark UK winter months
Prune out old yellowing climbing stems in early spring to encourage vigorous new shoots from the base
Check regularly for red spider mite and mealybugs which thrive in dry indoor UK growing conditions

items.name: Asparagus sprengeri
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters below seven degrees Celsius
Water thoroughly once top inch of soil dries then let drain fully to prevent tuberous root rot
Prune yellowing or bare stems at the base in early spring to stimulate lush new feathery growth
Repot in spring only when the vigorous roots crack or push out of the pot using loam-based compost
Position in bright indirect light avoiding direct midday UK summer sun which scorches the fronds

items.name: Asparagus squarrosus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural sand to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres in a heated propagator at twenty degrees.
Water sparingly during summer, allowing the compost to dry out completely between soakings.
Overwinter pots in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame to protect roots from freezing temperatures.
Prune yellowing stems back to the base in late autumn using sharp, sterilised secateurs.

items.name: Asparagus striatus
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet, cold UK winters.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to protect from hard frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out completely.
Prune back dead, yellowing stems in late autumn to maintain shape and prevent fungal disease.
Propagate by dividing the tuberous root clump in spring just as new growth begins to emerge.

items.name: Asparagus suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African ornamental in pots to easily move indoors before autumn frosts hit UK
Plant in free-draining loam mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, reducing to monthly in winter
Prune yellowing woody stems at the base in early spring to encourage fresh bright green needle growth
Watch for red spider mite in dry indoor winter air and mist the fine foliage regularly to deter them

items.name: Asparagus virgatus
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to protect young roots from wet UK winter rot.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of five millimetres using a free-draining gritty loam compost mix.
Water sparingly once established allowing the top three centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Prune the feathery stems back to the base in early spring before the new bright green shoots emerge.
Incorporate plenty of horticultural grit into heavy clay soils to prevent waterlogging in winter.

items.name: Asperugo procumbens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep to mimic natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, gravelly soils.
Grow in poor, well-drained alkaline soil to prevent the weak stems from becoming overly floppy.
Provide a low trellis or plant near sturdier shrubs to support its scrambling, hook-covered stems.
Monitor for powdery mildew in damp UK summers and space plants well to ensure good air circulation.

items.name: Aspidoglossum
items.growersTips:
Sow these South African grassland perennials in gritty, free-draining loam to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pots in full sun but bring them into a frost-free greenhouse or porch before November.
Water active growers moderately in summer, but keep the compost almost bone-dry throughout winter.
Check the tuberous roots regularly for vine weevil grubs, which love nesting in container compost.
Plant tubers just below the soil surface in spring, using terracotta pots to help moisture evaporate.

items.name: Aspidogyne
items.growersTips:
Grow this jewel orchid in a shallow, wide pot using a free-draining sphagnum moss and perlite mix.
Keep your plant in a warm, humid room out of direct UK sun to prevent the velvet leaves from burning.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than tap water, keeping the potting medium damp but never soggy.
Watch out for fungus gnats in the damp soil, using yellow sticky traps nearby to catch them early.
Propagate in spring by carefully snipping the creeping rhizome, ensuring each piece has two nodes.

items.name: Aspidosperma
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted quebracho indoors before the first autumn frost to survive cold UK winters.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in damp clay.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into your peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage it needs.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot in your garden to mimic warmth.
Check the undersides of leaves weekly in summer for glasshouse red spider mite and spray with water.

items.name: Aspidosperma australe
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors by October to shield its tender roots from wet British frosts.
Plant in a deep, loam-rich pot with extra grit to ensure the perfect drainage this tree craves.
Water thoroughly only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, keeping it drier in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the canopy and encourage fresh, glossy evergreen leaves.
Position your pot in a bright, south-facing conservatory or sunroom to mimic its sunny homeland.

items.name: Aspidosperma cylindrocarpon
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors for winter as it will not survive a frost-free UK winter outside.
Grow it in a container with John Innes No 3 and extra grit to ensure the roots never sit in wet clay.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of compost feel dry to touch during summer months.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost slow growth.
Place your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing patio sheltered from cold easterly winds.

items.name: Aspidosperma discolor
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian native in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant your specimen in a very free-draining, loam-based compost with added grit to prevent root rot.
Water thoroughly once the top inch of soil dries out, but keep it barely damp during cold winter months.
Place your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its warm tropical home.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost risk passes to shape the shrub and encourage new growth.

items.name: Aspidosperma macrocarpon
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical tree indoors for winter as it will not survive a frosty British frost.
Plant your specimen in deep, free-draining sandy loam to mimic its native dry forest soil.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil feel completely dry to prevent root rot.
Position your pot in the sunniest south-facing spot you have to maximise crucial summer warmth.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to August to boost indoor growth.

items.name: Aspidosperma megalocarpon
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical tree indoors for winter as it cannot survive a damp UK frost below ten degrees.
Grow it in a large container with a heavy loam-based grit mix to ensure the roots never sit in water.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, then let it drain completely.
Place your pot in a conservatory or south-facing room to maximise the limited UK summer sunshine.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to August to boost leaf growth.

items.name: Aspidosperma parvifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian native in a large pot so you can move it indoors before the autumn frost.
Use a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, reducing this to a minimum in winter.
Place your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing room to mimic its native tropical light.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to August to boost its slow growth.

items.name: Aspidosperma polyneuron
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian giant in a large pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant seeds just cover-deep in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent cold-season rot.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry, mimicking its native seasonal drought cycle.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs on the leathery leaves during damp British autumn months.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost risk passes to shape it and fit your indoor space.

items.name: Aspidosperma pyrifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a typical cold UK frost.
Grow it in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the roots never sit in wet soil.
Water it thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel completely dry to the touch.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the high light levels it absolutely craves.
Prune back any leggy stems in early spring just as the new growth starts to show to keep it bushy.

items.name: Aspidosperma quebracho-blanco
items.growersTips:
Bring your white quebracho indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters.
Plant in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy, free-draining soil to mimic its dry native habitat.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, then let it drain fully.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or patio spot to maximise summer light.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape it, as this slow-growing tree recovers very slowly.

items.name: Aspidosperma ramiflorum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a chilly UK frost.
Plant in a deep pot with peat-free loam and perlite to ensure the taproot has excellent drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, keeping it barely damp through winter.
Place your pot in a bright conservatory or near a south-facing window to mimic its sunny canopy.
Feed with a balanced liquid seaweed fertilizer once a month from April to September to boost growth.

items.name: Aspidosperma spruceanum
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted tree indoors to a heated conservatory before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to mimic its natural tropical dry season.
Mix plenty of perlite and grit into your peat-free compost to prevent winter root rot in the UK.
Place it in your brightest south-facing window to maximize the weak British winter sunlight.
Repot in spring using a deep container to accommodate its taproot without bending it.

items.name: Aspidosperma subincanum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a damp UK frost below ten degrees.
Grow it in a large terracotta pot filled with gritty, peat-free loam to ensure excellent drainage.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil feel completely dry to prevent root rot.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing room to maximise the bright, indirect sunlight.
Feed with a diluted balanced liquid fertiliser once a month only during the active spring growth.

items.name: Aspidosperma tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a damp British frost.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy loam to mimic its dry savannah home.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil feel bone dry to prevent root rot.
Wipe the fuzzy leaves with a dry microfiber cloth to keep dust off and boost sunlight intake.
Position it in your brightest south-facing window or heated conservatory for maximum light.

items.name: Aspidosperma triternatum
items.growersTips:
Bring this South American native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a wet UK frost.
Grow it in a loam-based compost with added grit to ensure the roots never sit in winter wet.
Place your pot in the sunniest spot on your patio to mimic its warm, native woodland habitat.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, then let it drain completely.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to keep its bushy shrub shape tidy.

items.name: Aspidosperma ulei
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical Brazilian tree indoors for winter as it cannot survive a damp UK frost.
Grow it in a heavy clay pot with added grit to stop the wind toppling its top-heavy canopy.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our cool climate.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer monthly from April to September to boost leaf growth.
Wipe the glossy leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and maximize scarce UK winter light.

items.name: Aspidosperma vargasii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical tree indoors for winter as it cannot survive a damp, freezing UK frost.
Grow it in a large, deep pot filled with a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, reducing this in winter.
Place your pot in a conservatory or south-facing room to maximise essential UK sunlight.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape the plant and encourage bushy, manageable indoor growth.

items.name: Aspidotis
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate fern in a gritty, neutral to acidic soil mix with plenty of leaf mould.
Keep it in a sheltered, damp rock crevice or alpine house to protect it from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, allowing the gritty compost to dry out between waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to feast on the tender new emerging fronds.
Propagate your plants by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes during mild spring weather.

items.name: Aspidotis californica
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate fern in a gritty, free-draining mix of leafmould and sand to mimic its wild home.
Keep it in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse over wet UK winters to prevent its crown from rotting.
Water it sparingly from below during summer, letting the compost dry out completely between drinks.
Tuck it into a sheltered, north-facing rockery crevice to shield its fronds from harsh midday sun.
Snip off any dead, brown fronds right at the base in early spring just before new growth starts.

items.name: Aspidotis carlotta-halliae
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate fern in a sheltered, frost-free spot with moist, acidic, leaf-mould-rich soil.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it into a cold greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Tuck it into a shady rockery crevice or stone wall to mimic its natural, well-drained cliff home.
Snip away any dead or tatty fronds in early spring just as the fresh new growth begins to unfurl.

items.name: Aspidotis densa
items.growersTips:
Plant this dainty fern in a sheltered, gritty rock crevice to mimic its native scree habitat.
Water sparingly in winter but keep the soil damp during dry UK summer spells to prevent browning.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to ensure the perfect free-draining conditions.
Tuck it next to small companion plants like saxifrages that won't crowd its delicate fronds.
Protect the crown with a layer of grit to prevent winter wet rot during damp British winters.

items.name: Astephanus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African climber in a pot so you can move it into a warm greenhouse for winter.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in a free-draining peat-free compost mixed with grit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to avoid rotting its delicate root system.
Prune back the tangled stems in early spring just as new shoots begin to emerge from the base.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in a dry UK conservatory during summer.

items.name: Asteranthera
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean beauty in moist, acidic woodland soil, ideally near a peat-free ericaceous bed.
Grow it up a north or east-walled trellis where its stems can cling to cool, damp masonry or bark.
Water with rainwater weekly to keep the soil consistently damp, as tap water is too alkaline.
Mulch every spring with leaf mould or pine needles to mimic its native temperate rainforest floor.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh winter winds with fleece if temperatures drop below -5C.

items.name: Asteridea
items.growersTips:
Sow these Australian annual seeds shallowly indoors in March to beat the damp UK spring chills.
Give them gritty, free-draining soil in your sunniest border to mimic their dry native habitat.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy British winter wet.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with beer traps or copper tape.
Snip off faded daisy heads regularly through August to keep the cheerful blooms coming.

items.name: Asteropyrum
items.growersTips:
Plant these delicate woodlanders in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous shrubs.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during dry UK spring and summer spells.
Protect the emerging early spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets.
Propagate by carefully dividing the rhizomatous clumps in early autumn after flowering ceases.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in November to mimic their natural forest floor habitat.

items.name: Asterostigma
items.growersTips:
Plant these tuberous aroids eight inches deep in rich, leaf-mold soil to protect from winter frost.
Keep the soil consistently damp throughout summer, but stop watering entirely once autumn arrives.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or shed for the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when the highly unusual, mottled stems first push up.
Mix lots of grit and composted bark into your clay soil to prevent the tubers from rotting in wet.

items.name: Astilbe
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade, incorporating plenty of leaf mould.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent the foliage from scorching and drying out.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour.
Leave faded flower heads intact over winter to protect the crown from severe UK frosts.
Plant alongside Hostas and Ferns in damp, shady borders where they thrive in identical conditions.

items.name: Astilbe × arendsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating well-rotted manure to prevent drying out.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate feathery plumes from the drying UK midday sun.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the foliage from crisping and browning at the edges.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and bloom.
Leave the spent flower heads over winter to provide structural interest and protect the crown from frost.

items.name: Astilbe chinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam enriched with leafmould to prevent the soil drying out.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch, keeping the soil constantly damp.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and size.
Plant alongside Hostas or Rodgersia in partial shade to create a self-shading damp-loving canopy.
Leave faded bronze flower heads intact over winter to provide structural interest in frosty gardens.

items.name: Astilbe japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the leaf margins from browning and curling.
Divide the root clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain flowering vigour.
Mulch annually in March with leaf mould to protect shallow roots from drying out in spring sun.
Plant alongside Hostas or Rodgersias in dappled shade to shield the delicate fronds from midday sun.

items.name: Astilbe simplicifolia
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted manure to keep UK clay soils moisture-retentive.
Plant crowns shallowly with the buds just below the soil surface to prevent crown rot in wet winters.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to stop the delicate crinkled leaves from scorching.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring just as the bronze-tinted shoots emerge.
Plant alongside Hostas or ferns to provide the dappled shade needed to protect the pale pink blooms.

items.name: Astilbe thunbergii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted manure.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent the delicate leaf margins from scorching.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and flowering potential.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect shallow roots from hard winter frosts and drying.
Position in partial shade alongside Hostas and Ferns to shelter the tall arching stems from wind.

items.name: Astilboides
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade to prevent leaf scorch.
Water copiously during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Shelter from strong winds to protect the massive, delicate umbrella-like leaves from tearing.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted manure every spring to retain vital soil moisture.
Protect emerging spring buds from late frosts using horticultural fleece or a layer of dry bracken.

items.name: Astridia
items.growersTips:
Bring your Astridia indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect it from wet UK winters.
Plant in a gritty cactus compost with extra perlite to ensure the roots never sit in damp soil.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then give it a good soak, but stop watering entirely in winter.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Propagate your Astridia in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous before potting.

items.name: Astrolepis
items.growersTips:
Plant these sun-loving ferns in a gritty, free-draining rockery to survive wet UK winters.
Grow them in terracotta pots of alpine compost so you can easily move them under glass in November.
Water them only from the base during summer to keep their beautiful fuzzy fronds from rotting.
Pair them with hardy sempervivums and sedums that thrive in the same dry, sunny crevices.
Watch out for slugs hiding under the fuzzy leaves during damp British spring nights.

items.name: Astrolepis cochisensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of loam and coarse grit.
Keep it under a glass porch or cold frame to shield it from wet UK winters, which will rot it.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, and always pour water around the base, never on the fronds.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum possible winter sunlight.
Do not prune the old shrivelled fronds in autumn as they naturally curl up to protect the crown.

items.name: Asyneuma
items.growersTips:
Plant your Asyneuma in gritty, sharp-draining soil to stop winter wet from rotting its taproot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, letting the soil dry out completely between times.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Cut the faded flower spikes right back to the base in autumn to keep the rosette tidy for winter.
Grow them in a sunny rock garden alongside alpine pinks or sedums that share their love of grit.

items.name: Asyneuma limonifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in sharp-draining limestone grit to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position your pot in full, baking sun on a south-facing patio to mimic its native Balkan cliffs.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this plant hates soggy roots.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs using organic wool pellets or copper grit barriers.
In autumn, cut back the faded flower spikes to the base to keep the rosette compact and tidy.

items.name: Asystasia

Grow Asystasia gangetica in pots so you can easily move them indoors before the first autumn frost.

Water your potted Asystasia only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to touch in summer.

Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering your plants in a heated conservatory.

items.name: Asystasia dalzelliana

items.name: Asystasia gangetica

items.name: Asystasia mysorensis

Bring this tender south Indian native indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it alive.
Water it deeply only when the top inch of soil feels dry, as it hates sitting in soggy UK mud.

Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage a bushier habit and more flower spikes.

items.name: Ateleia

Plant alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens to benefit from this annual legume's soil-fixing traits

items.name: Athrixia
items.growersTips:
Start your Athrixia seeds indoors in March to beat the late UK frosts, planting them 5mm deep.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only when the top two inches feel dry to your touch.

Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and way more daisy-like flowers.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or copper tape to protect them.

items.name: Athrotaxidoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant your Tasmanian cedar in deep, moist, acidic soil, ideally enriched with leaf mould or peat.
Give it a sheltered spot out of cold UK winds to prevent the delicate scale-like foliage bronzing.
Water young trees deeply during dry summer spells to mimic the damp Tasmanian rainforest climate.
Avoid pruning these slow growers, but if you must, lightly trim wayward shoots only in late spring.
Protect young saplings with fleece during harsh, freezing British winters to prevent frost damage.

items.name: Athrotaxis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Tasmanian cedar in a sheltered spot away from drying, cold easterly winds in winter.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or compost to create the acidic, moisture-retentive soil it loves.
Keep the soil consistently damp during dry UK summers, as this conifer cannot tolerate drought.
Avoid pruning this slow grower, but if you must shape it, do so lightly in late spring.
Watch out for scale insects on the scale-like foliage of Athrotaxis cupressoides in early summer.

items.name: Athrotaxis cupressoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Tasmanian conifer in a moist, acidic site to mimic its native boggy mountain home.
Give it a sheltered spot out of freezing winds to protect the delicate scale-like foliage.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Avoid pruning this slow-growing tree as it naturally forms a beautiful, neat conical shape.
Grow it alongside acid-loving heathers or pieris which thrive in the same damp, peat-free compost.

items.name: Athrotaxis laxifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Tasmanian conifer in deep, moist, acidic soil mimicking the damp Scottish Highlands.
Shelter your young tree from harsh easterly winter winds to prevent the scale-like leaves browning.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the root ball consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Do not prune this slow grower at all, except to gently remove dead wood in late spring with shears.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or composted bark to retain moisture and mimic forest soil.

items.name: Athrotaxis selaginoides
items.growersTips:
Give this Tasmanian conifer a sheltered, humid spot in wet UK regions like Wales or Scotland.
Plant your King William pine in highly acidic, moisture-retentive soil enriched with leaf mould.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to mimic the damp, cool conditions of its native rainforest.
Do not prune this slow grower at all, as it struggles to regenerate from old wood if cut back.
Protect young plants from dry, cold winter winds with a temporary fleece wrap in exposed gardens.

items.name: Atocion
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April at a depth of two millimetres into well-drained, gritty garden soil.
Position in full sun to prevent the weak stems of this annual from flopping in damp UK summers.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the top soil to dry out to prevent root rot.
Deadhead spent pink blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering window before the plant dies.
Sow alongside companion plants like English lavender to support pollinators in dry gravel borders.

items.name: Atocion armeria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the soil surface in spring, as they need light to germinate in UK gardens.
Grow them in gritty, fast-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet British winters.
Leave the faded flower heads on the stems in autumn so they can self-seed freely for next year.
Water young plants weekly until established, then leave them to thrive in dry, sunny borders.
Plant them alongside lavender or thyme in a rockery to create a gorgeous, drought-tolerant display.

items.name: Atocion rupestre
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your soil to mimic alpine scree, as this plant hates damp UK winter roots.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn so winter cold can trigger their spring germination.
Water sparingly once established, only during dry spells, to keep its compact cushion shape.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a tidy habit and fresh foliage.
Grow it alongside saxifrages in a raised bed or trough to ensure the sharp drainage it loves.

items.name: Austrocedrus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean cedar in deep, moist, well-drained acid to neutral soil to mimic its home wildwood.
Position your tree in full sun but shelter it from cold, drying winds that scorch its scale-like leaves.
Water deeply during dry summer spells for the first three years until its root system is established.
Prune lightly in late spring only to remove dead wood, as this conifer does not regenerate from old wood.
Watch out for phytophthora root rot in heavy clay, so dig in plenty of grit before planting.

items.name: Austrogramme
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate fern in a terrarium or heated greenhouse to survive chilly UK winter drafts.
Keep the compost consistently damp using tepid rainwater rather than cold, lime-heavy tap water.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and perlite into peat-free compost to mimic its tropical forest floor.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light, completely away from scorching direct midday sun.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to stop the fronds browning.

items.name: Avicennia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender mangrove in a heated greenhouse kept above fifteen degrees to survive UK winters.
Plant your seeds shallowly in heavy, waterlogged clay mixed with sea salt to mimic their estuary home.
Keep the soil constantly flooded with brackish water, never letting the root zone dry out at all.
Wipe the leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent salt crust buildup from blocking photosynthesis.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in summer and mist daily to keep the humidity high.

items.name: Avicennia alba
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical mangrove in a heated greenhouse kept above fifteen degrees to survive UK winters.
Plant your specimen in a heavy, brackish clay soil mix and keep the pot permanently waterlogged.
Use non-iodized sea salt in your watering can to mimic the coastal estuary water it craves.
Watch closely for spider mites and scale insects which thrive in the humid greenhouse air it needs.
Avoid pruning the delicate breathing roots or pneumatophores that emerge upward from the mud.

items.name: Avicennia germinans
items.growersTips:
Grow this black mangrove in a heated greenhouse with a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees.
Keep the roots constantly submerged in warm brackish water using a mix of sea salt and rainwater.
Use a deep pot filled with heavy, anaerobic clay soil or mud to mimic its native coastal swamp.
Wipe the leaves weekly with a damp cloth to remove the salt crystals they naturally excrete.
Provide maximum light using a strong LED grow light to compensate for dull UK winter days.

items.name: Avicennia marina
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender grey mangrove in a heated greenhouse over winter to survive the chilly UK frost.
Grow it in a sealed, undrained pot filled with heavy clay and waterlogged with salty pond water.
Mimic its natural habitat by adding roughly thirty-five grams of sea salt per litre of tap water.
Place your pot on the sunniest windowsill possible to maximise light during short British days.
Wipe the leaves weekly with a damp cloth to clear the salt crystals your plant naturally secretes.

items.name: Avicennia officinalis
items.growersTips:
To mimic its native mangrove swamp, grow this plant in a heated greenhouse with wet, brackish soil.
Keep the potting mix constantly waterlogged by sitting the container in a deep tray of warm water.
Maintain a high greenhouse temperature above fifteen degrees Celsius to survive chilly UK winters.
Add a small pinch of aquarium sea salt to your watering can to replicate its natural coastal habitat.
Watch out for root rot if the water stagnates, so use a highly porous, sandy compost base.

items.name: Avicennia schaueriana
items.growersTips:
Grow this salt-tolerant mangrove in a heated greenhouse to survive cold British winters.
Plant them in deep, heavy, waterlogged clay mixed with sea salt to mimic their natural estuary mud.
Keep the soil constantly submerged under a few inches of brackish water using rain and aquarium salt.
Wipe the leaves weekly with a damp cloth to remove the salt crystals they naturally excrete.
Position your pot in the brightest spot of a south-facing conservatory to maximise daily sunlight.

items.name: Azorina
items.growersTips:
Bring your Azorina pot indoors to a bright, frost-free conservatory before the first autumn frost.
Grow this Azores native in a terracotta pot using a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mix.
Water sparingly in winter, only when the top two inches of compost feel completely bone dry.
Position your potted Azorina in your sunniest, most sheltered south-facing patio spot for summer.
Snip off the faded bell-shaped flowers in late summer to keep the rosette looking neat and tidy.

items.name: Babiana

Plant corms in autumn eight centimetres deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from November to April.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep completely dry in summer when the foliage dies back.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic their native South African climate.
Protect new spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape around pots.

items.name: Babiana blanda

Plant Babiana blanda corms 8cm deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors to survive UK frosts.
Mix equal parts grit and peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage these South African bulbs need.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry during their summer dormant phase.
Position pots in your garden's hottest, most south-facing sun trap to mimic their native climate.
Overwinter pots in a cold greenhouse or unheated conservatory to protect corms from wet winter rot.

items.name: Babiana brachystachys
items.growersTips:

Grow in pots to easily move undercover before the first frosts, as they cannot survive UK winters.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, then increase watering only when active leaf growth begins.

Allow the foliage to die back naturally in summer to feed the bulb for the next spring flowering.

Plant corms in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil.

Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic the hot South African summer baking.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a sandy compost mix and expect flowers in three years.

items.name: Babiana dregei

Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic their hot South African habitat.
Watch for aphids on the pleated leaves in spring and treat immediately to prevent virus spread.

Position pots in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic the intense winter sun of the Cape.
Protect emerging winter foliage from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape on pots.

items.name: Babiana papyracea

Plant bulbs in autumn five centimetres deep in a gritty loam-based compost using deep terracotta pots.

Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in summer and keep the soil completely dry.

items.name: Babiana rubrocyanea
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.

items.name: Babiana sambucina
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, sharply draining loam to prevent winter wet rot.

Plant Babiana corms 8cm deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors to survive wet UK winters.
