items.name: Babiana tubiflora

items.name: Babiana villosa
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet root rot.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory during UK winters.

Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic South African sun and trigger blooms.
Protect emerging winter foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Bacopa

Keep them in pots or hanging baskets so you can easily move them indoors before the first UK frost.
Water them daily in summer to keep the compost damp, as they stop flowering if the soil dries out.
Mix plenty of grit and organic matter into your multi-purpose compost to ensure excellent drainage.
Trim back the stems by half in midsummer to encourage a fresh flush of those lovely white flowers.
Watch out for aphids in late spring and wash them off with a gentle spray from your garden hose.

items.name: Bacopa caroliniana
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Bacopa indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to survive chilly UK winters.
Plant stems five centimetres deep in wet soil at your pond edge so they do not float away in wind.
Prune the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and more blue summer flowers.

items.name: Bacopa crenata
items.growersTips:
Grow this bog-lover in a shallow pond edge or wet container to keep its roots constantly soggy.

Watch out for slugs during damp British springs, as they love to feast on the tender new shoots.

items.name: Bacopa monnieri
items.growersTips:
Grow it in a shallow pot of acidic peat-free compost kept constantly waterlogged or submerged.
Bring your pots indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frosts hit in October.
Snip the stem tips weekly during spring to encourage a bushier habit and prevent straggly growth.
Plant it alongside water forget-me-not in your garden pond margins for a beautiful blue contrast.

Bring container-grown plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse by late October to survive UK winters.
Plant it alongside native Marsh Marigold to create a lovely colour contrast in your bog garden.
Snip the stem tips in midsummer to encourage a bushier habit and prevent it from getting too leggy.
Watch out for pond snails in spring as they love to munch on the soft, fleshy submerged foliage.

items.name: Baeriopsis
items.growersTips:
Sow Baeriopsis seeds in free-draining sandy loam under a cold frame in April to survive UK spring damp.
Water these drought-tolerant annuals only when the top three inches of soil feel completely dry.
Plant them alongside thrift or sea rosemary to mimic their natural coastal cliffs in your rockery.
Avoid any pruning or pinching out, as this delicate annual naturally keeps a neat, compact shape.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British summers, using organic grit barriers around stems.

items.name: Bahiopsis

items.name: Baikiaea plurijuga

Grow this African teak as a warm, indoor conservatory annual in free-draining, sandy loam soil.
Soak the hard, woody seeds in warm water for 24 hours before sowing them 2cm deep in individual pots.
Keep the soil barely damp to mimic its dry native habitat, as overwatering will quickly rot roots.
Position your pots in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic the intense African sun.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites under cover and mist the surrounding air on hot days.

items.name: Baissea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African climber in a conservatory pot using peat-free loam with extra perlite.

Prune your vine right after its summer flowering to keep it tidy and fit your greenhouse space.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry glasshouse air and mist the leaves daily to deter them.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight during the active spring growth.

items.name: Baissea multiflora
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender African climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water it only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining compost mix have dried out completely.
Feed your plant monthly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer from May to August to boost blooms.
Prune the stems lightly in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its vigorous vines tidy.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor winter heating.

items.name: Balizia
items.growersTips:
Start Balizia seeds indoors in early April on a warm windowsill to beat the cool UK spring weather.
Sow Balizia seeds just five millimetres deep in free-draining peat-free compost and keep moist.
Plant your Balizia outdoors in late May once all risk of frost has passed in a sunny, sheltered spot.
Water Balizia at the base every morning during dry summer spells to avoid powdery mildew on leaves.
Feed Balizia weekly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertiliser from July to boost summer blooms.

items.name: Ballochia amoena
items.growersTips:
Plant this Yemeni native in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Keep your plant in a pot so you can move it inside to a bright, frost-free windowsill by October.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, cutting back to almost nothing in winter.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in late spring to encourage a bushier, more compact growth habit.
Pair it with hardy sedums in containers to mimic its natural dry, rocky Middle Eastern habitat.

items.name: Ballochia rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Arabian gem in a very gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by October.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as this species hates soggy roots.
Place your pot on a south-facing patio to maximise the precious British summer sunshine.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to maintain a compact, bushy shape.

items.name: Baphia
items.growersTips:
Sow Baphia seeds indoors in late April at a depth of one centimetre to protect them from UK frosts.
Mix plenty of grit into your garden soil before planting to ensure the sharp drainage they need.
Water your Baphia deeply once a week at the base, letting the soil dry out fully between soakings.
Pinch out the growing tips in early June to encourage a much bushier habit and more summer flowers.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with beer traps or copper tape barriers.

items.name: Barjonia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Barjonia in free-draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet British winters without rotting.
Position this perennial in full south-facing sun to help it thrive in our cooler UK summers.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and encourage fresh spring growth.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper tape barriers.

items.name: Barleria
items.growersTips:

Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plants indoors.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser from May to September for best blooms.

items.name: Barleria aculeata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African native in a pot of gritty loam so you can move it indoors before frost.

Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its warm origin.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering this spiny shrub in your conservatory.

items.name: Barleria albostellata
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted bush violet indoors before the autumn frosts hit, as it cannot survive UK winters.
Grow this African beauty in a free-draining mix of loam and grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water it generously throughout summer, but let the soil dry out completely between winter waterings.
Prune back the stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more white flowers.
Position your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing patio to get enough sun for blooming.

items.name: Barleria cristata
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Philippine violet indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it cozy all winter.
Plant it in a terracotta pot filled with gritty, peat-free compost to ensure excellent drainage.
Water generously in summer but let the top inch of soil dry out completely before watering again.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more purple flowers.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plant in the conservatory.

items.name: Barleria elegans
items.growersTips:
Bring this African beauty indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Grow it in a container with one-third grit to ensure the fast drainage this dry-loving shrub needs.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry, then let it drain completely.
Prune it back by half in early spring to stop it getting leggy and encourage more orange blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering it in your conservatory.

items.name: Barleria greenii
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African native indoors or to a heated greenhouse before the first autumn frost.

Prune the stems back by half in early spring to keep its naturally sparse habit bushy and compact.
Feed it weekly with a high-potash liquid tomato fertiliser from June to August to boost flowering.

items.name: Barleria lupulina
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Thai native indoors before October frosts and keep it on a sunny windowsill.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to prevent winter root rot in soggy UK weather.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, reducing to a light trickle during winter.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping it in your conservatory.
Prune the spiny stems by one-third in early spring to keep its bushy shape and encourage yellow blooms.

items.name: Barleria mysorensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Indian native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.

Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this plant hates soggy British winters.
Prune the stems back by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more purple flowers.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory for maximum light.

items.name: Barleria observatrix
items.growersTips:

items.name: Barleria obtusa

Bring your potted bush violet indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.

items.name: Barleria oenotheroides
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.

Prune stems back by half in late spring to encourage a bushy habit and maximize summer flowering.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic the bright light of its natural habitat.

items.name: Barleria prionitis
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted barleria indoors before the first autumn frost to protect it from cold UK winters.
Use a very free-draining sandy loam mix in pots to prevent root rot during wet British summers.

Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more yellow flowers.

items.name: Barleria repens

Bring your red bush violet indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.

items.name: Barleria siamensis

items.name: Barleria strigosa

Bring your potted blue sage indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.

items.name: Barleria tetracantha

items.name: Barlerieae

Bring your potted Barleria indoors by October to protect them from the wet, frosty UK winter.

items.name: Barnardia

items.name: Barnardia japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs in late spring about five centimetres deep in well-drained, gritty soil.

Water regularly during their active summer growth but keep them almost dry throughout the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in autumn when those delicate pink flower spikes finally emerge.
Divide overcrowded clumps in early spring just as the fresh green strap-like leaves start to show.

items.name: Barnebydendron
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using bottom heat to ensure germination.

Bring containers inside to a heated greenhouse or conservatory before the first autumn frosts hit.

items.name: Bartholina
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African orchid indoors for winter as it cannot survive frosty British temperatures.

Keep a sharp eye out for UK greenhouse pests like spider mites and aphids on the delicate fringed lip.

items.name: Basedowia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam to mimic its arid native soil.

Protect plants from slugs during damp UK summers by using grit barriers around the base of stems.

items.name: Baseonema

items.name: Baskervilla

Keep this rare orchid snug in winter by bringing your potted Baskervilla indoors before first frost.

items.name: Batesia
items.growersTips:
Sow Batesia seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres to protect from late UK frosts.

Water Batesia deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to avoid powdery mildew.
Pinch out the growing tips of young Batesia plants in May to encourage a bushier flowering habit.
Watch for black bean aphids on young Batesia shoots and spray them off with a firm jet of water.

items.name: Baynesia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Baynesia indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.

Propagate your plant by taking stem cuttings in late spring and letting them callous before potting.

items.name: Baynesia lophophora
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare staple succulent in a gritty loam-free mix with seventy percent pumice for drainage.
Keep it completely dry from October to March in a heated greenhouse or bright windowsill above 10C.
Water only when the tiny ribbed stems slightly wrinkle, soaking thoroughly then letting it dry out.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight stem joints, treating them quickly with rubbing alcohol.
Position your pot in a south-facing conservatory but shade it slightly during scorching July afternoons.

items.name: Beaumontia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a large pot so you can move it into a heated conservatory for winter.
Prune your vine hard right after its spring flowering to keep its vigorous growth under control.
Water generously during hot summer spells but let the compost dry out completely between waterings.

Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and mealybugs when keeping this plant indoors over winter.

items.name: Beckwithia
items.growersTips:
Grow this buttercup relative in gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its native alpine scree habitat.

items.name: Beesia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Beesia in a damp, shady spot under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland home.

Divide your Beesia clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to get free extra plants easily.

items.name: Begonia

Start tuberous begonias indoors in March, hollow side up, just level with the compost surface.

items.name: Begonia ‘Angel Wing’

items.name: Begonia × tuberhybrida

Start your tubers indoors in March by pushing them hollow-side up just level with the compost surface.

Pinch out the very first flower buds in June to encourage a much bushier plant with more blooms.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp August weather by spacing your pots to allow good airflow.
Lift the tubers after the first autumn frost, dry them off, and store in dry sand over winter.

items.name: Begonia × tuberhybrida ‘Kimjongilia’

Lift the tubers in October after the first frost, dry them, and store in dry sand over winter.

items.name: Begonia acerifolia

items.name: Begonia acetosa

items.name: Begonia aconitifolia

items.name: Begonia acutifolia

items.name: Begonia albococcinea

items.name: Begonia annulata

Bring this Indian native indoors by October to protect its stunning zoned leaves from UK frosts.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only when the top inch of compost feels dry to touch.

items.name: Begonia baccata

Bring this rare Sao Tome native indoors by October to protect it from wet and chilly UK winters.

Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent stem rot in our cool climate.

items.name: Begonia boliviensis

Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a cascade of blooms in your hanging baskets.

items.name: Begonia bowerae

Keep yours in a pot of peat-free compost with extra perlite to survive damp, chilly UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, keeping the fuzzy leaves completely dry.

Snip off any leggy stems in early spring to keep your Tiger Kitten cultivar compact and bushy.

items.name: Begonia brevirimosa

Keep this pink-variegated beauty indoors year-round as it cannot survive UK winter temperatures.
Water only when the top inch of soil dries out, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid leaf spotting.

items.name: Begonia capensis

Water only when the top inch of soil feels dry to prevent tuber rot in our damp climate.

items.name: Begonia carolineifolia

items.name: Begonia chitoensis

items.name: Begonia coccinea

Prune leggy stems by one-third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flowering side-shoots.

items.name: Begonia conchifolia

Bring your shell begonia indoors by October as it cannot survive a damp, chilly UK winter outside.

Snip off any leggy stems in early spring to encourage a much bushier, more compact growth habit.

items.name: Begonia consobrina

items.name: Begonia cubensis

Bring your cubensis indoors before October frosts as this Cuban native cannot survive a UK winter.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.

items.name: Begonia cucullata

items.name: Begonia davisii

items.name: Begonia decandra

items.description: Berberis aquifolium, the Oregon grape, holly-leaved barberry, or Mahonia, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is an evergreen shrub growing up to 3 metres (10 ft) tall and 1.5 m (5 ft) wide. It has pinnate leaves consisting of spiny leaflets, exhibiting dense clusters of yellow flowers in early spring, followed by dark bluish-black berries.

Watch out for slugs and snails which love to devour the emerging winter growth in damp weather.

items.name: Blennospora
items.growersTips:
Sow Blennospora seeds in April under glass, barely covering them with a very fine layer of grit.
Plant these Australian annuals in your sunniest, south-facing border once all spring frosts pass.
Mix plenty of horticultural sand into your soil to mimic their native well-drained sandy habitat.
Water sparingly from below only when the top inch of soil feels dry to prevent damp seedling rot.
Grow them alongside hardy annual grasses to support their delicate, wiry stems in breezy UK weather.

items.name: Blepharis
items.growersTips:
Keep these African beauties in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them inside for winter.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, letting the gritty compost dry out fully between drinks.
Sow your seeds shallowly in spring using a heated propagator to mimic their native desert warmth.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and mealybugs when overwintering your plants in a heated porch.
Trim back the faded spiky flower spikes in late autumn to keep your potted specimens neat and bushy.

items.name: Blepharis capensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African beauty in a pot so you can move it indoors before the autumn frosts hit.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive our wet, soggy UK winters.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil dries out completely to prevent crown rot.
Place your pot on your sunniest south-facing patio to mimic its hot, dry native habitat.
Wear thick gloves when handling it because those spiny, thistle-like leaves really sting.

items.name: Blepharis dhofarensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Arabian native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil rot.
Grow it in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of gritty sand and peat-free compost for drainage.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, then drench it and let it drain fully.
Place it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense Middle Eastern sun it loves.
Snip off faded flower spikes in late summer to keep this unusual spiny perennial compact and neat.

items.name: Blepharis edulis
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot with 50% grit to survive wet UK winters indoors.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly but never let the pot sit in water.
Sow the spiny seeds just under the surface in spring using a heated propagator to mimic warmth.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to get the maximum light and heat UK skies offer.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots in spring, so keep pots elevated off the ground outdoors.

items.name: Blepharis grossa
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African native in a very gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory by late October.
Water deeply only when the soil is bone dry, as this desert beauty is highly prone to root rot.
Position it on your hottest, brightest south-facing patio to mimic its sunny native habitat.
Prune back the spiny foliage lightly in spring to encourage fresh, compact new growth.

items.name: Blepharis maderaspatensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors by October to protect its delicate roots from wet UK winter frost.
Plant it in a terracotta pot filled with gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot in our rain.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this plant hates soggy British winter soil.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense sunlight of its natural home.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.

items.name: Blepharis mitrata
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frost.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix to prevent root rot during rainy summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, mimicking its natural arid habitat.
Position your pot in the brightest south-facing spot you have to mimic the intense African sun.
Snip off faded flower spikes in late autumn to keep the prickly foliage neat and compact.

items.name: Blepharis spiculifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this African native in a terracotta pot with 50% grit to survive wet UK winters indoors.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, then soak it thoroughly but gently.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill from October to April to mimic its desert home.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite in dry indoor air, misting occasionally to deter them.

items.name: Blepharodon
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of peat-free compost with perlite so you can move it inside by October.
Water your vine only when the top two inches of gritty soil feel dry to prevent winter root rot.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing porch to mimic its native tropical warmth.
Provide a sturdy bamboo trellis at planting time to support its twining stems as they search for light.
Check the leaf undersides weekly for glasshouse red spider mite, spraying with horticultural soap.

items.name: Bletiinae
items.growersTips:
Grow Bletilla striata in free-draining loam enriched with leafmould to survive wet UK winters.
Plant the pseudo-bulbs just two centimetres deep in spring so the warming sun triggers early growth.
Water your Chinese ground orchids generously from May to August, but keep them dry during dormancy.
Mulch the crowns with a thick layer of bracken or bark in November to protect them from hard frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to eat the tender emerging flower shoots.

items.name: Bletilla
items.growersTips:
Plant your Bletilla pseudobulbs just five centimetres deep in spring so the warming UK sun triggers growth.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into your soil to mimic a damp but free-draining woodland floor.

Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love to munch the tender new shoots.
Mulch the crown with a thick layer of bark chips in November to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.

items.name: Bloomeria aurea
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs five inches deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to survive UK wet.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormancy to prevent the bulbs from rotting underground.

Watch out for slugs and snails eating the fresh spring shoots as they emerge in chilly April.
Position your goldenstars in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic their warm native climate.

items.name: Bloomeria crocea
items.growersTips:
Plant your golden star bulbs five inches deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining sandy loam soil.

Keep watering minimal during summer dormancy to prevent the bulbs from rotting in damp British soil.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them into a dry greenhouse for winter shelter.

items.name: Blyttia
items.growersTips:
To grow Blyttia in the UK, plant it in a damp, shaded spot that mimics its native woodland home.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry British summer spells.

Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, tender new growth.
Propagate your Blyttia by dividing established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Bobartia
items.growersTips:
Plant Bobartia bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in sharply draining, gritty UK soil.

Water your Bobartia weekly during their spring active growth, but stop completely once they die back.

items.name: Bobgunnia madagascariensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twentyC

Feed your plants every fortnight with a high-potassium liquid seaweed to boost those unique blooms
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and mist the foliage regularly to keep humidity high

items.name: Bocconia
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep fertile loam in spring, burying the crown just level with the soil surface.
Position in full sun sheltered from strong UK winds to prevent the tall hollow stems from snapping.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to support the massive tropical foliage.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in late autumn and mulch heavily to protect from frost.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots and apply organic control early in the season.

items.name: Bocconia frutescens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a large pot to easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for UK winters.

items.name: Boea

Bring your Boea indoors before autumn frosts start, as they cannot survive a typical UK winter.

items.name: Boea hygroscopica
items.growersTips:
Bring this resurrection plant indoors before autumn frosts as it cannot survive a wet UK winter.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, pouring water at the base to avoid rotting the fuzzy leaves.

Propagate by dividing the offsets in spring when you see new green growth starting to emerge.

items.name: Bolandra
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native damp woodland canyon habitat
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged
Protect the delicate foliage from strong winds by planting near sheltered north-facing walls

Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they target the tender emerging shoots

items.name: Bolandra oregana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a moist, shaded rock garden or crevice using gritty, humus-rich, neutral to acid soil.
Water regularly in summer to mimic its native damp cliffs, but ensure sharp drainage to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for spring germination.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails during wet UK spring nights using organic grit.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Bolbitis
items.growersTips:
Tie your Bolbitis to bogwood or lava rock using black cotton thread rather than burying its rhizome.
Position this fern in a shady, draft-free indoor spot to mimic its native humid forest canopy.
Water with harvested UK rainwater to avoid the lime buildup from our typical hard tap water.
Snick off any older, tattered fronds right at the base during your spring houseplant tidy-up.
Keep your home thermostat above twelve degrees Celsius in winter so this tropical beauty stays cosy.

items.name: Bolbitis appendiculata
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical fern in a warm, humid greenhouse or terrarium to shield it from chilly UK drafts.
Grow it as an epiphyte by tying its rhizome to damp bark or lava rock rather than burying it in soil.
Mist the fronds daily with rainwater to mimic its native rainforest humidity in dry UK indoor air.
Position it in deep shade or filtered light, as direct UK summer sun will quickly scorch the fronds.
Divide the creeping rhizome in spring using sharp snips, ensuring each piece has a few healthy leaves.

items.name: Bolbitis heteroclita
items.growersTips:
Grow this slow fern as a houseplant or in a humid terrarium to survive chilly UK winter drafts.
Secure its rhizome onto bogwood or lava rock with thread rather than burying it in heavy compost.
Mist the fronds daily with rainwater to mimic tropical humidity in dry centrally heated rooms.
Keep the planting medium consistently damp but never soggy by watering from below once a week.
Snip off older yellowing fronds at the base in spring using sterilized shears to boost new growth.

items.name: Bolbitis heudelotii
items.growersTips:
Tie this aquatic fern to wood or stone with fishing line instead of burying its rhizome in gravel.
Keep your tank water between twenty and twenty-eight degrees to mimic its natural tropical home.
Position it in a shady spot of your aquarium to prevent algae from smothering its delicate leaves.
Prune older damaged fronds near the base in spring to encourage fresh green underwater growth.
Give it a boost by placing it near your filter outlet where the strong water flow mimics a stream.

items.name: Bolbitis quoyana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical fern in a warm, humid bathroom terrarium to mimic its native rainforest habitat.
Anchor its creeping rhizome onto damp lava rock or driftwood rather than burying it in heavy soil.

Keep winter indoor temperatures above fifteen Celsius and shield the fronds from cold window draughts.
Snip off any decaying lower fronds in spring using sterilized shears to encourage fresh green growth.

items.name: Bombycilaena
items.growersTips:
Sow Bombycilaena erecta seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect them from late UK frosts.
Plant this cotton-wool-like annual in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter wet rot.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, as this dry-loving plant hates soggy British soil.
Grow it alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to match its love for sun and poor, alkaline earth.
Collect the woolly seed heads in late autumn to sow next spring, as it rarely self-seeds in UK wet.

items.name: Bommeria
items.growersTips:
Plant Bommeria in free-draining, gritty soil under a sheltered UK wall to protect from winter wet.
Water sparingly in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty compost to dry out between drinks.
Sift leaf mould and sharp sand into your planting hole to mimic its natural rocky crevice habitat.
Bring potted specimens into a cold greenhouse by October to shield them from hard British frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the delicate, emerging spring fronds.

items.name: Bommeria elegans
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican fern indoors before the first frost, as it cannot survive a wet UK winter.
Plant it in a shallow pot with plenty of grit and perlite to ensure the roots never sit in soggy soil.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, mimicking its natural dry-season rest period.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light, like a east-facing windowsill, to avoid leaf scorch.
Group it with potted maidenhair ferns to help boost the local humidity without overwatering the soil.

items.name: Bonatea
items.growersTips:
Bring these African orchids indoors by October to protect them from the chilly, wet UK winter frost.
Plant tubers just below the soil surface in a very free-draining bark, perlite and loam compost mix.
Water them weekly during active summer growth but keep the soil almost bone dry throughout winter.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping your orchids in warm, dry indoor rooms.
Place your pots on a bright east-facing windowsill to get gentle morning sun without scorching them.

items.name: Bongardia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Bongardia tubers five inches deep in autumn using gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Grow this tuberous perennial in a greenhouse or cold frame to protect its foliage from frost damage.
Water your Bongardia only when it is actively growing in spring, then keep it bone dry all summer.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging fresh shoots.

items.name: Boraginoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant green alkanet in deep shade under deciduous trees where its taproot can break up heavy UK clay.
Sow borage seeds exactly two centimetres deep in April once the damp British spring soil warms up.
Cut pulmonaria back to the ground in July right after flowering to stop powdery mildew in its tracks.
Water comfrey deeply once a week during dry spells to keep those nutrient-rich leaves lush for mulch.
Grow wood forget-me-not alongside tulips to create a beautiful blue carpet that masks dying bulb foliage.

items.name: Borago
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in spring at 1.5cm depth in free-draining soil to avoid taproot transplant shock.
Position in full sun to maximise nectar production for UK bumblebees and encourage self-seeding.
Cut back hard after the first summer flowering to stimulate a second flush of fresh edible leaves.
Plant alongside strawberries to improve fruit set and deter common UK pests like tomato hornworm.
Grow the white-flowered Alba cultivar in damp UK summers as it resists powdery mildew better.

items.name: Borago officinalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors from April to June at a depth of one centimetre to avoid root damage.
Grow borage next to strawberries in UK clay soil to improve fruit yield and attract pollinators.
Water young plants weekly until established, then only during dry British summer spells.
Cut the plant back by half in July to encourage a second flush of fresh leaves and edible flowers.
Deadhead spent blooms promptly to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your vegetable beds.

items.name: Borago pygmaea

Plant this trailing borage in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Tuck it into a sunny rockery or raised bed where its delicate pale blue bells can cascade freely.
Cut back the faded stems in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of foliage before winter sets in.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp UK April mornings.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to ensure you have backup plants for hard frosts.

items.name: Borrichia
items.growersTips:
Try growing sea marigolds in containers so you can easily move them indoors before winter frosts.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in a very free-draining, sand-heavy compost mix.
Water them deeply once a week, letting the soil dry out completely between sessions to mimic dunes.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots during wet UK springs, using beer traps to protect them.

items.name: Boucerosia
items.growersTips:
Bring your Boucerosia indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from wet UK winter rot.
Plant them in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit for perfect drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep them completely dry from November through to March.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum possible winter light in the UK.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem joints, and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Bourreria
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Bourreria indoors to a bright conservatory before the first autumn frost hits.
Plant your strongback shrub in free-draining sandy loam mixed with plenty of grit to avoid wet feet.
Water thoroughly only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy UK winter soil.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites when overwintering your plant in indoor spaces.

items.name: Bourreria succulenta
items.growersTips:
Bring this Caribbean native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Grow it in a container with fifty percent perlite to ensure the sharp drainage it absolutely needs.
Water it only when the top two inches of compost are dry, as it hates soggy British winters.
Place it in your brightest south-facing conservatory or windowsill to mimic its native sunshine.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to keep its bushy shrub shape manageable.

items.name: Boykinia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive humus-rich soil in dappled shade to mimic native UK woodland edges.

Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Combine with ferns and hostas in damp shady borders for contrasting foliage textures.

items.name: Boykinia aconitifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil damp but avoid waterlogged conditions.

Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Boykinia major

Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Boykinia occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil in a sheltered, fully shaded border.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp, mimicking its native creek beds.

Cut back the faded flower stems and dead foliage to the ground in late autumn to prevent crown rot.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the emerging tender bronze foliage.

items.name: Boykinia richardsonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil in partial shade to mimic its native stream banks.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Plant alongside Astilbe or hostas in a bog garden to complement its white summer flower spikes.

items.name: Boykinia rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native damp woodland ravine habitat.
Sow seeds in pots in a cold frame during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the large rounded leaves from scorching.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside Astilbe or Hostas in bog gardens where soil never dries out completely.

items.name: Brachybotrys paridiformis
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland gem in deep shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native forest canopy.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your soil to recreate the rich humus it loves.

Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when the delicate new shoots first emerge from the ground.

items.name: Brachycorythis
items.growersTips:
Plant these terrestrial orchids in a mix of fine bark, perlite, and loam to mimic woodland soil.
Keep them damp but never soggy during summer, then cut back watering completely as they go dormant.
Grow them in pots so you can bring them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when the delicate new shoots first emerge from the soil.
Position your pots in bright, filtered light rather than direct, harsh UK afternoon sunshine.

items.name: Brachystegia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 1.5cm using a heated propagator to mimic tropical warmth.
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing border with grit added for sharp drainage.

Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp May nights.
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving ornamental grasses to complement this legume's natural soil chemistry.

items.name: Brachystegia bakeriana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twenty degrees
Grow in free-draining sandy loam amended with grit to mimic dry African soils and prevent root rot
Water sparingly once a week during summer, allowing the compost to dry out completely between sessions

Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp spring nights

items.name: Brachystegia boehmii

items.name: Brachystegia glaucescens

items.name: Brachystegia laurentii

items.name: Brachystegia spiciformis

items.name: Brachystele

Protect the delicate emerging shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in spring.
Position your pots in bright, indirect light to replicate the dappled shade of their native home.

items.name: Brachystelma

Plant your tuber shallowly with the top third exposed above a very gritty, free-draining soil mix.

items.name: Brachystephanus
items.growersTips:
Bring this African forest native indoors by October to shield its tender roots from UK frosts.

items.name: Brachystephanus kupeensis
