Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month from April through to September.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites, misting the leaves regularly to keep humidity high.

items.name: Brandzeia
items.growersTips:
Sow your Brandzeia seeds indoors in late March to beat the chilly UK spring and get a head start.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into your heavy clay soil to give this annual the drainage it loves.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering gently at the base to prevent any midsummer root rot.
Watch out for slugs on tender young Brandzeia shoots during those damp British May mornings.
Snip off the fading flowers regularly through July and August to keep new blooms coming.

items.name: Brassavola cucullata
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid mounted on cork bark or in very free-draining bark chips to prevent root rot.
Keep it on a warm, south-facing windowsill to get the high light it needs to trigger flowering.
Water heavily during summer growth, then let it dry out completely between waterings in winter.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of twelve degrees Celsius to keep this tropical beauty happy.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the distinctive, needle-like leaves during dry winter months.

items.name: Brassavola flagellaris
items.growersTips:
Mount this orchid on cork bark with a little moss to let its roots dry out rapidly in UK humidity.
Hang it in your brightest south-facing window or warm conservatory to mimic Brazilian sunshine.
Water copiously in summer but let it dry completely before winter when you must keep it nearly dry.
Maintain a minimum indoor winter temperature of twelve Celsius to keep this tropical beauty happy.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices of those distinctive whip-like terete leaves.

items.name: Brassavola martiana
items.growersTips:
Grow this Brazilian orchid mounted on cork bark to let its roots dry out fast in damp UK winters.
Hang it in your brightest south-facing window or heated conservatory to mimic its native sunshine.
Water heavily in summer then let it dry completely before watering again to prevent root rot.
Keep your winter thermostat above twelve degrees Celsius to protect this orchid from cold shocks.
Mist the roots daily during hot summer spells to keep humidity high without soaking the compost.

items.name: Brassavola nodosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a chunky bark mix or mounted on cork so the roots dry out rapidly after watering.
Hang it in your brightest south-facing window to mimic its native sun, but shield from midday burn.
Let the potting medium dry out completely between waterings, especially during dull UK winters.
Keep your home above twelve degrees Celsius at night, as this tropical beauty hates the British cold.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser every second watering in summer, then halt feeding in winter.

items.name: Brassavola subulifolia
items.growersTips:
Mount this orchid on cork bark with moss to mimic its wild home and prevent wet UK winter root rot.
Hang your orchid in a south-facing window to give it the intense bright light it needs to flower.
Only water when the potting bark is bone dry, then drench it thoroughly with tepid rainwater.
Keep it indoors year-round as it hates UK cold and needs a minimum night temperature of fifteen.
Mist the aerial roots daily in summer to boost humidity when your indoor heating dries the air.

items.name: Brassavola tuberculata
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid on a cork mount or in very free-draining bark to survive damp UK winters.
Give it a bright south-facing windowsill but shade it from scorching midsummer midday sun.
Water copiously in summer when active, then let it dry out completely before watering again.
Keep temperatures above twelve Celsius in winter by moving it away from drafty windowpanes.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the papery sheaths at the base of the slender pseudobulbs.

items.name: Brassavola venosa
items.growersTips:
Grow your Brassavola venosa in a very chunky bark mix or on a cork mount so the roots dry out fast.
Keep this orchid on a warm south windowsill but shade it from scorching midsummer midday sun.
Water weekly in summer letting it dry fully between times, then cut back drastically in winter.
Watch out for scale insects hiding in the papery sheaths at the base of the slender pseudobulbs.
Position it near a fan or open window because this orchid absolutely loves active fresh air flow.

items.name: Braunsia
items.growersTips:
Bring your braunsia indoors to a sunny windowsill by october to protect it from wet winter frosts
Grow this succulent in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat free compost
Water your braunsia only when the soil is bone dry and keep it completely dry throughout winter
Snip leggy stems in late spring using sharp scissors to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol

items.name: Braunsia apiculata
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African beauty in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes No 1 and half grit.
Keep it on a sunny indoor windowsill year-round, as our wet UK winters will quickly rot its roots.
Water only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle slightly, then drench it and let it dry fully.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints, especially during dry indoor winter heat.
Propagate in late spring by snipping stem cuttings, letting them dry for a week, then potting up.

items.name: Bravaisia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Bravaisia indoors to a bright, frost-free conservatory before the first autumn frost.
Water your Bravaisia deeply once a week in summer, letting the top two inches of soil dry out first.
Repot in spring using a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part grit for excellent drainage.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in late spring to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Feed your Bravaisia with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer every fortnight from May to September.

items.name: Brickellia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres to combat the cool wet British spring.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit-amended soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and increase the flower count.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or physical barriers.

items.name: Brighamia insignis
items.growersTips:
Bring your vulcan palm inside before October as it cannot survive UK winter temperatures below ten degrees.
Plant in a gritty cactus mix to ensure fast drainage and prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, then soak it and let the excess drain away.
Check the crown regularly for red spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor UK heating.
Keep it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic its native Hawaiian sunshine.

items.name: Brighamia rockii
items.growersTips:
Keep this Hawaiian gem indoors or in a heated conservatory as it cannot survive UK winter frosts.
Plant in a very gritty, fast-draining cactus mix to prevent its sensitive roots from rotting.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, then give it a good soak and let it drain fully.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air and mist the leaves regularly to deter them.
Place it on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum amount of daily British sunshine.

items.name: Brillantaisia
items.growersTips:
Bring your giant salvia indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Water deeply twice a week in summer, keeping the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge to prevent wilt.
Take softwood cuttings in July as backup plants in case the parent struggles through a cold winter.
Prune back the leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and more blue flowers.
Plant them alongside cannas or hostas in partial shade to create a lush, sheltered jungle look.

items.name: Brimeura
items.growersTips:
Plant your Brimeura bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in well-drained, gritty soil.
These Mediterranean beauties love a sunny UK rock garden or a spot under deciduous garden shrubs.
Keep the soil moist during their spring growing season but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they absolutely love the tender new foliage.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.

items.name: Brimeura amethystina
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in well-drained, gritty soil.
Grow them under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland home and keep them cool in summer.
Keep the soil moist during their spring growing phase but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they love to munch on the fresh new shoots.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in June so the bulb can store up energy.

items.name: Brocchinia micrantha
items.growersTips:
Bring this Venezuelan bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a very loose orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild cliffside home.
Keep the central leafy urn filled with rainwater but let the potting soil dry out between waterings.
Position your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to mimic high-altitude sun.
Watch out for scale insects in the leaf crevices and wipe them away with a damp cloth in spring.

items.name: Brocchinia reducta
items.growersTips:
Grow this carnivorous bromeliad in a bright conservatory or south windowsill to mimic Venezuelan sun.
Water only with rainwater or distilled water, keeping the central tubular pitcher filled at all times.
Use a very loose, acidic mix of two parts perlite to one part peat moss to prevent root rot in the UK.
Keep winter temperatures strictly above ten degrees Celsius, as this tropical plant cannot take frost.
Do not fertilise the soil; the plant gets all its nutrients from insects trapped in its yellow urn.

items.name: Brocchinia tatei
items.growersTips:
Grow this Venezuelan native in a warm conservatory, as it will not survive a chilly UK winter.
Plant it in a very loose, acidic orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to mimic its wild home.
Keep the central leaf urn filled with rainwater, but let the potting compost dry out between waterings.
Position your pot in the brightest spot possible, ideally a south-facing windowsill or greenhouse.
Watch out for scale insects and mealybugs hiding deep inside the leaf rosettes during dry summers.

items.name: Brodiaea
items.growersTips:
Plant Brodiaea bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight to ten centimetres in very free-draining soil.
Keep them damp during spring growth but stop watering completely once the foliage dies back in summer.
Grow them in your warmest, most south-facing border to mimic their native sunny Californian climate.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers.
Leave the dead foliage alone until it is completely straw-like to feed next year's blooms.

items.name: Brodiaea appendiculata
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in very gritty, free-draining garden soil.
Keep them damp during their spring growth but let the soil dry out completely once they go dormant.
Grow them in your sunniest south-facing spot or a warm gravel garden to mimic their native climate.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or pet-safe wool pellets.
Overwinter them in pots of gritty compost under a cold frame to shield them from wet UK winters.

items.name: Brodiaea californica
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs eight centimetres deep in autumn in a sharply draining, gritty south-facing bed.
Water them only during their spring growth, then keep them completely dry once summer dormancy hits.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Leave the faded foliage alone until it goes completely brown and papery in late summer before clearing.
Grow them in pots of gritty compost if your UK soil is heavy clay, so you can move them out of winter rain.

items.name: Brodiaea coronaria
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at least eight centimetres deep in very gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep them damp during spring growth but stop watering completely once the foliage dies back in summer.
Grow them in your sunniest south-facing border or a terracotta pot to mimic their dry US home.
Watch out for slugs eating the tender new shoots in damp UK springs by using organic beer traps.
Let the leaves die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.

items.name: Brodiaea elegans
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in a warm, south-facing border.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure sharp drainage and prevent winter bulb rot.
Leave them completely dry during their summer dormancy period after the foliage dies back.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using your preferred barrier method.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme to support the slender stems and show off the blue flowers.

items.name: Brodiaea filifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in very gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep them damp during spring growth but stop watering entirely once the foliage dies back in summer.
Grow them in pots so you can move them into a cold greenhouse to protect them from wet UK winters.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme to support their thin stems and keep weeds from choking them.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love eating the tender new shoots.

items.name: Brodiaea jolonensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in very sharply draining, gritty soil.
Keep them damp during their spring growth but let them bake completely dry once summer dormancy hits.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them under glass to protect them from wet UK winter rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the tender new shoots as they emerge in spring.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme to support the weak stems and mimic their native grassland.

items.name: Brodiaea kinkiensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs five inches deep in autumn using a gritty mix to survive wet UK winter rot.
Keep them bone dry in summer after the leaves die back to mimic their native dry California heat.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a cold frame to shelter from heavy winter rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love to devour the emerging shoots.
Pair them with low-growing thymes that won't crowd them out or block their need for full UK sun.

items.name: Brodiaea minor
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in your sunniest, sharpest-draining spot.
Mix plenty of grit into heavy UK clay soil to keep the bulbs dry and prevent winter rot.
Avoid watering them at all during their summer dormant phase after the foliage naturally dies back.
Grow them alongside low-growing sedums or thyme to support their thin stems and hide yellowing leaves.
Protect the tender spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers.

items.name: Brodiaea pallida
items.growersTips:
Plant these rare bulbs five inches deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent rot.
Keep them damp during spring growth but stop watering entirely once the foliage dies back in summer.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a cold greenhouse to survive wet UK winters.
Position them in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native hot Californian foothills.
Watch out for slugs eating the emerging spring shoots and protect them with pet-safe organic grit.

items.name: Brodiaea terrestris
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in a very sunny, south-facing spot.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because these California natives will rot in wet UK winter clay.
Keep them damp while they grow in spring, but stop watering completely once the leaves die back.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a greenhouse to dry out during wet UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love eating the tender new shoots.

items.name: Brodiaeoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at three times their depth in free-draining soil to survive UK winters.
Water them only during their spring growth, then keep them completely dry once the summer dormancy hits.
Protect new spring shoots from slugs and snails using grit barriers or beer traps in damp UK weather.
Plant them alongside shallow-rooted alpines or thyme to help soak up excess winter wet from the soil.
Leave the faded foliage alone until it turns completely yellow and papery to feed next year's blooms.

items.name: Bromelia antiacantha
items.growersTips:
Bring this spiky bromeliad indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a super-gritty, acidic ericaceous mix with orchid bark to mimic its native sandy soil.
Water only into the central rosette during summer, but keep this cup dry in winter to prevent rot.
Give it your brightest south-facing windowsill or conservatory spot to coax out those red bracts.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when pruning dead outer leaves because those curved spines really bite.

items.name: Bromelia balansae
items.growersTips:
Bring this spiky Brazilian indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a shallow pot using free-draining orchid bark mixed with grit to mimic its wild home.
Water only the central leaf cup during summer, keeping the surrounding soil barely damp to the touch.
Watch out for scale insects hiding under the sharp leaves and wipe them off with soapy water.
Position your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to coax out that red flush.

items.name: Bromelia binotii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Brazilian indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a shallow, extremely free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and peat-free compost.
Water only into the central rosette cup using tepid rainwater, keeping the soil barely damp.
Position it in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to mimic its native tropical sun.
Feed your plant with a highly diluted orchid mist sprayed onto the leaves once a month in summer.

items.name: Bromelia chrysantha
items.growersTips:
Bring this spiky bromeliad indoors by October as it cannot survive wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a shallow, gritty orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to ensure rapid drainage.
Water only into the central rosette during summer, keeping the surrounding soil barely damp.
Position your pot in your brightest south-facing conservatory to mimic its native hot sun.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding deep in the leaf crevices and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Bromelia hieronymi
items.growersTips:
Bring this Argentine native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant in a very gritty, free-draining peat-free acidic mix to mimic its dry woodland habitat.
Water into the central rosette during summer, but keep the soil almost bone dry throughout winter.
Use thick leather gloves when pruning dead leaves because those vicious marginal spines really bite.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to get the high light levels needed for flowering.

items.name: Bromelia humilis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender bromeliad in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water into the central leafy rosette rather than the soil, keeping it filled with rainwater.
Plant in a very free-draining mix of orchid bark and peat-free compost to prevent winter root rot.
Keep it on a bright south-facing windowsill during UK winters to mimic its sunny native habitat.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints and dab them off with organic neem oil.

items.name: Bromelia karatas
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical beauty in a pot so you can bring it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Plant it in a free-draining mix of orchid bark and peat-free compost to prevent UK winter root rot.
Water only into the central rosette during summer, keeping it dry in winter to stop fungal decay.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf axils, wiping them away with a damp cloth or spirit.
Give it your brightest windowsill or a heated conservatory to mimic its native sunny climate.

items.name: Bromelia laciniosa
items.growersTips:
Bring your Macambira indoors by October to protect this tender Brazilian native from UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a shallow, gritty orchid mix with perlite rather than heavy UK garden soil to prevent rot.
Water directly into the central rosette during summer, but keep it bone dry throughout damp winters.
Position it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic the bright Caatinga sun it loves.
Propagate by slicing off the offsets with a clean knife once they reach a third of the parent size.

items.name: Bromelia pinguin
items.growersTips:
Bring your pinguin indoors by October because UK frosts will quickly turn this tropical wild pine mush.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining orchid and peat-free compost mix to stop winter root rot.
Water only into the central leaf cup during summer, keeping the soil barely damp to the touch.
Watch out for scale insects hiding in the sharp leaf crevices and wipe them off with soapy water.
Wear thick leather gauntlets when pruning dead leaves because those curved spines will shred skin.

items.name: Bromelia serra
items.growersTips:
Bring this Argentine native indoors by October to protect its roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a very shallow, gritty orchid bark mix to mimic its natural dry woodland soil.
Water only into the central rosette during summer, keeping the surrounding soil barely damp.
Wear thick leather gloves when pruning because the hooked leaf spines will easily tear your skin.
Position it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to coax out its dramatic red flowering spike.

items.name: Bromelia sylvicola
items.growersTips:
Bring your Bromelia sylvicola indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Keep the central leaf cup filled with rainwater, flushing it weekly to prevent stagnant buildup.
Plant in a very gritty, peat-free orchid bark mix to mimic its natural free-draining woodland home.
Place it in a bright conservatory or on a south-facing windowsill, shaded from harsh midday sun.
Propagate by slicing off the offsets or pups in spring once they reach a third of the parent size.

items.name: Bromelia unaensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian native indoors by October to shield it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a super-chunky, free-draining orchid bark mix to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Water directly into the central rosette cup using tepid rainwater rather than hard UK tap water.
Keep it on a bright, south-facing windowsill to mimic the tropical sun it needs to flower.
Wipe the tough, spiky leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and check for mealybugs.

items.name: Brongniartieae
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in March on a warm windowsill to beat the chilly UK spring temperatures.
Plant them out in May after the last frost, spacing them twenty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water them deeply at the base once a week rather than giving them daily light sprinkles to rot roots.
Sow them alongside calendula to keep aphids away and attract helpful pollinators to your plot.
Snip off the fading flower heads regularly through July and August to keep new blooms coming.

items.name: Broussaisia arguta
items.growersTips:
Grow in a sheltered woodland border with acidic, humus-rich soil to prevent leaf yellowing.
Provide winter protection with a thick mulch layer to shield roots from severe UK frosts.
Water weekly with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the moisture-loving roots damp.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes, removing only dead or damaged stems.
Plant alongside shade-loving ferns and hostas which thrive in the same damp, dappled light.

items.name: Brownanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your Brownanthus indoors by October to protect this tender South African succulent from UK frost.
Plant them in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part compost for sharp drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely during winter.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum winter sunlight it craves.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the jointed stems and dab them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.

items.name: Brownea
items.growersTips:
Grow Brownea grandiceps in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept above fifteen degrees Celsius.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters in a heated propagator with bottom heat.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the acidic, peat-free loam-based compost consistently moist.
Mist the foliage daily with soft water to maintain the high humidity this tropical plant requires.
Feed fortnightly in spring and summer using a high-potassium liquid fertiliser at half strength.

items.name: Brownea coccinea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept above fifteen Celsius.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Plant in a large pot using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to maintain shape and remove dead wood.
Mist the foliage daily during dry summer months to simulate the high humidity of its native jungle.

items.name: Brownea grandiceps
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept strictly above fifteen Celsius.
Plant in a large pot with acidic, loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for fast drainage.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent rot.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent by placing the pot on a tray of wet clay pebbles.
Prune lightly only in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove dead wood.

items.name: Brownea leucantha
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse kept strictly above fifteen Celsius.
Plant in a large pot with acidic, loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for fast drainage.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent by placing the pot on a tray of wet clay leca pebbles.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to shape and remove dead wood safely.

items.name: Brownea macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a heated conservatory or greenhouse with minimum winter temperatures of 15C.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Plant in a large pot using a peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Mist the foliage daily or use a humidifier to maintain the high humidity this rainforest plant needs.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer to control size and remove dead wood.

items.name: Brownleea
items.growersTips:
Grow Brownleea orchids in a mix of fine bark and perlite to copy their wild African soil.
Keep these tuberous perennials damp in summer but let them dry out during their winter dormancy.
Protect your potted Brownleea from UK winter frosts by moving them into a cool, bright greenhouse.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the tender new shoots that emerge in late spring.
Repot your plants in early spring just as new growth starts, being very gentle with the tubers.

items.name: Brownleeinae
items.growersTips:
Tuck these African terrestrial orchids into a moist, peat-free acidic compost with plenty of grit.
Keep them damp but never soggy during summer, then cut back on watering once the foliage dies down.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when the delicate new shoots first emerge from the soil.
Give them bright, filtered light rather than direct UK sun to prevent their leaves from scorching.

items.name: Brunnera
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained soil in full shade to prevent the delicate leaves from scorching.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or well-rotted manure to retain crucial woodland moisture.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of healthy new foliage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or spring to propagate and maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Brunnera macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial shade to prevent the delicate leaves from scorching.
Water young plants regularly in summer to establish a deep root system in damp UK woodland borders.
Cut back faded flower stems in summer to encourage a fresh flush of attractive heart-shaped foliage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp weather.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or spring to propagate and maintain vigorous growth.

items.name: Brunoniella
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Aussie native in pots so you can bring it inside before the first UK frost hits.
Plant your blue-bells in free-draining, grit-amended loam to prevent winter root rot in wet soil.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, keeping it drier in winter.
Position your pots in a sheltered, south-facing spot to mimic its sunny native woodland edge.
Prune back the leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage a bushier shape and more flowers.

items.name: Brunoniella australis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant your blue trumpet in a free-draining peat-free grit mix to prevent winter root rot outdoors.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out, as this plant hates soggy British clay.
Position your pot in a south-facing conservatory to mimic the bright Australian sun it craves.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring when the plant active growth phase begins.

items.name: Brya
items.growersTips:
Sow Brya seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect their delicate taproots.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering only when the top two centimetres feel dry.
Grow Brya in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic the warmth of their native tropical climate.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimetres to encourage a bushier habit.
Plant alongside French marigolds to help deter the aphids that love targeting young Brya stems.

items.name: Bryobium
items.growersTips:
Bring your Bryobium orchid indoors before October frosts as they cannot survive a UK winter outside.
Grow them in a chunky bark and perlite mix rather than soil to prevent their delicate roots rotting.
Water thoroughly once a week in summer, but let the potting compost dry out completely between sessions.
Position your potted Bryobium on a bright east-facing windowsill to avoid scorching the small leaves.
Feed with a diluted orchid fertilizer every third watering during the active spring growing season.

items.name: Bucephalandra
items.growersTips:
Glue the rhizome to a rock or bogwood instead of burying it in soil, otherwise it will rot and die.
Keep your indoor tank water between twenty and twenty-six degrees to mimic their tropical home.
Use soft tap water or rainwater to prevent unsightly calcium deposits on their beautiful leaves.
Trim older leaves near the base in spring to encourage fresh colorful growth and prevent algae.
Pair them with slow-growing Anubias plants which share their low-light and liquid fertilizer needs.

items.name: Bufonia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained gritty soil to mimic the cold winter stratification they need.
Grow in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to prevent winter wet from rotting the delicate roots.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty substrate to dry out completely between feeds.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK spring weather.
Sow alongside companion plants like wild thyme or sedums that share its love for poor, alkaline soil.

items.name: Buglossoides
items.growersTips:
Try planting Buglossoides purpurocaerulea in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodlands.
Tuck the crown just level with the soil surface when planting in autumn so it settles before winter.
Give it a hard chop right down to the ground in late summer once those deep blue flowers fade away.
Mix plenty of grit into heavy UK clay to keep the roots dry and rot-free during wet winter months.
Propagate your clumps by taking root cuttings in early spring just as the soil begins to warm up.

items.name: Buglossoides arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn just below the soil surface to let UK winter frosts trigger spring germination.
Keep soil on the dry, sandy side and avoid rich fertilisers to prevent this wildflower flopping.
Grow it alongside red campion and wild carrot to create a stunning, authentic UK meadow display.
Watch out for flea beetles in early summer, which love to chew tiny holes in the hairy foliage.
Cut the stems back to the ground in late summer after seeding to keep your patch neat and tidy.

items.name: Buglossoides purpurocaerulea
items.growersTips:
Plant this purple gromwell in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its native UK woodland.
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted compost into heavy clay soil to improve drainage before planting.
Peg down the long, arching non-flowering stems in late summer to easily propagate new root systems.
Cut back the sprawling stems hard in autumn to keep this vigorous spreader from overtaking neighbours.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers until their deep, drought-tolerant roots establish.

items.name: Bulbophyllinae
items.growersTips:
Grow in shallow pans of open bark and sphagnum moss to match their shallow-rooting creeping habit.
Keep winter temperatures above twelve Celsius and water weekly to prevent pseudobulbs from shrivelling.
Position under fleece or shade cloth in summer to protect delicate leaves from direct UK sunlight.
Water with rainwater only to prevent salt build-up on the sensitive, thread-like roots of species.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight crevices between pseudobulbs and treat with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Burkea
items.growersTips:
Sow Burkea seeds indoors in April at a depth of 1cm using a heated propagator to mimic warm climates
Transplant seedlings outdoors in June into free-draining sandy loam after the last frost has passed
Water sparingly at the base only when the top 5cm of soil is dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or against a warm wall to maximise limited UK heat
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps as damp UK spring weather makes them highly vulnerable

items.name: Burkea africana
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early April using a heated propagator to mimic its native warm climate.
Plant your seedlings out in late May once frost has passed, choosing the sunniest spot in your garden.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this dry-land plant needs.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as it hates having soggy roots in wet UK summers.
Protect your young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps, as they love the tender new growth.

items.name: Burmeistera
items.growersTips:
Grow this Andean native in a conservatory or heated greenhouse to protect it from UK winter frosts.
Water with rainwater to keep the ericaceous, peat-free compost mix damp but never waterlogged.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser fortnightly from April to September to boost those quirky blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and mist the foliage regularly to keep the humidity high.
Repot in spring using a mix of bark, perlite and loam to mimic its natural cloud forest home.

items.name: Burnettia
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a peat-free, acidic compost mix that mimics its native boggy heathlands.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged by using rainwater instead of tap water.
Place your pot in a cool greenhouse or cold frame to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Do not prune this delicate perennial; just gently remove any dead leaves at the start of spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to munch on the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Buxus
items.growersTips:
Always plant your box so the rootball sits level with the soil, never bury the stem.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Prune your boxwood on a dry, overcast day in late May to prevent leaf scorch and blight.
Watch out for box moth caterpillars from April to October and handpick them off immediately.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit and compost into heavy UK clay to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Buxus balearica
items.growersTips:
Plant your Balearic box in a sheltered spot to protect it from harsh, drying UK winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the well-drained soil dry out between cuts.
Prune in late spring after the frost risk passes to shape it and avoid winter dieback on new shoots.
Check the dense foliage regularly for box moth caterpillars, which are becoming common in the UK.
Grow it in alkaline to neutral soil, adding a handful of grit to the planting hole to aid drainage.

items.name: Buxus citrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Caribbean native in a pot so you can move it indoors before the first UK frost hits.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry to touch.
Grow it in a peat-free, loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent drainage.
Position your pot in a bright, warm spot with indirect light, avoiding harsh afternoon summer sun.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape your shrub and encourage bushier, healthier new growth.

items.name: Buxus colchica
items.growersTips:
Plant your Colchic box in moist, well-drained soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted leaf mould.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, focusing on the roots to keep the foliage dry.
Prune your shrubs in late May or June, choosing a dry, cloudy day to prevent leaf scorch.
Watch out for box moth caterpillars and treat immediately with biological nematodes in spring.
Mulch annually with organic compost to keep roots cool and mimic its native woodland habitat.

items.name: Buxus harlandii
items.growersTips:
Plant this boxwood in a sheltered UK spot to protect its delicate narrow leaves from cold winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers, letting the soil dry out slightly between times.
Prune your shrub in late spring after the frosts to maintain its compact shape and encourage growth.
Check regularly for box moth caterpillars, as their larvae love the dense foliage of this species.
Mix plenty of grit and organic matter into heavy UK clay soils to ensure excellent winter drainage.

items.name: Buxus hildebrandtii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Somali boxwood in your sunniest, sheltered UK spot to protect it from harsh winter frosts.
Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the sharp-draining soil to dry out fully between soakings.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost risk passes, avoiding wet days to prevent box blight.
Mix plenty of grit and horticultural lime into your soil to keep it alkaline and free-draining.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a cold greenhouse during freezing winters.

items.name: Buxus macowanii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cape boxwood in a warm, sheltered microclimate to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but keep the soil much drier throughout winter.
Prune your shrub in late spring after the frost risk passes to encourage dense, bushy new growth.
Mix plenty of grit and leaf mould into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.
Watch out for box blight and caterpillars, keeping the foliage dry by watering only at the base.

items.name: Buxus microphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this boxwood in well-drained soil with a handful of grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving it daily light sprinkles.
Prune your shrubs in late May or June after the frost risk passes to avoid damaging new growth.
Watch out for box moth caterpillars from April to October and handpick them off immediately.
Mulch with garden compost in spring but keep it clear of the main stems to prevent rot.

items.name: Buxus natalensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African native in a pot so you can move it indoors to protect it from UK winter frosts.
Water your plant deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of soil dry out completely.
Plant it in a mix of peat-free compost, grit, and John Innes No 3 to ensure the sharp drainage it needs.
Prune your shrub in late spring after the frost risk passes to shape it and encourage bushy growth.
Check the glossy leaves regularly for scale insects, which love the sheltered microclimate of UK patios.

items.name: Buxus sempervirens
items.growersTips:
Plant box in well-drained soil with a handful of grit to prevent waterlogging in wet UK winters.
Trim Buxus on a dry, overcast day in late May or June to prevent sun scorch on newly cut leaves.
Check weekly from April to October for green box moth caterpillars and web-like silk in the foliage.
Water deeply at the base rather than overhead to keep leaves dry and reduce the risk of box blight.
Grow dwarf Suffolk Blue or Faulkner cultivars for better natural resistance to common UK diseases.

items.name: Buxus sinica
items.growersTips:
Plant this boxwood at the exact same depth as its nursery pot to prevent stem rot in damp UK soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry English summers rather than giving it frequent light sprinkles.
Keep a sharp eye out for box moth caterpillars from April to October and handpick them off immediately.
Prune your shrubs on a dry, overcast day in late May to avoid leaf scorch and prevent fungal spores.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into heavy UK clay to ensure the roots never sit in waterlogged soil.

items.name: Buxus vahlii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Caribbean boxwood in a deep pot to bring indoors before the first UK winter frost.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Watch out for box blight and caterpillars by checking the dense, leathery leaves every week.
Prune your shrub gently in late spring after the threat of frost has completely passed for the year.
Mix plenty of grit and organic matter into your peat-free compost to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Caccinia
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial in sharply draining gravelly soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position your Caccinia in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic its native hot, dry steppes.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural winter chill can break their dormancy.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails who love the juicy, borage-like leaves.

items.name: Caesalpinia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two centimetres after soaking them in warm water for a day.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure fast drainage.
Water young plants deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish deep roots.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach fifteen centimetres high to encourage bushy growth.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite if growing under glass or in a very sheltered urban courtyard.

items.name: Caesalpinia coriaria
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Caribbean shrub in a pot of gritty loam to move indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Water sparingly in winter but drench thoroughly once soil dries completely during summer active growth.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape the canopy and remove winter-damaged or crossing stems.
Blend thirty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to ensure the rapid drainage it needs.
Position in your hottest south-facing suntrap or unheated greenhouse to mimic its native warmth.

items.name: Caesalpinia mexicana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 1cm after soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours
Grow in pots of free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to allow winter greenhouse shelter
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out to prevent root rot in wet UKs
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot against a brick wall to maximise summer heat accumulation
Prune lightly in late spring to remove frost-damaged stems and maintain a compact container shape

items.name: Caesalpinia pulcherrima
items.growersTips:
Grow in containers using free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to move indoors for winter
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre after soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool UK summers
Place pots in the hottest south-facing spot or greenhouse to mimic the heat of its native climate
Prune back lightly in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flowers on the new wood

items.name: Caesalpinieae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to avoid disturbing their sensitive taproots.
Nick the hard seed coats with a file and soak them overnight before sowing to speed up germination.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their native warmth.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Add plenty of grit to your compost when planting out because these annuals hate cold, soggy clay.

items.name: Calacanthus
items.growersTips:
Give this rare Indian beauty a warm, sheltered spot in a heated UK greenhouse to mimic its home.
Water moderately during the summer active growth phase, but keep the soil almost dry in winter.
Plant in a very free-draining, peat-free loam compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the leaves to deter these pests.
Prune gently in early spring just as new growth starts, only to shape and remove dead stems.

items.name: Caladenia
items.growersTips:
Grow these delicate Aussie orchids in a gritty, free-draining mix of pumice and bark to avoid rot.
Keep them damp in winter but let them dry out completely once the leaves die back in summer.
Protect them from frost in a cold greenhouse or conservatory during chilly UK winters.
Repot your tubers in late summer just as they wake up, burying them about two centimeters deep.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Caladeniinae
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in late summer at a depth of twice their height in a highly gritty, free-draining mix.
Water sparingly in autumn to trigger growth, keeping the compost damp but never soggy over winter.
Keep pots in a cool, frost-free greenhouse or cold frame to protect from wet UK winter freezes.
Apply a very weak, low-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during the active winter growing phase.
Repot annually during the summer dormant period when the compost is completely dry to prevent rot.

items.name: Caladium
items.growersTips:
Start your tubers indoors in warm, moist peat-free compost during March to beat the cool UK spring.
Water only when the top inch of soil feels dry, using tepid rainwater to avoid shocking the roots.
Keep them in bright, indirect light away from draughty UK windows to prevent their leaves burning.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite by regularly misting the undersides of those lovely leaves.
Dig up tubers in October before the first frost, then store them in dry vermiculite over winter.

items.name: Caladium bicolor
items.growersTips:
Start your tubers indoors in warm propators by mid-March to beat the cool British spring weather.
Plant tubers knobbly side up about five centimetres deep in peat-free ericaceous compost.
Keep soil damp but never soggy, watering only with tepid rainwater to avoid shocking the roots.
Bring them inside before October night temperatures dip below twelve degrees to save them from rot.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping them in dry, heated indoor winter rooms.

items.name: Caladium lindenii
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical beauty cosy indoors at twenty degrees to survive chilly British drafts.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top inch of compost feels dry to prevent tuber rot.
Blend peat-free compost with plenty of perlite and orchid bark for the perfect airy root run.
Wipe the gorgeous white-veined leaves weekly with a damp cloth to stop spider mites in their tracks.
Cut back on watering in October to let the plant rest naturally in a warm cupboard for winter.

items.name: Caladium lindenii ‘Magnificum’
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical beauty in a warm, draft-free room above 18C to prevent it from dropping leaves.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top inch of compost dries, as cold tap water shocks it.
Plant in a peat-free mix with plenty of perlite and orchid bark to mimic its native jungle floor.
Mist the leaves daily or use a gravel tray to combat dry UK radiator heat and stop leaf crisping.
Wipe the gorgeous patterned foliage weekly with a damp cloth to clear dust and check for spider mites.

items.name: Calanthe
items.growersTips:
Plant hardy Calanthe discolor shallowly in humus-rich, well-drained soil, keeping the pseudobulb flush.
Water your Calanthe with rainwater to keep the soil damp in summer, but let it dry out in winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the tender emerging flower spikes.
Grow Calanthe alongside Hostas and Ferns in a sheltered, shady spot to mimic woodland conditions.
Protect evergreen Calanthe triplicata from harsh UK frosts by bringing it into a cool greenhouse.

items.name: Caleana
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Australian duck orchid in a cold greenhouse to protect it from harsh UK winter frost.
Use a very free-draining mix of fine bark, perlite, and peat-free compost to mimic its native soil.
Water with pure rainwater only, keeping the compost damp in summer but barely moist during winter.
Avoid adding any chemical fertilisers, as this orchid relies on delicate mycorrhizal fungi to live.
Watch out for glasshouse pests like spider mites and aphids, gently wiping them off with a damp cloth.

items.name: Calenduleae
items.growersTips:
Sow your seeds directly in April about one centimetre deep in a sunny patch of well-drained soil.
Water them only during dry spells once established, as too much dampness causes powdery mildew.
Snip off the faded flower heads weekly to keep new bright blooms popping up right until autumn.
Watch out for pesky aphids on the young shoots and simply wash them off with a gentle hose spray.
Plant them next to your tomatoes and potatoes to help deter those annoying whiteflies naturally.

items.name: California macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this native annual in autumn or early spring at a shallow depth of just two millimetres.
Sow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry grassland habitat and boost flowering.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Collect the corkscrew-like seed pods in late summer before they self-disperse across your borders.

items.name: Calla
items.growersTips:
Plant your bog arum rhizomes shallowly in muddy pond edges or boggy soil just below the water line.
Keep the soil permanently wet and muddy as this native UK wild bog plant cannot tolerate drying out.
Watch out for water snails and pond snails which love to munch on the lush emerging spring foliage.
Propagate your plants by dividing the creeping rootstocks in spring just as new growth starts.
Grow them alongside native marsh marigolds to create a beautiful and natural UK pond edge display.

items.name: Calla palustris
items.growersTips:
Grow this British native in shallow pond margins covered by no more than ten centimetres of water.
Plant the creeping rhizomes horizontally in aquatic baskets filled with heavy, unfertilised clay.
Watch out for water snails eating the young spring foliage and handpick them off on damp mornings.
Propagate by dividing the fleshy rhizomes in late spring once the water starts to warm up.
Position in full sun or partial shade to ensure those lovely white spathes develop fully in June.

items.name: Calliandra
items.growersTips:
Grow these tender beauties in pots so you can easily move them indoors before the first autumn frost.
Plant seeds just five millimetres deep in a heated propagator during March to get a head start.
Use a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the roots never sit in cold UK wet.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water to keep the soil damp but never soggy.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when you bring your potted plants indoors for winter.

items.name: Callianthemum
items.growersTips:
Plant these alpine beauties in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Keep them damp but never soggy during spring and summer by watering from the base, not the top.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the delicate new buttercup-like leaves in spring.
Tuck them into a raised scree bed or alpine trough where they get cool morning sun but midday shade.
Propagate your clumps by careful division immediately after they finish flowering in early summer.

items.name: Callianthemum miyabeanum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Japanese alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree bed to survive wet UK winters.
Top-dress the soil with alpine grit to keep the delicate foliage from rotting in damp conditions.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy during its spring growing and flowering phase.
Position in partial shade or a north-facing rockery to protect it from hot, drying summer sun.
Grow in a deep terracotta pot using a loam-based compost mixed with fifty percent horticultural grit.

items.name: Callichilia
items.growersTips:
Bring your callichilia indoors by October to protect this tropical beauty from chilly UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry to touch.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from May to September for best blooms.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in early spring to encourage a bushier, more compact shape.
Repot every two years in spring using a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.

items.name: Callistephus chinensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March then plant out in May after the last frosts to beat the UK damp.
Water them at the base in the morning to keep leaves dry and prevent devastating aster wilt.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are fifteen centimetres tall to get loads more flowers.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young plants during wet British spring nights using beer traps.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil to give these hungry annuals a rich, draining bed.

items.name: Callitriche antarctica
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy evergreen in boggy pond margins or shallow water up to ten centimetres deep.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in spring and pushing them directly into wet, muddy pond edges.
Clear fallen autumn leaves from your pond to stop them smothering this low-growing oxygenator.
Grow it alongside native marsh marigolds to provide light shade and keep the water cool in summer.
Watch out for pond snails in late spring, as they love to munch on the soft, delicate foliage.

items.name: Callitriche brutia
items.growersTips:
Plant this native starwort in a garden pond shelf about thirty centimeters deep for best growth.
Keep it in still or slow-flowing water as heavy winter pond currents will uproot its delicate stems.
Grow it alongside native hornwort to help control algae and keep your UK garden pond water crystal clear.
Watch out for pond snails in spring as they love to munch on the tender submerged evergreen foliage.
Propagate it in summer by simply pushing stem cuttings directly into aquatic compost baskets.

items.name: Callitriche cophocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this native oxygenator in still or slow-flowing garden ponds at a depth of 10 to 30 centimetres.
Anchor bare roots in heavy clay loam using aquatic baskets to prevent them from floating to the top.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris to provide shade and reduce algae growth around the young shoots.
Thin out dense mats in late summer to maintain open water and prevent the pond from choking.
Monitor for water snails in spring as they can rapidly consume the delicate submerged foliage.

items.name: Callitriche hamulata
items.growersTips:
Grow this native starwort in still or slow-moving water up to one meter deep to mimic UK streams.
Plant in a heavy clay and loam mix within aquatic baskets to prevent the fine roots from drifting.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and weighting them down into the pond substrate.
Clear fallen autumn leaves from the pond surface to maintain the high light levels this plant needs.
Introduce Ramshorn snails to your pond to naturally control algae growth on the delicate foliage.

items.name: Callitriche hermaphroditica
items.growersTips:
Plant this fully submerged aquatic perennial in still or slow-flowing neutral to alkaline garden ponds.
Anchor the delicate stems in heavy clay loam within shallow planting baskets to prevent them floating.
Position in partial shade to cool UK pond water and prevent filamentous algae from smothering stems.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and weighting them down in the muddy bottom of the pond.
Introduce Ramshorn snails to your pond to naturally control algae without damaging these fragile stems.

items.name: Callitriche heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this starwort in still or slow ponds up to forty centimetres deep to keep it happy and green.
Pop it in a sunny spot so those lovely floating rosettes can form a dense mat on the water.
Plant it alongside native hornwort to help keep your UK garden pond clear and free of algae.
Trim back the vigorous stems in late summer to stop it from taking over your garden pond.
Watch out for pond snails in spring as they love to munch on the tender new submerged leaves.

items.name: Callitriche marginata
items.growersTips:
Plant this starwort in your garden pond margins at a shallow depth of five to fifteen centimeters.
Grow it in a sunny spot to keep its delicate foliage dense and prevent it from getting leggy.
Anchor the roots in small baskets filled with heavy clay loam rather than standard potting compost.
Thin out the dense mats in late summer to keep the pond water clear and let light reach the bottom.
Watch out for pond snails in spring as they love to munch on the soft, tender submerged leaves.

items.name: Callitriche palustris
items.growersTips:
Plant this native oxygenator in still or slow-moving water up to thirty centimetres deep in spring.
Grow in full sun to partial shade in neutral to acidic pond soil or loam-filled planting baskets.
Thin out dense mats in late summer to prevent the plant from choking smaller garden ponds.
Watch for water snails which graze on the foliage but avoid chemical treatments in wildlife ponds.
Pair with native Caltha palustris in shallow margins to create structural contrast and shade.

items.name: Callitriche stagnalis
items.growersTips:
Pop this native starwort in your garden pond margin at a depth of ten to thirty centimetres deep.
Plant it in heavy clay loam using a mesh aquatic basket to stop it floating away in your pond.
Keep it in full sun or partial shade to help those lovely floating rosettes form on the water.
Thin it out by hand in late summer to stop it taking over and to keep the water oxygenated.
Watch out for pond snails which love to munch the leaves, so keep their numbers in check.

items.name: Callitriche truncata
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate oxygenator in still or slow-moving pond water at a depth of 10 to 30 centimetres.
Anchor the stems in small pots of heavy clay-based loam rather than nutrient-rich potting compost.
Grow this native starwort alongside hornwort to help suppress algae in your garden pond.
Watch out for pond snails in early spring as they love to munch on the soft, translucent foliage.
Keep it in partial shade to prevent summer sun from scorching the delicate submerged leaves.

items.name: Callitriche verna
items.growersTips:
Plant this native starwort in your garden pond margin at a water depth of ten to thirty centimeters.
Anchor the delicate roots in heavy clay loam rather than standard compost to stop it floating away.
Thin out the dense underwater mats in late summer to keep your pond oxygenated and prevent stagnation.
Watch out for pond snails eating the floating rosettes, and gently hose them off into the water.
Pair it with native marsh marigold to provide beautiful spring colour and shade for the pond life.

items.name: Callitris
items.growersTips:
Plant your Callitris in well-drained, sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position this conifer in full sun against a south-facing wall to shield it from harsh frost.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep it completely dry during the damp winter months.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape it, but never cut back into the old wood as it won't regrow.

items.name: Calochortus nuttallii

items.name: Calochortus obispoensis

items.name: Calochortus palmeri

items.name: Calochortus panamintensis

items.name: Calochortus persistens

items.name: Calochortus plummerae

items.name: Calochortus pulchellus

items.name: Calochortus raichei

items.name: Calochortus simulans

items.name: Calochortus splendens

items.name: Calochortus striatus

items.name: Calochortus subalpinus

items.name: Calochortus superbus

items.name: Calochortus syntrophus

items.name: Calochortus tolmiei

items.name: Calochortus umbellatus

items.name: Calochortus umpquaensis

items.name: Calochortus uniflorus

Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter rot in wet soil.

items.name: Calochortus venustus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in a mix of equal parts gritty John Innes No.3 and coarse horticultural sand

Water sparingly from winter foliage emergence until flowering, then stop watering as leaves yellow

items.name: Calochortus vestae
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil.

items.name: Calochortus weedii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in a mix of equal parts grit and loam to ensure rapid winter drainage.

Apply a high-potassium liquid feed once in spring when active leaf growth first appears.
Check foliage weekly in spring for scarlet lily beetles and handpick them to prevent defoliation.

items.name: Calomeria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late summer as they need light and winter cold to germinate in the UK
Overwinter young plants in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame to protect them from wet UK winters

Stake the tall flowering stems early in summer to protect them from strong winds and heavy summer rain
Monitor foliage regularly for aphids and glasshouse red spider mite which thrive on its sticky leaves

items.name: Calotropis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical milkweed in containers of gritty, free-draining soil so you can move it inside.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry, and keep it barely damp during winter.
Watch out for yellow aphids on new shoots and wipe them off with a damp cloth to protect monarchs.
Prune your giant milkweed in early spring to shape it and encourage bushy new growth for flowers.
Wear thick gloves when cutting stems to protect your skin from the highly toxic, irritating sap.

items.name: Calotropis gigantea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shrub in a pot so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Use a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, cutting back to almost nothing in winter.
Prune lightly in early spring to shape the plant and always wear gloves to avoid the toxic sap.
Place it in your brightest south-facing window or heated conservatory to get enough daily sun.

items.name: Calotropis procera
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender shrub in a pot of gritty cactus compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Keep it on your sunniest windowsill or in a heated conservatory as it needs constant warmth.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly and let all excess drain away.
Wear thick gloves when pruning in spring to protect your skin from its highly toxic milky sap.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and wipe the large felted leaves with a damp cloth.

items.name: Caltha
items.growersTips:
Plant Caltha palustris in heavy clay or boggy soil at the pond edge, submerged up to ten centimetres.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in late summer to maintain vigorous growth.
Water container-grown marsh marigolds daily in summer to keep the compost constantly saturated.
Cut back faded foliage and spent flower stems in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry UK summers and prune affected leaves to ground level immediately.

items.name: Caltha dionaeifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny Falkland native in a mix of peat-free compost and grit to mimic its boggy home.
Keep the soil constantly wet by sitting its pot in a shallow saucer of rainwater year-round.
Place it in a cool, bright spot but shield it from the scorching afternoon sun in midsummer.
Watch out for garden snails as they love to munch on the tight, succulent-like leaf cushions.
Propagate by carefully teasing apart the tiny rosettes in early spring just as new growth starts.

items.name: Caltha leptosepala
items.growersTips:
Plant this white marsh marigold in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil at the edge of your pond.
Keep the crown just at the water surface or submerged no deeper than five centimetres in your pool.
Watch out for powdery mildew in dry UK summers, so keep the soil consistently wet to prevent it.
Divide overgrown clumps right after they finish flowering in late spring to get free new plants.
Plant them alongside native UK moisture-lovers like Astilbe or Hostas for a gorgeous bog garden.

items.name: Caltha natans
items.growersTips:
Sink its roots into heavy, wet clay or shallow water up to ten centimetres deep in a sunny pond edge.
Keep the soil constantly muddy and never let this little white marsh marigold dry out in summer.
Propagate it by dividing the creeping runners in late summer once the dainty white flowers fade.
Watch out for powdery mildew in humid UK Augusts and space them out to keep the air flowing well.
Plant it alongside native water forget-me-nots to create a beautiful, damp-loving ground cover.

items.name: Caltha novae-zelandiae
items.growersTips:
Plant this little kiwi alpine in a gravelly, grit-rich scree bed that mimics cool mountain streams.
Keep the soil constantly moist but free-draining, mimicking wet alpine flushes in the UK rain.
Position it in partial shade to protect its delicate leaves from scorching during hot UK summers.
Surround it with sharp grit mulch to deter slugs and snails from eating the tender spring growth.
Divide the clumps right after flowering in early summer to keep this slow-growing perennial vigorous.

items.name: Caltha obtusa
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf white marigold in a permanently wet bog garden or right at your pond edge in full sun.
Press the seeds gently into wet, compost-rich mud in late summer rather than burying them deeply.
Keep an eye out for powdery mildew during muggy UK summers and space plants to improve air flow.
Divide the clumps right after they finish flowering in late spring to keep them vigorous and healthy.
Grow them alongside dwarf hostas or astilbes to shade their roots during hotter British summers.

items.name: Caltha palustris
items.growersTips:
Plant this native marginal in heavy clay or wet soil at the pond edge up to ten centimetres deep.
Water container-grown specimens daily with rainwater during dry UK summers to prevent soil drying.
Cut back faded foliage to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of leaves and autumn flowers.
Watch for powdery mildew in late summer and improve air circulation by thinning congested clumps.
Divide established clumps in early autumn or after flowering in May to maintain vigour and spread.

items.name: Caltha sagittata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Patagonian marsh-marigold right at the muddy edge of your garden pond in acidic soil.
Keep the soil constantly wet or submerged under shallow water up to five centimetres deep.
Position it in full sun or partial shade to mimic its cool, bright South American home.
Protect the young spring leaves from slugs and snails which love the damp conditions it grows in.
Propagate by dividing the root clumps in early spring just as the white flowers begin to fade.

items.name: Calydorea
items.growersTips:
Plant these South American bulbs 8cm deep in gritty, free-draining soil in a warm, south-facing spot.
Grow them in pots so you can bring them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory over winter.

Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the emerging grassy foliage.
Repot your bulbs every three years in late summer using a mix of peat-free compost and sharp sand.

items.name: Calylophus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.

Prune back the woody stems by half in early spring to stimulate fresh flowering growth for summer.
Protect young plants with fleece during prolonged UK winter frosts below minus five Celsius.

items.name: Calymmodon
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny tropical fern in a humid terrarium or glass jar to survive dry UK indoor heating.
Mount it on sphagnum-wrapped bark instead of potting soil to mimic its wild epiphytic home.
Mist daily with rainwater or distilled water, as UK tap water contains too much harsh lime.
Keep it in bright, indirect light near a north window, shielded from direct midday summer sun.
Maintain a cosy indoor room temperature above fifteen degrees Celsius throughout the chilly winter.

items.name: Calymmodon cucullatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny tropical fern in a warm terrarium to mimic its humid, high-altitude rainforest home.
Mount it on sphagnum moss and cork bark rather than potting it in standard UK compost mixes.
Mist daily with rainwater or distilled water to keep humidity high without waterlogging the roots.
Keep it in bright, indirect light but safely away from cold drafts and dry central heating vents.
Maintain indoor temperatures above fifteen degrees Celsius year-round to prevent cold shock.

items.name: Calypsoinae
items.growersTips:
Plant Calypso bulbosa in a mix of decayed pine needles and coarse sand to mimic UK coniferous woods.
Water with rainwater to keep the shallow soil damp but never soggy during the spring growing season.
Protect emerging shoots from slugs and snails in early spring using organic copper tape or barriers.
Position containers in deep shade facing north to prevent summer overheating in temperate UK gardens.
Do not disturb the delicate roots or repot unless essential, as they rely on specific soil fungi.

items.name: Calyptrion
items.growersTips:
Plant your Calyptrion in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding leaf mould to mimic woodland.
Position it in dappled shade to protect the delicate leaves from the harsh midday British sun.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering deeply at the base during dry summer spells.
Mulch annually in late autumn with well-rotted compost to insulate the roots from wet winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring, using beer traps to protect the tender new shoots.

items.name: Calyptrion arboreum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical violet tree in a heated conservatory to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.

Prune lightly in late autumn after flowering to maintain a compact shape for indoor growing spaces.

items.name: Camassia
items.growersTips:
Plant your camassia bulbs deep at around fifteen centimetres in autumn so they stay cool and damp.
Give them a generous watering during dry spring spells to keep their tall flower spikes lush.
They absolutely love heavy clay soil that stays moist in winter but does not get waterlogged.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year's show.
Grow them alongside late tulips or hostas to hide their fading leaves as summer gets underway.

items.name: Camassia cusickii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soils.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth but allow it to dry out after summer dieback.
Sow in borders alongside late-flowering tulips and hostas to hide the yellowing post-bloom foliage.
Leave the faded flower spikes intact to self-seed and naturalise in damp UK wildflower orchards.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they quickly damage the emerging young shoots.

items.name: Camassia howellii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to 15cm in moist, clay-heavy soil that mimics UK wet meadows.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth but allow it to dry out slightly in summer.
Position in full sun to partial shade to prevent the tall, delicate flower spikes from flopping.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in summer to feed the bulb for next year's spring blooms.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Camassia leichtlinii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in moisture-retentive, clay-friendly soil.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to prevent the flower spikes from aborting before they bloom.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally until July to feed the bulb for next year's spring display.
Plant alongside late-flowering perennials like hardy geraniums to hide the yellowing summer foliage.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Camassia quamash
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten to fifteen centimetres in moisture-retentive clay soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth but allow it to dry out after summer dieback.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in July to allow the bulb to store energy for next spring.
Plant alongside late-flowering perennials like hardy geraniums to hide the yellowing summer foliage.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Camassia scilloides
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in moisture-retentive, clay-heavy soil that mimics UK damp meadows.
Water thoroughly during dry spring spells to support flowering, but keep soil drier during winter.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy emerging young foliage.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in summer before cutting it down to feed next year's bulb.
Associate with late-flowering narcissi or damp-loving grasses in a naturalised UK wildflower lawn.

items.name: Camellia
items.growersTips:
Plant them shallow with the root flare just visible, as burying camellias too deep prevents flowering.
Water thoroughly with stored rainwater during July and August when next spring's buds are forming.
Prune them immediately after spring flowering finishes before they start growing their new shoots.
Mix plenty of ericaceous compost into the planting hole to keep our neutral UK soils nice and acidic.
