items.name: Camellia ×williamsii
items.growersTips:
Plant your williamsii in acidic soil with the root flare sitting just level with the ground surface.
Water deeply with rainwater from July to September to ensure next spring's flower buds develop well.
Prune your shrub immediately after flowering in late spring before the new growth begins to emerge.
Protect those early spring buds from morning sun by planting your camellia in a west or north aspect.
Mulch annually with composted pine needles or leaf mould to keep the shallow roots cool and acidic.

items.name: Camellia amplexicaulis
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Vietnamese beauty inside a warm greenhouse or conservatory before UK autumn frosts.
Plant in a pot using ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure it never sits in soggy soil.
Water only with stored rainwater to keep the soil acidic, keeping it damp but not waterlogged.
Prune very lightly just after spring flowering to shape it without losing next year's flower buds.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month from spring to late summer for lush leaves.

items.name: Camellia azalea
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare summer-bloomer in a pot of ericaceous compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Water only with stored rainwater to keep the soil acidic and prevent yellowing leaves in hard water.
Prune gently in late August right after flowering finishes to shape it without losing next blooms.
Position your pot in dappled shade facing west to protect delicate summer petals from midday sun.
Feed with a liquid sequestered iron fertiliser in spring to boost its glossy evergreen foliage.

items.name: Camellia chrysanthoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare yellow gem in ericaceous compost mixed with pine needles to mimic its forest home.
Protect the delicate winter-blooming buds by positioning it away from cold, drying easterly winds.
Water only with stored rainwater to keep the soil acidic, especially during dry mid-summer spells.
Prune very lightly just after spring flowering finishes so you do not cut off next year's buds.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which love eating the roots of container-grown plants.

items.name: Camellia crapnelliana
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in acidic, ericaceous compost and keep the root ball level with the soil surface.
Protect the bark from hard UK frosts by wrapping the main trunk in horticultural fleece in winter.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and buds developing.
Prune lightly immediately after spring flowering to shape the shrub without losing next year's buds.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in late summer, as they love chewing the roots of container plants.

items.name: Camellia cuspidata
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in a sheltered spot away from cold drying winds and harsh early morning UK sun.
Mix plenty of composted pine needles or ericaceous compost into your soil to keep the pH low.
Water thoroughly with stored rainwater during July and August when next spring's buds are forming.
Prune lightly right after flowering in late spring to shape it before the new growth starts.
Protect the delicate white blossoms from late frosts with a light fleece jacket on freezing nights.

items.name: Camellia euphlebia
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender species in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Mix plenty of composted pine bark into your peat-free ericaceous compost to ensure perfect drainage.
Water only with stored rainwater to keep the soil acidic and prevent leaf yellowing from tap water.
Keep it in a sheltered, dappled shade spot away from cold drying winds and harsh morning sunshine.
Prune very lightly immediately after spring flowering to shape it without losing next year's buds.

items.name: Camellia fraterna
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in a sheltered spot away from cold, drying winds to protect its delicate blooms.
Mix plenty of ericaceous compost into your soil before planting to keep this acid-lover happy.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to prevent the leaves from turning a sickly yellow.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in spring so you do not cut off next year's buds.
Apply a thick mulch of pine needles or bark in autumn to protect the shallow roots from UK frosts.

items.name: Camellia granthamiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare beauty in a sheltered, frost-free spot as its huge winter blooms hate cold winds.
Use a mix of peat-free ericaceous compost and pine needles to keep the soil acidic and free-draining.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to prevent the leaves turning a sickly yellow.
Prune very lightly immediately after spring flowering to avoid cutting off next year's flower buds.
Protect the early autumn buds from harsh morning sun to stop them from dropping off prematurely.

items.name: Camellia grijsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot with ericaceous compost to keep the soil acidic and drain well in UK rain.
Water with saved rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and prevent bud drop.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring before next year's buds start to form.
Wrap your potted grijsii in bubble wrap during freezing UK winters to protect its delicate roots.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots of your container-grown plants in autumn.

items.name: Camellia hengchunensis
items.growersTips:

items.name: Canbya aurea

items.name: Canbya candida

items.name: Canistropsis billbergioides

items.name: Canistropsis elata

items.name: Canistropsis marceloi

items.name: Canistropsis microps

items.name: Caralluma

items.name: Caralluma adscendens

items.name: Caralluma munbyana

items.name: Cardiocrinum

Plant the bulb shallowly with its nose just showing at the soil surface in a humus-rich woodland bed

Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in April
Sow the fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate in the UK

items.name: Cardiocrinum giganteum

items.name: Carissa

items.name: Carissa bispinosa

items.name: Carissa carandas

Grow this tender shrub in a pot so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.

items.name: Carissa haematocarpa

items.name: Carissa macrocarpa

Watch out for scale insects under the glossy leaves, wiping them off with a damp soapy cloth.

items.name: Carissa spinarum
items.growersTips:
Bring your natal plum indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits your garden.

Prune your shrub in late spring after the frost risk passes to shape it and keep those thorns tidy.

items.name: Carissa tetramera

Bring your sand-cherry indoors by October to protect this tender African shrub from frost.

items.name: Carlowrightia

Prune back the stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more purple flowers.

items.name: Carmona

items.name: Carpanthea

items.name: Carpanthea pomeridiana

items.name: Carpobrotus aequilaterus

items.name: Carpobrotus chilensis

items.name: Carpobrotus dimidiatus

Plant this South African native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it inside.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it, but stop watering completely from November.

Trim back the trailing stems in late spring using sterile shears to keep the plant compact.
Nestle it next to hardy Sedums in a sunny rockery to mimic its natural coastal sand dune home.

items.name: Carpobrotus edulis

items.name: Carpobrotus mellei

Plant this South African beauty in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive UK winter wet.
Bring your pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or bright windowsill before the first autumn frost.

Snip leggy stems in late spring to keep it compact and encourage those bright yellow-pink flowers.
Pair it with hardy Sedums in a gravel bed to create a stunning, drought-proof coastal display.

items.name: Carpobrotus modestus

Plant this pigface shallowly in sandy, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in UK rain.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Protect this tender perennial from frost by moving container-grown plants into a greenhouse by October.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring after the last frost to keep its spreading habit tidy.
Grow it alongside hardy sedums in a sunny rockery to create a beautiful, drought-tolerant display.

items.name: Carpobrotus muirii

Plant this South African native in your poorest, sharpest-draining sandy soil to prevent winter rot.
Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it indoors to a frost-free greenhouse before November frosts.

items.name: Carpobrotus quadrifidus

Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily overwinter backup plants on a bright indoor windowsill.
Position your pot in the brightest south-facing spot you have to mimic its sunny coastal home.

items.name: Carpobrotus rossii

Plant this Aussie pigface in your sunniest, poorest soil to mimic its coastal dunes, not rich loam.
Give it sharp grit drainage and protect it under glass or fleece when UK winter wet and frost hit.

Take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors as backup against harsh British winter rot.

items.name: Carpobrotus virescens

Give it a sunny south-facing wall or gravel bed to mimic its warm, dry native habitat.

items.name: Carruanthus

items.name: Carruanthus ringens

items.name: Cascabela

Bring your potted Cascabela indoors before the first autumn frost to keep this tender shrub alive.
Water deeply once the top two inches of soil dry out, then let it drain fully to avoid root rot.
Prune your plant in late winter using sharp shears to shape it and encourage bushy spring growth.

items.name: Cascabela thevetia

items.name: Catharanthus

Grow them in pots so you can easily move them indoors before the first autumn frosts hit the UK.

items.name: Cathaya

items.name: Cathaya argyrophylla

items.name: Catopsis berteroniana
items.growersTips:
Grow this epiphytic bromeliad in a warm conservatory or terrarium, never outdoors in chilly UK rain.
Pot it in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix rather than soil to mimic its natural tree-top home.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater, but let the potting bark dry out between light waterings.
Give it bright, indirect light on a south-facing windowsill, but shade it from scorching summer sun.

items.name: Catopsis floribunda

Grow this tropical air plant indoors year-round, as our UK winters are far too cold for them.
Keep rainwater in its central leafy reservoir, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnant rot.

Position it on a bright east-facing windowsill to give it the soft morning sun it loves so much.
Mist the leaves daily during dry winter heating months to keep the indoor humidity high enough.

items.name: Catopsis morreniana
items.growersTips:
Keep this Mexican native indoors year-round as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter outdoors.
Grow it in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix rather than standard UK peat-based composts.
Always fill its central leafy cup with soft rainwater instead of hard British tap water.
Place it on a bright east or west windowsill to get the soft morning or evening light it loves.
Flush out the central cup every month with fresh water to prevent stagnant rot in humid rooms.

items.name: Catopsis nitida
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical bromeliad in a warm conservatory or bright bathroom to escape UK frost.
Plant it in a free-draining orchid bark and perlite mix rather than standard British garden soil.

Position it in bright, indirect light near a south-facing window but shade it from scorching sun.
Mist the leaves twice a week in winter when indoor central heating dries out your home's air.

items.name: Catopsis sessiliflora

Grow this tropical bromeliad indoors year-round as it cannot survive chilly UK winter temperatures.

Position on a bright east or west windowsill to avoid harsh direct summer sun scorching the leaves.
Mist the foliage twice a week in winter when central heating dries out your indoor UK air.

items.name: Caudanthera
items.growersTips:
Give this rare perennial sharp-draining grit in your soil to survive wet British winters.
Protect its succulent stems from slugs and snails during damp spring nights with organic pellets.
Position your pot in a south-facing, unheated greenhouse to maximize precious UK summer sun.
Water sparingly only when the compost dries out completely, then keep it bone dry through winter.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in midsummer when the plant is actively growing and warm.

items.name: Caulophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant Caulophyllum thalictroides in deep, moist, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous trees.
Keep soil consistently damp with rainwater, especially during dry UK spring and summer spells.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn, as they need winter chill to germinate next spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails devouring the delicate, smoky-purple emerging shoots in April.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted leaf mould to mimic their natural forest floor habitat.

items.name: Caulophyllum giganteum
items.growersTips:
Plant this shade-lover in deep, moist, humus-rich acidic soil to mimic its native woodland home.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame, as they need two winters of UK chills to finally germinate.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, especially during our dry UK spring spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the emerging metallic-blue shoots.
Plant it alongside hepaticas and trilliums, which thrive in the same cool, sheltered UK conditions.

items.name: Caulophyllum thalictroides
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native forest canopy.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your soil to create the acidic, damp bed it loves.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love to feast on the emerging shoots.
Propagate by dividing the thick rhizomes in autumn once the foliage has naturally died back.

items.name: Cedrelinga
items.growersTips:
Start your Cedrelinga seeds indoors in early April using a heated propagator to mimic warm soils.
Plant out in late May after the last frost, spacing them forty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep root growth.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into heavy UK clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage they need.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them with organic copper tape barriers.

items.name: Cedrus
items.growersTips:
Give your cedar plenty of space in deep, well-drained acidic soil to avoid waterlogging in wet winters
Water young trees deeply once a week during dry UK summers, but let the soil dry out between drinks
Prune only dead or crossing branches in late autumn, never cut back into old wood as it won't regrow
Keep an eye out for giant conifer aphids in spring and wash them off with a gentle hose spray
Plant prostrate cultivars like Golden Horizon in smaller gardens to avoid them outgrowing your space

items.name: Cedrus atlantica
items.growersTips:
Give your Atlantic cedar plenty of room to spread because it hates being moved once established.
Plant it in deep, well-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Water young trees deeply during dry spring spells but leave mature ones to cope on their own.
Prune only in late autumn or winter to avoid sap bleeding and keep the gorgeous natural shape.
Watch out for the giant conifer aphid in summer and gently spray them off with your garden hose.

items.name: Cedrus deodara
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, well-drained loamy soil with a handful of grit to survive wet British winters.
Give young trees a thorough bucket of water once a week during dry UK spells for the first two years.
Check the trunk and lower branches for giant conifer aphids during mild, damp autumn weather.
Only prune in late autumn or winter to shape it and avoid bleeding sap when the tree is active.
Choose the compact Golden Horizon cultivar if your British suburban garden has limited space.

items.name: Cedrus libani
items.growersTips:
Plant your cedar in deep, well-drained loamy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Give young trees a deep soak weekly in dry summer spells, but never let the soil get waterlogged.
Prune only in late autumn or winter to avoid sap bleeding and deter the destructive cedar aphid.
Keep a sharp eye out for honey fungus, a common UK threat that can quickly kill mature cedars.
Choose the dwarf cultivar Sargentii if you have a smaller garden, as the species grows massive.

items.name: Cedrus libani var. brevifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cypriot cedar in a raised bed or gravelly soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Give young trees a deep soak once a week during dry summer spells, but leave them alone in winter.
Never prune the main central leader, just gently tidy up any competing double leaders in late winter.
Watch out for giant conifer aphids in spring; blast them off with a hose before they cause soot mould.
Mulch with pine needles or bark in spring to keep the soil acidic and replicate its native woodland.

items.name: Cenostigma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect young roots from late UK frosts
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to prevent root rot in damp UK clay
Watch for pea aphids in June and spray them with garlic infusion to protect the delicate foliage
Prune back spent summer blooms in late August to encourage a second flush of flowers before autumn
Mix grit and well-rotted manure into heavy UK soil before planting to ensure the required drainage

items.name: Centrolobium
items.growersTips:
Start your Centrolobium seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect the taproots.
Plant out in late May after frosts pass, choosing the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, strong roots.
Mix plenty of grit and compost into your soil to ensure the rapid drainage this exotic plant needs.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around stems.

items.name: Centromadia fitchii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in April to ensure light-induced germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained sandy soil to mimic its native habitat and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells as this annual is highly drought-tolerant.
Position in the absolute brightest, south-facing spot to cope with cool, overcast UK summers.
Sow alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to provide ground cover that supports its upright stems.

items.name: Centromadia perennis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring after frosts, barely covering them with a light dusting of gritty compost.
Grow in a terracotta pot with free-draining sandy soil to mimic dry Californian coastal conditions.
Water sparingly only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Position in your garden's brightest south-facing spot to maximize daily sunshine and flower opening.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly in summer to prolong the flowering season before autumn frost.

items.name: Centromadia pungens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April at a depth of three millimetres into gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border to mimic its native dry California habitat.
Water seedlings sparingly once established, allowing the gritty topsoil to dry out completely.
Wear thick gloves when weeding nearby to protect your hands from this plant's sharp, spiny bracts.
Leave the faded autumn flowerheads untouched to allow self-seeding for the following spring.

items.name: Centropogon
items.growersTips:
Grow your Centropogon in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during summer.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into ericaceous compost to mimic their native cloud forest soil.
Take softwood cuttings in late spring to guarantee fresh backup plants for the cold British winter.
Position your pot in dappled shade where it gets morning sun but is shielded from harsh midday heat.

items.name: Centropogon dissectus
items.growersTips:
Bring this Andean beauty indoors by October as it cannot survive a wet, freezing UK winter outside.
Grow it in a container using peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for sharp drainage.
Water it consistently to keep the soil damp like a cloud forest, but never let the pot sit in water.
Position your pot in dappled shade or morning sun, as harsh afternoon UK sun will scorch the leaves.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when you bring it inside your conservatory for the winter.

items.name: Centrostigma
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare African orchid in a heated greenhouse to survive damp, chilly UK winter freezes.
Plant tubers just below the soil surface in a gritty, free-draining compost to prevent rot.
Water actively during summer growth but keep the soil almost bone-dry throughout winter dormancy.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and slugs attracted to the tender emerging shoots.
Pair them with small ferns in pots to provide the dappled shade and high humidity they love.

items.name: Cephalanthera
items.growersTips:
Plant red helleborines in chalky soil under beech trees, keeping the rhizome just below the surface.
Water container-grown white helleborines with rainwater only during their active spring growth.
Watch out for slugs eating the tender emerging shoots of sword-leaved helleborines in damp Aprils.
Leave the fading autumn stems alone to naturally decay and feed the essential soil fungi.
Sow native woodland grasses nearby to provide the light dappled shade these wild orchids love.

items.name: Cephalantheropsis
items.growersTips:
Plant this terrestrial orchid in a mix of leaf mould and grit to mimic damp UK woodland soils.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, especially during our wet winter months.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse when frost hits.
Position your pot in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the emerging tender shoots.

items.name: Cephalipterum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March using gritty, free-draining compost to protect from damp UK spring cold.
Plant out in May in your sunniest border, spacing them fifteen centimetres apart for good airflow.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as these Aussie annuals hate wet feet.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your clay soil to mimic their dry, sandy native outback home.
Deadhead the paper-like yellow blooms weekly through summer to keep new daisy flowers coming.

items.name: Cephalophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow these in a gritty, free-draining mix of half potting compost and half horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping them completely dry from November through to March.
Bring your pots indoors to a bright windowsill by October to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.
Snip off dead, mushy leaves in spring with clean scissors to prevent rot spreading in damp weather.
Position them on a south-facing patio in full sun to trigger those brilliant midday daisy blooms.

items.name: Cephalophyllum pillansii
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African beauty indoors to a frost-free windowsill or heated greenhouse by October.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of grit and peat-free compost to survive wet British winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep it completely dry in winter.
Place your pot in the sunniest spot of your garden, like a south-facing patio, to trigger blooms.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when overwintering your plant indoors.

items.name: Cephalophyllum purpureo-album
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African succulent in a grit-rich, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or porch before November.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely during damp winter months.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing patio to trigger those stunning purple-and-white blooms.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the fleshy leaf joints, especially when keeping it indoors.

items.name: Cephalophyllum spissum
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half compost and half horticultural grit.
Keep it dry in winter by overwintering it in a cold greenhouse or on a very sunny windowsill.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then stop watering completely in winter.
Place it in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to trigger those bright magenta blooms.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the fleshy leaves, wiping them away with a dab of rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Cephalophyllum subulatoides
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African succulent indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first autumn frost.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep it completely dry from November through to March.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in June, letting the wounds callous for three days before potting.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Cerastium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Cut back hard by half immediately after summer flowering to keep the silver foliage neat and compact.
Water newly planted divisions weekly until established, then rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to rejuvenate growth and maintain vigor.
Position in full sun next to dark-leaved Sedums or purple Heucheras for striking foliage contrast.

items.name: Cerastium aleuticum
items.growersTips:
Recreate its subarctic home by planting in gritty, sharply draining soil with zero organic mulch.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells, as winter wet in UK climates will rot the roots.
Position in the brightest, most exposed spot in your rock garden to mimic wind-swept cliff tops.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by carefully dividing clumps in spring.
Protect from winter waterlogging by placing a pane of glass or a cloche over the plant from November.

items.name: Cerastium alpinum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil to prevent winter rot caused by wet UK autumns and winters.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery, to mimic its natural montane habitat.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry summer spells to avoid waterlogging.
Cut back the foliage hard after flowering in mid-summer to maintain a neat, compact cushion shape.
Propagate by dividing the clumps in early spring or taking softwood cuttings after summer flowering.

items.name: Cerastium arcticum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot caused by wet UK winters.
Water sparingly, only during prolonged dry summer spells, to mimic its dry arctic habitat.
Position in full sun and a raised bed or rockery to ensure maximum light and sharp drainage.
Propagate by dividing the clump in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Clear fallen autumn leaves quickly to prevent dampness from rotting the compact foliage cushion.

items.name: Cerastium arvense
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Propagate by dividing established clumps in early spring or immediately after flowering in summer.
Shear the foliage back hard after summer flowering to maintain a neat, compact carpet.
Water newly planted divisions sparingly, only during prolonged dry spells in the UK summer.
Position in full sun alongside rockery companions like Thymus serpyllum or Sedum acre.

items.name: Cerastium biebersteinii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Shear the foliage back by half immediately after summer flowering to keep the clump compact.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as this plant is highly drought-tolerant once established.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
Position in full sun alongside rock soapwort or sedums which share its love for dry conditions.

items.name: Cerastium brachypetalum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into poor, sharply draining soil with added grit.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry UK banks, avoiding any waterlogged winter areas.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as this annual thrives on neglect.
Allow the plant to set seed naturally in late summer to ensure its return the following spring.
Weed hand-around the delicate shallow roots carefully to prevent disturbing the young seedlings.

items.name: Cerastium diffusum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring at a depth of two millimetres in poor, sharply draining soil.
Grow this annual in full sun alongside Sedum or Thymum species to mimic its native coastal habitat.
Water seedlings sparingly during damp UK springs to prevent dampening-off in heavy garden soils.
Avoid adding any compost or fertiliser to the soil as excess nutrients cause floppy, weak growth.
Collect the seed capsules in midsummer before they split to control self-seeding in gravel paths.

items.name: Cerastium fontanum
items.growersTips:
Control this invasive lawn weed by hand-pulling damp soil to extract the shallow, fibrous root system.
Mow your lawn at a high setting of seven centimeters to shade out and weaken these light-loving seeds.
Apply a nitrogen-rich lawn fertilizer in spring to help grass outcompete this low-growing weed.
Spot-treat dense patches in autumn using a selective lawn weedkiller containing fluroxypyr or MCPA.
Aerate compacted clay soils in autumn with a hollow-tine fork to reduce the damp conditions it loves.

items.name: Cerastium glomeratum
items.growersTips:
Hand-weed young rosettes in early spring before they set seed in damp UK borders and gravel paths.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn using gritty compost to ensure winter chill.
Avoid watering established plants in wet UK winters to prevent root rot in heavy clay soils.
Shear back the foliage by half immediately after flowering in June to stop aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in well-drained rockeries to create a competitive ground cover.

items.name: Cerastium holosteoides
items.growersTips:
Keep this vigorous spreader in check by shearing it back hard immediately after flowering in July.
Grow in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent the plant from becoming excessively floppy and weak.
Water newly divided clumps weekly during dry UK spring spells until their shallow roots establish.
Divide congested mats every three years in autumn to maintain vigour and prevent center dieback.
Pair with robust rockery plants like Aubrieta to prevent this fast grower from smothering them.

items.name: Cerastium nigrescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty scree or a raised alpine bed to ensure the sharp winter drainage this UK native needs
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells and keep completely dry during wet British winters
Cut back gently after summer flowering to maintain its tight cushion habit and prevent rotting off
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to safeguard against winter wet losses
Position in full sun alongside non-vigorous alpine companions like Saxifraga to prevent smothering

items.name: Cerastium pumilum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in autumn on the surface of gritty, well-drained soil to mimic UK wild habitats.
Position in full sun in a rock garden or gravel path where winter wet will not rot the roots.
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells, allowing the growing medium to dry out completely.
Leave faded flowers intact in midsummer to allow this annual to self-seed for the following year.
Clear surrounding aggressive weeds in early spring to prevent this small plant from being smothered.

items.name: Cerastium regelii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water only during prolonged dry spells, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Trim back the foliage by half in late summer after flowering to maintain a tight, compact cushion.
Position in full sun next to Campanula portenschlagiana to mimic natural alpine scree conditions.
Propagate by dividing the dense mats in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.

items.name: Cerastium semidecandrum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn on well-drained sandy soil to mimic UK coastal dunes for spring blooms.
Water sparingly only during dry spring spells as this annual thrives in dry, nutrient-poor soils.
Position in full sun alongside Sedum acre or Thymum to prevent more vigorous weeds from choking it.
Watch for slugs on young seedlings during damp British springs and protect with grit barriers.
Allow seed heads to dry and self-sow naturally in late summer to ensure its return next spring.

items.name: Cerastium subtriflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun to maintain the compact, low-growing habit and prevent leggy growth.
Cut back hard after flowering in midsummer to encourage fresh foliage and prevent self-seeding.
Water only during prolonged dry spells, as this alpine species is highly drought-tolerant.
Propagate by division in early spring or autumn to rejuvenate older, woody clumps.

items.name: Cerastium sylvaticum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or boggy.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Shear back by half after summer flowering to promote fresh foliage growth and prevent self-seeding.
Plant alongside hostas or ferns in dappled shade to create a naturalistic woodland ground cover.

items.name: Cerastium tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Shear the foliage back by half immediately after flowering in July to keep the mat tight and neat.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives on neglect and dry conditions.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and prevent bald spots.
Plant alongside purple aubrieta or creeping phlox for a classic, contrasting dry stone wall display.

items.name: Cerastium utriense
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, as this alpine species hates soggy soil.
Trim back by half immediately after summer flowering to maintain a tight, cushion-like habit.
Position in full, unobstructed sun to mimic its native exposed limestone scree habitat.
Propagate by dividing the clump in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.

items.name: Ceratocapnos
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they need winter cold to break dormancy before spring growth.
Grow in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic their native woodland habitat.
Provide a fine trellis or allow them to scramble naturally through sturdy shrubs like sarcococca.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the delicate foliage from dying back early.
Collect the explosive seed pods in summer just before they split to control self-seeding in borders.

items.name: Ceratocapnos claviculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a shady woodland border with moist, acidic, humus-rich soil.
Provide a fine twiggy trellis or plant near shrubs to support its delicate climbing tendrils.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the shallow root system consistently damp.
Check young shoots in spring for slug damage and protect them using organic beer traps.
Let the plant self-seed naturally in late summer to ensure its return the following year.

items.name: Ceratocephala
items.growersTips:
Pop this little buttercup relative in gritty, sharply draining soil to mimic its dry native home.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the chilly UK winter naturally breaks their stubborn dormancy.
Keep watering very light during wet British winters to prevent the delicate roots from rotting.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tiny, vulnerable leaves first emerge.
Plant it alongside rock garden companions like sedums that won't crowd out this pint-sized gem.

items.name: Ceratocephalus testiculatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this buttercup relative in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK rain.
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to allow natural winter chilling for germination.
Water sparingly during the spring growing phase, allowing the soil to dry out completely between times.
Position in full sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent the plant from becoming leggy.
Plant alongside sedums or sempervivums in a rock garden to prevent vigorous plants from smothering it.

items.name: Ceratopteris
items.growersTips:
Grow this floating fern in a heated indoor tank or conservatory pond to survive chilly UK winters.
Anchor some stems in a muddy substrate of aquatic compost and sand to encourage submerged growth.
Thin out the dense surface fronds weekly in summer so light can still reach your underwater plants.
Watch out for pond snails in your tank as they love to feast on the delicate, lacy green fronds.
Propagate easily by letting the tiny plantlets that form on mature fronds break off and float free.

items.name: Ceratopteris thalictroides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical fern as a submerged aquarium plant or in a very warm, humid heated greenhouse.
Plant it in a mix of peat-free compost and sand, keeping the crown just above the wet mud level.
Water constantly to keep the soil muddy, or simply submerge the pot fully in a heated indoor pond.
Watch out for snails and slugs, which will quickly devour the soft, delicate fronds in warm areas.
Trim older decaying fronds regularly in summer to encourage fresh, bright green feathery growth.

items.name: Ceratostylis
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a mesh basket of chopped sphagnum moss to suit damp, humid UK bathrooms.
Water with room-temperature rainwater whenever the moss feels dry to the touch, avoiding tap water.
Keep it on a north-facing windowsill to protect the delicate leaves from strong UK summer sun.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense, grassy foliage clumps during mild winter months.
Bring your potted plants indoors by October before UK overnight temperatures drop below ten degrees.

items.name: Cerberiopsis
items.growersTips:
Bring this New Caledonian native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from UK frosts.
Grow it in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with added perlite to prevent winter wet.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, then let it drain completely.
Position your pot in a south-facing conservatory or sunroom to maximise crucial UK sunlight.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite in summer and mist the foliage weekly to deter them.

items.name: Cercestis
items.growersTips:
Bring your Cercestis mirabilis indoors by October to protect its tropical leaves from UK frosts.
Grow this climber in a peat-free, bark-rich orchid mix to mimic its natural African rainforest soil.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid root chill.
Position your plant in bright, filtered light near an east-facing window to prevent leaf scorching.
Provide a moss pole for the aerial roots to cling to, keeping the pole damp to boost humidity.

items.name: Cercestis dinklagei
items.growersTips:
Grow this African climber in a peat-free ericaceous potting mix kept above fifteen degrees Celsius.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out, as this rainforest vine hates soggy roots.
Provide a moss pole for its aerial roots to grip, mimicking its natural jungle climbing habit.
Position in bright, indirect light near a west-facing window to avoid scorching its deep green leaves.
Mist the foliage daily or use a gravel tray to combat dry UK central heating during winter months.

items.name: Cerinthe
items.growersTips:
Sow the large black seeds in pots indoors in March, burying them about one centimetre deep.
Plant them out in May in your sunniest border, as they need maximum UK light to get those blue bracts.
Water them sparingly once established, as soggy British winter soil will easily rot their roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love devouring the tender young shoots.
Collect the seeds in August when they turn black, so you can sow them again next spring for free.

items.name: Cerinthe major
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds individually in deep pots in March to protect their long taproots before planting out.
Soak the large, hard seeds in warm water overnight to kickstart germination before sowing them.
Plant them next to yellow wallflowers or orange geums to make those purple bracts really pop.
Watch out for slugs when seedlings are small, but once established, the snails will leave them be.
Let them self-seed in your gravel paths for the most natural, effortless displays next spring.

items.name: Cerochlamys
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African succulent in a mix of three parts grit to one part loam to survive UK damp.
Water only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle, keeping them bone dry from November to March.
Keep your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to get enough winter light.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
Repot in late spring using a shallow pan because their fibrous roots do not need deep soil.

items.name: Ceropegia
items.growersTips:
Keep your string of hearts in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive damp UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to once a month from November through February.
Hang your pot near a south-facing window to get enough bright, indirect British sun to keep variegation.
Press those little bead-like aerial tubers gently onto damp soil in spring to easily grow new vines.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when indoor heating goes on in the autumn.

items.name: Ceropegia ampliata
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African beauty in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix with extra perlite for drainage.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill in winter, keeping the temperature above ten degrees.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but never let the pot sit in a tray of water.
Provide thin bamboo canes or a small trellis for its twining, leafless green stems to scramble up.
Watch out for mealybugs in the stem joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Ceropegia candelabrum
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender climber indoors by October before UK frosts hit, keeping it above twelve degrees.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, then drench it and let the pot drain completely.
Use a mix of half peat-free compost and half perlite to prevent root rot in damp British winters.
Provide a small trellis or hoop in spring for its twining stems to climb toward the summer sun.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Ceropegia dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Bring this Canary Island native indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant in a mix of half peat-free compost and half grit to prevent root rot in damp British air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep it completely dry from November through to March.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic its bright, arid natural habitat.
Watch out for mealybugs in the stem joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Ceropegia discoidea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tuberous climber in a gritty cacti mix with fifty percent perlite for sharp drainage.
Keep it on a south-facing windowsill to mimic its native sun but protect it from frosty drafts.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then reduce this to a monthly splash during UK winters.
Tuck the tuber just below the soil surface, leaving the top crown exposed to prevent stem rot.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Ceropegia fusca
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant indoors by October to protect its succulent stems from chilly, wet UK winters.
Plant in a mix of half grit and half peat-free compost to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then soak it, but stop watering completely from Nov to March.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic the bright Canary Island sun it loves.
Watch out for mealybugs in the stem joints and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Ceropegia jainii
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Indian tuber in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent winter rot.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill indoors, as it needs warmth and cannot survive UK frost.
Water only when the soil dries out completely in summer, then keep it bone dry throughout winter.
Plant the small tuber shallowly, keeping the top level with the soil surface to avoid stem rot.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and treat them quickly with an organic neem oil spray.

items.name: Ceropegia linearis
items.growersTips:
Bring your string of needles indoors by October as it cannot survive a damp, freezing UK winter.
Water only when the potting mix is bone dry, usually once every fortnight during a warm UK summer.
Use a gritty cactus compost with half perlite to stop the tubers rotting in our humid climate.
Keep it on a bright south-facing windowsill to maintain those lovely purple leaf undersides.
Take stem cuttings in June by pinning nodes directly onto damp grit to easily back up your plant.

items.name: Ceropegia pusilla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny Indian native in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent winter root rot.
Keep it on a warm, sunny windowsill year-round as it cannot survive the chilly UK winter outdoors.
Water only when the soil dries out completely in summer, then keep it bone dry throughout winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the narrow, grass-like leaves and treat them with organic spray.
Repot in spring only when roots escape the bottom, keeping the tiny tuber just below the surface.

items.name: Ceropegia radicans
items.growersTips:
Keep this South African native indoors year-round as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter.
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely, cutting back to a monthly sip in winter.
Plant in a shallow pot of half peat-free compost and half perlite to prevent root rot.
Prune leggy stems in spring to encourage bushier growth and propagate the cuttings in water.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when indoor heating goes on in autumn.

items.name: Ceropegia rhynchantha
items.growersTips:
Plant this tuber shallowly in gritty, free-draining soil with the top just peeking above the surface.
Keep it cozy indoors during chilly UK winters and only water when the potting mix is bone dry.
Hang it in a bright, south-facing window to get enough UK sun to trigger those bizarre green flowers.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints, especially when indoor central heating goes on.
Propagate in late spring by snipping stems just below a node and rooting them in damp perlite.

items.name: Ceropegia sandersonii
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African vine in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix to survive damp UK winters.
Keep it on a bright, draft-free windowsill but shield the leaves from scorching mid-summer sun.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then reduce to a monthly splash from November to March.
Untangle the twining stems gently in spring and train them onto a small hoop trellis for support.
Check the parachute-shaped flowers regularly for mealybugs hiding in the intricate, fused petals.

items.name: Ceropegia stapeliiformis
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African gem in a gritty cactus mix with fifty percent perlite for sharp drainage.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill to mimic its native heat and encourage summer blooms.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but keep it completely dry through winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the jointed stems and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
Provide a small trellis or hoop for the snake-like stems to scramble up as they grow.

items.name: Ceropegia woodii
items.growersTips:
Pop your string of hearts in a gritty cactus mix with extra perlite to survive damp UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it, but never let the pot sit in a saucer of water.
Hang it in your brightest south-facing window to keep those gorgeous purple leaf backs vibrant.
Trim the vines in spring to encourage bushier growth and pop the cuttings back in the soil to root.
Watch out for mealybugs in winter when indoor heating dries the air, and dab them with soapy water.

items.name: Chaenorhinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this little gem in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring by just pressing them into damp compost, as they need light to sprout.
Give it a haircut after the first summer flush to trigger a fresh wave of dainty purple blooms.
Tuck it into sunny crevices of dry stone walls or gravel paths where it happily self-seeds.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps to protect them in damp UK weather.

items.name: Chaenorhinum origanifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant your dwarf snapdragon in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Tuck it into sunny crevices of dry stone walls or rockeries where it mimics its native scree.
Water newly planted plugs weekly until established, then leave them to survive on normal UK rain.
Cut back the faded stems in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of pretty lilac flowers.
Watch out for slugs in damp spring weather, as they love to munch on the tender new shoots.

items.name: Chaetymenia
items.growersTips:
Sow these annual seeds indoors in early April to beat the unpredictable British spring frosts.
Plant them out in May in a spot that gets at least six hours of direct British summer sunshine.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy by watering them deeply just once a week.
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach ten centimetres tall to encourage a much bushier habit.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK spells by using pet-safe wool pellets around stems.

items.name: Chalarothyrsus amplexicaulis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Acanthaceae perennial in a sheltered, frost-free spot or keep it in a pot indoors.
Water it consistently to keep the compost moist but never soggy, especially during dry UK summers.
Feed your plant with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from May through to August.
Cut back the leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more pink flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites if you are overwintering it in a heated greenhouse.

items.name: Chamaecyparis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lawson cypress so the soil level matches the pot line to prevent collar rot in UK rain.
Water your young conifer deeply once a week during dry British summers to establish deep roots.
Prune lightly in late spring but never cut back into old brown wood as it will not regrow.
Watch out for conifer aphid damage in May and spray them off with a firm blast of your garden hose.
Mix plenty of composted bark into heavy UK clay soil to ensure the excellent drainage they crave.

items.name: Chamaecyparis formosensis
items.growersTips:
Give this Taiwanese cypress shelter from cold UK winds in a moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil.
Water your young tree deeply every week during dry UK summers until its root system is established.
Prune lightly in late spring, only cutting young green wood as it will not regrow from old brown wood.
Mix plenty of composted bark into your planting hole to mimic its native mountain forest floor.
Watch out for phytophthora root rot in wet clay soils by planting on a slight mound to aid drainage.

items.name: Chamaecyparis lawsoniana
items.growersTips:
Plant this cypress in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil to avoid root rot in wet UK winters.
Water your young tree deeply once a week during dry summer spells until its roots are established.
Only trim the green foliage in spring or summer, as cutting back into old wood leaves permanent bare patches.
Watch out for cypress aphid infestations in late spring, which cause unsightly brown patches.
Choose compact cultivars like Ellwoodii for smaller UK gardens so they do not outgrow their space.

items.name: Chamaecyparis obtusa
items.growersTips:
Give your Hinoki cypress a sheltered spot out of harsh drying winds to prevent foliage browning.
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of compost to the hole.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells, especially while the young conifer is establishing.
Only prune lightly in late spring, as cutting back into old wood means it will not regrow.
Keep an eye out for juniper scale and treat early with organic sprays to protect the foliage.

items.name: Chamaecyparis pisifera
items.growersTips:
Plant your sawara cypress in acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of leaf mould to keep it moist.
Keep it watered during dry UK summers, especially while it is establishing in its first two years.
Prune lightly in late spring, but never cut back into old wood as it will not regrow from bare stems.
Protect golden cultivars like Filifera Aurea from strong midday sun to prevent the foliage burning.
Watch out for honey fungus in damp UK soils, as this conifer is unfortunately quite susceptible.

items.name: Chamaecyparis taiwanensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Taiwanese cypress in moist, acidic to neutral soil, adding leaf mould to mimic forest bed.
Water deeply during dry UK summers, especially in the first two years to establish its root system.
Position in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect its delicate foliage from icy winds.
Prune very lightly in late spring, only cutting new wood as it will not regenerate from old brown wood.
Watch out for juniper scale and cypress aphid, spraying with organic insecticidal soap if spotted.

items.name: Chamaecyparis thyoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Atlantic white cypress in wet, acidic soil near a pond where UK rain keeps it soggy.
Choose a sunny, open spot in your garden to prevent the dense foliage from thinning out and browning.
Never cut back into the old wood because this conifer won't regrow from bare branches.
Watch out for juniper scale insects in dry UK summers and blast them off with a strong hose stream.
Give young trees a thick mulch of pine needles or composted bark to keep the soil acidic and damp.

items.name: Chamaegastrodia
items.growersTips:
Grow these terrestrial orchids in a mix of leaf mould and grit to mimic native woodland floor soils.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy by watering with rainwater, especially during dry UK summers.
Shield these delicate plants from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or copper barriers.
Position them in deep shade under shrubs like ferns or hostas to protect them from direct sunlight.
Protect them from winter wet by placing a cloche over them during heavy UK winter rain and frosts.

items.name: Chamaenerion
items.growersTips:
Plant Chamaenerion angustifolium Album in partial shade to control its vigorous UK woodland spread.
Cut stems to the ground in late autumn to prevent self-seeding across damp British clay soils.
Grow in deep pots to restrict invasive rhizomes from choking out delicate cottage garden plants.
Water newly divided spring offsets weekly until established in free-draining acidic UK soils.
Monitor young spring shoots for elephant hawk-moth caterpillars and hand-pick them off gently.

items.name: Chamaenerion angustifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant white cultivar Album to enjoy the showy flowers without the aggressive self-seeding of pinks.
Chop stems to the ground in late autumn to prevent wind-blown seeds from invading your UK lawn.
Grow in large sunken bottomless buckets to restrict the highly invasive underground running roots.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK springs but stop once established to prevent floppy growth.
Plant alongside robust native ferns and nettles in damp woodland edges to naturally curb its spread.

items.name: Chamaeranthemum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Brazilian gem in a pot so you can easily bring it indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy by watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light to prevent the delicate patterned leaves from scorching.
Mix plenty of perlite and leaf mould into peat-free compost to mimic its native rainforest floor.
Snip off any leggy stems in spring to encourage a bushier habit and fresh, colourful new foliage.

items.name: Chamaescilla corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in pots to easily move undercover during wet UK winters, preventing waterlogged dormant roots.
Water moderately during active winter growth, then dry out completely after summer foliage dies back.
Position in full sun or a south-facing cold frame to mimic its native sunny Australian habitat.
Protect emerging winter shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Chamaescilla spiralis
items.growersTips:
Plant these Australian native bulbs 5cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive UK winters.
Grow in pots of loam-based compost mixed with 50 percent grit to prevent winter wet root rot.
Water moderately during their autumn to spring active growth, then keep completely dry in summer.
Position pots in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield them from heavy UK winter rainfall.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring when the highly twisted, spiral leaves first emerge.

items.name: Chamaexeros
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its roots from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant in a terracotta pot using fifty percent grit mixed with peat-free compost for fast drainage.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil feels bone dry, then soak it and let it drain.
Check the leaf bases weekly for mealybugs, which love hiding in the dense, grassy foliage clumps.
Divide established clumps in late spring once the soil warms up to help new divisions settle in.

items.name: Chamerion latifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant in poor well-drained gravelly soil to mimic its native subarctic riverbed habitat in the UK
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they require cold stratification and light to germinate
Water sparingly once established only during prolonged dry summer spells to prevent root rot in clay
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn after seed pods split to control self-seeding in borders
Grow alongside alpine plants like Saxifraga in a raised scree bed to prevent it being smothered

items.name: Chamorchis
items.growersTips:
To mimic its alpine home, plant this tiny orchid in extremely well-drained, gritty limestone soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy during its active spring and summer growth.
Do not prune this delicate perennial; just gently snip off any dead flower spikes in late autumn.
Protect emerging shoots from slugs and snails in early spring using pet-safe organic pellets.
Plant it alongside slow-growing alpine grasses to provide natural shelter without smothering it.

items.name: Champluviera
items.growersTips:
Plant your Champluviera in well-drained UK soil mixed with grit to stop winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to keep the clump tidy for winter.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so use beer traps or wool pellets early on.
Divide your mature Champluviera clumps every three years in spring to keep them vigorous.

items.name: Chasmanthe
items.growersTips:
Plant these African bulbs about ten centimeters deep in autumn using gritty, well-drained soil.
Give them a sunny, south-facing border or a warm patio pot to mimic their native South African heat.
Water them regularly through winter and spring, but let them dry out completely during summer dormancy.
Protect the early spring flower spikes from late UK frosts with a cozy layer of horticultural fleece.
Divide the congested clumps of corms every four years in late summer to keep the blooms coming.

items.name: Chasmanthe aethiopica
items.growersTips:
Plant these African bulbs five inches deep in autumn using gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Grow them against a south-facing house wall to trap extra warmth and shield them from hard frosts.
Keep the soil damp during their winter growing phase but stop watering completely when they go dormant.
Leave the faded foliage alone in summer so the bulb can recharge for those fiery winter blooms.
Mulch the crown heavily with bark in November to protect the tender bulbs from freezing UK soil.

items.name: Chasmanthe bicolor
items.growersTips:
Plant these African bulbs ten centimetres deep in spring using pots you can move inside for winter.
Give them a warm south-facing wall in grit-heavy soil to mimic their dry South African summers.
Water them weekly through spring but stop completely when the leaves die back in midsummer.
Watch out for slugs chewing the tender new shoots as they emerge during mild UK autumns.
Grow them alongside hardy cyclamen to keep the pots looking lovely during their summer dormancy.

items.name: Chasmanthe floribunda
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 10cm deep in autumn in well-drained soil, using grit in the hole to prevent winter rot.
Grow them against a south-facing wall to shield them from harsh UK frosts and cold winds.
Water deeply during their winter growing phase but keep them completely dry in their summer dormancy.
Cut the dead foliage back to the ground only after it turns yellow in midsummer to feed the bulb.
Mulch heavily with bark in autumn to protect the shallow root systems from severe British freezes.

items.name: Chasmatophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty rockery or alpine trough to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November until March.
Mix equal parts John Innes number two with horticultural grit to ensure super-fast drainage.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the fleshy leaves during damp spring nights.
Grow them alongside hardy Sempervivums or Sedums which thrive in the same sunny, dry conditions.

items.name: Cheilanthes
items.growersTips:
Plant these lip ferns in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and grit to survive wet UK winters.
Tuck them into south-facing crevice gardens or dry stone walls where excess rain drains instantly.
Water them only at the base during dry spells, keeping the delicate, furry fronds completely dry.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to hide in the dry crown during damp spring days.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under a cold glass frame for winter wet.

items.name: Cheilanthes acrostica
items.growersTips:
Plant this fern in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its native limestone crevices.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, as it hates having wet feet in UK winters.
Tuck it into a south-facing dry stone wall or rockery to shield it from heavy British downpours.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a porch to stay dry during damp winter months.
Tolerate its dry-season curling habit; it is not dead, just waiting for a light drink to unfurl.

items.name: Cheilanthes austrotenuifolia
items.growersTips:
Tuck this rock fern into a gritty, free-draining crevice or alpine trough to mimic its dry home.
Plant it shallowly with the crown just above the soil level to prevent winter wet from rotting it.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect it from wet UK winters by placing a pane of glass or cloche over the crown from November.
Snip away dead, shrivelled fronds in mid-spring just as the fresh new green growth begins to unfurl.

items.name: Cheilanthes distans
items.growersTips:
Plant this woolly distans fern in a gritty, free-draining rockery to survive wet UK winters.
Avoid watering the crown directly; instead, water the surrounding soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a cold greenhouse during heavy frosts.
Tuck it into south-facing crevices where limestone chippings will mimic its dry native habitat.
Snip away any dead, shrivelled fronds in late spring once the threat of hard frost has passed.

items.name: Cheilanthes sieberi
items.growersTips:
Plant this little fern in a raised bed with lots of grit to survive wet British winters.
Keep it in full sun or light shade, a rare treat for ferns that helps it thrive in UK gardens.
Water very sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks.
Tuck it into a dry stone wall or rockery to mimic its natural, free-draining rocky home.
Protect the crown from winter wet with a cloche or pane of glass during soggy UK Decembers.

items.name: Cheilanthoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant these lip ferns in gritty, free-draining limestone scree to survive wet British winters.
Keep them dry in winter by placing a pane of glass over the crown to shield them from heavy rain.
Water only at the base during dry summer spells, keeping the delicate, hairy fronds completely dry.
Tuck them into south-facing dry stone wall crevices where excess moisture drains away instantly.
Grow them in terracotta pots of alpine compost so you can move them into a cold greenhouse in November.

items.name: Cheiloplecton rigidum
items.growersTips:
Try growing this rare Mexican fern in a very free-draining gravelly loam to prevent winter wet rot.
Keep it in a pot so you can bring it inside a frost-free greenhouse when UK winter frosts arrive.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, letting the gritty compost dry out almost fully between drinks.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light rather than deep shade to mimic its natural cliff home.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your peat-free compost to ensure excellent root aeration.

items.name: Cheiridopsis
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Cheiridopsis indoors to a bright windowsill by October to survive wet UK winters.
Plant them in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part loam to prevent root rot.
Water only when the leaves start to wrinkle slightly, keeping them bone dry during summer dormancy.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints, especially during dry indoor winter spells.
Use shallow terracotta pots rather than plastic to help the soil dry out quickly in our damp climate.

items.name: Cheiridopsis caroli-schmidtii
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half potting compost and half grit.
Keep it on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water only from autumn to spring when it grows, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks.
Keep it bone dry during its summer dormant phase, resisting the urge to water even if it looks shriveled.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints, and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Cheiridopsis denticulata
items.growersTips:
Keep this South African beauty in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water it only from autumn to spring, then let it go completely dry and dormant during the summer.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to get the maximum winter sunlight.
Protect it from frost by keeping it indoors or in a heated greenhouse once temperatures hit 5C.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints during its active winter growing season.

items.name: Cheiridopsis peculiaris
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active succulent in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive UK wet.
Keep it completely dry from May to August during its dormant phase when the old leaves papery dry.
Water sparingly from September to March, only when the inner leaf pair begins to wrinkle slightly.
Place on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to mimic South African sun.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf crevices during winter and dab them with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Cheiridopsis pillansii
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half potting compost and half grit.
Keep it completely dry during its summer dormancy, only watering when new growth shows in autumn.
Overwinter your plant on a sunny windowsill or heated greenhouse to protect it from UK winter wet.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices between the fleshy, grey-green leaf pairs.
Never prune the leaves, just gently peel away the paper-dry old sheaths once they are fully dead.

items.name: Cheiridopsis purpurea
items.growersTips:
Plant this succulent in a gritty compost mix of half John Innes number two and half coarse grit.
Keep it completely dry from June to August during its natural summer dormancy to prevent root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry between September and May, its active growth phase.
Grow it on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to survive damp UK winters.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints and dab them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.

items.name: Cheiridopsis speciosa
items.growersTips:
Keep them in a gritty loam mix of two parts pumice to one part soil to survive wet UK winters.
Water them only from August to November, then keep them completely dry during their winter dormancy.
Grow them on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to get the high light levels they need.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the old papery leaf sheaths and peel them away to prevent rot.
Propagate by taking cuttings in late summer, letting the stems callous for a week before potting.

items.name: Cheirostylis
items.growersTips:
Grow these delicate jewel orchids indoors in a shallow, wide pot using a free-draining mossy mix.
Keep them in a humid, warm spot out of direct UK sun, like a north-facing bathroom windowsill.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top orchid moss feels dry, keeping the roots damp.
Watch out for fungus gnats and spider mites, which love the warm, humid air these orchids need.
Do not prune them, just gently snip off yellowing leaves at the base with sterilized scissors.

items.name: Chelidonium majus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in damp, shady borders to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Wear thick gloves when weeding to avoid skin irritation from the toxic bright orange sap.
Cut back foliage to the ground in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in damp soil.
Plant alongside shade-loving pulmonaria or hostas to mask the untidy post-flowering dieback.
Water young plants weekly in dry summer spells but leave established clumps to survive on rainfall.

items.name: Chelone lyonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink turtlehead in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soil that does not dry out in summer.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its woodland home and prevent the leaves from scorching.
Cut the stems back by half in May to encourage bushier growth and prevent the need for staking.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather when the fresh new shoots start to emerge.
Divide the congested root clumps in early spring every three years to keep the plant vigorous.

items.name: Chelone obliqua
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink turtlehead in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soil that never dries out in summer.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat and prevent leaf scorch.
Cut the stems back by half in May to encourage bushier growth and prevent the need for staking.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh new shoots as they emerge in the damp UK spring.
Divide the congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain its flowering vigour.

items.name: Chelonistele
items.growersTips:
Bring this delicate orchid indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix to mimic its natural mossy tree-branch home.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the potting bark feels dry to the touch, keeping it humid.
Place your pot on a gravel tray in bright, filtered light but away from direct midday summer sun.
Watch out for pesky scale insects and mealybugs hiding under the lush, evergreen foliage.

items.name: Cherleria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under a cold frame to protect from heavy UK spring downpours.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in damp British climates.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out fully between waterings.
Position in full sun to mimic their native alpine habitats and prevent leggy, weak growth.
Plant alongside sedums in rock gardens to provide compatible low-water companion conditions.

items.name: Cherleria biflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic alpine scree.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Position in full sun and surround the base with a fine grit mulch to keep the foliage dry.
Grow alongside Saxifraga or Sempervivum in a raised alpine trough to ensure perfect drainage.
Check regularly for slugs and snails during wet spring nights as they love the soft foliage.

items.name: Chiliadenus bocconei
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on free-draining grit to mimic Maltese rocky cliffs.
Keep water minimal and only water from below to prevent damp rot in damp UK weather.
Grow this sun-lover in a terracotta pot so you can move it indoors during wet autumns.
Mix plenty of limestone chippings into your peat-free compost to keep the soil alkaline.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers.

items.name: Chionodoxa
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs in autumn at about eight centimetres deep to keep them safe from UK frosts.
Pop them under deciduous shrubs so they get winter sun and summer shade as the canopy fills out.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in spring to feed the bulbs for next year.
Watch out for slugs nibbling the early buds during our damp British Februarys and Marchs.
Divide overcrowded clumps in late summer while they are dormant to spread the blue colour around.

items.name: Chionodoxa forbesii
items.growersTips:
Pop these little bulbs three inches deep in autumn so they survive the damp UK winter without rotting.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs like hazel so they get spring sun before the canopy blocks the light.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in May to feed the bulbs for next year's show.
They love our wet winters but need gritty, well-drained soil to avoid getting soggy bottoms in clay.
Combine them with yellow primroses for a classic, bee-friendly British spring colour explosion.

items.name: Chionolaena
items.growersTips:
Sow these half-hardy annual seeds indoors in March, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit.
Plant out in May after the last frost into gritty, sharply draining soil in your sunniest border.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out fully between drinks to prevent rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the young, woolly spring foliage.
Deadhead regularly throughout the British summer to keep those daisy-like blooms coming until autumn.

items.name: Chionophila tweedyi
items.growersTips:
Plant in a raised scree bed or alpine house using a gritty, sharply draining neutral to acid compost.
Water only from below or around the base in winter to prevent the crown from rotting in wet UK cold.
Position in a north-facing crevice or light afternoon shade to protect from hot midsummer UK sun.
Protect plants with a pane of glass or cloche from November to March to shield from persistent rain.
Watch closely for vine weevil larvae which target the roots of this alpine in container culture.

items.name: Chirita
items.growersTips:
Keep these indoor beauties in a peat-free, free-draining compost mix with plenty of added perlite.
Water them from the base only when the top inch of soil is dry to prevent any crown rot.
Place your pots on east or west-facing windowsills to avoid the harsh midday British summer sun.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love to munch on these delicate root systems.
Propagate your favourites in spring by taking leaf cuttings and placing them in a heated propagator.

items.name: Chlamydocardia
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender African perennial potted so you can easily move it indoors before autumn frosts.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top inch of compost feels dry to prevent root rot.
Position in bright indirect light near a west-facing window to mimic its natural woodland canopy.
Feed with a diluted high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertilizer once a month from April to August.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in early spring to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.

items.name: Chloraea
items.growersTips:
Keep these Chilean orchids in pots so you can move them into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.
Plant the tuberous roots shallowly, just two centimetres deep in a gritty, free-draining compost.
Water them only when active growth shows in autumn, then keep them barely damp through the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the emerging flower spikes.
