items.name: Cleretum bellidiforme
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on gritty compost, barely covering them, to plant out after May frosts.
Plant these sun-lovers in your sharpest draining soil, adding plenty of grit to survive UK rain.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as damp British soil will quickly rot their fleshy roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK summers, as they love to feast on the juicy leaves.
Deadhead faded blooms regularly through summer to keep the vibrant daisy-like flowers coming.

items.name: Cleretum clavatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African native in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winter rot.
Keep them in your sunniest, south-facing spot or a container to mimic their warm desert home.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, as these succulents hate soggy roots in cool weather.
Bring pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums in a rockery to create a beautiful, drought-tolerant display.

items.name: Cleretum herrei
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African ice plant in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Keep it in your sunniest, south-facing spot or a warm gravel garden to coax out the daisy flowers.
Protect your potted plants from frost by moving them into a cold greenhouse or conservatory in autumn.
Water sparingly, letting the soil dry completely between drinks, as damp roots will rot quickly.
Shield the fleshy leaves from slugs and snails, which love to munch on them in damp UK weather.

items.name: Cleretum maughanii
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet British winters.
Keep your pots in the sunniest spot possible, like a south-facing windowsill or warm patio.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as this succulent hates having wet feet in cool weather.
Bring your plants indoors before the first autumn frost, as they cannot cope with freezing cold.
Feed sparingly with a diluted low-nitrogen fertilizer during spring to boost those pretty blooms.

items.name: Cleretum papulosum
items.growersTips:
Plant this ice plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, as this succulent hates soggy roots.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on a sunny windowsill, barely covering them with a sprinkle of grit.
Protect the fleshy leaves from slugs and snails, which love to feast on them in damp spring weather.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under cover when heavy autumn rain starts.

items.name: Cleretum pinnatifidum
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African ice plants in your sunniest UK spot to mimic their warm native climate.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Protect these tender perennials from frost by moving container-grown plants into a greenhouse by October.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry, as they hate soggy roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs, as they love to munch the fleshy leaves.

items.name: Clermontia hanaulaensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian beauty indoors by November to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a deep pot filled with ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite for sharp drainage.
Water it thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, keeping it drier during winter.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites under the leaves if you keep it in a conservatory or porch.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light to mimic its natural forest canopy home without scorching.

items.name: Clermontia montis-loa
items.growersTips:
Treat this Hawaiian native as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen to shield it from UK winter frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, using rainwater to mimic its cloud forest home.
Plant it in a highly acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air, so mist the leaves daily to keep humidity high.
Do not prune this slow-grower; just gently pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage bushy growth.

items.name: Clermontia peleana
items.growersTips:
Grow this Hawaiian rare gem in a heated conservatory to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Use a very free-draining, acidic, peat-free compost mix with lots of perlite to mimic volcanic soil.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites and wipe leaves down with a damp cloth weekly.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light rather than harsh, direct midday British summer sun.

items.name: Clermontia pyrularia
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Hawaiian lobelioid in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Use a highly acidic, gritty ericaceous compost mix to mimic its volcanic woodland soil origins.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, as it hates wet feet.
Position your pot in dappled shade to protect the delicate foliage from strong afternoon UK sun.
Check regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and aphids, which love the soft, lush green leaves.

items.name: Clermontia samuelii
items.growersTips:
Grow this Hawaiian native in a pot of acidic, sandy loam so you can move it indoors for winter.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, mimicking its wet mountain forest habitat.
Place it in a bright conservatory or greenhouse to protect it from harsh UK frosts and winds.
Feed it monthly in spring and summer with a weak, balanced liquid fertiliser to boost growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and aphids when keeping it under glass during winter.

items.name: Clinacanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your Clinacanthus indoors by October to protect this tender tropical from chilly UK frosts.
Grow it in a container of peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit for sharp drainage.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, cutting back on watering during dark winter weeks.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and prevent legginess.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this plant in a warm conservatory or porch.

items.name: Clinacanthus nutans
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Thai native inside before October frosts and keep it on a sunny windowsill.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Feed with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed every fortnight from May to August to boost leafy growth.
Prune the stem tips in spring to encourage a bushy shape rather than a single leggy stem.
Plant in free-draining peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite to mimic its tropical soil.

items.name: Clintonia
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade using acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor.
Set rhizomes shallowly at five centimetres deep in autumn, spacing them fifteen centimetres apart.
Water regularly with rainwater during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but damp.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Propagate by dividing congested clumps in early spring just as the new growth begins to show.

items.name: Clintonia andrewsiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native redwood forest canopy in UK gardens.
Incorporate leaf mould and pine needles into acidic soil to keep the pH low and mimic forest floor.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the dry UK summer months of July and August.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Clintonia borealis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil enriched with pine needles or leaf mould to mimic native woodland conditions.
Sow fresh seed in autumn outdoors as they require a cold winter period of stratification to sprout.
Position in deep damp shade under deciduous trees to protect the delicate leaves from summer scorch.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water during dry spells to maintain the required low soil pH.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Clintonia udensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic soil mimicking UK woodlands.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in spring to retain soil moisture and mimic natural forest floors.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, keeping the rhizomes moist.

items.name: Clintonia umbellulata
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil, mimicking a UK woodland floor.
Set the rhizomes 5cm deep in autumn, spacing them 20cm apart in dappled shade under deciduous trees.
Keep soil consistently moist during dry UK spring spells, but avoid waterlogging the winter roots.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as the new growth begins to show.

items.name: Clintonia uniflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade in acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor.
Set the delicate rhizomes just two to three centimetres deep in autumn, spreading roots horizontally.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry summer spells.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or copper tape.
Mulch annually in late autumn with leaf mould or pine needles to maintain the required soil acidity.

items.name: Clistax
items.growersTips:
Bring your Clistax indoors or to a heated greenhouse before the first autumn frost hits the UK.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Feed your plant with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight during the summer.
Prune back leggy stems in early spring to encourage a bushier shape and more vibrant blooms.
Grow Clistax in pots using a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit for excellent drainage.

items.name: Clitandra
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African climber in a pot so you can move it into a warm conservatory for winter.
Plant it in a free-draining peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite to prevent root rot.
Water freely in summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings during winter months.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its climbing habit tidy.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mite when growing this vine under cover in the UK.

items.name: Cnicothamnus
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds indoors in March to beat the late UK frosts, then transplant them out in late May.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to keep their roots dry during wet British summers.
Water them deeply at the base once a week, but let the top inch of soil dry out completely first.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on young stems, especially during damp spring mornings.
Plant them alongside cosmos or marigolds to help support their stems and attract local pollinators.

items.name: Codon
items.growersTips:
Grow these desert borage relatives in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pots outdoors so winter cold can naturally break their dormancy.
Keep them bone dry during their summer dormant phase to prevent the fleshy roots from rotting away.
Protect the highly spiny foliage from slugs and snails when young shoots emerge in early spring.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame when heavy rain hits.

items.name: Codon royenii
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African desert native in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty grit and loam mix.
Keep the plant completely dry during its summer dormancy to prevent the fleshy roots from rotting.
Place the pot on a sunny, south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to mimic desert heat.
Water sparingly from below only when active growth appears in autumn, keeping foliage bone dry.
Protect the highly spiny leaves from slugs and snails which target the tender young growth.

items.name: Codonacanthus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender perennial in pots so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Use a peat-free gritty loam mix in partial shade to mimic its natural Asian woodland habitat.
Prune back the stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more white flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plants in a heated conservatory.

items.name: Codonacanthus pauciflorus
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender forest perennial indoors by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a container with peat-free compost and grit to easily move it out of cold drafts.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Snip back the leggy stems in early spring to encourage a bushier shape and more white flowers.
Position your pot in dappled shade under taller shrubs to mimic its natural woodland canopy home.

items.name: Codonanthe
items.growersTips:
Bring your Codonanthe indoors by October as these Brazilian natives cannot survive cold UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Hang them in a bright, east-facing window where they get morning sun but avoid harsh midday glass.
Snip back leggy stems in early spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier trailing habit.
Check the leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, which love the humid microclimates of UK bathrooms.

items.name: Codonanthopsis
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical trailer warm indoors or in a heated conservatory, never letting it drop below 15C.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of your peat-free, bark-heavy compost feels dry.
Hang it in bright, filtered light near an east-facing window, avoiding harsh direct midday UK sun.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a fortnight from April to September to boost those blooms.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them off immediately with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Codonanthopsis crassifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical epiphyte in a hanging basket of orchid bark and peat to mimic its canopy home.
Keep it indoors year-round as it hates UK cold, needing a bright spot away from chilly draughts.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of compost dries out, as tap water is too harsh.
Mist the leaves daily or use a gravel tray to boost humidity, especially when central heating is on.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away with a cotton bud dipped in soapy water.

items.name: Codonanthopsis macradenia
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical epiphyte indoors for winter as it will not survive a damp UK frost.
Mount it on bark or use a very free-draining orchid compost mix to prevent root rot.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top half of the compost feels dry to the touch.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the natural steam mimics its humid rainforest home.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a month during the active spring growing season.

items.name: Codonanthopsis uleana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical epiphyte in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix to prevent UK winter root rot.
Keep it cozy indoors above fifteen degrees Celsius as our British winters are far too cold for it.
Water only when the top half of the potting mix feels dry, using tepid rainwater if you can.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the high humidity mimics its native South American rainforest.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the leaves and wipe them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Codonoboea
items.growersTips:
Grow these tender perennials indoors or in a heated greenhouse to protect them from cold UK winters.
Water from below with tepid rainwater to keep the delicate, hairy leaves dry and prevent rotting.
Pot them in a very free-draining mix of peat-free compost and perlite to mimic their cliff habitat.
Place them on a north or east-facing windowsill where they get bright light but no harsh direct sun.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which love to eat the roots of these container plants.

items.name: Codonopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant your clematis-like climbers in moist, rich soil with their crown two inches below the surface.
Give these Himalayan beauties a spot in partial shade to mimic their native cool woodland canopy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love the tender emerging shoots.
Provide a twiggy pea-stick support early on so the delicate twining stems can scramble upward.
Leave the tubers completely undisturbed in winter and mulch them well to protect from UK frosts.

items.name: Codonopsis lanceolata
items.growersTips:
Plant this climber in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil in a partially shaded spot.
Sow seeds in pots in a cold frame during autumn, barely covering them as they need light to sprout.
Provide a sturdy trellis or plant next to a shrub so its twining stems can scramble upwards naturally.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails, which absolutely love to devour them.
Mulch the root area well in winter with leaf mould to protect them from wet and freezing UK soils.

items.name: Codonopsis pilosula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late winter on the surface of gritty compost as they need light and cold to germinate.
Grow this climber up a sturdy trellis in a sheltered spot to protect its delicate stems from wind.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry spells in July and August.
Mulch the crown heavily with bark in November to protect its fleshy roots from wet UK winter rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the tender new shoots at ground level.

items.name: Codonopsis subscaposa
items.growersTips:
Plant this climber with its tuber crown just two inches deep in gritty, free-draining woodland soil.
Give it a sturdy obelisk or twiggy hazel stems to help its delicate twining stems scramble upward.
Water gently but regularly in dry UK summers, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from hungry slugs and snails using organic beer traps or grit.
Mulch with leafmould in late autumn to shield the dormant tubers from wet, freezing winter rot.

items.name: Codonorchis
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in a well-drained, humus-rich acidic soil mix.
Grow in partial shade to mimic beech woodland, using leaf mould to keep the soil moist but not wet.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Keep soil barely damp during summer dormancy to prevent the delicate tuberous roots from rotting.
Avoid any root disturbance or division, as this orchid relies on fragile mycorrhizal associations.

items.name: Codonorhiza
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs five centimetres deep in pots of very gritty, free-draining compost.
Keep them completely dry in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame during their summer dormant phase.
Water them gently from autumn to spring only when the top few centimetres of soil feel totally dry.
Protect the delicate winter growth from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape.
Move your pots into full UK sunshine during winter to maximise light and encourage spring blooms.

items.name: Coeliopsidinae
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a warm greenhouse or indoors at fifteen degrees Celsius minimum in winter.
Plant in hanging baskets using coarse bark and charcoal to allow the pendant flower spikes to emerge.
Water heavily during summer growth but keep the compost barely damp during the winter rest period.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent using gravel trays to prevent red spider mite attacks.
Feed fortnightly with a weak high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during active spring growth.

items.name: Coelogyne
items.growersTips:
Grow Coelogyne cristata in a cool, draft-free room or frost-free greenhouse over UK winters.
Water heavily in summer but keep them almost bone dry from November until spring flowering ends.
Pot them in chunky pine bark mixed with perlite, never standard compost, to keep roots aerated.
Hang your orchid in the dappled shade of an apple tree during warm UK summer months to boost growth.
Never cut off the green pseudobulbs, as they store vital water and nutrients for next year.

items.name: Coelogyninae
items.growersTips:
Grow Coelogyne cristata in a chilly, drafty spare room or porch to trigger those winter blooms.
Keep compost soaking wet in summer, then completely dry them out from November until spring shoots.
Pot these orchids in chunky bark mixed with moss, never soil, to mimic their wild tree-hugging life.
Watch out for sneaky mealybugs hiding under the papery sheaths around the base of the plump bulbs.
Hang your baskets outside in dappled shade from June to September to mimic their humid forest home.

items.name: Coenoemersa
items.growersTips:
Plant Coenoemersa crowns five centimeters deep in rich, damp soil during the mild days of mid-autumn.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs, using organic beer traps to protect them.
Cut back the faded foliage right to the ground in late winter before the new spring shoots emerge.
Divide your mature clumps every three years in early spring to keep them vigorous and free-flowering.

items.name: Coespeletia palustris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring indoors using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to prevent dampening off.
Plant out in late May after the frosts in a sunny, sheltered spot with gravel around the collar.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two inches of gritty soil have dried out completely.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the tender young spring foliage.
Grow alongside thrift or sedums in a raised bed to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.

items.name: Cojoba
items.growersTips:
To grow annual Cojoba in the UK, sow seeds indoors in March at a shallow depth of one centimetre.
Keep your potted Cojoba in a humid, draft-free conservatory to mimic its native tropical climate.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of compost feels dry, avoiding soggy winter roots.
Feed your Cojoba fortnightly in summer with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed to boost leafy growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite under indoor glass and mist the foliage daily to deter them.

items.name: Coldenia
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a pot with fifty percent grit so it survives wet UK winters outdoors.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing patio to mimic its natural hot, arid habitat.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it fully but never let the pot sit in a saucer.
Protect the low, spreading stems from damp soil by mulching the pot surface with horticultural grit.
Bring the pot into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch from November to March to block winter rain.

items.name: Coldenia procumbens
items.growersTips:
Grow this frost-tender tropical plant in containers to easily move indoors before autumn frosts.
Use a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost mix to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Water only when the top three centimeters of soil are dry, as this species hates waterlogged roots.
Position pots in your garden's hottest, most sun-drenched spot to mimic its native warm climate.
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in early spring using a heated propagator set to twenty-one Celsius.

items.name: Colletogyne
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare perennial indoors by October to protect its tender tubers from wet UK winter rot.
Plant the tubers shallowly in spring, just two centimetres deep in free-draining ericaceous compost.
Water sparingly from below once growth starts, keeping the soil damp but never soggy to prevent rot.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light, mimicking its natural shady woodland canopy home.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this delicate species in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Collinsia bartsiifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April or May at a shallow depth of three millimetres in raked soil.
Grow in gritty, well-drained soil to prevent root rot during wet, cool British summer spells.
Water seedlings gently from the base to avoid flattening the delicate, slender stems of this annual.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to mimic its native cool woodland edge habitat.
Sow alongside low-growing Nemophila to create a contrasting blue and white spring ground cover.

items.name: Collinsia callosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural California winter cooling.
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK autumns and winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the top five centimetres of soil dry out between feeds.
Position in partial shade rather than full sun to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching.
Sow alongside low-growing native UK annuals like poached egg plant to support early pollinators.

items.name: Collinsia childii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn for early spring UK blooms.
Grow in moist but well-drained sandy loam with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland floor.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent strong midday UK summer sun scorch.
Water weekly to keep soil evenly damp but never waterlogged during dry British spring spells.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings and protect them with organic pellets.

items.name: Collinsia concolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into well-drained, gritty soil to avoid root disturbance
Position in full sun but provide light dappled shade during hot, dry UK midsummer afternoons
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out to prevent rot
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, using organic grit barriers to protect them
Sow alongside low-growing native annuals like poached egg plant to support local UK pollinators

items.name: Collinsia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they are to flower to benefit from winter cold stratification.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in spring to prevent mildew in damp UK weather.
Water the soil at the base weekly during dry spells to keep the shallow root system from drying out.
Sow alongside red campion in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat in UK gardens.
Deadhead spent blooms in midsummer to encourage a second flush of blue flowers before autumn frosts.

items.name: Collinsia heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in April at a depth of 3mm into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade.
Water seedlings weekly during dry UK spring spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Sow alongside native red campion or forget-me-nots to create a woodland-style pollinator border.
Deadhead spent Chinese houses blooms in midsummer to encourage a second flush of purple flowers.

items.name: Collinsia multicolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they are to flower to benefit from winter cold stratification.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in spring to prevent dampening off in damp UK weather.
Plant in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge habitat.
Water the soil at the base weekly during dry spring spells to keep the woodland soil evenly moist.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Collinsia parryi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring directly into well-drained, gritty soil to mimic alpine scree.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the spring active growing period.
Position in partial shade or dappled light to prevent the delicate blue flowers from bleaching.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Sow alongside low-growing spring bulbs like dwarf daffodils to provide natural support for stems.

items.name: Collinsia parviflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural UK winter cold stratification.
Grow in moist well-drained acidic soil in partial shade to replicate its native damp woodland edge.
Water gently at the base weekly during dry spring spells to keep the shallow fibrous roots damp.
Watch for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they quickly consume the delicate young stems.
Plant alongside native red campion or wild primroses which share its preference for dappled shade.

items.name: Collinsia sparsiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained grit-amended soil to mimic natural UK winter chilling.
Plant seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres and keep the soil damp until spring germination.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to replicate its native woodland edge habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top three centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Grow alongside native spring bulbs like wild daffodils to support early emerging UK bumblebees.

items.name: Collinsia tinctoria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn for early spring blooms in mild UK regions.
Water sparingly once established as this California native dislikes wet winter soil and root rot.
Sow directly into gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to mimic its natural scree habitat.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings during damp UK April weather and protect them.
Grow alongside low-water annuals like Eschscholzia californica to match its dry soil needs.

items.name: Collinsia torreyi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural cold stratification outdoors.
Grow in moist, well-draining acidic soil enriched with leaf mould to replicate redwood forest floors.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect delicate blooms from strong UK summer sun.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry post-spring spells.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Collinsia verna
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in autumn as they require winter cold stratification to germinate the next spring
Plant seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade
Water consistently to keep the soil damp but not waterlogged, mimicking damp UK woodland floors
Grow alongside native primroses or wood anemones which share the same spring shade requirements
Leave faded flowers to self-seed naturally in late summer to ensure a display the following year

items.name: Colobanthus acicularis
items.growersTips:
Plant this needle-leaved cushion in sharp gritty alpine compost to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil is dry to the touch, as damp conditions will rot its tight mound.
Protect it from slugs and snails in spring, as they love to nestle inside the dense foliage.
Grow it alongside saxifrages or sempervivums in a raised scree bed for perfect drainage.
Gently clear fallen autumn leaves off the cushion so it does not rot in the damp British winter.

items.name: Colobanthus muscoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Antarctic cushion in a gritty, free-draining alpine mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water it from below or use a gravel mulch to keep the tight foliage dome dry and rot-free.
Grow it in a cold frame or alpine house to protect the delicate green cushions from heavy rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding underneath the dense mat, especially during damp springs.
Propagate by gently teasing apart the tiny rosettes in late spring and potting them up in grit.

items.name: Colobanthus quitensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Antarctic pearlwort in a gritty, free-draining alpine compost to mimic its rocky home.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Grow it in a container so you can move it under a cold frame to shield it from wet winter rot.
Nestle it next to slow-growing saxifrages or sedums which won't crowd out this tiny, low cushion.
Watch out for garden slugs and snails, as they can quickly devour this delicate, slow grower.

items.name: Colocasia
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers deep in spring, about ten centimeters down, to protect them from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil constantly wet and boggy all summer; these thirsty plants love sitting in water.
Feed them weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid fertilizer from May to August to get those huge leaves.
Dig up the tubers in October after the first frost, dry them, and store them in dry peat over winter.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them indoors to a warm conservatory when the autumn chills hit.

items.name: Colocasia antiquorum
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers in spring five inches deep in rich, compost-heavy soil to kickstart growth.
Keep the soil constantly soggy and boggy throughout summer, as these plants absolutely love water.
Bring them indoors or lift tubers to store dry in a frost-free shed before the first autumn frost.
Watch out for red spider mites when growing them in dry UK conservatories or glasshouses in summer.
Feed them weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid fertiliser from May to August to boost leaf size.

items.name: Colocasia esculenta
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers ten centimetres deep in late March indoors to give them a head start before spring frost.
Feed them liquid seaweed weekly and keep the soil constantly soggy, they love sitting in wet mud.
Watch out for red spider mites when growing them in warm greenhouses or during dry UK summer spells.
Dig up the tubers in October after the first frost, dry them off, and store in dry compost indoors.
Grow the hardy Pink China cultivar if you want a variety that can survive UK winters in the ground.

items.name: Colocasia fallax
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf elephant ear in moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered spot with dappled shade.
Water heavily throughout the summer growing season but keep it almost dry during winter dormancy.
Dig up the small tubers in late October to store indoors in dry peat free of frost until spring.
Watch out for red spider mites when you bring them indoors or grow them in a dry summer greenhouse.
Grow this runner-spreading plant in a wide, shallow pot to give its stolons plenty of room to roam.

items.name: Colocasia gigantea
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers ten centimetres deep in rich, organic compost to kickstart strong spring growth.
Water them daily in summer and keep the pot sitting in a shallow tray of water to mimic a swamp.
Bring containers into a frost-free shed or greenhouse by late October to survive the cold UK winter.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertilizer from May to August for massive leaves.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping them indoors, and mist the leaves daily to deter them.

items.name: Colocasieae
items.growersTips:
Bring colocasias indoors by October before the first UK frost to overwinter them in a dry, warm shed.
Plant your tubers shallowly with the growing tip just showing above a rich, moisture-retentive soil.
Water them copiously with harvested rainwater during hot July spells to mimic their native monsoons.
Feed these hungry perennials weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertilizer from May to August.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping them in dry greenhouse air and mist the leaves daily.

items.name: Colophospermum mopane
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part loam to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Overwinter indoors under grow lights keeping temperatures above ten degrees Celsius to avoid frost.
Water deeply only when the soil dries out completely in summer then keep almost dry through winter.
Prune in late spring after new growth starts to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged stems.
Sow seeds in spring after soaking in warm water for twenty-four hours and burying one centimetre deep.

items.name: Columnea
items.growersTips:
Hang your goldfish plant in a bright, draught-free UK bathroom to mimic its native humid jungle.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid shock.
Repot in spring using a free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and peat-free compost.
Trim leggy stems back by a third after flowering in summer to encourage a bushier, fuller habit.
Watch out for mealybugs in winter when central heating dries the air, wiping them off with alcohol.

items.name: Columnea consanguinea
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical beauty warm indoors year-round, as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter outside.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of your bark-rich, orchid-style compost feels dry.
Hang it in bright, filtered light near an east window to mimic its natural rainforest canopy home.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser every two weeks from April to September to boost those red spots.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in spirit.

items.name: Columnea crassifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this trailing beauty in a hanging basket near a bright, east-facing window out of cold drafts.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free, gritty orchid compost dry out.
Keep winter temperatures above twelve degrees Celsius, as UK frost will quickly kill this tropical.
Prune leggy stems by one-third in spring right after flowering to promote a bushier, fuller habit.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Columnea domingensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Caribbean native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a chilly UK frost.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the high humidity mimics its natural tropical home.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry.
Feed with a weak high-potash liquid fertiliser monthly from April to September for red blooms.
Snip leggy stems back by a third in spring to encourage a much bushier trailing habit.

items.name: Columnea flexiflora
items.growersTips:
Bring this Ecuadorian rainforest gem indoors during chilly UK winters to keep it above fifteen degrees.
Grow it in a hanging basket with orchid bark and peat-free compost to mimic its wild tree-hugging life.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries out, as tap water ruins the roots.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the steamy air keeps its gorgeous fuzzy orange flowers happy.
Snip back the trailing stems right after flowering in late summer to encourage a bushier shape.

items.name: Columnea glabra
items.growersTips:
Keep it in a bright room but out of direct UK sun to prevent those glossy green leaves from scorching.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out, using lukewarm rainwater if yours is chalky.
Plant in a free-draining peat-free orchid mix with perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Trim the stems by a third right after flowering in summer to keep its trailing habit bushy and neat.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when indoor central heating goes on in autumn.

items.name: Columnea gloriosa
items.growersTips:
Hang your goldfish plant in a bright bathroom where high humidity mimics its natural tropical home.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to your touch.
Keep it indoors year-round as this delicate beauty will drop its leaves if temperatures hit ten degrees.
Snip back the trailing stems by a third in spring to encourage a bushier habit and more orange blooms.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away using a cotton bud dipped in soapy water.

items.name: Columnea hirta
items.growersTips:
Keep this trailing goldfish plant indoors in winter as it cannot survive UK frosts below ten degrees.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel completely dry.
Hang it in a bright UK bathroom where the high humidity mimics its natural tropical rainforest home.
Snip back the stems by a third in spring after flowering to encourage a bushier trailing habit.
Check the leaf axils weekly for mealybugs which love hiding in the fuzzy hairs of this plant.

items.name: Columnea linearis
items.growersTips:
Grow this indoor trailer in a peat-free, bark-rich orchid compost to mimic its wild tree-hugging life.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out, using lukewarm rainwater to prevent root shock.
Hang it in a bright, east-facing UK window where it gets gentle morning sun but no scorching midday heat.
Keep it cozy indoors over winter because this tropical beauty will suffer if temperatures drop below twelve degrees.
Snip the stem tips right after its pink summer flowering to encourage a bushier, trail-heavy shape.

items.name: Columnea microcalyx
items.growersTips:
Hang this trailing goldfish plant in a bright, humid bathroom away from cold UK drafts.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to the touch.
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potash tomato fertiliser to boost those orange blooms.
Prune leggy stems by one-third in spring right after flowering to keep your basket looking bushy.
Repot every two years in spring using a free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and compost.

items.name: Columnea microphylla
items.growersTips:
Hang this goldfish plant in a bright, warm room but keep it shaded from harsh direct summer sun.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to the touch.
Keep it cozy indoors year-round as it will drop its leaves if UK room temperatures fall below 15C.
Snip stem tips after spring flowering to encourage a bushier habit and more trailing orange blooms.
Mist the foliage daily during dry winter months to mimic the humid rainforests it loves so much.

items.name: Columnea minor
items.growersTips:
Grow this Ecuadorian native indoors in a hanging basket with bright, indirect light but no hot sun.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of your peat-free orchid compost mix feels dry.
Keep room humidity high by misting daily or placing your pot on a tray of wet clay pebbles.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser fortnightly from April to September to boost those yellow blooms.
Prune leggy stems by a third in spring right after flowering to keep its trailing habit bushy.

items.name: Columnea orientandina
items.growersTips:
Keep this Ecuadorian native in a warm, humid room or heated conservatory to survive UK winters.
Plant in a very free-draining orchid bark and peat-free compost mix to prevent root rot.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of compost have dried out completely.
Hang the pot in bright, indirect light near a north or east window to avoid leaf scorch.
Prune the trailing stems right after flowering in summer to encourage a bushier habit.

items.name: Columnea purpurata
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical beauty inside for winter as it cannot survive chilly British frosts outdoors.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to the touch.
Hang your pot in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to mimic its canopy home.
Feed with a weak high-potash liquid fertiliser every fortnight from April to September to boost blooms.
Snip back leggy stems by a third in spring just above a leaf node to keep your plant bushy and neat.

items.name: Columnea querceti
items.growersTips:
Bring your Columnea querceti indoors before autumn frosts start, as it cannot survive below ten degrees.
Water it with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost have dried out.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where high humidity levels mimic its native cloud forest habitat.
Prune the stems by a third right after spring flowering to encourage a bushier trailing habit.
Check the leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, which love the dense foliage of this trailing plant.

items.name: Columnea rubricaulis
items.growersTips:
Keep this trailing beauty in a warm, draft-free room with bright, indirect light to mimic canopy life.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of your peat-free orchid compost mix feels dry.
Mist the foliage regularly to boost humidity, but avoid spraying the bright red flowers directly.
Feed with a weak high-potash liquid fertilizer fortnightly from April to September to boost blooms.
Prune leggy stems by one-third in spring right after flowering to keep its trailing habit bushy.

items.name: Columnea sanguinolenta
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical epiphyte indoors for winter as it cannot survive frosty British temperatures.
Grow it in a hanging basket using a free-draining orchid compost mix to prevent root rot.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to the touch.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where high humidity mimics its native rainforest canopy.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in spring to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.

items.name: Colvillea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at 22C.
Grow in pots of gritty, free-draining loam-based compost to easily move indoors before autumn frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top three centimetres of soil have dried out to prevent root rot.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its native tropical warmth.
Monitor weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and treat early with biological control predators.

items.name: Colvillea racemosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator at twenty-five Celsius.
Grow this tropical beauty in a large pot so you can move it into a heated conservatory for winter.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Mix plenty of perlite into peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this Madagascan native needs.
Check leaves regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and mist them daily to keep the humidity high.

items.name: Colysis
items.growersTips:
Try growing this unusual fern in a terrarium or moist bathroom to mimic its native tropical home.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, as they hate sitting in cold wet mud.
Blend peat-free compost with plenty of orchid bark and perlite for the perfect free-draining mix.
Keep your plant in a warm, draught-free spot with bright but indirect light, away from hot radiators.
Watch out for pesky scale insects and gently wipe them off the fronds with a damp cotton wool bud.

items.name: Conandron
items.growersTips:
Grow this alpine gem in a shady rock crevice or a pot filled with gritty, acidic, leaf-mould soil.
Keep the compost damp all summer but ensure it drains rapidly to prevent winter wet from rotting it.
Tuck it into a north-facing stone wall where rainwater drains away from the crown during winter.
Protect the soft, crinkly leaves from slugs and snails which absolutely love to feast on them.
Bring potted plants into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch to shield them from hard UK frosts.

items.name: Conandron ramondioides
items.growersTips:
Plant your conandron in a shady, north-facing crevice or rock wall so water drains away from the crown.
Keep the compost damp in summer but let it dry out almost completely during its winter dormancy.
Protect the soft leaves from slugs and snails in spring using organic pellets or beer traps.
In cold UK regions, grow it in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Mix plenty of grit and leafmould into the soil to mimic its natural damp, rocky woodland home.

items.name: Conchidium
items.growersTips:
Grow these tiny orchids in bark-based compost under glass to survive the damp and cold UK winters
Water them with tepid rainwater only when the potting bark has dried out completely to avoid rot
Keep them on a bright UK windowsill but shaded from harsh direct summer sun to prevent leaf scorch
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in dry summers and mist the surrounding air to stop them
Give them a cool winter rest period in an unheated room to trigger their beautiful spring blooms

items.name: Condylocarpon
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of peat-free loam so you can move it into a heated greenhouse by October.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot.
Prune back unruly stems by a third in late spring once new growth starts to keep it tidy and vigorous.
Feed fortnightly from May to August with a high-potassium liquid seaweed to encourage those blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite under the leaves and mist regularly to keep humidity high.

items.name: Conicosia
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African ice plants in sandy, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly, only when the soil is bone dry, as damp roots will quickly rot in our climate.
Position your plants in your garden's brightest, most sun-drenched spot to encourage flowering.
Protect them with a dry winter mulch or move potted specimens into a frost-free greenhouse by November.
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty compost mix on a warm, sunny windowsill.

items.name: Conicosia elongata
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African ice plant in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive UK wet.
Give it a sunny south-facing spot and water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first November frost.
Sow the seeds shallowly in spring using a heated propagator to mimic its native warm environment.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs as they love to devour the fleshy succulent leaves.

items.name: Conicosia pugioniformis
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African succulent in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive UK wet.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing patio from May to September to mimic its native dune heat.
Bring the pot indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first autumn frosts hit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely over winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK spring nights as they love the fleshy tri-angled leaves.

items.name: Coniogramme
items.growersTips:
Plant your bamboo fern in shade-dappled, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor.
Water consistently to keep the soil moist but never soggy, especially during dry British summers.
Mulch the crown with leaf mould in late autumn to protect its shallow rhizomes from hard winter frosts.
Snip away any tattered, brown fronds right at the base of the plant in mid-spring to tidy it up.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the delicate new crosiers as they emerge in spring.

items.name: Connellia augustae
items.growersTips:
Bring this Venezuelan tepui native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Grow it in a gritty, acidic, peat-free orchid mix with perlite to mimic its rocky cliff habitat.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil moist but never soggy during summer.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the high light levels it craves in the UK.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight rosettes and dab them away using rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Connellia quelchii
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Venezuelan bromeliad in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK winters.
Use a very free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and acidic peat to mimic its tepid tepui home.
Water with pure rainwater directly into the central rosette, keeping the potting mix barely damp.
Position in the brightest spot possible, using supplementary LED grow lights during dark UK winters.
Keep minimum temperatures above ten degrees Celsius to prevent root rot and foliage damage in winter.

items.name: Conoclinium
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade to mimic its boggy habitat.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut the dead stems back to ground level in early spring just as new basal growth begins to emerge.
Divide overgrown clumps in March or April to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.
Protect young spring shoots from slug damage using organic pellets or beer traps in damp weather.

items.name: Conophytum
items.growersTips:
Water them only from late summer to winter, keeping them bone dry during their spring dormant phase.
Grow them in a gritty compost mix of one part John Innes number two to two parts horticultural grit.
Keep them on a sunny south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to survive damp UK winters.
Gently peel away the dry, papery old leaf sheaths in late summer to prevent rot and encourage bloom.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dry papery skins and treat them with a dab of rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Conophytum bilobum
items.growersTips:
Keep them in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes number two and half horticultural grit.
Water only from late August to winter when they wake up, keeping them completely dry all summer.
Place them on a south-facing windowsill to give them the maximum winter sunshine the UK can offer.
Do not peel off the papery, dried-up outer skins in summer; they protect the new leaves inside.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the dry sheaths and treat them with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Conophytum breve
items.growersTips:
Keep them in a gritty mix of equal parts pumice and loam to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Water only from late August to spring when they wake up, keeping them bone dry during summer dormancy.
Give them your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic South African sun and prevent stretching.
Peel away the dry, papery old leaf sheaths gently in autumn to stop pests nesting underneath.
Keep your greenhouse above five degrees Celsius in winter as they cannot survive a hard UK frost.

items.name: Conophytum burgeri
items.growersTips:
Grow this onion-shaped gem in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part John Innes number one.
Keep it completely dry from April to August while it rests safely inside its papery summer sheath.
Water very lightly from late August to November only when the translucent body starts to wrinkle.
Position on a south-facing UK windowsill with a minimum winter temperature of five degrees Celsius.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the old dried leaf sheaths during the autumn growing season.

items.name: Conophytum calculus
items.growersTips:
Give your calculus maximum winter light on a south-facing UK windowsill to prevent weak stretching.
Stop watering completely in late spring when the outer skin turns papery and starts to dry out.
Only water from late August when you see the new green bodies bursting through the old dry sheaths.
Pot them in a super-gritty mix of two parts horticultural grit to one part loam-based compost.
Keep your greenhouse or conservatory completely frost-free as these succulents hate winter damp.

items.name: Conophytum ficiforme
items.growersTips:
Mix seventy percent grit into your peat-free compost to stop autumn rots in damp UK weather.
Water them only from late August to March when the old papery leaf sheath naturally splits open.
Keep them on a south-facing windowsill to get enough winter light without needing grow lights.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the dry papery skins during their summer dormant phase.
Never water during their summer sleep from April to July or you will turn them into mush.

items.name: Conophytum flavum
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active gem in a gritty, soil-free mix of pumice and loam to prevent winter rot.
Water very lightly from August to March, then stop completely as they go dormant and sheathe over.
Keep them on your sunniest UK windowsill or in a greenhouse to get enough winter light to flower.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the dry, papery old leaf sheaths during the summer dormancy.
Never peel off the dry outer skins yourself; let the new leaves burst through naturally in autumn.

items.name: Conophytum hammeri
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny winter-active gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of seventy percent pumice and loam.
Keep it completely dry from April to August when it goes dormant and paper-dry sheaths form over it.
Position your pot on a south-facing UK windowsill to give it maximum light during dull winters.
Water very lightly from late August to trigger autumn flowering and help it break through its sheath.
Watch out for root mealybugs in winter by checking the pot base and using a neem oil drench if needed.

items.name: Conophytum jucundum
items.growersTips:
Grow them in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part loam to prevent winter root rot.
Water only from late August to spring, then keep them completely dry during their summer dormancy.
Keep them on a sunny UK windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect them from frost damage.
Peel away the papery, dead outer sheaths gently in late summer to help new succulent heads emerge.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dry leaf papery sleeves and treat them with a cotton swab.

items.name: Conophytum longum
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes 2 and pumice.
Water only from late August to spring, keeping them completely dry during their summer dormancy.
Place them on a south-facing windowsill to maximize the weak UK winter sun and prevent stretching.
Gently peel away the dry, papery old leaves in autumn once the new green bodies fully break through.
Keep your greenhouse or conservatory completely frost-free as they cannot tolerate freezing damp.

items.name: Conophytum minimum
items.growersTips:
Water them only from late summer to winter when new heads burst through their dry papery sheaths.
Grow them in a gritty mix of one part John Innes number two to two parts horticultural grit or pumice.
Keep them on a sunny south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to survive damp UK winters.
Leave the papery dead skins alone in summer as they protect the sleeping plants from strong sun.
Watch out for root mealybugs by checking the soil if your plants look wrinkled during their winter.

items.name: Conophytum minutum
items.growersTips:
Pot these pebbles in a gritty, free-draining mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent loam.
Water them only from late August to winter when the old papery summer skins have completely dried.
Keep them on your sunniest UK windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to prevent winter damp rot.
Never peel off the dry protective sheaths yourself as you will easily damage the new body beneath.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dry papery layers during their summer dormancy period.

items.name: Conophytum obcordellum
items.growersTips:
Plant them in a mix of seventy percent grit and thirty percent loam to survive damp UK winters.
Water them only from late August to spring, keeping them completely dry during their summer sleep.
Place them on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to get enough weak British winter sun.
Never peel off the papery brown sheath in summer as it protects the new leaves from scorching.
Watch out for root mealybugs in autumn by checking the drainage holes of your terracotta pots.

items.name: Conophytum pellucidum
items.growersTips:
Water these winter-growers only from August to March, keeping them bone dry during summer dormancy.
Grow them in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part John Innes number 1 for perfect drainage.
Keep them on a sunny south-facing windowsill to mimic South African light in our gloomy winters.
Never peel off the papery, dried sheath in summer; it protects the new leaves from sunburn.
Watch out for root mealybugs in winter, treating them with a diluted organic neem drench.

items.name: Conophytum piluliforme
items.growersTips:
Water from late August to spring, then keep them bone dry in summer when they sleep in paper sheaths.
Pot them in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part loam to survive damp UK winter humidity.
Give them the sunniest south-facing windowsill you have to mimic South African winter sunshine.
Watch out for sneaky mealybugs hiding under the dry, papery summer skins before autumn watering.
Gently peel away the papery old leaves in autumn only if they do not naturally split open first.

items.name: Conophytum stephanii
items.growersTips:
Keep this tiny fuzzy succulent bone dry during its summer dormancy from May until late August in the UK.
Grow it in a gritty mix of two parts pumice to one part John Innes number two to prevent root rot.
Water from below in autumn when the old papery sheath splits to reveal the new green heads inside.
Provide a bright windowsill or greenhouse shelf with maximum winter light and frost protection.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense hairs and use a fine cotton swab with alcohol to spot treat.

items.name: Conophytum truncatum
items.growersTips:
Water these winter-growers only from August to March, letting them dry completely during summer.

Mulch annually in spring with pine needles or compost to protect the shallow roots from drying out.

items.name: Cornus amomum
items.growersTips:
Plant this damp-lover near your UK pond or in clay soil that stays naturally moist all year round.
Cut the stems back to 10cm from the ground in March to get those brilliant purple winter twigs.
Mix lots of well-rotted leaf mould into the planting hole to mimic its favourite British woodland.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the branches and wipe them off with a damp cloth.
Grow it alongside yellow-stemmed golden dogwood to create a stunning winter contrast in your garden.

items.name: Cornus asperifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough shrub in damp clay soil near a pond to mimic its natural wet woodland habitat.
Prune hard in late March to encourage the brightest new stem colour for the following winter.
Mulch heavily with well-rotted leaf mould in autumn to keep the roots cool and damp through summer.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the stems and treat them with organic winter wash.
Grow it alongside snowdrops and winter aconites for a stunning cold-season ground display.

items.name: Cornus canadensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this creeping dogwood in acidic, peaty soil, adding ericaceous compost to your garden bed.
Position it in damp, dappled shade under trees to mimic its natural cool woodland habitat in the UK.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, watering deeply at the base of the plant.
Leave the plant unpruned to allow its delicate white bracts and red autumn berries to develop naturally.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, protecting the tender new emerging shoots with beer traps.

items.name: Cornus capitata
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen dogwood in sheltered, dappled shade to protect the delicate winter foliage.
In dry UK summers, give it a deep weekly soak to prevent the large strawberry-like fruits dropping.
Prune lightly in late spring only to remove dead wood, as it flowers on the previous year's growth.
Mix plenty of composted pine needles into neutral soil to mimic its preferred acidic woodland home.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, and protect the root zone with a thick leaf mould mulch.

items.name: Cornus controversa
items.growersTips:
Give this stunning pagoda tree plenty of room to show off its tiered layers in a lawn or border.
Plant it in moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil, adding lots of leaf mould to the hole.
Keep it well watered during dry summer spells for its first three years to establish deep roots.
Avoid pruning it unless absolutely necessary, as cutting branches ruins its natural tiered shape.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the bark and treat them with organic winter wash.

items.name: Cornus darvasica
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare dogwood in moist, well-drained loam enriched with plenty of well-rotted leaf mould.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge and protect leaves from hot UK sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove damaged stems and maintain its natural bushy perennial shape.
Watch out for slugs and snails on fresh spring shoots, protecting them with organic wool pellets.

items.name: Cornus disciflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare evergreen dogwood in deep, fertile, acidic to neutral soil to prevent leaf yellowing.
Position it in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds, which can easily scorch its lush foliage.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to maintain its elegant tree-like shape.
Protect young plants with a thick mulch of bracken or bark chips before the wet winter cold sets in.

items.name: Cornus drummondii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rough dogwood in moist, clay-heavy UK soils where other shrubs struggle to thrive.
Prune hard in late winter to encourage the bright reddish-purple young stems for winter colour.
Water deeply during dry British summers until its deep, soil-binding root system is established.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the bark and treat with organic plant oil sprays.
Underplant with native primroses or wild garlic to create a beautiful, damp woodland edge feel.

items.name: Cornus elliptica
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen dogwood in a sheltered spot to protect its glossy leaves from cold UK winds.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or compost into your clay soil to give its roots the drainage they crave.
Keep it well-watered during dry summer spells while it establishes over its first two years.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape it or remove any frost-damaged shoots.
Watch out for slugs on young spring growth and mulch annually with chipped bark to keep roots cool.

items.name: Cornus florida
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native woodland floor.
Water deeply weekly during dry UK summers to prevent shallow root scorch and leaf margin browning.
Prune only in late winter to remove dead wood as they dislike hard pruning and bloom on old wood.
Watch for powdery mildew in humid UK summers by spacing plants well to ensure good air circulation.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles to maintain the low soil pH they require.

items.name: Cornus foemina
items.growersTips:
Plant this dogwood in damp clay or near a UK pond where its roots can stay reliably moist all year.
Prune hard in late March to encourage the brightest new stem colour for your winter garden display.
Add a thick mulch of composted bark in spring to lock in moisture and mimic its native woodland soil.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the stems and treat them with organic horticultural oil.
Underplant with snowdrops and winter aconites to create a stunning contrast against the dark stems.

items.name: Cornus glabrata
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough shrub in damp, heavy clay where other plants struggle, as it loves wet UK soils.
Prune your brown dogwood hard in late winter to encourage fresh, vibrant new stem growth for spring.
Keep soil moist but not waterlogged during dry UK summers to stop the leaves from scorching.
Propagate easily by taking hardwood cuttings in autumn and popping them straight into the ground.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the branches during mild, damp British spring days.

items.name: Cornus hemsleyi
items.growersTips:
Plant this dogwood in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil to mimic its native woodland home.
Water your young shrub deeply once a week during dry UK summers to establish its deep root system.
Prune in late winter by removing a third of old stems to keep this large shrub from outgrowing space.
Underplant with shade-loving wood anemones or winter aconites for a lovely natural woodland look.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the branches, especially in damp British spring weather.

items.name: Cornus hongkongensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen dogwood in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect winter foliage.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into the soil to mimic its natural woodland habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove any frost-damaged stems.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch around the base in autumn to protect the roots from hard frosts.

items.name: Cornus kousa
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to avoid UK summer drought stress, keeping the root flare level with the soil surface.
Incorporate acidic leaf mould or peat-free compost into sandy or chalky UK soils to prevent chlorosis.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK spells for the first three years to establish fibrous roots.
Prune only in late winter to remove crossing branches, as spring pruning causes sap bleeding.
Watch for horse chestnut scale insects on stems and treat with organic winter wash in December.

items.name: Cornus macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this large dogwood in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil that doesn't dry out in summer.
Prune your tree in late winter to remove crossing branches and maintain that lovely tiered shape.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the bark, especially in damp UK spring weather.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to mimic its natural woodland floor habitat.
Underplant with shade-loving wood anemones or hostas to complement the high summer canopy.

items.name: Cornus mas
items.growersTips:
Plant this dogwood in a sunny UK spot with chalky or heavy clay soil to get the best spring blooms.
Prune lightly in late winter just to remove crossing branches before those yellow flowers burst open.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in autumn to keep the soil moist during dry British summers.
Grow underplantings like snowdrops and hellebores to create a stunning late-winter display.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the bark and wipe them off with a damp cloth.

items.name: Cornus nuttallii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Pacific dogwood in deep, fertile, acid to neutral soil that drains well but stays moist.
Give it a sheltered spot out of harsh winds to prevent late spring frosts damaging the bracts.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to stop the shallow roots from drying out in UK heatwaves.
Avoid regular pruning as it hates being cut back, just gently remove dead wood in late summer.
Watch out for dogwood anthracnose in wet UK summers by clearing fallen leaves to prevent fungus.

items.name: Cornus obliqua
items.growersTips:
Plant this dogwood in moisture-retentive, heavy clay soil near a pond or in a damp UK garden bog.
Prune stems hard to the ground in late March to encourage those vibrant new winter-coloured shoots.
Water deeply during dry UK spells in July and August to prevent leaf scorch on young shrubs.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted leaf mould to mimic its native damp woodland floor.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the older bark during mild British spring months.

items.name: Cornus officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this winter-flowering beauty in moist, well-drained clay to mimic its native woodland soil.
Prune your Cornus right after spring flowering to keep its shape and boost next winter's blooms.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in autumn to protect roots from wet, chilly UK winter waterlogging.
Position it in full sun or partial shade to guarantee that stunning, peeling orange-brown bark.
Keep an eye out for horse chestnut scale insects on the branches during mild British summers.

items.name: Cornus racemosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough shrub in damp clay or boggy spots where other plants struggle to thrive.
Prune hard in late winter to keep its size in check and encourage those lovely white berries.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the stems and treat them with organic plant oils.
Underplant with wood anemones or wild daffodils to create a beautiful, natural UK woodland look.
Mulch well in spring with leaf mould to mimic its native damp woodland soil and lock in moisture.

items.name: Cornus rugosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this round-leaved dogwood in dappled shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your clay or sandy soil to keep the roots cool and damp but not soggy.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help its fibrous roots establish in the first year.
Prune in late winter by removing a third of the oldest stems to encourage fresh, vigorous growth.
Keep an eye out for sawfly larvae in June, handpicking them off the large leaves to prevent damage.

items.name: Cornus sanguinea
items.growersTips:
To get those brilliant winter stems, hard prune your shrubs right down to the ground every March.
Plant them in moisture-retentive clay soil, adding well-rotted manure to the planting hole first.
Keep young plants well-watered during dry UK summers until their root systems are fully established.
Look out for horse chestnut scale insects on the stems and wipe them off with a damp cloth in May.
Underplant with snowdrops or winter aconites to create a stunning cold-season contrast in your border.

items.name: Cornus sericea
items.growersTips:
Prune stems to the ground in late March to encourage the brightest red winter colour on new growth.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or boggy soil near ponds to mimic its natural wet UK habitat.
Mulch annually in April with well-rotted manure to boost the vigorous growth needed for red stems.
Propagate easily in November using hardwood cuttings inserted directly into outdoor soil trenches.
Watch for horse chestnut scale insects on older wood and treat with organic plant oil sprays.

items.name: Cornus sessilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this dogwood in moisture-retentive, acidic soil, adding lots of compost to mimic woodland beds.
Keep the soil consistently damp, watering deeply during dry UK summers to prevent leaf scorch.
Prune in late winter before new growth starts, cutting back old stems to encourage fresh foliage.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the branches, especially in damp British springs.
Plant alongside winter aconites and snowdrops for a lovely woodland display under its yellow blooms.

items.name: Cornus suecica
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf cornel in acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of leaf mould.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a Scottish moor, watering with rainwater rather than tap water.
Position it in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.
Mulch annually in autumn with pine needles or composted bark to maintain the low soil pH it craves.
Propagate by gently detaching rooted runners in early spring just as the new growth starts to show.

items.name: Cornus unalaschkensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this creeping dogwood in acidic, humus-rich soil, mimicking a damp British woodland floor.
Set the rootball just level with the soil surface and mulch with pine needles to keep it acidic.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Grow it under shade-loving companions like dwarf ferns, hostas, or native wood anemones.
Propagate by gently detaching rooted runners in autumn to help this groundcover spread naturally.

items.name: Cornus walteri
items.growersTips:
Plant this Walter dogwood in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil to mimic its native woodland.
Prune in late winter to shape the tree and remove any crossing branches before the spring sap flows.
Water young trees deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help establish their deep root system.
Underplant with early spring bulbs like snowdrops to contrast beautifully with its dark winter bark.
Watch out for horse chestnut scale insects on the bark and treat with organic plant invigorator.

items.name: Cornus wilsoniana
items.growersTips:
Plant this ghost dogwood in moist, well-drained loamy soil, adding leaf mould to mimic woodland beds.
Water your young tree deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help those roots establish well.
Prune in late winter to remove congested branches, keeping its stunning mottled bark on full display.
Mulch annually in spring with compost, keeping it clear of the trunk to prevent any bark rot.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like snowdrops that thrive in its light, dappled shade.

items.name: Coronidium
items.growersTips:
Sow your paper daisy seeds indoors in March, barely covering them with a light dusting of grit.
Plant them out in May after the last frost, choosing the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as they hate soggy British winter wet.
Pinch out the growing tips when they are young to encourage a much bushier, flower-filled plant.
Cut the straw-like flowers just as they start to open so you can dry them for winter displays.

items.name: Corunastylis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare native Australian orchid in a cold glasshouse to protect it from wet UK winters.
Use a very free-draining compost of one part peat-free loam, one part perlite, and one part grit.
Water only when the slender autumn-flowering spike emerges, keeping the pot dry during summer.
Place pots in full sun on a gravel tray to mimic dry, open eucalyptus woodland conditions.
