Repot dormant tubers in late summer at a depth of three centimetres, handling brittle roots gently.

items.name: Corunastylis ciliata
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Aussie orchid in a gritty, free-draining mix of pumice and bark to survive UK wet.
Keep the compost damp in winter but let it dry out completely once the summer dormancy kicks in.
Sow seeds alongside established native grasses to provide the essential mycorrhizal fungi they need.
Overwinter your pots in a cold frame to protect them from heavy frost while keeping air circulating.
Watch out for slugs and snails during the damp autumn when the tiny green flower spikes emerge.

items.name: Corunastylis laminata
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare orchid in a very gritty, well-draining, acidic compost mix to mimic its native soil.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy during summer, then let it dry out almost completely in winter.
Grow it in a container so you can bring it into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame for the winter.
Avoid adding standard fertilizers, as this delicate orchid relies on sensitive mycorrhizal fungi.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the emerging single grassy leaf.

items.name: Corybas
items.growersTips:
Plant Corybas tubers just one centimetre deep in a mix of live sphagnum moss and fine bark.
Keep the compost damp but never waterlogged from autumn to spring using rainwater, not tap water.
Place your helmet orchids in a shady, draft-free spot indoors or in a heated greenhouse at fifteen degrees.
Watch out for tiny fungus gnats and slugs that love the damp moss and will quickly eat the flowers.
Let the pots dry out almost completely during their summer dormancy once the leaves die back.

items.name: Corycium
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African orchids in deep pots using a very gritty, sharply draining compost mix.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormant phase to prevent the tubers from rotting.
Water them from below during autumn and winter when you see the fresh green shoots emerging.
Grow them in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny conservatory to protect them from wet UK winters.
Repot them gently every two years in late summer just before their autumn growth spurt begins.

items.name: Corydalis
items.growersTips:
Plant blue Corydalis flexuosa in moist acidic soil to prevent summer dormancy in dry UK summers.
Sow fresh Corydalis solida seeds immediately in autumn as they lose viability rapidly if dried.
Plant tuberous Corydalis solida five centimetres deep in well-drained soil under deciduous trees.
Watch for slugs and snails on fresh spring shoots of Corydalis during damp UK April mornings.
Divide fibrous-rooted Corydalis ochroleuca in early spring just as new green growth appears.

items.name: Corydalis ambigua
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn in moist well-drained soil rich in leaf mould.
Keep soil consistently damp during spring growth but dry out slightly once summer dormancy begins.
Plant alongside snowdrops and wood anemones to fill the bare gaps left when it dies back in June.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Avoid disturbing the soil in summer when the plant has vanished to prevent damaging dormant tubers.

items.name: Corydalis aurea
items.growersTips:
Sow fresh seed in late summer in a cold frame as they need winter chilling to germinate in spring.
Plant in moisture-retentive but sharply draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter crown rot.
Water weekly during dry spring spells but keep relatively dry during their summer dormant phase.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their natural woodland edge habitat.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the delicate young foliage.

items.name: Corydalis caseana
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp UK woodland floor, keeping pH neutral to acidic.
Position in partial to full shade, ensuring the soil remains consistently moist even during summer.
Incorporate leaf mould and grit into the planting hole to provide moisture retention with drainage.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as the delicate new shoots emerge from the ground.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous rootstock in early spring just as the plant begins active growth.

items.name: Corydalis caucasica
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn in moist well-drained soil rich in leaf mould.
Siting is key so plant under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland shade and prevent summer baking.
Keep soil consistently moist during active spring growth but allow to dry out during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Do not disturb the soil or replant companions in summer when the delicate foliage has died back.

items.name: Corydalis cava
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five to eight centimetres deep in autumn to prevent them drying out in UK winters.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy clay soil to mimic the damp deciduous woodland floor they love.
Water only during spring growth and keep the soil relatively dry during summer dormant periods.
Plant under deciduous shrubs so they get spring sun before being shaded by summer leaf canopies.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the tender emerging shoots.

items.name: Corydalis cheilanthifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Sow fresh seed in autumn directly into cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to prevent the fern-like foliage from dying back early.
Position away from aggressive spreading plants to protect its delicate, slow-growing crown.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather which quickly devour the emerging yellow flowers.

items.name: Corydalis chelidoniifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in dappled shade to mimic its woodland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the following spring.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to prevent the delicate fern-like foliage from dying back early.
Position away from aggressive ground cover to protect its brittle stems and delicate root system.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate successfully.

items.name: Corydalis flavula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK spring.
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leafmould to mimic their native woodland floor.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect delicate foliage from hot summer sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells but allow soil to dry slightly when dormant in summer.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly consume the tender young shoots.

items.name: Corydalis flexuosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to prevent the plant from entering premature summer dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate blue-flowered shoots first emerge.
Let the foliage die back naturally in summer, then top-dress with leaf mould to nourish the tubers.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to propagate and maintain vigorous blue blooms.

items.name: Corydalis incisa
items.growersTips:
Plant this biennial in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Deadhead flowers before they set seed to prevent this highly invasive species from choking borders.
Sow fresh seeds in late summer in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring growth, especially during wet UK April weather.
Grow alongside robust ferns or hostas that can withstand this plant's aggressive self-seeding.

items.name: Corydalis intermedia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn in moist but well-drained soil under deciduous trees.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out when dormant in summer.
Plant alongside early snowdrops and wood anemones to mimic their natural UK woodland habitat.
Leave dying foliage intact after flowering in May to allow the tuber to store energy for next year.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly consume the tender emerging shoots.

items.name: Corydalis lutea
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mimicking UK woodland edge conditions.
Sow seeds immediately when ripe in summer, as they require winter cold to germinate next spring.
Do not overwater in winter; damp UK soils can cause the delicate tuberous roots to rot.
Grow in stone wall crevices or gravel paths where it self-seeds freely without overtaking beds.
Combine with shade-loving ferns and hostas to hide the foliage when it dies back in late summer.

items.name: Corydalis malkensis
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in late summer in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous trees or shrubs.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out during summer dormancy.
Sow fresh seed immediately in summer as dry stored seeds of this species quickly lose viability.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Associate with early snowdrops and winter aconites which share its woodland soil requirements.

items.name: Corydalis mucronifera
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in a cool, partially shaded rock garden or alpine house to shield it from hot summer sun.
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep almost dry during its summer dormancy.
Protect the delicate, blue-green foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.
Propagate by carefully dividing the fragile tuberous roots immediately after flowering in summer.

items.name: Corydalis nobilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge.
Sow fresh seed immediately in summer as they lose viability quickly and need winter cold to sprout.
Mark its location in summer because the foliage dies back completely after flowering in May.
Water during dry spring spells but keep soil relatively dry during its summer dormant period.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they target the emerging tender shoots and buds.

items.name: Corydalis pumila
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist but well-drained deciduous shade.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy UK clay soils to mimic their natural woodland floor habitat.
Allow the plant to die back naturally in summer and keep the soil relatively dry during dormancy.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they eagerly devour the emerging young foliage.
Associate them with snowdrops and wood anemones for a synchronized early spring woodland display.

items.name: Corydalis rutifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in autumn using gritty loam to mimic their native dry Mediterranean winters.
Water sparingly during summer dormancy to prevent the tuberous roots from rotting in wet UK soil.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Sow fresh seed in pots outdoors during summer so winter cold naturally triggers spring germination.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine house to shield the delicate pink flowers from heavy UK winter rain.

items.name: Corydalis solida
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 8cm deep in autumn in humus-rich, well-drained soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Keep soil moist during spring growth but allow tubers to dry out during their summer dormant phase.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they quickly devour the emerging tender flower shoots.
Plant alongside late-emerging hostas or ferns to cover the bare patches left when foliage dies back.
Avoid disturbing the soil from June onwards when the plant has completely disappeared underground.

items.name: Corymborkis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare terrestrial orchid in a heated conservatory to mimic its tropical forest home.
Use a very free-draining compost of orchid bark, perlite, and leaf mould to prevent root rot.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, using harvested rainwater instead of tap water.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light, shielding the delicate leaves from harsh midday sun.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a month during spring and summer to encourage growth.

items.name: Corytoplectus
items.growersTips:
Bring your Corytoplectus indoors by October to protect its tropical foliage from damp UK frosts.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid root shock.
Repot in spring using a peat-free mix with plenty of perlite and orchid bark for sharp drainage.
Position your plant on a north or east-facing windowsill to mimic its native shaded forest canopy.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away with a damp cloth or organic spray.

items.name: Cosentinia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mediterranean fern in a gritty, free-draining rockery to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, as this fern hates having permanently wet feet.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it indoors before the hard winter frosts hit.
Tuck it into a south-facing stone wall crevice where it can soak up the maximum summer warmth.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit and leaf mould into your soil to mimic its rocky native home.

items.name: Cosmianthemum
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted cosmianthemum indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frost.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as this tropical plant easily gets root rot.
Mix plenty of grit and leaf mould into your peat-free compost to mimic its native forest floor soil.
Keep an eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when growing them in your conservatory or greenhouse.
Snip off the faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage fresh foliage growth for next spring.

items.name: Cosmos
items.growersTips:
Pinch out the growing tips when they reach twenty centimetres to get bushier, flower-packed plants.
Sow seeds shallowly in April indoors, then plant out after the last May frosts to avoid slug damage.
Stake taller varieties like Sensation early on to protect them from strong British summer winds.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly right down to the next leaf node to keep flowers coming until October.
Avoid rich fertilizers or heavy feeding, as too much nitrogen gives you lush leaves but no flowers.
items.description: The cosmos is an alternative name for the universe or its nature or order. Usage of the word cosmos implies viewing the universe as a complex and orderly system or entity.

items.name: Cosmostigma
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of peat-free loam so you can move it into a heated greenhouse by October.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during summer, then cut watering right back over the winter months.
Watch out for red spider mites in your conservatory and mist the leaves daily to keep them away.
Prune back the tangled stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep it tidy and vigorous.
Feed it a high-potassium liquid tomato food every fortnight from May to September to boost blooms.

items.name: Cosmostigma cordatum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Indian climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant in loam-based peat-free compost with added grit to ensure the roots never sit in cold wet mud.
Water sparingly in winter but keep it damp and mist the leaves daily during hot UK summer spells.
Train the twining stems up a sturdy bamboo teepee as soon as new spring growth starts to appear.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for red spider mites when keeping this vine in a conservatory.

items.name: Cotoneaster ×watereri
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a wide hole twice the rootball width to establish roots before winter rains.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer to prevent leaf drop in sandy UK soils.
Prune in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing the winter berry display.
Watch for fireblight in warm damp UK summers by immediately cutting back blackened wilted branches.
Grow in well-drained loam enriched with garden compost to prevent waterlogging in wet British winters.

items.name: Cotoneaster acuminatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in UK clay.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems at the base to boost autumn berry display.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm in late spring and prune out infested silk-webbed shoots immediately.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus to create a wind-resistant screen that thrives in UK partial shade.

items.name: Cotoneaster acutifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK clay or loam at the same depth as the original nursery pot.
Water weekly during the first dry British summer, then leave to rely solely on natural rainfall.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain shape before spring sap starts to flow.
Check leaves in June for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars and remove webbing nests immediately.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus in sun or partial shade to boost local UK pollinator biodiversity.

items.name: Cotoneaster adpressus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-drained grit-amended soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water weekly during the first dry summer then leave to rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune wayward upright shoots in late spring to maintain the signature flat prostrate ground cover.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm wet springs by pruning out and burning any blackened stems.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum on sunny banks to match its dry soil needs and suppress weeds.

items.name: Cotoneaster apiculatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil, keeping the root flare exactly level with the ground.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to survive on natural UK rainfall.
Prune wayward stems in late winter to maintain the low, herringbone shape and maximise spring bloom.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in June, hand-picking them to protect the dense foliage.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to bring colour before the red berries and autumn leaves.

items.name: Cotoneaster atropurpureus
items.growersTips:
Plant this low-growing shrub in well-drained soil to prevent root rot in wet UK winter conditions.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring to shape the plant without losing autumn berries.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry summer spells until their root system is established.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and prune out infested branches immediately.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to provide color before the shrub leaf out in early May.

items.name: Cotoneaster bullatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained loamy soil at the same depth as the nursery pot during autumn leaf fall.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish its deep foraging root system.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems at the base to boost autumn berry production.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm wet springs and immediately prune out infected black branches.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like Narcissus to draw early pollinators to your shrub.

items.name: Cotoneaster cambricus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining limestone soil or add grit to mimic its native Great Orme cliff habitat.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK spring spells but keep established plants dry.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood without ruining its natural prostrate shape.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and handpick them to protect the foliage.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to help conserve this critically rare species.

items.name: Cotoneaster cashmiriensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained UK soil with the root flare exactly level with the surrounding ground.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers until the root system is fully established.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its low-growing, spreading carpet habit.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and remove their silk nests immediately by hand.
Grow in full sun to maximise the production of its signature white spring flowers and red autumn berries.

items.name: Cotoneaster cochleatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to establish roots before winter waterlogging occurs.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its low-growing, ground-hugging habit.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK summer spells until their deep root system adapts.
Watch for cotoneaster web moth caterpillars in June and remove infested silk webs immediately.
Grow on a sunny, sloping bank to prevent waterlogging and showcase the bright red autumn berries.

items.name: Cotoneaster conspicuus
items.growersTips:
Plant this shrub in well-drained soil at the same depth as its nursery pot to prevent stem rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish a resilient, deep root system.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing winter berries.
Watch for fireblight in warm UK springs, pruning out infected blackened branches immediately.
Grow alongside spring-flowering bulbs like daffodils to provide colour before the shrub blooms.

items.name: Cotoneaster coriaceus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-drained loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in UK clay.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems to the base to boost autumn berry display.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely solely on UK rainfall.
Inspect leaves in May for cotoneaster webmoth caterpillars and physically remove the silk nests.
Grow alongside Pyracantha to create a dense, burglar-proof wildlife hedge that deters intruders.

items.name: Cotoneaster dammeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to allow roots to establish in moist UK soil before the spring growing season.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer dry spells to establish a deep, drought-proof root system.
Prune in late spring after flowering to control spread and shape without sacrificing the red autumn berries.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils before planting to prevent root rot in wet winter conditions.
Watch for woolly aphid infestations in summer and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Cotoneaster divaricatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK clay or loam, keeping the root flare level with the soil surface.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune in late winter to remove rubbing branches and maintain the characteristic arching habit.
Watch for fireblight in warm, wet UK springs, cutting back infected wood well into healthy growth.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like crocus to add colour before the shrub leafs out.

items.name: Cotoneaster franchetii
items.growersTips:
Prune in late winter to shape the shrub and encourage berries without disrupting nesting birds.
Plant in well-drained soil with the root flare level with the ground to prevent collar rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Inspect leaves in spring for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars and prune out infested silk webs.
Grow alongside Pyracantha or Holly to create a dense, wildlife-friendly hedge for UK songbirds.

items.name: Cotoneaster frigidus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to allow winter rains to establish the deep root system in well-drained UK soils.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems to the base to boost autumn berry display.
Watch for fireblight in warm wet UK springs by pruning infected blackened shoots well back into healthy wood.
Grow the cultivar Cornubia for its exceptionally heavy berry yield and semi-evergreen winter foliage.
Underplant with Galanthus nivalis to utilise the light shade of its deciduous canopy in early spring.

items.name: Cotoneaster glaucophyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to let winter rain establish roots before summer dry spells.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing winter berries.
Watch for fireblight in warm UK summers, cutting infected branches back 30cm into healthy wood.
Grow in full sun to maximize the distinctive blue-green leaf hue and heavy autumn berry display.
Propagate in late summer using semi-ripe cuttings rooted in a cold frame under typical UK weather.

items.name: Cotoneaster horizontalis
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south or west wall using rawlplugs and wire to train the herringbone branches flat.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and keep the flat shape before new spring growth starts.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and cut out silk-webbed branches immediately.
Grow in well-drained UK soil as wet winter clay causes root rot; add grit to the planting hole.
Do not plant near pear orchards due to fireblight risk, a serious bacterial disease in the UK.

items.name: Cotoneaster integerrimus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining limestone or chalky soil to mimic its native UK limestone cliff habitat.
Water deeply once a week during the first summer, then leave to rely solely on UK rainfall.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain its naturally compact, rounded shape.
Watch for cotoneaster web moth caterpillars in spring and remove their silken webs immediately.
Plant alongside wild thyme or marjoram in sunny rock gardens to support native UK pollinators.

items.name: Cotoneaster integrifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape and control its low, spreading habit.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry summer spells until their root system is established.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm, wet springs, pruning out infected wood immediately.
Grow alongside companion plants like hardy geraniums or thymes that thrive in dry, sunny borders.

items.name: Cotoneaster kweitschoviensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a double-width hole backfilled with grit to prevent winter root rot in clay.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer then leave to rely on natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing autumn berries.
Check leaves in damp spring weather for fireblight and prune out infected branches immediately.
Grow alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to provide color before the shrub leafes out in May.

items.name: Cotoneaster lucidus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at the same depth as the pot to let winter rain settle roots in UK clay soils.
Prune immediately after flowering in June to preserve the autumn crop of black berries.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers for the first two years until fully established.
Watch for fireblight in warm wet springs, pruning out infected blackened shoots into healthy wood.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus to create a wildlife hedge that thrives in damp British climates.

items.name: Cotoneaster microphyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining UK soil at the same depth as the nursery pot to prevent crown rot in wet winters
Water weekly during the first dry UK summer then leave to rely solely on natural rainfall once settled
Prune back unruly shoots in late spring after flowering to maintain its low-growing groundcover shape
Watch for fireblight in warm damp UK springs by pruning out and burning any blackened dying branches
Grow on a sunny south-facing bank to maximise the autumn berry display and attract local UK pollinators

items.name: Cotoneaster nitidus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to establish roots before winter waterlogging occurs.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without losing winter berries.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first year to establish deep roots.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in June and remove their silk nests immediately by hand.
Grow in full sun to maximise the autumn crop of bright red berries that feed local UK songbirds.

items.name: Cotoneaster nummularius
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky soil on a sunny south-facing bank to mimic its native limestone habitat.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer, then leave fully drought-tolerant.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove congested stems and maintain its naturally arching habit.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in May and hand-pick them to protect the foliage.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer and rooting them in a cold frame.

items.name: Cotoneaster pannosus
items.growersTips:
Prune in late winter to shape the arching branches and avoid cutting off spring flowers.
Plant in well-drained soil with the root flare exactly level with the surrounding ground.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry UK summer to establish the deep root system.
Inspect leaves in summer for cotoneaster webworm and prune out any webbed branch tips immediately.
Grow alongside Pyracantha or Holly to create a dense wildlife hedge that feeds UK birds in winter.

items.name: Cotoneaster roseus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained chalky or loamy soil to establish roots before wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood without ruining the natural arching habit.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first year to prevent leaf drop.
Watch for fireblight in warm damp UK springs by checking for blackened, scorched-looking shoots.
Grow alongside hardy geraniums or salvias to cover the bare lower stems of this upright shrub.

items.name: Cotoneaster salicifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained UK soil to establish roots before the wet winter waterlogging sets in
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub without sacrificing winter berries
Watch for fireblight in warm wet UK summers and prune out infected blackened branches immediately
Grow alongside companion plants like hardy geraniums to cover the bare lower stems of older shrubs
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish deep roots

items.name: Cotoneaster scandinavicus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining UK chalk or limestone soils to mimic its native Scandinavian cliff habitat.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry British summer, then leave to rely on natural rain.
Prune lightly in late winter to shape, avoiding heavy cuts that ruin its arching natural form.
Watch for fireblight in warm UK springs, pruning out infected blackened shoots immediately.
Underplant with wild thyme or sedums to complement its low-growing, rock-loving coastal habit.

items.name: Cotoneaster simonsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a double-depth hole enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week during the first UK summer dry spells to establish its deep taproot system.
Prune in late winter by removing one-fifth of old stems at the base to boost autumn berry production.
Watch for fireblight disease in warm wet UK springs, cutting infected blackened branches back by 30cm.
Grow alongside Viburnum opulus to create a dense windbreak that attracts diverse UK garden wildlife.
items.description: Cotoneaster simonsii, the Himalayan cotoneaster, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. It is native to Nepal, the eastern Himalayas, Assam, and Myanmar, and has been introduced to a number of locales in Europe, the west coast of North America, and Australia as a garden escapee. The Royal Horticultural Society considers it to be an undesirable invasive non-native species.

items.name: Cotoneaster tauricus
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained chalky soil to mimic its native Crimean limestone habitat.
Water deeply once a week during the first UK summer, then leave to rely solely on natural rainfall.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain its compact, arching shrub shape.
Check regularly for fireblight in warm, wet UK springs, cutting back infected wood to healthy tissue.
Grow alongside Origanum vulgare or Thymus to complement its drought tolerance and attract pollinators.

items.name: Cotyledon
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Cotyledon indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first wet autumn frost hits.
Water very sparingly from November to March, only when the bottom leaves start to slightly shrivel.
Mix fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to stop our damp UK weather from rotting the roots.
Snip off any leggy spring growth to keep your shrubby Cotyledon compact and bushy for summer.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the chalky white leaves, and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: A cotyledon is a "seed leaf" – a significant part of the embryo within the seed of a plant – and is formally defined as "the embryonic leaf in seed-bearing plants, one or more of which are the first to appear from a germinating seed." Botanists use the number of cotyledons present as one characteristic to classify the flowering plants (angiosperms): species with one cotyledon are called monocotyledonous ("monocots"); plants with two embryonic leaves are termed dicotyledonous ("dicots"). Many orchids with minute seeds have no identifiable cotyledon, and are regarded as acotyledons. The Dodders

items.name: Cotyledon orbiculata
items.growersTips:
Bring your pig's ear indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first wet autumn frosts hit the UK.
Plant it in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing this to a tiny splash once a month during winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the powdery white leaf folds and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
Take stem cuttings in late spring, letting the cut end dry for a week before potting in dry grit.

items.name: Cotyledon tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Bring your bear paws indoors by October to protect them from wet and frosty British winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, keeping the fuzzy leaves completely dry.
Mix two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure the roots never sit in cold UK damp.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep those cute red claw tips looking sharp.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the woolly leaf joints and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Cotyledon tomentosa is a species of flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae, native to South Africa. It is a succulent evergreen shrub with large chunky ovate fuzzy green leaves. Its autonymous subspecies is known as the bear's paw because of the prominent "teeth" at the tips of its leaves. It forms large orange bell-shaped flowers in spring.

items.name: Cotyledon undulata
items.growersTips:
Bring your silver crown indoors by October to protect its powdery leaves from wet UK winter rot.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of grit and peat-free compost to ensure quick drainage after rain.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and always pour at the base to keep the white wax intact.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the wavy leaf folds, especially during dry indoor winter spells.
Cut back leggy stems in late spring using sharp shears to encourage a bushier, compact shrub shape.
items.description:
Cotyledon undulata, also known as silver crown or silver ruffles, is a small succulent shrub up to 50 cm tall. It has unusual grey undulating leaves that give it a very sculptural shape. Cotyledon undulata is perhaps the most widely grown Cotyledon.
The stems are covered with a thick, white, coating.
The leaves are shaped like scallop shells, grey-white to blue-grey, with wavy edges and a powdery waxy coating over the whole leaf. The flowers are orange to yellow.

items.name: Couma
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted cow-tree indoors before autumn frosts hit, as it cannot survive a UK winter.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in our damp air.
Feed your potted specimen with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight during summer.
Repot into a peat-free, free-draining loam mix with added perlite to ensure excellent drainage.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mite and wipe leaves down with a damp cloth weekly.

items.name: Crabbea
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Crabbea indoors to a frost-free conservatory before the damp UK autumn chill sets in
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to ensure sharp drainage, as wet winter soil will rot them
Water your Crabbea only when the top two inches of soil feel completely dry to prevent root rot
Position your plant on a south-facing patio to catch every bit of weak British summer sunshine
Snip off faded flower heads in late summer to encourage a second flush of their unusual blooms

items.name: Cranichidinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these terrestrial orchids in a free-draining, gritty compost mix mimicking UK woodland soil.
Keep them damp but never soggy by watering with rainwater, especially during their active spring growth.
Position your pots in cool, dappled shade to protect the delicate leaves from strong UK summer sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the tender emerging flower spikes.
Overwinter them in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to protect the roots from severe UK frosts.

items.name: Cranichis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender orchid in a draft-free greenhouse with a minimum winter temperature of ten degrees.
Pot them in a chunky, bark-based mix with perlite to mimic their natural cloud forest habitat.
Water thoroughly with rainwater once the top inch of compost dries, keeping them damp but not soggy.
Position your pots in bright, filtered light, making sure to shade them from harsh summer midday sun.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs on the undersides of those broad leaves during warm spring days.

items.name: Cranocarpus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm April to beat the chilly UK spring before transplanting out in late May.
Plant your Cranocarpus in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs during wet British summers, using beer traps around young stems.
Pinch out the growing tips in early June to encourage a much bushier habit and more flowers.

items.name: Crantzia
items.growersTips:
Plant this creeping perennial in moist, boggy soil or shallow water up to two inches deep.
Keep the soil consistently wet, as this native of damp habitats cannot tolerate drying out.
Grow it in full sun or partial shade to encourage a dense, carpet-like evergreen mat.
Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate new plants and keep the growth vigorous.
Watch out for aggressive garden weeds that can easily smother this low-growing groundcover.

items.name: Crassula
items.growersTips:
Bring your jade plant indoors before the first autumn frost to protect it from freezing wet soil.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of compost feel bone dry, then let the excess drain away.
Mix one part grit to two parts peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage these shrubs need.
Prune leggy stems in spring just above a leaf joint to encourage a bushier, more compact shape.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf crevices, wiping them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Crassula alata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on free-draining gritty compost as they need light to germinate.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Grow in pots to easily move plants indoors before autumn frosts as this annual cannot survive frost.
Mix horticultural grit into standard compost to mimic their native dry soils in wet UK climates.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to prevent leggy growth in weak British sunlight.

items.name: Crassula alba
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural sand or perlite.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in early spring using a heated propagator at fifteen degrees.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are dry and keep completely dry during winter damp.
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or porch to maximize light and protect from UK frost.
Inspect leaf axils weekly for mealybugs and treat infestations immediately with organic neem oil.

items.name: Crassula alpestris
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active annual in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with 50 percent grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry during its summer dormant phase.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in late summer to match its natural autumn growth cycle.
Keep containers in a frost-free greenhouse or south-facing windowsill to survive wet UK winters.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Crassula alstonii
items.growersTips:
Grow this succulent in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit.
Keep completely dry in winter indoors to prevent rot, watering only when the leaves begin to wrinkle.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or heated greenhouse to maximise essential UK winter sunlight.
Propagate by gently detaching leaf cuttings in late spring and laying them on dry gritty compost.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices and treat immediately with an alcohol-soaked swab.

items.name: Crassula aquatica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring on wet, acidic mud at pond edges, leaving them uncovered to receive light.
Keep the soil constantly saturated or submerged in shallow water, mimicking UK wetland habitats.
Grow in full sun in a garden pond margin to prevent this tiny annual from being shaded out by algae.
Protect from aggressive pond snails and smothering blanket weed which easily overwhelm this species.
Sow alongside slow-growing native oxygenators like Hottonia palustris to avoid being outcompeted.

items.name: Crassula arborescens
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts and keep in a bright unheated room until spring to prevent rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty compost is dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Repot in spring using a mix of two parts John Innes Number 2 to one part horticultural grit or sand.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushy habit and use the cuttings for propagation.
Check leaf crevices weekly for woolly aphids or mealybugs, treating with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Crassula atropurpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a shallow depth of two millimetres using a heated propagator
Grow in a free-draining gritty compost mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter root rot
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry then drench and let drain fully
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or porch to maximise crucial UK autumn sunlight
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn which chew the roots of these succulents in container pots

items.name: Crassula ausensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost without burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, reducing to a trickle in damp autumns.
Grow in pots to easily move them indoors before the first wet frost of a typical UK autumn.
Check the tight leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, which thrive in humid British glasshouses.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into peat-free compost to prevent winter root rot in the UK.

items.name: Crassula barbata
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the rosette completely dry to prevent winter rot.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse kept above five degrees.
Sow the dust-like seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them, keeping them humid.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf hairs and treat immediately with an organic neem oil spray.

items.name: Crassula barklyi
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep completely dry during winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill to protect from frost and damp UK winter weather.
Watch closely for mealybugs hiding between the tightly overlapping, scale-like leaves of the stem.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous for a week before potting.

items.name: Crassula biplanata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to prevent winter rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to a minimum during damp autumn days.
Position in a south-facing window or greenhouse to maximise scarce UK winter and spring sunlight.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in the compost and treat with nematodes in late summer or autumn.
Sow alongside hardy Sedums in pots to create a dry-tolerant display that copes with UK wet spells.

items.name: Crassula brevifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part loam to prevent winter root rot in UK damp.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry, reducing to once a month in winter.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to meet its high winter light needs.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.
Inspect leaf joints weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations immediately with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Crassula capitella
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as it cannot survive UK winters below five degrees Celsius.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, reducing to once a month during winter.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to trigger the vibrant red foliage of the Campfire cultivar.
Take stem cuttings in late spring by letting them callus for three days before potting in grit.

items.name: Crassula clavata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winters.
Water only when soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November to March to prevent rot.
Plant in a mix of fifty percent grit and fifty percent peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximize light and bring out the deep red leaf coloration.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Crassula closiana
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit or perlite.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep completely dry during winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill to protect from frost and damp UK winter rot.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings, letting them callus for three days before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Crassula colligata
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand to prevent rot.
Keep outdoors in summer but move indoors before the first autumn frost to protect from UK damp cold.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month or less during dark winter months.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings, letting them callus for three days before potting up.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Crassula colorata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a free-draining mix of half grit and half peat-free compost.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry, keeping it barely damp during winter.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first autumn frost arrives.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to maximise intense light and prevent leggy growth.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Crassula columella
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-free compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is completely dry from spring to autumn, keeping it dry throughout winter.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors as the damp UK winter cold will rot this tender succulent.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.
Inspect the tight column of velvety leaves regularly for mealybugs hiding in the dense crevices.

items.name: Crassula columnaris
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Keep indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK winter frost.
Do not prune this monocarpic succulent, as it dies naturally after its single, terminal summer bloom.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on the soil surface under glass, maintaining a temperature of 18C.

items.name: Crassula connata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of gritty, free-draining soil without burying them to aid light.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Grow in shallow pots outdoors in full sun to mimic their natural dry, gravelly habitat conditions.
Position near Sedum album in rock gardens to create a compatible, drought-tolerant succulent display.
Protect from heavy autumn rains by moving pots under a cold frame or greenhouse to prevent decay.

items.name: Crassula corallina
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural sand or grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the foliage completely dry to prevent winter rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass with bottom heat to combat cool UK spring soil.
Position in a south-facing cold frame or unheated greenhouse to maximise crucial UK sunlight hours.
Watch closely for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices, treating immediately with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Crassula cotyledonis
items.growersTips:
Bring potted plants indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost to prevent rot.
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of free-draining gritty compost without burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month in damp winter.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural grit to ensure the rapid drainage they need.

items.name: Crassula cultrata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on a gritty, free-draining compost mix without burying them deeply.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out completely to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Grow in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise the limited UK summer sunlight.
Pruning stem tips in early summer encourages a bushier habit and prevents leggy growth.

items.name: Crassula deceptor
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent loam to prevent winter root rot.
Water only from April to September when the soil is dry and keep completely bone dry all winter.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximise scarce UK winter sun.
Check the tight leaf crevices weekly for mealybugs using a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Propagate in late spring by gently detaching side offsets and letting them calloused before potting.

items.name: Crassula decumbens
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with 50% grit or perlite to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, and keep almost dry throughout winter.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect from UK frost.
Propagate in late spring by pressing stem cuttings lightly into damp, sandy compost to root.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during humid UK summers and treat with organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Crassula dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on free-draining gritty compost in spring, barely covering them with fine sand.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil dries completely to prevent stem rot in damp UK air.
Grow in pots on a south-facing windowsill or greenhouse to ensure maximum light and warmth in summer.
Watch for aphids and mealybugs in the leaf joints, treating them with a cotton swab dipped in alcohol.
Sow fresh seeds annually in March as this species is a true annual and will die after flowering.

items.name: Crassula elegans
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring on gritty compost and cover with a very fine layer of vermiculite.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK autumns.
Grow in a terracotta pot to ensure rapid drainage and move indoors before the first winter frosts.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural grit to recreate its native free-draining soil.
Inspect stem bases regularly for mealybugs which thrive in cool British greenhouse conditions.

items.name: Crassula ericoides
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill from October to April to survive UK winters.
Grow in a mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in wet weather.
Water only when the soil is bone dry in summer, and keep completely dry from November to March.
Prune leggy stems by one third in late spring after flowering to maintain a compact, bushy shrub habit.
Check the dense, scale-like foliage weekly for mealybugs, which hide easily in the tight leaf joints.

items.name: Crassula exserta
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny annual in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of equal parts John Innes No 1 and grit.
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly onto the soil surface without covering them with compost.
Water sparingly from below during the spring growing season, keeping the soil dry throughout winter.
Bring pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.
Position containers alongside hardy Sedums or Sempervivums to create a compatible low-water display.

items.name: Crassula glomerata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny annual in a gritty, free-draining soil mix of equal parts loam and horticultural grit.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in spring, keeping them indoors at fifteen degrees Celsius.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry, reducing to almost nothing in damp autumns.
Grow in pots to easily move them under glass or a porch to protect from persistent UK winter wet.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container compost and pick off aphids by hand during humid summers.

items.name: Crassula helmsii
items.growersTips:
Keep this highly invasive weed strictly in sealed garden ponds and never let it escape to waterways.
Grow it in a submerged container to restrict its rapid spread and prevent it choking other plants.
Rake out excess growth in autumn and compost it securely in a closed bin to avoid wild spread.
Check your pond weekly for tiny pink-white flowers in summer to monitor its rapid growth rate.
Do not introduce this plant to any natural UK water body as it is legally banned from the wild.

items.name: Crassula lactea
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts or grow year-round in a bright conservatory to prevent freeze damage.
Water only when the top three centimetres of gritty, peat-free compost is completely dry to the touch.
Prune leggy stems in late spring after winter flowering to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during winter when indoor heating makes air dry and stagnant.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into standard compost to ensure the rapid drainage it requires.

items.name: Crassula marnieriana
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Propagate in spring by snipping stems, drying for two days, then inserting 2cm deep in sharp sand.
Grow in a south-facing window or greenhouse to prevent the trailing stems from stretching out.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices, treating immediately with an alcohol-soaked swab.

items.name: Crassula moschata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty free-draining soil or rockeries to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full coastal sun or bright light to maintain its compact creeping mat-forming habit.
Water sparingly in summer only when soil is dry and keep almost completely dry during winter.
Propagate easily in spring by snipping stem cuttings and inserting them directly into sandy grit.
Protect from severe frosts below minus five Celsius using horticultural fleece or move containers.

items.name: Crassula multicava
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors or move to a frost-free greenhouse from October to April to survive UK winter wet.
Water only when the top three centimetres of gritty, free-draining soil mix has dried out completely.
Propagate easily by pinning the small plantlets that form on spent flower stems directly into compost.
Grow in partial shade rather than full sun to prevent the succulent green leaves from turning red.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in pots during autumn and drench with parasitic nematodes if found.

items.name: Crassula muscosa
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by late September to protect this frost-tender succulent from cold UK winter wet.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty compost are bone dry, reducing to monthly in winter.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for rapid drainage.
Propagate in spring by snipping three-inch stem cuttings and inserting them directly into dry grit.
Watch for mealybugs in the dense, scale-like foliage during dry summer spells under glass.

items.name: Crassula namaquensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a free-draining loam and grit mix to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, keeping it entirely water-free during damp winter days.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before autumn frosts.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to maintain its compact shape and leaf colour.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Crassula nudicaulis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters outside.
Water only when the potting mix is bone dry, reducing to once a month during dull winter months.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost.
Grow on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximise essential daily sunlight.
Propagate in spring by taking leaf cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.

items.name: Crassula ovata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winter temperatures below 5C.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, then drench fully and let it drain completely.
Repot in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free multi-purpose compost and horticultural grit for drainage.
Prune in spring by cutting back to a leaf joint to encourage a bushy, tree-like structure.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to prevent leggy growth and encourage red-edged leaves.
items.description: Crassula ovata, commonly known as jade plant, lucky plant, money plant or money tree, is a succulent plant with small pink or white flowers that is native to the KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape provinces of South Africa, and Mozambique; it is common as a houseplant worldwide. Much of its popularity stems from the low levels of care needed; the jade plant requires little water and can survive in most indoor conditions. It is sometimes referred to as the money tree; however, Pachira aquatica also has this nickname.

items.name: Crassula peduncularis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of free-draining gritty compost without burying them.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry, keeping it barely damp during winter.
Grow in shallow terracotta pots to prevent waterlogging during wet UK autumns and winters.
Position in full sun on a south-facing windowsill or in an unheated greenhouse to prevent legginess.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost and pick off any visible mealybugs with a cotton bud.

items.name: Crassula pellucida
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for essential drainage.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, reducing to once a month during dark winter months.
Take stem cuttings in late spring by letting them callus for two days before potting in sandy soil.
Position in a south-facing window or greenhouse to maintain the vibrant purple leaf margins.

items.name: Crassula perfoliata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October to protect this tender South African succulent from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow in a mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid drainage in damp air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from November through to March.
Position on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximize scarce UK winter sun.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Crassula perforata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African succulent in pots of 50% grit and 50% peat-free compost to ensure drainage
Bring pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect from wet UK winter frosts
Water only when the soil is dry to the touch in summer, and keep almost completely dry in winter
Take stem cuttings in late spring by letting the cut ends dry for three days before potting up
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol

items.name: Crassula picturata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on the surface of free-draining gritty compost in spring under a heated propagator
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Move pots indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect this tender succulent from frost
Snip off faded summer flower stalks at the base in autumn to keep the compact rosette foliage tidy
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into standard peat-free compost to ensure rapid winter drainage

items.name: Crassula pubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them as they need light to germinate.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Grow in a gritty mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural sand for drainage.
Bring pots indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect this tender annual from UK frosts.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more star-shaped flowers.

items.name: Crassula rubricaulis
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill as this succulent cannot survive UK frost
Plant in a gritty cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in wet autumns
Water only when the soil is bone dry then soak thoroughly and let drain completely to mimic drought
Take stem cuttings in June to propagate new plants easily before the cold autumn damp sets in
Position in full south-facing sun to bring out the vibrant red coloration on the leaf margins

items.name: Crassula rupestris
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month during the cold UK winter months.
Keep on a south-facing windowsill indoors or move to a sunny patio only when night temperatures exceed ten degrees.
Prune leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage bushier growth and propagate cuttings.
Check leaf crevices regularly for mealybugs, treating infestations with an organic neem oil spray.

items.name: Crassula sarcocaulis
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a rockery to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm house wall to mimic its native Drakensberg habitat.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then withhold water entirely in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the bonsai-like stems and remove dieback.
Provide fleece protection or move potted specimens under a cold glasshouse if temperatures drop below -5C.

items.name: Crassula sarmentosa
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters below freezing temperatures.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand.
Water thoroughly only when the soil dries out completely, then keep dry throughout winter.
Take stem cuttings in late spring to easily propagate new plants and maintain a compact habit.
Place on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to get the best red-edged leaf variegation.

items.name: Crassula setulosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month from October to March in UK wet cold.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them as they require light to germinate.
Protect from slugs and snails in damp UK springs using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or cold frame to shield from persistent autumn rain.

items.name: Crassula sieberiana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the surface of free-draining gritty compost without covering them with soil
Grow in unheated greenhouses or alpine sinks to protect the shallow roots from winter wet rot
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry and stop watering completely during winter dormancy
Position in full south-facing sun to prevent the delicate stems from stretching and losing color
Plant alongside sedums in shallow gravel scree beds to ensure rapid drainage during heavy UK rains

items.name: Crassula spathulata
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before the first autumn frost as this tender South African succulent cannot survive UK winters.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month during the dark, cold winter months.
Take stem cuttings in late spring to easily propagate new plants before the active summer growth.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximize light levels during the overcast British winter.

items.name: Crassula subaphylla
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining gritty loam with fifty percent horticultural sand to prevent winter root rot
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry and keep completely dry in winter
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or cold frame to maximise scarce UK winter sunlight
Protect from frost by moving pots indoors to a cool windowsill when temperatures drop below five C
Propagate from stem cuttings in late spring by letting them callus for three days before potting up

items.name: Crassula tecta
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, keeping it bone dry throughout the damp UK winter.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light and prevent the compact rosettes stretching.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this succulent cannot survive wet UK frosts.
Watch for mealybugs in the tight leaf crevices, treating infestations with an alcohol-soaked swab.

items.name: Crassula tetragona
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts or grow year-round in a bright south-facing UK windowsill.
Water only when the gritty compost is dry to the touch, reducing to once a month during winter.
Mix two parts horticultural grit with one part peat-free compost to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Prune leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushy, bonsai-like shrub habit.
Propagate easily in summer by drying stem cuttings for three days before inserting into dry grit.

items.name: Crassula tillaea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface of sharply draining gravelly paths to mimic UK wild habitats.
Water only during extreme summer droughts to prevent this damp-sensitive annual from rotting away.
Weed hand-pull competitors in spring to prevent vigorous garden plants from smothering this tiny succulent.
Plant alongside slow-growing stonecrops in gritty scree beds to prevent soil erosion on dry banks.
Allow the plant to turn red in full summer sun and self-seed naturally before it dies back in autumn.

items.name: Crassula umbella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they need winter light and cool UK temperatures to sprout.
Water only from below when the soil dries completely to prevent the delicate cup-shaped leaves from rotting.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural grit.
Keep in a frost-free greenhouse or bright UK windowsill as this winter-grower damages below five degrees.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in winter which target the shallow root system of this delicate succulent.

items.name: Crassula vaillantii
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil with 50 percent horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month in damp UK winters.
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly onto the soil surface without burying them.
Grow in shallow pots that can be moved indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill by October.
Position in full south-facing sun to bring out the vibrant red stress coloration on the foliage.

items.name: Crataegus × lavalleei
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough hybrid in full sun to get the very best autumn leaf colour and brightest red berries.
Prune your tree in late winter to keep its shape neat and remove any dangerous, sharp thorns.
Water deeply every week during its first dry UK summer to help the deep root system establish well.
Watch out for leaf blight in wet UK springs, clearing away fallen leaves to stop the fungus spreading.
Grow it in fertile, well-drained soil, but don't worry if your garden has heavy clay or alkaline chalk.

items.name: Crataegus ×media
items.growersTips:
Plant Pauls Scarlet in late autumn to let winter rains settle the roots before spring bud burst.
Prune your tree in midsummer after flowering to keep its shape without losing next years blossoms.
Watch out for leaf blight in wet UK summers by clearing fallen leaves to stop the fungus wintering.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to help the roots establish quickly.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like daffodils to bring colour before the hawthorn leaves emerge.

items.name: Crataegus aestivalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mayhaw in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil to mimic its native boggy home.
Give it a generous bucket of water weekly during dry UK summers, especially while it establishes.
Prune in late winter to shape the shrub and clear out any dead wood before the spring sap rises.
Watch out for fireblight in warm, wet UK springs, cutting back affected branches to healthy wood.
Underplant with moisture-loving native ferns or hostas to keep the root zone cool and damp.

items.name: Crataegus altaica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Altai hawthorn in deep, well-draining loam to copy its native cold, dry Asian hillsides.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers until its deep taproot is fully established.
Prune in late winter to shape the shrub and clear out crossing branches before spring growth starts.
Watch out for fireblight in warm, wet UK springs, pruning out any blackened twigs immediately.
Underplant with wild daffodils to create a lovely spring display that thrives in its light shade.

items.name: Crataegus ambigua
items.growersTips:
Plant this Russian hawthorn in autumn so UK winter rains can settle its roots deep into clay soil.
Prune your shrub in late winter to shape it, keeping an eye out for any signs of fireblight damage.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to lock in moisture and boost those gorgeous red berries.
Watch out for hawthorn sawfly larvae in June, which can quickly skeletonize the lovely foliage.
Grow it alongside native wild privet to create a wildlife-friendly, wind-resistant garden hedge.

items.name: Crataegus apiifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this parsley-leaved hawthorn in deep, fertile, moisture-retentive clay soil to mimic UK fens.
Prune lightly in late winter, focusing only on congested branches to keep its lovely weeping shape.
Watch out for fireblight in warm UK springs, cutting infected wood back to healthy green growth.
Water deeply once a week during dry English summers until its taproot system is fully established.
Underplant with wild garlic or wood anemones to create a natural, damp-loving British woodland edge.

items.name: Crataegus azarolus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mediterranean medlar in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to help the yellow fruit ripen.
Keep young plants well-watered during dry UK summers, but let the soil dry out between waterings.
Prune in late winter to remove crossing branches and keep the centre open for maximum sunlight.
Watch out for fireblight in warm, wet springs, and prune out any blackened shoots immediately.
Grow it in free-draining, chalky or loamy soil; avoid heavy clay that holds winter wetness.

items.name: Crataegus berberifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this hawthorn in autumn so UK winter rains can settle the roots before the spring growing season.
Keep a sharp eye out for pear slug sawfly larvae in summer and wash them off with a firm water spray.
Prune in late winter to shape the canopy and remove crossed branches while the plant is still dormant.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your clay soil before planting to help with drainage and grit.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers until the root system is fully established.

items.name: Crataegus brachyacantha
items.growersTips:
Plant this blue hawthorn in deep, moisture-retentive clay soil to mimic its native wet valley home.
Water deeply every week during dry UK summers until its root system is fully established in your lawn.
Prune in late winter before the buds burst to keep its shrubby, multi-stemmed habit nice and tidy.
Watch out for fireblight in warm, wet springs, cutting back affected branches to healthy wood.
Underplant with moisture-loving wood anemones to create a beautiful, naturalistic British woodland look.

items.name: Crataegus brainerdii
items.growersTips:
Plant this hawthorn in autumn so UK winter rains can settle the roots before the spring growth.
Prune in late winter before buds break to keep its shrubby shape and remove any crossing branches.
Watch out for leaf miners in summer; pick off affected leaves early to keep the foliage healthy.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your clay soil before planting to help with drainage.
Grow it near wild garlic or bluebells to create a lovely, natural British woodland edge look.

items.name: Crataegus calpodendron
items.growersTips:
Plant this pear hawthorn in deep, fertile, well-draining loam to prevent waterlogging in wet winters.
Prune in late winter before buds break, focusing on thinning the canopy to let UK summer light in.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells for the first two years to establish roots.
Watch out for fireblight in warm, wet springs, and prune out any blackened, dying shoots immediately.
Underplant with early spring bulbs like wild daffodils to bring color before the hawthorn leaves emerge.

items.name: Crataegus chlorosarca
items.growersTips:
Pop this black-berried hawthorn in a sunny spot with heavy clay soil to get the best autumn colour.
