Plant corms in late summer at a depth of 8cm in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in a cool, partially shaded rock garden or alpine house to mimic their native damp meadows.
Keep the soil consistently moist during their active late summer flowering and autumn growth phase.
Protect the delicate autumn blooms from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps.
Avoid dry summer baking by top-dressing the soil with leaf mould to retain cool moisture.

items.name: Crocus veluchensis
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8cm deep in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun or dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native Balkan woodland.
Avoid watering during their dormant summer phase from July to September to prevent the corms rotting.
Leave foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after spring flowering to feed next year's bloom.
Protect emerging spring buds from slugs and house sparrows using copper tape or physical barriers.

items.name: Crocus vernus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to protect them from winter frosts and foraging squirrels.
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winter clay will rot the bulbs; add grit to the planting hole.
Protect emerging spring buds from birds by placing physical barriers or black cotton thread nearby.
Let the foliage die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing lawns with crocuses.
Divide congested clumps in late spring after flowering to maintain vigorous blooms in future years.

items.name: Crocus versicolor
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm to 10cm in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in full sun to ensure the delicate striped petals fully open during cool UK spring days.
Protect emerging buds from mice and birds by covering the planting area with fine wire mesh.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing your lawn.
Divide congested clumps in late summer while the bulbs are dormant to maintain vigorous flowering.

items.name: Crocus vitellinus
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full south-facing sun to ensure the winter-blooming flowers open fully on cold days.
Keep soil dry during summer dormancy by planting under deciduous shrubs to mimic native dry heat.
Protect emerging winter buds from slugs and birds using copper tape or physical wire cloches.
Grow in terracotta pots of loam-based grit mix to easily shelter them from persistent UK rain.

items.name: Croptilon divaricatum
items.growersTips:
Sow these slender scratch-daisy seeds shallowly in April, barely covering them with gritty compost.
Keep them in your sunniest, sharp-draining border to mimic their native dry, sandy pineland soil.
Water young seedlings sparingly, only when the top two inches of gritty UK soil feel bone dry.
Watch out for damp October slugs, as our wet autumns can quickly rot their delicate, wiry stems.
Grow them alongside hardy UK coastal grasses to give their floppy, sprawling stems natural support.

items.name: Croptilon hookerianum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect these Texas natives from wet UK spring chills.
Keep soil gritty and sharply drained, mimicking their sandy home to prevent root rot in damp rain.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out fully between drinks to avoid mildew.
Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to help create the hot, dry microclimate they love.
Deadhead the yellow daisy-like blooms regularly through August to keep new flowers coming.

items.name: Croptilon rigidifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect them from late British spring frosts.
Plant them in very sandy, free-draining soil to mimic their native dry scrubland habitat.
Position this sun-lover in your hottest south-facing border to ensure it gets maximum summer light.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely to prevent root rot.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums and thymes which thrive in the same dry, nutrient-poor conditions.

items.name: Crossandra
items.growersTips:
Bring your firecracker flower indoors by October to protect it from chilly British winter frosts.
Water with lukewarm rainwater only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to touch.
Snip off faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of bright orange blooms.
Mist the leaves daily or place the pot on wet pebbles to counter dry indoor central heating air.
Repot in spring using a mix of multi-purpose compost and perlite to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Crossandra infundibuliformis
items.growersTips:
Bring your firecracker flower indoors by mid-September before UK night temperatures drop below 10C.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of peat-free, acidic potting mix feels dry.
Snip off faded flower spikes just above the leaves in autumn to keep new orange blooms coming.
Mist the leaves daily or use a wet pebble tray to tackle dry indoor air from central heating.
Check leaf undersides weekly for spider mites, especially during winter when radiators are on.

items.name: Crotalarieae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 1cm depth using a heated propagator to beat the cool British spring.
Water these drought-tolerant annuals only when the top 5cm of gritty, free-draining soil is dry.
Squeeze young stems in June to encourage a bushier habit and more of those yellow pea-like flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you are starting them early in a damp UK greenhouse.
Plant them alongside French marigolds to deter nematodes in your sunny, sheltered border soil.

items.name: Crudia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect young seedlings from late frosts
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure sharp drainage
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to support the deep taproot system
Check regularly for slugs and snails in June as they target the tender young Fabaceae foliage
Apply a potassium-rich liquid feed in July to encourage flowering before the autumn damp sets in

items.name: Crudia zeylanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator set to twenty-one Celsius
Grow in a south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to mimic its native tropical warmth and humidity
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the loam-based compost consistently moist but never waterlogged
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer to support its legume flowering
Monitor closely for glasshouse red spider mite and maintain high humidity to deter infestations

items.name: Crupina crupinastrum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in spring about five millimetres deep once the UK frost risk has fully passed.
Keep soil on the dry side and avoid heavy watering to prevent root rot in our damp UK climate.
Plant this annual in poor, sandy soil to stop it growing too leggy and flopping over in the wind.
Watch out for slugs and snails which love to devour the tender young seedlings in damp spring weather.
Grow them alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary to match their need for sharp drainage and sun.

items.name: Crupina vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of one centimetre directly into poor, well-drained soil in full sun.
Avoid watering this drought-tolerant annual once established to prevent root rot in damp UK clay.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails which love to devour the young seedlings in wet springs.
Grow it alongside gravel-loving companions like wild thyme and sedums that thrive in dry conditions.
Deadhead the purple flowers promptly in late summer to stop this vigorous self-seeder from spreading.

items.name: Cryptantha
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Water only during prolonged summer droughts keeping the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew issues
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in spring using beer traps or physical copper barriers
Grow alongside drought-tolerant alpines like Sedum or Sempervivum in containers to control moisture

items.name: Cryptantha affinis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to allow natural winter cold stratification.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet United Kingdom winters.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to mimic its native dry habitat.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise warmth and prevent damp-related fungal issues.
Plant alongside drought-tolerant sedums or wild thyme which share its low-nutrient soil needs.

items.name: Cryptantha ambigua
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet British winter rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells once the root system is fully established.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent leggy growth.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers in damp weather.

items.name: Cryptantha angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a gritty, free-draining alpine compost mix to prevent winter root rot.
Keep plants in pots to move under a cold frame or greenhouse to shelter them from wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry, mimicking its arid natural habitat.
Position in the brightest, south-facing spot of your garden to maximize essential summer sunlight.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a heated propagator to overcome cool British temperatures.

items.name: Cryptantha cinerea
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a mix of equal parts grit and compost to survive damp UK winters.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the soil dry out completely between sparse soakings.
Position your pot in the brightest, most sun-baked spot of your garden to mimic its home climate.
Protect it from winter wet by moving the pot into a cold frame or unheated greenhouse from October.
Grow it alongside hardy sedums in a raised alpine bed to ensure excellent drainage and companion fit.

items.name: Cryptantha clevelandii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural cold stratification.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet United Kingdom winters.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil is completely dry to the touch.
Position in a south-facing border or unheated greenhouse to maximise essential summer sunlight.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using physical barriers or organic pellets.

items.name: Cryptantha confertiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-heavy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm wall to mimic its native dry desert habitat.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, keeping the crown completely dry in winter.
Protect from winter wet using a rain shelter or cloche from October through to March.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to allow natural winter stratification.

items.name: Cryptantha crassisepala
items.growersTips:
Plant this thick-seeded borage in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy for spring.
Keep watering to a minimum, only soaking them during prolonged hot, dry summer spells.
Grow them in pots you can move under a cold frame to protect their roots from winter rot.
Plant alongside sedums in your rock garden to ensure they get the sharp drainage they crave.

items.name: Cryptantha crinita
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained alkaline grit or scree mix to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn under cold frames to mimic natural winter chilling for germination
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells keeping the crown dry to prevent fungal infections
Position in full south-facing sun against a warm wall to maximise summer heat in the UK climate
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring as new hairy foliage emerges in damp British weather

items.name: Cryptantha flava
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert beauty in a mix of three parts grit to one part compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a terracotta pot under a cold frame or porch to shield the crown from persistent rain.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting down to absolutely zero water from October to March.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors in a cold frame, barely covering them with a thin layer of fine grit.
Place your pot in the brightest, most south-facing sun trap in your garden to mimic its home.

items.name: Cryptantha flavoculata
items.growersTips:
Plant this yellow-flowered borage in a raised bed or rockery with fifty percent grit for drainage.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a glass cloche or cold frame during damp UK winters.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry North American habitat.

items.name: Cryptantha intermedia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in free-draining gritty compost to allow winter chilling for germination.
Grow in a raised bed or gravel garden to protect the taproot from wet UK winter rot.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to mimic its native dry habitat.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise warmth and prevent leggy growth in overcast UK weather.
Plant alongside native UK drought-lovers like Sedum to share the same dry, low-nutrient soil.

items.name: Cryptantha leiocarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to mimic natural cold winter stratification.
Grow in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, allowing the gritty substrate to dry fully.
Position in the brightest, south-facing spot possible to maximise essential British summer sunshine.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers.

items.name: Cryptantha microstachys
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in autumn to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet British winter rot.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between times.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent leggy growth.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using grit barriers or beer traps in damp weather.

items.name: Cryptantha minima
items.growersTips:
Grow this little borage family gem in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the seeds shallowly in autumn so the cold winter weather naturally triggers their germination.
Position this sun-lover in your brightest rock garden spot to mimic its native dry grasslands.
Water very sparingly, only during prolonged dry spells, as damp roots will quickly rot this plant.
Plant alongside low-growing thymes or sedums which won't crowd out its delicate, tiny white blooms.

items.name: Cryptantha muricata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost mix to mimic scree conditions.
Grow in terracotta pots to prevent root rot during wet UK winters and move under glass to stay dry.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry, reducing to zero watering during winter.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise limited UK summer warmth.
Surround the base with a sharp grit mulch to keep the foliage dry and prevent damp-induced decay.

items.name: Cryptantha nevadensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained, gritty soil or a raised scree bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn and leave pots outdoors to undergo natural winter chilling for germination.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in spring using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Position in the sunniest, most south-facing spot of your garden to mimic its native desert light.

items.name: Cryptantha osterhoutii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Utah native in a raised bed of 70% grit and 30% compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep watering to a absolute minimum, only drenching it during prolonged dry summer spells.
Sow the seeds in cold frames during autumn so UK winter chills can naturally break their dormancy.
Position this sun-lover in your hottest, south-facing spot, completely unshaded by larger plants.
Guard the gritty crown with a layer of pure granite chippings to prevent rot from damp UK soil.

items.name: Cryptantha pterocarya
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 2mm in a cold frame to mimic natural winter chilling.
Grow in a gritty, free-draining soil mix with 50 percent grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, reducing to zero watering during damp winter months.
Protect plants from slugs and snails in early spring using copper tape around pots or gravel mulches.
Position in a south-facing unheated greenhouse or gravel garden to maximise crucial summer sun.

items.name: Cryptantha roosiorum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a raised bed of ninety percent alpine grit and ten percent loam to survive wet UK winters.
Protect from autumn rain using a glass pane or open-sided cloche to prevent winter crown rot.
Water only during active spring growth when the top five centimetres of gritty substrate is dry.
Sow seeds in cold frames during January to allow natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Plant alongside low-growing Sempervivum in full south-facing sun to ensure rapid soil drainage.

items.name: Cryptantha scoparia
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert gem in a mix of three parts grit to one part compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a porch to shield it from heavy autumn rain.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, mimicking its native arid home, and stop watering by October.
Position your pot on a south-facing brick patio to soak up every bit of precious British sunshine.
Watch out for slugs in spring, as they love to munch on the fuzzy, bristly leaves of young plants.

items.name: Cryptantha subcapitata
items.growersTips:
Plant this dry-loving borage family gem in a raised gravel bed to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds in autumn just under the grit surface so winter chills can naturally trigger sprouting.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, letting the gritty soil dry out completely in between.
Protect the hairy foliage from rot by placing a glass cloche over the crown from November to March.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums and sedums which thrive in the same sharply drained UK soils.

items.name: Cryptantha virginensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a pot with ninety percent grit to survive wet British winters outdoors.
Keep it completely dry under a cold frame or greenhouse glass from October through to late March.
Plant seeds just barely covered in sandy compost during early spring on a sunny windowsill.
Position your pots in the absolute hottest, brightest south-facing spot in your garden.
Water only when the potting mix is bone dry, and never let water sit in the central rosette.

items.name: Cryptochilus
items.growersTips:
Grow Cryptochilus albidus in a free-draining bark, perlite and chopped sphagnum moss compost mix.
Position in bright, indirect light in a cool greenhouse or conservatory with winter lows of 10C.
Water thoroughly with rainwater when the potting medium dries out, reducing this frequency in winter.
Maintain high humidity around the orchid by placing the pot on a tray of wet clay pebbles or leca.
Repot only when the orchid outgrows its container, doing so in spring just as new growth commences.

items.name: Cryptocoryne
items.growersTips:
Grow these aquatic beauties in a warm indoor tank or a heated conservatory to beat the UK chill.
Plant them with their crowns just above the gravel to prevent rot in your indoor water garden.
Keep your tank water chemistry stable to stop the dreaded melt when you first bring them home.
Feed them with root tabs placed in the substrate rather than liquid fertilizers in the water.
Give them low to moderate light to prevent algae from smothering their slow-growing leaves.

items.name: Cryptocoryne ×willisii
items.growersTips:
Keep this aquatic plant in a heated indoor tank as our chilly UK climate is far too cold for outside.
Plant the crowns just above your aquarium gravel to prevent the delicate rhizome from rotting away.
Use root tabs in a clay-based substrate to feed this heavy root-feeder since UK tap water lacks iron.
Do not panic if it sheds leaves when first planted; it is just adjusting to your local water chemistry.
Keep aquarium lighting moderate and stable to prevent algae from smothering its slow-growing leaves.

items.name: Cryptocoryne albida
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical aquatic perennial in a heated indoor aquarium to survive the chilly UK climate.
Plant it with the crown just above the gravel to prevent rot in your indoor tank or heated terrarium.
Add a nutrient-rich root tab underneath the substrate to feed this slow-growing, heavy root feeder.
Keep water temperatures steady at twenty-two degrees Celsius to prevent the dreaded crypto melt.
Place it under moderate, diffused LED light to stop green algae from smothering its narrow leaves.

items.name: Cryptocoryne beckettii
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic plant submerged in your indoor tropical tank or in a warm, humid winter terrarium.
Plant the crown just above the gravel surface to prevent the delicate rhizome from rotting away.
Keep your tank water between twenty and twenty-six degrees Celsius to mimic its tropical home.
Do not panic if leaves melt after planting; they will soon grow back adapted to your local water.
Feed it with root tabs pushed deep into the substrate to provide a steady supply of iron.

items.name: Cryptocoryne spiralis
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic perennial submerged in a heated indoor aquarium to survive the chilly UK climate.
Plant its roots gently in a nutrient-rich aquarium soil, keeping the crown just above the gravel.
Feed this heavy root-feeder with aquarium root tabs pushed into the substrate every six months.
Prune decaying outer leaves at the base using sharp aquascaping scissors to prevent water rot.
Keep your tank water between twenty and twenty-eight degrees Celsius to avoid crypt melt.

items.name: Cryptocoryne walkeri
items.growersTips:
Keep this aquatic plant fully submerged in a heated indoor tank as it won't survive UK winter frost.
Plant the roots firmly in nutrient-rich aquarium soil but keep the crown just above the substrate.
Avoid moving it once planted to prevent melt, a shock response where all the leaves disintegrate.
Grow it alongside Anubias or Java fern which thrive in the same low-light and warm water conditions.
Trim decaying outer leaves at the base using sharp aquascaping scissors to encourage new growth.

items.name: Cryptocoryne wendtii
items.growersTips:
Plant this aquatic perennial in a heated indoor aquarium as it will not survive UK winter cold outdoors.
Keep the crown just above the gravel to prevent rot when planting this slow-growing rosette.
Add iron-rich root tabs to your substrate to prevent the leaves from melting in soft UK tap water.
Do not move it once planted because this fussy species hates root disturbance and will drop leaves.
Prune decaying outer leaves at the base in autumn to encourage fresh, compact growth for winter.

items.name: Cryptocoryneae
items.growersTips:
Keep these aquarium plants in indoor heated tanks as they cannot survive the chilly UK winter frost.
Plant them with their crowns just above the gravel to prevent the rhizome from rotting in your tank.
Avoid moving them once planted to prevent crypt melt, where they drop all their leaves from shock.
Feed these heavy root feeders by pushing clay nutrient tabs deep into the substrate near their base.
Pair them with low-light mosses or anubias that thrive in the same shady spots under your tank lights.

items.name: Cryptogramma acrostichoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this parsley fern in gritty, acidic scree or rock crevices to mimic its native scree slopes.
Water it consistently in dry summer spells but ensure the drainage is sharp to prevent winter rot.
Nestle it next to dwarf ericaceous shrubs or small hostas that thrive in cool, damp UK shade.
Avoid rich garden soil; instead, mix plenty of non-limestone grit and peat-free compost into the site.
Keep an eye out for slugs in spring, as they love the tender new unfurling fertile fronds.

items.name: Cryptogramma cascadensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Cascade parsley fern in a north-facing, lime-free rock crevice using acidic gritty compost.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Mimic its mountain home by top-dressing with granite chippings to keep the root crown cool and dry.
Protect the delicate fronds from drying out in summer by placing it in a humid, sheltered UK spot.
Grow it alongside dwarf acid-loving vacciniums or small ericaceous plants in a shaded alpine trough.

items.name: Cryptogramma crispa
items.growersTips:
Nestle this parsley fern into a north-facing rock crevice or scree bed to mimic its mountain home.
Mix lots of slate chippings or grit into acidic, lime-free soil to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Water regularly with stored rainwater, keeping the roots damp but never sitting in stagnant pools.
Leave the old fronds intact over winter to naturally shelter the crown from severe UK frosts.
Plant it alongside dwarf heathers or bilberries which thrive in the same acidic, rocky conditions.

items.name: Cryptogramma stelleri
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate fern in a sheltered, north-facing rock crevice to mimic its cool upland home.
Mix plenty of limestone grit into moist, alkaline soil to keep its roots happy and well-drained.
Water gently with harvested rainwater to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged during summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the soft, emerging fronds.
Grow it alongside small, shade-loving alpine plants like Saxifraga for a natural mountain look.

items.name: Cryptogrammoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant parsley ferns in acidic, gritty slate scree or rock crevices to mimic their native UK fells.
Keep the soil damp but exceptionally well-drained, as they hate winter wetness in soggy UK clay.
Tuck them into a north-facing rockery where they get cool shade and protection from midday sun.
Leave the dead fronds on over winter to protect the crown, then gently snip them away in April.
Grow them alongside dwarf heather or bilberry which love the same acidic, rocky upland conditions.

items.name: Cryptolepis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African vine in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for UK winters.
Water sparingly in winter but keep the soil damp during its active summer growing phase.
Plant it in a free-draining mix of loam and perlite to prevent root rot in damp British weather.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk in late spring to support its vigorous twining stems.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in warm, dry indoor winter conditions.

items.name: Cryptolepis africana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African climber in a pot so you can move it inside before the first UK winter frost.
Water it generously in summer but let the gritty, free-draining soil dry out fully between drinks.
Position your pot in your sunniest south-facing conservatory or patio spot to mimic its warm home.
Prune the stems lightly in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its vigorous vines tidy.
Feed it a diluted potash-rich liquid fertiliser once a month from May to August to boost its health.

items.name: Cryptolepis capensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into peat-free compost to keep the roots dry during wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this vine hates sitting in soggy compost.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk in spring to support its twining stems as they start to grow.
Check the leaf axils regularly for mealybugs, especially when keeping the plant indoors in winter.

items.name: Cryptolepis cryptolepioides
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender African climber indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from cold.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy, free-draining compost to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry, then let the pot drain fully.
Prune back unruly stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flowers.
Position your pot in a south-facing conservatory or sunny patio corner for maximum summer heat.

items.name: Cryptolepis decidua
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender African vine in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during wet British autumns and winters.
Water sparingly from May to September, letting the soil dry out completely between each watering.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk in spring to support its twining, leafless rush-like stems.
Keep a sharp eye out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in a warm, dry conservatory.

items.name: Cryptolepis dubia
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse before autumn frosts.
Plant in a very free-draining sandy loam mix to protect its delicate roots from wet UK winters.
Water generously through the summer growing season but let the soil dry out completely in winter.
Prune back lightly in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more of its small yellow flowers.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in warm, dry indoor or conservatory spaces.

items.name: Cryptolepis oblongifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare African climber indoors or into a heated conservatory before the first autumn frost.
Grow it in a very free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part grit to prevent rot.
Water only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, cutting back to once a month in winter.
Position your pot in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic its warm native habitat.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer once a month from May to August to boost leafy growth.

items.name: Cryptolepis sanguinolenta
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender African vine indoors before October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winters.
Grow it in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure fast drainage in damp weather.
Keep the soil barely damp during dark winter months, then water weekly once spring growth begins.
