items.name: Cyanea stictophylla
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian native indoors by October to protect its tender leaves from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a deep pot using acidic, ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, never letting it dry out or sit in water.
Position your pot in dappled shade to mimic its forest home and prevent the leaves from scorching.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in summer and mist the foliage daily to keep them away.

items.name: Cyanea superba
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Hawaiian palm-like plant indoors to a heated conservatory before autumn frosts hit.
Keep the compost moist but never soggy, using harvested rainwater instead of hard UK tap water.
Grow it in a large, deep pot filled with free-draining ericaceous compost mixed with perlite.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light, keeping it well away from cold draughty windows.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor winter heating.

items.name: Cyanea truncata
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian gem indoors by autumn to protect its frost-sensitive stems from UK freezes.
Grow it in a deep pot using a well-draining, acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mix.
Position your pot in dappled shade to mimic its natural forest home and prevent leaf scorch.
Keep the soil consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge, never letting it dry out or waterlog.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in winter and mist the leaves daily to deter them.

items.name: Cyanicula
items.growersTips:
Plant these delicate Australian orchids in a gritty, free-draining mix of peat and perlite.
Keep the tubers completely dry during their summer dormancy to prevent them from rotting.
Place your pots in a bright, frost-free greenhouse to shelter them from wet UK winters.
Water gently from autumn to spring, mimicking the damp but never soggy Mediterranean winter.
Repot the tiny tubers annually in late summer, burying them about three centimetres deep.

items.name: Cyclachaena
items.growersTips:
Pull up this invasive annual early in spring before its deep taproot makes manual weeding difficult.
Wear gloves when handling this plant to protect your skin from its highly irritating sap and pollen.
Snip off the greenish flower heads in July before they set seed to stop them invading your borders.
Grow it in poor, dry soil if you want to restrict its height and prevent it from swamping neighbours.
Do not compost any cleared plants; bag and dispose of them to prevent seeds spreading in the wind.

items.name: Cycladenia
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare gem in a cold frame to protect its delicate roots from relentless UK winter wet.
Mix plenty of gritty limestone chippings into your compost to mimic its native rocky Californian soil.
Water very sparingly from May to August, letting the gritty potting mix dry out completely between sessions.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this plant under cover in summer.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Cyclocodon lancifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan perennial in a sheltered, woodland-style spot with dappled shade to mimic its home.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into the soil to ensure it stays moisture-retentive.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Mulch heavily with autumn leaves in November to protect the root crown from severe winter frosts.

items.name: Cyclodium
items.growersTips:
Plant this shade-loving fern in moist, acidic woodland soil enriched with plenty of leaf mould.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering deeply during dry UK summer spells.
Apply a thick mulch of chipped bark in late autumn to protect its crown from severe winter frosts.
Snip off old, tattered fronds in early spring just as the fiddleheads begin to unfurl at the base.
Divide mature clumps in spring, replanting them at the same depth alongside hostas and astilbes.

items.name: Cyclodium meniscioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-loving fern in a sheltered, fully shaded spot to mimic its native rainforest.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted compost to create the acidic, humus-rich soil it needs.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summers.
Protect its delicate fronds from drying winds by planting it alongside hostas or astilbes.
Mulch the crown with bark in late autumn to insulate it from wet, freezing UK winter temperatures.

items.name: Cyclolepis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March to beat the cool UK spring, then transplant out after May frosts.
Plant them in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent root rot during our wet British summers.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails on young shoots during damp UK spring nights using beer traps.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly through August to keep the plants flowering right up until the autumn.

items.name: Cyclophorus
items.growersTips:
Grow this epiphytic fern in a highly porous, bark-rich orchid mix to survive damp UK winters.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of compost dries out to prevent root rot.
Keep your potted specimen indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it will not survive UK frosts.
Wipe the leathery fronds with a damp cloth in spring to clear dust and boost light absorption.
Group it with bird's nest ferns to create a humid microclimate that mimics its tropical home.

items.name: Cyclopogon
items.growersTips:
Grow this terrestrial orchid in a free-draining, bark-based compost to mimic its forest floor home.
Keep your plant in a warm, humid bathroom or terrarium to shield it from dry UK indoor heating.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than tap water, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Watch out for fungus gnats in spring and use yellow sticky traps near the pot to catch them early.
Position in bright, indirect light near an east-facing windowsill, avoiding harsh midday UK sun.

items.name: Cylindrocline commersonii
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to mimic their native heat.
Prick out seedlings into individual pots of gritty, free-draining compost to prevent root rot.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot on your patio once the late May frosts have fully passed.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top inch of soil feels dry, keeping the foliage dry.
Bring plants into a bright conservatory by October to prolong their unique silvery leaf display.

items.name: Cylindrocline lorencei
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March using a heated propagator to mimic its native tropical warmth.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering from below to prevent seedling rot.
Grow this critically endangered beauty in pots so you can move it inside before autumn frosts hit.
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potassium liquid seaweed to encourage healthy leaf growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this rare shrubby plant sheltered indoors.

items.name: Cylindrolobus aporoides
items.growersTips:
Keep this orchid in a warm conservatory as our chilly UK winters will kill it if left outdoors.
Water it only when the bark compost dries out completely to prevent its delicate roots from rotting.
Hang its trailing stems in a bright spot with filtered light to mimic its natural canopy home.
Feed it weekly with a weak orchid fertilizer during summer then stop entirely over the winter.
Repot every two years in autumn using a chunky bark mix to keep the drainage sharp and fresh.

items.name: Cylindrophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant your Cylindrophyllum in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep this South African native in a sunny pot so you can move it indoors before the first frost.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through March.
Tuck some pea gravel around the plant base to keep the succulent leaves from touching damp soil.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums in a shallow alpine trough for a lovely dry-garden display.

items.name: Cylindrophyllum calamiforme
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African succulent in a grit-heavy, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or porch by October.
Water only when the cylindrical leaves wrinkle slightly, and keep it completely dry through winter.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or patio to maximise the scarce UK summer sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense leaf clumps, and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Cylindrophyllum tugwelliae
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African succulent in a mix of half grit and half compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill by October.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through to March.
Protect the low fleshy leaves from slugs and snails which love to feast on them in damp UK springs.
Give it your sunniest south-facing patio spot to mimic its native desert and trigger summer blooms.

items.name: Cymbalaria
items.growersTips:
Tuck Cymbalaria muralis into damp mortar gaps or dry stone walls with just a pinch of gritty compost.
Water newly tucked-in plugs weekly during dry UK springs until their roots grip the brickwork.
Shear back the faded foliage in autumn to stop this enthusiastic self-seeder from overtaking lawns.
Watch out for slugs on tender new spring shoots, especially in damp, shaded corners of your garden.
Pair it with native hart's tongue ferns in shady, north-facing wall crevices for a lush green look.

items.name: Cymbalaria muralis
items.growersTips:
Tuck it into dry stone walls or paving gaps with just a pinch of gritty compost to anchor the roots.
Water newly tucked-in plants weekly, but once established in damp UK shade, leave them to dry rain.
Snip back the trailing stems in late autumn to keep this enthusiastic self-seeder from taking over.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love hiding under the damp, ivy-like leaves in mild UK winters.
Pair it with native hart's tongue ferns in shady, north-facing brickwork for a classic cottage look.

items.name: Cymbalaria pallida
items.growersTips:
Plant this Italian toadflax in gritty, well-draining soil in a sunny rock garden or wall crevice.
Water sparingly once established, only during dry summer spells to prevent the roots from rotting.
Trim back the trailing stems in late autumn to keep its spread neat and encourage fresh spring growth.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, especially during damp UK April weather.
Pair it with Sedum or Thymus in paving gaps where they can happily scramble together.

items.name: Cymbidiinae
items.growersTips:
Put your cymbidiums outdoors from June to September in light shade to trigger those winter blooms.
Water copiously once a week in summer, letting it drain fully so the roots never sit in soggy compost.
Feed with a high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer in spring, switching to high-potash from late summer.
Repot every three years in spring using a chunky bark-based orchid mix, keeping the pseudobulbs high.
Bring them inside before the first autumn frost to a cool room around ten to fifteen degrees Celsius.

items.name: Cynanchum
items.growersTips:
Tuck Cynanchum acutum into sharply draining chalky soil to mimic its native UK coastal habitats.
Water your established swallow-wort only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot.
Prune the vigorous twining stems right back to the base in late autumn to keep them in bounds.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids on the tender new spring shoots and wash them off with a hose.
Grow it up a sturdy trellis alongside hardy jasmines to support its scrambling climbing habit.

items.name: Cynanchum acidum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of gritty cactus compost so you can bring it indoors for winter.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly but never let the pot sit in water.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to mimic its hot origin.
Check the vine tips regularly for aphids and mealybugs, wiping them off with a damp cotton pad.
Provide a small trellis or bamboo canes in spring for its twining succulent stems to scramble up.

items.name: Cynanchum acutum
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in a sturdy root barrier to stop its invasive runners taking over.
Keep it in a sunny, sheltered spot to help it survive wet UK winters in well-drained soil.
Prune the stems hard to the ground in late winter before the sap starts flowing in spring.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between.
Watch out for aphids on the tender new shoots in May and simply blast them off with a hose.

items.name: Cynanchum daltonii
items.growersTips:
Bring this Cape Verde native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant in a gritty cactus mix with added perlite to prevent root rot during damp British summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, then drench it and let it drain completely.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mites when growing it in your sunroom.
Prune back any leggy, tangled stems in early spring just as the new growth begins to show.

items.name: Cynanchum ellipticum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender African climber in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frost.
Use a gritty loam-based compost with added perlite to ensure excellent drainage in wet UK winters.
Water generously during the summer growing season but let the soil dry out fully between soakings.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk in spring to support its vigorous twining stems as they shoot up.
Watch out for aphids and spider mites when you bring the plant inside your greenhouse for winter.

items.name: Cynanchum floribundum
items.growersTips:
Sow these Australian native seeds shallowly in free-draining grit under glass to handle UK damp.
Keep this tender climber in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between drinks in summer.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk early on to support its vigorous twining perennial stems.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering your plant indoors.

items.name: Cynanchum guehoi
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender perennial indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Grow it in a very gritty, free-draining loam mix to prevent root rot during damp spring days.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, cutting back to a monthly splash in winter.
Position your pot in a south-facing conservatory or sunny windowsill to mimic its native light.
Train its twining stems gently onto a small hoop trellis in spring to keep the growth tidy.

items.name: Cynanchum laeve
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous climber in a sturdy root barrier to stop its invasive runners taking over.
Keep it happy in wet UK winters by mixing plenty of coarse grit into your heavy clay planting hole.
Prune the stems right back to ground level in late autumn to keep the vigorous growth under control.
Snip off the seed pods in late summer before they split to stop windblown seeds invading your lawn.
Grow it in a container on a sunny patio to easily contain its roots and enjoy the white summer blooms.

items.name: Cynanchum socotranum
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Socotran succulent in a very gritty, free-draining cactus mix to prevent winter rot.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill inside, as it cannot survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, reducing this to a tiny splash once a month during winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem joints and dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Repot in spring only when roots crowd the pot, using a shallow container to avoid excess wet soil.

items.name: Cynanchum viminale
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender African succulent indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it warm and dry.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot during damp UK winters.
Water it only when the soil is completely dry, and keep it bone dry throughout the winter months.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give this sun-lover the maximum light it needs.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tangled, leafless joints and dab them with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Cynarospermum
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your UK clay soil to give this perennial the sharp drainage it needs to survive winter.
Sow the seeds just under the surface in spring, keeping the pot in a cold frame to protect from frost.
Watch out for slugs eating the fresh spring shoots, so protect them with beer traps or copper tape.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and prevent rot in damp weather.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers, but let the soil dry out completely between times.

items.name: Cynarospermum asperrimum
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Indian borage in a deep pot so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Mix plenty of grit into your peat-free compost to mimic the free-draining rocky soils of its origin.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering it indoors.
Prune back the woody stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more flowers.

items.name: Cynoglossum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into free-draining soil to benefit from winter cold stratification.
Plant in gritty, poor soil to prevent floppy growth and ensure survival through wet UK winters.
Water young plants weekly until established then leave dry to avoid crown rot in damp climates.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding around your borders.
Watch out for slugs and snails on fresh spring shoots by using beer traps or organic pellets.

items.name: Cynoglossum amabile
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in April once the chilly UK spring soil starts to warm.
Keep young plants damp but let established ones dry out to survive wet British summers without rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love devouring the soft young leaves during damp UK spring nights.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of those lovely blue blooms.
Plant them near wallflowers or tulips to create a gorgeous spring display in your cottage borders.

items.name: Cynoglossum cheirifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mediterranean native in your poorest, sharpest-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the seeds shallowly in spring, barely covering them with a light dusting of grit or compost.
Position it in your absolute hottest, sunniest spot, perhaps against a south-facing brick wall.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, as soggy roots will quickly rot this dry-loving plant.
Protect the young, woolly foliage from slugs and snails during damp British spring evenings.

items.name: Cynoglossum creticum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn as this biennial needs winter cold to trigger spring germination.
Plant them in poor, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water seedlings sparingly once established because this Mediterranean native hates soggy roots.
Watch out for caterpillars and slugs in spring, as they love the soft, hairy young foliage.
Grow them alongside lavender or rosemary to mimic their natural dry, sunny hillside habitat.

items.name: Cynoglossum germanicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn because this British native needs a winter chill to germinate successfully.
Plant them in partial shade under deciduous trees to mimic their natural woodland edge habitat.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to recreate the damp, chalky ground they love in the wild.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love the young foliage.
Leave the faded flower stems standing over winter so they can self-seed and feed local wildlife.

items.name: Cynoglossum grande
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in partial shade with moist, humus-rich soil to mimic its native canopy.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames so the natural winter chill can break their dormancy perfectly.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy during the active spring and summer growing months.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, protecting the tender emerging young foliage.
Mulch annually in late winter with leaf mould to replicate the rich forest floor it loves best.

items.name: Cynoglossum officinale
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 1cm depth so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy for spring.
Grow this British native in poor, well-drained chalky soil to stop it getting too tall and floppy.
Watch out for caterpillars of the beautiful scarlet tiger moth, which love feeding on the leaves.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late summer to prevent this vigorous self-seeder taking over.
Plant it alongside wild marjoram or viper's bugloss to create a stunning, drought-tolerant haven.

items.name: Cynoglossum virginianum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the UK winter cold naturally breaks their dormancy for spring.
Plant this wild comfrey in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its natural woodland home.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged using a weekly deep soak during dry spells.
Check the rough leaves regularly for slugs and snails which love damp UK shade and young foliage.
Clear away fallen autumn leaves around the crown to prevent winter rot in wet British soils.

items.name: Cynoglossum zeylanicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 5mm deep, then plant out in May after the last frosts have passed.
Grow this hound's tongue in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in damp UK wet.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely in between.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late autumn to keep the rosette tidy and prevent excessive seeding.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with beer traps or grit barriers.

items.name: Cynoglottis barrelieri
items.growersTips:
Plant this blue beauty in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in damp UK climates.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its woodland home and keep the delicate leaves from scorching.
Water young plants weekly until established, then let the UK rain do the work as they tolerate dry spells.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in midsummer to encourage a fresh flush of lush green foliage.
Watch out for slugs and snails on new spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers to protect them.

items.name: Cynometra
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator set to twenty-four Celsius
Grow in pots of acidic, peat-free loam-based compost mixed with thirty percent perlite for drainage
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during summer months
Position in the warmest, brightest spot of a heated greenhouse to mimic tropical humidity and light
Check regularly for red spider mites under leaves and mist daily to deter them in dry indoor air

items.name: Cynometra alexandri
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical tree in a heated conservatory at twenty degrees Celsius to mimic its rainforest.
Sow seeds two centimeters deep in a free-draining loam and peat-free compost mix with added grit.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during winter.
Mist the foliage daily with soft water to maintain the high humidity required in dry UK indoor air.
Feed monthly in spring with a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer to support slow container growth.

items.name: Cynometra beddomei
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare tropical annual in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to mimic its native warmth.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty-five Celsius.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the acidic, peat-free loam soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser to support its Fabaceae growth.
Monitor indoor plants closely for red spider mites and mist the foliage daily to maintain humidity.

items.name: Cynometra browneoides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical annual in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive cool UK summers.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the acidic, peat-free loam soil consistently moist but not wet.
Apply a high-potassium liquid seaweed feed every two weeks during the active summer growing phase.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mites under leaves and use biological controls if pests appear.

items.name: Cynometra cauliflora
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical tree in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive the cold UK climate.
Plant seeds five centimetres deep in a well-draining, acidic loam mixed with plenty of leaf mould.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius to prevent devastating leaf drop.
Watch closely for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the foliage daily to keep humidity high.

items.name: Cynometra lenticellata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical tree in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive the cold UK climate.
Sow seeds indoors at a depth of two centimeters in a well-draining, acidic loam soil mix.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Maintain high humidity levels above sixty percent using daily misting or wet gravel trays.
Monitor closely for glasshouse red spider mites and mealybugs under the leaves during winter.

items.name: Cynometra ramiflora
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical legume in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive the cold UK climate
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters in a free-draining acidic loam soil mix
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy
Maintain high humidity around the plant by misting daily or placing the pot on a wet pebble tray
Watch for glasshouse red spider mites and treat infestations early with biological controls

items.name: Cynometra travancorica
items.growersTips:
Grow as an indoor or heated greenhouse annual sowing seeds five centimeters deep in warm loam soil
Water consistently to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged using tepid rainwater in the UK
Provide a minimum temperature of eighteen degrees Celsius using grow lights to mimic tropical sun
Watch for spider mites in dry indoor winter air and mist the foliage daily to maintain humidity
Feed biweekly with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertilizer once the first true leaves expand

items.name: Cynorkis
items.growersTips:
Grow these Madagascan orchids in a free-draining bark and perlite mix to prevent winter root rot.
Keep them on a bright UK windowsill but shaded from harsh direct summer sun to avoid leaf scorch.
Water freely during active spring growth but keep them almost completely dry during winter dormancy.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites which love the dry air of centrally heated British homes.
Repot your tuberous perennial in early spring just as the fresh green growth begins to show.

items.name: Cypella
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in late spring at a depth of eight centimetres in free-draining sandy loam soil.
Keep them in pots so you can move them into a frost-free greenhouse or shed during wet UK winters.
Water them regularly in summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings to avoid rot.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme to support their slender stems and show off the exotic blooms.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to eat the tender emerging sword-like leaves.

items.name: Cyphia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African tuber in a gritty, free-draining loam mix to survive wet UK winters.
Plant the small tubers five centimetres deep in pots so you can easily move them indoors for winter.
Water sparingly during the spring growing season, letting the compost dry out between soakings.
Provide a tripod of thin bamboo canes early on to support the delicate, twining stems as they climb.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plants under glass.

items.name: Cyphia bulbosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a container with gritty, free-draining compost to survive UK rain.
Bury the small bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn and keep them completely dry during winter.
Place your pots in a sunny, unheated greenhouse or on a bright windowsill to mimic their home sun.
Water sparingly only when active green growth appears in spring, letting the soil dry out between.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to munch on the tender emerging shoots.

items.name: Cyphia digitata
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African climber in a deep, gritty mix using equal parts loam and horticultural grit.
Keep the tuber completely dry during its winter dormancy to prevent rot in our damp UK climate.
Provide a slender trellis or birch twigs for the delicate twining stems to climb as they grow.
Water sparingly only when active growth appears in spring, mimicking its natural dry-summer cycle.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory.

items.name: Cyphia volubilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African climber in a container with gritty, free-draining loam to protect from rot.
Keep the pot in a greenhouse or bright conservatory over winter to shield it from harsh UK frosts.
Water your Cyphia regularly during its active summer growth but keep the soil dry during dormancy.
Provide a delicate trellis or twiggy birch sticks for its twining stems to scramble up naturally.
Mix plenty of horticultural sand and perlite into your peat-free compost to mimic its native soil.

items.name: Cyphocarpus
items.growersTips:
Plant these Chilean bellflowers in sandy, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Give them a sheltered, south-facing wall to mimic their native warm, rocky scrubland habitat.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep them almost bone-dry during our cold winter months.
Sow seeds in early spring using a heated propagator to get a head start on our short UK summers.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Cypripedium acaule
items.growersTips:
Plant in extremely acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.0 using a mix of peat, sand, and pine needles.
Position in dappled shade under pine trees or birch, avoiding any direct midday UK summer sun.
Water with rainwater only to keep the soil damp but never soggy, as tap water minerals will kill it.
Plant the rhizome shallowly, just one centimetre below the surface, with the bud pointing upwards.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or copper tape.

items.name: Cypripedium arietinum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty, well-draining, neutral to slightly acidic mix of pumice, perlite, and leaf mould.
Position in dappled shade facing north or east to mimic its natural cool woodland understorey.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, using rainwater rather than chlorinated tap water.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using copper tape or organic beer traps.
Mulch annually in autumn with a thin layer of composted pine needles to maintain soil acidity.

items.name: Cypripedium calceolus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, gritty, alkaline soil using oyster shells to keep the pH between 6.5 and 7.5
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic native UK woodland light and avoid midday sun
Keep soil constantly moist but never waterlogged during the active spring and summer growing season
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or physical copper barriers
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud resting just two centimetres below the soil surface

items.name: Cypripedium californicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a constantly moist but free-draining mix of pumice, perlite, and composted pine bark.
Position in dappled shade or north-facing spots to mimic cool, damp Pacific Northwest ravines.
Water with rainwater to keep the root zone wet but never stagnant, especially during dry summers.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
Overwinter in the ground as they need UK winter cold to break dormancy, but shield from excess rain.

items.name: Cypripedium candidum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a gritty, alkaline mix of limestone chippings, perlite, and loam to mimic fen conditions.
Position in full sun to very light dappled shade to replicate its native open meadow habitat.
Keep the soil constantly moist but free-draining, never letting it dry out during summer growth.
Incorporate slow-release oyster shell grit annually to maintain the high soil pH this orchid craves.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or physical barriers.

items.name: Cypripedium dickinsonianum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a cold frame or alpine house to protect this tender species from wet UK winter rots.
Use a highly porous, alkaline mix of pumice, tufa, and perlite with very little organic matter.
Water with pure rainwater to keep the gritty compost damp but never waterlogged during summer.
Provide bright, filtered light but shade from hot midday sun to mimic its high-altitude habitat.
Keep compost barely damp and protect from deep frosts during its crucial winter dormancy period.

items.name: Cypripedium elegans
items.growersTips:
Plant in a mix of equal parts leafmould, perlite, and grit to mimic cool, free-draining woodland soil.
Position in a north-facing, dappled shade border to prevent summer leaf scorch in UK gardens.
Water with rainwater to keep soil damp but never soggy, reducing frequency during winter dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud resting just two centimetres below the soil surface.

items.name: Cypripedium fasciculatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a free-draining, gritty, neutral to slightly acidic compost mix using pumice and perlite.
Position in a sheltered, cool, north-facing spot to mimic its native damp woodland canopy shade.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during spring growth.
Apply a deep mulch of composted pine needles in autumn to protect shallow rhizomes from UK frosts.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.

items.name: Cypripedium flavum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, gritty, neutral to slightly alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland light levels.
Water thoroughly with rainwater during active spring growth but keep barely damp in winter dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud sitting just one centimetre below the soil surface.

items.name: Cypripedium formosanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a shallow 5cm deep mix of equal parts leafmould, perlite, and grit in partial dapple shade.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged from spring until leaves die back in autumn.
Protect the early emerging fan-shaped leaves from late spring frosts using a cloche or fleece.
Apply a slug barrier or copper tape around the plant in March as new shoots are highly vulnerable.
Grow in a container or raised bed to easily control the required acidic to neutral soil drainage.

items.name: Cypripedium franchetii
items.growersTips:
Plant in a free-draining, gritty, humus-rich soil mix of pumice, perlite, and composted pine bark.
Position in a sheltered, cool spot with dappled shade, avoiding direct hot afternoon summer sun.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during active growth.
Apply a deep mulch of leaf mould in autumn to protect the shallow rhizomes from severe winter frost.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or physical barriers.

items.name: Cypripedium guttatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a shallow 5cm deep mix of equal parts leafmould, perlite, and coarse grit for sharp drainage.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged from April to September using stored rainwater.
Position in a cold, north-facing spot with dappled shade to mimic its native Siberian woodland.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic ferrous phosphate pellets.
Ensure a cold winter dormancy below 5C to trigger flowering, avoiding any winter mulching.

items.name: Cypripedium henryi
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil using grit and leaf mould.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic UK woodland and avoid midday summer sun.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never soggy from autumn through to spring.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud just one centimetre below the soil surface.

items.name: Cypripedium irapeanum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Mexican orchid in a heated greenhouse as it cannot survive UK winter frosts outdoors.
Use a highly porous, inorganic potting mix of pumice, perlite, and Kanuma to prevent root rot.
Water with pure rainwater only, keeping the mix damp in summer and almost completely dry in winter.
Provide bright, filtered light but shade from direct midday sun to prevent the soft leaves burning.
Maintain high humidity around the pot using wet gravel trays while ensuring excellent air movement.

items.name: Cypripedium japonicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a mix of leaf mould, perlite, and loam, keeping it loose, airy, and neutral to acidic.
Position in deep, dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic UK woodland and prevent leaf scorch.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during active spring and summer growth.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted leaf mould to protect the shallow rhizomes from hard frost.

items.name: Cypripedium kentuckiense
items.growersTips:
Plant in a mix of 50 percent inorganic grit or pumice and 50 percent leaf mould to ensure drainage.
Position in dappled shade facing north or east to mimic UK woodland edges and prevent leaf scorch.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged from April to September using rainwater.
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud resting just two centimetres below the soil surface.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.

items.name: Cypripedium macranthos
items.growersTips:
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud just one to two centimetres below the soil surface
Incorporate plenty of coarse grit and perlite to create a free-draining but moisture-retentive soil
Water with rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during summer growth
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic natural woodland light and prevent scorch

items.name: Cypripedium montanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, gritty, neutral to slightly alkaline soil using perlite and bark chippings.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland edges and prevent leaf scorch.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the spring growth.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
Apply a light mulch of leaf mould in autumn to protect the shallow rhizomes from severe UK frosts.

items.name: Cypripedium parviflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a mix of 50% inorganic grit or pumice and 50% leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soils.
Position in dappled shade facing north or east to prevent strong midday sun from burning the leaves.
Water with rainwater to keep soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during the spring growth.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic copper tape.
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud resting just two centimetres below the soil surface.

items.name: Cypripedium passerinum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a moisture-retentive, gritty, alkaline mix of loam, perlite, and crushed limestone.
Position in a cool, north-facing spot with dappled shade to mimic its native boreal forest canopy.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged, using rainwater rather than tap water.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper barriers.
Ensure a cold winter dormancy by leaving pots outdoors, as this orchid needs frost to trigger blooms.

items.name: Cypripedium reginae
items.growersTips:
Plant in a mix of equal parts peat, perlite, and grit to mimic UK fens, keeping soil neutral to acid.
Position in dappled shade facing north or east to protect the foliage from scorching UK summer sun.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged during the growing season.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or physical copper barriers.
Plant the rhizome shallowly with the growing bud sitting just one centimetre below the soil surface.

items.name: Cypripedium tibeticum
items.growersTips:
Plant in 50% inorganic grit and pumice with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soils and prevent rot.
Position in a cool north-facing border or dappled shade to protect leaves from strong UK summer sun.
Water with rainwater to keep soil damp in spring but reduce watering in winter to avoid crown rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers in April.
Top-dress the soil annually in autumn with a thin layer of well-rotted beech or oak leaf mould.

items.name: Cypripedium yatabeanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a mix of 50% inorganic grit and 50% leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soil and ensure drainage.
Position in a cool north-facing border or dappled shade to protect leaves from strong UK summer sun.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never waterlogged using rainwater rather than tap water.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or physical barriers.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted leaf mould to protect the shallow rhizomes from hard frost.

items.name: Cyrtandra
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Pacific native in a pot of peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite.
Keep your pot indoors or in a heated greenhouse from October to May to protect it from UK frosts.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy, as cold tap water shocks the roots.
Place your pot in a humid, north-facing conservatory or bathroom to mimic its native rainforest home.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer once a fortnight from April to August to boost flowering.

items.name: Cyrtandra cleopatrae
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Philippine native in a heated conservatory to protect it from cold UK winters.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy by watering with tepid rainwater, not tap.
Provide high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to mimic its rainforest home.
Feed with a weak high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from April to September.
Position in bright, filtered light away from direct midday sun to prevent the leaves from burning.

items.name: Cyrtandra cyaneoides
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian native indoors by October to keep it safe from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a chunky, bark-rich orchid compost mix to mimic its natural mossy rainforest home.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries out, as tap water stunts it.
Position it in a humid, steamy bathroom window facing north or east to avoid scorched leaves.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in dry indoor air and mist the leaves frequently.

items.name: Cyrtandra heinrichii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender tropical indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a peat-free, ericaceous compost mix with added perlite to ensure sharp, free drainage.
Keep it in bright, filtered light away from direct midday sun to prevent the lush leaves burning.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water to keep the soil consistently moist but damp.
Feed weekly in spring with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertiliser to encourage those blooms.

items.name: Cyrtandra kaulantha
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian native indoors by September to protect it from wet and cold UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with perlite to mimic its natural volcanic soil.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent root rot.
Position it in a humid bathroom or on a pebble tray to stop the leaf tips from browning.
Feed with a weak orchid fertilizer once a month from April to August to encourage white blooms.

items.name: Cyrtandra platyphylla
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian native indoors by October to shield it from chilly, wet UK autumn frosts.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent root rot.
Pot it in a peat-free ericaceous mix with plenty of perlite to mimic its volcanic home.
Keep it in bright, indirect light like an east-facing windowsill to avoid scorching the leaves.
Mist the foliage daily or use a gravel tray to recreate the high humidity of tropical forests.

items.name: Cyrtandra waianaeensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian native indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a peat-free, bark-rich ericaceous compost mix to mimic its volcanic forest home.
Keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering only with lukewarm rainwater, never tap.
Place it in a humid, steamy bathroom window facing east to mimic its misty tropical canopy.
Feed weekly in spring with a highly diluted orchid fertiliser to boost those delicate white blooms.

items.name: Cyrtandra wawrae
items.growersTips:
Bring this Hawaiian forest perennial indoors by October to protect it from chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a peat-free, bark-rich compost mix that mimics the damp but airy forest floors it loves.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the soil damp, but never let the pot sit in a puddle.
Place it in a humid, steamy bathroom with bright but filtered light to stop the leaves from drying.
Feed with a very weak liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month only during the active summer growth.

items.name: Cyrtandromoea
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender perennial indoors by October to protect it from wet and cold UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a peat-free, ericaceous compost mix to mimic its preferred acidic rainforest floor.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water to avoid shocking its delicate root system.
Place it in dappled shade under a pergola to protect its soft leaves from harsh afternoon sun.
Mist the foliage daily in summer to boost humidity, but keep leaves dry during chilly winter days.

items.name: Cyrtomium
items.growersTips:
Plant your holly fern in moist, humus-rich soil under the dappled shade of a north-facing UK wall.
Water regularly during dry summer spells to keep the soil damp, but never let the roots sit in bog.
Snip away the tatty, old fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh green growth.
Protect your fern from dry, biting winter winds by tucking it next to shelter like a hardy Astilbe.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow your fern in a patio pot.

items.name: Cyrtomium falcatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Japanese holly fern in a sheltered, damp, shady border alongside hostas and astilbes.
Tuck it into humus-rich, well-drained soil, keeping the crown just level with the ground surface.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Cut back the old, tattered fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh growth.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or bark in autumn to protect its roots from severe winter frosts.

items.name: Cyrtomium fortunei
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy fern in damp, shady borders alongside hostas to create a lush foliage contrast.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted compost into your soil to mimic its natural woodland home.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, watering deeply at the base of the plant.
Cut back old, tatty fronds in late winter before the fresh new fiddleheads start to unfurl.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new spring growth, using organic beer traps to deter them.

items.name: Cyrtosia
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare parasitic orchid near rotting wood and oak trees so its host fungi can feed it.
Keep the soil constantly damp and rich in leaf mould to mimic a shady British woodland floor.
Never apply chemical fertilisers as they will instantly kill the vital underground fungal network.
Protect the emerging summer spikes from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Leave the seed pods to decay naturally on the ground to help the orchid spread across your garden.

items.name: Cyrtosia septentrionalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this parasitic orchid near rotting oak stumps so its roots can feed on the essential fungi.
Keep the soil constantly damp and shaded to mimic the cool, humid woodland floor of the UK.
Do not prune or cut back any stems, as this wild orchid relies on self-seeding to propagate.
Layer leaf mould over the planting area in autumn to insulate the soil and boost fungal activity.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the emerging fleshy shoots.

items.name: Cyrtosperma
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical swamp-lover in a heated conservatory or warm greenhouse above fifteen degrees.
Grow it in a heavy, clay-rich loam mixed with leaf mould, keeping the pot standing in shallow water.
Repot in spring, burying the thick rhizome just below the soil surface to encourage sturdy growth.
Wipe the giant leaves weekly with a wet sponge to boost humidity and deter red spider mites.
Feed weekly in summer with a diluted high-nitrogen liquid fertiliser to boost those massive leaves.

items.name: Cyrtosperma merkusii
items.growersTips:
Grow this giant swamp taro in a large, heated indoor conservatory or warm greenhouse all year round.
Keep its pot submerged in warm, shallow rainwater to mimic its natural tropical wetland habitat.
Use a rich, heavy loam mixed with plenty of leaf mould and well-rotted manure for hungry roots.
Wipe the massive leaves weekly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite infestations indoors.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius to stop the plant from dying back.

items.name: Cyrtostylis
items.growersTips:
Grow these tiny Australian orchids in a gritty, free-draining mix of peat alternative and perlite.
Keep the compost damp from autumn to spring, then let it dry out completely during summer dormancy.
Protect them from winter frost by keeping pots in a cold greenhouse or on a cool indoor windowsill.
Watch out for slugs and snails in autumn when the delicate single leaves first emerge from the soil.
Repot the small tubers annually in late summer, burying them about two centimetres deep in fresh mix.

items.name: Cystacanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Asian perennial indoors by October to shield it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top two inches of soil dry out between waterings.
Mix plenty of grit and leaf mould into your clay soil to give its roots the sharp drainage it craves.
Prune back the leggy stems by half in early spring to encourage a much bushier, flower-filled habit.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when growing this plant under cover in spring.

items.name: Cysticapnos
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn in a cold frame to mimic natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Grow in gritty, sharply draining neutral soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Provide a fine twiggy birch peastick support for this delicate climber to scramble up naturally.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells to avoid waterlogging the sensitive root system.
Watch closely for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots emerging in damp British gardens.

items.name: Cystorchis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare jewel orchid in a humid terrarium or greenhouse to survive chilly UK winters.
Use a very free-draining mix of chopped sphagnum moss, perlite, and fine bark instead of soil.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the moss surface feels dry, keeping it damp but never soggy.
Keep your pots in deep shade or dappled light, mimicking the dark tropical forest floor indoors.
Watch out for fungus gnats and slugs, which love the warm, damp conditions these orchids need.

items.name: Dactylicapnos
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 10cm deep in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in a sheltered, partially shaded spot
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or soggy
Provide a sturdy trellis or plant next to a deciduous shrub like Hydrangea for the stems to climb
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps in damp weather
Mulch the root zone with leaf mould in late autumn to protect the crown from severe British winter frosts

items.name: Dactylorhiza
items.growersTips:
Plant these native marsh orchids in a damp, humus-rich soil that mimics a wet UK meadow.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring and summer, never letting these orchids dry out.
Sow them alongside fine fescue grasses to provide the essential mycorrhizal fungi they need to grow.
Plant the tuber shallowly, just two centimetres below the surface, with the bud pointing upwards.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn once the foliage has completely died back for the winter.

items.name: Dalbergia
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect their sensitive taproots.
Sow them exactly one centimetre deep in a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of sharp grit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate sitting in cold UK winter wet.
Grow them in your brightest south-facing spot or a conservatory to mimic their native warmth.
Plant them alongside French marigolds to help deter aphids and spider mites in the greenhouse.

items.name: Damrongia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Damrongia indoors to a warm windowsill before the first autumn frost hits the UK.
Water your Damrongia only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot.
Mix plenty of perlite into peat-free compost to give these delicate roots the drainage they crave.
Keep a close eye out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints of your Damrongia during winter.
Propagate your Damrongia by taking leaf cuttings in late spring when the plant is growing actively.

items.name: Daniellia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using bottom heat to overcome UK chill.
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing spot with sharply draining sandy soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling to avoid rot.
In July pinch out the growing tips of young plants to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite in dry weather and mist the foliage with water to deter them.

items.name: Daniellia ogea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter the cool UK spring.
Grow in a south-facing glasshouse or conservatory to provide the high light levels this tree needs.
Water deeply once a week during summer, allowing the free-draining sandy loam soil to dry out fully.
Apply a low-nitrogen, high-potassium liquid feed monthly in summer to support its Fabaceae roots.
Check weekly for glasshouse red spider mite and use biological controls if infestations occur.

items.name: Daniellia oliveri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimetres using bottom heat to ensure germination
Grow in containers of gritty loam-based compost to easily move them under glass during wet summers
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is dry to prevent root rot in cool UK weather
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot available to mimic its native tropical light levels
Apply a low-nitrogen liquid fertiliser monthly in summer to support growth without scorching roots

items.name: Darmera
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade, keeping the crown at ground level.
Water copiously during dry UK summer spells to prevent the large, umbrella-like leaves from wilting.
Cut back the thick flower stems in late spring after flowering before the massive leaves expand.
Protect the emerging spring flower buds from late UK frosts using a temporary layer of fleece.
Divide the tough, creeping rhizomes in autumn or early spring using a sharp spade to propagate.

items.name: Darmera peltata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive boggy soil or shallow pond margins where the crown stays damp year-round.
Protect the early spring pink flower spikes from late frosts using a temporary fleece covering.
Position in partial shade to prevent the large umbrella leaves from scorching in afternoon sun.
Divide congested rhizomes in autumn or early spring using a sharp spade to propagate new plants.
Plant alongside Astilbe or Hostas which thrive in the same damp soil and mask the bare spring soil.

items.name: Darwiniothamnus lancifolius
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of three millimetres to beat the cool UK weather.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy by watering gently at the base every few days.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimetres to encourage a bushier habit.
Plant them outdoors in May alongside calendula to help deter aphids and attract local pollinators.
Watch out for slugs during wet British summers by using organic grit barriers around young stems.

items.name: Darwiniothamnus tenuifolius
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass as this rare Galapagos native needs early warmth to start.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty, well-draining soil dry out between drinks.
Keep these delicate annuals in your warmest, brightest spot, ideally a south-facing patio container.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the base of the stems.
Grow alongside potted lavender or thyme to match its love for dry, sunny, sheltered UK microclimates.

items.name: Dasynotus
items.growersTips:
Tuck your Dasynotus into gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters without rot.
Position this alpine beauty in a sheltered, sun-drenched rockery to mimic its native scree slopes.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, letting the gritty soil dry out between times.
Protect the soft foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic grit barriers in spring.
Propagate your Dasynotus by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to secure backup plants easily.

items.name: Daubenya aurea
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in late summer, burying the bulb exactly three centimeters deep in pots.
Keep it on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse, as it cannot survive wet UK winter frosts.
Water deeply only when active leaf growth appears in autumn, then keep the soil completely dry in summer.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost, coarse grit, and perlite to ensure the fast drainage it demands.
Watch out for slugs and snails in autumn, as they love to feast on the emerging low-hugging leaves.

items.name: Daubenya zeyheri
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix under glass to survive wet UK winters.
Set the bulbs about five centimetres deep in autumn, keeping them snug but not squashed in pots.
Water only when active growth appears in autumn, then keep them barely damp once summer dormancy hits.
Position your pots on a sunny, south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to mimic the Cape.
Watch out for slugs and snails during the damp winter months as they love the succulent green leaves.

items.name: Decalepis
items.growersTips:
Grow decalepis in deep pots of gritty, free-draining loam to protect its thick roots from wet rot.
Bring your potted decalepis indoors to a bright, frost-free windowsill from October until late May.
Water sparingly, letting the compost dry out fully between drinks to mimic its dry native climate.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser once a month during summer to boost root development.
Check the leaf undersides weekly for red spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor overwintering.

items.name: Decalepis arayalpathra
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Indian perennial indoors by October to protect its roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a gritty, free-draining loam mix with added perlite to prevent root rot in damp weather.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, cutting back to a light misting during winter.
Keep it in your brightest south-facing conservatory or windowsill to mimic its native sunny climate.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air, so mist the leaves weekly to keep humidity up.

items.name: Decalepis hamiltonii
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Indian climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Plant the tuberous roots in a very free-draining sandy loam to prevent rot during damp UK springs.
Water sparingly during winter dormancy, only dampening the soil when the top two inches are dry.

Keep a close eye out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in warm, dry indoor conditions.

items.name: Decanema
items.growersTips:
Dig a deep planting hole in spring and mix in plenty of grit to help this perennial drain in UK wet.
Protect the crown with a thick mulch of dry straw or bracken before the first sharp winter frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent shallow sprinkles.
Cut back the faded flowering stems right to the base in autumn to keep the clump tidy and healthy.
Grow it alongside hardy geraniums which love the same soil and help support its upright stems.

items.name: Decumaria
items.growersTips:
Plant against a warm south or west-facing UK wall to protect young stems from harsh winter frosts.
In spring apply a thick mulch of composted bark to keep the shallow root system cool and moist.
Prune immediately after summer flowering by cutting back wayward shoots to a strong side bud.
Grow in fertile moisture-retentive acidic to neutral soil as alkaline chalk causes chlorosis.
Provide a sturdy trellis or wire support until the aerial roots self-cling to the brickwork.

items.name: Decumaria barbara
items.growersTips:
Plant against a sheltered south or west wall to protect the delicate early summer buds from cold winds
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or composted bark to mimic its native woodland soil before planting
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years until its aerial root system establishes
Prune immediately after flowering in midsummer by cutting back overlong shoots to a strong side bud
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants and treat with beneficial nematodes in autumn

items.name: Deilanthe
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African succulents in a gritty, free-draining mix of half compost and half grit.

Water them only when the soil is bone dry, soaking the pot then letting it drain fully.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the velvety leaves, dabbing them with rubbing alcohol.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than the ground to easily control moisture in wet British summers.

items.name: Deinandra arida

Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect this rare desert daisy from UK damp.
Plant them in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix to mimic their dry Mojave home.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the foliage completely free of overhead moisture.
Position your pots in the hottest, brightest spot on a south-facing patio to catch maximum sun.
Watch out for slugs on young seedlings during wet British springs, using grit barriers to stop them.

items.name: Deinandra clementina
items.growersTips:
Sow these island-native seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect from cold UK rain.
Grow them in gritty, fast-draining soil to mimic their dry coastal home and prevent root rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out fully between drinks to avoid mildew.
Nip out the growing tips in late May to encourage a bushier habit and more daisy-like yellow blooms.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps to protect them in damp British weather.

items.name: Deinandra conjugens
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare annual seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect them from late British frosts.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to mimic their native dry scrub and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the tender young spring shoots of this annual.
Grow them alongside hardy UK herbs like thyme to share the same sunny, sharply-drained conditions.

items.name: Deinandra fasciculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in late spring directly into sandy, sharply drained soil to mimic dry hillsides.
Position in your sunniest, south-facing border as this Californian native needs maximum UK heat.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between sessions.
Leave the yellow flowers to self-seed naturally in autumn for a free display of blooms next summer.
Grow alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme and oregano which thrive in the same dry, sunny spots.

items.name: Deinandra greeneana
items.growersTips:
Sow these Californian annuals in April under glass to protect them from late British frosts.
Plant them out in May in free-draining sandy soil to mimic their native dry coastal bluffs.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry as they easily rot in our damp UK summers.
Give them the sunniest spot in your garden to encourage those bright yellow daisy-like blooms.
Deadhead regularly through August to keep them flowering right up until the first autumn frost.

items.name: Deinandra halliana
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in early spring under cover to protect them from late UK frosts before planting out.
Grow this Californian native in your poorest, fastest-draining soil to mimic its dry scrub habitat.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid rot.
Position them in your absolute brightest, most south-facing spot to get the best summer blooms.
Deadhead the spent yellow daisy flowers regularly to keep the plant blooming right up to autumn.

items.name: Deinandra increscens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April just dusting them with grit to let the weak UK spring light wake them up.
Give this California native your poorest gritty soil and avoid rich compost to prevent floppy growth.
Water sparingly only during dry spells as damp UK soils will quickly rot their drought-loving roots.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around them.
Plant them next to Mediterranean herbs like thyme to share the same dry sunny spot in your garden.

items.name: Deinandra kelloggii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in April directly into well-drained, gritty soil to mimic its native dry habitat.
Keep watering minimal once established, only soaking during prolonged hot, dry UK summer spells.
Position this annual in your sunniest, south-facing border to ensure it gets maximum summer light.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow flowers.
Collect the seed heads in autumn to sow next spring, as this annual will not survive UK frosts.

items.name: Deinandra lobbii
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect them from wet British frosts.
Plant them in very gritty, free-draining soil because they rot quickly in heavy clay garden beds.

Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage a bushier shape and more yellow summer flowers.
Water them only during long dry spells as these drought-tolerant annuals hate soggy compost.

items.name: Deinandra minthornii

items.name: Deinandra pallida

Sow seeds in late spring after frosts, just pressing them lightly into well-drained, sandy soil.

Place this California native in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic its warm home climate.

Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK summers, using beer traps to protect young seedlings.

items.name: Deinandra pentactis

Sow seeds in April under glass to protect this Californian native annual from late UK frosts.
Press the tiny seeds lightly into gritty, free-draining compost rather than burying them deep.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native arid drought conditions.
Plant alongside English lavender to attract the specific pollinators needed for its yellow blooms.
Scatter grit around the base of young stems to prevent damp-off during wet British summers.

items.name: Deinandra streetsii
items.growersTips:
Sow these rare annual seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect them from late British frosts.

Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to maximise summer blooms.
Watch out for slugs on young seedlings during damp British springs, using beer traps to protect them.

items.name: Deinanthe

items.name: Deinanthe caerulea
items.growersTips:

Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Deinostema

items.name: Deinostigma

items.name: Deiregyne

Grow this rare Mexican orchid in a gritty, free-draining loam to survive damp UK winter wet.

items.name: Delilia biflora

Sow seeds indoors in April at five millimetres deep to beat the cool British spring temperatures.

items.name: Delissea kauaiensis

items.name: Delissea rhytidosperma

Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out, keeping it almost completely dry over winter.

Place it in your sunniest south-facing spot or conservatory to mimic its hot native climate.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this plant indoors during the winter.

items.name: Delonix elata

Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre using a heated propagator at 21C.
Grow this tender tree in a pot of gritty, free-draining loam so you can move it inside for winter.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as this species hates soggy winter soil.

Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering your potted plant in a heated room.

items.name: Delonix floribunda

Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre using a heated propagator at twenty-one degrees.
Grow this tender annual in pots of gritty, free-draining compost so you can move it into a sunny greenhouse.

items.name: Delonix regia

Grow this tropical beauty in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn chills hit.

items.name: Delosperma

items.name: Delosperma aberdeenense

Plant this South African native in a raised bed or gravel garden to guarantee the sharp drainage it needs.

Water only when the soil is bone dry, focusing on a deep soak once a fortnight during hot summers.
Grow it alongside hardy sedums and sempervivums in a shallow terracotta bowl for a stunning display.
Trim back any leggy stems in late spring to encourage a tighter, more compact cushion of purple blooms.

items.name: Delosperma cooperi

Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep roots bone-dry during our wet, soggy UK winters.
Plant them on a south-facing slope or rockery where they can soak up every drop of British sunshine.

items.name: Delosperma echinatum

Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill by November.

items.name: Delosperma lavisiae

Plant this hardy ice plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of compost and sharp sand to survive wet UK winters.
Position your Delosperma in your garden's absolute sunniest spot so the daisy-like flowers fully open.

Protect the fleshy leaves from slugs and snails in spring by using grit barriers or organic pellets.

items.name: Delosperma lehmannii

items.name: Delosperma napiforme

items.name: Delosperma sutherlandii

Cut the faded flower spikes down to the ground in July to coax a second beautiful flush in autumn.

items.name: Delphinium

Stake your tall stems early in spring with birch brushwood to withstand those wet UK summer gales.

Cut the faded flower spikes right back to the ground in July to encourage a second flush in autumn.

items.name: Delphinium ×belladonna

Cut the spent flower spikes right back to the ground in July to trigger a second flush in autumn.
Feed weekly in spring with a high-potash liquid seaweed to boost those iconic blue flower spikes.

items.name: Delphinium ×cultorum

Stake your tall stems early in April with brushwood or canes to withstand wet UK spring winds.

Cut the faded flower spikes right down to the ground in July to encourage a second flush in autumn.
Plant them in fertile, moisture-retentive soil with the crown level with the ground, never buried.

items.name: Delphinium andersonii

Plant this desert native in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pot in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its hot Great Basin habitat.

items.name: Delphinium bakeri

Plant this rare beauty in deep, fertile, alkaline soil, adding grit to ensure it never sits in wet.
Water deeply at the base once a week in dry UK summers, keeping the lush foliage completely dry.

Cut the faded flower spikes right back to the ground in July to coax a second flush by autumn.
Stake the tall stems early in May using sturdy hazel twigs to withstand those sudden British winds.

items.name: Delphinium barbeyi

Plant this tall beauty in deep, fertile soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted garden compost.
Protect the emerging spring shoots early on from hungry slugs using organic beer traps or grit.
Stake the heavy flower spikes in mid-spring before the strong UK winds can snap their hollow stems.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the woodland soil damp.
Cut the faded flower spikes right back to the ground in July to encourage a second autumn flush.

items.name: Delphinium bicolor

Plant this low-growing beauty in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters.

Position it in full sun but sheltered from strong winds to keep those delicate blue stems upright.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in midsummer to encourage a cheeky second flush of autumn blooms.

items.name: Delphinium brunonianum

Plant this musk larkspur in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds in late winter, barely covering them with grit, and keep them cold to trigger germination.
Position this low-growing alpine in full sun but shelter its roots with a mulch of slate chippings.
Watch out for slugs early in spring, as they absolutely love the tender new emerging foliage.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of blue blooms.

items.name: Delphinium californicum

Plant this California native in very sharp-draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in full, bright sun but shelter the tall stems from strong, snapping UK winds.

Protect the emerging spring shoots from hungry UK slugs using beer traps or organic grit.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the ground in late summer to encourage a second flush.

Plant this red larkspur in your sunniest, sheltered spot to mimic its native warm California home.

Slugs absolutely love the young spring shoots so protect them early with beer traps or copper tape.
Cut the faded flower spikes right back to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush.

items.name: Delphinium carolinianum

Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep these wild American imports safe from wet UK winter rot.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the tray in a cold frame so our chilly winter naturally wakes them up.
Water deeply only when the top inch of soil dries out, as they hate soggy roots more than drought.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs in early spring, as they love to devour the fresh emerging shoots.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in midsummer to encourage a cheeky second flush of blue blooms.

items.name: Delphinium decorum

Plant this coastal native in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tender new shoots first emerge.

items.name: Delphinium denudatum

Plant this Himalayan beauty in gritty, sharp-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds in late winter on a cool windowsill, barely covering them with a sprinkle of vermiculite.

Cut the faded flower stems back to the ground in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.

items.name: Delphinium depauperatum

Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs using copper tape or beer traps as they love them.

items.name: Delphinium glareosum

Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.

items.name: Delphinium glaucum

items.name: Dichelostemma

items.name: Dicheranthus
