items.name: Dichocarpum

items.name: Dichodon cerastoides

items.name: Dichopogon strictus

items.description: Dieffenbachia, commonly known as dumb cane or leopard lily, is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Araceae. It is native to the New World Tropics from Mexico and the West Indies south to Argentina. Some species are widely cultivated as ornamental plants, especially as houseplants, and have become naturalized on a few tropical islands.

items.name: Dieffenbachia amoena

Keep it cozy indoors above fifteen Celsius year-round because our chilly UK winters will kill it.
Water only when the potting mix dries out completely, using tepid rainwater to avoid root rot.
Hang your basket in a bright bathroom where the natural shower steam keeps the humidity high.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding inside the hollow, pitcher-like leaves during the autumn months.

items.name: Dischidia nummularia
items.growersTips:
Treat it as an indoor plant because our chilly UK winters will kill this tropical beauty.
Water only when the bark mix is bone dry, as damp compost quickly rots its delicate roots.
Pot it in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix rather than standard British multipurpose compost.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the natural shower steam mimics its native humid rainforest.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the button-like leaves and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Dischidia oiantha
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical epiphyte indoors year-round as it cannot survive UK winter temperatures below 15C.
Grow it in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix rather than standard UK multipurpose potting compost.
Water only when the bark dries out completely, using tepid rainwater to avoid cold shock to roots.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where natural steam mimics the humid rainforest canopy it loves.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints, wiping them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Dischidia ovata
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical epiphytic vine warm indoors by avoiding cold windowsills below twelve degrees.
Water only when the chunky orchid bark mix dries out completely to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Hang it in bright indirect light to bring out those beautiful red leaf veins without scorching.
Boost humidity in dry centrally heated UK homes by placing a tray of wet pebbles right underneath.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and use cuttings to propagate.

items.name: Dischidia ruscifolia
items.growersTips:
Keep this plant indoors year-round as it hates UK cold, and pot it in a free-draining orchid bark mix.
Water only when the leaves feel slightly soft to the touch, using tepid rainwater if you can.
Hang it in a bright bathroom where the natural shower steam will mimic its native humid climate.
Trim the trailing stems in spring to keep it bushy and use the cuttings to propagate new plants.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense, heart-shaped foliage during the dry winter months.

items.name: Dischidia vidalii
items.growersTips:
Grow this exotic ant plant in a hanging basket of orchid bark and perlite for perfect drainage.
Keep it indoors in a bright spot with indirect sun, as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter.
Only water when the potting mix is dry, using lukewarm rainwater to keep its sensitive roots happy.
Mist the hollow pitcher leaves regularly to mimic the humid rainforests they naturally grow in.
Feed with a very weak orchid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost summer growth.

items.name: Dischistocalyx
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare tropical perennial indoors by October to protect it from wet and cold UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our humid climate.
Pot your plant in a mix of peat-free compost, orchid bark, and perlite for the drainage it craves.
Place it on a bright east-facing windowsill to mimic the dappled light of its natural rainforest.
Feed with a diluted high-nitrogen liquid fertiliser once a month from April through to September.

items.name: Diselma archeri
items.growersTips:
Plant this Tasmanian conifer in moist, acidic, well-drained soil using ericaceous compost in spring.
Position your Diselma in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland home and protect from hot sun.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
No pruning is needed, just gently snip away any brown or dead foliage in the mild days of mid-spring.
Protect young plants from harsh, drying winter winds with a temporary fleece wrap in cold regions.

items.name: Disinae
items.growersTips:
Keep Disa orchids in rainwater only, keeping their pots sitting in a shallow tray of water all summer.
Grow them in a mix of pure live sphagnum moss and perlite to match their native boggy hillside homes.
Bring them into a cool, frost-free greenhouse or bright porch in winter to survive wet UK freezes.
Watch out for greenfly aphids on the emerging flower buds in spring, washing them off with water.
Never use standard garden fertilisers; use a highly diluted orchid feed only during active growth.

items.name: Disperis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a frost-free greenhouse using a very free-draining, gritty compost mix.
Water them damp during their autumn-to-spring growth, but keep the tubers bone dry in summer dormancy.
Plant the delicate tubers shallowly, just two centimetres deep, with the growing tip pointing up.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring, as they love to devour the emerging flower spikes.
Keep winter temperatures around ten degrees Celsius to protect these tender South African natives.

items.name: Disphyma
items.growersTips:
Plant your Disphyma in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so winter rain drains away fast.
Position this sun-lover on your south-facing patio to soak up every drop of British summer warmth.
Stop watering entirely from November to March to prevent the fleshy roots from rotting in the damp.
Take stem cuttings in August and keep them on a dry windowsill indoors as a backup for hard frosts.
Snip off the withered pink flowers in late autumn to keep the succulent carpet looking tidy.

items.name: Disphyma australe
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand ice plant in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet winters.
Give it a sunny south-facing spot on a rockery or wall where rainwater drains away instantly.
Water only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle slightly, keeping it bone dry throughout winter.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors as insurance against severe UK frosts.
Surround the base with gravel mulch to keep the low-growing foliage from rotting on damp soil.

items.name: Disphyma crassifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant your purple dewplant in a raised bed or rockery with fifty percent grit to survive UK wet.
Keep this succulent bone dry during winter by sheltering it from heavy rain under a cold frame.
Cut back leggy stems in late spring to encourage a dense carpet of pink flowers and fresh leaves.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs as they love to feast on the fleshy foliage.
Grow it in your sunniest south-facing spot to ensure the flowers open fully during the day.

items.name: Disphyma crassifolium subsp. clavellatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Aussie native in the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have to mimic its warm home.
Pot it up in a gritty, free-draining mix of half compost and half horticultural grit to stop rot.
Only water this succulent when the soil is bone dry, and keep it completely dry throughout winter.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first UK frost.
Snip off leggy stems in late spring to keep its carpet-like trailing shape neat and tidy.

items.name: Disphyma papillatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing succulent in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and sharp sand to avoid rot.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot of your patio to mimic its native coastal light levels.
Move your containers into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch before the wet UK winter frosts hit.
Water only when the soil has dried out completely, then soak it thoroughly on a warm morning.
Snip off any leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more pink daisy flowers.

items.name: Ditassa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South American climber in a pot so you can move it indoors before autumn frosts hit.
Use a very free-draining peat-free grit mix to prevent winter root rot in our damp British climate.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this species hates sitting in soggy compost.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing porch to maximise the scarce UK summer sunshine.
Prune back unruly tangled stems in early spring just as new growth starts to show to keep it tidy.

items.name: Diuridinae
items.growersTips:
Grow in a mix of 70% coarse grit and 30% loam to mimic Australian soils in wet UK winters.
Keep tuberoids completely dry from June to August during their mandatory summer dormant phase.
Plant tuberoids 5cm deep in late August to protect them from early autumn frosts in the UK.
Water thoroughly once in autumn to trigger growth, then only when the grit mix is completely dry.
Overwinter pots in a cold greenhouse kept above 2C to prevent freezing while maintaining air flow.

items.name: Diuris
items.growersTips:
Plant these Australian donkey orchids in a gritty, free-draining mix of pumice, bark, and loam.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormancy, starting water only when autumn shoots appear.
Grow them in pots so you can move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for UK winters.
Feed weekly with a highly diluted, low-phosphorus orchid fertilizer during active winter growth.
Watch out for slugs and aphids on the tender spring flower spikes, using organic beer traps nearby.

items.name: Dolichoglottis lyallii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty compost mix to mimic their native alpine home.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering from below to prevent crown rot.
Plant them in a spot that gets cool morning sun but is shielded from the harsh afternoon heat.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on their tender alpine foliage in damp UK weather.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them under cover during our excessively wet winter months.

items.name: Doronicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring under glass or cold frames.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to prevent the shallow root system from drying out.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the emerging young foliage.
Deadhead faded yellow daisy flowers weekly in late spring to encourage a second flush of blooms.

items.name: Dorotheantheae
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African ice plants in your grittiest, sharpest-draining soil to survive UK wet.
Keep them in your sunniest, south-facing spot so the blooms actually open up on cloudy British days.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as damp roots will rot these succulents during cool spells.
Bring potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first October frost.
Mix them with hardy sedums in gravel beds to create a drought-tolerant, colorful ground cover.

items.name: Doryopteris
items.growersTips:
Grow your digit fern in a pot of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for sharp drainage.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy by watering from below with tepid rainwater.
Position your potted fern on a pebble tray in a bright bathroom to mimic the humid tropics.
Bring your plant indoors to a warm windowsill before the first autumn frosts hit your UK garden.
Snip off any brown or tatty fronds right at the base in spring to encourage fresh new growth.

items.name: Doryopteris angelica
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive frosty UK temperatures below ten degrees.
Plant it in a shallow pot using peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of horticultural grit.
Water with harvested rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Position your pot in a humid bathroom or kitchen away from direct summer sun to prevent frond scorch.
Snip off dead or tatty fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, bright green growth.

items.name: Dossinia
items.growersTips:
Bring your jewel orchid indoors before autumn frosts start to keep this tropical beauty warm.
Plant your Dossinia in shallow pots using a loose, airy mix of sphagnum moss and fine orchid bark.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top moss layer feels dry, keeping the roots damp not wet.
Position your pot in a humid bathroom or on a wet pebble tray to mimic its native damp rainforest.
Wipe those gorgeous pinstriped leaves with a damp cloth weekly to clear dust and check for thrips.

items.name: Downingia
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate annual in wet soil or shallow pond margins where it won't dry out in summer.
Sow seeds in spring on the soil surface of boggy areas, pressing them in gently without burying.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the tender young foliage in damp UK spring weather.
Grow them alongside marsh marigolds and water forget-me-nots for a stunning bog garden display.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames to get a head start on next year's vibrant blue flowers.

items.name: Downingia bacigalupii
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of wet mud in early spring without covering them with soil.
Grow them in a shallow bog garden or pond edge where the soil stays permanently wet and saturated.
Keep them in full sun to mimic their native pools, ensuring they get at least six hours of light.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using organic bait as wet conditions attract them.
Plant them alongside native UK marsh marigolds to create a beautiful, moisture-loving display.

items.name: Downingia bella
items.growersTips:
Grow this native pool-dweller in wet, muddy acidic soil at the shallow margins of your garden pond.
Sow the tiny seeds in autumn directly onto damp compost, leaving them uncovered to trigger sprout.
Keep the soil constantly soggy, mimicking a drying vernal pool as summer heat naturally arrives.
Watch out for pond snails and slugs that love to feast on the tender, low-growing spring foliage.
Plant alongside water forget-me-nots to create a beautiful, moisture-loving blue and white display.

items.name: Downingia bicornuta
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of wet, muddy soil in early spring without covering them.
Grow them in a shallow pond margin or a boggy container that stays completely wet all summer.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp spring weather.
Position your pots in full sun to mimic their native open pools and get the best blue blooms.
Bring potted plants into a cold greenhouse over winter to protect roots from severe UK frosts.

items.name: Downingia concolor
items.growersTips:
Grow this pool-loving beauty in wet, acidic boggy soil or shallow pond margins up to five cm deep.
Sow seeds in late autumn directly onto wet mud so the natural winter cold triggers spring growth.
Keep the soil constantly saturated during spring and summer; never let this damp-lover dry out.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love devouring the tender new shoots.
Plant it alongside native UK marsh marigolds to create a stunning, moisture-loving colour contrast.

items.name: Downingia elegans
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in spring, as they need light to germinate in the UK.
Grow this annual in wet, boggy soil or shallow pond margins, keeping it constantly soggy.
Position your pots in full sun to mimic their native pools and encourage those blue blooms.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK spring weather, as they love the tender young shoots.
Pair them with native UK marsh-marigolds in a bog garden to create a stunning damp-loving display.

items.name: Downingia laeta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on wet, acidic mud to mimic the UK's natural seasonal vernal pool cycles.
Grow this damp-lover in a bog garden or shallow pond margin where the soil never dries out.
Position in full sun to ensure these delicate, pale blue flowers bloom well in our cool summers.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the pond edge.
Do not prune, but let the plant self-seed naturally in damp gravel to maintain your colony.

items.name: Downingia pulchella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they need light and winter cold to germinate in the UK.
Keep the soil constantly soggy in spring to mimic their native vernal pools, then let it dry out.
Plant them alongside native UK rushes or dwarf sedges to give their weak stems natural support.
Grow them in shallow, peat-free acidic compost in a sunny spot to match their natural boggy home.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love eating the tender young shoots.

items.name: Downingia yina
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of wet, muddy soil in early spring without burying them at all.
Grow them in shallow, acidic pond margins or boggy containers to mimic their natural vernal pools.
Keep the soil constantly saturated from March to July, then let it dry out completely in late summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the tender young stems in damp UK spring weather.
Plant them alongside native UK bog plants like marsh marigolds to create a beautiful wetland display.

items.name: Dracontioides
items.growersTips:
Plant these bog-lovers in deep, heavy clay mud right at your pond edge so their roots never dry out.
Watch for slugs on the huge emerging spring leaves and use wildlife-safe wool pellets to deter them.
Mulch the crowns with a thick layer of autumn leaves to protect them from harsh UK winter frosts.
Give them space by planting alongside marsh marigolds which won't crowd their massive summer growth.
Propagate by carefully dividing the thick rhizomes in early spring just as the first green tips show.

items.name: Dracontioides desciscens
items.growersTips:
Since this rare Brazilian aroid loves warmth, grow it in a heated greenhouse or conservatory in the UK.
Keep its soil constantly soggy by sitting the pot in a shallow tray of rainwater all year round.
Plant the tuber in a chunky, acidic mix of peat, perlite, and orchid bark to mimic rainforest soil.
Maintain high humidity above sixty percent using a humidifier to stop the leaf tips from browning.
Watch out for red spider mites in winter when your indoor heating makes the air dry and stagnant.

items.name: Dracontium
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical oddity in a pot of peat-free compost mixed with perlite so you can move it inside.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during summer, then stop watering completely when it goes dormant.
Plant the tuber deep, about fifteen centimetres down, to support that single massive umbrella leaf.
Overwinter your pot in a heated greenhouse or warm conservatory to protect it from wet UK frosts.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this plant indoors during the dry summer months.

items.name: Dracontium gigas
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical giant in a large pot so you can bring it indoors before the autumn frosts hit.
Plant the tuber deep in a rich, well-draining mix of peat-free compost, orchid bark, and perlite.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during summer, then stop watering completely when it goes dormant.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this humidity-lover indoors during winter.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light to mimic the rainforest canopy and avoid leaf scorch.

items.name: Dracontium pittieri
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical gem in a deep pot of free-draining aroid mix so you can bring it indoors by October.
Plant the tuber at least fifteen centimetres deep to support that massive, umbrella-like single leaf.
Water heavily during summer but keep the tuber bone-dry in winter to prevent it rotting in the cold.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping it warm indoors during the dry winter months.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid fertiliser once the leaf spike emerges in late spring.

items.name: Dracontium spruceanum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical beauty in a well-draining, peat-free potting mix rich in leaf mould and perlite.
Keep it cozy indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it cannot survive UK winters below fifteen degrees.
Water generously during summer active growth but let the soil dry out slightly between waterings.
Watch out for spider mites and fungus gnats which thrive in the warm, humid air this plant loves.
Plant the tuber about ten centimetres deep in a wide pot to give its vigorous roots plenty of room.

items.name: Dracophilus
items.growersTips:
Grow these South African succulents in a gritty, free-draining loam to survive wet UK winters.
Water them only from spring to autumn, letting the soil dry out completely between drenches.
Keep them on a sunny windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to protect them from frost and damp.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
Mix fine gravel into the topsoil to keep the base of your plants dry and prevent rot.

items.name: Dracunculus
items.growersTips:
Plant your dragon arum tubers deep, about fifteen centimeters down, to protect them from UK frosts.
Grow them in fertile, sharply draining soil; add plenty of grit to stop winter wet rotting tubers.
Position them in full sun or light dappled shade to mimic their warm Mediterranean home climate.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when those dramatic, exotic shoots first push through.
Plant them near the back of borders so other summer plants can hide the foliage as it dies down.

items.name: Dracunculus canariensis
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers deep, about fifteen centimeters down, in autumn to protect them from UK frosts.
Add plenty of grit to your compost because these Canary Island natives hate having soggy winter feet.
Keep them well-watered during spring growth, then stop watering completely once the leaves die back.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or shed over the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love eating the tender new shoots as they emerge.

items.name: Dracunculus vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Plant the tubers deep, about fifteen centimeters down, in autumn to protect them from UK frosts.
Give them a spot in full sun with incredibly sharp-draining soil so the tubers do not rot in winter.
Wear thick gloves when handling them because the sap can cause quite nasty skin irritation.
Do not cut back the dying foliage until it has completely yellowed to feed next year's bloom.
Keep children and pets away from the berries that form after the dramatic spathe withers.

items.name: Drakaea
items.growersTips:
Grow hammer orchids in a cool glasshouse with free-draining sandy compost to mimic Western Australia.
Water them from below during their autumn growth spike, then keep them barely damp through winter.
Inoculate your potting mix with mycorrhizal fungi to help these tricky terrestrial orchids survive.
Keep a sharp eye out for UK greenhouse thrips and aphids that love to feast on the tender new leaves.
Do not prune these delicate perennials; just gently snip off the dead flower spikes in late spring.

items.name: Drakaeinae
items.growersTips:
Grow hammer orchids in a cold greenhouse with free-draining, gritty, low-nutrient terrestrial mix.
Water pots from below only during autumn and winter growth, keeping the soil dry during summer dormancy.
Do not fertilise these orchids as their sensitive mycorrhizal fungi partners will be destroyed.
Hand-pollinate the flowers yourself because their specific Australian wasp pollinator is absent in the UK.
Protect emerging autumn shoots from slugs and snails using copper tape around the greenhouse staging.

items.name: Draperia
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in very sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position your Draperia in a sheltered, partially shaded rock garden to mimic its woodland home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between sessions in summer.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails during damp British spring mornings.
Propagate by taking soft stem cuttings in early summer and rooting them in a sandy compost mix.

items.name: Dregea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of gritty loam so you can move it into a frost-free green house.
Water thoroughly in summer but let the compost dry out completely between sessions to avoid rot.
Prune your vine in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its vigorous size in check.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and wipe them off with a damp cloth in dry weather.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer every two weeks from May to September for more blooms.

items.name: Dregea arabica
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Arabian climber indoors before autumn frosts hit to keep it warm and thriving.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining loam mix to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water generously in summer when topsoil dries, but keep it barely damp throughout the winter.
Position your pot in a south-facing conservatory or sunny patio to mimic its native light.
Prune back any leggy stems in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more fragrant blooms.

items.name: Dregea sinensis
items.growersTips:
Give this climber a warm south-facing wall to shield it from harsh UK winter winds and frosts.
Plant it in extremely free-draining soil mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply only when the top few inches of soil dry out, as it hates soggy UK ground.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its size in check.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids on the tender new shoots during our damp British spring months.

items.name: Dregea volubilis
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender climber indoors before autumn frosts, keeping it in a bright conservatory at 10C.
Plant in loam-based compost with plenty of grit to ensure sharp drainage and prevent winter root rot.
Water freely during the summer growth spurt but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring to encourage fresh flowering wood and keep its size in check.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and wipe leaves down with damp fleece if you spot webs.

items.name: Drimia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Drimia bulbs shallowly in autumn so the top third of the bulb sits just above the soil.
Grow them in terracotta pots with gritty compost so you can easily move them indoors for winter.
Water your Drimia only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely during summer dormancy.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs in spring when those delicate, spear-like flower spikes first emerge.
Place your pots on a south-facing patio to give them the baking summer sun they need to flower well.

items.name: Drimia capensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a container so you can easily move it indoors before winter frosts.
Use a gritty, free-draining loam mix with plenty of horticultural sand to prevent winter bulb rot.
Water well during its autumn and winter growing phase, but keep it bone dry throughout summer dormancy.
Position your pot in the brightest, most sun-drenched spot of your patio to mimic its native habitat.
Watch out for slugs and snails targeting the emerging flower spikes during damp UK autumn nights.

items.name: Drimia elata
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs shallow with their necks just above the soil line in very free-draining gritty compost.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormancy, then start watering when the flower spike appears.
Bring pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill before the first autumn frosts hit.
Use a terracotta pot to help the soil dry out quickly and prevent the bulb from rotting in wet weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails in late summer as they love to munch on the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Drimia exuviata
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African bulb in a gritty, free-draining loam to survive wet UK winters.
Keep the bulb neck just at the soil surface to mimic its native habitat and prevent rot.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, then keep it completely dry during its summer dormancy.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frosts hit.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the unusual, papery peeling layers of its stem.

items.name: Drimia indica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Indian squill in well-drained gritty soil to survive wet winters without rotting.
Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it indoors to a frost-free greenhouse before winter hits.
Water moderately during its summer active growth but keep the bulb completely dry when dormant.
Plant the large bulb with its top third sitting just proud of the compost surface, not buried.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to feast on the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Drimia maritima
items.growersTips:
Plant your sea onion bulb shallowly in autumn with its neck poking just above the soil level.
Keep it bone dry during its summer dormancy, then start watering when the flower spike appears.
Grow this tender Mediterranean native in a pot so you can bring it inside before winter frosts hit.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to ensure the sharp drainage this bulb needs in damp UK weather.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the lush green foliage that emerges after autumn flowering.

items.name: Drimia media
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Set the bulb tips just level with the soil surface rather than burying them deep in the pot.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, then keep the compost almost dry during summer dormancy.
Bring your pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first winter freeze.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails when the delicate autumn flower spikes first emerge.

items.name: Drimiopsis
items.growersTips:
Bring your leopard lily indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive a UK winter.
Plant the bulbs with their necks just peeking out of a gritty, free-draining peat-free compost.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, then let the pot drain completely.
Keep an eye out for snails who love chewing the spotted leaves when kept in a damp garden spot.
Divide the congested bulb clumps in spring just as the new spotted leaves begin to push through.

items.name: Drimiopsis maculata
items.growersTips:
Bring this African bulb indoors by October as it cannot survive a wet, freezing UK winter outside.
Plant bulbs shallowly in spring with their pointed noses just peeking out of the compost surface.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, then reduce to a bare minimum during winter.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your peat-free compost to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to shred the beautiful spotted leaves in damp UK springs.

items.name: Drosanthemum
items.growersTips:

items.name: Echium creticum

items.name: Echium tuberculatum

items.name: Echium virescens

items.name: Echium vulcanorum

items.name: Echium vulgare

items.name: Echium webbii

items.name: Echium wildpretii

items.name: Eclipta

items.name: Ehrendorferia
