items.growersTips:
Give your epimediums a mulch of leaf mould in autumn to mimic their favourite British woodland soil.
Shear off the old leathery leaves in February so you can actually see the delicate new flowers open.
Plant them with the crown just level with the soil surface to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Water them weekly during their first British summer, but after that they can handle dry shade well.
Pair them with snowdrops and primroses for a lovely, classic spring display under deciduous trees.

items.name: Epimedium acuminatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen groundcover in moist, well-drained soil enriched with plenty of leaf mould.
Cut back the old, leathery foliage in late winter to let the delicate spider-like flowers shine.
Water regularly during dry UK summers until established, as it dislikes bone-dry woodland soil.
Shelter it from harsh, freezing winds which can scorch the beautiful bronze-tinted spring leaves.
Divide your clumps in autumn after flowering to easily propagate and fill other shady garden spots.

items.name: Epimedium alpinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine barrenwort shallowly in autumn so the rhizomes sit just below the soil surface.
Tuck it under deciduous shrubs where it gets winter light and damp shade during hot UK summers.
Shear off the old leathery leaves in late February to let the tiny red spring flowers shine.
Keep young plants damp but once established they will easily survive dry shade under mature trees.
Mulch yearly with leaf mould to mimic its native European woodland soil and boost leaf growth.

items.name: Epimedium franchetii
items.growersTips:
Pop your bare-root plant in the ground so the crown sits just below the soil surface in autumn.
Give it a deep weekly soak during dry UK summers to help those woodland roots establish properly.
Snip off the old leathery leaves in late February to let the bright yellow spring flowers shine.
Mulch with leaf mould in spring to mimic its natural damp, acidic woodland home in British gardens.
Plant it alongside shade-loving hostas and ferns to keep its delicate roots cool and protected.

items.name: Epimedium grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
To help your bishop's hat thrive in UK clay, dig in plenty of leaf mould to keep the soil acidic.
Cut back the old leathery foliage right to the ground in February before the new flower buds emerge.
Plant the shallow rhizomes just two centimetres below the soil surface so they do not rot in winter.
Keep the soil damp during dry May spells to help the delicate spring flowers last much longer.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing the roots of these woodland beauties.

items.name: Epimedium pinnatum
items.growersTips:
Cut back old leathery leaves in late February so the delicate yellow spring flowers can be seen.
Plant crowns just below the soil surface in autumn to let winter rain settle them into UK borders.
Mulch with leaf mould in spring to mimic their natural woodland home and keep the soil damp.
Keep them well watered during dry summer spells in their first year until the roots establish.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn after flowering to get free plants for dry shady spots.

items.name: Epimedium pubigerum
items.growersTips:
Cut back the old leathery foliage in late January so the delicate spring flowers can be seen clearly.
Plant them at the exact same depth as the pot in humus-rich, damp soil under deciduous UK trees.
Water weekly during dry summer spells for the first two years until their root system is established.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing the roots of these evergreen clumps.
Divide the woody rhizomes in autumn right after flowering finishes to easily make free new plants.

items.name: Epimedium sagittatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring, burying the crown just below the soil surface to protect it from late UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until its roots establish in your shady border.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing the roots of these woodland plants.
Shear back the old, leathery foliage in late February so the delicate new spring blooms can shine.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your clay soil before planting to mimic their natural woodland home.

items.name: Epimedium wushanense
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen in partial shade using leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soils before mulching.
Water deeply during dry UK summers until established, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged.
Snip off old tattered winter foliage in late February to let the spidery spring flowers shine.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in spring, as they love chewing the roots of your potted plants.
Pair it with hostas and ferns in a sheltered border to protect the long leaves from cold winds.

items.name: Epipactis
items.growersTips:
Plant marsh helleborines in damp, alkaline soil near a pond, keeping their rhizomes just shallow.
Water your broad-leaved helleborines only during dry summer spells once they are well established.
Watch out for slugs eating the tender new spring shoots, so protect them with organic wool pellets.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn using a sharp spade while the orchid is entering dormancy.
Grow them alongside native ferns and hostas to provide the dappled woodland shade they love.

items.name: Epipogiinae
items.growersTips:
Since ghost orchids need specific fungi, mix native beech leaf mould into your soil to help them feed.
Keep the soil constantly damp like a squeezed sponge, using rainwater rather than tap water.
Plant your delicate tubers shallowly, just two inches deep in a shady, sheltered woodland border.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the tender emerging flower spikes.
Never prune or cut back the stems after flowering, just let them die back naturally to save energy.

items.name: Epipremnum
items.growersTips:
Water your pothos only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to avoid root rot in UK damp.
Keep it in bright, indirect light to stop variegated varieties like Marble Queen turning solid green.
Cut stems just below a leaf node in spring to propagate easily in a jar of tap water on your sill.
Feed with a balanced liquid houseplant fertiliser once a month from April to September only.
Watch out for mealybugs in winter when central heating makes your indoor air dry and stuffy.

items.name: Epipremnum amplissimum
items.growersTips:
Keep this Solomon Islands native warm in winter by keeping it indoors away from chilly UK drafts.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Give its aerial roots a moss pole to climb so the narrow leaves can grow to their full size.
Feed with a weak liquid fertiliser monthly from April to September to boost its active growth.
Wipe the long leaves with a damp cloth regularly to clear UK household dust and maximise light.

items.name: Epipremnum aureum
items.growersTips:
Keep this leafy climber away from drafty UK windowsills in winter to protect it from chilly glass.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as damp UK winters easily cause root rot.
Feed your pothos with a liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month from April to September for growth.
Snip leggy stems just below a leaf node in spring to propagate new starts in a jar of tap water.
Wipe the glossy leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust so they get enough weak winter sun.

items.name: Epipremnum ceramense
items.growersTips:
Keep this Indonesian beauty in a warm room above fifteen Celsius to survive chilly UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to prevent root rot.
Give it a moss pole to climb so the leaves grow larger rather than trailing downwards.
Position in bright indirect light near an east window to avoid scorching the delicate foliage.
Feed with weak liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost active growth.

items.name: Epipremnum dahlii
items.growersTips:
Keep this rare climber in a warm room above fifteen Celsius to mimic its tropical island origin.
Plant in a chunky bark and perlite mix to prevent root rot during damp United Kingdom winters.
Water only when the top half of the pot is dry, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid leaf shock.
Provide a moss pole so the aerial roots can climb, which encourages the leaves to grow larger.
Wipe the glossy foliage weekly with a damp cloth to remove dust and prevent spider mite attacks.

items.name: Epipremnum falcifolium
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical climber warm in the UK by placing it in bright, indirect light near a radiator.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free soil dry out, as damp UK winters cause root rot.
Give it a moss pole to climb so the leaves can mature and split, mimicking its natural canopy.
Wipe the long leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and boost light absorption in winter.
Propagate in spring by snipping stems below a node and rooting them in water on a warm windowsill.

items.name: Epipremnum giganteum
items.growersTips:
Bring it indoors by October as this tropical giant cannot survive damp UK winters below ten degrees.
Grow it up a sturdy moss pole to mimic its natural habit and help those massive leaves split open.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in our gloomy winter light.
Wipe the huge leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear UK household dust and boost photosynthesis.
Repot in spring using a chunky mix of peat-free compost, orchid bark, and perlite for drainage.

items.name: Epipremnum pinnatum
items.growersTips:
Keep this climber warm indoors during UK winters, ensuring it stays well above fifteen degrees.
Let the top two inches of compost dry out completely before watering to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Give it a moss pole to climb, which encourages the leaves to split and grow much larger indoors.
Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and boost light absorption in gloomy winters.
Feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost active growth.

items.name: Episcia
items.growersTips:
Keep your episcia indoors year-round as our chilly UK drafts and winter nights will quickly kill it.
Water with lukewarm rainwater from the bottom to keep those gorgeous fuzzy leaves dry and rot-free.
Pot them in a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for that airy, free-draining moisture.
Pinch out the trailing runners in spring to encourage your plant to grow bushier and more compact.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the leaf joints, especially when your indoor heating goes on.

items.name: Episcia cupreata
items.growersTips:
Keep your flame violet in a humid bathroom or on a pebble tray to survive dry UK central heating.
Water from below with tepid rainwater to avoid spotting those gorgeous velvety, metallic leaves.
Grow this tropical beauty as a houseplant or in a heated conservatory, keeping it above fifteen.
Pot in a shallow, wide pan using peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Snip off the trailing runners in spring to easily propagate new baby plants for your friends.

items.name: Episcia lilacina
items.growersTips:
Keep this warm-loving gem indoors as a houseplant year-round, away from chilly UK window drafts.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries to prevent root and crown rot.
Plant in a shallow pot using a peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for fast drainage.
Snip off the trailing runners in late spring to propagate new plants and keep the parent tidy.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs hiding under the soft, velvety leaves during damp winter months.

items.name: Epithema
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical shade-lover in a warm, humid terrarium or heated conservatory to survive UK cold.
Plant in a peat-free, free-draining acidic compost mixed with plenty of perlite to prevent rot.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries, keeping the air around it humid.
Keep it in bright, indirect light but shield it from harsh afternoon sun to avoid leaf scorch.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the leaves regularly to keep these pests away.

items.name: Eranthemum
items.growersTips:
Bring your Eranthemum indoors by October to protect this tropical beauty from chilly UK frosts.
Grow it in a container using peat-free loam compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Water generously in summer when the top inch of soil dries, but keep it barely damp in winter.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage a bushy shape and more blue flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites on the leaf undersides when indoor heating goes on.

items.name: Eranthemum capense
items.growersTips:
Grow this blue sage in pots of loam-based compost so you can bring it inside before first frost.
Water thoroughly when the top inch of soil feels dry, but keep it barely damp during winter.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and more flower spikes.
Set your pots in bright, indirect light near a south-facing window to mimic its warm native home.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer every two weeks from May to September for best blooms.

items.name: Eranthemum pulchellum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender blue beauty in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frosts.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Give it a hard prune right after flowering in spring to keep its bushy shape and boost next blooms.
Place it on a bright, draft-free windowsill or in a heated conservatory to mimic its warm home.
Watch out for red spider mites and mealybugs, which love the dry indoor air of UK winter heating.

items.name: Eranthemum roseum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical beauty in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frosts hit.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Give it a light trim right after its winter flowering to keep the stems bushy and prevent legginess.
Place your pot on a tray of wet pebbles to boost the humidity levels in dry centrally heated rooms.
Keep a close eye out for red spider mites which love the dry indoor air of typical UK winters.

items.name: Eranthis
items.growersTips:
Plant Eranthis hyemalis tubers 5cm deep in autumn, soaking them in water overnight before planting.
Grow them in moist, well-drained soil rich in leafmould under deciduous trees to mimic woodland.
Divide congested clumps green immediately after flowering in spring rather than when they are dry.
Protect emerging yellow flowers from slugs and snails during wet UK winters using organic grit.
Sow fresh seed in summer as it loses viability quickly and needs winter cold to germinate.

items.name: Eranthis hyemalis
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in late summer at a depth of five centimetres and space them ten centimetres apart.
Soak the shrivelled tubers in water for twenty-four hours before planting to trigger active growth.
Grow in moist well-drained alkaline soil enriched with leafmould under deciduous trees or shrubs.
Associate with Galanthus nivalis and Cyclamen coum for a synchronized late winter colour display.
Propagate by lifting and dividing the congested clumps in green immediately after flowering in spring.

items.name: Erechtites
items.growersTips:
To stop this aggressive annual from taking over, pull it up by the roots before it seeds in July.
Sow seeds in spring just on the soil surface as they need UK light to germinate, rather than burying.
Keep the soil damp but not soggy during dry spells to prevent the plant from flowering too early.
Watch out for slugs and snails which absolutely love devouring the tender young spring seedlings.
Plant near heavy feeders like potatoes to help break up compacted clay soils in your veg patch.

items.name: Eremocrinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert gem in a raised bed with half grit to mimic its dry native Utah soil.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep the soil bone dry during winter by placing a cloche over the crown to prevent rot.
Water only during active spring growth, then completely stop once the leaves die back.
Plant it alongside hardy sedums and sempervivums which thrive in the same dry, sunny spots.

items.name: Eremogone
items.growersTips:
Incorporate sharp grit into UK clay soils to prevent winter wet root rot in these alpine perennials.
Sow Eremogone seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter stratification for spring.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once established to mimic dry scree conditions.
Trim back faded flower stems in late summer to maintain a tight cushion habit and prevent self-seeding.
Plant alongside Thymus serpyllum in raised beds for compatible low-nutrient and sharp-drainage needs.

items.name: Eremogone aculeata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in full, unobstructed sun to mimic its native high-elevation dry scree habitat.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts, keeping the crown dry to avoid decay.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by dividing established clumps in spring.
Protect from winter wet using a rain shelter or by top-dressing the soil with a thick layer of grit.

items.name: Eremogone bryophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine cushion in a gritty raised bed or scree to survive wet British winters.
Water only during dry spring spells, as damp soil will quickly rot its delicate, moss-like foliage.
Mix equal parts John Innes number one, sharp sand, and grit to mimic its native Himalayan scree.
Keep an eye out for slugs in autumn, as they love to hide under and devour the dense green cushions.
Grow it alongside saxifrages in a stone trough for a beautiful, well-drained miniature display.

items.name: Eremogone cliftonii
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native rocky habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by carefully dividing clumps in spring.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Eremogone congesta
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine native in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into your soil to mimic its rocky home and prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly once established, only giving it a drink during prolonged, dry UK summer spells.
Trim back the faded flower stems in late summer to keep the dense cushion shape neat and compact.
Protect the crown from damp winter weather by mulching around the base with a thick layer of grit.

items.name: Eremogone fendleri
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold winds, ideally in a raised bed or alpine rockery.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as this plant is highly susceptible to root rot.
Protect the crown from winter wet by top-dressing the surrounding soil with a layer of gravel.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or by dividing the clumps in spring.

items.name: Eremogone franklinii
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Nestle bare roots shallowly into gravelly scree or a rock garden, keeping the crown above soil level.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Protect the evergreen foliage from winter damp by placing a pane of glass or cloche over the plant.
Grow it alongside sedums or sempervivums in a sunny, south-facing raised bed to ensure sharp drainage.

items.name: Eremogone macradenia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mojave sandwort in a raised bed or rockery with fifty percent grit to survive UK winter wet.
Keep it in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic its native desert and prevent leggy growth.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks.
Trim the faded flower stems back to the foliage cushion in late August to keep the mound compact.
Surround the crown with a thick layer of gravel mulch to stop damp soil from rotting the leaves.

items.name: Eremogone saxatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position it in your sunniest spot, as it needs maximum light to mimic its native rocky screes.
Water sparingly, only during dry spells in summer, letting the soil dry out completely between runs.
Surround the collar with a deep layer of pea shingle to keep damp soil away from the crown foliage.
Prune back the spent flower stems in late summer to keep its tight cushion habit neat and compact.

items.name: Eremogone ursina
items.growersTips:
Plant this Bear Valley sandwort in sharp-draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winters.
Give it a sunny spot in your rockery or alpine trough where it gets maximum light and no shade.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells as this tough alpine hates having wet roots.
Keep invasive garden weeds cleared from around its low cushion to prevent it being smothered.
Mix it with slow-growing sempervivums or saxifrages which share its love for dry gritty scree.

items.name: Eremomastax
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors by October to protect its soft leaves from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with a mix of multi-purpose compost, perlite, and grit for drainage.
Keep the soil lightly damp from spring to autumn, but let the top inch dry out before watering.
Position your pot in a bright conservatory or on a south-facing windowsill to mimic its home sun.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and prevent leggy stems.

items.name: Eremomastax speciosa
items.growersTips:
Bring this African forest native indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winters.
Grow it in a fast-draining, peat-free loam mixed with plenty of perlite to prevent winter root rot.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy during summer, then cut watering right back in winter.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light, avoiding direct midday sun which scorches the leaves.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage a bushier shape and prevent it getting leggy.

items.name: Eremothera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April 1cm deep in free-draining sandy soil to prevent rot in wet UK spring weather.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as these drought-tolerant annuals dislike soggy British soil.
Watch for flea beetles in June, using fine insect mesh to protect young leaves from damage.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering season before autumn frosts arrive.
Sow alongside poached egg plants to attract hoverflies that naturally control aphids on the stems.

items.name: Eremothera boothii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under glass at a depth of three millimetres to combat wet UK winters.
Grow in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to mimic its native desert habitat and prevent root rot.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Position in the absolute sunniest spot of your garden to maximise the short UK summer heat.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers to protect them.

items.name: Eremothera chamaenerioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring directly into poor well-drained soil as they dislike root disturbance of potting
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic their native hot dry desert environment
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp British summers
Avoid adding compost or fertilizer to the soil as high nutrients cause floppy weak growth
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in autumn to ensure a display the following year

items.name: Eremothera refracta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a cold frame to protect them
Grow in sharply draining sandy soil mix with added grit to mimic its native dry desert habitat
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise essential summer heat levels
Protect young plants from slugs and snails which eagerly target the tender spring foliage in the UK

items.name: Erepsia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Erepsia indoors to a frost-free windowsill from October to April to survive winter.
Plant them in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part compost for sharp drainage.
Water your Erepsia only when the soil feels bone dry, then soak it thoroughly and let it drain.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most south-facing spot in your garden to mimic South Africa.
Snip off dead flowers in late summer to keep the plant tidy and prevent damp rot in autumn.

items.name: Eria
items.growersTips:
Grow Eria in a free-draining bark and perlite mix rather than soil to prevent winter root rot.
Position in a bright, unheated conservatory or east-facing windowsill to mimic cool UK spring light.
Water thoroughly with rainwater once a week in summer but keep almost dry from November to March.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of ten degrees Celsius to protect these tender orchids from frost.
Feed with a weak high-nitrogen orchid fertilizer only during the active growing season of May to August.

items.name: Eriaxis
items.growersTips:
Try growing this rare wild orchid in a gritty, acidic pine-bark mix to mimic its native soil.
Keep your potted orchid damp but never soggy by watering with rainwater, especially in summer.
Protect the tender roots from harsh UK frosts by overwintering the pot in a cool greenhouse.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to munch on the emerging green shoots.
Repot only when absolutely necessary in early spring, taking care not to disturb the fragile roots.

items.name: Eriinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these woolly orchids in a free-draining bark and perlite mix to survive damp UK winters.
Keep them in a bright conservatory but shade them from harsh afternoon sun to prevent leaf scorch.
Water weekly in summer but let the compost dry out completely between waterings during winter.
Mist the foliage daily in dry indoor air to mimic their natural humid cloud-forest habitat.
Repot only when the pseudobulbs spill over the pot edge, ideally right after spring flowering.

items.name: Erinus
items.growersTips:
Tuck fairy foxglove into gritty, free-draining mortar on sunny garden walls or rock crevices.
Water your young plants sparingly, only when the top inch of gritty alpine soil feels dry.
Look out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, as they love eating the tender new foliage.
Trim back the faded flower stems in late summer to keep the neat cushions compact and tidy.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames so the natural winter chill triggers spring germination.

items.name: Erinus alpinus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in wall crevices or rockeries to prevent winter wet root rot.
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly into the soil surface without covering them with compost.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Cut back faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a neat cushion habit and prevent self-seeding.
Grow alongside Sempervivum or Saxifraga in alpine troughs to create a complementary dry-loving display.

items.name: Eriobotrya japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant your loquat against a south-facing brick wall to trap extra winter heat and boost fruiting.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells while the young tree establishes its deep roots.
Prune in mid-spring after the frosts pass, focusing on removing crossed branches to let light in.
Protect autumn flower buds with fleece if the UK winter forecast threatens a dip below minus five.
Feed with a high-potash tomato fertilizer in summer to encourage better flower and fruit set.

items.name: Eriocapitella
items.growersTips:
Plant these autumn anemones in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent dry summer roots.
Mulch the crown with well-rotted manure in late autumn to protect young plants from harsh UK frosts.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to keep them flowering vigorously.
Watch out for leaf-mining sawfly larvae in June and pick off any blotched leaves immediately.
Water them deeply during dry spells in July and August to ensure a spectacular late-season show.

items.name: Eriocapitella ×hybrida
items.growersTips:
Plant these Japanese anemones in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent leaf scorch.
Mulch the crown with well-rotted manure in late autumn to protect roots from wet UK winter rot.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to control their vigorous spread and boost summer flowering.
Watch out for leaf-mining sawfly larvae in June and cut back any damaged foliage immediately.
Stake taller cultivars like Honorine Jobert in windy areas using discreet hazel twigs in May.

items.name: Eriocapitella hupehensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Japanese anemone in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to stop the roots drying out.
Spread a thick mulch of leaf mould or compost in autumn to protect young roots from hard UK frosts.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or after flowering to keep them vigorous and control spread.
Cut the dead woody stems back to ground level in late winter before the fresh new foliage emerges.
Keep a sharp eye out for caterpillars and leaf-mining sawflies which love chewing the lush leaves.

items.name: Eriochilus
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate Aussie orchid in a gritty, free-draining mix of pumice, peat, and sharp sand.
Keep the compost damp in winter but let it dry out completely during its summer dormant phase.
Protect these tiny winter-bloomers from frost by keeping them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house.
Repot your tubers during their summer dormancy, burying them about two centimetres deep in the soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails in autumn as they love to devour the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Eriodictyon
items.growersTips:
Grow yerba santa in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy soil so you can move it indoors for UK winters.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Prune your plant by one-third in late spring to stop it from getting leggy in low British light.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly if you overwinter your potted shrub in a conservatory or greenhouse.
Mix lots of horticultural grit into your planting hole to mimic its native dry Californian home.

items.name: Eriodictyon altissimum
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare California native in your sunniest, sheltered spot with gravelly, sharp-draining soil.
Keep young plants damp but let established ones dry out completely between waterings to avoid rot.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse over the wet UK winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and encourage fresh growth.
Watch out for root rot during humid British summers by keeping the foliage dry and well-ventilated.

items.name: Eriodictyon angustifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian native in your sunniest south-facing spot in extremely free-draining gravel.
Protect it from wet UK winters by growing it in a terracotta pot that you can move under glass.
Only water this drought-lover when the top five centimetres of soil have dried out completely.
Prune the stems back by a third in late spring once the risk of hard frost has fully passed.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to mimic its natural dry hillside habitat.

items.name: Eriodictyon californicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your poorest, sharpest-draining grit-heavy soil to avoid root rot.
Position it against a south-facing brick wall to mimic its hot homeland and survive wet UK winters.
Only water young plants during dry spells in their first summer, then leave them completely dry.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frosts pass to keep its naturally leggy habit nice and bushy.
Protect the resinous leaves from winter wet with a temporary rain shelter or cloche from November.

items.name: Eriodictyon capitatum
items.growersTips:
Give this rare Californian beauty a spot in your poorest, sharpest draining sandy soil to survive wet winters.
Plant your shrub in your sunniest, most sheltered south-facing border to mimic its native heat.
Water deeply only during dry summer spells once established, as damp soil will quickly rot the roots.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to keep its upright shape tidy.
Watch out for root rot during soggy UK winters by planting it on a slight mound to shed excess rain.

items.name: Eriodictyon crassifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian native in a terracotta pot with grit so you can move it dry for UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as damp UK autumns will quickly rot its woolly grey leaves.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape it and encourage fresh purple blooms.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into your compost to mimic its dry, rocky hillside home.
Watch out for powdery mildew during muggy UK summers, keeping it in a breezy, open spot to dry.

items.name: Eriodictyon sessilifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mexican native in a terracotta pot with 50% grit so you can move it dry into winter shelter.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing patio to mimic its Baja home and survive damp UK summers.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as damp roots in cool British weather will rot it instantly.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and encourage fresh resinous leaves.
Protect the foliage from winter wet with a rain shelter or fleece jacket from November to March.

items.name: Eriodictyon tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Plant this woolly California native in your sunniest, sheltered south-facing spot to mimic its home.
Mix lots of grit into your soil because this beauty will rot instantly in wet winter clay.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave it dry to prevent root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frosts pass to keep its lovely woolly shape compact.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a cold greenhouse to survive freezing winters.

items.name: Eriodictyon trichocalyx
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sunniest south-facing spot with gravel mixed deep into the soil.
Keep young plants damp but let established ones dry out completely between waterings to avoid rot.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse during wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and encourage fresh growth.
Watch out for powdery mildew during damp British summers and space plants out to improve airflow.

items.name: Eritrichium
items.growersTips:
Mix equal parts grit and John Innes number two to mimic alpine scree and prevent winter wet rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn and leave the pots outside to let winter frosts trigger germination.
Water only from the base during winter to keep the hairy foliage dry and prevent devastating rot.
Protect plants with a glass cloche from November to March to shield them from persistent UK rain.
Grow them alongside dwarf saxifrages in a raised alpine trough to ensure perfect sharp drainage.

items.name: Eritrichium nanum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, alkaline scree mix with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only from below or use a collar of pure granite grit to prevent the woolly foliage from rotting.
Protect with an open-ended glass cloche from October to March to shield from persistent UK rain.
Position in an unheated alpine house or cold frame with maximum ventilation and bright, cool light.
Propagate by carefully taking tiny rosette cuttings in early summer using a very sharp, sterile blade.

items.name: Erodiophyllum elderi
items.growersTips:
Sow these Australian desert annuals indoors in early spring using a very free-draining sandy loam.
Keep watering to a bare minimum once established, letting the compost dry out fully between drinks.
Position your pots in the sunniest, warmest spot of your patio to mimic their hot native habitat.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers as soon as you plant out.
Deadhead the daisy-like flowers regularly in summer to encourage a continuous flush of new blooms.

items.name: Erodium
items.growersTips:
Plant Erodium in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between watering sessions.
Cut back faded flowers and stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect alpine Erodium varieties from winter wet using a rain shelter or cloche from November.
Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants easily.

items.name: Erodium acaule
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native scree habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in late spring to ensure new plants establish before winter.
Protect the crown from excessive winter wet using a cloche or by mulching with horticultural grit.

items.name: Erodium botrys
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit or compost.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in full sun, such as a south-facing rockery or gravel garden, to mimic Mediterranean heat.
Deadhead spent flowers regularly in summer to encourage continuous blooms and prevent self-seeding.

items.name: Erodium chium
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, barely covering them with a thin layer of sharp grit.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Mediterranean coastal habitat.
Cut back faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.

items.name: Erodium chrysanthum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or rock gardens to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Greek cliffs and keep the silver foliage dry.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, as this plant is highly drought-tolerant.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in early summer rather than trying to divide the woody taproot.
Protect the crown with a layer of gravel mulch to shed water away from the fuzzy leaves in winter.

items.name: Erodium ciconium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring at a depth of three millimetres in free-draining sandy soil.
Grow in full sun and shelter from heavy UK winter wet by using a cold frame or gritty raised bed.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out completely between drinks.
Sow alongside companion plants like Thymus or Sedum that thrive in the same dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, protecting them with grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Erodium cicutarium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in free-draining sandy loam to mimic UK coastal dunes and ensure overwintering.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, nutrient-poor soil.
Hand-weed taproots before spring flowering to prevent aggressive self-seeding across gravel gardens.
Position in full south-facing sun to prevent winter rot in damp British clay soils.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in rockeries to provide essential drainage and matching low vigor.

items.name: Erodium cygnorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in sharply draining sandy loam to survive wet UK winters without rotting
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass at fifteen degrees Celsius before transplanting outdoors
Water only during prolonged dry spells as this hardy herb is highly drought-tolerant once established
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or gravel garden to mimic its hot natural habitat
Grow alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme and oregano which share its need for dry nutrient-poor soil

items.name: Erodium glandulosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised rockery to prevent winter wet rot in UK rain.
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native Pyrenean cliffs and maximize summer blooms.
Water sparingly only during dry spells once established, allowing the gritty soil to dry out fully.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in early summer or by carefully dividing the clump in spring.
Protect the crown from heavy winter wet using a pane of glass or by planting on a sloped crevice.

items.name: Erodium laciniatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in early spring using a cold frame.
Water only during prolonged dry spells once established to mimic its native Mediterranean habitat.
Position in a south-facing rockery or gravel garden to maximise essential daily sunlight.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of grit or gravel before the onset of winter wet.

items.name: Erodium lebelii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty compost mix to mimic UK shingle beach conditions.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells as this coastal native easily rots in damp soil.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to ensure the sharpest drainage during wet winters.
Watch for slugs and snails during damp UK springs as they target the delicate feathery foliage.
Plant alongside Thymus serpyllum to create a drought-tolerant gravel garden display.

items.name: Erodium malacoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer in free-draining sandy soil to mimic UK gravel garden conditions.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Protect young autumn rosettes from winter waterlogging by planting on a slope or in raised beds.
Cut back faded flower stems in midsummer to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your borders.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in full sun to provide excellent drainage and complementary blooms.

items.name: Erodium manescavi
items.growersTips:
Plant in grit-amended, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun to mimic its native Pyrenean habitat and ensure continuous summer blooms.
Cut back faded flower stems and tatty foliage in autumn to keep the rosette tidy for winter.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells in the height of UK summer.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn, as they require winter chilling to germinate by spring.

items.name: Erodium maritimum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or rock crevices to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full sun to mimic its native UK coastal cliffs and encourage compact, healthy growth.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a gritty compost mix and keep them in a cold frame.
Protect from slugs and snails during damp UK springs when young foliage is most vulnerable.

items.name: Erodium moschatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer in free-draining sandy soil to mimic UK coastal habitats.
Water sparingly once established, letting the gritty soil dry out fully between winter rains.
Watch for slugs and snails on young rosettes during damp UK autumns and protect with grit barriers.
Cut back the spent flowering stems in late summer to control its prolific self-seeding habit.
Grow alongside Thymus serpyllum in sunny rock gardens to provide essential winter drainage.

items.name: Erodium texanum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using grit-heavy compost to mimic its native dry habitat.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden with sharp drainage to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent crown rot in damp weather.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using copper tape or beer traps.
Plant alongside hardy sedums and thymes which share its strict requirement for low-nutrient soil.

items.name: Erymophyllum
items.growersTips:
Sow these Australian paper-daisy seeds indoors in March to beat the chilly UK spring frosts.
Plant your seedlings out in May in a spot that gets at least six hours of direct British sunshine.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep their roots dry during our frequent summer downpours.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy conditions.
Snip off the faded flower heads regularly to keep new daisy-like blooms popping up until autumn.

items.name: Erythronium
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in moist, humus-rich soil that mimics woodland conditions.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent the delicate foliage from scorching.
Mulch annually with leafmould in winter to retain moisture and replicate natural forest floors.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering while the foliage is still green and active.

items.name: Erythronium ‘Pagoda’
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs deep, about ten to fifteen centimeters down, so they stay cool during UK summers.
Mix lots of leaf mould or compost into your soil to recreate their favourite damp woodland home.
Never let the bulbs dry out before planting; get them in the ground the moment they arrive in autumn.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh new growth.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next spring.

items.name: Erythronium albidum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs pointy side up about ten centimetres deep in moist, leaf-mould enriched soil.
Keep the soil damp even in summer dormancy by adding a thick bark mulch to mimic woodland floors.
Sow them under deciduous shrubs like hazel so they get spring sun before the leaf canopy closes.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs as they love chewing the emerging buds.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year's show.

items.name: Erythronium americanum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs immediately in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres so they do not dry out.
Mix leafmould and grit into your soil to mimic a damp, free-draining British woodland floor.
Place them in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect the delicate yellow petals from sun.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring but let them dry out slightly when they go dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they love to eat the emerging mottled foliage.

items.name: Erythronium californicum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs ten centimetres deep in autumn so they stay cool and do not dry out in UK summers.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to recreate the damp, woodland floor they love so much.
Keep the soil moist during active spring growth but let them go relatively dry once they die back.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love to eat the emerging shoots.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs so they get spring sun before the canopy blocks out the light.

items.name: Erythronium caucasicum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs early in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres to keep them cool during UK winters.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to mimic their natural damp, deciduous woodland habitat.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged throughout their active spring growing phase.
Protect the emerging early spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or grit.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs like hazel so they get spring sun before the canopy shades them.

items.name: Erythronium citrinum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres, twice as deep as the bulb itself.
Choose a spot with moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil that mimics a woodland floor.
Position them under deciduous shrubs to give them spring dappled shade and summer dry dormancy.
Keep the soil damp while they grow, but let them dry out slightly once the leaves die back in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch the emerging marbled leaves.

items.name: Erythronium dens-canis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs five inches deep in autumn so they stay cool and never dry out during UK summers.
Mix lots of leaf mould into your soil to mimic the damp, deciduous woodland floor they love most.
Plant them under hostas or ferns which shade the soil just as the erythronium foliage dies back.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they absolutely love ruining the early blooms.
Leave the fading leaves alone after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next spring's show.

items.name: Erythronium grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs early in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in cool, moisture-retentive soil.
Recreate their native woodland edge habitat by planting them under the light shade of deciduous shrubs.
Keep the soil consistently damp during their spring growth but let it dry out slightly in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails which absolutely love devouring the fresh emerging spring shoots.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.

items.name: Erythronium helenae
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs early in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in humus-rich, well-draining soil.
Mimic their native woodland home by choosing a dappled shade spot under deciduous shrubs or trees.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during their active spring growing season.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in winter to protect the bulbs and replicate forest floor nutrients.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch on the emerging fresh foliage.

items.name: Erythronium hendersonii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs 10cm deep in autumn so they stay cool and moist during dry UK summers.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to mimic the damp, woodland floors they love.
Grow them under deciduous shrubs so they get spring sun but stay shaded in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they adore the emerging mottled leaves.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year.

items.name: Erythronium japonicum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics woodland floors.
Position in partial to full shade under deciduous shrubs to prevent summer sun from baking the soil.
Water during dry spring spells but keep soil barely damp, not soggy, during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Leave foliage to die back naturally to feed the bulb and avoid disturbing the soil in summer.

items.name: Erythronium klamathense
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs 10cm deep in moist, well-drained leafmould to mimic their native conifer woods.
Keep the soil damp throughout summer dormancy, as these delicate bulbs hate drying out completely.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in a cold frame, but be patient as they take five years to flower.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tender mottled foliage first emerges.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs to give them spring sun followed by cool summer shade.

items.name: Erythronium mesochoreum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs 8cm deep in autumn so the early spring roots stay cool and damp in UK weather.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into heavy clay soil to mimic the well-drained woodland floor they love.
Keep the soil damp during their active spring growth but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they adore eating the emerging flower buds.
Grow them alongside hepatica or wood anemone for a beautiful, natural-looking spring display.

items.name: Erythronium montanum
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine native deep, about ten centimetres down, so the bulbs stay cool during summer.
Mimic its rainy home by watering regularly in spring, but keep it drier once the leaves die back.
Mix plenty of leafmould and grit into your soil to get that perfect, free-draining woodland feel.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring, as they love to devour the emerging flower buds.
Grow them alongside dwarf ferns or hepatica to shade the soil when the bulbs go dormant in July.

items.name: Erythronium multiscapideum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-draining soil.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland canopy conditions.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow to dry out slightly during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by lifting and dividing congested clumps in late summer just as the foliage dies back.

items.name: Erythronium oregonum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimeters in moist, well-drained deciduous shade.
Mimic their native damp spring by watering weekly until June, then keep them dry during dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love the emerging fresh foliage.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your soil to recreate a rich woodland floor.
Plant them alongside wood anemones or small ferns which will cover the bare ground when they die back.

items.name: Erythronium pluriflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs ten centimeters deep in autumn so they stay cool and damp during hot UK summers.
Mix lots of leaf mould into your soil to mimic their natural shady woodland home before planting.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy from late winter until their leaves die back.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch the fresh emerging shoots.
Sow seeds immediately in cold frames if you want to propagate them, as dried seeds won't germinate.

items.name: Erythronium propullans
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny bulbs five centimetres deep in leaf-mould rich soil under deciduous garden trees.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during spring, then let them dry out slightly as they go dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate pink shoots first push through.
Grow them alongside wood anemones or miniature ferns to mimic their native woodland floor habitat.
Leave the bulbs completely undisturbed for years so they can slowly spread via their unique runners.

items.name: Erythronium purpurascens
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 10cm deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under deciduous trees.
Incorporate leafmould or composted bark to mimic UK woodland soil and prevent summer drying out.
Position in dappled shade as strong afternoon UK sun scorches the delicate purplish-green foliage.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but avoid waterlogging to prevent bulb rot.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Erythronium pusaterii
items.growersTips:
Plant these Sierra Nevada natives five inches deep in moist, leafy soil to mimic their mountain home.
Give them a spot in cool, dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to copy UK woodland edge conditions.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during winter, then let them dry out slightly as they go dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate, mottled leaves first push through.
Mulch with leaf mould in autumn to feed the bulbs and keep the soil structure beautifully open.

items.name: Erythronium revolutum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in moist but well-drained leafmould soil.
Mimic their native damp woodland home by planting them under the light dappled shade of deciduous shrubs.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring growth but let them dry out slightly when dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love devouring the emerging fresh shoots.
Combine them with wood anemones or miniature ferns which thrive in the same cool UK woodland conditions.

items.name: Erythronium rostratum
items.growersTips:
Plant these yellow trout lily bulbs deep, about ten centimetres down, so they stay cool in summer.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to recreate the damp, acidic woodland floors they love.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring but let them dry out a bit once they go dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love devouring the new shoots.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs to give them spring sunshine and essential summer shade.

items.name: Erythronium sajanense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native Siberian woodland habitat.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out slightly during summer.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect bulbs from severe UK winter wet and frosts.
Watch for lily beetle larvae in spring and handpick them immediately to prevent foliage damage.

items.name: Erythronium sibiricum
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs 10cm deep in late summer so they do not dry out in the UK's autumn winds.
Mix leafmould into your soil to mimic their native forest home and keep the roots damp but draining.
Position them under deciduous shrubs to give them spring sun but cool shade during hot UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs, as they love to eat the emerging flower buds.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year's display.

items.name: Erythronium sulevii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, acidic soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their natural woodland floor habitat.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but avoid waterlogging during summer dormancy.
Apply a thick leaf mould mulch annually in autumn to replicate woodland leaf litter and feed bulbs.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Erythronium taylorii
items.growersTips:
Plant these rare bulbs ten centimetres deep in rich, leaf-mould soil under deciduous garden trees.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during their spring growing and flowering phase.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Leave the dying foliage to yellow naturally in summer to feed the bulb for next year's yellow blooms.
In the UK, plant them alongside wood anemones or miniature ferns for a natural woodland aesthetic.

items.name: Erythronium tuolumnense
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil under deciduous trees or shrubs.
Incorporate leafmould or well-rotted manure before planting to mimic their native woodland floor.
Water during dry spring spells but keep the soil relatively dry and undisturbed during summer dormancy.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps in late summer just as dormancy ends, replanting the fragile bulbs immediately.

items.name: Erythronium umbilicatum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs ten centimetres deep in autumn so they stay cool and damp during hot UK summers.
Mix lots of leaf mould into your soil to mimic the damp deciduous woodlands they love to grow in.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy from late winter until their foliage dies back.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs like hazel to give them spring sun and deep summer shade.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh shoots.

items.name: Erythrophleum
items.growersTips:
Sow these tender seeds indoors in early spring using bottom heat to get a head start on our UK cold.
Scarify the tough seed coats with sandpaper before soaking them for twenty-four hours to aid growth.
Plant them out in late May once frosts pass, choosing the brightest, most sheltered spot you have.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving them daily splashes.
Protect your young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British spring nights.

items.name: Erythrophleum fordii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator at twentyC
Grow in free-draining acidic loam amended with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils
Position in the warmest south-facing border to maximise summer heat and protect from cold winds
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep the soil barely damp during autumn

items.name: Erythrophleum lasianthum
