items.growersTips:
Sow Falcataria seeds indoors in early April at a depth of one centimetre to beat late UK frosts.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently from below to protect seedlings.
Position your pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the weak British spring sunshine.
Watch out for slugs and snails when hardening them off outside in late May after the final frost.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertiliser once they are established in the ground.

items.name: Farfugium
items.growersTips:
Plant your Farfugium in a sheltered, damp spot under deciduous trees to mimic its woodland home.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your clay soil before planting to keep those roots cool and moist.
Slugs absolutely love those glossy leaves, so surround your plants with grit or organic pellets.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry summer spells to stop those huge leaves from wilting.
Mulch heavily with bark in late autumn to protect the crown from wet, freezing UK winter soil.

items.name: Farinopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant this shrub in a sheltered UK spot to protect its delicate leaves from harsh freezing winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry English summers, rather than giving it daily light sprinkles.
Prune your shrub in late spring right after flowering to keep its shape neat and compact.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into heavy clay soil to ensure the roots do not rot in wet winters.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which love to nibble on the roots of this shrub.

items.name: Faucaria
items.growersTips:
Bring your tiger jaws inside by October to protect them from wet and freezing British winters.
Gritty, free-draining soil is key; mix fifty percent John Innes number two with poultry grit.
Water only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle, keeping them bone dry from November to March.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sun.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the toothy leaf margins and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Faucaria bosscheana
items.growersTips:
Bring your Tiger Jaws indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect them from cold UK winters.
Plant in a gritty mix of equal parts potting soil, perlite, and horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep them completely dry from November through February.
Check the deep crevices of the fleshy leaves regularly for mealybugs hiding from the damp UK air.
Place them in a terracotta pot rather than plastic to help the roots breathe in our humid climate.

items.name: Faucaria britteniae
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts compost and horticultural sand.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill to mimic its native light and prevent winter stretching.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then keep it completely dry in winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the toothy leaf crevices and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
Bring your potted plant indoors by October as it will not survive a wet, freezing British winter.

items.name: Faucaria felina
items.growersTips:
Bring your tiger jaws inside by October to protect them from wet and freezing UK winter rot.
Plant them in a gritty mix of half potting compost and half horticultural grit for fast drainage.
Only water when the fleshy leaves start to feel slightly soft, keeping them bone dry all winter.
Position on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the jaw-like leaf crevices and dab them with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Faucaria subintegra
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes number two and half grit.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill inside, as it will not survive a wet UK winter outdoors.
Water deeply from April to September only when the soil is bone dry, then keep it totally dry in winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the fleshy leaf joints, dabbing them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.
Repot every two years in spring into a shallow terracotta pan to prevent the roots from rotting.

items.name: Faucaria tigrina
items.growersTips:
Bring your tiger jaws indoors by October to protect them from wet and freezing UK winter weather.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping them completely dry from November through to March.
Pot them in a gritty mix of equal parts John Innes number two, coarse grit, and perlite for drainage.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic their sunny South African home.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the toothy leaf folds and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Faucaria tuberculosa
items.growersTips:
Bring your tiger jaws inside by October to protect them from damp UK winter frosts on a sunny sill.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then keep it completely dry in winter.
Pot them in a gritty mix of fifty percent John Innes number two and fifty percent coarse perlite.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the bumpy leaf warts and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than plastic to help the roots dry out quickly in our climate.

items.name: Favratia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Favratia in well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position this perennial in a sheltered, south-facing spot to catch the maximum British summer sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry spells, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect the crown with a thick mulch of gravel in late autumn to shield it from heavy winter frosts.
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new growth starts, to keep your plants vigorous.

items.name: Fendlera
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun against a south-facing brick wall to mimic its native hot, dry canyon microclimate.
Incorporate heavy grit and limestone chippings into clay soils to ensure the sharp winter drainage.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry spring spells, then leave to establish without feed.
Prune immediately after summer flowering by cutting back flowered shoots to strong lower buds.
Protect young spring shoots from late UK frosts using fleece to prevent damage to the flower buds.

items.name: Fendlera rupicola
items.growersTips:
Plant in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot or against a warm wall to mimic Utah heat.
Incorporate plenty of grit and lime into the planting hole to ensure the sharp drainage it needs.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, as damp UK winters are its enemy.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer, cutting back flowered shoots to strong buds.
Watch for aphids on new spring growth and protect young plants from severe, wet winter frosts.

items.name: Fendlerella
items.growersTips:
Plant this drought-tolerant shrub in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native hot, arid US habitat.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot.
Prune lightly immediately after summer flowering to maintain its compact, mounded shape.
Protect young plants from severe winter frosts using a dry mulch of gravel around the base.

items.name: Fenestraria
items.growersTips:
Grow baby toes in a gritty mix of three parts pumice to one part loam to prevent UK winter rot.
Water only when the flat leaf tops wrinkle, keeping them completely dry from November to March.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to maximise weak UK winter sun and prevent leggy growth.
Keep the translucent leaf windows level with the soil surface when potting to mimic nature.
Watch out for split leaves, which mean your indoor humidity is too high or you have overwatered.

items.name: Fernaldia
items.growersTips:
Grow Fernaldia in a sheltered UK spot with moist, acidic soil rich in leaf mould to mimic woodland.
Plant your Fernaldia crown just level with the soil surface in spring to prevent winter crown rot.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the soil damp but never soggy.
Mulch with pine needles in November to protect the root zone from harsh British winter frosts.
Prune back dead foliage in late February to make way for fresh, vibrant spring growth.

items.name: Ferraria
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs in early autumn about eight to ten centimetres deep in gritty soil.
Keep them in your sunniest spot or a cold greenhouse to protect the winter foliage from hard frosts.
Water them weekly during their winter growing phase but keep them bone dry once they die back in June.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging flower buds.
Grow them in terracotta pots filled with loam-based compost mixed with plenty of horticultural grit.

items.name: Ferraria crispa
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in very gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Water them regularly throughout winter and spring, but keep them bone dry once they die back in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the unusual starfish-like buds start to emerge.
Position your pots in the sunniest, warmest spot in your garden to mimic their native South Africa.

items.name: Ficaria
items.growersTips:
Plant double-flowered Flore Pleno in damp, shady borders where they can safely spread without fuss.
Work plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted manure into your soil to mimic their native UK woodland home.
Divide congested clumps in late summer when they are dormant, replanting tubers about five cm deep.
Plant them alongside snowdrops and primroses for a beautiful, naturalised spring display in your lawn.
Keep an eye out for celandine rust fungus on leaves and pick off infected foliage to stop the spread.

items.name: Ficaria verna
items.growersTips:
Plant these tubers shallowly about five centimetres deep in autumn under deciduous garden trees.
To stop them spreading too fast, grow colourful cultivars like Brazen Hussy in sunken containers.
Keep the soil consistently damp in winter and spring, but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for the yellow rust fungus in spring and remove any distorted leaves immediately.
Plant them alongside snowdrops and wood anemones for a beautiful, classic UK woodland display.

items.name: Fieldia
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian native in a pot of ericaceous compost so you can move it indoors for winter.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, using rainwater to mimic its humid rainforest home.
Hang your pot in a sheltered, shady spot out of the harsh afternoon sun to prevent leaf scorch.
Prune lightly after spring flowering to keep its scrambling, epiphytic growth habit tidy.
Protect it from slugs and snails in spring when the delicate new trailing shoots begin to emerge.

items.name: Fieldia australis
items.growersTips:
Grow this Aussie gem in a hanging basket using a peat-free ericaceous mix with plenty of perlite.
Hang it in a sheltered, damp, shady spot to mimic its native cool temperate rainforest home.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, especially during dry UK summers.
Bring it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the first autumn frosts hit your area.
Propagate new plants by taking soft semi-ripe cuttings in late summer and using a heated propagator.

items.name: Filago
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the surface of gritty soil in autumn so winter cold triggers spring germination.
Grow this woolly annual in your poorest, sharpest-draining sand or gravel to prevent winter rot.
Avoid watering once established because this dry-land native thrives on UK rainfall alone.
Plant alongside wild thyme or stonecrop to create a naturalistic, drought-tolerant gravel garden.
Leave the faded seedheads intact over winter to self-sow naturally in your sunny patio cracks.

items.name: Filetia
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your heavy UK clay soil to give this damp-loving perennial the drainage it needs.
Plant your divisions in early spring at the exact same depth they were growing in their old pots.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells to keep the woodland-style soil consistently damp.
Cut the faded flowering stems back to the ground in autumn to encourage healthy new spring growth.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the tender new shoots during wet British spring mornings.

items.name: Fitchia
items.growersTips:
Start your Fitchia seeds indoors in early April to beat the cool UK spring and get a head start.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in our damp British climate.
Pinch out the growing tips when your plants are young to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.
Feed them with a high-potash liquid seaweed fertilizer every two weeks once the first buds appear.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet summer spells, using organic beer traps to protect them.

items.name: Fittonia
items.growersTips:
Keep your nerve in winter by keeping them away from drafty windowsills and radiator heat in the UK.
Water with tepid rainwater when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent their dramatic wilting.
Mix peat-free compost with plenty of perlite to stop their delicate roots rotting in damp UK light.
Snip off the growing tips in spring to encourage a bushy habit instead of leggy, trailing stems.
Mist them daily or pop them in a humid bathroom to mimic the rainforest in our dry central heating.

items.name: Fittonia albivenis
items.growersTips:
Keep your nerve-plant cozy indoors by misting it daily to mimic the humid UK glasshouse environment.
Water with lukewarm rainwater when the top inch of soil dries, as cold tap water shocks its roots.
Grow your fittonia in a shallow pot with peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Pinch off the stem tips in spring to stop it getting leggy and encourage a lovely bushy shape.
Place it on a north-facing windowsill to avoid the harsh summer sun scorching those colorful leaves.

items.name: Fittonia gigantea
items.growersTips:
Keep this rain-forest beauty cozy indoors at fifteen degrees minimum to survive chilly UK winters.
Drench the soil only when the top inch dries out, using tepid rainwater to avoid shocking its roots.
Mix three parts peat-free compost with one part perlite to stop soggy British damp from causing rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to stop this sprawling perennial from getting leggy and wild.
Mist the leaves daily or use a pebble tray to mimic the humid tropics in dry, centrally heated homes.

items.name: Fittonia verschaffeltii
items.growersTips:
Keep this Peruvian native warm and draft-free indoors, as UK winter windowsills get far too chilly.
Water whenever the top soil dries, but if she wilts dramatically, a quick misting will perk her up.
Mix lots of peat-free compost with perlite to prevent root rot in our damp, dark British winters.
Snip the growing tips regularly in spring to keep her trailing stems bushy rather than leggy.
Group her with ferns in a humid bathroom to mimic her rain forest home and stop leaf edges browning.

items.name: Fitzroya cupressoides
items.growersTips:
Give this slow-growing Chilean conifer plenty of space in deep, moist, acidic to neutral soil.
Plant your Fitzroya in a sheltered spot away from drying winds to protect its delicate foliage.
Water young trees deeply during dry UK summer spells to establish a strong, resilient root system.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to mimic its native temperate rainforest floor.
Avoid pruning this conifer altogether as it naturally forms a beautiful, weeping pyramidal shape.

items.name: Fitzwillia
items.growersTips:
Sow your Fitzwillia seeds in late spring once the UK frosts have fully passed for the year.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent these annual roots from rotting.
Plant them in a sheltered spot with plenty of sunshine to protect them from chilly British winds.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to nibble on the tender young leaves of this annual.
Mix plenty of well-rotted compost into your garden bed before planting to give them a great start.

items.name: Flaveria bidentis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in April, barely covering them, as they need warmth to germinate.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest spot, as this South American native craves full UK sun.
Water the soil deeply only when the top few inches dry out, avoiding soggy roots in wet UK summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow flower clusters.
Grow them alongside Mediterranean herbs like oregano to help drain the soil and deter common aphids.

items.name: Flaveria campestris
items.growersTips:
Start this sun-loving annual indoors in April to beat the UK chill, sowing seeds just on the surface.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent stem rot in damp UK summers.
Mix plenty of grit into your border soil to ensure the sharp drainage this wild plains native needs.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or copper tape to protect your plants.
Plant them next to purple salvias to create a stunning colour contrast that thrives in full sun.

items.name: Flaveria chlorifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Plant out in late May after the frosts in a south-facing spot to maximize our limited UK sunshine.
Water the base deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more vibrant yellow blooms.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots during damp British Junes by using organic wool pellets around them.

items.name: Flaveria floridana
items.growersTips:
Start this warm-climate annual indoors in April to beat the short, cool British growing season.
Plant your seedlings out in late May in a spot that gets at least six hours of direct UK sunshine.
Water the base deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage strong, deep roots.
Grow it in poor, sandy soil with grit added to ensure the roots never sit in cold winter wet.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier shape and get way more yellow flowers.

items.name: Flaveria linearis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of three millimetres to beat the cool UK spring temperatures.
Plant this yellow flare in poor, sandy soil to prevent it from getting too floppy in damp weather.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this plant hates soggy British winter wet.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier shape and more golden autumn flowers.
Grow it next to purple lavender to create a stunning contrast that thrives in dry, sunny borders.

items.name: Flaveria oppositifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow these tender annual seeds indoors in April, barely covered with compost, as they need light.
Plant them out in late May after the frosts, spaced thirty centimetres apart in your sunniest bed.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as they hate soggy British winter wet.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and far more yellow blooms.
Grow them alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary to help deter common UK greenhouse pests.

items.name: Flaveria trinervia
items.growersTips:
Sow these heat-lovers indoors in April at just two millimetres deep to get a head start on UK cold.
Plant them out in late May after frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full southern sun.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as they easily rot in damp British weather.
Mix plenty of grit into your clay soil to mimic their native dry, rocky Mexican home environment.
Snip off the faded yellow flower heads in August to keep them bushy and stop them self-seeding wild.

items.name: Fleischmannia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March at two millimetres deep to combat late UK spring frosts.
Water the soil base weekly to keep it moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs by using organic beer traps around stems.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers before autumn.
Grow alongside companion plants like marigolds to naturally deter aphids in typical UK borders.

items.name: Flickingeria
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a warm conservatory or terrarium to protect it from chilly UK winters.
Mist the aerial roots daily during summer and let the bark compost dry out slightly between waterings.
Mount it on cork bark with sphagnum moss instead of potting it in standard soil to prevent root rot.
Position it in bright, filtered light but shield it from direct midday sun in July and August.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser every third watering during its active spring and summer growth.

items.name: Flourensia cernua
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of 3mm using a free-draining sandy loam to prevent root rot.
Place pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light and keep soil temperature at 21C.
Water seedlings sparingly from below only when the top two centimetres of compost are bone dry.
Acclimatise plants outdoors in late May after the last frost and space them thirty centimetres apart.
Plant alongside rosemary or lavender in gravel beds to match their strict low-moisture requirements.

items.name: Fockea
items.growersTips:
Bring your Fockea indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a mix of half grit and half peat-free compost to stop the fat caudex from rotting.
Water deeply only when the soil is bone dry in summer, then keep it completely dry over winter.
Keep the lower round caudex shaded under the soil for a few years to help it swell up much faster.
Train the vigorous twining summer vines onto a small hoop trellis to keep them tidy indoors.

items.name: Fockea edulis
items.growersTips:
Bring your Fockea indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect its caudex from UK frosts.
Plant it with the fat caudex sitting mostly above a very gritty, free-draining cactus compost.
Water thoroughly only when the soil dries out completely, then keep it bone dry all winter long.
Check the tangled summer vines regularly for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints and crevices.
Prune back unruly leafy vines in early spring to keep the plant neat and encourage a fatter base.

items.name: Fockea multiflora
items.growersTips:
Keep this African succulent in a pot so you can bring it indoors before the damp UK autumn chills.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November to March.
Plant it with the fat caudex sitting proud above the soil line to prevent winter rot in our damp air.
Position it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense sunlight of its homeland.
Repot every two years in spring using a mix of fifty percent John Innes number two and fifty percent grit.

items.name: Fokienia
items.growersTips:
Give this rare Chinese cypress shelter from cold UK winds and plenty of sun to keep it happy.
Plant your Fokienia in moist, acidic to neutral soil, adding well-rotted leaf mould to the pit.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Prune your evergreen lightly in late spring only to remove dead wood or shape its fan-like sprays.
Grow this tender conifer in a large pot so you can move it into a greenhouse for winter protection.

items.name: Forsteronia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Forsteronia indoors before the first autumn frost to protect its tender roots.
Plant this woody climber in a peat-free, loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Position your container near a south-facing wall to give it maximum summer warmth and light.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as it hates waterlogged winter soil.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its vine habit tidy.

items.name: Forzzaea warasii
items.growersTips:
Bring your Forzzaea warasii indoors before October frosts, as they cannot survive UK winters.
Water sparingly from above only when the top two inches of compost feel completely dry to touch.
Grow them in a gritty, free-draining loam-based mix to prevent root rot during damp UK summers.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the weak autumn sunlight we get here.
Repot in spring using a shallow terracotta pan rather than a deep plastic pot to aid drainage.

items.name: Fragaria × ananassa
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in spring to prevent rot in wet UK weather.
Water heavily at the base during fruit swell, keeping foliage dry to avoid grey mould.
Tuck barley straw under developing berries in May to lift them off damp soil and deter slugs.
Cut back all foliage to five centimetres after the final harvest in August to stimulate new growth.
Plant alongside garlic or chives to naturally deter aphids and red spider mites in humid summers.

items.name: Fragaria ×vescana
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using well-rotted manure to help runners establish before the cold UK winter wet.
Space plants forty centimetres apart in raised beds to prevent fruit rot during damp UK summers.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during fruit swell to avoid powdery mildew on the foliage.
Cut back all runners in August to redirect energy into the crown for a stronger crop next summer.
Net the crop in May to protect the early ripening berries from blackbirds and thrushes.

items.name: Fragaria cascadensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, gritty, well-draining soil to mimic its native Cascade range pine-forest habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the crown dry to prevent rot in damp weather.
Prune runners in late summer to maintain a compact shrub habit and boost next year's berry yield.
Protect roots with pine needle mulch to maintain the low soil pH and suppress weeds in wet climates.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in autumn, as they target container-grown plants in damp UK gardens.

items.name: Fragaria chiloensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in well-drained, sandy soil with grit to mimic coastal dunes and prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply during dry summer spells but keep the crown dry to avoid fungal diseases in damp weather.
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in autumn to allow roots to establish before winter frosts.
Prune runners in late summer to focus energy on fruit production rather than invasive spreading.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK weather.

items.name: Fragaria daltoniana
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic to neutral, gritty loam to mimic its native Himalayan scree and prevent winter rot.
Plant the crown exactly level with the soil surface in autumn to ensure winter survival in the UK.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, keeping the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Propagate by pegging down runners into small pots of peat-free compost during July and August.
Protect the early spring white flowers from late UK frosts using a temporary fleece cover overnight.

items.name: Fragaria iinumae
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic, sandy-loam soil mimicking its native Japanese subalpine woodland habitat.
Provide partial shade and consistent moisture to prevent leaf scorch during dry UK summer spells.
Propagate via runners in late summer, potting them up in ericaceous compost to establish roots.
Protect the delicate white spring blossoms from late UK frosts using a temporary fleece cover.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants, treating with nematodes in autumn.

items.name: Fragaria iturupensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in acidic, sandy-loam soil with a pH of 5.5 to 6.5, mimicking its volcanic Kuril Island origin.
Provide winter cloche protection in wet UK regions to prevent crown rot from heavy winter rain.
Water consistently at the base during fruit set, keeping soil moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Propagate via runners in late summer, potting them in peat-free ericaceous compost for winter shelter.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants, treating with nematodes in autumn.

items.name: Fragaria moschata
items.growersTips:
Plant one male pollinator like Profumata di Tortona for every five female plants to ensure fruit set.
Grow in dappled shade rather than full sun to mimic its native European woodland edge habitat.
Mulch with straw in May to keep the low-hanging, delicate musk berries off wet British soil.
Net the bed in June as the intense aromatic scent attracts local birds far more than hybrid berries.
Clear away runners in autumn to keep the main crown productive and prevent overcrowding in damp air.

items.name: Fragaria moupinensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this wild strawberry in moist, well-drained acidic soil to mimic its native Sichuan woodland.
Water consistently during dry UK summers, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged to avoid rot.
Plant runners in autumn at crown level, ensuring the central bud sits exactly flush with the soil.
Protect the early spring white flowers from late UK frosts using a temporary fleece cover.
Prune away dead foliage and excess runners in late autumn to maintain a neat groundcover habit.

items.name: Fragaria nilgerrensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild strawberry in dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil to mimic its woodland home.
Water consistently during the summer fruiting period to prevent the shallow root system drying out.
Protect the delicate white alpine blooms from late UK spring frosts using a temporary fleece cover.
Propagate by pegging down the vigorous runners into small pots of compost during late summer.
Net the plants in June to protect the highly aromatic, pale white-pink berries from garden birds.

items.name: Fragaria nipponica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil to establish roots before UK winter frosts.
Water deeply once a week during summer fruiting, avoiding the crown to prevent rot in damp UK weather.
Clear runners in late summer to redirect energy into fruit production rather than invasive spreading.
Apply a thick straw mulch in spring to keep the low-hanging fruit off wet, slug-prone British soil.
Grow alongside alliums like chives to naturally deter aphids and red spider mites in humid climates.

items.name: Fragaria nubicola
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild strawberry in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its native forest home.
Incorporate leaf mould into well-drained, acidic to neutral soil before planting in autumn or spring.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, focusing on the root zone to prevent fruit rot.
Cut back runners in late autumn to keep the plant compact and focus energy on next spring's berries.
Protect the early spring blooms from late UK frosts by covering plants with horticultural fleece.

items.name: Fragaria orientalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained loam enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native Siberian woodland home.

Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails which actively target the young foliage.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in June to feed the bulb for next year.

items.name: Fritillaria pudica
items.growersTips:
Plant this yellow beauty in autumn at a depth of three times the bulb height to keep it insulated.
Give it gritty, fast-draining soil to survive wet UK winters, ideally in an alpine house or pot.
Keep the compost moist during spring growth, but let it go completely dry once the leaves die back.
Watch out for the red lily beetle in spring, as its larvae will quickly ruin the yellow blooms.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it under cover to shield it from heavy winter rain.

items.name: Fritillaria purdyi
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of three times their height in very gritty, free-draining soil.
Grow them in terracotta pots in an unheated greenhouse to protect them from wet UK winter rot.
Water them moderately during spring growth, but keep the bulbs completely dry during summer dormancy.
Watch out for red lily beetles and their larvae from spring onwards, as they will devour the leaves.
Top dress the pots with horticultural grit to keep the foliage and low flowers off damp compost.

items.name: Fritillaria pyrenaica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Pyrenean beauty 10cm deep in autumn, placing the bulb on its side so water cannot rot it.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to mimic its mountain home and prevent winter waterlogging.
Position this dark purple gem in light dappled shade where it won't get baked by midday summer sun.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring, hand-picking them off before they ruin the nodding bells.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in May to feed the bulb for next year's blooms.

items.name: Fritillaria raddeana
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 20cm deep in autumn on their sides to prevent water collecting in the hollow crown.
Incorporate plenty of horticultural grit to ensure sharp drainage in heavy UK clay soils.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade to mimic their native Central Asian hillside habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in May to feed the bulb for next year.

items.name: Fritillaria recurva
items.growersTips:
Plant this scarlet beauty deep at about fifteen centimetres down to keep the bulb cool in summer.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because this Californian native hates sitting in wet winter mud.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under cover to dry out during damp UK summers.
Watch out for the bright red lily beetle which will happily munch the leaves and ruin the flowers.
Give it a liquid tomato feed just as the first green shoots appear to boost those fiery bells.

items.name: Fritillaria reuteri
items.growersTips:
Plant this Persian beauty five inches deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Keep the soil moist during its spring growing season but let it dry out completely over the summer.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame to shelter from heavy winter rain.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring and gently handpick them off the delicate linear leaves.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme to support the slender stems and mask the dying foliage.

items.name: Fritillaria rhodia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Greek native in a gritty, free-draining mix in a pot to protect it from wet UK winters.
Set the delicate bulbs about eight centimetres deep in autumn, resting them on a bed of sharp sand.
Keep them damp but never soggy during spring, then let them bake completely dry once they die back.
Place your pots in a sunny greenhouse or cold frame to mimic the warm, bright Aegean hillsides.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring, squishing them immediately before they ruin the blooms.

items.name: Fritillaria rhodocanakis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Greek gem in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy, free-draining compost to mimic hills.
Bury the bulbs quite deep, about four inches down, to keep them cool during their summer dormancy.
Keep them damp through winter and spring, then dry them out completely once the foliage dies back.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring, as their larvae will quickly devour the flower buds.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate plum blooms from UK rain.

items.name: Fritillaria sewerzowii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Central Asian native deeply, about fifteen centimetres down, to protect it from UK frost.
Give it sharp drainage by mixing plenty of horticultural grit into your soil to prevent winter rot.
Keep it completely dry during its summer dormant phase by covering the spot or lifting the bulb.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring and pick them off by hand before they damage the foliage.
Grow it in a cold greenhouse or unheated alpine house if your local UK region gets very wet winters.

items.name: Fritillaria sinica
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in sharply draining, gritty loam to prevent rot
Grow in containers under cold glass to protect delicate stems from persistent UK winter wetness
Water moderately during the spring growing phase but keep the bulbs completely dry during dormancy
Top-dress pots with a thick layer of horticultural grit to deter slugs and prevent soil splashing
Position in bright but dappled light mimicking alpine scree rather than harsh direct UK midday sun

items.name: Fritillaria striata
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs about 10cm deep in late autumn, using plenty of grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Keep them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to shield them from relentless UK winter wet.
Water them regularly through spring, but let the pots dry out completely once the summer dormancy hits.
Watch out for the dreaded red lily beetle in spring, squashing any you spot on the fresh shoots.
Plant them in a soil mix of equal parts loam, leaf mould, and coarse grit for the perfect balance.

items.name: Fritillaria thunbergii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at least four times their own depth to keep them cool in UK summers.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because these bulbs will rot instantly in wet winter clay.
Keep them damp while they are growing in spring, but let them dry out completely once they die back.
Watch out for red lily beetles in April as they love to eat the delicate pale green bell flowers.
Plant them near low-growing hardy geraniums to hide the messy fading foliage in late summer.

items.name: Fritillaria tubiformis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in sharply draining, gritty, neutral to acid soil.
Position in a cool, partially shaded spot that mimics their native damp alpine meadow habitat.
Keep soil moist during spring growth but allow a dry, warm summer dormancy period without baking.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and red lily beetles using organic barriers or handpicking.
Grow in terracotta pots of gritty loam if your garden soil is heavy clay to prevent winter bulb rot.

items.name: Fritillaria usuriensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs five inches deep in rich leafmould to mimic their native woodland soil.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during spring, then let them dry out slightly in summer.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring, as they love chewing the delicate climbing tendrils.
Give them twigs or sturdy companion ferns to grab onto, as their leaf tips act like climbing vines.
Grow them in dappled shade rather than full UK sun to keep their delicate purple bells from fading.

items.name: Fritillaria uva-vulpis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at least 10cm deep in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Place the bulbs on their sides when planting so water does not collect in the hollow crown and rot.
Keep them in dappled shade or a cool spot to mimic their native woodlands and prevent drying out.
Watch out for bright red lily beetles in spring and pick them off immediately to protect the buds.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in May so the bulb can store energy for next year.

items.name: Fritillaria verticillata
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at least fifteen centimetres deep in gritty, well-draining soil to thrive.
Keep them in a spot with dappled shade to mimic their native woodland edges in our UK climate.
Add plenty of horticultural grit to the planting hole to prevent winter rot in wet British soils.
Watch out for red lily beetles in spring and gently handpick them off the delicate green foliage.
Let the leaves die back naturally after flowering in June so the bulb stores energy for next year.

items.name: Fuchsia
items.growersTips:
Plant hardy cultivars like Mrs Popple with the root crown five centimetres deep to survive UK frosts.
Water container fuchsias daily in summer, letting the top centimetre of soil dry out between feeds.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants after three sets of leaves to encourage bushy growth.
Prune hardy fuchsias hard down to ground level in March once the worst of the winter frosts pass.
Check leaves weekly for fuchsia gall mite, removing distorted tips immediately to stop its spread.

items.name: Fuchsia ×bacillaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring after frosts pass, placing the root ball 5cm deeper than soil level to protect buds.
Water deeply once a week at the base, increasing to twice in dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop.
Inspect leaf undersides weekly from June for fuchsia rust, removing infected orange-spotted leaves.
Prune stems back by half in April once new growth appears, removing any frost-damaged wood entirely.
Incorporate grit and leaf mould into heavy UK clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage they require.

items.name: Fuchsia apetala
items.growersTips:
Grow this tuberous species in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soil.
Plant the tuber five centimeters deep in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before first frost.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil damp during summer active growth to mimic cloud forest rain.
Prune back weak stems in early spring just as new buds emerge to encourage a bushy flowering habit.
Inspect the large soft leaves weekly for fuchsia gall mite and pick off infected tips immediately.

items.name: Fuchsia arborescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered south-facing border or container using loam-based John Innes No 3 with grit.
Bring potted plants into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the first November frosts.
Prune hard in April by cutting back stems to a low bud to encourage fresh pink-purple flower panicles.
Water copiously during dry summer spells but keep the compost barely moist during winter dormancy.
Watch for fuchsia gall mite damage on new shoot tips and prune out infested growth immediately.

items.name: Fuchsia boliviana
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this tender species cannot survive UK frosts.
Water copiously in summer to keep the rich, organic soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximize the pendulous blooms.
Position in dappled shade or morning sun to prevent the large, soft leaves from scorching in July.
Watch closely for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when keeping the plant under cover.

items.name: Fuchsia bracelinae
items.growersTips:
Plant this Brazilian native in a sheltered, dappled shade spot to mimic its natural woodland home.
Give it moist, free-draining soil enriched with leaf mould to prevent its delicate roots rotting.
Mulch the crown deeply with bark chips in late autumn to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Pruning is best done in spring once new growth appears, cutting back damaged stems to a strong bud.
Water consistently with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy.

items.name: Fuchsia campii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Ecuadorian native in a sheltered, south-facing UK border to protect from cold winds.
Mulch the crown deeply with 10cm of bark in autumn to protect the roots from wet UK winter rot.
Prune stems back to ground level in early spring only after the hardest winter frosts have passed.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells, targeting the base to keep the organic-rich soil moist.
Watch for fuchsia gall mite in summer, removing distorted shoot tips immediately to stop spread.

items.name: Fuchsia campos-portoi
items.growersTips:
Plant this Brazilian beauty in a sheltered UK spot with its root ball buried two inches extra deep.
Give it a thick mulch of bark in autumn to protect its crown from wet and freezing British winters.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells rather than giving it daily light sprinkles.
Prune stems right back to the ground in early spring once you see the first new green shoots appear.
Watch out for fuchsia gall mite damage and snip off any distorted leaf tips as soon as you spot them.

items.name: Fuchsia coccinea
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy Brazilian native 5cm deeper than its pot level in autumn to protect crown from frost.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers, targeting the base to prevent rust on the foliage.
Prune stems down to ground level in March after the worst winter frosts to stimulate fresh growth.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage this species requires.
Underplant with hostas in partial shade to create a barrier that deters vine weevil larvae.

items.name: Fuchsia corymbiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant in a deep pot of loam-based compost to easily move this frost-tender shrub indoors by October.
Water copiously in summer but keep the soil barely damp during its winter dormancy in a greenhouse.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to encourage the long, weeping red flower clusters to form.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite in dry summer conditions and mist the foliage to deter them.
Feed weekly with high-potassium liquid tomato fertiliser from May to September to boost flowering.

items.name: Fuchsia cyrtandroides
items.growersTips:
Treat this rare Andean native to a sheltered, frost-free greenhouse or conservatory over UK winters.
Plant in a rich, acidic to neutral loam mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent drainage.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never soggy, using harvested rainwater whenever possible.
Prune your shrub lightly in early spring to shape it and encourage fresh, flowering wood to grow.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite and apply biological controls if you spot fine webbing.

items.name: Fuchsia denticulata
items.growersTips:
Overwinter this tender species indoors in a heated greenhouse or conservatory kept above five degrees.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty, acidic soil to dry out.
Prune stems by one third in early spring to stimulate new flowering wood and maintain a bushy habit.
Plant in a sheltered spot with morning sun and afternoon shade to prevent the foliage from scorching.
Watch for fuchsia gall mite from May to September and immediately cut off any distorted shoot tips.

items.name: Fuchsia encliandra
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining loam enriched with leafmould to mimic Mexican oak woodland in partial shade.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Prune back by one-third in April after frosts pass to stimulate new flowering wood on young stems.
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or wrap in fleece as this species only tolerates light UK frosts.
Watch for fuchsia gall mite on shoot tips, removing infested distorted growth immediately to burn.

items.name: Fuchsia excorticata

Plant this New Zealand native in a sheltered, moisture-retentive, acid-to-neutral woodland soil.
Protect the distinctive peeling copper bark from hard UK winter frosts using a thick root mulch.
Water copiously during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp forest floor environment.
Prune established plants in late spring after frost risk passes to encourage fresh flowering wood.
Watch for fuchsia gall mite damage on young shoots and remove affected foliage immediately.

items.name: Fuchsia fulgens

Overwinter tubers in dry peat-free compost indoors at five degrees Celsius to survive UK frosts.

Water deeply once a week in summer, keeping the root ball damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Prune stems back to the tuberous base in early spring just as new green shoots begin to emerge.
Check leaf undersides weekly for fuchsia gall mite, removing infested distorted tips immediately.

items.name: Fuchsia glazioviana

Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect its delicate stems from harsh UK winter winds.
Mulch the crown deeply with bracken or bark in November to survive wet British winter freezes.
Prune stems back to ground level in early spring just as new growth appears from the base.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than daily shallow sprinkles.
Grow in moist but free-draining acidic to neutral soil to prevent root rot in heavy clay.

items.name: Fuchsia hatschbachii

Plant this Brazilian native in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect against cold UK winds.
Mulch the crown with ten centimetres of bark in November to protect roots from deep winter frosts.

Prune stems back to ground level in early spring once the risk of severe UK frosts has passed.
Grow alongside ferns or hostas in dappled shade to mimic its natural humid forest understorey.

items.name: Fuchsia jimenezii

Grow this tender Mexican species in a pot of loam-based grit mix to easily move it indoors for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil consistently damp from April to September during active growth.

Watch for fuchsia gall mite and move the plant to a cool greenhouse if temperatures drop below five.

items.name: Fuchsia loxensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining acidic loam enriched with leafmould to mimic its native Andean forest floor.
Water deeply twice a week in dry UK summers, keeping the root zone damp but never waterlogged.
Prune back hard to ground level in April after the last frosts to stimulate vigorous new stems.
Mulch the crown with a ten-centimetre layer of bark chippings in November to survive UK winters.
Watch for fuchsia gall mite from May, removing distorted shoot tips immediately to stop spread.

items.name: Fuchsia lycioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this dry-summer Chilean native in a sheltered south-facing border to survive wet UK winters.
In spring prune back frost-damaged stems to ground level to stimulate vigorous new flowering wood.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep soil virtually dry throughout the winter.
Incorporate grit and leaf mould into heavy clay soils to ensure the sharp drainage this species needs.
Protect the crown with a thick mulch of bark chippings in November to insulate it from hard frosts.

items.name: Fuchsia magellanica
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at least 5cm deeper than the pot level to protect the crown from deep UK frosts.
Prune hard to ground level in early spring once new growth appears at the base of the stems.

In cold northern UK regions, mulch the root zone with 10cm of bark chippings before winter starts.
Grow alongside shade-tolerant hostas and ferns in moist, well-drained soil with partial shade.

items.name: Fuchsia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining loam enriched with leafmould to mimic Mexican oak forest soil conditions.
Position in partial shade sheltered from cold UK winds to prevent winter stem dieback.
Water consistently in summer keeping soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot.
Prune hard in mid-spring after frosts pass to encourage fresh flowering wood and compact habit.
Mulch the crown deeply with bark chips in late autumn to protect roots from severe UK frosts.

items.name: Fuchsia paniculata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native cloud forest habitat.
Shed winter frost damage by pruning stems back to a low framework of buds in late April or May.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to prevent bud drop and support the berry crop.
Position in a sheltered site facing south or west to protect the delicate lavender-like blooms.
Mulch the root zone with a thick layer of bark chips in November to survive wet UK winter freezes.

items.name: Fuchsia parviflora

Grow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, adding grit to the planting hole to prevent winter rot.
Plant in a sheltered, partially shaded spot to protect the delicate, tiny flowers from strong winds.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Prune back hard in early spring after frosts pass to encourage fresh, floriferous new growth.
Overwinter in a cold greenhouse or wrap in fleece if temperatures drop below minus five Celsius.

items.name: Fuchsia perscandens

Plant this scrambling climber against a warm south-facing UK wall to protect it from cold winds.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top two inches of soil dry out between waterings.
