Mulch the root zone with five centimetres of compost in November to protect roots from UK freezes.
Grow in well-drained loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet British clay soils.

items.name: Fuchsia procumbens
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty loam to prevent winter root rot in wet, cold UK soils.
Protect from hard frost by overwintering in a cold greenhouse or under a thick dry mulch of bark.
Water moderately in summer but allow the top inch of soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Prune back untidy stems in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain a neat carpet habit.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots of container-grown plants during autumn and winter.

items.name: Fuchsia regia
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy climber 10cm deeper than its pot level to protect the root crown from UK frosts.
Prune hard in April down to a low woody frame once new buds appear to stimulate vigorous red shoots.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells rather than daily sprinkling to encourage deep roots.
Siting against a south or west-facing wall provides the microclimate needed for winter survival.
Mulch the root zone with 8cm of composted bark in November to insulate against wet UK winter rot.

items.name: Fuchsia simplicicaulis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Peruvian beauty indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive a UK winter.
Water thoroughly only when the top inch of compost feels dry, as its roots rot easily in wet soil.
Keep it in a bright spot but shaded from harsh midday sun to prevent those long red tubes fading.
Prune back the stems by half in early spring to encourage a bushier habit and more flower tassels.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid tomato food from May to September to boost the blooms.

items.name: Fuchsia splendens
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mexican native in a sheltered, west-facing border to protect its early spring blooms.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of gritty soil to dry out first.
Overwinter in a frost-free greenhouse or wrap the base in thick straw mulch before November frosts.
Prune back hard in April to encourage new wood, which produces the distinctive long orange flowers.
Grow in a terracotta pot using peat-free compost mixed with one-third perite for vital drainage.

items.name: Fuchsia thymifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this little beauty in a sheltered, west-facing spot to protect its tiny leaves from cold winds.
Mulch the base heavily with bark in late autumn to protect its roots from wet, freezing UK winters.
Wait until late spring to prune, cutting back dead stems only after new green shoots start to show.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry spells in July and August.
Watch out for capsid bugs in summer, which can quickly distort the lovely, delicate micro-foliage.

items.name: Fuchsia triphylla
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors before first frost as this tender species cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Pinch out growing tips in early spring to encourage a bushy habit and maximize the tubular blooms.
Position in bright filtered light or morning sun, avoiding harsh afternoon glare that scorches leaves.
Feed weekly in summer with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer to sustain the long flowering season.

items.name: Fuchsia vulcanica
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist well-drained acidic soil using ericaceous compost to mimic its volcanic habitat.
Overwinter indoors or under fleece as this species is tender and will not survive UK frosts.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Prune lightly in early spring to encourage bushy growth and remove any frost-damaged stems.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate foliage from scorching in direct afternoon sun.

items.name: Fumaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained, gritty UK soil at a shallow depth of five millimetres.
Grow alongside companion plants like wild pansies or campions to support native UK pollinators.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry, gravelly cottage gardens.
Hand-weed around young seedlings in spring rather than using hoes to protect their delicate stems.
Collect the ripe seed pods in late summer to control self-seeding in small UK garden borders.

items.name: Fumaria agraria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 5mm to allow winter cold stratification for spring germination.
Grow in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile sandy loam with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out fully between watering sessions.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to mimic its native Mediterranean scrub habitat.
Sow alongside native UK wildflowers like Papaver rhoeas to complement its scrambling growth habit.

items.name: Fumaria bastardii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in autumn to mimic natural UK seed drop cycles.
Grow in well-drained gritty soil with neutral to alkaline pH to prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to avoid waterlogging the roots.
Hand-weed surrounding soil early in spring to prevent aggressive native grasses smothering stems.
Plant alongside wild pansies or herb robert in sunny borders for compatible nutrient needs.

items.name: Fumaria bicolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to allow winter cold to break their dormancy.
Grow in well-drained chalky or sandy loam with a neutral to alkaline pH to mimic UK downland soils.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant plant prone to rot dislikes wet winters.
Watch for downy mildew in damp UK summers and space plants thirty centimetres apart for airflow.
Plant alongside wild pansies or salad burnet in sunny rock gardens to support native pollinators.

items.name: Fumaria capreolata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic UK wild hedge conditions.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as this plant thrives in dry, gravelly UK soils.
Watch for aphids on young spring shoots and blast them off with a sharp stream of garden hose water.
Cut back the scrambling stems to ground level in late autumn after seeds have dispersed naturally.
Plant alongside native red campion or wild geranium to support diverse UK pollinators in partial shade.

items.name: Fumaria densiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres depth to mimic natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Grow in well-drained chalky or sandy loam with a neutral to alkaline pH to match UK field habitats.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer dry spells as this species is highly drought-tolerant.
Hand-weed around young seedlings in spring to prevent faster-growing garden weeds smothering them.
Plant alongside wild pansies or field forget-me-nots which share its preference for open sunlight.

items.name: Fumaria flabellata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to allow winter chilling for spring germination.
Grow in well-drained chalky or sandy soil to mimic its native UK coastal cliffs and prevent rot.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established to prevent waterlogging the roots.
Plant alongside rosemary or wild thyme which share its preference for dry sunny limestone rockeries.
Cut back the sprawling stems in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and encourage fresh spring growth.

items.name: Fumaria muralis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres depth in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic UK wild habitats.
Water young plants sparingly only during dry summer spells to prevent root rot in damp UK clay.
Hand-pull plants in late summer before seed pods explode to control its aggressive self-seeding.
Grow alongside wild pansies or red campion in dappled shade for a natural cottage garden aesthetic.
Watch for powdery mildew in humid UK summers and thin out dense foliage to improve air circulation.

items.name: Fumaria officinalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of five millimetres to allow winter cold to break their dormancy.
Grow in well-drained, low-nitrogen soil to prevent excessive leaf growth at the expense of flowers.
Water newly sprouted seedlings sparingly, only during prolonged dry spells in the UK spring.
Hand-pull plants in midsummer before they set seed to control their rapid self-seeding habit.
Plant alongside winter wheat or spring barley in a cottage garden to mimic its natural arable habitat.

items.name: Fumaria parviflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at five millimetres deep in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic UK wild habitats.
Water sparingly only during dry spells as this drought-tolerant plant rots easily in wet UK clay.
Hand-weed around seedlings in spring to prevent aggressive garden grasses from smothering growth.
Grow alongside cornflowers and poppies in sunny borders to recreate a traditional UK arable meadow.
Collect the small nutlets in late summer before they self-seed aggressively across your borders.

items.name: Fumaria purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained, gritty soil to benefit from winter cold stratifying.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active spring and summer growth phases.
Monitor plants closely in damp UK springs for downy mildew and remove affected foliage immediately.
Cut back the sprawling stems to ground level in late autumn after the plant has finished seeding.
Plant alongside native primroses or wild strawberries to provide support for its climbing tendrils.

items.name: Fumaria schleicheri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 5mm to allow winter chilling to break dormancy naturally in the UK.
Grow in well-drained, alkaline to neutral chalky soil, avoiding heavy clays that rot the roots.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top 5cm of soil to dry out between waterings.
Position in full sun to light dappled shade to mimic its natural UK arable field margin habitat.
Watch for downy mildew in damp UK summers and space plants 20cm apart to improve air circulation.

items.name: Fumaria vaillantii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at 5mm depth in well-drained, chalky soil to mimic UK arable field conditions.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts to prevent root rot in damp UK clay soils.
Hand-weed surrounding areas carefully to avoid disturbing this plant's delicate, shallow roots.
Grow alongside wild pansies and field poppies in a sunny, gravelly border to support UK pollinators.
Collect the small nutlets in late summer before they drop to control self-seeding in small gardens.

items.name: Fumariola
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare alpine in gritty, sharply draining neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in a sheltered, partially shaded rock garden or alpine house to mimic its scree habitat.
Water moderately during the spring growing season but keep almost dry throughout the damp UK winter.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by carefully dividing the delicate rootstock in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Fumariola turkestanica
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply drained alkaline soil in a raised bed or alpine trough to prevent winter wet.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural winter chilling for successful germination.
Water sparingly from below during summer dormancy to prevent the delicate crown from rotting.
Protect from slugs and snails in early spring using organic pellets or copper tape around pots.
Position in a sheltered, partially shaded spot to mimic its native cool, rocky crevice habitat.

items.name: Funastrum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive UK winters.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory to get enough sunlight.
Water thoroughly only when the soil dries out completely, then keep it dry throughout the winter.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Provide a small trellis or bamboo hoop in spring for its twining stems to scramble up as it grows.

items.name: Funastrum cynanchoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender climber in a pot of gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive UK winters.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory to get enough summer sun.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to once a month during our cold, damp winters.
Keep a sharp eye out for greenhouse whitefly and red spider mites, which love dry indoor air.
Provide a small trellis or wire hoop in spring so the twining stems have immediate support to climb.

items.name: Funtumia
items.growersTips:
Bring your Funtumia indoors by October to protect this tropical tree from wet, freezing UK winters.
Grow Funtumia in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Water generously through summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings in winter.
Position your potted Funtumia in your brightest south-facing window or a heated conservatory.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor winter heating.

items.name: Furcraea
items.growersTips:
Plant your Furcraea in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first frost.
Mix fifty percent grit into your peat-free compost to stop the roots rotting in wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely from November.
Cut away the lower leaves at the stem in spring using sharp shears to keep that tidy trunk shape.
Watch out for snails nesting in the rosette base during damp autumn days and clear them out fast.

items.name: Furcraea andina
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with fifty percent grit to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this species cannot survive frost below zero.
Water thoroughly once a week in summer but keep completely dry from October to March to avoid rot.
Plant in a heavy terracotta pot to prevent the top-heavy mature rosette from blowing over in wind.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf bases and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Furcraea cabuya
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to ensure sharp drainage and prevent winter wet rot.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this tender species cannot survive UK frost below zero.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, then stop watering in winter.
Position in the brightest south-facing spot possible to mimic its native hot South American climate.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Furcraea foetida
items.growersTips:
Grow in a container with 50% grit to move indoors before the first autumn frost hits your area.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost is bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or conservatory to mimic its native tropical climate.
Cut away dead lower leaves at the base in spring using sterilized shears to prevent rot in damp air.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during winter storage and treat immediately with organic spray.

items.name: Furcraea hexapetala
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with 50% grit and 50% peat-free compost to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Bring indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the first autumn frost in October.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, and keep completely dry in winter.
Position in the brightest spot possible, ideally a south-facing patio wall to maximise UK summer heat.
Cut away dead lower leaves at the base in spring using sterilized shears to prevent rot in damp air.

items.name: Furcraea tuberosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to ensure sharp drainage and prevent winter rot.
Move the pot into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from October to April to survive UK cold.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Prune away the lowest damaged leaves in late spring using sterilized loppers to maintain the shape.
Watch for mealybugs in the leaf axils during winter and treat immediately with organic insect spray.

items.name: Fusifilum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs about eight centimetres deep in autumn so the UK frosts do not damage the roots.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent bulb rot in wet British winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp spring nights as they love to chew the fresh new shoots.
Add plenty of grit to your compost mix to ensure the heavy UK clay soil drains quickly and easily.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer but leave the green leaves to feed the bulb for next year.

items.name: Gadoria falukei
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in a sheltered, south-facing rockery or alpine house to maximise essential summer sun.
Water sparingly only when the soil dries completely, keeping the crown dry to avoid fungal decay.
Protect from heavy winter wet and frost using a removable glass cloche or cold frame from October.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer or sowing seed in a cold frame during spring.

items.name: Gaga
items.growersTips:
Try planting Gaga monstraparva in shallow, well-drained grit to mimic its native desert home.
Keep your Gaga dry in winter by sheltering it in a cold frame to survive damp British frosts.
Water your Gaga only when the compost is bone dry, using rainwater rather than tap water.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs hiding in the tight, fleshy crevices of your Gaga plants.
Propagate your Gaga in late spring by carefully dividing the offsets with a sterile knife.

items.name: Gagea
items.growersTips:
Plant Gagea lutea bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist, deciduous woodland soil.
Position these bulbs under deciduous shrubs to ensure winter sun and summer shade in UK gardens.
Avoid watering Gagea during their summer dormancy to prevent the bulbs from rotting in wet clay.
Propagate by lifting clumps in late spring just as the foliage dies back and separating offsets.
Grow Gagea alongside wild garlic or wood anemones in a dedicated naturalised damp shade border.

items.name: Gagea alberti
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 5cm in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade to mimic its native Central Asian steppe habitat.
Keep soil moist during spring growth but allow a dry summer dormancy period once foliage dies back.
Grow in alpine pans or raised beds to easily manage the essential sharp drainage in wet UK winters.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Gagea altaica
items.growersTips:
Plant Gagea altaica bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil.
Position this alpine bulb in full sun to mimic its native dry, exposed Central Asian grasslands.
Water sparingly in winter to prevent bulb rot, keeping the soil barely damp during dormancy.
Grow in a raised bed or alpine trough to protect the small bulbs from aggressive garden weeds.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as the delicate yellow star-like flowers emerge.

items.name: Gagea bohemica
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny bulb in early autumn at a shallow depth of about five centimetres in sharp grit.
Keep it in a terracotta pot of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of sand to mimic Welsh hills.
Position your pots in full winter sun to coax the delicate yellow flowers open during cold days.
Water very sparingly in winter and let the pot dry out completely once the foliage dies in summer.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they can easily devour the tiny emerging flower buds.

items.name: Gagea bulbifera
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn three times their depth in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow in containers of peat-free loam mixed with horticultural grit to mimic dry limestone screes.
Keep the compost moist during spring growth but allow it to bake dry in summer when foliage dies back.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames during autumn to experience natural UK winter chilling for germination.
Position pots in full sun on a south-facing patio to ensure the delicate yellow flowers fully open.

items.name: Gagea chrysantha
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty neutral soil.
Siting them in a rock garden or alpine trough mimics their native dry, stony Mediterranean habitat.
Keep the soil moist during winter and spring growth but allow a dry summer dormancy period.
Protect the emerging early spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets.
Position in full sun to ensure the small yellow star-like flowers fully open on bright days.

items.name: Gagea divaricata
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining, gritty loam to avoid rot.
Position in a rock garden or alpine house to mimic dry summer dormancy and shield from winter wet.
Water moderately during active spring growth but keep the soil almost completely dry during summer.
Protect the delicate emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.
In late summer carefully divide congested clumps of bulbs to propagate and maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Gagea fedtschenkoana
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent rot.
Position in a rock garden or alpine house to mimic its native dry, cold winter and hot summer cycle.
Water sparingly during the spring growing season and keep the soil almost completely dry in summer.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical grit barriers.
Grow alongside low-growing sedums or thymes that will not overcrowd this tiny, delicate spring bulb.

items.name: Gagea foliosa
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty loam to prevent rot.
Position in a rock garden or raised bed facing south to maximise crucial late winter UK sunshine.
Keep soil consistently moist during winter growth but allow to dry out completely during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Propagate by lifting the clump in late summer to gently separate and replant the tiny offset bulbs.

items.name: Gagea granatellii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil.
Siting in full spring sun is crucial to trigger the opening of the temperature-sensitive flowers.
Keep the soil moist during active winter growth but ensure it dries out completely during summer.
Grow in a dedicated alpine trough to prevent aggressive garden weeds from smothering this tiny bulb.
Protect the emerging early spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic ferrous phosphate bait.

items.name: Gagea granulosa
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm in well-drained, gritty loam that mimics UK deciduous woodland.
Keep soil consistently moist during spring growth but allow it to dry out during summer dormancy.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to match its natural UK woodland edge habitat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by lifting the clump after foliage dies back in June to separate and replant bulbils.

items.name: Gagea hiensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these small bulbs in autumn about five centimetres deep in well-drained, gritty alpine soil.
Keep the soil moist during their active spring growth but let them dry out during summer dormancy.
Grow them in pots or rock gardens to prevent larger, aggressive garden plants from crowding them out.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging tender shoots.
Position them in a spot that gets full sun to encourage the bright yellow star-like flowers to open.

items.name: Gagea lacaitae
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of five centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rot.
Position in full sun or dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its native open woodland edge.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil almost entirely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Grow in containers using a loam-based John Innes number two mix with fifty percent added grit.

items.name: Gagea liotardii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic alpine scree conditions.
Position in full sun or light dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to match UK woodland edge habitats.
Keep soil moist during winter and spring growth, but allow a dry summer dormancy once foliage dies.
Grow in shallow terracotta alpine pans using a loam, grit, and leafmould mix to prevent winter rot.
Avoid disturbing the soil around established clumps as they propagate slowly via delicate offsets.

items.name: Gagea lutea
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous trees.
Replicate woodland conditions by incorporating leaf mould into the soil before planting the bulbs.
Keep the soil consistently moist during winter and spring but allow it to dry out during summer dormancy.
Associate with early wild garlic or wood anemones to mimic natural UK deciduous woodland communities.
Avoid weeding or disturbing the soil in late spring to protect the delicate, dying foliage of bulbs.

items.name: Gagea minima
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny bulb five centimetres deep in autumn in a spot with damp, deciduous woodland shade.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to mimic their natural UK forest floor habitat perfectly.
Leave the fading leaves alone after spring flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch on the tender new shoots.
Grow them alongside wood anemones and primroses which share the same damp, shady UK growing needs.

items.name: Gagea pauciflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny bulb five centimetres deep in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent rot.
Place it in a rock garden or alpine trough where larger, aggressive plants won't crowd it out.
Keep the soil moist during its early spring growth, then let it dry out completely in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate yellow flowers first emerge.
Grow it in a container so you can move it under a cold frame to shelter it from heavy winter rain.

items.name: Gagea peduncularis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in sharply draining, gritty neutral to alkaline soil
Position in a rock garden or raised bed facing south or west to maximise crucial winter and spring sun
Keep soil moist during spring growth but allow the bulb to dry out completely during summer dormancy
Protect the delicate early spring flowers from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Associate with low-growing thymes or sedums to provide summer ground cover without smothering the bulbs

items.name: Gagea pratensis
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in well-drained, gritty soil.
Keep them in a spot that gets plenty of early spring sunshine before deciduous trees leaf out.
Avoid waterlogging in winter by mixing plenty of horticultural grit into your planting pockets.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in April to feed the bulb for next year.
Grow them alongside low-growing wild sedges or primroses to help support their delicate stems.

items.name: Gagea pusilla
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny bulbs in early autumn about five centimetres deep in gritty, well-drained soil.
Keep them in a sunny rock garden or container to mimic their native dry, limestone grasslands.
Avoid summer watering entirely once the leaves die back to prevent the bulbs from rotting.
Watch out for aggressive garden weeds that can easily smother this delicate, low-growing species.
Grow them alongside miniature spring bulbs like blue scilla for a lovely contrasting colour mix.

items.name: Gagea serotina
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny bulbs in autumn about five centimetres deep in very sharp-draining, gritty soil.
Position them in a rock garden or alpine trough where they get full winter sun but cool summer shade.
Keep the compost moist during their spring growth but let them dry out completely when dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch on the emerging flower buds.
Grow them alongside dwarf winter aconites or slow-growing sedums to protect the delicate bulbs.

items.name: Gagea spathacea
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of eight centimetres in moist, deciduous woodland-style leafmould.
Position in dappled spring shade under hazel or birch to mimic its native UK woodland habitat.
Keep the soil consistently damp during winter and spring but allow it to dry slightly in summer.
Avoid disturbing the soil in summer as this species relies on delicate bulbils for propagation.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.

items.name: Gagea tenera
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 5cm to 8cm in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in a rock garden or raised bed facing south or west to maximise crucial early spring sun.
Keep the soil moist during active spring growth but allow it to dry out completely during summer.
Avoid disturbing the soil in summer when the tiny bulbs are dormant and easily damaged by digging.
Grow alongside low-growing sedums or thymes which will not overcrowd this delicate, small species.

items.name: Gagea villosa
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny bulbs in autumn about five centimetres deep in sharp sand to ensure perfect drainage.
Give them a sunny, south-facing spot in rockeries or gritty containers to mimic their wild habitat.
Keep the soil barely damp in winter, then let them dry out completely once the foliage dies down.
Watch out for aggressive garden weeds that can easily smother these delicate, slow-growing shoots.
Grow them alongside dwarf sedums or thymes that won't compete for space or crowd them out of the sun.

items.name: Galearis
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy orchid in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, mimicking a leafy UK woodland floor.
Position your plant in dappled shade, safely tucked away from the harsh midday summer sun.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during the active spring growing season.
Protect the delicate emerging spring shoots from hungry slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.
Mulch annually in autumn with decayed leaf mould to feed the soil and protect roots from winter frost.

items.name: Galenia
items.growersTips:
Mix coarse grit into your soil to mimic South African dunes, as wet UK winters will rot the roots.
Grow this tender trailer in a hanging basket so you can easily move it into a greenhouse for winter.
Water your plant only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, especially during damp autumns.
Trim back the sprawling stems in late spring to keep the growth compact and encourage fresh foliage.
Pair it with hardy sedums in a sunny rockery to create a beautiful, drought-tolerant ground cover.

items.name: Galeola
items.growersTips:
Do not try to grow Galeola in UK gardens as it is a parasitic orchid requiring specific host fungi.
If attempting conservation, plant seeds directly next to decaying oak wood to provide host fungi.
Maintain constant dampness in acidic, leaf-mold rich soil to mimic native woodland conditions.
Provide deep shade and winter mulch to protect the delicate underground rhizomes from UK frosts.
Never apply standard garden fertilizers as chemical nutrients will kill the essential mycorrhizae.

items.name: Galeomma
items.growersTips:
Start your Galeomma seeds indoors in early spring to beat the unpredictable UK frost.
Plant them out in late May in well-drained soil, spaced fifteen centimetres apart for good airflow.
Water them at the base in the morning to keep the damp British weather from causing mildew.
Deadhead the faded blooms weekly through summer to keep new flowers coming until autumn.
Watch out for slugs during wet spells; use organic beer traps to protect tender young stems.

items.name: Galtonia
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15cm deep in autumn or spring in fertile, well-drained soil to protect from winter frost.
Water generously during the summer growing season but keep bulbs dry in winter to prevent rotting.
Apply a thick mulch of bark chips in November to protect the dormant bulbs from severe UK frosts.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring as they eagerly target the emerging fleshy Galtonia shoots.
Lift and store bulbs in a cool greenhouse over winter if gardening in cold, wet northern UK regions.

items.name: Gambelia juncea
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mexican bush snapdragon in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Mix loads of grit into your peat-free compost to mimic its native dry desert soil and prevent rot.
Water it only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, cutting back to almost nothing in winter.
Prune the stems back by a third in late spring to encourage bushy growth and more red flowers.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering it indoors.

items.name: Gambelia speciosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this showy island snapdragon in a terracotta pot so you can move it indoors for UK winters.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep those roots dry during our notoriously wet winters.
Prune the stems back by half in late spring to encourage a bushy shape and more red flowers.
Water deeply but only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, mimicking its native climate.
Watch out for aphids on the fresh spring shoots and blast them off with a gentle hose spray.

items.name: Gasteranthus
items.growersTips:
Grow these tropical gems in a warm conservatory or terrarium to shield them from chilly UK frost.
Plant them in a highly aerated mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part perlite for drainage.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries to prevent root rot in damp winters.
Position your pots in bright, indirect light near a north or east window to avoid scorching leaves.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away using a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Gasteranthus atratus
items.growersTips:
Keep this Ecuadorian rain forest native in a warm, humid greenhouse over the cool UK winter.
Plant in a very chunky, peat-free orchid bark mix to mimic its natural epiphytic leafy home.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy or waterlogged.
Position in dappled shade away from direct glass glare to prevent the dark leaves from scorching.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs hiding under the velvety foliage and wipe them away with alcohol.

items.name: Gasteranthus bilsaensis
items.growersTips:
Grow this Ecuadorian native indoors in a warm, humid terrarium to mimic its cloud forest home.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy by watering with lukewarm rainwater.
Position in bright, indirect light away from harsh UK summer sun to prevent leaf scorch.
Plant in a very airy, peat-free potting mix enriched with perlite and orchid bark.
Maintain a minimum room temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius to protect it from UK winter drafts.

items.name: Gasteranthus extinctus
items.growersTips:
Keep this Ecuadorian cloud forest native cozy in a heated UK greenhouse at a steady fifteen degrees.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the peat-free, mossy compost damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Mimic its misty home by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to boost the indoor humidity.
Position it in bright, filtered light but shield it from the harsh afternoon sun of a UK summer.
Feed with a very weak orchid fertiliser once a month during spring to encourage those orange blooms.

items.name: Gasteranthus quitensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this Ecuadorian rain forest beauty inside by October to protect it from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite to mimic its acidic home.
Keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, watering only with harvested rainwater if you can.
Position your pot in a humid, draft-free bathroom with bright but soft, filtered northern light.
Snip off the faded orange pouch-like blooms in late autumn to encourage fresh new spring growth.

items.name: Gasteranthus tenellus
items.growersTips:
Keep this delicate perennial in a humid, draft-free spot indoors or in a heated greenhouse year-round.
Water with room-temperature rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy to prevent root rot.
Pot it in a free-draining mix of peat-free compost, perlite, and orchid bark for healthy roots.
Place in bright, indirect light near a north or east window, avoiding harsh direct UK summer sun.
Feed with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertiliser once a month from April through to September.

items.name: Gastrodia
items.growersTips:
Plant this leafless orchid near established oak or beech trees to provide the essential fungi it needs.
Mix plenty of decaying leaf mould and rotting wood into your soil to mimic a damp UK woodland floor.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during our wet British autumn and winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails which love to devour the emerging flower spikes in early summer.
Leave the tubers completely undisturbed once planted as they rely on delicate underground networks.

items.name: Gaura
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Cut back hard to ground level in early spring rather than autumn to protect the crown from frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells only until established, then leave to tolerate drought.
Position in full sun to prevent the long, delicate flowering stems from flopping and seeking light.
Divide congested clumps in spring every three years to maintain vigor and prevent center die-out.

items.name: Gaura sinuata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Cut stems back to ground level in early spring to encourage fresh, bushy new growth.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells in the UK summer.
Position in full sun to prevent the delicate flower stems from flopping and seeking light.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in spring to replace short-lived parent plants.

items.name: Gavilea
items.growersTips:
Plant these Chilean orchids in well-drained, gritty, acidic soil to mimic their native Andean home.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy during spring growth, then dry them out completely in summer.
Protect the tubers from harsh UK winter frosts by lifting them or using a thick mulch of bracken.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch on the emerging fleshy shoots.
Grow them in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield them from excessive British winter wet.

items.name: Gayophytum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic their native scree beds.
Give these drought-tolerant plants a deep soak once a week only during dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around them.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and prevent self-seeding.
Plant them alongside hardy alpine sedums to create a beautiful, low-maintenance gravel garden.

items.name: Gayophytum diffusum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in late spring directly onto well-drained, gritty soil as they need light to sprout.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells to mimic their arid native North American habitat.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your gravel garden to maximize UK summer warmth.

Water your Gochnatia deeply once a week at the base, letting the top inch of soil dry out first.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on young shoots during damp British summer evenings.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly through August to encourage a continuous display of fresh flowers.

items.name: Gomphocarpus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender perennial in pots so you can easily move it indoors before the first winter frost.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on a warm windowsill to give them a crucial head start in the UK.
Water your swan plant deeply but let the compost dry out completely between waterings to avoid rot.
Keep a sharp eye out for yellow aphids, which love this plant, and wash them off with a hose.
Mix plenty of grit into your multi-purpose compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant craves.

items.name: Gomphocarpus fruticosus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK growing season.
Grow this tender African native in pots so you can easily move it into a greenhouse for winter.
Keep a sharp eye out for yellow aphids, as they absolutely love colonising the soft new stems.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil feels dry, but never let the pot sit in soggy compost.
Plant it alongside nectar-rich salvias to attract the pollinators needed for those iconic seedpods.

items.name: Gomphocarpus physocarpus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early March at five millimetres deep to give them the long UK season they need.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry to touch.
Watch out for yellow aphids in midsummer, brushing them off with soapy water to protect the stems.
Bring your potted plants into a frost-free greenhouse by October to keep them alive over winter.
Grow them alongside companion plants like marigolds to naturally deter pests from the balloon pods.

items.name: Gonatopus
items.growersTips:
Grow this African native in a pot of gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive UK wetness.
Keep it completely dry and frost-free indoors from October to March while the tuber is dormant.
Water deeply only when the soil dries out fully, mimicking its natural tropical dry-season cycle.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the distinctive leaf joints and wipe them off with rubbing alcohol.
Repot in spring just as new shoots appear, keeping the unusual tuber buried about two inches deep.

items.name: Gonatopus boivinii
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors by October to protect its tender tuber from wet UK winter rot.
Plant the tuber shallowly in free-draining cactus compost with the top third peeking above soil.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, then mimic summer rains with a thorough drenching.
Watch for spider mites in dry indoor air by misting the glossy, bipinnate leaves occasionally.
Propagate this unusual plant by tucking fallen leaflets into moist grit to sprout mini tubers.

items.name: Gonioma
items.growersTips:
Bring your South African Gonioma indoors or to a heated greenhouse before the first UK autumn frost.
Grow Gonioma in pots of gritty, peat-free loam to easily move them out of chilly winter wetness.
Water your Gonioma only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as they hate soggy roots.
Place your pot on a south-facing patio to soak up maximum summer sun and mimic its native warmth.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to keep this slow-growing shrub compact.

items.name: Goniorrhachis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator to beat UK cold.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the deep taproot system.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and increase the summer blooms.
Grow alongside nasturtiums to act as a sacrificial trap crop for black bean aphids in midsummer.

items.name: Gonolobus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse before autumn frosts.
Plant seeds just one centimetre deep in free-draining peat-free compost with added perlite for drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, then drench it and let the pot drain fully.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites which love the warm, dry indoor air they prefer.
Train the vigorous vines up a sturdy bamboo teepee to support the heavy, star-shaped green blooms.

items.name: Goodyera
items.growersTips:
Plant your creeping lady's tresses in a mix of leaf mould and grit to mimic UK pine forest soils.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering with rainwater rather than tap water to prevent rot.
Position them in deep shade, perhaps under a north-facing wall or beneath larger ferns and hostas.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the tender new evergreen rosettes.
Avoid burying the creeping rhizomes too deep; just press them gently into the top layer of moss.

items.name: Goodyera procera
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a mix of fine bark and moss to mimic its natural damp woodland floor habitat.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged, using rainwater instead of UK tap water.
Place your pot in bright, indirect light, shielding this delicate perennial from harsh midday sun.
Provide winter protection in a cool greenhouse or indoors, as it cannot survive hard UK frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails which love to feast on the tender emerging flower spikes in spring.

items.name: Goodyera pubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen orchid in a mix of leaf mould and pine needles to mimic UK woodland soil.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering with rainwater rather than tap water to avoid lime.
Position it in a shady, sheltered spot out of cold winds, ideally under deciduous garden shrubs.
Protect the gorgeous variegated leaves from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Avoid planting the shallow rhizomes too deep; just press them gently into the top layer of mulch.

items.name: Goodyera rubicunda
items.growersTips:
Grow this native orchid cousin in a shady, cold frame to protect it from wet UK winter rot.
Mix plenty of pine needles and leaf mould into your peat-free compost to mimic its forest floor home.
Water with harvested rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy, especially during hot summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the soft, evergreen rosettes in damp spring.
Propagate by gently dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Goodyera umbrosa
items.growersTips:
Nestle this woodland orchid in a shallow, damp bed of leaf mould and pine needles, never deep soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, using harvested rainwater rather than tap water.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the soft, velvety evergreen leaves.
Plant it alongside shade-loving ferns and native mosses to mimic its natural damp forest home.
Provide winter protection with a cloche or cold frame to shield the foliage from harsh UK frosts.

items.name: Goodyerinae
items.growersTips:
Plant your jewel orchids in a shallow mix of fine bark and chopped sphagnum to mimic forest floors.
Keep their compost damp but never soggy by watering with tepid rainwater from spring to autumn.
Position these shade lovers on a north-facing windowsill to protect their velvety leaves from sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the soft, succulent stems of these low growers.
Maintain high humidity around them by placing their pots on a tray of wet pebbles in winter.

items.name: Gordonia
items.growersTips:
Plant Gordonia in acidic, ericaceous soil mixed with leaf mould to mimic their native woodland home.
Position your shrub in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect late blooms from cold winds.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to ensure those autumn flower buds don't drop.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frosts have passed to shape the plant and remove dead wood.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark in spring to keep the shallow roots cool and damp.

items.name: Gordonia fruticosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen in acidic, ericaceous soil mixed with plenty of leaf mould to keep it happy.
Give it a sheltered, semi-shaded spot away from cold drying winds and harsh early morning UK sun.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and moist but well-drained.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to shape the shrub and remove any frost-damaged stems.
Apply a thick mulch of pine needles or composted bark every autumn to protect roots from hard frosts.

items.name: Gordonia lasianthus
items.growersTips:
Give this acid-loving beauty a sheltered, south-facing spot to shield it from cold UK winter winds.
Plant your loblolly bay in moist, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of leaf mould.
Water only with harvested rainwater to keep the soil acidic and prevent yellowing chlorotic leaves.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to shape and remove dead wood.
Mulch heavily with pine needles or composted bark every autumn to protect the roots from hard frosts.

items.name: Gorteria diffusa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to combat UK dampness.
Place pots on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sun these annuals need.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers.
Plant out in late May after frosts pass, spacing ten centimetres apart in rockeries or gravel.
Watch for slugs and snails on young seedlings during wet spring nights and use organic barriers.

items.name: Gorteria personata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to combat wet UK weather.
Plant out in late May in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native South African heat.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Watch for slugs on young seedlings as damp UK spring nights can quickly destroy this tender annual.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in summer to encourage continuous flowering until the first autumn frost.

items.name: Grammitids
items.growersTips:
Grow these delicate ferns in a chunky, bark-rich orchid mix to mimic their wild epiphytic homes.
Mist them daily with rainwater to survive dry UK indoor heating, keeping humidity above sixty percent.
Water only when the top moss feels dry, as their fine roots rot easily in soggy British winters.
Nestle them near hardy ferns or mosses in a terrarium to create a self-sustaining damp microclimate.
Keep them in bright, indirect north-facing light, safely away from harsh afternoon conservatory sun.

items.name: Grammitis
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate native fern in a moist, sheltered rock crevice or a mossy, acid-bark container.
Keep the compost constantly damp but never soggy, watering only with soft, lime-free rainwater.
Position your pot in a cool, shaded spot to mimic its damp, humid UK woodland ravine habitat.
Protect it from harsh winter frosts by bringing the pot into a cold frame or unheated greenhouse.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding in the damp fronds, especially during wet British springs.

items.name: Grammitis diminuta
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny fern in a humid terrarium or glazed pot to mimic the damp, sheltered UK woodland.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost constantly moist but never soggy or waterlogged.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and orchid bark for the perfect free-draining soil.
Keep it in a draft-free spot with bright, indirect light, away from direct midday UK sun.
Snip off any dead or brown fronds at the base in spring to encourage fresh, healthy new growth.

items.name: Grammitis nudicarpa
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate epiphyte in a highly porous, bark-based orchid mix rather than standard soil.
Keep your fern in a humid, draft-free spot out of direct sun, ideally in a steamy UK bathroom.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost damp, but never let the roots sit in soggy runoff.
Mist the fronds daily during dry summer spells to mimic its natural damp woodland habitat.
Watch out for scale insects on the fronds and gently wipe them off with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Grammitis stenophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate dwarf fern in a shallow, free-draining peat-free orchid compost mix, never deep.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost damp but not soggy, avoiding the crown to prevent rot.
Keep it in a humid, draft-free spot indoors or in a heated greenhouse to mimic its tropical home.
Position in soft, indirect light, avoiding harsh UK summer sun which easily scorches the fronds.
Snip off any dead or decaying fronds at the base in spring using sterilized mini pruning shears.

items.name: Grammitis wattsii
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate epiphyte in a highly porous, bark-based orchid mix rather than standard soil.
Keep your fern in a humid, draft-free spot indoors or in a heated greenhouse to mimic its home.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the roots damp but never soggy, avoiding chlorinated tap water.
Position it in bright, indirect light, shielding its fronds from harsh afternoon UK conservatory sun.
Mist the foliage daily during dry summer months or stand the pot on a wet gravel tray to boost humidity.

items.name: Grangea maderaspatana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass as this tropical annual needs early warmth to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to mimic its native damp paddy fields.
Plant it alongside moisture-loving mint or lobelia in a sunny, sheltered UK patio container.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the tender young leaves during wet British Mays.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow flowerheads.

items.name: Graptopetalum
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted ghost plant indoors to a bright windowsill before the first wet October frosts.
Plant them in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit for sharp drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep them completely dry from November through March.
Propagate new plants easily by wiggling off healthy lower leaves and laying them on damp compost.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight rosettes, especially during the damp winter months.

items.name: Graptopetalum amethystinum
items.growersTips:
Keep these chubby pink succulents in pots of gritty, free-draining soil so you can move them inside.
Water only when the leaves wrinkle slightly, then drench them, keeping them bone dry all winter.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep their lovely lavender-pink coloring.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints, especially during damp British winters indoors.
Propagate them easily in spring by gently wiggling off a plump leaf and laying it on dry compost.

items.name: Graptopetalum bartramii
items.growersTips:
Bring your Bartramii indoors by October to protect this delicate desert rosette from freezing UK wet.
Plant it in a gritty mix of fifty percent pumice and peat-free compost to prevent root rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry throughout the winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf rosettes during dry indoor winter spells.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum possible British sunshine.

items.name: Graptopetalum bellum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican native indoors by October to protect its delicate leaves from wet UK frosts.
Plant in a shallow pot using fifty percent grit and fifty percent peat-free compost for drainage.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly but never let the pot sit in water.
Check the tight leaf rosettes weekly for mealybugs, which love the dry indoor winter conditions.
Place on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the Mexican sun and boost pink summer blooms.

items.name: Graptopetalum macdougallii
items.growersTips:
Keep this Mexican native in a pot so you can move it indoors before the damp UK autumn frost hits.
Water only when the gritty compost is bone dry, keeping it completely dry throughout the winter.
Mix two parts horticultural grit to one part peat-free compost to prevent root rot in our wet climate.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight rosettes, especially during winter indoor storage.
Propagate new plants easily by detaching the long, thread-like runners in late spring or summer.

items.name: Graptopetalum paraguayense
items.growersTips:
Bring your ghost plant indoors to a bright windowsill before the first wet UK autumn frost hits.
Plant in a gritty fifty-fifty mix of John Innes number two and horticultural grit for drainage.
Only water when the leaves start to wrinkle slightly, then drench it and let it dry out completely.
Propagate easily in spring by wiggling off healthy lower leaves and laying them flat on dry soil.
Watch out for sneaky mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially during dry winter indoor storage.

items.name: Graptophyllum
items.growersTips:
Bring your caricature plant indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our cool climate.
Grow this tropical beauty in a pot using peat-free loam-based compost with added grit for drainage.
Prune active stems in late spring to encourage bushy growth rather than one tall, leggy stalk.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to get the bright indirect light needed for leaf color.

items.name: Graptophyllum excelsum
items.growersTips:
Bring your scarlet fuchsia inside by October because UK frosts will quickly kill this tender shrub.
Grow it in a pot of peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure fast drainage.
Water generously in summer but let the top two inches of soil dry out completely before watering.
Prune the stems by a third in early spring to keep it bushy and encourage those bright red blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering this Australian native indoors.

items.name: Graptophyllum ilicifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its holly-like leaves from UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a pot with John Innes No. 2 and extra grit to ensure the roots never sit in cold wet soil.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, cutting back to a bare minimum in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost passes to keep its bushy shape and encourage pink blooms.
Place your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing patio spot to mimic its sunny Queensland home.

items.name: Graptophyllum pictum
items.growersTips:
Bring your caricature plant indoors by October to protect it from chilly British winter frosts.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to avoid root rot in our damp air.
Prune the stems back by half in late spring to encourage bushy growth and stop it getting leggy.
Wipe the variegated leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and boost light absorption.
Feed with a high-nitrogen liquid fertiliser every fortnight from April to September for leaf colour.

items.name: Graptophyllum spinigerum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Grow it in a container of peat-free loam-based compost with added grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Position your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to mimic its sunny homeland.
Water only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, cutting back to a monthly splash in winter.
Prune the tips in early spring to encourage bushy growth and stop it from becoming leggy indoors.

items.name: Gratiola
items.growersTips:
Pop Gratiola officinalis into soggy soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep.
Keep your soil constantly wet or boggy because this marsh lover cannot tolerate drying out at all.
Grow this fast spreader in a submerged aquatic basket to stop it taking over your garden pond.
Cut the stems back to the base in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and promote fresh spring shoots.
Watch out for water snails munching the young leaves and handpick them off on damp UK evenings.

items.name: Gratiola amphiantha
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare aquatic annual in shallow acidic pond margins or mud flats under full UK summer sun.
Sow seeds in late spring by pressing them gently onto wet, peat-free ericaceous compost without burying.
Maintain constant water levels just covering the soil surface to mimic natural vernal pool habitats.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails which quickly consume the delicate submerged foliage.
Overwinter collected seeds in damp sand in a cold frame to undergo essential winter stratification.

items.name: Gratiola brevifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this bog-loving perennial in shallow pond margins no deeper than five centimetres of water.
Keep the soil constantly muddy and wet, especially during dry spells in our warm UK summers.
Divide the root clumps in early spring just as new green growth begins to emerge from the mud.
Watch out for water snails munching the young stems during mild, damp British spring mornings.
Grow it alongside native marsh marigolds to create a beautiful, moisture-loving pond edge display.

items.name: Gratiola heterosepala
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring on wet, muddy soil surfaces without covering them, as they need light.
Grow this obligate wetland annual in a bog garden or pond margin with water up to five cm deep.
Maintain a constant acidic to neutral pH by using rainwater rather than chlorinated UK tap water.
Position in full sun to mimic its vernal pool habitat and ensure successful summer flowering.
Collect seed capsules in late summer to resow next spring, as this annual will not survive winter.

items.name: Gratiola neglecta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of wet, acidic compost in spring as they need light to germinate in the UK.
Grow this mud-loving annual in bog gardens or pond margins with water levels up to five centimetres.
Keep the soil constantly saturated using rainwater rather than tap water to maintain low pH levels.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its natural North American wetland habitat in the UK.
Sow indoors in March to protect young seedlings from late UK frosts before planting out in May.

items.name: Gratiola officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in heavy clay or boggy soil at the pond edge with the crown submerged no deeper than five cm.
Keep the soil permanently wet or waterlogged, never allowing this marsh plant to dry out in summer.
Cut back the sprawling stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the clump tidy for spring growth.
Propagate by dividing the fibrous root rhizomes in early spring just as new green shoots appear.
Position in full sun to partial shade to ensure the small white flowers bloom reliably in July.

items.name: Gratiola peruviana
items.growersTips:
Grow this native bog plant in a permanently wet, acidic to neutral soil or shallow pond margin.
Plant crowns just below the soil surface in spring to allow roots to establish in warm mud.
Position in full sun to partial shade to mimic its natural damp UK meadow and creek habitats.
Propagate in spring by dividing the creeping rhizomes or taking softwood cuttings in early summer.
Cut back the dieback in late autumn to prevent decaying foliage from fouling small garden ponds.

items.name: Gratiola quartermaniae
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare limestone glade beauty in a gritty, alkaline soil mix to mimic its native habitat.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged, as it loves wet ledges and seasonal seeps.
Position your pot in full sun to light shade to copy the open, bright woodland glades it prefers.
Protect this delicate perennial from aggressive garden weeds that will easily crowd and smother it.
Bring container-grown plants into a cold frame for winter to shield them from excessive UK wet.

items.name: Greeneocharis circumscissa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, free-draining soil to allow winter cold to break dormancy
Grow in a raised scree bed or alpine trough to protect the roots from wet winter rot in UK climates
Water only during dry spring spells, allowing the gritty substrate to dry out completely between feeds
Position in full south-facing sun to mimic its native dry habitat and prevent leggy, weak growth
Surround the collar with fine granite grit to prevent damp soil from rotting the lower foliage

items.name: Greigia landbeckii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean bromeliad in acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp southern beech forest.
Position it in a sheltered, partially shaded spot to protect the exotic foliage from cold UK winds.
Water generously in summer but keep it relatively dry in winter to prevent the crown from rotting.
Mulch heavily with leaf mould in late autumn to insulate the shallow roots from harsh winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails nesting in the dense, spiky leaf rosettes during damp spring days.

items.name: Greigia pearcei
items.growersTips:
Bring this Chilean bromeliad indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before October.
Plant it in a gritty, acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of orchid bark.
Water deeply into the central leaf rosette during summer, but keep the soil barely damp in winter.
Position it in bright, dappled shade under a tree canopy to prevent the foliage from scorching.
Propagate by carefully slicing off the offsets at the base in spring using a sharp, sterile knife.

items.name: Greigia sphacelata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean bromeliad in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from cold UK winds.
Keep the soil gritty and free-draining by mixing in plenty of horticultural grit before planting.
Water directly into the central rosette during dry summer months to mimic its native rainforest.
Cover the crown with a thick layer of dry straw or fleece to survive wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant it alongside hardy ferns or winter-flowering heathers for a beautiful foliage contrast.

items.name: Greigia vulcanica
items.growersTips:
Grow this Chilean bromeliad in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Plant in a highly acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Nestle the plant shallowly with its crown just above the soil line to prevent winter crown rot.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the central leaf rosette moist.
Keep it in dappled shade under a canopy, mimicking its native Andean woodland home.

items.name: Griselinia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Griselinia littoralis in spring so the roots establish before the cold UK winter hits.
Trim your hedge in late spring or summer with secateurs, not shears, to avoid ugly sliced leaves.
Water young plants deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than giving them daily splashes.
Add a thick layer of organic mulch around the base in autumn to protect roots from hard UK frosts.
Choose the cultivar Variegata for shady spots to brighten up dark corners of your British garden.

items.name: Griselinia littoralis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Griselinia at the same depth it was in its pot, adding grit to help heavy UK clay drain.
Water deeply once a week during its first dry UK summer to help those glossy roots establish well.
Prune your hedge in late spring using secateurs, not shears, so you do not slice the lovely leaves.
Keep an eye out for leaf spot fungus during wet UK autumns and clear away fallen leaves quickly.
Shield young plants from freezing winter winds with horticultural fleece if you live up north.

items.name: Griselinia lucida
items.growersTips:
Plant this NZ native in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter winds.
Water your young shrub deeply once a week during dry English summers until its roots settle in.
Prune in late spring after the frosts pass to keep its lovely glossy foliage neat and compact.
Mix plenty of grit and compost into heavy clay soil to give its roots the sharp drainage it loves.
Keep an eye out for leaf spot disease during damp autumns and clear away any fallen debris quickly.

items.name: Guibourtia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters to protect them from late UK spring frosts.
Plant in well-drained, sandy loam soil mixed with grit to prevent waterlogging during wet summers.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry spells, allowing the topsoil to dry out between.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot of your garden to maximize limited UK summer heat.
Protect young shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or physical copper barriers.

items.name: Guibourtia coleosperma
items.growersTips:
Grow this frost-tender African shrub in a container of free-draining loam to move indoors by October.
Water only when the top five centimeters of soil dries out to prevent root rot in cool UK summers.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and remove winter dieback.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to maximize essential summer heat.
Feed monthly from May to August with a low-nitrogen fertilizer to support its legume root nodules.

items.name: Guibourtia sousae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using free-draining peat-free grit-amended compost.
Plant out in late May after frosts in a south-facing spot with maximum sun to mimic warm climates.
Water deeply once a week at the base only when the top 5cm of soil feels dry to prevent root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and increase the flower yield.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp UK spring nights.

items.name: Guilandina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres using bottom heat to ensure germination.
Scarify the hard seed coat with sandpaper before soaking in warm water for twenty-four hours.
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British spring nights.

items.name: Gunniopsis
items.growersTips:
Bring your gunniopsis indoors before the first autumn frost to keep this tender succulent alive.
Plant them in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, mimicking their arid native habitat.
Position your pots on a south-facing windowsill or patio to maximise scarce British sunlight.
