Grow in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position against a south-facing brick wall to maximize summer heat and shield from freezing winds.
Water only when the top five centimeters of soil is bone dry, reducing to zero during winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter-damaged stems.
Protect with fleece or move to a cold greenhouse when UK temperatures are forecast to drop below -5C.

items.name: Hazardia cana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in free-draining sandy loam to prevent waterlogging in wet UK weather.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, as this island native is highly rot-prone.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or a gravel garden to maximise scarce UK summer heat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic bait or copper tape during damp springs.
Grow in terracotta pots that can be moved under a cold frame to shield them from excessive autumn rain.

items.name: Hazardia detonsa
items.growersTips:
Grow in sharply drained gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Position in the warmest south-facing sun trap or against a brick wall to mimic its native climate.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells and keep completely dry during cold winter months.
Prunt lightly in late spring after frost passes to maintain a compact shape and remove dead wood.
Protect with fleece or move container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse during severe UK frosts.

items.name: Hazardia orcuttii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early spring under glass to combat wet UK soils.
Water sparingly only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot in damp UKs.
Grow in a gritty loam mix with fifty percent perlite to mimic its arid native Mexican habitat.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to maximise heat during cool British summers.
Monitor closely for slugs and snails which aggressively target young seedlings in damp spring weather.

items.name: Hazardia squarrosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil against a south-facing wall to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts once established to prevent root rot.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter dieback.
Protect with horticultural fleece during severe UK winter frosts below minus five Celsius.
Grow in a terracotta pot using a gritty loam-based compost to easily move indoors for winter.

items.name: Hazardia stenolepis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly loam to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position against a south-facing brick wall to maximise sun exposure and trap essential summer heat.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the soil completely dry throughout winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter-damaged stems.
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to easily move indoors before heavy winter frosts.

items.name: Hazardia whitneyi
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximize summer heat and protect from frost.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells once established, keeping the crown dry in winter.
Prune lightly in late spring after frost risk passes to maintain a compact, bushy shrub shape.
Protect with fleece or move container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse during severe UK freezes.

items.name: Hebe
items.growersTips:
Plant your hebe in free-draining soil with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Trim your hebe lightly with shears right after flowering in late summer to keep it neat and bushy.
Protect tender large-leaved hebes from harsh winter frosts with fleece if you live up north.
Water your newly planted hebe deeply once a week during its first dry UK summer to help it settle.
Grow compact hebes alongside lavender in sunny borders for a lovely, bee-friendly combination.

items.name: Hebe pimeleoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this silver-leaved beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Give it a light trim in late spring after the frosts pass to keep its neat, bushy shape.
Water your new shrub weekly during its first UK summer, then leave it to be quite drought-tolerant.
Protect it from freezing winter winds by planting it next to a warm, south-facing garden wall.
Group it with purple lavender or dark-leaved heucheras to make its pale blue flowers really pop.

items.name: Hebe recurva
items.growersTips:
Plant this silver-leaved beauty in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Give it a light trim in late spring after frosts pass to keep its naturally mounded shape compact.
Position it in full sun to bring out the best blue-grey leaf colour and encourage summer blooms.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in its first year, but let it dry out between waterings.
Watch out for downy mildew in damp autumns by spacing plants well to improve air circulation.

items.name: Hechtia argentea
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican beauty indoors by October to protect its silver leaves from wet UK winter rot.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two, grit, and perlite.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the central rosette dry to prevent rot.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill or patio to get the high light it needs to shine.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect yourself from those viciously spiny margins.

items.name: Hechtia caerulea
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican native indoors by October to protect its roots from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, then let the excess drain away completely.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or conservatory to keep those blue leaves vibrant.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from its viciously spiny leaf edges.

items.name: Hechtia capituligera
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican bromeliad indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet winter rot.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and fine gravel.
Water only when the soil is dry to the touch, pouring water directly into the soil, not the crown.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to maximise scarce UK sunlight.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf crevices; wipe them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Hechtia carlsoniae
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a shallow pot using two parts coarse grit to one part peat-free compost for drainage.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, keeping the central leaf rosette dry to prevent rot.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to maximise weak UK sunlight.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from its viciously spiny leaf margins.

items.name: Hechtia caudata
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two, grit, and perlite.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is dry, keeping the central leaf rosette completely dry.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse for maximum summer sun.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding deep within the spiny, overlapping bases of the tough leaves.

items.name: Hechtia epigyna
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and fine gravel.
Water only when the soil dries out completely, keeping the central rosette dry to prevent decay.
Place your pot on a sunny south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse for maximum light.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the spiny leaf bases and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Hechtia galeottii
items.growersTips:
Bring your Hechtia indoors by October to protect this Mexican native from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant in a shallow terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and coarse grit.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the central leaf rosette completely dry.
Place it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic its hot, bright native desert home.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from its viciously spiny leaf edges.

items.name: Hechtia glomerata
items.growersTips:
Bring your pot indoors to a bright windowsill before the first damp autumn frost hits the UK.
Plant in a gritty cactus mix with added perlite to stop waterlogging during wet British winters.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, keeping the central rosette completely free of water.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from those viciously sharp teeth.
Position this sun-lover in your brightest south-facing conservatory or greenhouse to boost color.

items.name: Hechtia laxissima
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of John Innes number two and grit to ensure the sharp drainage it needs.
Water deeply only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the central rosette completely free of water.
Place your pot on a sunny, south-facing patio in summer to mimic its hot, arid native cliffs.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding deep within the spiny leaf bases during dry indoor winter spells.

items.name: Hechtia lundelliorum
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican native inside to a sunny windowsill before the first wet autumn frosts arrive.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and fine gravel.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, pouring water directly into the soil, not the leaf rosette.
Keep it in your brightest south-facing spot or greenhouse to bring out its deep red leaf margins.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from the sharp, hooked leaf spines.

items.name: Hechtia lyman-smithii
items.growersTips:
Treat this terrestrial bromeliad like an alpine by potting it in a highly gritty, free-draining mix.
Bring your potted specimen indoors to a bright windowsill before the first damp autumn frost hits.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, pouring water directly into the soil rather than the crown.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing spot to bring out its striking, deep reddish leaf tones.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from its viciously spiny margins.

items.name: Hechtia marnier-lapostollei
items.growersTips:
Bring this frosty Mexican bromeliad inside by October to protect it from wet UK winter rot.
Plant it in a shallow pot with fifty percent grit to mimic its native limestone cliff home.
Water only when the potting mix is bone dry, keeping the central leaf rosette completely dry.
Place it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep those beautiful white leaf scales vivid.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the spiny leaf bases and dab them with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Hechtia montana
items.growersTips:
Grow this Mexican bromeliad in pots of gritty, free-draining cactus compost so you can move it inside.
Bring your potted plant indoors before the first autumn frost to protect it from cold UK winters.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, allowing the gritty soil to dry out completely between drinks.
Keep the plant completely dry during winter dormancy to prevent root rot in damp, unheated glasshouses.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a bright conservatory to mimic its native sun.

items.name: Hechtia mooreana
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter rot.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of John Innes number two and perlite for the sharp drainage it needs.
Water deeply only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the central rosette completely free of water.
Place your pot on a south-facing patio in summer to give it the baking hot sun it craves to thrive.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the spiky leaf bases and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Hechtia podantha
items.growersTips:
Bring this Mexican native indoors by October to protect its roots from wet UK winter rot.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two and horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the central rosette completely dry during winter.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot of a south-facing conservatory to mimic its desert home.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight, spiny leaf bases where they love to nest in UK homes.

items.name: Hechtia sphaeroblasta
items.growersTips:
Bring your Hechtia indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing British winter rot.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit for perfect drainage.
Water this terrestrial bromeliad deeply only when the top three inches of soil feel bone dry.
Position your pot on a south-facing patio in summer to give it the baking sun it needs to thrive.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling this plant to avoid its viciously sharp, spiny leaf edges.

items.name: Hechtia stenopetala
items.growersTips:
Bring your Hechtia indoors by October as it cannot survive wet UK winters and needs frost protection.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts John Innes number two, perlite, and gravel.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the central leaf rosette completely dry to stop rot.
Position it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or conservatory to mimic its Mexican home.
Wear thick leather gloves when repotting to protect your hands from its viciously spiny leaf edges.

items.name: Hechtia texensis
items.growersTips:
Keep your Texas false agave in a pot of gritty, peat-free cactus compost so you can move it inside.
Water it only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry from October through to March.
Place your pot on the sunniest, most south-facing windowsill you have to mimic its desert home.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight rosettes, dabbing them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.
Plant it alongside hardy sedums in summer containers to give it compatible, drought-loving friends.

items.name: Helenium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in gentle heat under glass in March to get a head start on our short UK growing season.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged to prevent early powdery mildew in dry summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and far more daisy-like flowers.
Plant alongside annual grasses like Briza maxima to support the heavy autumn flower heads naturally.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly to keep the colorful display going right up until the first UK frost.

items.name: Heliantheae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April, 1.5cm deep in peat-free compost, to beat the late UK spring frosts.
Slugs love young seedlings, so protect them with copper tape or beer traps after planting out in May.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, wind-resistant roots.
Stake taller varieties early in June using hazel twigs to protect them from strong British summer winds.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach 20cm high to encourage bushier growth and more blooms.

items.name: Helianthella
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April to protect young shoots from late UK frosts before planting out in May.
Mix plenty of grit into your clay soil to prevent winter root rot in our wet British climate.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, sturdy roots.
Protect young spring growth from hungry slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Plant them alongside lavender or salvias to create a beautiful, bee-friendly cottage garden look.

items.name: Helianthus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April indoors in peat-free compost, then plant out in May after the last frost.
Plant your sunflowers about twelve inches apart in a spot that gets at least six hours of sun.
Push a sturdy bamboo cane into the soil at planting time to support them against strong UK winds.
Water them deeply at the base once a week rather than giving them a light daily sprinkle.
Put copper tape or beer traps around young stems to stop slugs devouring them overnight.

items.name: Helichrysum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres and transplant out after the May frosts.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile gritty soil as rich soils cause floppy stems and fewer flowers.
Water young plants weekly until established then only during prolonged dry spells to avoid root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach fifteen centimetres to encourage bushy lateral growth.
Harvest strawflowers for drying just as the outer petals open before the yellow centre is visible.

items.name: Helicodiceros
items.growersTips:
Plant your dead horse arum tuber fifteen centimetres deep in fertile, sharp grit-drained soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist during its spring growth but let it dry out completely in summer.
Slay slugs and snails early in spring as they absolutely love to feast on the emerging spathe.
Position this stinky beauty in a sheltered, sunny UK spot to mimic its native warm Mediterranean.
Grow it in a container so you can banish the foul-smelling blooms away from your patio seating area.

items.name: Helicodiceros muscivorus
items.growersTips:
Plant your tubers 15cm deep in autumn using a very gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet winters.
Keep them dry during their summer dormancy, but water weekly once growth starts in late winter.
Grow this dead-horse arum in a deep pot so you can move it indoors when the smelly blooms open.
Position the pot in full sun and shelter it from cold winds to mimic its native Mediterranean cliffs.
Watch out for slugs eating the emerging shoots in early spring, as they love the tender new growth.

items.name: Heliomeris longifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native arid North American habitat.
Deadhead spent yellow blooms weekly from July to October to prolong the late-season flowering display.
Position near purple Salvia nemorosa to provide a structural and colour contrast in sunny borders.

items.name: Heliomeris multiflora
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April under glass to protect from late UK frosts.
Plant in free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to encourage deep, drought-tolerant roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to promote a bushier habit and increase the number of yellow blooms.
Position near dark-foliaged Physocarpus to create a striking colour contrast in UK borders.

items.name: Heliopsis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March, then transplant to a sunny, sheltered spot after May frosts.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil moist but not soggy.
Watch out for young slugs in spring, using beer traps or organic pellets to protect new shoots.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers come July.
Plant alongside purple Salvia nemorosa to create a stunning, bee-friendly colour contrast.

items.name: Heliosperma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring under glass to beat late UK frosts.
Water sparingly at the base only when the top two centimetres of gritty, alkaline soil feel dry.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around plants.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the short annual flowering window.
Plant alongside Dianthus or Sedum in raised beds to ensure the sharp winter drainage they require.

items.name: Heliosperma pusillum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame using a gritty compost mix to mimic UK alpine scree conditions.
Water sparingly from below to keep the foliage dry and prevent rot in damp British winters.
Position in a raised bed or rockery facing south to maximise scarce UK winter sunshine.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during wet spring weather.
Grow alongside Saxifraga or Sempervivum in shallow troughs to ensure perfect sharp drainage.

items.name: Heliotropioideae
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted cherry pie plant indoors to a frost-free windowsill before the October chills start.
Water your heliotropes in the morning, keeping the soil damp but never letting the roots sit in bog.
Feed these hungry plants with a high-potash tomato food every fortnight through the British summer.
Snip off the faded purple flower heads regularly to encourage fresh, vanilla-scented blooms.
Mix plenty of grit into your clay soil to give these sun-lovers the sharp drainage they crave.

items.name: Heliotropium
items.growersTips:
Overwinter potted heliotropes indoors at ten degrees Celsius to survive wet UK winter frosts.
Plant out in late May after the last frost in a south-facing border to maximise essential sunlight.
Water the base deeply twice a week in dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop and powdery mildew.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in spring to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.
Grow in peat-free compost mixed with one-third grit to ensure the fast drainage they require.

items.name: Heliotropium amplexicaule
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Overwinter container plants in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory to survive UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top soil to dry out completely.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage bushy growth and maximize summer flowering stems.
Watch for aphids and glasshouse whitefly when keeping plants indoors or under glass in spring.

items.name: Heliotropium angiospermum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter in a heated greenhouse or indoors as this tender perennial cannot survive UK frosts.
Grow in pots of free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its native dry-scrub habitat.
Prune back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent the stems from flopping.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites when keeping the plant indoors over the winter.

items.name: Heliotropium anomalum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender coastal shrub in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent horticultural grit
Overwinter containers in a heated greenhouse or conservatory kept strictly above five degrees Celsius
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters
Take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer to ensure replacement plants survive the cold British winter
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or against a warm brick wall to mimic its native habitat

items.name: Heliotropium arborescens
items.growersTips:
Overwinter plants indoors at 10C from October to May as they cannot survive UK frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top 2cm of soil dries to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage bushy growth and more cherry-pie scented blooms.
Grow in pots using peat-free compost mixed with 20 percent grit for essential wet-weather drainage.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise the intense vanilla fragrance on warm summer evenings.

items.name: Heliotropium arboreum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a free-draining sandy loam with neutral pH to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soils.
Position in a terracotta pot in full sun so you can move it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out, as this shrub hates waterlogged roots.
Prune back lightly in early spring after overwintering to encourage bushy new flowering growth.
Monitor closely for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when sheltering indoors over winter.

items.name: Heliotropium crispum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender perennial in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter rot.
Position in your warmest south-facing border or container to maximise essential UK summer sun.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out to avoid fatal root rot in damp climates.
Bring containers into a frost-free greenhouse by October before the first autumn frosts hit.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer to guarantee new plants survive the damp British winter.

items.name: Heliotropium curassavicum
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining sandy soil or gravel to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm coastal habitat.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Overwinter in a frost-free greenhouse or bring indoors as this plant is tender in UK winters.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late summer to ensure survival of the plant for next year.

items.name: Heliotropium dentatum
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty loam with a neutral pH to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep under glass in March keeping temperatures at twenty degrees.
Water moderately allowing the top two centimetres of soil to dry out fully between watering sessions.
Overwinter containers indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before late autumn frosts.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more flower spikes.

items.name: Heliotropium europaeum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly indoors in March and transplant out only after the last late-May frosts.
Water sparingly once established as this Mediterranean native thrives in dry, well-drained soil.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp UK spring weather.
Grow in pots to easily move indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before October.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in June to encourage a bushier habit and more blooms.

items.name: Heliotropium hirsutissimum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to protect roots from wet UK winters and rot.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot or unheated greenhouse to mimic its native Aegean heat.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent fatal root rot in damp UK air.
Overwinter indoors on a bright windowsill keeping the compost barely damp to survive frosts.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring to ensure backup plants for the next year.

items.name: Heliotropium indicum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at three millimetres deep using bottom heat of twenty degrees Celsius.
Plant out in late May after all frost risk has passed into a sheltered spot with full southern sun.
Water the soil deeply once a week at the base to prevent powdery mildew on the hairy foliage.
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when growing in UK conservatories or cold frames.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.

items.name: Heliotropium stenophyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy loam to survive wet UK winters and move indoors by October
Water only when the top three inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in cool British summers
Prune back by one third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent leggy stems
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot against a brick wall to maximize essential heat retention
Watch for glasshouse whitefly and spider mites when overwintering this tender shrub indoors

items.name: Heliotropium tenellum
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate wild heliotrope in a sharply draining, gritty loam to mimic its native dry soils.
Keep watering to a minimum, letting the top few inches dry out completely before you water again.
Sow the seeds shallowly, just dusting them with a fine layer of grit, in a warm propagator in March.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your patio to trap vital summer warmth.
Bring containers into a frost-free greenhouse by October as this plant cannot survive a wet UK winter.

items.name: Helleborus
items.growersTips:
Snip off the old leathery leaves in January to stop black spot and show off the new flowers.
Plant them shallowly with their crown just at the soil surface, as burying them too deep stops blooms.
Mix in plenty of well-rotted leaf mould to mimic their favourite damp, shady UK woodland soils.
Watch out for hellebore aphid in spring, blasting them off the flower backs with a sharp water spray.
Pair them with snowdrops and pulmonaria for a gorgeous, slug-resistant late winter display.

items.name: Helleborus argutifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained alkaline soil adding grit to the planting hole to prevent winter rot
Cut back flowered stems to ground level in late spring to encourage vigorous new basal growth
Position in partial shade sheltered from cold drying winds which scorch the architectural foliage
Water deeply during dry summer spells in their first year to help the deep root system establish
Watch for hellebore black spot in damp UK autumns and promptly remove and destroy affected leaves

items.name: Helleborus atrorubens
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty at the exact same depth it was in its pot, keeping the crown at soil level.
Give it a generous mulch of well-rotted leaf mould each autumn to mimic its native European forests.
Snip off the old leathery leaves in late winter just as the new flower buds start to peep through.
Watch out for hellebore black spot during wet UK springs and space plants well to improve airflow.
Damp, dappled shade under deciduous shrubs like witch hazel makes the perfect home for this perennial.

items.name: Helleborus cyclophyllus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Greek beauty in rich, alkaline soil with added grit to mimic its wild limestone home.
Snip off the old tattered leaves in late autumn to stop black spot and show off the green flowers.
Give it a deep weekly drench during dry UK summers, but keep the winter soil damp rather than soggy.
Nestle the crown just level with the soil surface, as burying it too deep stops it from flowering.

items.name: Helleborus foetidus

items.name: Helleborus lividus

items.name: Helleborus thibetanus

items.name: Helleborus viridis

items.name: Hemiboea

items.name: Hemidesmus

Grow this tender Indian sarsaparilla in a pot so you can move it indoors before the autumn frosts.

items.name: Hemidesmus indicus

items.name: Hemigraphis repanda

items.description: Hosta is a genus of plants commonly known as hostas, plantain lilies and occasionally by the Japanese name gibōshi. Hostas are widely cultivated as shade-tolerant foliage plants. The genus is placed in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Agavoideae, and is native to northeast Asia. Like many "lilioid monocots", the genus was once classified in the Liliaceae. The genus was named by Austrian botanist Leopold Trattinnick in 1812, in honor of the Austrian botanist Nicholas Thomas Host. Grow them in clay or heavy soil under deciduous trees where they will get winter wet and summer shade.
Keep them in pots or contained borders to stop them from hybridising with our native UK bluebells.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in May to feed the bulbs for next spring.
Water your potted bulbs occasionally during winter dry spells, but keep them damp, never soggy.

items.name: Hyacinthoides italica
items.growersTips:
Plant these Italian bluebells four inches deep in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil to avoid rot.
Give them a sunny, south-facing spot as they need much more warmth and light than our native species.
Water them weekly during active spring growth, but let the soil dry out completely over summer.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in June so the bulb can store energy for next year's blooms.
Divide congested clumps in late summer right after dormancy to keep your displays vigorous and neat.

items.name: Hyacinthoides lingulata
items.growersTips:
Plant these Mediterranean bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in very well-drained soil.
Keep them in a terracotta pot on a sunny patio to protect them from wet UK winter waterlogging.
Water them weekly during their active autumn growth, but keep them dry when they go dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as the delicate star-shaped blue flowers emerge.
Mix grit into your compost to mimic their native gravelly soil and prevent bulb rot in British rain.

items.name: Hyacinthoides non-scripta
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimeters in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous shade.
Water during dry spring periods but keep soil relatively dry during their summer dormant phase.
Avoid planting near Spanish bluebells to prevent hybridization and preserve the native UK species.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before clearing the leaves.
Divide congested clumps in late summer by lifting and replanting bulbs immediately to boost blooms.

items.name: Hyacinthus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm, about three times the bulb height, in well-drained soil.
Wear gloves when handling bulbs to prevent skin irritation caused by calcium oxalate crystals.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
After flowering, cut the dead flower spike but leave the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks.
For indoor winter blooms, use prepared bulbs chilled at nine degrees Celsius before forcing in pots.

items.name: Hyacinthus orientalis
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to 15cm to protect them from severe UK winter frosts.
Wear gloves when handling bulbs to prevent skin irritation caused by calcium oxalate crystals.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in November to insulate bulbs against wet UK winter rot.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in spring but leave foliage to die back naturally for six weeks.
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent bulb rot during damp British autumn and winter months.

items.name: Hyalis
items.growersTips:
Sow your Hyalis seeds indoors in early April to get a head start before the UK frosts have finished.
Plant them out in late May in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent their roots rotting in wet clay.
Position your Hyalis in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic their native warm environment.
Water them deeply once a week at the base, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect young shoots from slugs using beer traps during damp, typical British spring nights.

items.name: Hyalochlamys
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly under glass in April to protect them from late British frosts before planting.
Water the base gently early in the morning to avoid wetting foliage and causing damp-off in wet UK weather.
Mix plenty of grit into your heavy UK clay soil to give these annuals the sharp drainage they need.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails during damp British springs, as they love the young seedlings.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme to help suppress weeds and create a lovely sunny gravel bed.

items.name: Hyalosperma
items.growersTips:
Sow these Australian annual seeds indoors in March to beat the late UK frosts, using a sandy mix.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering gently from below to avoid damping off seedlings.
Plant them out in May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their hot native habitat.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage these little everlastings crave.
Deadhead the faded paper-like blooms regularly to keep new daisy-like flowers coming all summer.

items.name: Hybanthus
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare violet relative in free-draining, gritty loam to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so natural winter chills can break their dormancy.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy during our active spring growing season.
Protect the delicate emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic beer traps.
Plant them alongside woodland shade-lovers like dwarf ferns and primroses in dappled light.

items.name: Hybanthus calycinus
items.growersTips:
Give this Australian native sharp drainage by mixing plenty of grit into your UK soil before planting.
Keep it safe from harsh British frosts by growing it in a pot to move indoors over the winter months.
Water only when the top few inches of compost feel dry to avoid rotting its delicate root system.
Position your pot in a sunny, sheltered spot near a south-facing wall to mimic its warm homeland.
Prune back the stems by half in early spring to encourage fresh new growth and a bushier habit.

items.name: Hybanthus concolor
items.growersTips:
Plant this green violet in moist, rich woodland soil with plenty of leaf mould to mimic its home.
Position it in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect the delicate foliage from UK sun.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged during dry British summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to munch on the emerging tender shoots.
Propagate by carefully dividing the root clump in early spring just as new growth begins to show.

items.name: Hybanthus floribundus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Aussie native in a pot with grit-heavy ericaceous compost so you can move it in winter.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as wet UK winters will rot the roots fast.
Keep it in your brightest conservatory or unheated greenhouse from October to April to dodge frosts.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to keep its woody, shrubby habit neat and bushy.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you are overwintering it indoors under cover.

items.name: Hybanthus monopetalus
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors by October to protect its delicate roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant your spade-leaf violet in a gritty peat-free mix to mimic its natural free-draining sandstone.
Dapple the light using woodland companions like native ferns to prevent the leaves from scorching.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to avoid root rot in our damp British climate.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring when the plant is actively growing in warmth.

items.name: Hybanthus stellarioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in a warm, sheltered gravel bed to mimic its natural dry habitat.
Keep watering minimal once established, only soaking during prolonged hot, dry UK summer spells.
Overwinter your potted plants in a frost-free greenhouse to protect them from wet British winter rot.
Mix plenty of grit and perlite into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this perennial craves.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums and sempervivums which share their love for poor, well-drained soil.

items.name: Hybanthus vernonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Aussie native in acidic, sandy loam to mimic its wild soil and prevent winter root rot.
Keep soil barely damp in summer, then cut watering right back during our cold, wet UK winters.
Tuck it into a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect its delicate stems from harsh frost.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer when the plant is actively growing.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh new shoots.

items.name: Hydrangea
items.growersTips:
Prune mophead types in early spring by cutting back to the first pair of strong buds below the flower
Plant in moisture-retentive soil enriched with well-rotted manure to prevent summer drought stress
Water newly planted shrubs deeply twice a week during dry UK summers using rainwater to keep soil acid
Apply aluminum sulfate to acidic soil in autumn to turn pink macrophylla cultivars to deep blue
Leave faded flowerheads on the shrub over winter to protect tender new buds from hard UK spring frosts

items.name: Hydrangea anomala
items.growersTips:
Plant this self-clinging climber against a damp, north or east-facing wall to prevent leaf scorch.
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted manure deep into the planting hole to retain summer moisture.
Prune immediately after summer flowering by cutting back shoots that have grown away from the wall.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers until the root system is fully established.
Protect young spring shoots from late UK frosts using fleece if grown in exposed northern gardens.

items.name: Hydrangea arborescens
items.growersTips:
Prune hard to 30cm in March to encourage massive new-wood blooms on cultivars like Annabelle.
Plant in moisture-retentive soil enriched with well-rotted manure to prevent summer wilting.

Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells rather than spraying the foliage.
Grow in dappled shade to protect the delicate white bracts from scorching in midday sun.

items.name: Hydrangea aspera
items.growersTips:
Plant in dappled shade sheltered from cold winds to protect the large velvety leaves from scorch.
Incorporate leaf mould or composted bark to mimic woodland soil and retain moisture in dry summers.

Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted organic matter to keep the shallow root system cool.

items.name: Hydrangea bretschneideri
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland habitat

Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to prevent the large leaves from wilting in heat

Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and maintain the preferred acid soil

items.name: Hydrangea chinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chinese hydrangea in moist, acidic to neutral soil to keep its lacecap flowers blue.
Protect the early spring buds from late UK frosts using fleece to ensure you do not lose blooms.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer by cutting back spent stems to a strong side bud.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to keep the shallow root system from drying out.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles or leaf mould to retain moisture and acidity.

items.name: Hydrangea cinerea
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, adding a bucket of well-rotted manure to the planting hole.

Prune in late winter by cutting stems back to a strong pair of buds to encourage vigorous new growth.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould to maintain the cool, damp root run this shrub prefers.

items.name: Hydrangea heteromalla
items.growersTips:
Plant this large shrub in moist well-drained soil enriched with plenty of composted leaf mould.

Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch in the UK's increasingly hot Julys.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate lacecap summer blooms from strong afternoon sun.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture and feed the shallow roots.

items.name: Hydrangea hirta
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native woodland floor.
Position in dappled shade or a sheltered north-facing border to prevent the delicate leaves burning.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system constantly damp.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late summer, cutting back to a strong pair of buds.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain moisture and protect roots from winter frosts.

items.name: Hydrangea hydrangeoides
items.growersTips:
Plant against a sturdy north or east-facing UK wall to protect young spring shoots from late frosts.
Incorporate leaf mould into acidic soil to mimic its native woodland floor and retain summer moisture.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer by cutting back flowered shoots to a strong bud.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK spells in July and August to prevent leaf scorch.
Plant alongside shade-loving ferns and hostas which thrive in the same moist, dappled conditions.

items.name: Hydrangea integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this self-clinging climber against a sheltered north or east-facing wall to avoid leaf scorch.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into the planting hole to mimic forest soils.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers until the root system is fully established.
Prune immediately after summer flowering by cutting back overlong shoots to a strong lateral bud.
Protect young spring growth from late frosts using horticultural fleece on cold UK nights.

items.name: Hydrangea involucrata
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade sheltered from cold winds to protect the delicate felted leaves from scorch.
Mulch annually with leafmould in spring to maintain the moist acidic to neutral soil they prefer.
Prune in mid-spring by cutting back flowered stems to a strong pair of buds to encourage new growth.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the soft flower buds from drying out and dropping.
Protect the early spring emerging buds from late UK frosts using fleece on exceptionally cold nights.

items.name: Hydrangea macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent afternoon leaf scorch.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to support its repeat-blooming habit.

Prune in late winter by removing only dead wood and old flower heads, as it blooms on new wood too.
Add sulfur-based ericaceous fertiliser in March to turn flowers blue in neutral UK garden soils.

items.name: Hydrangea paniculata
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in early March down to a low framework of buds to guarantee massive current-season blooms.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.

Mulch annually in spring with compost to retain moisture and protect roots from drying out.
Select Limelight for strong upright stems that will not flop under heavy British summer rain.

items.name: Hydrangea peruviana
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare evergreen climber against a warm south-facing wall to protect it from harsh UK frosts
Water deeply twice a week during dry summer spells to establish its deep, moisture-loving root system

Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants and apply biological nematodes in autumn

items.name: Hydrangea petiolaris

Plant against a north or east-facing wall in fertile, moisture-retentive, neutral to acid soil.
Water deeply twice a week during the first two dry summers to establish the slow-growing root system.
Prune immediately after flowering in summer by cutting back overlong shoots to a healthy bud.
Secure young stems to a sturdy trellis until the self-clinging aerial roots grip the brickwork.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted leaf mould to mimic their natural woodland forest floor.

items.name: Hydrangea quercifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot with dappled shade to protect the large leaves from strong UK winds.
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted manure to mimic woodland soil and retain summer moisture.

items.name: Hydrangea radiata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil to keep the silver leaf-undersides vibrant.
Siting in dappled shade or morning sun prevents the delicate foliage from scorching in UK heatwaves.
Prune stems back to a strong pair of buds in early spring to encourage vigorous new flowering wood.
Mulch annually with composted pine needles or leaf mould to retain moisture and maintain soil acidity.

items.name: Hydrangea sargentiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered, north or east-facing spot to protect large, velvety leaves from wind scorch.
Incorporate plenty of leaf mould or well-rotted manure to mimic UK woodland soil before planting.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the massive foliage from drooping and drying out.
Prune in late spring by removing only dead wood and old flowerheads to safeguard the new buds.
Mulch annually in spring with compost to retain moisture and protect the shallow root system.

items.name: Hydrangea scandens
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich soil in dappled shade to mimic woodland edge conditions.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or compost to retain moisture and keep shallow roots cool.
Prune lightly immediately after summer flowering by cutting back spent shoots to a strong side bud.
Protect early spring buds from late UK frosts using fleece to safeguard the delicate white flowers.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.

items.name: Hydrangea serrata
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade to prevent UK midday sun from scorching the delicate, thin leaves.
Water deeply twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system moist.
Prune in spring by cutting back flowered stems to the first pair of strong, healthy buds.
Grow in acidic soil with sulfate of iron to maintain the blue colour of cultivars like Bluebird.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to protect roots from late UK frosts and retain moisture.

items.name: Hydrangea serratifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant against a sheltered south or west wall to protect the self-clinging stems from cold UK winds.
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted manure deep into the planting hole to retain summer moisture.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to establish the climbing root system.
Prune immediately after summer flowering by trimming back overlong shoots to a strong side bud.
Mulch the root zone annually in spring with compost to mimic its native damp woodland floor.

items.name: Hydrangea strigosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in dappled shade sheltered from harsh winds to protect the delicate velvety leaves from scorch
Incorporate plenty of leafmould or well-rotted manure to mimic the damp woodland soils they love
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the large soft foliage from wilting and drying out
Prune in spring by removing dead wood and old flower heads down to the first pair of strong buds
Protect the early spring leaf buds from late UK frosts using fleece if a sudden cold snap threatens

items.name: Hydrangea stylosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade with moist, well-draining soil, adding leaf mould to mimic UK woodland beds.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the shallow root system moist.
Prune in late spring after the last frosts, cutting back dead stems to a strong pair of healthy buds.
Protect young spring shoots from late UK frosts using horticultural fleece to prevent bud damage.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain soil moisture and suppress competing weeds.

items.name: Hydrangea xanthoneura
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil enriched with leafmould to mimic its native woodland habitat
Prune in late winter by removing deadwood and thinning congested stems to keep the shrub open

items.name: Hydrangeoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant pink or blue Hydrangea macrophylla in ericaceous compost to guarantee vibrant blue flowers.

items.name: Hydrophylloideae
items.growersTips:
Sow Phacelia seeds in early spring just five millimetres deep to jumpstart your garden beds.
Water your waterleaf plants deeply once a week rather than giving them daily shallow sprinkles.

items.name: Hydrophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant your waterleaf in damp, shady woodland borders alongside native UK ferns and wild primroses.
Keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy, especially during dry spells in July and August.
Mulch with leaf mould in late autumn to mimic the forest floor and protect roots from hard frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using beer traps or wool pellets.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate them easily.

items.name: Hydrophyllum appendiculatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native forest home.
Sow seeds in autumn because they need a cold UK winter to break dormancy and germinate in spring.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or compost into your clay soil to keep it moist but free-draining.
Keep the soil consistently damp during dry spring spells, but do not let it get waterlogged.
Grow it alongside native ferns and wild garlic to create a gorgeous, natural wildlife corner.

items.name: Hydrophyllum canadense
items.growersTips:
Plant this wood aster relative in moist, dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic UK woodlands.
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted compost into heavy UK clay to keep the soil moisture-retentive.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to support its lush foliage before it goes dormant in heat.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using organic beer traps to protect them.

items.name: Hydrophyllum capitatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural canopy.

Watch out for slugs early in spring as they adore the tender emerging hairy foliage.

items.name: Hydrophyllum fendleri
items.growersTips:
Plant your Fendler's waterleaf in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames, as UK frost helps break dormancy for spring germination.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry British summer spells.

items.name: Hydrophyllum macrophyllum

Plant this shade-lover in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees or shrubs.

Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or wool pellets.

items.name: Hydrophyllum occidentale

Plant this wood aster relative in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous garden trees.

Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, protecting the emerging young shoots early.

items.name: Hydrophyllum tenuipes

Plant this Pacific waterleaf in moist, humic soil under deciduous trees to mimic its native woods.
Keep the soil consistently damp during dry UK summers, but ensure it drains well so roots do not rot.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural British winter chill can break their dormancy.

items.name: Hydrophyllum virginianum

Plant this wood-lover in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland.

items.name: Hygrophila

Grow Hygrophila corymbosa in your indoor heated aquarium as it is too tender for UK outdoor ponds.

items.name: Hygrophila auriculata

Grow this tender marsh plant in a pond basket filled with heavy clay soil to stop it from floating.

Cut back the leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and more blue flowers.

items.name: Hygrophila corymbosa

Grow this aquatic perennial submerged in your indoor heated aquarium, as the UK climate is too cold.
Plant the stems two inches deep in nutrient-rich aquarium gravel to help the roots anchor quickly.

items.name: Hygrophila costata

Plant this bog-lover in wet soil by your pond edge or submerged up to fifteen centimetres deep.

Cut back the leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more white flowers.
Watch out for pond snails and slugs which love devouring the tender underwater foliage.
Grow it alongside native Marsh Marigolds to create a beautiful, moisture-loving contrast.

items.name: Hygrophila difformis

Keep this aquatic beauty in a heated indoor tank as our chilly UK climate is too cold for outdoors.
Plant stems two inches deep in nutrient-rich gravel, leaving space between them so lower leaves get light.
Prune the fast-growing tops weekly to encourage bushy side shoots and prevent it taking over your tank.
Watch out for melting leaves, a sign your water needs a boost of liquid iron fertilizer and more light.

items.name: Hygrophila pogonocalyx
items.growersTips:
Grow this bog-loving perennial in a shallow, muddy pond margin where water is just over the crown.

Cut the stems back by half in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and prevent winter rot in the water.

items.name: Hygrophila polysperma

Grow this fast-growing aquatic plant in a heated indoor aquarium to survive the chilly UK winters.
Plant the stems two inches deep in a nutrient-rich aquarium soil to anchor their rapid root growth.
Prune the stems weekly from the top to encourage bushy side shoots and prevent it blocking light.
Watch out for pond snails eating the soft leaves, and gently remove them by hand to protect stems.

items.name: Hylaeaicum pendulum
items.growersTips:
Keep this trailing epiphyte cozy indoors or in a heated greenhouse, as it cannot survive UK frosts.
Water with rainwater when the top inch of bark mix dries, mimicking its humid rainforest home.
Nestle its roots in a free-draining orchid compost mixed with perlite to prevent winter root rot.
Hang it in bright, filtered light near an east window to avoid scorching its delicate pendulous stems.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost its summer growth.

items.name: Hylaeaicum wurdackii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, frosty UK winter chill.
Plant it in a very chunky, free-draining orchid bark mix rather than standard heavy garden soil.
Water directly into the central rosette cup using collected rainwater instead of tap water.
Position it in bright, indirect light near a south-facing window to mimic its natural canopy home.
Feed it during spring by misting a highly diluted liquid seaweed fertilizer onto its foliage.

items.name: Hylomecon
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic their native woodland canopy habitat.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to keep soil damp but stop watering when they go dormant.
Plant alongside Hostas or ferns to cover the bare patches left when Hylomecon dies back in midsummer.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they quickly devour the tender emerging shoots.

items.name: Hylomecon japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist humus-rich acidic soil under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames as they require winter chilling to germinate the next spring.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to prevent the foliage from dying back prematurely in June.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in late summer once the plant has gone dormant to propagate new stock.

items.name: Hylomecon vernalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees to mimic its native woodland canopy conditions.
Sow fresh seed in late summer or divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth starts.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to prolong the delicate yellow flowering period in May.
Leave the dying foliage alone in summer as this plant naturally goes dormant and disappears early.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould to protect the shallow rhizomes from harsh UK winter frosts.

items.name: Hylotelephium
items.growersTips:
Plant your stonecrop in gritty soil to survive wet UK winters, keeping the crown level with the turf.
Cut the stems back by half in May using the Chelsea chop to keep your autumn display tidy and upright.
Leave the dried flower heads on all winter to give UK songbirds a treat and create beautiful frost.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in spring, as they love chewing the roots of container-grown plants.
Pair them with ornamental grasses like Stipa tenuissima for a gorgeous, drought-tolerant border.

items.name: Hylotelephium anacampseros
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen in poor, gritty soil with added sharp sand to survive wet British winters.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry completely to prevent root rot.
Tuck it into a sunny rock garden or stone wall crevice where its trailing stems can drape naturally.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums and sedums which thrive in the same dry, sunny conditions.
Prune back any leggy or winter-damaged stems in early spring to encourage fresh, compact growth.

items.name: Hylotelephium cauticola
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet, soggy UK winters.
Position your pot in full sun on a south-facing patio to get those deep pink autumn flowers.
Water sparingly during summer, only when the top few centimetres of soil are completely dry.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in early spring to make way for new blue-grey buds.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow this in a container.

items.name: Hylotelephium erythrostictum
items.growersTips:
Plant this stonecrop in a sunny, free-draining spot to prevent winter root rot in soggy UK soils.
Cut the stems back by half in late May using the Chelsea Chop to keep the plant compact and sturdy.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots of your potted plants during damp autumn months.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to keep the pink-tinged foliage vigorous.
Pair it with purple-leaved Heucheras for a gorgeous autumn contrast in your mixed herbaceous borders.

items.name: Hylotelephium ewersii
items.growersTips:
Pop this pink beauty in your grittiest, sharpest-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a sunny spot in a raised bed or rockery where soggy rainwater can easily drain away.
Only water this drought-lover when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely by October.
Leave the faded flower heads on over winter to protect the crown from harsh UK frosts and rot.
Grow it alongside hardy sempervivums and sedums in shallow pots to create a lovely alpine display.

items.name: Hylotelephium sieboldii
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink-edged beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Keep it in full sun on your patio to bring out those gorgeous, bright autumn leaf colours.
Water only when the top few inches of compost are bone dry, as it hates soggy roots.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in containers, they love to munch the roots in spring.
Leave the faded flower heads on all winter to protect the crown from harsh UK frosts.

items.name: Hylotelephium spectabile
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to stop winter wet from rotting its fleshy roots.
Chop stems back by half in late May to keep the plant sturdy and prevent it flopping in autumn rain.
Leave the dried flower heads on all winter to give UK songbirds seeds and create lovely frost shapes.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots, especially if you grow them in patio containers.
Divide the clumps every three years in spring to keep them vigorous and get free plants for friends.

items.name: Hylotelephium telephioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild stonecrop in grit-rich, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Position in full, baking sun to keep its naturally loose, shrubby stems compact and prevent flopping.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between your drenchings.
Leave the dried flower heads through winter to feed birds, then cut stems to the base in early spring.
Divide your clumps every three years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and prevent center dieback.

items.name: Hylotelephium telephium
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Do the Chelsea chop in late May to keep stems sturdy and prevent them from flopping.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this succulent thrives on neglect.
Leave faded flower heads intact over winter to provide structural frost interest and feed birds.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and protect young spring shoots from slugs.

items.name: Hymenaea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using a heated propagator kept at a constant 25C.
Grow this tropical annual in a heated greenhouse or south-facing conservatory to survive UK summers.
Water only when the top 5cm of sandy, free-draining loam dries out to prevent root rot.
Apply a high-potassium liquid feed fortnightly once the first flower buds appear in midsummer.
Monitor daily for glasshouse red spider mite and use biological controls at the first sign of webbing.

items.name: Hymenaea courbaril
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical tree in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive UK winter cold.
Sow scarified seeds two centimetres deep in a free-draining sandy loam mixed with perlite.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil dries out to prevent root rot.
Position in the brightest south-facing indoor spot to maximise essential UK summer sunlight.
Inspect regularly for glasshouse red spider mite and wipe leaves with a damp cloth to deter them.

items.name: Hymenaea oblongifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using bottom heat of 21C to counter cool UK spring soils.
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep the taproot moist while avoiding waterlogged clay.

Grow alongside nitrogen-fixing clover in sandy, well-draining soil to boost early vegetative growth.
Pinch out the growing tips in mid-July to encourage bushy lateral growth and more summer blooms.

items.name: Hymenaea stigonocarpa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of 2cm using a heated propagator to mimic warm soils.
Grow this tender species in pots of free-draining sandy loam so you can move them inside for winter.
Water deeply once the top 3cm of soil dries out, reducing moisture in autumn to prevent root rot.
Position pots in your sunniest south-facing spot or greenhouse to maximise crucial UK summer heat.
Feed monthly in spring and summer with a low-nitrogen fertiliser to support healthy legume growth.

items.name: Hymenaea verrucosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical tree as a container annual in a heated greenhouse or conservatory at 20C minimum.
Sow the extremely hard seeds in spring after scarifying with sandpaper and soaking in warm water.
Use a very free-draining loam and grit potting mix to prevent root rot during cool UK summers.
Water only when the top three inches of compost are dry, reducing moisture during overcast weeks.
Keep a vigilant watch for glasshouse red spider mite and mealybugs in dry indoor air conditions.

items.name: Hymenostegia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using peat-free compost to protect from late UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week at the base to prevent powdery mildew in humid UK summer weather.

Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 15cm high to encourage a bushier flowering habit.
Incorporate grit into heavy UK clay soils before planting to ensure the sharp drainage they need.

items.name: Hymenostegia bakeriana

Sow the seeds exactly one centimetre deep in a moist, peat-free seed compost mixed with perlite.

Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British summers by using beer traps around the stems.
Grow them alongside French marigolds to naturally deter aphids and boost your garden biodiversity.

items.name: Hymenothrix loomisii

Sow seeds shallowly indoors in early April then transplant out after the May frosts have passed.

Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to match its strict low-nutrient soil needs.
Snip off the fading cream flower heads in August to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.

Avoid transplanting established plants by sowing them directly where you want them to flower.

items.name: Hypecoum imberbe

Plant alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme and oregano which share its low-nutrient soil needs.

items.name: Hypecoum pendulum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained gritty soil as they dislike root disturbance.

Avoid overwatering by letting the soil dry out completely between waterings to prevent root rot.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Allow the plant to self-seed naturally in gravel gardens to ensure a display the following year.

items.name: Hypecoum procumbens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil to allow winter cold to naturally break dormancy.

Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers in wet weather.
Avoid transplanting established plants by sowing directly where they are to flower in the garden.

items.name: Hypoestes
items.growersTips:
Bring your polka dot plant indoors by October to protect it from chilly wet UK autumn frosts.
Pinch out the growing tips every few weeks in spring to stop it getting leggy and encourage bushiness.

items.name: Hypoestes floribunda

Mix plenty of grit into your multi-purpose compost to ensure the roots never sit in soggy soil.

items.name: Hypoestes forskaolii

Bring this tender perennial indoors by October to protect it from wet and freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in our cool climate.

items.name: Hypoestes phyllostachya

Keep this tropical beauty indoors on a bright UK windowsill, away from direct midday summer sun.

items.name: Hypseocharis

Protect from slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate new foliage emerges.
Overwinter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to shield from heavy UK frosts.

items.name: Iberodes
items.growersTips:
Plant your Iberodes linifolia in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winter rot.

items.name: Ichnocarpus

items.name: Ichthyothere

items.name: Ichtyoselmis macrantha

Propagate by careful division in early spring just as new growth begins to show above the ground

items.name: Ifloga

Watch out for damp UK autumn weather and clear away faded plants early to prevent grey mould.

items.name: Ilex × attenuata
items.growersTips:
Plant this hybrid holly in acidic to neutral soil, as UK chalk will cause yellowing leaves.

items.name: Ilex amelanchier

Plant this rare holly in acidic, moisture-retentive soil like a bog garden or damp woodland edge.

Watch out for leaf miners in spring; pinch off affected leaves early to keep the foliage healthy.

items.name: Ilex anomala

Plant this Hawaiian holly in a warm, sheltered spot to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.

items.name: Ilex arisanensis

Give this Taiwanese holly a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to prevent winter leaf scorch.
Plant your Arisan holly in moist, acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of composted pine bark.
Water deeply every week during dry British summers until its root system is fully established.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to shape this slow-growing evergreen.
Mulch the root zone every autumn with leaf mould to protect it from wet, freezing winter soil.

items.name: Ilex asprella
items.growersTips:
Plant this deciduous holly in moist, acidic soil rich in leaf mould to mimic its native woodland.
Water deeply every week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy.
Prune lightly in late winter to shape the shrub and remove any frost-damaged stems before spring.
Mulch annually with pine needles or bark to maintain the low soil pH and lock in vital moisture.
Watch out for leaf miners in spring, cutting off affected foliage immediately to keep it healthy.

items.name: Ilex bioritsensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this holly in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine bark.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its native forest edge, sheltered from harsh UK winter winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until its deep root system is fully established.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to shape and maintain its compact form.
Keep an eye out for holly leaf miner damage and simply pick off affected leaves to keep it tidy.

items.name: Ilex canariensis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Canary Island holly in a sheltered, south-facing spot to shield it from cold UK winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.
Prune your holly in late spring after any risk of frost has passed to keep its shape tidy.
Add a thick layer of bracken or leaf mould mulch in autumn to protect the roots from winter frost.
Watch out for leaf miners in spring and squish affected leaves immediately to keep foliage clean.

items.name: Ilex cassine
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender holly in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter winds.
Plant it in moist, acidic soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles to keep the pH low.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to mimic its native damp bog environment.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to shape and remove dead wood.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in autumn to protect the shallow roots from freezing UK soils.

items.name: Ilex chinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chinese holly in moist, well-drained acidic soil using plenty of composted pine bark.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help its shallow roots establish in your garden.
Prune your holly in late spring after the frosts to shape it and keep those red berries coming.
Watch out for holly leaf miner in May and squish any mined leaves you see to protect the foliage.
Pair it with shade-loving sarcococca to enjoy a lovely mix of winter scents and glossy green leaves.

items.name: Ilex colchica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Black Sea holly in moist, well-drained acidic soil, mixing in plenty of composted bark.
To get those bright red winter berries, you must plant a male cultivar nearby to pollinate her.
Give your young shrub a deep soak once a week during dry UK summers to help its roots settle in.
Prune your holly in late spring after the frosts to shape it and keep its glossy leaves looking neat.
Watch out for leaf miners making pale trails on the foliage, and just snip off any affected leaves.

items.name: Ilex coriacea
items.growersTips:
Plant this bayberry holly in acidic, ericaceous compost to prevent the leaves from turning yellow.
Keep the soil consistently damp as this bog-loving shrub thrives in damp UK clay and wet hollows.
Prune your large gallberry bush in late spring after the frost to keep its sprawling habit neat.
Watch out for the holly leaf miner pest which can disfigure the glossy foliage in mild UK winters.
Grow it alongside blueberries or heather since they all love the same damp, acidic UK soil conditions.

items.name: Ilex cornuta

Feed with an ericaceous fertiliser in spring if your garden soil is naturally chalky or alkaline.
Prune your shrub in late summer to shape it and keep those fiercely spiny leaves away from paths.
Watch out for holly leaf miner damage and simply pick off affected leaves to keep the plant tidy.

items.name: Ilex crenata

Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Prune your shrubs in late spring or early autumn to maintain that neat, cloud-pruned shape.

items.name: Ilex cymosa

Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy using tepid rainwater rather than cold tap water.
Pot it up in a well-draining, acidic ericaceous soil mix to mimic its native peat swamp habitat.
Place your pot in a bright conservatory or on a warm, humid windowsill away from cold draughts.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape the shrub and encourage bushier fresh green growth.

items.name: Ilex decidua

Plant your possumhaw holly in moist, acidic clay-heavy soil to mimic its native damp woodland home.

Keep the soil consistently damp during dry UK summers, especially while the roots are establishing.
Watch out for scale insects on the branches and treat them early with an organic plant oil spray.

items.name: Ilex denticulata

items.name: Ilex laevigata

Grow a male clone like Maryland Beauty nearby to ensure your female plants produce those red berries.

items.name: Ilex latifolia

Prune in late spring after frosts pass to shape it and remove any winter-damaged foliage.
Watch out for holly leaf miner in May and simply pick off and burn any blistered leaves.

items.name: Ilex longipes

Pair with shade-loving UK woodland plants like ferns and hostas for a beautiful texture contrast.

items.name: Ilex macropoda

Keep young trees well-watered during dry British summers until their root system is fully established.

items.name: Ilex malabarica

items.name: Ilex micrococca

Shelter it from harsh, cold winds by planting near a south or west-facing wall to protect the buds.
Watch out for leaf miners in spring, snipping off and burning any blotchy leaves you spot.

items.name: Ilex mitis

Plant this African holly in a sheltered, frost-free spot as UK winters can bite its tender leaves.

items.name: Ilex montana

Plant this mountain holly in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic soil to mimic its native woodland.
Water deeply every week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but not waterlogged.
Prune your shrub in late winter to shape it and encourage fresh berry-bearing wood for next year.
Plant a male pollinator like Ilex verticillata nearby to guarantee a heavy crop of bright berries.

items.name: Ilex mucronata

items.name: Ilex myrtifolia

Position it in a sheltered, sun-drenched spot to protect those delicate narrow leaves from cold winds.

Prune gently in late spring after any frosts to shape the bush and encourage dense, bushy growth.

items.name: Ilex obcordata

Plant this slow-growing holly in moist, well-drained acidic soil to prevent yellowing leaves.
Give it shelter from cold, drying winds which can scorch the delicate, heart-shaped foliage.
