Keep young plants well-watered during dry spells, especially in sandy southern UK soils.
Grow it alongside acid-loving companion plants like dwarf rhododendrons or heathers.

items.name: Ilex opaca
items.growersTips:
Give this American holly a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to prevent winter leaf scorch.
Plant your holly in acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of composted pine needles to the hole.

items.name: Ilex pedunculosa

Plant this long-stalked holly in acidic to neutral soil, adding compost to keep it moist but well-drained.

Prune lightly in late spring to shape your holly, avoiding late autumn cuts which invite frost damage.

items.name: Ilex perado

items.name: Ilex pernyi

Plant this slow-growing holly in a spot with moist, well-drained acidic to neutral soil.

Watch out for holly leaf miner in May; just snip off and burn any blotchy leaves you spot.

items.name: Ilex pubescens
items.growersTips:
Give this Chinese holly a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter winds.
Plant your shrub in moist, acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of composted pine bark to the hole.

Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to maintain its neat, bushy shape.

items.name: Ilex rotunda

Plant this holly in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect its glossy evergreen leaves.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit and leaf mould into heavy clay soil to ensure excellent drainage.
Water your young tree deeply once a week during dry British summers to help the roots establish.
Prune in late spring after the frosts have passed to shape it and remove any winter damage.

items.name: Ilex rugosa

items.name: Ilex sapiiformis

Plant this rare holly in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic soil to mimic its native damp habitat.

items.name: Ilex serrata

Plant your Japanese winterberry in acidic to neutral soil, adding well-rotted pine needles to prep.

items.name: Ilex triflora

items.name: Ilex uraiensis

Plant this rare Taiwanese holly in a sheltered, west-facing spot to shield it from cold UK winds.

items.name: Ilex verticillata
items.growersTips:
Plant a male cultivar like Southern Gentleman near your female bushes to guarantee those red berries.
Keep the soil consistently damp as this bog-loving holly hates drying out in hot UK summers.
Mix plenty of ericaceous compost into your soil to keep the pH acidic and prevent yellow leaves.
Prune them in late winter while dormant to shape the shrub without losing the current winter berries.
Watch out for leaf miner pests in spring by picking off and burning any blotchy or tunnelled leaves.

items.name: Ilex vomitoria
items.growersTips:
Grow this American native in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Plant it in acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of composted pine bark to keep the pH low.
Water deeply once a week during dry English summers until its deep root system is fully established.
Prune your shrub in late winter to shape it before the new spring growth starts to emerge.
Watch out for scale insects and treat them early with organic horticultural oil in midsummer.

items.name: Ilex vulcanicola
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare holly in acidic, humus-rich soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine bark first.
Protect its roots from harsh UK frosts by applying a thick layer of bracken or leaf mould mulch.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to mimic its natural damp mountain environment.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape it, as this slow grower dislikes heavy winter cutting.
Keep a close eye out for leaf miners in May and pick off any blistered leaves immediately.

items.name: Illecebrum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring by pressing them lightly into damp, acidic, sandy soil without burying them.
Grow this damp-loving annual in bog gardens or pond edges to mimic its native UK heathland habitat.
Water frequently with rainwater to keep the soil consistently wet, as tap water is too alkaline.
Position in full sun to ensure the tiny white axillary flowers bloom fully from July to September.
Clear competing weeds by hand regularly because this prostrate plant is easily smothered by turf.

items.name: Illecebrum verticillatum
items.growersTips:
This little pink-stemmed gem loves soggy feet, so plant it right at the margins of your garden pond.
Sow the tiny seeds in spring by pressing them gently into wet, acidic peat-free compost, no deeper.
Keep the soil constantly wet and boggy, mimicking its native UK damp gravelly heathland habitats.
Watch out for aggressive garden mint trying to smother this delicate, low-growing carpet weaver.
Let it self-seed naturally in damp gravel paths to create a lovely, wild-looking ground cover.

items.name: Indigofereae
items.growersTips:
Sow your indigo seeds indoors in March using deep root trainers to avoid disturbing the taproot.
Scarify the tough seeds with sandpaper and soak them in warm water for a day before sowing in April.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure excellent drainage in wet UK winters and prevent rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimeters high to encourage a bushier habit.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.

items.name: Inga
items.growersTips:
Start Inga seeds indoors in warm April, sowing them two centimetres deep in peat-free compost.
Grow your Inga in large pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Water your Inga deeply once a week, letting the top inch of soil dry out between waterings.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites under the leaves and mist regularly to keep them away.
Feed your Inga monthly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser from June to promote strong growth.

items.name: Ingeae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth using peat-free compost to beat the cool UK spring soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.

Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils before planting to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Plant alongside brassicas as companions to benefit from the nitrogen-fixing nodules on the roots.

items.name: Inocarpus
items.growersTips:
Sow Inocarpus seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep using a heated propagator to mimic tropical warmth.
Keep the compost consistently wet like a marsh, watering with tepid rainwater rather than tap water.
Grow this Tahitian chestnut in a container so you can move it inside before first autumn frosts hit.
Feed fortnightly in summer with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed to boost its lush canopy growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites under the leaves and mist daily to keep humidity high.

items.name: Intsia bijuga
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical legume in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive cool UK temperatures.
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of two centimeters after scarifying and soaking them in warm water.
Water deeply once the top three centimeters of free-draining, sandy loam soil has dried out completely.
Apply a low-nitrogen, high-potassium liquid fertilizer monthly during the active summer growth.
Inspect regularly for glasshouse red spider mites and maintain high humidity to deter infestations.

items.name: Intsia palembanica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical tree indoors in a heated conservatory to mimic its native warm rainforest habitat
Sow seeds in spring after scarifying and soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours to sprout
Water consistently to keep the acidic loamy soil moist but never waterlogged during summer months
Provide a minimum winter temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius using grow lights to prevent leaf drop
Watch for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the foliage daily to maintain high humidity levels

items.name: Iostephane heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of three millimetres to protect them from late frosts
Plant out in late May in a south-facing border with free-draining soil to maximise summer warmth
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily to prevent root rot in damp UK summers
Deadhead faded blooms weekly through August to prolong the flowering display until the first frost
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical copper barriers

items.name: Ipsea
items.growersTips:
Bring your yellow clay orchid indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Grow this orchid in a gritty, free-draining mix of fine bark and perlite to prevent root rot.

Position your potted orchid on a bright, east-facing windowsill to mimic its native sunny grassland.
Repot in early spring just as new growth appears, keeping the pseudobulbs level with the soil surface.

items.name: Irideae
items.growersTips:
Plant your iris bulbs in autumn at twice their depth in gritty, well-drained soil facing south.

items.name: Iridoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant dwarf reticulata bulbs four inches deep in autumn for a brilliant splash of early spring colour

Feed your spring irises with a low-nitrogen fertiliser just as they finish flowering in May

items.name: Iris
items.growersTips:
Plant dwarf bulbs like Iris reticulata in autumn at a depth of three times the bulb height in pots.
Ensure sharp drainage by mixing grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter bulb rot in wet weather.
Force potted bulbs indoors in December for early winter blooms then transplant outside in spring.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in March.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally and turn yellow before removing it to feed next years bulb.

items.name: Iris × germanica
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to the UK sun to bake and ensure reliable flowering.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter rot in wet British conditions.
Cut foliage back to a clean five-inch fan in autumn to reduce wind rock and prevent leaf spot.
Divide congested clumps every three years in late summer after flowering to maintain plant vigour.
Watch for iris sawfly larvae in spring and handpick them to prevent rapid defoliation of leaves.

items.name: Iris ×hollandica
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres, about twice the height of the bulb itself.
Choose your sunniest border with free-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter wet from rotting them.
Once the flowers fade in early summer, let the foliage turn fully yellow and die back naturally.
Watch out for slugs and snails eating the emerging spring shoots, especially during wet UK springs.
Plant them alongside shallow-rooted annuals to hide the untidy, dying leaves later in the summer.

items.name: Iris acutiloba
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate bulb in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in a very gritty, sharp soil.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormancy to mimic their native dry Middle East climate.
Grow this iris in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the blooms from heavy UK winter rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the emerging flower buds.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the foliage starts to die back in late spring.

items.name: Iris acutiloba subsp. lineolata

Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of twice their height in sharply draining, gritty compost.
Keep them completely dry in summer by using a cold frame to mimic their dormant desert home.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than open borders to protect them from wet UK winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the delicate emerging shoots.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot in your garden to help bake the bulbs after flowering.

items.name: Iris alberti
items.growersTips:
Plant this iris in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in well-drained, grit-amended soil.

items.name: Iris albicans

Divide the congested clumps every three years in late summer right after they finish flowering.

items.name: Iris alexeenkoi

Plant these tiny bulbs in autumn at twice their depth in gritty, sharp-draining soil to stop rot.
Pop them in your sunniest south-facing rockery or a raised bed to mimic their dry mountain home.
Give them a dry summer rest by covering the soil or lifting bulbs once the foliage dies down.
Watch out for slugs chewing the delicate spring blooms, so use grit barriers around your pots.
Grow them in terracotta pots of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to survive wet winters.

items.name: Iris aphylla

Plant this little native of dry grasslands in a gritty, free-draining soil to survive UK winters.

items.name: Iris aphylla subsp. hungarica

items.name: Iris arenaria

items.name: Iris atrofusca

Plant this Middle Eastern beauty in a terracotta pot with grit so you can move it out of winter rain.

items.name: Iris atropurpurea
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in your sunniest, south-facing spot.
Ensure your soil is mixed with plenty of grit to survive wet UK winters without the bulbs rotting.
Keep them dry during their summer dormant phase by covering the soil or lifting them after flowering.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch on the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Iris attica
items.growersTips:
Plant this little gem just two inches deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to stop winter rot.
Give it a baking hot, south-facing spot in your rockery to mimic its sunny Greek hillside home.

items.name: Iris aucheri

items.name: Iris auranitica

Plant this Syrian beauty in a terracotta pot to easily move it under glass during wet UK winters.

items.name: Iris barnumiae
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Iraqi native in a raised bed of gritty, sharply draining soil to survive UK wet.
Keep the rhizome completely dry during its summer dormancy by covering it with a glass cloche.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot possible, ideally a south-facing unheated greenhouse.

items.name: Iris bicapitata
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn about ten centimetres deep in extremely well-drained, gritty UK soil.

items.name: Iris bismarckiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this oncocyclus iris in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to survive wet UK winters.
Position the rhizome, not bulb, right at the soil surface so the British summer sun can bake it.
Keep it bone dry in summer by covering with a rain cloche or cold frame during its dormant phase.
Water very sparingly from October to spring, only when active green growth is visibly showing.

items.name: Iris boissieri
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Portuguese bulb in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in very sharp grit.
Give it a hot, dry summer baking by covering the soil with a slate tile once the leaves die down.
Grow it in a terracotta pot in a cold greenhouse to protect its roots from wet UK winter rot.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to ensure water drains away instantly.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to chew the emerging flower buds.

items.name: Iris bostrensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny Syrian bulb in autumn about eight centimetres deep in your sharpest-draining UK soil.
Keep it bone dry in summer by covering the bed or lifting bulbs to mimic its native desert heat.
Grow this dwarf wild iris in a gritty alpine trough to protect its delicate roots from winter wet.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they love chewing the emerging narrow leaves and flower buds.
Saturate the soil only during its brief spring growing phase, then stop watering as flowers fade.

items.name: Iris bracteata
items.growersTips:
Plant your Siskiyou iris in acidic, gritty soil as they absolutely hate lime and wet winter feet.
Keep the rhizomes near the surface, barely covered with grit, rather than burying them like bulbs.
Water them during dry spring spells but leave them completely dry once summer dormancy sets in.
Watch out for slugs eating the delicate yellow spring blooms, so use organic pellets early on.
Avoid moving them once planted because these wild beauties have fragile roots that hate disturbance.

items.name: Iris bucharica
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in a super gritty, free-draining soil.
Give them a hot, sunny spot against a south-facing wall to bake the bulbs after they flower.
Keep them dry during their summer dormancy to prevent the delicate fleshy roots from rotting away.
Watch out for slugs early in spring as the fresh, bright green shoots start pushing through.
Let the foliage die back naturally in summer so the bulb can gather energy for next spring.

items.name: Iris bulleyana
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in reliably damp, humus-rich acid soil near a pond or in a boggy border.
Position your plant in full sun or partial shade to mimic its native damp Chinese meadow habitat.
Divide congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep the plant vigorous and blooming well.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted leafmould to retain moisture and feed the soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK spring weather as they love the tender new emerging shoots.

items.name: Iris caucasica
items.growersTips:
Plant this little bulb five inches deep in autumn so the winter frost can trigger its spring blooms.
Give it a gritty, sharply draining soil mix to survive our wet UK winters without rotting away.
Place it in your hottest, sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native dry mountain home.
Stop watering completely in summer once the leaves die back to let the bulb bake and rest.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the delicate early spring shoots as they emerge in March.

items.name: Iris chrysographes
items.growersTips:
Plant this black beauty in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil, never letting it dry out.
Position your gold-veined iris in full sun or partial shade to bring out those dark, moody velvet tones.
Divide the rhizomes—not bulbs—every three years in late summer to keep the plant vigorous and flowering.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in spring to lock in the dampness this damp-loving Chinese native craves.
Watch out for slugs eating the young spring shoots, so protect them early in the damp UK weather.

items.name: Iris chrysophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate Oregon native in free-draining, gritty, acidic soil to mimic its pine-woods home.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during its active spring growing season.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, as they love to munch the slender, grassy leaves.
Divide the creeping rhizomes, not bulbs, in late summer after flowering to keep the clump vigorous.
Plant them alongside dwarf conifers or heathers to provide the light dappled shade they prefer.

items.name: Iris clarkei
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in boggy, acidic soil near your pond rather than in dry borders.
Keep the soil consistently damp during dry UK summers, as this Himalayan native hates drying out.
Plant the rhizomes, not bulbs, just below the soil surface in spring, spaced thirty centimetres apart.
Divide congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep them vigorous and blooming well.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love to feast on the fresh new shoots.

items.name: Iris confusa
items.growersTips:
Plant this bamboo-like iris in a sheltered, dappled shade spot to protect leaves from cold UK winds.
Mulch the shallow rhizomes with leaf mould in autumn to protect them from hard British winter frosts.
Prune out the old flowered stems right to the base in late summer to keep the clump looking tidy.
Keep the soil reliably moist during its spring growing season, but never let it sit in soggy mud.
Grow it alongside hostas or ferns in humus-rich, neutral to acid soil for a lush woodland look.

items.name: Iris cristata
items.growersTips:
Plant your crested iris rhizomes shallowly, barely covered with a light leaf-mould and grit mix.
Give them dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native woodland edge habitat.
Water regularly during dry spring spells to help the delicate blue flowers establish and bloom.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, as they love to munch the tender new shoots.
Divide the creeping clumps every three years right after flowering to keep them vigorous and neat.

items.name: Iris croatica
items.growersTips:
Plant your Croatian iris bulbs in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in free-draining soil.
Give them a sunny, south-facing spot to mimic their native Balkan hills and survive wet UK winters.
Avoid overwatering these bulbs once established, as they only need a drink during dry spring spells.
Cut the flower stems right back to the base after flowering in July to keep the bulb energised.
Watch out for slugs in damp British springs, protecting the new shoots with grit or beer traps.

items.name: Iris crocea
items.growersTips:
Plant this tall yellow beauty in autumn about ten centimeters deep in heavy, moisture-retentive soil.
Give it a sunny, damp spot like a pond edge or bog garden where the UK rain keeps the soil wet.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring and summer but let it go slightly drier in winter.
Cut the faded flower stems right down to the base in late summer to keep the plant looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the fresh new shoots as they emerge in early spring.

items.name: Iris cycloglossa
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs eight centimetres deep in late autumn using a very gritty, free-draining compost.
Keep them damp during their spring growth but completely dry them out once they die back in summer.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate petals from heavy UK rain.
Feed them with a high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the first flower buds begin to show.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging, tender young shoots.

items.name: Iris danfordiae
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs deep at about ten to fifteen centimetres to stop them splitting into non-flowering offsets.
Give them a hot, dry summer baking by planting them against a south-facing wall or in a raised bed.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because these bulbs will rot quickly in wet winter UK clay.
Feed them with a high-potash fertiliser just as the green leaves push up to help next year's bud.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can move them under cover to dry out after the foliage dies.

items.name: Iris delavayi
items.growersTips:
Plant these moisture-lovers in damp, acidic soil near your pond edge or in a boggy garden border.
Plant the rhizomes—not bulbs—shallowly, keeping the tops just showing at the soil surface in autumn.
Keep them well-watered during dry UK summers, as they hate drying out and love wet feet.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in late summer to keep the plant looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging green shoots.

items.name: Iris dichotoma
items.growersTips:
Plant this Vesper iris in free-draining gravelly soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors during autumn so the natural winter cold breaks their dormancy easily.
Give them a spot in full sun facing south or west to ensure those late-afternoon summer blooms open.
Keep watering regular but light in summer, then let them dry out almost completely during winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the tender emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Iris domestica
items.growersTips:
Plant your blackberry lily bulbs eight centimeters deep in well-drained soil to survive wet winters.
Site them in your warmest, most sun-drenched border to ensure they actually flower in UK summers.
Water them regularly through active growth, but keep them bone dry in winter to prevent bulb rot.
Leave the gorgeous seedheads intact over winter for striking leopard-spotted architectural interest.
Protect the tender new spring shoots from hungry slugs using beer traps or physical barriers.

items.name: Iris douglasiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen rhizome, not a bulb, shallowly with its top just showing in acid to neutral soil.
Water your young plants weekly during dry UK spring spells until their deep root system establishes.
Tuck them into light dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic their native woodland edge habitat.
Snip away dead foliage and faded flower stems in late summer to keep the clump tidy and pest-free.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, especially during damp British Aprils.

items.name: Iris ensata
items.growersTips:
Plant your Japanese water iris in rich, acidic soil, avoiding any lime which turns their leaves yellow.
Keep them soaking wet in spring and summer, ideally placing pots on a shallow tray of rainwater.
Move potted plants out of the water in winter to prevent their crowns from rotting in cold soggy mud.
Feed them heavily with an ericaceous liquid fertilizer every fortnight during their spring growth.
Divide the congested rhizomes every three years in late summer to keep those huge blooms coming.

items.name: Iris fernaldii
items.growersTips:
Plant this native of woodland edges in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its home turf.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into your soil to keep these bulbs damp but never waterlogged.
Plant your bulbs about eight centimetres deep in late autumn before the first hard frost hits.
Watch out for slugs chewing the delicate spring shoots and use organic wool pellets to stop them.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.

items.name: Iris filifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in your sunniest, most sheltered spot.
Add plenty of grit to your planting hole to ensure the sharp drainage this Mediterranean native needs.
Keep the soil moist during their active spring growth but let them bake completely dry in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails as the delicate new shoots begin to emerge through the damp soil.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year's blooms.

items.name: Iris flavescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this bearded iris in shallow soil with the top of the rhizome exposed to the warm UK sun.
Give it a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to prevent wet winter rot in soggy British weather.
Divide the congested clumps every three years in late summer to keep the pale yellow blooms coming.
Cut the faded flower stems right down to the base in July to save the plant's energy for next year.
Watch out for iris rust and snails hiding in the fan-shaped leaves during damp spring mornings.

items.name: Iris florentina
items.growersTips:
Plant this rhizome, not a bulb, shallowly with its top exposed to the warm UK summer sun to flower.
Settle it into very sharp-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet British weather.
Cut the fan-shaped leaves down to a neat V-shape in autumn to stop wind-rock loosening the roots.
Divide the congested clumps every three years in late summer right after they finish flowering.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding under the flat leaves during damp UK spring mornings.

items.name: Iris foetidissima
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough native in dry shade under trees where other plants struggle to grow.
Leave the autumn seedpods on the stems for spectacular bursts of bright orange winter colour.
Cut back tatty old leaves right to the ground in early spring to make way for fresh green growth.
Divide congested clumps in late summer after the seeds have dispersed to propagate new plants.
Watch out for iris sawfly larvae in summer and handpick them off to save the evergreen foliage.

items.name: Iris formosana
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen rhizome, not a bulb, shallowly with its top exposed to the warm UK summer sun.
Tuck it into a sheltered, south-facing border to protect its delicate early spring blooms from frost.
Keep the soil gritty and free-draining, as damp winter clay will quickly rot its roots.
Divide the congested clumps right after flowering in summer to keep the plant vigorous and healthy.
Watch out for hungry slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love the fresh new foliage.

items.name: Iris fosteriana
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in your sharpest-draining gritty soil.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or bulb frame to protect the delicate winter blooms from UK rain.
Keep the soil completely dry during their summer dormant phase to prevent the bulbs from rotting.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging flower buds.
Feed them with a high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the foliage begins to die back in spring.

items.name: Iris fulva
items.growersTips:
Plant your copper iris in a soggy spot or pond margin where the soil never dries out in summer.
Give this Southern US native your sunniest south-facing UK border to help the rhizomes bake and flower.
Feed them with a high-potash tomato fertiliser in early spring to boost those unusual copper blooms.
Mulch heavily with leaf mould in autumn to protect the shallow rhizomes from hard UK winter frosts.
Divide the congested clumps right after flowering in July to keep them vigorous and blooming well.

items.name: Iris furcata
items.growersTips:
Plant this little beauty in autumn just five centimetres deep in gritty, free-draining soil.
Give it a sunny spot in your rockery to mimic its native dry slopes and prevent winter wet rot.
Water gently during spring growth but keep it dry once it goes dormant in the damp UK summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch the delicate emerging spring flower buds.
Divide the bulbs every three years in late summer to keep them vigorous and flowering well.

items.name: Iris gatesii
items.growersTips:
Plant this oncocyclus iris in a gritty, alkaline soil mix inside a cold greenhouse to shield it from UK rain.
Bury the rhizome shallowly, leaving the very top exposed to catch whatever rare UK summer sun we get.
Stop watering completely in summer after flowering to give the bulb its essential dry dormant bake.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, as they love the tender new growth.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under glass when the autumn wet begins.

items.name: Iris giganticaerulea
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant water iris in a heavy clay soil enriched with lots of well-rotted garden compost.
Grow this moisture-lover in shallow pond margins or a bog garden that never dries out in summer.
Position it in your sunniest south-facing spot to get those huge blue flowers in our cool climate.
Protect the shallow rhizomes with a thick layer of organic mulch before the harsh winter frosts hit.
Divide the congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep them vigorous and blooming well.

items.name: Iris glaucescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this little beauty in autumn just three inches deep in your grittiest, sharpest draining soil.
Keep it in your sunniest, most baked spot to mimic its dry Siberian home and prevent bulb rot.
Only water during dry spring spells, then let the bulb go completely dry and dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs chewing the early spring shoots by using pet-friendly wool pellets around them.
Grow them in terracotta pots to easily move them under a cold frame during our wet UK winters.

items.name: Iris gracilipes
items.growersTips:
Nestle this woodland gem in dappled shade using leafy, acidic soil that mimics a British forest.
Plant the delicate rhizomes just at the soil surface, never deep, and mulch lightly with leafmould.
Keep the soil reliably moist throughout our spring growing season, but avoid soggy winter wet.
Protect the tender emerging spring shoots from hungry slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.
Divide the congested clumps right after their late spring flowering to keep them vigorous and happy.

items.name: Iris graeberiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in very gritty, free-draining soil.
Give it a sunny, sheltered spot like a south-facing rockery to mimic its native Central Asian home.
Water it weekly during spring growth, but keep the bulb completely dry once the summer dormancy hits.
Watch out for slugs chewing the delicate pale blue flowers as they emerge in April and May.
Gently divide the clumps every three years right after flowering to keep the bulbs vigorous.

items.name: Iris graminea
items.growersTips:
Plant this plum-scented beauty in moist, well-drained soil with the rhizome tops just under the surface.
Tuck it into partial shade rather than full sun to stop the delicate grassy foliage from scorching.
Give it a generous mulch of leaf mould in autumn to mimic its native damp woodland edge habitat.
Divide overgrown clumps in late summer after flowering to keep the blooms from getting congested.
Position it near a path or in a raised bed so you can easily smell that lovely ripe plum fragrance.

items.name: Iris grant-duffii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in very sharp, free-draining gritty soil.
Give them a hot, dry summer baking by covering the soil with a pane of glass to mimic their homeland.
Water them generously during their active winter and spring growth, but keep them dry in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, as they love the tender new foliage.

items.name: Iris halophila
items.growersTips:
Plant this rhizome, not a bulb, just below the soil surface in autumn so the UK sun can bake it.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring but let it dry out a bit once flowering finishes.

Cut the faded flower stems right down to the base in July to keep the plant looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs eating the new spring shoots, especially during our wet UK April weather.

items.name: Iris hartwegii
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild beauty in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters unscathed.
Position your pots in full sun to mimic its native California heat and get those blooms popping.
Water gently during spring growth but keep the soil almost bone dry throughout the summer dormancy.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from hungry slugs using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to let the natural UK winter chill trigger spring germination.

items.name: Iris haynei
items.growersTips:
Plant your Iris haynei bulbs in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in very gritty, sharp soil.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormant phase by using a rain shelter or cold frame.
Position them in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic the hot, dry Middle Eastern hillsides.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they love chewing the emerging flower buds.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than open borders so you can easily control the moisture levels.

items.name: Iris hermona
items.growersTips:
Plant these Golan irises in the sunniest spot you have, ideally in a raised bed or a gravel garden.
Plant your bulbs in autumn about ten centimeters deep in extremely sharp-draining, gritty soil.
Stop watering completely in summer to give the bulbs the baking-hot dry rest period they crave.
Cover them with a cold frame in wet UK winters to protect the dormant bulbs from rotting in damp.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the emerging flower buds.

items.name: Iris hexagona
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes shallowly in heavy clay soil, leaving the tops exposed to catch the UK sun.
Keep their soil constantly soggy or submerged in a shallow pond margin, as they hate drying out.
Give them a thick mulch of leaf mould in late autumn to protect the crown from severe British frosts.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in July to keep the plant tidy and prevent rot.
Divide congested clumps in late summer every three years to keep them flowering beautifully.

items.name: Iris histrio
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in early autumn at a depth of ten centimetres to protect them from UK winter frosts.
Choose a gritty, free-draining soil mix to prevent the bulbs from rotting during wet British winters.
Place them in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic their native dry, bright Mediterranean home.
Protect the early January blooms from slugs and snails by scattering organic grit around the shoots.
Keep them dry in summer by planting under a wall or lifting bulbs once the foliage naturally dies back.

items.name: Iris histrioides
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs in autumn about eight to ten centimeters deep to protect them from UK frosts.
Add plenty of grit to your soil because these bulbs will rot fast in wet, heavy British winter clay.
Position them in your brightest, sunniest spot so they get baked and dry out during summer dormancy.
Watch out for hungry slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch the emerging blue buds.
Grow them in shallow terracotta pots so you can bring them close to the house to enjoy the scent.

items.name: Iris hoogiana
items.growersTips:
Plant these Regelia bulbs in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in your sunniest border.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your soil to ensure the sharp winter drainage they crave.
Cover the bed with a cloche from July to September to give them the dry summer bake they need.
Watch out for slugs eating the delicate new shoots as they emerge during mild UK spring weather.
Grow them alongside low-growing thymes which won't shade them but will help absorb excess moisture.

items.name: Iris hookeri
items.growersTips:
Plant this little beauty in autumn about eight to ten centimeters deep in gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep it happy in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its coastal home.
Water well during spring growth, but let the soil dry out completely over the damp UK summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging shoots.
Tuck some grit right around the crown to prevent winter rot in our wet British weather.

items.name: Iris hookeriana
items.growersTips:
Plant this little Himalayan beauty about five centimeters deep in grit-heavy, free-draining soil.
Keep it quite dry during its winter dormancy to prevent the bulb from rotting in wet UK clay.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot you have to mimic its bright, native alpine slopes.
Watch out for slugs and snails during the damp British spring when the fresh shoots first emerge.
Feed it with a high-potash liquid fertilizer just after flowering to help next year's bulb develop.

items.name: Iris humilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this little bulb just three inches deep in late autumn so it can chill over the UK winter.
Mix lots of grit into your soil because this alpine beauty will rot quickly in wet UK winter clay.
Put it in your sunniest rock garden or a raised bed to mimic its dry, native rocky hillsides.
Keep watering to a minimum once the leaves die back to give the bulbs a dry summer rest period.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they love to munch the delicate yellow flowers as they emerge.

items.name: Iris iberica
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate Turkish native in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to survive wet UK winters.
Keep the bulb completely dry during its summer dormant phase by using a cloche or cold frame.
Set the bulb just below the soil surface, about two inches deep, in your sunniest south-facing spot.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the emerging exotic blooms.
Mix lots of horticultural grit and limestone chippings into your soil to mimic its mountain home.

items.name: Iris imbricata
items.growersTips:
Plant this rhizome, not a bulb, just at the soil surface so the UK summer sun can bake it dry.
Give it sharp drainage by mixing plenty of grit into your heavy UK clay soil to prevent winter rot.
Water it only during dry spring active growth, then leave it dry once the yellow flowers fade.
Cut the fan of leaves back into a neat V-shape in autumn to stop wind rock and clear away pests.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots and divide the clumps every three years in midsummer.

items.name: Iris innominata
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen rhizome, not a bulb, shallowly with the top just showing in acid, peaty soil.
Position your iris in dappled shade under a deciduous shrub to mimic its native woodland edge.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil acidic and damp during dry UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to feast on the tender new grassy foliage.
Divide established clumps in early autumn after flowering to help them settle before winter frosts.

items.name: Iris japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant this shallowly with its rhizomes just showing, as deep planting stops it flowering in the UK.
Give it a spot in partial shade under deciduous trees to protect its delicate winter-green foliage.
Water it weekly during dry spring spells, but let the soil dry out a bit throughout the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, as they love to munch on the fresh new flower buds.
Divide the congested clumps every three years right after flowering in June to keep them vigorous.

items.name: Iris juncea
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten to fifteen centimetres in your sunniest border spot.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp winter drainage this Mediterranean native needs.
Keep the soil damp during spring growth but let them bake completely dry once summer dormancy starts.
Protect the emerging winter foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or pet-friendly pellets.
Grow them in terracotta pots if your UK garden has heavy clay so you can move them out of wet weather.

items.name: Iris junonia
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Turkish bulb five inches deep in autumn in a gritty, sharply draining UK soil mix.
Give it a hot, dry summer baking by placing it near a south-facing brick wall to mimic its home.
Water well during its active spring growth, but keep it completely dry once the foliage dies back.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the emerging spring shoots during damp British April days.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it under glass to escape relentless winter rain.

items.name: Iris kashmiriana
items.growersTips:
Plant this bearded iris in your sunniest UK spot with the top of the rhizome exposed to bake in summer.
Give it sharp-draining, alkaline to neutral soil to prevent winter rot in wet British weather.
Divide the rhizomes every three years in late summer just after flowering to keep them blooming well.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs as they love to feast on the fresh new shoots.
Cut the faded flower stems down to the base in July but leave the fan of leaves to gather energy.

items.name: Iris kemaonensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf Himalayan iris in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position the bulbs in a sunny rock garden or raised bed so they get baked by the summer sun.
Water them moderately during active spring growth but keep them almost dry during winter dormancy.
Protect the early spring blooms from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide the congested clumps right after flowering in late spring to keep the plants vigorous.

items.name: Iris kolpakowskiana
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight to ten centimeters in very gritty, sharp soil.
Keep them bone dry in summer by covering them or lifting them once the foliage naturally dies back.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate early blooms from UK rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in February when the gorgeous purple flowers first start to emerge.
Feed them with a high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the leaves begin to push up in late winter.

items.name: Iris korolkowii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in your sunniest, sharp-draining spot.
Mix plenty of grit and horticultural sand into your soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK weather.
Keep them dry during their summer dormant phase by covering them or lifting them after flowering.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love the tender emerging foliage.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame during heavy rain.

items.name: Iris lactea
items.growersTips:
Plant your lactea rhizomes just below the soil surface in autumn, keeping the very tops exposed.
Position them in your sunniest south-facing border to ensure they get the summer bake they need.
Water young plants weekly during dry spring spells, but let established clumps dry out in summer.
Cut back the faded foliage to the ground in late autumn to prevent slugs harboring in the clumps.
Divide congested clumps every four years in late summer right after their flowering period ends.

items.name: Iris lacustris
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny beauty in gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its native Great Lakes limestone home.
Keep the shallow, creeping rhizomes just visible at the soil surface rather than burying them.
Grow it in a container or alpine trough to protect it from rampant UK weeds and damp winter rot.
Position your pot in dappled shade as our strong afternoon summer sun can easily scorch the leaves.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the delicate emerging buds.

items.name: Iris laevigata
items.growersTips:
Grow in heavy clay or boggy soil at a planting depth of up to fifteen centimetres of standing water.
Position in full sun to ensure reliable flowering during the typical British midsummer wet season.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomes, not bulbs, in late summer after the flowering period has ended.
Cut back dead foliage to the ground in autumn to prevent rot in damp UK winter conditions.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris to create a vibrant colour contrast in pond margins.

items.name: Iris latifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in a spot that gets full UK sun.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure excellent drainage so the bulbs do not rot in winter.
Water them well during their spring growing phase but let the soil dry out completely in summer.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the fresh young shoots as they emerge in early spring.

items.name: Iris lazica
items.growersTips:
Plant this shade-lover in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, unlike its sun-worsor cousin unguicularis.
Keep the rhizome nestled just at the soil surface, not buried deep, so the cool UK sun can reach it.
Tidy up the evergreen foliage in late spring by snipping away any tatty, winter-damaged leaf tips.
Watch out for sneaky snails hiding in the dense clumps, as they love to chew the winter blooms.
Grow it alongside snowdrops or hellebores to create a gorgeous, damp-loving winter woodland display.

items.name: Iris lineata
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in very gritty, free-draining soil.
Give them a hot, dry summer dormant period by covering the soil with a cloche to mimic Kabul.
Water them only during their active spring growth, then stop completely once the foliage dies back.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate blooms from heavy UK rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to eat the emerging flower shoots.

items.name: Iris longipetala
items.growersTips:
Plant this moist-loving iris in heavy clay or boggy soil that stays damp even through dry UK summers.
Bury the rhizomes just below the soil surface in autumn, keeping them shallower than true bulbs.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet spring days as they love chewing the fresh new foliage.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer but leave the semi-evergreen leaves to overwinter.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn every four years to keep your blooms vigorous and healthy.

items.name: Iris lortetii
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate Oncocyclus iris in a gritty, free-draining raised bed or an unheated greenhouse.
Plant the rhizomes shallowly in late summer so the top of the rootstock is fully baked by the sun.
Keep them bone dry from July to October to mimic their native Middle Eastern summer dormancy period.
Water very sparingly only during their active winter and spring growth to prevent root rot.
Protect the early spring blooms from heavy UK rain by using a temporary cloche or cold frame.

items.name: Iris lutescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf iris in late summer just beneath the soil surface so the rhizome gets baked by sun.
Keep them in gritty, sharply draining soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Water them only during dry spring active growth, then let them dry out completely over the summer.
Divide the congested clumps every three years right after flowering in July to keep them blooming.
Watch out for slugs eating the early spring buds, so protect them with grit barriers in February.

items.name: Iris maackii
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-loving iris in damp, boggy soil near your pond edge or in a heavy clay border.
Set the creeping rhizomes just at the soil surface rather than burying them deep like true bulbs.
Give them full sun to partial shade to mimic their native Siberian wetlands in your UK garden.
Divide congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep them vigorous and blooming well.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the fresh spring shoots as they emerge in damp UK weather.

items.name: Iris macrosiphon
items.growersTips:
Plant this native beauty in very well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Place your iris in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural woodland home.
Keep the soil damp during spring growth but let it dry out completely during the summer dormant phase.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the tender new emerging foliage.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomes, not bulbs, in late summer after the flowering has finished.

items.name: Iris magnifica
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb deeply at fifteen centimeters in well-drained, gritty soil to support its tall stem.
Give it a warm, south-facing spot by a wall to mimic its native dry Central Asian summer bake.
Water it weekly during spring growth but keep the bulb completely dry once the foliage dies back.
Watch out for slugs early in spring as they love to feast on the emerging fleshy leek-like shoots.
Leave the fading leaves alone until they are fully yellow and papery before gently pulling them away.

items.name: Iris maracandica
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny bulbs in autumn about five centimeters deep in extremely sharp-draining gritty soil.
Keep them bone dry during their summer dormant phase by covering them or lifting them into a greenhouse.
Grow them in a cold frame or alpine house to protect the delicate early spring blooms from UK rain.
Water them very sparingly only when active growth starts in late winter, never let the bulbs sit wet.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the emerging shoots during damp February nights.

items.name: Iris mariae
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert iris in a pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet British winters.
Keep the pot completely dry under glass from July to September to mimic its natural summer baking.
Water it sparingly only from October to April when you see active green growth appearing.
Place the container on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or in a very bright cold greenhouse.
Watch out for aphids in spring and gently wipe them off to prevent viruses from ruining the blooms.

items.name: Iris marsica
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Italian wild iris in autumn at a depth of about ten centimeters in well-drained soil.
Choose your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic its warm native Apennine mountain habitat.
Add plenty of grit to your planting hole to prevent winter waterlogging in wet UK clay soils.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love to feast on the fresh shoots.
Let the foliage die back naturally in late summer so the bulb can store energy for next spring.

items.name: Iris masia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Turkish native in your sunniest UK spot using sharp sand to guarantee dry winter roots.
Bury these small bulbs about eight centimetres deep in autumn, pointing the growing tips upwards.
Keep soil barely damp during summer dormancy to mimic its dry, baked Middle Eastern home climate.
Surround your bulbs with low-growing sedums to keep the soil structure open and prevent waterlogging.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as the delicate purple-blue petals begin to emerge from the soil.

items.name: Iris meda
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate Iranian native in a raised bed with sharp grit to survive wet UK winters.
Set the bulbs five centimetres deep in late autumn, ensuring the point faces directly upwards.
Keep them bone dry during their summer dormant phase by covering the soil with a cloche or pane.
Grow them in a terracotta pot so you can easily move them under glass when heavy autumn rain hits.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as the fine, grassy foliage first begins to push through.

items.name: Iris mesopotamica
items.growersTips:
Plant your rhizomes shallowly in late summer so the top sits exposed to the baking UK sunshine.
Slightly slope your planting bed to ensure winter wet drains away from the roots to prevent rot.
Mix plenty of coarse grit and organic matter into heavy clay soil to mimic dry Mediterranean hills.
Divide the congested clumps every three years right after summer flowering to keep them blooming.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from hungry snails using pet-safe organic iron phosphate pellets.

items.name: Iris milesii
items.growersTips:
Plant this deciduous rhizome, not a bulb, just at the soil surface so the UK sun can bake it.
Give it moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking its natural Himalayan forest home.
Protect the fresh spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Divide the congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep the blooms coming every year.
Mulch the crown heavily in late autumn to protect it from wet, freezing British winter rot.

items.name: Iris minutoaurea
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny gem just below the soil surface in a gritty, free-draining raised bed or alpine pot.
Keep the soil moist during spring growth but let it dry out during its summer dormant period.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they can easily devour the tiny emerging flower buds.
Divide the congested clumps in late summer right after the foliage dies back to boost flowering.
Grow it alongside miniature narcissi or thymes in a stone trough to prevent it being smothered.

items.name: Iris missouriensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild iris in a boggy spot that dries out completely in late summer to mimic its home.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors during autumn so the cold UK winter naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep the soil damp during spring growth but stop watering entirely once the foliage dies back.
Give it a position in full sun to get the best purple blooms in our cool British climate.
Watch out for slugs on the fresh spring shoots by using beer traps or organic grit barriers.

items.name: Iris munzii
items.growersTips:
Keep this tender Californian in a cold greenhouse to shield its winter foliage from harsh UK frosts.
Plant the rhizomes, not bulbs, shallowly in very gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Give it a hot, dry summer baking from July to September by withholding all water during dormancy.
Feed weekly with a high-potash liquid seaweed once active growth starts in the chilly spring.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Iris nigricans
items.growersTips:
Plant your black iris bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in a warm, south-facing spot.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this dry-loving bulb absolutely needs.
Water them only during active spring growth, then keep the soil bone dry throughout summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs in damp UK springs, as they love to feast on the emerging dark purple buds.
Protect the bulbs from winter wet with a cloche or grow them in terracotta pots you can move indoors.

items.name: Iris notha
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in a spot that gets full UK sun.
Keep the soil damp during spring growth but let them dry out completely once summer dormancy hits.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure sharp drainage, as damp winter clay will rot them.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the fresh spring shoots, so use pet-safe barriers early on.
Leave the foliage alone after flowering until it turns yellow so the bulb can store energy.

items.name: Iris orchioides
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in a gritty, free-draining sunny spot.
Keep them dry during their summer dormancy to prevent the bulbs from rotting in wet UK soil.
Grow them in a raised bed or alpine house to protect the delicate spring blooms from heavy rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to feast on the emerging shoots.
Feed them with a high-potash fertiliser just as the flowers fade to help next year's bulbs grow.

items.name: Iris orientalis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Turkish iris bulbs in autumn about ten centimetres deep in moist, well-draining soil.
Give them a generous watering during dry spring spells to help those tall flower stems develop.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in July to keep the clump looking neat and tidy.
Watch out for slugs nibbling the fresh spring shoots by using pet-safe organic wool pellets.
Divide congested clumps every four years in late summer to keep your blooms big and beautiful.

items.name: Iris orjenii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Orjen iris in well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Keep the bulb tip just peeping out of the soil surface when planting in your sunny borders.
Water sparingly during summer dormancy to mimic its native dry Balkan mountain habitat.
Protect the early spring shoots from slugs using grit barriers or beer traps in damp UK weather.
Plant alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to keep the soil surface cool and weed-free.

items.name: Iris pallida
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes shallowly in late summer so the baking UK sun can ripen them for next year.
Give them a spot in your garden with sharp drainage, adding grit to heavy clay to prevent winter rot.
Cut the elegant grey-green foliage back into a neat fan shape in autumn to stop wind rock in storms.
Watch out for iris sawfly larvae in spring and squish them before they ruin the beautiful blooms.
Divide the congested clumps every three years right after flowering to keep them blooming strongly.

items.name: Iris paradoxa
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb in early autumn at a depth of about ten centimetres in your sunniest border.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this dry-loving species craves.
Keep the soil completely dry during its summer dormant phase to prevent the bulb from rotting.
Protect the early spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.
Grow this delicate beauty in a terracotta pot so you can move it under cover during wet winters.

items.name: Iris petrana
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert iris in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy, sharp-draining compost to mimic Jordan.
Keep the bulb completely dry during its summer dormancy by moving the pot into a sunny greenhouse.
Water only from autumn to spring when you see active growth, letting the soil dry out between drinks.
Position the pot in your sunniest, south-facing spot to give it the intense light it craves.
Watch out for slugs on the tender new spring shoots, using organic wool pellets around the pot rim.

items.name: Iris planifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in early autumn about five centimeters deep in extremely sharp-draining gritty soil.
Keep them bone dry during their summer dormant phase by covering them or lifting them into a greenhouse.
Grow them in terracotta pots to easily move them under cover and protect flowers from harsh UK rain.
Position your pots in the absolute sunniest spot you have to mimic their hot Mediterranean home.
Watch out for slugs and snails in mild winter wet spells as they love chewing the emerging shoots.

items.name: Iris pontica
items.growersTips:
Plant this little bulb five centimetres deep in autumn so it gets the cold winter chill it needs.
Give it sharply draining gritty soil to stop the bulb rotting in our wet British winters.
Keep it damp during spring growth but let it bake in dry soil once the leaves die back in summer.
Watch out for slugs chewing the delicate spring blooms by using gravel mulch around the base.
Grow it in a container or rock garden so this tiny treasure does not get lost under bigger plants.

items.name: Iris potaninii
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny dwarf iris in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Tuck the bulbs just two inches deep in a sunny rock garden or a raised bed to mimic its alpine home.
Water sparingly in summer as this little beauty prefers a dry, baked dormancy after it finishes blooming.
Protect the early spring buds from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic grit barriers.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame during relentless winter rain.

items.name: Iris prismatica
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in acidic, boggy soil near your pond or in a damp border that never dries out.
Position your plant in full sun to partial shade to mimic its native damp meadow habitat in the UK.
Unlike typical garden irises, this species grows from slender rhizomes, not bulbs, so plant them shallowly.
Mulch with leaf mould in autumn to keep the soil acidic and protect the roots from harsh UK frosts.
Divide congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep them vigorous and propagate new plants.

items.name: Iris pseudacorus
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly with the tops exposed to the sun in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil.
Position at the margins of a garden pond up to twenty centimeters deep to control its vigorous spread.
Cut the foliage back to the ground in autumn to prevent rotting leaves from polluting pond water.
Divide congested clumps in late summer using a sharp spade to maintain vigor and control size.
Wear thick gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from the toxic sap of this native plant.

items.name: Iris pseudocaucasica
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in a very sharply draining grit mix.
Give it a hot, dry summer dormancy by covering the soil with a cloche to mimic its native climate.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot possible to help the bulb bake and trigger next spring's bloom.
Water sparingly in winter, only keeping the soil barely damp to prevent the bulb from rotting.
Grow this delicate beauty in a container so you can easily move it shelter when heavy UK rain hits.

items.name: Iris pseudopallida
items.growersTips:
Plant this rhizome shallowly in late summer so the top sits just proud of your well-drained UK soil.
Give it a sunny, south-facing spot to bake the rhizomes, mimicking its native dry Balkan cliffs.
Water sparingly once established, only drenching during prolonged, unusually dry British summers.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base in July to keep the fan of foliage looking tidy.
Watch out for slugs in damp spring weather, as they love to chew the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Iris pseudopumila
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny Mediterranean bulbs about eight centimetres deep in autumn so they survive UK frost.
Give them a gritty, sharply draining soil mix because wet winter clay will rot their bulbs fast.
Keep them in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic their native hot Sicilian hillsides.
Water them weekly during their spring growing phase but keep them bone dry throughout summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs eating the delicate early spring blooms, so protect them with grit barriers.

items.name: Iris pumila
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer with the tops exposed to the UK sun to ensure next springs bloom
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rhizome rot during wet British winters and springs
Place in full south-facing sun to mimic their native dry hillsides and prevent shade-induced failure
Divide congested clumps every three years in July after flowering to maintain vigor and flower yield
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the low-growing early buds

items.name: Iris purdyi
items.growersTips:
Plant these woodland gems in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native canopy.
Add plenty of grit and leaf mould to your soil to ensure the perfect free-draining, acidic mix.
Water them gently during dry summer spells but keep them relatively dry throughout our wet winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the delicate new shoots.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to help the rhizome build energy for winter.

items.name: Iris regis-uzziae
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare desert bulb five centimetres deep in autumn, using a terracotta pot to control water.
Give it a sharp, gritty compost mix with plenty of horticultural sand to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it completely bone-dry during its summer dormancy by moving the pot under a greenhouse pane.
Water very sparingly from November to March, only when the top few centimetres of grit feel dry.
Watch out for slugs chewing the delicate pale blue winter blooms during damp January spells.

items.name: Iris reichenbachii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Balkan native in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position your iris in full sun, ideally in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its mountain home.
Bury the rhizomes shallowly, leaving the tops exposed to the UK sun to bake and trigger blooms.
Water sparingly during summer dormancy, only giving a splash if the soil becomes bone dry.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they love to munch on the emerging delicate flower buds.

items.name: Iris reticulata
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres to protect them from severe UK winter frosts.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to prevent bulb rot during wet British autumn and winter months.
Apply a high-potash liquid feed after flowering to help the bulbs build energy for next spring.
Plant alongside low-growing sedums to cover the untidy, dying foliage as it yellows in late spring.
Grow in terracotta pots to easily move them under cover and keep them dry during summer dormancy.

items.name: Iris robusta
items.growersTips:
Plant your Iris robusta rhizomes, not bulbs, shallowly in heavy, wet UK clay soil by a pond edge.
Divide congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep them blooming well in British gardens.
Keep the soil consistently damp or boggy, as this hybrid absolutely thrives with wet feet year-round.
Cut the dead foliage back to the ground in autumn to prevent pests like slugs overwintering in them.
Grow them alongside moisture-loving marsh marigolds to create a stunning spring colour contrast.

items.name: Iris rosenbachiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this winter-hardy bulb five inches deep in gritty, free-draining soil to survive UK wetness.
Keep it bone-dry in summer by sheltering the pot in a greenhouse or cold frame during dormancy.
Give it a sunny, south-facing spot in a raised bed or rockery to catch the weak early spring sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails in February when the delicate, colorful shoots first push through.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertilizer just as the flowers fade to build up next year's bulb.

items.name: Iris rossii
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland gem in moist, well-drained, acidic soil under the dappled shade of deciduous trees.
Set the delicate rhizomes just below the soil surface, about two inches deep, in early autumn.
Keep the soil consistently damp during spring growth, but let it dry out slightly over the summer.
Protect the tender spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in winter to mimic its native forest floor and keep roots cool.

items.name: Iris ruthenica
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes just below the surface in gritty, well-drained soil to prevent winter wet rot.
Give them a sunny spot in your rockery or border edge to mimic their native dry grassland home.
Water weekly during dry spring spells, but let the soil dry out completely over the damp UK winter.
Tuck some grit right around the crown to shield the base from slugs and snails during wet springs.
Divide the congested clumps right after their late spring flowering to keep them blooming happily.

items.name: Iris sambucina
items.growersTips:
Plant this elder-scented iris in late summer, keeping the rhizome top exposed to the warm UK sun.
Give it sharp drainage by mixing plenty of grit into your heavy UK clay soil before planting.
Water newly planted rhizomes weekly in dry spells, but let established clumps survive on rain alone.
Divide your congested clumps every three years in July to keep the purple and yellow blooms coming.
Watch out for slugs on tender spring shoots, using beer traps to protect the emerging foliage.

items.name: Iris sanguinea
items.growersTips:
Plant your Iris sanguinea rhizomes shallowly in autumn, leaving the very tops exposed to UK sun.
Keep the soil consistently damp during our dry spring spells to ensure those blue blooms pop.
Divide your crowded clumps every three years right after flowering in July to keep them vigorous.
Mix plenty of compost into your soil to keep it acidic and moisture-retentive, just how they like.
Watch out for slugs on tender new spring shoots, especially during our damp British April nights.

items.name: Iris sari
items.growersTips:
Plant this Turkish beauty in late summer, burying the rhizome shallowly with its top exposed to sun.
Keep it bone dry during its summer dormancy by using a rain shelter or cloche to mimic its homeland.
Pot it up in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to munch on the emerging flower buds.
Give it a high-potash feed just as active growth starts in spring to boost those exotic blooms.

items.name: Iris scariosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this dry-land beauty in a raised bed or gravel garden to survive wet UK winters.
Mix lots of grit and horticultural sand into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage it craves.
Water very sparingly in summer, mimicking its native dry steppe climate during its dormant phase.
Protect the rhizomes from slugs and snails in spring when the delicate new shoots first emerge.
Place it in your sunniest, south-facing spot to get the baking heat it needs to flower next spring.

items.name: Iris schelkownikowii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare bulb 10cm deep in late autumn in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to avoid rot.
Stop watering completely from July to September to give the bulb the hot, dry summer dormancy it needs.
Grow it in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate spring blooms from UK rain.
Add plenty of horticultural grit and limestone chippings to your compost to mimic its wild soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to eat the emerging flower buds.

items.name: Iris ser. Californicae
items.growersTips:
Plant these in acidic to neutral soil as they absolutely hate lime and will yellow in alkaline beds.
Move or plant them only in autumn when you see new white roots active, never during summer dormancy.
Water them with stored rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH nice and low in your garden.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they love ruining the fresh foliage.
Mulch with leaf mould or pine needles annually to mimic their native woodland edge habitat perfectly.

items.name: Iris ser. Hexagonae
items.growersTips:
Plant these Louisiana irises in a sunny, damp spot or pond edge, keeping the rhizomes near the surface.
Water them generously during dry UK summers to mimic their native wetlands and ensure rich blooms.
Mulch heavily in late autumn with organic matter to protect the shallow root systems from hard frosts.
Feed them in early spring with an acid-loving fertiliser to suit their preference for low pH soils.
Divide overcrowded clumps in late summer every three years to keep them vigorous and flowering well.

items.name: Iris ser. Laevigatae
items.growersTips:
Plant these moisture-lovers in heavy, acidic clay soil or right at the edge of your garden pond.
Keep their crowns submerged under shallow water up to ten centimetres deep during the UK spring.
Plant the rhizomes, not bulbs, just below the soil surface in a sunny spot to bake in summer.
Divide your clumps every three years in late summer after flowering to keep them blooming well.
Watch out for water snails eating the young leaves and handpick them off on damp spring mornings.

items.name: Iris ser. Longipetalae
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes, not bulbs, just below the soil surface in autumn so the UK rain settles them.
Give them heavy clay soil that stays damp in winter but drains well enough to dry out in summer.
Water them deeply during dry spring spells to ensure you get those beautiful blue-veined blooms.
Cut the dying foliage right back to the ground in late autumn to prevent any overwintering pests.
Divide congested clumps every four years in late summer to keep your plants flowering vigorously.

items.name: Iris ser. Ruthenicae
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes, not bulbs, just below the soil surface in gritty, well-drained neutral loam.
Give them a sunny rock garden spot or a raised bed to mimic their native dry, alpine conditions.
Water gently during dry spring spells but keep them relatively dry throughout the damp UK winter.
Divide the congested clumps right after their late spring flowering to keep them blooming well.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK weather, as they love to feast on the delicate new shoots.

items.name: Iris ser. Sibiricae
items.growersTips:
Plant these bareroot in moist, acidic to neutral soil during mild autumn days so roots settle early.
Keep them well-watered during dry May spells to ensure your early summer blooms really stretch out.
Cut the faded foliage back to the ground in late autumn to prevent pests overwintering in the clump.
Divide congested clumps every three years in late summer to keep their flowering vigor at its peak.
Mulch them annually with damp leafmould in March to lock in the moisture their fibrous roots crave.

items.name: Iris ser. Spuriae
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes shallowly with their tops just showing in heavy clay soil that retains moisture.
Water them deeply during their spring growth spurt but let them dry out completely over the summer.
Cut the dying foliage right back to the ground in autumn to stop slugs overwintering in the clumps.
Give them a mulch of well-rotted manure in late winter but keep it clear of the central growing tip.
Leave them undisturbed for years as they hate being moved and take ages to settle back in to bloom.

items.name: Iris ser. Syriacae
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of three times their height in your sunniest, warmest spot.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage they need to survive wet UK winters.
Let them bake in dry soil after summer flowering to mimic their native Middle Eastern climate.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs as they love to devour the emerging shoots.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under cover to shelter from winter rain.

items.name: Iris ser. Tripetalae
items.growersTips:
Plant these beauties in damp, acidic soil near your pond edge where they can soak up the UK rain.
Bury the rhizomes just below the surface in autumn, keeping them shallower than true bulb species.
Watch out for slugs in mild, wet British springs as they love to feast on the emerging new shoots.
Divide the congested clumps right after summer flowering to keep them vigorous and blooming well.
Grow them alongside moisture-loving ferns or primulas for a gorgeous, natural bog garden display.

items.name: Iris serotina
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-summer beauty 10cm deep in your sunniest, most baking-hot border to mimic Spain.
Keep the soil bone-dry during winter by using a rain shelter or planting in a very gritty raised bed.
Give it a weekly drenching in late spring to mimic Mediterranean rains and trigger strong growth.
Look out for slugs devouring the emerging flower spikes in August, as they bloom later than others.
Surround it with low-growing thyme to keep the soil warm and prevent weeds from shading the bulb.

items.name: Iris setosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in boggy soil or pond edges where its roots never dry out in UK summers.
Set the rhizomes shallowly just at the soil surface rather than burying them deep like Dutch bulbs.
Divide overcrowded clumps in late summer after flowering to keep them blooming well year after year.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, especially in damp British weather.
Pair them with marsh marigolds or astilbes for a gorgeous, damp-loving UK garden display.

items.name: Iris sibirica
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes just below the soil surface in autumn, keeping them moist but well-drained.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to ensure robust flowering in the UK's early summer.
Cut the foliage back to the ground in late autumn after it turns yellow to prevent pests.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early autumn to maintain plant vigour.
Grow in moisture-retentive, slightly acidic soil alongside primulas or astilbes in damp borders.

items.name: Iris sintenisii
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen iris in a spot that gets full sun to help the purple flowers pop in June.
Tuck the rhizomes, not bulbs, just below the soil surface in well-drained, neutral to acid loam.
Give it a good soak during dry spring spells, but keep it fairly dry once winter dormancy hits.
Cut back the tough, grassy foliage right to the ground in early spring to tidy up the clump.
