Watch out for slugs chewing the delicate new flower buds as they emerge from the grassy leaves.

items.name: Iris songarica
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare iris in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot of your patio to mimic its native hot, dry Asian summers.
Give it a deep drenching during spring growth, then keep it bone dry once summer dormancy sets in.
Protect the emerging spring foliage from slugs using beer traps, as damp UK weather brings them out.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural winter chill triggers spring germination.

items.name: Iris speculatrix
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare evergreen iris in a sheltered, warm spot with dappled shade to mimic its woodland home.
Use a gritty, humus-rich soil mix that stays moist in summer but drains fast to prevent winter rot.
Protect the delicate foliage from harsh frosts using a cloche or dry winter mulch in colder UK areas.
Keep watering consistently through spring and summer, but let the soil dry out more during winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the emerging flower spikes.

items.name: Iris sprengeri
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Turkish beauty in early autumn about 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under glass to stay bone-dry during summer dormancy.
Keep it in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic the hot, dry Asiatic hillsides it loves.
Water weekly during active spring growth, but stop completely once the foliage starts to die back.
Watch out for slugs in damp UK springs, as they easily ruin the delicate, veined flowers.

items.name: Iris spuria
items.growersTips:
Plant your spuria rhizomes shallowly with the tops just showing to catch the weak UK autumn sun.
Give them a deep weekly soak during their spring growing phase, then let them dry out in summer.
Cut the dead foliage right back to the ground in autumn to stop slugs overwintering in the clumps.
Prepare your soil with plenty of well-rotted manure to keep these heavy feeders happy for years.
Divide your clumps in late summer only when flowering drops, as they hate being moved too often.

items.name: Iris stenophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in very sharp, free-draining soil.
Keep them under a cold frame or alpine house in winter to protect them from excessive UK wetness.
Give them a dry summer rest by baking the bulbs in dry compost under glass after the leaves die back.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate blue flowers first push through.
Grow them alongside dwarf narcissi or crocus in pots of gritty compost for a stunning spring show.

items.name: Iris stolonifera
items.growersTips:
Plant these rhizomes, not bulbs, just two inches deep in very sandy, free-draining soil in full sun.
Give them a dry summer rest by covering the soil with a cloche to mimic their native desert climate.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under cover when the autumn rains start.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as those fresh, emerging shoots are an absolute magnet for them.
Feed them with a high-potash tomato food in spring to encourage those spectacular striped blooms.

items.name: Iris suaveolens
items.growersTips:
Plant this little beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to stop winter wet from rotting its rhizome.
Position your pot in full sun on a south-facing patio to mimic its sunny Balkan mountain home.
Plant the rhizome shallowly, leaving the very top exposed to the UK sun to bake and form next blooms.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs, as they love to munch the delicate dwarf buds.
Divide the congested clumps right after summer flowering to keep them vigorous and blooming well.

items.name: Iris subbiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this Iberian native in your sunniest UK spot, keeping the rhizome top exposed to bake in summer.
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil, as wet winter clay will quickly rot these Mediterranean bulbs.
Water sparingly once established, only giving them a drink during prolonged, dry UK spring spells.
Cut back the fan of leaves by half in autumn to stop strong UK winds rocking and loosening the roots.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs, as they love to munch the emerging flower buds.

items.name: Iris subg. Hermodactyloides
items.growersTips:
Plant these little bulbs in autumn at about ten centimetres deep in gritty, sharply draining soil.
Position them in your sunniest south-facing border or a gravel garden to bake the bulbs in summer.
Avoid watering them at all during their summer dormancy to prevent the bulbs from rotting underground.
Watch out for slugs eating the delicate early spring blooms, especially during wet UK Februarys.
Grow them in terracotta pots if your garden has heavy clay, using a mix of half grit and half compost.

items.name: Iris subg. Iris
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs in autumn about ten centimetres deep in a spot that gets plenty of warm UK sunshine.
Make sure your soil drains really well by mixing in lots of grit to prevent winter bulb rot.
Once they finish flowering in spring, let the foliage die back naturally to feed next year's blooms.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who just love to feast on the emerging fresh spring shoots.
Grow them alongside shallow-rooted annuals like forget-me-nots so they do not compete for nutrients.

items.name: Iris subg. Limniris
items.growersTips:
Plant your rhizomes shallowly with their tops exposed to the UK sun to bake and trigger next blooms.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during our dry spring spells.
Divide your crowded clumps every three years in late summer right after they finish flowering.
Cut the foliage down to a neat V-shape in autumn to prevent wind rock and tidy up the borders.
Watch out for slugs and snails on new spring shoots, using organic grit barriers to deter them.

items.name: Iris subg. Scorpiris
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in your sunniest, most sheltered border.
Add plenty of horticultural grit to your soil to ensure the sharp winter drainage they absolutely need.
Keep them dry during their summer dormant phase by covering the spot with a cloche if it rains heavily.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to chew the emerging fleshy leaf fans.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering so the bulb can store energy for next year.

items.name: Iris subg. Xiphium
items.growersTips:
Plant your Dutch iris bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres to protect them from UK frosts.
Choose a baking hot, south-facing spot with sharp drainage so the bulbs do not rot in wet winters.
Feed them with a high-potash tomato fertiliser weekly once the first green flower buds appear.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in July to feed the bulb for next spring.
Watch out for slugs eating the emerging spring shoots and use organic wool pellets to stop them.

items.name: Iris susiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mourning Iris bulb in autumn about ten centimeters deep in sharp sand for sharp drainage.
Keep it bone dry in summer by covering with a cloche or lifting the bulb after foliage dies back.
Grow this delicate beauty in a terracotta pot so you can move it under glass during wet UK winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love devouring the emerging flower buds.
Feed with a high-potash fertilizer in spring to help those huge, dark, dramatic blooms develop.

items.name: Iris tectorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this roof iris shallowly with the top of the rhizome just visible above the soil surface.
Give it a spot in light dappled shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat in UK gardens.
Water regularly during the spring growing season but keep it much drier throughout the damp winter.
Protect the lush fan-shaped leaves from slugs and snails which absolutely love the tender new growth.
Divide the congested clumps every three years right after flowering in midsummer to keep them happy.

items.name: Iris tenax
items.growersTips:
Plant this native of woodland edges in acidic to neutral soil, as it hates lime and chalky beds.
Unlike most irises, this species grows from tough fibrous roots, so do not bury any fleshy bulbs.
Sow your seeds in autumn in cold frames to let the British winter chill naturally break dormancy.
Keep the soil moist during spring growth but let it dry out a bit once summer flowering finishes.
Divide established clumps in early autumn, taking care to protect the delicate, sensitive roots.

items.name: Iris tenuifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight centimetres in very sharply draining gritty soil.
Keep them dry during their summer dormant phase by covering the soil or planting under a house eve.
Grow them in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native dry, sunny Asian steppe climate.
Protect the early spring blooms from slugs and snails using beer traps or pet-friendly grit barriers.
Pair them with low-growing thymes or sedums that won't overcrowd them or compete for precious light.

items.name: Iris tenuissima
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate woodland iris in dappled shade, mimicking its native open pine forest canopy.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into your soil to keep it acidic, moist, yet sharply drained.
Sow fresh seeds in cold frames during autumn to let natural UK winter chills trigger germination.
Water gently throughout the active spring growing phase but keep the soil drier during the summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love to munch the tender new shoots.

items.name: Iris tigridia
items.growersTips:
Plant these tiny bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn using a very gritty, free-draining soil mix.
Keep them in a cold frame over wet UK winters to protect the dormant bulbs from rotting in damp soil.
Water them weekly during their spring growing phase but stop completely once the foliage dies back.
Grow them in terracotta pots alongside dwarf sedums to easily manage their strict dry summer needs.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to eat the emerging flower buds.

items.name: Iris tingitana
items.growersTips:
Plant these Moroccan beauties extra deep, about fifteen centimetres down, to protect them from frost.
Give them your baked, south-facing border in gravelly soil so the bulbs get the summer bake they need.
Keep them dry during their summer dormancy, as wet UK summers will easily rot the resting bulbs.
Watch out for slugs chewing the early spring shoots, and use copper tape or grit to protect them.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them under a cold glass frame for winter shelter.

items.name: Iris typhifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in well-drained, gritty, neutral soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist during their spring growing season but dry during winter dormancy.
Position them in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native dry, bright summer habitat.
Snip off the faded flower stems in July right at the base to stop them wasting energy on seeds.
Watch out for slugs on the fresh spring shoots, using beer traps or organic pellets to save them.

items.name: Iris unguicularis
items.growersTips:
Plant this winter-flowering beauty shallowly with its rhizomes baked by the sun against a south wall.
Cut back the untidy old foliage in October to let the winter sun reach and open the hidden buds.
Keep them in poor, sharply drained alkaline soil; too much rich compost actually stops them flowering.
Watch out for snails hiding in the dense clumps of leaves, as they love to chew the emerging buds.
Divide congested clumps in spring just after flowering to keep them vigorous and blooming well.

items.name: Iris uniflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this little gem just two inches deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet winters.
Give it a sunny, sheltered rock garden spot to mimic its native dry, sunny Asian hillside home.
Water sparingly only during spring growth, then leave it completely dry during its summer dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, as they love to munch the delicate new shoots.
Divide the congested clumps right after its late spring flowering to keep the blooms coming back.

items.name: Iris variegata
items.growersTips:
Plant your rhizomes shallowly in late summer so the UK sun can bake the tops and trigger next blooms.
Keep them in sharp-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet British clay.
Divide the congested clumps every three years in July to keep the variegated stripes vivid.
Watch out for snails hiding in the fan bases during damp spring mornings and clear them off.
Pair them with low-growing thyme to cover the bare soil without shading the iris rhizomes.

items.name: Iris vartanii
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs 8cm deep in autumn in a gritty, free-draining mix to survive wet UK winters.
Give them a hot, dry summer dormancy by covering the soil with a cloche during July and August.
Grow this winter-bloomer in a terracotta pot so you can move it under cover to protect the flowers.
Top the soil with a layer of sharp grit to keep the delicate, pale blue petals clean from mud.
Watch out for slugs and snails in January as they love to eat the early emerging flower buds.

items.name: Iris verna
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in acidic, humus-rich soil, avoiding any lime or alkaline compost.
Unlike typical bulbs, keep the rhizomes just under the soil surface rather than burying them deep.
Give it dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural open woodland home in the UK.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during the spring growing season, then let it dry out in summer.
Watch out for UK slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the tender new flower buds.

items.name: Iris versicolor
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in wet soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep in full sun.
Divide the rhizomes, not bulbs, every three years in late summer to maintain vigorous UK flowering.
Cut back the dying foliage to the ground in autumn to prevent the common iris rust fungus overwintering.
Watch for iris sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent severe leaf damage.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris in boggy areas to provide contrasting early spring yellow blooms.

items.name: Iris virginica
items.growersTips:
Plant this native of wet areas in shallow water or boggy soil at the edge of your garden pond.
Keep the soil consistently damp or submerged, as this plant cannot tolerate drying out in summer.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in late summer after flowering to keep the plant vigorous and tidy.
Watch out for snails and slugs on the young spring shoots, especially in damp UK garden spots.
Grow it alongside marsh marigolds or water forget-me-nots for a lovely, natural British pond look.

items.name: Iris warleyensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Juno bulb in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in a very sharp, gritty compost.
Keep it bone dry during its summer dormancy by covering the soil or moving your pot into a greenhouse.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot possible to mimic its native Central Asian mountain slopes.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to devour the emerging fleshy foliage.
Feed with a high-potash liquid fertiliser just as the blue-violet flowers start fading in spring.

items.name: Iris wattii
items.growersTips:
Plant this bamboo-like iris in a sheltered, frost-free spot as UK winters can bite its tall stems.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during its active spring growth.
Mulch heavily with leaf mould in autumn to protect its shallow rhizomes from hard British frosts.
Cut down the flowered canes right to the ground in late summer to encourage strong new shoots.
Grow it in light dappled shade under a south-facing wall to mimic its native woodland edge home.

items.name: Iris westii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Oncocyclus iris in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to survive wet UK winters.
Keep the bulb completely dry during its summer dormant phase by using a glass cloche overhead.
Plant the bulbs shallowly in autumn, ensuring the top of the rhizome sits just below the soil.
Water sparingly in early spring, then stop watering entirely once the foliage begins to die back.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, as they love to feast on the emerging buds.

items.name: Iris willmottiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this Juno iris bulb at least ten centimetres deep in late autumn to protect it from UK frosts.
Choose a south-facing border with sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter wet rotting bulbs.
Water sparingly in spring, then keep the soil completely dry during its summer dormant period.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the delicate emerging shoots during damp British springs.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year's blooms.

items.name: Iris wilsonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in reliable boggy soil or beside your garden pond so it never dries out.
Position your iris in full sun or very light dappled shade to ensure those yellow blooms pop.
Unlike dry-land bulbs, this species thrives in acidic to neutral soil, so avoid adding lime.
Divide the congested clumps in late summer after flowering to keep the plant vigorous and healthy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK spring weather as they love the tender new shoots.

items.name: Iris winogradowii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of about eight to ten centimeters in very well-drained soil.
Keep them damp during spring but make sure they stay quite dry and baked throughout the summer months.
Add plenty of grit to your compost to survive wet UK winters and prevent the bulbs from rotting.
Watch out for hungry slugs and snails in early spring as they love eating the emerging yellow buds.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them under a cold frame to shelter from heavy winter rain.

items.name: Iris xiphium
items.growersTips:
Plant these Spanish iris bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in a super sunny, warm spot.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because these bulbs will rot if they sit in wet winter ground.
Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering in July to feed the bulb for next year.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the tender new shoots as they emerge in early spring.
Plant them alongside shallow-rooted annuals to hide the iris leaves when they start to look untidy.

items.name: Ischnolepis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare African perennial in a gritty, free-draining loam to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pot in a south-facing, sheltered spot to mimic its native sunny grassland habitat.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil are dry, then keep it barely damp during winter.
Bring the container into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory from late October until May.
Propagate by carefully dividing the root clump in early spring just as new growth begins to show.

items.name: Ischnolepis natalensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Grow it in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix to prevent root rot during damp spring days.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, cutting back to once a month in winter.
Keep it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic the bright African light it craves.
Feed it with a highly diluted succulent fertiliser just twice a year during the active summer growth.

items.name: Isoberlinia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth in peat-free compost to protect from late UK spring frosts.
Plant out in June in a south-facing border with grit added to clay soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry July spells rather than daily light sprinklings.
Protect young shoots from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British spring nights.
Grow alongside nitrogen-loving leafy greens like spinach to benefit from this legume's root nodules.

items.name: Isoberlinia doka
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in peat-free compost to beat the chilly UK spring weather.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering gently at the base every three days.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots; protect them using beer traps or copper tape around pots.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach 15cm high to encourage a bushier, stronger habit.
Plant out in late May alongside French marigolds to deter pests and boost your garden border.

items.name: Isodendrion
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Hawaiian shrub indoors before autumn frosts hit, keeping it in a bright conservatory.
Water sparingly in winter, letting the top two inches of compost dry out completely between drinks.
Pot your plant in a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite under leaves, spraying with tepid water to boost humidity.
Prune lightly in late spring after the flowering flush to maintain a compact, bushy shape in pots.

items.name: Isodendrion pyrifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare Hawaiian shrub indoors before autumn frosts as it cannot survive UK winter cold.
Grow it in a highly free-draining, acidic loam-based compost mix with plenty of added perlite.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil dry out, keeping it drier during winter.
Place your pot in a bright conservatory or south-facing windowsill to mimic its sunny habitat.
Prune lightly in late spring after any flowering to maintain a compact shape and bushy growth.

items.name: Isoglossa
items.growersTips:
Bring your Isoglossa indoors by October to protect this tender perennial from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow them in pots of peat-free loam compost so you can easily move them inside when temperatures drop.
Water your Isoglossa only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot in cool weather.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage a bushier habit and prevent leggy, weak stems.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering them indoors.

items.name: Isoglossa woodii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender South African perennial indoors before the first autumn frost hits your garden.
Grow it in a pot with peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure excellent drainage.
Water it only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as it hates sitting in soggy winter wet.
Keep it in a bright, draught-free conservatory or on a sunny windowsill over the UK winter.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage a bushier habit and prevent it getting leggy.

items.name: Isophysis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Isophysis bulbs in autumn at a depth of three times their height in acidic, sandy peat.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, mimicking their damp Tasmanian home.
Grow them in containers so you can move them into a cold greenhouse to protect from wet UK winters.
Position your pots in partial shade where they get morning sun but are shielded from midday heat.
Top-dress the soil with a layer of grit to prevent winter rot around the neck of the bulbs.

items.name: Isophysis tasmanica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Tasmanian gem in acidic, peaty, very gritty soil to mimic its native alpine moorland.
Keep the compost constantly moist but never soggy, using rainwater rather than tap water if you can.
Grow it in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate blooms from heavy UK winter rain.
Give it maximum winter light but position it in light afternoon shade during hot British summers.
Propagate by carefully dividing the rhizome-like bulbs just after the summer flowering finishes.

items.name: Isopyrum
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic their native UK woodland edge habitat.
Incorporate leaf mould into moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil before planting in autumn.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during their active spring growing period.
Propagate by dividing the delicate rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has died back.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Isopyrum thalictroides
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate wood anemone cousin in autumn under deciduous shrubs to mimic UK woodland floors.
Mix lots of leaf mould or well-rotted compost into heavy UK clay soils to ensure perfect drainage.
Keep the soil consistently moist through spring, but let it dry out slightly once it goes dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tender carrot-like shoots first emerge.
Divide the fragile tuberous roots in late summer once the foliage has completely died back.

items.name: Isotoma
items.growersTips:
Tuck your Isotoma into free-draining soil mixed with grit to prevent winter wet rotting the roots.
Water them deeply once a week in dry summer spells, letting the top inch of soil dry out first.
Protect these tender perennials by bringing pots into a frost-free greenhouse before November.
Trim back the stems by half in late summer to encourage a fresh flush of those starry blue flowers.
Wear gloves when dividing clumps in spring because the milky sap can irritate your skin.

items.name: Isotoma anethifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring as they need UK light to trigger germination.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in our damp British winters.
Move pots to a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame by October to protect them from severe freezes.
Snip off faded blue star flowers regularly through summer to keep the blooms coming until autumn.
Wear gloves when pruning because the milky sap can irritate your skin and is toxic to pets.

items.name: Isotoma axillaris
items.growersTips:
Bring your pots indoors before the first autumn frost because this tender Aussie won't survive UK winters.
Water them only when the top inch of soil feels dry, as soggy British winters will rot their roots.
Wear gloves when pinching out the stem tips in May, because the milky sap can really irritate skin.
Mix plenty of grit into your multi-purpose compost to ensure the sharp drainage they absolutely crave.
Plant them alongside yellow bidens in patio pots for a gorgeous, long-lasting summer colour contrast.

items.name: Isotoma fluviatilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this blue star creeper in moist, free-draining soil to stop winter rot in wet UK climates.
Water it deeply once a week during dry British summers until its creeping root system establishes.
Tuck it between paving stones or garden path gaps where light foot traffic actually helps it spread.
Divide your clumps in spring after the last frost to easily propagate and fill bare garden patches.
Keep a lookout for slugs and snails during damp spring nights as they love the tender new shoots.

items.name: Isotoma hypocrateriformis
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in early spring, as they need light to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse before winter frosts hit.
Pinch out the growing tips when young to encourage a much bushier habit and far more blue flowers.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using beer traps or grit to protect them.

items.name: Isotoma petraea
items.growersTips:
Bring this Australian native indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters.
Sow the tiny seeds on top of damp, peat-free compost in spring, as they need light to germinate.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this plant hates soggy British winter wet.
Wear gloves when pruning back in autumn to protect your skin from its toxic, milky sap.
Grow it in pots alongside trailing lobelia so you can easily move it to a sunny, sheltered patio.

items.name: Isotoma pusilla
items.growersTips:
Tuck this tiny Australian gem into gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this little plant hates soggy roots.
Protect its low foliage from slugs and snails during damp British spring nights with grit barriers.
Plant it alongside dwarf sedums in a sunny rockery where larger plants won't crowd it out.
Give it a light trim after the first flush of summer flowers to encourage a second show.

items.name: Isotoma scapigera
items.growersTips:
Grow this Australian native in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent winter wet rotting the roots.
Plant it in full sun but keep it sheltered from cold, drying winds that sweep across UK gardens.
Water moderately in summer but let the soil dry out slightly between waterings to avoid root rot.
Bring containers of this tender perennial into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Propagate by dividing the root clumps in spring just as new growth begins to show.

items.name: Isotria
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare orchid in a shady, damp spot mimicking British oak woodlands with acidic soil.
Mix plenty of decayed leaf mould into the soil to mimic its natural, fungi-rich woodland home.
Water with harvested rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy, especially during dry summers.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Leave the plant completely undisturbed once planted, as its delicate roots hate being moved.

items.name: Isotria medeoloides
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare orchid in a very acidic, well-draining leaf mould mix to mimic its native woodland.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only with stored rainwater to avoid tap water lime.
Grow it in a shaded cold frame to protect the delicate stems from harsh UK wind and heavy rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they will quickly devour the emerging single flower.
Surround it with slow-growing mosses to help maintain the high humidity this woodland native loves.

items.name: Isotria verticillata
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare orchid in acidic, leaf-mold rich soil that mimics a damp British woodland floor.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never waterlogged, using rainwater instead of tap water.
Position it in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect the delicate leaves from hot sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the emerging single-whorled shoots.
Leave the roots completely undisturbed once planted, as this species hates being moved around.

items.name: Ivesia
items.growersTips:
Grow this alpine shrub in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet, cold UK winters.
Plant your Ivesia in a raised bed or rockery to keep its roots from rotting in heavy clay.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry spells, letting the soil dry out completely between times.
Tuck some horticultural grit right around the crown in autumn to protect it from damp winter rot.
Lightly trim the foliage in late spring to keep its compact, mounded shape looking tidy.

items.name: Ixia
items.growersTips:
Plant your ixia bulbs in autumn about ten centimetres deep in a very sunny, sheltered UK border.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure sharp drainage so the bulbs do not rot in wet winters.
In colder UK regions, lift the bulbs in October and store them in dry peat-free compost over winter.
Water your ixias regularly during their spring growing period but keep them dry once they die back.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme to support their slender stems and keep the bulbs warm.

items.name: Ixia curta
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using pots of gritty compost to easily move them indoors for winter.
Grow in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic South African heat and trigger flowering.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep bulbs bone dry from July to October during dormancy.
Protect from hard UK frosts by overwintering pots in a cold greenhouse or bright conservatory.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into heavy UK soils to prevent bulb rot in wet winter weather.

items.name: Ixia dubia
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors to protect them from wet UK winters.
Mix equal parts grit and peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage these South African bulbs need.
Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely after summer flowering to allow the bulb to bake.
Position pots against a south-facing brick wall to maximise sun exposure and mimic their native heat.
Overwinter containers in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame once autumn temperatures drop below 5C.

items.name: Ixia flexuosa
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Grow in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame during wet UK winters.
Water weekly during spring growth but stop watering completely after summer flowering to dry them.
Position in your warmest south-facing border against a brick wall to maximize essential UK sunlight.
Lift bulbs in October if grown in cold northern UK regions and store them in dry peat over winter.

items.name: Ixia maculata
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, free-draining mix to prevent winter waterlogging rot.
Grow in containers to easily move them under a cold frame or unheated greenhouse during UK winters.
Position in your garden's absolute warmest, most south-facing spot to ensure full summer flowering.
Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely after flowering to let the corms dry out.
Lift corms in late autumn in cold northern UK regions and store them in dry sand away from frost.

items.name: Ixia micrandra
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using pots of gritty compost to easily move them indoors for winter.
Grow in the sunniest, south-facing spot possible to mimic their native South African light levels.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep bulbs completely dry in summer once the foliage dies back.
Overwinter pots in a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame as these bulbs will not survive UK freezes.
Mix horticultural grit into your soil to prevent bulb rot during wet British autumns and winters.

items.name: Ixia monadelpha
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using pots of gritty compost to easily move them indoors for winter.
Water sparingly in winter but keep soil moist during their active spring growth and flowering phase.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot possible to mimic their native South African heat.
Dry out the bulbs completely after summer dieback by storing the pots in a dry greenhouse or shed.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails which quickly destroy the flower buds.

items.name: Ixia odorata
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent rot during wet UK winters.
Grow in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame from November to April.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry once foliage dies back in summer.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border against a warm wall to mimic their South African heat.
Do not cut yellowing leaves in summer; let them die back naturally so the bulb stores energy to flower.

items.name: Ixia paniculata
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, sharply draining soil mix to prevent winter rot.
Grow in containers to easily move them under glass or into a cold frame to survive UK winter frosts.
Water weekly during spring growth but stop watering completely once foliage dies back in summer.
Position in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic their native South African heat.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Ixia polystachya
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8cm deep in autumn using a gritty, free-draining mix to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil
Position in your warmest south-facing border or against a brick wall to maximize essential sunlight
Lift corms in October after foliage dies back and store dry in a frost-free shed over UK winters
Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely once flowering ends to allow summer dormancy
Grow in terracotta pots to easily move them under glass and protect from heavy UK winter rains

items.name: Ixia scillaris
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm to 10cm in sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot.

Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil completely dry once summer dormancy begins.
Position in the sunniest, most south-facing spot available to mimic their native South African heat.
Apply a thick dry mulch of bark or straw in late autumn to protect bulbs from severe UK frosts.

items.name: Ixia viridiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 8cm deep in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Grow in pots to easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame from November to April.
Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely after summer flowering to allow a dry dormancy.
Position in your warmest south-facing suntrap to mimic their native South African baking conditions.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Ixiolaena
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March to beat the late UK frosts, pressing them lightly into gritty compost.

items.name: Ixodia
items.growersTips:
Sow your Ixodia seeds indoors in early spring using a very free-draining sandy compost mix.

Shield young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during wet British springs.

items.name: Jacobsenia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Jacobsenia indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water only when the leaves wrinkle slightly, keeping them bone dry from November to March.

items.name: Jagrantia

Plant your Jagrantia tubers six inches deep in autumn to protect them from harsh UK winter frosts.

Mix plenty of well-rotted grit into your heavy clay soil to give Jagrantia the drainage it loves.

items.name: Jamesia
items.growersTips:
Plant Jamesia americana in sharply draining, gritty, neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter rot.

items.name: Jamesia americana

items.name: Jamesioideae

items.name: Jamesonia
items.growersTips:
Grow these Andean ferns in a highly acidic, gritty peat-free compost mix to mimic their moorland home.

Position them in a bright spot with high humidity but shield them from direct midday summer sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails nesting in the dense, hairy fronds during damp spring mornings.

items.name: Jasione
items.growersTips:
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep Jasione laevis happy during wet UK winters.
Plant these little blue buttons in full sun where they can bask in the bright British summer light.

items.name: Jasione corymbosa

Plant this Spanish native in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.

items.name: Jasione laevis

Plant this Jasione in gritty, sharply draining soil to stop its roots rotting in wet UK winters.

items.name: Jasione montana

items.name: Jasminanthes

items.name: Jefea brevifolia

items.name: Jeffersonia

items.name: Jensenobotrya

items.name: Jordaaniella

items.name: Juniperus bermudiana

Grow this tender Bermudiana in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for UK winters.

items.name: Juniperus blancoi

items.name: Juniperus brevifolia

items.name: Juniperus californica

items.name: Juniperus cedrus

items.name: Juniperus communis

items.name: Juniperus deltoides

items.name: Juniperus durangensis

items.name: Juniperus excelsa

Watch out for juniper scale insects in summer and spray them with organic plant oils immediately.

items.name: Juniperus flaccida

items.name: Juniperus foetidissima

items.name: Juniperus formosana

Plant your Formosan juniper in a raised bed or gravelly soil to survive wet British winters.

items.name: Juttadinteria

Plant this desert succulent in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice to survive damp UK winters.
Keep it completely dry from November to March in a greenhouse to prevent rot in our cold climate.
Soak the soil only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle slightly, then let it dry out fully.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the weak British winter sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints during warm, humid spring spells.

items.name: Juttadinteria deserticola
items.growersTips:
Keep this desert succulent in a gritty loam-based compost with seventy percent sand or perlite.
Bring your plant indoors to a bright windowsill before the first wet autumn frosts arrive.
Water only when the leaves slightly wrinkle, keeping the soil completely dry throughout winter.
Use a shallow terracotta pot to prevent water from pooling around the delicate root system.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints and dab them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.

items.name: Kalanchoe
items.growersTips:
Bring your kalanchoe indoors by mid-September before the damp UK autumn chill and frosts set in.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, peat-free compost are bone dry to prevent root rot.
Prune back leggy stems by half after the spring blooms fade to keep your shrub compact and bushy.
Keep an eye out for vine weevil grubs in your pots, as they love chewing through kalanchoe roots.
Give your plant six weeks of fourteen-hour dark nights in autumn to trigger those winter flowers.

items.name: Kalanchoe ×houghtonii
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender succulent indoors before the first autumn frost to keep it safe from UK damp.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are bone dry, then soak and drain it completely.
Pot it in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit for perfect drainage.
Snip off the spent flower spikes in late spring to help your plant focus on fresh new leaf growth.
Watch out for tiny plantlets dropping into nearby pots, as they root quickly and can take over.

items.name: Kalanchoe arborescens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting mix with fifty percent perlite to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, then drench and drain fully.
Position on a south-facing indoor windowsill to maximise crucial winter light levels in the UK.
Move outdoors only from June to August when night temperatures consistently stay above ten degrees.
Prune leggy stems in early spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier growth habit.

items.name: Kalanchoe beauverdii
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Provide a sturdy trellis or bamboo cane support for its scrambling, vining stems to climb up.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, then reduce to once a month during damp UK winters.
Overwinter indoors on a south-facing windowsill as this succulent cannot tolerate UK frosts.
Take stem cuttings in late spring to propagate new plants before the autumn temperature drop.

items.name: Kalanchoe beharensis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by October as this Madagascar native cannot survive wet UK winters below five degrees.
Water only when the top five centimetres of gritty, free-draining cactus compost is completely dry.
Propagate in spring by pinning a single mature leaf flat onto damp sand to trigger new plantlets.
Prune leggy stems in April just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Wipe the felted leaves with a dry brush rather than water to prevent rot and powdery mildew.

items.name: Kalanchoe bentii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of free-draining gritty compost in early spring under heated glass at 18C.
Keep pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the intense sunlight this desert species craves.
Water only when the potting mix dries out completely, then drench and let all excess drain away.
Overwinter indoors in a heated room or greenhouse as this tender succulent cannot survive UK frosts.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with an organic insecticidal soap spray.

items.name: Kalanchoe blossfeldiana
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by September before UK frosts hit as they cannot survive temperatures below ten degrees
Water only when the top two inches of gritty peat-free compost have dried out completely to avoid rot
Deadhead spent flower stems at the base in spring to encourage a second flush of colourful blooms
Place on a south-facing windowsill to get the daily four hours of direct sun needed for bud growth
To trigger winter flowering cover the plant for fourteen hours daily in autumn to mimic short days

items.name: Kalanchoe bouvetii
items.growersTips:
Bring pots indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from wet and freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost have dried out completely.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring without burying them, as they need light to germinate.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and prevent leggy stem growth.
Position in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise limited UK summer sunlight.

items.name: Kalanchoe daigremontiana
items.growersTips:
Grow indoors in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, reducing to once a month from November to March.
Keep pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light levels during overcast British winters.
Pick off the plantlets from leaf margins before they drop and weed them out of adjacent housepots.
Maintain indoor temperatures above ten degrees Celsius to protect this succulent from frost damage.

items.name: Kalanchoe delagoensis
items.growersTips:
Bring pots indoors before first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry then drain fully to prevent root rot.
Grow in a gritty mix of fifty percent peat-free compost and fifty percent horticultural sand.
Remove the tiny plantlets from leaf tips regularly to stop them invading neighbouring pots.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise winter light and prevent leggy growth.

items.name: Kalanchoe farinacea
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Water only when the top three centimeters of gritty, free-draining soil mix has dried out completely.
Grow in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to provide the maximum daily sunlight UK offers.
Propagate in late spring by taking stem cuttings and letting them callous for three days before potting.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and treat immediately with organic insecticidal soap or alcohol.

items.name: Kalanchoe fedtschenkoi
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this tender succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes
Water only when the top three centimetres of gritty compost are completely dry to prevent root rot
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage bushier growth and propagate the cuttings in sand
Grow in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils during winter when indoor heating creates dry stagnant air

items.name: Kalanchoe garambiensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring under glass as they need light to germinate.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Bring pots indoors by September before the first autumn frost to protect this tender succulent.
Mix fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this plant requires.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow flowers.

items.name: Kalanchoe gastonis-bonnieri
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters below ten degrees.
Propagate in summer by detaching the plantlets that form on leaf tips and potting them in grit sand.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty loam are dry to prevent root rot in humid UK weather.
Use a free-draining mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part perlite for outdoor summer pots.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices during autumn when moving containers into indoor glasshouses.

items.name: Kalanchoe laciniata
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Christmas bells indoors by October to protect them from wet and frosty UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining soil are bone dry to prevent root rot.
Prune your shrubby stems in early spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent them from going leggy.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints, especially during dry indoor winters.
Mix plenty of perlite and horticultural sand into standard compost to mimic their dry native soil.

items.name: Kalanchoe laetivirens
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty peat-free loam with fifty percent perlite to survive damp UK autumn humidity.
Water only when the top three centimetres of soil are bone dry, keeping completely dry in winter.
Keep indoors on a south-facing windowsill from October to May to protect from frost and wet rot.
Scrape off the tiny plantlets from leaf margins in spring to prevent them invading nearby pots.
Check leaf crevices weekly for mealybugs, treating infestations with an organic neem oil spray.

items.name: Kalanchoe lanceolata
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant indoors by October to protect this tender African succulent from wet UK winters.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, then soak it and let it drain fully.
Mix fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to stop root rot in our damp British climate.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier, more compact shrubby habit.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints during dry indoor winter months.

items.name: Kalanchoe longiflora
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before October frosts as this succulent cannot survive wet cold UK winter conditions
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK climates
Grow in a mix of two parts peat-free compost to one part horticultural grit for sharp drainage
Prune leggy stems in spring to encourage bushy growth and propagate the cuttings in dry soil
Place on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light and develop the signature red leaf margins

items.name: Kalanchoe luciae
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winters below five degrees.
Grow in a gritty loam-based potting mix with fifty percent perlite or horticultural sand for drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry then drench fully, keeping the central leaf rosette dry.
Place on a south-facing windowsill to get maximum sunlight which triggers the red leaf margins.
Propagate in spring by taking leaf cuttings and letting them callus for three days before potting.

items.name: Kalanchoe manginii
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted plants indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits the UK.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, then let the excess drain out completely.
Mix half peat-free compost with half grit or perlite to keep its delicate roots from rotting.
Trim the trailing stems right after the spring blooms fade to keep your plant bushy and compact.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the fleshy leaves, especially during dry winter heating.

items.name: Kalanchoe marmorata
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant indoors by October to protect its fleshy leaves from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry, then drench it and let it drain fully.
Mix equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural grit to keep its roots dry in our damp climate.
Snip off any leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier shape and fresh spotted leaves.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots if you keep your potted shrub outdoors in summer.

items.name: Kalanchoe marnieriana
items.growersTips:
Bring it indoors by October because UK winter frosts will quickly kill this tender Madagascan shrub.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining soil are bone dry to prevent root rot.
Propagate easily in spring by snipping leggy stems, drying them for two days, then potting in sand.
Position on your brightest south-facing windowsill to get those lovely pinkish-red leaf margins.
Wipe the blue-grey leaves gently with a damp cloth in spring to clear dust and check for mealybugs.

items.name: Kalanchoe millotii
items.growersTips:
Bring your millotii indoors by October before the damp autumn chill and frost damage set in.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty soil are bone dry, then drench and drain completely.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to help this velvety shrub maintain a compact, bushy shape.
Repot in spring using a mix of half peat-free compost and half horticultural grit for fast drainage.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the fuzzy leaves, and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Kalanchoe orgyalis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first autumn frost as this succulent cannot survive wet UK winter freezes.
Water only when the gritty compost dries out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK climates.
Grow in a pots with fifty percent perlite or grit to ensure the rapid drainage this plant needs.
Place on a south facing windowsill to maximise light levels during dark British winter months.
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage bushier growth and maintain the bronze leaf colour.

items.name: Kalanchoe pinnata
items.growersTips:
Grow in pots of peat-free grit mix so you can move them indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Propagate by placing a mature leaf flat on damp compost to trigger plantlets along the margins.
Keep in a south-facing conservatory or windowsill to maximise limited UK winter sunlight hours.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in the compost during spring and treat with beneficial nematodes.

items.name: Kalanchoe poincarei
items.growersTips:
Bring your poincarei indoors by October to protect this tender shrub from wet UK winter frosts.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, keeping it drier in winter.
Blend fifty percent grit with peat-free compost to stop root rot in our damp British climate.
Prune leggy stems in late spring after flowering to keep this shrubby succulent bushy and neat.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them off with a damp cloth or organic spray.

items.name: Kalanchoe porphyrocalyx
items.growersTips:
Keep this Madagascar native potted so you can easily bring it inside before the autumn frosts hit.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, then drench it and let the pot drain fully.
Mix plenty of grit into peat-free compost to prevent root rot during damp British winters.
Prune back the stems by half right after the pink bell flowers fade in spring to keep it bushy.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints when you move your plant indoors for the winter months.

items.name: Kalanchoe pumila
items.growersTips:
Bring your frost-tender pumila indoors to a bright windowsill before the first chilly UK autumn frost.
Water only when the top few centimetres of gritted compost are bone dry, especially in winter.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring after flowering to keep its lovely mounded shrub shape.
Mix fifty percent horticultural grit into your peat-free compost to prevent soggy UK winter root rot.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the dusty grey-pink leaves when indoor heating goes on.

items.name: Kalanchoe rhombopilosa
items.growersTips:
Keep your rhombopilosa in a pot so you can bring it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, which in wet UK winters might mean just once a month.
Mix fifty percent grit or perlite into standard peat-free compost to prevent winter root rot.
Place it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep those lovely silver leaf markings vivid.
Propagate fallen fan-shaped leaves in spring by just resting them on dry gritty soil to root.

items.name: Kalanchoe robusta
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by late September to protect this frost-tender succulent from damp UK autumn chills.
Water only when the top three centimeters of gritty, free-draining loam soil is completely dry.
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring on the surface of damp compost under a clear polythene cover.
Position in your brightest south-facing windowsill or conservatory to prevent leggy, weak growth.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers and treat with UK-approved nematodes in late summer.

items.name: Kalanchoe scandens
items.growersTips:
Bring your scandens indoors by October to protect its succulent leaves from wet, frosty UK winters.
Grow this climber in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, cutting back to once a month in winter.
Prune the trailing stems right after its late winter flowering to keep its vining habit bushy.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when keeping it in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Kalanchoe sect. Bryophyllum
items.growersTips:
Bring potted mother of thousands indoors by October to survive the wet, freezing UK winter frosts
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost are bone dry to touch
Pick off and discard the falling plantlets from leaves to stop them invading nearby garden pots
Provide maximum winter windowsill light to prevent leggy growth and weak stems in gloomy UK months
Watch for mealybugs in leaf crevices and dab them with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol

items.name: Kalanchoe sexangularis
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted shrub indoors to a bright windowsill before the first UK autumn frost hits.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it and let all the excess drain away.
Mix half peat-free compost with half grit or perlite to keep its roots dry and happy.
Place it in your sunniest south-facing spot to turn those leaf edges a gorgeous deep red.
Snip off leggy stems in late spring to keep your plant bushy and encourage fresh new growth.

items.name: Kalanchoe suarezensis
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors by late September to protect this frost-tender succulent from cold UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost have dried out completely.
Grow in a terracotta pot rather than open soil to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Position on a south-facing windowsill to ensure it receives the six hours of daily sun it requires.
Pick off the tiny plantlets that form on leaf margins to propagate new plants easily in spring.

items.name: Kalanchoe tetraphylla
items.growersTips:
Keep this succulent in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first wet UK autumn frost.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, then soak it and let all excess drain away completely.
Plant in a gritty mix of fifty percent peat-free compost and fifty percent horticultural grit.
Place it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep those leaf margins a vibrant red.
Wipe the large paddle leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and check for mealybugs.

items.name: Kalanchoe thyrsiflora
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost with fifty percent perlite to prevent root rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench thoroughly, keeping the central rosette dry.
Move indoors to a south-facing windowsill by October to protect from damp UK autumn frosts.
Position in maximum direct summer sun to trigger the vibrant red leaf margins on Flapjack foliage.
Propagate by taking leaf cuttings in late spring, allowing the wound to callus before potting.

items.name: Kalanchoe tomentosa
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining grit-heavy compost on a south-facing UK windowsill to maximise daily light.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, reducing to once a month during damp UK winter months.
Keep indoors year-round as this succulent cannot survive UK frost and needs temperatures above 10C.
Snip leggy stems in spring just above a leaf node to encourage a bushier, more compact habit.
Inspect the fuzzy silver leaves weekly for mealybugs which hide easily in the dense leaf hairs.

items.name: Kalanchoideae
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted kalanchoe indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Water only when the top two inches of gritty, free-draining cactus compost have dried out completely.
Prune back leggy stems by half after spring flowering to encourage a bushier, more compact shape.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Feed with a diluted succulent fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost next year's blooms.

items.name: Kamettia
items.growersTips:
Plant Kamettia in well-drained loam enriched with grit to survive wet, cold UK winters without rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, letting the top inch of soil dry out between.
Prune back old stems in late autumn to protect the crown from frost damage and encourage spring growth.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or copper tape around your containers.
Divide mature clumps every three years in early spring to keep them vigorous and free-flowering.

items.name: Kanahia
items.growersTips:
Bring this African shrub indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow your Kanahia in a deep pot filled with gritty loam to easily move it inside when autumn hits.
Water heavily in midsummer to mimic its native riverbeds, but keep it barely damp during winter.
Watch out for aphids on the milky sap of new spring shoots and wash them off with warm soapy water.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more cream flowers.

items.name: Karpatiosorbus badensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Baden whitebeam in deep, fertile, well-drained loam to mimic its native limestone soil.
Water your young shrub deeply once a week during dry UK summers to establish its deep rooting system.
Prune only in late winter to remove crossing branches, preserving its natural neat, upright shape.
Keep a sharp eye out for fireblight and aphids, which can occasionally trouble this Sorbus relative.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted leaf mould to keep the roots cool and mimic forest soils.

items.name: Karpatiosorbus bristoliensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Bristol whitebeam in deep, fertile, well-drained loam to mimic its native Avon Gorge home.
Water your young shrub deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help its deep root system establish.
Prune only in late winter to remove crossing branches before the active spring sap starts to flow.
Keep a sharp eye out for fireblight in warm, wet British springs, cutting back any blackened twigs.
Underplant with wild marjoram or thyme to create a limestone-loving community that deters weeds.

items.name: Kashmiria
items.growersTips:
Plant your Kashmiria in free-draining UK soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week in dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between times.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in late autumn to keep the perennial clump neat for winter.
Watch out for slugs on tender new spring shoots, especially during wet British April weather.
Divide your mature clumps every three years in early spring to keep the plant vigorous and healthy.

items.name: Kashmiria himalaica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan gem in free-draining, gritty soil to survive wet, cold UK winter root rot.
Position it in dappled woodland shade to mimic its native mountain home and prevent leaf scorch.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the soil consistently damp but never soggy.
Protect the crown with a dry winter mulch of bark chippings or gravel to shield it from heavy frost.
Divide the clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to keep the plant vigorous and healthy.

items.name: Keckiella antirrhinoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian native in your sunniest, sheltered UK south-facing border to mimic its home.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure fast drainage and prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Water sparingly once established, only giving a drink during prolonged, dry British summer spells.
Prune back lightly in late spring after the last frost to shape the shrub and encourage new blooms.
Protect the root zone with a thick dry mulch in late autumn to help it survive cold UK winters.

items.name: Keckiella breviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sunniest south-facing spot with gravel mixed deep into the soil.
Keep young plants damp but let established ones dry out completely between waterings to avoid rot.
Protect the crown with a thick layer of dry grit before wet winter frosts hit your UK garden plot.
Prune back the woody stems by half in late spring once you see the first signs of fresh green growth.
Grow it alongside rosemary or lavender to match its love for sharp drainage and baking hot sun.

items.name: Keckiella cordifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian beauty against a south-facing brick wall to shield it from cold UK winds.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to ensure the roots never sit in winter wet.
Prune the woody stems back by half in late spring once the threat of hard UK frosts has passed.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Take softwood cuttings in midsummer as an insurance policy against exceptionally harsh UK winters.

items.name: Keckiella corymbosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian beauty in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs.
Cut stems back by half in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more bright red summer blooms.
Water deeply once a week during its first UK summer, then leave it to establish deep drought tolerance.
Grow it against a south-facing brick wall to trap extra heat and protect it from cold winter winds.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of grit or gravel in autumn to prevent rot from cold British rain.

items.name: Keckiella rothrockii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mojave native in a raised bed with half grit to mimic its dry desert canyon home.
Protect it from wet UK winters by planting under a south-facing wall or keeping it in a pot.
Water only during extreme summer droughts once established, as damp soil will rot the roots.
Prune back by a third in late spring after frosts pass to keep its woody, shrubby habit tidy.
Grow it alongside rosemary or lavender which love the same sharp drainage and baking sun.

items.name: Keckiella ternata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian native in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic its warm home climate.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to ensure the sharp winter drainage it craves.
Water deeply but very rarely once established, letting the soil dry out fully between soakings.
Cut the woody stems back by half in late spring to encourage fresh, bushy growth and more flowers.
Protect the root zone with a thick autumn mulch of gravel to shield it from wet UK winter frosts.

items.name: Keteleeria
items.growersTips:
Plant your Keteleeria in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, watering deeply during dry summer spells.
Watch out for late spring frosts, which can easily damage the delicate new needle growth.
Add plenty of leaf mould or compost to your planting hole to mimic its preferred forest soils.
Avoid pruning this conifer unless you are removing dead wood, which is best done in late autumn.

items.name: Keteleeria davidiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this conifer in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect young spring growth from UK frosts.
Provide deep, acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native forest floor.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells while the young taproot establishes in your garden.
Keep a sharp eye out for phytophthora root rot if your British clay soil gets waterlogged in winter.
Avoid pruning this tree at all, as it naturally forms a beautiful, balanced conical shape.

items.name: Keteleeria evelyniana
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender Chinese fir in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.
Grow it in acidic to neutral soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles or leaf mould first.
Avoid pruning this conifer altogether, as it naturally forms a beautiful, neat pyramidal shape.
Protect young trees with fleece during freezing winters until they are established and hardier.

items.name: Keteleeria fortunei
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare conifer in deep, acidic, sandy loam to mimic its native warm woodland habitat.
Position it in a sheltered, south-facing spot to protect young spring growth from late UK frosts.
Water deeply during dry summer spells for the first five years until its taproot is fully established.
Avoid pruning this tree as it naturally forms a beautiful, balanced pyramidal shape on its own.
Mulch the root zone every autumn with composted pine needles to maintain the low soil pH it loves.

items.name: Khadia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Khadia in a gritty, free-draining mix of half potting compost and half horticultural grit.
Keep these South African succulents completely dry during the damp UK winter to prevent root rot.
Position your potted Khadia on a south-facing windowsill or in a sunny greenhouse for maximum light.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, then let all excess water drain away completely.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight foliage clumps during the warm summer months.

items.name: Khadia acutipetala
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes No. 2 and half grit.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it under glass to escape wet UK winter rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry from November to March.
Position your pot on a south-facing patio to maximise the summer baking it needs to trigger flowers.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints, dabbing them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.

items.name: Khadia borealis
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes No. 2 and half grit.
Keep it in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or porch for winter.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, then leave it alone to prevent root rot.
Position your pot on a south-facing patio to soak up every bit of scarce British summer sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight, fleshy leaf joints during dry indoor winter spells.

items.name: Krapfia

items.name: Kreodanthus

items.name: Laeliinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these orchids in a chunky bark mix with perlite, never in standard UK multipurpose compost.

Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the papery sheaths around the base of the new pseudobulbs.
Move them outdoors to a sheltered spot in June and July to trigger autumn blooms with cool nights.

items.name: Lagenandra

Grow Lagenandra meeboldii in a warm indoor terrarium or heated greenhouse to survive UK winters.

Watch out for fungus gnats in the damp soil and use yellow sticky traps to catch them early.

items.name: Lagophylla
items.growersTips:

Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or organic pellets to protect them.

items.name: Lampranthus

Plant this sun-lover in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet British winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly, but stop watering entirely in winter.

Trim back the leggy stems by one third in late summer after flowering to keep the clump compact.
Grow it alongside hardy sedums in a south-facing rockery to guarantee excellent drainage.

items.name: Lampranthus aureus

Plant this sun-lover in a terracotta pot with 50% grit so you can move it indoors before UK frosts.

Prune back leggy stems by one-third in late spring to keep your plant bushy and full of blooms.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your garden soil to prevent root rot during rainy autumns.

items.name: Lampranthus bicolor

Plant this sun-lover in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so winter rain drains away fast.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or bright windowsill before November.
Take stem cuttings in late summer as a cheap insurance policy against wet UK winter losses.
Only water when the compost is bone dry, then give it a good soak but never let the pot sit in water.
Snip off the faded daisy-like flowers in late summer to keep the succulent foliage neat and bushy.

items.name: Lampranthus glaucoides

Plant this South African beauty in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it inside.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then give it a good soak but never let it sit in a saucer.
