Tuck it next to hardy sedums in your rockery to mimic its natural dry, sun-baked cliffside home.
Prune back leggy stems by one third in late spring to encourage a dense carpet of orange blooms.

items.name: Lampranthus glaucus
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing succulent in a south-facing gravel bed or terracotta pot to catch max UK sun.
Mix fifty percent grit into your soil because this coastal beauty will rot in damp winter clay.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering entirely from November.
Take stem cuttings in late August to keep on a bright windowsill indoors as insurance against frost.
Trim back the leggy stems by one third in late spring to encourage a dense carpet of neon flowers.

items.name: Lampranthus multiradiatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing beauty in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Pop your plant in the sunniest south-facing spot you have so the daisy-like flowers actually open.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through to March.
Take stem cuttings in late summer as cheap insurance against a harsh, wet British winter frost.
Snip off faded blooms in late summer to keep the foliage tidy and encourage next year's buds.

items.name: Lampranthus roseus
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it inside for winter.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then give it a good soak but never let the pot sit in water.
Take stem cuttings in August to overwinter on a windowsill as insurance against wet winter rot.
Cut back leggy stems by half in late spring after the first flush of pink flowers to keep it bushy.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum heat in our cool UK summers.

items.name: Lampranthus sociorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African beauty in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and sharp sand to survive wet winters.
Give it a sunny, sheltered spot by a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm climate.
Water sparingly, only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, to prevent root rot.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first winter frost.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily propagate and safeguard your collection against cold snaps.

items.name: Lampranthus spectabilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing succulent in a gritty compost mix with extra perlite to survive UK winter wet.
Keep it in your sunniest south-facing spot to guarantee those brilliant magenta flowers open fully.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, then keep it almost completely dry throughout the winter.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors as insurance against severe UK frosts.
Trim back the leggy stems by one-third in late spring to encourage bushy new flowering growth.

items.name: Lampranthus tenuifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing ice plant in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so it survives wet winters.
Give it a hard prune by one third in late August to stop the stems from getting woody and sparse.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap extra heat during cool British summers.
Stop watering completely from November to March to prevent the roots from rotting in the damp cold.
Bring your containers into an unheated greenhouse or porch before the first autumn frost hits.

items.name: Lampranthus zeyheri
items.growersTips:
Plant this trailing succulent in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and sharp sand to survive UK rain.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot of your patio to coax those magenta flowers into fully opening.
Bring your containers indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first autumn frost.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to a tiny splash once a month during winter.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily overwinter new plants as insurance against wet winters.

items.name: Lamprocapnos spectabilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil to prevent early summer dormancy.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould or compost into the planting hole to mimic British woodland soil.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to prolong the delicate heart-shaped pink blooms.
Cut back yellowing foliage to ground level in midsummer once the plant naturally dies back.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Lankesteria
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical beauty in a pot so you can bring it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering only with lukewarm rainwater.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light, avoiding the harsh midday sun of a south-facing window.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from May to September to boost blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the leaves regularly to keep the humidity high.

items.name: Lapeirousia
items.growersTips:
Plant Lapeirousia laxa corms 5cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Grow them in pots to easily move them indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or cold frame by October.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep them completely dry during their summer dormant phase.
Position pots in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native South African warmth.
Overwinter outdoors only in mild UK coastal zones under a thick 10cm layer of dry bark mulch.

items.name: Lapeirousia angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors.
Mix equal parts grit and peat-free compost to mimic their native well-draining sandy soils.
Keep the soil completely dry during their summer dormant phase to prevent the bulbs from rotting.
Water them weekly once green shoots appear in late autumn, keeping the compost damp but not soggy.
Bring pots into a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill before the first UK winter frosts hit.

items.name: Laphangium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using free-draining peat-free compost indoors
Transplant outdoors in late May after frosts into a sheltered south-facing spot with full sun
Water the base only when the top two centimetres of soil is dry to prevent stem rot in damp UK weather
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic wool pellets or beer traps
Grow alongside thyme or rosemary in gravel gardens to mimic its natural dry, rocky habitat conditions

items.name: Lapidaria margaretae
items.growersTips:
Bring your Karoo rose indoors to a bright south windowsill before the first damp autumn frost hits.
Plant this mimicry succulent in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent loam.
Only water when the inner pair of fleshy leaves feels slightly soft to a gentle squeeze.
Do not water at all during the dark winter months to prevent root rot in our damp UK climate.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight fissures between the stone-like leaf pairs.

items.name: Lappula
items.growersTips:
Plant perennial Lappula squarrosa in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winter rot.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn at just five millimetres deep so cold winter temperatures trigger them.
Water young plants weekly in spring, but leave established ones dry to mimic their native steppes.
Snip off the burr-bearing seed heads in August before they stick to your pets and spread rapidly.
Plant them alongside lavender or thyme which love the same dry, sunny British gravel garden spots.

items.name: Lappula occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a depth of 3mm into gritty, free-draining soil to mimic UK winter chilling.
Position in full sun and water only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK clay.
Watch for slugs on young spring rosettes and clear surrounding weeds to prevent damp microclimates.
Plant alongside thyme or sedum in gravel gardens to provide the sharp drainage this species craves.
Cut back the flowering stems in late summer before seed drop if you want to limit its self-seeding.

items.name: Lappula squarrosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres in autumn to mimic natural UK winter chilling.

Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this annual is highly rot-prone in wet soil.
Wear thick gloves when clearing dead summer plants to avoid the painful, hook-spined burr seeds.
Plant alongside wild marjoram in sunny borders to attract native UK pollinators to the blooms.

items.name: Laricoideae
items.growersTips:
Plant your larch in moisture-retentive, acidic soil with plenty of leaf mould dug into the pit.
Water young trees deeply once a week during dry UK summers to prevent the needles from browning.
Prune your larch in late winter before new growth starts to keep its shape neat and manageable.
Watch out for larch adelgid woolly aphids in spring and spray them off with a sharp blast of water.
Underplant your larch with acid-loving heather or wood anemones for a lovely woodland look.

items.name: Larix
items.growersTips:
Plant your larch in deep, moist but well-drained acidic soil, avoiding chalky spots in your garden.
Water your young larch deeply once a week during dry UK summers until its roots are well established.
Prune deciduous larch trees only in midwinter when they are fully dormant to prevent sap bleeding.
Watch out for larch adelgid, a woolly white aphid, and spray it off with a sharp blast of water.
Grow dwarf cultivars like Larix decidua Little Bogle if you have a smaller UK patio or rock garden.

items.name: Larix × czekanowskii
items.growersTips:
Plant this hybrid larch in deep, moist but well-drained acidic soil to mimic its native Siberian home.
Water your young tree deeply during dry UK summers to establish its root system in the first two years.
Prune only in late winter when dormant to prevent sap bleeding and shape the canopy before bud burst.
Watch out for larch adelgid woolly aphids and treat them early with organic insecticidal soap.
Give it a sunny, open spot in your garden because this tree absolutely hates being in the shade.

items.name: Larix decidua
items.growersTips:
Plant this larch in deep, moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil where it gets full sun.
Water young trees deeply during dry UK summers to help their deep taproots establish properly.
Prune your larch in midwinter when it is dormant to shape it and remove any congested branches.
Watch out for larch adelgid woolly aphids, spraying them off with a sharp blast of hose water.
Plant understory wild daffodils or bluebells around the base to enjoy a classic British spring look.

items.name: Larix gmelinii
items.growersTips:
Plant this larch in moist, acidic to neutral soil that never dries out, especially in dry UK summers.
Give it the brightest spot in your garden because this tree absolutely hates being in the shade.
Prune your bonsai or dwarf cultivars in late winter before the gorgeous new green needles emerge.
Watch out for larch adelgid, a woolly aphid that looks like tiny white fluff on the branches.
Water young trees deeply during dry spells in May and June to help them establish in UK weather.

items.name: Larix griffithii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan larch in deep, moist, acidic soil to mimic its native mountain valleys.
Keep young trees well-watered during dry UK summers, especially in southern, less-humid counties.
Avoid pruning this conifer unless you are removing dead wood, which is best done in late winter.
Watch out for larch adelgid, a woolly aphid-like pest that thrives in damp British spring weather.
Give it plenty of space to grow, keeping it away from overhead lines and tight property boundaries.

items.name: Larix himalaica
items.growersTips:
Plant your Himalayan larch in deep, moist, acidic to neutral soil that never completely dries out.
Position this high-altitude beauty in a bright, open spot to avoid any shade from larger trees.
Water your young larch deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep its delicate root system cool.
Do any necessary shaping or pruning in midwinter when the tree is fully dormant and leafless.
Watch out for larch adelgid aphids, spraying them off with a sharp blast of water from your hose.

items.name: Larix kaempferi
items.growersTips:
Plant Japanese larch in deep, moist but well-drained acidic soil, avoiding shallow chalky spots.
Water young trees deeply during dry UK spring spells to help their shallow roots establish well.
Prune your larch in midwinter when dormant to shape it or manage its size before the sap rises.
Watch out for larch adelgid woolly aphids in early summer, spraying them off with a sharp hose jet.
Underplant with acid-loving heather or dwarf gorse to mimic its natural upland companion habitat.

items.name: Larix laricina

Plant your tamarack larch in a boggy, acidic spot where other trees struggle with wet winter soil.

items.name: Larix lyallii

items.name: Larix occidentalis

Water your young tree deeply during dry UK summers to help its extensive root system establish well.

items.name: Larix olgensis

Give it a spacious, sunny spot in your lawn so its wide-reaching root system has room to spread.

Prune only in midwinter when dormant to shape the canopy and avoid messy, sticky sap bleeding.
Watch out for larch canker in damp British springs, cutting away infected branches immediately.

items.name: Larix potaninii

items.name: Larix sibirica

Water your young tree deeply during dry UK summer spells to help its shallow root system establish.

items.name: Larryleachia cactiformis

items.name: Larryleachia perlata

Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum UK winter light it craves.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem ridges; dab them with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Lasia

Bring your Lasia indoors by October to protect its tropical rhizomes from wet, freezing UK winters.

items.name: Lasimorpha senegalensis

Use a heavy loam soil enriched with aquatic compost to support its thick, creeping rhizome growth.

items.name: Lasioideae
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Lysichiton indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before November.
Grow Symplocarpus in deep, permanently boggy, acidic soil near your pond to mimic wild wet woods.

Divide overcrowded clumps in early spring just as new growth starts, replanting them immediately.

items.name: Lastreopsis

Water these ferns deeply at the base once a week during dry UK summers to keep the compost damp.
Tuck them into a sheltered, fully shaded spot to protect the delicate fronds from cold drying winds.
Snip away the old dead fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh green croziers.
Mulch annually with leaf mould in autumn to protect their shallow rhizomes from hard winter frosts.

items.name: Lastreopsis decomposita
items.growersTips:
Plant this fern in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acidic soil to mimic its native forest floor.

items.name: Lastreopsis hispida

Snip off old tattered fronds in April just as the fresh bronze-green new growth starts to unfurl.

items.name: Lastreopsis marginans
items.growersTips:
Tuck your border fern into rich, leaf-mould compost that mimics a damp UK woodland floor.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering extra during dry British summers.
Plant it in a sheltered, fully shaded spot to protect the delicate fronds from cold drying winds.
Prune away the old, tattered fronds in early spring just as the new fiddleheads begin to unfurl.

items.name: Lastreopsis nephrodioides
items.growersTips:

items.name: Lastreopsis silvestris

Snip away the dead, tatty fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh growth.

items.name: Lavrania
items.growersTips:

items.name: Lawrencella davenportii

items.name: Lawrencella rosea
items.growersTips:
Sow these Australian pink everlastings indoors in March to shield seedlings from late UK frosts.
Plant seeds just two millimetres deep in gritty, free-draining compost as they need light to sprout.

items.name: Laxmannia squarrosa

items.name: Layia discoidea

items.name: Layia elegans

items.name: Lecanopteris
items.growersTips:
Grow these ant ferns in gritty orchid bark and moss to mimic their natural tree-dwelling habitat.

items.name: Lecanopteris carnosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this unusual ant fern in a very free-draining orchid bark and perlite mix, never standard soil.
Water with rainwater only when the mossy surface feels dry, keeping humidity high but never soggy.
Keep it indoors year-round near a bright east window, as it cannot survive cold UK winter drafts.

Mount it on a cork bark slab with sphagnum moss to mimic its natural epiphytic tree-dwelling habit.

items.name: Lecanopteris deparioides
items.growersTips:
Grow this unusual ant fern in a warm, humid bathroom to mimic its tropical rainforest home.
Plant it in a very chunky orchid bark and sphagnum moss mix to ensure its hollow rhizomes never rot.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the moss feels dry, keeping the air around it misted daily.
Keep it in bright, indirect light but safely away from cold winter draughts and direct radiators.
Check the hollow rhizome chambers regularly for scale insects and wipe them off with soapy water.

items.name: Lecanopteris sinuosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this ant fern in a warm, humid bathroom with bright, indirect light to mimic its tropical home.
Mount it on bark with sphagnum moss rather than potting it in soil to prevent its rhizomes rotting.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the moss feels dry, as UK tap water is too harsh for it.
Keep indoor temperatures above fifteen degrees Celsius year-round to protect it from UK winter drafts.
Check the hollow rhizomes regularly for scale insects, which love to hide in the natural cavities.

items.name: Lecanorchis
items.growersTips:
These are wild parasitic orchids that need specific woodland fungi to survive, so do not buy them.
Never try to pot them up as they lack chlorophyll and cannot grow in standard garden soil mixes.
If you find them in your woodland garden, leave the surrounding leaf litter and soil undisturbed.
Keep the canopy overhead dense and shady to mimic their natural damp UK beech wood habitat.
Avoid using any chemical fungicides nearby as you will kill the underground host mycelium.

items.name: Lecocarpus darwinii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep in early spring under glass with gentle bottom heat.
Grow in free-draining gritty loam to prevent root rot during wet, cool British summer periods.
Water only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry, as this Galapagos native hates wet feet.
Position in your sunniest south-facing border or a container to maximise scarce UK summer warmth.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp spring nights.

items.name: Lecocarpus pinnatifidus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at three millimetres deep under glass in April to combat cool UK spring soil.
Water the base weekly to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to prevent root rot in damp climates.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border to maximise heat for this rare Galapagos native.
Protect young plants from slugs using beer traps during wet British spring and summer nights.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to mimic its natural volcanic island habitat.

items.name: Ledebouria
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Ledebouria indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Plant bulbs shallowly with their tops just peeking out of a gritty, free-draining compost mix.
Let the soil dry out completely between waterings, especially during the cold winter dormancy.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in the UK, which love to chew through these tender bulb roots.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser only during active growth from April to September.

items.name: Ledebouria cooperi
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs shallowly with their necks just peeking out of the grit to prevent winter rotting.
Give them a dry winter rest by moving pots into a cold frame or unheated greenhouse from October.
Mix equal parts John Innes number two and horticultural grit to keep their roots dry and happy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring when those lovely purple-striped leaves first emerge.
Divide the congested clumps right after they finish flowering in late summer to get free plants.

items.name: Ledebouria ovatifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted African hosta indoors by October to protect its tender bulbs from UK winter frosts.
Plant the bulbs shallowly in free-draining gritty compost with the top third showing above soil.
Water only when the soil dries out in summer, then keep it completely dry during winter dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to shred those beautiful spotted emerging leaves.
Set your pot on a south-facing windowsill to get the bright light needed to keep its purple spots vivid.

items.name: Ledebouria revoluta
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs shallowly in the UK, keeping the top third of the bulb above the soil.
Use a very gritty potting mix of half peat-free compost and half horticultural grit to prevent rot.
Bring your pots indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect them from wet UK winter frosts.
Water them only when the soil dries out completely in summer, then stop watering entirely in winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the emerging patterned leaves.

items.name: Ledebouria socialis
items.growersTips:
Bring your leopard lily indoors before October frosts as it cannot survive a damp UK winter outside.
Plant the purple bulbs half-exposed above a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to a monthly splash during dark winter months.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the papery bulb scales and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
Grow them in terracotta pots on a south-facing windowsill to mimic their sunny South African home.

items.name: Legenere
items.growersTips:
Pop this rare wetland beauty in a bog garden or pond edge where its roots stay wet but never drowned.
Sow the tiny seeds on wet, muddy compost in spring without burying them, as they need light to grow.
Keep an eye out for UK pond snails that love to munch on the delicate submerged stems in summer.
Plant it alongside native marsh marigolds to provide some light shade during hot July afternoons.
Divide the clumps gently in early autumn to help your plants survive the damp British winter chill.

items.name: Legousia
items.growersTips:
Sow Legousia seeds shallowly in autumn so UK winter frosts can naturally break their dormancy.
Grow them in gritty, free-draining soil to stop the roots rotting during wet British winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out to mimic their dry Mediterranean home.
Plant them alongside yellow violas or wild pansies to create a stunning, natural cottage look.
Watch out for slugs in early spring, as they love to munch on the tender new emerging shoots.

items.name: Legousia hybrida
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in autumn so the UK winter chill can naturally trigger their germination.
Give them a spot in poor, well-drained chalky soil to mimic their favourite British wildflower downs.
Scatter them near winter wheat or wild poppies to recreate a gorgeous, traditional cornfield look.
Leave the seedlings alone in spring because they hate root disturbance and won't survive transplanting.
Let the faded summer flowers drop seed naturally to guarantee a fresh carpet of blooms next spring.

items.name: Legousia speculum-veneris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they are to flower so the winter cold naturally breaks dormancy.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimeters apart in spring to give their delicate stems room to spread.
Plant them in your poorest, well-drained chalky soil as rich borders make them floppy and weak.
Water only during prolonged dry spells since these British wild annuals hate soggy winter soil.
Sow alongside yellow corn marigolds for a stunning, authentic UK cottage meadow color contrast.

items.name: Leichhardtia
items.growersTips:
Bring your Leichhardtia indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Grow this climber in a loam-based compost with added grit to ensure the fast drainage it needs.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing patio to maximise precious UK summer sunshine.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, then let the pot drain fully.
Provide a sturdy trellis or bamboo teepee in spring to support its vigorous twining growth habit.

items.name: Leichhardtia australis
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted bush tucker vine indoors to a warm windowsill before the first chilly UK frost.
Plant seeds just five millimetres deep in free-draining cactus compost mixed with plenty of grit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry, as this desert native hates soggy roots.
Train the climbing stems onto a small bamboo trellis in spring to support its natural vining habit.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry conservatory air and mist the leaves weekly to deter them.

items.name: Leichhardtia liisae
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender Australian climber indoors by October to protect it from wet, frosty UK winters.
Grow it in a terracotta pot filled with free-draining peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this vine hates having soggy roots in winter.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing window to give it the maximum UK sun it craves.
Provide a sturdy trellis or moss pole early on so its twining stems can climb naturally indoors.

items.name: Leichhardtia micradenia
items.growersTips:
Bring this Aussie native indoors for winter as it cannot survive a wet, freezing UK frost.
Grow it in a gritty, free-draining loam-based compost to prevent root rot during damp UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, keeping it nearly bone dry through the winter.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum possible sunlight in the UK.
Check the leaf joints regularly for mealybugs, which love the dry indoor air this plant prefers.

items.name: Leipoldtia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Leipoldtia in a gritty mix of equal parts potting compost and horticultural sand.
Keep your plants in pots so you can easily move them indoors before the damp UK winter frost hits.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, but stop watering entirely in winter.
Place your pots on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to get maximum British sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the fleshy leaf joints and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Lellingeria

Grow this delicate tropical epiphyte in a hanging basket of damp sphagnum moss and orchid bark.

Keep it in bright, indirect light but shield it from the harsh afternoon sun in UK summers.
Bring it indoors before autumn nights drop below ten degrees to protect it from chilly drafts.

items.name: Lemmaphyllum
items.growersTips:
Mount this creeping fern on cork bark with damp sphagnum moss rather than potting it in heavy UK soil.
Hang your mounted fern in a humid, steamy bathroom to mimic its native Asian rainforest habitat.
Water with harvested UK rainwater to prevent tap water lime buildup on its delicate green fronds.
Keep it indoors year-round as our frosty British winters will quickly kill this tropical creeper.
Propagate in spring by snipping a piece of rhizome with two fronds and pinning it to damp moss.

items.name: Lemmaphyllum microphyllum

Keep this delicate fern damp but never soggy by misting its creeping rhizomes daily in dry weather
Mount it on bark with sphagnum moss rather than potting it in heavy, water-retaining UK garden soil

Position it in dappled shade away from direct afternoon sun to prevent its tiny fronds from burning

items.name: Lemna
items.growersTips:
To keep duckweed from taking over your UK pond, scoop out excess growth weekly with a fine net.
Grow it alongside native hornwort to compete for nutrients and naturally limit duckweed spread.
Overwinter a small jar of it in a frost-free shed so you can restock your pond come spring.
Use it as a nutrient-rich mulch for your vegetable beds after scooping it out of the water.
Keep it in a shaded pond area to slow down its rapid growth during warm British summer days.

items.name: Lemna aequinoctialis
items.growersTips:
Keep it in shallow, still water under five centimeters deep to mimic warm UK greenhouse ponds.
Skim off three-quarters of the crop weekly in summer to stop it choking your pond oxygen levels.
Grow it alongside water lilies which provide the dappled shade this duckweed needs to thrive.
Bring a small starter clump indoors to a sunny windowsill in October to save it from UK frosts.
Feed your pond with organic compost tea in spring to boost the high nitrogen levels it loves.

items.name: Lemna gibba
items.growersTips:
Scoop out excess gibbous duckweed weekly in summer to keep it covering under half your pond surface.
Float this rootless weed in a sunny, still wildlife pond with nutrient-rich water to help it thrive.
Add hornwort as a companion plant to compete for nutrients if this duckweed starts growing too fast.
Watch for water snails in autumn as they naturally graze on the fronds and keep the spread in check.
Compost your excess winter scoopings as they make a fantastic nitrogen-rich mulch for your borders.

items.name: Lemna minor
items.growersTips:
To keep duckweed from taking over your pond, skim it regularly with a fine net to compost the excess.
Grow it in partial shade to prevent rapid summer algae blooms from choking out your floating plants.
Pair it with hornwort to absorb excess nutrients and keep your garden pond water crystal clear.
In autumn, clear decaying leaves from the water surface so your duckweed can photosynthesise well.
Keep it out of fast-moving water features as this plant thrives best in still, calm UK garden ponds.

items.name: Lemna minuta
items.growersTips:
Net this tiny duckweed out of your pond in autumn to stop it rotting and depleting winter oxygen.
Scoop it regularly to keep it from shading out oxygenating pond plants like hornwort or elodea.
Compost your excess duckweed scoopings as they are packed with nitrogen for your vegetable beds.
Grow it alongside water lilies whose floating leaves block the light and naturally curb its spread.
Keep it in a dedicated garden tub if you want to feed it to chickens as a high-protein treat.

items.name: Lemna obscura
items.growersTips:
Pop this tiny duckweed into a sunny garden pond where the water stays still and warm in summer.
Keep it contained in a floating ring or bucket so it does not completely smother your pond plants.
Scoop out excess growth weekly with a fine net during June to keep water oxygen levels high.
Overwinter a small scoopful in an indoor jar of water to protect it from harsh UK winter freezes.
Grow it alongside water lilies which provide the dappled shade this little floater loves in July.

items.name: Lemna perpusilla
items.growersTips:
Float this tiny duckweed in a shallow garden pond or container with zero water current to let it thrive.
Scoop out excess growth weekly in summer to keep it from blocking light to your underwater plants.
Grow it alongside hornwort to help absorb excess nutrients and keep your garden pond water crystal clear.
Bring a small clump indoors to a sunny windowsill jar over winter so it survives the harsh UK frosts.
Keep your pond water slightly acidic to neutral as this little plant hates highly alkaline conditions.

items.name: Lemna trisulca
items.growersTips:
Pop Ivy Duckweed under water as it prefers to float submerged rather than on the pond surface.
Anchor it in a shady UK pond spot using mesh so chilly winter winds do not blow it away.
Thin out the tangled mats in late summer to keep your pond oxygenated and stop it choking.
Pair it with Water Crowfoot to create the perfect submerged shelter for native UK newts.
Watch out for pond snails in spring as they love to munch through these delicate green fronds.

items.name: Lemna turionifera
items.growersTips:
Keep it in a dedicated pond container to stop this vigorous UK native from taking over your garden.
Scoop out excess plants in late summer before they drop winter-hardy turions to the pond bottom.
Grow it alongside hornwort to help shade the water and naturally limit this duckweed's rapid spread.
Use a fine-mesh net weekly during warm British summers to manage its dense, oxygen-blocking mats.
Add it to shallow, sunny wildlife pools to provide instant cover and food for local UK amphibians.

items.name: Lemna valdiviana
items.growersTips:
Keep this tiny duckweed in a sheltered garden pond to stop strong UK winds blowing it all to one side.
Scoop out excess growth weekly in summer with a fine net to keep it from blocking pond light.
Grow it alongside hornwort to help absorb nutrients and prevent unsightly blanket weed takeovers.
Bring a small clump indoors to a sunny windowsill over winter to save it from deep UK pond frosts.
Avoid using tap water to top up its pond because the chlorine can easily yellow these tiny fronds.

items.name: Lemnoideae
items.growersTips:
Pop some native Lemna minor in your garden pond to naturally outcompete ugly summer algae blooms.
Keep your duckweed in check by scooping excess plants out with a fish net to compost every June.
Grow them alongside deeper water lilies whose floating leaves will shade and shelter your duckweed.
Overwinter a small jar of duckweed indoors on a bright windowsill to protect it from deep UK frosts.
Choose a sheltered, still-water pond spot as strong wind and fountain spray will drown these plants.

items.name: Lenophyllum
items.growersTips:
Bring your lenophyllum indoors by October to protect this tender succulent from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant them in a fifty-fifty mix of grit and peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage they need.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to just once a month during damp winter months.
Propagate new plants easily in spring by laying fallen leaves flat on top of damp, gritty compost.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, wiping them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Leontice
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in autumn using a gritty mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep them completely dry during their summer dormant phase by covering them or using a cold frame.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the tender new shoots as they emerge in spring.
Grow them in a terracotta pot so you can easily move them under glass when heavy winter rain hits.
Pair them with dwarf winter irises which share their love for sharp drainage and early spring sun.

items.name: Leontice incerta
items.growersTips:
Plant this tuberous perennial deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to mimic its dry Central Asian home.
Keep it completely dry under a cold frame or alpine house during its summer dormancy to prevent rot.
Water gently from autumn through spring, allowing the compost to dry out slightly between waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the delicate, unique foliage first emerges.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it under cover to protect it from wet UK winters.

items.name: Leontice leontopetalum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tuber deep at fifteen centimetres in sharply draining gritty soil to mimic its dry home.
Keep it bone dry in summer when it goes dormant by sheltering it from heavy UK rain under a cloche.
Grow it in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the early spring blooms from frost damage.
Feed with a high potash liquid fertiliser just as the shoots emerge in late winter to boost blooms.
Use a terracotta pot filled with equal parts loam and grit to ensure the roots never sit in wet.

items.name: Leontopodium
items.growersTips:
Plant your edelweiss in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet British winters without rot.
Keep watering very sparse, letting the soil dry out completely to mimic its dry alpine habitat.
Protect the fuzzy leaves from heavy autumn rain by placing a glass cloche over the crown.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit and limestone chippings into your pots to mimic mountain scree.
Position your pots in the brightest spot possible to keep that signature white woolly coating thick.

items.name: Leopoldia
items.growersTips:
Plant Leopoldia bulbs in autumn at twice their depth in gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Grow these Mediterranean natives in your sunniest, south-facing border or a hot gravel garden.
Water them during active spring growth but keep the soil bone-dry during their summer dormancy.
Leave the faded foliage to die back naturally so the bulb can store energy for next spring.
Watch out for slugs in damp UK springs, protecting the emerging flower spikes with grit barriers.

items.name: Leopoldia gussonei
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn about 8cm deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet winters.
Keep them in your sunniest, south-facing spot or a gravel garden to mimic their native Sicily.
Leave the foliage to die down naturally in summer to feed the bulb for next spring's blooms.
Grow them in terracotta pots of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of horticultural grit.
Water them very sparingly during their summer dormant phase to prevent the bulbs from rotting.

items.name: Lepidagathis
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender perennial in pots so you can bring it inside before the first autumn frost hits.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to help this dry-loving plant survive wet British winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as this species hates having soggy roots.
Give it a light trim in late spring to encourage bushy growth and stop it from getting too leggy.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are overwintering it in your conservatory.

items.name: Lepidagathis cuspidata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Himalayan perennial in a pot so you can easily move it into a greenhouse for winter.
Plant it in free-draining loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Water it deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of soil dry out between waterings.
Prune the stems back by half in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more purple flowers.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering this plant indoors.

items.name: Lepidagathis floribunda
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender perennial in a container so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frost.
Use a very free-draining gritty compost mix to prevent root rot during wet UK winters and springs.
Water sparingly once the top inch of soil dries out, keeping it barely damp during winter dormancy.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its warm origin.
Prune back any leggy stems in early spring to encourage bushy new growth as the weather warms up.

items.name: Lepidagathis keralensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical Indian native indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Grow it in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy peat-free compost to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as wet roots in UK damp will cause rapid rot.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the weak UK sunlight during winter months.
Prune back leggy stems by one-third in late April to encourage a bushier habit for the summer.

items.name: Lepidogyne
items.growersTips:
Try growing this rare orchid in a humid, shaded cold frame to mimic its native tropical forest.
Keep the compost damp but free-draining using a mix of fine bark, perlite, and chopped moss.
Watch out for greenhouse thrips and scale insects which love the tender, evergreen foliage.
Protect it from frost by bringing pots indoors to a warm, bright windowsill before October.
Repot gently in spring only when the roots crowd the pot, as they hate being disturbed.

items.name: Lepidospartum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to get a head start on UK warmth.
Plant your broom-shrubs in sandy, free-draining soil to mimic their native dry wash conditions.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using beer traps to protect the tender stems.
Position these sun-lovers in your hottest, south-facing border to maximise our limited UK sunshine.

items.name: Lepisoreae
items.growersTips:
Grow these epiphytic ferns in a moist, bark-based orchid mix rather than heavy UK garden soil.
Position your ferns in dappled shade under a canopy to mimic their natural woodland home.
Water with harvested rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy during chilly UK winters.
Tuck them into sheltered stone wall crevices where they can easily survive mild British winters.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they love the tender new fronds.

items.name: Lepisorus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lepisorus in a shady crevice or tree fork using leaf mould to mimic its woodland home.
Water these ferns only with rainwater to prevent lime buildup from harsh UK tap water on fronds.
Protect evergreen fronds from drying winter winds by planting them next to a sheltering hart's tongue.
Divide your Lepisorus clumps in mild April weather just as the new spring growth begins to unfurl.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs hiding in the damp fronds during wet British summer evenings.

items.name: Lepisorus thunbergianus
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy Japanese weeper on a mossy, damp stone wall or in a rock crevice to mimic its home.
Mix lots of pine bark and leaf mould into your soil to give its shallow rhizomes the drainage they need.
In dry UK summers, mist the fronds weekly and keep the soil damp but never soggy to prevent browning.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in mild April weather just as new fronds start unfurling for more plants.
Pair it with native British hart's tongue ferns in deep shade where their textures contrast beautifully.

items.name: Leporella
items.growersTips:
Keep this Australian orchid in a cool greenhouse over winter to protect it from wet UK frosts.
Plant the tubers shallowly in a gritty, free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and peat.
Water very sparingly from autumn to spring, allowing the compost to dry out between waterings.
Keep the pots completely dry during their summer dormancy period to prevent the tubers from rotting.
Grow them alongside other winter-green terrestrial orchids to easily manage their dry summer regime.

items.name: Leptadenia
items.growersTips:
Grow Leptadenia in containers with half grit and half compost so you can bring them inside for winter.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, as these desert plants hate wet roots.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated conservatory to get enough UK sunlight.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in late spring using sharp shears to encourage bushier growth.
Check the leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, which love the dry indoor air these plants prefer.

items.name: Leptadenia pyrotechnica
items.growersTips:
Bring this desert shrub indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters.
Grow it in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of gritty sand and peat-free compost.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it and let all excess drain away completely.
Place your pot on the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing patio spot you have all summer.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints when you bring the plant inside for winter.

items.name: Leptarrhena
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic peat-free compost mixed with grit to mimic Scottish highland bog conditions.
Position in partial shade to protect the evergreen leaves from scorching during dry UK summer heat.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH this alpine needs.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early autumn before the first frost wet weather sets in.
Watch for vine weevil larvae in container-grown plants during damp British autumn and winter months.

items.name: Leptarrhena pyrolifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil mimicking UK bog gardens using a mix of peat-free compost and sand
Position in partial shade to prevent the evergreen leathery foliage from scorching in midday sun
Water frequently during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge
Grow alongside Astilbe or Primula japonica in a damp woodland border for compatible moisture needs

items.name: Leptoceras
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a gritty, free-draining compost mix of bark, perlite and loam.
Keep the compost damp through winter but let it dry out completely once the leaves die back.
Protect these delicate tubers from hard UK frosts by keeping them in a cold greenhouse or frame.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early autumn when the fresh, single leaves begin to emerge.
Repot your tubers during their summer dormant phase, planting them about three centimeters deep.

items.name: Leptolobieae
items.growersTips:
Sow these annual seeds indoors in early April at a depth of one centimetre to beat the UK spring chill.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering them gently at the base every third day.
Watch out for young slugs in May; protect fresh shoots with beer traps or copper tape around pots.
Mix plenty of grit into your garden soil to ensure the excellent drainage these annuals crave.
Plant them alongside French marigolds to naturally deter aphids and boost your garden's colour.

items.name: Leptorhynchos
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect them from late UK frosts before planting.
Water your plants at the base only when the top inch of soil feels completely dry to prevent rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs as they love chewing the young shoots.
Mix plenty of grit into your heavy UK clay soil to give these plants the sharp drainage they need.
Plant them next to native bluebells or sea thrift to create a beautiful, well-drained gravel bed.

items.name: Lessingia arachnoidea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect this rare Californian native from late UK frosts.
Plant out in May into the sharpest draining, gritty soil you can manage to prevent winter root rot.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, as this drought-lover hates the damp British summer humidity.
Position in your hottest, most south-facing border to mimic its sunny chaparral home environment.
Watch closely for slugs in spring, as they find the young, woolly foliage absolutely irresistible.

items.name: Lessingia germanorum
items.growersTips:
Sow these San Francisco native seeds indoors in early spring to beat the cool, wet UK weather.
Plant them in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to mimic their natural coastal dune habitat.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot of your garden to help them thrive in the British summer.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely to prevent root rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the young, tender seedlings in damp springs.

items.name: Lessingia glandulifera
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the surface of sandy, well-drained soil in April as they need light to germinate.
Keep young seedlings on a sunny windowsill and only water when the top two inches of compost dry out.
Plant them out in June alongside hardy succulents or thyme to match their extreme drought tolerance.
Watch out for slugs during wet UK summers, so protect young stems with grit barriers or beer traps.
Deadhead the yellow button flowers in late August to encourage a second flush before the autumn frost.

items.name: Lessingia hololeuca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect this woolly Californian from wet UK springs.
Plant out in late May in your sunniest gravel garden or raised bed to ensure rapid drainage.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as this drought-lover rots easily in damp British soil.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and more purple blooms.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Lessingia lemmonii
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect them from damp UK frosts.
Grow them in gritty, fast-draining soil because wet winter ground will rot their roots instantly.
Water them only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, as they hate soggy British summer days.
Plant them alongside drought-tolerant thyme or sedum to create a beautifully dry, gravel-garden look.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with organic wool pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Lessingia leptoclada
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect this California native from cold UK spring rain.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest border using gritty, free-draining soil to avoid rot.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells as this annual hates soggy British soil around its roots.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more purple-pink autumn flowers.
Collect the fluffy seed heads in October to store indoors for sowing next spring before frosts hit.

items.name: Lessingia micradenia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to protect them from the unpredictable UK wet.
Plant these in your poorest, sharpest draining sandy soil as they hate sitting in damp winter clay.
Position them in your absolute sunniest spot to mimic their native dry California chaparral home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between your waterings.
Watch out for slugs when seedlings are young, as damp British springs make them prime targets.

items.name: Lessingia nemaclada
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in April, as they need light to trigger germination.
Keep your pots on a sunny windowsill because this California native needs all the warmth it can get.
Water only when the top inch of soil is bone dry to prevent root rot in our damp UK climate.
Mix plenty of grit into your multi-purpose compost to mimic the sandy, free-draining soils it loves.
Watch out for slugs and snails early on, as they will quickly devour the delicate young seedlings.

items.name: Lessingia tenuis
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in early spring under glass because they need warmth to germinate in our cool climate.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest border using grit to ensure the soil drains super fast.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry as they easily rot in damp UK weather.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on young shoots during those wet British spring nights.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums or thymes which love the same dry, sunny conditions in your garden.

items.name: Lessingia virgata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect this rare Californian annual from UK spring frost.
Plant them out in late May in your poorest, sharpest-draining soil to mimic their native gravelly home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely to prevent root rot in wet summers.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, which absolutely love devouring the tender young shoots.
Collect the tiny seeds in autumn to sow next year, as this plant is hard to find in UK garden centres.

items.name: Leucaena
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in April using deep pots to protect their long taproots before planting out.
Soak the hard seeds in hot water for twenty-four hours to break dormancy before sowing.
Plant them in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic the warmth they need to thrive.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, drought-tolerant roots.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps during wet UK spring nights.

items.name: Leucaena diversifolia
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in early spring using deep pots to protect their long, sensitive taproots.
Soak the hard seeds in warm water for twenty-four hours before sowing to help them germinate.
Plant them out in May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their warm native climate.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily to encourage the roots to search deep into the soil.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape during damp UK nights.

items.name: Leucaena greggii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre to give this sun-lover a head start.
Plant it out in late May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic its warm native climate.
Grow this tender shrub in a container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply but infrequently, letting the gritty soil dry out fully between drinks to prevent rot.
Feed monthly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser through summer to encourage those yellow blooms.

items.name: Leucaena retusa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using a heated propagator to boost warmth.
Grow this tender plant in a terracotta pot filled with gritty, free-draining loam-based compost.
Water deeply only when the top five centimeters of soil feels completely dry to prevent root rot.
Place your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum summer heat in our cool climate.
Bring the pot inside a heated greenhouse or conservatory by October before the first autumn frost.

items.name: Leucaena salvadorensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April indoors at 2cm deep after soaking them in warm water overnight to boost sprouting.
Grow this tender tree in a large pot so you can easily wheel it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top soil dry out completely before watering again.
Feed with a low-nitrogen liquid fertiliser monthly in summer to support foliage without leggy growth.
Check the leaf axils weekly for mealybugs, which love the warm indoor winter spots this plant needs.

items.name: Leucanthemum ×superbum
items.growersTips:
Divide clumps every three springs to maintain vigour and prevent the centre of the plant dying out.
Deadhead spent blooms down to the next lateral bud to trigger a second flush of late summer flowers.
Plant in free-draining soil with grit to prevent winter wet from rotting the crown in UK winters.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in spring, keeping it clear of the emerging stems.
Watch for aphids and earwigs on young buds, especially during damp British spring mornings.

items.name: Leucanthemum heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass, barely covering them with a light sprinkle of grit.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during dry spells to prevent premature seeding.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimeters to encourage a much bushier habit.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly through summer to prolong the flowering display right into the autumn.
Watch out for aphids on young shoots and blast them off with a gentle spray from your garden hose.

items.name: Leucanthemum ircutianum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or early spring, barely covering them with a fine layer of grit.
Keep young plants damp but not soggy to prevent damping off in our cool, wet UK spring weather.
Watch out for leaf miners in early summer, pinching off any mined leaves to keep the foliage clean.
Deadhead regularly through summer to encourage fresh blooms and prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Sow alongside red campion and ragged robin for a classic, wildlife-friendly British meadow look.

items.name: Leucanthemum maximum
items.growersTips:
Plant Shasta daisies in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK winters.
Divide your clumps every three years in early spring to keep the blooms vigorous and healthy.
Deadhead faded flowers down to the next lateral bud to trigger a second flush of late summer blooms.
Watch out for aphids and blackfly on the young spring shoots and wash them off with a garden hose.
Add a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in autumn to protect the crown from heavy UK frosts.

items.name: Leucanthemum paludosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in trays indoors in March or direct outdoors in May at a shallow depth of just two millimetres.
Plant them in free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings are ten centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as these daisy-like annuals hate soggy roots.
Deadhead spent flowers weekly through summer to keep the blooms coming right up until the first frost.

items.name: Leucanthemum rotundifolium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under cover to get a head start on the short UK summer.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in damp British weather.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly through summer to encourage a continuous display of fresh flowers.
Watch out for slugs and snails which absolutely love devouring the young spring foliage.
Mix plenty of grit into heavy clay soils to improve drainage before planting them out.

items.name: Leucanthemum vulgare
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn at a depth of two millimetres to mimic natural UK self-seeding cycles.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil to prevent excessive floppy vegetative growth.
Cut back faded stems to ground level in late summer to trigger a second flush of autumn flowers.
Divide established clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flowering.
Plant alongside red campion and yellow rattle in wildflower patches to balance competitive grasses.

items.name: Leucocasia gigantea
items.growersTips:
Plant your massive tuber shallowly in spring, just below the soil surface in a nice deep pot.
Keep this thirsty giant boggy with daily watering in summer, but dry it out completely in winter.
Bring the pot indoors before the first autumn frost, as UK winters will turn the tuber to mush.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil to feed its appetite for massive elephant ears.
Watch out for red spider mites when you bring the plant inside your warm conservatory for winter.

items.name: Leucochloron
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early March to give this tender annual a long, warm UK growing season.
Plant them out in late May after the last frosts in a sunny spot with well-draining, sandy soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, strong roots.
Pinch out the growing tips when the young plants are six inches tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Keep an eye out for slugs during wet British summers by using organic wool pellets around the stems.

items.name: Leucochrysum
items.growersTips:
Sow your seeds indoors in March on top of the compost as they need light to germinate in UK spring.
Plant them out in May in your sunniest gravel garden or raised bed to ensure the sharpest drainage.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry because they hate soggy British winter.
Pinch out the growing tips when they are ten centimetres tall to encourage lots of papery flowers.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK May nights.

items.name: Leucocrinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this sand lily in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Grow it in your sunniest south-facing rockery or a cold greenhouse to mimic its dry native home.
Plant the delicate fleshy roots about five centimetres deep in autumn, handling them very gently.
Water only when active growth shows in spring, then keep it completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect the early spring buds from slugs and snails which love to feast on the low-lying flowers.

items.name: Leucocrinum montanum
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-rich soil to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun in a raised bed or rockery to mimic its native dry mountain habitat.
Plant the fleshy roots five centimetres deep in autumn while the plant is dormant.
Withhold all watering during its summer dormant phase to prevent the crown from rotting.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers.

items.name: Leucogenes
items.growersTips:
Grow these alpine beauties in a gritty, free-draining compost mix to survive wet UK winters.
Water them from below or use a gravel mulch to keep the woolly foliage dry and prevent rot.
Protect your plants under a cold frame or alpine house from November to March to shield from rain.
Plant them alongside dwarf conifers or sempervivums in a sunny rock garden for great company.
Trim back the spent flower heads in late summer to keep the silver rosettes neat and compact.

items.name: Leucophyta
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK autumns.
Water sparingly, allowing the top two inches of compost to dry completely between drinks.
Position in full south-facing sun to maintain the intense silver foliage colour.
Trim lightly in midsummer to keep the cushion shape compact and prevent leggy growth.
Pair with purple-flowered heathers in autumn containers for a striking colour contrast.

items.name: Leucospora
items.growersTips:
Plant your Leucospora in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position this sun-lover in your brightest south-facing spot to mimic its native limestone glades.
Water deeply but let the soil dry out completely between waterings to prevent root issues.
Trim back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to keep its compact, mounded shape tidy.
Sow seeds in cold frames during early spring so natural UK temperature drops help them germinate.

items.name: Leysera
items.growersTips:
Sow these sun-loving annuals indoors in March, barely covering the tiny seeds with fine grit.
Plant them out in May in your sandiest, sharpest-draining soil to survive wet British summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as they hate soggy roots in our climate.
Position them next to Mediterranean herbs like thyme to match their strict dry-soil needs.
Deadhead the daisy-like yellow blooms weekly through August to keep new flowers coming.

items.name: Libertia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Libertia bulbs in spring five inches deep in free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Water your young Libertia weekly during dry UK summers until its root system is fully established.
Cut back any dead, tatty leaves right to the base in mid-spring to keep the clump looking fresh.
Grow Libertia grandiflora alongside purple heucheras to create a stunning foliage colour contrast.
Protect the crown with a thick layer of autumn mulch to shield it from wet and freezing UK winters.

items.name: Libertia chilensis
items.growersTips:
Plant your Libertia bulbs about eight centimetres deep in autumn so they survive chilly UK winters.
Tuck them into gritty, well-draining soil to stop the bulbs rotting during wet British winters.
Give them a good soak once a week during their first dry summer, then leave them to do their thing.
Snip away any tatty, browned leaves right at the base in mid-spring to keep them looking tidy.
Grow them alongside purple heucheras to make those lovely white, star-like flowers really pop.

items.name: Libertia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand iris in spring at the same depth it was in its pot to help it settle fast.
Give it a spot in full sun or light shade with free-draining soil so the roots do not rot in winter.
Snip off faded flower stems in late summer to keep it neat and prevent too many self-sown seedlings.
Pull away dead, tatty outer leaves by hand in spring to tidy the clump without damaging new growth.
Divide congested clumps in spring every few years to boost flowering and get free plants for friends.

items.name: Libertia paniculata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean iris five inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil during the mild spring days.
Water your young plants weekly in summer, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh UK winter winds with a thick mulch of bark around the base.
Snip off faded flower stems in late summer to keep the plant tidy and prevent unwanted self-seeding.
Divide overcrowded clumps in spring to propagate new plants and keep the parent bulb vigorous.

items.name: Libertia peregrinans
items.growersTips:
Plant your orange Libertia in full sun to get the brightest coppery foliage colour in UK gardens.
Grow this New Zealand iris in free-draining sandy soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Slightly bury the rhizomes just below the soil surface rather than planting them deeply like bulbs.
Comb through the grassy clumps with gloved hands in spring to pull out dead leaves and tidy them up.
Water your newly planted Libertia weekly during its first UK summer to help the roots establish.

items.name: Libertia pulchella
items.growersTips:
Plant this little Kiwi iris in a sheltered, damp, shady spot to mimic its native forest home.
Mix lots of leaf mould or compost into acidic soil to keep its delicate, shallow roots happy.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry British summer spells.
Mulch the crown with bark in autumn to protect it from harsh UK frosts and freezing winter winds.
Gently divide the clumps in spring after the last frost to propagate and refresh the plant.

items.name: Libidibia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimeters using bottom heat to overcome UK cold.
Plant out in June after the last frost in a south-facing border with free-draining sandy soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the taproot system.
Pinch out the growing tips in early July to encourage a bushier habit and more summer flowers.
Watch for glasshouse red spider mite when starting young plants under glass in early spring.

items.name: Libocedrus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Libocedrus in deep, moist but well-drained acidic soil to mimic its native rainy slopes.
Shelter young trees from cold drying UK winds by planting them near a south or west-facing wall.
Water your tree deeply once a week during dry British summers until its root system is established.
Prune lightly in late spring only to remove dead wood, as they do not regenerate well from old wood.
Watch out for scale insects and treat them early with organic insecticidal soap in mid-summer.

items.name: Libocedrus bidwillii
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand native in a sheltered spot to protect its young foliage from cold UK winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.
Grow it in acidic to neutral soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles or leaf mould first.
No regular pruning is needed, just gently snip away any frost-damaged tips in late spring.
Watch out for phytophthora root rot by avoiding heavy, waterlogged clay soils in your garden.

items.name: Libocedrus plumosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this gorgeous Kiwi native in a sheltered spot away from drying, cold UK winter winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.
Grow it in acidic to neutral soil, mixing in plenty of composted bark before you plant it.
No pruning is needed, just gently snip away any frost-damaged tips in late spring after frosts pass.
Watch out for scale insects and protect young trees with fleece during exceptionally hard freezes.

items.name: Ligeophila
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical orchid in a warm conservatory or terrarium to shield it from chilly UK winters.
Use a moist, airy bark and sphagnum moss mix to mimic its natural damp rainforest floor habitat.
Water with tepid rainwater rather than tap water to keep the sensitive roots damp but never soggy.
Place it in bright, indirect light near a north window to prevent the delicate leaves from burning.
Mist the foliage daily to boost humidity, especially when indoor central heating dries the air.

items.name: Lilieae
items.growersTips:
Plant Lilium bulbs in autumn at three times their depth to protect them from winter frost and wind.
Apply organic mulch in spring to keep roots cool and damp while keeping the foliage in UK sun.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their grubs from spring onwards to prevent total defoliation.
Grow lilies in pots of ericaceous compost if your UK garden soil is alkaline to prevent yellowing.
Cut spent flower stems back to the base only in autumn after the foliage has turned completely brown.

items.name: Lilioideae
items.growersTips:
Plant Lilium bulbs in autumn at three times their depth in well-drained, acidic soil to avoid rot.
Handpick bright red lily beetles and their sticky larvae from April onwards to prevent defoliation.
Water container-grown lilies deeply from the base, keeping the compost moist but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in winter to protect Fritillaria bulbs from hard UK frosts.
Stake tall Cardiocrinum stems early in spring using bamboo canes to withstand strong UK winds.

items.name: Lilium
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs at three times their depth in acidic soil for Asiatic and alkaline for Madonna lilies.
Water deeply at the base in early morning to prevent botrytis blight in damp UK summer weather.
Handpick red lily beetles and their grubs from April onwards to protect emerging spring foliage.
Keep lily pots in a sheltered spot over wet UK winters to prevent the bulbs from rotting in cold mud.
Cut stems back to ground level only in autumn after the foliage has turned completely yellow.

items.name: Lilium albanicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Balkan native in sharply draining, gritty, alkaline soil to mimic its mountain home.
Set the bulbs 10cm deep in autumn in a spot that gets morning sun but stays cool and shaded later.
Keep watering minimal in summer as this lily hates soggy soil and is highly prone to bulb rot.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from scarlet lily beetles by hand-picking them off early on.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to manage UK winter wet easily.

items.name: Lilium amabile
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs three times their depth in gritty, acidic soil to keep their roots cool and damp.
Give them a mulch of composted pine needles in autumn to mimic their native Korean woodland home.
Watch out for scarlet lily beetles in spring, squishing them by hand before they ruin the buds.
Plant them among low-growing ferns to shade the soil while letting the stems reach the UK sun.
Water them regularly during dry spring spells, but keep them completely dry during the winter.

items.name: Lilium auratum
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep pots or borders at least 15 to 20cm deep in ericaceous compost as they are lime-haters.
Provide shade at the roots using low-growing companion plants while keeping the flower heads in sun.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the acidic soil conditions they require to thrive.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in autumn to protect the bulbs from wet UK winter rot.
Watch for red lily beetles from spring onwards, removing them and their larvae by hand immediately.

items.name: Lilium bakerianum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs deep at fifteen centimetres in well-drained, gritty, acidic soil to mimic Tibet.
Keep them moist during active spring growth but bone dry in winter by using a cold frame or cloche.
Guard the emerging spring shoots diligently from red lily beetles and slugs using organic barriers.
Grow them in pots of ericaceous compost so you can easily move them under cover during wet winters.
Provide dappled shade for their roots while letting the delicate bell-shaped flowers reach the sun.

items.name: Lilium bolanderi
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in gritty, ericaceous soil to mimic its native habitat.
Position in partial shade with its roots kept cool and damp while its head reaches into the sun.
