Plant bulbs 15-20cm deep in late autumn to allow stem roots to develop and anchor the tall stems.
Grow in ericaceous compost or acidic soil as this species cannot tolerate lime or alkaline conditions.
Position in partial shade with the base shaded by low shrubs to mimic its native woodland edge.
Watch for red lily beetles from spring onwards and hand-pick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active summer growing season.

items.name: Lilium superbum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 15cm in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Position in a sheltered spot with the roots in cool shade and the flower heads in full morning sun.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick annual mulch of leafmould or composted pine needles in spring to maintain soil acidity.
Handpick red lily beetles and their grubs daily from April onwards to prevent total defoliation.

items.name: Lilium tsingtauense
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland lily in dappled shade to mimic its native forest home and prevent leaf scorch.
Plant bulbs deep at fifteen centimetres in humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil that drains freely.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active spring and summer growth.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Leave the stems to die back naturally in autumn to return vital nutrients to the bulb for winter.

items.name: Lilium wallichianum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Himalayan beauty deep, at least 20cm down, in gritty soil to protect bulbs from UK frosts.
Keep it damp during the summer growing season but virtually bone dry in winter to prevent bulb rot.
Grow it in a container so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for winter.
Watch out for red lily beetles from early spring and pick them off immediately to save the foliage.
Provide dappled shade and acidic to neutral leaf-mould enriched soil to mimic its woodland home.

items.name: Lilium washingtonianum
items.growersTips:
Plant the bulbs deep at twenty centimetres in extremely free-draining, gritty, neutral to acid soil.
Position in dappled shade to mimic woodland edges, keeping the bulb cool and the flowers in sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep the soil almost dry during its dormant late summer period.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and red lily beetles using organic nematodes or grit.
Avoid moving established bulbs as this species resents root disturbance and takes years to recover.

items.name: Limbarda
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining sandy loam during early April
Water sparingly once a week only when the top five centimetres of soil has dried out completely
Position pots in full south-facing sun to mimic coastal cliffs and prevent damp winter root rot
Sow alongside sea lavender in gravel gardens to match natural salt-tolerant coastal conditions
Monitor young spring shoots closely for slug damage during typical wet UK April weather spells

items.name: Limnophila
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic beauty in a heated indoor tank or a very sheltered, sunny UK garden pond in summer.
Plant the stems in nutrient-rich pond soil or aquatic compost, burying the bottom two nodes deeply.
Pinch out the growing tips regularly during spring to encourage a bushier, more attractive habit.
Watch out for pond snails and aphids on the emergent leaves, washing them off with a gentle spray.
Propagate your plants easily by taking stem cuttings and pushing them directly into wet substrate.

items.name: Limnophila aquatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical aquatic herb in a heated indoor aquarium as it cannot survive UK winter cold.
Plant stems two inches deep in nutrient-rich aquatic soil capped with gravel to prevent floating.
Provide intense LED lighting for ten hours daily to prevent the lower leaves from rotting away.
Prune the fast-growing stem tops weekly in summer using sharp aquascaping scissors to promote bushiness.
Inject carbon dioxide gas into the water to maintain the vibrant lime-green colour of the foliage.

items.name: Limnophila aromatica
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender herb in a heated greenhouse or indoor windowsill as it cannot survive UK winters.
Plant in a soil mix of acidic peat and sand kept constantly wet to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Provide at least six hours of direct supplemental grow lighting to maintain its purple leaf colour.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and prevent leggy growth.
Watch for aphids on new shoots during humid summer months and wash them off with a gentle water spray.

items.name: Limnophila repens
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated indoor aquarium or warm greenhouse pond as this tropical herb cannot survive UK frost
Plant stems individually two centimetres deep in nutrient-rich aquatic soil using long tweezers
Prune the fast-growing stem tops weekly in summer to encourage bushy lateral growth and red leaves
Maintain high light levels and inject carbon dioxide to prevent the lower leaves from rotting away
Pair with slow-growing Cryptocoryne species to balance the tank layout and prevent nutrient spikes

items.name: Limnophila sessiliflora
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic herb submerged in a heated indoor aquarium as it cannot survive UK winter cold.
Plant stems individually spaced two centimeters apart in nutrient-rich aquarium soil to prevent rot.
Prune the fast-growing stems weekly from the top to encourage bushy lateral growth in your tank.
Provide high light and dose liquid carbon to prevent the delicate whorled leaves from shedding.
Keep water temperature between twenty and twenty-eight degrees Celsius using an aquarium heater.

items.name: Limodorum
items.growersTips:
Since violet limodore is a parasitic orchid, plant it near pine or oak roots to feed its mycelium.
Keep your soil chalky, dry, and alkaline, as this wild orchid hates rich, wet, or acidic garden loam.
Never prune or cut back the stems; let them die down naturally to return nutrients to the fungus.
Watch out for slugs eating the emerging purple shoots in spring, so use organic grit around them.
Do not move or repot this orchid once settled, as disturbing the root fungus will kill the plant.

items.name: Linaria
items.growersTips:
Plant Linaria purpurea seeds just on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate.
Grow these in poor, sharply draining UK soil to stop them getting floppy and falling over.
Cut the spent flower spikes right back to the base in August to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp UK summers by spacing plants to keep the air flowing freely.
Divide your established clumps every three years in early spring to keep the plants vigorous.

items.name: Linaria algarviana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in April directly into poor, well-drained soil to prevent floppy, weak stems.
Position in full sun and shelter from cold winds to mimic its native warm Portuguese coast.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, as this annual is highly susceptible to rot.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring seedlings, protecting them with grit or beer traps.
Leave spent flower spikes in autumn to self-seed naturally for a display the following spring.

items.name: Linaria alpina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the surface of gritty, sharply draining soil to allow winter cold to break dormancy.
Position in full sun in a scree garden or wall crevice to mimic its native alpine gravel habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in the damp UK climate.
Leave faded flowers intact to allow the plant to self-seed freely and persist in your garden.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Linaria amethystea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in autumn or early spring directly into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun.
Cover seeds with just a very fine dusting of sharp sand as they need light to trigger germination.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK spring weather.
Leave spent flower spikes in late summer to allow this annual to self-seed naturally for next year.
Grow alongside thyme or sedums in gravel gardens to provide the sharp drainage this species craves.

items.name: Linaria arenaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring in a gritty, free-draining sandy loam to mimic coastal dunes.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres and do not cover them, as they require light to germinate.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden, such as a south-facing gravel bed or rockery.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spells and avoid any watering once the plants are established.
Leave the faded flower spikes intact at the end of summer to allow self-seeding for next year.

items.name: Linaria bipartita
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly outdoors in April at a depth of three millimetres in a sunny, well-drained spot.
Water seedlings lightly twice a week until established, then only during prolonged dry UK summers.
Shear back the stems by half after the first flush of flowers in July to encourage a second bloom.
Sow alongside Nigella damascena to provide physical support for the slender, floppy Linaria stems.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Linaria dalmatica
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they require light to germinate.
Cut flower spikes to the base in August to prevent aggressive self-seeding in your garden.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts once the deep taproot is established.
Grow alongside Origanum or Stachys byzantina which thrive in the same dry, sunny borders.

items.name: Linaria genistifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or spring just pressing them into free-draining gritty soil for light.
Water sparingly only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives in dry UK gravel gardens.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Plant alongside companion plants like Thymus or Sedum that share its love for poor alkaline soils.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots especially during wet UK spring weather.

items.name: Linaria maroccana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly outdoors in April or May just 2mm deep as they need light to germinate in UK soil.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil to prevent floppy stems in wet UK summers.
Water seedlings lightly until established then leave to tolerate dry spells without extra watering.
Shear back the faded stems by half in midsummer to encourage a second flush of blooms by autumn.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Linaria purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn onto well-drained grit to let UK winter cold trigger germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent floppy stems and encourage self-seeding in gravel.
Cut flower spikes to the base in August to prompt a second flush and control prolific self-seeding.
Plant alongside dry-loving UK partners like Nepeta or Lavender in full sun to prevent root rot.
Watch for rosemary beetle damage in dry summers and hand-pick them off the purple flower spikes.

items.name: Linaria repens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in autumn to allow winter cold to trigger germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky soil to prevent the plant from flopping and becoming invasive.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK springs, then leave established plants to rely on rainfall.
Cut back faded flower spikes in August to prevent excessive self-seeding in small cottage gardens.
Plant alongside wild marjoram or thyme in sunny gravel borders to support native UK pollinators.

items.name: Linaria ricardoi
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic its native dry Mediterranean habitat.
Position in the sunniest, south-facing spot of your UK garden to maximize summer flowering potential.
Water sparingly only during prolonged dry spells, as this annual is highly prone to root rot in wet.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Allow the seed heads to dry on the plant in late summer to encourage self-seeding for next year.

items.name: Linaria triornithophora
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at the same depth as the pot in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings.
Cut back the spent flowering stems to ground level in autumn to encourage fresh basal growth.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flowering.

items.name: Linaria triphylla
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in April directly into poor, well-drained soil to prevent floppy, weak growth.
Water seedlings sparingly, only during dry spells, as this Mediterranean native hates wet roots.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with pet-safe organic grit.
Deadhead spent flower spikes weekly in summer to prolong the blooming season into early autumn.
Plant alongside thyme or sedums in gravel gardens to match its preference for dry, sunny spots.

items.name: Linaria tristis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April by pressing them into a gritty, free-draining soil mix without covering.
Water seedlings sparingly only during dry spells to prevent root rot in damp UK spring weather.
Watch for slugs and snails on young shoots during wet British nights and protect with organic grit.
Plant alongside thyme or sedum in gravel gardens to provide the sharp drainage this species craves.
Deadhead spent blooms in midsummer to encourage a second flush of flowers before the autumn frosts.

items.name: Linaria vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or early spring directly into poor, well-drained sandy or gravelly soil.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry UK spells, then leave established plants to thrive on rainfall.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in small gardens.
Grow alongside wild marjoram or thyme in sunny borders to attract native UK pollinators and bees.
Watch for linaria pug moth caterpillars in summer and tolerate them as they are harmless to plants.

items.name: Lindelofia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lindelofia in gritty, well-drained soil to help it survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position this Himalayan native in partial shade so our strong summer afternoon sun does not scorch it.
Keep watering consistent during dry spring spells to help its deep taproot establish in your garden.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer to encourage a neat shape and potential second flush.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp spring weather, as they love targeting the fresh new shoots.

items.name: Lindmania holstii
items.growersTips:
Bring this Venezuelan bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining peat-free orchid compost mix to prevent root rot in our damp air.
Water the central rosette with rainwater rather than tap water to avoid lime buildup on the leaves.
Position your pot on a bright south-facing windowsill to mimic its native high-altitude sunshine.
Propagate by carefully slicing off the offsets with a sharp knife once they reach a third of its size.

items.name: Lindmania navioides
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare bromeliad in a gritty, free-draining acidic mix of bark and perlite to avoid rot.
Keep it in a bright conservatory or greenhouse as it will not survive a wet, frosty UK winter.
Water the soil directly rather than the central rosette, letting it dry out between waterings.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf crevices during dry summer spells indoors.
Propagate by carefully detaching the offsets at the base in spring using a sharp, clean knife.

items.name: Lipochaeta
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in March to give these Hawaiian natives enough warmth before planting out.
Sow the seeds just two millimetres deep in a free-draining sandy compost mix to prevent rotting.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry as they hate soggy British winter wetness.
Plant them alongside French marigolds to help deter aphids which love their tender summer growth.
Pinch out the growing tips in late May to encourage a much bushier habit and more yellow blooms.
items.description: Lipochaeta, common name nehe, is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae that is endemic to Hawaii.

items.name: Liriodendron
items.growersTips:
Plant Chinese tulip shrub chinense in fertile deep loam sheltered from cold drying UK easterly winds
Water young shrubs deeply once a week during dry British summers to establish a deep root system
Prune Liriodendron only in late winter to avoid sap bleeding and preserve its natural shape
Grow in acidic to neutral soil as chalky UK soils cause leaf yellowing and stunt shrub growth
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture in sandy UK garden soils

items.name: Liriodendron chinense
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep moisture-retentive acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered spot to mimic woodland edges
Water young trees deeply once a week during dry UK summers to establish the sensitive root system
Prune only in late winter to remove damaged stems before the sap rises to prevent bleeding wounds
Protect young spring foliage from late frosts using horticultural fleece in colder northern UK regions
Position away from exposed windy corners to prevent the large characteristic leaves from shredding

items.name: Liriodendron tulipifera
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep fertile moisture-retentive acidic to neutral soil in a sheltered sun-drenched spot.
Water young trees deeply every week during dry UK summers until their root systems are established.
Prune only in winter to remove dead wood as spring pruning causes sap to bleed heavily and weaken.
Protect the brittle young branches from strong prevailing winds by staking securely at planting.
Watch for aphids on new spring growth and treat immediately to prevent disfiguring sooty mould.

items.name: Lithodora
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with grit added to the planting hole to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in July to keep the growth compact and prevent leggy stems.
Water only during prolonged dry summer spells once established as they prefer drought to damp soil.
Position in full sun to maximise the intensity of the blue flowers and prevent the foliage thinning.
Protect young plants from slugs in damp UK springs using organic grit barriers around the base.

items.name: Lithodora fruticosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil or a raised bed to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native warm Mediterranean climate.
Prune lightly in late summer after flowering to prevent the woody stems from becoming leggy.
Water newly planted shrubs sparingly and only during prolonged dry spells once established.
Propagate by taking semi-ripe cuttings in midsummer to safeguard against severe winter losses.

items.name: Lithophragma
items.growersTips:
Plant woodland stars in humus-rich, well-drained soil that mimics a damp British deciduous forest.
Sow bulbils just two centimetres deep in autumn to ensure they establish before the winter frosts.
Water weekly during spring growth but keep soil completely dry during their dormant summer phase.
Shed light shade over them by planting alongside native UK ferns and primroses in a woodland border.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Lithophragma affine
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in autumn three centimetres deep in humus-rich soil that drains rapidly during winter
Position under deciduous shrubs to mimic woodland shade and prevent summer baking during dormancy
Water weekly during spring growth but stop completely in summer when the foliage naturally dies back
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps
Combine with native wood anemones or primroses which share its preference for damp spring soil

items.name: Lithophragma cymbalaria
items.growersTips:
Plant bulblets 3cm deep in autumn in well-drained, gritty loam to mimic its native woodland habitat.
Water weekly in spring during active growth, then stop watering completely as it goes dormant in July.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect delicate white blooms from midday sun.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames in autumn, allowing natural UK winter chills to trigger germination.
Guard emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Lithophragma glabrum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulblets 3cm deep in autumn in sharply draining gritty soil to mimic their native rocky slopes.
Water sparingly in spring, then keep completely dry during their summer dormancy to prevent bulb rot.
Sow in UK cold frames in autumn as seeds require winter chilling to break dormancy and germinate.
Grow in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to replicate their natural woodland edge habitat in UK.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Lithophragma heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulblets 3cm deep in autumn in gritty, well-drained soil under deciduous shrubs or trees.
Water only during dry spring spells, then keep the soil completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Do not prune the dying summer foliage; let it wither naturally to feed the underground bulbils.
Associate with native UK woodlanders like Primula vulgaris in partial shade to mimic its habitat.

items.name: Lithophragma maximum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral loam in partial shade to mimic its woodland edge.
Sow seeds shallowly in cold frames during autumn to benefit from natural UK winter stratifying.
Water consistently during spring growth but reduce watering in summer when the plant goes dormant.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth appears to propagate successfully.

items.name: Lithophragma parviflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a gritty, free-draining loam mix to mimic its native dry woodland habitat.
Sow bulbils or seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in cold frames during autumn.
Water moderately in spring but keep almost entirely dry during its summer dormant period.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect from intense midday summer sun.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers and protect emerging spring foliage from slugs.

items.name: Lithophragma tenellum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth of 5cm in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter bulb rot.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat.
Water only during spring growth, then keep the soil almost entirely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or physical barriers.
Propagate by carefully separating the tiny bulbils from the parent plant in late summer.

items.name: Lithops
items.growersTips:
Plant them deep in 90 percent grit or pumice so only their flat tops peep out of the soil.
Only water them from May to September when they shrivel, keeping them bone dry all winter.
Place them on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic the strong South African sun.
Never water when they are splitting and growing new leaves, as the old ones must dry up.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in their root systems during the damp UK autumn.

items.name: Lithops amicorum
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lithops amicorum in seventy percent coarse grit to thirty percent soil to stop UK rot.
Keep them completely dry from October to April while they absorb their old leaves in winter.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sun.
Only water when the top window of the succulent wrinkles slightly during their summer growth.
Never mist them because the damp British air will quickly cause these desert plants to turn to mush.

items.name: Lithops aucampiae
items.growersTips:
Use a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent soil to stop rot in damp UK winters.
Only water when the top flat face wrinkles, usually from May to September, then keep totally dry.
Keep them on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to get the intense light our British sky lacks.
Stop watering completely when they start splitting in autumn so the new leaves can eat the old ones.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dry paper-like leaf sheaths and dab them with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Lithops bromfieldii
items.growersTips:
Keep them in your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic their native South African light levels.
Plant them deep in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent peat-free compost.
Stop watering completely from October to April while they absorb their old leaves to grow new ones.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in the deep fissures between their two fleshy leaves.
Never mist them in winter because the damp UK air can easily cause their delicate skin to split.

items.name: Lithops coleorum
items.growersTips:
Keep them in a gritty, free-draining mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent John Innes.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to prevent them from stretching in UK light.
Stop watering completely from October until their old leaves have shrivelled away in spring.
Sow seeds in spring using a heated propagator to cope with chilly British indoor temperatures.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dry leaf papery layers during the damp winter months.

items.name: Lithops comptonii
items.growersTips:
Ditch standard soil and pot your Lithops comptonii in ninety percent grit to survive UK dampness.
Give them a deep soak in autumn when they flower, then stop watering completely until spring.
Never water when they are splitting and growing new leaves, or the old ones will rot and mush.
Keep them on your sunniest south-facing windowsill because our grey UK winters lack enough light.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in the deep fissure between their two stone-like leaves.

items.name: Lithops dinteri
items.growersTips:
Plant this dinteri in a mix of seventy percent grit and thirty percent soil to stop UK rot.
Give it a deep soak only when the leaves wrinkle in summer, then keep it bone dry all winter.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to get the maximum possible British winter light.
Never water when the old leaves are splitting and transferring their moisture to the new pair.
Watch out for sneaky mealybugs hiding in the dry leaf papery sheaths during the damp spring.

items.name: Lithops dorotheae
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on top of gritty compost in spring, barely covering them with a thin layer of fine sand.
Keep your pots on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sun they crave.
Only water when the old leaves have completely shriveled up and the new pair has fully emerged.
Mix three parts horticultural grit to one part loam-based compost to ensure rapid winter drainage.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the central fissure during the damp UK autumn and winter months.

items.name: Lithops francisci
items.growersTips:
Pop your Lithops francisci in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice to survive damp UK winters.
Give them a sunny south-facing windowsill to mimic their native Namibian sun and prevent stretching.
Stop watering completely from October until their old outer leaves have shrivelled away in spring.
Only water them when the top wrinkles slightly in summer, soaking the pot then letting it dry out.
Watch out for sciarid flies in moist peat, so always use a top dressing of dry quartz gravel.

items.name: Lithops fulviceps
items.growersTips:
Plant your fulviceps in 80 percent grit to survive damp UK winters, keeping the leaf tops flush with the soil.
Water only from May to September when the sides wrinkle, then stop completely as they split in winter.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill, as they need more light than other Lithops.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in the dry, papery sheaths of the old leaves in spring.
Sow seeds in April using a heated propagator to get a head start on our short UK growing season.

items.name: Lithops gesineae
items.growersTips:
Keep your gesineae in a gritty, soil-free mix of eighty percent pumice to survive damp UK winters.
Only water them from April to October, completely stopping when they start splitting in winter.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sun.
Plant them deep enough so only the flat, patterned tops show, keeping the delicate necks buried.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in the fissure between the leaves during damp autumns.

items.name: Lithops gracilidelineata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on top of gritty compost in spring, barely covering them with a light dusting of fine sand.
Keep them completely dry from October to April while new leaves absorb the moisture from old ones.
Plant them in a mix of seventy percent horticultural grit and thirty percent John Innes number two.
Place them on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense light of their native home.
Watch out for greenflies in early summer and gently brush them off the fissures with a soft artist brush.

items.name: Lithops hallii
items.growersTips:
Keep your Lithops hallii in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent John Innes.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense South African sunlight.
Only water from May to September when the leaf tops wrinkle, then keep them bone dry all winter.
Never water while they are actively splitting and growing their new pair of leaves in spring.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf fissures and dab them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Lithops hermetica
items.growersTips:
Grow this Namibian native in a gritty, soil-free mix of ninety percent pumice to prevent root rot.
Keep them completely dry from October to April while they absorb their old leaves in our damp winters.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense desert sun they crave.
Plant them deep with only the flat tops showing, then top-dress with matching grey river pebbles.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in the fissure during the warm UK summer active growth.

items.name: Lithops herrei
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lithops herrei in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice to prevent UK winter damp rot.
Keep them on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to mimic their bright South African habitat.
Water only from April to October, completely stopping when they start splitting to grow new leaves.
Never let the tap root sit in water, so always use terracotta pots with large drainage holes.
Watch out for greenhouse mealybugs hiding in the fissure between their two stone-like leaves.

items.name: Lithops hookeri
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lithops hookeri in a gritty mix of seventy percent pumice and thirty percent John Innes.
Keep them completely dry from October to April while they absorb their old leaves in the UK winter.
Place them on your sunniest south-facing windowsill to prevent them from stretching and losing shape.

items.name: Lopezia
items.growersTips:
Grow Lopezia coronata in free-draining loam mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK soil.
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in spring under glass with gentle bottom heat of fifteen C.
Overwinter these tender perennials in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory kept above five degrees.
Prune back stems by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more mosquito-like flowers.
Water weekly in dry summer spells but allow the top three centimetres of compost to dry out first.

items.name: Lopholaena festiva
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in early spring under glass to beat the cool UK weather before planting out in May.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep their roots dry during those wet British summer spells.
Water them only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry to prevent any root rot issues.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch on their tender young spring foliage.
Plant them alongside drought-tolerant companions like sedums to create a beautiful low-water bed.

items.name: Lophospermum
items.growersTips:
Grow your lophospermum in a pot so you can easily move it indoors to overwinter before November frosts.
Plant them in peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to keep the roots dry during wet UK springs.
Water deeply once a week in summer, letting the top inch of soil dry out completely between pours.
Prune back the woody stems by half in early March to encourage a flush of fresh, flowering growth.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly when growing them in your conservatory or sunny UK greenhouse.

items.name: Lophospermum atrosanguineum
items.growersTips:
Plant in late May after frosts in free-draining soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of compost to dry out completely.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk immediately at planting to support its rapid twining stems.
Overwinter indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory kept at a minimum of five degrees.
Take softwood cuttings in late summer as insurance against wet UK winters which often kill the plant.

items.name: Lophospermum erubescens
items.growersTips:
Plant in late May after frosts in free-draining soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk at planting to support its rapid two-meter climbing habit.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out.
Take stem cuttings in August to overwinter indoors as insurance against wet UK winter losses.
Prune back hard to thirty centimeters in early spring only if overwintered in a heated greenhouse.

items.name: Lophospermum purpusii
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory as this tender climber cannot survive UK winter frost.
Plant in free-draining loam-based compost with added grit to prevent root rot during wet UK summers.
Water deeply once a week in summer, allowing the top two inches of soil to dry out between waterings.
Prune back hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new flowering shoots from the base of the plant.
Provide a sturdy trellis or netting for the self-clinging leaf petioles to climb up in late spring.

items.name: Lophospermum scandens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimetres using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees
Grow in pots of peat-free loam-based compost so you can move them into a frost-free greenhouse by October
Water copiously from June to September keeping soil damp but never allow the pot to sit in standing water
Provide a trellis or netting for the self-clinging leaf petioles to climb up as soon as shoots appear
Check young spring growth daily for aphids and glasshouse whitefly which thrive in sheltered UK patios

items.name: Louteridium
items.growersTips:
Grow this Mexican native in a large pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.
Plant in a warm, sheltered spot in well-draining loam mixed with plenty of grit to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week in summer, but keep the soil almost dry during the cold winter dormancy.
Prune back the woody stems in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more purple flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and red spider mite when overwintering your plants indoors.

items.name: Loxogramme
items.growersTips:
Try growing this delicate fern in a moist, shaded crevice of a damp garden stone wall or rockery.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged by misting the fronds during dry UK summers.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into your soil to mimic the woodland floor they naturally love.
Plant them alongside shade-loving mosses and small dwarf hostas to keep their shallow roots cool.
Protect these evergreen fronds from harsh, freezing winter winds by tucking them under a cloche.

items.name: Loxogramme dictyopteris
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen fern in a sheltered, damp rock crevice or a hanging basket to mimic its wild home.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering with rainwater rather than tap water.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into the soil to ensure excellent drainage in wet UK winters.
Position it in deep or partial shade, away from harsh midday sun which easily scorches the fronds.
Protect the crown from severe winter frosts with a light covering of dry bracken or fleece.

items.name: Lucilia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April under glass to protect young seedlings from late UK spring frosts.
Plant out in free-draining sandy loam once all risk of frost has passed in late May.
Water deeply at the base once a week to prevent powdery mildew in damp British summers.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more abundant blooms.
Deadhead faded flowers weekly through August to prolong the display until the first autumn frost.

items.name: Ludisia
items.growersTips:
Grow this jewel orchid in a shallow pot of peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite for drainage.
Keep it in a warm room away from direct sun, as strong UK winter light can scorch the dark leaves.
Water only when the top inch of soil feels dry, using tepid rainwater instead of cold tap water.
Wipe the velvety leaves with a soft, damp cloth monthly to clear dust and check for mealybugs.
Snip off the flower spikes at the base once the white winter blooms fade to boost leaf growth.

items.name: Ludwigia
items.growersTips:
Grow Ludwigia palustris in boggy pond margins or wet soil under three inches of water in full sun.
Prune stems in midsummer by cutting just above a leaf node to encourage bushy, colorful side shoots.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris to provide spring color before Ludwigia reaches peak summer growth.
Bring container-grown plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or bright windowsill over winter.
Propagate in spring by taking four-inch stem cuttings and inserting them directly into wet compost.

items.name: Ludwigia adscendens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender aquatic perennial in a basket submerged no deeper than fifteen centimetres in water
Overwinter plants indoors in a frost-free greenhouse as they will not survive a typical UK winter
Prune aggressive floating stems weekly in midsummer to prevent them from choking pond oxygenators
Plant in heavy clay loam topsoil without added organic compost to prevent pond water eutrophication
Pair with native Marsh Marigold to provide early spring structure before this late-starter emerges

items.name: Ludwigia alternifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this native wet-loving perennial in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil at a pond edge or bog.
Ensure the crown sits no deeper than five centimetres below water level to prevent winter crown rot.
Prune stems back to the base in late autumn to encourage bushy new growth and vibrant red stems.
Water daily in dry summer spells if planted in borders to maintain the essential boggy conditions.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris to provide early spring cover before this late-emerging plant wakes.

items.name: Ludwigia decurrens
items.growersTips:
Grow this moisture-lover in a bog garden or pond shelf submerged under no more than tencm of water.
Overwinter it indoors in a frost-free greenhouse as our chilly UK winters will easily kill it off.
Prune the stems hard in late spring to encourage bushy growth and prevent it from getting leggy.
Plant it alongside native UK marsh marigolds to create a beautiful, moisture-loving contrast.
Watch out for water snails in your garden pond as they love to munch on the soft, tender stems.

items.name: Ludwigia glandulosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this marginal plant in a pond basket submerged no deeper than ten centimetres below the surface.
Propagate in late spring by taking five-inch stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet compost.
Plant in a heavy clay-loam aquatic soil topped with pea gravel to prevent fish from digging it up.
Position in full sun to ensure the foliage develops its signature deep red and purple coloration.
Cut back dead stems to the water level in late autumn to prevent rotting vegetation in your pond.

items.name: Ludwigia grandiflora
items.growersTips:
Do not plant this in the UK as it is a highly invasive banned weed that must be reported if found.
If you spot this plant in your pond, dig it out completely and burn or compost it away from water.
Never dispose of this plant in the wild or wash fragments down the drain as it grows from tiny stems.
Keep a close watch on your garden pond margins in summer for its distinctive bright yellow flowers.
Report any sightings to the GB Non-Native Species Secretariat to help protect UK waterways.

items.name: Ludwigia hexapetala
items.growersTips:
Report sightings of this invasive weed to the GB Non-Native Species Secretariat as it is illegal to grow.
Do not plant this in UK garden ponds or waterways as it is a banned invasive species of concern.
If found on your property eradicate it completely by digging out all roots and drying them thoroughly.
Dispose of plant material by burning or landfill rather than composting to prevent vegetative spread.
Never transfer water or pond plants from an infested site to prevent spreading stem fragments.

items.name: Ludwigia hirtella
items.growersTips:
Grow in wet acidic soil or boggy pond edges using ericaceous compost to mimic its native habitat
Overwinter container plants indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this species cannot survive UK frost
Position in full sun to maximize the striking red stem coloration and yellow summer blooms
Prune leggy stems in late spring to encourage bushier growth and prevent the plant from becoming untidy
Check regularly for water lily beetles and sawfly larvae which damage foliage in damp UK gardens

items.name: Ludwigia hyssopifolia
items.growersTips:
Treat this water-loving plant as a tender annual in the UK, starting seeds indoors in early spring.
Keep the soil constantly wet or submerge the pot under two inches of water in your garden pond.
Plant it in a heavy, loam-based soil mix to stop the nutrients from washing away in your pond.
Place your pots in the sunniest spot of your garden to help this tropical beauty cope with UK summers.
Bring container-grown plants into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the autumn chills.

items.name: Ludwigia murchisonae
items.growersTips:
Grow in full sun in a clay-heavy, nutrient-rich soil to bring out the deep red foliage coloration.
Plant in shallow pond margins or bog gardens at a maximum water depth of ten centimeters.
Protect young shoots from late spring frosts using fleece if grown outside of a greenhouse.
Prune aggressively in late summer to maintain a bushy shape and prevent invasive leggy growth.
Propagate in spring by taking stem cuttings and rooting them directly in wet, muddy compost.

items.name: Ludwigia octovalvis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a pond basket filled with heavy loam and submerge no deeper than fifteen centimetres.
Overwinter indoors in a heated greenhouse or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive frost.
Water daily with harvested rainwater to keep the soil saturated if growing in a bog garden border.
Prune leggy stems by half in late spring to encourage bushier growth and more yellow flowers.
Check submerged foliage regularly for water snails and manually remove them to prevent leaf damage.

items.name: Ludwigia palustris
items.growersTips:
Plant in wet mud or submerged up to thirty centimetres deep at pond edges in full sun for red leaves.
Prune aggressively in midsummer by pinching stem tips to encourage bushy growth and prevent leggy stems.
Grow in acidic to neutral clay loam enriched with organic compost to mimic UK wetland conditions.
Pair with shallow-water companions like Caltha palustris to provide shade and suppress green algae.
Watch for water snails in late spring which rapidly consume the soft submerged foliage of this plant.

items.name: Ludwigia peploides
items.growersTips:
Keep this highly invasive weed strictly contained in sealed garden ponds to prevent environmental escape.
Prune stems aggressively in late summer to prevent the plant from smothering native pond oxygenators.
Overwinter a small stem cutting indoors in a jar of water to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Plant in heavy clay loam within a submerged aquatic basket to restrict its rapid root spread.
Dispose of all excess plant material by burning or bagging it to comply with strict UK wildlife laws.

items.name: Ludwigia peruviana
items.growersTips:
Grow this invasive tender perennial in a submerged container to prevent aggressive spread in ponds.
Overwinter containers indoors or in a heated greenhouse as it cannot survive frost below five degrees.
Prune stems hard in late spring to encourage bushy growth and maximize the yellow summer blooms.
Plant in heavy clay loam with a slow-release aquatic fertilizer tablet to support rapid summer growth.
Check foliage weekly in summer for water lily aphid infestations and wash them off with a hose.

items.name: Ludwigia polycarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this marginal perennial in shallow water up to fifteen centimetres deep in a sunny garden pond.
Plant in heavy clay loam using aquatic baskets to prevent the roots from spreading invasively.
Propagate in midsummer by taking stem cuttings and inserting them directly into wet pond-side mud.
Cut the dying stems back to the pond basket level in late autumn to prevent winter water pollution.
Check foliage regularly in spring for water lily beetle larvae which skeletonise the green leaves.

items.name: Ludwigia repens
items.growersTips:
Grow this aquatic perennial in UK garden ponds at a planting depth of fifteen to thirty centimetres.
Propagate in spring by snipping healthy stem cuttings and inserting them directly into clay soil.
Prune aggressively in midsummer to prevent the rapid growth from choking out slower pond plants.
Position in full sun to ensure the leaves develop their signature deep red autumn coloration.
Overwinter submerged below the UK pond ice line to protect the crown from severe winter freezes.

items.name: Ludwigia sedoides
items.growersTips:
Overwinter indoors in a heated tank or conservatory as this tropical plant cannot survive UK frosts.
Plant in heavy loam soil within a shallow aquatic basket submerged exactly five to fifteen centimeters.
Position in your pond's absolute brightest spot to ensure the foliage develops its red coloration.
Check regularly for water snails and aphids which quickly disfigure the delicate floating rosettes.
Group with deeper water lilies to provide wind protection and keep the floating mosaic stable.

items.name: Ludwigia sphaerocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this aquatic perennial in a heavy clay loam soil enriched with iron-rich root tabs.
Keep water levels consistently above the crown or grow in a bog garden that never dries out.
Position in full sun to achieve the characteristic deep bronze-orange foliage in UK summers.
Prune the stems in late spring by pinching the growing tips to encourage a bushier habit.
Overwinter indoors or in a heated greenhouse as this species is tender and will not survive UK frost.

items.name: Luina hypoleuca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March to beat late UK frosts, barely covering them with a light grit layer.
Plant out in May in a sunny, free-draining gravel bed to mimic their native rocky mountain home.
Water sparingly once established, only when the top three inches of soil feel completely dry.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during damp British nights.
Snip off faded yellow flower heads in late summer to encourage a second flush of fresh blooms.

items.name: Lutheria
items.growersTips:
Try growing them in pots of peat-free ericaceous compost to suit their need for acidic conditions.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a bright windowsill before the first harsh UK autumn frosts.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH consistently low.
Feed them with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month during the active spring growing phase.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping them in a warm conservatory over winter.

items.name: Lychnis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April on damp compost and cover with a very fine layer of vermiculite.
Water young seedlings gently at the base twice a week to prevent dampening off in cool UK springs.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new growth during wet May nights using organic beer traps.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering season until the first autumn frosts.
Grow alongside companion plants like Nigella or Briza media in free-draining, gritty UK soil.

items.name: Lymania alvimii
items.growersTips:
Grow this Brazilian bromeliad in a pot of orchid bark and peat so you can bring it indoors by October.
Keep the central urn filled with rainwater but let the potting mix dry out before watering again.
Place your pot in bright, indirect light near a west window to mimic its native forest canopy home.
Flush the central reservoir every fortnight with fresh water to prevent stagnant rot and pests.
Feed during active summer growth by spraying a very weak liquid seaweed fertilizer onto the leaves.

items.name: Lymania smithii
items.growersTips:
Bring this Brazilian bromeliad indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly British winters.
Nestle its roots shallowly in a chunky orchid bark and peat-free compost mix for perfect drainage.
Water directly into the central rosette cup using tepid rainwater, keeping it topped up weekly.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light near a bathroom window to mimic its humid jungle home.
Flush out the central urn with fresh water monthly to prevent stagnant rot in our cooler climate.

items.name: Lyperanthus
items.growersTips:
Grow these Australian orchids in a gritty, free-draining mix of peat and perlite to mimic bushland.
Keep the tubers bone dry during their summer dormancy to prevent them from rotting in wet UK soil.
Water them from below during winter growth to keep the foliage dry and avoid damp-off in cold weather.
Protect emerging winter shoots from slugs using copper tape around your pots or organic pellets.
Place your pots in a frost-free greenhouse or bright windowsill to survive chilly British winters.

items.name: Lysichiton
items.growersTips:
Plant your skunk cabbage in deep, wet mud at the boggy edge of a garden pond where it won't dry out.
Watch out for slugs and snails early in spring as they love to munch on the emerging flower spikes.
Give them plenty of space because their massive glossy leaves will easily spread over a metre wide.
Plant them alongside moisture-loving astilbes or hostas to mask the foliage as it dies back in autumn.
Avoid planting the yellow species near wild waterways as it is classified as invasive in the UK.

items.name: Lysichiton americanus
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant in rich, deep mud right at your pond edge where its roots can stay wet all year.
Wear gloves to cut back the massive leaves in late autumn before they rot and smell like wet dog.
Grow it in partial shade to stop the gorgeous yellow spathes from scorching in our UK spring sun.
Watch out for self-seeded babies around your bog garden as this vigorous beauty loves to spread.
Pair it with native marsh marigolds to mask the messy summer dieback of those huge floppy leaves.

items.name: Lysichiton camtschatcensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this white skunk cabbage in boggy mud or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep.
Position it in partial shade to mimic its native woodland swamps and prevent leaves from scorching.
Propagate by sowing fresh seed in late summer directly into wet, peat-free ericaceous compost.
Watch out for slugs and snails which love to shred the massive, glossy emerging spring foliage.
Plant alongside marsh marigolds and water irises to create a stunning, natural pond-edge display.

items.name: Lysidice
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimeters to combat the cool UK spring soil.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep taproot growth.
Watch for black bean aphid infestations on young shoots during humid British midsummer afternoons.
Incorporate well-rotted grit into heavy UK clay soils to prevent winter root rot in wet conditions.
Plant alongside sweet peas to maximize nitrogen fixation and attract essential UK pollinators.

items.name: Lysiloma
items.growersTips:
Start Lysiloma seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant them out in June after the last frost, choosing your sunniest, most sheltered south-facing wall.
Mix plenty of grit and compost into heavy clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage these plants need.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep, resilient roots.
Sow them alongside French marigolds to help deter aphids and whiteflies from their delicate foliage.

items.name: Lysionotus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Lysionotus in a gritty, acidic ericaceous compost mix to mimic their native woodland home.
Position your pot in dappled shade, as harsh UK afternoon sun will quickly scorch the delicate leaves.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH low and the roots happy.
Bring your potted Lysionotus into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the first November frost.
Propagate your favourite plants by taking soft stem cuttings in early summer using a heated propagator.

items.name: Lysipomia aretioides
items.growersTips:
Grow this Andean alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree compost to survive wet UK winters.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during its active spring growing phase.
Protect this cushion plant from winter wet by placing a glass pane or cloche over it from November.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to nestle under its tight, low-growing foliage cushions.
Propagate by carefully dividing the small offsets in late spring once the risk of hard frost passes.

items.name: Lysipomia laricina
items.growersTips:
This rare Andean alpine needs a gritty, free-draining soil mix to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it constantly moist but never waterlogged during the dry summer months using rainwater.
Grow this tiny cushion plant in a raised scree bed or alpine trough to prevent slugs eating it.
Protect it with a winter cloche or cold frame to shield the foliage from heavy UK winter rain.
Propagate by carefully dividing the delicate clumps in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Mabrya acerifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender cliff-dweller in a gritty alpine mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep it in a frost-free greenhouse or sunny conservatory during our freezing, damp winter months.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, mimicking its natural arid Spanish canyon habitat perfectly.
Position your pot in full UK sun to encourage those lovely, snapdragon-like yellow-green blooms.
Watch out for glasshouse pests like spider mites and mealybugs that love dry, sheltered spots.

items.name: Machaerium
items.growersTips:
Start your Machaerium seeds indoors in April to beat the chilly UK spring and get a head start.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to ensure excellent drainage during wet British summers.
Water these annuals deeply once a week at the base to keep roots damp without soaking the foliage.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots during damp May nights and protect them with copper tape.
Plant them alongside French marigolds to help deter common pests in your sunny border displays.

items.name: Machairophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half compost and half horticultural grit.
Keep it dry in wet UK winters by moving your potted plants under the shelter of a cold greenhouse.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to almost nothing from November to March.
Place your pots on a south-facing patio to soak up every drop of our precious, fleeting UK sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf crevices and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Machairophyllum brevifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African beauty indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes number two and half horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry during the damp UK winter months.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints, especially during dry indoor winters.
Grow it in a shallow terracotta pot to help the roots breathe and prevent waterlogging in our wet climate.

items.name: Mackaya
items.growersTips:
Bring your Mackaya indoors or to a heated greenhouse by October to protect it from UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a container with peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with grit to ensure sharp drainage.
Keep the soil damp in summer but let the top two inches dry out completely before watering in winter.
Prune the stems back by half in late spring right after flowering to keep its bushy shape compact.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light near a west-facing window to mimic its forest canopy home.

items.name: Mackaya bella
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender South African beauty in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Keep soil barely damp in winter but water weekly from May to September to mimic its rainy season.
Prune stems back by half in late spring just after flowering to keep its shrubby habit compact.
Add plenty of grit to your peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this forest plant needs.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you keep it indoors or in a conservatory year-round.

items.name: Macleaya
items.growersTips:
Plant Macleaya microcarpa Kelways Coral Plume in deep moist soil to prevent windburn in dry UK summers
Control aggressive underground runners in small gardens by planting inside a buried bottomless bucket
Cut the hollow stems right down to ground level in late autumn to prevent winter wet rotting the crown
Wear gloves when pruning to avoid skin irritation from the toxic orange sap typical of Papaveraceae
Stake the tall stems in spring using hazel twigs before the heavy summer rain bends them to the lawn

items.name: Macleaya cordata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun or partial shade, sheltered from strong UK winds.
Control its invasive rhizomes by planting inside a buried, bottomless bucket or deep root barrier.
Cut the hollow stems right back to ground level in late autumn or winter using sharp secateurs.
Wear gloves when pruning to avoid skin irritation from the toxic, staining orange-yellow sap.
Propagate in spring by dividing the root clump or taking root cuttings before new growth starts.

items.name: Macleaya microcarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moist, well-drained loam in full sun or partial shade to reach its full height.
Install a root barrier at planting to contain its invasive, fast-spreading underground runners.
Wear gloves when cutting back dead stems in late winter to avoid irritation from the orange sap.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn or winter when the plant is dormant.
Stake the tall stems in late spring to protect them from strong winds in exposed UK gardens.

items.name: Macledium spinosum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of five millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet British summer spells.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to mimic its arid native habitat.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or greenhouse to maximise essential summer warmth.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the flowering display before autumn.

items.name: Macledium zeyheri
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of five millimetres to combat the cool UK climate.
Grow in free-draining sandy loam with added grit to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top two inches of gritty soil to dry out completely.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border or greenhouse to maximise essential summer heat.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using copper tape or beer traps in damp spring weather.

items.name: Macodes
items.growersTips:
Keep your jewel orchid in a shallow pot of pure sphagnum moss or a chunky, bark-heavy peat-free mix.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top moss feels dry, as UK tap water minerals burn roots.
Place them in a humid, north-facing room away from drafty windows and harsh direct British sun.
Keep a close eye out for fungus gnats and wipe the velvety leaves gently with a damp cloth weekly.
Maintain a cosy indoor temperature above fifteen degrees Celsius during our chilly British winters.

items.name: Macowania
items.growersTips:
Sow Macowania seeds indoors in early April to protect the young annuals from late UK spring frosts.
Plant them out in May in a south-facing spot with sharp-draining soil to mimic their native heat.
Water the base weekly during dry summer spells, but let the gritty soil dry out fully between waterings.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are ten centimetres tall to encourage a bushier flowering habit.
Deadhead spent blooms regularly through August to keep this annual flowering until the autumn damp.

items.name: Macroditassa
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender perennial indoors by October to shield it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from May to August to boost blooms.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth for the summer ahead.
Pot in a free-draining mix of peat-free compost and plenty of grit to mimic its native drainage.

items.name: Macrolobium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm depth in peat-free compost using bottom heat of 21C to start early.
Plant out in June after frosts in a south-facing border with grit added to clay soil for drainage.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry July spells to prevent early pod drop in dry soil.
Watch for black bean aphid on young shoots in June and wash them off with a firm spray of water.
Grow alongside sweet alyssum to attract hoverflies that naturally control pests on the foliage.

items.name: Macrolobium pittieri
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical legume in a heated conservatory or greenhouse to survive cold UK winters.
Plant in acidic to neutral loam mixed with orchid bark to mimic its native rainforest floor.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged or soggy.

items.name: Mahonia

items.name: Mahonia aquifolium

Plant in autumn in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, keeping the root flare level with the ground.

Underplant with shade-loving UK native wood anemones or winter aconites to mask bare lower stems.

items.name: Mahonia bealei
items.growersTips:
Plant this shade-lover in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil, adding leaf mould to the pit.

Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until its deep taproot system is fully established.
Underplant with snowdrops and hellebores to create a stunning, shade-tolerant winter display.

items.name: Mahonia duclouxiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender beauty in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect its winter blooms.

items.name: Mahonia fremontii
items.growersTips:

items.name: Mahonia japonica

items.name: Mahonia leschenaultii
items.growersTips:
Plant this tender Himalayan beauty in a sheltered, woodland-style spot away from harsh UK frosts.

Prune lightly in spring right after flowering to keep its leggy, architectural stems under control.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep its glossy, holly-like leaves from scorching.

items.name: Mahonia nervosa
items.growersTips:
Plant your Oregon grape in moist, acidic woodland soil, mixing in plenty of composted pine needles.
Water it deeply once a week during dry UK summers until its shallow, creeping roots are established.

Watch out for rust fungus on the leaves during damp autumns, and quickly clear away any fallen foliage.
Grow it under the shade of a silver birch alongside autumn-flowering cyclamen for lovely contrast.

items.name: Mahonia oiwakensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this shrub in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect those long, delicate leaves.
Give it moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of composted leaf mould.

Watch out for rust and powdery mildew during damp UK autumns, clearing away fallen leaves quickly.
Water your young Mahonia regularly during dry summer spells until its deep root system establishes.

items.name: Mairia burchellii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of 3mm using a free-draining, gritty compost mix.

Water sparingly from below once seedlings emerge, allowing the topsoil to dry to prevent damp-off.
Acclimatise plants outdoors in May after the last frost, spacing them 15cm apart in full sun.
Protect young foliage from slugs using organic grit barriers during wet British summer spells.

items.name: Mairia coriacea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass, as they need warmth and light to germinate well.
Grow them in sharply draining, gritty loam to mimic their native dry soils and prevent winter rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between light waterings.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to soak up the UK summer heat.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails early on using beer traps or copper tape around pots.

items.name: Mairia crenata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early April indoors to protect young seedlings from late UK spring frosts.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy, watering at the base to avoid damp foliage.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British summers, using organic beer traps to save them.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme or sedum to keep soil moisture even and suppress weeds.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly through August to encourage a continuous display of fresh flowers.

items.name: Mairia hirsuta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in early spring under glass at a depth of five millimetres to beat the chilly UK weather.

Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs by using organic wool pellets around stems.

items.name: Mairia robusta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of three millimetres to protect them from late UK frosts.
Plant out in May in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on leaves.
Deadhead spent daisy-like flowers weekly in July and August to prolong the summer blooming period.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Malaxidinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these native bog orchids in a mix of live sphagnum moss and acidic peat, keeping it wet.
Keep pots in a cold frame over winter to mimic the damp, chilly UK bogs without freezing solid.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the tender emerging green shoots.
Sit the pot in a shallow tray of rainwater or distilled water, never tap water, to keep it soggy.
Propagate by gently dividing the tiny pseudobulbs just as new growth starts in early spring.

items.name: Malephora
items.growersTips:
Plant your Malephora in a gritty loam mix and raise the bed slightly to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil are bone dry, then soak it thoroughly.

Trim back leggy stems in late spring to encourage compact growth and more daisy-like flowers.

items.name: Malephora crassa

Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to almost nothing from November to March.
Protect your potted plants indoors or under glass once autumn frosts threaten to freeze them.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily propagate new plants and guarantee winter backups.

items.name: Malephora crocea

Plant this South African native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive UK winter wet.
Bring your pots indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first autumn frosts hit.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, cutting back to once a month during our dark winter days.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily overwinter backup plants on your kitchen windowsill.
Squeeze the fleshy leaves occasionally; if they feel soft, it is time to give them a good soak.

items.name: Malephora lutea

Bring your potted ice plant indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill before October.

Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily propagate new plants as backup against winter losses.
Position them in your garden's hottest, most south-facing spot to mimic their native sunshine.

Bring your containers indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first UK freeze.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to easily propagate new plants as backups against winter losses.

Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like Narcissus to attract early pollinators to the blossoms.

items.name: Malus ×micromalus

Prune out crossing branches in late winter before buds swell to keep the compact canopy open.
Watch for apple scab during damp British springs and clear away fallen leaves to stop it spreading.

items.name: Malus ×robusta

Prune in late winter to remove congested branches and keep the centre open to prevent apple scab.
Watch out for aphids in spring and simply blast them off with a sharp spray from your garden hose.

items.name: Malus baccata

Plant your Siberian crabapple in autumn so the damp UK winter soil helps its roots settle in well.

items.name: Malus crescimannoi

Grow a pollinator partner nearby like Scrumptious or Katy because Beacon is not self-fertile.

items.name: Malus domestica 'Cox's Orange Pippin'

Plant Cox in a sunny sheltered spot to protect its delicate blossoms from late UK spring frosts.

items.name: Malus domestica ‘Gascoyne’s Scarlet’

items.name: Malus domestica 'Golden Delicious'
items.growersTips:
Plant your tree in a sunny, sheltered spot to help this late-ripening variety sweeten up in UK sun.
Grow near a pollination partner like Braeburn or Gala because Golden Delicious is not self-fertile.
Prune in winter to open up the canopy and prevent scab, which thrives in damp British weather.
Thin the young fruits in July to avoid biennial bearing and ensure you get a good crop every year.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to keep the soil moist and feed its hungry root system.

items.name: Malus domestica 'Granny Smith'
items.growersTips:
Plant in the sunniest UK spot possible to ensure this late-ripening variety gets enough autumn heat.

Prune in late winter to open the canopy and maximise sunlight penetration to the ripening fruit.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells to prevent bitter pit in the developing apples.

items.name: Malus domestica 'King of the Pippins'
items.growersTips:
Plant this self-fertile tree in deep, well-draining loam to prevent waterlogging in wet UK winters.

items.name: Malus domestica ‘Mutsu’

Plant this triploid Mutsu in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect its late-opening blossoms from frost.

Prune in late winter to keep the center open, preventing powdery mildew in damp UK summers.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells to stop the large, heavy fruits from dropping early.
Watch out for bitter pit by applying a calcium foliar spray to the leaves during mid-summer.

items.name: Malus domestica ‘Tsugaru’
items.growersTips:
Grow this sweet Japanese apple in full sun to boost its red skin colour in cooler UK summers.
Prune in late winter using the spur-bearing method to encourage heavy crops on older wood.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells to prevent bitter pit in the ripening fruit.
Watch for apple scab in damp UK springs by clearing fallen leaves to stop fungal spores.
Plant with a pollination partner from group three like Cox or Gala for a successful fruit set.

items.name: Malus domestica 'Wealthy'
items.growersTips:
Plant Wealthy in a sunny spot with deep, fertile soil, keeping the graft union 10cm above ground level.
Water your young tree deeply every week during dry UK summers to help its shallow roots establish.
Prune in late winter to thin out the heavy crop, preventing biennial bearing and snapped branches.
Keep a sharp eye out for apple scab in damp British spring weather by clearing away fallen leaves.
Grow chives or clover nearby to attract pollinators and help deter common pests like aphids.

items.name: Malus domestica var. Fuji
items.growersTips:
Fuji apples need our sunniest, most sheltered spot to ripen well before the autumn frosts hit.
Prune your Fuji in midwinter to open up the canopy so every bit of rare UK sunshine reaches the fruit.
Grow Fuji near a self-fertile partner like Braeburn to ensure successful pollination in our climate.
Keep a sharp eye out for woolly aphid in spring, as Fuji bark is particularly prone to infestations.
Mulch well in spring to keep the soil damp, as dry roots make Fuji apples prone to bitter pit disease.

items.name: Malus domestica var. Jonathan
items.growersTips:

items.name: Meconella oregana
