Sow seeds on the soil surface in autumn as they need winter cold and light to trigger germination.
Grow in gritty, neutral to slightly alkaline soil to mimic their native dry, rocky habitat.
Water sparingly only during winter and spring, then keep completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect the tiny, delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in spring.
Plant alongside slow-growing alpine saxifrages to prevent this small wildflower from being smothered.

items.name: Meconopsis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic soil enriched with leaf mould in a sheltered spot with dappled woodland shade.
Water copiously with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the soil constantly damp but not wet.
Cut back flowered stems of monocarpic species like Meconopsis napaulensis before they set seed.
Protect emerging spring crowns from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps of perennial blue poppies in early spring just as new growth commences.

items.name: Meconopsis aculeata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the surface of damp, gritty compost in winter as they need light and cold to germinate
Plant in acidic, humus-rich, moist but sharply draining soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UKs
Position in dappled shade sheltered from strong winds to protect the delicate, sky-blue petals
Water copiously with rainwater during the summer growing season to mimic their damp Himalayan home
Protect the young rosettes from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp spring weather

items.name: Meconopsis betonicifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp, cool Scottish woodland floor.
Water with rainwater to keep soil constantly moist but never waterlogged during dry UK summers.
Protect emerging spring crowns from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut back faded flower stems in autumn to prevent self-seeding and encourage strong winter crowns.
Plant alongside shade-loving Hostas or Ferns to shelter the delicate blue blooms from harsh winds.

items.name: Meconopsis gakyidiana
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil in dappled shade mimicking cool Scottish woodland conditions.
Water with rainwater to keep soil constantly damp but never waterlogged during dry summer months.
Protect emerging spring crowns from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.
Do not cut back the fading foliage until late autumn to allow the plant to store energy.
Plant alongside Hostas or Ferns to provide essential shade and shelter for the delicate roots.

items.name: Meconopsis grandis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of leafmould or compost.
Position in dappled shade sheltered from strong winds to protect the delicate, large blue petals.
Water copiously during the spring and summer growing season to ensure the soil never dries out.
Remove the flower spikes in the first year to force the plant to establish a strong perennial clump.
Protect emerging spring crowns from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Meconopsis horridula
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late winter on compost surface, leaving them uncovered as they need light to germinate.
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of leafmould or compost.
Position in dappled shade sheltered from strong winds to prevent the fragile stems from snapping.
Water copiously during dry summer spells to keep soil constantly damp but never waterlogged or boggy.
Protect the winter rosette from excessive wet by placing a pane of glass or cloche over the crown.

items.name: Meconopsis napaulensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of leafmould or compost.
Position in dappled shade sheltered from strong winds to protect the tall, fragile flower spikes.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Protect the winter rosette from excessive wet by covering with an open-sided cloche or pane of glass.
Sow fresh seed in late summer on the soil surface as they need light and winter cold to germinate.

items.name: Meconopsis simplicifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral humus-rich soil, incorporating plenty of leaf mould to retain moisture.
Position in dappled shade sheltered from strong winds to prevent the delicate blue petals tearing.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark annually in autumn to protect the crown from winter wet.
Watch for slugs and snails in early spring as they eagerly devour the emerging hairy leaf rosettes.

items.name: Medeola
items.growersTips:
Plant Medeola virginiana tubers 8cm deep in autumn in moisture-retentive, acidic deciduous woodland soil.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic its native UK-hardy woodland habitat.
Keep soil consistently damp but not waterlogged during spring growth, reducing water after flowering.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by carefully dividing the fragile tuberous rhizomes in late autumn once foliage dies back.

items.name: Medeoloideae
items.growersTips:
Plant these woodland bulbs about eight centimetres deep in moist, well-drained leaf mould in autumn.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during spring, then let them dry out slightly as they go dormant.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the delicate whorled leaves just as they emerge in April.
Grow them under the light dappled shade of deciduous shrubs to mimic their native forest canopy.
Mix leaf mould and grit into your clay soil to prevent the fragile bulbs from rotting in wet winters.

items.name: Mediocalcar
items.growersTips:
Grow this miniature creeping orchid on a cork bark mount with live sphagnum moss to mimic tree bark.
Water daily in summer with rainwater to keep the moss damp, but reduce to misting in winter cold.
Keep in a cool greenhouse or shady windowsill, ensuring winter temperatures stay above ten Celsius.
Position in bright indirect light, avoiding direct UK summer sun which quickly scorches the leaves.
Propagate in spring by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes, ensuring each piece has three bulbs.

items.name: Megalochlamys
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Megalochlamys indoors to a warm windowsill before the first harsh UK autumn frost.
Water very sparingly in winter, letting the soil dry out completely to prevent root rot in damp UK air.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mixed with perlite to mimic its dry native habitat.
Position your plant in the sunniest south-facing spot in your garden or greenhouse for maximum warmth.
Feed with a weak liquid succulent fertiliser just once a month during the active spring growing phase.

items.name: Megalorchis
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare perennial in late autumn, burying the tuber exactly five centimetres deep in loam.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, then keep the soil almost dry throughout winter.
Watch out for slugs eating the tender spring shoots; use organic grit barriers around the base.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into your soil to mimic the damp, free-draining British woodland.
Grow it alongside native ferns or wood anemones which share its love for dappled, partial shade.

items.name: Megaskepasma
items.growersTips:
Bring your Brazilian red cloak indoors by October as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter frost.
Water it thoroughly once the top inch of soil dries out, but keep it much drier during winter.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more vibrant flowers.
Feed it weekly in summer with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer to boost those huge red bracts.
Grow it in a large pot using peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit for excellent drainage.

items.name: Megastylidinae
items.growersTips:
Grow Megastylidinae in a cool greenhouse using a free-draining mix of fine bark and perlite.
Water thoroughly with rainwater once the top inch of compost dries, keeping it drier in winter.
Maintain a minimum winter temperature of ten degrees Celsius to prevent frost damage to tubers.
Apply a highly diluted orchid fertilizer fortnightly during the active spring and summer growth.
Repot every two years in spring just as new root growth begins to avoid damaging the root system.

items.name: Megastylis
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a very chunky, bark-based mix to mimic its native New Caledonia home.
Keep it in a humid greenhouse or conservatory to protect it from chilly UK winter temperatures.
Water with rainwater only, letting the potting medium dry out slightly before you water it again.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away with a damp cotton bud.
Repot only when the roots completely fill the pot, doing this in spring as new growth starts.

items.name: Melanoxylum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator to offset UK cold.
Plant out in late May into free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells rather than daily light sprinkling.
Position next to brassicas as companions to utilise the nitrogen-fixing benefits of this legume.
Monitor young shoots closely in June for black bean aphid attacks and wash them off with water.

items.name: Melanthera
items.growersTips:
Start Melanthera seeds indoors in April using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant them out in June in a south-facing spot with sandy, free-draining soil to mimic coastal dunes.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry July spells rather than daily shallow sprinkles.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a bushier habit and more yellow blooms.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around stems.

items.name: Melicytus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Melicytus ramiflorus in a sheltered spot away from cold, drying northerly UK winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frosts pass to shape the shrub and remove winter damage.
Grow this New Zealand native in well-drained, humus-rich soil, adding grit to heavy clay gardens.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using organic wool pellets around the base.

items.name: Melicytus alpinus
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand native in free-draining gravelly soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it full sun and shelter from cold winds, especially in chilly northern UK gardens.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape the tangled stems or remove winter dieback.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to nibble on the tender new spring shoots.

items.name: Melicytus angustifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant this narrow-leaved mahoe in a sheltered spot to protect its delicate foliage from chilly UK winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry spells in July and August.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost passes to maintain its elegant, upright shrubby shape.
Add a thick layer of organic mulch around the base in November to insulate its roots from winter frost.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, and protect them with pet-safe wool pellets or grit.

items.name: Melicytus crassifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough Kiwi shrub in sharply draining soil, adding grit to the hole to survive UK wet.
Keep it in full sun or light shade, but give it a sheltered south-facing wall to block cold winds.
Water it weekly during its first UK summer, then leave it alone as it is highly drought-tolerant.
Prune lightly in late spring only to shape it or remove stems damaged by harsh winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs chewing the low, tangled branches, and clear fallen autumn leaves from its base.

items.name: Melicytus dentatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this spiky New Zealand native in well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a sheltered spot against a south-facing wall to protect those tiny yellow flowers from frost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between times.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frosts pass to shape the bush and remove any winter dieback.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots, and use copper tape around your pots to keep them safe.

items.name: Melicytus flexuosus
items.growersTips:
Plant this NZ native in well-drained, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Position your shrub in a sheltered spot against a south-facing wall to protect it from frost.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost passes to maintain its unique tangled, wiry shape.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out fully between waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding in the dense, twiggy base during damp autumn months.

items.name: Melicytus lanceolatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand native in a sheltered spot away from cold drying winds to prevent leaf singe.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your soil to mimic its natural damp woodland floor habitat in the UK.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost risk passes to shape it and remove dead wood safely.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young plants when the tender new growth begins to emerge in spring.

items.name: Melicytus novae-zelandiae
items.growersTips:
Plant this coastal Kiwi shrub in free-draining sandy loam to mimic its native seaside habitat.
Keep your young shrub sheltered from harsh UK winter winds with a thick mulch of organic compost.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out fully between drinks.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to shape and remove winter damage.
Grow it alongside hardy evergreen companions like Griselinia to create a tough, wind-resistant screen.

items.name: Melicytus orarius
items.growersTips:
Plant this coastal kiwi shrub in free-draining sandy loam to mimic its native shoreline habitat.
Give it a sheltered south-facing wall to protect its delicate winter flowers from harsh UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely in between.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain its compact, bushy evergreen shape.
Propagate this dioecious plant by taking semi-ripe cuttings in late summer for the best success.

items.name: Melicytus ramiflorus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Kiwi native in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect its glossy evergreen leaves.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Add a thick layer of organic mulch around the base in late autumn to insulate roots from winter frosts.
Prune lightly in late spring after any frost risk has passed to shape it and remove winter damage.
Grow it in fertile, well-draining neutral soil, mixing in plenty of well-rotted compost before planting.

items.name: Melodinus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot of loamy ericaceous compost so you can move it inside for winter.
Water your vine deeply once a week in summer, but let the top two inches of soil dry out first.
Prune the stems right after flowering in late summer to keep its vigorous climbing habit in check.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping this plant in a warm, dry UK greenhouse or conservatory.
Feed it a high-potassium liquid fertiliser every fortnight from April to September to boost blooms.

items.name: Melpomene
items.growersTips:
Plant these delicate Andean ferns in a moist, peat-free acidic compost mix with plenty of perlite.
Keep them in a humid, draft-free spot out of direct UK sun, mimicking their misty cloud forest home.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil consistently damp but not wet.
Watch out for greenhouse pests like scale insects and gently wipe them off with a damp cotton pad.
Bring them indoors or into a heated conservatory before the first autumn frosts hit your garden.

items.name: Memoremea scorpioides
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native European woodland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy in the UK.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil evenly damp but never waterlogged.
Watch for slugs and snails in spring, as they target the tender emerging borage-like foliage.
Propagate by dividing established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to appear.

items.name: Mendoncia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical climber in a heated conservatory to protect it from chilly UK winters.
Plant in a pot with peat-free loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite for sharp drainage.
Water generously with lukewarm rainwater in summer, but let the top inch of soil dry out first.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its size manageable.
Keep a close eye out for red spider mites, which love the dry air of indoor heated glasshouses.

items.name: Merciera
items.growersTips:
Plant your Merciera in sandy, sharply draining soil to survive wet, cold UK winters without rotting.
Keep your Merciera in a pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse during winter.
Water your Merciera only when the top few inches of soil are dry, as it hates soggy British ground.
Prune your Merciera lightly in late spring after the frost passes to encourage bushy new growth.
Grow Merciera alongside hardy sedums in a sunny rockery to match its dry, low-nutrient soil needs.

items.name: Mertensia
items.growersTips:
Plant Mertensia maritima in free-draining gritty soil to mimic UK shingle beaches and prevent rot.
Sow Mertensia virginica seeds in autumn to let winter cold break dormancy naturally in UK gardens.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Water Mertensia virginica consistently in spring but allow it to dry out when it goes dormant in July.
Plant Mertensia virginica alongside hostas to cover the bare patches left when it dies back in summer.

items.name: Mertensia lanceolata
items.growersTips:
Plant this prairie native in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position your bluebells in light dappled shade to mimic their natural open woodland edge habitat.
Water deeply once a week during dry spring spells, but let them go completely dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love the tender emerging shoots.
Sow seeds in pots outdoors in autumn because they need winter cold to trigger spring germination.

items.name: Mertensia maritima
items.growersTips:
Plant this oyster plant in very gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Protect the young blue leaves from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic grit barriers.
Water sparingly once established, mimicking the dry, salty shingle of its native UK coastlines.
Position your pot in full sun but keep the roots cool by using a light-coloured terracotta container.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the natural winter cold breaks their dormancy for spring growth.

items.name: Mertensia oblongifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this bluebell in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the natural winter cold breaks their dormancy for spring growth.
Position your pot in light dappled shade to mimic its native cool montane woodland habitat.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep the soil almost dry when it goes dormant in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love the tender new shoots.

items.name: Mertensia sibirica
items.growersTips:
Plant your Siberian bluebells in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp woodland.
Position them in dappled shade to keep the delicate foliage from scorching in midday summer sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to support their lush leaf growth and blue blooms.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tender young shoots first emerge.
Let the foliage die back naturally in summer to allow the plant to store energy for next year.

items.name: Mertensia virginica
items.growersTips:
Plant them under deciduous shrubs so they get spring sun but cool shade when they go dormant in summer.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during spring using a thick leaf mould mulch.
Sow seeds in autumn as they need the cold UK winter chill to trigger germination the next spring.
Mark their spot with a cane because they die back completely by July and you might dig them up.
Plant them alongside late-emerging hostas or ferns to beautifully fill the gap when they disappear.

items.name: Merwilla
items.growersTips:
Plant your Merwilla plumbea bulbs shallowly in spring with the neck sitting just above the soil.
Grow them in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the bulbs outdoors.
Place pots in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their hot, dry South African summer home.
Bring containers into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the first harsh UK autumn frost.
Water them thoroughly but infrequently during summer, then keep them completely dry through winter.

items.name: Merwilla plumbea
items.growersTips:
Plant this African beauty in a terracotta pot with grit-heavy compost to survive wet UK winters.
Bury the large bulb with its neck poking just above the soil surface to prevent it from rotting.
Water it freely from spring to autumn but keep the bulb bone-dry during its winter dormancy.
Bring your potted Merwilla indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or sunny windowsill by late October.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh new shoots.

items.name: Mesadenella
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical orchid indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a free-draining mix of orchid bark and perlite to mimic its natural damp forest floor.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil slightly damp but never soggy.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to avoid scorching leaves.
Watch out for glasshouse spider mites in dry indoor air and mist the surrounding foliage weekly.

items.name: Mesechites
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Caribbean vine in a conservatory to protect it from chilly UK winter frosts.
Water your plant thoroughly only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to the touch.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser during spring to boost those summer blooms.
Prune back unruly stems in late winter to keep its vigorous climbing habit tidy and manageable.
Provide a sturdy trellis or moss pole in the pot for its twining stems to grip as they grow.

items.name: Mesembryanthemum
items.growersTips:
Plant these in gritty, sharply draining soil or containers, as wet UK winter soil will rot them.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, mimicking their native South African home.
Pinch out the growing tips in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and far more summer flowers.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors, protecting them from harsh UK frosts.
Position them in your absolute sunniest spot so the daisy-like blooms actually open up fully.

items.name: Mesembryanthemum cordifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring your pots indoors by October because these South African beauties cannot survive a UK frost.
Mix fifty percent grit into your peat-free compost to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, but stop watering completely in winter.
Take stem cuttings in August to easily overwinter new mini plants on a sunny windowsill indoors.
Plant them alongside hardy sedums in south-facing rockeries to mask bare patches during winter.

items.name: Mesembryanthemum crystallinum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring on gritty compost, barely covering them as they need light to grow.
Plant them out in May after the last frost in your poorest, sharpest-draining soil in full sun.
Water sparingly only when the soil is bone dry, as damp UK soil will quickly rot their roots.
Protect them from slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the juicy, glistening leaves.
Bring a few potted plants indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to keep them alive over winter.

items.name: Mesembryanthemum nodiflorum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring using a free-draining grit mix to prevent damp dampening-off.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, as this coastal succulent easily rots in wet UK winters.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or porch for winter.
Mix lots of horticultural sand into your borders to mimic their native dry, rocky habitats.
Plant them alongside hardy sedums which share their love for baking hot, sunny UK south-facing walls.

items.name: Mesembryanthemum tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African native indoors by October to protect its fuzzy leaves from UK winter wet.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit for perfect drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, keeping the hairy foliage completely dry.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse to maximise vital UK summer sunshine.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense, woolly leaf joints and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Mesembryanthemum tortuosum
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African succulent indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first autumn UK frost.
Plant your Sceletium in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free soil.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, reducing this to a tiny splash once a month during winter.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, dabbing them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Take stem cuttings in late spring, letting them callow for three days before potting in dry grit.

items.name: Mesocyparis
items.growersTips:
Plant this cypress relative in moist, well-drained acid soil to avoid yellowing foliage in dry UK summers.
Give young plants a deep soak weekly during dry spells, rather than frequent light sprinkles.
Prune lightly in late spring after the last frost, avoiding cutting back into old wood.
Watch out for conifer aphid infestations in early summer and blast them off with a garden hose.
Shelter it from cold, drying winter winds by planting near a west-facing wall or fence.

items.name: Mestoklema
items.growersTips:
Bring your Mestoklema indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Grow this succulent in a gritty mix of fifty percent pumice and loam to prevent root rot in damp air.
Water deeply only when the soil is bone dry, then stop watering completely from November to March.
Prune the stems in early spring to expose the thick, bonsai-like caudex as it grows larger.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints during dry indoor winter storage.

items.name: Metalasia cephalotes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in a free-draining, gritty compost mix to prevent dampening off.
Grow in containers to easily move plants under a cold frame during excessively wet UK autumn weeks.
Water sparingly, allowing the top 5cm of soil to dry completely before repeating to prevent root rot.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic the intense light of its native South Africa.
Blend horticultural grit into standard UK garden loam to achieve the required rapid drainage.

items.name: Metalasia compacta
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 3mm in free-draining sandy loam to prevent waterlogging in wet UKs.
Water sparingly only when the top 5cm of soil is dry to mimic its native drought-tolerant habitat.
Position in full south-facing sun to maximise summer heat and prevent mildew in humid UK weather.
Sow alongside companion plants like English lavender to attract pollinators and aid seed dispersal.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in late summer to prolong flowering and prevent unwanted self-seeding.

items.name: Metalasia densa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in free-draining sandy loam during early spring.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp UK springs.
Deadhead faded flower heads weekly in summer to prolong the blooming season and prevent self-seeding.
Grow in full sun alongside companion plants like lavender and thyme to ensure excellent drainage.

items.name: Metalasia divergens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at 2mm depth in April using free-draining sandy loam to prevent waterlogging.
Water only when the top 5cm of soil is dry, as this South African native hates wet UK winters.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp May nights.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July to prolong the flowering season of this annual daisy.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme in a south-facing border to mimic its natural dry habitat.

items.name: Metalasia erubescens
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in April using a free-draining sandy loam compost mix.
Place pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise light before transplanting after May frosts.
Water sparingly only when the top two centimetres of soil are dry to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Protect young seedlings from slugs using organic wool pellets during wet British spring nights.
Plant alongside lavender or thyme in raised beds to ensure the sharp drainage this species needs.

items.name: Metalasia fastigiata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass using a gritty, free-draining peat-free compost mix.
Position in the sunniest spot of your garden to mimic its native South African light requirements.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Plant alongside hardy annuals like Calendula to attract pollinators and boost local biodiversity.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the flowering season before first frost.

items.name: Metalasia muricata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass using a gritty, free-draining compost to prevent damping.
Plant in full sun and poor, sandy soil to mimic its native coastal habitat and prevent leggy growth.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the soil to dry out completely between watering sessions.
Protect young plants from severe UK winter frosts using a dry mulch or move containers indoors.
Prune lightly after flowering in late summer to maintain a compact shape and prevent woody stems.

items.name: Metalasia serrata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring using a free-draining sandy loam mix.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the top five centimetres of soil to dry out completely.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails during wet UK springs using organic copper barriers.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native South African light requirements.
Deadhead faded flower heads weekly in late summer to prolong the overall blooming period in the UK.

items.name: Metalasia tricolor
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at two millimetres deep in early spring under glass to protect from UK frosts.
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil with low nutrients to mimic its native South African habitat.
Water sparingly only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK weather.
Position in the sunniest south-facing spot of your garden to maximise summer flowering potential.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in July and August to prolong the display of papery flower heads.

items.name: Metaplexis
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous climber in a sturdy container to easily control its invasive underground runners.
Plant seeds in spring just five millimetres deep using a free-draining gritty loam to avoid rot.
Position your pot against a warm south-facing brick wall to mimic its native Asian climate.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then keep the soil almost dry throughout our wet UK winters.
Prune the vines hard back to ground level in late autumn after the seed pods have split open.

items.name: Metarungia
items.growersTips:
Bring your Metarungia indoors by October as these tender African shrubs cannot survive UK frosts.
Grow them in pots using loam-based John Innes No. 3 mixed with grit to ensure excellent drainage.
Water generously through summer but let the top two inches of soil dry out completely in winter.
Prune the stems back by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more red flowers.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering them in your conservatory.

items.name: Metasequoia
items.growersTips:
Plant your dawn redwood in a boggy spot or near a pond where its roots can drink deeply year-round.
Give young trees a thick mulch of chipped bark in autumn to protect their shallow roots from UK frosts.
No need to prune this beauty, just snip off any dead lower branches in late winter before sap rises.
Watch out for late spring frosts which can scorch the lovely soft new needles of gold-leaved cultivars.
Grow it alongside damp-loving yellow marsh marigolds to contrast beautifully with its autumn bronze.

items.name: Metasequoia glyptostroboides
items.growersTips:
Plant your dawn redwood in a boggy spot or near a pond, as they absolutely crave wet UK soil.
Add a thick layer of composted bark mulch every spring to lock in that essential ground moisture.
Give young trees a deep bucket of water every week during dry spells in our increasingly hot summers.
Grow it as a single leader by snipping off competing vertical stems in the dormant winter months.
Underplant with hostas and astilbes that love the same damp, dappled shade beneath its canopy.

items.name: Metasequoia occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Give this dawn redwood plenty of space in wet, boggy soil near a UK pond or stream to thrive.
Plant your young tree in a deep hole enriched with leaf mould to mimic its native forest floor.
Water it deeply every week during dry UK summers while it establishes its root system.
Prune only in winter when dormant to remove competing leaders and keep its neat pyramidal shape.
Protect the tender spring needles from late UK frosts by planting it away from cold frost pockets.

items.name: Metastelma
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender climber indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winter soil.
Plant your Metastelma in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during rainy summers.
Water only when the top five centimetres of soil feel dry, as this plant hates soggy roots.
Give it a sturdy trellis or obelisk in a south-facing, sunny spot to help its vines scramble.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping it in your greenhouse or conservatory during spring.

items.name: Meyenia
items.growersTips:
Grow Meyenia in pots of peat-free loam-based compost so you can easily move them indoors by October.
Water deeply once a week in summer, then let the top two inches of soil dry out before watering again.
Prune your Meyenia back by a third in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more summer blooms.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plant in a conservatory.
Feed with a high-potash tomato fertiliser every two weeks from May to September to boost flowering.

items.name: Meyenia hawtayneana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Indian climber in a pot so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy during the active spring and summer growth.
Prune back the stems by half in late winter to keep its vigorous scrambling habit under control.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer from May to September to boost those blue blooms.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping it indoors.

items.name: Meyerophytum
items.growersTips:
Bring your meyerophytum indoors by October to protect this tender South African succulent from frost.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining mix of two parts pumice to one part loam to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the leaf pairs shrivel, usually from autumn to spring, keeping it dry in summer.
Position on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense light of its native home.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight gaps between the fused leaves during dry summer rests.

items.name: Mezobromelia capituligera
items.growersTips:
Grow this exotic bromeliad in a pot of peat-free orchid compost so you can bring it inside for winter.
Keep the central leafy reservoir filled with rainwater, flushing it out weekly to prevent stagnation.
Stand the pot on a tray of wet gravel to boost humidity, which helps copy its native rainforest home.
Place it in bright, filtered light near a south-facing window, but shield it from hot midday sun.
Feed it monthly in spring by spraying a very weak, diluted liquid seaweed fertilizer onto the leaves.

items.name: Mezoneuron
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of 2cm using bottom heat of 20C to counter cool UK springs.
Plant out in June in a south-facing border with grit added to the soil to ensure sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to establish the taproot system.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them using beer traps or copper tape barriers.
Grow alongside nitrogen-hungry leafy brassicas to benefit from this legume's soil enrichment.

items.name: Michauxia
items.growersTips:
Plant these stately biennials in deep, gritty soil to accommodate their long, taproot system.
Sow seeds in late spring on the surface of compost as they need light and UK summer warmth to sprout.
Protect the fleshy winter rosettes from slugs and wet rot by mulching with gravel, not manure.
Stake the tall flowering spikes early in spring to prevent wind damage from sudden UK gales.
Let them self-seed in your borders because these short-lived plants die after they finish blooming.

items.name: Michauxia campanuloides
items.growersTips:
Plant this biennial in deep, gritty, alkaline soil so its long taproot won't rot in wet UK winters.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring; they need light and a cold frame's warmth to germinate.
Stake the tall flowering spikes early in May to protect them from strong, gusty British winds.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry summer spells, keeping moisture off the leaves.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they absolutely love targeting the fresh new growth.

items.name: Mickelia
items.growersTips:
Plant this fern in moisture-retentive, acidic soil with plenty of leaf mould to mimic UK woodlands.
Keep the compost consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summers.
Position your fern in deep or partial shade, sheltered from harsh, drying winds that scorch fronds.
Apply a thick mulch of bark chippings in autumn to protect the shallow root system from hard frosts.
Snip away dead or damaged fronds in early spring just as the new fiddleheads begin to unfurl.

items.name: Micklethwaitia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at a depth of two centimetres to protect young roots from late UK frosts.
Plant in free-draining chalky soil mixed with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet British clay.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily misting to encourage deep drought-resistant roots.
Position next to lavender or rosemary to attract bumblebees needed for successful pod pollination.
Watch for early signs of black bean aphid on new shoots and spray with organic horticultural soap.

items.name: Micranthemum
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate pond carpet in shallow margins where UK sun can reach and warm the water.
Push the tiny roots gently into a heavy, clay-based aquatic compost to stop them floating away.
Trim the creeping stems back in late summer to keep them from choking your oxygenating plants.
Watch out for pond snails in spring as they love to munch on the tender new green shoots.
Divide the dense mats in May when the water warms up to easily propagate new patches.

items.name: Micranthemum callitrichoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny carpeting plant in a warm indoor aquarium or heated greenhouse to survive UK winters.
Press small clumps gently into a rich, fine aquatic soil substrate, leaving just the leaves exposed.
Provide very high light and inject carbon dioxide to stop this delicate stem plant from rotting away.
Trim the carpet regularly with curved scissors to prevent the lower layers from losing light and dying.
Pair it with peaceful cherry shrimp in your tank to naturally keep hair algae off the tiny leaves.

items.name: Micranthemum micranthemoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate stem deeply in fine UK pond soil so the buoyant shoots do not float away.
Trim the fast-growing stems weekly in summer to keep this oxygenator dense and prevent rotting.
Group it with Hornwort in your garden pond to help compete against stubborn UK blanket weed.
Keep your pond water slightly acidic to neutral to prevent this sensitive plant from melting.
Bring a few stems indoors to over-winter in a bright fish tank before the first UK hard frost.

items.name: Micranthes
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist, gritty, acidic to neutral soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden or scree bed.
Water consistently during dry UK spring spells to mimic natural alpine snowmelt without waterlogging.
Plant crowns exactly level with the soil surface and surround with a thick layer of grit to prevent rot.
Propagate by carefully detaching and potting up offsets in late summer after the flowering period.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which target the roots of these compact alpine perennials.

items.name: Micranthes aprica
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in a rock garden to prevent winter wet root rot in UK rain.
Position in partial shade or a north-facing crevice to protect from hot, drying summer afternoon sun.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep almost dry during damp, cold UK winter dormancy.
Propagate by carefully detaching offsets in late spring after flowering to increase your stock.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers, which eat the roots of these small alpine perennials.

items.name: Micranthes bryophora
items.growersTips:
Grow in gritty, free-draining acidic soil in a rock garden or alpine trough to mimic mountain scree.
Position in a north-facing site or partial shade to protect from hot, direct UK summer afternoon sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep dry in winter by using a rain shelter to prevent crown rot.
Propagate by carefully detaching the tiny vegetative bulbils that form in the leaf axils in autumn.
Protect from slugs and vine weevil grubs which target the fleshy foliage and roots in damp weather.

items.name: Micranthes californica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in gritty, free-draining soil at a depth where the crown sits level with the surface.
Water only during dry spring spells, then stop watering in summer when the plant goes dormant.
Protect from winter wet by placing a layer of horticultural grit around the base of the rosette.
Grow alongside companion plants like dwarf ferns or Primula vulgaris in a cool, semi-shaded rockery.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and treat with nematodes if you notice notched leaf margins.

items.name: Micranthes ferruginea
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic humus-rich soil in a cool north-facing rockery to mimic Scottish scree habitats
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged or stagnant
Surround the crown with granite grit to prevent winter wet rot during damp British winters
Propagate by gently detaching the small offsets produced in late summer and potting them in peat-free compost
Keep a vigilant watch for vine weevil grubs which frequently attack the roots of Saxifragaceae species

items.name: Micranthes hieraciifolia
items.growersTips:
Grow in a permanently moist, acidic peat-free compost mixed with grit to mimic UK mountain flushes.
Position in a cold, north-facing rockery or alpine trough to protect from hot UK summer afternoon sun.
Water using collected rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low pH this alpine requires.
Sow seeds in autumn in a cold frame as they need winter chilling to break dormancy in UK climates.
Surround the crown with sharp grit to prevent winter wet rot during damp UK winters.

items.name: Micranthes integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, gritty soil in a rock garden or scree bed to mimic alpine conditions.
Water consistently during dry UK spring months to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate foliage from strong afternoon summer sun.
Propagate by carefully dividing the rosettes in early autumn after the flowering period ends.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Micranthes micranthidifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a permanently wet, acidic bog garden or beside a garden stream in partial to deep shade.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames, leaving pots outdoors to experience winter chill for spring.
Keep soil consistently saturated year-round, mimicking its native Appalachian mountain seep habitat.
Protect young spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic beer traps or physical barriers.
Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Micranthes nelsoniana
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden spot.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to mimic its native damp, subarctic stream habitats.
Position away from aggressive spreading plants, using slow-growing dwarf conifers as companions.
Propagate by dividing the rosettes in early spring just as new growth begins to emerge.
Protect from slugs and snails in wet spring weather using organic beer traps around the foliage.

items.name: Micranthes nidifica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth equal to the root ball in gritty, free-draining acidic soil mix.
Water weekly during dry spring periods but keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in UK peat-free composts and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Position in a north-facing rockery or crevice to mimic alpine conditions and avoid midday sun.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in early summer to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Micranthes nivalis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a gritty, free-draining scree bed or alpine trough to mimic its native UK mountain habitat.
Water only during dry spring spells, then keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot from wet cold.
Plant shallowly in autumn with the crown level with the soil, topped with a thick layer of grit.
Position in a cool, north-facing rock crevice to shield it from intense, direct summer afternoon sun.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in containers, which eat the roots and cause the rosette to collapse.

items.name: Micranthes occidentalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty neutral to acid soil to mimic UK upland scree and prevent winter crown rot.
Position in a north-facing rockery or alpine trough to provide essential cool summer shade.
Water moderately during dry spring growth but keep almost dry during damp UK winter dormancy.
Sow fresh seed in autumn in cold frames to trigger germination via natural UK winter chills.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.

items.name: Micranthes odontoloma
items.growersTips:
Grow in constantly moist humus-rich soil mimicking UK stream edges, never letting the roots dry out.
Position in partial to full shade, ideally on a north-facing slope or cool woodland garden spot.
Plant crown level with the soil surface in autumn to prevent winter waterlogging rot of the base.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
Protect emerging spring foliage from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.

items.name: Micranthes oregana
items.growersTips:
Plant in permanently wet boggy soil or pond edges in full sun to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface as they need winter cold stratification to germinate in UK.
Keep the crown at soil level when planting to prevent rot in the damp conditions it requires.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes in late summer.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.

items.name: Micranthes palmeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining acidic soil mimicking UK scree gardens to prevent winter crown rot.
Position in partial shade facing north or east to protect delicate foliage from harsh midday sun.
Water moderately during dry spring spells but keep virtually dry during dormant wet UK winters.
Surround the base with a thick layer of granite grit to keep foliage off wet soil and deter slugs.
Propagate by carefully detaching offsets in late spring after flowering has finished.

items.name: Micranthes pensylvanica
items.growersTips:
Plant in boggy neutral to acid soil near ponds to mimic its native North American wetland habitat
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chill to germinate in the UK climate
Keep the soil consistently wet or saturated year-round never allowing this perennial to dry out
Position in partial shade to protect the lush foliage from scorching during hot dry UK summers
Divide the rhizomatous crown in early spring every three years to maintain plant vigour and health

items.name: Micranthes petiolaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic soil using leafmould to mimic UK woodland floor conditions.
Position in partial to full shade to protect the delicate foliage from scorching UK summer sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged or soggy.
Propagate by carefully dividing the rosettes in early autumn after the flowering period ends.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails using organic barriers or beer traps in damp weather.

items.name: Micranthes rufidula
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in a rock garden or alpine trough to survive wet UK winters.
Position in partial shade or a north-facing crevice to protect the foliage from hot summer sun.
Water moderately during spring growth but keep almost dry during the damp autumn and winter months.
Surround the plant crown with a layer of granite grit to prevent rot from contact with wet soil.
Propagate by carefully dividing the small rosettes in early spring just as new growth commences.

items.name: Micranthes scopularum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining neutral to acid soil to mimic its native rocky alpine habitat.
Position in a partially shaded, north-facing rockery to protect it from hot UK summer midday sun.
Water moderately in spring but keep almost dry in winter to prevent the crown from rotting in wet.
Propagate by carefully detaching and potting up offsets in late spring after the flowering phase.
Protect from slugs and vine weevil grubs which target the fleshy foliage in damp British springs.

items.name: Micranthes stellaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in a permanently moist, acidic, gritty scree mix or a bog garden to mimic UK mountain rills.
Position in a cool, north-facing spot with shade from midday sun to prevent the foliage scorching.
Water frequently with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the required low soil pH.
Propagate by carefully detaching and potting up the small offsets in late spring after flowering.
Protect the delicate rosettes from winter waterlogging by top-dressing the soil with granite grit.

items.name: Micranthes tolmiei
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining acidic scree or alpine troughs to survive wet UK winters.
Position in a cool, north-facing rock crevice to shield the roots from hot summer afternoon sun.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the preferred low soil pH.
Top-dress the soil surface with a thick layer of granite grit to prevent crown rot from damp.
Propagate by carefully detaching rooted offsets in late spring after the main flowering flush.

items.name: Micranthes virginiensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, well-drained acidic to neutral soil to mimic its native rocky woodland habitat.
Position in partial shade under deciduous shrubs to protect the delicate foliage from hot UK sun.
Water consistently during dry spring spells but keep the crown dry in winter to prevent rot.
Propagate by carefully dividing the small rosettes in early autumn after the summer dormancy.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow natural UK winter chilling for spring germination.

items.name: Micranthus
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs five inches deep in autumn in a warm, sheltered, south-facing border.
Keep the gritty soil moist during spring growth, but let them bake dry once summer flowering ends.
Protect the dormant bulbs from wet UK winters by covering the soil with a thick mulch of dry bark.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the tender emerging shoots during damp British spring days.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme to provide natural support for their slender flowering stems.

items.name: Micranthus alopecuroides
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn, using grit for sharp drainage.
Keep them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse over wet UK winters.
Water weekly during their active spring growth, but keep them bone dry once the foliage dies back.
Pair them with low-growing thymes in a sunny rockery to keep the soil warm and suppress weeds.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as the delicate new shoots emerge from your containers.

items.name: Microberlinia
items.growersTips:
Grow zebrawood in a large pot with ericaceous compost to easily move it indoors before UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer then keep the soil barely damp during the cold winter dormancy.
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain a compact shrub shape in patios.
Check the undersides of the leaves weekly for glasshouse red spider mite during hot dry UK summers.
Feed monthly from April to August with a high-potassium liquid fertilizer to boost root resilience.

items.name: Microberlinia brazzavillensis
items.growersTips:
Grow in a heated conservatory or greenhouse as this tropical West African shrub cannot survive UK frost
Pot in free-draining acidic loam mixed with orchid bark to mimic its native rainforest floor soils
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in winter
Prune lightly in late spring after new growth starts to maintain shape and manage its indoor height
Inspect regularly for spider mites and mealybugs which thrive in dry indoor winter heating drafts

items.name: Microbiota decussata
items.growersTips:
Plant this Siberian cypress in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Give it a light trim in late spring to keep it compact and prevent the center from going bare.
Watch for the bronze winter color shift; it is totally natural and not a sign of a dying plant.
Grow it alongside winter-flowering heathers for a lovely, contrasting groundcover display.
Water regularly during dry summer spells in its first year, then leave it to be drought-tolerant.

items.name: Microchilus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender terrestrial orchid in a warm indoor terrarium to mimic its native tropical home
Keep the peat-free sphagnum moss compost consistently damp but never waterlogged to prevent rot
Place your pot in bright, indirect light near a north or east window, avoiding harsh UK summer sun
Watch closely for fungus gnats in the damp soil and use yellow sticky traps to catch them early
Repot gently in spring only when the creeping rhizomes begin to spill over the edge of the container

items.name: Microchirita
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Asian beauty indoors or in a heated conservatory to protect it from UK winter frost.
Water from the bottom with tepid rainwater to keep the delicate, hairy leaves dry and prevent rot.
Pot your plant in a free-draining mix of equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and vermiculite.
Place it on a north or east-facing windowsill where it gets bright light but no scorching midday sun.
Watch out for aphids and thrips in spring, gently dabbing them off with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Microchirita lavandulacea
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender plant indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Keep the compost moist but never soggy, watering only from the base to avoid rotting the stems.
Grow it in a bright conservatory or windowsill, shielded from the harsh afternoon summer sun.
Plant in a free-draining mix of equal parts peat-free compost, perlite, and fine horticultural grit.
Watch out for aphids and glasshouse whitefly, treating them early with an organic insecticidal soap.

items.name: Microgramma
items.growersTips:
Grow this epiphytic fern in a chunky orchid bark and sphagnum moss mix to mimic its wild tree home.
Keep your plant in a humid bathroom or mist it daily to survive dry UK winter central heating.
Water only when the moss feels dry, using rainwater to avoid the tap water minerals they hate.
Mount it on cork bark with fishing line so the creeping rhizomes can spread naturally indoors.
Position it in bright, indirect light near a north window, keeping it safe from strong summer sun.

items.name: Microgramma lycopodioides
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical epiphyte on cork bark in a humid, warm terrarium to survive chilly UK winters.
Mist the creeping rhizomes daily with rainwater rather than tap water to prevent mineral buildup.
Position in bright, indirect light near a north window to mimic its natural shaded canopy home.
Bind the roots gently with fishing line onto damp sphagnum moss instead of burying them in soil.
Keep indoor temperatures above fifteen degrees Celsius year-round to stop this fern dropping fronds.

items.name: Microgramma megalophylla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical epiphyte on cork bark in a humid UK terrarium rather than planting it in soil.
Mist the creeping rhizomes daily with rainwater to mimic its natural rainforest canopy home.
Position it in bright, indirect light near a north window to prevent the delicate fronds from burning.
Keep your home heating above fifteen degrees Celsius in winter to protect this tender fern from frost.
Propagate by cutting a rhizome section with at least three leaves and pinning it to damp sphagnum moss.

items.name: Microgramma nitida
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical epiphyte in a chunky orchid bark mix rather than standard UK potting compost.
Mist the creeping rhizomes daily to mimic rainforest humidity in centrally heated British homes.
Mount it on cork bark with sphagnum moss to let its shallow roots breathe and spread naturally.
Keep it in bright, indirect light near a north or east window to avoid scorching the fronds.
Water only when the moss feels dry to the touch, using rainwater rather than hard UK tap water.

items.name: Microgramma squamulosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical epiphytic fern in a hanging basket of orchid bark and moss, never in standard soil.
Keep it indoors year-round or in a heated greenhouse, as it will not survive a damp UK winter frost.
Mist the creeping rhizomes daily with rainwater to mimic its native humid South American rainforest.
Position it in bright, indirect light near a north or east window, avoiding harsh direct UK sun.
Propagate in spring by cutting a rhizome section with at least three fronds and pinning it to moss.

items.name: Microloma
items.growersTips:
Bring these South African climbers indoors by October to protect them from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix in spring.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, then let any excess drain away completely.
Give them a sturdy twiggy tripod to climb on as soon as those delicate twining stems start to grow.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites in summer and mist the leaves gently to keep them away.

items.name: Microloma calycinum
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African climber in a pot of gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive UK rain.
Keep it on a sunny windowsill or heated greenhouse as it cannot survive wet UK winter frosts.
Water sparingly from below only when the soil dries out completely, mimicking its native dry cycle.
Provide a small wire trellis or twiggy sticks early on so its twining stems can climb naturally.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs in summer and wipe them off with a damp cotton bud immediately.

items.name: Microloma sagittatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African climber in a gritty, free-draining loam to survive wet UK winters.
Grow it in a pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse when autumn temperatures drop.
Water sparingly from below during summer, letting the compost dry out completely between drenches.
Provide a slender trellis or birch twigs early on for its delicate twining stems to scramble up.
Watch out for red spider mites when keeping this vine in your conservatory during warmer months.

items.name: Microloma tenuifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African native in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive UK wet spells.
Keep it in a pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory for the winter.
Water it only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, then give it a light, careful drink.
Provide a small, delicate trellis or twiggy sticks for its twining stems to climb up naturally.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping this delicate climber indoors over winter.

items.name: Microparacaryum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames to allow winter chilling to break dormancy before spring growth.
Plant in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters and damp springs.
Position in full sun against a south-facing wall to mimic its native dry montane microclimate.

items.name: Minuartia groenlandica
