Water only from below during the autumn growing season to prevent water collecting in the crown.
Keep the pots completely dry and cool during their summer dormancy to prevent the tubers rotting.
Watch out for glasshouse slugs and snails that love to chew the emerging flower spikes in autumn.

items.name: Nama
items.growersTips:
Bring nama indoors over winter as our UK frosts will easily kill this tender perennial.
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot using fifty percent grit to ensure ultra-sharp drainage.
Water nama only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, as damp UK soil causes root rot quickly.
Place your potted nama on a south-facing patio to maximise the precious summer sun it craves.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering your nama in a heated conservatory.

items.name: Nama aretioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree bed to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Protect the low foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers during damp spring nights.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a cold frame to shield it from winter rain.
Topdress the soil with a thick layer of fine gravel to keep the collar dry and prevent damp rot.

items.name: Nama demissa
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, mimicking its natural arid habitat to prevent root rot.
Position your pot on a south-facing patio to catch every bit of precious British summer sunshine.
Keep a close eye out for slugs and snails, as they love to feast on its succulent-like foliage.
Bring your potted plant indoors to a bright windowsill before the first autumn frosts arrive.

items.name: Nama densa
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are bone dry, keeping it completely dry over winter.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot of your garden, ideally against a south-facing brick wall.
Protect this delicate perennial from frost by moving the pot into a cold greenhouse by October.
Mix horticultural sand into your compost to mimic its natural sandy soil and prevent root rot.

items.name: Nama hispida
items.growersTips:
Plant this Texas native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pot in the sunniest south-facing spot you have to mimic its hot desert home.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly but never let the pot sit in water.
Bring the pot into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch from October to April to stop winter rot.
Prune back the woody stems by half in early spring to encourage fresh, bushy new summer growth.

items.name: Nama lobbii
items.growersTips:
Plant this woolly mountain native in a raised bed with lots of grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot possible to mimic its natural dry Californian slopes.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, as damp roots will rot this plant.
Protect the fuzzy foliage from winter wet by placing a cloche over it from November to March.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to ensure you have backups for cold snaps.

items.name: Nama pusilla
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny desert native in a gritty, free-draining alpine compost mix to survive wet winters.
Keep it safe from damp UK cold by overwintering your potted plants in a bright, unheated greenhouse.
Water very sparingly from below only when the soil is bone dry, keeping the foliage completely dry.
Top-dress your pots with fine granite grit to keep the delicate collar safe from rotting in rain.
Position your pots in the absolute sunniest, south-facing spot in your garden to mimic its home.

items.name: Nama rothrockii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Californian native in extremely sharp-draining gravelly soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position your Rothrock's nama in your hottest, most south-facing gravel garden or sunny raised bed.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails who love the tender new growth in damp springs.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late winter to back up your plants against severe UK frosts.

items.name: Namaquanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your Namaquanthus indoors to a sunny windowsill before the damp autumn frosts arrive.
Plant this succulent in a fifty-fifty mix of grit and peat-free compost to prevent root rot.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely during the dark winter months.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints; dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Grow them in terracotta pots rather than the open ground to manage the wet UK weather easily.

items.name: Namibia
items.growersTips:
Try mixing seventy percent grit into your peat-free compost to stop this desert gem rotting.
Only water this succulent when its stone-like leaves wrinkle, keeping it totally dry all winter.
Grow your Namibia on a south-facing windowsill to give it the intense UK sunshine it craves.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints; dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Sow seeds in spring on damp sand, then cover the pot with cling film to keep the humidity high.

items.name: Namibia cinerea
items.growersTips:
Bring this succulent indoors by October to protect it from wet, frosty UK autumns and winters.
Grow it in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes number two and half horticultural grit.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, keeping it completely dry from November through to March.
Place it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic its native southern African sun.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints, dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

items.name: Nananthus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Nananthus in a mix of equal parts John Innes number two and grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only on sunny mornings from April to September, letting the gritty soil dry out completely.
Keep these low-growing gems in pots on a sunny patio so you can move them under glass when frost hits.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight rosette foliage during dry spells in your greenhouse.
Grow them alongside hardy Sedums in a alpine trough to create a beautiful, free-draining display.

items.name: Nananthus vittatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this South African gem in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes No 2 and half grit.
Keep it on a sunny windowsill or in a cold greenhouse to shield it from wet UK winter rot.
Water thoroughly only when the soil is bone dry from April to September, then keep completely dry.
Plant the tuberous root crown slightly raised above the soil line to prevent neck rot in damp air.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf crevices and treat them with a cotton bud in alcohol.

items.name: Nandina
items.growersTips:
Plant in a spot sheltered from cold UK winds to stop those gorgeous winter berries from dropping.
Feed with an ericaceous fertiliser in spring if your garden has the typical heavy UK clay soil.
Give it a light prune in mid-spring, just cutting back any leggy stems to keep the shape compact.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers until the root system is fully established.
Grow the dwarf cultivar Firepower in a patio pot if you want the best fiery red winter foliage.

items.name: Nanorrhinum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface in spring, pressing lightly without burying them deep.
Water sparingly once established, allowing the gritty compost to dry out fully between waterings.
Cut back faded stems in autumn to encourage a compact habit and prevent the plant from flopping.
Grow alongside Sedums or Sempervivums in rock gardens to match their low-water, high-drainage needs.

items.name: Nanorrhinum scoparium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Canary Island native in your sunniest, sheltered UK gravel garden or a very gritty pot.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, as this plant hates soggy winter roots.
Protect it from harsh UK frosts by moving containers into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch.
Prune back the wiry stems by half in late spring to encourage fresh, bushy new flowering growth.
Grow it alongside sedums or thymes in poor, sharply draining soil to mimic its wild rocky home.

items.name: Naravelia
items.growersTips:
Grow Naravelia in a large pot of loam-based compost so you can move it into a heated greenhouse for winter
Water deeply once a week in summer but keep the compost barely damp from November to March to prevent rot
Prune stems back by half in April to encourage bushy growth and more yellow-green flowers on new wood
Provide a sturdy trellis in a sheltered south-facing spot to support its leaf-tip climbing tendrils
Watch for clematis slime flux on damaged stems in wet UK springs and prune out affected wood immediately

items.name: Naravelia zeylanica
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical climber indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a deep pot using free-draining loam mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Position your pot in a conservatory or south-facing window so it gets the maximum possible UK sun.
Provide a sturdy trellis or obelisk early on so its sensitive leaf-tendrils have support to climb.
Water generously in summer but let the top inch dry out completely before watering during winter.

items.name: Nautilocalyx
items.growersTips:
Grow these tropical beauties in pots of peat-free compost with perlite to survive damp UK winters.
Keep them on a warm, east-facing windowsill to mimic their native rainforest canopy light.
Water only when the top inch of soil dries out, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid shocking roots.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles, but never let the roots sit in water.
Feed them fortnightly with a half-strength high-potash liquid fertiliser from April to September.

items.name: Nautilocalyx bicolor
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical beauty indoors year-round as it cannot survive a chilly British winter outside.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of compost dries out to avoid shocking the roots.
Grow in a peat-free houseplant mix enriched with perlite to ensure the roots never sit in soggy soil.
Place on a pebble tray filled with water to boost humidity levels in dry, centrally heated UK homes.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertilizer once a fortnight from April to September for lush leaves.

items.name: Nautilocalyx ecuadoranus
items.growersTips:
Grow this Ecuadorian beauty in a pot indoors or in a heated greenhouse to shield it from UK frosts.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy by watering with tepid rainwater from below.
Place it in bright, filtered light near a north or east window to avoid scorching the soft leaves.
Feed with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertilizer every fortnight from April through September.
Maintain high humidity around the plant by placing its pot on a tray of wet clay pebbles or leca.

items.name: Nautilocalyx glandulifer
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical perennial warm indoors over winter as UK frost will quickly kill it.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of compost dries to avoid root rot.
Grow in a peat-free, free-draining mix of equal parts coir, perlite, and orchid bark.
Position in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to prevent leaf scorch.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to stop leaf drop.

items.name: Nautilocalyx melittifolius
items.growersTips:
Bring this Caribbean beauty inside for winter as it cannot survive a chilly UK frost outdoors.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy using lukewarm rainwater to avoid root shock.
Position in bright indirect light near an east window to mimic its natural shaded forest canopy.
Mix plenty of perlite and orchid bark into peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage it loves.
Snip off the faded red flowers in autumn to keep the plant looking tidy and encourage fresh growth.

items.name: Neatostema
items.growersTips:
Plant this native borage relative in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors so the cold winter weather naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep watering minimal once established, as this dry-pasture lover hates soggy summer soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the young, hairy spring foliage.
Grow it alongside wild thyme or biting stonecrop to mimic its natural gravelly habitat.

items.name: Negria
items.growersTips:
Bring this Lord Howe Island native indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winters.
Grow your Negria in a pot with ericaceous compost and grit to keep the soil acidic and free-draining.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to prevent lime buildup and keep the foliage healthy.
Place your pot in bright, filtered light near a window, avoiding the harsh direct midday sun.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping this plant in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Nelsonia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Nelsonia in a warm greenhouse using grit-heavy soil to survive damp UK winters.
Water sparingly from below during winter to prevent crown rot in our cool British climate.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when growing this tender perennial under cover.
Propagate your Nelsonia by taking softwood cuttings in late spring when active growth begins.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn frosts hit.

items.name: Nelsonia canescens
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical creeper in a heated greenhouse or conservatory to survive chilly UK winters.
Plant it in a free-draining, peat-free loam compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent root rot.
Water generously during active summer growth but let the top inch of soil dry out between drinks.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites which thrive in dry indoor air during summer.
Propagate by taking softwood stem cuttings in late spring and rooting them in a heated propagator.

items.name: Nelsonioideae
items.growersTips:
Grow these tender African natives in pots of peat-free loam so you can move them indoors by October.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out, keeping them barely damp during winter.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and treat early with organic insecticidal soap under the leaves.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your compost to ensure the sharp drainage these plants need.
Sow your seeds shallowly in early spring on a heated propagator mat set to twenty-one degrees.

items.name: Neltuma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to avoid disturbing their sensitive taproots.
Plant out in late May in your sunniest south-facing spot with grit added for sharp drainage.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or copper tape around pots.
Grow alongside rosemary or lavender to match their love for poor soil and baking hot sun.

items.name: Nemacladus
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny threadstem seeds on the surface of gritty, free-draining soil in early UK spring.
Keep watering minimal, letting the sandy compost dry out completely between light mistings.
Grow them in pots so you can move them under glass to protect against wet, cold UK winters.
Place containers on a south-facing patio to maximise the bright sun these desert natives crave.
Watch out for slugs and snails which will quickly devour the delicate, thread-like stems.

items.name: Nemacladus glanduliferus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in sandy, free-draining grit to mimic their native dry desert soils.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the soil dry out completely between light sprinkles.
Protect these delicate plants from slugs and snails which love to feast on their tender stems.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them indoors to escape wet, freezing UK winter weather.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot of your garden to give them the maximum light they crave.

items.name: Nemacladus rigidus
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of gritty, free-draining compost in early spring, do not bury.
Keep them in a cold frame to mimic chilly UK springs, watering only from below to prevent rotting.
Plant them alongside hardy sedums in a sunny, sheltered rock garden to shield them from wet winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails in May as they love to devour the delicate, thread-like new stems.
Avoid rich soil and fertilizers, as these starved beauties actually thrive best in poor, sandy grit.

items.name: Nemacladus sigmoideus
items.growersTips:
Grow this tiny threadplant in gritty, sharply draining alpine compost to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the dust-like seeds on the soil surface in early spring, pressing lightly without covering.
Keep potted plants in a cold frame to shelter them from relentless British winter rain and rot.
Water sparingly from below during summer, letting the gritty potting mix dry out between drinks.
Watch out for slugs and snails, which can quickly devour this delicate, thread-like plant.

items.name: Nemacladus twisselmannii
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare desert native indoors for winter to protect it from wet UK frosts and damp soil.
Grow it in a gritty cactus compost mix with fifty percent perlite to ensure perfect drainage.
Water very sparingly only when the soil is bone dry to prevent root rot in our cool climate.
Keep it on a south facing windowsill to mimic its natural bright California desert habitat.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Nemastylis
items.growersTips:
Plant your celestial lily bulbs five inches deep in autumn to protect them from cold UK frosts.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil because these bulbs will rot in wet, heavy British winter clay.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a greenhouse or cold frame when winter wet hits.
Water them regularly during their spring growth but keep them completely dry once they go dormant.
Position them in your warmest, most sheltered south-facing spot to mimic their sunny native home.

items.name: Nemastylis floridana
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn in a warm, sheltered spot to mimic Florida heat.
Grow them in pots of gritty, free-draining compost so you can easily move them indoors for winter.
Water them generously throughout their summer active growth, but keep them bone dry during winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to devour the emerging tender green shoots.
Position them next to low-growing sedums to support their floppy stems and show off the blue flowers.

items.name: Nemastylis geminiflora
items.growersTips:
Plant these prairie bulbs five inches deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors for winter.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to keep their roots dry during wet British winters.
Water them weekly during their spring growth but stop completely when they go dormant in July.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the emerging pleated leaves.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme to support their thin stems and protect them from wind.

items.name: Nematanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your goldfish plant indoors by autumn as it cannot survive a damp, chilly UK winter outside.
Water only when the top two inches of compost dry out to prevent root rot in our humid climate.
Hang it in a bright, east-facing window to get morning sun without scorching the delicate leaves.
Prune leggy stems by one-third in spring to encourage bushy growth and more orange blooms.
Repot every two years in spring using a free-draining peat-free compost mixed with orchid bark.

items.name: Nematanthus gregarius
items.growersTips:
Keep your goldfish plant indoors in winter as our UK frost will kill this tender Brazilian native.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp air.
Hang it in a bright, east-facing window to get the morning sun without scorching those glossy leaves.
Prune leggy stems by one-third in spring to encourage bushy growth and way more orange blooms.
Feed with a high-potash tomato fertiliser every fortnight from April to September for maximum flowers.

items.name: Nemophila
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April as they dislike transplanting in our damp UK spring weather.
Cover seeds with just five millimetres of soil because they need total darkness to germinate well.
Water the soil gently at the base to keep it moist without wetting the delicate saucer-shaped blooms.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love devouring the tender young foliage during wet British Mays.
Plant them alongside yellow violas to create a beautiful contrasting carpet in your border edges.

items.name: Nemophila aphylla
items.growersTips:
Sow these woodland natives in autumn just beneath the soil surface so winter cold breaks their dormancy.
Keep the soil consistently damp but not soggy, mimicking a shaded British stream bank in spring.
Plant them alongside native primroses and ferns to create a natural, moisture-loving shade community.
Watch out for slugs during wet UK springs, as they find the tender, low-growing foliage irresistible.
Avoid hot midday sun by choosing a sheltered, dappled spot under deciduous garden trees or shrubs.

items.name: Nemophila heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate native in partial shade to mimic its natural woodland edge habitat in the UK.
Sow seeds shallowly at just three millimetres deep in autumn for early spring blooms next year.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during our dry late spring spells.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Grow it alongside native ferns or primroses which thrive in the same damp, dappled shade spots.

items.name: Nemophila maculata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April or May, just five millimetres deep, where you want them to bloom.
Water gently at the base to keep soil moist but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love eating the young, tender foliage during damp British springs.
Sow alongside yellow violas or red poppies for a stunning, contrasting cottage garden colour mix.
Grow this as a hardy annual in the UK, pulling up spent plants in autumn to let them self-seed.

items.name: Nemophila menziesii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April at 5mm depth, as they hate root disturbance from transplanting.
Water the soil gently at the base to keep it damp but never soggy, especially during dry May spells.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, which absolutely love devouring these tender young shoots.
Plant them alongside yellow violas or spring bulbs to create a gorgeous, contrasting colour display.
Sow a second batch in late June to extend those beautiful sky-blue blooms right through to autumn.

items.name: Nemophila parviflora
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds shallowly in early spring, just barely covering them with a light grit layer.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, especially during our cool, wet UK spring days.
Watch out for slugs and snails who absolutely love devouring the tender young spring foliage.
Plant them alongside native woodlanders like wild primroses to mimic their natural shady habitat.
Clear away the spent summer growth in autumn to let the self-sown seedlings emerge for next year.

items.name: Nemophila pedunculata
items.growersTips:
Sow these low-growers in early spring just two millimeters deep so light can trigger germination.
Water them gently at the base twice a week to keep the soil damp without rotting their delicate stems.
Watch out for slugs in damp UK springs by using organic wool pellets around your young plants.
Grow them alongside spring bulbs like yellow daffodils for a gorgeous blue and gold contrast.
Shear them back by half in midsummer after flowering to encourage a fresh flush of green leaves.

items.name: Nemophila phacelioides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring just 3mm deep in moist soil, as they need darkness to germinate.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, mimicking the cool, wet UK spring they love.
Watch out for slugs and snails in May, as they absolutely love devouring the tender young foliage.
Plant them alongside spring bulbs like daffodils to hide the fading bulb foliage as they spread out.
Cut the stems back to the ground in late summer once they finish flowering to encourage fresh growth.

items.name: Nemophila spatulata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn or early spring just 3mm deep in well-drained, gritty soil to mimic mountain scree.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the tender young foliage during wet spring nights.
Plant them alongside dwarf spring bulbs like crocus to cover the bare soil as the bulbs fade away.
Grow this low alpine in a raised bed or alpine trough to ensure the sharp drainage it absolutely needs.

items.name: Nemosenecio nikoensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they need light to germinate in the cool UK climate.
Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic its native Japanese woodland habitat.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but not waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails which target tender Asteraceae foliage in damp spring.
Plant alongside hostas or ferns in a woodland border to provide the dappled shade it requires.

items.name: Neocallitropsis pancheri
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare New Caledonia conifer in a large pot so you can move it indoors before winter frosts.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining ericaceous compost mix to mimic its native ultramafic soil needs.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH slightly acidic to neutral.
Position your pot in the brightest, sunniest spot on your patio to replicate its tropical light.
Check regularly for mealybugs in the dense, scale-like foliage during dry summer spells.

items.name: Neocheiropteris
items.growersTips:
Try growing Neocheiropteris palmatopedata in a moist, peat-free ericaceous compost with added grit.
Position this fern in deep shade under a north-facing wall to mimic its native forest floor habitat.
Water consistently with harvested rainwater to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged in winter.
Mulch the rhizomes with leaf mould in November to insulate them from harsh UK winter frosts.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on the tender new fronds as they unfurl in early spring.

items.name: Neohenricia
items.growersTips:
Bring your scented Neohenricia indoors by October to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant this night-bloomer in a grit-heavy, free-draining mix of two parts pumice to one part loam.
Water only when the tiny, toothy leaves feel slightly soft, keeping it bone dry from November.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to mimic its sunny South African home.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense, low-growing mat of highly textured foliage.

items.name: Neohenricia sibbettii
items.growersTips:
Grow this nocturnal beauty in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost with extra perlite or pumice.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill indoors, as it will not survive a wet UK winter outside.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through to March.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices of its highly textured, coral-like leaves.
Repot in spring only when the clump crowds the pot edge, using a shallow container to prevent rot.

items.name: Neoholmgrenia
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in boggy soil or pond edges to mimic its natural damp habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames so the natural UK winter chill can break their dormancy.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British springs as they love the tender new shoots.
Leave the faded foliage intact over winter to protect the crown from severe UK frosts.
Divide mature clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to keep the plant vigorous.

items.name: Neoholmgrenia andina
items.growersTips:
Grow this Andean alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree bed to survive wet UK winters without rot.
Keep soil barely damp in summer, watering only from below to protect its delicate, low-growing foliage.
Shield the plant with a pane of glass from November to March to mimic dry, cold mountain conditions.
Plant it alongside saxifrages in a raised alpine trough to create a natural, well-drained community.
Watch out for slugs in early spring, as they love to devour the tender new shoots of this perennial.

items.name: Neolepisorus fortunei
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen fern in a sheltered, shady spot with acidic to neutral leaf-mould enriched soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Mulch the shallow rhizomes with bark in late autumn to protect them from severe British winter frosts.
Snip away any tatty, wind-damaged fronds in mid-spring just as the fresh new growth begins to emerge.
Divide overcrowded clumps in spring and pot them up to propagate new plants for your woodland borders.

items.name: Neomarica
items.growersTips:
Bring your walking iris indoors before the first autumn frost as they cannot survive UK winters.
Plant the rhizomes shallowly with the tops just showing in a rich, acidic, well-draining soil mix.
Water them generously throughout the summer but let the soil dry out completely during the winter.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping these plants in your conservatory or porch.
Cut back the flowered stems only after the new baby plantlet at the tip has rooted into the soil.

items.name: Neomarica candida
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted false iris indoors before the first autumn frost to protect it from UK freezes.
Plant the rhizomes shallowly with their tops just peeking out of a gritty, well-draining soil mix.
Water your plant generously in summer but let the compost dry out between waterings in winter.
Keep an eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are overwintering them in a warm conservatory.
Snip off the faded flowers at the base to encourage the plant to produce healthy new leaf fans.

items.name: Neomarica northiana
items.growersTips:
Bring your walking iris indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive UK winters.
Grow this beauty in a pot so you can easily move it inside to a bright conservatory for winter.
Keep the compost moist but not soggy during summer, then water much less throughout the winter.
Plant the rhizomes shallowly with their tops just showing above a free-draining, gritty soil mix.
Let the spent flower stems arch to the ground so the new baby plantlets can root in nearby pots.

items.name: Neotinea
items.growersTips:
Plant these native UK orchids in well-drained, chalky or limestone soil to mimic their wild downs.
Keep the soil damp through winter and spring, but let them go completely dry once they die back.
Plant the tubers shallowly in autumn, just two inches deep, with the pointed growing tip facing up.
Sow wild fescue grasses nearby to provide the vital mycorrhizal fungi these orchids need to thrive.
Watch out for slugs in early spring as they love to eat the emerging flower spikes of burnt orchids.

items.name: Neottia
items.growersTips:
Plant these native orchids in deep shade under beech trees where they can feed on leaf mould fungi.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy by mimicking a damp woodland floor with a thick leaf mulch.
Do not use standard fertilisers as they destroy the vital mycorrhizal fungi these plants need.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love eating the emerging flower spikes.
Leave the soil completely undisturbed after planting so you do not damage the delicate root system.

items.name: Nephelaphyllum
items.growersTips:
Grow these terrestrial orchids in a shallow, free-draining mix of fine bark, perlite, and chopped moss.
Keep them in a warm, humid bathroom or heated greenhouse to mimic their tropical forest floor home.
Water with tepid rainwater to keep the compost damp but never soggy, especially during chilly winters.
Position in bright, indirect light as strong UK summer sun will easily scorch their mottled leaves.
Watch out for fungus gnats in the damp compost and treat with biological control nematodes in spring.

items.name: Nephthytis
items.growersTips:
Keep this West African native potted indoors as UK winters are far too cold for it to survive outside.
Water only when the top two inches of peat-free compost dry out to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Wipe the arrow-shaped leaves with a damp cloth monthly to clear dust and keep photosynthesis active.
Place your pot in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to avoid scorching the foliage.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost active growth.

items.name: Nephthytis swainei
items.growersTips:
Grow this African native in a warm conservatory or terrarium to shield it from chilly UK drafts.
Keep the compost evenly moist but never soggy, using lukewarm rainwater to avoid shocking the roots.
Position your plant in bright, indirect light, avoiding direct midday sun which scorches the leaves.
Feed with a weak liquid seaweed fertiliser once a month from April to September for lush growth.
Repot every two years in spring using a free-draining mix of peat-free compost, orchid bark, and perlite.

items.name: Neptunia
items.growersTips:
Keep your sensitive Neptunia oleracea floating in a warm, sunny garden pond from June to August.
Grow this tender annual in a shallow container of water indoors until the late May frosts pass.
Plant the roots in heavy clay loam at the bottom of a basket submerged just ten centimetres deep.
Watch out for pond snails eating the delicate feathery leaves and clear them off by hand weekly.
Bring your potted water mimosa inside to a bright windowsill before autumn night temperatures drop.

items.name: Neptunia oleracea
items.growersTips:
Grow this sensitive water-mimosa in a sunny indoor pond or heated conservatory to escape UK chills.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in rich, wet compost before submerging the pot in water.
Keep the water temperature above twenty degrees Celsius using a small aquarium heater in your pond.
Watch out for aphids on the floating stems and gently wash them off with a lukewarm water spray.
Bring your plants indoors by late September before the first autumn frosts damage the foliage.

items.name: Nerieae
items.growersTips:
Plant Nerine bowdenii bulbs in summer with their noses just peeking out of well-drained soil.
Situate your nerines against a south-facing brick wall to trap vital extra warmth in UK winters.
Divide congested clumps in summer right after the foliage dies back but before autumn flowering.
Water container-grown nerines weekly in summer but keep them completely dry during winter dormancy.
Protect emerging autumn flower buds from slugs by scattering organic grit around the bulb clumps.

items.name: Nesocodon
items.growersTips:
Grow this Mauritian beauty in a pot so you can bring it inside before the first UK autumn frost.
Water only when the top inch of compost feels dry, as its roots will rot quickly in damp UK soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails, as they absolutely love devouring the rare red nectar it produces.
Repot in spring using a very free-draining mix of peat-free compost, perlite, and horticultural grit.
Keep it on a warm, bright windowsill in winter, away from cold drafts and central heating radiators.

items.name: Neuracanthus
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted Neuracanthus indoors to a heated greenhouse before the first autumn frost hits.
Grow this African native in a free-draining mix of two parts grit to one part peat-free compost.
Water only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, as this plant easily rots in damp UK clay.
Position your pots on a south-facing windowsill to maximise the weak British winter sunlight.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser once a month from May to August to boost flowering.

items.name: Neuracanthus aculeatus
items.growersTips:
Bring this African native indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining loam to prevent root rot during our damp British summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, mimicking its natural dry-season cycle.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum daily sunlight the UK offers.
Snip back leggy stems in late spring to encourage a bushier habit and more compact growth.

items.name: Neurolaena
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early April to give this warmth-loving annual a head start in the UK.
Plant them out in late May in free-draining sandy loam enriched with well-rotted garden compost.
Water deeply once a week at the base to keep the soil moist but never soggy during dry summer spells.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around stems.
Sow alongside marigolds to help deter common UK pests while boosting your patch's overall health.

items.name: Neuwiedia griffithii
items.growersTips:
Keep this rare orchid relative in a warm conservatory as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter.
Plant it in a free-draining mix of orchid bark and peat free compost to mimic its forest floor home.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent fatal root rot.
Position it in bright indirect light away from harsh afternoon sun which easily scorches the leaves.
Maintain high humidity by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to stop the leaf tips browning.

items.name: Neuwiedia zollingeri
items.growersTips:
Bring this orchid indoors by October as it cannot survive a damp, freezing UK winter outside.
Grow it in a free-draining mix of orchid bark and perlite, keeping the soil damp but never soggy.
Place your pot in bright, indirect light like a east-facing windowsill to mimic its forest home.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a month during spring to encourage its yellow blooms.
Watch out for spider mites in dry indoor air, misting the leaves occasionally to keep them away.

items.name: Newtonia
items.growersTips:
Sow your Newtonia seeds indoors in April, then plant out in May once the final frost has passed.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering gently at the base to prevent stem rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach ten centimeters to encourage a bushier habit.
Position these annuals in your sunniest border spot to maximize their short summer flowering run.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots; use beer traps or copper tape around your pots to deter them.

items.name: Newtonia buchananii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early April at a depth of one centimetre to protect them from late UK frosts.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this annual needs in wet UK summers.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than spraying the leaves to prevent powdery mildew.
Keep a sharp lookout for slugs and snails which love to devour the tender young spring shoots.
Plant alongside calendula to help deter pests and attract beneficial pollinators to your garden.

items.name: Nicoteba
items.growersTips:
Plant Nicoteba tubers five inches deep in rich, well-drained loam after the last late May frost.
Water thoroughly once a week at the base, keeping leaves dry to prevent damp-loving UK mildews.
Protect tender spring shoots from hungry slugs using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Cut back the faded flowering stems to the ground in autumn to encourage strong return next spring.
Mulch the crown heavily with bark chippings in November to shield roots from wet British winters.

items.name: Nicoteba betonica
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial in spring after frosts, placing the root crown level with your UK soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry British summers rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Watch out for slugs and snails on fresh spring shoots, using beer traps or organic pellets.
Cut back the dead stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the plant tidy over winter.
Mix plenty of well-rotted compost into heavy UK clay soil before planting to ensure good drainage.

items.name: Nidularium amazonicum
items.growersTips:
Keep this Brazilian beauty in a pot so you can bring it indoors before the first autumn frost hits.
Water directly into the central rosette using rainwater, keeping it topped up but never stagnant.
Plant in a peat-free orchid compost mix with added perlite to ensure the roots never sit in soggy soil.
Place it on a bright UK windowsill but shield it from direct summer sun to prevent leaf scorching.
Flush the central urn with fresh water monthly to prevent stale salt build-up from tap water.

items.name: Nidularium atalaiaense
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant indoors by October to protect its tender leaves from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Water directly into the central rosette cup using tepid rainwater, keeping it topped up weekly.
Pot it in a free-draining mix of orchid bark and peat-free compost to prevent soggy root rot.
Position it in bright, filtered light near an east window to mimic its natural canopy home.
Flush the central cup with fresh water monthly to stop stagnant mineral buildup in hard-water areas.

items.name: Nigella
items.growersTips:
Sow Nigella seeds directly into raked UK soil in September for much earlier flowers next spring.
Thin your seedlings to fifteen centimeters apart so they grow sturdy stems and do not flop over.
Leave the beautiful seedpods on the stems to dry out so you can collect seeds for next year.
Grow them alongside your carrots to help deter the pesky carrot fly with their feathery foliage.
Give them a sunny spot in well-drained soil, as they hate sitting in wet winter mud.

items.name: Nigella arvensis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn to let UK winter cold naturally trigger spring germination.
Grow them in poor, sharply draining chalky soil to mimic their native dry UK downland habitats.
Water seedlings sparingly during damp UK springs as they hate sitting in cold, waterlogged soil.
Sow alongside wild marjoram or field scabious to create a perfect native UK pollinator haven.
Leave the gorgeous horned seed pods over winter to feed local birds and encourage self-seeding.

items.name: Nigella ciliaris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly into well-drained, gritty soil to mimic its native dry Mediterranean winter.
Keep watering minimal once established, only soaking during prolonged hot UK summer dry spells.
Plant alongside rosemary or thymes in full sun to match their shared love for sharp drainage.
Leave the unique bristly seed pods on the plant over winter for beautiful structure and self-seeding.
Protect young spring shoots from damp-loving slugs using grit barriers around the base of the plant.

items.name: Nigella damascena
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in spring or autumn at a depth of one centimetre to avoid root disturbance.
Water seedlings lightly until established then leave to tolerate dry UK summer soil without rotting.
Thin emerging seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart to prevent mildew in damp British weather.
Leave the decorative balloon-like seed pods on the stem to self-seed naturally for the next spring.
Sow alongside calendula to attract beneficial ladybirds that control aphids in UK cottage gardens.

items.name: Nigella gallica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in spring into well-drained, gritty soil as they hate root disturbance.
Water sparingly once established, only during dry spells, to mimic their dry Mediterranean home.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with pet-safe grit barriers.
Deadhead regularly to prolong the blue blooms, but leave some seedpods for winter structure.
Plant them alongside silver-foliaged herbs like thyme and oregano which love the same sunny spots.

items.name: Nigella hispanica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April directly where they will flower as they dislike root disturbance.
Water young plants weekly until established then let the UK rain do the work in well-drained soil.
Watch out for slugs on tender spring shoots by using beer traps or organic wool pellets around them.
Deadhead regularly to prolong the summer blooms or leave seed pods for beautiful winter structure.
Plant them alongside companion herbs like rosemary and thyme which love the same sunny dry spots.

items.name: Nigella orientalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April or May, just barely covering them with a light dusting of soil.
Thin your seedlings to fifteen centimeters apart so these upright plants don't crowd each other out.
Water them only during dry spells as they absolutely hate sitting in wet, heavy UK winter clay.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids on the young shoots and wash them off with a gentle hose spray.
Let the unusual green and purple seed pods dry on the stem to collect next year's seeds in autumn.

items.name: Nigella sativa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outside in April at a depth of one centimetre, as they hate root disturbance.
Water your plants only during dry spells, as this Mediterranean native rots in soggy UK soil.
Watch out for slugs eating the young seedlings during damp British spring nights using beer traps.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before sowing to ensure the sharp drainage these plants crave.
Grow them next to your potatoes to help deter common pests and add a lovely splash of blue.

items.name: Nigella segetalis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they will flower to let UK winter cold naturally break dormancy.
Sow shallowly at just five millimetres deep in sharply draining grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water seedlings weekly during dry spring spells, but leave established plants alone to brave droughts.
Position near lavender or rosemary to give this wild Mediterranean beauty the dry, sunny bed it craves.
Leave the decorative seed pods intact over winter to feed local birds and encourage self-seeding.

items.name: Nigritella
items.growersTips:
Grow vanilla orchids in a cold frame using a gritty, free-draining alkaline soil mix to mimic Alps.
Water these alpine orchids only with rainwater, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the emerging shoots.
Sow fresh seed in autumn directly onto a mossy top layer so they can get the winter chill they need.
Plant them alongside slow-growing alpine grasses to provide the natural root support they crave.

items.name: Niphaea
items.growersTips:
Keep your Niphaea cozy indoors or in a heated greenhouse as they cannot survive chilly UK frosts.
Plant the small rhizomes just one centimetre deep in a light, free-draining peat-free compost mix.
Water with lukewarm rainwater to keep the soil damp but never soggy during the active growing season.
Watch out for glasshouse whitefly and treat early with organic insecticidal soap to save the leaves.
Let the plant die back naturally in autumn then keep the soil almost dry over the cold winter months.

items.name: Niphidium
items.growersTips:
Grow Niphidium crassifolium in a peat-free, bark-rich orchid mix to mimic its wild epiphytic home.
Keep this tender fern indoors or in a heated greenhouse, as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter.
Water your Niphidium only when the top two inches of compost dry out, using lukewarm rainwater.
Position your pot in bright, filtered light near an east-facing window to avoid scorching leaves.
Mist the fronds daily or place the pot on a wet pebble tray to mimic tropical humidity indoors.

items.name: Niphidium crassifolium
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender rainforest fern in a pot of orchid bark and peat-free compost to drain UK rain.
Bring your potted fern indoors before October frosts because it cannot survive cold UK winters.
Water with rainwater when the top inch of soil dries, keeping it damp but never soggy or waterlogged.
Place it in a humid bathroom or mist it often to mimic its native tropical canopy environment.
Wipe the thick fronds with a damp cloth in winter to clear dust and maximize low British light.

items.name: Nissolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April using deep pots to protect the long taproots before planting out in May.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to keep these dry-land annuals safe from wet UK winter rot.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to mimic home.
Keep an eye out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps to protect the tender growth.
Plant alongside rosemary or thyme to give them the sunny, sharply drained companion spot they love.

items.name: Nivenia
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs five inches deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive UK wet.
Keep them bone dry during their winter dormancy by overwintering pots in a frost-free greenhouse.
Water them generously once a week from April to August to mimic their active summer growing season.
Pair them in pots with hardy sedums to help absorb excess moisture around the bulb base.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when growing them under cover during damp British springs.

items.name: Nivenioideae
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs five inches deep in autumn using pots you can move inside for winter.
Mix equal parts grit and peat-free compost to give their roots the sharp drainage they absolutely need.
Water them weekly from spring until they finish flowering, then keep the soil bone dry over summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, so use beer traps or wool pellets early.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums in a sunny gravel bed to keep the soil warm and mimic their home.

items.name: Noisettia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Noisettia in well-drained loamy soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted garden compost.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, focusing on the roots to avoid powdery mildew.
Prune back the woody stems by one-third in late February to encourage vigorous new spring growth.
Protect the crown with a thick layer of straw mulch in November to survive wet British winters.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots in spring, using beer traps or grit barriers to deter them.

items.name: Nolina
items.growersTips:
Plant your Nolina in a terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and coarse grit.
Keep it outside in summer but bring it indoors before the first autumn frost wets the compost.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it thoroughly and let the excess drain away.
Never prune the main stem, just gently peel away the brown, dead lower leaves in early spring.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf bases, wiping them off with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Nolina beldingii
items.growersTips:
Plant your Nolina in a terracotta pot using fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Keep it bone dry from November to March to prevent the central crown from rotting in cold damp weather.
Position your pot against a south facing brick wall to maximize summer heat and shield it from wind.
Prune away only the fully dead bottom leaves in late spring to keep the trunk neat and pest free.
Check the tight leaf bases regularly for mealybugs which love the dry microclimate of this plant.

items.name: Nolina bigelovii
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet British winters outdoors.
Keep it bone dry from November to March to prevent the central growing crown from rotting in the damp.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to soak up maximum summer heat and rain shelter.
Surround the base with a thick layer of gravel to keep the lower leaves off wet soil and stop decay.
Move it into an unheated greenhouse or porch when temperatures threaten to drop below minus five.

items.name: Nolina brittoniana
items.growersTips:
Bring your pot inside a frost-free greenhouse or sunny porch to survive wet, freezing UK winters.
Plant your bear grass in a gritty, free-draining mix of half peat-free compost and half sharp sand.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting down to once a month from October through to March.
Keep an eye out for mealybugs hiding in the tight, grassy leaf bases during warm summer spells.
Avoid cutting the main crown and only trim away brown, dead leaf tips in late spring with shears.

items.name: Nolina cismontana
items.growersTips:
Plant this chap in a 50 percent grit mix to survive wet UK winters, keeping the root crown elevated.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering entirely from October.
Keep it in a heavy terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse during winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf bases, and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
Never cut the green leaves, just gently pull off the lower dead brown ones to reveal the trunk.

items.name: Nolina erumpens
items.growersTips:
Plant your Mexican grass tree in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it inside for winter.
Only water this desert plant when the compost is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to soak up maximum heat and shelter from rain.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs hiding deep inside the crown, dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
Never cut the green leaves, just gently pull away the dead, dry lower foliage to keep it tidy.

items.name: Nolina greenei
items.growersTips:
Plant this hardy succulent in a raised bed of fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Keep it in a pot so you can easily move it under a porch or greenhouse to shield it from winter rain.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, cutting it back to absolutely nothing from November to March.
Protect the crown from rot by mulching with a thick layer of gravel rather than organic compost.
Position your pot in the brightest spot you have, ideally against a south-facing brick wall for heat.

items.name: Nolina interrata
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare succulent in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it inside for winter.
Only water your Dehesa beargrass when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely in winter.
Position your pot in the brightest, most south-facing spot in your garden to mimic its home sun.
Check the leaf bases regularly for mealybugs, which love to hide in the dense, spiky foliage.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a rain shelter or cloche if you leave it outdoors.

items.name: Nolina lindheimeriana
items.growersTips:
Plant this Texas native in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely from November.
Keep it in your brightest south-facing spot or a cold greenhouse to mimic its sunny home climate.
Cut back the dead, straw-like outer leaves in late spring to keep the grassy clump looking tidy.
Watch out for snails nesting deep inside the crown during damp autumns and clear them out by hand.

items.name: Nolina microcarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a mix of equal parts grit and compost to survive wet British winters.
Keep your plant in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it under cover during freezing rains.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely from October.
Snip away dead, brown leaf tips in spring with sharp shears to keep the rosette looking tidy.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the dense leaf bases, especially if you overwinter it indoors.

items.name: Nolina nelsonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this blue yucca in a raised bed or gravel mulch to keep the root crown dry during wet winters.
Mix fifty percent grit or perlite into your soil to ensure the ultra-fast drainage this plant needs.
Water deeply once a fortnight in summer, but stop watering entirely from October through to March.
Keep a lookout for mealybugs nestled deep inside the leaf bases and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
Avoid pruning the blue-green leaves; only trim away the dead, brown lower foliage in late spring.

items.name: Nolina parryi
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert native in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it under cover for winter.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering entirely from October to March.
Position your pot against a south-facing brick wall to soak up maximum heat during damp UK summers.
Watch out for snails hiding in the dense leaf crown, as they love chewing the tender new growth.
Never cut back the green leaves; just gently pull away the dead, dry lower foliage in late spring.

items.name: Nolina texana
items.growersTips:
Plant this Texas sotol in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and horticultural grit to survive wet winters.
Site your pot-grown Nolina in full sun against a south-facing wall to maximise summer heat and light.
Water deeply once a fortnight in summer, but keep the soil virtually dry from October to March.
Protect the crown from rot by covering it with a temporary rain shelter during soggy winter months.
Prune away only the dead, brown outer leaves in late spring to keep the architectural shape tidy.

items.name: Nolletia gariepina
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of three millimetres to beat the cool UK weather.
Plant them in a gritty, free-draining soil mix to prevent root rot during wet British summers.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this desert native hates soggy roots.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its hot homeland.
Protect young seedlings from slugs and snails using copper tape around your patio containers.

items.name: Nomocharis
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs deep, about fifteen centimetres down, in cool, dappled shade to mimic woodland.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and grit into your soil to keep it moist but free-draining.
Water them regularly in spring with rainwater to keep the soil damp, never letting it dry out.
Protect the tender spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or copper tape.
Leave the stems to die back naturally in autumn so the bulb can gather energy for next year.

items.name: Nomocharis aperta
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs ten centimetres deep in rich, acidic leafmould to mimic their native woodland soil.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy during the spring growing season using rainwater if possible.
Protect the delicate emerging shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in May.
Grow them in dappled shade under rhododendrons or ferns to shield the soft pink blooms from hot sun.
Leave the stems to die down naturally in autumn and mulch with leafmould to insulate against frosts.

items.name: Nonea
items.growersTips:
Try planting Nonea lutea seeds just five millimetres deep in autumn so winter cold breaks dormancy.
Grow your Nonea in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Water young Nonea weekly, but once established, let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Cut Nonea back to the base right after flowering in July to stop it self-seeding all over your beds.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new Nonea shoots during damp UK spring mornings.

items.name: Nonea caspica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using gritty compost to mimic its native dry, rocky steppe habitat.
Grow this borage relative in full sun and very free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between sparse waterings.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with gravel barriers.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late summer to encourage neat, compact perennial growth.

items.name: Nothocalais alpestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring using a gritty, free-draining compost to mimic alpine scree.
Keep the soil barely damp during cool UK springs to prevent the delicate seedlings from rotting.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around your alpine troughs.
Position your pots in full sun to catch every bit of weak British sunshine during the summer.
Avoid feeding these low-nutrient specialists as rich garden soil will cause leggy, weak growth.

items.name: Nothocalais cuspidata
items.growersTips:
Sow these prairie seeds in autumn in gritty compost so UK winter cold naturally breaks their dormancy.
Keep them in your sunniest spot with sharp drainage to mimic their dry, native North American soil.
Water only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry as they hate sitting in damp winter wet.
Protect the young spring shoots from slugs using copper tape around your pots or raised beds.
Grow them alongside low-growing fescues to give their slender stems natural support in wind.

items.name: Nothocalais troximoides
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in autumn or early spring just 2mm deep in a gritty, free-draining sunny bed.
Water young seedlings weekly during dry UK springs, but let the soil dry out fully between waterings.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your soil to mimic its native dry, rocky habitat and prevent rot.
Protect the tender spring foliage from hungry garden snails and slugs using pet-friendly grit barriers.
Plant alongside low-growing UK alpines like stonecrop to support its upright, dandelion-like stems.

items.name: Notholaena
items.growersTips:
Grow these desert ferns in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts potting compost and perlite.
Keep them in pots so you can bring them inside to a dry, frost-free greenhouse for the wet winter.
Water from below to keep the delicate, hairy fronds dry and prevent them from rotting in UK damp.
Place your pots on a south-facing windowsill to give them the maximum winter sunlight they crave.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs hiding in the dense, powdery undersides of the fronds in spring.

items.name: Notholaena californica
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert fern in a terracotta pot with fifty percent grit so it survives wet UK winters.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, and always water from below to keep the fronds dry.
Bring your potted fern indoors to a bright windowsill from October to April to protect from frost.
Plant it alongside hardy succulents like Sempervivum which love the same sharp drainage and sun.
Never prune the shrivelled fronds in dry spells because they naturally uncurl when moisture returns.

items.name: Notholaena standleyi
items.growersTips:
Plant this desert fern in a gritty, free-draining mix of three parts poultry grit to one part loam.
Keep it in a pot so you can bring it inside to a dry, frost-free greenhouse before autumn wet hits.
Water only from below during summer, letting the soil dry out completely before you damp it again.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense sunshine of its native home.
Never mist the fronds because trapped moisture will quickly rot this dry-loving rock dweller.

items.name: Notholirion
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs five centimetres deep in leaf-mould rich, well-drained soil in partial woodland shade.
Keep the soil consistently moist through spring but let them dry out slightly after summer flowering.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they love to devour the emerging young shoots.
These bulbs die after flowering, so save the tiny offset bulblets to replant for future blooms.
Mulch heavily with bark in autumn to protect the shallow bulbs from severe British winter frosts.

items.name: Notholirion macrophyllum
items.growersTips:
Plant this bulb in early autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in humus-rich, acidic woodland soil.
Position it in dappled shade with shelter from strong winds to mimic its native Himalayan home.
Keep the soil consistently moist through spring but ensure it drains freely to prevent winter rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the emerging shoots.
Propagate by carefully detaching the tiny offset bulbils when the main flowering stem dies back.

items.name: Nothotsuga
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare conifer in deep, acidic, sandy loam to mimic its native mountain forest floor.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Shelter your young tree from harsh easterly winter winds which can scorch the delicate needles.
Prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead wood, as it naturally maintains a lovely shape.
Keep a watchful eye out for woolly aphids in spring, spraying them off with a sharp jet of water.

items.name: Notobasis syriaca
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly where they will flower to survive mild UK winters and bloom early.
Grow this thistle in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Give it a spot in full, unobstructed south-facing sun to mimic its native Mediterranean heat.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling this plant to protect your hands from its vicious spines.
Deadhead the purple flower heads before late summer to stop this vigorous self-seeder taking over.

items.name: Notogrammitis angustifolia
items.growersTips:
Keep this delicate alpine fern constantly damp but never waterlogged using rainwater, not tap water.
Grow it in a very well-draining, gritty, acidic leafmould mix to mimic its native damp rock crevices.
Position it in a cool, sheltered, fully shaded spot in your garden to prevent the fronds from burning.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the tender new emerging fronds.
Protect it with a cloche or fleece during harsh UK winter frosts to keep the evergreen foliage tidy.

items.name: Notogrammitis billardierei
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate alpine fern in a shady, moist rock crevice or a shallow terracotta pan of grit.
Water with rainwater to keep the compost damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry summers.
Mix equal parts peat-free ericaceous compost, perlite, and fine bark to mimic its wild forest home.
Protect it from harsh winter wet and drying winds by placing it under a cold frame or alpine house.
Plant it alongside miniature hostas or small filmy ferns which love the same cool, humid conditions.

items.name: Notogrammitis heterophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this native fern in a moist, sheltered rock crevice or a gritty, peat-free acidic soil mix.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged by watering gently from the base, not above.
Position it in deep or partial shade, away from drying winds and harsh afternoon UK summer sun.
Protect the delicate fronds from winter frost damage using a light covering of dry bracken or fleece.
Tuck it near companion plants like dwarf hostas or mosses to help maintain high local humidity.

items.name: Nuttallanthus
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in early spring, as they need light to germinate.
Plant them in poor, sharply draining sandy soil to mimic their natural gravelly US habitat.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells to prevent root rot in UK damp.
Cut back the spent flower spikes in autumn to encourage a fresh flush of basal foliage for winter.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or organic grit to protect them.

items.name: Nuttallanthus canadensis
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the compost surface in spring, as they need light and UK sun to germinate.
Plant them in poor, sandy, well-drained soil to stop this wild toadflax from rotting in wet winters.
Let this short-lived perennial self-seed in gravel paths to keep your garden stocked year after year.
Grow them alongside low-growing thyme or sedums which won't crowd out their delicate, slender stems.
Cut faded flower spikes in late summer to encourage a second flush of pretty violet blooms for bees.

items.name: Nuttallanthus texanus
items.growersTips:
Sow these tiny seeds on the surface of well-drained sandy soil in autumn to mimic UK winter chill.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings in summer.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails which will devour the delicate young spring shoots.
Cut back the spent flowering stems in late summer to encourage a second flush of violet blooms.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme or sedum in a sunny gravel garden to help suppress weeds.

items.name: Nyssa
items.growersTips:
Plant your tupelo in deep, moist, acidic to neutral soil to avoid the yellow leaves of chlorosis.
Position your Nyssa in full sun to catch the autumn light, which coaxes out those fiery red tones.
Water young trees deeply every week during dry UK summers to keep their thirsty roots happy.
Avoid pruning your Nyssa unless absolutely necessary, and only do it in winter when fully dormant.
Choose the cultivar Forest Glory if your garden is small and you need a reliable, compact habit.

items.name: Nyssa aquatica
items.growersTips:
Plant this water tupelo in boggy soil or right at your pond edge where its roots can stay wet.
Add plenty of leaf mould to your planting hole to mimic its native acidic woodland soil.
Position your tree in full sun to guarantee those brilliant fiery red autumn colours in UK weather.
Protect young saplings with a tree guard to stop rabbits chewing the bark during damp UK winters.
Avoid pruning this tree unless you are removing dead wood in late summer when the sap has slowed.

items.name: Nyssa biflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this swamp lover in the wettest part of your garden, like a bog garden or beside a pond.
Mix plenty of composted bark into your soil to keep it acidic and mimic its native peat bog.
Water it deeply every week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently wet, not just damp.
Avoid pruning this tree as it hates being cut back; just remove dead wood in late winter if needed.
Plant it alongside moisture-loving ferns or astilbes which thrive in the same soggy, acidic soil.

items.name: Nyssa ogeche
items.growersTips:
Plant your Ogeche lime in a permanently damp, boggy spot or near a pond to mimic its native swamps.
Protect young trees with fleece during harsh UK winters until they develop woody frost resistance.
Mix plenty of acidic leaf mould or peat-free ericaceous compost into the planting hole to lower pH.
Avoid pruning this tree unless you are removing dead wood in late winter while it is fully dormant.
Keep it heavily mulched with bark chippings to lock in soil moisture during dry British summers.

items.name: Nyssa sinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chinese tupelo in deep, moist, acidic soil to get those fiery autumn colours in the UK.
Give your young tree a thick mulch of composted pine needles every spring to keep the soil acidic.
Water it deeply during dry summer spells, as this tree hates drying out in our changing UK climate.
Only prune in late winter when dormant to remove crossing branches, as it bleeds sap if cut in spring.
Shelter it from cold, drying winds which can scorch the delicate, emerging bronze spring foliage.

items.name: Nyssa sylvatica
items.growersTips:
Plant this tupelo in a damp, acidic spot to guarantee those famous fiery red autumn colours.
Avoid chalky soils by digging in plenty of composted pine needles or sulphur before planting.
Water your young tree deeply every week during dry UK summers to stop the leaves from dropping.
Leave your shears in the shed as this tree hates pruning and naturally grows a beautiful shape.
Protect the young trunk from rabbits with a spiral guard during its first few British winters.

items.name: Nyssa yunnanensis
items.growersTips:
Plant your young Yunnan tupelo in a deep, sheltered spot to protect its delicate leaves from cold UK winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry British summer spells.
Grow this rare tree in acidic to neutral soil; add plenty of composted pine needles to the planting hole.
Avoid pruning this specimen unless absolutely necessary, and only do so in late winter when dormant.
Watch out for late spring frosts in northern UK regions by wrapping young trees in horticultural fleece.

items.name: Ochagavia litoralis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean coastal gem in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in UK rain.
Position your pot in the sunniest spot possible, moving it to a cold greenhouse for winter frosts.
Water sparingly from spring to autumn, then keep the rosette crown completely dry throughout winter.
Watch out for slugs hiding in the spiky lower leaves during damp British spring evenings.
Propagate by carefully slicing off offsets with a sharp knife in late spring to share with friends.

items.name: Ochrosia
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender tropical in a pot of peat-free loam so you can move it indoors before first frost.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Wipe the glossy leaves with a damp cloth in winter to stop spider mites in dry heated indoor air.
Prune lightly in late spring just as active growth starts to keep its bushy shape manageable.
Mix plenty of perlite into your potting soil to ensure the sharp drainage this island native needs.

items.name: Oclemena nemoralis
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in early spring under glass to get a head start on our short UK growing season.
Keep the boggy soil constantly wet by planting it near your pond edge or in a damp wildflower patch.
Mix plenty of acidic peat-free compost into your clay soil to mimic its native British peatland home.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the tender young spring shoots in damp UK gardens.
Plant alongside bog pimpernel or marsh marigold for a beautiful, moisture-loving native display.

items.name: Oddoniodendron
items.growersTips:
Sow these annual seeds indoors in warm propagators during March to beat the chilly UK spring soils.
Plant out in late May after the final frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Watch out for young slugs on damp June nights and protect tender stems with copper tape or grit.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly throughout July and August to keep fresh flowers coming until autumn.

items.name: Odontadenia
items.growersTips:
Bring your odontadenia indoors or to a heated conservatory by October to survive chilly UK winters.
Plant this vigorous climber in a large pot with grit-heavy, free-draining loam to prevent root rot.
Water generously with tepid rainwater in summer, but let the top soil dry out completely in winter.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its size manageable.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites, especially when central heating goes on.

items.name: Odontadenia macrantha
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical beauty inside for winter as it cannot survive UK frosts below ten degrees.
Grow it in a large container with a tall, sturdy trellis to support its vigorous climbing habit.
Water generously in summer but let the top inch of soil dry out completely before watering again.
Feed every two weeks in spring and summer using a high-potassium liquid fertilizer for best blooms.
Prune lightly in late winter to shape the vine and encourage fresh flowering wood for the summer.

items.name: Odontochilus
items.growersTips:
Grow this terrestrial orchid in a free-draining mix of fine bark, chopped moss and perlite.
Keep your pots in a shaded, humid spot like a bathroom windowsill to mimic woodland humidity.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top centimetre of the orchid compost feels dry.
Maintain a winter temperature above twelve degrees Celsius to keep these tender perennials happy.
Watch out for slugs and snails which love to feast on the succulent, velvety patterned leaves.

items.name: Odontonema
items.growersTips:
Bring your firespike indoors by October to protect it from the damp, freezing British winter.
Grow it in a container of peat-free loam-based compost so you can easily move it inside.
Water thoroughly when the top inch of soil feels dry, but keep it barely damp during winter.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to encourage bushy growth and more autumn flowers.
