Sow seeds in spring just below the surface in pots kept on a sunny windowsill or cold frame.
Avoid winter wet by planting them in a raised bed or rockery with a thick gravel mulch top dressing.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, only giving them a drink during prolonged hot, dry UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the low-growing foliage in damp spring weather.

items.name: Olsynium
items.growersTips:
Plant your Olsynium bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep them moist during their winter growing phase but completely dry during their summer dormancy.
Grow them in terracotta pots to easily move them under a cold glass frame during wet UK summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love chewing the tender new grass-like leaves.
Propagate by gently dividing the congested bulb clumps right after they finish flowering in June.

items.name: Olsynium douglasii
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in well-drained, gritty, neutral soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist during their winter and spring growing season, but do not let it bog.
After they flower in spring, let the bulbs dry out completely during their summer dormant phase.
Grow them in a cold greenhouse or alpine house to protect the delicate early blooms from UK rain.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they love to eat the emerging grassy foliage.

items.name: Omalotheca
items.growersTips:
Sow Omalotheca seeds in March on free-draining sandy loam, barely covering them with fine grit.
Keep soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering gently from below to protect tiny seedlings.
Plant them alongside low-growing fescues or wild thyme to mimic their natural UK upland habitats.
Watch out for slugs in damp spring weather by using organic wool pellets around your young plants.
Do not prune these annuals, just let them self-seed in autumn to guarantee flowers next summer.

items.name: Omphalodes
items.growersTips:
Pop your cherry-tart Omphalodes cappadocica into damp, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, shady spot.
Water your navelwort regularly during dry UK summers to keep the woodland soil consistently moist.
Snip off the faded flower stems in late spring to encourage a fresh flush of lush green leaves.
Watch out for sneaky slugs and snails who love devouring the tender new spring foliage in wet weather.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn to propagate new plants and keep the parent clump vigorous.

items.name: Omphalodes cappadocica
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodland beauty in moist, humus-rich soil under the dappled shade of deciduous trees.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to keep them vigorous and propagate new plants.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging foliage.
Plant alongside snowdrops and primroses for a gorgeous, naturalised spring display in your borders.

items.name: Omphalodes linifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in spring or autumn just under the soil surface where you want them to flower.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the tender young spring foliage.
Plant them alongside forget-me-nots or hostas in partial shade for a gorgeous woodland look.
Let them self-seed naturally around your borders to ensure a beautiful display year after year.

items.name: Omphalodes verna
items.growersTips:
Tuck your creeping forget-me-not into moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in autumn.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to stop the shallow roots from drying out in dry shade.
Divide congested clumps right after spring flowering to easily propagate new ground cover.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the tender new spring foliage in damp British weather.
Plant them alongside yellow primroses and spring bulbs for a classic woodland colour contrast.

items.name: Oncidiinae
items.growersTips:
Grow these orchids in a bark-based mix, never soil, to keep their roots well-drained in UK damp.
Water them weekly in summer but let the potting mix almost dry out before watering in winter.
Place them on a east-facing windowsill to get bright morning sun without scorching their leaves.
Keep a lookout for mealybugs in the tight leaf joints, wiping them away with a damp cotton bud.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser every third watering during their active spring growing phase.

items.name: Oncosiphon pilulifer
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass as this South African annual needs warmth to germinate.
Plant them out in May in your sunniest, poorest soil to mimic their dry, native Karoo habitat.
Water sparingly once established because damp UK autumns will quickly rot their delicate roots.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, so protect them with grit barriers or beer traps.
Deadhead the yellow button flowers weekly in summer to keep the plant blooming until first frost.

items.name: Oncosiphon suffruticosus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect this South African annual from cold UK springs.
Plant out in late May in your sandiest, poorest soil to mimic its dry, coastal native habitat.
Water sparingly only during dry spells, as this plant hates soggy roots in damp British summers.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings are young to encourage a bushier, more floriferous habit.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the young, feathery foliage in damp spring weather.

items.name: Onosma
items.growersTips:
Plant your golden drops in sharp-draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet British winters.
Nestle Onosma against a south-facing stone wall or rockery to maximize crucial summer sunshine.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, only dampening the soil when it has dried out completely.
Protect the hairy foliage from winter rot by placing a pane of glass or cloche over the crown.
Prune back the faded flowering stems in late summer to keep your perennial neat and compact.

items.name: Onosma fruticosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this subshrub in a raised bed with lots of grit to survive wet British winters.
Give it a sunny south-facing spot next to rosemary to mimic its dry Mediterranean home.
Water only during dry summer spells and keep the hairy foliage completely dry in winter.
Prune back the woody stems lightly in late spring after the yellow flowers fade to keep it tidy.
Guard the young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or copper tape.

items.name: Onosma taurica
items.growersTips:
Plant this golden drop in a raised bed or rockery with grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water only during prolonged dry spells in summer, as this plant absolutely hates soggy soil.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch on the young, hairy spring foliage.
Trim back the faded flowering stems in late summer to keep the clump compact and tidy.
Position it next to purple thyme or sedums for a gorgeous, drought-tolerant sunny display.

items.name: Onosmodium virginianum
items.growersTips:
Plant this wild job's tears in a sunny border with gritty, free-draining soil to mimic its US home.
Sow your seeds in autumn in a cold frame, as they need winter cold to trigger spring germination.
Water newly planted divisions weekly until established, then let the UK rain do the work for you.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British springs, as they love chewing the fuzzy young shoots.
Leave the faded stems over winter to protect the crown from frost and feed the local garden birds.

items.name: Onychium
items.growersTips:
Plant your Onychium japonicum in a sheltered, damp spot to protect its delicate fronds from dry winds
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the dry UK summer months
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your clay soil to create the perfect leafy loam
Move your potted claw ferns into a cold greenhouse or unheated conservatory to survive winter frosts
Snip away any dead or tattered fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh growth

items.name: Onychium japonicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this carrot fern in a sheltered, damp spot with dappled shade to mimic its native woodland.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or compost into your soil to keep it acidic, moist, and free-draining.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering at the base to avoid rotting the crown.
Protect the delicate fronds from harsh, drying winds which can quickly turn the foliage brown.
In cold UK regions, mulch the crown with straw or fleece in late autumn to survive heavy frosts.

items.name: Oophytum
items.growersTips:
Grow these winter-active gems in a gritty, soil-free pumice mix to prevent rot in damp UK winters.
Water only from September to March, then let them bake completely dry in their papery summer sheaths.
Keep them on your sunniest south-facing indoor windowsill to mimic South African winter sunshine.
Set the pot on a tray of dry gravel to keep the base dry and prevent collar rot in humid UK air.
Never peel off the papery summer skin yourself; let the new green lobes burst through naturally.

items.name: Oophytum nanum
items.growersTips:
Grow this winter-active gem in a mix of seventy percent grit to survive damp UK winters rot-free.
Keep it completely dry from May to August when its papery sheath forms to protect the resting body.
Place your pot on a south-facing windowsill to give it the maximum possible winter light in the UK.
Water very lightly from September onwards only when the body starts to wrinkle during its growth.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding under the dry summer sheath and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Oparanthus
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm March to beat the late UK frosts, then plant out when May warms up.
Sow seeds shallowly, just five millimetres deep, keeping the compost moist but never soggy.
Give them a sunny, sheltered spot next to your tomatoes to block chilly British winds.
Water them deeply at the base once a week rather than giving them daily light sprinkles.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots; beer traps work wonders in damp UK weather.

items.name: Ophionella
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare South African succulent in a grit-heavy, free-draining mix to survive damp UK winters.
Keep your plant on a sunny south-facing windowsill to mimic its native warm, dry climate.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through March.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stems, especially during dry indoor winter heating.
Propagate by taking stem cuttings in late spring, letting them callus over before potting.

items.name: Ophiopogon
items.growersTips:
Plant your black mondo grass in moist, well-drained soil enriched with plenty of leaf mould.
Keep the soil consistently damp during dry UK summers, but never let it sit in soggy winter wet.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding in the dense tufts, especially during mild, damp springs.
Gently comb through the foliage with your gloved hands in spring to clear out any dead, brown leaves.
Pair the dark Ophiopogon planiscapus Nigrescens with bright green ferns for a striking shade contrast.

items.name: Ophiopogon chingii
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf mondo grass in moist, well-drained acid to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Tuck it into a sheltered, partially shaded spot to protect the delicate leaves from harsh frost.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to nest in and chew the dense evergreen tufts.
Gently divide the clumps in spring to propagate new plants and keep the parent patch looking fresh.

items.name: Ophiopogon japonicus
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf mondo grass in moist, well-drained acid to neutral soil in partial or dappled shade.
Space your plugs ten centimetres apart in spring to help them knit together into a lush evergreen lawn.
Water regularly during dry UK summers until established, as dry soil stunts their slow growth rate.
Watch out for slugs and snails in damp British weather, as they love hiding in the dense foliage clumps.
Comb through the tufts with your gloved hands in late winter to clear out dead leaves and debris.

items.name: Ophiopogon planiscapus
items.growersTips:
Plant this black grass with its crown level with the soil, as burying it too deep causes crown rot.
Plant it next to bright yellow Hakonechloa macra grass for a stunning, high-contrast UK border look.
Divide congested clumps in mild spring weather using two forks to easily propagate new free plants.
Keep soil moist but well-drained, especially during dry UK summers, to prevent the leaf tips browning.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding in the dark foliage during damp British spring evenings.

items.name: Ophryosporus
items.growersTips:
Sow these tender annual seeds indoors in early April using a heated propagator kept at twenty degrees.
Prick out seedlings into individual 9cm pots of peat-free compost once they show their first true leaves.
Plant them out in late May after the last frost, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water the base deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the free-draining soil moist.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots and protect them with organic wool pellets or beer traps.

items.name: Ophrys
items.growersTips:
Grow them in a very gritty, free-draining mix of alpine grit, perlite, and loam to prevent rot.
Water them from autumn to spring when they grow, but keep them bone dry during their summer dormancy.
Protect them from winter wet in the UK by keeping your pots in an unheated greenhouse or cold frame.
Watch out for slugs and snails in autumn as they love to eat the emerging winter leaf rosettes.
Plant the tubers about two inches deep in late summer, making sure the growing point faces upwards.

items.name: Oplonia
items.growersTips:
Bring your oplonia indoors before the first autumn frost as it cannot survive a chilly UK winter.
Water your oplonia only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot in damp clay.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to give this plant the sharp drainage it needs to thrive.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse whitefly when growing this tender beauty in your conservatory.
Prune your oplonia lightly in late spring to encourage bushy growth and remove any winter damage.

items.name: Oplonia spinosa
items.growersTips:
Bring this Caribbean native indoors by October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a terracotta pot filled with free-draining peat-free loam and plenty of added grit.
Water only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, as wet roots will quickly rot in UK damp.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring after new growth starts to keep its spiny habit compact.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping it in a heated conservatory over winter.

items.name: Orbea
items.growersTips:
Bring your Orbea indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect it from wet UK winter rot.
Use a gritty mix of equal parts John Innes number two and perlite to ensure excellent drainage.
Only water when the compost is bone dry, keeping them completely dry from November to March.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs hiding in the deeply grooved joints of the star-shaped stems.
Place them on a south-facing patio in summer but use fleece if night temperatures drop below ten.
items.description: Orbea is a bicycle manufacturer based in Mallabia, Spain. It is part of the Mondragón Cooperative Corporation and Spain's largest bicycle manufacturer. Orbea manufactures and assembles bikes at their own factories in Spain and Portugal.

items.name: Orbea ciliata
items.growersTips:
Grow this starfish cactus in a gritty, free-draining mix of equal parts potting soil and perlite.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill inside, as it cannot survive wet UK winters outdoors.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through March.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem crevices, and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.
Propagate easily by snipping a stem segment in summer, letting it callus, then potting it up.

items.name: Orbea decaisneana
items.growersTips:
Bring this Moroccan native indoors by October to keep it safe from damp UK winter frosts.
Plant your stems in a shallow mix of half John Innes number two and half grit for fast drainage.
Water only when the compost is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November to March.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem joints, and dab them off with a cotton bud in alcohol.
Position it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense desert sun it loves.

items.name: Orbea variegata
items.growersTips:
Bring your starfish flower indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to protect it from UK frosts.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit for perfect drainage.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and keep it completely dry from November through to March.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the stem crevices, and dab them off with rubbing alcohol.
Grow it in a shallow terracotta pot rather than a deep one to prevent the roots from rotting.

items.name: Orbeanthus
items.growersTips:
Grow your Orbeanthus in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost to survive damp UK winters.
Keep this tender perennial indoors on a sunny south windowsill from October until late May.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it, but never let the pot sit in a saucer of water.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints; dab them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Propagate new plants in summer by taking stem cuttings, letting them dry for three days before potting.

items.name: Orchidinae
items.growersTips:
Plant native marsh orchids in wet, acidic soil mixed with grit to mimic UK bog conditions.
Keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged during the active spring growing season.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs as they love chewing tender new orchid shoots.
Leave the faded flower spikes intact until winter to allow these perennials to self-seed naturally.
Grow them alongside damp-loving companion plants like ragged robin or marsh marigold in your garden.

items.name: Orchipedum
items.growersTips:
Keep this rare orchid in a warm greenhouse or indoors as it cannot survive chilly UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a chunky orchid bark and sphagnum moss mix to ensure its delicate roots never sit soggy.
Water with lukewarm rainwater rather than cold tap water to avoid shocking its tropical root system.
Place it in bright, filtered light but shield it from direct midday sun to prevent leaf scorching.
Keep a close eye out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Orchis
items.growersTips:
Plant these native tubers in early autumn about five centimetres deep in well-drained, gritty soil.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during spring, then let them dry out completely when dormant.
Grow them alongside fine fescues or wild thyme to provide the essential mycorrhizal fungi they need.
Never use chemical fertilisers or weedkillers nearby as they easily destroy the friendly soil fungi.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring when the tender green rosettes first emerge.

items.name: Oreocarya humilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine borage in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Protect its hairy foliage from winter wet by placing a cloche over it from November to March.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pots outside to let UK winter frosts naturally break dormancy.
Plant it alongside creeping thymes and sedums in a sunny rock garden to match its dry soil needs.
Water only during prolonged summer dry spells, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks.

items.name: Oreocharis
items.growersTips:
Grow Oreocharis in free-draining, gritty compost under the dappled shade of a north-facing wall.
Water them from below in winter to keep their fuzzy leaves dry and prevent crown rot in UK damp.
Plant them alongside hardy ferns and hostas in a sheltered, moist rockery or woodland border.
Bring your potted Oreocharis indoors to a cool, frost-free greenhouse before the November frosts.
Gently propagate them by taking leaf cuttings in early summer when the plant is actively growing.

items.name: Oreomecon nudicaulis
items.growersTips:
Sow these Arctic poppies on the soil surface in autumn as they need cold UK winter chill to sprout.
Plant them in gritty, fast-draining soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Water sparingly from below only when the top inch of soil is dry to keep their crowns from rotting.
Protect the delicate hairy leaves from slugs and snails during damp spring nights with grit barriers.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in summer to encourage a continuous display of bright crepe flowers.

items.name: Oresbia
items.growersTips:
Sow your Oresbia seeds indoors in March to beat the cool UK spring, planting them just 5mm deep.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering only at the base to prevent dampening-off disease.
Plant them out in May after the frosts, choosing a sunny spot with gritty, free-draining soil.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots, using organic wool pellets around the stems as a barrier.
Deadhead the faded blooms weekly through August to keep this lovely annual flowering until autumn.

items.name: Ormocarpum
items.growersTips:
Start your Ormocarpum seeds indoors in warm propagators by March to beat the cool British spring.
Plant these annuals out in June once frosts pass, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water them deeply at the base twice a week during dry summer spells to keep the taproot hydrated.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are growing them under glass or in a polytunnel.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to ensure the excellent drainage they require.

items.name: Ormosieae
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds indoors in March at a depth of two centimetres to get a head start on UK spring.
Plant them out in May after the last frost, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water them deeply once a week at the base rather than dampening the leaves to prevent powdery mildew.
Keep an eye out for slugs on young shoots and protect them with copper tape or organic pellets.
Grow them alongside calendula to naturally deter pests and attract beneficial pollinating insects.

items.name: Ornithoboea
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Asian perennial in a pot of peat-free compost with perlite to move indoors by October.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy, watering only from the base to avoid rotting the hairy leaves.
Place your pot on a bright east-facing windowsill to protect the delicate blue flowers from hot sun.
Watch out for glasshouse mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them off with a damp cotton bud.
Feed with a weak high-potash liquid fertiliser every two weeks from May to September for more blooms.

items.name: Ornithogalum
items.growersTips:
Plant Ornithogalum umbellatum bulbs eight centimetres deep in autumn to keep them safe from UK frosts.
Water your Star of Bethlehem only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, as they hate wet feet.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, especially during wet British springs.
Cut back the faded flower stems in summer but let the leaves die down naturally to feed next year.
Grow tender Ornithogalum dubium in pots so you can easily bring them indoors before the first frost.

items.name: Ornithogalum arabicum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimeters in your sunniest, most sheltered border.
Keep the soil gritty and free-draining to prevent the bulbs from rotting during wet UK winters.
Water them weekly during their spring growing phase, then stop completely once the foliage dies down.
Lift the bulbs in autumn and store them in dry sand if your garden gets hard winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the tender emerging flower buds during damp spring mornings.

items.name: Ornithogalum candicans
items.growersTips:
Plant your bulbs 15cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter wet rot.
Water them deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out between waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the tender new spring shoots as they emerge from the soil.
Cut the flower spikes right down to the base in autumn only after the foliage has turned yellow.
Grow them alongside purple salvias or lavender to beautifully contrast their nodding white bells.

items.name: Ornithogalum divergens
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn about eight centimetres deep in well-drained soil to mimic Mediterranean dry summers.
Water them only during active spring growth and let the soil dry out completely over the summer months.
Grow them alongside hardy geraniums or thyme to cover up their untidy foliage as it dies back in June.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, especially during wet UK Aprils.
Divide overcrowded clumps in late summer after the leaves have completely withered away to boost blooms.

items.name: Ornithogalum dubium
items.growersTips:
Plant your orange star bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn using pots you can move inside for winter.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into peat-free compost to stop the bulbs rotting in wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, then let the pot drain completely every time.
Keep your pots on a south-facing patio in summer but bring them indoors before the first autumn frost.
Cut the faded flower stems right back to the base to encourage a second flush of bright orange blooms.

items.name: Ornithogalum maculatum
items.growersTips:
Plant these South African bulbs 5cm deep in autumn using pots you can move indoors before winter.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into peat-free compost to prevent winter wet from rotting bulbs.
Water sparingly from autumn to spring, only letting the soil dry out slightly between drinks.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids and slugs on the tender new spring shoots as they emerge.
Position your pots in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic their native warm baking sun.

items.name: Ornithogalum narbonense
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in a sunny, south-facing border.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure sharp drainage and prevent winter bulb rot.
Water them only during active spring growth, then let the soil dry out completely in summer.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb for next year.
Protect the emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic pellets.

items.name: Ornithogalum pyrenaicum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil.
Keep the soil consistently moist during spring growth but let it dry out completely in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails damaging the tender young flower spikes as they emerge in May.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally after flowering in June to feed the bulb for next year.
Grow them in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic their native UK woodland habitat.

items.name: Ornithogalum saundersiae
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs ten centimetres deep in spring using grit for drainage to survive wet UK winters.
Move pots of these tender giants into a frost-free greenhouse or shed before the first autumn frost.
Water them thoroughly once active growth starts but let the soil dry out completely between drinks.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the emerging strap-like leaves in early spring.
Plant them alongside purple salvia or dark heucheras to make those starry white flowers really pop.

items.name: Ornithogalum thyrsoides
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in spring at a depth of about ten centimetres in a warm, south-facing sunny spot.
Bring potted bulbs indoors or lift them in autumn as they will not survive wet UK winter frosts.
Water them thoroughly when active growth starts, but let the soil dry out between waterings.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage these South African beauties need.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the emerging fresh shoots.

items.name: Ornithogalum umbellatum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in well-drained soil to survive wet UK winters.
Grow in containers or sink pots to restrict the highly invasive bulbils from overtaking lawns.
Withhold summer watering once foliage dies back to allow bulbs a dry dormant period in clay soil.
Cut back spent flower stems in June before seed heads mature to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Wear gloves when handling bulbs to avoid skin irritation caused by toxic calcium oxalate crystals.

items.name: Ornithogalum viridiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs 10cm deep in autumn using gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Keep them damp during spring growth, but let the soil dry out completely once summer flowering ends.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse or shed for the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the emerging green flower spikes in spring.
Position them in your sunniest, south-facing spot to mimic their native South African warmth.

items.name: Ornithogalum xanthochlorum
items.growersTips:
Plant these bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in your sunniest, sheltered border.
Keep the soil gritty and free-draining to prevent winter rot during wet UK winters.
Water them generously during active spring growth, then let the soil dry out completely in summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails targeting the fresh, fleshy emerging shoots in early spring.
Grow them in terracotta pots so you can easily move them into a frost-free greenhouse for winter.

items.name: Orontioideae
items.growersTips:
Grow golden club in shallow pond margins under six inches of water to mimic UK wetland habitats.
Plant Orontium aquaticum in heavy clay loam within aquatic baskets to stop soil washing away.
Watch out for water snails eating the young spring spadix shoots and clear them off by hand.
Divide the thick rhizomes in late spring once the UK weather warms up to propagate new plants.
Place these bog lovers in full sun to ensure those bright yellow flower spikes pop in May.

items.name: Orontium
items.growersTips:
Plant your golden club in a pond basket filled with heavy loam, topped with gravel to stop fish digging.
Position the planting basket so the crown sits about ten to fifteen centimetres below the water line.
Place them in your pond's sunniest spot to ensure those bright yellow poker flowers bloom in spring.
Divide the thick rhizomes in late spring after flowering to keep the clump healthy and make new plants.
Watch out for water snails in early summer, as they love to munch on the beautiful velvety leaves.

items.name: Orontium aquaticum
items.growersTips:
Plant golden club in a sturdy aquatic basket using heavy clay loam, not standard compost, to stop it floating.
Submerge the crown under five to fifteen centimetres of water in a sunny, still UK garden pond.
Watch out for water snails munching the young spring leaves, and gently pick them off by hand.
Propagate your clump by dividing the thick rhizomes in late spring once the water starts to warm up.
Position it alongside native marsh marigolds to create a beautiful, contrasting spring display.

items.name: Orontium mackii
items.growersTips:
Plant this golden club relative in heavy clay loam under six inches of still pond water.
Keep it in full sun to partial shade, as our cool UK summers need maximum light for flowering.
Watch out for water snails in spring, which love to nibble on the emerging spadix and leaves.
Propagate by dividing the thick rhizomes in late spring once the water temperature starts to rise.
Grow it alongside native marsh marigolds to create a beautiful, staggered spring pond margin display.

items.name: Orontium wolfei
items.growersTips:
Since this is a prehistoric fossil species, try growing its modern cousin Golden Club in UK ponds.
Plant the tubers in aquatic baskets filled with heavy clay soil, topped with gravel to stop fish.
Submerge the young plant in shallow water first, then gradually lower it to about twelve inches.
Keep it in full sun to mimic its ancient climate, which helps those bright yellow spikes bloom.
Watch out for water snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging leaves.

items.name: Orostachys
items.growersTips:
Plant your Orostachys in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely from November.
Watch out for slugs in spring, as they love to devour the tender rosettes of Chinese Dunce Cap.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them under a porch to shield them from heavy winter rain.
Propagate by snipping off the little offsets in summer and pressing them gently into gritty compost.

items.name: Orostachys japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant your rock pine in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep them in a terracotta pot so you can move them under a porch during relentless winter rain.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, stopping completely from November.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding in the rosette clumps during damp British spring nights.
Propagate by gently detaching the little side offsets in summer and pressing them into gritty compost.

items.name: Ortegia
items.growersTips:
Plant Ortegia in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position your Ortegia in full sun, ideally tucked into a south-facing rock garden or gravel bed.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks in summer.
Protect the crown with a layer of gravel mulch to keep damp soil off the lower leaves.
Propagate Ortegia by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to ensure you have backup plants.

items.name: Ortegia hispanica
items.growersTips:
Plant this Spanish native in a raised bed with lots of grit to survive wet British winters.
Give it a spot in the absolute fullest sun you have to mimic its hot Mediterranean home.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as wet soil in autumn will quickly rot the roots.
Prune the woody stems back lightly in early spring to keep its cushion-like shape nice and tidy.
Grow it alongside creeping thyme or sedums in a gravel garden for a perfect dry-loving community.

items.name: Orthanthera
items.growersTips:
Bring this rare desert shrub indoors by October to protect its tender roots from wet UK winters.
Plant your specimen in a gritty, free-draining loam mix with fifty percent perlite or sharp sand.
Water only when the soil is completely dry, cutting back to once a month from November to March.
Position your pot on a south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to maximise summer sun.
Propagate during the active growing season in June by taking semi-ripe cuttings in warm propagator.

items.name: Orthoceras
items.growersTips:
Grow this native orchid in a wet, acidic peat-free compost mix to mimic its boggy home.
Keep the pot sitting in a shallow tray of rainwater year-round so the roots never dry out.
Position your pot in a bright, unheated greenhouse to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to devour the emerging flower spikes.
Avoid using any standard garden fertilisers because these sensitive orchids thrive in poor soils.

items.name: Orthopterum
items.growersTips:
Grow this South African succulent in a grit-heavy, free-draining loam to survive damp UK winters.
Keep it on a sunny south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse to mimic its native habitat.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn, then keep completely dry all winter.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf joints and treat them quickly with an organic spray.
Propagate by carefully dividing the clumps in late spring just as the active growth phase begins.

items.name: Orthopterum waltoniae
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African gem indoors by October to protect its succulent leaves from wet UK frosts.
Plant in a gritty, free-draining cactus compost mix to stop winter root rot in damp British weather.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, cutting back to a light monthly splash from November to March.
Position on your brightest south-facing windowsill to mimic the intense sunshine of its homeland.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints and dab them away with rubbing alcohol.

items.name: Orthosia
items.growersTips:
Plant your Orthosia in moist, well-drained soil during early autumn to establish strong roots.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, using organic grit barriers to deter them.
Cut back the faded foliage in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent winter rot.
Divide overgrown clumps every three years in spring to keep your plants vigorous and healthy.

items.name: Orthrosanthus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Orthrosanthus in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect its delicate blooms from UK winds.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure the sharp drainage this Australian native needs to survive.
Bring container-grown plants into a cold greenhouse or unheated porch before the first winter frost.
Water them weekly in active spring growth, but let the soil dry out completely during winter dormancy.
Divide the congested clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to keep them flowering well.

items.name: Oscularia
items.growersTips:
Plant your oscularia in a gritty succulent mix, keeping the root flare level with the soil surface.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak thoroughly, stopping completely from November to March.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs in the leaf joints, especially when overwintering them indoors.
Prune back leggy stems in late spring after flowering to keep your plant bushy and full of blooms.
Grow them in pots so you can easily move them inside before the first wet UK winter frosts hit.

items.name: Oscularia caulescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this succulent in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep it in your sunniest, south-facing spot to encourage those bright pink stems and daisy flowers.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely from November through February.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a frost-free greenhouse or windowsill before the first UK frost.
Take stem cuttings in summer to easily propagate new plants and back up your collection for winter.

items.name: Oscularia cedarbergensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African native indoors to a frost-free windowsill from October through to April.
Plant in a gritty mix of two parts horticultural sand to one part peat-free compost for drainage.
Water only when the fleshy leaves start to wrinkle slightly, usually once every two weeks in summer.
Take stem cuttings in June by letting them dry for three days before popping them into gritty soil.
Position your pot in the sunniest south-facing spot in your garden to mimic the Cape climate.

items.name: Oscularia deltoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this succulent in a gritty, free-draining mix of half compost and half grit to survive wet winters.
Bring your potted plants indoors to a bright windowsill before the first harsh autumn frosts arrive.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then soak it thoroughly, keeping it completely dry in winter.
Take stem cuttings in summer to easily propagate new plants as backups against cold UK winters.
Position in your sunniest south-facing spot or gravel garden to encourage those pink daisy flowers.

items.name: Oscularia piquetbergensis
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African native indoors to a frost-free windowsill from October to April in the UK.
Plant in a mix of equal parts peat-free compost and horticultural grit to prevent winter root rot.
Water only when the fleshy blue leaves start to wrinkle slightly, then drench them thoroughly.
Take stem cuttings in June or July, letting the wounds dry for three days before potting in sand.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot on your patio to mimic its hot native cliffs.

items.name: Osmadenia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April under glass to protect this delicate annual from late UK frosts.
Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, mimicking its native dry-summer chaparral habitat.
Mix plenty of grit into your compost to ensure the sharp drainage this sensitive root system needs.
Watch out for slugs and snails in May, as they find the tender young spring shoots irresistible.
Plant alongside low-growing thyme in a sunny, south-facing border to trap crucial summer warmth.

items.name: Ostrowskia
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant bellflower deep, at least fifteen centimetres down, in ultra-gritty, sharp soil.
Keep the tuber bone-dry in summer after flowering by covering it with a cloche during UK rains.
Protect the early spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Position the crown in your sunniest, south-facing border against a warm wall to mimic its homeland.
Avoid moving it once planted, as the brittle, deep taproot hates being disturbed or transplanted.

items.name: Otochilus
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid in a chunky bark mix with perlite, never in standard UK garden soil.
Keep it in a humid, frost-free greenhouse or bright bathroom, as it cannot survive UK winters.
Water copiously in summer but let the compost dry out almost completely during winter dormancy.
Position in bright, filtered light but shield from direct midday sun to prevent leaf scorch.
Divide the pseudobulbs in spring only when the plant completely outgrows its current pot.

items.name: Ourisia alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant this Patagonian alpine in a gritty, moisture-retentive soil mix that never dries out completely.
Position your plant in a cool, north-facing rockery or semi-shaded bed to mimic its damp mountain home.
Surround the crown with a thick layer of horticultural grit to prevent winter wet from rotting it.
Water regularly with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the shallow roots cool and damp.
Propagate by gently dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins.

items.name: Ourisia breviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining compost mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position it in a cool, partially shaded spot mimicking its native damp, rocky mountain crevices.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry summer spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the tender new foliage.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes after flowering in late summer or autumn.

items.name: Ourisia breviflora subsp. breviflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in moist, gritty, acidic soil in a cool, north-facing rockery or crevice.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins.
Provide a winter mulch of fine gravel around the crown to prevent rot from persistent UK rain.

items.name: Ourisia breviflora subsp. uniflora
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny alpine in gritty, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp Scottish mountain crevice.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Position it in partial shade where it is protected from the scorching afternoon midsummer sun.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the clump.
Grow it in a cold greenhouse or alpine sink to shield it from excessive winter wet and rot.

items.name: Ourisia caespitosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in grit-rich, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Position your plant in partial shade to mimic its native cool, damp New Zealand mountain home.
Topdress the surrounding soil with horticultural grit to keep the creeping foliage off wet earth.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil moist but never allow it to sit waterlogged.
Divide the creeping mats in early spring to propagate new plants and keep the parent clump vigorous.

items.name: Ourisia calycina
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand native in a gritty, free-draining soil mix that stays moist but never soggy.
Position your pot in partial shade to mimic its natural cool, damp mountain home in the UK climate.
Top-dress the soil with a layer of fine grit or gravel to keep the foliage dry and prevent rot.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the compost slightly acidic to neutral.
Protect the evergreen leaves from harsh, drying winter winds with a temporary cloche or fleece.

items.name: Ourisia chamaedrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine creeper in a gritty, free-draining soil mix to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Tuck it into a cool, north-facing rockery pocket so the hot midday summer sun doesn't scorch it.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, watering it more during dry, warm spring spells.
Watch out for slugs and snails in early spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh shoots.
Propagate by gently detaching rooted runners in autumn and potting them up to overwinter in a cold frame.

items.name: Ourisia coccinea
items.growersTips:
Grow this Chilean gem in moist, acidic soil rich in leafmould to mimic its native woodland home.
Plant the creeping rhizomes just below the soil surface in a spot with cool, dappled partial shade.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh, drying winter winds with a mulch of composted pine needles.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the fresh, emerging red flowers.

items.name: Ourisia coccinea subsp. coccinea
items.growersTips:
Give this Chilean native a damp, cool spot in partial shade, mimicking its natural woodland home.
Plant the creeping rhizomes shallowly, just below the soil surface, in rich, acidic leaf mould.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh, drying winter winds with a light mulch of bark chippings.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging flower stems.

items.name: Ourisia confertifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine gem in a gritty, free-draining scree bed or crevice garden to survive UK winter wet.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the dry, warm summer months.
Nestle it next to dwarf ferns or small saxifrages to provide some light, dappled afternoon shade.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Top-dress the soil with a layer of fine granite chippings to keep the crown dry and rot-free.

items.name: Ourisia crosbyi
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand alpine in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil that mimics its native stream banks.
Position your plant in a cool, damp, north-facing spot or woodland edge to shield it from dry heat.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil damp, but ensure it never sits in bog.
Mulch with leaf mould or grit in autumn to protect the roots from winter wet and hard frosts.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to feast on the lush, low-growing evergreen foliage.

items.name: Ourisia fragrans
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean alpine in a gritty, moisture-retentive, acidic soil mix to mimic its scree home.
Position it in a cool, north-facing rockery or container to shield it from harsh afternoon sun.
Water consistently with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the shallow roots damp but free.
Protect the evergreen foliage from wet winter rot with a pane of glass or a cold frame overhead.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth starts to keep the clump vigorous.

items.name: Ourisia fuegiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this Patagonian alpine in a gritty, moisture-retentive, acidic soil mix to mimic its scree home.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering with rainwater rather than tap water in dry spells.
Position it in cool, partial shade, away from midday sun, perhaps on a north-facing UK rockery slope.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails with organic grit barriers or evening patrols.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth starts to keep the clump vigorous.

items.name: Ourisia integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine creeper in moist, acidic peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit for drainage.
Position it in a cool, north-facing rockery or crevice to shield it from the hot UK summer sun.
Water regularly with rainwater to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged or stagnant.
Protect the delicate evergreen foliage from winter wet with a pane of glass or a cloche.
Gently divide the creeping mats in early spring to propagate new plants and keep the clump vigorous.

items.name: Ourisia macrocarpa
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand alpine in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic soil in a cool, shady spot.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Protect the shallow roots from winter wet by top-dressing the soil with a layer of grit or gravel.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging foliage.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to show.

items.name: Ourisia macrophylla
