Plant this New Zealand native in a spot with reliable, year-round moisture that mimics a stream edge.
Position it in dappled shade under shrubs to prevent the delicate leaves from scorching in summer.
Topdress the soil annually with leafmould to mimic the rich, acidic forest floors of its homeland.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the emerging fresh green foliage.
Propagate by dividing the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to show.

items.name: Ourisia macrophylla subsp. lactea
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand native in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil to mimic its mountain woodland home.
Find a sheltered spot in partial shade, as hot afternoon UK sun will quickly scorch its lush leaves.
Water regularly during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh winter winds with a mulch of leaf mould in late autumn.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, which love to feast on the low-growing rosettes of leaves.

items.name: Ourisia macrophylla subsp. macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand native in a spot with damp, humus-rich soil that mimics its mountain home.
Give it partial shade under shrubs to protect its delicate white flowers from the strong midday sun.
Water it consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil moist but never waterlogged or soggy.
Mulch with leaf mould in autumn to protect its shallow roots from hard frosts and retain moisture.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging green foliage.

items.name: Ourisia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree bed or rock crevice to survive wet UK winters.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil mix slightly acidic.
Tuck it into a north or east-facing crevice to shield its delicate roots from hot midday sun.
Protect the evergreen foliage from winter wet by placing a glass collar or cloche over the crown.
Propagate by gently detaching rooted runners in spring and potting them in a gritty peat-free compost.

items.name: Ourisia modesta
items.growersTips:
Plant this creeping New Zealand native in a spot with damp, humus-rich soil that never dries out.
Give it partial or full shade to mimic its natural woodland home and prevent the leaves scorching.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the tender new creeping stems.
Propagate it easily in autumn by gently dividing the rooted runners and replanting them shallowly.
Grow it alongside miniature hostas or small ferns which thrive in the same cool, moist UK conditions.

items.name: Ourisia muscosa
items.growersTips:
Grow this Andean alpine in a gritty, free-draining compost mix inside a cold frame to mimic scree.
Water from below during wet UK winters to prevent the dense, moss-like foliage from rotting away.
Plant it alongside dwarf ferns or gentians that thrive in cool, partially shaded rock crevices.
Protect the delicate roots from summer heat by top-dressing your pots with a thick layer of grit.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love to eat the shallow root system of this herb.

items.name: Ourisia pygmaea
items.growersTips:
Keep this alpine treasure happy in a gritty, free-draining peat-free compost with added perlite.
Plant it in a cool, north-facing rockery or crevice to shield it from harsh UK midday summer sun.
Water with rainwater to keep the soil consistently damp, never letting it dry out in hot August.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails in spring using pet-friendly organic pellets.
Top-dress the soil with a layer of fine grit to keep damp compost away from the crown and leaves.

items.name: Ourisia remotifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand alpine in a gritty, acidic soil mix to mimic its native mountain home.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Position it in partial shade, as hot afternoon sun will quickly scorch its delicate foliage.
Protect the crown from winter wet using a slate collar or a layer of sharp alpine grit.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the fresh new growth.

items.name: Ourisia ruellioides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean native in a damp, shady spot like a woodland edge or beside a UK garden pond.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or compost into acidic soil to mimic its natural damp forest floor habitat.
Water regularly during dry UK summers to keep the soil constantly moist but never waterlogged.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh, drying winter winds with a mulch of bark or dry leaves.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in early spring to propagate new plants and keep the clump vigorous.

items.name: Ourisia serpyllifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree bed to survive wet UK winters.
Water it consistently in summer to mimic its native damp mountain home, never letting it dry out.
Tuck it into a north or east-facing rock crevice to protect its delicate roots from hot midday sun.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to feast on its prostrate, mat-forming foliage.
Propagate by carefully dividing the creeping rooted stems in spring just as new growth starts.

items.name: Ourisia sessilifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining compost mix so its roots never sit in winter wet.
Place it in a cool, north-facing rockery crevice to shield it from the hot midday summer sun.
Water with harvested rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil acidic and damp.
Watch out for slugs and snails during damp UK springs, as they love the soft, hairy foliage.
Divide your clumps right after flowering in summer to keep the plant vigorous and healthy.

items.name: Ourisia sessilifolia subsp. sessilifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining scree bed to mimic its snowy New Zealand home.
Keep the soil moist but never soggy during dry UK summers, using rainwater rather than tap water.
Position it in cool, dappled shade or a north-facing rockery to protect it from midday summer sun.
Watch out for slugs and snails, which absolutely love devouring its soft, hairy rosettes of leaves.
Top-dress the surrounding soil with fine granite grit to prevent the foliage from rotting in winter.

items.name: Ourisia sessilifolia subsp. splendida
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in a gritty, free-draining scree bed or rockery to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in a cool, north-facing spot or light dappled shade to mimic its native mountain home.
Water regularly with stored rainwater, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged during summer.
Protect the soft, hairy rosettes from winter wet by placing a pane of glass or cloche over them.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails, which love to feast on the tender, low-growing foliage.

items.name: Ourisia simpsonii
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Zealand alpine in a gritty, free-draining compost mix in a cool, north-facing rockery.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summers.
Protect its delicate evergreen foliage from winter wet with a simple glass or plastic cloche.
Grow it alongside dwarf ferns or small hostas that thrive in the same damp, semi-shaded conditions.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to feast on the tender new flower stems.

items.name: Ourisia spathulata
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining compost mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during our dry, warm spring and summer spells.
Position your pot in a cool, north-facing spot to mimic its native damp, shaded New Zealand cliffs.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in spring.
Divide the creeping rhizomes gently in early autumn to propagate new plants and keep the clump tidy.

items.name: Ourisia vulcanica
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in a gritty, free-draining compost mix to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy during dry summer spells using harvested rainwater.
Position your pot in partial shade, mimicking its native cool, damp volcanic crevice habitat.
Protect the delicate foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the base.
Divide the creeping rhizomes in early spring to propagate new plants and maintain parent vigor.

items.name: Oxygraphis
items.growersTips:
Plant these alpine gems in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters without rot.
Keep them damp but never soggy during spring, mimicking the melting snow of their native habitat.
Protect the delicate yellow spring blooms from slugs and snails using organic beer traps nearby.
Tuck them into a raised scree bed or alpine trough where they will not get choked out by larger plants.
Give them a top dressing of fine granite grit to keep damp soil away from their sensitive crowns.

items.name: Oxypetalum
items.growersTips:
Sow Oxypetalum caeruleum seeds indoors in March, barely covering them with a light dusting of grit.
Move your potted tweedia indoors to a frost-free conservatory or sunny windowsill by mid-October.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as they hate soggy winter roots.
Wear gloves when pruning leggy stems in spring to avoid irritation from the sticky white sap.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potash tomato food from June to September to boost those blue blooms.

items.name: Oxypetalum coeruleum
items.growersTips:
Bring your potted oxypetalum indoors to a sunny windowsill by October to survive the cold UK winter.
Sow the seeds shallowly in early spring, just barely covering them with a fine layer of vermiculite.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil dries out, but keep it much drier during the winter months.
Provide a small trellis or obelisk for its twining stems to climb as soon as active growth starts.
Wear gloves when pruning back leggy stems in spring to avoid irritation from its milky white sap.

items.name: Oxysepala grandimesensis
items.growersTips:
Keep this Australian orchid indoors in winter; it hates UK frost and needs a bright, warm windowsill.
Water it only when the bark mix dries out, mimicking its natural dry-season tropical habitat.
Pot it in a chunky orchid bark and perlite mix to ensure the roots never sit in soggy UK soil.
Feed it weekly with a very weak orchid fertiliser during its active summer growing phase.
Watch out for mealybugs in the tight leaf joints, wiping them off with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Oxystelma
items.growersTips:
Bring this tender climber indoors before autumn frosts and keep it in a bright, heated greenhouse.
Plant it in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of grit to ensure the roots never sit in water.
Water it freely during the summer growing season but let the soil dry out completely in winter.
Train the vigorous twining stems onto a sturdy trellis or hoop to manage its rapid summer growth.
Check the soft new shoots regularly for aphids, especially when you bring the plant indoors.

items.name: Oxystelma esculentum
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender climber in a pot so you can overwinter it indoors before the first autumn frost.
Plant your seeds just five millimetres deep in free-draining peat-free compost with added grit.
Water generously through summer but let the soil dry out completely between waterings in winter.
Prune back the vigorous vine stems in early spring to encourage bushy new growth and more blooms.
Keep a sharp eye out for aphids and red spider mites when you bring the pot inside for winter.

items.name: Oziroe arida
items.growersTips:
Plant this Chilean bulb five centimetres deep in autumn using extremely gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep it completely dry during its summer dormancy to prevent the bulb from rotting in wet UK soil.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for the winter.
Position your pot in the brightest, most sun-drenched spot in your garden to mimic its home desert.
Water it sparingly only from autumn to spring, allowing the gritty compost to dry out between drinks.

items.name: Ozothamnus
items.growersTips:
Pop your ozothamnus in a sunny, south-facing spot with gritty, free-draining soil to mimic the dunes.
Water young plants once a week during dry spells, but let established ones dry out completely.
Prune lightly in late spring after the frost to shape them and encourage those lovely button flowers.
Keep an eye out for root rot in soggy UK winters, so raise your beds or add plenty of gravel.
Plant them alongside lavender or rosemary for a gorgeous, drought-tolerant Mediterranean display.

items.name: Pachycarpus
items.growersTips:
Grow these South African gems in gritty loam and keep them in pots to move indoors before UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week in summer but let the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid rot.
Sow seeds in spring using a heated propagator to mimic their native warm grassland temperatures.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using beer traps or copper tape on pots.
Position your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to maximise summer heat.

items.name: Pachyelasma
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect the taproot before late May planting.
Mix plenty of grit into your clay soil to prevent winter rot in wet British garden beds.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep drought resistance.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs on young spring shoots by using beer traps around the damp borders.
Plant alongside calendula to naturally deter aphids and attract beneficial pollinators to the blooms.

items.name: Pachyphytum
items.growersTips:
Bring your Pachyphytum indoors by October to protect its chubby leaves from wet UK winter frosts.
Plant in a gritty mix of fifty percent pumice and peat-free compost to prevent root rot in damp air.
Water only when the lower leaves feel slightly soft, keeping them completely dry during winter.
Avoid touching the leaves because your finger oils will rub off their beautiful powdery blue bloom.
Place them on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep their compact, rosette shape tight.

items.name: Pachyphytum bracteosum
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant inside by October to protect its fleshy leaves from wet and freezing UK winters.
Mix fifty percent grit into your peat-free compost to stop the roots rotting in damp British air.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, then soak it, but never get water on the powdery blue leaves.
Keep it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to stop the stems stretching out and losing color.
Propagate new plants in spring by gently twisting off a healthy leaf and laying it on dry compost.

items.name: Pachyphytum compactum
items.growersTips:
Bring your little jewel plant indoors by October to protect its chubby leaves from cold UK frosts.
Plant it in a fifty-fifty mix of potting compost and grit so the roots never sit in damp winter soil.
Only water when the leaves start to wrinkle slightly, then give it a good soak and let it dry out.
Place it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to keep those lovely purple leaf tips vibrant.
Gently brush away any white fluffy mealybugs from the tight leaf crevices with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Pachyphytum hookeri
items.growersTips:
Bring your plant indoors to a frost-free windowsill before the damp UK autumn chill sets in.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, which might mean just once a month during cold UK winters.
Mix two parts grit to one part peat-free compost to stop the roots rotting in our humid climate.
Keep a sharp eye out for mealybugs hiding in the tight crevices of those lovely powdery leaves.
Propagate new plants in spring by gently twisting off a healthy leaf and laying it on dry grit.

items.name: Pachyphytum oviferum
items.growersTips:
Bring it indoors by October to protect those chubby leaves from harsh UK frosts and winter wet.
Water only when the leaves feel slightly soft to the touch, keeping it bone dry from Nov to March.
Plant in a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit to ensure rapid drainage.
Keep it on your brightest south-facing windowsill to maintain that lovely pinkish-purple blush.
Avoid touching the leaves so you do not rub off the delicate, powdery white protective coating.

items.name: Pachypodium
items.growersTips:
Keep it in a gritty, free-draining cactus mix on a south-facing windowsill to mimic its native sun.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then stop completely from October to spring when leaves drop.
Keep winter temperatures above twelve degrees Celsius to prevent this tender succulent from rotting.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and dab them away with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.
Repot in spring every two years using a shallow pot to accommodate its fibrous, shallow root system.

items.name: Pachysandra
items.growersTips:
Plant Pachysandra terminalis in moist, acidic to neutral soil under deciduous UK trees for best shade.
Water your new plants weekly during dry UK summers until they establish their spreading root system.
Trim the tips in early spring with shears to encourage a thicker, bushier carpet of green leaves.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow them in patio containers.
Combine them with shade-loving UK natives like ferns and hostas to create a lush woodland garden.

items.name: Pachysandra axillaris
items.growersTips:
Plant it in moist, acidic woodland soil in spring, burying the root crown just level with the ground.
Give it a deep weekly soak during dry UK summers until its underground runners are well established.
Snip back any leggy stems in late spring after flowering to keep its evergreen carpet nice and dense.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow this in patio containers.
Pair it with shade-loving ferns and hostas to create a lush, weed-smothering groundcover scheme.

items.name: Pachysandra procumbens
items.growersTips:
Plant this native beauty in moist, acidic clay soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodlands.
Water weekly during dry British summers until established, keeping the soil damp but never soggy.
Divide your clumps in early spring just as new growth starts to easily fill bare shady borders.
Snip away old winter-damaged leaves in March to let the lovely new mottled green foliage shine.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails during wet UK springs, as they love to nibble the young shoots.

items.name: Pachysandra terminalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this shade-lover in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil to avoid yellowing leaves.
Water your new plants weekly during dry UK summers until their shallow roots are fully established.
Shear the foliage back to the ground in early spring to encourage fresh, bushy new growth.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow them in patio pots.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or spring to easily fill bare patches under your trees.

items.name: Pachystachys
items.growersTips:
Bring your lollipop plant indoors to a warm, bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of compost feels dry to prevent root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in early spring to encourage a bushier shape and more golden bracts.
Feed fortnightly from April to September with a high-potash liquid tomato food for better blooms.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for red spider mites, which thrive in dry indoor UK heating.

items.name: Pachystachys coccinea
items.growersTips:
Bring your cardinal guard indoors by October as it cannot survive UK frosts below ten degrees.
Grow it in a peat-free loam compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure the roots never sit wet.
Water generously from May to September but let the top two inches of soil dry out during winter.
Prune the stems back by half in early spring to stop it getting leggy and promote bushy flowering.
Mist the leaves daily in dry centrally heated rooms to prevent red spider mites from taking over.

items.name: Pachystachys lutea
items.growersTips:
Bring your lollipop plant indoors to a warm, bright windowsill before the first autumn frost hits.
Water weekly in summer but let the top inch of compost dry out completely before you pour again.
Prune stems back by half in early spring to stop your plant from getting too leggy and sparse.
Check the leaf undersides regularly for glasshouse whitefly, especially during dry winter months.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid tomato fertilizer every fortnight from May through to September.

items.name: Pachystegia insignis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Marlborough rock daisy in well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a sheltered, south-facing spot against a warm wall to mimic its native coastal cliffs.
Water sparingly once established, only drenching during prolonged dry spells in the summer months.
Protect the young foliage from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using organic grit barriers.
Avoid hard pruning, just lightly trim the spent flower stems in late summer to keep it tidy.

items.name: Pachystoma
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare orchid in a warm greenhouse using a free-draining mix of fine bark and perlite.
Keep the soil damp but never soggy during spring growth, then cut back on watering in winter.
Position your pots in bright, filtered light but shield them from direct midday UK summer sun.
Watch out for glasshouse spider mites and wipe the leaves down with a damp cloth to deter them.
Repot only when the orchid mix begins to break down, ideally just as new root growth starts.

items.name: Palafoxia arida
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in March with bottom heat to mimic their native desert warmth before May.
Use a gritty, free-draining soil mix with fifty percent perlite to survive damp UK summer rain.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry to prevent root rot in our cool climate.
Position your pots in the absolute sunniest, south-facing spot you have to maximise summer blooms.
Sow seeds just two millimetres deep and do not cover them, as they need direct light to germinate.

items.name: Palafoxia callosa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at a shallow depth of three millimetres to beat the cool British spring.
Grow these Texas natives in your sunniest spot in sharply draining soil mixed with plenty of grit.
Water them only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry to prevent lethal root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to encourage a bushier habit and more of those pink blooms.
Plant them alongside Mediterranean herbs like thyme to match their strict low-water requirements.

items.name: Palafoxia integrifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow these heat-loving seeds indoors in early April at a shallow depth of just three millimetres.
Plant them out in late May only after the final frost, choosing your absolute sunniest border.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil first to mimic the dry, sandy coastal plains they love.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between light waterings.
Deadhead the faded pink blooms weekly in August to keep new flowers coming until the autumn chill.

items.name: Paliavana
items.growersTips:
Bring your paliavana indoors to a frost-free conservatory or greenhouse before the first UK frosts.
Grow this Brazilian shrub in a large pot with grit-heavy compost to ensure excellent winter drainage.
Water deeply only when the top three inches of soil feel dry, as paliavana hates soggy winter roots.
Prune back leggy stems by a third in early spring to encourage a bushier habit and more purple blooms.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot in your garden to mimic its native warmth.

items.name: Pallenis
items.growersTips:
Mix grit into your soil to help this Mediterranean annual survive wet, soggy UK summer downpours.
Sow seeds shallowly in April, barely covering them with compost as they need light to germinate.
Water deeply once a week only during dry spells, as overwatering causes root rot in our climate.
Snip off faded yellow daisy heads weekly in July to keep the plant producing fresh summer blooms.
Sow seeds directly next to purple lavender to create a gorgeous, drought-tolerant cottage border.

items.name: Palmerella
items.growersTips:
Grow this delicate lobelia relative in moist, acidic soil rich in leafmould to mimic its damp home.
Plant your Palmerella in a sheltered, partially shaded spot to protect it from harsh UK winds.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged, especially during dry British summer spells.
Mulch heavily with bracken or bark in late autumn to protect its tender roots from deep winter frost.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging new shoots.

items.name: Paloue
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators in March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Plant your Paloue in free-draining sandy loam enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Position them in your sunniest, south-facing border to mimic their native tropical warmth.
Water deeply once a week at the base, letting the top inch of soil dry out between drinks.
Apply a high-potassium liquid feed every fortnight in July to boost their summer flowering.

items.name: Papaver
items.growersTips:
Plant your perennial poppies in deep, well-drained soil as their long taproots hate wet winter feet.
Cut the faded foliage right back to ground level in July to trigger a fresh flush of green leaves.
Protect the tender new spring growth from hungry slugs using organic grit or beer traps.
Divide your mature clumps in autumn only, taking care not to damage that sensitive main taproot.
Sow seeds directly where you want them to bloom because these plants absolutely detest being moved.

items.name: Papaver aculeatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn so UK winter cold naturally triggers their spring germination.
Grow them in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter wet from rotting their taproots.
Position them in your sunniest border next to low-growing thyme to support their wiry stems.
Water only during dry spells in summer, letting the soil dry out completely between sessions.
Leave the prickly seed heads on the plant until autumn to let them self-seed around your garden.

items.name: Papaver alpinum
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine poppy in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Tuck seeds into gravelly scree beds or rock crevices in autumn for natural cold-stratification.
Water sparingly once established, only during dry spells, as this mountain beauty hates soggy feet.
Deadhead faded blooms regularly through summer to encourage a continuous flush of new pastel flowers.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to devour the delicate, feathery new foliage.

items.name: Papaver arenarium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly onto well-drained, gritty soil as they need winter cold to germinate.
Keep watering very light, only dampening the soil during dry spells to prevent root rot in UK rain.
Position in your brightest, most south-facing spot to mimic their native sunny, gravelly slopes.
Scatter grit around the base of young plants to protect the delicate foliage from slugs and damp.
Leave the seed heads intact over winter to self-sow naturally in your gravel paths and borders.

items.name: Papaver armeniacum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn so UK winter cold naturally triggers their spring germination.
Grow them in gritty, fast-draining soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Water only during dry spells in summer as these alpine poppies hate soggy roots.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly in July to encourage a second flush of delicate orange flowers.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme to support their stems and keep weeds at bay.

items.name: Papaver atlanticum
items.growersTips:
Pop this Spanish poppy in poor, well-drained soil in full sun so it doesn't get soggy in UK winters.
Sow the tiny seeds shallowly in spring by just pressing them into the soil surface without burying.
Deadhead regularly to keep those lovely apricot blooms coming and stop it self-seeding everywhere.
Watch out for downy mildew in damp UK summers by spacing plants well to keep the air flowing.
Divide the clumps in early spring or take root cuttings in winter to easily get free new plants.

items.name: Papaver bracteatum
items.growersTips:
Plant these deep taproots in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn so the natural winter chill triggers successful spring germination.
Cut faded stems right back in July to trigger a fresh flush of lush green foliage by September.
Water deeply only during dry spring spells, then leave them alone once summer dormancy sets in.
Watch for slugs on young spring shoots, and prop heavy flower heads before May winds damage them.

items.name: Papaver californicum
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds in autumn directly where they will bloom, as they hate having their roots disturbed.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil to ensure sharp drainage, preventing winter rot in wet UK clay.
Position them in your sunniest border to mimic their native warm slopes and encourage daily blooms.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry spells, to keep them from getting leggy.
Deadhead regularly in summer to prolong flowering, but leave the last seed heads to self-sow naturally.

items.name: Papaver cambricum
items.growersTips:
Sow the seeds in autumn directly onto damp, gritty soil so winter cold naturally triggers growth.
Grow them alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade where their bright yellow blooms pop beautifully.
Cut back the faded flower stems in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage a second flush.
Water young plants weekly during dry spells, but let established clumps rely on typical UK rain.
Watch out for downy mildew in damp summers by spacing them well to keep air flowing through leaves.

items.name: Papaver commutatum
items.growersTips:
Sow these Ladybird poppy seeds directly outdoors in spring as they hate their roots being disturbed.
Thin your seedlings to twenty centimetres apart in May so they have room to show off those red cups.
Pick a spot in full sun with poor, well-drained soil to stop them getting floppy in UK drizzle.
Leave the gorgeous seed heads on the stems in autumn so they self-seed naturally for next summer.
Watch out for slugs when the shoots are tiny, using organic grit to protect the young leaves.

items.name: Papaver dahlianum
items.growersTips:
Tuck this arctic poppy into gritty, sharply draining scree or rock gardens to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the tiny seeds shallowly on the soil surface in autumn so winter cold can naturally wake them up.
Water very sparingly only during dry summer spells, keeping the gritty collar around the crown dry.
Position in your windiest, most exposed sunny spot to mimic its native harsh Svalbard environment.
Protect the delicate blue-green rosettes from damp-loving slugs using organic grit barriers.

items.name: Papaver degenii
items.growersTips:
Plant this rare Alpine poppy in extremely gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position your pot in full sun but protect it from heavy rain using a cold frame or alpine house.
Water very sparingly from below during winter to prevent the fuzzy grey foliage from rotting away.
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface because they need a winter chill and light to germinate.
Surround the collar with a thick layer of granite grit to keep damp soil off the delicate leaves.

items.name: Papaver dubium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the soil surface in spring, as they need light to germinate in UK weather.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out to mimic its native gravelly habitats.
Scatter seeds directly where you want them, as their taproots hate being moved or transplanted.
Snip off fading seed heads in summer if you want to stop this enthusiastic self-seeder taking over.
Grow them alongside hardy annuals like cornflowers to create a classic, low-maintenance UK meadow.

items.name: Papaver glaucum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in March directly where they will flower as they hate having their roots disturbed.
Thin the seedlings to twenty centimetres apart in late spring so the tulip-like blooms have room.
Water young plants sparingly only during dry spells because they rot easily in wet British soil.
Watch out for slugs and snails when the first delicate grey-green leaves emerge in early spring.
Leave the architectural seed heads to dry on the stem in autumn to self-seed for next summer.

items.name: Papaver heterophyllum
items.growersTips:
Sow these Wind Poppy seeds shallowly in autumn so UK winter chill can naturally break their dormancy.
Give them sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent their roots from rotting during wet UK winters.
Position them in a sheltered, south-facing spot to mimic their native warm, sunny hillside homes.
Water them sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between sparse drinks.
Plant them alongside low-growing thyme or sedums to support their slender, delicate stems in wind.

items.name: Papaver hybridum
items.growersTips:
Sow these rough poppy seeds very shallowly in autumn so UK winter chills can trigger germination.
Keep them in your poorest, well-drained gritty soil as rich UK border soil makes them floppy.
Water seedlings sparingly during dry spring spells, then leave established plants to brave droughts.
Leave the bristly seed heads on over winter to let them self-seed naturally around your gravel path.
Sow them alongside wild chamomile or cornflowers to create a classic British cottage meadow look.

items.name: Papaver lapponicum
items.growersTips:
Plant this arctic poppy in gritty, sharply draining raised beds to survive wet UK winter rot.
Sow seeds directly onto the soil surface in autumn, as they need cold winter chills to germinate.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the gritty soil dry out completely between soakings.
Position them in your garden's windiest, most exposed spot to mimic their native open tundra.
Protect the low rosettes from slugs and snails during damp UK springs using beer traps or grit.

items.name: Papaver lateritium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Armenian poppy in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring, just pressing them into the soil surface as they need light to sprout.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in July to encourage a second flush of orange blooms in autumn.
Position it alongside silver-foliaged companion plants like stachys to complement the orange petals.
Divide established clumps in autumn every three years to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.

items.name: Papaver orientale
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil to accommodate the long taproot and prevent winter rot.
Cut the entire plant back to ground level in July after flowering to stimulate fresh new foliage.
Propagate by taking three-inch root cuttings in late autumn or winter when the plant is dormant.
Support heavy flower stems in May using hazel twigs or metal hoops before the blooms open and flop.
Plant alongside late-summer perennials like dahlias to mask the unsightly yellowing summer foliage.

items.name: Papaver pinnatifidum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn so UK winter cold naturally triggers their spring germination.
Grow them in gritty, fast-draining soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Water only during dry spring spells, then let the soil dry out completely as they go dormant.
Plant them alongside lavender or thyme to help support their floppy, delicate summer stems.
Cut faded foliage to the ground in late summer to encourage fresh, healthy autumn regrowth.

items.name: Papaver pygmaeum
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny alpine poppy in a gritty, free-draining scree bed to survive wet UK winters.
Sow the seeds shallowly in autumn on the soil surface because they need light to germinate.
Protect the delicate grey foliage from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in spring.
Water sparingly from below in summer, keeping the collar dry to prevent crown rot in damp weather.
Grow them alongside dwarf saxifrages in a raised alpine trough to mimic their rocky mountain home.

items.name: Papaver radicatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Arctic poppy in extremely gritty, sharply draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Keep them in your coldest, most exposed rock garden spot as they hate our humid summer heat.
Sow seeds directly on the soil surface in autumn because they need winter cold to germinate.
Avoid watering them at all once established, relying only on natural UK rainfall to prevent rot.
Grow them in shallow alpine troughs or raised scree beds to mimic their native gravelly slopes.

items.name: Papaver rhoeas
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly onto finely raked soil in spring or autumn as they need light to germinate.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in spring to prevent mildew in damp UK weather.
Grow in poor well drained soil in full sun to prevent floppy stems and encourage more blooms.
Deadhead faded flowers weekly to prolong blooming or leave seedheads to self sow for next year.
Sow alongside cornflowers and chamomile in autumn for a classic British cottage garden display.

items.name: Papaver rupifragum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or spring, barely covering them as they need UK light to germinate.
Give this Spanish poppy sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Cut faded stems back to the base in summer to trigger a second flush of bright apricot blooms.
Plant them alongside silver-leaved Mediterranean herbs like thyme to naturally support their stems.
Leave some late-season seed heads intact so they can self-sow freely in your gravel paths and walls.

items.name: Papaver setigerum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly in autumn directly onto well-drained, gritty soil for robust spring growth.
Keep seedlings barely damp in winter as wet UK soil will quickly rot their delicate taproots.
Thin your emerging seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in April so they have room to spread.
Scatter grit around the base of young plants to protect the soft foliage from hungry garden slugs.
Leave the beautiful dried seed heads intact through autumn to easily self-seed for next summer.

items.name: Papaver somniferum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly onto finely raked soil in spring, as they hate having their roots disturbed.
Thin your seedlings to thirty centimeters apart so the heavy flower heads get plenty of support.
Water the young plants gently during dry spells, but leave them alone once they are established.
Watch out for damp UK slugs when shoots are small, and use beer traps to protect the tiny leaves.
Leave the beautiful seed heads to dry on the stem in autumn if you want them to self-sow for next year.

items.name: Papaver umbonatum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn, barely covering them, so UK winter cold can trigger germination.
Plant these poppies in gritty, free-draining soil to stop the roots rotting during wet UK winters.
Water only during dry spells in spring, as they hate soggy soil and prefer a dry summer dormancy.
Cut back faded stems in July to encourage a second flush of those beautiful orange-red blooms.
Grow them alongside Mediterranean herbs like rosemary to help support their delicate, floppy stems.

items.name: Papaveroideae
items.growersTips:
Sow perennial poppy seeds shallowly in autumn so UK winter cold can trigger their germination.
Give your poppies gritty, sharp-draining soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Cut Welsh poppies right back after flowering in July to stop them aggressively self-seeding.
Water your poppies deeply at the base once a week during dry spells to avoid powdery mildew.
Plant poppies alongside hardy geraniums to hide the messy, dying foliage after summer blooms fade.

items.name: Paphiopedilum acmodontum
items.growersTips:
Keep this warm-growing orchid in a draft-free room above fifteen degrees Celsius all winter long.
Water once a week with tepid rainwater to keep the bark mix damp but never soggy or waterlogged.
Grow in a medium-grade bark and perlite mix to let air reach the roots while holding some moisture.
Position on a north or east windowsill to shield the delicate mottled leaves from hot summer sun.
Feed with a weak half-strength orchid fertilizer every third watering during the spring and summer.

items.name: Paphiopedilum appletonianum
items.growersTips:
Grow this orchid indoors on a north or east windowsill to shield it from harsh UK summer sun.
Water with rainwater when the bark mix is almost dry, keeping it damp but never soggy or waterlogged.
Pot in a free-draining medium-grade bark and perlite mix to mimic its natural forest floor habitat.
Keep winter room temperatures above thirteen degrees Celsius to protect this tender orchid from frost.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the leaf fan joints and dab them off with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Paphiopedilum argus
items.growersTips:
Keep this mottled-leaf orchid in a warm, draft-free room, never in an unheated UK greenhouse.
Water with rainwater when the bark mix starts to dry, but never let the roots sit in soggy soil.
Repot every spring into a fresh, free-draining fine bark and perlite mix to prevent root rot.
Position on a north or east-facing windowsill to avoid scorching the beautiful patterned leaves.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf joints, wiping them away with a damp cotton bud.

items.name: Paphiopedilum armeniacum
items.growersTips:
Keep this orchid in a cool, bright draft-free spot but shade it from strong summer sun in the UK.
Water with rainwater only, keeping it damp in summer but letting it dry out slightly in winter.
Add crushed oyster shells to a bark mix to mimic the limestone cliffs of its native home.
Give it a cool winter rest around twelve degrees to trigger those beautiful bright yellow blooms.
Repot every two years in spring using a fine bark and perlite mix to keep the roots breathing.

items.name: Paphiopedilum barbatum
items.growersTips:
Keep it snug in a small pot of fine bark and perlite, as its roots hate deep, soggy compost.
Water with rainwater when the mix is almost dry, never letting this slipper orchid sit in a puddle.

Keep it cool in winter, around twelve degrees, to trigger those stunning, glossy varnished blooms.
Feed it with a very weak orchid fertiliser every third watering during its active summer growth.

items.name: Paphiopedilum wardii
items.growersTips:
Keep its mottled leaves out of direct UK sun by placing it on a bright north or east windowsill.
Water with rainwater just as the bark mix dries out, keeping it damp but never soggy at the roots.
Pot this terrestrial orchid in a chunky bark, perlite, and sphagnum moss mix for drainage.
Maintain cosy indoor temperatures between fifteen and twenty-two degrees to mimic its warm home.
Feed with a very weak orchid fertiliser every third watering during the active spring growing phase.

items.name: Paphiopedilum wenshanense
items.growersTips:
Keep this Chinese native in a lime-rich, free-draining bark mix with oyster shells, never standard soil.
Water with tepid rainwater weekly in summer, keeping the moss damp but never letting the pot sit in water.
Place on a north or east windowsill to get bright, indirect UK light without scorching the leaves.
Maintain a winter minimum of twelve degrees Celsius to mimic its natural cool-dry resting period.
Watch out for mealybugs hiding in the tight leaf fans, especially when central heating goes on.

items.name: Pappobolus
items.growersTips:
Sow Pappobolus seeds indoors in April to beat the late UK frosts, planting them just 5mm deep.
Keep young seedlings damp but never soggy, watering only from below to prevent damping-off disease.
Plant them out in June in a sunny spot with gritty soil to help them survive wet British summers.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love eating the tender young leaves of these annuals in spring.
Plant them next to calendula to help draw away aphids and bring more pollinators to your garden.

items.name: Papuacedrus papuana
items.growersTips:
Give this tender Papuan cypress a warm, sheltered south-facing wall to survive chilly UK winters.
Plant it in deep, highly acidic to neutral soil that drains rapidly so the roots never sit in wet.
Water thoroughly during dry summer spells but keep it almost dry in winter to prevent root rot.
Never prune back into old wood as this slow-growing conifer will not regenerate from bare branches.
Protect young trees with fleece during hard frosts and watch out for scale insects in late spring.

items.name: Paracaleana
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Australian duck orchid in a cold greenhouse to protect it from wet UK winters.
Plant the tiny tubers shallowly in a highly gritty, free-draining mix of pine bark and perlite.
Water only from below during spring growth, keeping the compost damp but never waterlogged.
Allow the pot to dry out completely during its summer dormancy to prevent the tuber from rotting.
Watch out for common UK greenhouse pests like fungus gnats that can damage the delicate roots.

items.name: Paracaryum
items.growersTips:
Plant your Paracaryum in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK weather.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural winter chill can break their dormancy easily.
Position these borage relatives in full sun to mimic their native dry, rocky mountain habitats.
Protect young spring growth from slugs and snails, which love their soft, forget-me-not-like leaves.
Avoid rich fertilisers as too many nutrients make the plants floppy and reduce their blue flowers.

items.name: Paradisea
items.growersTips:
Plant St. Bruno's lily in well-drained, humus-rich soil that stays moist but never waterlogged.
Position your Paradisea in full sun or light dappled shade to mimic its native alpine meadow home.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill can trigger germination.
Mulch the crown with leaf mould in November to protect roots from severe, wet British frosts.
Divide overcrowded clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to keep them flowering well.

items.name: Paradisea liliastrum
items.growersTips:
Plant St Bernard's lily in moist, free-draining soil with grit to survive wet UK winter rot.
Plant the fleshy roots shallowly, just five centimetres deep, in early spring for the best start.
Give them a spot in full sun or light dappled shade to mimic their native alpine meadow habitat.
Keep soil consistently damp during their spring growing season, but let them dry out a bit in winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they absolutely love devouring the fresh new shoots.

items.name: Paradrymonia hypocyrta
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical beauty indoors in a warm, humid bathroom to mimic its native rainforest home.
Water with tepid rainwater only when the top inch of your peat-free, bark-rich compost feels dry.
Keep it away from cold draughts and chilly UK windowsills, especially during damp winter months.
Feed with a weak orchid fertiliser once a month from April to September to boost healthy growth.
Watch out for mealybugs in the leaf joints and wipe them away with a damp cotton bud immediately.

items.name: Paradrymonia lineata
items.growersTips:
Grow this tropical beauty in a warm conservatory or terrarium to shield it from chilly UK winters.
Water with tepid rainwater when the top inch of peat-free compost dries out to avoid root shock.
Feed with a diluted high-potassium liquid fertiliser fortnightly from April to September.
Place in bright, indirect light near an east-facing window to prevent the delicate leaves burning.
Keep humidity high by placing the pot on a tray of wet pebbles to stop the leaf tips turning brown.

items.name: Paragymnopteris
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate fern in a sheltered, frost-free spot or container using free-draining grit.
Water your potted specimens from below during winter to prevent crown rot in damp UK weather.
Mix plenty of leaf mould and perlite into the soil to mimic its natural limestone crevice habitat.
Grow it alongside hardy maidenhair ferns or small hostas in a cool, shaded rockery or alpine house.
Check the undersides of the fronds regularly for scale insects, especially in humid glasshouses.

items.name: Parahancornia
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical fruit indoors by mid-October to protect it from wet, chilly UK winter rot.
Plant seeds exactly two centimeters deep in a heated propagator kept at twenty-five degrees.
Water only when the top three centimeters of soil feel dry, as they hate soggy British winters.
Feed with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertilizer every fortnight from May through September.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites when keeping your plant in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Parakmeria
items.growersTips:
Plant this Magnolia relative in deep, fertile, acidic to neutral soil that mimics woodland floor.
Position your shrub in a sheltered spot away from cold UK winds to protect its glossy evergreen foliage.
Water deeply and regularly during dry summer spells to keep the moisture-loving root system happy.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering only to shape or remove any frost-damaged branches.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark to retain soil moisture and mimic its forest habitat.

items.name: Parameria
items.growersTips:
Bring your Parameria indoors by October to protect this tender tropical vine from UK winter frosts.
Grow it in a loam-based compost mixed with plenty of perlite to ensure the sharp drainage it needs.
Water generously in summer but let the top inch dry out completely before you reach for the can.
Prune back unruly stems in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its climbing habit neat.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry conservatory air and mist the leaves regularly to deter them.

items.name: Paramoltkia doerfleri
items.growersTips:
Plant this Balkan gem in a raised bed or rockery with lots of grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water it only during dry spring spells, then let the soil dry out completely over the summer.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh winter winds with a temporary cloche or fleece wrap.
Grow it alongside companion plants like saxifrages or dwarf campanulas that love alkaline soil.
Propagate your plant by taking semi-ripe cuttings in mid-summer rather than trying to find seeds.

items.name: Parapiptadenia
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in warm propagators in early March to beat the short UK summer season.
Sow the seeds exactly one centimetre deep in a free-draining peat-free compost with added perlite.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to prevent root rot during damp British Junes.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertiliser once you spot the very first flowers.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are keeping them under cover in a humid greenhouse.

items.name: Parapiptadenia rigida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre using a heated propagator at twentyC.
Grow this tropical annual in pots of gritty loam so you can move it to a warm greenhouse in autumn.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil dry out to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Feed fortnightly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertilizer once the first true leaves show.
Place your pots in the sunniest south-facing spot in your garden to mimic its native South America.

items.name: Parapolystichum acuminatum
items.growersTips:
Plant this delicate fern in a sheltered, damp spot out of the cold, drying UK winds.
Mix plenty of leaf mould or composted bark into your soil to mimic its natural woodland floor.
Water regularly to keep the soil consistently moist, especially during dry British summers.
Mulch the crown with fallen leaves in late autumn to protect it from hard winter frosts.
Snip away any dead or tattered fronds in early spring just as the fresh new growth starts to unfurl.

items.name: Parapolystichum munitum
items.growersTips:
Plant this Western Sword Fern in moist, acidic to neutral soil enriched with plenty of leaf mould.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back dead or tattered fronds right to the base in late winter to make way for fresh spring growth.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to protect the fronds from harsh afternoon sun.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted bark to protect the crown from severe winter frosts.

items.name: Paraquilegia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in a deep crevice or a raised bed with sharp, gritty scree drainage.
Keep it sheltered from wet UK winters under an alpine house glass or a simple makeshift cloche.
Water generously from below during spring growth, but keep the crown dry to prevent winter rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to devour the delicate, buttercup-like spring foliage.
Grow it alongside dwarf ferns or gentians in a cool, north-facing spot away from midday sun.

items.name: Paraquilegia anemonoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine beauty in a crevice or gritty raised bed with sharp drainage to survive wet winters.
Protect its delicate crown from winter rain by placing a glass collar or cloche over it from November.
Water it from below in summer to keep the foliage dry and prevent rot in our humid UK climate.
Watch out for slugs and snails early in spring as they absolutely love eating the tender new buds.
Grow it in a container with fifty percent grit so you can easily move it out of heavy winter downpours.

items.name: Paraquilegia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine gem in a crevice or gritty raised bed to protect its roots from winter wet.
Shield its delicate crown from heavy UK rain by placing a collar of sharp granite grit around it.
Water it moderately in spring but keep it almost dry during its dormant winter rest period.
Grow it in a container so you can move it into a cold greenhouse to escape damp winter weather.
Pair it with dwarf slow-growing ferns or saxifrages that share its love for cool, shady crevices.

items.name: Pararchidendron
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre to combat chilly UK April weather.
Water your plants deeply at the base once a week to mimic their native subtropical wet-dry cycles.
Blend plenty of grit into your compost to ensure the roots do not rot during damp British summers.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings reach fifteen centimetres to encourage a bushier habit.
Keep a close eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are raising them in a UK conservatory.

items.name: Pararuellia
items.growersTips:
Try growing this tender perennial in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before UK frosts hit.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering only when the top inch feels dry.
Give it a spot with bright, indirect light to mimic its natural woodland canopy home.
Feed your plant with a diluted balanced liquid fertiliser once a month throughout the spring.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites and mist the leaves regularly to keep humidity high.

items.name: Pararuellia delavayana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender Chinese beauty in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the autumn frosts.
Plant it in a free-draining peat-free compost mixed with plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot.
Position your pot in dappled shade to mimic its woodland home and keep the delicate leaves green.
Water generously through the summer but let the soil dry out almost completely during the winter.
Propagate by taking softwood cuttings in late spring to ensure you have backup plants for winter.

items.name: Parasenegalia
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early spring to give this tender annual a head start on the cool UK season.
Plant them out in late May after the last frost in a sheltered, south-facing spot to catch the sun.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than daily sprinkles to encourage strong, deep roots.
Mix plenty of grit into your soil before planting to ensure the excellent drainage this plant needs.
Pinch out the growing tips in early summer to encourage a much bushier shape and more lush growth.

items.name: Paraserianthes
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre using a heated propagator to sprout.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy to prevent your young seedlings from rotting.
Plant them out in May after the last frost in a sheltered spot that gets full southern sun.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser once they start growing rapidly in summer.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are starting them early in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Pardoglossum
items.growersTips:
Plant Pardoglossum cheirifolium in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to give them the winter chill they need to germinate.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, protecting them with gravel or copper tape.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late summer to keep the clump tidy and encourage fresh foliage.

items.name: Pardoglossum cheirifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mediterranean beauty in your sharpest-draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in late summer in cold frames, barely covering them with a very thin layer of fine grit.
Position your pot in the sunniest, most sheltered spot of your garden to mimic its native habitat.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drinks to avoid rot.
Protect the soft, velvety foliage from slugs and snails during damp British spring evenings.

items.name: Parkerioideae
items.growersTips:
Plant your floating water ferns in a sheltered garden pond to protect them from cold UK winds.
Keep these aquatic perennials in acidic to neutral water, adding rainwater to your pond to do this.
Thin out the dense floating mats in late summer so your other pond plants can still get some light.
Compost any excess ferns you scoop out, as they make a wonderfully rich mulch for your veg beds.
Bring a few small clumps indoors to overwinter in a bright, frost-free fish tank before UK frosts.

items.name: Parkia
items.growersTips:
Start your Parkia seeds indoors in warm propagators in April to beat the cool British spring weather.
Grow Parkia in deep pots filled with a loam-based compost to accommodate their long taproot systems.
Water your Parkia deeply once a week at the base, letting the soil dry out slightly between times.
Position your potted Parkia against a south-facing brick wall to maximise essential summer heat.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when growing Parkia under cover in damp UK summers.

items.name: Parkia bicolor
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect their sensitive taproots.
Plant them out in late May in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their native warmth.
Water deeply once a week at the base rather than giving daily light sprinkles to encourage roots.
Feed monthly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed to boost their strength against damp UK summers.
Watch out for slugs on young shoots by using beer traps or copper tape around your patio pots.

items.name: Parkia biglobosa
items.growersTips:
Start your African locust bean indoors in April at 25C to beat the short, cool UK summer.
Nick the tough seed coat with sandpaper and soak in warm water for 24 hours before sowing.
Grow this tender annual in a large pot of sandy, free-draining loam so you can chase the UK sun.
Water deeply once the top inch of soil dries out, keeping it drier during cool, cloudy weeks.
Move your pot into a heated greenhouse or sunny conservatory by September to finish pod ripening.

items.name: Parkia filicoidea
items.growersTips:
Start your African locust bean seeds indoors in April using deep root trainers to protect taproots.
Use a heat mat set to twenty-five degrees to mimic the warm tropical soils these seeds require.
Grow this tender annual in a polytunnel or sunny greenhouse to shield it from chilly UK summers.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage those deep roots to search down.
Feed your plants with a low-nitrogen seaweed extract to boost foliage without ruining bean yield.

items.name: Parkia javanica
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early April at a depth of two centimetres using a heated propagator.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy to prevent the young taproots from rotting.
Move your pots outside only after late May frosts have passed, choosing your sunniest, warmest spot.
Grow this tropical annual in a large container so you can easily move it shelter during wet spells.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid seaweed fertilizer once the feathery leaves start to expand.

items.name: Parkia pendula
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early spring using deep pots to protect their long, sensitive taproots.
Use a heat mat to keep the soil at twenty-one degrees Celsius for successful UK germination.
Plant them out in June in your sunniest, most sheltered spot to mimic their native tropical warmth.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep root systems.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are starting them early in a warm conservatory.

items.name: Parkia speciosa
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early spring using deep pots to protect the sensitive taproot.
Keep the compost consistently moist but never soggy to mimic the humid tropical climate.
Place your potted plant in the sunniest spot of your greenhouse to maximize summer warmth.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air and mist the leaves regularly to deter them.
Feed weekly with a high-nitrogen liquid fertilizer once the first true leaves fully expand.

items.name: Parkia timoriana
items.growersTips:
Keep this tropical annual warm by starting seeds indoors in April on a heated propagator mat.
Sow the large seeds exactly two centimetres deep in free-draining peat-free compost with grit.
Water only when the top inch of soil feels dry to prevent damp-off in our cool UK spring.
Grow your potted tree in a south-facing conservatory or sunny patio once night temperatures exceed twelve.
Watch out for red spider mites in dry indoor air and mist the leaves weekly to keep them away.

items.name: Parkinsonia
items.growersTips:
Sow your seeds indoors in early spring after soaking them in warm water for twenty-four hours.
Plant them in a super-gritty, free-draining compost mix to survive our damp UK spring weather.
Keep your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot on your patio to mimic their desert home.
Water them deeply only when the soil is bone dry, then let them drain completely to avoid rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when they are young to encourage a bushier habit in our short summers.

items.name: Parkinsonia aculeata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in spring after soaking them in warm water to help them germinate in our cool UK air
Grow this frost-tender beauty in a pot so you can easily move it into a heated greenhouse for winter
Use a very gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent root rot during wet British summers
Water sparingly only when the top few inches of soil are bone dry, as it hates soggy roots
Prune lightly in late spring to shape it and keep its thorny branches safe from garden pathways

items.name: Parkinsonia africana
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one centimetre using a heated propagator at twenty-one degrees.
Grow this tender plant in pots of gritty, free-draining loam so you can move it indoors for winter.
Water deeply only when the top five centimetres of soil is bone dry, as it hates soggy UK winter wet.
Place your pot against a south-facing brick wall to trap maximum summer heat and block cold winds.
Prune lightly in late spring to remove dead tips, always wearing thick gloves to avoid the sharp thorns.

items.name: Parkinsonia florida
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in hot water, then grow this desert tree in a pot to move inside for winter.
Plant in a gritty cactus compost mix to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Water deeply only when the soil is bone dry, mimicking its native desert rain patterns.
Prune lightly in late spring to shape it and remove frost-damaged branches after winter.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites when overwintering your plant indoors.

items.name: Parkinsonia microphylla
items.growersTips:
Start your seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator to mimic desert heat.
Sow seeds in a very gritty, free-draining cactus compost to prevent winter rot in wet UK soil.
Grow this desert native in a terracotta pot so you can move it into a frost-free greenhouse by October.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, then drench it, but stop watering completely over winter.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mite when overwintering your plant indoors.

items.name: Parkinsonia praecox
items.growersTips:
Grow this desert native in a pot with fifty percent grit so you can move it indoors for winter.
Sow the hard seeds in spring after nicking the coat and soaking them in warm water for 24 hours.
Keep watering to a bare minimum, letting the gritty compost dry out completely between drenches.
Place your pot in the hottest, sunniest spot against a south-facing brick wall to mimic Mexico.
Watch out for root rot during damp UK autumns by keeping the pot raised on feet off the ground.

items.name: Parma Violet Group
items.growersTips:
Keep these tender beauties in pots so you can bring them into a cold greenhouse before winter frosts.
Mix plenty of leafmould and grit into your compost to mimic their favourite damp woodland soil.
Water them from the base to keep the delicate double blooms dry and prevent unsightly grey mould.
Snip off the runners in summer to channel all the plant's energy into next spring's fragrant flowers.
Watch out for red spider mites when growing them under glass and keep the air nice and humid.

items.name: Paronychia
items.growersTips:
Plant this alpine in sharp-draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet British winters without rotting.
Tuck it into sunny rock crevices or raised beds where its delicate papery bracts stay mud-free.
Water newly planted divisions sparingly, only during dry spells, as damp roots are its main enemy.
Keep an eye out for slugs in early spring when the tiny green leaves first begin to carpet the ground.
Propagate by gently detaching rooted creeping stems in late spring to fill gaps in your paving.

items.name: Paronychia ahartii
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your grittiest alpine mix to survive wet British winters.
Keep it safe from damp by planting the crown shallowly and top-dressing with pea gravel.
Water only during dry summer spells, letting the soil dry out completely between soakings.
Position it in your brightest, most south-facing rockery to mimic its sunny home habitat.
Protect the delicate mat-forming foliage from winter rot by using a temporary rain cloche.

items.name: Paronychia argentea
items.growersTips:
Plant this silver carpet in your poorest, sharpest-draining grit to stop winter wet rotting roots.
Give it a sunny spot next to creeping thyme so they can mingle and smother out any garden weeds.
Water it only during prolonged dry spells in summer, as this tough plant hates soggy UK soil.
Trim the edges back with shears in early autumn to keep its tight, mat-forming shape looking neat.
Check the dense foliage for slugs during damp spring nights, as they love to hide underneath it.

items.name: Paronychia chartacea
items.growersTips:
Plant this paper-forkwort in a raised bed with sixty percent grit to survive wet UK winters.
Keep watering to a minimum, only dampening the soil when it has dried out completely.
Protect this delicate groundcover from slugs and snails during damp spring nights.
Do not prune this slow grower; just gently clear away fallen autumn leaves by hand.
Grow it alongside potted alpines like sempervivums to match its dry, sunny needs.

items.name: Paronychia drummondii
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn in a gritty compost mix, barely covering them to let light trigger germination.
Water only when the top three inches of soil are bone dry, as this plant hates soggy winter roots.
Plant it alongside creeping thyme or sedums in a sunny, raised rockery to ensure excellent drainage.
Protect your plants from winter wet by placing a glass cloche over them during heavy UK rain spells.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your soil before planting to mimic its native sandy habitat.

items.name: Paronychia fastigiata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn using a gritty, free-draining compost mix left outside for winter cold action.
Plant this alpine in a raised bed or rockery to ensure its roots never sit in wet winter UK soil.
Water very sparingly, only during dry summer spells, as this plant thrives on drought-like neglect.
Keep an eye out for slugs in early spring when the delicate green carpet starts its new growth.
Trim the mat lightly in late summer after flowering to keep its prostrate habit neat and compact.

items.name: Paronychia franciscana
items.growersTips:
Plant this tough alpine in a gritty, free-draining raised bed to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly only during dry summer spells, as damp soil will quickly rot its roots.
Tuck it into sunny rock crevices or gravel paths where it can freely spread its low carpet.
Trim the edges in early spring to keep its creeping mats neat and prevent it from overtaking.
Watch out for slugs in damp spring weather, as they love to hide under its dense foliage.

items.name: Paronychia rugelii
items.growersTips:
Plant this dry-loving US native in a raised bed or rockery with fifty percent grit for wet UK winters.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts, as this plant is highly prone to rot in damp British soil.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who love to hide under its low-growing, mat-forming foliage.
Trim the outer edges gently in late spring to keep its neat, carpet-like shape and prevent dieback.
Grow it alongside sedums and sempervivums which share its love for baking sun and sharp drainage.

items.name: Parsonsia
items.growersTips:
Grow Parsonsia capsularis in a sheltered south-facing spot to protect it from harsh UK winter frost.
Water your vine deeply once a week in summer, then let the soil dry out before watering again.
Prune your plant in early spring just as new growth starts to keep its vigorous climbing in check.
Mix plenty of grit and compost into heavy UK clay soil to ensure the roots never sit in winter wet.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse red spider mites if you are growing this climber in a greenhouse.

items.name: Parthenium
items.growersTips:
Sow your seeds indoors in April using a gritty compost to protect them from the damp UK spring.
Keep the soil barely damp to prevent root rot, watering only when the top two inches feel dry.
Wear gloves when handling this plant to protect your skin from its highly irritating sap.
Position your pots in the sunniest spot of your patio to mimic their native warm environment.
Deadhead the fading flowers weekly through summer to stop this aggressive self-seeder spreading.

items.name: Patersonia
items.growersTips:
Plant these Australian native bulbs five centimetres deep in autumn using a very gritty, free-draining soil.
Keep them dry in winter by placing containers under a house pane or in an unheated greenhouse.
Water them thoroughly once a week from April to August, but let the compost dry out between drinks.
Protect the evergreen foliage from harsh UK frosts by wrapping the pots in fleece during January.
Divide the congested clumps right after their late spring flowering to keep them blooming well.

items.name: Patersonia babianoides
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native three inches deep in gritty, sharply draining soil to survive UK wet.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse for the winter.
Water it weekly during its spring growth spurt, but keep it almost bone dry throughout the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring as they love to chew the emerging pleated, iris-like leaves.
Pair it with hardy succulents or alpine gravel plants that won't crowd its sun-loving, low habit.

items.name: Patersonia drummondii
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native in a warm, south-facing gravel bed or a pot to mimic its home soil.
Protect the bulb from wet UK winters by planting in extremely free-draining sandy loam or grit.
Water moderately in spring and summer, but keep the soil almost bone dry during winter dormancy.
Bring potted plants into a frost-free greenhouse or conservatory before the first autumn frost.
Group with hardy succulents like Sedum to create a beautiful, drought-tolerant sunny border.

items.name: Patersonia fragilis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Australian native bulb five centimeters deep in sharply draining, gritty, acidic soil.
Keep it damp in spring but let the soil dry out between waterings during wet UK winter months.
Grow it in a container so you can easily move it into a frost-free greenhouse when winter hits.
