Snip off faded flower stems at the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Grow them alongside hardy sedums in sunny rockeries so they do not get shaded out by bigger plants.

items.name: Pelargonium sidoides
items.growersTips:
Bring this South African beauty indoors before the first frost, as it cannot survive UK winters.
Plant your pelargonium in a gritty, free-draining mix of loam and sharp sand to prevent root rot.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, and keep it completely dry during winter.
Snip off faded dark purple flowers in late summer to encourage a flush of fresh autumn blooms.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which love to eat the roots of container-grown plants.

items.name: Pelargonium tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Bring your peppermint geranium indoors to a sunny windowsill before the first harsh autumn frost.
Water only when the top two inches of soil feel bone dry to prevent root rot in damp UK winters.
Give it plenty of elbow room because its sprawling, velvety stems easily spread over a metre wide.
Take stem cuttings in late summer to guarantee fresh young plants survive the cold winter months.
Plant it in a gritty, free-draining compost mix using terracotta pots to help shed excess rain.

items.name: Pelargonium triste
items.growersTips:
Plant this winter-grower in a gritty, free-draining mix of half John Innes No. 2 and half perlite.
Keep the tuber completely dry in summer, then start watering weekly in autumn when green shoots appear.
Grow your plant in a terracotta pot so you can easily move it indoors to protect from UK winter frosts.
Position it on your sunniest south-facing windowsill or in a heated greenhouse for maximum light.
Gently brush the carrot-like foliage to enjoy the night-scented fragrance of its yellowish flowers.

items.name: Pelargonium vitifolium
items.growersTips:
Bring your balm-scented pelargonium indoors by October to shield it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of compost feel dry to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Prune back leggy stems by half in early March to encourage a bushy habit and fresh lemon scent.
Mix plenty of grit into peat-free compost to ensure the sharp drainage this South African native needs.
Take stem cuttings in August as insurance against winter losses, rooting them on a sunny windowsill.

items.name: Pelargonium zonale
items.growersTips:
Pinch out the growing tips in March to encourage a bushier plant with way more summer blooms.
Water them only when the top two inches of compost feel dry, as they hate soggy roots.
Bring them indoors before the first autumn frost, keeping them on a bright, cool windowsill.
Feed them weekly with high-potash tomato food from June to September for non-stop flowers.
Snip off faded flower stems at the base to prevent botrytis mould in our damp UK summers.

items.name: Pelexia
items.growersTips:
Grow this terrestrial orchid in a free-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and leaf mould.
Keep it in a bright spot out of direct UK sun to prevent those gorgeous leaves from scorching.
Water with rainwater when the top inch of compost dries, keeping it barely damp through winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails during humid spells, as they love to feast on the tender new shoots.
Maintain a cosy indoor or heated greenhouse temperature above twelve degrees during chilly winters.

items.name: Pellaea
items.growersTips:
Bring your button fern indoors for winter as most Pellaea species cannot survive a wet UK frost.
Plant Pellaea in a shallow terracotta pot using a gritty, free-draining peat-free compost mix.
Water only when the top half of the soil is dry, as these ferns hate soggy British winters.
Snip off dead, dry fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, neat green growth.
Keep a close eye out for scale insects hiding on the undersides of the leathery leaflets.

items.name: Pellaea andromedifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant this coffee fern in extremely well-drained, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters.
Position it in a sheltered, partially shaded rockery or a dry stone wall to mimic its wild home.
Water sparingly once established, letting the compost dry out completely between soakings.
Protect the fronds from heavy winter wet by placing a glass cloche over the crown from November.
Grow it alongside hardy succulents or sedums that share its love for dry, sunny crevices.

items.name: Pellaea brachyptera
items.growersTips:
Plant this Sierra cliff-brake in gritty, alkaline soil with lots of limestone chippings for drainage.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this fern hates wet winter feet in the UK.
Tuck it into a south-facing rockery crevice to mimic its dry, sunny native mountain habitat.
Protect the crown from heavy UK winter wet by placing a slate pane over it from November to March.
Prune away the old, dry fronds in early spring just as the new fiddleheads begin to unfurl.

items.name: Pellaea breweri
items.growersTips:
Plant this Brewer's cliffbrake in gritty limestone scree or a rock crevice to mimic its alpine home.
Water it sparingly from below, letting the gritty soil dry out completely between sparse waterings.
Protect this hardy fern from wet winter rot by planting it on a slope or under a rain-shadow ledge.
Watch out for slugs and snails hiding in its tight crown, especially during damp UK spring nights.
Give it a position in partial shade, mimicking the cool mountain crevices of its native habitat.

items.name: Pellaea bridgesii
items.growersTips:
Plant this cliff-dwelling fern in gritty, sharply draining neutral to acid soil to mimic its home.
Water sparingly only when the top few inches of soil are dry, as it hates wet winter feet in the UK.
Grow it in a terracotta pot so you can move it under a porch to shield it from heavy winter rain.
Tuck it into a sheltered rock garden crevice or scree bed facing north or east to avoid midday sun.
Snip off any dead, shrivelled fronds in mid-spring just as the new fiddleheads begin to unfurl.

items.name: Pellaea calidirupium
items.growersTips:
Plant this fern in gritty, alkaline soil mixed with limestone chippings to mimic its native rocks.
Keep it in a container so you can bring it inside to a frost-free greenhouse during wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of grit are dry, as this species hates having soggy roots.
Position your pot in a sheltered, partially shaded spot that mimics a cool, rocky crevice.
Gently snip away any brown, dead fronds at the base in early spring to encourage fresh new growth.

items.name: Pellaea calomelanos
items.growersTips:
Plant this cliff-dwelling fern in gritty, sharply draining alkaline soil to mimic its rocky home.
Water sparingly from below only when the top few inches of soil are dry to prevent crown rot.
Keep it in a container so you can bring it indoors to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Position it in bright, indirect light rather than deep shade to keep its blue-green fronds vibrant.
Snip off old, dead fronds at the base in early spring just as the fresh new growth begins to emerge.

items.name: Pellaea falcata
items.growersTips:
Bring your sickle fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive a wet UK frost below minus five.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy by watering from the base only when the top inch feels dry.
Mix plenty of grit and leaf mould into your peat-free compost to mimic its rocky woodland home.
Tuck it into a shady north-facing border or cool bathroom away from drying radiator draughts.
Snip away the old tattered fronds right at the base in early spring to make way for fresh growth.

items.name: Pellaea glabella
items.growersTips:
Plant this limestone-loving fern in alkaline gritty soil with crushed oyster shells or chalk mixed in.
Nestle it into a dry stone wall or rockery crevice where winter rain drains away instantly from roots.
Water it only during prolonged dry spells in summer as this hardy fern hates soggy British winters.
Snip off the old dead fronds in mid spring just as the fresh new fiddleheads begin to unfurl.
Keep an eye out for slugs and snails who love hiding in the damp crevices around its crown.

items.name: Pellaea mucronata
items.growersTips:
Plant this cliff-brake fern in a gritty, free-draining rockery to survive wet UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry, as this species hates soggy roots.
Keep it safe from harsh winter frosts by planting it next to a warm, south-facing stone wall.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit and leaf mould into your soil to mimic its native crevices.
Snip away dead, brown fronds in early spring to make room for fresh, bright green growth.

items.name: Pellaea nana
items.growersTips:
Grow this tender fern in a pot so you can easily move it indoors before the first autumn UK frosts.
Keep the compost damp but never soggy, watering only when the top inch of soil feels dry to touch.
Mix plenty of grit and leaf mould into peat-free compost to mimic its rocky, well-draining home.
Place your pot in bright, indirect light like a north or east windowsill to prevent leaf scorch.
Snip off any dead or tatty fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, tidy new growth.

items.name: Pellaea paradoxa
items.growersTips:
Plant this fern in a gritty, alkaline soil mix using crushed limestone to mimic its natural habitat.
Keep it in a container so you can easily move it indoors to protect it from wet, freezing UK winters.
Water only when the top two inches of soil dry out, as this hardy species hates soggy roots in winter.
Position your pot in dappled shade or a bright bathroom to give it the high humidity it loves.
Snip off any tatty, brown fronds right at the base in early spring to encourage fresh, tidy growth.

items.name: Pellaea rotundifolia
items.growersTips:
Bring your button fern indoors for winter as it cannot survive UK frosts below five degrees.
Water only when the top inch of soil dries out to prevent root rot in our damp climate.
Blend peat-free compost with plenty of grit and perlite to ensure the sharp drainage it loves.
Keep it in a draught-free room with bright, indirect light away from harsh afternoon sun.
Snip off faded, dry fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, tidy new growth.

items.name: Pellaea truncata
items.growersTips:
Plant this cliff-brake in gritty, alkaline soil using crushed limestone to mimic its rocky home.
Keep it in a terracotta pot so the roots dry out quickly between your light watering sessions.
Position your pot in a bright, draft-free spot indoors or a very sheltered, dry gravel bed outside.
Watch out for winter wet rather than cold, as damp soil will quickly rot this desert fern's roots.
Snip away any dead, shrivelled fronds right at the base in early spring to encourage fresh growth.

items.name: Pellaea viridis
items.growersTips:
Bring your green cliff brake indoors for winter as it cannot survive a wet UK frost below five degrees.
Grow this fern in a gritty, free-draining peat-free compost mixed with plenty of perlite or sand.
Water only when the top two inches of soil are dry to prevent root rot in our damp British climate.
Position your pot in bright, indirect light like an east-facing windowsill to avoid scorching fronds.
Snip off dead or tatty outer fronds at the very base in spring to encourage fresh, tidy new growth.

items.name: Peltandra
items.growersTips:
Plant your arrow arum in heavy clay soil about fifteen centimetres deep at the edge of a pond.
Keep the soil constantly wet or submerged in up to thirty centimetres of water all year round.
Cut back the dead foliage in late autumn to keep your garden pond looking neat and tidy.
Watch out for water snails damaging the young spring leaves and clear them off by hand.
Divide the thick root clumps in early spring to easily propagate new plants for your pond.

items.name: Peltandra virginica
items.growersTips:
Plant this bog lover in heavy clay soil up to fifteen centimeters deep at the edge of your pond.
Keep it constantly wet by placing it in a shallow UK garden pond margin or a boggy, damp hollow.
Cut back the faded foliage in late autumn to keep your pond tidy and prevent rotting in the water.
Watch out for water snails in spring as they love to munch on the fresh, emerging green shoots.
Grow it alongside native UK marsh marigolds to create a beautiful, contrasting spring display.

items.name: Peltandreae
items.growersTips:
Plant Arrow Arum in heavy clay soil enriched with well-rotted garden compost or organic manure.
Position your planting baskets in shallow pond margins no deeper than fifteen centimeters.
Mulch crowns with a thick layer of straw in late autumn to survive harsh UK winter frosts.
Watch out for water snails feeding on the lush foliage during the damp spring months.
Divide overgrown clumps in early spring just as the first new green shoots begin to emerge.

items.name: Peltoboykinia
items.growersTips:
Plant this woodlander in deep shade under a deciduous canopy to mimic its native forest home.

Divide the creeping rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins to propagate them.

items.name: Peltogyne mexicana
items.growersTips:
Start your Mexican purpleheart seeds indoors in April using a heated propagator to beat the UK chill.
Plant them out in June after the last frost in a south-facing spot to get maximum British sunshine.
Water deeply once a week at the base, letting the top inch of sandy, free-draining soil dry out first.
Sow them alongside French marigolds to keep aphids and whiteflies away from your young plants.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertilizer in July to boost their summer growth.

items.name: Peltogyne purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 1cm depth in peat-free compost to beat the cool UK spring weather.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent damping off in our damp UK climate.
Watch out for slugs and snails on young shoots by using organic wool pellets around the base.
Plant alongside marigolds in sunny borders to deter pests and boost your summer flower display.
Pinch out the growing tips in June to encourage a bushier habit and more flowers before autumn.

items.name: Peltophorum
items.growersTips:
Start your Peltophorum seeds indoors in March using a heated propagator to mimic their native warmth.
Soak the hard seeds in warm water for twenty-four hours before sowing them one centimetre deep.
Grow them in pots of gritty, free-draining compost so you can move them under glass when it rains.
Feed your young plants weekly with a high-potassium liquid fertiliser to boost their summer growth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you are keeping them in a conservatory or greenhouse.

items.name: Peltophorum africanum
items.growersTips:
Bring this African beauty indoors by October to shield its tender roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds in spring after soaking them in warm water for 24 hours to help break their tough dormancy.
Mix plenty of grit into your multi-purpose compost to ensure the fast drainage this plant craves.
Water deeply only when the top two inches of soil feel dry, keeping it drier during winter months.
Place your potted specimen in your sunniest south-facing spot to mimic its native African warmth.

items.name: Peltophorum dasyrhachis
items.growersTips:
Sow these tropical seeds indoors in early spring using a heated propagator set to twenty degrees.
Grow them in pots of peat-free compost with added grit so you can move them inside before frosts.
Water thoroughly only when the top two inches of soil feel dry to avoid rotting the young roots.
Place your pots in the sunniest, most sheltered spot on your patio to mimic their native warmth.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite when keeping these delicate seedlings under cover in May.

items.name: Peltophorum dubium
items.growersTips:
Bring this tropical annual indoors by October before the first UK frost chills its roots.
Sow seeds in March using a heated propagator kept at twenty-four degrees to kickstart growth.
Feed weekly with a high-potassium liquid seaweed fertilizer once summer flowers begin to bud.
Plant in free-draining sandy loam mixed with grit to prevent winter rot in wet British soils.
Watch out for glasshouse red spider mite if you are growing this specimen under cover in spring.

items.name: Peltophorum pterocarpum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in early spring at a depth of one inch, using a heated propagator to mimic the heat.
Water your potted copperpod deeply once a week, letting the free-draining sandy soil dry out between.
Keep a sharp eye out for glasshouse spider mites when overwintering this tropical beauty indoors.
Prune back any leggy stems in late summer to encourage a bushier habit before the winter chill.
Repot annually in spring using a mix of peat-free compost, perlite, and grit for ultimate drainage.

items.name: Pennellianthus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Japanese alpine in gritted, acidic soil to mimic its native volcanic scree slopes.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry UK summers, letting the gritty soil dry out between drinks.
Protect the crown from wet winter rot by mulching with a thick layer of slate chippings or gravel.

Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails who love to munch the tender new spring shoots.

items.name: Penstemon
items.growersTips:
Cut back the old stems in mid-spring rather than autumn to protect the crown from harsh UK frosts.
Take softwood cuttings in mid-summer as insurance because some varieties are short-lived in wet mud.
Plant them in free-draining soil with grit to stop their roots rotting in damp British winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving them daily shallow sprinkles.
Deadhead spent flower spikes regularly in July and August to keep fresh blooms coming until autumn.

items.name: Penstemon acaulis
items.growersTips:
Plant this tiny Utah native in a raised scree bed or alpine trough to survive wet UK winters.
Mix equal parts grit and John Innes No. 1 to give its roots the super-sharp drainage it craves.
Protect the low cushions from winter wet with a pane of glass or a cold frame from November.
Water very sparingly only during dry spring spells, then leave it dry once flowering finishes.
Watch out for slugs and snails who love to hide under the dense, ground-hugging evergreen mats.

items.name: Penstemon acuminatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this sand-loving beauty in sharp-draining grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winter rot.
Keep watering minimal once established, only soaking them during prolonged dry summer spells.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Leave the old foliage intact over winter to protect the crown from harsh UK frosts, pruning in spring.
Take softwood cuttings in midsummer to propagate new plants as this species can be short-lived here.

items.name: Penstemon alamosensis
items.growersTips:
Plant this New Mexico native in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs.
Cut back the spent flowering spikes in late autumn to keep the plant tidy and prevent self-seeding.
Water deeply but infrequently during dry summer spells, allowing the soil to dry out completely.
Grow it alongside hardy rosemary or lavender to match its love for poor, alkaline UK soils.
Protect the crown with a dry mulch of grit in November to guard against wet British winter rot.

items.name: Penstemon albidus
items.growersTips:
Plant this white beardtongue in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet British winters.
Cut the spent flower spikes back to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Avoid winter wet by planting them in raised beds or containers filled with a gritty compost mix.
Leave the old foliage intact over winter to protect the crown from harsh UK frosts, pruning in spring.
Propagate your plants by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to ensure backup against cold damp.

items.name: Penstemon albomarginatus
items.growersTips:
Grow this rare Mojave native in a raised bed of pure grit and sand to survive wet UK winters.
Sow seeds in autumn and leave the pot outdoors to get the winter chill needed to trigger growth.
Place your pot against a south-facing wall to mimic the baking desert heat this plant craves.
Water only during dry spells in summer, then keep the soil completely dry throughout the winter.
Watch out for slugs and snails in spring, as they love to eat the tender new desert shoots.

items.name: Penstemon alluviorum
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in rich, damp soil near a pond edge to mimic its native wetland habitat.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry UK summers, as this species hates drying out completely.
Leave the faded flower stems intact over winter to protect the crown from harsh British frosts.
Cut the old stems back to the ground in April once you see fresh new shoots starting to emerge.
Propagate your plants by taking softwood cuttings in early summer to ensure you have backup stock.

items.name: Penstemon ambiguus
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink-flowered beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winter root rot.
Position in your hottest, most south-facing border to mimic its native dry desert sun.
Leave the old woody stems intact over winter to protect the crown from harsh UK frosts.
Prune back hard to new growth in mid-spring once the risk of severe frost has passed.
Propagate via softwood cuttings in midsummer as this species can be short-lived in the UK.

items.name: Penstemon anguineus
items.growersTips:
Plant your Siskiyou beardtongue in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Cut back the faded flowering stems in late autumn to encourage a healthy, bushy habit next spring.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp UK Mays.
Water newly planted divisions deeply once a week until established, then let the soil dry out.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn so the natural UK winter chill can break their dormancy.

items.name: Penstemon angustifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant this broad-leaved beardtongue in extremely gritty, sharp-draining soil to survive wet winters.
Avoid organic mulches and use gravel around the crown to prevent winter rot in damp UK climates.
Water deeply only during prolonged dry summer spells as this species is highly drought-tolerant.
Cut back the faded flower stems in late spring rather than autumn to protect the crown from frost.
Grow it alongside companion plants like hardy thymes or sedums that share its love for poor soil.

items.name: Penstemon arenicola
items.growersTips:
Give this sandy-soil lover sharp drainage by mixing plenty of grit into your UK garden planting hole.
Keep watering to a minimum once established, letting the soil dry out completely between splashes.
Protect its crown from wet UK winters by mulching with gravel rather than damp-holding compost.
Prune back the old stems in late spring rather than autumn to protect new shoots from hard frosts.
Plant it alongside sea thrift or lavender to create a gorgeous, drought-tolerant sunny border.

items.name: Penstemon arkansanus
items.growersTips:
Plant this Arkansas native in sharply draining, gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position it in full sun, but give it light afternoon shade if you live in the hot south of England.
Water young plants weekly during their first dry UK summer, then leave them to be quite drought-hardy.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in late summer to encourage a tidy, leafy winter rosette.
Watch out for slugs and snails on the fresh spring shoots, using organic grit barriers to stop them.

items.name: Penstemon attenuatus
items.growersTips:
Plant this sulphur penstemon in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position it in full sun or light dappled shade to mimic its native open woodland habitat perfectly.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers, but let established clumps dry out between drinks.
Cut the faded yellow flower stems back to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Grow it alongside blue salvias or hardy geraniums for a gorgeous, pollinator-friendly colour contrast.

items.name: Penstemon auriberbis
items.growersTips:
Plant this Colorado native in your sunniest spot using grit-heavy soil to survive wet UK winters.
Avoid rich fertilizers and heavy compost as this wild beauty thrives on starvation-level soils.
Water deeply only during dry summer spells, keeping the crown completely dry to prevent rot.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in late summer to help the plant conserve its energy.
Protect the evergreen foliage from soggy winter slush by placing a cloche over it from November.

items.name: Penstemon azureus
items.growersTips:
Plant this blue beauty in sharply draining, gritty soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK climates.
Give it a sunny south-facing spot and water only weekly during dry spells once it is established.
Cut the faded flowering stems back to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Leave the old foliage intact over winter to protect the crown, then prune it hard in mid-spring.
Grow it alongside silver-leaved Mediterranean herbs like thyme or lavender which love the same soil.

items.name: Penstemon barbatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass, barely covering with compost, for blooms the next year.
Cut spent flower spikes back to the base in August to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps every three years in April to maintain plant vigour and flower quality.

items.name: Penstemon barrettiae
items.growersTips:
Plant this evergreen beauty in a raised bed or gravel garden to guarantee the sharp drainage it needs.
Give it a sunny, south-facing spot to mimic its native gorge habitat and survive wet UK winters.
Avoid rich soil and fertilisers, as too many nutrients will make your plant floppy and short-lived.

items.name: Penstemon bicolor
items.growersTips:
Plant this Mojave native in a raised bed or gravel garden to ensure the sharp winter drainage it needs.
Mix plenty of horticultural grit into your soil to mimic its natural gritty, alkaline habitat.

items.description: Penstemon bicolor is a species of penstemon known by the common name pinto penstemon. It is native to the desert mountains and valleys of southern Nevada, eastern California, and western Arizona, where it grows in scrub, woodland, and other local habitat. It is a perennial herb which may exceed one meter in maximum height.

items.name: Penstemon brevisepalus
items.growersTips:
Plant this short-sepalled beauty in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet British winters.
Give it a weekly deep soak during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out fully between waterings.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in August to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Leave the old foliage intact over winter to shield the crown from hard frosts, then tidy in April.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots by using organic wool pellets around the base of the plant.

items.name: Penstemon californicus
items.growersTips:
Plant this California native in your sunniest spot with sharp grit to survive wet UK winters.
Water sparingly once established, letting the soil dry out completely between drenches in summer.
Prune back the woody stems by half in late spring, only after the last UK frosts have passed.
Protect young plants from slugs and snails in spring using beer traps or physical barriers.

items.description: Penstemon californicus is a species of penstemon known by the common name California penstemon. It is native to the Mexican state of Baja California but is also found in a few places in the American state of California. It grows in the forest and woodland habitat of the Peninsular Ranges and nearby slopes.

items.name: Penstemon calycosus
items.growersTips:
Plant this calycosus at the same depth as its pot in free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, but let the soil dry out completely between sessions.
Cut the faded flower stems back to the base in autumn to encourage a second flush of foliage.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with beer traps or copper tape.
Divide established clumps every three years in spring to keep them vigorous and flowering well.

items.name: Penstemon canescens
items.growersTips:
Plant this eastern US native in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Sow the seeds in cold frames during autumn so they get the winter chill they need to germinate.
Leave the faded stems intact over winter to protect the crown from severe UK frosts, pruning in May.
Grow it alongside native UK wildflowers like wild marjoram to create a magnet for local bumblebees.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells, but let the soil dry out completely between times.

items.name: Penstemon cardinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant this scarlet beauty in sharp-draining grit to help it survive wet, cold UK winters.
Cut the faded flower spikes down to the base in late summer to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Avoid rich soil and heavy manure, as this plant thrives best in poor, alkaline to neutral earth.
Leave the old foliage on over winter to protect the crown from frost, then prune back in April.
Take softwood cuttings in early summer to easily propagate and back up your plants against hard frost.

items.name: Penstemon centranthifolius
items.growersTips:
Plant scarlet bugler in a raised bed with lots of grit to survive wet British winters.
Cut back the spent flower spikes in autumn to encourage a second flush of those red tubes.

Keep a sharp eye out for slugs and snails from March onwards, using beer traps or organic pellets.
Plant June in rich, moisture-retentive soil with plenty of compost, keeping the crown at soil level.
Divide your established clumps in early spring just as the new shoots start poking through the soil.
items.description: Blue-edged gold heart.

items.name: Hydrangea 'Annabelle'
items.growersTips:
Prune your Annabelle hard in March down to about thirty centimetres to get those massive blooms.
Push sturdy hazel branches into the soil around the base in spring to support the heavy flower heads.
Plant her in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade to stop those delicate petals scorching.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil when planting to keep her thirsty roots happy.
Mulch generously in April with leaf mould to lock in that crucial British spring moisture.
items.description: Huge white mophead.

items.name: Hydrangea 'Endless Summer'
items.growersTips:
Feed them in spring with ericaceous fertiliser if you want blue blooms in our UK clay soils.
Prune only the dead wood in April, leaving new stems to produce those lovely repeat summer flowers.
Water them deeply twice a week during dry spells, especially if planted in sandy southern soils.
Plant them in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the leaves from scorching.
Mulch with leaf mould in November to protect the crown from wet, freezing British winter weather.
items.description: Reblooming blue/pink.

items.name: Hydrangea 'Nikko Blue'
items.growersTips:
Keep your soil acidic with sulfate of iron or ericaceous compost to stop those blue petals turning pink.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry UK summers, as these big leaves get thirsty very fast.
Prune in late spring after the last frosts, cutting back to the first pair of strong, healthy buds.
Leave the faded flowerheads on all winter to protect the delicate new spring buds from harsh frosts.
Plant in dappled shade to stop the midday sun from scorching those beautiful blue summer blooms.
items.description: Classic blue mophead in acid soil.

items.name: Hydrangea 'Pia'
items.growersTips:
Pia is a dwarf shrub so plant it in a pot or at the front of a border so it does not get shaded out.
Keep your soil neutral to alkaline with garden lime if you want to preserve its natural pink colour.
Prune in late spring by cutting back dead stems to a strong pair of buds just as new growth starts.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry UK summers to keep its shallow roots from drying out.
Protect the early spring buds from late frosts with fleece to ensure you do not lose summer blooms.
items.description: Dwarf pink mophead.

items.name: Helleborus 'Double Ellen Red'
items.growersTips:
Snip off old leaves in late January so the gorgeous double red blooms can be seen clearly.
Mulch with leaf mould in autumn to mimic their native woodland soil and boost spring flowering.
Plant with the crown just level with the soil surface to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Position in dappled shade under deciduous shrubs to protect those dark red petals from scorching.
Watch out for hellebore black spot in damp weather and remove affected foliage immediately.
items.description: Double dark-red blooms.

items.name: Helleborus 'Pretty Ellen Pink'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in moist, well-drained soil enriched with plenty of well-rotted leaf mould.
Snip off the old leathery leaves in late winter to show off those lovely nodding pink blooms.
Watch out for black spot disease and quickly remove infected foliage to keep the plant healthy.
Water your new division deeply during dry summer spells while it establishes its deep roots.
Plant them alongside snowdrops and hostas for a gorgeous, shade-loving woodland display.
items.description: Double soft pink.

items.name: Helleborus 'Anna's Red'
items.growersTips:
Snip off the old leathery leaves in late January so those gorgeous magenta-red blooms can shine.
Plant the crown exactly level with the soil in rich, heavy clay that stays damp but never sodden.
Mulch them every autumn with well-rotted leaf mould to mimic their favourite British woodland soil.
Watch out for black spot disease on leaves and quickly burn any affected foliage to stop it spreading.
Position them next to snowdrops or gold-leaved hostas for a stunning shade-loving colour contrast.
items.description: Marbled foliage, wine-red blooms.

items.name: Echinacea 'Magnus'
items.growersTips:
Plant Magnus in well-drained soil with the crown level with the surface to prevent winter wet rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than light daily sprinkles to build deep roots.
Leave the gorgeous dark seedheads standing all winter to feed goldfinches and add frosty structure.
Watch out for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots using beer traps or organic pellets.
Divide your established clumps every three years in spring to keep the pink blooms large and vigorous.
items.description: Reliable purple coneflower.

items.name: Echinacea 'White Swan'
items.growersTips:
Plant this perennial in spring at crown level in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Leave the gorgeous cone seedheads on all winter to feed goldfinches and add lovely frost structure.
Protect the tender new spring shoots from hungry slugs using beer traps or organic copper tape.
Divide your clumps every three years in early spring to keep the white blooms vigorous and healthy.
items.description: Crisp white coneflower.

items.name: Echinacea 'Cheyenne Spirit'
items.growersTips:
Plant this short-lived perennial in spring, barely covering the root ball in gritty, free-draining soil.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers, letting the soil dry out fully between soakings.
Leave the faded autumn flower heads intact to feed local goldfinches and protect the crown from frost.
Snails love the young spring shoots, so protect them early with organic wool pellets or beer traps.
Divide the clumps every three years in spring to keep the mixed red, orange and yellow blooms vivid.
items.description: Mixed warm shades, seed-grown.

items.name: Echinacea 'Green Envy'
items.growersTips:
Plant these unique green coneflowers in full sun and rich, well-draining soil to boost their color.
Water them deeply once a week during dry UK summers, keeping the crown dry to prevent winter rot.
Watch out for slugs and snails chewing the young spring shoots, so protect them with grit barriers.
Leave the faded flower heads on over winter to feed goldfinches and provide structural frost beauty.
Divide the clumps every three years in spring to keep your plants vigorous and flowering well.
items.description: Unusual green-petalled cultivar.

items.name: Geranium 'Rozanne'
items.growersTips:
Give Rozanne plenty of room to scramble because she easily spreads over a metre wide by late summer.
Chop her back to the ground in August if she looks scruffy to get a fresh flush of autumn flowers.
Plant her in moisture-retentive UK clay improved with grit so she does not dry out or get soggy.
Divide your clumps in spring every three years to keep her vigorous and get free plants for free.
Grow her alongside yellow roses or orange geums for a stunning, long-lasting colour contrast.
items.description: Long-blooming violet-blue cranesbill.

items.name: Geranium 'Johnson's Blue'
items.growersTips:
Chop the whole plant down to the ground after the first summer flowering to get fresh new blue blooms
Give it space to sprawl in a sunny front border because it tends to flop over its neighbours
Divide the root clump every three years in early spring to keep this vigorous grower full of energy
Plant the crown level with the soil in well-drained loam to prevent winter wet from rotting roots
Watch out for sawfly larvae eating holes in the leaves during damp British spring weather
items.description: Classic mid-blue hardy geranium.

items.name: Geranium 'Ann Folkard'
items.growersTips:
Give this scrambler plenty of room to weave through sturdy neighbors like rose bushes or shrubs.
Tuck it into well-drained soil in full sun to get those chartreuse leaves looking their brightest.
Cut the whole plant back to the ground after the first flush of flowers to get fresh new growth.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots if you are growing this beauty in patio pots.
Propagate your plant by taking root cuttings in late autumn once the top growth has died back.
items.description: Magenta with gold foliage.

items.name: Clematis 'Nelly Moser'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in partial shade to stop those gorgeous pink striped flowers from fading in the sun.
Bury the root ball deep, about six inches below the soil level, to protect it from clematis wilt.
Give it a light trim in late winter and another right after the first big flush of spring blooms.
Keep its roots cool and damp by planting low shrubs or placing a few heavy flat stones over the base.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, and water deeply during dry UK spells to prevent wilt.
items.description: Pale pink with darker bar.

items.name: Clematis 'The President'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty deep with the crown five centimetres below soil level to prevent clematis wilt.
As a Group Two clematis, just prune it lightly in late February and again after its June bloom.
Keep its roots cool in hot UK summers by planting low-growing companion cranesbills at its base.
Feed it weekly with tomato fertiliser from April to keep those huge purple blooms coming.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using organic wool pellets to protect the new growth.
items.description: Rich purple, free-flowering.

items.name: Clematis 'Niobe'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Niobe deep with the root ball five inches down to protect it from devastating clematis wilt.
Feed your plant weekly in spring with tomato food to boost those stunning deep ruby-red UK blooms.
Prune hard in February by cutting all stems back to strong buds about thirty centimetres above ground.
Give Niobe shady roots and sunny shoots by planting low shrubs to shade the base from midday UK sun.
Keep a sharp eye out for slugs in damp UK springs as they absolutely love the tender new Niobe shoots.
items.description: Deep ruby red.

items.name: Camellia 'Adolphe Audusson'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in acidic soil with the root flare just visible above the ground to avoid rot.
Water thoroughly with stored rainwater during summer to ensure those gorgeous red buds set for spring.
Protect the early spring blooms from harsh morning sun by planting it in a sheltered westerly spot.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring before the new season buds start to form.
Drench with a liquid sequestered iron tonic in spring to keep the glossy evergreen leaves deep green.
items.description: Semi-double red, classic mid-season.

items.name: Camellia 'Bob Hope'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Bob Hope in ericaceous compost as it hates alkaline soil and needs that acidic boost.
Give it rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil acidic and prevent its leaves yellowing.
Protect the early spring buds from cold morning sun by planting it in a sheltered westerly spot.
Prune your shrub immediately after flowering in late spring before it starts setting next year's buds.
Mulch with pine needles or bark in autumn to protect its shallow roots from harsh UK winter frosts.
items.description: Deep red double, late.

items.name: Camellia 'Pink Perfection'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in acidic soil or use ericaceous compost in a pot to prevent yellowing leaves.
Protect the delicate buds from freezing east winds and morning sun by planting near a west wall.
Water thoroughly with rain water during August and September when next spring's buds are forming.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in spring before the new growth buds start to swell.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots if you are growing this one in a patio container.
items.description: Formal double pink.

items.name: Buxus 'Suffruticosa'
items.growersTips:
Plant this dwarf boxwood at the same depth it was in its pot to prevent stem rot in damp UK soil.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells, keeping the leaves dry to prevent box blight.
Trim your plants once a year in late August to avoid soft new growth getting damaged by autumn frost.
Watch out for box tree moth caterpillars from April to October and clear them off your plants fast.
Mix plenty of well-rotted grit and compost into heavy clay soil to give the roots the drainage they need.
items.description: Dwarf box for low edging.

items.name: Buxus 'Elegantissima'
items.growersTips:
Give this lovely variegated box a shallow planting depth to keep its root flare just above the soil.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers, focusing on the base to keep the white-edged leaves dry.
Prune in late August after the main growth flush to avoid frost damage on the delicate new foliage.
Watch out for box moth caterpillars by checking the dense variegated leaves weekly from April onwards.
Feed in spring with a handful of seaweed meal to keep those beautiful creamy-white margins bright.
items.description: Variegated cream margins.

items.name: Magnolia 'Exmouth'
items.growersTips:
Plant this grandiflora in a sheltered south or west facing spot to protect the buds from frost.
Add plenty of leaf mould to your neutral-to-acid soil when planting to mimic its native woodland.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to stop those huge, glossy evergreen leaves from dropping.
Prune your Exmouth in spring just as new growth starts if you need to shape it or remove frost damage.
Watch out for scale insects on the undersides of those large leaves and wipe them off with soapy water.
items.description: Hardy English-grown evergreen magnolia.

items.name: Magnolia 'Goliath'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in a warm, sheltered spot against a south-facing wall to protect from cold UK winds.
Water your young tree deeply every week during dry summer spells until its roots are well established.
Prune lightly in mid-spring to shape it and remove any unsightly winter frost damage from the leaves.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to keep the soil acidic and lock in vital moisture.
Watch out for scale insects on the stems, gently wiping them off with a damp cloth if you spot them.
items.description: Huge waxy white blooms.

items.name: Dianthus 'Doris'
items.growersTips:
Pop your Doris in a spot with gritty, alkaline soil as she hates wet winter feet in soggy UK clay.
Give her a good haircut by chopping spent flower stems right to the base in August for a second flush.
Water only when the top inch of soil is bone dry, as this pink thrives on neglect once established.
Take easy heel cuttings in July to propagate new free plants and keep your stock young and vigorous.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with gravel barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Salmon-pink pink with darker eye.

items.name: Dianthus 'Mrs Sinkins'
items.growersTips:
Pop this historic pink in sharp-draining, gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in damp UK wet.
Plant her shallowly with the crown just above the soil line to stop the stems from rotting away.
Deadhead spent blooms regularly in summer to encourage a second flush of those clove-scented flowers.
Support her heavy, split-calyx blooms with subtle twiggy pea sticks before the summer rains hit.
Take cuttings in summer to replace the parent plant, as she gets woody and tired after three years.
items.description: Fragrant white pink.

items.name: Malus 'Bramley's Seedling'
items.growersTips:
You need to plant a different apple nearby because Bramley is sterile and cannot pollinate itself.
Prune your Bramley in winter to keep its vigorous, spreading branches from taking over your garden.
Thin out the young fruits in July so the remaining apples grow huge and do not break the branches.
Mulch well in spring to help the roots retain moisture in our increasingly dry UK summers.
Watch out for apple scab during wet springs by clearing away fallen leaves to stop the fungus.
items.description: Classic cooking apple, sharp and tart.

items.name: Malus 'Cox's Orange Pippin'
items.growersTips:
Plant this fussy cultivar in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the delicate blossoms from UK frosts.
Mulch yearly with well-rotted manure to feed its hungry roots and keep the soil moist but free-draining.
Prune in winter to open up the canopy, which improves air circulation and prevents apple scab disease.
Thin out the young fruits in July to avoid biennial bearing and ensure you get large, juicy apples.
Keep a watchful eye out for woolly aphid and canker, as Cox is sadly very susceptible to both in the UK.
items.description: Aromatic dessert apple, late September.

items.name: Malus 'Egremont Russet'
items.growersTips:
Mulch the base in late winter with well-rotted manure to keep its preferred moist soil from drying.
Prune in January to keep its upright spur-bearing habit open and prevent congested fruit clusters.
Thin out the tiny developing apples in July to avoid biennial bearing and get larger russet crops.
Watch for bitter pit by spraying calcium in summer, as this cultivar is quite prone to the disease.
Plant with a pollination partner like Cox or Discovery nearby since it is not fully self-fertile.
items.description: Nutty russet dessert apple.

items.name: Malus 'Discovery'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early-fruiting apple in full sun to keep its skin bright red and sweeten the flesh.
Mulch well in spring to help the shallow roots retain moisture during dry UK summer spells.
Prune in winter, focusing on thinning the canopy to let light in and prevent scab in damp weather.
Pick the apples in August as soon as they turn red, because Discovery does not keep well at all.
Grow it near a pollination partner like Cox or Scrumptious to ensure you get a bumper crop.
items.description: Crisp early dessert apple.

items.name: Malus 'Gala'
items.growersTips:
Plant Gala in full sun and well-drained soil, keeping the graft union 10cm above the ground level.
Water your young tree deeply once a week during dry UK summers to help those sweet fruits swell.
Prune in winter when dormant, thinning the centre to let light in and prevent scab in damp UK weather.
Watch out for aphids and apple scab; space your branches well to keep the air flowing freely.
Grow Gala near a pollination partner like Scrumptious or Self-Fertile Cox to get a bumper crop.
items.description: Sweet red-striped dessert apple.

items.name: Malus 'Worcester Pearmain'
items.growersTips:
Plant this classic UK apple in a sunny, sheltered spot to help its sweet strawberry flavour develop.
Prune in late summer rather than winter because this lovely traditional variety is a partial tip-bearer.
Keep an eye out for apple scab during wet British springs, and clear away fallen leaves to stop it.
Water deeply every week during dry summer spells while the delicious red fruits are swelling up.
Grow near a pollination partner like Cox or James Grieve to guarantee a bumper crop of autumn apples.
items.description: Strawberry-scented red apple.

items.name: Malus 'Russet'
items.growersTips:
Plant this bare-root in late autumn so its roots settle before the damp UK winter frost sets in.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the soil moist during dry British summer spells.
Prune in January to open up the center, which prevents scab in our notoriously damp UK climate.
Watch out for codling moth traps in May to protect the unique, rough skin from tunneling larvae.
Grow near a pollination partner like 'Cox's Orange Pippin' to ensure a heavy harvest of russets.
items.description: Rough-skinned heritage dessert apple.

items.name: Malus 'James Grieve'
items.growersTips:
Plant this dual-purpose apple in a sunny spot with moist, well-drained soil to boost its juicy crop.
Prune in winter, focusing on thinning congested branches to let light reach the ripening fruit.
Watch out for apple scab in damp UK springs, clearing fallen leaves away to stop the fungus.
Mulch with garden compost in spring to keep the roots cool and damp during dry summer spells.
Since it is self-sterile, plant a Scrumptious apple nearby to ensure successful pollination.
items.description: Dual-purpose dessert/cooking apple.

items.name: Malus 'Howgate Wonder'
items.growersTips:
Plant your tree with the graft union sitting at least ten centimetres clear of the damp UK soil.
Give this heavy cropper a sturdy stake and tie to support the massive weight of its cooking apples.
Prune in late winter by thinning out congested branches to let the weak British summer sun ripen fruit.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells while the young tree is establishing its roots.
Thin out the tiny developing fruits in July so the remaining apples can grow to their giant size.
items.description: Heavy cropping cooking apple.

items.name: Fragaria 'Cambridge Favourite'
items.growersTips:
Plant Cambridge Favourite in autumn so its roots settle before the damp UK winter frost sets in.
Keep the crown level with the soil surface when planting to prevent rot in our wet British climate.
Tuck dry straw under the leaves in May to stop the heavy berries touching damp soil and rotting.
Net your plants in June because UK blackbirds love these bright red, sweet berries as much as we do.
Cut back all the old foliage to five centimetres after fruiting to stop mildew in damp autumns.
items.description: Reliable mid-season strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Honeoye'
items.growersTips:
Plant Honeoye in autumn so the roots settle in before the damp UK winter, keeping the crown at soil level.
Water the base deeply when the green berries swell, but avoid wetting the leaves to prevent grey mould.
Tuck clean barley straw under the trusses in May to lift your ripening berries off the damp soil.
Snip off the runners as they appear in summer to keep the mother plant focused on next year's fruit.
Watch out for slugs during wet British Junes, using beer traps or wool pellets around your plants.
items.description: Early heavy-cropping strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Florence'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-season beauty in spring with the crown sitting exactly level with the soil surface.
Keep soil moist but not soggy from flowering until harvest to get those huge, juicy late-July crops.
Throw a net over your patch by mid-June to stop greedy UK blackbirds from stealing the ripening fruit.
Cut back all the old foliage in autumn to keep next year's crop safe from nasty crown rot diseases.
Tuck some straw under the trusses in June to keep your heavy berries clean and safe from damp soil.
items.description: Late-season strawberry, disease resistant.

items.name: Fragaria 'Mara des Bois'
items.growersTips:
Plant crown level with the soil in spring; burying it too deep will rot this alpine-crossed gem.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to keep those gourmet berries juicy.
Snip off the first flush of spring flowers to boost your autumn harvest of intensely fragrant fruit.
Tuck straw under the leaves in May to stop damp British soil from rotting the low-hanging berries.
Watch out for slugs during wet spells and protect the ripening red fruits with fine netting from birds.
items.description: Wild-strawberry-flavoured everbearer.

items.name: Fragaria 'Symphony'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-season Scottish star in raised beds to protect its heavy summer crop from damp soil.
Give the roots a weekly deep drench at their base during dry spells, keeping the leaves bone dry.
Tuck straw under the trusses in May to keep these heavy, juicy berries off wet British mud.
Snip off the runners as soon as they appear to keep all the plant's energy in fruit production.
Net the plants securely in June before the local blackbirds spot those bright red berries ripening.
items.description: Late summer strawberry, large fruits.

items.name: Fragaria 'Pegasus'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-summer star in UK soil enriched with well-rotted manure to boost its heavy crop.
Space your Pegasus crowns at soil level, exactly 45cm apart, so wet British summers do not rot them.
Tuck straw under the leaves in May to keep these juicy, soft berries off damp UK soil and stop rot.
Water Pegasus deeply at the base during dry spells, keeping moisture off the leaves to avoid mildew.
Cut back all runners in autumn to keep this compact plant focused on producing next year's fruit.
items.description: Mid-season strawberry, resistant to mildew.

items.name: Solanum 'Gardener's Delight'
items.growersTips:
Plant this cordon type deep in the soil up to its first leaves in May after the last frosts pass.
Pinch out the side shoots weekly in summer to keep this vigorous vine focused on its sweet fruit.
Water consistently at the base to prevent the thin skins of these cherry tomatoes from splitting.
Feed weekly with high-potassium liquid seaweed once the first tiny green fruits start to form.
Strip lower leaves in August to let the weak British sun ripen the dense trusses of tomatoes.
items.description: Reliable cordon cherry tomato.

items.name: Solanum 'Sungold'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in mid-March at 6mm deep, keeping them on a warm, bright windowsill at 20C.
Plant them out in late May only after the last frost, choosing your sunniest, most sheltered spot.
Pinch out the side shoots weekly to keep this vigorous, vine-like grower to a single main stem.
Water them consistently at the base to prevent the thin-skinned, sugary orange fruits from splitting.
Pick the cherries when they turn a deep, warm orange rather than yellow for the sweetest flavour.
items.description: Orange cherry tomato, super sweet.

items.name: Solanum 'Black Russian'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March and keep them on a warm, sunny windowsill before planting out in June.
Mix plenty of well-rotted manure into your soil to satisfy this hungry variety's heavy feeding needs.
Water deeply at the base, not the leaves, to prevent blight during wet, humid UK summer spells.
Pinch out the side shoots weekly to keep this vigorous vine focused on ripening its dark fruits.
Stake the heavy main stem early because those large, juicy purple-black tomatoes will weigh it down.
items.description: Dark-fruited heirloom beefsteak.

items.name: Solanum 'San Marzano'
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm March then plant out in a greenhouse or sunny patio spot after May frosts.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food once the first tiny green fruits appear on the trusses.
Keep the soil consistently damp because uneven watering causes blossom end rot in this long variety.
Pinch out the side shoots regularly to keep this vine-like grower trained to a single main stem.
Strip away the lower leaves in late August to let the weak British autumn sun ripen the green fruit.
items.description: Italian plum tomato, ideal for sauce.

items.name: Solanum 'Moneymaker'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 6mm deep, keeping them at 18C on a warm windowsill before May planting.
Plant them deep up to their first leaves in late May to help their roots establish in cooler UK soil.
Pinch out the side shoots weekly and snap off the main growing tip once four fruit trusses form.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, especially during dry UK summer spells.
Watch out for late blight during wet British Augusts and harvest fruits early to ripen indoors.
items.description: Heavy-cropping greenhouse classic.

items.name: Solanum 'Tigerella'
items.growersTips:
Start your Tigerella seeds indoors in warm March to beat the short UK summer and get early fruit.
Plant them deep up to their first leaves in late May to help these tall vines grow strong roots.
These are vigorous cordons, so pinch out the side shoots weekly and tie the main stem to a stake.
Water consistently at the base to prevent the thin, striped skins of Tigerella from splitting.
Feed with high-potassium tomato food once the first tiny green fruits appear to boost your yield.
items.description: Striped red-and-yellow heirloom.

items.name: Solanum 'Brandywine'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March then plant out in a greenhouse or sunny, sheltered spot by late May.
Give these heavy feeders a deep weekly soak at the base to prevent blossom end rot in dry spells.
Prune out all side shoots weekly to keep this vigorous vine to a single stem for better ripening.
Pinch out the main growing tip in late August so the plant focuses on ripening the existing fruit.
Watch out for late blight in wet UK summers and remove any yellowing lower leaves to boost airflow.
items.description: Pink heirloom beefsteak, rich flavour.

items.name: Capsicum 'Bell Boy'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors by mid-March using a heated propagator to beat the cool British spring weather.
Move your plants into their final 23cm pots of peat-free compost once the first flowers appear.
Pinch out the growing tip when plants are 20cm tall to encourage a bushy habit and more peppers.
Water consistently to keep soil damp but not soggy to prevent blossom end rot in your greenhouse.
Support the heavy crop of blocky green fruits with a sturdy bamboo cane before they snap the stems.
items.description: Heavy-cropping bell pepper.

items.name: Capsicum 'Sweet Banana'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short UK summer growing season.
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy to prevent blossom end rot in cool British weather.
Stake these heavy-fruiting plants early so the weight of the long yellow peppers doesn't snap stems.
Pick the first few fruits when yellow to encourage the plant to keep producing more peppers.
Watch out for aphids under the leaves when you move your potted plants into the greenhouse in May.
items.description: Long yellow sweet pepper.

items.name: Capsicum 'Hungarian Hot Wax'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Keep compost damp but never soggy to prevent root rot in our unpredictable British summer weather.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are twenty centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Harvest these chillies when they turn pale yellow for the best mild heat and crunchy texture.
Watch out for aphids under the leaves when moving your pots into a sunny greenhouse or conservatory.
items.description: Mild-to-hot yellow pepper.

items.name: Capsicum 'Cayenne'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors by February in a heated propagator to beat the short, cool UK growing season.
Keep plants in pots on a sunny windowsill or greenhouse, as they rarely thrive in open UK soil.
Water only when the top inch of compost is dry, as soggy British soil leads to fatal root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are twenty centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Feed weekly with high-potash tomato food once the first tiny white flowers begin to show.
items.description: Slim red chilli pepper, dries well.

items.name: Capsicum 'Jalapeño'
items.growersTips:
Start seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to beat the short, cool UK summer season.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are fifteen centimetres tall to encourage a bushier habit.
Water consistently but let the top soil dry out slightly to avoid root rot in damp UK weather.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato food once the first tiny green fruits begin to set.
Harvest some pods green to boost yields, leaving others to turn red for a sweeter, milder heat.
items.description: Classic Mexican mid-hot chilli.

items.name: Brassica 'Calabrese'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April to June at 1.5cm deep, transplanting when they have five true leaves.
Net your plants immediately to stop cabbage white butterflies and pigeons ruining your crop.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkling to encourage deep, strong root systems.
Harvest the main central head while buds are tight to trigger lots of delicious side shoots.
Firm the soil down really well with your boots before planting to prevent wind rock in winter.
items.description: Sprouting broccoli with central head.

items.name: Brassica 'Purple Sprouting'
items.growersTips:
Net your young plants immediately after planting out to stop pigeons and cabbage white butterflies.
Stake these top-heavy plants in autumn to prevent strong UK winter winds from blowing them over.
Give them firm, alkaline soil by treading down the bed before planting to help them form tight spears.
Space them at least sixty centimetres apart because they grow into massive bushes by the spring.
Harvest the central spear first in spring to trigger a massive flush of smaller side shoots.
items.description: Hardy purple-sprouting broccoli.

items.name: Brassica 'Cavolo Nero'
items.growersTips:
Net your plants early to stop the cabbage white butterfly from laying eggs on those lovely dark leaves.
Plant them deep right up to the lowest leaves and firm the soil with your boots to stop wind rock.
Give them a liquid nitrogen feed in late summer to boost that gorgeous deep blue-green leaf growth.
Harvest the lower leaves first from autumn onwards, leaving the crown to keep producing all winter.
Add garden lime to your soil before planting to keep the pH high and ward off nasty clubroot disease.
items.description: Tuscan black kale.

items.name: Brassica 'Red Drumhead'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April in a seedbed then transplant them in June, burying stems up to the first leaves.
Space these big cabbages at least forty-five centimetres apart so they have room to form huge heads.
Tread the soil down firmly before planting because loose soil prevents them from forming tight heads.
Net your crop immediately to keep those pesky cabbage white butterflies and hungry pigeons away.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving them daily light sprinkles.
items.description: Compact red cabbage.

items.name: Daucus 'Nantes 2'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to July at a depth of one centimetre to avoid transplant shock.
Thin seedlings to three centimetres apart on a warm evening to keep the carrot root fly away.
Grow under a fine insect mesh barrier to stop the low-flying carrot root fly from ruining your crop.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage long straight roots to grow down.
Grow them alongside spring onions or rosemary as their strong scent naturally deters flying pests.
items.description: Sweet sweet stump-rooted carrot.

items.name: Daucus 'Autumn King'
items.growersTips:
Sow these seeds directly from April to July at a depth of about one centimetre in stone-free soil.
Sift your soil deeply and avoid manure to stop these long, tapered roots from forking or splitting.
Cover your crop with a fine insect mesh immediately after sowing to block the devastating carrot fly.
Water the soil deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Leave this hardy winter variety in the ground and harvest them fresh right up until next February.
items.description: Heavy long-rooted maincrop.

items.name: Daucus 'Purple Haze'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to July at 1cm deep in stone-free, sandy soil to keep roots straight.
Cover your crop with fine insect mesh immediately after sowing to block the devastating carrot fly.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage those purple roots to grow long.
Sow alongside spring onions or rosemary; their strong scents help confuse searching carrot flies.
Harvest these sweet treats by late autumn before heavy UK frosts turn their purple skins bitter.
items.description: Purple-skinned heritage carrot.

items.name: Daucus 'Paris Market'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to July at just one centimetre deep to avoid disturbing their roots.
Since they are short and round, they grow brilliantly in shallow containers or heavy clay soils.
Water them evenly but sparingly to stop the roots splitting when the unpredictable UK rain arrives.
Sow alongside spring onions or rosemary to mask the scent and deter the pesky carrot rust fly.
Harvest them when they reach golf ball size, as leaving them too long makes them woody and tough.
items.description: Round baby carrot, ideal for shallow soil.

items.name: Lavender
items.growersTips:
Improve heavy UK clay by mixing in grit and planting on a mound to prevent winter root rot.
Prune annually in late August after flowering by cutting back green stems but avoiding old wood.
Water newly planted lavender weekly in dry spells but leave established plants entirely to rain.
Grow alongside rosemary or thyme in full sun to match Mediterranean drainage and watering needs.
Choose Hidcote or Munstead cultivars as they tolerate damp British winters better than French types.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Lavender cultivars.

items.name: Lavender 'Hidcote'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Hidcote in a raised bed or gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Prune your Hidcote in late August by cutting back flowered stems but never into the old bare wood.
Water newly planted Hidcote weekly during its first UK summer, then leave it to thrive on rain.
Add a handful of lime to your planting hole if your UK garden has acidic soil to keep it happy.
Keep Hidcote away from damp, shady walls and plant it in full south-facing sun to prevent splaying.
items.description: Compact dark-purple lavender; classic edging.

items.name: Lavender 'Munstead'
items.growersTips:
Pop this compact beauty in a spot with full sun and incredibly gritty, free-draining soil to thrive.
Only water young plants; once established in our damp UK climate, they hate wet feet and soggy soil.
Prune gently in late August after flowering, cutting back green stems but never into the old wood.
Plant them alongside rosemary or thyme, which love the same dry, sunny conditions in British gardens.
Watch out for rosemary beetles in summer; just hand-pick them off to keep your Munstead healthy.
items.description: Soft-blue early-flowering lavender.

items.name: Lavender 'Loddon Pink'
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink beauty in a raised bed or gritty soil to survive wet UK winters without root rot.
Prune your Loddon Pink in late August right after flowering to keep its compact, mounded shape.
Cut back to just above the woody base, but never prune into old wood or it won't grow back.
Avoid feeding this lavender or watering it once established, as rich soil ruins its pink colour.
Grow it next to rosemary or sage in full sun to create a classic, drought-tolerant UK herb border.
items.description: Soft pink spires.

items.name: Lavender 'Alba'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Alba in free-draining gritty soil to stop UK winter wet from rotting its roots.
Prune right after its white flowers fade in August, cutting back to just above the woody stems.
Water your new Alba weekly until established, then leave it alone to thrive in dry summer spells.
Give this white-flowered beauty maximum sunshine, ideally next to a south-facing brick wall.
Keep Alba compact by avoiding rich fertilizers, which only make it floppy and reduce those blooms.
items.description: Pure white lavender.

items.name: Lavender 'Imperial Gem'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Imperial Gem in full sun and very gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters.
Prune your bush back by a third every August right after flowering, but never cut into old wood.
Keep watering to a minimum once established, only soaking them during prolonged dry summer spells.
Plant them alongside rosemary or thyme to create a drought-tolerant, bee-friendly Mediterranean bed.
Give this compact dwarf variety space to breathe so damp autumn air doesn't cause any root rot.
items.description: Deep violet; long flowering.

items.name: Rose
items.growersTips:
Prune your UK shrubs in late winter, cutting just above an outward-facing bud to keep air flowing.
Plant your rose with the graft union buried five centimetres deep to protect it from harsh frosts.
Feed your soil with well-rotted manure in spring to help clay soils retain moisture through summer.
Water deeply at the base every week in dry spells, keeping the leaves dry to stop blackspot spread.
Underplant with lavender or salvias to naturally deter aphids and mask any bare stems at the base.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Rose cultivars.

items.name: Rose 'Gertrude Jekyll'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Gertrude deep with the graft union three inches below ground to stop those wild suckers.
Prune her back by half in late January to keep this vigorous shrub from getting too tall and leggy.
Give her a rich mulch of well-rotted manure in March to fuel that famous, heavy first flush of scent.
Keep a sharp eye out for blackspot in damp UK summers and strip infected leaves off immediately.
Train her main stems horizontally along a fence to trigger loads of flowering side-shoots.
items.description: David Austin English rose; richly fragrant pink.

items.name: Rose 'Graham Thomas'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Graham Thomas deep with the graft union three inches below the soil to stop wind rock.
Give it a heavy drench weekly at the base rather than light sprinkles to stop blackspot in UK rain.
Prune this vigorous climber-shrub by one third in late February to keep those yellow blooms at eye level.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to satisfy its greedy appetite in our damp British soils.
Watch out for sawfly larvae in May which love eating these soft, buttery leaves down to the veins.
items.description: Apricot-yellow English rose.

items.name: Rose 'Munstead Wood'
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep with the graft union three inches below soil level to protect it from cold UK winds.
Feed with high-potassium rose food in March and July to keep those heavy, dark crimson blooms coming.
Prune hard in late February, cutting back by half to keep this naturally floppy shrub quite bushy.
Mulch damp soil in spring with well-rotted manure to stop blackspot spores splashing onto leaves.
Plant next to silver-leaved lambs ears to beautifully contrast the deep velvet purple of the petals.
items.description: Deep velvety crimson.

items.name: Rose 'Iceberg'
items.growersTips:
Prune your Iceberg in late February to open up the center and prevent mildew in damp UK weather.
Plant the graft union three centimeters below the soil to protect it from harsh British winter frosts.
Watch out for blackspot in humid UK summers by watering only at the base, never wetting the leaves.
Feed with rose food in April and July to keep those repeat-flowering white blooms coming all summer.
Underplant with lavender or salvia to mask bare lower stems and deter common pests like aphids.
items.description: Reliable white floribunda.

items.name: Rose 'Mister Lincoln'
items.growersTips:
Plant this deep with the graft union three inches below soil level to protect it from harsh UK frosts.
Feed weekly with high-potassium tomato food in summer to boost those iconic, highly scented blooms.
Prune hard in late February down to about ten inches to encourage strong stems that won't flop.
Watch out for blackspot in damp UK summers, so strip any affected leaves immediately to stop spread.
Water deeply at the base every week during dry spells, keeping the lush foliage completely dry.
items.description: Dark red hybrid tea, strong scent.

items.name: Rose 'Peace'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Peace rose graft union two inches below the soil to protect it from harsh UK winter frosts.
Prune hard in late February, cutting stems back to an outward-facing bud to keep the shrub compact.
Water generously at the base every week in summer to stop powdery mildew ruining the glossy leaves.
Feed with high-potassium rose food in March and July to boost those massive pink-flushed blooms.
Underplant with lavender or salvia to mask bare lower stems and deter common UK aphids naturally.
items.description: Classic yellow-pink hybrid tea.

items.name: Rose 'Queen Elizabeth'
items.growersTips:
Plant this tall beauty deep enough to bury the graft union three inches down to stop wind rock.
Give her a hard prune down to two feet in late February to keep those sky-high blooms at eye level.
Watch out for blackspot in damp UK summers and strip any spotted leaves the moment you see them.
Feed with high-potassium rose food in April and July to keep those gorgeous pink flushes coming.
Underplant with lavender or salvia to hide her bare, leggy stems and deter pesky greenflies.
items.description: Tall pink grandiflora.

items.name: Rose 'The Pilgrim'
items.growersTips:
Plant this pale yellow beauty deep, keeping the graft union five centimetres below the soil surface.
To stop blackspot in damp UK weather, space it well and prune out the centre for good airflow.
Give it a sturdy obelisk or trellis early on, as its long, flexible stems love to climb.
Feed it twice a year with rose food, once in March and again after its first summer bloom.
Prune in late winter by cutting back main stems by one-third to encourage bushy, repeat flowering.
items.description: Soft yellow English rose, very floriferous.

items.name: Wood Sage
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Cut back faded flower spikes to the ground in July to trigger a second flush of blooms in autumn.
Leave dead stems intact over winter to protect the crown from frost, then clear them in March.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain plant vigour and flower size.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Wood Sage cultivars.

items.name: Wood 'Caradonna'
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK winters.
Cut the dark purple stems right back to the ground in May to keep your plant compact and bushy.
Deadhead faded flower spikes in July to encourage a second flush of blooms that lasts into autumn.
Divide the root clump every three years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and free-flowering.
Keep young spring shoots safe from slugs and snails using beer traps or pet-safe organic pellets.
items.description: Dark-stemmed violet spires.

items.name: Wood 'Mainacht'
items.growersTips:
Pop this Salvia in free-draining soil with grit, as soggy UK winter wet will rot its roots.
Cut faded flower spikes right back to the ground in July to trigger a fresh flush in late summer.
Plant the crown level with the soil surface in full sun to prevent rot and encourage maximum blooms.
Watch out for slugs eating the tender new shoots in spring, so protect them with organic pellets.
Divide the clump every three years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and free-flowering.
items.description: Indigo flowers, early.

items.name: Wood 'Amethyst'
items.growersTips:
Cut back faded stems to the ground in July to trigger a second flush of purple blooms by autumn.
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to help this Salvia survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full sun next to silver-foliaged Lambs Ears to make the amethyst flowers really pop.
Divide the clump every three years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and free-flowering.
Watch out for slugs on young spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers to protect them.
items.description: Light purple, long flowering.

items.name: Wood 'Schwellenburg'
items.growersTips:
Pop this salvia in a sunny, free-draining spot to stop its roots rotting in our wet UK winters.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in July to encourage a second flush of deep purple blooms by autumn.
Avoid heavy clay by digging in plenty of grit and compost before planting to keep the roots happy.
Watch out for slugs and snails targeting the fresh, tender spring shoots as they first emerge.
Divide your mature clumps every three years in early spring to keep the plant vigorous and healthy.
items.description: Bright pink.

items.name: Yarrow
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on the surface in spring as they need light to germinate in the UK climate.
Grow in poor well-drained soil to prevent floppy stems and avoid adding rich compost or manure.
Deadhead faded flowers in July to encourage a second flush of blooms before the autumn frosts.
Divide established clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent center rot.
Avoid overwatering once established as this native wildflower is highly drought-tolerant in summer.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Yarrow cultivars.

items.name: Yarrow 'Cerise Queen'
items.growersTips:
Plant this pink beauty in your poorest, well-drained soil as rich UK soil makes the stems flop over.
Chop the faded flower heads right back to the ground in July to trigger a second flush of blooms.
Give it a wide berth from thirsty plants, watering only during prolonged, severe UK summer droughts.
Divide the clump every three years in spring to keep the vibrant cerise colour from reverting to white.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp autumns by spacing them well to keep the British breeze flowing.
items.description: Bright cerise pink.

items.name: Yarrow 'Paprika'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Paprika in poor, well-drained soil in full sun to stop the stems getting floppy and weak.
