Divide the clump every three years in spring to keep that brilliant red flower colour from fading.
Cut the faded red flower heads right back to the ground in July to trigger a second flush of blooms.
Water sparingly once established, as wet winter soil in the UK will quickly rot its roots.
Watch out for powdery mildew in muggy UK summers, so space them well to keep the air flowing freely.
items.description: Brick-red yarrow, fading to peach.

items.name: Yarrow 'Moonshine'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in your poorest, sharpest-draining soil to stop those lovely grey leaves rotting.
Give it a hard chop right to the ground in autumn to keep the clump tight and tidy for next spring.
Plant it alongside English lavender or purple salvias for a gorgeous, bee-friendly colour contrast.
Divide the root clump every three years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and flowering well.
Avoid rich fertilisers and heavy watering, as too much food makes the flower stems flop over.
items.description: Soft yellow with silvery leaves.

items.name: Daylily
items.growersTips:
Plant your daylilies with the crown just two centimetres below the soil to prevent crown rot.
Give them a deep soak once a week during dry UK summers rather than light daily sprinkles.
Watch out for the daylily gall midge in May and pinch off any swollen, distorted flower buds.
Cut the flower stems right back to the ground in autumn to stop pests overwintering in the foliage.
Divide your clumps every three years in spring to keep them flowering beautifully in our climate.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Daylily cultivars.

items.name: Daylily 'Stella de Oro'
items.growersTips:
Split and replant congested clumps every three years in spring to keep those yellow blooms coming.
Saturate the soil weekly during dry UK summers to stop this thirsty dwarf variety going dormant.
Plant the crown just two centimetres below the soil surface so it does not rot in damp UK winters.
Snip off faded flowers and green seed pods daily to trigger a second flush of late-summer buds.
Watch out for those pesky orange daylily gall midge grubs ruining your early June flower buds.
items.description: Compact reblooming yellow daylily.

items.name: Daylily 'Pardon Me'
items.growersTips:
Plant this red beauty in spring with its crown sitting exactly one inch below your soil surface.
Give it a weekly deep soak during dry UK summers to keep those repeat-blooming buds coming.
Snip off faded flowers and green seed pods daily in August to encourage a second flush of red.
Divide your clumps every four years in autumn to keep this compact variety flowering vigorously.
Watch out for gall midge in May by pinching off and destroying any unnaturally swollen flower buds.
items.description: Compact crimson daylily, evening fragrance.

items.name: Daylily 'Happy Returns'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in full sun and rich, damp soil to keep those yellow blooms coming all summer.
Divide your clumps every three years in autumn to keep them vigorous and flowering like mad.
Deadhead faded flowers daily in July and August to encourage a constant supply of fresh buds.
Watch out for the daylily gall midge in spring, pinching off any swollen, distorted flower buds.
Give them a generous mulch of well-rotted compost in spring to lock in that vital UK moisture.
items.description: Bright lemon-yellow reblooming.

items.name: Rhododendron
items.growersTips:
Plant your rhododendron shallowly with the root ball top just at soil level to prevent stem rot.
Always water them with harvested rainwater because UK tap water is too alkaline for their liking.
Prune them immediately after flowering in June so you do not cut off next year's developing buds.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark to keep their shallow roots cool and acidic.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and notch damage on leaves in damp UK autumns.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Rhododendron cultivars.

items.name: Rhododendron 'Cunningham's White'
items.growersTips:
Mix plenty of composted pine bark into your UK clay soil to keep this beauty happy and rot-free.
Plant it shallow with the root ball top just showing, as deep planting kills Cunningham's White.
Water with saved rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil acidic and leaves healthy.
Deadhead spent blooms in June by snapping them off gently at the base to boost next year's show.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow this one in a patio pot.
items.description: Reliable hardy white.

items.name: Rhododendron 'Nova Zembla'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in acidic soil using ericaceous compost and keep the root ball level with the turf.
Rainwater is best for watering, especially during dry spells in July when next year's buds form.
Deadhead spent red trusses gently in June to boost growth, taking care not to snap new buds below.
Mulch annually with pine needles or bark chippings to keep the shallow roots cool and moist.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots and leaf-cutter bees making neat notches in summer.
items.description: Deep red, very hardy.

items.name: Rhododendron 'Cynthia'
items.growersTips:
Give Cynthia plenty of elbow room because this vigorous shrub easily grows over three meters wide.
Plant her shallow with the rootball top just visible, as deep planting causes root rot in UK clay.
Tuck her into dappled shade to protect those gorgeous hot-pink spring blooms from bleaching in sun.
Mulch annually with pine needles or composted bark to keep her shallow roots damp and happily acid.
Snap off faded flower truss stems carefully in June to boost next year's buds without losing wood.
items.description: Classic rose-pink rhododendron.

items.name: Japanese Maple
items.growersTips:
Plant in a site sheltered from cold easterly winds to prevent spring frost damage to emerging leaves.
Incorporate ericaceous compost and grit to ensure a slightly acidic, moist yet free-draining soil.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch on delicate foliage.
Prune only during mid-winter dormancy to avoid sap bleeding which weakens the tree and invites rot.
Position red-leaved cultivars in dappled sunlight to prevent leaf scorch while maintaining color.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Japanese Maple cultivars.

items.name: Japanese 'Bloodgood'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Bloodgood with the root flare level with the soil to prevent stem rot in damp UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than light daily sprinkles to build deep roots.
Prune only in late autumn or midwinter when fully dormant to stop this sap-heavy maple from bleeding.
Mix plenty of composted pine needles into your soil to keep the pH slightly acidic and free-draining.
Shelter your Bloodgood from harsh easterly winds to prevent the delicate purple leaves from scorching.
items.description: Deep red-purple Japanese maple.

items.name: Japanese 'Dissectum Atropurpureum'
items.growersTips:
Plant it with the root flare just visible, as burying the stem of this dwarf shrub causes rot.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers to prevent the delicate purple leaf tips from scorching.
Prune only in late autumn or winter to stop the sap bleeding and keep its weeping umbrella shape.
Mix plenty of ericaceous compost into your clay soil to keep this acid-loving beauty happy.
Shelter it from harsh easterly winds to protect the finely cut, lace-like foliage from shredding.
items.description: Cut-leaved purple weeping form.

items.name: Japanese 'Sango-kaku'
items.growersTips:
Plant its root flare level with the soil in a spot sheltered from cold drying UK easterly winds.
Keep the soil consistently moist but never soggy, watering deeply during dry British summer spells.
Only prune in late winter when dormant to prevent the sap bleeding that attracts nasty diseases.
Grow it in acidic to neutral loam, adding plenty of compost to mimic a rich forest floor.
Watch out for aphids on new spring shoots and shield the bark from harsh, direct midday sun.
items.description: Coral-bark maple, red winter twigs.

items.name: Chinese Wisteria
items.growersTips:
Prune twice a year in July or August to five buds and again in January or February to two buds.
Plant grafted wisteria with the graft union at least five centimetres above the soil level.
Water newly planted wisteria deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to establish roots.
Grow in fertile well drained soil against a sunny south or west facing wall to ripen flowering wood.
Train main stems horizontally along sturdy wires spaced thirty centimetres apart to encourage blooms.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Chinese Wisteria cultivars.

items.name: Chinese 'Prolific'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Prolific in a south or west facing spot to get the warm UK sun it needs to bloom well.
Prune the new shoots back to five buds in August, then down to two buds in January for massive blooms.
Give your young vine a bucket of water weekly during dry UK summers until its roots are established.
Plant it in fertile, well-drained soil with the graft union sitting just above the ground level.
Avoid high-nitrogen feeds which only make leaves grow, using potash in spring to boost those flowers.
items.description: Free-flowering lilac-blue Chinese wisteria.

items.name: Chinese 'Alba'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Alba in a sunny, south-facing spot to help those white blooms bake and bud in UK summers.
Prune twice a year, cutting back green shoots to five buds in August, then to two buds in January.
Give it a weekly deep soak during dry summer spells while it establishes to prevent bud drop.
Enrich heavy UK clay with plenty of well-rotted grit and compost before planting to ensure drainage.
Train the main stems horizontally early on to trigger way more of those gorgeous white racemes.
items.description: White Chinese wisteria.

items.name: Houseleek
items.growersTips:
Plant in a 50 percent grit and peat-free compost mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full south-facing sun as British overcast skies will cause rosettes to lose color.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter.
Gently pull away dead outer leaves in late spring to prevent dampness and deter slugs and snails.
Propagate by snipping off offsets in summer and pressing them shallowly into gritty soil to root.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Houseleek cultivars.

items.name: Houseleek 'Atropurpureum'
items.growersTips:
Plant these in a shallow gritty mix with a top layer of gravel to keep rain from rotting the collar.
Water them only when the soil is bone dry, and hold off watering entirely during damp UK winters.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs chewing the roots, especially if you grow them in terracotta pots.
Keep their deep purple colour intense by placing them in the brightest, most sun-drenched spot.
Gently pull away the mother rosette once it dies after flowering to let the baby chicks fill in.
items.description: Burgundy houseleek.

items.name: Houseleek 'Silverine'
items.growersTips:
Plant Silverine shallowly in gritty, free-draining soil so the rosette sits right on the gravel.
Only water when the soil is bone dry, and never let water sit in the central crown during winter.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and protect them from wet winter rot under a cloche.
Gently pull away dead bottom leaves in spring to keep the silvery-purple rosettes looking tidy.
Plant them alongside Sedum album in a shallow terracotta pot to highlight their metallic sheen.
items.description: Silver-grey rosettes.

items.name: Houseleek 'Royal Ruby'
items.growersTips:
Plant Royal Ruby with its crown just above the gritty soil line to prevent winter wet rotting it.
Water only when the soil is bone dry, and stop watering completely during damp UK winter months.
Tuck horticultural grit under the rosette leaves to keep them off wet soil and stop slugs invading.
Gently pull out any rosettes that have flowered and died to make room for the new baby offsets.
Mix fifty percent grit into your peat-free compost to help this alpine survive heavy British rain.
items.description: Deep ruby rosettes.

items.name: Showy Stonecrop
items.growersTips:
Do the Chelsea chop in late May to reduce the height of stems and prevent the heavy clumps splaying.
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in free-draining grit to prevent winter wet crown rot.
Water only during severe summer droughts as wet UK soil causes floppy growth and root rot.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots in autumn and slugs damaging new spring shoots.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Showy Stonecrop cultivars.

items.name: Showy 'Autumn Joy'
items.growersTips:
Give your Autumn Joy gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in soggy UK wet spells.
Do the Chelsea chop in late May, cutting stems back by half to keep the heavy autumn blooms upright.
Leave the faded copper flower heads intact over winter to provide structural frost beauty and seeds.
Water sparingly once established, only during prolonged dry summer spells to avoid floppy growth.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and slugs targeting fresh, fleshy spring shoots.
items.description: Pink-to-rust autumn flowers.

items.name: Showy 'Brilliant'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Brilliant in poor, well-drained soil to stop the heavy autumn flowerheads from flopping.
Water newly planted sedums weekly, but once established, leave them to dry out in the UK drizzle.
Do the Chelsea Chop in late May, cutting stems back by half to keep the plant compact and sturdy.
Leave the dried, rusty-red winter seedheads intact to feed hungry birds and protect the crown.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots, especially if you grow your sedum in patio pots.
items.description: Bright rose-pink heads.

items.name: Saxifrage
items.growersTips:
Plant alpine types in gritty, free-draining soil to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Tuck silver saxifrages into vertical crevice gardens or rock gaps so rain drains off their crowns.
Water your mossy saxifrages during dry summer spells to stop their lush green mounds turning brown.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn after flowering to keep them vigorous and free-flowering.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in spring, as they love chewing through the roots of container plants.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Saxifrage cultivars.

items.name: Saxifrage 'Tumbling Waters'
items.growersTips:
Plant this beauty in a crevice or angled pot so winter rain drains away from its silver rosette.
Give it gritty, alkaline soil or add limestone chippings to match its natural mountain home.
Water only when the soil is dry, focusing on the base to avoid rotting the delicate foliage.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing through the fibrous roots.
Cut the main rosette away after it flowers, leaving the small side offsets to grow for next year.
items.description: Cascading white rockery saxifrage.

items.name: Saxifrage 'Peter Pan'
items.growersTips:
Plant this mossy saxifrage in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter wet rotting its roots.
Tuck it into a north or east-facing rockery to protect the delicate pink flowers from hot UK sun.
Water gently around the base rather than from above to keep the dense, mossy cushion from splitting.
Give it a light trim after flowering in June to keep the mound compact and prevent a brown centre.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which love to eat through these shallow, fibrous roots.
items.description: Compact pink mossy saxifrage.

items.name: Primrose
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root primroses in autumn at crown level so the base of the leaves sits flush with the soil
Water thoroughly during dry summer spells to mimic damp UK woodlands and prevent leaf scorch
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating roots in autumn and apply biological nematode controls in September
Divide congested clumps every three years immediately after spring flowering to maintain plant vigour
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to ensure moisture-retentive loam
items.description: Reference parent species for the Primrose cultivars.

items.name: Primrose 'Wanda'
items.growersTips:
Divide your Wanda clumps every three years in late summer to keep their purple blooms vigorous.
Plant them with their crowns flush at the soil level to prevent winter rot in wet UK weather.
Mix plenty of leaf mould into your clay soil to replicate their favourite damp woodland home.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots if you grow these purple beauties in patio pots.
Snip off the faded stems in late spring to encourage a cheeky second flush of autumn flowers.
items.description: Deep purple primrose.

items.name: Primrose 'Belarina'
items.growersTips:
Plant these double beauties in partial shade with their crown sitting exactly level with the soil.
Keep the soil consistently damp but never soggy, especially during dry spells in spring and autumn.
Watch out for vine weevil grubs eating the roots, and drench with nematodes in August or September.
Snip off faded flowers at the base of the stem to encourage a second flush of gorgeous blooms.
Divide the clumps every three years right after flowering to keep them vigorous and free-flowering.
items.description: Double-flowered primrose series.

items.name: Pear
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, well-drained loam in a sheltered, south-facing UK spot for sun.
Prune in winter when dormant to establish a strong central leader and remove congested branches.
Water deeply every fortnight during dry summer spells, especially while the young tree establishes.
Watch for pear midge in spring; pick and burn deformed, blackened fruitlets before larvae escape.
Mulch annually in early spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main woody stem.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Pear cultivars.

items.name: Pear 'Conference'
items.growersTips:
Plant this self-fertile pear in a sunny, sheltered UK spot to protect early spring blossoms from frost.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the soil moist and feed its greedy root system.
Prune in mid-winter to thin crowded branches and encourage those classic, heavy-cropping spurs.
Keep an eye out for pear midge in spring, picking off any swollen, blackening baby fruits early on.
Thin out congested fruit clusters in July so the remaining pears grow big, juicy, and sweet.
items.description: Reliable self-fertile pear.

items.name: Pear 'Doyenné du Comice'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Comice near another pear like Concorde because it is self-sterile and needs a partner.
Grow this variety against a warm south-facing wall to help the fruit ripen in our cool UK summers.
Prune in winter by thinning congested branches to let light in and prevent scab in damp UK weather.
Water deeply during dry spells in July and August to stop the heavy, juicy fruits dropping early.
Wrap grease bands around the trunk in autumn to stop winter moth caterpillars ruining next year's crop.
items.description: Buttery flesh, finest dessert pear.

items.name: Pear 'Williams' Bon Chrétien'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Williams in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the early spring blossom from UK frosts.
Water deeply every week during dry summer spells while the young pears are swelling on the branch.
Prune your pear in midwinter, cutting back some older spurs to keep the fruit size big and juicy.
Pick the pears while they are still green and firm, then let them ripen indoors for the best flavor.
Watch out for pear midge in spring, and quickly pick off any tiny, blackening fruitlets you see.
items.description: Classic Bartlett pear.

items.name: Pear 'Beurré Hardy'
items.growersTips:
Give this vigorous pear plenty of space and prune in winter to keep its upright growth in check.
Plant your bareroot tree in late autumn so the roots settle before the wet UK winter sets in.
Watch out for pear midge in spring by checking for unnaturally swollen, blackening young fruit.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to keep the soil rich and retain crucial moisture.
Grow a pollination partner like Conference nearby since Beurre Hardy is not fully self-fertile.
items.description: Russet pear, melting flesh.

items.name: Pear 'Concorde'
items.growersTips:
Plant Concorde with the graft union sitting at least five centimetres above the damp UK soil line.
Prune your tree in winter to encourage a strong central leader since Concorde loves to grow upright.
Thin out the heavy clusters of tiny pears in July so the remaining fruits grow big and juicy.
Keep a lookout for pear midge in spring and pick off any swollen, blackening baby fruits quickly.
Grow Concorde on Quince C rootstock if your UK garden has limited space or heavy clay soil.
items.description: Conference × Comice; compact heavy cropper.

items.name: Sweet Cherry
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root whips between November and March in deep, moist, well-drained loam to aid rooting.
Prune strictly in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease and bacterial canker infections.
Water deeply every fortnight during the first dry summer to establish the shallow root system.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in spring, keeping it clear of the collar to prevent rot.
Watch for black cherry aphid in May and encourage ladybirds or lacewings as a natural control.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Sweet Cherry cultivars.

items.name: Sweet 'Stella'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Stella on a south-facing wall to trap the UK sun and protect early spring blossoms from frost.
Prune your Stella only in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease, never during the damp winter.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to keep the shallow roots damp during dry UK summer spells.
Hang shiny CDs or netting in June to stop blackbirds from stealing the cherries before they ripen.
Apply a grease band to the trunk in autumn to stop winter moth caterpillars climbing up your tree.
items.description: Self-fertile dark sweet cherry.

items.name: Sweet 'Sunburst'
items.growersTips:
Plant this cherry in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the delicate early spring blossom from frost.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late February to feed its heavy crops and keep the soil moisture in.
Only prune in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease, keeping the center open for air and light.
Net the tree securely in July because UK blackbirds will strip the sweet, dark red fruit in days.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells while the young cherries are swelling on the branch.
items.description: Self-fertile large dark red cherry.

items.name: Sweet 'Sweetheart'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Sweetheart on a Gisela 5 rootstock to keep this vigorous shrub to a manageable 3m height.
Prune in late July or August to avoid silver leaf disease, focusing on keeping the center open.
Water deeply once a week during June fruit-swell to prevent the cherries from splitting in UK rain.
Apply a high-potassium feed in early spring to boost the heavy crops this self-fertile variety yields.
Net the bush in June before the fruit turns red, as UK blackbirds will strip the crop overnight.
items.description: Late-cropping self-fertile cherry.

items.name: Sweet 'Victoria'
items.growersTips:
Thin your Victoria plums in May to stop the heavy fruit crop from snapping the branches in summer.
Prune your tree only in midsummer to protect it from silver leaf disease and bacterial canker.
Plant with the graft union clear of the soil and water deeply weekly during dry UK spring spells.
Watch out for plum moth caterpillars by hanging pheromone traps in your tree from May to August.
Grow chives or garlic nearby to help ward off fungal diseases common in damp British weather.
items.description: Self-fertile dessert/cooking plum.

items.name: Sweet 'Marjorie's Seedling'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-season plum in a sunny, sheltered spot to help the late September fruit ripen fully.
Prune your Marjorie's Seedling in mid-summer, never winter, to prevent silver leaf disease spores.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells while the heavy crop of purple plums is swelling.
Thin out congested branches in July so the heavy, late-fruiting branches do not snap under weight.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in spring to keep the soil moist and feed the roots.
items.description: Late-cropping dark cooking plum.

items.name: Sweet 'Czar'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Czar at the same depth as its nursery pot, keeping the graft union well above the soil.
Prune your Czar only in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease, which thrives in wet UK winters.
Thin out the dense green fruits in May so the remaining plums grow big and do not snap the branches.
Drench the roots weekly during dry British summers while the plums are swelling to prevent splitting.
Watch out for plum moth caterpillars in July by hanging pheromone traps in your tree by late May.
items.description: Hardy cooking plum, very reliable.

items.name: Sweet 'Peregrine'
items.growersTips:
Plant this peach against a warm south-facing brick wall to trap the essential summer heat it needs.
Protect early spring blossoms from frost using fleece to guarantee a great crop of juicy peaches.
Prune your bush in late spring when the leaves emerge to prevent the nasty silver leaf disease.
Water deeply weekly while the fruit swells in summer, keeping the base clear of thirsty weeds.
Watch out for peach leaf curl by keeping rain off the emerging spring buds with a plastic screen.
items.description: Hardy white-fleshed peach for UK walls.

items.name: Sweet 'Rochester'
items.growersTips:
Protect your Rochester peach from January to May with a plastic cover to prevent peach leaf curl.
Plant your tree in a sunny, south-facing spot against a warm wall to help the fruit ripen in August.
Thin out the tiny green peaches in May so there is a hand-width gap between each fruit for size.
Prune your peach tree in midsummer, never in winter, to avoid the deadly silver leaf disease.
Mulch yearly with well-rotted manure to keep the soil moist, as dry roots make the fruit drop early.
items.description: Yellow-fleshed reliable peach.

items.name: Raspberry
items.growersTips:
Prune summer-fruiting canes to the ground in autumn, but cut autumn-fruiting ones down in February.
Plant bare-root canes between November and March at the same depth they were previously growing.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in March to retain moisture in sandy or chalky UK soils.
Net the ripening fruit in summer to protect your harvest from hungry blackbirds and thrushes.
Grow in slightly acidic to neutral soil, avoiding wet clay areas to prevent Phytophthora root rot.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Raspberry cultivars.

items.name: Raspberry 'Glen Ample'
items.growersTips:
Plant this spine-free variety in rich, acidic to neutral soil, keeping the crown just at soil level.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to feed the roots and keep the damp UK soil moist but drained.
Prune fruited canes to the ground in autumn, leaving the new green ones to produce next year's crop.
Tie the vigorous, heavy-yielding canes to a sturdy wire support system to stop them snapping in wind.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in June; pick off any damaged berries to save your harvest.
items.description: Heavy summer-fruiting raspberry, spine-free.

items.name: Raspberry 'Autumn Bliss'
items.growersTips:
Cut all canes right down to ground level in February so you get a bumper crop of new fruit in autumn.
Plant them with the root plug just below the soil surface to prevent rot in wet UK winter weather.
Water deeply at the base during dry July spells to stop the heavy berries from shrivelling up.
Give them a mulch of well-rotted manure in spring to feed the soil and lock in crucial moisture.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in August and hand-pick them to save your autumn harvest.
items.description: Autumn-fruiting raspberry, fruits on new canes.

items.name: Raspberry 'Polka'
items.growersTips:
Cut these autumn-fruiting canes right down to ground level every February to get a huge summer crop.
Plant bare-root Polka canes in sunny, sheltered UK spots from November to March just below the soil.
Polka hates wet feet so mix plenty of well-rotted manure into clay soil to assist with drainage.
Keep your Polka well-watered during dry spells in July when those heavy berries are swelling up.
Tie your heavy Polka canes to a simple wire support so the massive autumn crop does not touch the soil.
items.description: Heavy autumn primocane raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Tulameen'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Tulameen in a spot sheltered from wet UK winds to protect its exceptionally tall canes.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to feed this hungry variety and keep its shallow roots damp.
Prune out the fruited floricanes right down to the ground in autumn, leaving the new green ones.
Water the base deeply during summer fruit swell to stop the large, sweet berries from crumbling.
Keep a sharp eye out for raspberry beetle grubs which love Tulameen's late July ripening window.
items.description: Large-fruited summer raspberry, sweet flavour.

items.name: Raspberry 'Loch Ness'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Loch Ness in autumn or spring so the crown sits exactly level with your garden soil.
Give it a weekly deep soak at the base during dry summer spells to keep those juicy berries plump.
Prune out the old, fruited canes to ground level in winter, leaving the new green ones for next year.
Feed with a high-potash organic mulch in March to help this heavy cropper thrive in UK clay soils.
Tie the vigorous, thornless canes securely to a sturdy wire trellis to protect them from UK winds.
items.description: Thornless heavy-cropping blackberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Oregon Thornless'
items.growersTips:
Plant this blackberry in a spot with damp, acidic soil and give it a sturdy three-wire trellis.
Prune out the fruited canes in November, then tie in the new green ones for next year's crop.
Watch out for the blackberry gall mite, which stops the green berries from ripening properly.
Give it a thick mulch of composted bark in March to keep the shallow roots damp and happy.
Keep watering the base deeply during dry July spells to ensure your berries plump up nicely.
items.description: Parsley-leaved thornless blackberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Black Butte'
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant blackberry in early spring, keeping the crown exactly level with the UK soil line.
Give it a sturdy three-wire trellis to support those heavy, incredibly long and vigorous canes.
Prune out fruited canes in autumn, training new green ones to the wires for next summer's crop.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs by checking the hulls of the earliest ripening giant berries.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in March to keep the shallow roots damp during dry spells.
items.description: Huge berries, early ripening.

items.name: Blackcurrant
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root bushes in late autumn 5cm deeper than the nursery mark to encourage strong new stems.
Prune in winter by removing one-third of the oldest dark wood at the base to stimulate new growth.
Water newly planted bushes weekly during dry spring spells to ensure fruit swells in June and July.
Mulch annually in March with well-rotted manure to keep the shallow root system cool and damp.
Net bushes in early summer to protect ripening berries from bullfinches and blackbirds.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Blackcurrant cultivars.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Ben Sarek'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Ben Sarek two inches deeper than the pot level to encourage a bushy, multi-stemmed base.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late winter to keep the shallow roots cool and damp in UK summers.
Since it is a compact dwarf, prune out only the oldest, darkest wood in winter to keep it fruiting.
Watch for the big bud mite in early spring and pick off any swollen, rounded buds immediately.
Net the bush in June because UK blackbirds love these heavy-cropping, easy-to-reach low branches.
items.description: Compact blackcurrant for small gardens.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Ben Hope'
items.growersTips:
Plant Ben Hope two inches deeper than the pot level in autumn to encourage strong new basal shoots.
Prune in winter by removing a third of the oldest wood to keep this vigorous variety productive.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the shallow roots damp during dry UK spring spells.
Watch for gall mite in spring and immediately pick off any unnaturally swollen, rounded buds.
Net the bush in June because UK blackbirds love Ben Hope berries just as they start to ripen.
items.description: Heavy-cropping blackcurrant, aphid resistant.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Ben Lomond'
items.growersTips:
Plant this variety two inches deeper than the pot level to encourage a bushy base of strong new stems.
Prune out about a third of the oldest dark wood in winter to keep this heavy cropper productive.
Watch for big bud mite in spring and immediately pick off any abnormally swollen rounded buds.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the soil damp and feed this hungry UK favorite.
Net the bush in June because local blackbirds love these sweet late-ripening berries as much as you.
items.description: Reliable mid-season blackcurrant.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Jonkheer van Tets'
items.growersTips:
Plant your bare-root shrub in autumn so it settles well before the wet UK winter sets in.
Prune in late winter by cutting back a third of the old wood to keep the bush productive.
Watch out for early frosts in spring and cover the blossoms with fleece to protect your crop.
Feed with a high-potassium mulch in early spring to encourage a bumper harvest of juicy berries.
Keep the soil consistently moist during dry summer spells to prevent the fruit from dropping early.
items.description: Heavy early-cropping redcurrant.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Red Lake'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Red Lake three centimeters deeper than its pot to encourage a strong, bushy base of stems.
Prune out a third of the oldest, dark wood in winter to keep this heavy-cropping shrub productive.
Water your shrub weekly at the base during dry summer spells to stop the juicy berries from dropping.
Protect the early spring blooms from late UK frosts by draping fleece over the shrub on cold nights.
Net the bush in June because local birds love these sweet, translucent red berries as much as you do.
items.description: Mid-season redcurrant, long sprigs.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'White Versailles'
items.growersTips:
Plant your bush 5cm deeper than its pot level in autumn to encourage a strong, multi-stemmed base.
Prune out a third of the oldest, dark wood in winter to keep this white currant highly productive.
Net the bush in June because UK blackbirds will strip these sweet, translucent berries in a day.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the shallow roots cool and damp during dry spells.
Grow them as a space-saving flat cordon against a north wall if your UK garden is short on sun.
items.description: Translucent white-currant.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Invicta'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Invicta gooseberry two inches deeper than the pot level to encourage a sturdy bush shape.
Prune in winter by clearing the center to keep it airy, which stops mildew on this tough variety.
Water deeply at the base during dry UK spells to stop the skins splitting on those juicy berries.
Watch out for sawfly caterpillars in mid-spring; they can strip your Invicta leaves in days.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late winter to feed the soil and lock in that vital moisture.
items.description: Mildew-resistant gooseberry.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Hinnonmaki Red'
items.growersTips:
Plant this gooseberry slightly deeper than its pot level to encourage a sturdy, multi-stemmed bush.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late winter to keep the shallow roots damp during dry UK springs.
Prune in winter by keeping the centre open like a goblet so air flows and prevents powdery mildew.
Keep a sharp eye out for sawfly larvae in May, as they can strip the leaves of your bush overnight.
Net the ripening red berries in June to stop local blackbirds from stealing your entire harvest.
items.description: Dessert gooseberry, dark red when ripe.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Whinham's Industry'
items.growersTips:
Plant Whinham's Industry in autumn so the damp UK winter soil helps its roots settle before spring.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the soil damp and feed this hungry, heavy cropper.
Prune in winter, keeping the center open to let air flow and prevent American gooseberry mildew.
Watch out for sawfly larvae in May, they love eating the leaves of Whinham's Industry to the veins.
Plant it in partial shade as this traditional red cultivar actually prefers it to baking hot sun.
items.description: Heritage red gooseberry, heavy cropper.

items.name: Highbush Blueberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in ericaceous compost with pine needles to keep the soil pH strictly between 4.5 and 5.2.
Water only with stored rainwater because UK tap water contains calcium that raises soil pH.
Prune in late winter by removing wood older than three years to stimulate productive new stems.
Cover bushes with fine netting in July to prevent UK blackbirds from stripping the ripening fruit.
Grow two different cultivars like Duke and Bluecrop nearby to ensure successful cross-pollination.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Highbush Blueberry cultivars.

items.name: Highbush 'Bluecrop'
items.growersTips:
Mix lots of ericaceous compost and pine needles into your soil to keep the pH between 4.5 and 5.2.
Always water your Bluecrop with stored rainwater because UK tap water will make the soil too alkaline.
Prune in late winter by removing wood older than three years to keep those big berries coming.
Cover your bush with fine netting in July before the local blackbirds strip all the ripening fruit.
Plant a Sunshine Blue nearby to boost pollination and get a much heavier harvest of sweet berries.
items.description: Reliable mid-season blueberry.

items.name: Highbush 'Duke'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early-fruiting beauty in pure ericaceous compost as our UK soils are rarely acidic enough.
Rainwater is best for Duke, so tap water is out; keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge.
Prune in late winter by removing old wood to keep this upright shrub from overproducing small fruit.
Net your Duke securely by June because UK blackbirds will strip the early berries before they ripen.
Plant Duke near Bluecrop to boost pollination, even though it is technically self-fertile.
items.description: Early blueberry, big sweet berries.

items.name: Highbush 'Chandler'
items.growersTips:
Mix lots of pine needles and ericaceous compost into your soil to keep the pH between 4.5 and 5.5.
Water only with stored rainwater because UK tap water is too alkaline for Chandler's shallow roots.
Prune in late winter by removing any twiggy growth and one or two of the oldest, woodiest stems.
Net the shrub securely in July because UK blackbirds will strip the giant berries before they ripen.
Plant Chandler near Duke or Spartan blueberries to boost pollination and get even bigger harvests.
items.description: Late-summer blueberry, huge berries.

items.name: Highbush 'Patriot'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Patriot in ericaceous compost as it hates UK chalk and needs a low pH to survive.
Water it only with collected rainwater because tap water contains lime that will turn leaves yellow.
Net the bush in July because UK blackbirds absolutely love these huge, early-ripening berries.
Prune in late winter by removing low branches; Patriot has a spreading habit that sags under fruit.
Mulch with pine needles or composted bark every spring to keep the shallow roots cool and damp.
items.description: Hardy blueberry, attractive autumn colour.

items.name: Grape Vine
items.growersTips:
Prune in midwinter to prevent bleeding sap and thin the summer canopy to expose grapes to UK sun.
Plant against a south-facing wall in well-drained soil with the graft union 10cm above ground level.
Water deeply at the base every ten days during dry summer spells, avoiding the foliage entirely.
Watch for powdery mildew in damp UK summers and space branches widely to maximise air circulation.
Select cold-hardy cultivars like Brandts or Boskoop Glory that reliably ripen in cooler UK climates.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Grape Vine cultivars.

items.name: Grape 'Black Hamburgh'
items.growersTips:
Grow this classic in a cold greenhouse as our UK summers are rarely warm enough to ripen it outside.
Prune your vine strictly in December or January to prevent the sap bleeding from the cuts in spring.
Pinch out the growing tips two leaves beyond each flower cluster to focus energy on the grapes.
Water deeply at the roots weekly during summer, but never splash the leaves to avoid powdery mildew.
Thin out half the young grapes in each bunch with scissors in July so the remaining fruit grows big.
items.description: Classic glasshouse black dessert grape.

items.name: Grape 'Müller-Thurgau'
items.growersTips:
Plant this vine against a south-facing wall to help its grapes ripen in our cool UK summers.
Prune in midwinter while fully dormant to prevent the vine from bleeding sap and losing vigor.
Grow it in poor, well-drained soil because rich earth makes too many leaves and fewer grapes.
Watch out for powdery mildew in damp British weather by thinning leaves to improve airflow.
Mulch with gravel rather than manure to reflect extra heat and light up onto the low-hanging fruit.
items.description: Reliable white grape for UK outdoors.

items.name: Grape 'Phoenix'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Phoenix vine in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to help the grapes ripen.
Prune your vine in midwinter while it is fully dormant to prevent the stems from bleeding sap.
Pinch out the growing tips of fruiting shoots two leaves past the bunch to focus energy on grapes.
Watch for powdery mildew in damp UK summers by thinning the summer foliage to improve airflow.
Give your vine a deep soak at the base once a week during dry summer spells while fruit is swelling.
items.description: Disease-resistant white wine grape.

items.name: Grape 'Regent'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Regent vine in the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have to help the grapes ripen in UK autumns.
Prune your vine in midwinter when it is dormant to prevent the stems from bleeding sap and weakening.
Pinch out the growing tips of fruiting shoots two leaves past the grape bunches in midsummer.
Thin out the dense summer foliage around the fruit bunches to let the weak UK sun ripen the grapes.
Keep a lookout for wasps and birds in September, using fine netting to protect your ripening crop.
items.description: Hardy red wine grape.

items.name: Lettuce
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep every two weeks from March to July for continuous crops.
Water early in the morning directly at the base to prevent downy mildew in damp UK summer weather.
Protect young leaves from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during wet British spring nights.

Plant your Idared grafting union at least ten centimetres above the soil to stop it rooting itself.
Prune your Idared in late winter, thinning the center to prevent mildew in damp UK summers.
Give this late-harvest apple a sunny, sheltered south-facing wall to help the fruit ripen by October.
Add a partner like Egremont Russet nearby because Idared needs a pollination buddy to set fruit.
Hang codling moth traps in your Idared tree around May to protect the developing autumn crop.
items.description: Bright-red dessert apple, stores well.

items.name: Malus 'Jupiter'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Jupiter deep in moist, well-draining soil, keeping the graft union 10cm above ground.
This triploid needs a partner nearby, so plant a self-fertile Cox or Scrumptious to pollinate it.
Prune your tree in late winter to open up the canopy and prevent the dreaded UK apple scab disease.
Water deeply every week during dry summer spells to help those huge, juicy fruits swell up nicely.
Mulch the root area in spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main woody trunk.
items.description: Cox-style dessert apple, modern.

items.name: Malus 'Keswick Codlin'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early cooker in a sunny spot to help those large, ribbed green fruits ripen by August.
This variety is tip-bearing, so prune it in winter by only cutting back branches that have fruited.
Keep it well-watered from June as the heavy crop develops, preventing bitter pit in the dry weeks.
Watch out for woolly aphid on the old wood; brush them off with soapy water during your spring walks.
Add a thick mulch of well-rotted manure each March to feed its hungry roots in damp British soil.
items.description: Cumbrian heritage cooker.

items.name: Malus 'Kingston Black'
items.growersTips:
Plant this cider apple in deep, well-draining loam with plenty of organic compost to boost growth.
Watch out for apple scab in damp UK springs by clearing away fallen leaves to stop the fungus.
Prune your tree in winter while it is dormant to keep its shape and encourage a healthy harvest.
Grow wildflowers nearby to attract the bees needed to pollinate its beautiful spring blossoms.
Water your young tree deeply once a week during dry summer spells to help the roots establish.
items.description: Cider apple, classic vintage variety.

items.name: Malus 'Lane's Prince Albert'

Plant this tree with the graft union sitting at least ten centimetres clear of the damp UK soil.

Watch out for codling moth in June by hanging pheromone traps in the branches of your tree.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in early spring but keep it clear of the main trunk to avoid rot.

items.name: Malus 'Lord Derby'

Prune your tree in winter, focusing on keeping the center open to prevent brown rot in wet UK weather.

Grow it near a pollination partner like Falstaff or Golden Delicious to guarantee a heavy crop.

items.name: Malus 'Newton Wonder'

items.name: Quince 'Champion'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Champion in a warm, sheltered, south-facing spot to help the large fruits ripen in UK sun.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in late winter to keep the soil moist and feed its shallow root system.
Prune lightly in dormant winter, focusing on keeping the centre open so damp UK air doesn't trap rot.
Water deeply during dry summer spells while the heavy pear-shaped fruits are swelling to stop drops.
Watch out for leaf blight in wet British springs, and quickly clear away any fallen spotted leaves.
items.description: Pear-shaped heritage quince.

items.name: Quince 'Meech's Prolific'
items.growersTips:
Plant this quince in full sun, sheltered from cold UK winds, to help the delicate pink spring buds.
Prune in winter when dormant to keep an open center, allowing light to ripen the heavy autumn fruit.
Give it deep weekly watering while the fruit swells in summer to stop the skins from splitting open.
Watch out for leaf blight in damp UK summers, and clear away fallen leaves to stop it overwintering.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to keep the soil rich and moist, but keep it off the trunk.
items.description: Heritage US quince, large fruit.

items.name: Quince 'Portugal'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Portugal quince in full sun but shelter it from cold UK winds to protect spring blossom.
Prune in winter by removing crowded branches to let light ripen the exceptionally large fruits.
Water deeply during dry summer spells while the heavy, pear-shaped quinces are swelling.
Watch out for quince leaf blight in wet British summers and rake up fallen leaves to stop spread.
Mulch annually in early spring with well-rotted manure to feed this vigorous, hungry cultivar.
items.description: Heritage Portuguese quince.

items.name: Quince 'Serbian Gold'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Serbian Gold in full sun to help the fruit ripen in our cool UK autumns.
Prune in winter while dormant to keep the center open for air and light to prevent leaf blight.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to keep the soil moist, as quinces hate drying out.
Watch for brown rot on the fruit during wet UK summers and remove affected quinces immediately.
Pick your golden quinces in late October before the first hard frost ruins their lovely aroma.
items.description: Serbian heritage quince, golden.

items.name: Quince 'Vranja'
items.growersTips:
Plant Vranja in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the early pink spring blossom from cold UK winds.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into your soil before planting to keep the roots moist and happy.
Prune your Vranja in winter while it is dormant to remove crowded branches and keep the centre open.
Watch out for leaf blight in wet UK summers and quickly clear away fallen leaves to prevent spread.
Give your tree a deep bucket of water every week during dry spells while the heavy fruits are swelling.
items.description: Yugoslav heritage quince, large.

items.name: Medlar
items.growersTips:
Plant Nottingham Fruiting or Nottingham graft-union two inches above soil to prevent rotting.
Mulch with damp compost in March to lock in rain before our dry UK spring spells hit.
Prune in late winter by removing crossing branches to let light reach the ripening fruit.
Watch for leaf blight in wet Welsh or English summers and rake up fallen leaves to stop spread.
Plant chives nearby to help ward off scab and encourage pollinators to visit the white blooms.
items.description: Reference parent species for the Medlar cultivars.

items.name: Medlar 'Bredase Reus'
items.growersTips:
Plant this Dutch giant in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the delicate spring blossom from frost.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into clay soil to help the deep roots establish in wet UK winters.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove rubbing branches and keep the centre open for ripening sun.
Water your young tree deeply every week during dry summer spells to prevent the heavy fruit dropping.
Harvest the large fruits after the first November frost, then store them eye-down until they blet.
items.description: Large heritage Dutch medlar.

items.name: Medlar 'Iranian'
items.growersTips:
Plant this Iranian beauty in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect its delicate spring blossom from frost.
Add well-rotted manure to clay soil before planting to keep its roots damp but never waterlogged.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove rubbing branches and keep its lovely weeping shrub shape.
Watch out for leaf blight in damp UK summers, and clear away fallen leaves to stop it spreading.
Harvest the fruit in late October, then let them blet indoors until soft and brown before eating.
items.description: Iranian heritage medlar.

items.name: Medlar 'Nottingham'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Nottingham grafted union strictly above soil level to prevent it reverting to hawthorn.
Give it a deep bucket of water weekly during dry UK summers while those unique fruits are swelling.
Prune lightly in late winter only to remove crossing branches and keep that lovely weeping shape.
Watch out for leaf blight in damp British springs and clear away fallen leaves to stop it spreading.
Pick the fruit after the first hard autumn frost then let them blet on wood shavings until soft.
items.description: Heritage English medlar.

items.name: Medlar 'Royal'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Royal in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect its beautiful, delicate spring blossoms.
Keep the soil consistently moist but well-drained, especially during dry summer spells.
Prune your shrub in winter to remove crossing branches and maintain an open, goblet shape.
Let the fruit experience the first autumn frosts before harvesting to start the bletting process.
Watch out for leaf blight in wet UK summers and clear fallen leaves to prevent it spreading.
items.description: Heritage medlar, large fruits.

items.name: Fragaria 'Elsanta'
items.growersTips:
Plant Elsanta crowns level with the soil in spring to stop rot in wet UK weather.
Water your Elsanta plants deeply at the base, not over the leaves, to prevent grey mould.
Protect early Elsanta blossoms from late UK spring frosts by covering them with fleece.
Lay straw under developing Elsanta berries in June to keep them off damp British soil.
Replace your Elsanta plants every three years to keep fruit size big and avoid disease.
items.description: Dutch maincrop strawberry, large red fruits.

items.name: Fragaria 'Sonata'
items.growersTips:
Pop these mid-season gems in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with the crown level with the earth.
Water them deeply at the base when the fruit swells, keeping the leaves dry to prevent grey mould.
Net your plants in June to stop greedy UK blackbirds and squirrels stealing your ripening berries.
Snip off the runners during the summer so your plant puts all its energy into those sweet berries.
Tuck straw under the fruit in May to keep them off damp British soil and stop them rotting away.
items.description: Dutch mid-season strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Marshmello'
items.growersTips:
Plant this sweet variety in mid-autumn so the roots settle well before the chilly UK winter.
Give them a mulch of straw in late spring to keep the heavy berries clean and off the damp soil.
Net your plants early in May because UK blackbirds absolutely love these juicy, sweet fruits.
Snip off the runners in summer to keep all the plant's energy focused on next year's big crop.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells, keeping the leaves dry to avoid mildew.
items.description: Heavy-cropping late strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Pandora'
items.growersTips:
You must plant a pollinator cultivar nearby like Florence because Pandora is completely female-sterile.
Give them a deep weekly soak at the base during dry UK spells to keep those big berries swelling nicely.
Tuck plenty of fresh straw under the leaves in May to stop our damp British soil rotting the fruit.
Cut back all the old foliage in late summer after fruiting to keep next year's crop disease-free.
Keep a sharp eye out for vine weevil grubs in autumn, as they love chewing Pandora's roots to bits.
items.description: Late strawberry, large fruits.

items.name: Fragaria 'Rhapsody'
items.growersTips:
Plant these late-season strawberries in late summer to establish strong roots before the UK winter.
Water your Rhapsody plants deeply at the base when the green fruit starts swelling in early summer.
Watch out for slugs and snails during wet British Junes by using organic beer traps around plants.
Cut away all old runners and dead leaves in autumn to prevent crown rot in damp winter weather.
Mulch with barley straw in May to keep the heavy trusses of red berries off the damp soil.
items.description: Late summer strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Royal Sovereign'
items.growersTips:
Give this heritage beauty rich, slightly acidic soil with plenty of well-rotted manure before planting.
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in autumn so they establish before the cold UK winter hits.
Water generously at the base while fruit swells, but keep leaves dry to prevent grey mould damage.
Protect the ripening berries from damp soil and slugs by tucking a fresh layer of straw underneath.
This variety is prone to virus, so replace your plants with certified stock every three years.
items.description: Heritage British strawberry, prized.

items.name: Fragaria 'Fenella'
items.growersTips:
Plant Fenella in crown-level soil by March so the wet UK spring doesn't rot the central growing tip.
Water deeply at the base during June fruiting to keep those large, juicy berries from splitting.
Lay straw or mats under the trusses in May to protect Fenella's heavy low-hanging fruit from slugs.
Cut back old leaves and runners in late August to help this late-season variety bud for next year.
Give Fenella extra space in your beds because its dense, bushy canopy needs good UK breeze to dry.
items.description: Disease-resistant mid-season strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Vibrant'
items.growersTips:
Plant these early-fruiting strawberries in late summer to get a bumper crop the following spring.
Give them a generous drenching at the base every morning once the white flowers start to open.
Tuck dry straw under the leaves in May to keep the low-hanging berries off wet British soil.
Snip off the runners as they appear in summer so the mother plant keeps its energy for fruiting.
Throw a net over the patch by mid-May to stop greedy blackbirds from stealing the ripening fruit.
items.description: Very early strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Christine'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early-season star in late summer so its roots settle before the damp UK winter sets in.
Pop straw under the berries in May to keep Christine's heavy, low-hanging fruit off the wet soil.
Watch for frost in April and cover the early blossoms with fleece to save your precious crop.
Give them a deep soak at the base twice a week when fruiting, keeping the leaves dry to stop rot.
Cut back all the old foliage to the ground in August to keep next year's plants disease-free.
items.description: Early strawberry, sweet flavour.

items.name: Fragaria 'Gariguette'
items.growersTips:
Plant these French treats in late summer so they establish strong roots before the UK winter chills.
Give them a mulch of straw in May to keep those long, slender berries off our damp British soil.
Water deeply at the base when flowering to prevent the shallow roots drying out in dry UK springs.
Net them early in May because UK blackbirds absolutely love the intense fragrance of Gariguette.
Cut away the runners in autumn to keep all the plant's energy focused on next May's delicious crop.
items.description: French heritage gourmet strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Korona'
items.growersTips:
Plant them with the crown level with the soil surface to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Water deeply at the base when the fruits start to swell, keeping the leaves dry to avoid grey mould.
Net your plants in June to stop greedy blackbirds and starlings from stealing the bright red berries.
Cut back all the old foliage in late summer after fruiting to encourage fresh, healthy autumn growth.
Tuck straw under the ripening berries in May to keep them off the damp British soil and stop slugs.
items.description: Dutch mid-season strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Manille'
items.growersTips:
Plant this French mid-season gem in well-drained, slightly acidic soil enriched with rotted manure.
Give these strawberries a deep soak at the base twice a week during dry UK summer fruiting spells.
Tuck straw or mulch under the low-growing fruit trusses in May to stop damp soil rotting your crop.
Snip off the runners on your young plants until late summer to boost next year's berry harvest.
Net your patch in June to keep greedy local blackbirds from stealing the ripening red berries.
items.description: Heavy-cropping strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Maxim'
items.growersTips:
Give these giant-fruiting plants extra space by planting them 45cm apart to prevent grey mould.
Water deeply at the base when the huge fruits are swelling, but keep the foliage dry to stop rot.
Tuck plenty of fresh straw under the heavy trusses in June to keep these massive berries off wet soil.
Snip off the runners during the summer so your plant puts all its energy into those giant fruits.
Net your patch early in May because UK blackbirds will target these exceptionally large red berries.
items.description: Very large fruited maincrop.

items.name: Fragaria 'Sweetheart'
items.growersTips:
Pop your Sweetheart runners in soil by late August so they establish before the chilly UK winter.
Water them deeply at the base, not over the leaves, to stop grey mould during damp British summers.
Tuck straw under the fruit in May to keep your berries clean and safe from damp soil pests.
Snip off the first spring blossoms in their first year to get a much bigger harvest later on.
Net your plants securely in June because local birds love these sweet red berries just as much as you.
items.description: Compact strawberry for hanging baskets.

items.name: Fragaria 'Albion'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Albion crowns in spring with the soil level exactly halfway up the central green bud.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry UK summers, keeping the leaves and developing fruit dry.
Cut off the early spring runners to force this perpetual variety to focus on big autumn berries.
Tuck straw under the trusses in June to stop damp British soil from rotting your ripening crop.
Net your plants in July to stop greedy blackbirds and starlings from stealing the red berries.
items.description: Day-neutral everbearer.

items.name: Fragaria 'Cambridge Late Pine'
items.growersTips:
Plant this strawberry with the crown level with the soil line to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Water deeply at the base during dry spells, keeping the foliage dry to prevent grey mould.
Net your plants in June to stop blackbirds from stealing the delicious pine-flavoured berries.
Cut back old leaves in autumn and clear debris to prevent slugs harbouring in the damp UK weather.
Plant near borage to attract pollinators and boost your Cambridge Late Pine berry yield.
items.description: Heritage Cambridge strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Cambridge Vigour'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early-fruiting variety in August so it establishes well before the cold UK winter.
Give them a mulch of straw in May to keep the low-hanging berries clean and dry in damp UK weather.
Watch out for mildew on these leaves, so water only at the base and space them forty centimetres apart.
Pick off the runners in summer to keep the parent plant strong and packed with sweet, juicy fruit.
Net your patch by late May because local blackbirds absolutely love these bright red early berries.
items.description: Heritage Cambridge strawberry, sweet.

items.name: Fragaria 'Loran'
items.growersTips:
Plant these deep pink beauties in early spring, keeping the crown level with the soil surface.
Water your Loran plants at the base, not the leaves, to prevent grey mould in damp UK summers.
Tuck straw under the leaves in May to keep those heavy, sweet berries clean and off the wet soil.
Snip off any runners as they appear to force your Loran to focus all its energy on big berries.
Net your plants in June or the greedy local blackbirds will eat the red fruits before you do.
items.description: Mid-season strawberry, vigorous.

items.name: Fragaria 'Ostara'
items.growersTips:
Pluck off the very first spring flowers so your plant puts its energy into a huge autumn harvest.
Keep watering consistently as fruits swell, aiming right at the base to avoid grey mould on leaves.
Plant them with the crown level with the soil; too deep and they rot, too shallow and they dry out.
Snip off the runners as they appear through summer to keep all the growing power in the main plant.
Tuck some straw under the ripening berries in July to stop damp UK soil from rotting your harvest.
items.description: Perpetual strawberry, all-summer.

items.name: Fragaria 'Tarda Vicoda'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-season beauty in spring, burying the crown exactly level with your soil surface.
Give it a weekly deep soak at the base to keep the heavy late-summer berry crop swelling nicely.
Tuck straw under the trusses in July to stop damp UK soil from rotting these huge, juicy fruits.
Snip off the runners on young plants to force all the energy into a massive August harvest.
Net the patch in summer because British blackbirds love these bright red, late-fruiting berries.
items.description: Italian heritage strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Eve's Delight'
items.growersTips:
Plant this everbearer in early spring, keeping the crown exactly level with the soil to prevent rot.
Give them a liquid tomato feed every fortnight from May to September for a continuous summer harvest.
Tuck straw under the leaves in May to keep the heavy rain from splashing mud onto your ripening fruit.
Snip off the runners during the summer so the parent plant pours all its energy into juicy berries.
Pop a net over them in June because UK blackbirds will spot those bright red berries before you do.
items.description: Heavy-cropping June strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Hapil'
items.growersTips:
Plant Hapil crowns level with the soil in late summer to let roots settle before the UK winter cold.
Give Hapil extra water when the berries start swelling to prevent dry soil from ruining your crop.
Lay straw or use mats under the heavy trusses in May to stop Hapil fruit from resting on damp soil.
Net your plants in June because UK blackbirds love Hapil berries just as much as you do.
Snip off the runners on your Hapil plants until late summer so they put all energy into big fruit.
items.description: Belgian midseason strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Aromel'
items.growersTips:
Plant this everbearer in spring with the crown flush with the soil to prevent rot in wet UK weather.
Snip off the very first spring flowers so the plant puts its energy into a huge late-summer crop.
Water deeply at the base every morning during dry spells, keeping the leaves dry to avoid mildew.
Tuck straw under the trusses in June to stop damp British soil from rotting your ripening berries.
Snip off the runners as soon as they appear so your plant focuses entirely on making sweet fruit.
items.description: Perpetual fragrant strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Mae'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early-season star in spring, keeping the crown level with the soil so it does not rot.
Give these thirsty berries a deep soak at their base every morning while the fruit is swelling.
Lay down a thick bed of dry straw in May to keep those low-hanging berries clean and off damp soil.
Snip off the runners as soon as they appear in summer to keep all the energy in your berry crop.
Cover the patch with fine netting in June to stop greedy local blackbirds stealing your red fruit.
items.description: Modern early strawberry.

items.name: Fragaria 'Malling Pearl'
items.growersTips:
Plant this everbearer in late spring when the soil warms up, keeping the crown level with the earth.
Water deeply at the base, not the leaves, to stop grey mould in our damp British summers.
Snip off the early spring runners to channel all the plant's energy into those juicy autumn berries.
Net your plants in July to stop greedy blackbirds and starlings stealing your precious red harvest.
Tuck straw under the leaves in May to keep the low-hanging fruit clean and safe from damp soil.
items.description: UK breeding strawberry, sweet.

items.name: Raspberry 'Glen Magna'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late summer beauty in acidic to neutral soil, adding well-rotted manure to the trench.
Space your canes 45cm apart and support their vigorous 1.5m growth with a sturdy wire trellis system.
Prune fruited canes to the ground in autumn, leaving the new green ones to overwinter for next year.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells to ensure those large, dark berries swell nicely.
Keep a close eye out for raspberry beetle grubs in July, as this late variety can attract them.
items.description: Modern summer raspberry, large fruit.

items.name: Raspberry 'Glen Coe'
items.growersTips:
Prune out the dark purple fruited canes right to the ground in autumn once they finish cropping.
Plant bare-root in autumn or winter, keeping the crown level with the soil to avoid crown rot.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to feed this hungry purple hybrid and keep the roots damp.
Give them a sturdy post and wire support system to keep these vigorous, arching canes off the lawn.
Net the ripening purple berries in July to stop greedy UK blackbirds from stealing your harvest.
items.description: Purple raspberry, very sweet.

items.name: Raspberry 'Joan J'
items.growersTips:
Cut this autumn-fruiter right to the ground in February so you get a huge crop on new summer wood.
Give them a thick mulch of garden compost in March to lock in moisture and feed the shallow roots.
Keep these spineless stems well-watered from July to September while the heavy berries are swelling.
Tie the heavy, fruit-laden canes to a simple wire trellis to stop them collapsing in autumn winds.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in July, and pick them off early to save your autumn harvest.
items.description: Spine-free autumn raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Malling Jewel'
items.growersTips:
Plant this bareroot in late autumn so its roots settle in the damp UK soil before spring growth.
Support these compact, slightly floppy canes with a simple two-wire fence to keep berries off the wet ground.
Prune fruited canes right down to the ground in autumn, leaving the new green ones for next year.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to feed the shallow roots and keep the soil damp.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in June; pick them off early to save your summer harvest.
items.description: Heritage UK summer raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Octavia'
items.growersTips:
Plant Octavia in autumn with the root flare just at soil level to avoid rot in wet UK winters.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to keep the acidic, sandy, or loamy soil moist and fertile.
Prune out all fruited brown canes to ground level in late August, leaving young green ones for next year.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during July fruiting to prevent the berries from shrivelling.
Drape netting over the canes in June to stop blackbirds stealing the late-summer ripening berries.
items.description: Late summer raspberry, very large.

items.name: Raspberry 'Glen Lyon'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early summer fruiter in acidic to neutral soil, keeping the crown level with the turf.
Mulch with damp bark in March to protect its shallow roots from drying out in dry UK spring spells.
Cut fruited floricanes to the ground in autumn, leaving new green primocanes to bear next year.
Watch out for raspberry beetle larvae in June; net the plants to keep the adult beetles away.
Feed with rose food in late winter to boost its heavy yield of firm, easy-to-pick berries.
items.description: Heavy-cropping summer raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Glen Moy'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early-fruiting summer variety in a sunny, sheltered spot to protect the delicate blooms.
Mulch with acidic well-rotted manure in March to keep the shallow roots damp during dry UK springs.
Cut all fruited canes right down to the ground in August, leaving the new green ones for next year.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in June; use pheromone traps nearby to keep your berries clean.
Support these virtually spine-free canes with a simple post and wire system to stop them snapping.
items.description: Early summer raspberry, large fruit.

items.name: Raspberry 'Glen Prosen'
items.growersTips:
Plant this spine-free variety in autumn in a sunny spot with rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil.
Since it is a summer-fruiting floricane, prune out the brown, woody fruited canes right after harvest.
Keep the soil consistently damp during July fruiting but avoid waterlogging to prevent root rot.
Tie the vigorous, upright canopy to a sturdy post-and-wire support system to protect from UK winds.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in the berries by checking the white flowers in May and June.
items.description: Spine-free summer raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Heritage'
items.growersTips:
Cut these autumn-fruiting canes right down to ground level in February to get a huge crop by August.
Plant them with the crown just at soil level in a sunny spot sheltered from wet UK winter winds.
Give them a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in spring to keep their shallow roots damp and fed.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in July, especially if you want to eat them straight from the bush.
Grow them near garlic or chives to help keep those pesky aphids off your delicious autumn berries.
items.description: Autumn primocane raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Leo'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-summer raspberry in fertile, acidic soil with a generous layer of composted bark.
Support these tall, vigorous canes on a sturdy wire system to protect them from strong UK winds.
Prune Leo by cutting all fruited canes to the ground in winter, leaving the new green ones to fruit.
Water deeply at the base during dry July spells to ensure those late-season berries swell up plump.
Keep a close eye out for raspberry beetle grubs in August when these late fruits are ripening.
items.description: Late summer raspberry, large firm fruit.

items.name: Raspberry 'Malling Promise'
items.growersTips:
Plant this early cropper in autumn in free-draining, slightly acidic soil to avoid root rot.
Tie the vigorous, floppy canes securely to sturdy wire supports to keep heavy summer fruit off damp soil.
Prune fruiting canes right down to the ground in August, leaving new green ones for next year.
Lay a thick mulch of compost in March to keep shallow roots damp during dry UK spring spells.
Net your bushes in June to stop local blackbirds from stealing the berries just as they turn red.
items.description: Heritage early summer raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Sceptre'
items.growersTips:
Plant this autumn-fruiting primocane in a sunny, sheltered UK spot with rich, acidic to neutral soil.
Cut all canes right down to ground level in February to get a huge crop of late-summer berries.
Water deeply at the base during dry British spells to keep those juicy Sceptre berries swelling.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in spring to feed the roots and keep weeds at bay.
Watch out for raspberry beetle larvae in summer and use organic traps to protect your harvest.
items.description: Modern primocane autumn raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Tadmor'
items.growersTips:
Plant this late-season beauty in acidic to neutral soil, adding well-rotted manure to the trench.
Since Tadmor fruits on last year's canes, prune out only the brown, fruited wood each November.
Keep soil consistently damp but not soggy from flowering to harvest to ensure those huge berries swell.
Support these exceptionally tall canes by tying them securely to a strong three-wire fence system.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in July, as Tadmor's late harvest overlaps with their cycle.
items.description: Modern raspberry, very tasty.

items.name: Raspberry 'Terri Louise'
items.growersTips:
Plant this autumn in moist, acidic to neutral soil, burying the root ball just below the surface.
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry UK summers to keep those heavy, sweet berries juicy.
Prune all canes right down to ground level in late winter since this is an autumn-fruiting variety.
Watch out for raspberry beetle larvae in July; use organic traps to save your delicious harvest.
Give these vigorous shrubs a sturdy post-and-wire support system to keep heavy autumn crops upright.
items.description: Modern autumn raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Valentina'
items.growersTips:
Plant Valentina in autumn to let its roots settle in the damp UK winter before spring growth starts.
This apricot beauty fruits on last year's wood, so only prune stems that have finished cropping.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to feed the soil and keep those shallow roots damp in June.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in July; pick them off to keep your orange berries pristine.
Give Valentina a sunny, sheltered spot to bring out that unique, sweet apricot-peach flavour.
items.description: Apricot-coloured raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Zeva'
items.growersTips:
Plant your Zeva bareroot in autumn, setting the crown just two centimetres below the soil surface.
Prune this autumn-fruiting variety by cutting all canes down to ground level in February.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the berries plump and juicy.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in spring to give Zeva the rich, acidic soil it absolutely loves.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in July, especially if you see dry, shrivelled fruit tips.
items.description: Swiss autumn raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'Erika'
items.growersTips:
Plant Erika bare-roots in late autumn with the crown just at soil level to avoid rot in wet UK clay.
As a double-cropper, cut half the canes to the ground in February and leave the rest to fruit in July.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in March to feed Erika's heavy demand for rich, moisture-retentive soil.
Water deeply at the base during dry spells in June to stop the heavy autumn crop from shrivelling up.
Watch out for raspberry beetle grubs in July, especially if you see dry patches near the stalk end.
items.description: Italian primocane raspberry.

items.name: Raspberry 'All Gold'
items.growersTips:
Prune all canes to the ground in February so your autumn crop grows strong on fresh new wood.
Plant your bare-root canes in winter with the root bud sitting just two inches below the soil.
Drench the roots weekly during dry UK summers to keep those sweet yellow berries plump and juicy.
Net your bushes in July because British blackbirds love these yellow fruits just as much as red ones.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Jubilee'

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Keepsake'

Watch out for the gooseberry sawfly caterpillar in spring, which can strip the leaves overnight.

items.description: Heritage gooseberry, long picking.

items.description: Heritage UK gooseberry, large dark fruit.

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Pax'

items.name: Blackcurrant 'Surprise'

items.name: Highbush 'Brigitta'
items.growersTips:
Plant Brigitta in a pot of ericaceous compost, as most UK garden soils are simply not acidic enough.

items.name: Highbush 'Concord'

Plant your Concord in a pot of ericaceous compost because our UK garden soils are rarely acidic enough.

items.description: Late mid-season blueberry, large berry.

Prune hard in January while dormant, leaving just two main buds on each spur to prevent overcrowding.
Watch out for powdery mildew in humid UK summers by thinning the leaves around your grape bunches.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry spells, but stop watering once the grapes turn yellow.

items.name: Grape 'Concord'

Plant your Concord in the sunniest, most sheltered south-facing spot to help the fruit ripen in the UK.
Prune your vine in midwinter when fully dormant to prevent the stems from bleeding sap and weakening.
Mulch with well-rotted manure in early spring to feed the roots and help retain vital soil moisture.
Thin out the dense summer foliage to let sunlight reach the grape bunches and prevent powdery mildew.

Plant your Dornfelder in a south-facing, sheltered spot to help the grapes ripen in UK summers.

items.name: Grape 'Madeleine Sylvaner'

items.name: Grape 'Orion'
